3d-artist.heading: 3D artist questions
qs: Why do most artists model in quads, and when are triangles fine?
Whether you understand topology beyond a rule you were taught.
Quads give clean subdivision and deformation. Triangles are fine where nothing bends, since real-time engines triangulate every mesh anyway.

Quads subdivide predictably and give clean edge loops, so a face or an elbow bends without pinching. For a static prop in a game, triangles are fine: the engine turns every mesh into triangles anyway. What I avoid are n-gons, faces with more than four sides, on curved surfaces, because they triangulate unpredictably and cause shading artifacts.
What is texel density, and why does it matter across a set of assets?
Your grasp of how texture resolution is spread over a scene.
Texture pixels per unit of surface, kept consistent so no asset looks sharper or blurrier than its neighbor.

It is how many texture pixels cover a given area of the model, for example pixels per meter. If a crate next to a wall has twice the density, it looks crisp while the wall looks blurry, and the eye catches it. I agree on a target with the team, check it with a density checker, and only raise it for hero items the player sees up close.
A junior's base color texture has shadows and highlights painted into it. What do you tell them?
Whether you understand the physically based material workflow.
Lighting belongs to the renderer. The base color holds only the surface's own color, and roughness, metalness and occlusion maps do the rest.

In a physically based workflow the engine does the lighting. If shadows are painted into the base color, the asset looks wrong under any light that does not match, and the shadows double up. I would have them flatten the base color to the plain surface color, keep ambient occlusion in its own map, and put wear and shine into the roughness map.
Which texture maps should be read as sRGB and which as linear, and what goes wrong if you mix them up?
Your technical care with texture settings in the engine or renderer.
Color maps like base color in sRGB; data maps like normal, roughness and metalness in linear. A data map read as sRGB gets its values shifted.

Base color and emissive are color, so they are sRGB. Normal, roughness, metalness, height and ambient occlusion are data, so they are linear. If a roughness map is flagged as sRGB, the renderer applies a gamma curve, the mid values get darker and the surface looks shinier than I painted. A normal map read that way gives bent, wrong lighting.
Walk me through how you would light a product shot of a polished steel watch.
How you use light to show form and material.
Lights the reflections, not just the object: large soft sources, a clean highlight along the form, dark cards for contrast, and a check for glare.

Polished metal shows what it reflects, so I light the reflections more than the object. I use a large soft key from one side, a long strip light to draw a clean highlight along the case, and black cards so the steel has contrast. I watch the glass for glare over the dial, then check the image in grayscale to make sure the shapes read.
Your normal map bake shows hard seams and warped details on the low poly. How do you fix it?
Whether you find the cause of a baking problem instead of painting over it.
Adjusts the cage or ray distance, splits UVs at hard edges, matches triangulation and tangent space with the engine, and adds edge padding.

Warped details usually come from the ray direction, so I adjust the cage until it covers the high poly cleanly. For seams, I make sure every hard edge has a UV split, the mesh is triangulated before the bake, and the baker uses the same tangent space as the engine. I also check the green channel convention and add enough edge padding.
A character's shoulder collapses when the arm goes up. Where do you look?
Whether you understand how topology and rigging work together on a character.
Edge loops around the joint first, then skin weights, then corrective shapes or helper joints if those are not enough.

First the topology: the shoulder needs enough loops that follow the muscle, or there is nothing to bend. Then the skin weights, since a hard split between the arm and chest joints causes pinching. If the volume still collapses, I ask the rigger for a helper joint or sculpt a corrective shape that turns on as the arm rises.
How would you build the same wooden chair differently for a game and for a film?
Whether you know how real-time and offline rendering change the work.
Game: tight triangle and texture budgets, baked detail, lower-detail versions for distance. Film: real geometry, subdivision and displacement at render time.

For a game I keep a low poly mesh, bake the carved detail from a high poly into a normal map, share a texture set with other props and make lower-detail versions for distance. For film the renderer can handle far more, so I keep real geometry, subdivide at render time, use displacement for the carving and spread textures over several tiles for close-ups.
The art director wants more detail on a hero prop, but it is already at its triangle budget. What do you do?
How you balance the look against technical limits.
Moves small detail into maps, cuts geometry that does not earn its cost, and raises the budget question openly instead of quietly going over.

First I check where the triangles go. Small bevels and flat areas can often move into the normal map, and faces the camera never sees can be cut. That frees budget for the silhouette, which is what geometry is really for. If it still is not enough, I show the art director and the tech artist the cost and let them decide, rather than quietly going over.
Tell me about a time an asset you delivered broke further down the pipeline.
How you own a mistake and change the way you work.
A specific error, a quick fix, and a check added so it does not happen again.

I delivered 40 props exported in the wrong units, so they came into the engine a hundred times too small. A level designer flagged it the same day. I fixed the export settings, re-exported everything that afternoon and checked each prop in a test scene. Since then I keep a human-scale reference in every file and run a checklist: scale, pivot, naming and frozen transforms.
How do you decide where to put UV seams, and how do they relate to hard edges?
Whether you unwrap with both the texture artist and the normal bake in mind.
Seams hidden where the camera rarely looks, and every hard edge also split in UVs, while a UV split does not need a hard edge.

I hide seams under arms, on inner edges and along natural breaks between materials. Every hard edge gets a UV split, because each side of the edge needs its own pixels in the normal map. A UV split without a hard edge is fine. I also cut where stretching appears and straighten islands so they pack tightly.
In a metal/roughness workflow, what values do you put in the metallic map, and why?
Your grasp of physically based materials, not just painting by eye.
Metallic treated as a mask of 0 or 1, grey only in small transitions, metal color in base color, no pure black or white for non-metals.

Metallic is a mask: bare metal is 1, everything else is 0. Paint, rust and dirt on top of metal are 0 too. Grey values belong only in thin blends like chipped edges. The tint of gold or copper goes into base color. For non-metals I avoid pure black or pure white base color, because no real surface reflects all or no light.
How do you lay out the edge loops on a face that has to talk and emote?
Whether your character topology is built for animation, not just for a still render.
Loops around eyes and mouth like the muscles, a line for the nasolabial fold, poles kept away from the parts that bend most.

I run circular loops around the eyes and mouth, following the muscles that close them, so lids and lips can open, close and squash cleanly. Another set runs from the wing of the nose past the mouth corners for the smile fold. I keep poles away from the mouth corners and put density where the face moves, lighter on the skull.
Seams on a game asset look fine up close but show colored lines at a distance. What is happening?
Whether you understand mipmaps and texture padding.
Mipmaps average neighboring pixels, so islands need spacing and edge dilation scaled to the texture size.

That is mip bleeding. The engine uses smaller versions of the texture at a distance, made by averaging pixels, so colors from the background or a nearby island creep into the edge. I give islands more spacing on larger maps and set the baker to dilate each island's edge color outward, so the shrunk versions still have the right color at the seam.
When would you skip a high poly bake and use a mid-poly with weighted normals instead?
Your range of hard-surface methods for real-time work.
Knows the trade: no bake and free use of tiling textures, at the cost of more vertices, with bakes kept for unique detail.

For large hard-surface pieces like vehicles or architecture I model bevels into the mesh and use weighted normals, so big flat faces shade flat and the bevels carry the curve. No high poly, and the mesh works with tiling textures and trims. The cost is more vertices. I still bake small unique details like bolts or vents when the asset needs them.
You have to texture a whole city block for a game. How do you plan it?
How you balance quality against memory and production time at scale.
Tiling textures and trim sheets for most surfaces, decals and vertex blending against repetition, unique bakes only for hero props.

Unique textures for every building would cost too much memory and months of work. I plan a small set of tiling materials and a trim sheet, one texture with strips for moldings, panels and edges that many meshes map onto. Decals and vertex-painted blends hide repetition. Unique bakes go only to the props a player walks up to and inspects.
Walk me through how you build LODs for a prop and check them.
Whether you can make an asset hold up across distances without wasting performance.
Silhouette kept, inner detail removed first, UVs and normals preserved, and the result checked in engine at the real switch distances.

I keep the silhouette and remove what sits inside it first: small bevels, interior loops, parts that become a few pixels. As a starting point each level cuts roughly half the triangles. UVs and normals have to stay close so the same material still reads. Then I check in engine at the switch distances and fix anything that visibly pops.
Your interior render is still noisy after you doubled the samples. What do you do?
How you diagnose a render problem instead of throwing time at it.
Find the source with render passes, fix the cause (lights, portals, clamping), use the denoiser last and check it for smearing.

I split the render into passes to see where the noise lives: indirect light, glossy reflections or one small bright light. Then I fix that cause. I add portals at windows so sky light is sampled well, make tiny lights a bit larger, and clamp indirect light to kill fireflies, knowing it darkens slightly. The denoiser comes last, checked on fine texture detail.
A batch of props you exported arrives in the engine 100 times too small and rotated. How do you fix it for good?
Whether you fix pipeline problems at the source instead of patching them downstream.
Units checked, transforms applied, pivots and axes set, a saved export preset, and no fixes left in the engine.

That is a unit mismatch: my scene was in centimeters on one side and meters on the other, plus a different up axis. I fix it in the source file: set scene units, apply scale and rotation so transforms read clean, put pivots where they belong, and save an export preset. Patching scale in the engine breaks again on the next re-export.
A junior hands you a finished game prop. What do you check before it goes into the build?
Your standards as a senior and how you pass them on.
A repeatable checklist run in engine, covering geometry, UVs, materials and setup, with notes the junior can act on.

I open it in engine, not only in the modeling tool. I check scale against a reference character, pivot, naming, n-gons, flipped normals, overlapping UVs, a lightmap UV channel if we bake lighting, texel density, material count, LODs and collision. Then I give notes as a short list they can tick off, so the next asset comes in cleaner.

account-executive.heading: Account executive questions
qs: What is the difference between a champion and an economic buyer?
Whether you know who actually approves a deal.
A champion sells for you inside the account. The economic buyer controls the budget and can say yes alone. Sometimes one person is both, but often not.

A champion wants my solution to win and pushes for it internally, usually because it solves their problem. The economic buyer owns the budget and can approve the spend without asking anyone else. A friendly user who loves the demo is not automatically either one. I test a champion by asking them to do something, like getting me a meeting with the buyer.
How do you run a demo so it is not just a feature tour?
How you tie the product to what the buyer said they need.
It starts from the problems found in discovery, shows only what solves them, and checks in with the buyer often.

I open by repeating the two or three problems they told me about and asking if anything changed. Then I show only the workflows that fix those problems, in their words, and stop after each one to ask how it compares to how they work today. Anything they did not ask about waits. I end by agreeing on the next step before we hang up.
What is a mutual action plan, and when do you bring it up?
Whether you manage the steps to signature together with the buyer.
A shared, dated list of steps both sides own, from evaluation to signature. You raise it once there is real interest, not at the very end.

It is a simple shared document: every step left before go-live, who owns it on each side, and a date. Security review, legal, budget approval, signature, kickoff. I bring it up after a good second meeting, framed as how we get you live by the date you need. If the buyer will not commit to any dates, that tells me the deal is less real than it looked.
Why do you multi-thread a deal, and how do you do it?
How you avoid a deal that depends on a single contact.
Relationships with several people in different roles, reached with the champion's help, with a clear reason for each meeting.

If my only contact leaves, goes on leave or loses the internal argument, the deal dies. So I ask my champion who else will be affected and who might push back, and I ask for help meeting them. Each person gets a reason to talk: IT gets a security session, finance gets a cost model. By the proposal stage I want at least three people who know me, including the buyer.
What do you need to see before you put a deal in commit?
Your forecasting discipline.
Evidence confirmed by the buyer: budget approved, decision maker engaged, signing process known, dated close plan. Not a gut feeling.

Commit means I would bet my number on it. I need the economic buyer to have said yes to the solution and the price, a known signing process with names and dates, and no open legal or security review that could run long. If any of those is a guess, the deal stays in best case. I would rather forecast low and pull a deal in than explain a miss.
A prospect asks if the product can do something it cannot. What do you say?
Your honesty when a sale is on the line.
A clear no, then a question about the underlying need, and a check with product before mentioning any roadmap or workaround.

I say no, it does not do that today. Then I ask what they are trying to achieve, because sometimes another feature or an integration covers it. If it is on the roadmap, I check with product before saying anything about dates, and I never put an unreleased feature in a contract on my own. Overpromising wins a signature and loses the renewal.
Your champion stops answering two weeks before the planned close date. What do you do?
How you handle a stalled deal without panicking or pestering.
One short, useful message, contact with the other people in the account, and an honest update to the forecast.

First I send one short note with something useful, like the security answers they asked for, and a direct question: is the timeline still the same? Then I contact the other people I have met there, not to go around my champion but to learn what changed. If I hear nothing in a few days, I move the deal out of commit and tell my manager why.
Procurement asks for 15% off the day before signature. How do you respond?
How you trade for value instead of giving away price.
Nothing for free. Any concession is traded for something, like a longer term, upfront payment or a bigger order, and stays within approval rules.

I do not say yes on the call. I ask what is behind it, since procurement is often measured on savings and needs a win to show. Then I trade: a lower price for a two-year term, upfront payment or more seats. Anything beyond my discount authority goes to my manager with the reason. If I give in on the first ask, they learn there was more room.
The prospect already uses a competitor and is mostly happy. How do you win the deal?
How you sell against an incumbent without attacking them.
Finds the real cost of staying put, respects the current vendor, and makes switching feel low-risk.

I never attack the competitor, because the buyer chose them and that insults their choice. I ask what they would change if they could, and what it costs them today in hours or lost business. If the gap is real, I make switching feel safe: a migration plan, a reference customer who moved over, maybe a pilot. If they are truly happy, I stay in touch until their renewal.
A deal you called commit slips to next quarter. How do you handle it with your manager?
Whether you own a forecast miss and learn from it.
Tells the manager early, says plainly what was missed, gives a new dated plan, and changes the forecasting habit that failed.

I tell my manager the day I know, not on the last day of the quarter. I say what happened plainly: I had the champion's word but never spoke to the CFO, and the budget was moved. Then I share the new close plan with dates the buyer has confirmed. And I change my rule: no commit until I hear yes from the person who signs.
What is a paper process, and when do you start mapping it?
Whether you know how a deal actually gets signed after the buyer says yes.
The steps after a verbal yes: legal, security, procurement and signers. Mapped early, during discovery, not in the last week.

It is every step between a verbal yes and a signed contract: legal review, security questionnaire, procurement, vendor setup, and who signs above which amount. I ask about it in discovery, usually by asking how they bought their last tool of this size. A deal with a known process rarely slips because of paperwork.
How do you work out how much pipeline you need for the quarter?
Whether you plan pipeline from your own numbers instead of a rule of thumb.
Gap to quota divided by your real win rate, adjusted for cycle length, so the pipeline exists in time.

I start with the gap: say $400,000 left to close. If I win about 25% of qualified pipeline by value, I need $1.6 million that can still close this quarter, so 4 times coverage. If my cycle is 90 days, most of that had to exist when the quarter began, so I build next quarter's pipeline now.
What is a compelling event, and what do you do when a deal has none?
How you deal with a common loss in sales: the buyer decides to do nothing.
A dated reason with a real cost of waiting. Without one, you build the cost of inaction with the buyer or keep the deal out of the forecast.

It is something with a date that forces a decision, like a contract renewal, a new regulation or a product launch. If there is none, I work with my champion to put a number on waiting: what each month of the current problem costs them. If we cannot find one, the deal stays in pipeline but out of my forecast.
You inherit a territory of 200 accounts. How do you spend your first 90 days?
How you set priorities across a territory instead of working whoever calls back.
Open deals and renewals checked first, accounts tiered by fit and buying signals, and a plan the manager can see.

Week one, I check open opportunities and anything renewing soon, because that is revenue at risk. Then I tier the accounts: about 20 top tier on fit and buying signals, 60 middle, the rest light touch. Top tier gets researched outreach to several people. I share the tiers with my manager by day 30 and review what is moving at day 60.
How do you build a business case that a CFO will accept?
Whether you can turn value into numbers a finance leader trusts.
The customer's own numbers, conservative assumptions and a plainly stated payback. Built with the champion, not handed over.

I use their figures, not ours: hours spent today, error rates, what a lost customer costs. My champion confirms each input, so it is their model. I keep assumptions conservative, show the full cost including setup and training, and state the payback period. A CFO who catches one inflated number stops trusting the rest.
An RFP arrives from a company you have never spoken to. Do you answer it?
Your judgement on where to spend time, and whether you can spot an RFP written for a competitor.
Qualify before writing: who wrote it, can you talk to the buyer, does it fit. Willing to decline.

Not automatically. If the requirements read like a competitor's feature list and I have met no one there, I am probably the third quote. I ask for a call with the buyer before the deadline. If they refuse and the fit is weak, I decline politely. A 200-question response takes days that my real pipeline needs.
Their legal team sends back redlines on the liability cap and indemnity. What is your role?
Whether you know the limits of your authority and keep a deal moving through legal.
You do not agree to legal terms yourself. You bring in your legal team, learn the buyer's real concern and keep dates on track.

I do not agree to legal terms myself; that is our legal team's call. My job is to find out what drives the ask, for example a past vendor breach, and pass that context to our counsel. Then I set a call with both lawyers and put it on the mutual plan with a date, so the redlines do not sit in an inbox for three weeks.
The buyer wants a three-year price lock and payment terms of net 90. How do you think about it?
How you trade concessions instead of giving them away.
Every give has a get. You know what each term costs your company and check with finance before agreeing.

Both cost us something: a price lock limits future increases, and net 90 delays our cash by three months. I check with finance and deal desk first. Then I trade: a three-year lock in exchange for a three-year term, and longer payment terms only if they sign this month or add seats. I never give two things for nothing.
You sent a proposal with a price below what was approved, and the customer accepted it. What do you do?
How you own a mistake that affects both your company and the customer.
Tells the manager right away, does not quietly change the price, and lets the company decide whether to honor it.

I tell my manager the same day: the approved price, what I sent, and the gap. I do not quietly send a new quote. Often the company honors it and I learn from it. If it cannot, I call the customer myself, own the error plainly and offer something fair. Trust lost over a hidden fix costs more than the discount.
Your manager wants you to offer a big discount to pull a deal into this quarter, though the buyer never asked for one. What do you do?
Your judgement when this quarter's number and the account's long-term value pull apart.
States the trade-off with numbers, offers other ways to close sooner, and follows the final decision openly.

I would show what the discount does: less revenue on this deal, and a buyer who now expects a discount at every renewal and quarter end. Then I offer options, like asking the buyer if an earlier start date helps them, with no discount. If my manager still decides to discount, I do it, but I tie it to a real ask, like a longer term.
What was your quota attainment last year, and what were your average deal size and sales cycle?
Whether you know your numbers and can explain them, not only quote them.
Attainment as a percentage of quota for each of the last two or three years, the average deal size, the usual cycle length, and one sentence on why a weak year was weak.

Last year I closed 112% of a $900K annual quota; the year before, 94%, because two large deals slipped into January. My average deal was about $45K, and most closed in 60 to 90 days. I can show the numbers from the CRM if you would like to check them.
How much of your pipeline did you source yourself?
Whether you can create deals, or only close the ones marketing and SDRs hand you.
A rough share you sourced yourself, the channels that worked, and the weekly routine behind it.

About 40% of my pipeline came from my own outbound; the rest came from SDRs and inbound. I block two mornings a week for prospecting: research on 25 accounts, then calls, emails and LinkedIn messages. Referrals from existing customers gave me my two largest deals last year.
Walk me through your sales process. Do you use a framework such as MEDDIC?
Whether you qualify deals on purpose, and can name the steps instead of improvising each deal.
The stages from first call to signature, what must be true to move a deal to the next stage, and a framework only if you really use it.

I qualify on the first two calls: the problem and what it costs them, who decides and who signs, and when they need it solved. I use MEDDIC as a checklist, so a deal without an identified economic buyer or a decision process does not go into commit. Then a demo built around their problem, a mutual action plan with dates, the proposal, and procurement.

account-manager.heading: Account manager questions
qs: What is the difference between gross and net revenue retention?
Whether you know the numbers an account team is judged on.
Gross counts only revenue kept after downgrades and churn, so it caps at 100%. Net also adds expansion from the same customers.

Gross retention shows how much of the recurring revenue we started with we kept after downgrades and cancellations, so it can never go above 100%. Net retention also adds expansion from those same customers, like upsells. Net can pass 100% while gross falls, which means growth is hiding churn, so I watch both.
You inherit a book of 60 accounts. What do you do in your first 30 days?
How you sort a portfolio by risk and value before you start calling.
A clear order based on renewal date, revenue and health, with early calls to listen, not to sell.

I sort the book by renewal date and revenue, then pull usage and support tickets. Accounts renewing in the next 120 days, and large ones with falling usage, get a call in the first two weeks. I ask what they wanted when they bought and whether they got it, and note who decides and who signs. Smaller healthy accounts get a short email and an open slot on my calendar.
When do you start working on a renewal, and what happens in that time?
Your renewal timeline and whether you plan for the buyer's process.
Starting months ahead, proving value, mapping signers and procurement, and closing before the end date.

For a mid-size account I start about 90 to 120 days out, longer if they need procurement or a security review. First I confirm the value they got, with numbers. Then I check who signs, their paperwork process and budget cycle. I want terms agreed at least 30 days before the end date, so there is no last-week scramble and no gap in service.
What early signs tell you an account may not renew?
Whether you spot churn risk before the customer tells you.
Concrete signals like falling usage, a silent champion or a new leader, and a quick, direct response.

Logins and usage dropping, a champion who stops answering, support tickets that turn sharp, or a new executive who did not choose us. Questions about the contract end date or exporting data are a big warning. When I see two of these together I call that week, ask plainly how things are going, and bring a plan to fix the gap, not a discount.
Your main contact at a large account leaves the company. What do you do?
How you protect an account that depends on one person.
Fast contact with the successor, a fresh case for value, and more relationships across the account.

I reach the replacement or their manager within days, before someone else tells the story. I review the value we delivered and ask about their goals now. Then I widen the circle: users, the budget owner and IT, so the account never hangs on one person again. I also keep in touch with the old contact, who may bring us into their new company.
How do you run a business review that the customer finds worth their time?
Whether your account reviews are about the customer's results, not your product.
An agenda set with the customer, results in their terms, open issues faced honestly, and clear next steps.

I send a short agenda a week ahead and ask what they want to cover. I open with their goals and results in their numbers, like hours saved, not our feature list. Then the problems we still owe answers on, and one or two roadmap items that matter to them. I end with next steps and owners. If an upsell fits, it comes from their goals, not a forced slide.
A customer is using more seats than their contract covers. How do you handle it?
How you raise a money issue without damaging the relationship.
Checking the data first, framing growth as a good sign, and offering fair options instead of a surprise bill.

First I check the data is right. Then I raise it as a fact, not an accusation: usage grew, which usually means the tool works for them. I show the contract terms and the numbers and offer options: pay for the extra seats now, add them at renewal, or remove inactive users. Most customers settle it fairly when it does not arrive as a surprise invoice.
You see an upsell that would help your number, but you doubt it helps the customer. What do you do?
Your judgement when your quota and the customer's interest pull apart.
Putting the long-term account first, testing the need honestly, and knowing unused purchases hurt renewals.

I do not push it. If they buy something they do not use, it becomes shelfware, software they pay for and ignore, and it puts the whole renewal at risk. I tell them what I see, ask whether the problem it solves is real for them, and suggest a small pilot if they are unsure. I would rather miss a quarter's number than lose their trust.
You have to pass on a price increase at renewal. How do you tell the customer?
How you deliver bad news on price and keep the renewal.
Early notice within the contract terms, a plain reason, value shown, and trade-offs ready instead of a flat discount.

I tell them early, with at least the notice the contract requires and never by invoice. I say the number plainly, give the reason in a sentence or two, and tie it to the value they have had. Then I offer options, like locking a longer term at a lower rate or adjusting scope. If I give something, I get something back, such as a longer commitment.
A key customer had a long outage, renewal is in two months, and they want a credit. How do you handle it?
How you handle a real failure on your side right before a renewal.
Owning the failure, getting the facts from engineering, honoring the contract terms, and rebuilding trust before renewal.

I own it first. I get the incident report from engineering and walk them through what broke, why, and what changed so it will not repeat. I check the service level agreement in their contract to see what credit they are owed and get it approved fast. I keep the credit separate from renewal talks, then set regular check-ins to rebuild confidence before the date.
How do you decide which accounts in your book get most of your time?
How you tier a book of business instead of answering whoever calls loudest.
A clear basis such as revenue, growth potential and churn risk, with a lighter touch, not no touch, for small accounts.

I tier the book on three things: current revenue, room to grow, and risk of churn. The top tier gets a written plan, monthly contact and quarterly reviews. The middle gets regular check-ins. Small, stable accounts get email and webinars, but I still look at their usage every month so a problem does not surprise me.
How do you multi-thread an account, and how do you know when you have enough contacts?
Whether you lower the risk of one relationship carrying the whole account.
Contacts at the user, manager and budget level, each with a real reason to talk to you, not just names in the CRM.

I want at least a daily user, the person who owns the outcome, and the person who approves the budget. Each needs their own reason to meet me: training for users, results for the owner, cost and risk for the buyer. I know it is enough when the account would still renew if my champion left tomorrow.
Your champion loves the product, but you have never met the person who signs. Renewal is in four months. What do you do?
How you reach the economic buyer without going around your champion.
Working with the champion to get the meeting, and bringing the buyer something of value, like results stated in money or time.

I tell my champion plainly that renewals get questioned at the budget level and I want to help them defend it. We build a one-page summary of results together, in dollars or hours saved, and they invite their boss to a short review. I do not go around them. If they block it, that is a risk I flag in my forecast.
A customer wants to cut seats by 40% at renewal. How do you handle it?
How you respond to a downsell without fighting the customer's real usage.
Finding out why first; accepting a right-size when usage supports it, and protecting trust and future growth.

First I find out why: a budget cut, layoffs, or low adoption. If 40% of the seats really sit unused, I agree to right-size, because charging for software nobody uses costs trust and later the whole account. If it is adoption, I offer a plan to get those users active, maybe a smaller cut now with a check-in halfway through the term.
Procurement asks for a 15% discount at renewal with nothing else changing. What do you do?
Your negotiation discipline: trading concessions, not giving them away.
No free discount. Any concession is traded for value such as a longer term, more volume, prepayment or an earlier signature.

I ask what is behind the number, since procurement often has a savings target to hit. Then I trade. A lower price could come with a two-year term, more seats, prepayment, or signing before quarter end. If they want nothing to change, the price does not change either, and I show the value they got last year to back that up.
The customer will sign a three-year deal if you cap yearly price increases. How do you structure it?
Whether you understand multi-year terms, their trade-offs and your approval limits.
A cap is a fair trade for a longer commitment; agree the cap, term and billing within limits set by finance or deal desk.

A three-year commitment is worth something to us, so a cap on yearly increases is a fair trade. I would propose a fixed percentage cap per year, annual billing, and added seats at the contracted rate. Before I offer it, I check with finance and the deal desk on what cap I can give, so I do not promise terms that get rejected later.
A customer says they will renew only if a feature on your roadmap ships by spring. What do you do?
Whether you avoid promising what you do not control.
No roadmap date in the contract or in writing; bring in product, give honest timing, and find a way to meet the need now.

I would not put a roadmap date in the contract or promise it by email, because dates move and that becomes a broken promise. I would bring a product manager to hear the need and share what they can honestly say. Then I look for a workaround that solves the problem today, so the renewal rests on what they already have.
How do you forecast your renewals for the quarter, and what makes a deal “commit”?
How accurate and honest you are about what will close.
Clear criteria tied to what the buyer has done, such as a yes from the signer and paperwork in process, not a good feeling.

I place each renewal in a category based on what the customer has done, not what I hope. Commit means the signer said yes, the price is agreed and the order form is with their legal or procurement team. Best case means good signals but something still open. I would rather call a deal at risk early than surprise my manager on the last day.
A customer sends a notice that they will not renew. The contract ends in 60 days. What do you do?
How you handle a churn notice: a real save attempt, learning, and a clean exit.
A quick call to learn the real reason, an offer only if it fixes that reason, and a respectful, helpful exit if not.

I call the same day, ask what led to it, and listen. If the reason is something we can fix, like a missing integration or poor onboarding, I bring a concrete plan and the right people. If they chose a competitor for good reasons, I make the exit smooth, help with their data, and ask for honest feedback. A clean exit leaves the door open.
How do you find expansion in an account that already uses your core product fully?
Whether you find growth by understanding the customer's business, not by pushing products.
Looking for other teams, use cases or company goals where the product solves a real problem, with a sponsor who will make the case.

I look sideways: which other departments have the same problem, and who in the account knows them. I ask my sponsor about next year's goals and where they collide with work still done by hand. Then I offer the new team a small pilot, with results from the team already using it. Growth that solves a real problem renews; growth pushed in does not.

accounting.heading: Accounting questions
qs: A client buys $5,000 of services on credit and pays 30 days later. What are the journal entries?
Whether you have debits and credits down cold.
Both entries are right: revenue when earned against receivables, then cash against receivables when paid, with no revenue booked twice.

When the work is done and invoiced, I debit accounts receivable $5,000 and credit revenue $5,000. When the payment arrives 30 days later, I debit cash $5,000 and credit accounts receivable $5,000. Revenue is recorded once, when earned. The payment only turns the receivable into cash.
What is the difference between a prepaid expense and an accrued expense?
Your grasp of the timing between paying for something and using it.
Prepaid is paid before it is used and sits as an asset. Accrued is used before it is billed or paid and sits as a liability.

A prepaid expense is paid first and used later, like a year of insurance paid in advance. It sits as an asset and is expensed month by month. An accrued expense is the reverse: we used the service, say January electricity, but have no bill yet. I book the expense and a liability so January carries its own cost.
What is a three-way match in accounts payable, and why does it matter?
Whether you know the basic control before a vendor gets paid.
Purchase order, receiving record and invoice agree on item, quantity and price before payment. It stops paying for things not ordered or not received.

Before I approve an invoice, I compare it with the purchase order and the receiving report. The PO says what we agreed to buy and at what price, the receiving report says what actually arrived, and the invoice says what the vendor bills. If quantity or price do not agree, I hold the invoice and ask purchasing or the vendor before it gets paid.
Why do you need a W-9 before you pay a new vendor?
Whether you know the vendor tax paperwork that payables handles.
The W-9 gives the legal name, taxpayer ID and tax classification needed to decide on and file 1099s. Getting it up front avoids a year-end scramble.

The W-9 gives me the vendor's legal name, taxpayer ID number and entity type. That tells me whether the vendor will need a 1099 at year-end, for example a sole proprietor we pay for services. If I wait until January, some vendors never answer. If a vendor will not give a valid ID, backup withholding may apply, so I flag it before the first payment.
The office buys a $3,000 laptop. Do you expense it or capitalize it?
How you apply a capitalization policy.
Follows the company's written threshold and useful life. If capitalized, the laptop becomes a fixed asset depreciated over its life.

I check our capitalization policy first. If the laptop is above the threshold and will be used for more than a year, I record it as a fixed asset and depreciate it, for example straight-line over three years, so about $83 a month. If it is below the threshold, it goes straight to expense. Either way, I apply the policy the same way every time.
A customer pays $12,000 on January 1 for a year of service. How do you record it?
Whether you know that revenue follows delivery, not cash.
Cash comes in with deferred revenue as a liability, then revenue is recognized as the service is delivered, here $1,000 a month.

On January 1, I debit cash $12,000 and credit deferred revenue, a liability, because we still owe the service. If the service is delivered evenly, each month-end I debit deferred revenue $1,000 and credit revenue $1,000. By December 31 the liability is zero and the full $12,000 is in revenue for the year.
It is January 31. A contractor did $8,000 of work this month, but the invoice will come in February. What do you do?
Whether you handle cutoff with accruals and reversals.
Accrue the cost in January with support, reverse it on February 1, then book the real invoice so the cost is not counted twice.

I book an accrual on January 31: debit the expense $8,000, credit accrued liabilities, with the email or contract as support. On February 1 the entry reverses. When the invoice comes in, accounts payable books it normally and the reversal offsets it. If the invoice is $8,400, only the $400 difference lands in February.
How do you estimate the allowance for doubtful accounts?
Your judgement on receivables that may not be collected.
Uses the aging with loss rates based on history and current conditions, reviews large past-due accounts one by one, and books the change to bad debt expense.

I start with the accounts receivable aging. Each age bucket gets a loss rate from our own history, adjusted if conditions have changed, so older buckets carry higher rates. Large past-due balances I review by name with the credit team. Then I adjust the allowance to that total and book the difference to bad debt expense. A truly uncollectible account is written off against the allowance.
A vendor emails asking you to send future payments to a new bank account. What do you do?
How you guard against payment fraud.
No change on email alone: call the vendor at a number already on file, get a second approval, and watch the first payment.

I do not change anything based on the email. I call the vendor using the phone number already in our vendor file, not the one in the email, and confirm with someone I know there. Then a second person approves the change in the system, and I tell the controller. Fake bank-change requests are a common fraud, and wired money is often gone for good.
You find an expense booked to the wrong month three months ago, and that period is closed. What do you do?
How you own and fix an error in closed books.
Tells the controller, sizes the error, corrects it in the open period if immaterial with a clear note, and fixes the cause. Material errors may need restating.

First I size it and tell my controller. I do not reopen a closed period on my own. If it is immaterial, the usual fix is a correcting entry in the current month, with a memo that explains it and links the support. If it is material, the controller decides on restating prior periods. Then I look at why it happened, like a missed cutoff check, and fix that step.
On a bank reconciliation, which reconciling items need a journal entry on your books and which do not?
Whether you know which side of a bank reconciliation each item belongs to.
Fees, interest and returned checks get book entries. Timing items get none, and bank errors are fixed by the bank, not in your ledger.

Outstanding checks and deposits in transit are timing. The bank will catch up, so I book nothing. Bank fees, interest earned and customer checks returned for insufficient funds are things the bank knew first, so I book them. If the bank made an error, I ask the bank to correct it and leave my books alone.
We sell a machine that cost $50,000, with $35,000 of accumulated depreciation, for $18,000 cash. Walk me through the entry.
Your handling of a fixed asset disposal from start to finish.
Depreciation brought up to the sale date first, the asset and its accumulated depreciation removed, and the $3,000 gain worked out correctly.

First I make sure depreciation is booked through the sale date, so the $35,000 is current. Book value is $15,000, so an $18,000 sale is a $3,000 gain. I debit cash $18,000 and accumulated depreciation $35,000. I credit equipment $50,000 and gain on sale $3,000. Then I remove the machine from the fixed asset register.
Some of our inventory now sells for less than it cost us. How do you account for that?
Your knowledge of inventory write-downs under US GAAP.
Lower of cost and net realizable value for FIFO or average cost, a write-down in the current period, and the lower amount becoming the new cost basis.

Under FIFO or average cost, inventory is carried at the lower of cost and net realizable value. That is the expected selling price minus the costs to complete and sell. If a $40 unit now nets only $32, I write it down $8 and charge the loss to cost of goods sold. The $32 becomes the new cost, so a later price recovery does not reverse it in the annual statements.
Why is depreciation on our books often different from depreciation on the tax return, and what does that difference create?
Whether you understand temporary differences between book and tax.
Different methods for different purposes, creating a temporary difference and usually a deferred tax liability when tax deductions come first.

The books follow US GAAP, usually straight-line over the useful life. The tax return can use faster schedules, like MACRS or bonus depreciation. Over the asset's life the difference reverses; only the timing changes. When tax deductions run ahead of book depreciation, we pay less tax now and more later, so we record a deferred tax liability.
We sign a five-year office lease. How does it show up on the balance sheet under ASC 842?
Whether you know current lease accounting rather than the old off-balance-sheet rules.
A lease liability at the present value of payments and a matching right-of-use asset, with the 12-month short-term exception mentioned.

At the start date I record a lease liability at the present value of the payments. I discount at the rate in the lease or, usually, our incremental borrowing rate. The right-of-use asset starts at the same amount, adjusted for prepaid rent or incentives. As an operating lease, it shows one straight-line lease cost. Only leases of 12 months or less can stay off the balance sheet.
A customer pays $120,000 for a software license plus two years of support. How do you recognize the revenue?
How you apply the ASC 606 five steps to a contract with more than one promise.
Two performance obligations, the price split by standalone selling price, the license recognized at a point in time and support recognized over time.

Under ASC 606 I identify the contract, then the promises. The license and the support are usually distinct, so there are two performance obligations. I allocate the $120,000 by standalone selling prices, say $90,000 and $30,000. License revenue is recognized when the customer can use the software. Support is spread over 24 months, $1,250 a month.
Legal says we will probably lose a customer lawsuit, with a payout between $200,000 and $500,000. What do you book?
Your knowledge of loss contingency rules under ASC 450.
Accrue when a loss is probable and estimable. With no best estimate in the range, accrue the low end and disclose the possible higher amount.

A loss that is probable and can be reasonably estimated must be accrued. If legal has a best estimate inside the range, I book that. If no amount is more likely than another, ASC 450 says to accrue the minimum, $200,000, and disclose that it could reach $500,000. If the loss were only reasonably possible, I would disclose it and book nothing.
Our year ended December 31. On February 10, before the statements are issued, a big customer files for bankruptcy. Does that change December?
Whether you know the difference between recognized and nonrecognized subsequent events.
It depends on whether the condition existed at year end. Adjust the allowance if it did; disclose if an event after year end caused it.

Under ASC 855 I ask whether the condition existed at the balance sheet date. If the customer was already in trouble in December, with late payments and losses, the bankruptcy confirms it, so I adjust the December allowance. If a sudden event after year end caused it, like a fire in January, I leave December alone and disclose it if it is material.
At month-end, one subsidiary shows a $48,000 receivable from another, which shows only $45,000 payable. How do you handle it?
How you work through intercompany differences before consolidation.
Both sides matched and the cause found before elimination, not a plug to make the consolidation balance.

Intercompany balances have to match before I eliminate them, or the consolidation is wrong. I pull both ledgers and match them line by line. Usually it is timing, such as an invoice one side booked and the other has not, or a currency rate difference. Once I find the $3,000, the side that is wrong books the correction. I never plug it, and I fix the cause, like a shared cutoff date.
Your controller asks you to hold a $60,000 accrual until next month so the quarter hits its target. What do you do?
Your integrity when the numbers are under pressure from above.
A calm refusal to misstate the period, openness to a better estimate, and escalation if the pressure continues.

I would say I can't do it. The expense belongs to this quarter under accrual accounting, and leaving it out misstates the results. I would show the support for the amount and ask if there is a real reason to doubt it, because a better estimate is fine. If the request stands, I would take it to the CFO or the audit committee and keep notes of what was asked.

accounts-payable.heading: Accounts payable specialist questions
qs: What is a three-way match, and why do we use it?
Whether you know the basic control behind every purchase-order invoice.
Purchase order, receiving record and invoice must agree on item, quantity and price before payment, so we only pay for what we ordered and received.

I compare three documents: the purchase order, the receiving report and the vendor invoice. Items, quantities and prices must agree. If the PO says 100 units at $4 and the dock received 90, I pay for 90, not 100. The match stops us from paying for goods we never ordered or never got.
An invoice says "2/10 net 30." What does that mean, and would you take the discount?
Your grasp of payment terms and what early-payment discounts are worth.
Full amount due in 30 days, 2% off if paid within 10. Paying 20 days early for 2% is worth roughly 37% a year, so take it when cash allows.

The full amount is due in 30 days, but we can take 2% off if we pay within 10. Paying 20 days early to save 2% works out to roughly 37% a year, so if we have the cash it almost always beats keeping the money in the bank. I schedule those invoices to pay near day 10, not earlier.
An invoice arrives with no purchase order number and no approval. What do you do?
Whether you hold to approval rules instead of paying because a bill looks real.
Do not pay. Log it, find who ordered it, get approval from the right person under the approval limits, and keep the record.

I log it so it does not get lost, then find out who ordered it, from the vendor contact or the department. I send it to that budget owner for approval within their limit. If nobody claims it, I ask the vendor for proof of the order. It does not get paid until someone with authority signs off.
The invoice price is higher than the price on the purchase order. How do you handle it?
How you deal with price differences and tolerances.
Check the company's tolerance; above it, put the invoice on hold and send it to the buyer, not quietly pay or short-pay without a record.

First I check our match tolerance. If the gap is within it, the system lets it through. If not, I put the invoice on hold and send it to the buyer with both prices. Either the buyer updates the PO with a reason, or the vendor sends a corrected invoice or credit memo. I note the outcome on the invoice record.
How do you make sure the same invoice is never paid twice?
Your methods for catching duplicate payments before money leaves.
System checks on vendor plus invoice number, plus manual review for near-matches: same amount and date, typos, copies or statements sent as invoices.

The system blocks the same invoice number for the same vendor, but duplicates sneak past that: a dash added, a zero dropped, or a copy sent to a second person. So before each payment run I review a report of same vendor, same amount, close dates. I also never pay from a statement or a "second notice" without checking the original.
What tax forms do you collect from vendors, and how do they tie to year-end reporting?
Whether you know the W-9 and 1099 process for US vendors.
A W-9 before the first payment, flags for 1099-reportable vendors, tracking payments for services, and awareness of exceptions like corporations and attorneys.

I get a signed W-9 before the first payment: legal name, tax ID and entity type. Individuals and most LLCs paid for services get flagged for a 1099-NEC. Corporations are mostly exempt, but attorneys' fees are reported anyway. Payments by credit card are left out, since the card processor reports those. Without a valid tax ID, backup withholding applies.
You get an email from a regular vendor asking you to send future payments to a new bank account. What do you do?
Whether you spot payment fraud and follow verification steps.
Treat it as possible fraud: call the vendor at a number already on file, never one in the email, and have a second person approve the change.

I change nothing based on an email. Fake vendor emails are one of the most common ways companies lose money. I call the vendor at the phone number already in our file, not the one in the message, and confirm with someone I know. The change needs a written form and a second person's approval. I also watch the first payment to the new account.
A senior manager asks you to pay an urgent invoice today and skip the usual approval. How do you respond?
Your judgement when pressure meets internal controls.
Help with speed, not by dropping controls: get the right approval fast, document it, and escalate if pushed, since urgency is a common fraud tactic.

I say I want to get it paid today and ask who the approver is so I can reach them now. Most of the time a quick call gets the sign-off within the hour. If the manager insists I skip it, I explain I cannot, and I bring in my supervisor. Urgent requests to bypass approval are exactly what fraudsters use, so the rule protects both of us.
Cash is tight this week and you cannot pay every bill that is due. How do you decide what gets paid?
How you weigh priorities and who you involve when there is not enough cash.
Use the aging report, put critical items first (payroll taxes, key suppliers, items with penalties), and get the decision approved by the controller.

I run the aging report and group bills by risk. Taxes, payroll-related items, rent, and suppliers who would stop shipping go first, then bills with late fees. Bills not yet due can wait. I bring the list to the controller to decide, since it is not my call alone. Then I call the vendors we delay and give them a real payment date.
A vendor's statement lists three invoices you have no record of. How do you work it?
How you reconcile a vendor statement line by line instead of just paying the balance.
You get copies, check whether they were keyed under another number or already paid, and confirm receipt and approval before entering them.

I ask the vendor for copies and search our system by amount, date and PO number, in case they were keyed under a different invoice number. Then I check with receiving and the buyer that we actually got the goods. Only valid, approved invoices get entered. I note each item on the reconciliation so next month starts clean.
At month-end, goods have arrived but the invoice has not. What do you record?
Your grasp of accruals and period cutoff in accounts payable.
An accrual for the received goods at the PO price, reversed next period when the real invoice is entered.

The cost belongs to the month we received the goods, so I book an accrual, usually from the received-not-invoiced report, at the PO price. It reverses on the first day of next month, and the real invoice is entered as normal. I check large items with the buyer so we do not accrue for a shipment that was rejected.
A vendor in another state sold us taxable equipment and charged no sales tax. What happens?
Whether you know when the buyer owes use tax.
Unless an exemption applies, the buyer self-assesses use tax to the state where the item is used and keeps a record of it.

If the item is taxable where we use it and the seller did not collect tax, we generally owe use tax ourselves. I check whether an exemption applies, like goods bought for resale with a certificate on file. If not, I flag it so use tax is accrued and reported on our return for that state. I keep a list so these are not missed.
Which vendor payments go on a 1099-NEC, which on a 1099-MISC, and which on neither?
Your detailed knowledge of 1099 reporting rules.
NEC for services by non-employees, MISC for rents and royalties; goods, most corporations and card payments are left off, with attorney fees as an exception.

Fees for services from contractors go on the 1099-NEC, including legal fees. Rents and royalties go on the 1099-MISC. Payments for goods are not reported, and payments to corporations generally are not, except attorney fees and medical payments. Anything we paid by credit card is left off, because the card processor reports it on a 1099-K.
The IRS sends a notice saying several vendors' names and tax ID numbers do not match. Walk me through what you do.
Whether you know the B-notice and backup withholding process.
Check for your own keying errors, send B-notices with a W-9 request on time, and start backup withholding if no valid number comes back.

That is a CP2100 notice. First I compare it to the W-9s on file, since some are our own typos. For the rest I mail a B-notice with a blank W-9 within 15 business days. If no corrected W-9 comes back, backup withholding must start no later than 30 business days after we received the notice, and it is reported on Form 945 and the vendor's 1099.
You find vendor checks from two years ago that were never cashed. What do you do with them?
Whether you know how unclaimed property rules apply to payables.
Contact the vendor and reissue if owed; if unclaimed, report and remit to the state after the dormancy period instead of writing it off.

I would not write them back to income. First I check whether the vendor was paid another way or still holds the check. If they are owed, I reissue. If I cannot reach them, the money is unclaimed property. We send a due diligence letter, then report and remit it to the state of the vendor's last known address once that state's dormancy period passes.
You discover a vendor was paid twice for the same invoice last month. How do you get the money back?
How you recover an error and fix its cause, not only the symptom.
Confirm it, ask for a refund or a credit against open invoices, book it correctly, and find out why the control missed it.

I confirm both payments cleared the bank and that it truly is one invoice. Then I call the vendor, ask for a refund or a credit against our next invoices, and put it in writing. I record a receivable until it is settled. Last, I find why our check missed it, say an invoice number keyed once with a dash, and tighten the duplicate rule.
In a well-run AP team, who should not be able to do what?
Your understanding of segregation of duties in payables.
The person who sets up or changes vendors does not enter invoices or release payments, and every vendor change is reviewed.

The person who creates or changes vendor records, especially bank details, should not also enter invoices or release payments. Approvers should not be the people who pay. In a small team I add a review: a weekly report of every vendor master change, checked by someone outside AP. That way no one person can invent a vendor and pay it.
Before a payment run goes to the bank, what do you check?
How carefully you review a payment run before money leaves the company.
Totals tie to the approved list, no duplicates or unverified bank changes, discounts taken, and a positive pay file sent for checks.

I tie the run total and count to the approved proposal. I scan for duplicate amounts to the same vendor, new vendors, and any bank detail changed since the last run, and confirm each change was verified by a callback. I check that discounts due were taken. For checks, I send the positive pay file so the bank only clears checks we issued.
The auditor asks you to show that payables are complete at year-end. How do you support that?
Whether you know how unrecorded liabilities are searched for and proven.
A search of payments and invoices after year-end, plus received-not-invoiced items, showing each was booked in the right period.

Completeness means nothing we owed at year-end is missing. I pull payments made and invoices received in the weeks after year-end, show which relate to goods or services from before the cutoff, and show each was accrued. I add the received-not-invoiced report and vendor statements. Anything we missed, I book as an adjustment and explain.

accounts-receivable.heading: Accounts receivable and collections specialist questions
qs: What is DSO, and how do you calculate it?
Your grasp of the main measure of how fast customers pay.
The formula, the period it covers, and what a rising number tells you.

Days sales outstanding is the average number of days it takes to collect a sale. I take accounts receivable at period end, divide it by credit sales for the period, and multiply by the days in the period. If DSO climbs from 38 to 47 days, cash is coming in slower, and I go to the aging to see which customers are behind.
What do you look at first on an AR aging report?
How you find where the collection risk sits.
Focus on the oldest buckets and the biggest balances, plus a check for credits that distort the totals.

I look at the buckets past 60 and 90 days and at who owns most of the money there. One customer with $40,000 at 75 days matters more than twenty small invoices at 35. I also check for credits and unapplied cash in the report, because they make the totals look better or worse than they really are.
Walk me through a first call to a customer who is 30 days past due.
How you run a collection call that ends in a firm commitment.
Right contact, clear facts, a question about what is blocking payment, and a promise with an amount and a date.

I confirm I am speaking with the person who handles payables, then give the invoice number, amount and due date. I ask if they received it and whether anything is holding it up. Often it is a missing PO number or a wrong billing address. I end with a specific promise, an amount and a date, and send an email the same day that restates it.
What rules do you follow when you call a customer about money they owe?
Whether you know where collection law applies and collect fairly anyway.
Knows the FDCPA mainly targets third-party collectors of consumer debt, and keeps every call honest and private.

The federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act mostly covers third-party collectors of consumer debt, not a company collecting its own business invoices. Some states, like California, extend similar rules to creditors. Either way I keep the same habits: no threats, nothing untrue, reasonable calling hours, and I never discuss the debt with anyone but the customer or their authorized contact.
A $12,480 ACH payment arrives with no remittance detail. How do you apply it?
Your cash application method when the payment does not say what it pays.
Uses bank details and invoice matching, and parks the cash as unapplied rather than guessing.

First I check the bank detail for the payer name and any reference number. Then I search that customer's open invoices for an exact match or a set of invoices that adds up to 12,480. If I cannot match it with confidence, I post it as unapplied cash on their account and email their AP team for the remittance. A wrong guess creates two problems instead of one.
A customer pays $9,200 on a $10,000 invoice. What do you do with the missing $800?
How you handle short payments and deductions.
Leaves the gap open, finds the reason, gets it validated, then credits it or collects it.

I apply the 9,200 and leave the 800 open as a deduction, not a write-off. Then I find the reason: a price difference, damaged goods, or an early-pay discount taken after the discount date. I send it to sales or shipping to confirm. If the deduction is valid we issue a credit memo. If not, I go back to the customer with the backup, like the signed delivery receipt, and collect it.
What is the difference between the allowance for doubtful accounts and a write-off?
Your understanding of how bad debt is recorded.
The allowance is an estimate booked ahead; a write-off removes a specific invoice against that allowance.

The allowance is our estimate of what we will not collect, booked ahead as bad debt expense, often as a percentage of each aging bucket. A write-off removes a specific invoice once we decide it is uncollectible: debit the allowance, credit accounts receivable. Under the allowance method the write-off itself does not hit expense a second time.
You discover you applied a payment to the wrong customer two weeks ago. What do you do?
How you own and fix a cash application mistake.
Reports it, reverses and reapplies, contacts any customer affected, and closes the gap that caused it.

I tell my lead right away, then reverse the application and reapply the cash to the right account and invoices. I check whether either customer got a statement or a reminder letter in the meantime, and if so I call them to correct it. Then I look at the cause, say two similar company names, and start matching on customer number, not just name.
Your largest customer is over its credit limit, and sales wants a new order shipped today. What do you do?
Your judgement between protecting cash and keeping a key customer.
Gets facts and a payment commitment fast, then gives the decision maker a clear recommendation in writing.

I do not just say no or just release it. I check how old the balance is and whether recent payments are on time. Then I call their AP and ask for a payment on the oldest invoices today. The release is the credit manager's call, so I bring the numbers, my recommendation and the risk in writing, so sales gets an answer within the hour.
We have old credit balances sitting on customer accounts. What do you do with them?
Whether you know a credit balance is money owed back, not income.
Researches each one, refunds or applies it, and knows unclaimed balances may have to be reported to the state.

A credit balance is money we owe the customer, so it cannot just be moved to income. I research each one: an overpayment, a duplicate payment, a credit memo never used. Then I offer a refund or apply it to open invoices and document the contact. If the customer cannot be reached, the balance may have to be reported to the state as unclaimed property, so I work with accounting on that.
What is a lockbox, and how does it change the way you apply cash?
Whether you know how payments reach the company and what that means for your daily work.
The bank receives and deposits checks and sends images and data. You work the exceptions instead of keying every check.

With a lockbox, customers mail checks to a bank address. The bank deposits them and sends us a file with check images and remittance data. Most payments then match to open invoices automatically, and my day is the exceptions: no invoice number, short pays, or one check covering ten invoices with a few missing.
A customer on 2/10 net 30 terms pays $9,800 on a $10,000 invoice on day 25. How do you handle it?
How you enforce payment terms without damaging the relationship.
You see an unearned discount, follow the written policy, and recover or approve the $200 openly instead of quietly writing it off.

The 2% discount was only earned if they paid within 10 days, so the $200 is unearned. I apply the $9,800, leave $200 open, and send a short note with the invoice date, terms and payment date. If it is a good account, I may ask my manager to allow it once, documented, and tell the customer the next one will be billed.
A big retail customer short-pays every month with chargebacks for late delivery and labeling errors. How do you manage that?
Whether you can work deductions as a process, not one dispute at a time.
Codes each deduction, pulls proof, disputes invalid ones within the customer's deadline, and reports root causes to shipping and sales.

I log every deduction with a reason code. For each one I pull the proof of delivery, the bill of lading and the retailer's routing guide. Invalid ones I dispute in the retailer's portal before its deadline. Valid ones I clear with approval. Each month I show shipping and sales which causes cost the most, because fixing one labeling problem beats fighting a hundred claims.
How do you set a credit limit for a new customer?
Your judgement in extending credit before any sale is made.
A credit application, references, a credit report and, for large limits, financial statements, sized to expected orders and reviewed later.

I start with a signed credit application, then check trade references and a business credit report for payment habits, liens or judgments. For a large request I ask for financial statements. I set the limit near expected monthly purchases, start lower if the data is thin, and review it after six months of payments.
Why should the person who applies cash not also be able to issue credit memos or write off balances?
Whether you understand the controls that protect receivables from theft.
Explains how one person could steal a payment and hide it, including lapping, and the approval and review that stop it.

If one person can take in payments and also clear balances, they can steal a payment and hide it with a credit memo or write-off. Another trick is lapping: covering customer A's stolen payment with customer B's payment, and so on. Credits and write-offs should need someone else's approval, and customers should get statements so they would notice.
DSO went up five days last month, but the share of past-due AR went down. How can both be true?
How you read a metric before drawing a conclusion from it.
Points to sales timing: a late-month sales spike adds AR that is not yet due and raises simple DSO. Confirms with the aging or a countback.

Simple DSO divides ending AR by average daily sales. If a lot of sales landed in the last week of the month, ending AR jumps with invoices that are not even due yet, so DSO rises while collections are fine. I would confirm with the aging and a countback DSO, which matches AR against the most recent months of sales.
A customer pays an invoice we wrote off last year. How do you record it?
Whether you can record a recovery correctly under the allowance method.
Reinstates the receivable against the allowance, then records the cash against it, so the customer's history shows the payment.

Under the allowance method I first reverse the write-off: debit accounts receivable, credit the allowance for doubtful accounts. Then I record the receipt as usual: debit cash, credit accounts receivable. That way the account shows the customer paid, which matters if they ask for credit again.
A customer says they paid last month's invoices to a new bank account from an email that looked like ours. What do you do?
How you respond to payment fraud aimed at your customers.
Acts fast: escalates, has the customer ask their bank for a recall, keeps invoices open, checks for a breach and warns other customers.

I escalate to my manager and IT within the hour, since speed is the best chance to get money back. I ask the customer to call their bank now to request a recall. The invoices stay open until we are paid. We check whether our email was breached, and remind customers we never change bank details by email and they should confirm by phone at a number they already have.
A customer with $85,000 open files for Chapter 11. What do you do?
Whether you know what bankruptcy changes for collections and how to protect the company's claim.
Stops collecting pre-filing debt because of the automatic stay, files a proof of claim, and checks for priority on goods received in the 20 days before filing.

The automatic stay means I stop all calls and letters about the $85,000 right away and put the account on hold. I tell sales and legal, and we file a proof of claim before the deadline. Goods the customer received in the 20 days before filing may get priority, so I pull those delivery dates. Any new sales go on approved terms, often cash in advance.
A customer has missed three promised payment dates on a 75-day-old balance. Walk me through what you do next.
How you escalate firmly and in order when a customer stops keeping its word.
Moves to a decision-maker, credit hold, a written demand with a date, then an agency or attorney with approval, documenting each step.

I stop accepting vague promises. I ask for someone who can approve payment, like the controller, and get a specific amount and date, or a written payment plan. The account goes on credit hold. If that fails, I send a final demand letter with a deadline, then recommend to my manager placing it with an agency or attorney. Every call and promise is in my notes.

actuary.heading: Actuary questions
qs: What is IBNR, and why does an insurer have to hold it?
Whether you know the basic pieces of a claims reserve.
Claims incurred but not yet reported, often also covering growth on known claims. It is held because the insurer already owes for events that have happened.

IBNR stands for incurred but not reported. The accident has already happened, so the insurer owes for it, but the claim has not reached us yet. In practice the bulk IBNR usually also covers future growth on claims we already know about, beyond the case reserves adjusters set. Without it, the balance sheet would understate what the company owes.
Walk me through the chain-ladder method.
Your grasp of the most common reserving method.
Triangle, age-to-age factors, selections and a tail, factor to ultimate, then IBNR. Also the assumption that past patterns repeat.

I lay out cumulative losses in a triangle by accident year and age. I compute age-to-age factors, look at several averages, and select a factor for each age, plus a tail factor. Multiplying them gives a factor to ultimate for each year. Ultimate minus reported losses is IBNR. The method assumes past development will repeat, so I check that first.
Long-term interest rates drop by one percent. What happens to a pension plan's liability, and why?
Whether you understand discounting and duration in pension work.
The liability goes up because future payments are discounted at a lower rate. The size is roughly duration times the rate change.

The liability rises. It is the present value of benefits paid decades out, so a lower discount rate makes each payment worth more today. A quick estimate is duration times the rate change: a plan with a duration of 12 sees its liability rise about 12%. Bond assets may rise too, so I would look at funded status, not just one side.
When would you use the loss ratio method instead of the pure premium method to set rates?
Your knowledge of the core ratemaking methods.
Loss ratio gives a change to current rates and needs on-level premium. Pure premium gives a rate directly from exposures and suits new products.

The loss ratio method compares projected losses to premium restated at current rate levels, so it gives a percent change to existing rates. It needs a reliable rate history. The pure premium method divides projected losses by exposures and loads for expenses and profit, so it gives a rate directly. I use it for a new product or when past rate changes are hard to rebuild.
A small employer group ran far better than the manual rate last year. How much should their renewal reflect that?
How you use credibility to weigh a group's own data against the wider book.
A blend of group experience and the manual rate, with a credibility weight that grows with size, and the point that one good year is often luck.

Not fully. For a small group, one quiet year is mostly chance. I would give their experience a credibility weight based on size, for example the square root rule against a full-credibility claim count, and put the rest on the manual rate. If credibility is 20%, a result 40% better than manual moves their rate about 8%. That is fair to them and protects the pool.
For the most recent accident year, the chain-ladder result looks unreliable. What would you use instead?
Whether you know where chain ladder breaks down and what replaces it.
Bornhuetter-Ferguson or an expected loss ratio method, because large early factors magnify noise. BF uses an expected loss for the unreported part.

For a green year the factor to ultimate can be 5 or more, so one large early claim gets multiplied many times. I would use Bornhuetter-Ferguson: reported losses plus expected losses times the share still unreported, which is one minus one over the factor to ultimate. As the year matures, the method moves toward the chain-ladder answer on its own.
The latest diagonal of your reported loss triangle jumps well above past patterns. What do you do?
How you investigate a change in the data before it flows into the reserve.
Check the data and ask the claims team first: a large loss, stronger case reserves, faster closing, a system change. Then adjust the method to fit the cause.

First I check the data for duplicates, a new claims system or a coding change. Then I talk to the claims department. If one large loss drove it, I may treat it separately. If they strengthened case reserves, old factors would overstate IBNR, so I would lean on paid data or restate case reserves to a consistent level, as in the Berquist-Sherman approach. I document what I found.
