The information is linearly decodable there, not that the model uses it. Proof of use needs a causal test, plus controls such as the same probe on a random model.

Only that the information is present and linearly readable at that layer. The model might never use it, and a strong probe can partly learn the task itself. I would compare against baselines, such as the same probe on a randomly initialized model. Then I would intervene along the probe direction and see whether the model's behavior actually changes.
Walk me through how you would use activation patching to find which components drive a behavior.
Your hands-on grasp of a core causal method in interpretability.
Clean and corrupted runs that differ minimally, patching one component at a time, and a clear metric such as the logit difference between right and wrong answers.

I build pairs of prompts that differ in one detail, like the subject name in a fact recall task. I run the corrupted prompt, copy in the activation of one layer or head from the clean run, and measure how much of the logit difference comes back. Components that restore most of it are candidates, which I then confirm with ablations.
For a dangerous-capability eval, do you report pass@1 or pass@k, and why?
Whether your metric matches the threat model rather than leaderboard habit.
pass@k when a misuser can retry and check results, computed with the unbiased estimator from n samples, not by sampling exactly k once.

A real attacker can try many times and keep what works, so pass@1 understates the risk. I sample n attempts per task, more than k, and use the standard unbiased estimator for pass@k. I report several k values and note whether the attacker could tell a success from a failure, since retries only help if they can.
Changing the answer format from letters to full text moves a model's score by 10 points. How do you report the eval?
How you handle results that depend on incidental choices in the eval.
Treat format as a source of variance: test several reasonable templates, report the spread, and say which one the headline number uses and why.

A 10-point swing means the format is part of what we measure. I would run a small set of reasonable templates, report the mean and the range, and fix one template before comparing models, so nobody picks the format that flatters theirs. I would also read failures to see whether they are parsing errors rather than missing knowledge.
How would you test whether a model's chain of thought reflects what actually drove its answer?
Whether you test faithfulness instead of trusting the written reasoning.
Interventions: add a hint that changes the answer and see if the reasoning admits it; edit or cut the reasoning and see if the answer follows.

I would plant a hint in the prompt, like a note suggesting an answer, and find cases where the hint flips the model's answer. If the reasoning never mentions the hint, it was not faithful. I would also truncate the reasoning or insert a mistake into it. If the final answer never changes, the written steps were not doing the work.
You are setting up an eval where a model agent can run code and browse the web. How do you contain it?
Your safety practice when the model under test can act, not just answer.
Isolated environment, no real credentials, network allowlists, limits on time and resources, full logging, and a human able to stop runs.

Each run gets a fresh isolated container or VM with no production credentials, only fake accounts. Network access goes through an allowlist, with mocks for anything risky. I cap time, compute and spending, log every command and page, and review transcripts, not just the final score, because the interesting failures show up in the actions.
A colleague says a sparse autoencoder found a 'deception feature.' How would you check the claim?
How you test an interpretability label before it guides decisions.
Look beyond top examples, test on held-out cases with known labels, and show a causal effect through steering or ablation, with reconstruction error in mind.

Top activating examples are where labels mislead, so I would look at weak and random activations too. Then I would test it on a held-out set where we know which answers are deceptive and measure false positives and negatives. Finally I would clamp the feature up or down and see if behavior changes as claimed. A label is a hypothesis until those pass.
After results went to leadership, you find a grading bug that inflated a safety score. What do you do?
Your honesty and process when your own work turns out to be wrong.
Report it fast to the people who used the number, give corrected results and the decisions they affect, then add a check that would have caught it.

I tell the people who received the number the same day, before the fix is done, so no decision rests on it. Then I rerun with the fix and send the corrected score with a short note on the cause and which conclusions change. Last, I add a check, like hand-graded spot checks on a sample, so this kind of bug is caught before results leave the team.
Before a release, a capability eval lands just under the risk threshold your team committed to. How do you advise the decision?
Your judgement when evidence sits near a line with real consequences.
Uncertainty stated plainly, elicitation gaps named, the threshold not quietly reinterpreted, and a clear recommendation with what would change it.

Just under is not the same as safe. I would give the confidence interval, say how hard we tried to elicit the capability, and list what we did not test. If the interval crosses the threshold, we cannot rule it out, so I would recommend more elicitation or the safeguards set for the higher level. Changing the threshold after seeing the score is off the table.

ai-trainer.heading: AI trainer and data annotation questions
qs: In your own words, why does the quality of one label matter to a model?
Whether you understand what your work feeds into.
Models learn patterns from many examples. Wrong or inconsistent labels teach wrong patterns, and those errors are hard to find later.

A model learns from thousands of examples like mine. If I label carelessly, it learns my mistakes as if they were true, and nobody may notice until the model behaves badly. One label looks small, but the same slip repeated across a batch becomes a pattern the model copies.
You see two model responses to the same prompt and must pick the better one. How do you decide?
How you compare responses against clear criteria instead of gut feeling.
Read the prompt first, then check accuracy, instruction following, safety and clarity in the order the guideline sets. Length and polish are not the goal.

I reread the prompt to know what the user actually wanted. Then I check each answer for errors, whether it follows every instruction, and whether anything is unsafe. Only then do I look at tone and clarity. I try not to reward the longer answer just because it looks thorough, and I write a short reason for my choice.
The guideline does not cover the item in front of you. What do you do?
Whether you flag gaps instead of quietly inventing your own rule.
Apply the closest rule and its intent, flag the item or ask in the project channel, and note the case so the guideline can be updated.

I look for the closest example in the guideline and the reason behind it. If I am still unsure, I use the skip or flag option if the project has one, or ask the lead with the item ID. I do not make up a rule, because other annotators would choose differently and the data would become inconsistent.
How do you fact-check a model's answer on a subject you do not know well?
Your method for verifying claims with reliable sources.
Break the answer into separate claims, check each against primary or authoritative sources, not other AI output, and mark what could not be verified.

I split the answer into single claims: names, dates, numbers, cause and effect. For each one I look for a primary or official source, like the original study, a government page or the organization's own site. I don't use another chatbot as proof. If I can't confirm a claim in reasonable time, I say it is unverified instead of guessing.
A response is clear and well written but contains one wrong fact. How do you rate it?
Whether a confident tone can fool you.
Accuracy outweighs style. A wrong fact stated with confidence is a real problem, and the rating should follow the rubric's severity rules.

I rate it down, and I name the exact error in my comment. A polished answer with a false fact is risky because readers trust it. How far down depends on the rubric: a wrong date in a side note is minor, while a wrong fact the whole answer depends on, like a wrong safety instruction, makes the answer fail.
Walk me through writing a prompt and an ideal response for a training set.
Whether you can write examples worth learning from.
A realistic prompt and a response that is accurate, complete and follows every constraint, checked against the guideline before submitting.

I write a prompt a real user might send, with a clear task and maybe one constraint, like a word limit. Then I write the answer I'd want a model to give: correct, direct, in the right format. I check every fact, count the words, and reread it as a strict reviewer would. If any part is something I'd guess at, I change the prompt.
Your project pays per task and you notice you are falling behind the expected pace. What do you do?
How you balance speed against accuracy when time pressure is real.
No cutting quality to hit numbers. Find where time goes, raise it if hard items need longer, and gain speed through habits, not shortcuts.

First I look at where my time goes. Often it is rereading the guideline, so I make a one-page summary for myself. If certain items truly take longer, I tell the lead with examples instead of rushing them. A fast wrong label gets caught in review and costs everyone more than a slow right one.
Is it ever fine to use an AI tool to help you with annotation tasks?
Your judgement about project rules and confidentiality.
Only if the project explicitly allows it. Many forbid it, and pasting task content into outside tools can break confidentiality agreements.

Only when the project rules say so in writing. Many projects forbid it, because they want human judgement, not a model grading a model. Task content is usually confidential too, so pasting it into an outside tool could break my agreement. If the rules are unclear, I ask before I try anything.
As a reviewer, you find an annotator who makes the same error on many items. How do you handle it?
How you give quality feedback that fixes the cause, not just the item.
Correct the items, give specific feedback with examples and the rule, check whether the guideline itself is unclear, and recheck the next batch.

I fix the items I'm responsible for and write the annotator a short note: the rule, two of their examples, and the correct label. Then I ask myself whether the guideline invited the error; if three people make the same mistake, the text is the problem. I spot-check their next batch to see that it stuck.
Two annotators agree on only about 60% of items for a label. What does that tell you, and what do you do?
Whether you can diagnose a guideline problem from agreement data.
Low agreement usually means an unclear definition or a truly ambiguous category. Study the disagreements, sharpen the definition with examples, and re-test.

It usually means the label is defined loosely, not that both people are careless. I pull the items they disagreed on and sort them by reason. Then I rewrite the definition with clear borderline examples, have both annotators label a fresh sample, and compare again. Some metrics, like Cohen's kappa, also correct for agreement that would happen by chance.
A prompt asks for exactly three bullet points in under 50 words. The response is accurate and helpful but has four bullets. How do you rate it?
Whether you treat the user's explicit limits as part of the task.
The broken constraint counts as a real failure under the rubric. Good content does not excuse it.

I mark it down on instruction following, because the user asked for three bullets and got four. Good content does not cancel that; the user may need exactly three for a slide. I still note that the facts are right, so my rating shows what worked and what failed. If another response follows the format with similar content, that one wins.
While labelling customer chat logs, you find a full name, home address and phone number in one item. What do you do?
How you handle personal data you were not meant to see.
No copying or sharing and no looking the person up. You follow the project's personal-data rule and flag the item through the official channel.

I do not copy the details into notes, chats or my own files, and I do not look the person up. I check the guideline for a personal-data rule; many projects have a flag or a redact label for this. If there is none, I report only the item ID to the lead through the official channel and hold off on that item until I hear back.
A user asks, “How do I kill a Python process that froze?” and the model refuses because it sounds violent. How do you rate that?
Whether you can tell a harmful request from one that only sounds harmful.
It is an over-refusal and gets a low rating. A refusal is not automatically the safe or correct choice.

That is an over-refusal. Here “kill” is the normal word for stopping a program, and the request carries no risk. I rate it low on helpfulness and explain why, since the model should learn from context, not keywords. A good answer would say: find the frozen process and end it in Task Manager on Windows, or with the kill command on Mac or Linux.
The prompt says, “Explain why Einstein won the Nobel Prize for relativity.” What should an ideal response do?
Whether you catch a false premise instead of answering around it.
It politely corrects the premise: the prize cited the photoelectric effect, not relativity. Then it still gives the user something useful.

It should not play along. Einstein's 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics cited his services to theoretical physics and especially his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect. Relativity was not named. A good response says that kindly, then adds context: the committee was cautious about relativity at the time. That way the user still learns something.
A model's answer cites three studies with authors, years and journals. How do you check them?
How you catch invented or misused sources.
You confirm each source exists and actually supports the claim. One made-up citation is a serious error.

For each one I search the exact title and authors in a scholarly search engine or on the journal's site, and I check that the year and journal match. Then I read the abstract or the text to see if it says what the answer claims. Models sometimes invent a real-sounding paper, or tie a real paper to the wrong claim. A made-up source is a major error, even if the sentence is true.
You are rating two answers that contain code. Neither is obviously wrong. How do you decide which is better?
Whether you test code rather than judging it by how it looks.
You run or trace the code on normal and edge cases and check it does what was asked. Only then do you weigh clarity and safe habits.

I run both if the project gives me a sandbox, or trace them by hand if not. I try a normal input, then edge cases like an empty list or a zero. Then I check that each one does what was asked, not a close version of it. Only after that do I weigh clarity, comments and risky habits, such as a password written into the code. Working code beats pretty code.
Reviewers on your team keep preferring the longer of two responses. Why is that a problem, and how would you check for it?
Whether you know that rater habits can teach a model the wrong lesson.
The model learns that padding wins. Check how often the longer answer wins, and test raters with pairs where the shorter answer is clearly better.

If raters reward length, the model learns that padding wins, and users get long answers to simple questions. I would pull a sample of ratings and see how often the longer response won, including cases where the extra text added nothing. Then I would add test pairs where the short answer is clearly better, and a line in the guideline: length is not quality.
Annotators agree on 90% of items for a spam label. Why might that number still hide a problem?
Your understanding of agreement measures beyond raw percent agreement.
With a rare label, much of the agreement can come from chance. Use a chance-corrected measure such as Cohen's kappa and look at the rare label on its own.

If only 5% of items are spam, two people who label everything “not spam” agree on every item and still catch no spam. So I would use a measure that corrects for chance, like Cohen's kappa for two annotators. I would also check agreement on the spam items alone. That is where the label matters most, and where real disagreement usually hides.
A guideline says only: “Label a comment toxic if it is offensive.” Walk me through making that rule consistent.
How you turn a vague rule into one that different people apply the same way.
You define the label by what can be seen in the text, add examples and near-misses, settle edge cases, and test the draft on real items.

“Offensive” depends on the reader, so I would define toxic by what is in the text: insults aimed at a person, slurs, threats or harassment. Then I add clear examples and near-misses, like swearing with no target, or quoting a slur in order to report it. I write a rule for each edge case, test the draft with two annotators on 50 items, and fix every spot where they split.
Halfway through a project, the client changes a guideline. Five thousand items are already labelled under the old rule. What do you do?
How you keep a dataset consistent when the rules change.
You version the guideline, measure how many old items the change affects, and offer a relabel or a version tag. Everyone knows the exact switch date.

First I make sure everyone works from the new version, with a dated change note. Then I measure the impact: I pull a sample of old items and count how many would get a different label. If it is a few, we relabel just those. If it is many, I propose a relabel pass or tagging each item by guideline version, and the client decides. Mixed rules with no record is what I avoid.

aml-kyc.heading: AML and KYC analyst questions
qs: What is the difference between customer due diligence and enhanced due diligence, and what triggers the second?
Whether you know how risk-based checks scale with the customer.
Due diligence for everyone, enhanced checks for higher risk, with real triggers like PEPs, high-risk countries or an unclear source of funds.

Due diligence is the standard check for everyone: who you are, what you will use the account for, and a risk rating. Enhanced due diligence goes deeper, for higher-risk customers: a politically exposed person, ties to a high-risk country, or flows that do not fit the profile. Then I ask for source of funds and source of wealth, with documents, and get senior sign-off.
What on-chain patterns make you look twice at a deposit?
Your knowledge of how laundering looks on a blockchain.
Specific patterns such as mixers, peel chains, chain hopping and fast pass-through, treated as reasons to look, not proof.

Funds that came through a mixer. A peel chain, where a wallet sends off small amounts hop after hop. Chain hopping through bridges and swaps in a short time. Many small deposits from fresh wallets that leave in one withdrawal within minutes. Each is a reason to dig, not a verdict. I check how it fits the customer's profile before I decide.
Your blockchain analytics tool shows a deposit with indirect exposure to a darknet market, four hops back. How do you weigh it?
How you read analytics alerts instead of just obeying the risk score.
Explains direct versus indirect exposure, then weighs the share of funds, the hops and the customer's history together.

Direct exposure means the funds came straight from the risky wallet; indirect means they passed through others first. Four hops back can be noise, or it can be layering. I check what share of the deposit traces there, whether the hops were quick and deliberate, and whether the customer's history fits. A small, old trace usually closes; a large, fast one gets escalated.
A new customer's name is a close match to someone on the OFAC sanctions list. How do you clear or confirm it?
Whether you can handle a sanctions hit without guessing.
Compares identifiers beyond the name, documents the reason, and holds the account until a true match is ruled out.

A name alone proves nothing. I compare date of birth, nationality, address and ID number against the list entry and its aliases. If strong identifiers clearly differ, I close it as a false positive and write down exactly why. If they line up or I cannot tell, the account stays on hold and I escalate. A true match means funds are blocked and reported to OFAC; that is a legal duty, not a choice.
A 72-year-old customer who has only bought small amounts suddenly sends most of her balance to a new wallet, saying an online advisor told her to. What do you do?
Whether you spot a likely scam victim and act to protect her.
Recognises an investment or romance scam, contacts the customer, uses the holds policy allows, and reports it.

This looks like a pig butchering scam: someone builds trust online, then drains the victim. I would pause the transfer if our policy allows and call her. I ask how she met the advisor and whether she has ever withdrawn from his site. I check the receiving wallet for scam links and file a SAR if it fits. I stay kind; she may be embarrassed.
Walk me through how you write a SAR narrative.
Your ability to write a suspicious activity report that law enforcement can use.
Covers who, what, when, where, why and how in plain language, with amounts, dates and wallet addresses, and no guessing.

I open with a summary: who, what total, over what dates, and why it is suspicious. Then the facts in time order: account details, amounts, wallet addresses, transaction hashes and how the funds moved. I say what we checked and what the customer told us. I write plainly, so an investigator who never saw our system understands it. Facts, not accusations.
A customer whose account you restricted calls and asks if you reported him to the government. What do you say?
Whether you know the rule against tipping off a customer about a SAR.
Never confirms or denies a SAR, which is confidential by law, and gives a neutral, honest answer about next steps.

I cannot tell him whether a report exists. A SAR, and even the fact that one was filed, is confidential by law, and disclosing it could mean penalties for me and the firm. I say the account is under review, tell him what documents would help, and give a realistic timeline if I have one. I stay calm and polite, and I note the call in the case file.
Sales wants a high-volume client onboarded today, but his source of wealth is still unclear. How do you handle the pressure?
Your judgement when business goals press against compliance.
Holds the line on the missing checks, explains the risk in business terms, and offers a quick path to yes.

I would not open the account until the source of wealth makes sense; that gap is exactly where laundering hides. I tell sales what is missing and why, and offer to call the client myself to speed it up. Often one document fixes it, such as a sale contract or tax return. If sales still pushes, I escalate to my manager in writing, so the decision and the reason are on record.
You closed an alert as low risk. A month later, the same wallet is publicly linked to a hack. What do you do?
How you own a mistake and fix its consequences.
Reopens and escalates at once, checks what else is affected, and learns from it without hiding or blaming.

I tell my lead the same day and reopen the case. I check what the customer has done since, whether funds are still here to restrict, and whether other customers touched the same wallets. We decide on a SAR and any freeze. Then I look honestly at my reasoning: was the link visible then, or new? If I missed something, I say so and we adjust the rule or checklist.
What is OFAC's 50 percent rule, and how does it change the way you screen a corporate customer?
Whether you know sanctions reach beyond the names printed on the list.
Entities owned 50% or more in total by blocked persons are blocked too, so ownership must be traced, not just names screened.

If one or more blocked persons own 50 percent or more of a company in total, directly or indirectly, that company is blocked even if its name is on no list. So for a business customer I screen the owners, not just the company, and I add up the stakes held by listed people. Two listed owners at 25 percent each make the company blocked.
How does the Travel Rule apply to crypto, and what do you do when the other side is an unhosted wallet?
Your grasp of the Travel Rule and its gap with self-hosted wallets.
Above the rule's threshold, sender and recipient details travel with the transfer between institutions; for unhosted wallets you collect and verify what you can.

FinCEN applies the Travel Rule to crypto transfers by money transmitters: above the threshold, we must pass the sender's and recipient's details to the receiving institution and keep records. An unhosted wallet has no institution behind it, so nothing can be passed. I still record who the customer says owns it and may ask for proof, like signing a message with that wallet.
A 20-year-old customer receives dozens of small deposits from unrelated wallets and cashes each one out to his bank within hours. What is happening, and what do you check?
How you spot a money mule account and build the case.
Names the mule pattern, traces where the deposits come from, compares with the customer's profile, and escalates instead of settling on one explanation.

Many senders, fast cash-out and nothing held looks like a mule account, often recruited through fake job ads. I trace the senders for scam or fraud exposure, compare the volume with his stated income and purpose, and check for devices shared with other accounts. If it holds up, I restrict the account and file a SAR, noting he may be a victim too.
Funds you are tracing go through a cross-chain bridge and then a decentralized exchange on another chain. How do you keep following them?
Your tracing skill when funds change chains and assets.
Matches the bridge deposit to the release on the other chain by amount, timing and bridge data, then follows the swap, and says where confidence drops.

I find the deposit into the bridge contract, then the matching release on the destination chain. Amount minus fees, timing and the bridge's own event data usually line them up. Then I follow the swap on the exchange to the new asset and address. When several transfers match equally well, I say so in the file and call it a probable link, not a certain one.
A verified customer's logins suddenly come from an Iranian IP address. What do you do?
How you act on a sanctions red flag that is not a name match.
Restricts activity at once, checks for VPN use or travel, escalates to the sanctions officer, and reviews past trades for possible disclosure.

Iran is under comprehensive US sanctions, so I restrict the account first and ask questions second. I check the login history, the device and whether the IP is a VPN exit point, and I ask the customer for an explanation and proof of residence. I escalate to our sanctions officer, because if he traded from Iran, legal must decide on next steps and on a voluntary self-disclosure to OFAC.
A deposit arrives from a wallet address that is listed on the SDN list. Walk me through what happens next.
Whether you know the blocking and reporting duties when sanctioned funds land.
Confirms the exact address, blocks the funds instead of returning them, reports to OFAC within 10 business days, and reviews the customer for a SAR.

I confirm the address matches the listed one exactly; with crypto, a match is not a fuzzy name question. Then the funds are blocked: held, not sent back, since returning them would itself be a prohibited transaction. We report the blocked property to OFAC within 10 business days, review the customer's other activity, and decide on a SAR.
Much of our inbound volume comes from an offshore exchange with weak KYC. How do you assess that counterparty?
Whether you can do due diligence on another exchange, not just on a person.
Looks at licensing, KYC and sanctions controls, and on-chain exposure, then sets limits or extra monitoring rather than an all-or-nothing call.

I check where it is licensed, whether it serves US persons, and what its KYC and sanctions controls look like, through a questionnaire and public enforcement records. On chain, I measure its exposure to mixers, scams and sanctioned addresses. If the risk is high but manageable, I lower limits and watch its flows more closely; if it serves sanctioned users, we stop taking its funds.
Our monitoring rules produce thousands of alerts a month and almost none lead to a SAR. How would you tune them without opening a gap?
How you tune rules with evidence instead of just cutting workload.
Uses data on which alerts were useful, tests activity just below proposed thresholds, documents each change, and checks results after go-live.

First I see which rules and thresholds produce the few useful alerts. Before raising a threshold, I sample cases just below the proposed new line to see whether real suspicious activity sits there. Every change gets a written reason and sign-off, and I re-check results a few months later. The goal is better alerts, not fewer, and an examiner should be able to follow each step.
You learn the sanctions list in our screening tool has not updated for six days. What do you do?
How you handle a control failure that may already have let something through.
Fixes the feed, rescreens everything from the gap, escalates and documents, and treats any hit found as a live sanctions case.

I tell my manager and the sanctions officer right away and get the feed fixed. Then we rescreen all customers and transactions from those six days against the current list. Any true hit is handled as a real case, with blocking and reporting as required. I write up the cause, the gap and the lookback results, and we add a check so a stale list is caught within a day next time.

analog-engineer.heading: Analog and mixed-signal engineer questions
qs: Why does a decoupling capacitor need to sit right next to the supply pin?
Whether you understand fast supply current and why distance from the pin matters.
Trace inductance resists fast current changes. A close capacitor with a small loop supplies the charge locally.

When the circuit switches, it pulls short bursts of current. The trace back to the regulator has inductance, so it cannot deliver those bursts fast, and the rail dips. A capacitor right at the pin supplies that charge locally. I keep the loop from pin to capacitor to ground small, because loop area sets the inductance.
What does an anti-aliasing filter do, and why can't you fix aliasing after the ADC?
Your grasp of sampling and the Nyquist limit.
Content above half the sample rate folds into the band and looks like real signal, so it must be filtered before sampling.

A sampler cannot tell a tone above half the sample rate from one below it. The high one folds down and lands in my band, and after sampling it looks exactly like real signal, so no digital filter can remove it. The analog filter in front must attenuate anything that would fold into the band until it sits below the noise floor I care about.
How does a bandgap reference produce a voltage that barely changes with temperature?
Whether you know the core idea behind the most common on-chip reference.
A falling base-emitter voltage plus a scaled rising PTAT term, so the slopes cancel to first order near 1.2 V.

The base-emitter voltage of a bipolar transistor falls as temperature rises, about 2 mV per degree. The difference between two Vbe values at different current densities rises in proportion to absolute temperature. Scale that difference and add it to a Vbe, and the slopes cancel to first order. The result sits near 1.2 V, close to silicon's bandgap.
You need to make a 1.8 V analog rail for an ADC from 3.3 V. LDO or buck converter?
How you weigh efficiency against noise when choosing a power supply.
It depends on current: an LDO is quiet but wastes the drop as heat; a buck is efficient but its ripple must be kept out of the band.

For a small current I would use an LDO. It is quiet and simple, and losing about 45% of the power is fine at tens of milliamps. For a large current I would use a buck for efficiency, then filter its ripple, maybe with an LDO after it, and pick a switching frequency whose harmonics stay out of the signal band.
What is kT/C noise, and how does it set the size of a sampling capacitor?
Your understanding of the noise limit behind ADC power and area.
Sampled noise is the square root of kT/C, independent of switch resistance; halving it takes four times the capacitance.

The noise sampled onto a capacitor has an rms voltage of the square root of kT over C, whatever the switch resistance. So noise, not speed, sets the capacitor size. Each extra bit halves the LSB, so I need about four times the capacitance per bit. That costs area and driver power, which is why high-resolution ADCs get large.
How do you check that a feedback amplifier is stable, and what margin do you aim for?
Whether you verify stability with the right method across all conditions.
Loop gain and phase margin from a proper loop-break, checked over corners and loads, confirmed by a step response.

I break the loop in simulation with a method that keeps the loading right, such as a stability probe, and plot loop gain and phase. I read the phase margin where loop gain crosses one. I want at least 45 degrees, ideally near 60, across corners and loads, and I check gain margin too. A transient step then confirms it: ringing means trouble.
How would you lay out a differential input pair so the two transistors match well?
Your layout sense for mismatch, which sets offset in analog circuits.
Common-centroid interleaving, same orientation, dummy devices at the edges, symmetric routing, away from heat and noise.

I split each transistor into fingers and interleave them in a common-centroid pattern, so a gradient across the die hits both sides equally. Same orientation, same surroundings, and dummy fingers at the ends so the outer devices see the same edges. I keep the pair away from hot or noisy blocks and route both sides symmetrically so parasitics match.
Your ADC measures a SINAD of 62 dB on a full-scale sine. How many effective bits is that, and what next?
Whether you can turn a measurement into a diagnosis.
About 10 bits from (SINAD minus 1.76) over 6.02, then reading the FFT to separate distortion from noise.

ENOB is SINAD minus 1.76, divided by 6.02, so about 10 bits. On a 12-bit converter I have lost two bits. Next I look at the FFT: strong harmonics point to linearity, a raised floor points to noise or clock jitter. I also confirm the input really was full scale, since a smaller input lowers SINAD on its own.
Some of your first chips power up with the reference stuck at zero volts. What do you suspect?
How you trace a silicon failure back to a design weakness.
The zero-current state of the bandgap core and a weak start-up circuit, reproduced on the bench and in simulation.

A bandgap core usually has two stable states: the normal one and one where no current flows. I would check the start-up circuit first: does it inject current on slow supply ramps and at cold, and does it switch off cleanly afterward? I would reproduce it with a slow ramp at cold on the bench, then simulate the same ramp across corners.
A day before tape-out, Monte Carlo shows comparator offset fails spec in 2% of runs. What do you do?
Your judgement when schedule and yield pull in different directions.
Confirm the result, put a yield cost on it, check if trim covers it, and take options to the lead rather than hiding it.

First I check it is real: enough runs, the right models, the right spec. Then I put a number on it: 2% fallout in one block is yield lost on every wafer. I ask whether trim or calibration can catch it. I bring the lead options with costs: larger input devices, a trim plan, or a short slip. I do not quietly tape out with it.
How do you use gm/Id when you size a transistor?
Whether you size devices with a method rather than by trial and error.
Chooses gm/Id from the trade-off of efficiency against speed, then gets current density and W from simulated curves.

gm/Id tells me how much transconductance I get per unit of current. High values, near weak inversion, save power but are slow and need big devices. Low values, in strong inversion, are fast. I pick gm/Id for each device's job, get gm from the bandwidth or noise target, then read current density from simulated curves to set W at my chosen length.
Your low-frequency amplifier is dominated by 1/f noise. How do you bring it down?
Your knowledge of flicker noise and the circuit techniques that beat it.
Bigger gate area for the input pair, a lower-flicker device type if the process has one, or chopping to move the signal away from the noise.

Flicker noise falls as gate area grows, so I first make the input pair larger in width and length, accepting more capacitance. In many processes PMOS shows less flicker than NMOS, so I check the models. If that is not enough, I chop: move the input up above the 1/f corner, amplify, bring it back down, then filter the ripple that chopping leaves.
Why does a fully differential amplifier need common-mode feedback, and what can go wrong with it?
Whether you understand the second loop hidden inside every fully differential design.
The output common mode is otherwise undefined with high-gain loads; the CMFB loop needs its own stability check and must not load the outputs.

With high-impedance loads, a tiny current mismatch drives the output common mode to a rail, because the differential loop does not control it. A CMFB circuit senses the average output and adjusts a bias current. It is a separate loop, so I check its phase margin on its own, and make sure the sensing circuit does not load the outputs or cut the swing.
What is latch-up, and what do you check in layout to prevent it?
Your knowledge of a failure that layout choices cause or prevent.
Explains the parasitic PNPN path between wells and substrate, and the cures: close well and substrate taps, and guard rings near I/O.

The NMOS, PMOS, well and substrate form a parasitic PNPN thyristor. If a pin is driven past a rail and injects current, it can trigger and short the supply until power is cycled. I check that well and substrate taps are close enough per the rules, add guard rings around I/O and large drivers, and keep NMOS and PMOS apart near the pads.
Your design passes at the typical corner. What do you run before you call it done?
How you plan verification across process, voltage and temperature.
Process corners crossed with supply and temperature limits, Monte Carlo for mismatch, plus startup, transient and post-layout runs.

I run the process corners, including the skewed ones where NMOS and PMOS move apart, crossed with the supply range and the temperature range in the spec. Then Monte Carlo for mismatch, with enough runs to support the yield claim. I also check power-up and power-down, load steps and every mode, and repeat the key cases on the extracted layout.
After extraction, your amplifier's bandwidth drops by a third. How do you find and fix the cause?
How you debug layout parasitics instead of guessing.
Finds the node that moved before changing anything, then fixes routing or device layout before resizing the circuit.

First I find which node moved: I compare node capacitance between schematic and extracted views, or add parasitics back one net at a time. Usually it is a high-impedance node or the input gates with long wiring. I work with the layout designer to shorten that route, reduce metal overlap or reshape the device fingers, and only resize the circuit if layout cannot recover it.
A 14-bit ADC must sample a 100 MHz input. How much clock jitter can you allow?
Whether you can do a quick budget that links clock quality to converter performance.
Uses SNR = -20·log10(2π·f_in·σ_jitter) and lands near 80 fs rms for about 86 dB, before any margin.

Jitter-limited SNR is -20·log10(2π·f·σ), with σ the rms jitter. An ideal 14-bit converter gives about 86 dB, so 2π × 100 MHz × σ must be about 5×10^-5, which is roughly 80 fs rms. That is the whole budget, so the real clock must be well below it, since quantization and thermal noise also take their share.
How do you choose the loop bandwidth of a PLL for low phase noise?
Your judgement of noise trade-offs in a frequency synthesizer.
Inside the loop bandwidth the reference path dominates; outside, the VCO does. Set the bandwidth near where they cross, then check stability and spurs.

Within the loop bandwidth the output follows the reference path: reference, divider, phase detector and charge pump noise, scaled up by the divide ratio. Outside it, the VCO's own noise shows through. I plot both and set the bandwidth near where they cross to minimize integrated jitter, then check phase margin, settling and reference spurs, which a wider loop filters less.
On the bench, your ADC spectrum shows a spur that simulation never showed. How do you track it down?
How you debug real silicon methodically, separating the chip from the test setup.
Rules out the setup first, then uses the spur's frequency and how it moves to point to a source such as a clock, supply or substrate coupling.

I first check the setup: another signal source, a clean filter, the board's supplies. Then I note the spur's frequency and change one thing at a time: input frequency, sample clock, digital activity. If it tracks a digital clock, I suspect supply or substrate coupling, and try turning blocks off or shifting digital edges away from the sampling instant.

analytics-engineer.heading: Analytics engineer questions
qs: What does the grain of a table mean, and why do you settle it first?
Whether you know the first decision behind every data model.
Grain is what one row stands for. It is stated before building and tested, because unclear grain causes double counting.

Grain is what one row stands for, such as one row per order line. I write it at the top of every model and test that the key columns are unique. If I cannot say the grain in one sentence, the model is usually mixing two things, and that is where double counting starts.
What is the difference between a fact table and a dimension table?
Your grasp of the basic building blocks of a dimensional model.
Facts hold events and measures with keys. Dimensions hold the descriptive attributes used to filter and group, joined to facts on those keys.

A fact table holds events or measurements, like one row per payment with the amount and keys for who, what and when. A dimension holds the descriptions you filter and group by, like customer name, plan and region. Facts grow fast; dimensions change slowly. Analysts join the two on the keys.
Which tests do you put on a new model as a minimum?
Whether testing is a habit for you and what it covers.
Unique and not null on the primary key, relationship tests on foreign keys, accepted values, plus freshness or reconciliation checks on key tables.

Every model gets unique and not null tests on its primary key. Foreign keys get a relationship test, so every order points to a customer that exists. Status columns get an accepted values test. For key tables I add a freshness check on the source and a row count or total check against the source, so a silent drop shows up.
How do you lay out the layers of a project, from raw data to the tables analysts use?
How you organize models so logic lives in one place.
Light staging per source, shared logic in an intermediate layer, business-facing marts, so each rule is defined once.

Staging models sit one to one on raw sources: rename columns, cast types, fix time zones, nothing more. Intermediate models hold joins and logic that several outputs share. Marts are the facts and dimensions analysts query, named in business terms. Each rule lives in one place, so a fix flows to every report.
After you added a join, revenue on a dashboard doubled. How do you find the cause?
Whether you recognize and fix join fan-out.
Suspects a one-to-many join, compares row counts before and after, fixes the grain before joining and adds a test.

I suspect fan-out: the joined table has more than one row per key, so each order repeats. I compare row counts before and after the join and count keys that appear twice on the right side. The fix is to bring that table to one row per key before the join, then add a uniqueness test so it cannot come back.
A customer moves from one sales region to another. How do you keep last year's revenue in the old region?
Your knowledge of slowly changing dimensions.
A type 2 history with valid from and valid to dates, joined on the date of the event; type 1 overwrite when history is not needed.

I keep a type 2 history: a new row each time the region changes, with valid from and valid to dates and a current-row flag. Sales join where the sale date falls between those dates, so last year's revenue stays with the old region. Where nobody needs history, I simply overwrite the value; that is type 1.
When do you build a model incrementally instead of rebuilding it every run, and what can go wrong?
How you weigh speed and cost against correctness.
Incremental for large, append-heavy tables, with a unique key and lookback window; knows about late rows, duplicates and logic changes.

I go incremental when a full rebuild of a big event table takes too long or costs too much. Each run loads only rows newer than what is there, with a lookback window for late data. Risks: missed late rows, duplicates without a unique key to merge on, and logic changes that only reach new rows, so I run a full refresh after changing logic.
Two teams report different numbers for active users. What do you do?
How you turn a conflicting metric into one agreed definition.
Finds the definitional gap, gets the owner to agree on one, builds it once, documents it, and names any variant differently.

I find out exactly how each team counts: which events, which time window, whether internal and test accounts are excluded. Usually it is a definition gap, not a bug. I bring both to the metric owner to agree on one, build it once in a shared model with documentation, and point both dashboards at it. A variant that is truly needed gets its own name.
You need to rename a column that thirty dashboards use. Walk me through how you do it.
Whether you change shared tables without breaking the people who rely on them.
Checks lineage, runs old and new names side by side, announces a date, migrates users, confirms no use, then removes.

I check lineage for every model and dashboard that reads the column. I add the new name next to the old one, so both work for a while, and announce the date the old one goes away. I move the dashboards or help their owners do it, and check query logs to confirm nobody still reads the old name. Only then do I drop it.
A uniqueness test fails on the orders model at 6 a.m., before the morning reports go out. What do you do?
How you handle a data incident under time pressure.
Stops bad data from publishing, tells users, traces the cause upstream, fixes at the right layer, and writes up how to catch it earlier.

I keep the failing model from publishing, so reports show yesterday's correct numbers rather than wrong ones, and tell report users the data is delayed. Then I pull the duplicate keys and trace them upstream; often a source loaded a file twice. I fix it at the right layer, rerun, and write up the cause and the earlier check that would have caught it.
Why can you add up daily sales across days but not daily account balances?
Whether you know which measures add up across time and which do not.
Calls balances semi-additive: they sum across accounts but not across days, so you report the closing or average value.

Sales are events, so a week is the sum of its days. A balance is a snapshot of a state. Adding seven daily balances gives a number seven times too big that means nothing. Across accounts on one day the sum is fine. For a week I report the closing balance or the average daily balance, and the docs say which one.
A dashboard shows daily revenue. Which time zone do you use, and where in the pipeline do you convert?
How you handle timestamps so that a day means the same thing in every report.
Store in UTC, convert to the business time zone once, before cutting to a date, and handle daylight saving correctly.

I keep raw timestamps in UTC and convert to the business's local zone in one model, before I cut the timestamp to a date. If I truncate in UTC first, evening orders on the West Coast land on the next day. I use a named zone like America/Los_Angeles, not a fixed offset, so daylight saving days come out right.
A customer can belong to several segments, and a segment has many customers. How do you model that?
Whether you can model a many-to-many relationship without double counting.
A bridge table with one row per customer and segment, and a clear rule for reports whose totals must add up.

I build a bridge table with one row per customer per segment, with start and end dates if membership changes. Revenue stays on the order fact. Revenue by segment then adds up to more than the company total, since a customer counts in each segment. I say so on the dashboard, or give each customer one primary segment for reports that must add up.
How do you decide whether a model should be a view or a table?
Your judgement on the trade-off between freshness, query speed and compute cost.
Views for light logic that is rarely read; tables for heavy joins or models that dashboards query all day, checked against real usage.

A view runs its SQL every time someone queries it, so it costs compute on each read. A table is built once per run and is fast to read. Staging models that only rename and cast columns are usually views. Anything with heavy joins that a dashboard hits all day becomes a table. I check query history to see how often a model is actually read.
Where should the definition of a metric like net revenue live, and why?
How you keep one business definition from splitting into several versions.
In one governed place in code, a modeled column or a semantic layer, with a named owner and written rules, not inside each dashboard.

In one place in the code, either a column in a modeled table or a metric in a semantic layer, with a named business owner. If each dashboard computes it, someone forgets to remove refunds or tax and we get three numbers. The docs state the rule in plain words: what is in, what is out, and which date the revenue counts on.
Your revenue model is 3% lower than the number finance reports for last month. How do you reconcile them?
How you track down a gap between your model and an official source.
Agree the definition first, then break both totals down until the gap sits in specific rows, then fix or document it and add a test.

First I ask finance exactly what their number includes: tax, shipping, refunds, which date. Then I split both totals by day and payment type. Once the gap was orders placed late on the last evening of the month, which my model dated in UTC and pushed into the next month. I fixed it and added a test comparing monthly totals with finance.
An upstream team renamed a column in their database and your pipeline broke overnight. How do you stop that happening again?
Whether you protect your models from source changes, not just repair the break.
A quick fix in the staging layer, then tests and freshness checks on sources and an agreed change process with the source owners.

First I handle the rename in the staging model, so the rest of the project is untouched. Then I meet the owning team and we write a simple contract: the columns we depend on, and notice before they change. I add tests on those source columns and a freshness check, so the next break shows up as a clear alert, not as a wrong dashboard.
The warehouse bill doubled last month. How do you find out why?
Your ability to trace compute cost back to specific models, queries and schedules.
Ranks cost from query history, finds the few big causes, and fixes them with materialization, filters or schedules, plus an alert.

I pull the warehouse's query history and group cost by model, user and schedule. A few items usually explain most of it: a large table rebuilt in full every hour, a dashboard refreshing every five minutes on a heavy view, or a new job scanning all history with no date filter. I fix the top ones and set a budget alert.
A customer asks to have their personal data deleted under a privacy law. How do you make sure the warehouse complies?
Whether you know personal data spreads into copies and how to remove it from all of them.
Knows where personal data lives, including snapshots and derived tables, and runs a repeatable, logged deletion process.

Personal columns are tagged in our docs, so I can list every table that holds them. Deleting from the source is not enough: snapshots, history tables and exports keep copies. I run a deletion job keyed on the customer ID across all of them, rebuild what depends on them, and log what was removed. I ask legal about backups and retained copies.
Tell me about a time you shipped a wrong number. What happened and what did you change?
How you own a mistake and turn it into a lasting safeguard.
A specific error told plainly, fast notice to the people using the number, and a test or process change that stops a repeat.

I changed a join in the subscriptions model and dropped customers with no plan record, so churn looked 4 points better for two days. A sales lead noticed. I told dashboard users what was wrong and which dates, fixed the join and rebuilt. Then I added a row-count test against the source, and now I compare key metrics before and after any change to a core model.

android-developer.heading: Android developer questions
qs: What is the difference between minSdk, targetSdk and compileSdk?
Whether you know how an app declares which Android versions it supports.
minSdk is the oldest version that can install the app, compileSdk is the API set you build against, targetSdk is the behavior the app has opted into.

minSdk is the oldest Android version that can install the app. compileSdk is the API level I compile against, so it decides which APIs I can call. targetSdk tells the system which version's behavior changes the app is ready for. If I call an API newer than minSdk, I guard it with a check on Build.VERSION.SDK_INT.
A user rotates the phone and the form they were filling in goes blank. What happened and how do you fix it?
Your grasp of the activity lifecycle and configuration changes.
Rotation destroys and recreates the activity; keep data in a ViewModel and save small user input so it also survives process death.

By default rotation is a configuration change, so the activity is destroyed and created again, and anything held only in it is lost. I move the form data into a ViewModel, which survives that change. For text the user typed I also use SavedStateHandle or rememberSaveable, because a ViewModel does not survive the system killing the process in the background.
Where do you launch a network call for a screen, and what happens to it when the user leaves?
Whether you use coroutines with the right scope and the right thread.
Launch in viewModelScope so the work is canceled with the screen, keep blocking work off the main thread, and avoid GlobalScope.

I launch it from the ViewModel in viewModelScope. When the ViewModel is cleared because the user left the screen for good, the coroutine is canceled and no result goes to a dead screen. The repository switches to Dispatchers.IO for blocking work, so callers can stay on the main thread. I avoid GlobalScope, since nothing would ever cancel that work.
How do you ask for location permission so that users actually grant it?
How you handle runtime permissions and a user who says no.
Ask when the feature needs it, explain why, request the least access that works, and keep the app usable after a denial.

I ask only when the user taps the feature that needs location, not at first launch. If shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale returns true, I first show a short screen saying why. I ask for approximate location if that is enough. If they deny, the feature still works another way, like typing a ZIP code, and after repeated denials I point them to app settings instead of asking again.
The app must upload photos even if the user closes it. How do you build that?
Whether you pick the right tool for background work on modern Android.
WorkManager with constraints and retries for work that must finish; a foreground notification only when the user should see ongoing work.

I enqueue the upload with WorkManager, with a network constraint and a backoff policy for retries. It stores the job, so it still runs after the app is closed or the phone restarts, and it respects battery rules like Doze. Each photo is its own unit of work, so one failure does not restart the batch. For a large upload the user is waiting on, I run the work in the foreground with a notification.
Users report an App isn't responding dialog. What causes it and how do you track it down?
Whether you know what blocks the main thread and how to find it.
The main thread was blocked too long by disk, network or a lock; find it with ANR traces and StrictMode, then move the work off the main thread.

An ANR means the main thread could not handle an input event or broadcast in time; for input that is about five seconds. Common causes are database reads, a network call or waiting on a lock on the main thread. I read the ANR stack traces in the store's vitals reports, turn on StrictMode in debug builds to flag disk and network access on the main thread, and move that work to a background dispatcher.
What is a common way an Android app leaks an activity, and how do you find it?
Whether you know how context references cause memory leaks.
A long-lived object holds an activity, like a singleton or a listener never removed; find it with a heap dump, fix it by scoping or the application context.

A classic one is a singleton or static field holding an activity context, or a listener registered in onStart that is never removed. After a rotation the old activity cannot be garbage collected. I catch it with a leak detection library in debug builds or a heap dump in the memory profiler. The fix is the application context, or unregistering in the matching lifecycle callback.
A list built with Jetpack Compose stutters when you scroll. What do you check?
Whether you understand recomposition and how to keep it cheap.
Measure in a release build, then stable item keys, no heavy work inside composables, remember and derivedStateOf, and stable data passed to items.

First I measure in a release build, because debug builds of Compose run much slower. Then I look at recomposition counts in the layout inspector. Usual fixes: give LazyColumn items a stable key, move sorting and formatting out of the composable into the ViewModel or a remember block, use derivedStateOf for values like show the scroll-to-top button, and pass immutable data to items.
A teammate put a paid API key in the app's code and says R8 will hide it. What do you say?
Your judgement about secrets that ship inside an APK.
Anything shipped in the APK can be extracted; obfuscation is not protection. The key belongs on a server, and the leaked key should be rotated.

R8 shrinks and renames code; it does not encrypt strings, and anyone can unpack an APK and find the key. I would move that call behind our own backend, which holds the key, checks the user is signed in and applies rate limits. Then we rotate the key, because the one already shipped has to be treated as leaked.
You released to 10% of users and the crash rate jumps on one phone model. What do you do?
How you handle a bad release when an installed app cannot be rolled back.
Halt the staged rollout, group crashes by device and OS, ship the fix as a new build with a higher version code, and use a remote flag if there is one.

I halt the staged rollout in the store console so no new users get the build. People who already updated keep it, since I cannot push an older version, so the fix ships as a new build with a higher versionCode. I group the crashes by device and OS version to find the cause. If the crash sits in a feature behind a remote flag, I switch the flag off right away.
How do you collect a Flow from a ViewModel in the UI, and when would you pick StateFlow over SharedFlow?
Whether you know how to observe data without wasting work or missing updates.
Collection tied to the lifecycle, StateFlow for screen state, and a clear view on one-off events.

In Compose I use collectAsStateWithLifecycle, and in views repeatOnLifecycle with STARTED, so collection stops when the app goes to the background. StateFlow always holds a current value, so it fits screen state. For one-off things like a snackbar I prefer a flag in the state that the UI clears, because a SharedFlow event can be lost if nobody is collecting.
A release on Google Play has a serious bug. Can you roll it back?
Whether you know how Play releases actually work.
No true rollback: halt the rollout, and ship a fix or the old code under a higher versionCode.

Not in the usual sense. Play needs every new release to have a higher versionCode, so I cannot push the old build again. If it is a staged rollout I halt it first, so no new users get it. Users who already updated keep it. Then I ship a fix, or rebuild the last good code with a new, higher versionCode.
A teammate wraps a suspend call in runCatching and the screen keeps loading after the user leaves. What is wrong?
Your grasp of how coroutine cancellation works.
Knowing that catching CancellationException breaks cancellation, and how to rethrow it.

runCatching catches every Throwable, including CancellationException. When the ViewModel scope is canceled, that exception is swallowed, so the code carries on as if nothing happened. I catch the specific exceptions I expect, like IOException, or rethrow CancellationException before handling the rest, so cancellation still travels up.
How do you unit test a ViewModel that launches coroutines?
Whether your tests of async code are fast and reliable.
Replace the Main dispatcher, inject the others, use runTest and control when work runs.

I use a test rule that calls Dispatchers.setMain with a StandardTestDispatcher and resets it after. The ViewModel gets its IO dispatcher through the constructor, so the test passes the same test dispatcher. Inside runTest, delays are skipped, and I call advanceUntilIdle before checking the state. No real waiting, no flaky sleeps.
How do you check that your app survives process death?
Whether you test the case most developers forget.
A real way to kill the process in the background, and knowing what is restored and what is lost.

I open a screen, fill in some data, press Home, then run adb shell am kill with the package name and reopen the app from recents. The system restores the back stack and saved state, but the ViewModel is new. Anything that matters must come back from SavedStateHandle or disk. I keep that state small, because a large Bundle can throw TransactionTooLargeException.
The debug build works, but the release build crashes when parsing a server response. What do you suspect?
How you deal with problems that only appear after code shrinking.
Suspecting R8 renaming or removing classes used by reflection, fixing with rules, and testing release builds.

R8 likely renamed or removed fields that a reflection-based JSON parser needs, so the names no longer match the JSON. I add keep rules or annotations for those models, or move to a parser that generates code at compile time. I run the minified build in CI, and upload the mapping file so stack traces from users are readable.
Your App Links open the browser instead of the app. How do you find out why?
Your knowledge of how Android verifies links to a website.
Checks the manifest, the assetlinks.json file and the signing key fingerprint, with a tool to see the status.

I run adb shell pm get-app-links with the package name to see the verification state. Then I check the intent filter has autoVerify set and https links, and that assetlinks.json is served at /.well-known/ over HTTPS without redirects. The usual culprit: the file lists the upload key's SHA-256, not the app signing key that Play uses.
Cold start takes too long. Walk me through how you would improve it.
How you measure and fix startup, not just guess.
Measure first with a benchmark, cut work at launch, and use Baseline Profiles for code compiled ahead of time.

I measure first with a Macrobenchmark startup test, so I have a number to beat. Then I look at Application.onCreate and move anything not needed for the first screen to later or lazy init. I add a Baseline Profile so the startup path gets compiled ahead of time at install. I call reportFullyDrawn when the real content shows, and measure again.
You join a large app built with XML views, and the team wants to rewrite it in Compose. What do you recommend?
Your judgement on a big technical change that carries business risk.
An incremental plan using interop, starting where the risk is low, rather than a big rewrite.

I would not stop features for a rewrite. Compose works inside views through ComposeView, and views work inside Compose through AndroidView. I would start with new screens and small shared components, set up one theme for both, and move old screens when we touch them anyway. We track startup and scroll performance as we go, so problems show early.

api-developer.heading: API and SDK developer questions
qs: When should an API return 401 and when should it return 403?
Whether you know the HTTP status codes that client developers rely on.
401 means the caller is not authenticated; 403 means the caller is known but not allowed. The difference tells the client what to fix.

401 means we do not know who you are: the token is missing, expired or invalid, and the client should get a new one. 403 means we know who you are but you may not do this, so retrying with the same token will not help. I keep that split strict because SDKs use it to decide whether to refresh a token.
Which of these are breaking changes: adding a response field, adding a required request parameter, adding a new enum value to a response?
Your sense of what can break code you cannot see.
A new required parameter clearly breaks callers. A new response field is usually safe. A new enum value can break clients that handle every case, so it needs care.

A new required parameter breaks every existing caller, so it is out unless it gets a default. A new response field is normally safe if clients ignore unknown fields, which we document. A new enum value is the sneaky one: a client with a strict switch statement can crash, so we warn in the docs that new values may appear and announce them ahead.
Offset pagination or cursor pagination: which would you pick for a list endpoint, and why?
Whether you understand how pagination behaves on real, changing data.
Cursors stay correct when rows are added or removed and stay fast deep in the list. Offsets are simpler but skip or repeat items and get slow on large tables.

For most public lists I use a cursor, an opaque token that marks the last item returned. If new records arrive while a client pages through, offsets shift and the client skips or repeats items; a cursor does not. Large offsets also make the database read and throw away many rows. Offsets are fine for small admin lists where users jump to page 5.
A client goes over its rate limit. What should the API send back, and how should your SDK react?
How you design limits that clients can handle cleanly.
Status 429 with a Retry-After header, and an SDK that waits as told, backs off with jitter, caps its retries and then raises a clear error.

The API returns 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header, and I like to add headers showing the limit and what is left. The SDK waits for Retry-After if present, otherwise backs off exponentially with random jitter so many clients do not retry at the same moment. After a few tries it raises a rate-limit error the developer can catch.
Would you generate your SDKs from an OpenAPI spec or write them by hand?
Your judgement on keeping several SDKs consistent with the API.
A clear trade-off: generation keeps languages in sync with the spec, hand-written layers make the SDK feel natural. Often a mix of both.

With five languages, I generate the low-level layer from the OpenAPI spec so a new field reaches every SDK the same day and nothing drifts. Generated code often feels clumsy, so I hand-write a thin layer on top: pagination helpers, retries, typed errors and names that fit each language. The spec stays the single source of truth.
How do you make webhooks secure and reliable for the people receiving them?
Whether you know how push events go wrong in practice.
Signed payloads with a timestamp, retries with backoff, and guidance to dedupe by event ID, reply fast and not assume order.

Each event is signed with HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body plus a timestamp, using a secret per endpoint. Receivers check the signature with a constant-time compare and reject old timestamps to block replays. Delivery is at least once with retries, so every event has an ID to dedupe on. I tell receivers to return 2xx quickly, process later, and not assume order.
A partner wants to put their API key in their mobile app to call your API directly. What do you tell them?
Your grasp of authentication for clients that cannot keep a secret.
Anything shipped in an app can be extracted. Use OAuth with PKCE for user-scoped tokens, or route calls through their own backend.

I would say no. Anyone can unpack the app and read the key, then call our API as them with full rights. If the app acts for a user, they should use the OAuth authorization code flow with PKCE, so each user gets a short-lived, limited token. If it is their own data, the app should call their backend, which holds the key on a server.
What is different about writing code that runs inside someone else's application?
Whether you think like an SDK author rather than an app developer.
Few dependencies, no global side effects, configurable logging, thread safety, and errors that are typed and never silently swallowed.

My SDK is a guest. I keep dependencies minimal because each one can clash with a version the app already uses. I never print to the console, change global settings or log tokens; logging goes through a hook the developer controls. Errors are typed so they can catch a rate limit apart from a bad request, and clients are safe to share across threads.
An old endpoint still gets traffic from a few hundred customers. How do you retire it?
How you remove something without breaking customers.
Measure who still uses it, announce a date early, warn in docs and responses, contact heavy users directly, and only switch off after usage drops.

First I check the logs to see exactly which accounts still call it and how often. Then we publish a sunset date months out, add a deprecation note to the docs and a warning header to responses, and email the top users with a migration guide. I watch usage weekly. Near the date we may do a short planned brownout so anyone left notices before the real switch-off.
You fix a bug in a response, and a large customer's integration breaks because it depended on the bug. What do you do?
How you handle a fix that turns out to be a breaking change.
Restore service for the customer first, then treat the fix as a breaking change: versioned or opt-in, announced, with a migration window.

First I unblock them: roll back or put the old behavior behind a flag for their account the same day. Then I accept the lesson: once clients depend on behavior, changing it is a breaking change even if it was wrong. I would ship the fix in a new version or as opt-in, announce it, give a deadline, and add a contract test so we notice such changes before release.
What is the difference between PUT and PATCH, and which of them is idempotent?
Whether you know HTTP method semantics well enough to design and document them.
PUT replaces the whole resource and is idempotent by definition. PATCH applies partial changes and is idempotent only if the patch format makes it so.

PUT sends the full new state of the resource, so sending it twice leaves the same result: it is idempotent. PATCH sends a set of changes. A merge patch that sets a field is safe to repeat, but a patch like “add 5 to the balance” is not. So I document for each endpoint whether a retry is safe.
What should a good error response from an API contain?
How you design errors that both a program and a person can act on.
A stable machine-readable code, a human message, the field at fault and a request ID. A standard shape such as RFC 9457 Problem Details is a plus.

The right status code, then a stable error code the client can branch on, like card_declined, because messages change. A plain message for the developer, which field was wrong, and a request ID they can send to support. I use one shape everywhere, often RFC 9457 Problem Details, so the SDK can turn every error into a typed exception.
A client asks for a report that takes ten minutes to build. How should the endpoint behave?
Whether you can design long-running operations instead of holding a request open.
Return 202 Accepted with a link to a status resource, let the client poll or get a webhook, and have the SDK hide the waiting.

I would not keep the HTTP request open for ten minutes; proxies and clients time out long before that. The POST returns 202 Accepted and a Location header pointing to an operation resource with its status. The client polls it, honoring a Retry-After hint, or gets a webhook when it is done. The SDK offers a wait helper so most users never write the polling loop.
Two users edit the same record through your API at the same time, and one change silently overwrites the other. How do you prevent that?
Your grasp of optimistic concurrency in HTTP APIs.
ETags with If-Match: the server rejects a stale write with 412 Precondition Failed, and the client reloads and tries again.

This is the lost update problem. Each GET returns an ETag, a version tag for the resource. The client sends it back in an If-Match header on the update. If the record changed in between, the tag no longer matches and the server answers 412 Precondition Failed instead of writing. The client fetches the new version, merges and retries. The SDK can carry the ETag automatically.
A third-party app needs to read your users' data with their consent, and a partner's backend needs to call your API with no user present. Which OAuth flows fit each?
Whether you can match OAuth 2.0 flows to the type of client.
Authorization code with PKCE for apps acting for users, client credentials for server-to-server. No implicit or password grant.

For the third-party app, the authorization code flow: the user signs in with us, approves the scopes, and the app swaps the code for tokens. I require PKCE, which ties the code to the app that asked for it. For the partner's backend, the client credentials flow, with the secret kept on their server and narrow scopes. I would not offer the implicit or password grants.
Your SDK supports a language version that has reached end of life. Is dropping it a breaking change?
How you apply semantic versioning to a client library, not just to an API.
Yes for users still on that runtime. Ship it in a major version or under a published support policy, with notice and a supported last release.

For anyone still on that runtime, the new version will not install or run, so I treat it as breaking and ship it in a major release. If we publish a policy that we follow the language's end-of-life dates, some teams do it in a minor release, but only with advance notice. Either way, the last version that supports it gets security fixes for a stated period.
What do you think about before adding a third-party dependency to an SDK?
Whether you see that your dependencies become your customers' dependencies.
Each dependency can clash with the customer's own versions and adds size and security risk. Prefer the standard library and wide tested version ranges.

My dependencies end up inside their application. If I need version 2 of a JSON library and they are on version 1, they may not be able to install both. So I lean on the standard library, accept the widest version range I have tested, and avoid pulling in a big framework for one helper. Each dependency also brings its security alerts into their scans.
How would you catch a breaking API change before it reaches customers?
Your process for protecting backward compatibility automatically.
Automated checks in CI: diff the API spec against the released one, run contract tests, and test old SDK versions against the new server.

The OpenAPI spec lives in the repo, and CI diffs it against the last released spec and fails on removed fields, new required parameters or changed types. We run the test suites of the last few SDK releases against the new server, since old SDKs stay in use for years. A person still reviews behavior changes a diff cannot see, such as a new default sort order.
You find out that last week's minor SDK release renamed a public method and broke customers. What do you do?
How you recover from a semantic versioning mistake.
Restore the old method fast in a patch release, mark it deprecated, tell users, keep removal for the next major, and add a check so it cannot recur.

First I ship a patch release that brings the old name back as an alias of the new one, marked deprecated, so anyone affected is fixed by upgrading again. I post a note in the changelog and the issue tracker. The removal waits for the next major version. Then I add a public API diff check to the release pipeline, so a renamed or removed method fails the build.
Design a batch endpoint that creates 500 records in one call. What happens when 3 of them fail?
How you handle partial failure, one of the hardest choices in API design.
Decide all-or-nothing or per-item results up front, report each item's status in order, and make the whole batch safe to retry.

First I choose: all-or-nothing, or partial success. If partial, the response lists each item in request order with its own status, and either the new ID or the error code. Then 497 records exist, and the client resends only the 3 that failed. I add an idempotency key so a retried batch does not create duplicates, and the SDK returns successes and failures separately.

application-security.heading: Application security engineer questions
qs: A developer builds a SQL query by joining strings with user input. What do you tell them?
Whether you know the real fix for injection, not a weak one.
