I'd write: “Thanks for writing to us. I checked your order, and it was placed 45 days ago, which is past our 30-day refund window, so I can't refund it. If the item is faulty, it may still be covered by its warranty, and I'm glad to start that for you now.” I'd also leave the ticket open until they answer.
An email thread has passed between three agents over two weeks, and the customer now writes “Is anyone actually reading this?” You pick it up. What do you do?
How you take ownership of a case that has already gone wrong.
Reads the whole thread first, admits the delay plainly, gives one clear status with a date, and stays the owner until it is closed.

I read the whole thread and notes before replying, so I don't ask for anything they already sent. Then I write that I'm sorry they had to repeat themselves, that I'm handling it personally now, what the real status is, and when they'll hear from me next. I keep the ticket assigned to me and write on that date even if there is no news yet.
What do you look at before you write the first word of a reply?
Whether you gather context first so the customer does not have to repeat themselves.
Ticket history, account and order details, what the customer already tried, and any known issues. Then the reply fits the real situation.

I read the whole thread and the customer's past tickets, then check the account: plan, order status, recent changes. I look at what they say they already tried, and I check our status page for a known issue. That takes a minute and saves me from asking a question they answered last week.
Halfway through a chat, the customer asks: "Am I talking to a real person?" How do you answer?
Your honesty and how you rebuild trust when a customer suspects canned replies.
A truthful answer, said plainly, and a change in style if the replies have felt scripted. Honest about any bot step in the process.

I answer honestly: "Yes, I'm Dana, a real person, and I'm staying with you until this is sorted." The question usually means my replies felt canned, so I drop the template and write the next line in my own words. If a bot handled the start of the chat, I say so and say where I took over.
A customer writes in a language you do not speak. What do you do?
How you serve a customer in another language without risking accuracy or privacy.
Check for a colleague or queue in that language first; if using translation, only an approved tool, with short plain sentences and no idioms.

First I check whether we have an agent or queue for that language and route it if we do. If not, I use the translation tool our team approves, never a random website, since the message may hold personal data. I write short, plain sentences with no idioms, and I say I'm using translation so they can reply simply.
An outage starts and 200 tickets arrive about the same problem in an hour. Walk me through how you handle them.
How you keep replies fast, consistent and accurate during an incident.
Link tickets to the incident, use one approved message, promise no fix time that engineering has not given, and follow up with everyone when it is fixed.

I confirm the incident in our internal channel, then tag every related ticket so they can be updated together. We send one approved message: what we know, that the team is on it, and that we'll write again. I never guess a fix time. When it's resolved, we send a follow-up to every tagged ticket, not just to the people who chased us.
A colleague told a customer the fix would ship Friday. Friday passes and it has not shipped. You own the ticket now. What do you do?
How you handle a broken promise and stop it from happening twice.
Write to the customer first, own it without blaming the colleague, give no new date unless confirmed, and raise the issue of promising dates.

I write before the customer has to ask. "We told you Friday and we missed it. I'm sorry." I don't blame my colleague; to the customer, we are one team. I check with engineering and only share a new date if they commit to it; otherwise I say when I'll update them. Then I raise it with my lead so we stop quoting dates we don't control.
A customer asks for a refund, and you see they have already filed a chargeback with their bank for the same charge. What do you do?
Whether you know how a card dispute works and avoid paying the same money back twice.
No refund while the dispute is open; explain kindly that the bank now handles it, note the ticket and route it to billing per policy.

Once a chargeback is open, the bank is deciding where the money goes. If I refund as well, the customer could be paid twice. So I explain kindly that their bank is handling it now and that we'll respond to the bank. I add an internal note and send it to our billing team, who manage disputes. If they'd prefer a refund from us, billing can tell them the right steps.
A customer writes: "Delete all my data." How do you handle it?
Whether you treat a privacy request as a formal process, not a quick fix.
Verify the person, use the company's privacy process instead of deleting things yourself, and explain what happens and that some records may be kept by law.

I treat it as a privacy request. I confirm they own the account using our verification steps, then log it through our privacy process rather than deleting things myself in the admin tool. Some state laws, like California's, give people a right to ask for deletion, so the request has deadlines. I tell them what happens next and that some records, like invoices, may be kept where the law requires.
In a chat about a billing issue, the customer writes that they do not see the point of living anymore. What do you do?
How you respond to a possible crisis while following your company's protocol.
Take it seriously, respond as a person, follow the crisis protocol, share 988, call 911 if danger is immediate, and bring in a supervisor.

I stop talking about billing. I write something human: "I'm really sorry you're feeling this way. I'm glad you told me." I follow our crisis protocol and alert my supervisor right away. I share the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline: they can call or text 988 any time. If they say they're in immediate danger, I tell them to call 911 and follow our steps for that.
You are reviewing a newer agent's tickets for quality. What do you score, and how do you give the feedback?
Your standard for a good ticket and how you coach others.
Accuracy and resolution first, then security and policy, then tone and clarity. Feedback is specific, uses the ticket's own words, and includes what went well.

First: was the answer correct, and did it solve the problem or set up the next step? Then: did they verify identity and follow policy? Then tone, clarity, and whether the internal note would let someone else pick it up. In feedback I quote their own sentence, show a better version, and name one thing they did well, so it reads as coaching, not grading.
Your first response time is the best on the team, but your reopen rate is the highest. What does that tell you, and what do you change?
How you read your own numbers and find the cause behind them.
Sees that speed may be costing completeness, reviews reopened tickets to find the pattern, and changes habits rather than chasing one metric.

It tells me I'm fast but not finishing. I'd pull my last 30 reopened tickets and sort them by reason. Usually it's things like answering one of three questions, skipping a check, or closing before the fix was confirmed. Then I'd change the habit: reread the customer's message before sending, and end with what happens next. A slightly slower first reply that ends the ticket is better.

chief-of-staff.heading: Chief of staff questions
qs: How is a chief of staff different from an executive assistant?
Whether you understand the scope of the role.
A clear split: the assistant manages the executive's time and logistics; the chief of staff manages priorities, follow-through and special projects.

An executive assistant runs the calendar, travel and correspondence, and that work is essential. I work on what the time is spent on: the priorities, the operating rhythm of the leadership team, and projects that cross departments. The best setups have us working closely, because my plans fail if they never reach the calendar.
How do you learn how a new executive likes to work?
How you build the working relationship in the first weeks.
Asks directly and observes: how they want information, what they decide alone, what to escalate. Then confirms it in writing.

In week one I ask for an hour on their goals for the year, how they want updates, written or spoken, and what they want to hear about at once versus weekly. Then I watch a few weeks of meetings and email. I write a short page of working agreements and ask them to correct it. We revisit it after 90 days.
The weekly leadership meeting runs two hours and decides nothing. Walk me through how you would fix it.
Your skill in designing meetings that lead to decisions.
Starts with the purpose, separates updates from decisions, uses pre-reads, owners and time limits, then checks whether it worked.

First I ask the executive what the meeting is for. Then I move status updates into a written note sent the day before, so room time goes to two or three decisions, each with an owner and a clear question. I set a time for each item, close by reading back decisions and actions, and after a month I ask attendees whether it is better.
What goes into the brief you prepare before your executive's big meeting?
Whether you can prepare an executive in minutes, not hours.
One page: purpose, who is in the room and what they want, the decision or ask, key facts, risks and a recommended position.

One page, read in five minutes. Why the meeting exists and what we want to leave with. Who attends, what each person wants and any history between us. The three facts that matter, the likely pushback, and my recommended position. Background goes in an appendix they can skip. I send it the evening before, not in the hallway.
How do you make sure the decisions made in a meeting actually happen?
How you run follow-through across the leadership team.
One log of decisions and actions, each with a single owner and a date, sent quickly and reviewed at the next meeting.

Before people leave I read back each decision and action, with one owner and a due date. Within a few hours I send that list and add it to a shared tracker. The next meeting opens with overdue items. If something slips twice, I talk to the owner privately first, so the meeting does not become a public scolding.
How would you check whether your executive's time matches their priorities?
Whether you can run a calendar audit and act on it.
Tags past weeks of the calendar by priority, shows the gap with numbers, and proposes concrete cuts or delegations.

I take the last four to six weeks of the calendar and tag each meeting against the executive's stated priorities, plus a bucket for everything else. Last time the top priority got about 10% of the hours. I showed that on one page and proposed dropping three recurring meetings and sending a delegate to two others. We freed six hours a week.
When do you make a call on behalf of your executive, and when do you take it to them?
Your judgement about decision rights and the limits of your role.
Rules agreed in advance: decides on reversible matters where the executive's view is known; escalates new direction, people decisions and anything hard to undo.

We agree the lines early. I decide on things that are reversible, low cost, and where I already know the executive's position, like meeting changes or which team leads a small project. I escalate anything new in direction, anything about people's jobs or pay, and anything hard to undo. When unsure I ask, and I report calls I made in their name.
A vice president asks you privately whether the rumored reorganization is real. You know it is. What do you say?
How you protect confidential information without lying.
Neither confirms nor lies; says it cannot be discussed, and tells the executive the rumor is spreading.

I would say: I can't talk about organization plans, and I would not rely on hallway talk either way. I would not deny it, because a lie would cost me their trust later. Then I would tell the executive that the rumor has reached the VP level, so they can decide whether to move up the announcement.
A direct report of your executive tells you that you are blocking their access to the boss. How do you respond?
Whether you see yourself as a bridge, not a gatekeeper.
Listens without defending, checks the facts, fixes the process, and never stands between direct reports and their manager.

I would thank them and ask for examples. Direct reports should always be able to reach their own manager; my job is to make that time well used, not to ration it. If my process slowed them down, say by asking for pre-reads on urgent items, I would change it and tell the executive about the complaint myself, so they hear it from me first.
You sent a note to the company in your executive's name, and it promised more than they had agreed to. What do you do?
How you own a mistake made with someone else's authority.
Tells the executive at once, brings a correction, fixes it quickly and openly, and changes the approval step.

I would go to the executive right away, explain what went out and what it promised, and bring a draft correction. A short, plain follow-up the same day is better than letting people plan around a wrong promise. Then I would fix the cause: from then on, any message in their name gets their sign-off on the final text, not an earlier draft.
How would you explain OKRs to a leadership team that has never used them, and what mistake do teams make most often?
Whether you understand the planning tool many executive teams use.
Objectives are qualitative goals; key results are measurable outcomes, not task lists. Names a common failure, such as having too many OKRs.

An objective says where we want to go, in words people remember. Key results are the two to four numbers that prove we got there. The most common mistake is writing tasks as key results, like 'launch the pricing page,' instead of the outcome, like 'raise trial-to-paid conversion from 8% to 11%.' The second is having so many OKRs that nothing is a priority.
A decision touches product, sales and finance, and nobody knows who owns it. How do you sort out decision rights?
How you make ownership clear when a decision crosses teams.
One accountable owner named early, with clear roles for who is consulted and who is only informed, using a simple framework like RACI.

I would write it down as a RACI: who is Responsible for the work, the one person Accountable for the call, who is Consulted before, and who is Informed after. The key rule is a single A. I get my executive and the three leaders to agree on that page before the debate starts, so the argument is about the decision, not about who makes it.
Walk me through how you would prepare your executive for a quarterly board meeting.
Your grasp of the board cycle and how far ahead the work has to start.
A plan worked backward from the meeting date, a storyline before slides, materials sent ahead as a pre-read, and practice on the hard questions.

I start about six weeks out with the agenda and the two or three topics the board needs to discuss. Then a storyline before anyone builds slides, drafts from each owner, and a review with the CEO and the general counsel. The pre-read goes out a week ahead so the meeting is discussion, not presentation. Last, a dry run on the hardest questions a director could ask.
Your executive wants a two-day leadership offsite next quarter. How do you design it?
How you design a meeting around outcomes rather than an agenda of updates.
Starts from what must be decided or aligned by the end, uses pre-work and interviews, protects time for hard topics, and ends with owners and dates.

First I ask my executive what must be true when people leave: a decision, a shared plan, repaired trust. Then I interview each leader for 20 minutes to find the real tensions. Updates go into pre-reads. The hard topic gets the morning of day one, when energy is high. We close with a written list of decisions, owners and dates, sent out within 48 hours.
You get a 40-page strategy draft from a business unit, and your executive has ten minutes. What do you give them?
Whether you can turn a long document into something an executive can act on.
A one-page summary that leads with the ask and a view on it, flags weak points and the decisions needed. Not a shorter copy of the draft.

One page, with the bottom line first: what the unit is asking for, and my view of it. Then three lines on the strategy, the two or three assumptions it rests on, and where it is thin, for example a revenue plan with no hiring to support it. I end with the questions I suggest asking the unit head. The full draft stays attached for anyone who wants it.
In your first 90 days here, how would you decide what to take on and what to leave alone?
How you earn trust in a new role before you start changing things.
Listening first, a short list agreed with the executive, a few visible early wins, and care not to take over work that belongs to other leaders.

The first month is mostly listening: one-on-ones with each direct report and a look at how decisions and meetings actually run. Then I bring my executive a short list of what I heard and propose two or three things to own, such as the operating rhythm and one stuck project. I avoid taking work from leaders who do it well, because that costs trust I will need later.
At a public company, you see the quarterly results two weeks before they are announced. What rules do you follow?
Whether you handle market-sensitive information the way securities law requires.
Treats it as material nonpublic information: no trading or tipping, follows the insider trading policy and blackout windows, shares only on a need-to-know basis.

That is material nonpublic information. I do not buy or sell company stock, and I do not hint at it to anyone, including family, since tipping is illegal too. I follow the insider trading policy, which usually means trading only in open windows and with pre-clearance. I keep the files in restricted folders, share them only with people who need them, and ask legal when unsure.
Your executive and a peer executive are openly at odds, and it is slowing both teams. Your executive asks you to handle it. What do you do?
How you work across executives without becoming a messenger or taking sides.
Finds the real disagreement, frames it as one decision with options, and gets the two leaders in a room instead of fighting the battle by proxy.

I would not carry messages between them; that keeps the conflict alive. I talk with the other leader's chief of staff or deputy to find what the dispute is really about, often a shared resource or unclear ownership. Then I write it up as one decision with options and set a 30-minute meeting for the two. If they still cannot agree, the page goes to their common boss.
You argued against a decision, and your executive made it anyway. What do you do next?
Whether you can disagree in private and support the decision in public.
Commits fully and does not signal dissent to the organization, while knowing the exception: anything illegal or unethical goes to legal or the proper channel.

If it is a judgement call, I commit. I do not let anyone guess I argued the other side, because a chief of staff who undercuts the boss is useless to both. I do set a checkpoint, for example a review in 60 days on the numbers we agreed. The exception is anything illegal or unethical: then I say so plainly and, if needed, go to legal or the ethics line.
Your executive asks you to coordinate planning for a layoff of about 8% of staff. How do you run it?
How you lead the most sensitive project a chief of staff runs, with the right people and rules.
A small need-to-know group, HR and legal from day one, WARN Act and state rules checked, one announcement day, and care for those leaving and staying.

I keep a small, named planning group with HR and employment counsel in it from the start. Legal checks the federal WARN Act, which can require 60 days' notice for larger layoffs, plus any stricter state law, and reviews the selection for bias. I plan one day: managers trained, packages ready, a script, then a note to everyone staying about what changes and why.

civil-engineer.heading: Civil engineer questions
qs: What does a Proctor test tell you, and how is it used in the field?
Whether you understand the basis of soil compaction control.
Lab maximum dry density and optimum moisture, a spec stated as a percentage of that, and field density compared against it.

A Proctor test compacts a soil sample at several moisture contents to find its maximum dry density and optimum moisture. The spec then asks for a percentage of that, often 95% under pavement. In the field the tester measures density, usually with a nuclear gauge, and compares it with the lab value for that same soil.
What slopes do you design to for an accessible route across a parking lot?
Your working knowledge of ADA site design limits.
Running slope up to 1:20 before it is a ramp, cross slope up to 1:48, ramps up to 1:12, and a margin for construction tolerance.

Under the 2010 ADA Standards, a route can run up to 1:20 before it counts as a ramp, and the cross slope can be no more than 1:48. A ramp can be up to 1:12, with landings, and handrails once the rise is over 6 inches. I design below the limits, like 1.5% instead of 2.08%, because concrete never lands exactly on grade.
When would you use the rational method, and what are its limits?
Whether you know the basic runoff method and where it stops working.
Q = CiA explained, peak flow only, intensity tied to time of concentration, and use limited to small areas per the local manual.

Q equals C times i times A: a runoff coefficient, the rainfall intensity for a storm as long as the time of concentration, and the area in acres, giving cubic feet per second. It gives a peak flow only and assumes even rain over the area, so I use it for small areas like inlets and parking lots, within the size limit the local drainage manual sets.
Why do you check the hydraulic grade line in a storm sewer, and not just pipe capacity?
How well you understand storm sewer hydraulics beyond pipe sizing.
Tailwater and structure losses can flood a pipe that has capacity; you work upstream from the outfall and keep the HGL below rims with freeboard.

A pipe can have room on paper and still flood if water backs up from downstream. The hydraulic grade line shows how high water rises in each structure, counting tailwater, friction and losses at junctions. I start at the outfall and work upstream, and check the line stays below every rim and inlet with the freeboard the local manual requires.
On a site visit after a storm, you see muddy water running past the silt fence into a creek. What do you do?
How you handle an erosion control failure under a stormwater permit.
Immediate notice and repair, finding why it failed, documenting it under the SWPPP, and updating the plan if the control was wrong.

I take photos, note the time, and tell the superintendent right away so the fence is repaired and sediment cleaned up. Then I look at why it failed: often the fence runs downhill or drains too big an area. The SWPPP inspection log must record it, the plan may need a sediment trap instead, and if the permit requires reporting the discharge, the operator reports it.
A compaction test under the pavement fails, and the contractor wants to pave tomorrow anyway. What do you say?
Your judgement when schedule pressure meets a failed test.
No paving over a valid failure; confirm the test is right, have the area reworked and retested, and keep the delay short and in writing.

I would not let them pave over a failed test. Once asphalt is down, a soft spot becomes a pothole and a fight over who pays. I check the test first: right Proctor value for that soil, moisture in range. If it holds, they rework the area, adjust moisture, recompact and retest. I put the decision in writing and line up a quick retest.
Your 28-day concrete cylinder breaks come back below the specified strength. Walk me through what you do.
Whether you know the acceptance rules and the steps before talking about removal.
Applies the ACI 318 acceptance criteria, checks testing and curing, then cores reviewed by the engineer of record before any tear-out.

First I check if it is truly a failure: under ACI 318, the average of three consecutive tests must reach f'c, and no single test may fall more than 500 psi below it when f'c is 5,000 psi or less. Next I check curing and handling at the lab. If doubt remains, we take cores and the engineer of record judges them before anyone talks about tearing out.
The geotechnical report says the building sits on expansive clay. How does that change your site and foundation design?
How you turn a geotechnical finding into design decisions.
Explains swell and shrink, follows the geotech's options for soil and foundation, and controls water around the building.

Expansive clay swells when wet and shrinks when dry, so it can lift and crack a slab. I follow the geotechnical engineer's recommendations, which might be replacing the top few feet with non-expansive fill, moisture conditioning, or a post-tensioned slab or piers. I also grade so water drains away and keep downspouts and irrigation off the foundation.
The contractor finds your new sanitary sewer would cross just above an existing water main. How do you handle it?
How you resolve a utility conflict while protecting drinking water.
Verifies actual locations, checks the state separation rule, adjusts grade or uses an approved alternative, and gets regulator approval.

I have the real depths surveyed first; record drawings are often off. Then I check the state separation rule, which in many states wants the water line 18 inches above the sewer at a crossing. If I cannot lower the sewer enough, I use an approved alternative such as pressure-rated pipe or encasement at the crossing, and get the regulator's approval.
After the curbs are poured, you find your grading plan sends parking lot water toward the building entrance. What do you do?
Whether you own a design mistake and fix it fast.
Tells the client and manager quickly with a fix ready, picks the cheapest fix that works, and changes the review process.

I tell my manager and the client the same day, with the cause and a proposed fix, not just the problem. Then I find the cheapest fix that works, maybe a trench drain at the low spot or regrading pavement not yet placed. I document the change, and afterward I add a check of flow arrows against finished floor elevations to my review list.
How do you set the slope of a small sanitary sewer, and why not just make it as flat as the site allows?
Whether you design sewers so they clean themselves.
A self-cleansing velocity of at least 2 ft/s flowing full, a minimum slope for each pipe size, and a check against the local standard.

I design for at least 2 feet per second flowing full, the Ten States Standards rule many agencies use. That sets a minimum slope for each pipe size, 0.40 percent for an 8-inch line. Too flat and solids settle and the sewage turns septic. I always check the local standard too, since it can be stricter.
Your grading plan shows cut and fill in balance, yet the contractor says he will need to import fill. Who is right?
Whether you account for shrinkage and soil losses in earthwork.
Soil compacted in fill takes less room than it did in the ground. A real balance applies the geotech's shrink factor and subtracts topsoil and unsuitable soil.

Probably the contractor. Soil dug from a cut and compacted in a fill takes less volume than it did in place, often 10 to 20 percent less. Stripped topsoil and soft material can't go into structural fill either. I'd rerun the numbers with the shrink factor from the geotechnical engineer and raise or lower finished grades to rebalance.
What controls the length of a crest vertical curve on a new road?
Your grasp of sight distance in vertical alignment.
Stopping sight distance at the design speed, using AASHTO eye and object heights, which gives a minimum K value multiplied by the grade change.

Mostly stopping sight distance. A driver at design speed must see a 2-foot object beyond the crest in time to react and stop. AASHTO uses a 3.5-foot eye height and 2.5 seconds to react. That gives a minimum K, the curve length per percent of grade change. I multiply K by the difference in grades, then check that a long, flat top still drains.
A horizontal curve on a county road is too tight for its design speed. What are your options?
How you balance radius, superelevation and side friction on curves.
Uses e + f = V²/15R, respects the agency's maximum superelevation, and treats a lower design speed as a last resort needing approval.

The check is e plus f equals V squared over 15R, with speed in mph and radius in feet. First I try a flatter curve within the right of way. Next, more superelevation, the banking of the road, but only up to the agency maximum, which is lower where ice is common. Lowering the design speed is last, with the owner's approval and advisory signs.
How is designing a curb inlet in a sag different from one on a continuous grade?
Whether you know why sag inlets are the critical ones.
On grade, bypass flow moves to the next inlet; in a sag it has nowhere to go, so you size for all flow, allow for clogging and often add flanking inlets.

On a grade I space inlets so the spread of water stays within the allowed width, and some flow can bypass to the next inlet. In a sag, everything ends at one spot, including that bypass. So I size it for the total flow, assume part of the grate clogs, and often add a flanking inlet on each side. I also check where water goes if they all plug.
How do you restrain a 12-inch water main at a 45-degree bend?
Your knowledge of thrust forces in pressure pipe.
Thrust of about 2PA sin(θ/2) at test pressure, resisted by a thrust block sized on soil bearing or by restrained joints over a calculated length.

The thrust is about 2 times pressure times pipe area times the sine of half the bend angle, and I use the test pressure. Then I either size a concrete block poured against undisturbed soil, using the bearing value from the geotech, or I specify restrained joints over a length worked out from soil friction. Where people may dig later, I prefer restrained joints.
Your post-development peak flow comes out lower than pre-development before you add any detention. What do you check?
Whether you question a result that should not happen.
Assumes an error first: drainage areas, existing cover and soil groups, runoff coefficients or curve numbers, and time of concentration on the paved site.

Paving a site should raise the peak, so I assume a mistake. I check that drainage areas match on both maps, that the existing condition uses the real cover and soil group, and that the paved site doesn't have a longer flow path than it should. A long time of concentration on pavement is a common slip. If it still holds, I ask a second engineer to review it.
A client wants to place fill in the regulatory floodway on their parcel. What does that require?
Your knowledge of FEMA floodplain rules for development.
An engineered hydraulic analysis showing no rise in base flood elevation; if there is a rise, the community must first get a CLOMR from FEMA.

In a floodway the rule is no rise in the base flood elevation, the 1-percent-annual-chance flood level. I'd run a hydraulic model, usually starting from the effective FEMA model, and certify that the fill causes no increase. If it does, the community must get a Conditional Letter of Map Revision from FEMA first. Usually I'd advise moving the fill out of the floodway.
The contractor submits HDPE pipe as a substitute for the reinforced concrete storm pipe under a road. How do you review it?
How you judge a material substitution in a submittal.
Checks owner standards, cover limits for traffic, hydraulics, and backfill, since flexible pipe depends on side support, plus a deflection test.

First, does the owner's standard allow plastic pipe under a public road? If so, I check cover against the maker's minimum and maximum for traffic loads, and the hydraulics, since diameter and roughness can differ. Flexible pipe gets its strength from the soil around it, so I'd require proper backfill and compaction and a mandrel deflection test after backfill.
Halfway through grading, you learn the benchmark on your plans was off by 0.8 foot. What do you do?
How you own and contain a design error found in the field.
Holds affected work, confirms with the surveyor, lists what is built, shifts or redesigns, and tells the owner in writing early.

I'd ask the contractor to hold work that depends on elevations and have the surveyor confirm from two other control points. Then I'd list what is built: pads, pipe inverts, curb. Often I can shift the whole design by 0.8 foot if outfalls and tie-ins still work. Any part that doesn't gets redesigned. I'd tell the owner the same day, in writing.

client-services.heading: Client services manager questions
qs: How is managing client accounts different from working a support queue?
Whether you understand the account side of the role, not only ticket work.
Ownership of the whole relationship over time: goals, renewals, several contacts, and problems spotted before the client raises them.

In a queue I solve the ticket in front of me and move on. With accounts I own the same clients for months. I know their goals, who signs the contract, and what went wrong last quarter. A lot of the job is spotting problems before they call, and making sure the service still fits what they need at renewal.
You inherit twenty accounts from a manager who left. What do you do in your first weeks?
How you take over relationships without dropping anything.
Reading the history, ranking accounts by risk and renewal date, and meeting each key contact early instead of waiting for problems.

First I read each account's notes, open issues, contract terms and renewal date. I rank them: anything with an open complaint or a renewal in the next few months goes first. Then I call each main contact, introduce myself, and ask what is working and what is not. I write down every promise the last manager made so nothing gets lost in the handover.
What is an SLA, and what do you do when your team is about to miss one?
Your grasp of service commitments and how you act before a breach.
A service level agreement is a written promise, such as response or fix times. Telling the client before the deadline passes, with a new time and the reason, beats silence.

An SLA, or service level agreement, is the part of the contract that sets measurable promises, like how fast we respond or fix an issue. If we are about to miss one, I tell the client before the deadline, not after. I say what is late, why, and when they will have it. Then I check whether the contract gives them a credit and make sure it is applied without them having to ask.
A client asks your team for extra work that is not in their contract. How do you handle it?
Whether you can protect the scope of the contract without hurting the relationship.
Acknowledging the need, checking the contract, and turning the request into a priced change order or a clear decision, not quietly absorbing it.

I first check the contract to be sure it really is out of scope. Then I tell the client it is a fair request and explain it falls outside what we agreed. I get an estimate from the team and send a short change order with cost and timing. If it is tiny and good for the account, my manager and I might do it once, but we say so openly so it does not become the new normal.
Walk me through how you would run a quarterly business review with a client.
Your ability to run a structured review that shows value and sets next steps.
Prepared numbers tied to the client's goals, honesty about problems, a focus on their next quarter, and an ending with owners and dates.

Before the meeting I ask the client what they want to cover and pull the numbers that match their goals, like volume, response times and open issues. In the meeting I start with their goals, show results against them, and name anything we missed and what we changed. Then we plan the next quarter. I send a summary the same day with each action, its owner and its date.
What early signs tell you a client might not renew?
Whether you can spot the risk of losing a client before the renewal talk.
Concrete signals such as falling usage, a quiet or departed main contact, new decision makers, late payments, or questions about exporting data.

Usage dropping is the clearest one. Others: my main contact stops answering, a new executive arrives, invoices start being paid late, or they ask how to export their data. Complaints are actually a better sign than silence, because they still care. When I see two or three signals together I flag the account and set up a call to ask directly how things are going.
Your main contact at a big client leaves their company. What do you do?
How you protect an account that depended on one person.
Quickly meeting the new owner, recapping the value delivered, and having more than one contact at every account so it does not happen again.

If I can, I ask the departing contact who takes over and get an introduction. I meet the new person soon, with a short recap of what we do for them, the results so far and open items. I treat it like a new sale, because they did not choose us. Afterward I make sure I know at least two or three people there, including someone senior.
A client's executive emails your CEO to complain and skips you. How do you respond?
How you handle an escalation over your head without getting defensive.
Owning it quickly, briefing your leaders with facts, reaching the executive with a plan, and finding out why they felt they could not come to you.

I would not take it personally; it means the problem felt big to them. I give my CEO a short brief the same day: what happened, what we have done, and what I propose. Then I call the executive, with my leader if that helps, and give a plan with dates. Later I ask my usual contact what made them go higher, so I can fix the gap.
Our system sent a client a report with wrong numbers, and they have already used it. How do you tell them?
How you communicate an error your own company made.
Telling them fast and plainly: what is wrong, the impact and what you are doing, then a follow-up with the cause and the fix, without excuses.

I call before they find it, then confirm in writing. I say plainly which report was wrong, which numbers, and since when. I send the corrected figures or a time when they will have them, and offer to help explain it to anyone who used the report. Once we know the cause, I send a short note on what happened and what we changed so it does not repeat.
Your company is raising prices, and your largest client will be upset. How do you deliver the news?
How you handle a hard commercial message while keeping the client.
Notice as the contract requires or earlier, a personal call before the letter, the reason tied to value, and knowing in advance what flexibility you have.

I check the contract for the notice it requires and tell them well before that, by phone, before any formal letter. I explain the reason and remind them of the results we delivered this year. Before the call I agree with my manager what we can offer, like a phased increase or a longer term at a fixed rate, so I am not inventing deals on the spot. Then I follow up in writing.
What would you put into a client health score, and how would you know it works?
How you turn scattered signals into an early warning you can trust.
A few weighted signals tied to outcomes, plus a check that low scores actually came before past churn.

I would mix usage, support ticket trends, sentiment from the main contacts, whether we have an executive sponsor, and billing problems. I keep it to five or six signals so people trust it. Then I test it: look back a year and see whether the accounts that churned scored red months earlier. If they did not, I change the weights before anyone acts on it.
How do you map who matters inside a client account?
Whether you build relationships beyond one friendly contact.
Names the roles: who signs, who owns the budget, the champion, daily users, possible blockers. Keeps more than one relationship per account.

For each key account I write down who signs the renewal, who owns the budget, who champions us, who uses the product daily and who might argue against us. Then I check where I depend on a single person. If my only relationship is the daily admin, I ask them to introduce me to their manager before renewal, framed as a review of results, not a sales pitch.
A client is using 30% of the licenses they pay for, and renewal is in 90 days. What do you do?
How you handle a renewal risk early and honestly.
Find out why before renewal talks, run an adoption plan, and be ready to reduce seats rather than lose the client.

First I find out why: a rollout that stalled, a team that left, or a product that does not fit their workflow. If adoption stalled, I set up training for the teams not using it and agree on a target with the sponsor within 30 days. If they truly need fewer seats, I would rather renew a smaller contract we can grow than defend a number that loses the whole account.
Someone at a client emails asking to be made an admin and to change the billing address. They are not an authorized contact. What do you do?
Whether you protect the client's account and data, even when it slows things down.
No change until an authorized contact confirms through a channel already on file. Polite with the requester, and fraud signs get flagged.

I make no change yet. I reply politely that for security we need approval from an authorized contact, and I reach that contact through the phone number or email already on file, not the details in the request. A billing change from an unknown person is a classic fraud pattern, so if anything looks off I also flag it to our security team.
In the handoff from sales you learn the rep promised a feature we do not have. The client expects it next month. How do you handle it?
How you fix a broken promise without hiding it or blaming a colleague in front of the client.
Confirm the facts internally first, then tell the client early and plainly, with what is possible instead.

First I check with the rep and product what was said and whether anything is planned. Then I call the client before they find out on their own. I say plainly the feature will not be there next month, without blaming the rep, and bring options: a workaround, a real date if one exists, or a contract change my manager approves. Then I fix the handoff process.
At renewal, the client asks for a 20% discount or they will look at a competitor. How do you respond?
Your ability to negotiate a renewal without giving away value.
Find the real reason, show the value delivered, and trade any concession for something: a longer term, a smaller scope, or a reference.

I ask what is behind it: budget cuts, a cheaper quote, or doubt about value. Then I show what they got this year in their own numbers. If a concession makes sense, I trade it rather than give it: a lower price for a two-year term, fewer seats, or a reference. I agree my limits with my manager before the call so I am not making up numbers in the room.
Your biggest client wants a feature the product team has said no to. How do you push for it?
How you influence teams you do not manage.
Turns the request into the client's real problem, backs it with evidence and revenue at stake, and accepts the answer honestly.

I find the problem behind the request, since product may solve it another way. Then I bring evidence: how many accounts ask for something similar, the revenue they represent, and what this client does today instead. If the answer is still no, I tell the client honestly and help with a workaround. I never promise what product has not committed to.
A client has had three serious outages this quarter and says one more means they leave. What is your plan?
How you lead a recovery when trust is already low.
Own it, bring the root cause and fixes in writing with a senior engineer, set regular updates, and apply contract credits without being asked.

I meet the sponsor with someone senior from engineering, not alone. We explain the root cause of each outage in plain words and what is changing, with dates. I set a weekly update until the fixes are done, and I make sure any service credits their contract allows are applied without them having to ask. Then we review the next 90 days together.
Tell me about an account you lost. What would you do differently?
Whether you learn from churn instead of blaming price or the product.
An honest story, the warning signs that were missed, and a specific change in how you work now.

I lost a client of about 40 users after two years. Looking back, the signs were there: our champion was promoted, logins dropped, and they stopped coming to reviews. I read it as a busy season. Now I track sponsor changes and usage drops every month, and any account with both gets a call with a senior contact within two weeks, not at renewal time.

clinical-research.heading: Clinical research and medical affairs questions
qs: What does ALCOA mean for source documents?
Whether you know the basic standard for trial data.
Each letter explained with what it looks like at a site, plus awareness that ALCOA+ adds more qualities.

Attributable, Legible, Contemporaneous, Original and Accurate. At a site I can see who wrote each entry and when, it was recorded at the time, corrections are a single line with initials, date and reason, and the chart matches the case report form. ALCOA+ adds complete, consistent, enduring and available.
What is the difference between an adverse event and a serious adverse event?
Your grasp of safety definitions that drive reporting.
Seriousness is defined by outcome, not intensity, and the candidate can name the criteria.

An adverse event is any unfavorable medical occurrence in a participant, related to the study drug or not. It is serious if it causes death, is life-threatening, requires or prolongs a hospital stay, causes lasting disability, is a birth defect, or is an important medical event. Serious is about outcome, not intensity: a severe headache can be non-serious.
What is the Form FDA 1572, and who signs it?
Whether you know the investigator's commitments in an FDA drug study.
It is the Statement of Investigator under an IND, signed by the principal investigator, and kept up to date.

It is the Statement of Investigator for a drug or biologic study under an IND. The principal investigator signs it and commits to follow the protocol, personally supervise the study, use IRB review and informed consent, and report as required. It lists sub-investigators, sites and labs, so I update it when those change. Device studies use an investigator agreement instead.
During a monitoring visit you find a participant signed an older version of the consent form. What do you do?
How you handle a consent problem without losing sight of the participant.
Re-consent on the current approved version, document and report the deviation, and check every other participant.

I confirm which version the IRB had approved on that date. If the participant signed a superseded form, the site re-consents them on the current version at the next visit, or sooner if the change affects safety. I note it in my report, the site logs it as a deviation and reports it per IRB rules, and we check every other consent that day.
The study drug fridge log shows the temperature went out of range over the weekend. What happens next?
Your handling of investigational product when storage fails.
Quarantine, document, let the sponsor decide on use, dose no one meanwhile, and find the cause.

The site quarantines the affected kits, labels them do not use, and keeps them at the right temperature. We record the highest or lowest reading and how long it lasted, then send that to the sponsor, who decides if the drug is usable. No patient gets those kits until then. I also look at why: the alarm, the power, who checks the log.
You discover a participant who did not meet one inclusion criterion was enrolled and has already been dosed. How do you handle it?
How you balance participant safety, data integrity and honest reporting.
Safety first, the sponsor's medical monitor decides on continuation, the deviation is reported, and the cause is fixed.

First I tell the investigator, who checks the participant is safe. The sponsor's medical monitor then decides whether they stay on drug and how their data are handled; the site does not decide alone. It is reported as an important deviation to the sponsor and to the IRB if its rules require. Then we fix the cause, for example a second person checking eligibility before randomization.
A physician asks you, as a medical science liaison, about using your product for an unapproved indication. How do you respond?
Whether you know the line between scientific exchange and off-label promotion.
Answer only an unsolicited request, stay balanced and narrow, document it, and keep sales out of it.

If the question came unprompted, I can answer it. I give a balanced scientific answer limited to what was asked, say clearly the use is not approved, and share the data, including weak or negative results. I log the request through medical information. I never raise the topic myself and never pass it to sales to follow up.
An investigator calls at night wanting to unblind a participant who is in the emergency room. What do you advise?
Your judgement on emergency unblinding in a blinded trial.
Unblind when knowing the treatment changes care, use the proper system, limit it to one participant, and document it.

Safety comes first. If knowing the treatment would change how the patient is treated, the investigator can unblind; a quick call to the medical monitor helps, but they need no permission. If care is the same either way, stopping the drug may be enough. They use the randomization system, unblind only that participant, keep others blinded, and document why and when.
How do you decide what to check when you cannot verify every data point at a site?
Whether you can apply risk-based monitoring sensibly.
Focus on data critical to safety and the main result, and use central data trends to target visits.

I start with what protects participants and the main result: consent, eligibility, serious adverse events, study drug, and the primary endpoint. Those get full checks. For the rest I follow the monitoring plan and central data: sites with unusual query rates, late entry or odd patterns get more on-site time. ICH E6 supports this risk-based approach.
A site enrolls twice as fast as the others and its data look almost perfect. What concerns you, and what do you do?
How you spot possible misconduct and escalate it properly.
Knows real data are messy, looks for concrete evidence, and escalates to quality assurance instead of accusing.

It might just be a great site, but real data are messy. I would look for identical vital signs, visits on days the clinic is closed, or lab dates that do not match. I compare source to outside records like pharmacy or lab reports. If it does not add up, I take the evidence to my manager and quality assurance rather than accusing the site myself.
What has to happen before the first participant can be dosed under a new IND?
Whether you know the regulatory steps that must be complete before a study can start.
The 30-day rule and clinical hold, plus the site-level pieces: IRB approval, a signed 1572 and controlled drug supply.

The sponsor submits the IND. It goes into effect 30 days after FDA receives it unless FDA places a clinical hold, or earlier if FDA says so. Each site also needs IRB approval of the protocol and consent and a signed 1572 from the investigator. I would not release drug to a site until all of that is on file.
A participant says they want to stop the study. What do you do first?
Whether you separate stopping study treatment from withdrawing from the study.
Ask what they mean, offer continued follow-up, keep data already collected, and document the decision clearly.

I ask what they mean: stop the study drug, or leave the study completely. Many want to stop the drug but are fine with visits or a phone call, and that follow-up keeps their data useful. If they withdraw consent fully, we stop collecting new data and document it. Data collected before withdrawal stay in the study, as FDA expects.
What can a principal investigator delegate, and what can't they?
Your understanding of investigator responsibility and real oversight at a site.
Tasks can be delegated to qualified, trained staff on the log. Responsibility cannot, and medical judgments need qualified people.

The PI can delegate tasks to trained staff listed on the delegation log, but never the responsibility. Medical judgments, like eligibility calls or whether an adverse event is related, go to people qualified to make them, usually sub-investigators. I look for proof of supervision: signed reviews and regular meetings, not just a signature on the log.
New safety data mean the protocol dosing should change today, but the amendment is not approved yet. Can the site act?
Whether you know the one exception to getting IRB approval before a protocol change.
Yes, only to eliminate an apparent immediate hazard. Then the IRB and FDA are notified. All other changes wait for approval.

Yes, but only to eliminate an apparent immediate hazard to participants. The site can make that change right away. The IRB is then notified promptly, and the sponsor submits a protocol amendment to FDA. Any change that is not about an immediate hazard waits for IRB approval, even if it looks small.
What makes an adverse event reportable to FDA in an IND safety report, and how fast?
Your command of IND safety reporting rules and timelines.
Serious, unexpected and a suspected adverse reaction. The 15-day and 7-day calendar-day clocks, with causality judged on evidence.

It must be serious, unexpected compared with the investigator's brochure, and a suspected adverse reaction, meaning a reasonable possibility the drug caused it. The sponsor reports within 15 calendar days of deciding it qualifies. If it is unexpected and fatal or life-threatening, the limit is 7 calendar days from first receiving the information.
Who is responsible for ClinicalTrials.gov, and what are the main deadlines?
Whether you know the registration and results reporting duties for applicable clinical trials.
The responsible party, registration within 21 days of first enrollment, and results generally within one year of primary completion.

For an applicable clinical trial, the responsible party, usually the sponsor, registers it no later than 21 days after the first participant is enrolled. Results are generally due within one year of the primary completion date. Delays are allowed only in specific cases, such as a product not yet approved. I also keep status updates current.
A site wants to record source data directly in a new electronic system. What do you check?
How you judge whether electronic source records will be trustworthy and inspection-ready.
Validation, a secure audit trail, unique role-based logins, monitor access, retention, and certified copies where paper is used.

I check that the system is validated for this use and has a secure audit trail showing who changed what and when. Access must be by role, with unique logins and no shared passwords. I ask how monitors get read-only access and how records stay retrievable for the full retention period. Any printouts used as source must be certified copies.
Why should the sponsor's study team not see the unblinded interim results the data monitoring committee reviews?
Your understanding of how trial integrity is protected during interim analyses.
Knowing the comparison can bias decisions on conduct. An independent statistician reports to the committee and the team gets only its recommendation.

If the people running the trial know how the arms compare, it can quietly shape their choices: which sites to push, how to chase missing data, whether to amend the protocol. That damages the trial's credibility. So an independent statistician prepares the unblinded reports for the committee, and the team hears only the recommendation, such as continue or stop.
A physician asks for drug and funding to run their own study. How does medical affairs handle it?
How you keep investigator-initiated research scientific, independent and separate from sales.
Formal review on scientific merit, no sales role, the investigator acts as sponsor, a written contract, and freedom to publish.

It goes through our formal review for investigator-initiated studies, judged on scientific merit and real evidence gaps, never on the doctor's prescribing. Sales has no role. If we support it, the investigator is the sponsor and holds any IND needed. We provide drug or a grant under a contract, and they are free to publish the results, including negative ones.
An FDA inspection ends with a Form 483. How do you lead the response?
How you turn inspection findings into a credible, timely corrective plan.
A written response within about 15 business days, with root cause, correction, prevention and evidence for each observation.

At close-out I make sure we understand each observation. Then I lead a written response within 15 business days, because FDA generally considers responses received in that window before deciding next steps. For each item I give the root cause, the correction, the step that prevents it happening again, and evidence with dates. Promising training alone rarely convinces.

cloud-engineer.heading: Cloud engineer questions
qs: What makes a subnet public or private in a cloud network?
Whether you know how traffic really enters and leaves a cloud network.
The route table decides it: a public subnet routes to an internet gateway, a private one does not.

It is the route table, not the name. A public subnet has a route that sends internet traffic to an internet gateway, so servers with public IPs can be reached. A private subnet has no such route. Its servers go out through a NAT gateway that sits in a public subnet, and nobody on the internet can start a connection to them.
How are security groups different from network ACLs?
Your grasp of the two firewall layers and when each one matters.
Security groups are stateful and attach to instances. Network ACLs are stateless, work per subnet and can deny.

A security group attaches to an instance's network interface, has only allow rules, and is stateful: if traffic is let in, the reply goes out automatically. A network ACL sits on the subnet, has allow and deny rules checked in number order, and is stateless, so I must also allow return traffic on the high ephemeral ports. I do most work in security groups.
Your team will connect a new VPC to the office network later. How do you choose its IP range?
Whether you plan address space before it becomes a problem.
A range that does not overlap with other networks, with room to grow, recorded in one shared plan.

First I check the ranges already used by the office, the VPN and our other VPCs, because overlapping ranges cannot be peered or routed cleanly. I pick a free private range, size it bigger than today's need, say a /16 split into /20 subnets per zone, and write it into our shared IP plan so the next team does not collide with it.
What is the state file in an infrastructure-as-code tool, and how do you keep it safe on a team?
Whether you have run infrastructure as code with more than one person.
State maps the code to real resources. It lives in a remote, locked, encrypted store and is never edited by hand.

The state file records which real resource each block of code created, so the tool knows what to change. On a team I keep it in a remote backend with locking, so two people cannot apply at once, plus encryption and tight access, because it can hold secrets in plain text. Nobody edits it by hand; if it must change, we use the tool's own state commands.
A server in a private subnet cannot download updates. Walk me through how you find the cause.
How you trace a network path step by step instead of guessing.
Following the packet: DNS, security group, ACL, route table, NAT gateway, and the NAT's own route out.

I follow the packet. Does DNS resolve? Does the security group allow outbound on 443? Does the subnet's ACL allow that port out and the return traffic on ephemeral ports? Does the route table send 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway? Is that NAT in a public subnet whose route goes to the internet gateway? Flow logs then show me where packets get rejected.
Someone changed a setting by hand in the console, and now your plan wants to undo it. What do you do?
How you handle drift between the code and what is really running.
Not applying blindly: finding out why it changed, then putting the fix into code or reverting it on purpose.

I do not just apply. I find who changed it and why; often it was a fix made during an incident. If the change is right, I put it into the code so the plan comes back clean. If it was wrong, I agree with the owner when to revert it. Then I raise how to stop it recurring, such as read-only console access in production.
When would you buy committed-use discounts, and when would you use spot instances?
Whether you match pricing models to how a workload behaves.
Commitments for the steady baseline, spot for work that can be interrupted, on-demand for the rest.

I look at usage over a few months. The floor that never goes away, like core databases and always-on services, gets a one- or three-year commitment. Spot capacity is much cheaper, but the provider can take it back with short warning, so I use it only for batch jobs, build runners or stateless workers that can restart. Spiky, unknown load stays on demand.
A developer asks for full admin rights to get unblocked today. How do you respond?
How you hold the line on access without blocking people's work.
Solving the real need with a narrow role and short-lived credentials, never a standing admin grant.

I ask what exactly they are trying to do. Usually it is one service, so I give a role scoped to that service and that environment, used through temporary credentials rather than long-lived access keys. If it is urgent I add a time limit and review it afterwards. Admin in production stays with a small group, with every action logged.
The monthly bill jumped 40% and nobody launched anything new. How do you find out why?
How you investigate cost the way you would investigate an outage.
Breaking the bill down by service, account, tag and usage type, then checking the common hidden drivers.

I open the cost report and split the increase by service, then by account and tag, then by usage type. Hidden growth is often data transfer, traffic through a NAT gateway, log volume or old snapshots. Last time a config change made a nightly job copy data across regions. After the fix I added a budget alert and anomaly detection so we hear in days, not at month end.
Your plan shows it will destroy and recreate the production database. What do you do?
Whether you stop and understand a dangerous change before applying it.
Stopping the apply, finding the field that forces replacement, protecting the data, and changing the approach.

I stop and do not apply. The plan marks which attribute forces replacement; often it is a renamed resource, a changed subnet group or an engine setting. A rename I fix by moving the state address, not by recreating. For a real change I take a snapshot, plan a migration with the data owner, and make sure deletion protection is on so one bad apply cannot drop the database.
Your company has grown to 30 VPCs connected by peering. Why does that become a problem, and what would you use instead?
Whether you know how cloud network links scale beyond a few networks.
Peering is not transitive, so a full mesh grows fast. A central hub with separate route tables keeps it manageable and keeps environments apart.

Peering joins exactly two VPCs, and traffic cannot pass through one to reach a third. Thirty VPCs in a full mesh means 435 links, plus routes in every table. I would move to a central hub, such as a transit gateway, with separate route tables so production and test stay apart. A pair that moves a lot of data might keep a direct peering, since the hub charges per gigabyte.
You are moving a public service to a new load balancer with a new address. How do you handle DNS so the cutover is quick and reversible?
How you plan a DNS cutover around caching.
Lower the TTL well ahead of the change, by at least the old TTL, keep the old target running for rollback, then raise the TTL once stable.

Resolvers cache a record for its TTL, the time it may be kept. If the TTL is a day, I lower it to about 60 seconds at least a day before the move, so every cache holds the short value. Then I switch the record, watch traffic shift, and keep the old load balancer running so I can switch back. Some clients cache too long, so I wait before turning it off, then raise the TTL again.
Your NAT gateway costs more each month than the servers behind it. What is usually going on?
Whether you know where hidden network charges come from.
NAT charges for every gigabyte it processes. Measure the traffic first, then send heavy flows to storage and provider services through private endpoints.

A NAT gateway charges for every gigabyte it processes, on top of its hourly fee. Often servers are pulling large files from object storage through it. I check flow logs to see where the bytes go. For object storage, a gateway endpoint carries that traffic with no extra charge. For other services, I weigh an interface endpoint's hourly fee against the NAT savings.
Finance wants each team to see its own share of the cloud bill. How do you make that possible?
Whether you can turn a shared bill into numbers each team owns.
An account or project per team where possible, a few required tags that are enforced in code and policy, and an agreed rule for shared costs that tags cannot reach.

A separate account or project per team and environment gives the cleanest split. On top of that, a short list of required tags, like team and environment, set in our modules and enforced by policy so untagged resources fail. Some costs, like shared networking, carry no team tag, so we agree on a rule to split them, for example by traffic. Then a monthly report each team lead actually reviews.
How would you split infrastructure code and state across environments and teams?
Your judgement about blast radius and speed in infrastructure code.
Separate state per environment and per layer, shared modules with versions, and a path that promotes changes from staging to production.

I keep separate state for each environment and for layers that change at different speeds, like network, data and apps. One bad apply then touches one slice, and plans stay fast. Shared pieces live in versioned modules, so production pins a version that already ran in staging. Teams read each other's outputs rather than editing each other's state.
You want to move existing resources into a new module without rebuilding them. How do you do it safely?
Whether you can change code structure without touching live resources.
Tell the tool the address changed, with a declared move or a state move. Confirm the plan shows nothing to add or destroy before applying.

To the tool, a new address looks like a new resource, so a plain refactor plans a destroy and a create. I take a state backup, then declare the move in code with a moved block, or move the entries with a state command. I run a plan and expect zero to add and zero to destroy. If anything shows a replace, I stop and fix the mapping before applying.
A teammate set a rule to move all logs to the coldest storage class after a week, and the bill went up. Why could that happen?
Whether you know the fine print of cheaper storage tiers.
Cold tiers have per-object transition fees, minimum storage periods and sometimes minimum billed sizes. Many small, short-lived files can cost more there.

Cheap tiers come with fine print. Each object moved costs a request fee, and with millions of small log files that adds up. Cold tiers bill a minimum stay, often months, so files deleted early are charged anyway, and some bill small objects as if they were larger. I would check object count, size and retention, bundle small files, and move only what we keep long enough to pay off.
We acquired a company whose network uses the same IP range as ours, and two apps must talk next month. What are your options?
How you solve a network problem that has no clean fix.
Knows peering cannot join overlapping ranges. Offers private service endpoints or NAT as a bridge, with re-addressing as the lasting fix.

Peering and most routed links will not work, because one address would point to two places. For next month I would expose only the services needed through private service endpoints, which give each side a local address inside its own network. If that does not fit, NAT through a non-overlapping range in between. In parallel I would plan to re-address one side for good.
Every server behind the load balancer went unhealthy at once, but the servers were fine. The health check calls the database. What went wrong, and how would you fix the design?
How you design health checks that do not turn a small fault into an outage.
A deep check tied to a shared dependency fails everywhere at once. Keep the load balancer check to the process itself and watch dependencies separately.

The database had a slow moment, every check failed together, and the load balancer pulled every server, so a partial problem became a full outage. I would make the load balancer check answer only whether this process can serve requests, with no calls to shared systems. Database health goes to monitoring and alerts instead, where a person can judge it.
A developer pushed a cloud access key to a public repository an hour ago. What do you do, in order?
How you respond to a live credential leak, step by step.
Disable the key first, then check audit logs for what it did, remove anything created and fix the cause. Deleting the commit alone is not enough.

First I deactivate the key, because bots scan public repos within minutes, and I give a new one to whoever needs it. Then I search the audit logs for every call made with that key since the push, in all regions, looking for new users, keys or servers. I remove what was created and check the bill. Rewriting the commit history comes last, since the key is already copied.

cloud-security.heading: Cloud security engineer questions
qs: What does the shared responsibility model mean for a team running virtual machines versus a managed database?
Whether you know where the provider's job ends and your team's job begins.
The provider secures the cloud itself; the customer secures what it puts in the cloud, and the line moves with the type of service.

The provider always owns the data centers, the hardware and the hypervisor. On virtual machines we own the operating system, patching, firewall rules and access. On a managed database the provider patches the engine, but we still own who can connect, encryption settings, backup retention and the data itself. Bad access settings are always on us.
In AWS, how is a security group different from a network ACL?
Your grasp of the basic network controls in a cloud account.
Security groups are stateful, attach to instances and have allow rules only; network ACLs are stateless, apply to subnets and have both allow and deny rules.

A security group sits on the network interface, has only allow rules, and is stateful: if inbound traffic is allowed, the reply goes back out on its own. A network ACL covers a whole subnet, has numbered allow and deny rules checked in order, and is stateless, so I must allow the return traffic myself, usually the ephemeral port range.
Why do you push teams to use roles instead of long-lived access keys?
Whether you understand why temporary credentials are safer than stored secrets.
Roles hand out short-lived credentials that expire on their own; static keys get copied into code and logs and stay valid until someone rotates them.

A role gives temporary credentials that expire after a set time, by default one hour when a role is assumed, and nothing has to be stored in code. Static keys end up on laptops, in build logs and in repos, and they work until someone rotates them. For workloads I use instance roles or workload identity; for people, single sign-on into roles.
How do you lock down the root user of a new AWS account?
Your habits for protecting the most powerful identity in an account.
Strong MFA, no access keys, a controlled process to use it, an alert on every sign-in, and daily work done through other identities.

I put a hardware MFA key on it, delete any access keys, and keep the credentials in a vault that needs two people to open. Daily work goes through single sign-on and roles. I set an alert on every root sign-in, so the team knows within minutes. Root is only for the few tasks that require it, like closing the account.
An engineer asks you to open SSH to 0.0.0.0/0 on a production server to debug an outage. How do you respond?
How you balance urgent business needs against exposing a server to the internet.
You help fix the outage fast but through a logged, narrow access path, and you make sure any temporary rule gets removed.

I would not open port 22 to the whole internet, but I would not block the fix either. I would get them in through Session Manager, which needs no open inbound port and logs the session, or allow only their IP for a set time with a ticket to remove it. After the outage, we make the logged path the default.
A scanner flags an S3 bucket that is open to the public. What do you do in the first hour?
How you contain an exposure while keeping the evidence you need.
Confirm it is not public on purpose, close access, save the old policy, check what was exposed and who read it, then fix the cause.

First I make sure it is not a public website bucket by design. If not, I turn on Block Public Access and save the old policy as evidence. Then I check what data it holds and search access logs or CloudTrail data events for outside reads. I tell the owner and the incident lead, then find how the setting got there so it stays fixed.
A developer pushed an AWS access key to a public code repository an hour ago. What now?
Whether you treat a leaked secret as already used and act in the right order.
Disable the key at once, give the app a new one, search the audit logs for what the key did, and only then clean up the code history.

Bots scan public repos within minutes, so I assume the key was used. I deactivate it right away and issue a new one to the app. Then I search CloudTrail for that access key ID: new users, new roles, servers started in odd regions. Removing the commit comes last, because the key has already been copied.
What logging do you set up in a new cloud environment, and how do you stop an attacker from erasing it?
Whether you can build an audit trail that survives a compromised account.
Audit logs for every account and region, sent to a separate locked account with write-once storage, plus an alert if logging is changed.

I turn on an organization-wide CloudTrail trail for all regions, plus VPC flow logs and DNS logs where they help. The logs go to a separate log-archive account that workload admins cannot touch, into a bucket with Object Lock, so nobody can delete them during the retention period. I also alert if anyone stops or edits the trail.
Why does it matter whether EC2 instances use IMDSv2?
Your knowledge of a common path from a web bug to stolen cloud credentials.
IMDSv2 needs a session token from a PUT request, which blocks most server-side request forgery attempts to read the instance role's credentials.

The metadata service hands out the instance role's credentials. With version 1, a server-side request forgery bug can trick the app into fetching them with a plain GET. Version 2 first needs a PUT request that returns a token, sent back in a header, which most such bugs cannot do. I require it in launch templates and flag any instance still allowing v1.
How do you stop a risky setting across 200 AWS accounts instead of fixing it one by one?
Whether you can secure an organization with guardrails rather than manual cleanup.
Preventive controls at the organization level, such as service control policies, plus detective checks and code review for what gets past them.

I use service control policies in AWS Organizations to deny actions outright, like turning off CloudTrail or using unapproved regions. An SCP never grants access; it only caps what any role in the account can do. Then I add AWS Config rules to flag drift, and check infrastructure-as-code templates before they deploy.
A role has an allow for s3:GetObject, but the call still fails with Access Denied. How does AWS decide, and where do you look?
Whether you know how AWS evaluates policies, not just how to write them.
An explicit deny anywhere wins, an allow is required, and SCPs, boundaries or session policies can cap it. The bucket policy and KMS key matter too.

An explicit deny anywhere wins, and with no allow the result is a default deny. So I look for a deny in the bucket policy, an SCP, a permission boundary or a session policy that caps the role. If the object uses a KMS key, the role also needs decrypt rights on that key. The error message often names the policy type that blocked the call.
A monitoring vendor wants a role in our account that they can assume. How do you set up the trust policy?
Whether you know the confused deputy problem and how to prevent it.
Trust only the vendor's account, require the external ID they assign to you, keep permissions read-only and scoped, and give the role an owner.

I trust the vendor's AWS account as the principal and add a condition requiring the sts:ExternalId value they assign to us. That stops another of their customers from tricking the vendor into using our role, the confused deputy problem. Permissions stay read-only and limited to what the product needs, and the role gets an owner and a yearly review.
A developer has no IAM write rights, only iam:PassRole on all roles and permission to create Lambda functions. Is that safe?
Whether you can spot privilege escalation paths that do not look like admin rights.
No: they can attach a powerful role to code they control. Limit PassRole to specific role ARNs and add an iam:PassedToService condition.

No. With PassRole on every role, they can create a function, attach the most powerful role in the account and have their code do whatever that role can. It is admin in two steps. I would limit PassRole to the one or two execution roles they need, by ARN, and add an iam:PassedToService condition so those roles can only be passed to Lambda.
Our build pipeline deploys to AWS with stored access keys. How would you replace them, and what goes in the trust policy?
