How you remove long-lived secrets from automation without opening a new hole.
OIDC federation for short-lived sessions, with a trust policy that checks the audience and pins the subject claim to the right repository and branch.

I register the CI system as an OIDC identity provider in IAM, and each job trades its signed token for a short session on a deploy role. The key part is the trust policy: it checks the audience and pins the subject claim to our repository and main branch. Without that, other projects on the same CI service could assume our role. Then I delete the old keys.
On a Kubernetes cluster in AWS, every pod can use the node's IAM role. Why is that a problem, and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand workload identity for containers.
One compromised pod gets every right on the node. Give each service its own role, keep the node role minimal, and block pods from instance metadata.

The node role usually holds rights for every workload on the node, so one compromised pod gets all of them. I give each service its own role through IAM Roles for Service Accounts or EKS Pod Identity, trim the node role, and require IMDSv2 with a hop limit of 1, so pods that are not on the host network cannot reach the node's credentials.
A product team asks for a permanent exception to the rule that no database may be publicly reachable, for a partner integration. How do you handle it?
Your judgement in weighing risk against the business, and how you record the decision.
Find the real need, offer a safer design first, and if an exception is granted, it has limits, extra controls, a named owner and an expiry date.

First I ask what the partner actually needs. Often a private connection, a site-to-site VPN or an API in front of the database does the job. If none works in time, I grant a limited exception: only the partner's IP ranges, TLS required, strong authentication, extra alerting, and a named owner who accepts the risk. It expires in 90 days and gets reviewed.
How do you make sure a sensitive S3 bucket can only be read from our own network and organization, even with stolen credentials?
Whether you can design controls that still hold when credentials leak.
A data perimeter: bucket policy denies requests outside your VPC endpoints and organization, and endpoint policies stop copying data out to foreign buckets.

I add a deny to the bucket policy for requests that do not come through our VPC endpoint, using aws:SourceVpce, or from principals outside our organization, using aws:PrincipalOrgID. Stolen keys used from a laptop then fail. A VPC endpoint policy blocks copying data to buckets we do not own. I test first, since this also blocks console access.
An EC2 instance is mining crypto and calling out to a known bad IP. How do you contain it without destroying evidence?
How you balance fast containment with keeping evidence.
Isolate, do not terminate. Know that tracked connections can survive a security group change, preserve disks and memory, and cut off its credentials.

I do not terminate it. I turn on termination protection, detach it from its autoscaling group, and swap in a security group with no rules. Tracked connections can survive that change, so I add a network ACL deny too. Then I snapshot the volumes, capture memory if possible, and revoke the role's older sessions so stolen credentials stop working.
You rolled out a service control policy, and an hour later production deployments started failing. What do you do, and what do you change?
How you own a mistake in a control that affects every team.
Roll back fast, tell affected teams, find the blocked call. Then test in a sandbox OU, check CloudTrail before enforcing, and roll out in stages.

I detach or revert the policy first, since broken production deploys cost more than a few hours without the guardrail, and I post what happened in the incident channel. Then I find the call it blocked. Next time it goes to a sandbox OU first, I check CloudTrail for who makes those calls before enforcing, and I roll it out one OU at a time.

commercial-counsel.heading: Commercial and product counsel questions
qs: Which carve-outs from a limitation of liability clause do you usually accept, and why?
Your working knowledge of the clause that most often decides how much a deal can cost the company.
A short standard list with a reason for each, and a sense of where a separate higher cap works better than unlimited liability.

I usually accept carve-outs for fraud, gross negligence or willful misconduct, breach of confidentiality, and our indemnity for third-party IP claims. A party controls those risks, or a normal cap would make the promise empty. When a customer wants all data breaches uncapped, I offer a separate, higher cap instead.
What is the difference between a warranty and an indemnity?
Whether you can separate two promises that business teams often treat as the same thing.
A warranty is a promise about a fact or quality; an indemnity is a promise to defend and cover losses from set events, usually third-party claims.

A warranty is a promise that something is true, for example that the software will perform as the documentation says. If it fails, the remedy is often repair, replace or refund. An indemnity is a promise to defend and pay if a set event happens, usually a third-party claim, such as someone suing the customer for patent infringement over our product.
We signed our master agreement with a customer, and now their purchase order arrives with their own preprinted terms on the back. What do you do?
How you handle the battle of the forms in day-to-day contracting.
Relying on an order of precedence clause in the master agreement, not on whoever sent the last form, and fixing the process so it does not repeat.

First I check that our master agreement says its terms control over any purchase order terms, and that preprinted PO terms have no effect. For sales of goods, UCC 2-207 can let a form with different terms still form a contract, so I do not count on having the last word. If the clause is missing, I send a short written note and fix the template.
Engineering wants to use an AGPL-licensed library in our hosted SaaS product. What do you check?
Your understanding of open source license obligations as they apply to a real product.
Knowing that the AGPL can reach network use, and asking whether the code is modified and how it connects to the product before deciding.

The AGPL differs from the GPL because it reaches network use: if we modify the library and users interact with it over the network, we must offer them the source of our modified version. So I ask whether we will change it, how tightly it links to our code, and whether a permissively licensed option exists. Many companies simply keep AGPL code out of the product.
Marketing wants the launch page to say we are “the most secure platform on the market.” How do you review it?
Whether you know the rules on advertising claims before a launch.
Treating it as an objective comparative claim that needs proof in hand before it runs, and offering wording the team can support.

The FTC expects a company to have a reasonable basis for an objective claim before it runs, not after. “Most secure on the market” reads as a comparison buyers can rely on, so I ask what testing compares us to competitors. Usually there is none, so I suggest a claim we can prove, like naming the specific certifications we hold.
We are launching a monthly subscription that renews automatically. What do you build into the sign-up and billing flow?
Your knowledge of federal and state automatic renewal rules.
Clear terms before payment, express consent to the renewal, and an easy way to cancel, with a check of the strictest states where customers live.

Before we take card details, the page must clearly show the price, that it renews, how often and how to cancel. The customer must agree to those terms, not just to a buried link, and gets a confirmation that repeats them. Cancelling must be simple; if they signed up online, they should be able to cancel online. I design to the strictest state law, like California's.
A customer sends back our template with 80 redlines two days before quarter end. Walk me through how you handle it.
How you triage a negotiation under time pressure without giving away what matters.
Sorting changes into accept, trade and hold, using an approved playbook, and telling sales early which points need a business decision.

I go through all 80 once and sort them. Wording and clarity edits I accept. Points with a fallback in our playbook, like payment terms, I trade. The few that touch liability, IP ownership or data I hold, and I tell the sales lead the same day which ones need a business call. Then I ask for a call with their counsel to clear the big items live.
A large customer insists on unlimited liability for any data breach. How do you respond?
Your judgement on a high-stakes ask that can block a big deal.
Understanding the customer's real worry, sizing our exposure and insurance, and offering a structured answer such as a higher separate cap.

I ask what they fear most: regulator fines, notification costs or their own customers suing. Then I check our cyber insurance limits with finance. Usually I offer a separate data breach cap, a multiple of annual fees, plus clear coverage of notification costs. That answers their worry without betting the company on one account.
After a deal closes, you find a sales email promising the customer a custom service credit that is not in the contract. What do you do?
How you handle a side promise that can create legal and accounting problems.
Not hiding behind the entire agreement clause: bringing in sales and finance and then either papering or withdrawing the promise.

The entire agreement clause helps, but I would not rely on it alone; the customer may have signed because of that email. I speak with the rep, then tell finance, since a side promise can affect revenue. We decide together: document it in an amendment, or have the account owner clearly walk it back. Then I add side letters to sales training.
The product team wants to train an AI model on data our customers have already given us. What do you check before saying yes?
Whether you can trace data rights through contracts, privacy notices and regulator expectations.
Checking contract use rights and privacy promises, and knowing that a material retroactive change to data use needs affirmative consent.

I check three things. First, what our customer contracts allow us to do with their data; many limit use to providing the service. Second, what our privacy notice told users. Third, whether we would be changing terms after the fact: the FTC has long said a material retroactive change in how collected data is used needs affirmative consent. If the rights are not there, we use opt-in or new data.
A supplier's NDA includes a residuals clause. What is it, and how do you handle it?
Whether you spot a clause that quietly weakens confidentiality.
Knows it lets people use information kept in unaided memory. Strikes it, or narrows it hard, especially for code and roadmaps.

A residuals clause lets the other side's people use what they remember from our confidential information, as long as they kept no notes. For a supplier who will see our roadmap or code, that is a hole in the NDA. I strike it. If they insist, I limit it to general know-how, exclude source code and product plans, and make clear it grants no patent or copyright license.
The draft excludes “consequential damages.” Why is that not enough to protect us on lost profits?
Your grasp of damages categories and how courts read them.
Explains direct versus consequential damages. Knows courts differ on whether lost profits are direct, so the clause should name them.

Consequential damages arise from special circumstances of the injured party, not from what naturally follows any breach of that kind. Lost profits can land on either side of that line, and courts disagree. So I name the excluded categories: lost profits, revenue, data and goodwill. Then I check that the list does not wipe out damages we would need to recover.
Design wants the sign-up page to say “By continuing you agree to our Terms,” with the link in small gray text below the button. What do you tell them?
Whether you know what makes online terms enforceable.
Clear notice plus a clear act of agreement: a visible link next to the button, wording tied to the click, and a record of which version was accepted.

Courts enforce online terms when the user had reasonably conspicuous notice and clearly showed agreement. Light gray text under the button invites a fight. I ask for the notice right above the button, with readable contrast, a working link, and wording tied to the action, like “By clicking Create account.” Then we log the user, the time and the terms version so we can prove it later.
Marketing is paying creators to post about our new app. What do you require?
Your knowledge of FTC rules on endorsements.
Clear and conspicuous disclosure of the paid relationship and honest claims, all written into the creator contract, plus a plan to monitor posts.

The FTC's Endorsement Guides say a material connection, like payment or free product, must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously. So the contract requires a plain disclosure such as “ad” or “paid partner” in the post itself, not buried in hashtags. Creators say only what they really think and make no claims we could not back up. We monitor posts and fix the ones that miss.
A product manager copies you on every email about a feature “to keep it privileged.” Is it?
Whether you understand the limits of privilege for in-house lawyers.
No. Privilege covers communications made to get legal advice. Copying a lawyer or adding a label does not protect a business discussion.

Not by itself. Privilege protects confidential communications made to get or give legal advice. Copying me on a pricing debate does not change its purpose, and courts look at substance, not labels. I tell the team to send legal questions to me directly, keep them separate from business threads, and not forward my advice widely.
Why does it matter whether we are a “service provider” under California's privacy law, and what makes us one?
Your command of the CCPA's contract requirements.
Knows the status depends on a written contract with required limits. Without it, the data transfer may count as selling or sharing.

If we qualify, a customer can hand us personal data without it counting as a sale or share. That needs a written contract that limits us to named business purposes, bars us from selling or sharing the data or combining it with other data except as the rules allow, and requires us to comply with the law. Then the product must really work that way.
Our product will depend on software from a 30-person startup. How do you protect us if they fail?
How you plan for a supplier that may not survive the contract.
Uses the bankruptcy protection for licensees, escrow with real release triggers, data export and transition help, not just a right to terminate.

I make sure the deal is framed as a license of intellectual property, since section 365(n) of the Bankruptcy Code lets a licensee keep its rights if a bankrupt licensor rejects the contract. I add source code escrow with triggers like bankruptcy or end of support, and a check that the deposit actually builds. Plus data export in a usable format and paid transition help.
A big customer asks for a most-favored-customer clause on pricing. How do you respond?
Your judgement on a clause that binds future deals.
Sees the hidden cost to future pricing, brings in sales and finance, and narrows scope, term and comparison instead of just refusing.

An MFN means any better price we give another customer could flow back to this one, so sales loses room to negotiate. I ask finance what it could cost. If we agree, I narrow it: same product, similar volume and terms, a fixed period, a price adjustment as the only remedy, and no audit of our books. Often a one-time discount gives them what they really want.
We are being acquired. How do you review our customer and supplier contracts for the deal?
How you find the contracts that a sale could put at risk.
Sorts by revenue and dependency, looks for anti-assignment, change of control, exclusivity and IP license limits, and knows deal structure matters.

I start with the contracts that carry the most revenue or that we cannot run without. In each I look for anti-assignment and change-of-control clauses, termination rights, exclusivity or non-competes that would bind the buyer, and licensed-in IP. Whether a merger counts as an assignment depends on structure and state law, especially for IP licenses, so I flag consents early.
A vendor tells us late Friday that an attacker got into a system holding our customers' personal data. What do you do in the first hours?
How you lead the legal side of a security incident under time pressure.
Gets facts with privilege in mind, preserves evidence, checks notice deadlines in contracts and state laws, and makes no statement that guesses.

I join the incident team and bring in outside counsel, who engages the forensic firm to support privilege. We ask the vendor what data, whose, and whether it is contained, and tell them to preserve logs. I pull our customer contracts, since many require notice within set hours, and map which state breach laws may apply. Nothing goes out that guesses at scope.

communications.heading: Communications and PR questions
qs: What is the difference between on the record, on background and off the record?
Whether you know the ground rules for talking to reporters.
Clear definitions, plus the point that terms must be agreed before speaking, since outlets read them differently.

On the record, the reporter can quote me by name. On background, they can use what I say but credit it to something like “a company spokesperson.” Off the record usually means they cannot use it at all. Outlets read these terms differently, so I agree on them before I say anything, never after.
What is a press embargo, and how do you use one?
Your grasp of a common tool for timing news coverage.
An agreement not to publish before a set time. It rests on trust, not law, so it goes only to reporters who have agreed to it.

It is an agreement that a reporter gets the news early but does not publish before a set date and time. It gives them time to write a better story. It is a courtesy, not a contract, so I ask first, get a yes before sending, state the time with the time zone, and keep the release ready in case it breaks early.
Walk me through how you build a press release for a product launch.
Whether you can write the core document of the job.
Inverted pyramid: the news in the headline and first paragraph, a quote that adds something, the facts, the boilerplate and a media contact.

The headline states the news, not an adjective. The first paragraph answers who, what, when, where and why, so a reporter can stop there. Then the details and one quote that gives a view or a reason, not “we are thrilled.” I close with the boilerplate, the standard paragraph about the company, and a named media contact with a phone number.
How do you prepare an executive for a tough media interview?
How you get a spokesperson ready to speak for the company.
Research on the reporter, two or three key messages with proof, a mock interview with the hardest questions, and clear ground rules.

I write a one-page brief: who the reporter is, what they have written lately, the likely angle. We agree on three messages and the proof for each. Then I run a mock interview with the questions they hope will not come up. I remind them nothing is off the record unless agreed first, and that “I don't know, I'll find out” is a fine answer.
How do you show that a PR campaign worked?
Whether you measure outcomes, not just the number of articles.
Measures tied to a goal set at the start, such as message pickup, coverage quality, site traffic or inquiries, and not advertising value equivalency.

I set the goal before the campaign and measure against it. Article counts are a start, but I check whether coverage hit the right outlets and carried our key message, and whether it moved something: site visits, demo requests, sign-ups. I don't use advertising value equivalency, the ad cost of the space. The industry's own measurement principles reject it.
You find a wrong figure in a press release that went out an hour ago. What do you do?
How you own and fix a public error.
A fast correction: tell your manager, issue a corrected release that says what changed, contact reporters who used it, then fix the cause.

First I tell my manager and confirm the right number with its owner. Then we send a corrected version through the same channel, marked as a correction, with the change noted. I contact each reporter who already used it and update our website. Afterward I add a step so the owner of every number signs off before release.
Your company is announcing layoffs. In what order do people hear the news?
Your judgement on the timing of internal and external messages.
Affected staff first, privately and from their managers, then all employees, then the public close behind, with HR and legal involved early.

People losing their jobs hear first, in person or by call from their manager, with HR present. Then the rest of the staff, from the CEO, before it can reach the news. The public statement follows within the hour. I bring in HR and legal early, since rules like the federal WARN Act can require advance notice for large layoffs.
Walk me through the first hour after a crisis breaks, such as a data breach.
How you act when facts are incomplete and pressure is high.
Gather facts, convene the crisis team, issue a short holding statement, brief staff, and set the next update time, with no guessing.

I get the crisis team on a call: leaders, legal, IT security, HR. We list what we know and what we don't. Within the hour a holding statement goes out: we are aware, we are investigating, here is what customers should do now, next update at a set time. Staff get the same message. I don't guess at numbers or causes.
The CEO wants to post a personal view on a divisive public issue from the company account. How do you advise?
Your judgement and your nerve when advising leaders.
You weigh the link to the business, staff and customers, and whether actions back the words, give a clear recommendation, and let the leader decide.

I ask a few questions. Does the issue touch our business, our people or our customers directly? Do our actions back up the words? Who will be upset, and will we still stand behind it a week later? If it passes, I help write it. If not, I say plainly that I recommend against it and why, and offer a better route, like a note to staff.
Walk me through how you build a message house for a new initiative.
How you turn a strategy into messages that everyone repeats the same way.
One umbrella message, about three supporting pillars, each backed by proof points, tested with the people who will use it.

The roof is one sentence that says why this matters, in words a customer would use. Under it go three pillars, for example cost, safety and speed. Each pillar gets proof points: a figure, a customer story, a third-party source. I test it on the spokespeople and a few staff. Then it feeds the release, the FAQ and the talking points, so everyone says the same thing.
When would you give one outlet an exclusive, and what does it cost you?
Your judgement in trading reach for depth with the press.
An exclusive buys a bigger story with one outlet, at the price of others possibly skipping it. The terms are agreed up front.

I offer one when the story fits one outlet's beat and depth matters more than reach, like a feature in the trade press our buyers read. The cost is that other reporters may ignore a story a rival broke. So I agree the terms first: what is exclusive and until when. Right after it runs, I brief the others with a fresh angle.
A reporter's story about us has a factual error. How do you handle it?
Whether you can tell a real error from coverage you simply dislike.
Separates errors of fact from unflattering framing, asks politely for a correction with evidence, and lets tone complaints go.

First I check that it is a fact, not a framing we dislike. If our revenue is wrong by a digit, I email the reporter, not the editor first, with the correct figure and a source, and ask for a correction. Most fix it within the day. If the angle is unflattering but accurate, I let it go and note what we could have explained better in the interview.
Half our staff work on a factory floor with no company email. How do you get an important change to them?
How you reach employees who never sit at a desk.
Uses supervisors and shift meetings, gives managers a script and an FAQ, covers every shift, and checks that the message landed.

Supervisors are the channel, so they hear it first, with a one-page script, an FAQ and a contact for hard questions. They share it at the start-of-shift huddle on every shift, including nights and weekends. I back it with posters by the time clock. A week later I ask a few supervisors which questions came up, and I fill the gaps.
We want employees and some paid creators to post about our new product. What rules do you set?
Your knowledge of the FTC rules on endorsements.
Anyone with a material connection, such as pay, free product or a job, must disclose it clearly, and the company monitors the posts.

Under the FTC's Endorsement Guides, anyone with a material connection to us must disclose it clearly in the post, not hidden behind a link or in a pile of hashtags. That covers paid creators, people who got free product and our own employees. I give them simple wording like “#ad” or “I work here,” ask for honest views only, and we check posts and fix any that miss it.
Legal wants our apology to say we “regret any inconvenience.” You want a real apology. How do you resolve it?
How you work with lawyers when legal risk and public trust pull apart.
Learns legal's exact concern, proposes wording that is human but sticks to known facts, and escalates to the owner of the risk if needed.

I ask what exactly worries them, usually an admission of legal fault. Then I propose wording that is human but sticks to facts we know: “Customers were charged twice. We are sorry, and here is how we are fixing it.” If we still disagree, I take both versions to the executive who owns the risk and let them decide with both costs in view.
Our company is public, and the CEO wants to tease big news in a podcast interview next week. What is your advice?
Whether you know how securities rules shape what a public company can say.
Sees that material news must reach all investors at once through a proper public release, coordinated with legal and investor relations.

If the news could move the stock, it is material and must reach all investors at once, usually by press release and an SEC filing. A hint on a podcast can leak unevenly, and Regulation FD bars sharing material news with some investors before others. So legal, investor relations and I set a proper announcement date, and the CEO discusses it after that.
A reporter has one of our internal memos and asks us to confirm it is real. How do you respond?
Your judgement under pressure when the company has lost control of a document.
Verifies the document first, never lies about it, decides with leaders whether to confirm with context, and tells staff before the story runs.

I ask the reporter to send it, then check with the author whether it is real and final or an old draft. I never deny a real document; that lie becomes the story. If it is real, we usually confirm and give context, like the decision it led to. Then I tell employees before they read it in the news, and I flag the leak to leadership without starting a witch hunt.

community-manager.heading: Community manager questions
qs: What are the most common scams in a crypto Discord, and how do you set up a server to resist them?
Whether you know how members actually lose funds in community spaces.
Names fake support DMs, impersonators and fake links, and pairs each with a concrete server setting or rule.

The big ones are fake support DMs, admins impersonated by copied names, and fake mint or airdrop links. I pin a rule that staff never DM first and never ask for a seed phrase, use a verification gate, block links in busy channels, and give staff a distinct role color so fakes stand out.
A member asks in general chat when the token will be listed and whether the price will go up. How do you answer?
How you handle price talk without making promises the team cannot back.
No predictions, no hints about listings, and a pointer to official announcements. The tone stays friendly, not robotic.

I would say I can't talk about price or unannounced listings, and that anything official will come through the announcements channel first. Then I steer to something I can help with, like what the team shipped this month. I never hint or wink, because a hint from staff gets read as a promise.
How do you set up roles and permissions for a moderation team?
Your grasp of access control as a security issue, not just an organization issue.
Least privilege, two-factor required for moderator actions, few admins, tight control of bots, webhooks and mass mentions.

Each role gets only what it needs. Mods can time out, delete and ban, but not edit roles or webhooks. Only two or three people hold admin. I turn on the setting that requires two-factor for moderator actions, limit who can ping everyone, and review bot permissions, since a hacked bot or webhook is a common way servers get drained.
Walk me through how you run an AMA with the founders.
How you plan a live event so it is useful and does not create risk.
Questions gathered ahead, a mix of popular and hard ones, a review of sensitive topics, a moderator on chat, and a written recap.

A week before, I collect questions in a thread and let members upvote them. I pick a mix, including two critical ones, and flag anything on price or legal matters for the team to decide on. During the AMA a second mod watches chat for scammers. Within a day I post a written recap and list the questions we owe answers to.
Member count went from 20,000 to 60,000 in a month. How do you tell whether the community actually grew?
Whether you measure engagement rather than headline numbers that bots inflate.
Looks at active and returning members, message quality, support resolution, and checks where the joins came from.

I would look at how many people post weekly, how many come back the next month, and whether questions get answered. Then I check the source of the joins. A jump right after a quest campaign with almost no new posters usually means farmers or bots. If active members rose 10% while joins tripled, that 10% is the real growth.
Your quest program is being flooded by airdrop farmers using many wallets. What do you change?
How you design member programs that reward real people, not sybil accounts.
Rewards tied to effort that is hard to fake, sybil checks before payout, and no promised rewards that invite gaming.

I would stop rewarding cheap actions like follows and reposts, and reward things that take real effort: good bug reports, guides, helping newcomers. Before any payout I'd check for wallets funded from the same source or acting in lockstep. I'd also stop announcing exact reward amounts in advance, since a fixed price per action is what draws the farms.
How do you turn a month of Discord chatter into a feedback report the product team will act on?
Your ability to turn noise into clear, ranked input for builders.
Groups issues by theme, counts them, adds real quotes and links, separates bugs from wishes, and suggests priority.

I tag feedback as it comes in, then group it by theme. The report opens with the top five issues, each with a count, two short member quotes and links to the threads. Bugs go separately with steps to reproduce. For example: 43 reports that a bridge transfer looked stuck, mostly mobile users. I close by noting what we fixed since last month.
A moderator banned a long-time member who had been loudly criticising the team. What do you do?
Your judgement on criticism versus rule-breaking, and how you hold moderators to the rules.
Checks what rule was broken. Criticism alone is not grounds for a ban; reverses it if needed and talks to the moderator privately.

I read the messages and the rules first. If he was harsh but not abusive or spamming, the ban was wrong and I lift it, with a short note to him. Then I talk to the mod in private, not in public. Banning critics tells everyone their voice doesn't count, and they'll take the complaint to places we can't answer it.
A moderator's account gets hacked and posts a fake mint link to the whole server. Walk me through your first hour.
How you respond to a compromise fast and in the right order.
Removes access first, deletes the posts, warns members clearly, tells victims how to revoke approvals, then finds the cause.

First I strip the account's roles and lock posting in public channels. Then I delete the messages and check webhooks and bots for anything new. Next I post a warning: do not click, and if you connected a wallet, revoke the approvals you gave that site and move funds if you signed anything. After that I find how the account was taken and write it up.
At 2 a.m. members report that funds are draining from the protocol, and the team has not confirmed anything. What do you post?
How you communicate in a crisis without speculating or spreading false advice.
Acknowledges quickly, states only what is known, gives no unverified instructions, escalates to the team, and sets a time for the next update.

I wake the on-call engineer first. Within minutes I post: we're aware of reports and investigating; updates will come only in the announcements channel. I don't guess at causes or tell people what to do until the team confirms it. I turn on slow mode, delete fake help links, and post an update every 30 minutes, even if it's only to say we're still looking.
A raid of brand-new accounts floods general chat with spam links in the middle of a launch. What levers do you pull?
Whether you know the server tools well enough to act in minutes.
Fast, layered steps: slow the channels, raise the entry bar, cut the abused invite, clean up, then a short calm note to members.

I turn on slowmode in the hit channels and raise the server verification level so new accounts must wait or verify a phone. I pause the invite link being abused and tighten AutoMod for links and mention spam. Mods ban from the join log. Then I post that it was spam, nothing was compromised, and the team never DMs first.
You have twelve moderators across five time zones. How do you make sure they apply the rules the same way?
How you build consistent moderation that does not depend on who is online.
Written rules with examples, a clear escalation ladder, every action logged with a reason, and regular review of the hard cases.

The rule book has real examples of what is and is not allowed. We use one ladder: warning, timeout, then ban, with a few offences like scam links going straight to a ban. Every action goes in a mod log with a reason. Each week we review a few borderline cases together so the team learns the same judgement.
A member says they lost funds after signing something on a fake site linked from our server. How do you help them?
Whether you can support a victim correctly and limit further damage.
Believes them, moves to an official private channel, is honest that transactions cannot be reversed, and focuses on stopping more loss and warning others.

I open a private ticket and say plainly that on-chain transactions cannot be undone. Then we stop further loss: revoke token approvals with a block explorer's approval checker, and if the seed phrase may be exposed, move what is left to a new wallet. I collect the transaction hash and contract, report it to security and warn the server.
You are hosting a side event at a big conference with 300 RSVPs. How do you prepare?
Your practical event planning for an in-person crypto crowd.
Plans for no-shows and capacity, safe check-in, a code of conduct and an incident contact, plus follow-up afterwards.

Free events lose many RSVPs, so I set numbers from our past show rate and keep a waitlist, never above the venue's capacity. Check-in is by name list, not by asking people to connect a wallet. A code of conduct is posted and one staff member handles incidents. Within a week everyone gets a short survey and the links we promised.
Our ambassadors are paid in tokens to post about the project on social media. What rules do you give them?
Whether you know the US disclosure rules for paid promotion.
Clear disclosure of the paid relationship in each post, as the FTC expects, plus no price promises and official links only.

Every post about us must say clearly that they are paid by the project, for example in tokens, in the post itself. A note in the bio is not enough under FTC guidance. They make no price predictions or promises of returns and link only to official channels. I spot-check posts and remove people who break the rules.
How do you run regional communities in languages you do not speak?
How you keep message and safety consistent across languages.
One official source text, checked translations, limits on what regional moderators can claim, and a regular sync.

Official announcements are written once in English and translated, with a second native speaker checking before posting. Regional mods follow the same rules but cannot make product or token claims on their own. We hold a weekly call where they flag local issues, and I keep a shared FAQ so the answers match everywhere.
Engineering tells you a promised upgrade is delayed three weeks because the audit found an issue. How do you tell the community?
How you handle bad news without losing trust.
Early, one clear announcement: what happened, what is known and unknown, when the next update comes, and no new date the team cannot keep.

I post the same day: the audit found an issue, we will fix it before launch, and safety comes before speed. I say what we know and what we do not. I give the date of the next update, not a guessed launch date. The post is pinned, mirrored on every channel, and mods get a short FAQ so answers stay the same.
How do you get token holders to take part in a governance vote without steering the result?
Your judgement on running governance fairly.
Raises turnout through clear information and a fair process, while staying neutral on the outcome.

I run a discussion period before voting and publish a neutral summary of the arguments for and against, checked by both sides. Before voting opens I post the dates, rules and how voting power is counted. I remind holders to vote and explain delegation, but I never tell them how to vote. Team members disclose their own votes.
Leadership wants you to tell the community the coming launch will make the token go 10x. What do you do?
Whether you recognise legal and trust risk and can push back usefully.
Refuses price promises, explains why in plain terms, involves legal, and offers a stronger message about what is actually shipping.

I would push back. Promising price gains damages trust and can add legal risk, because one test US regulators use for a security is whether buyers expect profit from the team's work. I would bring in legal and offer a better message: what the launch delivers, the dates, and how to stay safe from scams.
Tell me about a community decision you got wrong and what you changed after.
Whether you own mistakes and turn them into better process.
A real mistake, owned publicly, a fair fix for members, and a lasting change in how the work is done.

I let us announce a points program before the rules were final. When we changed the formula, early members felt cheated and said so loudly. I apologized publicly and honoured the old points for that month. Since then nothing launches until rules, dates and anti-abuse checks are written and reviewed.

compensation-benefits.heading: Compensation and benefits questions
qs: What is a compa-ratio, and how is it different from range penetration?
Your command of the basic measures used to read where someone sits in a pay range.
Correct formulas: salary over midpoint, and position between minimum and maximum, with a sense of when each is more useful.

Compa-ratio is salary divided by the range midpoint. At 1.0 the person is paid at midpoint; at 0.85 they are well below it. Range penetration shows where pay falls between minimum and maximum, so 25% means the lower quarter. I use both, because the same compa-ratio means different things in a narrow range and a wide one.
Walk me through how you benchmark a job using salary survey data.
Whether you can turn survey data into a market rate you can defend.
Matching on job content, not title, using several sound surveys, aging data to one date, and reading percentiles against the pay philosophy.

I match on duties, not title: I read the survey job description and only accept the match if most of the work fits. I use two or three surveys with similar company size and industry, age the data forward to a common date, and look at the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles. Then I check the result against our pay philosophy, such as paying at median for most roles.
A manager wants a new role slotted one level higher than you think it belongs. How do you decide the level?
How you level jobs on objective criteria and hold the line with a manager.
Leveling the role, not the person, against a framework and peer roles, and asking what the role owns that the lower level does not.

I level the role, not the person. I compare the job against our leveling guide on scope, complexity, independence and impact, then against roles already at each level. I ask the manager what decisions this role owns that the lower level does not. If there is a real answer, I move it up. If not, I explain why, and that title follows level, not the reverse.
What decides whether a job is exempt or non-exempt under the Fair Labor Standards Act?
Your knowledge of federal overtime classification rules.
The salary basis, salary level and duties tests, overtime for non-exempt staff over 40 hours, and that titles and state law matter.

Non-exempt employees get overtime at one and a half times their regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek. To be exempt, a role usually must pass three tests: paid on a salary basis, paid at least the minimum salary level, and doing exempt duties such as executive, administrative or professional work. Job title never decides it, and some states set stricter rules.
A hiring manager wants to offer a candidate 15% above the top of the range. What do you do?
Your judgement when one offer could break the pay structure.
Asking whether the range or the case is the problem, using other tools first, and checking the effect on current team pay.

First I ask why. If the market data shows our range is out of date, I fix the range for everyone in the job. If it is one exceptional candidate, I look at a sign-on bonus or a higher level if the scope supports it. Before any offer, I check what the current team earns, so we do not create a fairness problem on day one.
Tell me about a time you found pay compression and how you fixed it.
How you spot and correct new-hire pay catching up with tenured staff.
Data to size the problem, a costed fix phased within budget, and a change to ranges so it does not come back.

New engineers were being hired at almost what five-year staff earned. I pulled pay, compa-ratios and tenure for the team and found 14 people paid below recent hires in the same level. I proposed targeted raises costing about 3% of team payroll, phased over two cycles, and updated the ranges so offers and existing pay move together.
How are RSUs, nonqualified stock options and incentive stock options taxed for the employee?
Whether you understand equity well enough to explain it to employees correctly.
RSUs taxed at vesting, NSO spread taxed at exercise, ISOs with possible AMT at exercise and the holding periods for capital gain treatment.

RSUs are taxed as ordinary income on the share value when they vest and are delivered. With NSOs, the gap between exercise price and market value is ordinary income at exercise. ISOs have no regular income tax at exercise, but the gain can trigger alternative minimum tax. Holding the shares two years from grant and one from exercise makes the gain long-term capital gain.
Our medical plan renewal comes in 12% higher. What would you look at and propose?
How you manage benefit costs without simply shifting them onto employees.
Understanding the cause, modeling several levers, showing the cost to employees at different pay levels, and checking ACA rules.

I would ask the broker what drives it: overall trend, a few large claims or our demographics. Then I would model options: market the plan to other carriers, change deductibles or copays, add a high-deductible plan with an HSA, or change contributions. For each, I would show cost to the company and to employees at several pay levels, and confirm we still pass ACA affordability.
You discover a role paid as exempt does not meet the duties test. What do you do?
How you handle a classification mistake that carries legal and money risk.
Counsel involved early, reclassifying going forward, paying back overtime owed, telling the employee clearly, and checking similar roles.

I bring in legal counsel first. We reclassify the role as non-exempt going forward and start tracking hours. With counsel, we estimate the overtime owed for past workweeks and pay it. I tell the employee plainly that this is a classification fix, not a demotion, and explain how hours and overtime work now. Then I review similar roles for the same issue.
Walk me through how you would run a pay equity analysis.
Your method for finding and fixing pay gaps that legitimate factors do not explain.
Regression on valid factors, review of small groups by hand, work done with counsel, adjustments for unexplained gaps, and fixing the root cause.

I run a regression of pay on legitimate factors such as level, job family, location, tenure and performance, then see if gender or race still explains a gap. Groups too small for statistics I review one by one. We usually do this with counsel so it is privileged. Unexplained gaps get adjusted, and I look for the cause, often starting pay, so it does not return.
How do you age salary survey data, and why does it matter?
Whether you can bring market data to a common date before you use it.
Each survey is moved to one target date with an annual market movement rate, prorated for the months in between.

Surveys have different effective dates, so the raw numbers do not compare. I pick a target date, like our next merit date, and apply an expected annual market movement for the months in between. If a survey is dated April 1 and the target is January 1, that is nine months. At 3% a year, I add about 2.25%. Then I blend the sources.
How do you set midpoint progression and range width when you build a salary structure?
Your grasp of how a pay structure is put together.
Correct definitions, wider ranges at senior levels, and grade steps checked against real promotions and market data.

Midpoint progression is the percentage gap between one grade's midpoint and the next. Range spread is the maximum minus the minimum, divided by the minimum. I keep entry ranges narrower, because people move through fast, and senior ranges wider, because growth inside the job takes longer. Then I check that a promotion gives a real raise, not a move inside overlapping ranges.
Walk me through building a merit matrix that fits a 3.5% budget.
How you turn a budget into fair guidelines that managers can use.
Performance and position in range drive the cells, and the grid is costed against real payroll before it goes out.

I set rows by performance rating and columns by where people sit in their range. A top performer low in the range gets the biggest increase. A solid performer above midpoint gets less. I apply the grid to our actual employee file, add up the cost, and adjust cells until the total lands at 3.5% of eligible payroll, with a small reserve for exceptions.
An employee wants to drop her spouse from the medical plan in March because money is tight. Can she?
Whether you know the mid-year election rules for pre-tax benefits.
Section 125 elections are fixed for the plan year unless a permitted event occurs, and any change must be consistent with that event.

Not for that reason alone. Her premiums are paid pre-tax under a Section 125 plan, so her elections are fixed for the plan year unless she has a qualifying event, such as a divorce or her spouse gaining other coverage. Then she must ask within the window our plan sets, often 30 days. Otherwise I would show her the cheaper options for the next open enrollment.
When would you move a fully insured medical plan to self-funding, and what protects the company?
Your judgement on funding risk in benefits design.
Group size and stable claims come first. Stop-loss limits the risk, and the trade-offs in cash flow, compliance and volatility are named.

It fits a group large and stable enough for claims to be predictable. We pay claims ourselves through an administrator, skip insurer margins and premium taxes, and ERISA generally frees us from state insurance mandates. Specific stop-loss pays claims above a set amount for any one person. Aggregate stop-loss covers total claims above an agreed level. A bad year still hits cash flow.
The board asks why our equity burn rate is up. What is burn rate, and how is it different from overhang?
Whether you can explain equity plan dilution to a board.
Correct definitions of both, and why shareholders and proxy advisors watch them as measures of dilution.

Burn rate is the shares granted in a year divided by the weighted average common shares outstanding. Overhang is outstanding awards plus shares left in the plan, as a share of fully diluted shares. Burn rate shows the pace of granting. Overhang shows total potential dilution. If burn rose because the stock fell and we grant by dollar value, I would say so.
A strong engineer is moving from San Francisco to a lower-cost city and keeping her job remotely. How do you handle her pay?
Your judgement in applying a geographic pay policy fairly.
A written policy applied the same way to everyone, early and honest talk with the employee, and a humane path such as freezing pay instead of cutting it.

I follow our location policy, not a case-by-case deal. If her new area is in a lower pay zone, her pay may sit above the new range. Rather than cut it, I would usually red-circle her: hold her salary and limit raises until the range catches up. Her manager and I would tell her before she moves, so she decides with the numbers in front of her.
Our private company's founder wants to grant new options at last year's lower strike price to reward early hires. What do you advise?
Whether you know the Section 409A rules on option strike prices.
The strike must be at or above fair market value on the grant date, backed by a current independent valuation. Discounted options bring tax penalties.

An option priced below fair market value on the grant date counts as deferred pay under Section 409A, and the employee can owe tax at vesting plus an extra 20% and interest. ISOs also need a strike at least at fair market value. I would use a current independent valuation, under 12 months old with no major event since, and reward early hires with more options instead.
Our 401(k) failed the ADP test this year. What happens now, and how do you stop it happening again?
How you handle a retirement plan compliance failure.
The correct fixes, refunds to highly compensated employees or company contributions for others, done on time, plus a design change such as safe harbor.

Highly paid staff deferred too much compared with everyone else. We either refund the excess to them as taxable income or put qualified nonelective contributions in for the others. Refunds within 2½ months after year end avoid a 10% excise tax. Going forward, a safe harbor design removes the test, and auto-enrollment lifts participation.
A sales rep closes a huge, unplanned deal and the plan has no cap. Leadership wants to cut the payout. What do you do?
How you balance cost, trust and legal risk in incentive plans.
Pay what the written plan promises, since earned commissions are wages in many states, then fix windfall rules for future plans with legal.

First I read the plan document. If it has no windfall or discretion clause, we pay as written. Earned commissions are wages under many state laws, and California requires commission plans in writing. Cutting it would cost more in trust than the payout. Then, with legal, I would add a rule for next year: deals above a set size get a review under terms agreed up front.

compliance.heading: Compliance questions
qs: Why is a US crypto exchange treated as a money services business, and what does that require?
Whether you know the legal base of crypto AML in the US.
Names the Bank Secrecy Act, FinCEN registration, a written AML program, reports and records, plus state licenses.

Under FinCEN guidance, a business that accepts and transmits convertible virtual currency for others is a money transmitter under the Bank Secrecy Act. So we register with FinCEN, run a written AML program, file SARs and keep records. Most states also require a money transmitter license, and New York has its own virtual currency license.
How do you set a risk rating for a new customer?
How you apply a risk-based approach at onboarding.
Several factors weighed together, a clear rule for what each rating triggers, and a fresh review when the facts change.

I look at who they are, where they are, what they say they will do, and how they fund the account. A US retail user buying small amounts is low risk. A business with a complex ownership chain, or someone planning large transfers to other platforms, is higher. Each rating sets the checks: high risk means source of funds, closer monitoring and a periodic review.
A customer deposits $15,000 worth of bitcoin in one go. Do you file a Currency Transaction Report?
Whether you know which reports apply to crypto and which do not.
No: a CTR is for physical cash. The deposit can still need review, and a SAR if something about it is suspicious.

No. A CTR covers physical currency, coins and paper money, above the reporting threshold, so a crypto deposit does not trigger one. That does not end it. I check whether the size fits the customer's profile and where the coins came from. If it looks off, it goes to investigation and possibly a SAR. A bitcoin ATM taking cash is a different story.
Our blockchain analytics tool flags a deposit with indirect exposure to a darknet market, three hops back. What do you do?
How you read analytics alerts with judgement rather than by reflex.
Weighs how much value came from the source, how the funds moved and the customer's history, then documents the decision either way.

Three hops back can be noise, since busy wallets touch many things. I check what share of the deposit traces to the market, whether the hops look like a peel chain, small amounts split off wallet after wallet to hide the source, and whether the customer has done this before. A small share in a normal pattern I close with a written reason. A large share or a repeat goes to investigation.
A deposit arrives from an address on OFAC's sanctions list. Walk me through your next steps.
Whether you know how sanctions blocking works, not just screening.
Block and hold the funds, do not send them back, report to OFAC on time, and review the customer and linked accounts.

I make sure the funds are frozen and held, not returned, because sending them back would itself be a prohibited dealing in blocked property. We file a blocking report with OFAC within ten business days. Then I review the customer, their other activity and linked accounts, and check whether our screening worked as it should. If there is more to the story, we consider a SAR.
A retired customer wants to send most of her savings to an investment site a new online friend recommended. What do you do?
How you protect a likely scam victim while staying within your role.
Spots the scam pattern, contacts the customer, uses holds the terms allow, escalates, and considers a SAR.

This fits a common scam pattern: a new online friend, an unknown platform, a large first transfer. I would hold the withdrawal for review where our terms allow and have someone call her with open questions, not accusations. I would check the receiving address against scam reports, escalate, and file a SAR if the facts support it. It is her money, but she deserves a clear warning.
The business wants to launch a new product next quarter. How do you write the AML policy and procedures for it?
How you turn a new product's risks into rules people can follow.
Starts with a risk assessment, separates policy from procedure, works with the product team, and gets approval, training and testing before launch.

I start with a risk assessment: who will use it, how money moves, and how it could be abused. The policy states what we require and who owns it; the procedures say step by step what analysts do. I draft with the product and engineering teams so the controls are actually built in. Then senior management approves it, staff are trained, and we test it before launch.
You find out a transaction monitoring rule was switched off by mistake six months ago. What do you do?
How you handle a compliance failure honestly and fix it.
Restores the control, tells leadership at once, runs a lookback, files any SARs found, fixes the root cause, and documents it all.

First I turn the rule back on and check that it fires. I tell the BSA officer, who runs our AML program, and management that day. Then we run a lookback: apply the rule to the six missed months, review every alert, and file SARs where warranted. Last, I find how it was switched off, require sign-off for rule changes, and keep a full record for auditors and examiners.
What does the Bank Secrecy Act require in the AML program of a money services business like ours?
Whether you know the required parts of an MSB program, not just the words.
The four parts: written policies and controls, a named compliance officer, training, and an independent review, each sized to the firm's risk.

The program must be written and fit our risk. It needs internal policies and controls for identifying customers, filing reports and keeping records. It needs a named person responsible for compliance, training for the staff who need it, and an independent review. The reviewer can be an outside firm or an employee who does not run the program.
How does the Travel Rule apply when a customer withdraws to another exchange, and when the customer withdraws to a self-hosted wallet?
Your grasp of the Travel Rule for crypto and where it stops.
Between exchanges, the required details travel with transfers of $3,000 or more. A self-hosted wallet has no institution to receive them, so risk controls fill the gap.

When a customer sends $3,000 or more to another exchange, we must pass the sender's name, address and account, the amount and date, and the recipient details to that exchange. A self-hosted wallet has nobody to receive them. We keep our own records and, on a risk basis, ask who controls the wallet, sometimes with a signed message proving it.
A customer whose account we are investigating calls support and asks if we reported him to the government. What should the agent say?
Whether you know SAR confidentiality and can turn it into a script for frontline staff.
Never confirm or deny a SAR, even by hint. A neutral script, a route to compliance, and training so agents do not improvise.

The agent neither confirms nor denies any report; the law forbids revealing a SAR or anything that would show one exists. I give support a plain script: the account is under a routine review under our terms, and we will contact you when it is done. Agents escalate the call to compliance and never guess or explain how our monitoring works.
A customer withdraws about $2,950 in bitcoin five or six times a day, each time to a new address. What do you make of it?
How you read a pattern built to stay just under a threshold.
Sees amounts kept just under the $3,000 Travel Rule line as a red flag, investigates the whole picture and considers a SAR.

Amounts kept just under $3,000, the Travel Rule line, look designed to avoid recordkeeping. I pull the full history, check linked accounts, run the addresses through our analytics tool and compare with what the customer told us at onboarding. With no sound business reason, this is well above the $2,000 SAR threshold for an MSB, and I would file a SAR.
A customer verified as a US resident starts logging in from IP addresses in a comprehensively sanctioned country. Walk me through your response.
How you handle sanctions risk that the KYC file did not show.
Restricts the account fast, investigates beyond the IP address, and brings in counsel on blocking, reporting or disclosure to OFAC.

OFAC can penalize violations even without intent, so I restrict the account first. Then I check device data, past logins, signs of a VPN and the KYC documents, and ask the customer to explain. If the person is really in that country, I offboard them under our sanctions policy and work with counsel on whether anything must be rejected, reported or voluntarily disclosed to OFAC.
One of our monitoring rules produces almost nothing but false positives. How do you tune it without creating a gap?
Your method for tuning rules with evidence and proper approval.
Uses past alerts and SARs as data, tests above and below the new threshold, and documents and approves the change before it goes live.

I start with the alerts that led to SARs and check whether the new setting would still catch them. Then I run below-the-line testing: I sample activity just under the proposed threshold to see if real risk sits there. I write up the data, the change and the reason, get approval from the BSA officer, and review the results again a few months later.
Funds that came to us from another US exchange look like proceeds of a scam. How would you use 314(b) to work with that exchange?
Whether you know how voluntary information sharing works and where its limits are.
Both firms registered with FinCEN, sharing only for money laundering or terrorist financing purposes, kept secure, with no mention of SARs.

Section 314(b) lets financial institutions share information about possible money laundering or terrorist financing with a safe harbor from liability. We need a current notice filed with FinCEN, renewed every year, and I confirm the other exchange has one too. I share only what the case needs, keep it secure, and never say whether we filed a SAR.
A foreign exchange wants to open an institutional account and run its users' flows through us. What due diligence do you do?
How you assess a nested exchange whose end customers you cannot see.
Checks license, AML program, owners, Travel Rule ability and US exposure, then sets limits and monitoring because the end users are hidden.

Their users are hidden from us, so this is high risk. I check their home license, AML and sanctions program, owners, Travel Rule capability and adverse media, and whether FinCEN has named them a primary money laundering concern. If they do real business with US customers, they may have to register with FinCEN themselves. Then I set limits and watch the flows closely.
You join and find 6,000 alerts older than 60 days, with a regulatory exam in two months. What do you do?
How you fix a serious program weakness honestly and in order of risk.
Triage by risk, more trained reviewers with quality checks, no bulk closing, the root cause fixed, and leadership and examiners told the truth.

First I triage: sanctions hits and high-risk customers go to the front. I add trained reviewers with quality checks, and I never bulk-close alerts to make the number look better. I report the backlog and a dated plan to the BSA officer and the board, fix the cause, whether staffing or bad rules, and show the examiner the plan instead of hiding the problem.

compliance-officer.heading: Compliance officer questions
qs: What does an effective compliance program need to have?
Whether you know the framework that regulators and prosecutors use to judge a program.
The seven elements from the federal sentencing guidelines, plus risk assessment, and the point that a program must work in practice, not only exist on paper.

The federal sentencing guidelines list seven elements: written standards, oversight by senior leaders, care about who gets authority, training, monitoring with a way to report concerns anonymously, consistent discipline and incentives, and fixing problems once found. I add a regular risk assessment, because it tells you where to point all the rest.
How is the compliance function different from legal and from internal audit?
Your grasp of where compliance sits among the company's lines of defense.
Legal advises on what the law means. Compliance builds and monitors controls as a second line. Internal audit independently tests both as a third line.

Legal tells us what a law requires and defends the company. Compliance turns that into policies, training and monitoring, and challenges the business, which owns the risk day to day. Internal audit is the third line: it reports to the audit committee and tests whether we all do our jobs. I want audit to find my gaps before a regulator does.
Walk me through how you would run a compliance risk assessment for a business you just joined.
How you decide where to spend limited time and budget.
A clear method: list the rules that apply, rate likelihood and impact, look at existing controls, and rank the remaining risk with the business owners.

First I map which laws apply, by product, country and activity. Then I sit with each business owner and rate each risk for how likely it is and how bad it would be. I check which controls exist and how well they work, which gives the remaining risk. The top items get a plan, an owner and a date. I redo it yearly or when the business changes.
How would you show the board that the program works in practice and not just on paper?
Whether you measure results rather than activity.
Evidence beyond completion rates: control testing, hotline data, how fast cases close, repeat findings, and what employees actually know.

A 98% training completion rate says little. I test samples of transactions against the policy, track hotline volume and how quickly cases close, and watch for repeat findings. Short surveys show whether staff know how to raise a concern and trust that they can. If a region has no hotline reports at all, I treat that as a warning, not good news.
An anonymous hotline report says a manager is splitting purchases to stay under his approval limit. What do you do first?
How you triage a report and start an investigation without harming it.
Log it, protect the reporter, quietly preserve records, decide who investigates, and keep the manager out of the loop until the facts are gathered.

I log the report and reply through the hotline so the reporter can answer follow-up questions. Before anyone talks to the manager, I pull the purchase records and approvals and ask IT to preserve his email. I check for links to the vendors involved. Then I agree with legal on who investigates, and I make sure nobody tries to identify the reporter.
Your top salesperson broke the gifts policy, and the sales VP wants it handled quietly. How do you respond?
Whether you hold to consistent discipline under pressure.
Same rules for stars as for everyone, because regulators check whether discipline is consistent, and staff notice when it is not.

I tell the VP the outcome has to match what we did for others with the same breach, or the policy stops meaning anything. Prosecutors ask directly whether high performers get a pass. I bring the facts and past cases to HR so the result is fair, not harsher because of who he is. If the VP keeps pushing, I raise it through my reporting line, up to the board.
We want to hire a sales agent in a country with high corruption risk. What due diligence do you do, and what red flags stop the deal?
Your practical knowledge of third-party bribery risk under the FCPA.
Knows the company can be liable for an agent's bribes, checks ownership and ties to officials, and names real red flags such as odd payment requests.

Under the FCPA we can be liable for bribes an agent pays on our behalf, and looking away from obvious signs is no defense. I check ownership, links to officials, reputation and the business reason for the hire. Red flags: a commission well above market, requests for cash or payment to a third country, a referral from an official, or refusal to sign anti-bribery terms.
You are sitting in on an internal investigation interview with company counsel. What has to be said at the start, and why?
Whether you know how to run a fair interview that protects privilege.
The Upjohn warning: counsel represents the company, not the employee, and the company may choose to share what is said. Plus a reminder that retaliation is banned.

Counsel gives what is called an Upjohn warning: the lawyer represents the company, not the employee. The talk is privileged, but the privilege belongs to the company, which may decide to share it, even with the government. We ask the employee to keep it confidential and remind them retaliation is not allowed. Someone takes careful notes.
You learn that routine email deletion kept running for two weeks after the company received a subpoena. How do you handle it?
How you respond to a preservation failure honestly and fast.
Stop deletion now, try to recover data, document what was lost and why, and let counsel decide how to disclose it. No hiding it.

First I have IT suspend deletion for the people and systems covered and confirm in writing that it stopped. Then we check backups and devices to recover what we can. I document what ran, when, and what may be lost, and give that to counsel, who decides how to disclose it. Then I fix the gap: legal holds now go straight to IT with a named owner and a confirmation step.
Our review finds a violation that no regulator knows about. How do you decide whether to recommend self-disclosure?
Your judgement on one of the hardest calls in the job.
Weighs it with counsel: any legal duty to report, the credit given for disclosure and fixes, the chance of discovery. Stops and fixes the conduct either way.

Some rules require reporting, so I first ask counsel whether we have a legal duty. If not, we weigh it: DOJ and many regulators give real credit for voluntary disclosure, cooperation and fixing the cause, and that credit is lost if a whistleblower gets there first. We stop the conduct and remediate regardless. I give the board my recommendation in writing.
What makes a written policy one that employees actually follow?
Whether you can write rules for the people who must use them.
Plain language, a clear owner, who it covers, what to do and who to ask, a review date, and steps that match how the work is really done.

I write for the reader, not the regulator: who it covers, what they must do, what they must not do, and who to call. I keep the why short. Each policy has an owner and a review date. Before release I test it with a few people who do the work. If they cannot follow it on a busy day, I fix the process or the wording.
How do you decide who gets which compliance training, and how do you know it worked?
How you target training by risk and measure more than completion.
Training matched to roles and risks, judged by more than completion rates: quiz results, questions coming in, fewer repeat errors.

Everyone gets the code of conduct basics. Then I map risk to roles: sales and procurement get anti-bribery with real scenarios, finance gets controls and expense rules. Completion only proves attendance. I look at short scenario quizzes, the questions people bring us afterward, and whether the errors we saw in testing drop over the next two quarters.
You have a small team. How do you decide what to test and monitor this year?
Whether your testing plan follows risk rather than habit.
A plan built from the risk assessment, past findings and changes in the business, with clear test steps and follow-up on every failure.

I start from the risk assessment and rank areas by likelihood and impact, then add anything new, like a new product, market or system. High risks get tested every year, lower ones on a rotation. I use data where I can, such as scanning all expense claims for split amounts, instead of small manual samples. Every failed test gets an owner and a fix date.
A regional head asks for a permanent exception to the third-party approval policy because it slows deals. How do you handle it?
Your judgement when a control and the business collide.
Finds the real bottleneck, refuses a blanket exception, and offers a faster path or a narrow, logged, time-limited exception.

First I ask where the time goes; often it is one slow step, not the whole policy. A permanent exception creates an uncontrolled channel, so I would not grant one. I might set up a fast track for low-risk vendors, or a time-limited exception with a named approver and extra checks. Every exception goes in a log that I review and report.
You discover that a report we filed with a regulator last quarter contains an error. What do you do?
How you handle a mistake in a filing that is already in.
Confirms the error and its scope, brings in legal, corrects it promptly under the regulator's rules, and fixes the root cause.

I confirm the error and how far it goes: one report, or every report built from the same data. I bring in legal and the report owner, and we check the regulator's rules for amending. We correct it promptly and say plainly what changed and why. Then I fix the cause, such as a manual step or a missing review, and record the decision.
Legal sends you a draft separation agreement with a broad confidentiality clause. What do you look for?
Whether you know that agreements cannot block employees from reporting to regulators.
Knows the SEC rule against impeding whistleblowers and insists on a clear carve-out for reporting to agencies and receiving awards.

I check that nothing stops the person from reporting possible violations to the SEC or any other agency, or from receiving a whistleblower award. The SEC's rule against impeding whistleblowers covers clauses like this, and it has fined companies for them. I want a clear carve-out saying they may contact regulators without telling us or asking us first.
Our screening tool flags a new customer as a possible match on the OFAC sanctions list. Walk me through it.
Your grasp of sanctions screening and the duties that follow a true match.
Holds the transaction, compares identifiers, checks ownership under the 50 Percent Rule, and blocks or rejects and reports a true match.

Nothing moves until it is resolved. I compare the details: full name, date of birth, address, nationality and ID numbers. Most hits clear that way, and I document why. I also check owners, since a company owned 50% or more, alone or together, by blocked persons is blocked too. If it is a true match, we block or reject as the rules require, report to OFAC on time and bring in legal.
You learn that traders and managers settle business on personal messaging apps. Why does that matter, and what do you do?
Whether you know the recordkeeping and evidence risks of off-channel messages.
Knows firms like broker-dealers must keep business messages, regulators have fined off-channel use, and responds with approved tools, policy and testing.

If we are a broker-dealer, we must keep business communications, and the SEC and CFTC have fined many firms for messages on unapproved apps. Even outside that, we lose evidence we may need. I would give people an approved, archived tool, set a clear rule, have staff confirm it in writing, test with sampling, and treat repeat use as a disciplinary matter, starting at the top.
A credible report alleges that the CFO approved false invoices. How do you run this differently from an ordinary case?
How you keep an investigation of a senior leader independent.
The audit committee and outside counsel lead, data is preserved without tipping anyone off, and the CFO is kept out of the process.

The CFO cannot be in the reporting line for this case. I tell the general counsel, unless they are conflicted, and the audit committee chair. The committee usually hires outside counsel so the work is independent and privileged. We quietly preserve the CFO's email and files first, then interview others before the CFO. Findings go to the committee, not to management.
We are buying a smaller company in a high-risk market. What compliance work do you do before and after closing?
How you handle the risk a company inherits in a deal.
Risk-based diligence before the deal, then fast integration after it: policies, training, third-party review, testing and prompt disclosure of misconduct found.

Before closing I review its agents, government contacts, licenses, sanctions exposure and past issues. After closing I move fast: our code and training, a review of its third parties, and testing of high-risk payments. DOJ policy gives credit for promptly disclosing and fixing misconduct found in an acquired company, so speed matters.

computer-vision.heading: Computer vision engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between semantic, instance and panoptic segmentation?
Whether you know the basic output types of vision models.
Clear definitions, and a sense of which task needs which: counting separate objects needs instances.

Semantic segmentation gives each pixel a class, so three touching cars become one car blob. Instance segmentation separates each object, so you get car 1, car 2 and car 3. Panoptic does both: every pixel gets a class, countable objects also get their own ID, and regions like road or sky stay as one area.
What is IoU, and how is it used to score an object detector?
Your grasp of how detection results are measured.
IoU as overlap divided by union, a threshold that makes a box a hit, and mAP averaged over classes and sometimes thresholds.

IoU, intersection over union, is the area where the predicted box and the true box overlap, divided by the area they cover together. A prediction counts as a hit if IoU passes a threshold, often 0.5. Average precision is computed per class from the precision-recall curve, then averaged into mAP. Some benchmarks also average over thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95.
Your detector puts five boxes on the same pedestrian. What is happening, and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand non-maximum suppression and its limits.
Explains non-maximum suppression step by step and knows the threshold trade-off in crowded scenes.

Detectors predict many overlapping candidates, and non-maximum suppression should clean them up. It keeps the highest-scoring box, drops same-class boxes that overlap it above an IoU threshold, and repeats. If duplicates survive, the threshold may be too high.
