Set it too low and it deletes real people standing close, so I test on crowded images.
Which data augmentations would you avoid, and why?
Whether you choose augmentations that keep the label true.
Augmentations must not change what the image means, with examples like flips on text, road signs or left-right anatomy.

I avoid any change that makes the label wrong. A horizontal flip turns a left-turn arrow into a right-turn arrow and mirrors text. On chest X-rays it puts the heart on the wrong side. Strong color shifts are a bad idea when color is the signal, like ripe versus unripe fruit. I always look at a batch of augmented images before training.
You have 200 hours of video from 40 cameras. How do you split it into training and test sets?
Whether you can spot data leakage in image and video data.
Split by camera, site or recording, never by random frames, so the test set shows truly new scenes.

Not by random frames: neighboring frames are almost identical, so the test score would mostly measure memory. I split by camera, holding out, say, 8 whole cameras for test and a few for validation. I check that night, rain and each site type appear in every set. For medical scans the same rule applies per patient.
Two annotators label the same images and disagree on 15% of the boxes. What do you do?
How you manage label quality, the base of every vision model.
Finds where and why they disagree, fixes the guideline with examples, measures agreement again, and routes hard cases to review.

First I sort the disagreements by type: missed objects, loose boxes, or class confusion. Usually the guideline is unclear, for example whether to label a half-hidden bike. I add rules with picture examples, retrain the annotators and re-measure agreement on a shared sample. Truly ambiguous cases go to an expert reviewer or get an ignore label.
You can pay to label 5,000 more images out of 500,000 unlabeled ones. How do you choose them?
Your judgement on spending a labeling budget where it helps most.
Targeted selection from known failures, model uncertainty and diversity, plus a small random slice, not a random draw only.

I start from error analysis: if the model fails at night or on bikes, I pull those images first. Then I add images where the model is unsure, and use image embeddings to avoid picking hundreds of near-duplicates. I keep a small random slice so I still see normal data. After labeling I retrain and check that those failures improved.
A model that scored well in testing drops sharply on a customer's new camera. Walk me through how you find the cause.
How you debug a model that fails after deployment.
Checks the pipeline first (color channel order, resizing, normalization), then compares the images themselves before retraining.

First I rule out bugs: I run one image through the training code and the production code and compare the inputs. Common culprits are BGR versus RGB channel order, a different resize or crop, or missing normalization. If those match, I compare the images: resolution, lens distortion, compression, lighting. Then I label a small set from the new camera and fine-tune if needed.
Your detector misses small objects, like distant people in drone footage. What can you try?
Your toolbox for a common detection weakness.
Resolution and architecture fixes such as larger input, tiling, multi-scale features and fitting anchor sizes, with the speed cost of each.

Small objects often shrink to a few pixels when the image is resized down. I would try a larger input size, or cut the frame into overlapping tiles and merge the results. I check that the model uses fine, multi-scale feature maps and that anchor sizes fit small boxes. Each step costs speed, so I measure recall on small objects separately.
The model must run at 30 frames per second on a small device, and it runs at 8. How do you get there without losing much accuracy?
How you optimize a model for real hardware.
Profiles first, then uses levers like input size, quantization with calibration, pruning or distillation, checking accuracy after each step.

I profile first to see whether time goes to the model, preprocessing or copying data. Then the cheap wins: a smaller input size and the chip vendor's optimized runtime. Next, 8-bit quantization calibrated on a few hundred real images, or quantization-aware training if accuracy drops. If still slow, a smaller model trained by distillation from the big one.
What do a camera's intrinsic and extrinsic parameters describe, and how do you get them?
Whether you know the geometry that links pixels to points in the real world.
Intrinsics are focal length, principal point and lens distortion; extrinsics are the camera's rotation and position. Both are estimated from views of a known target.

Intrinsics describe the camera itself: focal length in pixels, the principal point, and lens distortion. Extrinsics are the rotation and translation that place the camera in the world or next to another sensor. I shoot a checkerboard from many angles, solve for both, and check the reprojection error. If someone changes the zoom or focus, I recalibrate.
A paper reports mAP at IoU 0.5 and our team reports COCO mAP. Why can't you compare the two numbers directly?
Your grasp of how detection metrics differ and what each one rewards.
mAP at 0.5 accepts loose boxes; COCO mAP averages over IoU thresholds from 0.50 to 0.95, so it rewards precise boxes and usually comes out much lower.

mAP at 0.5 counts a detection as correct if it overlaps the ground truth by at least 0.5 IoU. COCO mAP averages AP over ten thresholds, 0.50 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05, so sloppy boxes cost points. A model can look strong at 0.5 and only fair on COCO mAP. I'd run both models through the same evaluation code on the same test set before comparing.
We are mounting a camera on a fast warehouse robot. Rolling shutter or global shutter, and why?
Whether you understand how the sensor itself distorts what the model sees.
Rolling shutter reads rows at different moments, so fast motion skews shapes; global shutter avoids that, with trade-offs in cost and image quality.

A rolling shutter reads the sensor row by row, so when the robot turns fast, straight shelves look slanted and objects stretch. That hurts detection and any geometry. I'd pick a global shutter, which exposes every pixel at once, and accept the cost. I'd also keep exposure short, because motion blur is a separate problem a global shutter does not fix.
When can a single homography correctly map points from one image to another?
Your knowledge of the geometry behind stitching, rectifying and ground-plane mapping.
Two cases: the points lie on one plane, or the camera only rotates about its optical center. Any other motion with depth creates parallax.

A homography is a 3x3 matrix that maps one image plane to another. It is exact when the scene points lie on one plane, like a road surface or a document, or when the camera only rotates around its optical center, as in panorama stitching. If the camera moves and the scene has depth, near and far objects shift by different amounts, and one homography cannot fit them all.
Your stereo camera gives clean depth at 2 meters but noisy depth at 20 meters. Why, and what can you change?
How well you understand depth from disparity and its limits.
Depth is focal length times baseline over disparity, so a fixed matching error grows roughly with distance squared. Wider baseline, longer lens or more pixels help.

Depth equals focal length times baseline divided by disparity. Far objects have tiny disparities, so a quarter-pixel matching error is a big share of the signal, and depth error grows roughly with the square of distance. I'd widen the baseline, use a longer focal length or higher resolution, or improve sub-pixel matching. Each has a cost: a wider baseline loses overlap up close.
The model scores well in Python but gives poor results inside the C++ app, on the same images. Where do you look first?
How you debug a deployment pipeline when the model itself is probably fine.
Suspects preprocessing first: color order, normalization, resize method, tensor layout. Compares the actual input tensors, then layer outputs.

Same images means the input is the likely problem. I dump the input tensor from both pipelines for one image and diff them. Usual culprits: OpenCV loads images as BGR while training used RGB, missing mean and std normalization, a stretch instead of a letterbox resize, or HWC versus CHW layout. If the inputs match, I compare outputs layer by layer.
Your tracker keeps swapping IDs when two people cross paths. How do you reduce the ID switches?
Whether you know how multi-object trackers associate detections over time.
Explains motion-only matching and why it fails at crossings, then adds appearance features, occlusion handling and a tracking metric to measure progress.

A tracker like SORT predicts each track with a Kalman filter and matches detections by IoU using the Hungarian algorithm, so when people overlap, motion alone is ambiguous. I'd add an appearance embedding to the matching cost, keep lost tracks alive for a few frames so they can be re-matched after occlusion, and measure with IDF1 and ID switch counts, not detection accuracy.
The planning team uses your scores as probabilities, but at 0.9 confidence the model is right only 70% of the time. What do you do?
Whether you can make model outputs trustworthy for the systems that consume them.
Names it as miscalibration, measures it on held-out data, and fixes it with a post-hoc method like temperature scaling, rechecked per deployment condition.

The model is overconfident, which is common for deep networks. I'd plot a reliability diagram on held-out data and compute calibration error. Then I'd fit temperature scaling on a validation set: one learned number that divides the logits. It keeps the class ranking, so accuracy doesn't change, but a 0.9 starts to mean 90%. I'd recheck it per camera type.
A chest X-ray model reaches 97% accuracy in validation. How do you check it isn't learning a shortcut?
Your judgement about confounders that make a model look better than it is.
Looks for site, scanner, text markers or treatment devices as hidden signals; slices results, probes with masking, and tests on an outside hospital's data.

Models have learned the hospital, text markers or chest tubes placed after treatment instead of the disease. I'd break results down by site, scanner and patient position, and test whether the model can predict the hospital from the image. I'd mask suspect regions, treat saliency maps as hints only, and test on data from a hospital it never saw.
Tell me about a time your offline results turned out to be wrong. What had you missed?
How you own an evaluation mistake and change your process because of it.
A specific flaw, such as leakage from near-duplicate images, how it was found, the corrected number, and the check added afterward.

On a shelf product recognition project our test accuracy was 94%, but a pilot showed about 80%. Many test images were near-duplicates of training ones: same item, same shelf, shot seconds apart. I found them with image embeddings, grouped them, and resplit by store. The honest number was 83%. Now I run a duplicate check before any split.

construction.heading: Civil engineering and construction questions
qs: Walk me through how a submittal moves from a subcontractor to approval.
Your grasp of the paperwork that controls what gets built and installed.
The sub prepares it, the contractor checks it against the specs, the design team reviews it, and a log ties every due date to the schedule.

The sub sends shop drawings or product data. I check them against the specs and drawings before they go to the architect or engineer, so we do not waste their review time. They return it approved, approved as noted, or revise and resubmit. I keep a log with due dates tied to the schedule, because a late steel submittal delays fabrication, not just paper.
Before we grade a 12-acre site, which environmental permit do you check for, and what does it require on site?
Your knowledge of the stormwater permit that comes with almost every large site.
NPDES construction stormwater coverage for disturbing one acre or more, a written plan, controls installed before grading, and regular inspections.

Disturbing an acre or more needs coverage under the NPDES construction stormwater permit, issued by EPA or, in most states, the state agency. That means a written stormwater pollution prevention plan, silt fence, inlet protection and a stabilized construction entrance in place before mass grading, inspections on the permit schedule, and records kept on site.
A crew wants to dig a 6-foot trench for a duct bank and get in quickly before the rain. What has to be in place first?
Whether you know the excavation rules that prevent cave-ins.
A protective system at 5 feet or deeper unless it is stable rock, a competent person inspecting, safe access and spoil set back. Rain calls for more care.

At 5 feet or deeper OSHA requires a protective system: sloping, shoring or a trench box, unless it is all stable rock. A competent person inspects before work and after rain. Spoil stays at least 2 feet back from the edge, and a ladder must be within 25 feet of each worker since it is over 4 feet deep. Rain weakens the walls, so I would not rush it.
Halfway through the schedule you have spent 55% of the budget. Is the job over budget?
Whether you measure cost against work done, not against time or spending alone.
You cannot tell without earned value: compare the budgeted value of the work actually done with actual cost and with planned value.

Not necessarily. I need the earned value, the budget for the work actually in place. If 60% of the work is done, we are under budget and ahead. If only 45% is done, the cost performance index is 45 over 55, about 0.82: we spend a dollar for 82 cents of work, and I dig into which cost codes are driving it.
A subcontractor bills 80% complete on its electrical work, and your walk says it is closer to 60%. What do you do?
How you control cost without damaging the working relationship.
Verify in the field against the schedule of values, pay for what is in place, document it, and keep retainage and lien waivers in order.

I walk the work with their foreman, line by line against the schedule of values: conduit, wire pulled, gear set, terminations. We agree a number and I approve that, with notes on why. I hold retainage per the contract and collect conditional lien waivers with the payment. Overpaying early leaves no leverage if they walk off the job.
On a data center, how do you deal with switchgear, generators and transformers that take many months to arrive?
Whether you plan procurement as part of the schedule, not after it.
Long-lead items are named early, released ahead of final design if needed, tracked through fabrication, and tied to the schedule.

I list long-lead equipment at the start and put procurement in the schedule: submittal, approval, release, fabrication, shipping. Often the owner orders gear early on approved specs before drawings are final. I ask for factory progress reports and witness test dates, and plan a fallback, like temporary power, if a unit slips.
Excavation hits soil that smells of fuel and is not in the geotechnical report. What do you do?
Whether you protect people and the contract when the ground is not what was expected.
Stop in that area, protect workers, notify the owner in writing promptly per the contract, bring in an environmental consultant, and track cost.

I stop digging there, move the crew back and keep that spoil separate and covered. I notify the owner in writing the same day, because differing site condition clauses have notice deadlines. An environmental consultant tests it and sets handling and disposal. Meanwhile I photograph everything, track time and equipment on a separate cost code, and move crews to other work.
The 28-day cylinder breaks for a foundation come back below the specified strength. What happens next?
How you handle a quality failure in work that is already built.
No panic and no hiding: check the tests, compare with the acceptance rules, tell the engineer of record, and take cores if needed.

First I check the test itself: how the cylinders were made, cured and handled, since poor field curing lowers breaks. Then I compare results with the spec's acceptance rules, which usually follow ACI 318. I tell the engineer of record right away. If more data is needed we take cores from the structure, and the engineer decides if it is fine, needs strengthening or must be replaced.
How would you plan commissioning for a data center so it is ready for the owner's load on day one?
Whether you see commissioning as a planned phase, not a final checklist.
Levels from factory tests to an integrated systems test, planned into the schedule early, with load and failure scenarios proven before handover.

I plan it from the start with the commissioning agent, in levels: factory witness tests, delivery inspection, startup, functional tests of each system, then an integrated systems test. That last one uses load banks to simulate IT load and cuts utility power to prove generators and cooling take over. I leave real float before handover, because problems show up there.
What is the difference between total float and free float, and who owns the float on a job?
Whether you read a CPM schedule beyond the critical path.
Correct definitions, and the point that float ownership is set by the contract, not by whoever uses it first.

Total float is how long an activity can slip before it delays the project finish. Free float is how long it can slip before it delays the early start of the next activity. Who owns float depends on the contract; many say it is shared by the project. If the contract is silent, I raise it early, because quietly using float is how delay disputes start.
Who hires the special inspector on a building job, and what do they check?
Your knowledge of how the building code verifies structural work.
The owner or the owner's agent hires them, not the contractor. They work from the statement of special inspections and report to the building official.

Under the International Building Code the owner or the owner's agent hires the inspection agency, not us, so it stays independent. It follows the engineer's statement of special inspections: rebar before a pour, concrete placement, structural welds, high-strength bolts, fill compaction. My job is to call them in time and never cover work they have not seen.
What is the difference between a conditional and an unconditional lien waiver, and when do you collect each?
Whether you protect the owner and the company from liens when money moves.
Conditional waivers come with the payment request, unconditional ones after payment clears, from lower tiers too, and some states require their own forms.

A conditional waiver gives up lien rights only when the payment actually clears. An unconditional one gives them up at once, paid or not. I collect conditional waivers from the sub and its main suppliers with each pay application, then the unconditional one for that amount once the money has cleared. Several states require statutory forms, so I use those where they apply.
You have three bids for the electrical package, and the low one is 25% under the other two. What do you do before you award?
How you buy out a trade package without buying a scope gap.
Levels the bids line by line against the documents, has the low bidder confirm the scope, and checks its capacity before awarding.

A gap that size usually means missing scope, not a better price. I level the bids on one sheet, line by line against the drawings and specs: gear, temporary power, fire alarm, testing, cleanup. Then I walk the scope with the low bidder. If they confirm it all, I check their backlog, bonding and references. If not, I add the missing scope so the comparison is fair.
Walk me through what goes into a lift plan for setting a 40-ton transformer with a mobile crane.
Whether you can plan a heavy lift and not just approve one.
Full load with rigging, chart capacity at the real radius, ground support, buried utilities and power lines, wind, exclusion zone and qualified people.

I start with the true load: the manufacturer's weight plus rigging and the hook block. Then crane setup, radius and the load chart, giving percent of capacity. Ground bearing under outrigger mats, buried utilities, power line clearance, wind limit, exclusion zone, and a named qualified rigger, signal person and certified operator. The crew reviews it at the pre-lift meeting.
You see a subcontractor's crew working at a roof edge with no fall protection. They are not your employees. Why is it your problem?
Whether you know your legal duty for workers you do not employ.
Knows OSHA's multi-employer policy and the controlling employer's duty. Stops the work at once and follows up in writing.

As the general contractor we control the site, and under OSHA's multi-employer policy a controlling employer can be cited for hazards it should have found and corrected, even for another company's workers. So I stop the work right there, get them back from the edge and call their foreman. Work resumes when protection is in place, and I document it and raise it with the sub.
Your excavator hits rock at 4 feet where the boring logs showed clay to 15 feet. What do you do in the first 24 hours?
How you protect the contract position when the ground is not what the documents showed.
Prompt written notice under the differing site conditions clause before the area is disturbed further, separate cost tracking, and the engineer called in.

I stop digging in that area and photograph it. Then I send written notice to the owner right away under the differing site conditions clause, before the condition is disturbed further, so they can see it. I ask the geotechnical engineer to come out, track crew and equipment time on a separate code, and start a schedule impact. Late notice is how valid claims get lost.
The owner needs a change done now, but you cannot agree on the price. How do you proceed?
Whether you can keep work moving without giving up the right to be paid.
Proceeds only on a written directive, tracks actual cost separately with signed daily tickets, and settles it as a change order later.

On an AIA-style contract that is a construction change directive: the owner and architect sign a written directive, we proceed, and price and time are settled later. I never start on a verbal okay. I open a separate cost code, record labor, equipment and materials daily, and have the owner's rep sign the tickets. The change order is then built from real cost, not argument.
You need to tie new switchgear into a data hall that is already live. How do you plan the work?
How you work beside a running facility where one mistake drops the customer's load.
A written method of procedure approved by operations, redundancy kept, back-out steps, an agreed window, and de-energized work under lockout.

Nothing happens without a method of procedure: a step-by-step script approved by the owner's operations team. It lists each step, who does it, hold points, how redundancy stays up, and how to back out if a step fails. Circuits we touch are de-energized and locked out. We rehearse it, work in an agreed window, and stop if anything differs from the script.
The owner was late approving a design change, and in the same weeks your steel erector fell behind. You want a time extension. How do you build the case?
Whether you can prove delay with the schedule, not with opinion.
A time impact analysis on the schedule in force at the time, concurrent delay separated out, and knowing it usually earns time but not money.

I run a time impact analysis on the schedule update from just before the delay: I insert the owner's delay as a fragnet, a small chain of new activities, and see what it does to the critical path. If both delays drove the finish over the same period, that is concurrent delay, which usually earns time but no money. I claim cost only where the owner's delay alone was critical.

construction-manager.heading: Construction project manager questions
qs: What is the difference between an RFI, a submittal and a change order?
Your grasp of the basic paperwork that controls scope, cost and time.
An RFI asks for clarification. A submittal shows what will be installed, for review. A change order changes the contract's scope, price or time.

An RFI is a written question to the design team when the documents are unclear. A submittal is shop drawings, product data or samples sent for review before we buy or build. A change order is a signed change to the contract's scope, price or time. An RFI answer that adds work is not a change order by itself. I still have to price it and get it signed.
Walk me through how you review a subcontractor's monthly pay application.
How you protect the owner and the job before money goes out.
Checks billing against work actually in place, approved changes, stored materials, retainage and lien waivers before approving.

I compare each line of the schedule of values to what I see in the field, not to what the sub says. I check that change orders are approved before they are billed, that stored materials are documented, and that retainage is held per the contract. I also need a conditional lien waiver for this payment and an unconditional one for the last payment before I sign off.
The framing inspection fails the day before drywall is set to start. What do you do?
How you react to a failed inspection without losing control of the schedule.
Gets the correction list, fixes the items fast, rebooks the inspection, and moves crews instead of covering anything up.

First, nobody hangs a board in the failed areas. Covering work before it passes means tearing it out later. I get the inspector's correction list, assign each item to the right sub with a deadline, and book the reinspection right away. If only part of the building failed, I ask whether the areas that passed can proceed and move the drywall crew there.
The owner asks your superintendent in the field to move a wall. How do you handle it?
Whether you control scope changes and protect the contract.
No work on verbal direction alone: the request in writing, priced with its schedule impact, and a signed change order or directive before work starts.

I get the request in writing and route it through the architect so the drawings and code review are updated. I price it with the subs, including the schedule impact, and submit a change order. If it cannot wait, I ask for a signed construction change directive so work can go ahead while we settle the price. My supers know not to act on verbal changes.
A subcontractor on the critical path is two weeks behind. What steps do you take?
How you recover a schedule and use the contract without burning the relationship.
Finds the cause, gets a recovery plan with crew numbers, documents everything, and follows the subcontract's notice steps if nothing improves.

I sit down with the sub's owner, not just the foreman, and find out why: manpower, material or money. I ask for a written recovery plan with crew sizes and dates and track it daily. I look at resequencing to help. If they still miss, I send the written notice the subcontract requires, because any later right to supplement their crew depends on that paper trail.
Your excavator hits old concrete footings that are not on any drawing. What happens next?
Whether you know how to handle a differing site condition.
Stops work in that area, documents it, gives written notice promptly and before the condition is disturbed, then waits for direction.

I stop digging in that spot, take photos and measurements, and note the time and location in the daily log. Then I send written notice to the owner and architect right away, because most contracts require prompt notice before the condition is disturbed. I get a price for removal and the schedule impact, and we proceed once there is written direction.
What has to happen between substantial completion and final payment?
Your knowledge of closeout and handover.
Punch list, final inspections and the certificate of occupancy, closeout documents, owner training, and final waivers before retainage is released.

We walk the punch list with the architect and close every item. We finish final inspections so the building department can issue the certificate of occupancy. I collect warranties, operation and maintenance manuals and as-built drawings, and set up training for the owner's staff. Final lien waivers from every sub come in before final payment and release of retainage.
Halfway through the job, your forecast shows the project finishing over budget. What do you do?
How you manage cost and deliver bad news early.
Finds where the overrun comes from, separates owner changes from own losses, looks for real savings, and tells the owner early with numbers.

I break the forecast down by cost code to see where it is: a subcontract that came in high, extra labor, or unpriced changes. Owner-driven changes get priced and submitted. For our own losses I look at contingency and savings ideas the owner must approve. Then I tell my executive and the owner now, with a number and a plan, not at the last pay app.
Tell me about a scope gap you missed in buyout and how you dealt with it.
Whether you own mistakes and fix the process, not just the problem.
Admits the miss, gets the work done without fighting the subs, takes the cost honestly, and changes how scopes are written.

On a medical office job, neither the drywall sub nor the carpentry sub had wall blocking for cabinets in their contract. I caught it at framing, got a price from the carpenter, and covered it from our savings instead of forcing it on either sub. Now I use a checklist across trades when I award subcontracts, so blocking and firestopping always have a named owner.
What is the difference between total float and free float, and who owns the float on your jobs?
Whether you read a CPM schedule the way a scheduler does.
Correct definitions, and the point that the contract decides who owns float, not whoever uses it first.

Total float is how long an activity can slip before it pushes the project finish. Free float is how long it can slip before it delays the early start of the next activity. Who owns float depends on the contract. Many say it belongs to the project, so I don't let a sub or the owner use it up quietly. I track it at every update.
How is an allowance different from contingency, and how do you track each one?
Your grasp of where the money in a budget is allowed to go.
An allowance covers a known but undefined item and is trued up by change order; contingency covers unknown risk. Each is reported on its own.

An allowance is a set amount carried for a known item not yet chosen, like door hardware or tile. When the real cost comes in, the difference is adjusted by change order. Contingency covers unknown risk. Contractor contingency is for our own risks, like buyout gaps. Owner contingency is for owner changes. I report each one separately so nobody spends from the wrong pot.
When do you accept a conditional lien waiver, and when do you need an unconditional one?
Whether you protect the owner and the job from liens while paying subs on time.
Conditional waivers take effect only when payment is received; unconditional ones are final on signing. Statutory forms where the state requires them.

With a pay app, I collect a conditional progress waiver. It only takes effect once the sub is actually paid. Next cycle, I collect the unconditional waiver for the payment that cleared, from lower-tier subs and suppliers too. At closeout I need final waivers. Where the state has statutory forms, I use the exact form, because a custom one may not be valid.
A subcontractor's schedule of values puts a third of the contract on mobilization and submittals. What do you do?
How you protect the job's cash against front-loaded billing.
Rejecting it before the first pay app and tying line items to measurable work, so billing follows real progress.

I send it back before the first pay application. Mobilization should reflect its real cost, which is a small slice. I ask them to break the big items into measurable pieces, like per floor or per area, so I can check percent complete in the field. If a sub is overpaid early and then defaults, the money left won't cover finishing their work.
How does your approach change between a lump-sum job, a GMP job and a cost-plus job?
Whether you know where the cost risk sits under each contract type.
Lump sum puts cost risk on the contractor; GMP is open book with a cap and shared savings per contract; cost-plus without a cap puts risk on the owner.

On lump sum, the cost risk is ours, so I guard the scope and price every change. On a GMP, the owner pays actual cost plus fee up to a cap. It's open book, so my cost records must stand up to an audit, and savings are split as the contract says. On cost-plus with no cap, the owner carries the risk, so I report costs early and often.
What is the difference between a pay-when-paid and a pay-if-paid clause, and why does it matter to your subs?
Your understanding of payment risk down the contract chain.
Pay-when-paid sets timing; pay-if-paid shifts the risk of owner nonpayment to the sub, and some states will not enforce it.

Pay-when-paid means I pay the sub within a set time after the owner pays me. If the owner never pays, courts usually still expect me to pay within a reasonable time. Pay-if-paid makes owner payment a condition, so the sub carries that risk. Some states won't enforce pay-if-paid, so I check the state law and keep our subcontract wording clear.
Under OSHA's multi-employer policy, can the general contractor be cited for a hazard a subcontractor created?
Whether you know your legal duty as the controlling employer on site.
Yes: as controlling employer, the GC can be cited if it did not use reasonable care to prevent, or to find and correct, the hazard.

Yes. OSHA looks at four roles: the employer who created the hazard, the one whose workers are exposed, the one responsible for correcting it, and the controlling employer, which is usually us. We can be cited if we didn't use reasonable care to prevent it or find and fix it. So we walk the site regularly, write up hazards and follow up until they're fixed.
The owner wants the building six weeks before the contract date. How do you work out whether it can be done?
How you weigh cost, risk and contract terms when a schedule is compressed.
Focus on the critical path, crashing versus fast-tracking with their costs and risks, and a signed change order before any acceleration.

I start with the critical path, since only those activities move the finish. Then two tools: crashing, which adds crews or overtime and costs money, and fast-tracking, which overlaps tasks and risks rework. I price the cheapest mix, flag what I can't control, like inspections or long-lead equipment, and start only once a change order sets the new date and price.
A bonded drywall subcontractor stops showing up and won't return calls. Walk me through your next two weeks.
How you handle a default by the contract without losing the schedule or your rights.
Written notice and cure per the subcontract, the surety involved early, everything documented and a replacement lined up.

Day one, I send written notice under the subcontract, give the cure period it requires and copy the surety. I photograph and list the installed work and stored material. I hold their payments and get quotes from replacement subs. If they don't cure, we terminate per the contract and work with the surety on completion, keeping every cost record.
A late owner decision on finishes held up your interiors for three weeks. How do you prove the delay and get the time?
Whether you can build a delay request that holds up, not just ask for more days.
Written notice within the contract deadline, a time impact analysis on the schedule, and honest handling of any concurrent delay.

I give written notice within the contract's deadline, since missing it can waive the claim. Then I do a time impact analysis: I add a fragnet, a short chain of activities for the wait, to the last update before the delay and show how the finish moves. If our own work was late at the same time, I say so. Concurrent delay often gets time but no money.

content-designer.heading: Content designer and UX writer questions
qs: What is the difference between voice and tone in product writing?
Whether you know the basic tools of a content style guide.
Voice stays the same across the product; tone shifts with the user's situation and mood, especially when something goes wrong.

Voice is who the product is, and it stays the same everywhere: say, plain, warm and direct. Tone is how that voice adjusts to the moment. On a success screen we can be a little lighter. On a failed payment or a locked account we drop the jokes and get straight to what happened and what to do next.
A user types a date in the wrong format and sees "Invalid input." How would you rewrite that message?
How you write an error message that helps someone fix the problem.
Says what went wrong and how to fix it, in plain words, next to the field, without blame. Bonus for asking whether the error can be avoided.

I'd say how to fix it, right under the field: "Enter the date as MM/DD/YYYY, for example 03/14/2025." No "invalid," no blame, no error code unless support needs it. Then I'd ask the designer whether the field can accept several formats or use a date picker, so the error rarely shows at all.
Why shouldn't placeholder text inside a form field be used as the field's label?
Your grasp of accessible, usable form copy.
Placeholders vanish when typing starts, are often low contrast, and are not a dependable label for assistive tech. Use a visible label and helper text.

Placeholder text disappears as soon as someone starts typing, so people lose the hint while they still need it. It's usually light gray and hard to read, and it isn't a dependable label for screen readers. I put a visible label above the field and move format hints into helper text below it.
A designer hands you a finished mockup full of lorem ipsum and needs the words by tomorrow. What do you do?
How you work with design when content comes in last.
Delivers on time but asks about the goal, the user and real data, and flags where real words may change the layout.

I'd ask three things fast: what the user is trying to do here, what we want them to do next, and what real data shows up, like long names. Then I'd write real copy by tomorrow and flag spots where it won't fit the layout. Next time I'd ask to join earlier, at the wireframe stage, so the words shape the design.
On a confirmation dialog for deleting a project, what goes on the buttons, and why?
Whether you write clear labels for destructive actions.
Specific verbs instead of Yes/No or OK, a title naming the action, and a plain note on whether it can be undone.

Not "Yes" and "No." The title says what will happen: "Delete Q3 Budget project?" The body says what gets lost and whether it can be undone. The buttons read "Delete project" and "Cancel," with the delete button styled as dangerous. Someone who reads only the buttons still knows what they're agreeing to.
How would you test whether new onboarding copy works before it launches?
Your methods for checking words with real users.
Task-based usability testing with a few real users, think-aloud, no leading questions, plus a simple method like a highlighter test.

I'd run a short usability test with five or six people who match our users. I give a task, like "set up your first invoice," and ask them to think aloud, without reading the copy to them or hinting. I'd also try a highlighter test: green for what's clear, red for what's confusing. Where people hesitate or misread, I rewrite and test again.
When would you use a card sort, and when a tree test, to work on a product's navigation?
Your knowledge of information architecture research.
Card sorting helps build a structure from users' mental models; tree testing checks whether people can find things in a proposed structure.

A card sort helps me build the structure: people group topics and, in an open sort, name the groups, so I learn how they think. A tree test checks a structure: people see only the text menu, no visual design, and try to find where they'd go for a task. I'd sort first, draft the menu, then tree test it and fix labels where people got lost.
Legal asks you to put three paragraphs of terms directly on the sign-up screen. How do you handle it?
How you balance legal requirements with a usable flow.
Respects legal's goal, asks what must be shown versus linked, proposes a clear alternative, and gets sign-off rather than overriding them.

I'd ask what the actual requirement is: what must appear on screen, what can be linked, and whether we need active consent. Often a checkbox with a one-line plain summary and a link to the full terms meets it. I keep their exact wording wherever it's required, show them the two versions side by side, and get their sign-off before it ships.
The product is launching in German and Japanese. What changes in how you write the strings?
Whether you write content that survives translation.
No string concatenation, full sentences with placeholders, notes for translators, room for longer text, no idioms or text in images.

I stop building sentences from fragments, because word order changes between languages; I write full strings with placeholders like {name}. I add notes so translators know where a string appears and how much space it has. I leave room, since German often runs longer. I cut idioms and puns, let the code handle plurals, and keep text out of images.
You renamed a menu item, and the next week support tickets about finding that feature went up. What do you do?
How you own a content mistake and fix it with evidence.
Checks the data before assuming, says it openly, looks at what words users search, and fixes or rolls back fast, then tests the label.

First I'd confirm it's the label: did anything else ship that week, and what do the tickets actually say? If people are searching for the old name, that's my answer. I'd tell the team, roll back or add the old term as a search keyword right away, then run a quick tree test on two or three label options so the next change is based on users, not taste.
A new user opens the reports page and has no reports yet. What goes on that empty screen?
Whether you treat empty states as a chance to guide the user, not a dead end.
Says what the page will hold and why it is empty, then gives one clear action to fill it.

First, a short line on what lives here: "Your reports will appear here." Then one button that starts the task, like "Create your first report." I skip jokes if the user may be stuck or stressed. I would also write a separate version for empty search results, because that state needs a fix, like checking spelling, not a fresh start.
A toolbar has five icon-only buttons, and a page has six links that all say "Learn more." What do you flag?
Whether you write for screen reader users, not only for people who see the screen.
Each icon button needs a written accessible name. Each link needs text that makes sense on its own or from clear context.

A screen reader announces a button by its accessible name, so an icon with no name may be read as just "button." I write a short name for each, like "Share report," and the developer adds it as hidden text or a label. Many screen reader users jump through a list of links, so six "Learn more" links sound the same. I rewrite them as "Learn more about billing" and so on.
Security says the login error can't tell users whether the email or the password was wrong. Product says that hurts users. Where do you land?
How you balance clear copy against a real security risk.
Knows the risk of account enumeration, keeps the generic message, and helps the user recover in other ways.

Security is right. If the message says "No account with this email," anyone can test which emails are registered. So I keep "Email or password is incorrect" and make the next step easy: a visible "Forgot password?" link and a reset screen that says "If an account exists for this email, we sent a link." The user still has a clear way out.
The team wants to call a new feature "Smart Sync." How do you decide what it should be called?
Your process for naming things so users can find and understand them.
Starts from words users already use, tests a few options, and checks the name fits the product's existing terms.

I check what users call the task now: support tickets, search logs, interview notes. Then I list three or four names and ask whether each says what it does. "Smart Sync" says nothing about what syncs. I test the options with a quick comprehension test, make sure none clash with existing terms, and add the winner to our terminology list.
A readability checker says your onboarding copy is at a sixth-grade level. Is that enough to call it clear?
Whether you know what readability formulas measure and what they miss.
Formulas count sentence length and syllables. They cannot tell whether a reader understands or can act, so you still test with people.

It is a useful warning light, nothing more. Formulas like Flesch-Kincaid count sentence length and syllables per word. A short sentence full of our internal terms can score well and still confuse people. So I check our terms against the words users use, and I watch a few people try the task. If they do the right thing without help, the copy is clear.
A product manager wants the decline button on an upgrade offer to say "No thanks, I like paying more." What do you do?
How you push back on manipulative copy with arguments a business will listen to.
Names it as confirmshaming, explains the cost in trust and regulatory risk, and brings a neutral option plus a way to measure it.

I call it what it is: confirmshaming, a dark pattern that guilts people into a choice. It may lift clicks for a while, but it costs trust, and the FTC has been looking hard at dark patterns. I offer a plain "No thanks" and put a stronger reason on the upgrade button instead. Then I suggest we test it, so the decision rests on data, not taste.
You find out a pricing screen in production says "per month" but customers are billed yearly. What do you do in the first hour?
How you handle a high-stakes copy error once it is live.
Treats it as an incident: alerts the owner, legal and support at once, gets a fix shipped, and helps decide who must be told.

I raise it right away with the product owner in the incident channel, not as a ticket in a queue. Wrong price words can mean refunds and legal exposure, so legal and support hear about it the same hour. I write the corrected string and push for a hot fix. Then I help draft the note to affected customers and a support reply, and later find out how it got past review.
You inherit a product with 3,000 strings and no style guide. Where do you start?
How you set priorities in a large content audit.
Starts with the flows that matter most and fail most, builds a terminology list early, and fixes in batches, not everywhere at once.

I don't start at string one. I pull the busiest flows, like sign-up, checkout and errors, plus the screens with the most support tickets. I audit those first and list every term used for the same thing. That gives me a short glossary and a few rules, which become the first style guide. Then I fix by flow, so each release makes one journey fully consistent.
Leadership asks what content design has actually delivered this year. How do you show it?
Whether you can tie word changes to outcomes the business tracks.
Uses before-and-after numbers tied to specific changes, is honest about what caused what, and counts saved effort like fewer tickets.

I pick a few changes with clean measures. After we rewrote the payment errors, successful retries rose from 52% to 61% and related tickets fell by a third over two months. Where we ran an A/B test I say so. Where it is only before-and-after, I note what else shipped at the same time. I also show the glossary and guidelines that sped up other teams.
There are 12 product teams and only two content designers. How do you keep the writing good without reviewing every string?
How you scale content quality through systems instead of personal review.
Builds guidance into the design system and tools, trains others to write well, and saves personal review for the highest-risk flows.

I put the guidance where people already work. Each design system component gets content rules and examples, like how to write a button or an error. We keep a shared glossary and, where possible, a check that flags banned terms. I run short training for designers and PMs. My partner and I then review only high-risk flows: payments, privacy, legal text and blocking errors.

content-writer.heading: Content writer and editor questions
qs: What is search intent, and how does it change the article you write?
Whether you understand what search optimization is really for.
Intent is the need behind the query. The format and depth of the piece follow from it, not from the keyword alone.

Search intent is what the person typing the query actually wants: to learn, to compare, to buy or to find a page. Someone searching “how to descale a kettle” wants steps, fast, so I lead with a numbered list. Someone searching “best electric kettles” wants a comparison, so I build a table and explain how we chose. I check the top results to see what format readers expect.
Walk me through how you edit a colleague's 2,000-word draft.
How you organize an edit instead of fixing commas at random.
Separate passes from big to small: structure, then sentences, then facts and style. Notes explain the changes.

I read it once without touching anything, to see if the argument holds and the order works. Then I fix structure: moving sections and flagging gaps. Next comes the line edit for clarity and length, then a copy edit for style, names, numbers and links. I use tracked changes and leave short comments saying why, so the writer learns and can push back.
How do you prepare for an interview with a source, and what do you do during it?
Your interviewing method, from research to recording.
Research first, open questions, permission to record, and checking spellings and titles before the call ends.

I read what the person has already said publicly so I don't waste time on basics. I write five or six open questions, ranked, and expect to drop half. I ask permission to record, since some states require everyone's consent. I ask follow-ups like “Can you give me an example?” and end by confirming name spelling, title and how they want to be described.
How do you write the title tag and meta description for an article?
Whether you know how a page appears in search results.
Main topic first, short enough not to be cut off, a promise the page keeps, and knowing search engines may rewrite both.

The title tag is the clickable headline in search results, so I put the main topic near the front and keep it short enough that it isn't cut off. The meta description is the snippet below. It doesn't directly affect ranking, but it affects clicks, so I say plainly what the reader gets. Search engines sometimes rewrite both, so the page itself has to match the promise.
A client wants the keyword used 15 times in an 800-word post. How do you respond?
How you handle a request that would hurt both the piece and the client.
Explaining that keyword stuffing reads badly and is treated as spam, then offering a better plan for placement and related terms.

I'd explain that repeating a phrase that often makes the text read like spam, and search engines' spam policies name keyword stuffing directly. I'd offer a plan instead: the keyword in the title, the first paragraph and one subheading, then natural variations and related questions readers ask. I'd show them a sample paragraph written both ways so they can judge.
You find a striking statistic on a blog. What do you do before you use it?
Your fact-checking habits.
Tracing the number to the original study, checking date, sample and what it measures, and linking the primary source.

I follow the trail back to the original source, often a survey or a government dataset, because blogs copy each other and numbers drift. I check the year, who was surveyed and what the number actually measures. Once a “70% of shoppers” figure turned out to be 70% of 300 people in one survey. If I can't find the original, I don't use it.
A source asks to approve the article before it goes live. What do you say?
Your judgement on accuracy versus editorial control.
Knowing the publication's policy, offering to check quotes and facts for accuracy, and keeping the editorial decisions.

First I check our policy, because a brand blog and a news site differ. Usually I offer to read back their quotes and technical facts so nothing is wrong, but I explain that the angle and the edit stay with us. If they want to change what they said, not just fix an error, I talk to my editor before agreeing to anything.
Our article recommends products and we earn a commission on sales. What does the piece need?
Whether you know the FTC disclosure rules for affiliate content.
A clear, conspicuous disclosure in plain words near the recommendations, not hidden in a footer or behind a link.

The FTC expects a material connection, like a commission, to be disclosed clearly and conspicuously. So I put a plain sentence near the top, before the first link: “We earn a commission if you buy through links on this page.” Not only in the footer, and not behind a vague word like “partners.” The commission also can't change what we honestly say about the products.
A reader emails to say a fact in your published article is wrong. What do you do?
How you handle a mistake that is already public.
Verify fast, fix it, add a dated correction note instead of erasing it quietly, thank the reader and tell the editor.

I check the claim against the source that same day. If the reader is right, I fix the text and add a short note at the bottom with the date and what changed, rather than silently editing. I tell my editor, reply to the reader with thanks, and look at how it slipped through. Once it was a misread table, so now I check every number against the original twice.
Traffic to an older guide has dropped by half. How do you decide what to do with it?
How you diagnose and refresh existing content.
Data first: lost queries, what now ranks, outdated facts, overlapping pages. Then update, merge with a redirect, or retire.

I start with our search data: which queries it lost and what now ranks for them. Often the guide is out of date, or a newer page on our own site competes with it. If it's outdated, I update facts and screenshots and add what readers now ask. If two pages overlap, I merge them and set a 301 redirect from the weaker one. If nobody searches for it anymore, I retire it.
How do you set up the headings and images in a long guide, and why does it matter beyond looks?
Whether you build pages that work for screen readers, skimmers and search engines.
One clear H1, levels used in order, headings that say what follows, and alt text that describes the image's purpose.

I use one H1 for the title, then H2s for main sections and H3s inside them, never skipping a level just for font size. Screen reader users jump between headings, so each must make sense alone. Alt text says what the image shows and why it is there; purely decorative images get empty alt text.
What goes into a content brief you hand to a freelance writer?
How you turn a plan into instructions another writer can follow without guessing.
Reader, purpose, angle, target query, outline, sources, length range, links, deadline and what done looks like.

I name the reader and the one job the piece must do for them. Then the main query, the angle that sets us apart, a rough outline, must-use sources, internal links to include, a length range and the style rules that trip people up. I add one example we liked and the deadline for the first draft.
Your best quote from an interview is rambling and ungrammatical. Can you clean it up?
Your standards for accuracy in quotes.
No changing words inside quote marks beyond trivial fixes; paraphrase or quote a shorter clean part instead.

Not inside quotation marks. A direct quote has to be what the person said. I can trim with an ellipsis if the meaning stays the same, quote only the strong clause, or paraphrase the rest without quote marks and attribute it. If I am unsure what they meant, I call them back and ask.
Two of our articles target almost the same search query. What do you look at, and what do you do?
How you handle pages competing with each other in search.
Checks whether intent truly overlaps, then merges with a 301 redirect or gives each page a distinct angle.

First I check whether they serve the same intent, using the search results and which page Google shows for which queries. If they overlap, I merge the best of both into the stronger URL and 301 redirect the weaker one. If the intents differ, I sharpen each title and angle and link them to each other.
How do you plan internal links for a new article?
Whether you treat linking as part of the structure of a site, not an afterthought.
Links out to relevant pages and in from existing ones, with descriptive anchor text and no orphan pages.

I link from the new piece to the pages a reader would want next, using anchor text that says where the link goes, never "click here." Then I go back to three or four older related articles and add links to the new one, so it is not an orphan. I avoid stuffing the same exact-match anchor everywhere.
What does E-E-A-T mean, and how does it show up in your writing?
Your grasp of how Google describes quality content and how to show it on the page.
Experience, expertise, authoritativeness, trust; a concept from Google's rater guidelines, shown through real detail, sourcing and clear authorship.

It stands for experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trustworthiness, from Google's search quality rater guidelines. It is not one score you can tune. I show it with first-hand detail, a named author with a real bio, an expert review where the topic needs it, and claims linked to strong sources.
How do you use AI writing tools, and where do you draw the line?
Your judgement on speed versus accuracy and search risk.
Uses tools for support, checks every fact, adds original value, and knows mass-produced pages can break Google's spam policies.

I use them for outlines, headline options and tightening sentences. I never publish a fact I have not checked against a source, because they invent things. The value has to come from our own reporting and expertise. Google's spam policies target content mass-produced to game rankings, however it was made, so volume is never the goal.
While editing, you find paragraphs that closely match another site. What do you do?
How you handle possible plagiarism fairly and firmly.
Confirms the match, keeps it out of print, talks privately with the writer, and decides based on intent and pattern.

I run the full draft through a plagiarism checker and compare the passages side by side. The piece does not go live as is. I ask the writer privately how it happened; sometimes it is sloppy notes. Either way the text gets rewritten and properly credited, and if it is a pattern I tell the managing editor.
Your manager wants to change the "last updated" date on 50 old posts to look fresh. How do you respond?
Whether you push back on a misleading shortcut and offer a better plan.
Explains that a new date should mean a real update, and proposes updating the posts that matter most.

I would say a new date without real changes misleads readers, and Google's own guidance says not to change dates without significant updates. Instead I would pull the 50 posts' traffic and accuracy, update the ten that matter most with new facts and examples, and change those dates honestly.
How would you show leadership that our content program is worth what it costs?
Whether you can tie content work to business results, not just pageviews.
Links pieces to goals like signups or sales, uses assisted conversions, and compares cost per piece with return.

I start with what the business needs, say trial signups. I track organic traffic to pages that matter, signups those pages start or assist, and email growth from guides. Then cost per piece against results. Last year, in my example, 12 guides drove 40% of signups, so we cut thin posts and wrote more guides.

contract-manager.heading: Contract manager questions
qs: What is the difference between a master agreement and a statement of work, and why does the order of precedence clause matter?
Whether you understand how a set of contract documents fits together.
The MSA holds the general legal terms and the SOW the specific work. The precedence clause says which document wins when they conflict.

The master agreement sets the terms for every deal: liability, IP, payment, termination. Each SOW describes one project: scope, deliverables, price, dates. The precedence clause decides which wins in a conflict. Usually the MSA wins unless the SOW expressly overrides a named section. Without that clause, a loose SOW can quietly rewrite the MSA.
How is an indemnity different from a limitation of liability?
Your grasp of the two clauses that move the most risk.
An indemnity shifts specific losses, often third-party claims, to one party. A limitation caps or excludes damages. How the two interact matters most.

An indemnity is a promise to cover certain losses, often claims a third party brings, like an IP infringement suit, including defense costs. A limitation of liability caps what one side can recover from the other and often excludes indirect damages. I always check whether the indemnities sit inside the cap or are carved out of it.
Once a contract is signed, how do you make sure nothing is missed?
How you manage obligations and dates after signature.
A central record with key terms, a named owner for each duty, and alerts set before notice deadlines, not just before the end date.

Every signed contract goes into our repository with the key data pulled out: term, renewal type, notice period, price increases, reporting duties, insurance certificates. Each item gets an owner. Alerts fire before the notice deadline, not the end date, usually 90 and 30 days ahead. Each month I send owners a short list of what is coming due.
The other side sends back a clean version and says they only changed two clauses. What do you do?
Whether you verify a counterparty's changes yourself.
You run a compare against your last version every time and raise any unmarked change openly and calmly.

I never rely on a summary. I run a document compare of their version against the last one we sent, so every change shows, marked or not. Once that caught a payment term moved from 30 to 60 days that nobody mentioned. I raised it politely as a likely oversight, put it back, and from then on asked for tracked changes only.
A customer sends a purchase order with its own preprinted terms that conflict with our signed agreement. How do you handle it?
Whether you know which document governs and how to protect it.
Check what the master agreement says about PO terms, confirm in writing, and bring in counsel when there is no master agreement.

First I check whether our master agreement says preprinted PO terms do not apply; well-drafted ones do. If so, I reply in writing that we accept the PO under the master agreement only. If there is no master agreement, it is a battle of the forms, which UCC 2-207 governs for goods, and I bring in legal rather than assume the last form sent wins.
A supplier tells you it cannot perform because of force majeure. What do you check in the contract?
How you read a clause under pressure instead of assuming it applies.
The exact wording decides it: covered events, notice, which duties are excused, mitigation, and the right to exit a long delay.

In the US, force majeure mostly turns on the contract wording, so I read the clause closely. Is the event listed or caught by the general words? Did they give notice on time and in the required form? Does it excuse only delay or also payment? Must they mitigate? Can we terminate if it lasts past a set period? Meanwhile I line up a backup source.
Sales needs a deal signed today, and the customer refuses any cap on our liability. What do you do?
Your judgement on risk when the business is pushing hard.
Neither blocking nor caving: offer workable options, explain the exposure, and get the decision from someone with authority, in writing.

I would not just say no. I offer options: a cap tied to fees paid, a higher cap for data breaches, or no cap only for the risks they fear most. If they still refuse, I send the deal owner and approver a short note: what is exposed, rough size, what insurance covers. Signing uncapped is their documented call, not something I approve quietly to hit a date.
After signing, you find an email in which our sales rep promised the customer a free extra year of support. How do you handle it?
How you deal with promises made outside the signed contract.
Find out whether it could bind the company, involve the rep's manager and legal, settle it openly with the customer, and prevent repeats.

I check the entire agreement clause and the rep's authority, and ask legal whether that email could still bind us. Then I talk to the rep and their manager. If we honor it, it goes into a signed amendment. If not, the account owner tells the customer directly and soon. Then I remind sales that only signed paper commits the company.
You missed a notice deadline, and a software contract renewed for a year at a higher price. What now?
How you own and repair a costly mistake.
Telling your manager quickly, looking for options in the contract and the law, negotiating with the vendor, and fixing the tracking gap.

I tell my manager the same day, with the cost. Then I reread the contract: any right to reduce seats, a cap on price increases, termination for convenience. Some states have auto-renewal notice laws, so I ask legal whether one applies. Then I call the vendor; many will trade a better price for a longer commitment. Last, I find out why the alert failed and fix it.
A key supplier is being bought by one of our competitors. Walk me through what you check.
How you find your rights and risks when a counterparty changes hands.
Assignment and change of control clauses, termination rights, confidentiality and data terms, and a realistic exit plan.

I pull every contract with that supplier. I check assignment and change of control: do they need our consent, or can we terminate? Then confidentiality and data use, because our pricing and forecasts must not reach a competitor. I check termination notice, transition help and how long a switch takes. Then I brief the business with options and dates.
When does Article 2 of the UCC apply to a contract, and why do you care?
Whether you know which body of law governs the deal in front of you.
Goods fall under UCC Article 2, services under common law, and mixed deals usually follow the predominant purpose. It changes warranties and gap-filling terms.

Article 2 covers sales of goods. Pure services fall under each state's common law. For a mixed deal, like equipment plus installation, most courts ask what the main purpose was. It matters because Article 2 adds implied warranties and fills gaps like delivery and price. So if goods are involved, I make sure our warranty disclaimers and terms are drafted with it in mind.
A supplier agrees to use “best efforts” instead of “commercially reasonable efforts.” Does that wording settle anything?
How you handle efforts language that courts read differently.
Knowing US courts give these phrases no single fixed meaning, so the real protection is defining the steps or the result expected.

Not much on its own. Best efforts is usually seen as the stronger promise, but US courts do not agree on exactly what each phrase requires. If the obligation matters, I spell it out: named resources, milestones, a ceiling on what they must spend, or a firm deliverable with a date. Then nobody argues later about what the words meant.
A supplier sends a certificate of insurance listing us as additional insured. Is that enough?
Whether you know what a certificate of insurance does and does not prove.
A certificate is for information only and does not change the policy. The contract should require the coverage, and an endorsement should actually add you.

No. A standard certificate says on its face that it confers no rights and does not amend the policy. Additional insured status comes from an endorsement to the policy, so I ask for a copy of it. The contract should require the coverage types, limits, additional insured status and notice of cancellation. I also track the expiry date and ask for a renewed certificate.
We are paying an outside contractor to build custom software. Is a work-made-for-hire clause enough to give us the code?
Your grasp of how ownership of intellectual property actually transfers under US law.
Software by an independent contractor usually falls outside the statutory work-for-hire categories, so a written assignment of rights is needed as well.

Usually not alone. For an independent contractor, work made for hire under the Copyright Act covers only nine listed categories, with a signed writing, and ordinary software generally is not one of them. So I keep that language and add a present assignment, “hereby assigns,” of all rights in the deliverables, plus a license to any of their existing tools built into the code.
Our standard terms exclude consequential damages. What falls into that bucket, and what do you carve out?
How well you understand damages exclusions and where they leave us exposed.
Consequential damages are knock-on losses beyond the natural result of the breach. Carve-outs usually cover confidentiality, indemnity and willful misconduct.

Direct damages flow naturally from the breach, like the cost of replacing a failed part. Consequential damages depend on the other party's own situation, such as profits lost on other deals or a shut-down line. I keep the exclusion but carve out confidentiality and data breaches, indemnified third-party claims, and gross negligence or willful misconduct, where the real harm is often indirect.
The other side's NDA has a residuals clause. What is it, and would you accept it?
Your knowledge of a quiet clause that can undo confidentiality.
It lets the recipient use what its people remember without notes. Accept it only narrowly, if at all, and never for trade secrets or as a license to patents.

A residuals clause lets the recipient use ideas and know-how its staff keep in unaided memory, meaning without looking at notes. That can make the NDA close to useless for our real secrets. If we are the side sharing, I strike it. If they insist, I limit it to general skills, exclude source code, pricing and trade secrets, and state it grants no patent or copyright license.
A customer wants a fixed late-delivery charge of $5,000 per day in our supply contract. What do you check before agreeing?
Whether you know when a liquidated damages clause holds up and when it becomes our risk.
Courts enforce a set amount that reasonably estimates hard-to-measure harm and strike penalties. You also cap it and limit it to delays we cause.

First, whether $5,000 is a fair forecast of what a late day really costs them. US courts enforce liquidated damages that are a reasonable estimate when real harm is hard to measure, and refuse ones that work as a penalty. Then our side: a total cap, a grace period, no charge for delays they or a force majeure event cause, and the charge as their sole remedy for lateness.
A cloud supplier offers service credits as our sole and exclusive remedy for downtime. How do you respond?
How you weigh service credits against the right to real damages and to walk away.
Credits are fine as a first remedy, but you keep termination for chronic failure and do not let credits be the only remedy for serious breaches.

Credits are often a few percent of the monthly fee, so as the only remedy they can cost the supplier less than fixing the problem. I accept them for ordinary misses, but I add a right to terminate for repeated failures, say three missed months in a row or any outage over a set length. I also keep normal damages for data loss and security breaches.
You discover a plant manager signed a three-year supplier contract well above his signing authority. What do you do?
How you handle a contract signed outside the company's delegation of authority.
Not assuming it is void: the company may be bound by apparent authority or by accepting performance. Assess, then ratify, renegotiate or exit, and fix the control.

I would not tell the supplier it is void. If he looked authorized and we have taken deliveries, we could well be bound. I check the price and terms against what we would have approved, then take it to someone with real authority to ratify it, renegotiate or plan an exit. Then I fix the gap: publish signing limits and tell key suppliers who can sign.
You are asked to let sales close standard deals without legal or contracts review. How would you set that up?
Whether you can build a system that scales the contract function safely.
A template, a playbook with preapproved fallbacks, clear triggers for escalation, and regular checks of what actually got signed.

I would start with our standard template and a playbook for the ten clauses customers push on most. For each: our position, one or two preapproved fallbacks, and the red lines that need my review, like uncapped liability or giving away our IP. Deals under a set value on our paper go straight through. Each quarter I sample signed deals and update the playbook.

controller.heading: Financial controller questions
qs: Walk me through how you run the month-end close.
Whether you run the close as a planned process, not a scramble.
A dated checklist with owners, a clear order (subledgers, accruals, reconciliations, review), and a review of big changes before results go out.

I keep a close calendar with each task, its owner and its due day. Subledgers close first: payables, receivables, payroll, fixed assets. Then accruals and reclasses, then balance sheet reconciliations. Before I sign off, I review the reconciliations and a flux analysis that explains large changes from last month. Only then does the package go to leadership.
What is the difference between an accrued expense and a prepaid expense?
Your grasp of accrual accounting and matching costs to the right period.
Accrual: cost incurred but not yet billed, booked as a liability. Prepaid: paid before use, held as an asset and expensed over the period it covers.

An accrued expense is something we used but have not been billed for yet, like contractor hours in the last week of the month. I book the expense and a liability, then reverse it when the invoice arrives. A prepaid is paid in advance, like a year of insurance. It sits as an asset and I expense one twelfth each month.
What does a good balance sheet reconciliation look like?
Whether you know a reconciliation must prove a balance, not just make two numbers match.
Ties the ledger to independent support, explains every reconciling item with its age, has a separate preparer and reviewer, and clears old items.

It ties the general ledger balance to something outside the ledger: a bank statement, a subledger, a loan schedule. Every reconciling item is listed with a date and a reason, and anything older than 60 days gets chased. One person prepares it, another reviews and signs with a date. A plug to make it tie is not a reconciliation.
Explain the five steps of revenue recognition under ASC 606.
Your knowledge of the US revenue standard.
The five steps in the right order, with a sense of where the judgement sits, such as finding the separate promises in a contract.

First, identify the contract with the customer. Second, identify the performance obligations, the distinct promises in it. Third, determine the transaction price, including variable consideration. Fourth, allocate it to the obligations based on standalone selling prices. Fifth, recognize revenue when or as each one is satisfied. Step two is where most hard calls are.
Your accounting team is three people. How do you handle segregation of duties?
How you build controls when you cannot fully separate duties.
Separate the riskiest pairs, such as vendor setup and payment release, and add compensating controls like independent review where overlap can't be avoided.

No one can both create a vendor and release a payment to it, and the person who records cash does not reconcile the bank. Where overlap is unavoidable, I add a compensating control: each month I review the bank reconciliation, a report of vendor master changes and the payment runs, and the owner approves payments above a set amount.
Accounts payable gets an email from a long-time vendor asking to change the bank account for its payments. What do you do?
Whether you recognize a common payment fraud and stop it.
Treat it as possible fraud: confirm by calling the vendor at a number already on file, not one in the email, and require a second approval for the change.

Nothing changes based on an email. Someone calls the vendor at the phone number we already have on file, not the one in the message, and confirms with a known contact. The change needs a second person to approve it, and I watch the first payment to the new account. Business email compromise often looks exactly like this request.
Two days before quarter end, the CEO asks you to book revenue on a large order that will ship next week. How do you respond?
Your independence when leadership pushes on the numbers.
A clear, respectful no grounded in the rule that control has not passed to the customer, an offer of what can be shown honestly, and escalation if pressed.

I would explain that for a product sale, revenue is recognized when control passes to the customer, usually at shipment or delivery under the contract terms. Booking it now would misstate the quarter, and the auditors would find it. I can show the order as backlog in the board report. If the pressure continued, I would raise it with the audit committee.
Your auditors propose an adjustment you believe is wrong. How do you handle it?
How you work with auditors when you disagree with them.
Learn their reasoning, answer in writing with the standard and the evidence, escalate properly, and accept the adjustment if they turn out to be right.

I ask them to walk me through their reasoning and the guidance they rely on. Then I write a short memo with our position, the specific standard and the documents that support it. Often a missing fact is the issue, and the evidence settles it. If we still disagree, I take it to the CFO and, if needed, the audit committee. If I am wrong, we book it and move on.
Your close takes 12 business days and the CFO wants it in 5. Walk me through how you would get there.
Whether you can redesign a process instead of just pushing people to work faster.
