Map the close to find the bottleneck, move work before month end, use thresholds for estimates, automate repeat entries, and shorten in stages.

I would map every task with its work time and wait time to find the critical path. Then I move work earlier: reconcile steady accounts during the month, accrue from estimates above a set threshold instead of waiting for invoices, and agree cutoff dates with other departments in advance. I automate recurring entries and drop low value steps. I would aim for 8 days first, then 5.
A customer has sued the company. When do you book a liability, and when do you only disclose it?
Whether you know the loss contingency rules under ASC 450.
Accrue when a loss is probable and can be reasonably estimated; disclose when it is reasonably possible. Knows what to book when only a range is known.

I accrue when a loss is probable and I can reasonably estimate it. If I only have a range, I book the best estimate in it, or the low end if no amount is more likely. If the loss is only reasonably possible, I disclose it without booking. I get counsel's view in writing, because their read on the case drives the call.
Three weeks after year end, before the statements are issued, a major customer files for bankruptcy. Does that change your year-end numbers?
Whether you can tell a subsequent event you record from one you only disclose.
Asks whether the condition existed at the balance sheet date. If the customer was already failing, adjust the allowance; if a new event caused it, disclose.

It depends on when the problem started. Bankruptcy usually comes from a decline that was already there at year end, so I would adjust the credit loss allowance on that receivable. If a sudden event after year end caused it, like a fire at their plant, I would disclose it and leave the year-end numbers as they are.
Under ASC 842, how does an operating lease differ from a finance lease in the financial statements?
Your grasp of lease accounting under the current standard.
Both put a right-of-use asset and a lease liability on the balance sheet; the difference is the expense pattern and the cash flow classification.

Both go on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability, unless we elected to keep short-term leases of 12 months or less off. An operating lease shows one straight-line cost. A finance lease shows amortization plus interest, so expense is front-loaded. Finance lease principal payments are financing cash flows; operating lease payments are operating.
Your FIFO inventory includes a product line that now sells below cost. How do you account for it?
Whether you apply the inventory valuation rules correctly.
Writes the inventory down to net realizable value through cost of sales, and knows US GAAP does not allow reversing the write-down later.

Under FIFO the rule is lower of cost and net realizable value, meaning the expected selling price less the costs to complete and sell. I write the units down to that amount and charge cost of goods sold. That becomes the new cost basis; US GAAP does not let me reverse it if prices recover. I also check purchasing so we stop buying more.
Gross margin fell four points this month and nobody expected it. How do you find out why before you close?
How you investigate an unexpected result instead of explaining it away.
Rules out booking errors such as cutoff or missed accruals, then splits the change into price, mix and cost, and confirms with operations.

First I rule out our own errors: revenue cutoff, a missed inventory receipt, a freight accrual booked twice, a standard cost update. Then I split the change by product and customer to see whether it is price, mix or cost. If it is real, I confirm it with sales and operations and write the explanation down before the numbers go to the CFO.
At consolidation, intercompany balances between two subsidiaries are off by $85,000. What do you do?
How you handle intercompany differences and the process behind them.
Finds the cause instead of plugging it, has the wrong side book the fix, and adds a cutoff and matching step so it does not repeat.

I do not plug it. I match the two ledgers line by line; the usual causes are an invoice one side booked and the other did not, timing, or exchange rates when the entities use different currencies. The entity that is wrong books the fix. Then I set an intercompany cutoff date and a monthly matching step, so gaps surface before consolidation.
What do you look for when you review manual journal entries?
Whether you know where manual entries hide errors and fraud.
Looks at who posted, when, to which accounts and with what support; targets revenue, cash, reserves and entries made after close.

I want support and a reviewer who is not the preparer. Then I look for warning signs: entries posted after close or on weekends, round numbers, entries by people who rarely post, odd pairings like debit receivables and credit revenue with no invoice, and reserve changes without a memo. I run a monthly report of those, so the review is not just a sample.
You find an error in last year's audited statements. How do you decide what to do?
Whether you know the ways to correct a prior-period error under ASC 250.
Assesses materiality by amount and nature; knows reissuance restatement, revising comparatives, and correcting in the current period apart.

I size it, by amount and by nature, with the auditors and audit committee involved early. If it is material to last year, those statements are restated and reissued. If it is immaterial to last year but fixing it now would distort this year, we revise the prior-year figures in the next filing. If it is small both ways, I correct it this period. Then I find the control that missed it.
Your auditors find a control deficiency in revenue. How do you judge whether it is a material weakness?
Whether you can grade a control deficiency the way auditors and regulators do.
Uses the definition: a reasonable possibility a material misstatement is not prevented or detected in time. Weighs what could happen and other controls.

I ask how big a misstatement the gap could let through, not just what did happen. A material weakness means there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement would not be prevented or detected on time. A significant deficiency is less severe but still merits the audit committee's attention. I test whether another control would catch it, and I fix the gap either way.
The company will likely breach a loan covenant in six months. What does that mean for the statements you are about to issue?
Your judgement on going concern when the company's financing is at risk.
Evaluates substantial doubt within one year after issuance, tests management's plans, discloses either way, and brings the auditors in early.

Management must judge whether there is substantial doubt we can continue as a going concern within one year after issuance. A likely breach that makes the loan callable is that kind of condition. I test our plans, like a waiver or refinancing: are they probable, and would they solve it? Either way the notes describe it; if doubt remains, they say so plainly. I tell the auditors early.

controls-engineer.heading: Controls and PLC engineer questions
qs: What happens during one PLC scan?
Whether you understand how the controller actually runs your logic.
Read inputs, solve logic in order, write outputs, handle communications, and know what that means for fast signals.

Each scan, the PLC reads all inputs into an input image, runs the logic top to bottom using that snapshot, then writes the output image to the real outputs and handles communications. An input that changes mid-scan is seen next scan, and a very short pulse can be missed unless I use a fast input or an interrupt.
Why is a stop button usually wired normally closed, and how does that look in the ladder logic?
Whether you design so that a wiring failure stops the machine.
A broken wire drops the input and stops the machine. The candidate knows the ladder contact type differs from the field contact type.

Wired normally closed, the input is on while all is well. If a wire breaks or a terminal comes loose, the input drops and the machine stops, so the failure is safe. In the ladder I use a normally open contact, examine if closed, in series with the run rung, so the rung is true only while the button is not pressed.
A PNP sensor is wired to an input card and the input never turns on. What do you check?
Your grasp of sinking and sourcing I/O.
A PNP sensor sources current and needs a sinking input; NPN is the reverse. Mismatch means no current flows.

A PNP sensor is sourcing: when it switches, it supplies +24 V to the input. That needs a sinking input card, which takes the current and returns it to the 0 V common. If the card is a sourcing type, meant for NPN sensors, nothing flows. I check both data sheets, the common wiring, and measure the voltage at the terminal before swapping parts.
A pressure transmitter sends 4 to 20 mA for 0 to 150 psi. The input reads 12 mA. What pressure is that, and what would 2 mA tell you?
Your skill with analog scaling and live-zero signals.
75 psi, from linear scaling over a 16 mA span. A reading below 4 mA points to a fault, not a real pressure.

4 mA is zero and the span is 16 mA. 12 mA is 8 mA above zero, half the span, so 75 psi. A reading of 2 mA is below the live zero, so it most likely means a broken wire, lost loop power or a failed transmitter. I raise it as a signal fault instead of showing a negative pressure or letting the logic act on it.
You find the same output coil written on two different rungs. Why is that a problem?
Whether you know how duplicate outputs behave and mislead troubleshooting.
The last rung to write the coil in the scan wins. The fix is to drive each output from one place.

Outputs are written at the end of the scan, so the last rung that writes the coil wins and the earlier one has no effect. A technician sees the first rung true and the motor off and loses an hour. I would build intermediate bits for each condition and drive the output from a single rung, with a comment saying why.
A heated zone overshoots its setpoint by 15 degrees on every startup. How do you tune it?
How you approach PID tuning methodically.
Check the basics first, change one term at a time, test with setpoint steps and record results. Reduce integral before anything else.

First I confirm the thermocouple reads right, the output scaling is correct and the heater responds. Overshoot on a slow thermal zone often means too much integral action, so I reduce it, make a setpoint step and watch the trend. I change one term at a time and log each try. I add derivative only if needed, with filtering, because sensor noise makes it jumpy.
Walk me through an I/O checkout on a new machine during commissioning.
Your commissioning discipline before anything moves.
Point by point, with the real field device, a checklist, a clear area and every wiring fix marked on the drawings.

I check the panel against the drawings and verify power first. For each input I actuate the real device, like blocking the photo eye, and confirm the right tag changes. For outputs, with the area clear and the mechanical crew told, I turn on one at a time and confirm the right device moves. Each point gets ticked on a checklist, and every wiring fix goes on the redlines.
A customer wants the emergency stop to be just an input to the standard PLC program. What do you tell them?
Whether you know safety functions do not belong in ordinary PLC logic.
E-stop works through safety-rated hardware sized by a risk assessment; the standard PLC only monitors. Reset must not restart the machine.

I would advise against it. A hung program, a forced bit or a welded output could leave the machine running. The E-stop should remove power through a safety relay or a safety-rated controller, chosen from the risk assessment. The standard PLC reads its status to show the alarm and stop the sequence. Resetting the E-stop must not restart the machine by itself.
Production asks you to fix a nuisance stop with an online edit while the line is running. How do you decide?
Your judgement on changing live logic.
Weighs what the change touches, backs up first, informs operators, tests before accepting, and waits for downtime if unsure.

I look at what the rung affects. Changing an alarm timer preset is low risk; anything touching motion or an interlock waits for a planned stop. Before editing I save a copy of the running program, tell the operators and the shift lead, and test the edit before I accept it. If I cannot fully predict the effect, it waits for downtime.
You download your program and the line behaves differently than yesterday. The PLC had online changes your file did not. What do you do?
How you recover from a version control mistake and stop it happening again.
Makes the line safe, restores the known good version, merges the lost edits with their owners, then fixes the process.

First I stop the line safely and restore the upload I took before downloading, so production runs as before. Then I compare that upload with my file, find the missing edits, and merge them with whoever made each one. I test the merged version at a planned stop. Afterward I push for one master copy under version control and a rule: upload and compare before every download.
When would you use a latch instruction instead of a seal-in rung for a motor start, and what happens to each after a power loss?
Whether you know how retentive bits behave and why that matters for restarts.
A seal-in drops out on power loss, so the motor needs a new start. A latch stays set, so it must be cleared on purpose at power-up.

For a motor start I use a seal-in: start in parallel with the run contact, stop in series. If power drops, the rung goes false and the motor stays off until someone presses start. A latched bit is retentive, so after power returns it is still set. I only latch things like a fault memory, and I clear any run latches in a first-scan routine.
You read a 32-bit floating-point value from a Modbus TCP meter and the number is nonsense. What do you check?
Your hands-on knowledge of how Modbus addresses and data types really work.
The register offset by one and the word or byte order, checked against a known value on the meter's own display.

First the address: register 40101 in a manual is usually offset 100 in the protocol, so I may be one register off. Then word order: a float spans two 16-bit registers and vendors disagree on which comes first, so I try swapping words, then bytes. I compare with the reading on the meter's front panel until they match.
A timer in a subroutine sometimes never finishes, and an output in that routine stays on. What is going on?
Whether you understand that logic only runs when it is scanned.
The routine is called conditionally. When it is not called, its timers and outputs freeze in their last state. Fix the design, not the symptom.

Most likely the routine is only called when a condition is true. When that condition drops, the routine is not scanned, so the timer stops updating and its outputs keep their last state. I would call it every scan and move the condition into the rungs, or reset its outputs on the way out. Then I would look for other routines called the same way.
You need to take voltage readings inside a live 480 V panel to find a fault. What has to be in place before you open the door?
Whether you follow NFPA 70E in practice, not just in name.
Qualified person, arc flash label or risk assessment read, matching PPE, a rated meter checked on a known source, boundaries kept. Any repair done de-energized.

I have to be qualified on that equipment. I read the arc flash label or the risk assessment and wear the PPE it calls for, and I keep others outside the boundary. My meter must be rated for the panel, and I check it on a known live source before and after. Readings only: if I need to touch a wire, I lock out and test for absence first.
How do you structure the logic for a machine sequence with 30 steps and several fault paths?
How you design logic that others can read and troubleshoot.
A state machine: one step number, clear transitions, a timeout per step, faults handled in one place, and the current step shown on the HMI.

I use one integer for the current step and only one place in the code that changes it. Each step has its outputs, its transition condition and a timeout that raises a specific fault like "Step 12: clamp not closed after 5 s". The HMI shows the step and what it is waiting for, so night shift can clear most stops without calling me.
Operators ignore the alarm banner because there are always 150 active alarms. How do you fix that?
Your grasp of alarm management, beyond adding more alarms.
Rationalize with operations: every alarm needs a cause, an operator action and a priority. Uses ISA-18.2 or a similar method and measures the result.

I pull the alarm history and find the worst offenders; usually a few chattering points cause most of the noise. Then we rationalize with operations following ISA-18.2: if an alarm needs no operator action, it becomes an event or a log entry. I add deadbands and delays, suppress alarms that follow from one root cause, and track alarm rates every month.
A drive takes its speed command over EtherNet/IP and someone unplugs the cable. What should happen, and who decides?
Whether you design for communication loss instead of hoping it never happens.
The drive's comm-loss action is set on purpose, usually fault and stop, agreed with the risk assessment and tested by pulling the cable.

The drive has a setting for comm loss: fault and coast, ramp to stop, hold last speed and so on. Holding last speed is rarely acceptable, because the PLC can no longer stop it. I agree the action with the process owner and the risk assessment, usually a fault with a controlled stop, and at commissioning I test it by actually pulling the cable.
After a big draw-off, a level loop holds its fill valve at 100% for an hour. When the level recovers, it overshoots badly. What is happening?
Your understanding of PID behavior beyond tuning numbers.
Integral windup: the integral keeps growing while the output is saturated. Fix with anti-windup and correct output limits, not by detuning.

That is integral windup. While the valve is pinned at 100%, the error stays large, so the integral term keeps adding up. When the level reaches setpoint, that stored integral takes time to unwind, so the valve stays open too long. I would check that anti-windup is active and the output limits match the real valve range, rather than just slowing the loop down.
A flow totalizer stored as a 32-bit REAL stopped increasing after a few months, but the flow is still there. Why?
Whether you know the limits of floating-point math in a PLC.
A 32-bit float holds about 7 significant digits, so a tiny increment added to a big total is lost. Fix with integer rollover or a 64-bit type.

A 32-bit float keeps only about seven significant digits. Once the total is in the millions, adding 0.001 gallons each scan rounds to nothing, so it stops counting. I would accumulate into a small float that rolls into an integer total each whole unit, or use a 64-bit LREAL if the controller supports it, and base each increment on the real elapsed time.
You are asked to replace a 25-year-old PLC on a running line. There are no current drawings and the original programmer is gone. How do you approach it?
How you plan a migration with real risk and limited downtime.
Captures the running program and real wiring first, converts logic deliberately, tests offline, and plans the cutover with a way back.

First I upload the running program and keep two backups, then trace the field wiring and fix the drawings. I walk each section through with operators, since converted code keeps old quirks. I test the new program on a bench rack or simulation, plan the cutover for a shutdown with every I/O point checked, and keep the old rack ready to go back in.

corporate-trainer.heading: Corporate trainer questions
qs: What makes teaching adults at work different from teaching in a school?
Whether you know how adults learn on the job.
Adults want relevance to their real tasks, bring experience you can build on, and need to practice, not just listen.

Adults walk in asking how this helps them on Monday morning. So I open with a real task they struggle with, draw on their experience in discussion, and keep lecture short. They have work waiting, so every activity has to earn its time. Many also have bad memories of school, so I keep practice low-stakes and never put anyone on the spot.
How do you write a learning objective?
Your grasp of the basics of instructional design.
An action you can observe, the conditions and a standard. Not vague verbs like “understand” or “know”.

I start with what the learner will do, using a verb I can see, like “process a return” instead of “understand returns.” Then I add conditions and a standard: “Using the point-of-sale system, process a customer return with no errors in under three minutes.” If I can't watch someone do it, it isn't an objective yet.
Walk me through how you would build a course from scratch.
Whether you follow a structured design process.
A clear sequence such as ADDIE: analysis, design, development, a pilot, delivery and evaluation, with stakeholder sign-off along the way.

I use a version of ADDIE: analyze, design, develop, implement, evaluate. I confirm the business goal and the audience, write objectives, then outline activities and assessments and get sign-off before I build materials. I pilot with a small group, fix what confused them, then roll out. After launch I check results against the goal I started with.
How do you keep people engaged in a live virtual session?
How you run live online training, not just slides on a video call.
An interaction every few minutes (polls, chat, breakouts), shorter sessions, and a co-host for tech so the trainer can keep teaching.

I plan an interaction every few minutes: a poll, a chat question, a quick breakout. I call on people by name, kindly, so they expect to take part. I split a long course into 90-minute sessions with practice in between. And I ask for a co-host to handle tech problems and the chat so I can stay focused on teaching.
When would you choose e-learning instead of a live class, and when not?
Your judgement in picking the right delivery format.
E-learning for consistent knowledge across large or spread-out groups; live sessions for skills that need practice and feedback; often a blend.

E-learning fits knowledge that is the same for everyone and rarely changes, like a policy update for 2,000 people in five time zones. It is consistent and easy to track. For skills that need practice and feedback, like coaching conversations or handling a tough customer, I want a live session with role plays. Often I blend them: short e-learning for facts, live time for practice.
A subject matter expert gives you a 120-slide deck and wants all of it covered in two hours. How do you handle it?
How you work with experts and cut content down to what learners need.
Respect for the expert, steering by the objectives, need-to-know versus nice-to-know, and reference material moved into job aids.

I thank them, because their knowledge is the raw material. Then we sort the slides together against the objectives: what people must do on the job versus what they can look up. Usually the must-know fits in about 30 slides plus practice. The rest becomes a reference guide. I keep the expert involved by asking them to review the practice scenarios.
A manager asks you for customer service training because complaints are up. What do you do first?
Whether you check that training is the right fix before you build anything.
A needs analysis first: find the performance gap and its cause. If the cause is a process, tool or incentive, training will not fix it.

I ask for the complaint data and talk to a few reps before designing anything. Once a request like this turned out to be a refund policy reps couldn't apply without a supervisor, so customers waited. The fix was a policy change and a one-page job aid, not a full-day course. If skills really are the gap, I build the training around those specific calls.
How do you make sure people actually use what they learned once they are back at their desks?
Whether you plan for the transfer of learning to the job.
Managers involved before and after, practice on real tasks, job aids, and reinforcement spread over the following weeks.

Before the course I brief managers so they know what their people will learn and can set a goal with them. In class we practice on real cases from their work. Afterward they get a one-page job aid and short refreshers at one, two and four weeks. Managers get a few coaching questions for one-on-ones, because what the manager reinforces is what sticks.
A senior leader sits in on your workshop and keeps taking over the discussion. What do you do?
How you manage power in the room without embarrassing anyone.
Acknowledge the input, use structure to bring others in, and talk privately at a break, framed as helping the team speak up.

I thank them for the point and then use structure: “Let's hear from people who haven't spoken yet,” or small-group work so they can't steer every table. At the break I tell them privately that the team tends to go quiet when they speak first, and ask if they would share their view at the end. Most leaders take that well because they want honest input too.
Halfway through a rollout, you realize you taught one step of the new process wrong. What do you do?
How you own and correct a mistake that has already spread.
Tell the process owner and your manager at once, fix the materials, reach everyone already trained, and check for work done the wrong way.

I'd confirm the correct step with the process owner and tell my manager the same day. I'd fix the slides and job aid before the next session. For people already trained, I'd send a short correction with a screenshot and ask team leads to mention it in huddles. I'd also ask whether anyone already processed work the wrong way, so it can be checked and fixed.
What does SCORM actually track, and when would you want xAPI instead?
Whether you know how e-learning talks to a learning management system.
SCORM packages a course so the LMS can launch it and record completion and scores. xAPI records learning that happens outside the LMS.

SCORM is a standard for packaging e-learning so any compliant LMS can launch it and store completion, pass or fail, score and time. That is about all it covers. If I need to track a simulation, a mobile app or on-the-job practice, I use xAPI. It sends statements like 'Ana completed the forklift check' to a learning record store.
A director wants the course redesigned for visual, auditory and hands-on learners. How do you respond?
Whether you know the research on learning styles and can disagree politely.
Studies have not shown that matching teaching to a preferred style improves learning. Fit the method to the content instead, and do it without lecturing the director.

I'd agree with the goal, which is a course that works for everyone. Then I'd explain briefly that research hasn't found that teaching to a person's preferred style helps them learn more. What helps is fitting the method to the skill: a diagram for a workflow, hands-on practice for software, role-play for a hard conversation.
How do you write a quiz question that tests whether someone can apply a rule, not just repeat it?
Your skill at writing assessments that match the objective.
Scenario-based items where the learner makes the decision the job requires, with wrong answers that reflect real mistakes.

I start from the verb in the objective. If it says 'decide whether a refund is allowed', the question gives a short customer case and asks what to do. The wrong options are mistakes people really make, taken from the floor, not silly fillers. I avoid 'all of the above' and keep the options the same length, so nobody can guess from the format.
Walk me through the first two weeks of an onboarding program you would build for new customer support hires.
How you pace onboarding so new hires become productive without being overloaded.
Access and paperwork ready before day one, a buddy, and learning spread over time with real tasks early. Planned check-ins with the manager.

Before day one, I make sure IT access and paperwork are done, so the first morning isn't spent waiting. Day one is people and purpose: the team, the customer, a buddy. Then mornings of short lessons and afternoons shadowing real calls. By day eight they take easy tickets with the buddy listening. The manager and I check in at day five and day ten against a skills checklist.
What do you check before you publish an online course so that employees with disabilities can use it?
Whether you build accessibility in from the start instead of adding it at the end.
Concrete checks against a standard such as WCAG 2.1 level AA: captions, alt text, keyboard-only use, color contrast and screen reader testing.

I test against WCAG 2.1 level AA, a common target. Every video has accurate captions, not just auto-generated ones, and a transcript. Images that carry meaning have alt text. I go through the whole course using only the keyboard, and again with a screen reader. I check color contrast and make sure no instruction relies on color alone, like 'click the green button'.
You need 40 managers to deliver a new training to their own teams. How do you keep the quality consistent?
How you scale delivery through train-the-trainer without losing the message.
A detailed facilitator guide, a teach-back where each manager practices and gets feedback, and spot checks after launch.

I give them a facilitator guide with timings, the key points word for word where accuracy matters, and the questions people usually ask, with answers. Each manager does a ten-minute teach-back in a small group and gets feedback before running it. After launch I sit in on a few sessions, collect the questions they couldn't answer, and send a short FAQ to all 40.
Legal asks you to show who completed last year's harassment prevention training and what they were taught. What records do you keep?
Whether you document compliance training so it holds up in an audit or a legal claim.
Names, dates, completion status, assessment results and the exact version of the content, kept for the retention period legal sets.

For each learner I keep the date, completion status and quiz score from the LMS, plus sign-in sheets for live sessions. Just as important, I archive the exact version of the course they took, because the content changes every year. I log who delivered each live session. I follow the retention period our legal team sets rather than guessing at one.
Your workshop scores 4.8 out of 5 on evaluations, but managers say nothing has changed on the job. What do you make of that?
Whether you know that liking a course and changing behavior are different results.
High satisfaction does not prove behavior change. Find the cause in the work environment, manager support or the content before redesigning anything.

It tells me people enjoyed it, not that they can or will do it. I'd observe or interview a few learners and their managers. Often the cause is outside the room: the old process still works, nobody asks for the new one, or there's no time to practice. If the course is the problem, I'd cut the talking and add practice on real cases.
During a workshop break, a participant tells you a colleague in the room has been harassing her. What do you do?
Your judgement when a serious issue comes up that training cannot fix.
Listen, do not promise secrecy, and report it promptly through the company's channel, usually HR. Do not investigate or confront anyone yourself.

I'd find a private spot, listen, and thank her for telling me. I wouldn't promise to keep it secret, because once the company knows, it may have to act. I'd tell her I'm passing it to HR today and how she can contact them herself. I wouldn't confront the colleague or investigate. In the session I'd set up group work so she isn't paired with him.
The CFO asks what return the company got on a leadership program. How do you answer?
Whether you can link training to money credibly, without claiming every gain as your own.
Measures agreed before launch, the program's effect isolated from other causes, gains turned into dollars, and net benefit compared with the full cost.

I'd use measures we agreed on before launch, like turnover on the leaders' teams. I'd compare trained managers' teams with a similar group not yet trained, so I don't count gains from other changes. I turn the difference into dollars, like the cost to replace a leaver, subtract the full program cost including participants' time, and divide by that cost. I'd show my assumptions.

cpp-developer.heading: C++ developer questions
qs: What is RAII, and why does it matter in C++?
Whether you understand the idea that C++ resource handling is built on.
A resource is tied to an object's lifetime and released in its destructor, so cleanup happens on every exit path, including exceptions.

RAII means a resource is acquired in a constructor and released in the destructor. A std::lock_guard locks a mutex and unlocks it when it goes out of scope, even if an exception is thrown. So I don't write cleanup code by hand on every return path, and leaks of memory, files or locks become much rarer.
When do you use unique_ptr and when do you use shared_ptr?
How you think about who owns an object.
unique_ptr by default. shared_ptr only when ownership is truly shared, knowing it costs a control block and atomic reference counts.

unique_ptr is my default: one owner, no overhead beyond a raw pointer in the usual case, and it can be moved. I reach for shared_ptr only when several parts really share the lifetime, like a cache entry used by many threads. It has a control block and atomic reference counting, so it costs more, and cycles need weak_ptr to avoid leaks.
What does std::move actually do?
Whether you understand move semantics beyond the name.
It moves nothing. It is a cast to an rvalue that lets a move constructor or move assignment be chosen. The moved-from object stays valid but unspecified.

std::move is just a cast. It turns its argument into an rvalue so overload resolution can pick the move constructor or move assignment, which may take over the buffer instead of copying it. If the type has no move operations, you get a copy. After a move, a standard library object is valid but unspecified, so I don't read its value until I assign a new one.
What is undefined behavior, and why should a C++ developer care?
Your grasp of the rule that makes C++ both fast and dangerous.
The standard places no requirements on it. The optimizer may assume it never happens, so the bug can show up anywhere, often only in optimized builds.

Undefined behavior is code the standard gives no meaning to, like signed integer overflow, reading past an array, or using a pointer after delete. The compiler is allowed to assume it never happens, so it may remove a check I wrote or reorder code. The program can seem fine in testing and break with a new compiler or flag. I use sanitizers in CI to catch it early.
A class hierarchy has a base class without a virtual destructor. What can go wrong?
Whether you know a classic object lifetime trap.
Deleting a derived object through a base pointer is undefined behavior. The fix is a public virtual destructor or a protected non-virtual one.

If code deletes a Derived through a Base pointer and Base's destructor is not virtual, the behavior is undefined. In practice the derived destructor usually never runs, so its members leak. If the base is meant for polymorphic delete, I make the destructor public and virtual. If it is not, I make it protected and non-virtual so that delete through the base won't compile.
A loop over a std::vector crashes now and then after a teammate added a push_back inside it. Why?
How you spot iterator invalidation.
push_back can reallocate, which invalidates all iterators, pointers and references. Fix by looping by index or collecting changes and appending after the loop.

When push_back exceeds capacity, the vector moves its elements to a new buffer, so every iterator, pointer and reference into the old one dangles. It crashes only sometimes because that happens only when capacity runs out. I would loop by index, or collect new items in a second vector and append them after the loop.
We insert into the middle of a list of a few thousand items often. Would you use std::list or std::vector?
Whether you reason about real hardware, not only big-O.
Usually vector: contiguous memory is cache-friendly and often beats a linked list despite slower inserts on paper. Then measure with a benchmark on real data.

My first choice would be std::vector. A list insert is O(1) once you have the position, but finding it means walking nodes scattered in memory, with a cache miss at almost every step. A vector shifts elements, but a few thousand contiguous items move fast. I would still write a small benchmark with realistic sizes and decide on numbers, not on theory.
Two threads increment a shared int counter and the total comes out wrong. What is happening, and how do you fix it?
Your understanding of data races and the basics of the C++ memory model.
++ is a read-modify-write, and unsynchronized writes are a data race, which is undefined behavior. Fix with std::atomic or a mutex, then check with ThreadSanitizer.

Increment is read, add, write. Two threads can read the same value and both write back the same result, so counts are lost. In C++ this is a data race, which is undefined behavior, not just a wrong number. For a plain counter I'd use std::atomic<int> with fetch_add. If it guards more state, a mutex. Then I run ThreadSanitizer to check for other races.
Two threads each update their own counter, yet the code runs much slower with two threads than with one. What would you suspect?
Whether you know performance problems that come from the CPU cache.
False sharing: separate variables on one cache line bounce between cores. Fix by giving each its own line or counting locally, and confirm with a profiler.

I'd suspect false sharing. If the two counters sit next to each other, they likely share one cache line, often 64 bytes. Each write forces the other core to reload that line, so the cores keep fighting over it. I'd align each counter to its own line with alignas, or have each thread count locally and combine at the end, then confirm the gain with a profiler.
A bug crashes the optimized release build but never the debug build. How do you track it down?
How you hunt bugs that hide behind compiler optimizations.
Suspects undefined behavior, uninitialized data or timing. Builds optimized with debug symbols and runs sanitizers instead of guessing.

That pattern usually points to undefined behavior, an uninitialized variable or a race that debug timing hides. I build with optimization plus debug symbols so the crash still happens with a readable stack. Then I run AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, plus ThreadSanitizer if threads are involved. Full compiler warnings often point at the line too.
A teammate changed a function to return std::string_view instead of std::string, and callers now read garbage. What went wrong?
Whether you understand that a view does not own the data it points to.
The view points into a string that was destroyed; the fix is returning an owning string or keeping the source alive.

A string_view is just a pointer and a length. It owns nothing. If the function builds a local std::string and returns a view of it, the string is destroyed at return and the view dangles. I would return std::string here, and keep string_view for parameters, where the caller's data outlives the call.
Why should a move constructor be marked noexcept?
Whether you know how the standard library chooses between moving and copying.
std::vector moves elements on reallocation only if the move cannot throw, or if copying is impossible; otherwise it copies to keep the strong guarantee.

When a vector grows, it uses std::move_if_noexcept. If my move constructor is not noexcept and the type is copyable, the vector copies every element to keep its strong exception guarantee. So a missing noexcept can quietly turn cheap moves into expensive copies. A defaulted move constructor is noexcept automatically when all members' moves are.
Walk me through how you find where the time goes in a slow C++ program.
Your method for measuring before optimizing.
Profile an optimized build with symbols under realistic load, read the hot paths, change one thing, measure again.

First I reproduce the slowness with realistic input. I build with optimizations and debug symbols, for example -O2 -g, run a sampling profiler such as perf, and read a flame graph for the widest stacks. If the hot spot looks memory-bound, I check cache misses with hardware counters. I change one thing at a time and rerun the same measurement.
Two threads each need to lock the same two mutexes, and the program sometimes freezes. How do you fix it?
How you prevent deadlock when more than one lock is needed.
Name the lock-order cycle, then use one fixed order or std::scoped_lock, which locks several mutexes without deadlock.

Thread A holds mutex 1 and waits for 2, thread B holds 2 and waits for 1, so both wait forever. The simplest fix is std::scoped_lock over both mutexes, which acquires them with a deadlock-avoidance algorithm. Where that is not possible, I set one lock order and document it. Better still, I ask whether one lock or less shared state would do.
What does a virtual function call really cost, and when would you avoid it?
Whether you know the real cost of dynamic dispatch, not the myth.
The indirect call is cheap; the bigger cost is lost inlining and mispredicted branches in hot loops. Options: final, templates, or grouping by type.

The call is a load of the vtable pointer, a load of the function address and an indirect jump. In most code that is noise. In a hot loop over mixed types, it blocks inlining and can mispredict. There I would mark classes final so the compiler can devirtualize, use templates for static dispatch, or store objects grouped by type.
A particle update loop reads only position and velocity, but each particle struct has 20 fields. How would you speed it up?
Whether you think about cache lines and data layout, not just algorithms.
Each cache line loaded carries unused fields; moving hot fields into their own arrays (struct of arrays) saves memory bandwidth and helps vectorizing.

The CPU loads memory in cache lines, usually 64 bytes on x86. With 20 fields per struct, most of each line is data the loop never touches. I would move position and velocity into separate contiguous arrays, a struct-of-arrays layout. The loop then streams only what it needs, and the compiler can vectorize it more easily. I would measure before and after.
Your microbenchmark says a new hash function is 50 times faster than the old one. Why might you not believe it?
How you spot a benchmark that measures the wrong thing.
The compiler may have removed the work, the data may sit in cache, or the run is too short; check the assembly and use realistic inputs.

A 50x gain usually means the optimizer deleted the work because the result was never used, or computed it at compile time. I would make sure the result is consumed, for example with a benchmark library's DoNotOptimize, read the generated assembly, use realistic key sizes, warm up, and repeat runs to see the spread. Then I would test it inside the real program.
Thread A fills a buffer and then sets an atomic flag; thread B waits for the flag and reads the buffer. Which memory orders do you use, and why?
Your grasp of the C++ memory model beyond the default ordering.
A release store on the flag and an acquire load in the reader; relaxed on both could let the reader see the flag but stale buffer data.

Thread A stores the flag with memory_order_release; thread B loads it with memory_order_acquire. If B's load sees the value A stored, everything A wrote before that store is visible to B after the load. With relaxed on both, B could see the flag set and still read stale buffer contents, especially on ARM. The default seq_cst also works, at some extra cost on some CPUs.
In a trading system the median latency is fine, but the 99.9th percentile has spikes. Where do you look?
How you hunt rare latency spikes on a hot path.
Work that happens only sometimes: heap allocation, locks, system calls, page faults, blocking logs, OS scheduling. Pre-allocate, pin threads, measure percentiles.

Spikes usually come from work that runs only now and then. I check for heap allocations on the hot path, a vector growing, lock contention, logging that blocks, and page faults on first touch. I pre-allocate and pre-touch memory, move logging to another thread, and pin the hot thread to an isolated core. I track a latency histogram, not an average.
You maintain a shared library. A teammate adds a private member to a public class and ships only the new .so, and apps start crashing. Why, and how do you prevent it?
Whether you understand binary compatibility, not just source compatibility.
Apps built against the old header use the old size and layout, so adding members breaks the ABI. Use pimpl, change the soname on breaks, check ABI in CI.

The apps were compiled with the old header, so they allocate the old size and use the old member offsets. Private members still count, because stack objects and inline code depend on layout. The new library then writes past the end. I would hide data behind a pimpl pointer, bump the soname when a break is unavoidable, and add an ABI check to CI.

creative-director.heading: Creative and design director questions
qs: What goes into a good creative brief, and what do you do when a brief arrives incomplete?
Whether you know the document the whole job starts from.
Names the core parts: objective, audience, single message, deliverables, budget, deadline, approver. Pushes back before work starts, not after.

A good brief says what we want people to think or do, who they are, the one thing we must say, what we deliver, the budget, the deadline and who approves. If the objective or the approver is missing, I go back to the requester before anyone designs. A vague brief always turns into extra rounds later.
How do you give feedback in a design critique without redesigning the work yourself?
How you guide designers while leaving them ownership of their work.
Feedback tied to the brief, framed as problems to solve rather than fixes to copy, with a clear priority order.

I start with what works, then name the problems against the brief: the headline gets lost, the hierarchy is unclear on mobile. I say what has to change and why, not how to draw it. I rank the notes so the designer knows what matters most, and I only sketch myself if we are stuck on the same point twice.
A client looks at your concept and says, "Make it pop." What do you do?
How you turn vague client feedback into something the team can act on.
Asks questions to find the real concern, ties it back to the goal, and confirms the change before redoing work.

I ask what they want people to notice first and what feels flat to them. Usually it is the product or the offer getting lost. I might show two quick options, one with stronger contrast and one with a bigger hero image, and agree which direction we take before the team spends a day on it.
How do you keep a brand consistent when many designers, freelancers and agencies are producing work?
Your ability to build systems that keep quality up without you checking every file.
Clear guidelines, shared templates and asset libraries, a defined review point, and examples of what is and is not on brand.

I keep one source of truth: brand guidelines with logo, color, type and tone rules, plus templates and a shared asset library. Each guide shows good and bad examples. New partners get an onboarding call, and work goes through a set review step. When the same mistake shows up twice, I fix the guideline, not just the file.
How do you make sure your team's work is accessible?
Whether you know accessibility standards and build them into the work.
Knows WCAG basics such as contrast ratios, not relying on color alone, alt text and captions, and checks them during review, not after launch.

I build it into the design system so nobody has to remember it. Body text meets the WCAG AA contrast ratio of 4.5 to 1, large text 3 to 1. We never use color alone to carry meaning. Images get alt text and video gets captions. I check contrast with a tool during review, not after launch.
You find out a designer used an image from a web search in a final ad. What do you do?
Your grasp of image rights and how you prevent the problem from coming back.
Knows images online are copyrighted by default, stops the asset, licenses or replaces it, and adds a process step.

I pull it before it goes anywhere. An image found online is copyrighted by default, even with no notice on it, so we need a license or permission. I find the source and license it properly or replace it. Then I add a step: every asset in a final file has its source and license logged before I approve it.
You hire a freelance illustrator for a campaign. What do you need in writing before work starts?
Whether you understand who owns commissioned creative work under US law.
Knows the freelancer owns copyright unless there is a written assignment or a qualifying work-for-hire agreement, and covers scope, fee and usage.

Under US copyright law, the freelancer owns what they create unless we agree otherwise in writing. So I want a signed contract that assigns the rights we need, or a work-made-for-hire clause where the category qualifies. It also covers scope, usage, fee, rounds of changes, deadlines, and confirms any stock or fonts they use are licensed for us.
The CEO wants a change at the last minute that you believe weakens the work. How do you handle it?
How you defend the work while respecting who has the business decision.
Argues from the goal and evidence, offers an alternative, then commits fully once the decision is made.

I ask what is behind the request; often it is a real concern said as a design fix. I explain the risk in business terms, like the offer getting buried, and show a version that solves their concern without that cost. If they still want their change, it is their call. I make it look as good as it can and do not grumble to the team.
A print run of 20,000 brochures comes back with a wrong phone number on it. What do you do?
How you own a mistake and fix the process that let it through.
Stops distribution, tells the client fast with options and costs, takes responsibility, and fixes the proofing step.

I stop distribution first, then call the client the same day with the facts and options: a reprint, a printed correction sticker, or a redirect from the old number if that is possible. I own it, not the junior who typed it. Then I add a rule: phone numbers, prices and dates get checked against the source by a second person at final proof.
A test shows the version you thought was weaker performs better. How do you respond?
How you balance your own taste against evidence about what works.
Respects the data, checks the test was sound, looks for why it won, and uses that to make better work rather than defending taste.

First I check the test was fair: enough traffic, same audience, one clear difference. If it holds up, the weaker-looking version won and we use it. Then I ask why. Maybe the plain layout made the price clearer. My job is work that looks good and works, so I take that lesson and design the next version to keep both.
What makes an idea a campaign platform rather than a single good ad?
Whether you can tell a lasting idea from one clever execution.
A platform is a thought that can drive many executions across channels and years. A single ad cannot be extended.

A platform is a thought about the brand that can produce ten different executions in ten channels without repeating itself. My test: can the team write three more ads, a social post and a store moment from it in an hour? If every new piece needs a fresh idea, we have an ad, not a platform.
Walk me through how you build a brand identity system from scratch.
Your process from strategy to a system other people can use.
Research and strategy first, then a few directions tested on real pieces, then a full system written into guidelines.

I start with discovery: interviews, audience, competitors, what the brand must stand for. That becomes a short positioning. Then two or three directions, each tested on real items like a web page, packaging and a social post, not just a logo on white. The chosen one becomes a system: logo, type, color, grid, imagery, voice, and guidelines with do's and don'ts.
How many concepts do you show a client, and how do you choose them?
Your judgement in curating work before it reaches the client.
A few distinct options you would be glad to produce, with a clear recommendation. Never a weak one added as filler.

Usually three, sometimes two. Each must answer the brief and differ in strategy, not just in color. I never include one I would not want to make, because clients have a habit of picking it. I say which one I recommend and why, and tie each back to the goal in the brief.
You are art directing a photo shoot for a national campaign. What do you have in place before the shoot day?
Whether you prepare a shoot so nothing is left to chance on the day.
Shot list, approved references and paperwork settled early: a license that covers the planned usage and signed releases for recognizable people and private locations.

A shot list tied to every placement, with crops for each format, and a mood board the client has signed off. The photographer's license must cover the media, territory and time period we need. Every recognizable person signs a model release, and private locations sign a property release. On the day, I check shots against the list before we strike a set.
Your best concept needs twice the production budget the client has. What do you do?
How you protect an idea when money is short.
Finds what the idea truly depends on, keeps that and cuts around it, and offers clear costed options instead of a quietly weaker version.

I ask what the idea really needs. Often it is the thought, not the scale: one hero film instead of three, stills shot on the film set, a smaller cast. I bring the client two or three costed options and say plainly what each one loses. If the idea only works at full budget, I say so and we pick a concept that fits.
A company with a 40-year-old brand wants a rebrand. How do you decide what to keep?
Whether you respect the brand equity that already exists before changing it.
An audit of what customers already recognize and link to the brand, keeping strong distinctive assets and changing what holds the brand back.

I start with an audit: which colors, shapes, characters or phrases do customers recognize as this brand without seeing the name? Those took decades to build, so I keep or refine them. What is weak, dated or unrecognized can change. Many failed rebrands threw away a distinctive asset only because the people inside were tired of it.
A new logo is approved and launch is in a month. What checks do you insist on before rollout?
Whether you protect the company from legal and production problems with a new mark.
A trademark clearance search by legal counsel, plus tests at small sizes, in one color and on every surface where the mark will appear.

First, legal runs a clearance search so we do not launch a mark too close to an existing one in our line of business, and decides on filing with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office. Then production tests: tiny sizes, one color, reversed, embroidered, on a vehicle and on a busy photo. I want final master files and a rollout list before anything is printed.
A designer wants to use AI-generated images as the main visuals of a client campaign. What do you weigh?
Whether you understand the legal and brand risks of generative AI in client work.
Knows the US Copyright Office will not register material lacking human authorship, so the client may not own it exclusively; also checks tool terms and likeness risks.

Ownership first. The US Copyright Office will not register material made by AI without enough human authorship, so the client may not be able to stop a competitor from using similar images. I also read the tool's terms for commercial use, avoid anything that resembles a real person, and get the client's informed approval in writing before we go ahead.
Over several rounds of approvals, a campaign has been diluted until the idea is almost gone. What do you do?
Whether you notice and stop the slow dilution of an idea across rounds of feedback.
Puts the first and current versions side by side against the brief, names what was lost, and resets the work with the real decision maker.

I put round one and the current version side by side with the brief and ask: does this still do what we agreed? Then I meet the real decision maker, not the chain of reviewers, and show what each change cost. Usually we restore the core and keep some notes. Next time I agree up front who approves and how many rounds there are.
Tell me about a campaign you led that did not work. What did you change afterward?
Whether you own a failure and change your process because of it.
A real failure, an honest share of the blame, a clear cause and a lasting change in how the work is done.

We launched a clever outdoor campaign for a regional bank built on a pun. Recall tests showed people remembered the joke but only about one in five could name the bank. My mistake was approving it on the team's enthusiasm without checking branding. Now every concept gets a quick test: show it for three seconds and ask who it is from.

credit-analyst.heading: Credit analyst questions
qs: How do you calculate debt service coverage, and what does a ratio of 0.9 tell you?
Your grasp of the core repayment ratio.
Cash flow available for debt service divided by scheduled principal plus interest; below 1.0 the cash does not cover the payments.

I take cash flow available for debt service, usually EBITDA less taxes, unfinanced capital spending and distributions, and divide it by the year's scheduled principal and interest. At 0.9 the business earned 90 cents for every dollar owed to lenders. The gap was covered somehow, by new debt, owner cash or a shrinking cash balance, and I need to know which.
What is the difference between a primary and a secondary source of repayment?
Whether you know what a loan should be repaid from.
Primary is ongoing cash flow; secondary is collateral or a guarantor. A deal that only works on the secondary source is a weak deal.

The primary source is the borrower's own cash flow from running the business. Secondary sources are the fallback if that fails: selling collateral or calling on a guarantor. I want the primary source to work on its own. If I only get comfortable by counting on selling equipment, I am lending against assets, and that is a riskier loan.
Why is EBITDA not the same as cash available to repay debt?
How you look past an earnings figure to real cash.
Lists what EBITDA ignores: taxes, capital spending, working capital needs and owner distributions.

EBITDA leaves out cash that really goes out the door. Taxes get paid. A trucking company has to replace trucks, so capital spending is not optional. Growth ties up cash in receivables and inventory. Owners of pass-through companies often take distributions to pay their personal taxes. I subtract those before I decide what is left for the lender.
A borrower's sales grew 30% last year but its cash fell. Where do you look?
Whether you can read working capital and spot growth that eats cash.
Checks receivable and inventory days, payables, and whether the credit line is funding growth or hiding a problem.

Fast growth often eats cash, so I start with working capital. I compare days sales outstanding and inventory days to the prior year. If receivables grew faster than sales, customers are paying slower or some invoices may not be collectible. I pull the aging report and look for one large slow payer. Then I check whether payables were stretched to cover the gap.
The company's statements show $900,000 of net income, but its tax return shows $300,000. What do you do?
How you handle conflicting numbers from the same borrower.
No assumption either way: reconciles the two line by line, asks the borrower or CPA, and escalates if the gap stays unexplained.

Some difference is normal; tax depreciation, for example, is often faster than book depreciation. So I reconcile line by line: depreciation, revenue timing, other book and tax differences. If most of the $600,000 gap is bonus depreciation, fine. If not, I ask the borrower's CPA, and if I still can't tie it out, I tell my manager. I don't lend on numbers I can't trust.
What covenants would you put on a five-year equipment loan to a mid-sized manufacturer, and why?
Whether you can structure protection that fits the risk.
Financial covenants tied to the real risks, like minimum coverage and maximum leverage, plus reporting and limits on new debt or distributions.

I'd set a minimum debt service coverage ratio tested annually, and a maximum total debt to EBITDA so they can't pile on borrowing. I'd require yearly reviewed or audited statements and tax returns, and limit distributions and new debt without our consent. I set levels with room below their projections, so a covenant warns early instead of tripping on one normal bad quarter.
A relationship manager wants a deal approved by Friday and says the client will walk otherwise. You have concerns. What do you do?
How you keep independent judgement under sales pressure.
Names the specific risks, offers structures that could fix them, and writes the view honestly rather than softening it.

I'd tell the relationship manager exactly what bothers me, for example thin coverage and one customer at 40% of sales. Then I'd offer fixes: a shorter term, more equity, a personal guarantee, or a covenant on that concentration. If none work, my memo says so plainly. Losing a client is a cost; a loan that goes bad is a bigger one.
A borrower you've had for eight years misses its coverage covenant for the first time. Walk me through what you do.
How you handle an early warning on an existing loan.
Finds the cause, judges if it is temporary, updates the risk rating and collateral, then picks a waiver, amendment or tighter terms for a stated reason.

First I find out why: one bad quarter from a lost contract is different from margins slowly sliding. I get current numbers and aging reports and talk to the owner. I update the risk rating and collateral values. If it's temporary, a waiver with a fee or extra reporting may fit. If it's a trend, I tighten terms or add collateral while the business can still give it.
What separates a special mention loan from a substandard one?
Whether you know the regulatory risk rating categories US banks use.
Special mention has potential weaknesses; substandard has a well-defined weakness that puts repayment at risk.

Special mention means potential weaknesses that deserve management's close attention. If nothing changes, repayment could suffer later. Substandard means a well-defined weakness: the loan is not adequately protected by the borrower's current paying capacity or by the collateral, and the bank could lose money if it is not fixed.
On an income property loan, why look at debt yield as well as loan-to-value and debt service coverage?
Your grasp of commercial real estate sizing measures.
Debt yield is NOI over the loan amount, and it does not depend on the interest rate, amortization or the cap rate.

Debt yield is net operating income divided by the loan amount. A property with $800,000 of NOI and a $10 million loan has an 8% debt yield. It does not move with the interest rate, the amortization or an appraiser's cap rate, so it shows how much income backs each dollar I lend even if rates or values change.
A borrower's days sales outstanding went from 45 to 70 in one year. What do you look into?
How you read working capital trends and what they mean for cash.
Checks for timing effects, reads the aging, finds the cause, and links slower collections to cash needs and collateral quality.

First I check whether a big year-end month inflated it. Then I read the aging: is one large customer paying late, are there disputes, or did they loosen terms to win sales? Slower collections tie up cash, so I would expect heavier draws on the line and ask whether those receivables are still good collateral.
Walk me through how you build a borrowing base for an asset-based revolving line.
Whether you can turn receivables and inventory into a safe lending limit.
Removes ineligible items, applies advance rates, compares to the outstanding balance, and verifies with agings and field exams.

I start with total receivables and remove ineligibles: invoices past 90 days, related-party and foreign accounts, and amounts subject to offsets. I apply an advance rate, often around 80%, then add inventory at a lower rate. I compare the total to the line balance and test the numbers against the aging and field exam results.
A client wants to buy its building using its revolving line of credit. What concerns you?
How you match the loan structure to the purpose and the asset.
Spots the mismatch of short-term funding for a long-term asset and offers a better structure.

The line is meant to fund receivables and inventory that turn into cash within months. A building pays back over decades, so the line would stay drawn and could not be cleaned up, and the client would lose room for working capital. I would offer a separate real estate term loan, amortized to fit the asset, with the building as collateral.
How do you build a global cash flow for a business owner who guarantees the loan?
Your method for combining business and personal repayment capacity.
Adds outside personal income, subtracts personal obligations, covers related entities, and avoids counting cash twice.

I start with the business's cash available for debt service, then add the owner's outside income, like other wages or rental income. I subtract personal debt payments, taxes and living costs, and include other companies the owner owns or guarantees. Distributions from the borrower count only once. Total cash over total debt service gives global coverage.
The borrower's EBITDA includes $400,000 of owner add-backs. How do you judge them?
Whether you can tell real one-time costs from inflated earnings.
Sorts add-backs by evidence, rejects recurring ones, and sizes the loan only on what can be supported.

I sort them one by one. A documented one-time lawsuit settlement may be fair. Owner pay above market counts only if the owner will really take less and a replacement would cost less. A one-time cost that shows up every year is not an add-back. I ask for support and size the loan on EBITDA with only the add-backs I can prove.
How do you stress test a borrower with a floating-rate loan?
How you measure the cushion before a borrower cannot pay.
Raises rates and cuts cash flow, alone and together, finds the break-even point, and ties the result to structure.

I rebuild debt service at higher rates, for example 200 and 300 basis points above today, and see where coverage falls below our minimum. Then I cut revenue or margin to match their worst past year and combine both. I report how far things can move before coverage hits 1.0. If the cushion is thin, I ask for a rate hedge or lower leverage.
On an annual review, you see the UCC filing on a borrower's equipment lapses next month and nobody has continued it. What do you do?
Whether you know how lien perfection works and act fast on a collateral problem.
Knows filings lapse after five years, files the continuation in the six-month window, verifies it, and fixes the tracking gap.

A UCC financing statement generally lapses five years after filing, and a continuation can only be filed in the six months before that. We are inside that window, so I get it filed now and confirm with a new search. Then I check the tracking system to find out why it was missed and whether other loans have the same gap.
Tell me about a credit you got wrong. What did you miss?
Whether you learn from losses and change how you underwrite.
Names a specific miss, owns it without excuses, and shows a concrete change in method since then.

I approved a line for a distributor with strong coverage, but 40% of its sales came from one customer. I noted it but did not stress it. When that customer switched suppliers, coverage fell below 1.0 within two quarters. We restructured and were repaid, but now I model the loss of any customer above about 20% of sales.

custody-wallets.heading: Crypto custody and wallet specialist questions
qs: How do you decide what share of client assets sits in hot, warm and cold wallets?
How you balance speed of withdrawals against exposure to theft.
Hot holds only what normal withdrawals need, sized from real flow data. Cold holds the rest, with a planned refill path through warm storage.

I size the hot wallet from withdrawal history: enough for a normal day plus a buffer, with a hard cap. Warm storage refills hot within hours, under approvals. Everything else sits cold, offline. If hot drops below its floor, a refill request goes to signers. If it goes above the cap, the excess is swept down.
What is a seed phrase, and what does a derivation path do?
Whether you know how one backup can recover many keys and addresses.
The mnemonic encodes the seed. A path picks which key in the tree is used. A wrong path or passphrase makes the wallet look empty, not lost.

A seed phrase, usually 12 or 24 words under the BIP-39 standard, encodes the random value the whole wallet grows from. BIP-32 builds a tree of keys from that seed, and the derivation path, such as m/44'/60'/0'/0/0, says which branch to use. If a restore shows zero balance, I check the path and any optional passphrase before anyone panics.
Multisig or MPC: how do they differ, and when would you choose each?
Your grasp of the two main ways to require several parties to approve a transaction.
Multisig is enforced on-chain with separate keys. MPC splits one key into shares that sign together into one normal signature. Trade-offs named for each.

With multisig, say 2-of-3, the chain itself checks that enough separate keys signed, and the setup is visible on-chain. It depends on each chain supporting it. With MPC, multi-party computation, the key is never whole; shares on different machines produce one ordinary signature, so it works on almost any chain, but I rely on the MPC code being correct.
What does a hardware security module add to a signing setup?
Whether you know where keys live and how they are protected.
Keys are generated and used inside tamper-resistant hardware and never leave in plain form. You still need a policy deciding what it is allowed to sign.

An HSM generates the key inside the device and signs there, so the raw key never sits in server memory or on disk. I check which FIPS 140 level it is validated to and whether it supports secp256k1, the curve Bitcoin and Ethereum use. It still signs whatever it is told to, so the approval policy in front of it matters just as much.
A trader asks you to allowlist a new withdrawal address urgently. What happens next?
How you apply withdrawal controls under time pressure.
The normal process holds: verify the address through a second channel, a quorum approves, any cooling-off period applies, and a small test transfer goes first.

I follow the same steps as any other day. I confirm the address with the trader by calling a number we already have, not the chat the request came from. Two approvers sign off in the policy engine, the address waits out our cooling-off period, and we send a small test amount first. Urgency is a common sign of social engineering.
What is address poisoning, and how do you protect operators from it?
Whether you know a common attack on people who copy addresses.
An attacker plants a look-alike address in your history with a tiny transfer. Defense is allowlists and full-address checks, never copying from history.

An attacker creates an address with the same first and last characters as one we pay often, then sends a tiny or zero-value transfer so it shows in our history. An operator who copies from history pays the attacker. We only pay allowlisted addresses, our tool shows the full address, and we hide dust transfers from the view operators use.
Walk me through a key generation ceremony for a cold vault.
Your hands-on knowledge of creating root keys with no single point of trust.
Scripted steps, air-gapped devices, several witnesses, recording and logs, backups split and stored apart, and a test restore before funding.

We use a written script, air-gapped machines checked beforehand, and at least two witnesses plus a recording. Keys or shares are generated on the devices, backups go into numbered tamper-evident bags, and each holder signs for theirs. Before funding, we restore from backup on a separate device and confirm it derives the same addresses. Backups then go to sites in different cities.
An Ethereum withdrawal from the hot wallet is stuck pending, and every later withdrawal is queued behind it. What do you do?
How you handle transaction ordering without paying a customer twice.
Replace the stuck transaction using the same nonce and a higher fee. Never resend the withdrawal with a new nonce, since both could confirm.

Transactions from one address confirm in order of their nonce, a counter, so one low-fee transaction blocks the rest. I rebroadcast it with the same nonce, recipient and amount, and higher fees. I never send a fresh copy with a new nonce, because both may land and the customer gets paid twice. Then I find out why our fee estimate was too low.
You learn that a laptop holding one MPC key share may have been compromised. What are your first steps?
Your incident response when key material may be exposed.
Freeze outbound activity, revoke that device, then refresh shares or move funds to new keys, depending on whether the threshold could have been reached.

I pause withdrawals from that vault and revoke the device from the signing group. Then I check logs for any signing requests from it. If only one share was exposed and the threshold is two of three, a share refresh makes the old share useless. If I cannot rule out a second share, we move funds to a newly generated wallet. Then we write up the root cause.
What does a proof of reserves show, and what can it miss?
Whether you can judge what a reserve attestation really proves.
It shows control of on-chain assets at one moment. It can miss liabilities left out, off-chain debts, and assets borrowed just for the snapshot.

It usually pairs signed messages proving we control certain addresses with a Merkle tree of customer balances, so each customer can check they are included. It is a snapshot. It does not show other debts, and funds could be borrowed for the day of the check. I would add frequent reconciliations of our ledger against the chain and an outside audit of liabilities.
Why is reusing a signing nonce in ECDSA so dangerous, and how do signers avoid it?
Whether you understand the math risk behind a signature, not just the tools.
Two signatures from one key with the same nonce let anyone compute the private key. Deterministic nonces (RFC 6979) or a sound random source prevent it.

Each ECDSA signature uses a secret one-time number, the nonce. If one key signs two different messages with the same nonce, anyone who sees both signatures can compute the private key. Good libraries derive the nonce from the key and the message, as RFC 6979 describes, so it never repeats. In MPC the nonce is made jointly, so I review that part of the protocol too.
Walk me through signing a Bitcoin withdrawal on an air-gapped device using a PSBT.
How you move a transaction across an air gap without moving the key.
The online machine builds the PSBT. The offline signer shows outputs and fee on its own screen. Only the signed file comes back to be broadcast.

A watch-only online wallet builds a Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction, the BIP 174 format. I move it by QR code or a fresh USB stick. The offline device shows the destination, amount, change address and fee on its own screen. I check them against the approved request, then sign. The signed PSBT goes back, is finalized and broadcast. The key never leaves the device.
How do you decide how many confirmations to wait before crediting a deposit?
Your grasp of finality and reorg risk on different chains.
It depends on the chain's finality model and the amount. On probabilistic chains, bigger deposits wait for more blocks. On finality-based chains, you wait for finalization.

On Bitcoin, finality is probabilistic: the risk of a reorg falls with each new block. So I require more confirmations for larger deposits and for smaller chains that are cheaper to attack. On Ethereum I credit large deposits once the block is finalized, roughly two epochs, about 13 minutes. I review these settings after any reorg on a chain we support.
Your Bitcoin hot wallet holds thousands of small UTXOs. Why does that matter, and what do you do?
Whether you manage fees and wallet health before they become a problem.
Many small inputs make each withdrawal larger and costlier, worst during fee spikes. Consolidate when fees are low, and leave dust that costs more to move than it holds.

Every unspent output I spend adds an input, and fees are paid per virtual byte of transaction size. With thousands of small ones, a withdrawal during a fee spike costs far more than it should. I consolidate into fewer outputs when the mempool is quiet and fees are low. I leave dust alone if moving it costs more than it is worth.
Why can signing an off-chain message be as dangerous as sending a transaction?
Whether you know how token permits and typed signatures can drain a wallet.
A signed EIP-712 permit can let someone else move your tokens. Signers must decode and check every message, not approve it as harmless text.

Some tokens accept a permit: a typed message, signed under EIP-712, that grants a spender an allowance. Signing it costs no gas and sends nothing, yet the spender can submit it and move the funds. So our policy treats typed messages like transfers. We decode the fields, check the spender, amount and deadline, and block any spender we do not know.
What does a key share refresh in an MPC wallet do, and what can it not fix?
Your depth on the MPC life cycle beyond the first key generation.
A refresh issues new shares of the same key, so the address stays and old stolen shares stop working. It cannot help once an attacker holds a signing threshold.

A refresh runs a protocol between the share holders that produces new shares of the same private key. The address does not change, but old shares no longer combine with new ones. A share stolen last month becomes useless, as long as every party deletes its old share. If an attacker already holds enough shares to sign, a refresh is too late: I move the funds to a new key.
