A client sent a stablecoin to their deposit address, but on the wrong EVM network. Can you recover it?
How you think through a misdirected deposit before promising anything.
It depends on what controls that address on the other chain. A plain key-based address can be recovered with the same key; a contract wallet may not exist there.

First I check what the address is. If it is a plain address from a key we hold, that key controls it on every EVM chain. We can usually recover the tokens once we add that chain to our signing setup and pay gas there. If it is a smart contract wallet, the contract may not exist on that network, and recovery may be impossible. I promise nothing until I have checked.
A client wants to stake ETH held in custody. What failure do you design against first?
Whether you know how validator slashing happens and how custody setups avoid it.
Double signing, usually from one validator key running in two places after a failover. Keep a single active signer and keep the slashing protection data.

Slashing. The usual cause is our own redundancy, not an attacker: the same validator key runs on two machines, for example after a failover, and signs two conflicting messages. I keep exactly one active signer per key, carry the slashing protection database when a validator moves, and make failover manual, with a check that the old node is truly off.
A smart contract multisig transaction you must sign makes a delegatecall to an unknown contract. What do you check?
Whether you can spot a signing request that hands over control of the whole wallet.
Delegatecall runs outside code with the wallet's own storage, so it can rewrite the wallet. Refuse unless the target is known, reviewed and expected.

Delegatecall runs the target's code inside the wallet's own context, with its storage and its balance. A malicious target can overwrite the slot that points to the wallet's logic and take every asset in one step. I decode the call on a separate device, not only the signing screen, and confirm the target is an audited, allowlisted contract. If anything is unexpected, I do not sign and I escalate.
How would you design withdrawal controls so that two colluding employees cannot drain the vault?
How you build controls that hold against insiders, not only outside attackers.
Separate who requests, approves and signs; quorums across teams and sites; limits and delays enforced by the system; alerts no single team can silence.

I split the roles. The person who requests a withdrawal cannot approve it, and approvers cannot change the policy. Large moves need a quorum of more than two people from different teams and sites. Velocity limits and a delay for new addresses are enforced in the signing system itself, and alerts go to a team outside operations. Two people working together still hit a wall.

customer-education.heading: Customer education specialist questions
qs: How is customer education different from onboarding and support?
Whether you understand where your work fits in the customer journey.
Education teaches skills to many customers ahead of need; onboarding gets one account live; support fixes one problem. Each feeds the others.

Support solves one customer's problem after it happens. Onboarding gets a new account set up and live. Education teaches many customers at once, before they get stuck, and keeps going after onboarding ends. I read support tickets and onboarding notes to choose what to teach next.
How do you decide whether a topic needs a help article, a short video or a full course?
How you match the format to what the customer is trying to do.
By the task: quick lookups get an article, hard-to-describe steps get a short video, new skills that need practice get a course.

If someone needs one answer in the middle of their work, an article they can scan is best. If the steps are hard to describe in words, a two-minute video helps. If they must build a new skill, like designing reports, that needs a course with practice and feedback. I also ask how often the screen changes, since video costs the most to update.
What are SCORM and xAPI, and when does the difference matter?
Your knowledge of the standards behind learning platforms.
SCORM packages courses for an LMS and tracks completion and scores; xAPI records learning activity anywhere and sends it to a learning record store.

SCORM is an older standard for packaging a course so a compliant LMS can launch it and record completion, time and score. xAPI records statements like “Ana completed lab 3” and sends them to a learning record store, even from outside the LMS, such as a product sandbox. If we want to track hands-on practice in the product, xAPI matters.
Walk me through turning a new feature into a course.
Your process from product spec to finished training.
Starts with who uses the feature and what they must be able to do, then objectives, practice, expert review and a pilot with real users.

I meet the product manager to learn which customers the feature is for and what problem it solves. Then I write two or three objectives as tasks, like “set up an approval rule.” I build short lessons around a hands-on exercise, get the product expert to check accuracy, and pilot it with a few customers before launch day.
How do you keep a webinar for 300 customers from becoming a one-way demo?
How you build interaction into a large live session.
Planned interaction every few minutes, a second person handling chat and questions, and a clear follow-up.

I open with a poll on what attendees want to do, so I can adjust my examples. Every ten minutes or so there is a poll, a chat question or a quick task to try in their own account. A colleague moderates chat and groups questions for me. Afterward everyone gets the recording, the slides and a link to the next step.
The product interface changes every few weeks. How do you stop courses from going out of date?
How you plan content so it can be maintained.
Short modular pieces, a link to the release process, an owner and review date for each asset, and teaching the concept more than the click path.

I build short modules, so one change means re-recording three minutes, not an hour. I join release planning to see changes early and keep a list of which assets show which screens. Each asset has an owner and a review date. Where I can, I teach why and when to use a feature, which lasts longer than which button to press.
Support sees the same setup question again and again. What do you do?
Whether you use tickets to find learning needs, and know when training is not the fix.
Reads the tickets to find the real gap, puts help where users get stuck, and tells product when the design itself is the problem.

I read a sample of the tickets to see exactly where people fail. If it is missing knowledge, I write a short guide and ask to link it inside the product at that step and in support replies. If the screen itself is confusing, I tell product with the ticket count; training should not cover for a design flaw. Then I watch whether tickets drop.
Certified customers renew at a higher rate. Leadership wants to say certification drives renewals. What do you tell them?
Whether you can tell correlation from cause when reporting on education.
Points out that engaged customers are the ones who certify, and proposes a fairer comparison before claiming cause.

I would say the link is real but not proof. Customers who certify are often already committed, so they may have renewed anyway. I would compare certified accounts with similar ones by size, age and usage before certifying, or offer the program to some accounts first. If the gap holds, we can claim more with confidence.
You find out a course has taught a wrong setting for a month. What do you do?
How you handle your own error when customers may already have acted on it.
Fixes the content at once, finds and tells affected learners with the correct step, briefs support, and changes the review process.

I pull or correct the lesson the same day. I ask support and the product team how much harm the wrong setting can do. Then I use the LMS records to email everyone who took that lesson, with the right step and how to check their setup. I give support a note for related tickets, and I add a product expert review before any course goes live.
How do you write learning objectives for a product course?
Whether you design from what the learner must do, not from the feature list.
Each objective starts with an observable verb and names a real task. Each is tied to a practice step and a check.

I write them as tasks a learner can show me: 'Build a report that filters by region and share it with a team,' not 'Understand reports.' A word like 'understand' cannot be checked. Every objective then gets a practice activity and a question or task that proves it. Content that serves no objective gets cut.
How do you write a quiz question that tests judgement, not recall?
Your skill at writing assessments that go beyond 'which menu is this button in'.
A short realistic scenario with one clearly best answer. The wrong options are based on mistakes customers really make.

I start with a scenario: 'An admin wants managers to see only their own team's data. What should they set up?' The options are all real features, and the wrong ones are mistakes support sees, like giving everyone admin rights. I avoid 'all of the above' and trick wording, so the question measures the decision, not reading skill.
Your live demo breaks halfway through a webinar for a few hundred customers. What do you do?
How you stay in control when the product fails in front of an audience.
Calm, honest acknowledgment and a backup ready ahead of time, like recorded clips or a second account. Any promised follow-up is kept.

I say plainly that the demo environment has a problem, then switch to the backup I prepare for every live session: a short recording of the same steps or a second test account. A co-host checks whether it is a real product bug and alerts support. The follow-up email includes the recording and, if customers were affected, what we found.
The courses will be translated into five languages next year. What do you do differently now?
Whether you plan content so that translation later is cheap and accurate.
Text kept out of images, room for longer translations, plain sentences without idioms, and a glossary of product terms.

I keep all on-screen text editable, not baked into images or video, so translators do not need a designer. I leave space in layouts because many languages run longer than English. I write short sentences without idioms or jokes. I start a glossary of product terms now, including which ones stay in English. Voiceover goes on a separate track.
What makes a video course accessible?
Your working knowledge of accessibility for training content.
Accurate captions, a transcript, spoken descriptions of key visuals, a keyboard-usable player and readable contrast, with WCAG AA as the usual target.

Captions checked by a person, not just auto-generated, plus a transcript. When I click something, I say what I am clicking, so a learner who cannot see the screen still follows. The player and quizzes must work with a keyboard and a screen reader. Normal text needs a contrast of at least 4.5 to 1 under WCAG AA, and color is never the only signal.
Only 18% of people who start our core course finish it. How do you find out why?
How you diagnose a learning problem with data before redesigning anything.
Looks at where people drop off, who they are, and whether they got what they came for, before assuming the course is bad.

First I look at drop-off by lesson. If most people leave at one point, that lesson has a problem: too long, a broken lab, or a hard jump. Then I split by role. End users may leave once they have the part they need, which can be fine. I would talk to five people who left. Often the fix is splitting one long course into shorter role-based paths.
What does a customer academy need from an LMS that an employee LMS often does not?
Whether you know the tools of external training, not only internal training.
Self-registration and single sign-on, learners grouped by customer account, checkout if paid, branding, and data that flows to the CRM.

Customers must sign up on their own, ideally with single sign-on from the product, so there is no second password. Learners need to be grouped by customer account so a customer success manager can see one account's progress. If training is paid, we need checkout and seat licenses. Completion data should reach the CRM, next to usage and renewal data.
How do you build a certification exam that would hold up if a customer challenged their score?
Your knowledge of how a defensible certification exam is built.
A job task analysis, a weighted blueprint, items written and reviewed by experts, a beta with item analysis, and a documented pass-mark method.

I start with a job task analysis: what a competent admin actually does and how often. That becomes a blueprint that weights each area. Experts write and review items against it. I beta test, then drop items that are too easy, too hard, or that strong candidates miss more than weak ones. The pass mark comes from a method like Angoff, and every step is documented.
You find your certification exam questions posted on a public website. What do you do?
How you protect the value of a credential when its security fails.
Gets the content taken down, retires exposed items, checks score data for misuse, and acts on candidates only with evidence and policy.

I ask legal to help with a takedown request, since the questions are our copyrighted content. I retire the exposed items and swap in backup items, which is why I keep a pool larger than one exam form. I check scores since the leak for odd patterns, like very fast perfect scores. Any action on a candidate follows the candidate agreement and the evidence.
Leadership wants to start charging for training that is free today. How do you advise them?
Your judgement on the business model of customer education.
Keeps what customers need for basic success free and charges for premium value. Weighs fee revenue against adoption and churn.

I would keep anything a customer needs to get basic value from the product free, because blocking it can hurt adoption and renewals more than the fee brings in. Certifications, live workshops and advanced tracks can be paid. I would test first on one offer and watch enrollment, and include training credits in larger contracts so key accounts are not blocked.

customer-experience.heading: Customer experience manager questions
qs: What is the difference between NPS, CSAT and customer effort score, and when do you use each?
Whether you know the core CX metrics and what each one actually measures.
Correct NPS math, and each metric matched to its use: loyalty overall, satisfaction with one contact, ease of a task.

NPS asks how likely someone is to recommend us, from 0 to 10. Promoters give 9 or 10, detractors 0 to 6, and the score is percent promoters minus percent detractors. It tracks loyalty. CSAT asks how satisfied someone was with one interaction, so I send it after a support case. Effort score asks how easy a task was, like a return.
How do you write a customer survey that gets honest, useful answers?
Your survey design basics and how you avoid biased questions.
Short, neutral wording, one idea per question, sent soon after the event, with an open question and answers tied to the account.

I keep it to two or three questions: the score first, then one open question, such as what is the main reason for your score. I avoid leading words like how great was, ask one thing per question, and send it soon after the event while memory is fresh. I also link answers to the account so I can follow up and split results by segment.
Walk me through how you build a customer journey map.
How you turn scattered data into a clear picture of the customer's path.
One persona and goal, every stage and touch point, real data plus interviews, pain points marked, and an internal owner for each step.

I pick one customer type and one goal, like a small business owner opening an account. I list every stage, from the first ad to the first bill, using tickets, survey comments, web analytics and a handful of interviews. For each step I note what they do, feel and where they get stuck. Then I name who inside owns each step, so every fix has an owner.
What does closing the loop mean in a voice of the customer program?
Whether you know feedback must lead to action for the person and for the business.
Both loops: a quick personal follow-up with the customer, and fixing the root cause with the owning team, then telling customers what changed.

The inner loop is following up with the person, especially a detractor, within a few days, by someone who can actually help. The outer loop is fixing the cause: grouping feedback into themes, taking the top ones to the team that owns them, and telling customers what changed. Without both, people stop answering surveys.
Our NPS went from 32 to 28 this quarter. What do you do first?
How you react to a score change without panic or guessing.
First check whether the drop is real given sample size and normal noise, then segment it, then read the comments before naming a cause.

First I check whether it is real: how many responses we got, and whether a 4-point move is within the normal swing for that sample. Then I split it by segment, channel and product to find where it came from, and read the detractor comments for the period. Last time I did this, the whole drop sat in one region after a delivery partner changed.
Survey response rate fell from 18% to 6%, and most comments are now angry. How do you treat the results?
Whether you understand non-response bias and how it distorts a score.
Does not report the score as-is; finds what changed, compares responders to the customer base, and checks behavior data that does not depend on who answers.

I would not report the score as if nothing changed. I check what changed: send time, channel, email delivery, survey length. I compare who answered with the full customer base by segment and tenure, and flag or weight the result if they differ. I also look at behavior like repeat orders and cancellations, which does not depend on who chooses to answer.
You have thirty known pain points and room to fix three this quarter. How do you choose?
Your judgement in ranking problems by impact, not by who complains loudest.
Sizes each by reach, harm (contacts, drop-off, churn) and cost to fix, weighs high-value segments, and makes the ranking visible to owners.

I size each one by how many customers hit it, how much it hurts, such as extra contacts, drop-off or churn among those who hit it, and what a fix costs. A clumsy password reset that 40,000 people hit a month beats a rare billing glitch, unless that glitch is losing big accounts. I share the ranking openly so the choice is clear, not political.
The support director wants to cut average handle time, and you think it will hurt the experience. How do you settle it?
How you handle a conflict between efficiency targets and customer outcomes.
Brings data, not opinion: handle time next to repeat contacts and CSAT, and proposes a test judged on cost per resolved issue.

I would bring data. I would put handle time next to repeat contacts and CSAT for the same cases. If shorter calls mean customers call back, the saving is not real. Then I would propose a four-week pilot: one team aims at lower handle time, one at solving it on the first contact, and we compare cost per resolved issue and satisfaction.
You redesigned onboarding, CSAT for onboarding went up, but churn did not move. What might have gone wrong?
Whether you can question your own success metric and find the real driver.
Sees that the metric may not sit on the path to churn, considers who answered, and goes to churned customers for the real reasons.

Maybe we measured the wrong thing. The survey rated the new onboarding screens, but people may leave later over price or a missing feature. Maybe the happier responders were customers who would have stayed anyway. I would read exit reasons, interview a few churned accounts, and check whether onboarding is even linked to churn before spending more there.
How do you convince a finance leader that a customer experience project is worth the money?
How you link experience to revenue and cost in a way finance trusts.
Uses the company's own data to tie experience to retention and cost to serve, gives a range with stated assumptions, and agrees on a measure upfront.

I tie it to money with our own data. For example, I compare renewal rates of customers who had a bad support case with those who did not, and show what that gap means in revenue. Then I add savings, like fewer calls once a confusing bill is fixed. I give a range, state my assumptions, and agree before launch on the number we will check after.
Two regions both report an NPS of 40. Why might they still need very different plans?
Whether you look past the single score to what is under it.
You know NPS is the share of promoters minus the share of detractors, so the same score can hide very different mixes of customers.

NPS is the percent of promoters, who score 9 or 10, minus the percent of detractors, who score 0 to 6. Region A might have 60% promoters and 20% detractors. Region B might have 45% and 5%. A has an angry group to rescue fast. B has many lukewarm passives to win over. Same number, different work.
When would you run a relationship survey and when a transactional one?
Your grasp of which survey design fits which goal.
Relationship surveys track the overall bond on a schedule. Transactional surveys capture one specific contact soon after it happens.

A relationship survey goes out on a schedule, say twice a year, and asks how customers feel about us overall. It shows the trend in loyalty. A transactional survey goes out right after a contact, like a support case or a delivery, and asks about that moment. I use it to find which step breaks. I also set rules so nobody gets both in the same week.
How is a service blueprint different from a journey map, and when do you need one?
Whether you know service design tools beyond the journey map.
The blueprint adds what staff and systems do behind the scenes, split by a line of visibility, so you see where internal work causes customer pain.

A journey map follows the customer: steps, feelings, pain points. A blueprint lines those steps up with what frontline staff do, the backstage work customers never see, and the systems that support it, with a line of visibility between them. I use one when the fix is inside our operation, like a refund that stalls because two systems do not talk.
You have 12,000 open-text survey comments from last quarter. How do you turn them into something leaders act on?
How you analyze voice of the customer data at scale.
A clear codebook, a check that coding is consistent, and themes tied to scores and volume, not just a word cloud.

I read a random few hundred first and build a codebook of themes with clear definitions. Two people code the same sample to see if we agree, and we fix vague codes. Then a text tool or the team codes the rest, and I spot-check it. I report each theme by how often it appears and how much lower scores are when it does, with real quotes.
How would you find out which parts of the journey matter most to overall satisfaction?
Your method for key driver analysis and its limits.
Relates step scores to the overall score, then checks the result, because a correlation alone does not prove a step drives loyalty.

I would ask customers to rate key steps and give an overall score, then run a driver analysis, often a regression, to see which steps move most with the overall score. I plot importance against current performance. High importance and low score comes first. Steps often overlap, so I confirm with interviews or a test before I promise a result.
We want to change the returns process in every store. How would you test it before a full rollout?
How you apply service design to a pilot that gives real evidence.
Prototype cheaply, pilot against a comparison group, and agree in advance on what results mean go or stop.

First I would walk a few customers and staff through a paper or role-play version to catch obvious problems. Then I would pilot in eight stores and pick eight similar stores as a comparison. Before starting we agree on the measures: customer effort, return time, repeat contacts and cost per return. After six weeks we compare and decide.
Leadership wants a chatbot to handle 30% of support contacts this year. How do you protect the experience?
Your judgement when a cost goal can hurt customers.
Counts issues solved, not just contacts kept away from agents, keeps an easy path to a person, and watches repeat contacts.

I would accept the goal but define it as resolved, not just contained. A customer who gives up and calls later is not a win. I would start with simple, high-volume questions, give a clear way to reach a person with the chat history passed along, and track repeat contacts within seven days and CSAT for bot chats next to agent chats.
You find out some agents are asking customers to give them a 10 on the survey. What do you do?
How you handle gaming of customer feedback metrics.
Treats it as a system problem: stop it, find why the incentive pushed people there, and fix the measure rather than only punish agents.

I would first check how widespread it is, using comments and score patterns by agent. Then I would tell the team clearly that it stops, because those scores are now useless for decisions. I would also look at why: if bonuses ride on one score, people will chase it. I would move pay away from single survey scores and coach on behaviors instead.
Teams agree with your findings, but the fixes never ship. How do you set up governance so they do?
How you get other departments to own and deliver customer experience work.
Named owners, a regular forum with executive backing, fixes placed in each team's own roadmap, and progress reported openly.

I would set up a monthly customer council with an executive sponsor and the heads of product, operations and support. Each top pain point gets one named owner, a target date and a measure. Fixes go into that team's own roadmap, not a separate CX list. I report status to the council every month, so a stalled item is visible and gets a decision.
After you presented a finding to executives, you discover a data error that changes the conclusion. What do you do?
Your integrity and how you repair trust in customer data.
Corrects it quickly and openly, explains what changes, and fixes the process so the same error cannot happen again.

I would confirm the error, then tell the sponsor the same day, before anyone acts on it. Once a data join double-counted customers with two accounts, which made one churn driver look twice as big. I sent a short correction with the new numbers and what it changed, then added a second-person check on every data pull before a leadership deck.

customer-success-manager.heading: Customer success manager questions
qs: What is the difference between customer success and customer support?
Whether you understand what the role is for.
Support reacts to problems; success works ahead of them to get the customer to their goals and to renewal.

Support fixes what is broken when the customer asks, ticket by ticket. Success is proactive. I learn what the customer bought the product to achieve, track whether they are getting there, and step in before a problem shows up at renewal. I work closely with support, but I own the account's outcome, not a single ticket.
Walk me through how you run onboarding for a new account.
How you get a new customer to first value quickly.
A kickoff that confirms goals and owners, a dated plan with an early first win, and a clean handoff from sales.

Before kickoff I read the sales notes so the customer does not repeat themselves. At kickoff we agree on two or three goals, who owns each task on their side, and dates. I aim for one visible win in the first few weeks, like the first team going live. I send a short recap after every call and flag slipping dates early.
What would you put into a customer health score, and where can it mislead you?
Whether you can read account risk beyond a single number.
A mix of usage, engagement, support and sentiment signals, plus awareness that a green score can hide a lost sponsor.

I would combine usage against what they bought, active users, escalated tickets, whether we still have an engaged sponsor, and survey answers. I check the weights against accounts that actually churned. It misleads when usage looks fine but the buyer has left or a budget cut is coming, so I treat it as a prompt to look closer, not a verdict.
You own 60 accounts. How do you decide where your time goes?
How you manage a book of business with limited hours.
Segmenting by value and risk, scaled one-to-many touches for smaller accounts, and a weekly look at what changed.

I group accounts by revenue and by risk. Large or at-risk accounts get regular calls. Healthy smaller ones get scaled touches: webinars, emails triggered by usage, open office hours. Each week I check health changes and renewals due in the next 90 to 120 days, and those move to the top. Time follows risk and value.
How do you prepare a business review that the customer's executive will find worth the time?
Whether you can show value in the customer's terms, not yours.
Results tied to the goals they set, honesty about gaps, and a forward plan they agree to; not a feature tour.

I start from the goals we agreed at onboarding and show progress in their terms, like hours saved, not logins. I name what is behind and what we are doing about it. Then I propose next quarter's priorities and ask what has changed on their side. I send the deck to my contact a few days early, so nothing surprises the executive.
When do you raise an upsell with a customer, and when do you hold off?
Your judgement on expansion without damaging trust.
Expansion follows proven value and a real need; you hold off while the customer is unhappy or not using what they have.

I raise it when the customer has hit their goals and a need shows up that the extra product solves, like a new team asking for seats. I hold off if they use a fraction of what they bought, have an open escalation, or are unhappy, because pushing then puts the renewal at risk. When it fits, I bring in the account executive if they own the commercial side.
At kickoff you learn sales promised a feature the product does not have. What do you do?
How you handle a broken expectation without blaming a colleague.
Clarify quickly and honestly, offer a workaround or path, loop in sales and product, and fix the handoff for next time.

I would not let it ride, because it surfaces at renewal anyway. I confirm with the sales rep what was said, then tell the customer plainly what the product does today, show the closest workaround, and bring in product if it is on the roadmap. I keep it about the customer, not whose fault it was. Afterward I ask sales to add a check to the handoff notes.
Usage at an account fell 40% over two months and renewal is in 90 days. What do you do?
Whether you dig for the cause before you react.
Finding out why first, from data and from people, then a dated recovery plan shared with the sponsor.

First I check the data: which teams or features dropped, and when. A sudden drop often means a reorg, a lost admin or a broken integration. Then I call my contact and ask what changed, without pitching. Once I know the cause, we agree a dated recovery plan with the sponsor. I flag the renewal risk to my manager now, not in the final weeks.
Your main champion at a key account just left the company. What do you do?
How you protect a relationship that rested on one person.
Moving fast to find and win the new owner, proving value again, and seeing that relying on one contact was the real risk.

I ask the departing champion, if I can, who takes over and for an introduction. I meet the new owner quickly, learn their goals, and show what the account has achieved, since they did not choose us. I mark the account at risk and build contacts with other users and an executive. The real lesson: every key account needs several relationships, not one.
How do you define time to value for a new customer, and how do you shorten it?
How you tie onboarding to the customer's first real result.
A first value moment the customer would name themselves, measured in days, with setup trimmed or done in parallel to reach it sooner.

I ask the customer what result would make them say this was worth buying, then pick an early, measurable version of it, like the first report their manager actually uses. Time to value is the days from signature to that point. To shorten it, I limit setup to what that milestone needs and leave the nice-to-haves for later.
What goes into a success plan, and who owns it?
Whether your plans are shared commitments rather than a document only you read.
Customer goals, measures, milestones, and owners and dates on both sides, agreed with the customer and reviewed on a regular schedule.

It has two or three business goals in the customer's words, how we will measure each, the milestones to get there, and a named owner and date for every step, on their side and ours. The customer agrees to it, not just sees it. We review it each month or quarter, and it becomes the backbone of the business review.
How do you spot that you are single-threaded in an account, and what do you do about it?
How you build relationships beyond one contact before you need them.
Mapping stakeholders by role and influence, finding the gaps, and earning access by offering value to each person, not by going around the champion.

If every email, meeting and decision runs through one person, I am single-threaded. I map who signs, who uses, who pays and who blocks, and look for the gaps. Then I ask my champion to bring others in, with a reason that helps them: a training for their team or a short results summary for their boss. The champion should feel helped, not bypassed.
A customer tells you they are evaluating a competitor. What do you do?
How you respond to a competitive threat without panic or reflexive discounting.
Find out why and who is driving it, show value against their goals, address real gaps, and bring in leaders early. No discount before the reason is known.

First I thank them for telling me and ask what started the review and who is leading it. Usually it is one unmet need or a new leader. I take that need seriously: I show what they have achieved with us in numbers, and fix or plan for the gap with my product team. I tell my manager the same day. I do not offer a discount before I know the real reason.
At renewal the customer asks for a 25% discount or they will leave. How do you handle it?
How you negotiate a renewal while protecting value and margin.
Separating real budget pressure from a tactic, trading any concession for something in return, and staying within your approval limits.

I ask what is behind it: a budget cut, low usage, or a competitor's quote. If usage is low, a smaller plan that fits may be better than a discount. If I give anything, I trade it, for example for a two-year term or a reference. I stay within my approval limits, bring my manager in early, and never let "or we leave" set the price alone.
Several accounts are at risk over the same product gap. How do you get the product team to act?
How you turn customer feedback into a case product leaders can weigh.
Pooled evidence: accounts affected, revenue at risk, renewal dates and the problem customers need solved, plus honest workarounds in the meantime.

I gather the accounts affected, the recurring revenue at stake and the renewal dates, and describe the problem customers are trying to solve, not the button they asked for. One page, with quotes. I bring it to the product manager and ask for a decision and a date. Meanwhile I give customers a workaround and an honest answer on timing, never a promise product has not made.
The executive sponsor stopped coming to business reviews, but usage is healthy. Is that a problem?
Your judgement on a risk that usage numbers do not show.
Yes: the buyer decides the renewal, not the users. Re-engage with outcomes the executive cares about, in a short format that fits their time.

Yes. Users may love it, but the sponsor signs the renewal and sets the budget. I would ask my main contact what the executive cares about this year and offer something short: a 20-minute call or a one-page summary tying our results to that priority. If our leader can meet theirs, I set that up. Healthy usage with a silent buyer is a risk I flag.
You forecast a renewal as safe and it churned. Walk me through how you review what happened.
Whether you learn from a loss honestly and change how you forecast.
A blameless timeline of the signals missed and why, the customer's real reason from an exit talk, and one concrete change to the forecast process.

I would ask the customer for a short exit call to hear the real reason, then build a timeline of signals: usage, meetings, contacts, tickets. Usually the sign was there, like a new leader we never met. I would own my part and share it with the team. Then I change something real, for example requiring contact with the budget holder before any account counts as safe.

customer-success-specialist.heading: Customer success specialist questions
qs: What is the difference between customer support and customer success?
Whether you understand what this role is for.
Support reacts to problems as they come in. Success works ahead of them so customers reach their goals and renew.

Support answers when a customer asks for help: fix the problem, close the ticket. Success starts before the customer asks. I look at how each account uses the product, find who is stuck or drifting, and reach out with the next step. The goal is that they get value and renew, not just that their tickets are closed.
What does time to value mean, and how would you shorten it for a new small customer?
Your grasp of onboarding as the stage that often decides whether a customer stays.
A clear definition, one first outcome to aim for, and steps that remove setup friction early.

It is the time from signing up to the first real result the customer cares about. For a small account I pick one early win, like their first report sent, and build the first emails around it: a short checklist, a two-minute video, and an offer of a 15-minute call if they have not finished setup by day five.
Which signs tell you a low-touch account might churn before they say anything?
Whether you can read usage data and spot risk early.
Several signals, not one: falling logins, unused key features, fewer active users, billing trouble, repeated tickets, unanswered emails.

Logins dropping week over week, fewer active seats, and the core feature going unused are the big ones. I also watch for a failed payment, a run of support tickets on the same problem, and emails that stop getting answers. One sign alone can be noise, like a holiday. Two or three together means I reach out now.
You own 400 accounts and have time for about 15 calls this week. How do you choose them?
How you spend scarce one-to-one time across a large book of accounts.
A clear rule based on risk, revenue and timing, with everyone else covered by email or webinars.

I sort by risk and timing first: accounts with renewals in the next 60 to 90 days and a falling health score. Then I weigh revenue and a clear chance to help, like a team that is stuck mid-setup. The rest get a targeted email or an invite to the next webinar. I note why I chose each call so I can check later whether the rule worked.
Walk me through how you would plan a webinar for customers who are not using a key feature.
Whether you can run one-to-many sessions that change what customers do.
A narrow goal, the right audience picked from usage data, a live demo of a real task, a follow-up, and a check of usage afterward.

I would pull the list of accounts that have not used the feature in 30 days and invite only them. The session is 30 minutes: why it matters in one slide, then a live demo of one real task, then questions. Everyone gets the recording and a one-step guide. Two weeks later I compare how many attendees started using it with those who did not attend.
You sent an email about a new feature. Open rates were good, but almost nobody used the feature. What do you look at?
How you diagnose a campaign that got attention but no action.
Checking clicks, the call to action, the steps after the click and whether the audience fit, then testing one change.

Opens only tell me the subject line worked. I would check clicks next: if few clicked, the message or the button was weak. If many clicked but did not use it, the problem is after the click, like a confusing setup or the wrong audience. I would call two customers, fix the biggest gap, and send a revised version to a small test group.
Your main contact at a small account leaves the company. What do you do?
Whether you know how to handle a champion leaving, one of the top churn risks.
Act fast: find the new owner, re-onboard them, check that admin access moved, and spread contacts across more people.

I treat it as a risk right away. I look in the account for other active users and write to the most active one to ask who owns the tool now. I offer that person a short call to show what the team uses it for and what results they have had. I make sure admin access moved over, and from then on I keep at least two contacts per account.
The health score says an account is green, but a user tells you they are looking at a competitor. What do you do?
Your judgement when the data and what a customer says disagree.
Trust the customer, ask why, act on the reason, and flag the gap so the health score can be improved.

The customer's words win over the score. I would ask what is pushing them to look: price, a missing feature, or a bad experience. Then I would act on that reason, maybe a workflow they have not found or a talk with my manager about pricing. I would also tell whoever owns the score, since it missed a real risk and may lean too much on logins.
What is the difference between gross revenue retention and net revenue retention?
Your understanding of the main numbers a success team is judged on.
Both track the same customers' revenue. Gross counts only losses and cannot exceed 100%; net also adds expansion and can.

Both take the recurring revenue from a group of customers at the start of a period and compare it with what those same customers pay at the end. Gross retention counts only losses from churn and downgrades, so it tops out at 100%. Net retention also adds upgrades and added seats, so it can go above 100% when growth beats losses.
Before renewal, you see a customer pays for 20 seats but only 8 are used. What do you do?
Whether you put the customer's long-term value ahead of short-term revenue.
Raise it honestly and early: try to grow adoption first, and if the seats will not be used, support a right-sized plan instead of risking a surprise churn.

I raise it well before the renewal date, not after. First I ask about the other 12: are they people who never got invited, or seats no one needs? If it is an adoption gap, I help them onboard those users. If they truly need eight, I tell my manager and support a smaller plan. A customer who feels overcharged often leaves entirely; one who gets an honest fit usually stays.
We started the quarter with 200 customers, lost 10, and signed 30 new ones. What was our logo churn rate?
Whether you can calculate churn the standard way without mixing in new sales.
5%: the ten lost divided by the 200 at the start. New customers stay out of the math, so they cannot hide losses.

Five percent. Logo churn counts customers lost against the customers we had at the start, so 10 out of 200. The 30 new ones do not belong in that number; adding them would make retention look better than it was. I would report growth separately, since we ended the quarter at 220 customers.
What is the difference between a leading and a lagging indicator of churn, and which do you act on?
Whether you know which signals still leave time to save an account.
Cancellations are lagging; drops in usage or engagement are leading. You act on leading signs and check later whether they predicted churn.

A cancellation or a missed renewal is lagging: by the time I see it, the decision is made. Leading signs come earlier, like fewer weekly logins, a key feature no longer used, or the admin no longer opening emails. I act on those because there is still time to help, and later I check whether they really predicted churn.
A new customer signed three weeks ago, has not finished setup, and ignored three onboarding emails. What do you do next?
How you restart an onboarding that has stalled.
A new channel and a new message, not a fourth copy of the same email, plus one small, clear next step and a named owner.

Another email of the same kind will not work. I check who signed and who was meant to set up, since they are often different people. Then I try a short call or a personal note offering 15 minutes to finish setup together, naming the one missing step. If the buyer is not the user, I ask who should own setup.
A small customer keeps hitting their plan's usage limit. How do you bring up an upgrade without sounding like a salesperson?
How you handle expansion while keeping the customer's trust.
Starting from the customer's goal and data, offering real options including staying put, and a clean handoff if they want to buy.

I start from what they are trying to do. I tell them they hit the limit four times this month, show what that cost them, like blocked work, and give options: an upgrade, or ways to use less if budget is tight. If they want to buy, I pass it to sales or the self-serve page with the context, so they do not repeat themselves.
A customer says they will not renew unless they get 30% off. How do you handle it?
Your judgement in a renewal under price pressure.
Finding the real reason before talking price, and knowing who approves discounts and what to offer or ask in return.

First I ask what changed: is it budget, or are they not getting enough value? Often it is low use, and a discount only delays the churn. If value is the issue, I make a plan to fix it. If budget is real, I bring options to whoever approves pricing, like a smaller plan or a longer term, rather than promising 30% myself.
You send a campaign to 3,000 customers and it opens with "Hi {first_name}" instead of their names. What do you do?
How you own a mistake made at scale and recover from it.
Stopping further damage first, telling your manager, a calm judgement on whether to apologize, and a fix to the process.

I pause any scheduled sends in that campaign first so it does not spread. Then I tell my manager and check how many got the broken version. For a cosmetic error I usually skip a mass apology, since it draws more attention than the mistake. I reply kindly to anyone who writes in, and I add a test send with real data to our checklist.
A product change will remove a feature that about 150 of your accounts use. How do you tell them?
How you manage a change that hurts some customers.
Early notice to the affected accounts only, saying what changes, when, why, and what to do instead, with extra care for heavy users.

I pull the list of accounts that used the feature recently and write only to them, well before the date. The message says what changes, when, why, and the workaround, with a short guide or a webinar. The heaviest users get a personal note or a call. I also give support the same text so everyone answers the same way.
How do you turn what you hear from hundreds of small customers into feedback the product team acts on?
Whether you can make the voice of many customers useful to product.
Tagged, counted requests tied to revenue and churn, describing the customer's problem, not only the feature they asked for.

I log every request with a tag, the account, its plan value and the problem behind it, not just the feature they named. Once a month I bring the top themes with counts, the revenue tied to them, and a few quotes. A request linked to three lost renewals gets more weight than one loud email. Then I tell customers when something ships.
Most churned accounts picked "too expensive" on the exit survey. How far do you trust that?
How critically you read churn data before acting on it.
With caution: price is often the easy answer for low value. Checking usage before they left shows which it really was.

Price is the polite, quick answer, so I treat it as a starting point. I would compare those accounts' usage in the months before they left. If most barely used the product, the real problem is adoption, and cutting prices would not fix it. I would also call a handful of them; a five-minute talk often gives a truer reason than a dropdown.
How would you show that your webinar program actually reduces churn?
Whether you can tell a real effect apart from customers who were already engaged.
Seeing that attendees choose themselves, so a fair comparison is needed: matched accounts or a group not invited, compared on renewals.

Comparing attendees to everyone else is not enough, because people who join webinars are already more engaged. I would compare them with similar accounts that did not attend, matching plan, size and earlier usage. Better still, invite a random half of a segment first and compare renewals and feature use over a quarter. Then I report the gap honestly, even if small.

customer-support.heading: Customer support questions
qs: How do you use a saved reply without sounding like a robot?
How you use macros, the saved replies most help desks have, and still answer the actual person.
The macro is a base: you add the customer's details, cut what does not apply, and check that it answers their exact question.

I treat the macro as a first draft. I open with a line that shows I read their message, like naming the order they mentioned, and I delete steps that don't fit their case. Before sending, I reread their question once more and check that my reply answers it. If I edit the same macro every time, I suggest a fix to whoever owns it.
Why does it matter how you tag or categorize a ticket?
Whether you see that ticket data is used beyond the single ticket.
Tags feed reports, routing and bug counts. Careless tags hide trends and send work to the wrong people.

Tags are how the team sees patterns. If twenty people write about a login error and half are tagged billing, the product team never sees how big the problem is. Tags can also route tickets to the right queue. So I pick the most specific tag that fits, and if none fits, I ask my lead instead of guessing.
On a call, you need two minutes to look something up. Walk me through what you say and do.
Your phone habits around hold time and silence.
Ask before placing someone on hold, give a time, check back if it runs long, and thank them when you return.

I say what I'm checking and ask, “Is it okay if I place you on a short hold, about two minutes?” I wait for a yes. If it runs longer, I come back on the line, tell them where I am and ask if they can hold a bit more. When I return, I thank them for waiting and give the answer first.
Walk me through how you structure an email reply to a customer.
How you organize a written answer so the customer can act on it.
The answer up front, steps numbered, all needed questions asked at once, and a clear next step: what you will do and what they need to do.

First line: a short acknowledgment and the answer, or what I'm doing about it. Then the steps, numbered, one action each. If I need information, I ask for all of it in one place, so we don't go back and forth. I end with what happens next and when. Then I reread it as the customer would, on a phone screen, and cut anything they don't need.
A customer pastes their full credit card number into the chat. What do you do?
Whether you protect payment data when the customer does not.
Do not repeat or copy the number, redact it or flag it as your policy says, and tell the customer kindly not to share it.

I don't copy it, repeat it or use it. If our tool lets me redact the message, I do that right away; if not, I flag it to whoever handles that, following our policy. I tell the customer, without blaming them, that we never need the full card number in chat and that I've removed it. Then I help with their actual question.
A caller wants to change the email on an account but cannot pass verification. They are upset. What do you do?
Whether you hold the security line under pressure.
No change without verification, however convincing the story. Explain why, and offer the official path to prove ownership.

I don't make the change. Someone trying to take over an account can sound just as upset and convincing as the real owner. I explain that the check protects them, and I walk them through the other ways our process allows, such as a reset link sent to the email on file. If they still can't verify, I note the attempt and pass it to the team that handles account recovery.
A customer says, “Let me speak to your manager.” What do you do?
How you handle an escalation demand without getting defensive.
Find out what they need, try once to solve it, and if they still want a supervisor, follow the process without arguing or promising outcomes.

I don't take it personally. I say, “I can do that. Can you tell me what you'd like to happen, so they have the full picture?” Sometimes I can solve it right there. If not, or if they still want a manager, I follow our escalation process and write a short summary so they don't have to repeat themselves. I don't promise what the manager will decide.
You posted an internal note as a public reply, and the customer saw it. What do you do?
How you handle a ticketing mistake that the customer can see.
Tell the lead at once, check what was exposed, follow up with the customer honestly, and change your habit so it does not happen again.

I tell my lead right away, because the note might hold something sensitive, like another customer's details or a blunt comment. If the tool allows, we hide or delete it. Then I write to the customer: a short apology, a plain explanation that it was a note meant for my team, and the real answer. Since then I check whether the reply box says public or internal before every send.
In one hour, fifteen customers report the same error. What do you do?
Whether you spot a wider incident and act on it, not just ticket by ticket.
Alert the lead or engineering early with examples, link the tickets, use one agreed message, and never promise a fix time you were not given.

After the third or fourth one, I tell my lead or post in the incident channel with ticket numbers, times and screenshots, so engineering can check quickly. I tag and link the tickets so we can update everyone at once later. I reply with the agreed message: we know, we're working on it, we'll update you. I don't give a fix time unless engineering has given one.
A customer replies “still not working” for the third time. What do you change?
How you break a loop when your usual steps are not working.
Stop repeating steps, reread the thread from the start, switch to a call or screen share if available, and escalate with what was tried.

Three rounds means my approach isn't working, not just the fix. I reread the whole thread for something I missed, like the device or the exact error text. Then I change how we talk: I offer a call or screen share if we have one, so I can see what they see. If I still can't solve it, I escalate with a list of everything tried and tell the customer who has it now.
What is an SLA in support, and what do you do when a ticket is about to breach it?
Whether you know how support teams commit to response times.
Defines it as a promised response or resolution time, and acts before the breach: reply, update, or flag it.

An SLA, a service level agreement, is the time we promise to respond or resolve, often different by plan or priority. If a ticket is close, I send a real reply first, even a short update with a next step. If I cannot, I flag it to my lead before it breaches, not after, so someone can take it.
A customer stops replying halfway through a ticket. When and how do you close it?
How you follow up without dropping customers or leaving tickets open forever.
Follows the team's follow-up rule, sends a clear last message, and makes it easy to reopen.

I follow our team's rule, for example one reminder after two days and closing a few days later. The reminder repeats the one thing I need from them. The closing message says what we tried and that replying to the same thread reopens it, so they never have to start from zero.
You find a help center article with a wrong step. What do you do?
Whether you take care of the knowledge base, not only your own tickets.
Confirms the error, fixes or reports it through the proper process, and follows up with customers it may have misled.

I check the step myself in the product to be sure. Then I fix it if I have edit rights, or send the owner the exact wrong line and the correct one with a screenshot. I also search recent tickets that linked the article and follow up with anyone it may have sent the wrong way.
A customer asks whether a feature they need is coming soon. What do you say?
Whether you avoid promises the company has not made.
Honest about what is public, no unofficial dates, logs the request, and offers what works today.

If it is on the public roadmap, I share what is published and nothing more. If not, I say I cannot promise it or give a date, and that I am logging their request with their use case. Then I show the closest thing that works today, so they leave with something useful.
A customer says they will dispute the charge with their bank. What do you do?
How you handle a chargeback threat calmly and inside policy.
No arguing or warnings; tries to fix the cause within policy, and notes the account so billing knows.

I don't argue, since disputing a charge is their right. I ask what went wrong and check whether a refund or fix within policy solves it, because a dispute is slower for them and usually costs us a fee. I note the account and tell billing, so nobody refunds twice if the dispute also goes through.
A customer asks you to delete their account and all their data. What do you do?
Whether you treat privacy requests as a process, not a quick favor.
Verifies identity, uses the company's formal privacy process, and explains what happens next, since some state laws set rights and deadlines.

First I verify the person is the account owner, because deleting the wrong account cannot be undone. Then I log it through our formal privacy request process instead of deleting things by hand, since some states give a legal right to deletion with deadlines. I tell them what will be removed, what we may have to keep, like billing records, and when to expect confirmation.
How do you bring a pattern you see in tickets to the product team so they act on it?
Whether you can turn customer pain into a case a product team will act on.
Counts and links tickets, shows impact in customers' words, and ends with one clear ask, not a vague complaint.

I tag the tickets so I can count them, then write one short note: how many tickets in what period, which plans, two or three customer quotes, and the cost, like handle time or refunds. I end with one clear ask. “Customers hate exports” gets ignored; “42 tickets in May about wrong dates in CSV exports” gets looked at.
Your manager wants lower average handle time. How do you cut it without hurting quality?
How you balance speed against getting it right the first time.
Removes wasted time, not care: better saved replies and notes, fewer back-and-forths, while watching reopens and satisfaction.

I would look at where my time goes: searching for answers, slow tools, or asking for details I should have asked for in the first reply. I fix those with better saved replies and notes. I would not rush customers off the phone, because a reopened ticket costs more. So I watch reopens and satisfaction next to handle time.
Satisfaction scores on one type of ticket dropped this month. How would you find out why?
Whether you can investigate a quality problem with data, not guesses.
Reads the low-rated tickets and comments, and looks for what changed: a release, a policy, a saved reply, or staffing.

I would pull the low-rated tickets in that category and read twenty of them with the survey comments. Then I ask what changed this month: a release, a new policy, an edited saved reply, new agents. Often the score is about the policy or a bug, not the agent, and that changes who needs to fix it.
You see a teammate give credits outside policy to keep their scores high. What do you do?
Your integrity and how you raise a problem about a colleague.
Asks the teammate privately first, then brings facts to the lead; no gossip and no silence.

I would first ask them privately, in case there is an approval I don't know about. If not, I would tell our lead with ticket numbers, not opinions. Those credits cost money, teach customers to push, and are unfair to teammates who say no correctly. What happens next is the lead's decision.

customs-trade.heading: Customs and trade compliance specialist questions
qs: Walk me through how you classify a product you have never seen before.
Whether you follow the legal method for tariff classification.
Facts about the product first, then the General Rules of Interpretation in order, starting with heading text and notes, and a ruling when in doubt.

First I get the facts: what it is made of, how it works, what it is used for, plus a spec sheet or photo. Then I apply the General Rules of Interpretation in order. Under GRI 1, the heading text and the section and chapter notes decide first. I check past CBP rulings in the CROSS database. If it is still unclear and the duty matters, I ask CBP for a binding ruling.
We use a customs broker. Who is responsible if an entry is wrong?
Whether you know the importer's legal duty of reasonable care.
The importer of record stays responsible. A broker files for you but does not take over the duty to classify, value and declare correctly.

The importer of record. The law puts the duty of reasonable care on us, even when a licensed broker prepares and files the entry. So I give the broker accurate product data, review their classifications and values, and keep a classification database so the same part is entered the same way every time.
What goes into the customs value of an import besides the invoice price?
Your grasp of transaction value, the main US valuation method.
Knows the additions, like assists, royalties, packing and selling commissions, and that international freight and insurance are not part of US value.

Transaction value starts with the price actually paid or payable. Then I add packing costs, selling commissions, assists, certain royalties and license fees, and resale proceeds that go back to the seller. An assist is something we give the supplier free or cheap, like a mold. International freight and insurance are left out, because the US values goods on a foreign-port basis.
What does substantial transformation mean when you decide country of origin?
Whether you understand how origin is decided, not just where goods ship from.
Processing that makes a new article with a new name, character or use. Shipping from a country or simple repacking does not change origin.

Origin is where the goods were made or last substantially transformed, not where they shipped from. Substantial transformation means processing that turns the inputs into a new and different article with a new name, character or use. Repacking or labeling does not count. Trade agreement preference is a separate question with its own rules, so I check both and document how we decided.
Before we ship a product abroad, how do you decide whether we need an export license?
Your method for export control classification under US rules.
Jurisdiction first, then ECCN or EAR99, then destination, end user and end use. Never assumes an ordinary item is always license free.

First I check jurisdiction: a defense article on the US Munitions List falls under ITAR. Otherwise it is under the EAR, and I find its ECCN on the Commerce Control List or confirm it is EAR99. Then I check the country chart for that ECCN and screen the end user and end use. Even EAR99 items can need a license for embargoed places or banned parties.
Screening flags a new customer as a possible match on a restricted party list. What do you do?
How you handle a screening hit without guessing.
Holds the order, compares full details to the list entry, documents the decision, and escalates a true or unclear match instead of shipping.

I put the order on hold first. Then I compare the full name, address, country and other identifiers with the list entry, using the Consolidated Screening List and OFAC's list. If it is clearly a different party, I write down why and release it. If it matches or I cannot rule it out, it goes to our compliance lead. Nothing ships while it is open.
You find a part has been classified wrong for two years and we underpaid duty. What do you do?
Whether you correct errors properly with CBP.
Fixes new entries at once, corrects entries still open with Post Summary Corrections, considers a prior disclosure for older ones, and pays what is owed.

First I fix the classification so new entries are right. For entries still open for correction, I file Post Summary Corrections. For older ones I gather the numbers and recommend a prior disclosure to CBP, made before CBP opens an investigation, with the extra duty paid. That greatly reduces penalties. Then I find out why the error happened so it does not repeat.
A foreign national engineer joins our team next week. Is there an export issue?
Whether you know about deemed exports.
Knows that releasing controlled technology to a foreign person in the US counts as an export to their country and may need a license first.

Possibly. Under the EAR, releasing controlled technology or source code to a foreign person inside the US is a deemed export to that person's country. So I check what technical data the job needs, its ECCN, and the person's citizenship. If a license is needed, access waits until we have it, and IT limits access in the meantime.
CBP detains a shipment under the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act. How do you respond?
How you handle a forced labor detention and the proof it demands.
Knows goods tied to Xinjiang or listed entities are presumed made with forced labor, and that release takes full supply chain records back to raw materials.

Under that law, goods made wholly or partly in Xinjiang, or by listed entities, are presumed made with forced labor. I pull records back to raw materials: purchase orders, invoices, production and shipping records for every tier. If we can show the goods have no such tie, we submit that to CBP. If we cannot, the goods may be excluded, and we must rethink that supplier.
Sales wants to ship today, but the buyer will not say what the product will be used for. What do you do?
Your judgement when business pressure meets an export red flag.
Treats evasive end-use answers as a red flag, holds the shipment until it is resolved, and explains the risk to sales plainly.

A buyer who dodges end-use questions is a classic red flag in export rules. I hold the shipment, ask for an end-use statement, and check whether the order fits the buyer's business. I tell sales plainly: a late order costs a day, but shipping to a banned end use can bring fines, loss of export privileges and even criminal charges. No answers, no shipment.
A retail kit has a flashlight, batteries and a nylon pouch, sold together in one box. How do you classify it?
Whether you can apply the General Rules of Interpretation beyond GRI 1.
Checks that it meets the set criteria first, then classifies the whole kit by the item that gives essential character under GRI 3(b).

First I check that it is a retail set: different items from different headings, put together for one use, and sold to the user without repacking. If so, GRI 3(b) says to classify it by the item that gives the essential character. Here that is likely the flashlight, by function and value. If I could not decide, GRI 3(c) takes the heading that comes last in numerical order.
Beyond the HTS duty rate, what else can add duty to an import, and how do you keep track?
Your grasp of the special duties that sit on top of the normal rate.
Names Section 301, Section 232 and AD/CVD orders, knows how they are reported on the entry, and follows CBP notices as they change.

Section 301 duties on many goods from China, Section 232 duties on steel, aluminum and some other goods, and antidumping or countervailing duty orders set by Commerce. Other tariffs can come and go. They stack on the normal rate and are reported with Chapter 99 numbers or AD/CVD case numbers. I follow CBP's CSMS messages and check each part against the current lists.
When does a foreign-trade zone save us money, and when is it not worth it?
Whether you can weigh a duty savings program against its cost and limits.
Knows deferral, no duty on re-exports and inverted tariff relief, and that goods under Section 301 or 232 often must enter in privileged foreign status.

A zone pays when we re-export a lot, since goods shipped abroad from the zone pay no US duty, or when the finished product has a lower rate than its parts. But goods under Section 301 or 232 generally must be admitted in privileged foreign status, which keeps the parts' rate. Then setup, inventory control and audit costs can outweigh the savings.
A supplier in Mexico says its product qualifies for USMCA. What do you need before we claim it?
Whether you know who carries the burden when a preference claim is made.
The importer owns the claim: a certification with the required data, a check of the actual rule of origin, and records kept at least five years.

I need a certification of origin with the required data elements; there is no set form, and it can cover a blanket period of up to 12 months. But a certificate alone is not proof. I check the product-specific rule, usually a tariff shift or regional value content, and ask for the bill of materials if needed. We keep records at least five years, because CBP can verify the claim.
CBP sends us a CF-28 on an entry. What is it and how do you handle it?
How you handle a request from CBP without creating new problems.
Knows it is a request for information, not a penalty; answers on time, accurately and only what is asked, and asks for more time if needed.

A CF-28 is a request for information about an entry, often on classification, value or origin. It is not a penalty, but how we answer matters. I note the due date, gather exactly what is asked and check it against the entry before sending. If I need more time, I ask the officer for an extension in writing. If the answer shows an error, I talk with counsel about correcting it.
We find an error on an entry from four months ago. How do you choose between a post-summary correction, a protest and a prior disclosure?
Your command of the correction tools and the timing of liquidation.
Ties the tool to liquidation: a PSC before liquidation, a protest within 180 days after it, a prior disclosure when there may be a violation.

It depends on liquidation. If the entry has not liquidated, I file a post-summary correction, within 300 days of entry and at least 15 days before scheduled liquidation. If it has liquidated, a protest is possible within 180 days of liquidation. If the error points to a violation, like duty underpaid through a lack of reasonable care, I look at a prior disclosure with counsel.
How would you set up a first sale program, and what can make CBP reject it?
Whether you can use a valuation method that saves duty and defend it in an audit.
Knows the conditions: a bona fide sale, goods clearly destined for the US at the first sale, an arm's length price, and full factory documents.

First sale lets us declare the price the middleman paid the factory instead of what we paid the middleman. It works only if that first sale is a real sale, the goods are clearly meant for the US when sold, and the price is at arm's length. The weak point is usually paperwork: the middleman must share factory invoices, payment proof and the order chain. Without that, CBP will not accept it.
We buy from a related company abroad, and finance makes a year-end transfer pricing adjustment that raises the price. What happens on the customs side?
How you connect tax transfer pricing to customs value for related-party imports.
Sees that a higher price means more duty, plans with flagged Reconciliation entries or corrections, and can show CBP the price is at arm's length.

An upward adjustment raises the customs value, so we likely owe more duty on those entries. Ideally the entries were flagged for value under Reconciliation, so we report the final value once it is known. If not, we correct by post-summary correction or prior disclosure. I also check our pricing against CBP's related-party tests, since tax and customs judge arm's length differently.
Engineering says a new part is just a commercial item, but it was designed for a military customer. How do you decide between ITAR and the EAR?
Whether you can make a jurisdiction call that carries serious penalties if wrong.
Reviews the US Munitions List first, including the specially designed test, and asks DDTC for a commodity jurisdiction ruling when it is unclear.

I start with the US Munitions List: if the part is described there, it is under ITAR whatever engineering calls it. Military design work can make it specially designed, so I check that definition and its release criteria with engineering. If it is clearly off the list, it falls under the EAR and I find the ECCN. If it is still unclear, I ask DDTC for a commodity jurisdiction ruling and hold exports.

cybersecurity.heading: Cybersecurity questions
qs: How should an application store user passwords, and why not just encrypt them?
Whether you know the difference between hashing and encryption.
A slow, salted, one-way password hash such as Argon2 or bcrypt; encryption can be reversed by anyone who gets the key.

Passwords should go through a slow hashing function built for passwords, like Argon2 or bcrypt, with a unique random salt per user. Hashing is one-way, so at login we only compare hashes. Encryption is reversible: steal the database and the key, and you have every password. The salt stops cracking many accounts at once with precomputed tables.
How does SQL injection work, and what actually stops it?
Your grasp of a common web attack and its real fix.
User input gets read as part of the query; parameterized queries are the fix, not filtering characters.

It happens when an app builds a query by pasting user input into the SQL text, so input like a quote followed by OR 1=1 changes what the query does. The real fix is parameterized queries, where the database treats input only as data. Input checks and a low-privilege database account limit damage, but hand-escaping characters is not a fix I trust.
Walk me through threat modeling a new feature that lets customers upload files.
How you think like an attacker before the code ships.
A structured method: map the data flow, list what can go wrong at each step, for example with STRIDE, and tie each threat to a control.

I draw where the file goes: browser, upload service, storage, and whatever opens it later. Then I ask what can go wrong at each step. Someone uploads malware or a script disguised as an image, a huge file fills the disk, or a crafted filename writes outside the folder. My controls: check type by content, cap size, rename files, store them outside the web root and scan them.
You get an alert: one user signed in from Ohio and from overseas 40 minutes apart. What do you do?
How you triage an alert without overreacting or ignoring it.
Rule out benign causes such as a VPN fast, then treat signs of takeover seriously: revoke sessions, reset credentials, review what the account did.

First I check if it is real: does the overseas address belong to our VPN or a cloud provider, and did MFA succeed or get pushed again and again? If it looks like a takeover, I revoke active sessions, reset the password and confirm with the user by phone, not email. Then I review what the account touched: mailbox rules, file downloads, new MFA devices.
A scanner flags a critical flaw on a Linux server, but the admin says the package is already patched. How do you settle it?
Whether you verify findings instead of trusting the scanner or the admin blindly.
Checking evidence: distributions often backport fixes without changing the version number, so you read the advisory and compare package releases.

Scanners often go by version number, and Linux distributions often backport security fixes into an older version. So I look up the distribution's advisory for that CVE, see which package release fixes it, and compare it to what is installed. If it is fixed, I mark a false positive with that proof attached. If not, it goes back in the queue.
Why might you not want to wipe or shut down a compromised machine right away?
Whether you protect evidence while containing an incident.
Shutting down loses memory evidence; isolate the host from the network first and capture volatile data, unless damage is ongoing and cannot be stopped otherwise.

Memory holds things that vanish on shutdown: running processes, network connections, sometimes keys or injected code. Wiping also destroys the disk evidence that shows how they got in. So I usually cut the host off the network, capture memory and a disk image, then rebuild. If it is actively encrypting files and isolation fails, stopping the damage comes first.
Tell me about a time a security change you made broke something. What did you do?
How you own a mistake and fix the process behind it.
A quick rollback, honest communication, and a change to how such changes are tested or rolled out.

I pushed a firewall rule to block an old protocol and it cut off a payroll export that still used it. Within about 20 minutes I rolled it back and told the payroll lead what happened. Then we found every system using that protocol, moved them, and re-applied the block. Since then I run new blocking rules in log-only mode for a week first.
An actively exploited flaw hits an internet-facing system, and the business wants to wait two weeks for a launch. What do you do?
Your judgement when security and business goals collide.
No flat no and no silent yes: offer compensating controls, put the risk in writing, and have the system owner formally accept it.

I explain in plain terms what an attack would mean for them, not just the severity score. Then I offer options: patch in a short window this week, or add controls now, like a web application firewall rule blocking the exploit and extra monitoring. If they still wait, the system owner signs off on the risk with an end date. Their call, but on record.
After an intrusion, how do you know the attacker is really out of the network?
How deep your incident response goes beyond the obvious cleanup.
