Scoping and hunting for persistence before eviction, removing all footholds at once, resetting credentials broadly, then watching closely.

Before evicting them, I scope every host and account they touched and hunt for persistence: scheduled tasks, new services, new admin accounts, web shells. Then we remove them all at once, reset exposed credentials, and in Active Directory reset the KRBTGT password, the key behind all Kerberos tickets, twice. Then we watch closely for weeks.
What is the difference between OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, and why does it matter?
Whether you know which protocol proves who the user is and which only grants access.
OAuth grants an app access to an API; OpenID Connect adds an ID token saying who signed in. Using an access token as proof of login is a known flaw.

OAuth 2.0 is about authorization: it gives an app an access token to call an API for the user. It does not tell the app who the user is. OpenID Connect sits on top of OAuth and adds an ID token, a signed record of who signed in, which the app must validate: signature, issuer, audience and expiry. Treating an access token as login proof lets a token issued to another app be replayed.
Push-notification MFA is turned on everywhere. Why might that not be enough?
Your understanding of how attackers get past common MFA methods.
Push prompts and codes can be spammed or relayed by a fake site; FIDO2 keys and passkeys are tied to the real site's domain, so a phishing page gets nothing usable.

Attackers spam push prompts until a tired user taps approve, or run a fake login page that relays the password and code in real time. Number matching helps with the spam. Phishing-resistant methods like FIDO2 security keys or passkeys are better: the key signs a challenge bound to the real site's domain, so a look-alike domain gets nothing it can reuse. I would start with admins and remote access.
Before any incident happens, which logs do you make sure you have, and how do you keep them useful?
Whether you prepare the evidence an investigation will need.
Identity, endpoint, network edge, cloud audit and key app logs, stored centrally, time-synced, kept long enough and out of an attacker's reach.

I want sign-in and directory logs, endpoint detection data, firewall, VPN and DNS logs, cloud audit logs, and logs from apps that hold sensitive data. They go to a central system that the admins of the source servers cannot delete from. All clocks sync to the same time source so timelines line up. Retention is set by how long attackers often stay unseen, not by what storage is cheapest.
How do you set up backups that survive a ransomware attack?
How you protect the last line of recovery from an attacker with admin rights.
At least one immutable or offline copy, managed with separate credentials, plus regular restore tests with known recovery times.

Ransomware crews go after backups first, often with stolen domain admin rights. So I keep at least one copy immutable or offline, managed with separate accounts and MFA that are not tied to the main domain. I follow 3-2-1: three copies, two kinds of media, one offsite. And I run real restore tests, because the business needs to know how many days a full rebuild actually takes.
A developer's cloud access key turns up in a public code repository. What do you do, in order?
Your order of actions when a secret is exposed.
Disable the key first, then check audit logs for its use, then clean up. Deleting the commit alone fixes nothing, since public repos are scanned by bots.

First I deactivate the key. I don't start by deleting the commit, because bots scan public repos and often find keys within minutes. Then I check the cloud audit logs for every call made with that key since the push: new users, new keys, new servers, data reads. Anything an attacker created gets removed. Then the developer moves to short-lived role credentials, and we add secret scanning before commits.
A detection rule fires 400 times a day and almost every alert is a false positive. What do you do with it?
How you tune detections without creating blind spots.
Tune with data rather than mute: find what the noise has in common, narrow the rule tightly, and test that it still catches the real attack.

I would not just disable it; the rule exists for a reason. I pull a week of alerts and group them. Usually a few sources make most of the noise, like a backup server or an IT script. I exclude those narrowly, by host and process, not by whole subnet, and write down why. Then I replay a simulated attack to confirm the rule still fires, and track its true positive rate after.
Explain Kerberoasting and how you would defend against it.
Your depth on a common Active Directory attack path.
Any domain user can request service tickets encrypted with a key from a service account's password and crack them offline; strong managed passwords and monitoring stop it.

Any signed-in domain user can request a Kerberos service ticket for an account that runs a service. Part of the ticket is encrypted with a key made from that account's password, so the attacker cracks it offline, with no lockouts. I defend with managed service accounts that use long random passwords, AES instead of RC4, and alerts on odd ticket requests, like RC4 tickets in event 4769.
During an authorized penetration test, you find signs that a real attacker is already inside. What do you do?
Whether you know the limits of your authorization and when to escalate.
Pause, call the emergency contact in the rules of engagement right away, preserve evidence, and do not investigate or clean up beyond scope.

I stop testing in that area and call the emergency contact named in the rules of engagement right away, not in the final report. I write down exactly what I saw, with times and hosts, and I don't change or delete anything, because it is now evidence. I don't chase the attacker beyond my scope. The client decides whether the test pauses while their incident team takes over.
You learn that a package your build pipeline uses was replaced with a malicious version for two days. How do you work out the damage?
How you handle a software supply chain compromise.
Find the builds that pulled the bad version, treat build runners and their secrets as exposed, and trace what reached production.

I check lockfiles, build logs and the software bill of materials for every build in that window that pulled the bad version. Malicious packages often run code at install time, so any runner that installed it is suspect, along with every secret it could read: deploy keys, cloud tokens, signing keys. I rotate those, rebuild from a pinned safe version, and check what shipped to production or customers.
You find that a firewall change you made a week ago left remote desktop open to the internet. What do you do?
Your honesty and method when the security gap is your own mistake.
Close it, report it yourself at once, and check the logs for access during the exposure before calling it harmless; then fix the change process.

I close the rule first, then tell my lead and the incident team that same hour; hiding it would be worse than the mistake. Then I check the week: firewall connection logs, and successful and failed Windows sign-ins on the exposed hosts from outside addresses. If anything got in, it becomes an incident. Afterwards I add peer review and an automatic check for internet-exposed admin ports.

data-analyst.heading: Data analyst questions
qs: Walk me through how you check your numbers before a report goes out.
Whether you have a routine for catching your own errors before others do.
Concrete checks: totals against a trusted source, row counts through joins, filters and dates, and a sense check of whether the number is plausible.

I compare the total against a source I trust, like the finance system or last month's report. I check row counts before and after each join, look for nulls and duplicates in the keys, and confirm the date range and filters match the request. Then I ask if the number makes sense. If revenue doubled overnight, I assume a bug before a miracle.
Sales are up 30% in December compared with November. Is that good news?
Whether you account for seasonality before calling a change good or bad.
Not on its own: compare with the same period last year and check calendar effects and promotions before judging.

Not on its own. December is a peak month for many businesses, so I compare it with last December, year over year, and check that the number of weekend days and promotions line up. If December was up 40% over November last year, a 30% jump actually points to a weaker season.
A colleague reports the overall conversion rate as the average of the regional conversion rates. What is wrong with that?
Whether you know how to combine ratios correctly.
A simple average of rates ignores group size; the overall rate is total conversions divided by total visits, or a weighted average.

It gives a tiny region the same weight as a big one. If a region with 200 visits converts at 10% and one with 20,000 visits converts at 2%, the simple average says 6%. The true overall rate is 420 conversions out of 20,200 visits, about 2.1%. I divide totals by totals instead.
Two teams report different numbers of monthly active users. How do you settle it?
How you reconcile metric definitions across teams.
Finds the definition differences first, tests both on the same data, and ends with one written, agreed definition and an owner.

Usually the definitions differ, not the math. I write down each team's rule: what counts as active, which time zone, whether test accounts and bots are removed, and whether a person on two devices counts once. I run both rules on the same data, explain the gap, and get the owners to agree on one written definition for the dashboard.
After you join orders to another table, total revenue is suddenly twice what finance reports. What happened?
Whether you recognize a join that multiplies rows.
Spots a one-to-many join counting each order more than once, proves it with row counts and key checks, and fixes it by aggregating first.

Most likely the join fanned out. One order matched several rows on the other side, say one row per shipment, so its revenue was counted more than once. I compare row counts before and after the join and check that the key is unique where I expected. The fix is to sum the many side up to one row per order first, or join on the full key.
Marketing surveyed current customers and found 90% love the product. What would you warn them about?
Whether you can spot selection bias in how data was collected.
Only customers who stayed were asked, so unhappy ones who left are missing; the result describes current customers, not everyone.

Only people who stayed got the survey. Customers who left, maybe over price or a bug, are not in the sample, so the picture looks better than reality. I would label the result as what current customers think, and add an exit survey or look at what churned customers did before leaving to see the other side.
What is Simpson's paradox? Give an example of how it could fool a business.
Your grasp of how combining groups can reverse a trend.
A trend that holds in every group reverses when the groups are combined, usually because the group mix differs; the fix is to look at segments and the mix.

It is when a pattern holds inside every group but flips when you combine them. Say a new checkout converts better on both mobile and desktop, yet worse overall. That can happen if far more of its traffic came from mobile, which converts lower. The mix changed, not the checkout. I always break results down by the main segments before I trust a total.
Three days into a two-week A/B test, the result is significant and the product manager wants to stop and ship. What do you say?
Whether you understand the risk of stopping a test early when it looks good.
Explains that peeking and stopping at the first significant result inflates false positives; keeps the planned length or uses a sequential method set up in advance.

If we stop the first time the p-value dips under 0.05, our real false positive rate is much higher than 5%, because results swing a lot early on. I would run the test to the planned sample size and full weeks, to cover weekday patterns. If the team needs early reads next time, we can plan a sequential testing method before the test starts.
You split test results into 20 customer segments, and one shows a significant effect. How do you report it?
Whether you know the multiple comparisons problem.
With many tests, some will be significant by chance; treat it as a lead, adjust the threshold, and confirm with a new test.

With 20 tests at a 5% threshold, I would expect about one significant result by luck alone. So I report it as a lead, not a finding. I check whether that segment was named before the test, apply a correction like Bonferroni, which here means a threshold of 0.0025, and if it still looks real, I retest that segment on its own.
A director asks you to leave an unfavorable number out of a board presentation. How do you handle it?
Your integrity and how you push back on pressure to shade results.
Refuses to hide a number that changes the conclusion, offers a fair way to frame it, and escalates calmly if needed.

I would say I am glad to lead with the good news, but I cannot drop a number that changes the conclusion. If someone finds it later, we lose the decision and our credibility. I would offer to frame it well: the problem, its likely cause and the plan to fix it. If the director still insists, I would raise it with my own manager.
Conversion went from 4% to 5%. A slide says conversion rose 1%. Is that right?
Whether you keep relative change and percentage points apart.
It rose 1 percentage point, which is a 25% relative increase. The slide should name which one it means.

Not as written. The rate went up 1 percentage point, from 4 to 5. Relative to where it started, that is a 25% increase. Both are true, but "1%" is neither. I would write "up 1 point, from 4% to 5%" so nobody reads it as a tiny change or a huge one.
Someone adds up 30 days of daily active users and calls it monthly active users. What is wrong with that?
Whether you know which metrics can be added up and which cannot.
Distinct counts are not additive: a user active on many days is counted many times. Monthly users must be counted distinct over the whole month.

A person who opens the app every day gets counted 30 times. The sum is user-days, not users. To get monthly actives I count distinct user IDs across the 30-day window in one query. The same goes for weekly totals or adding unique visitors across regions when people appear in more than one.
Yesterday's revenue on your dashboard keeps rising for three days after the fact. How do you report it?
How you handle late-arriving data without misleading readers.
Find how long data takes to settle, mark recent days as provisional or hide them, and compare like with like.

I would first measure the lag: what share of a day's final revenue has arrived after one, two and three days. If it settles by day three, I mark the last three days as provisional on the chart. I also make sure nobody compares a partial day with complete ones, because that looks like a drop that is not real.
A customer moves from the West region to the East. Should last year's sales follow them to East?
Whether you understand how changing attributes affect historical reports.
Depends on the question. Usually past sales stay with the region at the time of sale, which means keeping the attribute history, not overwriting it.

For regional performance, no. West earned those sales, so they should stay there. That means the customer table needs history: the region with start and end dates, joined by order date. If we only keep the current region, every move silently rewrites last year's numbers. For questions about today's customer base, the current region can be fine.
The 20 worst stores last quarter got a coaching program, and this quarter they improved a lot. Did the coaching work?
Whether you spot regression to the mean.
Stores picked for a bad quarter tend to improve anyway. A fair test needs a comparison group of similar low stores without coaching.

Not proven. If you pick stores because they had their worst quarter, some of that was bad luck, and they tend to drift back toward their normal level on their own. I would compare them with similar low performers that were not coached, ideally chosen at random. If coached stores improved more than those, then I would credit the program.
Support agents are now judged on average time to close a ticket. What could go wrong?
Whether you think about how people react to a metric.
Once a number becomes a target, people can game it. Pair it with a counter-metric such as reopen rate or satisfaction.

Agents can close tickets fast without solving them, or close and reopen hard cases to reset the clock. The average then improves while customers suffer. I would track reopen rate and customer satisfaction next to it, and look at the full distribution, not just the average, so a few long tickets do not get rushed or hidden.
Your A/B test was set to split traffic 50/50, but the groups came out 52/48 on a million users. What do you do?
Whether you catch a sample ratio mismatch before trusting a test.
At that size the gap is far beyond chance. Stop reading results, test the split formally and find the cause first.

I would run a chi-square test on the counts. With a million users, a 52/48 split is almost impossible by chance. That usually means a bug: a redirect losing users, bots filtered in one arm, or events logged differently. Until I find the cause, I do not trust the lift, because the two groups may no longer be comparable.
A product manager wants to detect a 0.5% lift, but the page gets little traffic. How do you advise them?
Your grasp of statistical power and the trade-offs it forces.
Smaller effects need far more data; halving the effect roughly quadruples the sample. Offer real options instead of running an underpowered test.

I would run a power calculation. A tiny lift on low traffic could need months, and halving the effect you want to detect roughly quadruples the users needed. Options: test a bolder change, measure a more frequent metric earlier in the funnel, or accept that we can only detect larger effects. Running a short test and calling it "no effect" would be the worst choice.
A feature launched only in Texas, with no control group. How would you estimate its effect?
How you measure impact when you cannot randomize.
Compare Texas's change with the change in similar states over the same period, and check they moved together before launch.

I would use difference-in-differences. Take the change in Texas from before to after launch, and subtract the change in comparable states over the same weeks. That removes seasonality and company-wide shifts. It only holds if the states trended alike before launch, so I would plot the pre-period first and say clearly that it is an estimate, not a controlled test.
You find an error in a report that leadership already used for a decision. What do you do?
Your honesty and process when your own work was wrong.
Tell your manager quickly, size the impact, send a clear correction and fix the cause so it does not repeat.

Once I found I had double-counted refunds, so margin looked 3 points better than it was. I told my manager that day, reran the numbers and sent a short correction: what changed, by how much, and whether it affected the decision. Then I added a check that compares refunds with the finance total before any report goes out.

data-center.heading: Data center operations questions
qs: What is a hot aisle and cold aisle layout, and why do blanking panels matter?
Whether you understand how air moves through a data hall.
Racks face each other so server intakes share cool air, and panels stop hot exhaust from looping back to the front.

Rows of racks face front to front, so servers pull cool air from the cold aisle and blow hot air into the hot aisle behind. An empty slot is a hole: hot exhaust gets pulled back to the front and raises intake temperatures. A blanking panel closes that gap, so I put one in every time I remove a server.
How do you protect parts from static when you work inside a server?
Whether ESD protection is a habit for you.
A tested, grounded wrist strap, parts kept in anti-static bags, and handling by the edges.

I wear a wrist strap clipped to a ground point or the ESD mat, and I test the strap at the start of my shift. Parts stay in their anti-static bags until I install them, and I hold memory and cards by the edges. A failed part goes back into a bag, never loose on a floor tile.
A 70-pound server has to go near the top of a half-full rack. How do you do it?
How you handle heavy equipment without hurting yourself or tipping a rack.
Question the position first, check the rack's rating and anti-tip feet, mount rails first, and never lift it alone.

First I ask if it can go lower, since heavy gear belongs near the bottom. If the top is required, I check the rack's weight rating, put the stabilizer feet down and make sure no other server is pulled out on its rails. Rails go in first, then two of us lift it, or we use the server lift. I never lift that weight above my shoulders alone.
What do you do before you plug in a fiber patch cable?
Your fiber handling and eye safety.
Match the fiber type to the optic, inspect and clean both ends, and never look into a fiber end.

I check that the cable matches the optic: single-mode or multimode, and the right connector, usually LC. Then I inspect both ends with a fiber scope, clean them with a click cleaner or a lint-free wipe, and inspect again. Dirt is the most common cause of a bad link. I never look into a fiber end, because the laser light can be invisible.
A ticket says to replace a failed drive in a RAID 5 array. Walk me through it.
Whether you verify before you pull and understand what is at risk during a rebuild.
Confirm the array is degraded, not failed, and identify the exact drive by bay, serial and locator LED before pulling.

First I check the RAID controller: one drive failed, the array is degraded but still online. I match the bay and serial number to the ticket and turn on the locator LED. If it is hot-swap, I pull only that drive, insert the new one and watch the rebuild start. In RAID 5 a second failure before the rebuild finishes loses data, so pulling the wrong drive is the real danger.
A server will not boot after a memory upgrade. How do you find the cause?
Your hardware diagnostic method.
Start from what changed, read the management controller's log, check slot population rules, then isolate step by step.

I start with what changed: the memory. I read the event log in the management controller, the small built-in computer that monitors the server; it often names the failing slot. I confirm the modules are a supported type and sit in the slots the vendor's guide gives. I reseat them, and if it still fails I boot on the old memory and add new modules back a few at a time.
A server has two power supplies. How do you plug it in, and what do you check on the circuits?
Whether you understand redundant power and how a failover can overload a circuit.
One supply on the A feed and one on B, with total load small enough that one feed can carry it all if the other fails.

One power supply goes to the A-side PDU and the other to the B-side, which come from separate power paths. Then I check the load. If A drops, B suddenly carries everything, so the combined load of both sides must fit on one circuit within its continuous limit, normally 80% of the breaker rating. Adding one more server can quietly break that.
A customer asks you to power-cycle the server in rack 12, slot 20, but the label there shows a different hostname. What do you do?
Your judgement when the instructions and the hardware disagree.
Stop, touch nothing, verify with the customer by serial or locator light, and record the mismatch.

I stop and do not touch it. I take a photo of the label and the slot, contact the customer and ask them to confirm by serial number or by turning on the locator light remotely. A power cycle on the wrong box can take down someone's database. I also note the label mismatch in the ticket so the records get fixed.
You pulled a cable and then realize it was the wrong one. What do you do in the next few minutes?
How honestly and quickly you handle your own mistake.
Put it back if you are sure where it goes, tell the operations center at once, and write it up honestly.

If I am sure where it came from, I plug it back in right away. Then I call the network operations center, the team that watches the systems, and give them the port and the exact time so they can check what went down. I do not wait to see if anyone notices. Afterward I write it up and look at why the labels let me make that mistake.
A vendor wants a failed drive back for a warranty credit, but the drive held customer data. What do you do?
Whether you put data security and chain of custody ahead of convenience.
Follow the data-handling policy: the drive stays in custody and is wiped or destroyed by the approved method.

The drive stays with us unless policy says it may leave. Many sites buy a keep-your-drive option from the vendor for this reason. I log the serial number, lock the drive in the secure bin and track it until it is wiped or shredded by the approved method, with a certificate. A small warranty credit is not worth a data breach.
How do you tell single-mode from multimode fiber on the floor, and why does mixing them matter?
Whether you know the cable plant well enough to avoid a link that never comes up.
Jacket color and print as clues, the optic's label as proof, and an understanding that the fiber and both optics must match.

By the usual color code, single-mode jackets are yellow, and multimode is aqua for OM3 and OM4 and lime for OM5. Colors can lie on old runs, so I also read the print on the jacket and the label on each optic. A single-mode optic on multimode fiber, or the reverse, gives a dead or flaky link. The cable, the patch panel and both optics must match.
What is out-of-band management, and when would you use it instead of walking to the server?
How you use the server's management controller to work faster and with less risk.
Knows the controller has its own network port and works while the server is off, and uses it for console, logs and power before touching hardware.

Most servers have a baseboard management controller, a small computer on the board with its own network port. It keeps working while the server is powered off, as long as the power cords are in. Through it I can see the console, read the hardware event log, check sensors and power-cycle. I check it first, so I walk to the rack already knowing which part failed.
Someone in a vendor shirt walks up behind you at a badge door and asks you to hold it. What do you do?
Whether you keep physical security even when it feels rude.
Politely refuses, sends the person to the security desk, and calls security if they push.

I do not let them in, however friendly they are. I say every person badges in on their own and point them to the security desk, where visits are checked against a ticket. If they argue or try to follow me, I keep the door shut and call security. A shirt and a toolbag are not access. Many break-ins start with someone simply being polite.
One rack keeps throwing high inlet temperature alarms, but the room readings look normal. What do you check?
How you track down a hot spot instead of just making the whole room colder.
Measures at the server intakes, then looks for hot exhaust getting back to the front or cold air not arriving.

I measure at the front of the servers, at the top, middle and bottom, since the room sensor may be far away. Then I look for hot air coming back around: open rack spaces, gaps at the sides, a missing seal. On a raised floor I check that the perforated tile in front is in place and not blocked by boxes or cables. If the rack's load grew, I tell facilities.
On a walk-through you see both the A and B power strips of a rack at 60% of their breaker rating. Is that fine?
Whether you understand that redundant power only works if one side can carry the whole load.
No: if one feed fails, the other jumps to about 120% and trips. The combined load must fit safely on one circuit.

No, it only looks fine. The servers split their load across both supplies, so if feed A drops, feed B picks up everything, about 120% of its rating, and the breaker trips. Then the whole rack goes dark. The combined load has to fit on one circuit, under the 80% continuous-load limit most sites follow. I would open a ticket, stop new installs there and plan to move load.
Walk me through bringing a new rack of 20 servers from the loading dock to production-ready.
Whether you can run a full install and leave records that others can trust later.
Inventory against the order, racking to the elevation plan, labels and records updated, power watched, and tests before handover.

I check every box against the packing list and record serial numbers before anything is racked. I mount to the rack elevation drawing, heaviest at the bottom, and label both ends of every cable. I power up a few servers at a time and watch the circuit load. Then I update the asset records, run hardware diagnostics, and hand over serials, ports and any parts replaced.
A fiber link is up, but the switch shows a growing count of CRC errors. Walk me through how you fix it.
How you troubleshoot a dirty or weak optical link step by step.
Reads the optic light levels first, inspects and cleans every connector, then swaps one part at a time to isolate the fault.

First I read the optic diagnostics on both ends: receive power near the low limit points to loss in the path. I inspect each connector with a scope, clean it and inspect again, patch panel ports included. Then I look for a tight bend or a crushed cable. If errors continue, I swap the patch cable, then one optic, then the other, and watch the counter after each change.
A server reboots on its own every few days and the operating system logs show nothing. How do you find the cause?
Your method for an intermittent hardware fault that will not show itself on demand.
Reads the hardware event log, looks for a pattern, changes one part at a time, and proves the fix under load.

I start with the hardware event log in the management controller and line up its timestamps with the reboots. Rising memory errors on one DIMM, a power supply dropping out or a thermal trip each point somewhere different. I check the firmware is current, then swap one suspect part at a time, never three at once. Before I close the ticket I run a stress test for at least a day.
A breaker feeding a rack has tripped and the customer wants you to flip it back on right now. What do you do?
Your judgement when pressure to restore service meets an electrical safety risk.
No blind reset: a trip means overload or a fault. Follows site procedure, brings in facilities or electricians, and finds the cause first.

A breaker trips for a reason, an overload or a fault, and resetting it into a short can cause an arc or a bigger outage. I tell the customer I am on it and call our facilities team, as our site procedure says. While they come, I check the power readings before the trip and whether new gear was added. Power comes back only once the cause is known, a few servers at a time.
The pre-discharge alarm of the clean agent fire suppression system sounds while you are mid-install in the data hall. What do you do?
Whether you know the life-safety steps for a gas suppression system and follow them without hesitation.
Stops work and leaves at once, does not go back in until cleared, and uses an abort switch only if trained and the site procedure allows it.

I drop the work and leave by the nearest exit, taking anyone near me along. The delay before the gas releases is for getting out, not for saving a server. At the meeting point I tell the person in charge where I was working. I use an abort switch only if I am trained on it and the site procedure allows it, and nobody goes back in until the room is cleared.

data-engineer.heading: Data engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between ETL and ELT, and when would you pick each?
Whether you know the two basic ways to move data into a warehouse.
The order of the steps explained clearly, plus a real reason to choose each one, such as masking data before it lands.

In ETL I transform the data before loading it into the warehouse. In ELT I load the raw data first and transform it inside the warehouse with SQL. I usually pick ELT because cloud warehouses scale well and keeping raw data lets me rebuild models. I pick ETL when data must be cleaned or masked before it lands, like personal data that should never be stored raw.
What is a star schema, and what goes in a fact table versus a dimension table?
Your grasp of the most common way to model data for analysts.
Facts are measured events at a stated grain, dimensions describe them, and the grain is decided first.

A fact table holds events or measurements, for example one row per order line, with numbers like quantity and price and keys to the dimensions. Dimension tables describe the who, what, where and when: customer, product, store, date. Analysts filter and group by dimension columns and sum the facts. I always write down the grain of the fact table before anything else.
Why store large analytics tables in a columnar file format instead of CSV?
Whether you understand how storage choices affect query speed and cost.
Queries read only the needed columns, compression is better, and the schema and types travel with the file.

Analytics queries usually read a few columns across many rows. A columnar format stores each column together, so the engine reads only the columns it needs and compresses them well because similar values sit side by side. It also keeps the schema and data types, which CSV does not. CSV is fine for a small file sent to a person, not for a big table queried every day.
A customer moves to a new city. How do you keep their address history so old orders still show the old address?
Whether you can model data that changes over time.
A Type 2 slowly changing dimension: close the old row, add a new one with dates and a surrogate key, never overwrite.

That is a Type 2 slowly changing dimension. I do not overwrite the row. I close the old row by setting its end date and setting its current flag to false, then insert a new row with a new surrogate key, a start date and the current flag true. Facts store the surrogate key that was valid at the time, so old orders keep the old address.
What does it mean for a pipeline to be idempotent, and how do you build one?
Whether your pipelines survive retries and reruns without corrupting data.
Running a job twice gives the same result; loads replace a partition or merge on a key, and the run date is a parameter.

It means running the same job twice for the same period gives the same result, not double the rows. Jobs fail and get retried, and backfills rerun old dates, so this matters all the time. I make loads replace a date partition or merge on a business key instead of appending, and I pass the run date in as a parameter instead of reading the current time.
How do you load a large source table incrementally, and how do you handle records that arrive late?
How you move only new data without losing or duplicating rows.
A watermark on a change timestamp, a lookback window for late rows, a merge on the key, and a plan for deletes.

I keep a watermark, the highest updated_at value I loaded, and on the next run I pull rows changed since then. Because records can arrive late, I go back a safety window, say three days, and merge on the primary key so rows already loaded are updated, not duplicated. Deletes need care: I ask the source for a deleted flag or read its change data capture log.
Which data quality checks do you put on a pipeline, and what happens when one fails?
Whether you catch bad data before analysts do.
Concrete checks on freshness, volume, keys and values, and a clear split between checks that block a load and checks that only alert.

Freshness: did data arrive on time. Volume: is the row count in a normal range. Keys: no nulls or duplicates in the primary key, and foreign keys find a match. Values: amounts not negative, dates not in the future. A failed key check stops the load before analysts see bad data; an odd volume alerts the owner but lets the data through.
The source team renamed a column without telling you, and the nightly job failed. Walk me through what you do.
How you handle a broken pipeline and prevent the same break next time.
Users told first, a fix that shields downstream tables, a rerun with checks, then an agreement and an early schema check.

First I tell the users of the table that today's data is late and when I expect it. Then I confirm the rename in the source and map the new name in our staging layer, so downstream tables keep the old name. I rerun the failed date and check row counts. Afterwards I agree with the source team on notice before schema changes and add a check that fails early with a clear message.
You discover the revenue table has held duplicate orders for the past week. What do you do?
Your judgement when bad data has already reached the business.
Warn the affected users at once, find the root cause, fix and backfill, reconcile with the source, and add a test.

I tell finance and the dashboard owners right away which dates and reports are affected, so nobody shares wrong revenue. Then I find the cause, for example a retried job that appended instead of replacing. I fix the job, dedupe on order ID, rebuild the week and compare totals with the source system. Last, I add a uniqueness test on order ID so it cannot happen silently again.
Your streaming system delivers events at least once. How do you keep counts and totals correct?
Whether you understand delivery guarantees in streaming and how to design around them.
Duplicates are expected after failures; a unique event ID plus an idempotent write or a dedupe step keeps results exact.

At-least-once means that after a failure some events are delivered again, so a plain count can come out too high. I make sure every event carries a unique ID set by the producer, and I make the sink idempotent: an upsert on that ID, or a dedupe on it within a time window before aggregating. Then a replay overwrites the same rows instead of adding new ones.
What is the grain of a fact table, and what goes wrong when you mix grains?
Whether you understand modeling well enough to prevent double counting.
A clear definition of grain and a concrete case of a number repeating across finer rows, with a fix.

Grain is what one row stands for, for example one row per order line. Trouble starts when a number at a coarser grain sits on finer rows. If I join order-level shipping fees onto order lines, an order with three lines shows its fee three times and the total is triple. I either keep shipping in an order-level fact table or split the fee across lines with a stated rule.
How do you choose a partition key for a large event table?
Your sense of physical table design and how it affects query cost.
Partition by how people filter, usually date, and avoid high-cardinality keys that create many tiny files.

I start with how people filter. For event data that is almost always the event date, so a query for last week reads seven partitions, not the whole table. I avoid a key like user ID: millions of partitions mean millions of tiny files and slow planning. I also check file sizes and compact small files so each one is in the hundreds of megabytes.
Two dashboards show different revenue for the same month. How do you find out why?
How you trace a number through the pipeline and settle metric definitions.
Tracing one record through both paths, naming typical causes, and ending with one shared definition.

I take one order and trace it through both. Usually the definitions differ: one counts gross sales, the other subtracts refunds; one groups by order date, the other by payment date; one uses UTC, the other local time. Once I find it, I agree one definition with finance, build it in one shared model, and point both dashboards at it.
A team asks for real-time data. How do you decide between batch and streaming?
Whether you match freshness to the business need instead of to the request.
Asking what decision the data drives and how fast, and weighing the higher cost and harder fixes of streaming.

I ask what decision the data feeds and how fast someone acts on it. A fraud check that blocks a payment needs seconds, so that is streaming. A sales dashboard read each morning does not. Streaming costs more to run and is harder to fix and rerun, so I often find a batch every fifteen minutes covers what people mean by real time.
How would you capture changes from a busy production database without slowing it down?
Your knowledge of change data capture and its trade-offs.
Log-based capture over repeated full queries, an initial snapshot, and knowing an updated_at column misses deleted rows.

I would not run big SELECTs on the primary every hour. I prefer log-based change capture: a connector reads the database's transaction log and emits every insert, update and delete, with little extra load. I take one snapshot first, then apply changes in order. If logs are not available, I query an updated_at column on a read replica, knowing that misses hard deletes.
A distributed join has run for hours, and one task is stuck while all the others finished. What is going on?
Whether you recognize data skew and know the standard fixes.
Naming skew, checking key counts, and fixes like handling NULL keys, broadcasting a small table, or salting.

That is almost always skew: one join key has far more rows than the others, so one task does most of the work. I check the key counts. Often it is NULL or a default ID like 0, and I filter or handle those separately. If one side is small, I broadcast it so nothing is shuffled. For a truly hot key I add a random salt to spread it across tasks.
You changed the logic of a core table and need to rebuild two years of history. How do you do it safely?
How you plan a large backfill without breaking daily loads or surprising users.
Rerunnable partition-by-partition loads into a new table, limited parallelism, reconciliation, and a planned switch.

I write the new logic so it rebuilds one date partition at a time and overwrites it, so a rerun is safe. I run it into a new table, a month at a time, with a cap on parallel jobs so the nightly loads still finish. Then I compare row counts and totals per month with the old table, explain each gap, and swap only after consumers know the numbers change.
Your warehouse bill doubled this month. Walk me through how you find the cause.
Your habit of treating cost as something an engineer measures and owns.
Starting from query history ranked by cost, naming common culprits, fixing the largest first, then adding alerts.

I open the warehouse's query history and rank cost by user, job and table, this month against last. Usually one thing stands out: a dashboard refreshing every few minutes, a new job scanning a whole table because it lacks a date filter, or compute left running all weekend. I fix the worst first, then add budget alerts and a named owner for each big job.
A customer asks the company to delete their personal data. How do you design the platform so that is possible?
Whether you build privacy into the data model rather than patching it later.
Personal data kept in few places by design, deletion that reaches raw files and backups, and a record that it was done.

Several US state laws, California's among them, give people a right to request deletion, with exceptions. I keep names, emails and addresses in a few tables keyed by an internal ID, and events carry only that ID. A request then removes or masks those rows and rewrites the affected raw files. Backups age out on a set schedule, and I log each request and when it was done.
Tell me about a change you made that broke something downstream. What did you change in how you work?
How you own a mistake and turn it into a lasting safeguard.
An honest story with the real impact, and specific process changes such as lineage checks, notice, and before-and-after tests.

I added a filter to drop canceled orders from a sales table. It was right for finance, but a churn model read the same table and its scores shifted for a week before anyone noticed. Since then I check lineage to see who reads a table, announce changes in advance, and compare row counts and totals against production before I merge.

data-governance.heading: Data governance and quality questions
qs: What is the difference between a data owner and a data steward?
Whether you know the basic roles a governance program runs on.
The owner is accountable and decides; the steward does the daily care. A strong answer also places IT as the custodian.

The data owner is a business leader accountable for a domain, like customer data. They approve access and set the quality bar. The steward works day to day: keeps definitions current, reviews quality reports and routes issues. IT is the custodian that runs the systems where the data lives.
How do a business glossary, a data dictionary and a data catalog differ?
Whether you can separate the core tools of the trade.
Glossary defines business terms, dictionary describes technical fields, catalog is the searchable inventory that links the two.

The glossary says what a business term means, like what counts as a customer. The dictionary describes fields in a system: name, type, allowed values. The catalog is the searchable inventory of data assets that links each column to its glossary term, owner and lineage.
What are the main dimensions of data quality, and how would you measure one of them?
Your grasp of data quality as something you can measure, not a feeling.
Names the common dimensions and turns one into a metric with a threshold agreed with the owner.

The usual ones are completeness, accuracy, validity, consistency, timeliness and uniqueness. For completeness, I would count the share of customer rows with a required field filled, like email. I track it daily and alert when it drops below a threshold the owner agreed to, say 98%.
What should a catalog entry for a table contain so that people actually use it?
Whether you build a catalog for its users, not just to fill it.
Plain description, owner and contact, definitions, sensitivity, freshness, quality status and how to get access.

A plain sentence on what the table holds and what it is good for. The owner and steward to contact. Column definitions linked to the glossary. A sensitivity label, refresh schedule, quality score and lineage. And a clear button or link for requesting access, or people go back to asking in chat.
Why does data lineage matter? Give an example of using it.
How you use lineage for impact analysis and root cause.
Lineage shows where data comes from and where it goes, so you can predict what a change breaks and trace errors back.

Lineage maps data from source through each transformation to reports. Once an engineer wanted to rename a revenue column. Lineage showed 12 dashboards and a finance extract depended on it. We warned the owners, planned the switch together and nothing broke on the release day.
How do you decide who gets access to a dataset with personal information?
Whether you apply least privilege and protect personal data in practice.
Minimum access by role and purpose, owner approval, masking where identity is not needed, and regular reviews.

I start from least privilege: people get only what their role needs. Requests name a purpose and the data owner approves. If analysts do not need identities, they get a view with names and emails masked. Access is reviewed on a schedule, and people who leave or change roles lose it.
Two departments report different numbers for active customers. How do you resolve it?
How you settle a conflicting business definition.
Find both definitions, show why they differ, get owners to agree on one certified term, name any variant clearly.

I collect both definitions and trace each number. Often one counts 30 days of activity and the other 90, or one includes trials. I bring both owners together with the facts. We agree on one certified definition in the glossary, and any other version gets its own clear name.
Six months after you launch a data quality program, nobody looks at the dashboards. What went wrong, and what do you do?
How you own a governance failure and make the work useful to the business.
Admits the program measured what was easy, not what mattered, and ties fixes to business pain and named owners.

Likely we tracked hundreds of rules nobody cared about, with no owner for each. I would ask owners which errors cost them money or time, cut the dashboard to those, and assign each rule a person. Alerts would go to that owner directly, and I would report fixes in business terms.
How do you choose which data elements to treat as critical?
How you focus effort where bad data does the most harm.
Ties critical fields to regulatory reports, money and key decisions, and keeps the list short enough to really monitor.

I start from the outputs that hurt most when wrong: regulatory filings, financial reporting, billing and the few metrics leadership runs on. I trace back to the fields that feed them, like customer ID, account status and amount. Each one gets an owner, a definition and quality rules. I would rather monitor 40 fields well than 400 on paper.
What is the difference between role-based and attribute-based access control, and when would you use each?
Your grasp of access models beyond simple permission lists.
Roles grant access by job; attributes are checked at request time. Roles for broad access, attribute rules for fine-grained cases like region or sensitivity tags.

With role-based control, a person gets access because they hold a role, say finance analyst. Attribute-based control checks attributes when the request is made: the user's department, the data's sensitivity tag, the region. Roles are easy to audit but multiply fast. I use roles as the base and attribute rules for things like masking columns tagged as personal.
What is the difference between pseudonymized and anonymized data, and why does it matter for governance?
Whether you know when data still counts as personal data.
Pseudonymized data can be linked back with a key or other fields, so it keeps personal-data controls; anonymization must be tested against re-identification.

Pseudonymized means names or IDs are replaced with tokens, but someone with the key, or enough other fields, can link records back to a person. So it keeps personal-data controls. Anonymized means no reasonable way to re-identify, which is harder than it sounds: ZIP code, birth date and sex together can single out many people. I treat “anonymous” as a claim to test.
If we handle patient data, what are the two ways HIPAA allows health data to be de-identified?
Your knowledge of a US rule that shapes how health data can be shared.
Names Safe Harbor (remove the listed identifiers, no actual knowledge of identifiability) and Expert Determination (a qualified expert finds the risk very small).

Safe Harbor means removing the 18 kinds of identifiers the rule lists, such as names, all date elements except the year, and small geographic units, and having no actual knowledge the rest could identify someone. Expert Determination means a qualified expert applies statistical methods and documents that the re-identification risk is very small. The expert route can keep more useful detail.
Walk me through how you would build a golden record for customers who appear in several systems.
Your practical knowledge of master data management.
Standardization, match rules for duplicates, survivorship rules per field, and a steward queue for uncertain matches instead of blind merging.

First I standardize names, addresses and phones. Match rules then find likely duplicates: exact on email or tax ID, fuzzy on name plus address. Survivorship rules pick each field's value: billing wins for address, most recent wins for phone. Low-confidence matches go to a steward queue, not an auto-merge, because a wrong merge is harder to undo than a missed one.
What is a data contract, and what would you put in one?
Whether you can make quality the producer's job, not only the consumer's.
An agreement between producer and consumers on schema, meaning, quality and change process, enforced in the pipeline rather than kept as a document.

It is an agreement between the team that produces a dataset and the teams that use it. Mine covers schema and data types, the meaning of key fields, checks like no null order IDs, freshness, an owner, and how changes are announced, for example 30 days notice before a column is removed. It only works if the checks run in the pipeline and fail the build when broken.
Would you run governance centrally or federated across business domains? What would you keep central?
How you design a governance operating model that scales.
Usually federated with central standards: policy, classification, tooling and shared terms central; ownership and stewardship in the domains.

In most companies I pick a federated model. The center sets policy, the classification scheme, the catalog and the quality tooling, and owns company-wide terms like customer and revenue. Each domain names its own owners and stewards and writes its rules within those standards. Fully central becomes a bottleneck; fully local gives you five definitions of customer.
A quality rule fails on the nightly load: 3% of orders have no customer ID. Do you stop the pipeline or let it run?
Your judgement on blocking data versus letting it flow with a known defect.
Decides by impact and severity agreed in advance, quarantines bad rows where possible, alerts users and fixes the problem at the source.

It depends on the severity we agreed for that rule. If finance reports revenue by customer from this table, I would move the 3% to a quarantine table, load the rest, and flag the gap on the dashboard. The source owner gets a ticket with sample rows. A full stop is for failures that make every number wrong, like a load that ran twice.
The business wants to change the definition of a governed metric, such as active customer, that many reports already use. How do you handle it?
How you manage change to shared definitions without breaking trust.
Treats it as a release: owner approval, parallel run, versioned definition with an effective date, lineage to find users, and clear handling of history.

I treat it like a release. The owner approves the new definition, and we run old and new side by side for a while so people see the gap, say 4% fewer active customers. The glossary keeps both versions with an effective date, lineage shows which reports use it, and their owners get notice. Past figures are restated or clearly marked, never silently changed.
A scan finds Social Security numbers in a table classified as internal and open to 400 analysts. What do you do?
How you handle a real exposure of sensitive data.
Contains first, brings in security, privacy and legal, reviews access logs, then fixes the source, reclassifies and improves detection.

First I restrict the table or mask the column right away; the explanation can wait, the exposure cannot. I bring in security and privacy, since whether it is reportable is their call with legal, and pull access logs to see who queried it. Then I find how the field got there, fix the source, reclassify the table and add the pattern to our scanner.

data-leader.heading: Head of data and analytics questions
qs: Would you run the data team centrally or embed analysts in the business units?
How you think about team structure and its trade-offs.
Knows both sides and often picks a hybrid: shared standards and platform at the center, analysts close to the teams they serve.

A central team keeps standards and definitions consistent, but it can feel far from the business. Embedded analysts know their area well but drift into their own versions of the truth. I usually run a hub and spoke: analysts sit with product or sales day to day, but report to data, share one platform and go through the same code review.
When would you buy a data tool instead of having your team build it?
How you weigh build versus buy for the data stack.
Buys common pieces like data ingestion, builds where the company has an edge, and counts upkeep and staff time, not only the license price.

If the work is the same at every company, like copying data from common apps into the warehouse, I buy; my engineers' time costs more than the license, and upkeep never ends. I build where our logic is unique, like our pricing models. Before deciding I compare total cost over three years, including who maintains it when the builder leaves.
The CFO and the head of sales bring two different revenue numbers to the same meeting. What do you do?
How you settle conflicting metric definitions.
Finds the difference in definitions, gets one owner to sign off on the official one, and builds it once in a shared, governed place.

First I find out why they differ; it is usually definitions, like booked versus recognized revenue, or how refunds are timed. Often both numbers are right for their purpose. I write each definition down, have the CFO own the official one, give the other a different name, and build both once in the shared model so every dashboard pulls from there.
An analyst asks for full access to customer tables, including names and emails, to speed up their work. How do you respond?
Your judgement on privacy and access to personal data.
Least privilege: give what the task needs, mask identifiers, log access, and know that privacy laws and contracts limit use.

Most analysis does not need names or emails, so I would give access to a version where those are masked or replaced with an ID. If a task truly needs them, access is approved for that purpose, time-limited and logged. State privacy laws and our customer contracts limit how we use personal data, and the fewer people who see it, the smaller any breach.
A product team checks its A/B test every day and wants to stop it the first day it looks significant. What do you tell them?
Whether you understand experiment discipline well enough to set rules for other teams.
Stopping at the first significant look raises the false positive rate; fix sample size and run time up front, or use a method built for monitoring.

Each extra look is another chance for noise to cross the line, so stopping on the first good day makes false wins far more likely than the error rate they planned for. I ask them to set the sample size and run time before launch, usually whole weeks to cover weekday patterns. If they truly need to watch daily, we use a sequential test designed for that.
Your cloud data warehouse bill has doubled in three months. Walk me through what you do.
How you manage platform cost without slowing the business.
Finds what drives cost by job, user and dashboard, fixes the worst offenders, and sets budgets and alerts so the next jump is seen early.

I pull usage by job, user and dashboard; usually a handful cause most of the spend. Common culprits are a dashboard refreshing every five minutes that nobody opens, full table rebuilds that could be incremental, and oversized compute left running. We fix those first, then set budgets and alerts per team so the next jump shows up in a week, not a quarter.
A dashboard your team built showed the board a wrong number last quarter. How do you handle it?
How you own a data error and stop it from happening again.
Tells leaders quickly with the corrected figure, finds the root cause, and adds a test or sign-off that would have caught it.

I would tell the CEO and CFO the same day, with the right number and what it changes. Then we trace the cause; in one case I had, a source system started sending duplicate orders after an update. We fixed the model, added a uniqueness test and a row-count alert, and I put a sign-off step on any figure that goes to the board.
The CEO wants an AI project this year. How do you decide what, if anything, to build?
Whether you tie machine learning and AI work to business value and data readiness.
Starts from a business problem with a measurable outcome, checks the data and a simple baseline first, and pilots small before committing.

I ask which decision or task we want to improve and how we would measure success, like fewer hours spent on support tickets. Then I check whether we have the data, and what a simple rule or existing tool already achieves. If a pilot beats that baseline on a small slice, we scale it. If not, I would rather say so than ship a demo nobody uses.
You join and find 400 dashboards, low trust in the numbers and a long request backlog. What do you do in your first 90 days?
How you diagnose a data function and set a plan for your first quarter.
Listens first, restores trust in a few core metrics, cuts unused work, and shows an early win before any big rebuild.

The first month I talk with leaders about the decisions they make and check usage logs; often most dashboards are barely opened. I pick the five to ten metrics leadership runs on and make them correct, tested and documented. We retire unused dashboards and set up an intake process. By day 90 I want one trusted weekly report and a roadmap agreed with the exec team.
What makes a good north star metric for a company, and what makes a bad one?
Whether you can pick a company metric that tracks real customer value.
A metric tied to value customers get and to future revenue, that teams can move, with guardrail metrics beside it so it is not chased at any cost.

A good one measures value delivered, like weekly active teams sharing files in a collaboration tool, and leads revenue instead of lagging it. A bad one is a vanity count, like total signups ever, which only goes up. I always pair it with two or three guardrails, such as churn and support tickets, so nobody wins the main number by hurting customers.
In a data governance model, what is the difference between a data owner and a data steward?
Your grasp of who is accountable for data in a governance model.
The owner is a business leader accountable for a data domain; the steward handles definitions and quality day to day. Ownership sits with the business, not the data team.

The owner is the senior person accountable for a domain, for example the VP of finance for revenue data. They decide who may use it and sign off on definitions. The steward does the daily work: keeps definitions in the catalog, triages quality issues and answers questions. My team runs the platform, but we should not own the sales data.
Conversion went up in every marketing channel last quarter, but overall conversion went down. The CEO asks which number is lying. What do you say?
Whether you can explain a mix effect to an executive in plain words.
Neither is wrong: traffic shifted toward lower-converting channels. This is Simpson's paradox, and you show the mix change next to the rates.

Neither is lying. Each channel improved, but more of our traffic came from paid social, which converts much lower than search, so the blended rate fell. I would show one chart of rates by channel and one of traffic share. The real question is whether we chose that shift in spend, and whether the cheaper traffic still pays back.
Product engineers keep renaming columns and breaking your pipelines. How do you fix this for good?
How you set data quality expectations with the teams that produce the data.
An agreed contract on schema and meaning, checks in the producers' release process, and named owners, rather than constant firefighting by your own engineers.

I would agree a data contract with the product teams for the few tables that matter most: field names, types, meaning and how fresh the data must be. Then we add an automated check to their release process so a breaking change fails before it ships, not in our dashboards. Each contract has an owner on both sides, and we review breaks monthly.
Marketing ran a national TV campaign with no holdout and asks you to prove it worked. What do you do?
How you estimate impact when there was no controlled experiment.
A quasi-experimental method, such as comparing against a forecast or against regions with less exposure, with the uncertainty stated, and a holdout planned next time.

Without a holdout I cannot prove it, but I can estimate it. I would forecast sales from the past two years and compare actual results against that, and check whether regions with heavier airtime moved more than lighter ones. I would give a range, not one number, and agree that the next campaign keeps a few markets without ads as a control.
Support agents got a bonus for lower average handle time. It dropped 25%, but customer satisfaction fell. What went wrong and what do you change?
Whether you know how targets distort the metrics they are tied to.
Goodhart's law: once a measure becomes a target, people optimize the measure. Pair it with outcome metrics and check what changed in behavior.

Once a number pays a bonus, people move the number, and the fastest way to cut handle time is to rush or transfer calls. I would check repeat contacts and transfers to confirm it. Then I would suggest the bonus rest on resolution and satisfaction, with handle time watched as a cost metric, and test any new target on one team first.
A California customer asks the company to delete their personal data, and your warehouse copies it into dozens of tables and extracts. How do you make sure it is really deleted?
How you build privacy rights into the data platform, not just the policy.
Know where personal data lives through a catalog and lineage, delete or de-identify it everywhere by one key, log it, and let legal rule on exceptions and backups.

It only works if we know where personal data flows. I tag personal fields in our catalog and use lineage to find every downstream copy. The request feeds an automated job keyed on the customer ID that deletes or de-identifies the rows in each table and writes a log. Legal decides exceptions, such as records we must keep, and how backups are handled.
Your budget is cut by a third next year. What do you cut first, and what do you protect?
Your judgement about which data work truly earns its cost.
Cuts based on usage and business value, not on what is newest; protect core pipelines and the metrics leaders run the company on, and say clearly what will stop.

First I cut what nobody uses: dashboards with no views in 90 days, unused tool seats and idle warehouse jobs. Then projects with no named business owner. I protect core pipelines, finance and revenue reporting, and the quality checks. I also publish a short list of requests we will stop taking, so leaders hear it from me, not from a missed deadline.
The head of sales asks you to adjust the forecast model so next quarter lands on the plan number for the board. What do you do?
Whether you keep the numbers honest under pressure from senior people.
The model is not bent to fit a target. You show the gap, what drives it and what could close it, and escalate if the pressure continues.

I would say no to changing the model and offer something more useful: a clear view of the gap. For example, the forecast is 8% under plan, mostly from slower renewals in one region. Sales can present that gap with a plan to close it. If the pressure continued, I would take it to the CFO, because a forecast the board cannot trust is worse than a miss.
Tell me about a data initiative you led that did not deliver. What did you change afterward?
How you own a failure and what you learned from it.
A real failure with your own part in it, a clear cause, and a concrete change in how you work now.

I led a project to build a single view of every customer. It took nine months and was barely used. My mistake was building for every team at once with no one owner who needed it. Now I start with one use case, a named sponsor and a usage target at 90 days. The next project, a churn risk list for account managers, was in daily use within six weeks.

data-product-manager.heading: Data product manager questions
qs: What makes a dataset a product rather than just a table someone built?
Whether you understand what data product management adds to plain data work.
Named users, an owner, documentation, quality and freshness promises, and a way to get support and hear about changes.

A table is output. A product has users it was built for and an owner who answers for it. It has documentation, a stated refresh time, quality checks, a support channel and a change policy. If nobody would notice it broke, or nobody would fix it, it is not a product yet.
What goes into a data contract between the team that produces data and the teams that use it?
Your grasp of how data teams agree on what they deliver to each other.
Schema, field meanings, freshness and quality expectations, ownership, and how changes are announced. All written down, and ideally checked automatically.

The schema with field types and meanings, which fields can be empty, the refresh schedule and how late is too late, quality rules like unique IDs, the owner, and how much notice users get before a breaking change. I like the schema part enforced in the pipeline, so a breaking change fails a check instead of a dashboard.
An internal data platform earns no revenue. How do you show it is working?
How you pick success measures for a product whose users are your colleagues.
Adoption, reliability and trust measures tied to time or decisions saved, not row counts or the number of tables.

I track active users and queries by team, how often data lands on time, incidents and time to fix, and how long a new analyst takes to answer a first question. Then I tie a few to outcomes, like a report that took two days now refreshing on its own. Number of tables is not a measure; more tables can mean more mess.
A sales leader asks for real-time data in their dashboard. How do you respond?
Whether you weigh the cost of fresher data against the decision it supports.
Asks what decision changes with fresher data, matches the refresh speed to that, and explains the extra cost and complexity of streaming.

I ask what they would do differently if the number were minutes old instead of a day old. Often the answer is a morning review, so hourly or daily is enough. Streaming costs more to build, run and test. If a decision truly needs minutes, like stopping fraud, I make the case for it. Otherwise I offer the cheapest refresh that fits.
An upstream team renamed a column overnight and your customer-facing feed broke. Walk me through your morning.
How you run a data incident and keep it from happening again.
Contain, tell affected users early, fix or roll back, refill the missed data, then fix the process: contract, schema checks, change notice.

First I confirm the scope: which feeds, which customers, since when. I post a status note to affected users before I have a fix. With engineering we map the new name or roll back, rerun the missed loads and check the counts. Then the follow-up: a schema check that blocks publishing, and the upstream team added to our contract and change process.
Two dashboards show different numbers for active customers. How do you settle it?
Your approach to metric definitions and a single source of truth.
Traces both definitions and sources, gets the business owner to choose one, documents it in one shared place and retires the other version.

I trace both: source tables, filters, time windows and what counts as active. Usually one uses 30 days and one counts any login. I bring the difference to the metric's business owner to pick one, document it in our shared metric definitions, and point both dashboards there. The old version is removed, so it does not come back.
A team wants customer email addresses and exact locations added to a shared dataset. What do you check first?
Whether you handle personal data with care, not as just another column.
Purpose and real need, whether less identifying data would do, privacy or legal review, access limits, masking and how long it is kept.

I ask what they are trying to do, because often a hashed ID or a city works instead of an email and exact location. If they truly need it, I check with privacy or legal that our notice and terms allow that use, since several state laws give people rights over their data. Then access only for named roles, masking for others, and a retention limit.
You want to retire an old dataset that 40 scheduled jobs still query. How do you do it?
How you shut down a data product without breaking the people who depend on it.
Finds every user through query logs and lineage, offers a replacement and migration help, announces dates, then removes access in stages.

I use query logs and lineage to list every job and its owner. I make sure the replacement covers their needs, with a field-by-field mapping. Then I announce a date, contact owners directly and track who has moved. Near the end I mark it deprecated, then revoke access for a week before deleting, so anything we missed fails loudly and can be restored.
Your data warehouse bill doubled this quarter. What do you do?
Whether you manage the cost of a data product as part of the product.
Breaks cost down by team, job and table, finds the few heavy drivers, cuts waste and agrees on budgets or cost visibility with users.

I break the bill down by team, job and query; usually a few things drive most of it. I look for queries scanning whole tables that could read one date range, dashboards refreshing every few minutes that nobody opens, and duplicate pipelines. Then I show each team its own cost, so new heavy usage starts with a conversation, not a surprise.
A paying customer of your data feed finds wrong values that already went into their own reports. How do you handle it?
How you own a quality failure with outside customers who rely on your data.
Fast, honest notice of what was wrong and for which dates, corrected data with a clear note, a check of contract terms, and a lasting fix.

I confirm it, then tell every affected customer, not only the one who found it: which fields, which dates, and when corrected data arrives. We redeliver the corrected history with a clear note on what changed. I check the contract for any credits owed. Then we add the test that would have caught it, such as a range or row-count check before delivery.
What is the difference between an SLI, an SLO and an SLA for a dataset?
Whether you can set reliability promises for data in exact terms.
Clear roles: the SLI is the measurement, the SLO is the internal target, the SLA is the promise to a customer with consequences.

An SLI is the measurement itself, for example the share of days the table is loaded by 7 a.m. An SLO is our internal target for it, say 99% of days in a quarter. An SLA is the promise to a customer and what happens if we miss it, like a credit. I keep the SLO stricter than the SLA so we see trouble before we break a promise.
Walk me through writing the definition of monthly active users for the company metrics catalog.
How precisely you define a metric so every team computes the same number.
The exact rule, time zone, window, exclusions, grain, source, owner and worked examples, plus sign-off from the teams that use it.

I start with the business question, then write the exact rule: which events count as active, which time zone, the calendar or rolling window, and who is excluded, like test and internal accounts. I add the grain, the source table, an owner and a few worked examples with expected results. Finance and product sign off before it goes in the catalog.
A director asks you for a churn dashboard. How do you run the first interview?
How you find the decision behind a data request instead of taking the request as the spec.
Questions about the decision, past behavior and the current definition, then a playback that may change what gets built.

I ask what decision the dashboard will change and who makes it. Then I ask about the last time they needed this number: what they did, where they got stuck. I ask how they define churn today, since teams differ. I play back the decision and the definition. Sometimes the right product is one weekly alert, not a dashboard.
A customer moves from the West region to the East region. How should last year's revenue by region report?
Your grasp of how history is kept in dimension tables and why it matters to users.
Knows overwrite (Type 1) versus kept history with dates (Type 2), ties the choice to the use case and documents it.

It depends on the question, so I make it a choice, not an accident. If we overwrite the region, a Type 1 change, last year's revenue moves to East and old reports change. If we keep history with start and end dates, a Type 2 dimension, last year stays in West. Sales compensation usually needs history. I document which view each report uses.
Late transactions arrive after a month's numbers were already published. What is your restatement policy?
Whether you treat corrections to published numbers as a product rule agreed in advance.
A close window and a threshold agreed with users, versioned numbers, a stated reason and direct notice to those who used the old figure.

I agree the rule with users before it is needed. A month stays open for a set number of days. After close, we restate only if the change passes an agreed threshold. When we do, we version the numbers, note the reason and size of the change, and tell the people who used the old figure. Silent changes do more damage than late ones.
You need to make a breaking change to a data feed that outside customers use. How do you plan it?
How you manage change for external data consumers without breaking their work.
Knows what counts as breaking, runs old and new versions side by side, gives mapping docs and a dated window, and follows up per customer.

First I classify the change. Adding a column is usually safe; renaming, removing or changing a field's meaning breaks users. I ship a new version next to the old one, publish a changelog with a field-by-field mapping and sample files, and set a dated deprecation window. I track who has switched and call those who have not well before the cutoff.
Sales wants to package a third-party dataset we license into a product we sell. What do you check?
Whether you know that licensed data comes with use limits that shape the product.
Reads the license with legal first: redistribution, derived data, attribution, term and exit terms, and pricing for commercial use.

I read the license with legal before anything goes on the roadmap. Many licenses allow internal use only, ban redistribution, or allow derived data only if the source cannot be rebuilt from it. I check attribution, the term, what happens to delivered data if the contract ends, and commercial pricing. If resale is not allowed, we negotiate or find another source.
A consumer makes a deletion request under a state privacy law. How does your data platform make that work?
How you design a data platform so privacy requests can be honored everywhere the data lives.
