Knowing where personal data sits, deleting it from derived data too, stopping reloads, letting legal set exceptions, and logging completion.

It starts with lineage and a catalog, so we know every table holding personal data. Requests go to a tracked queue. We delete or de-identify the person in source tables and derived datasets, and make sure pipelines cannot reload them from raw copies. Legal decides exceptions, like records we must keep. We log each request as completed on time.
Your roadmap has three new dataset requests and a backlog of quality issues on your most used table. How do you decide?
How you weigh data quality work against new features on a data product roadmap.
Sizes both by user impact using usage and incident data, and explains the trade-off openly to the people who must wait.

I size both by impact. Query logs show how many teams and decisions rely on the existing table. Incident history shows how often wrong numbers reached users and what it cost. New datasets built on a shaky table inherit its problems. Usually I fix the top issues first, ship one new dataset, and show requesters the trade so they see why theirs waits.
A team's bonus is tied to a metric you own, and the number keeps rising while the real outcome does not. What do you do?
Your judgement when a metric you own is being gamed and people's pay depends on it.
Rules out a data bug first, brings evidence to the sponsor, proposes a guardrail and changes the definition on an agreed date, not midway.

First I rule out a data bug by breaking the metric into its parts. If people found a way to move the number, like closing tickets and reopening them as new ones, I take examples to the metric's sponsor. I propose a guardrail metric that must hold too, and we agree a date for the new definition so nobody's bonus math changes mid-period.

data-scientist.heading: Data scientist questions
qs: What is the difference between L1 and L2 regularization?
Whether you know how models are kept simple, not just that they can be.
L1 can set weights to exactly zero, so it selects features. L2 shrinks all weights smoothly. Features should be scaled first.

Both add a penalty for large weights to the loss. L1, used in lasso, penalizes the absolute values and pushes some weights to exactly zero, so it drops features. L2, used in ridge, penalizes the squared values and shrinks weights without zeroing them, which helps when features are correlated. Either way I scale the features first, or the penalty hits them unevenly.
What is data leakage? Give an example you have seen or caught.
Whether you can spot a model that looks good only because it saw the answer.
A clear definition and a real case, such as a feature known only after the outcome, or preprocessing fit on all the data before the split.

Leakage is when the model trains on information it will not have at prediction time. In a churn model I once saw 98% accuracy. The cause was a cancellation reason field filled in only after a customer left. I removed it and accuracy fell to a believable 81%. I also fit scalers and imputers on the training set only, never on all the data.
Only 1% of transactions are fraud. How do you build and judge a model for that?
How you handle rare events, where accuracy says almost nothing.
Precision, recall or PR AUC instead of accuracy, class weights or resampling on training data only, and a threshold set by the cost of each error.

A model that calls everything legitimate is 99% accurate and useless, so I look at precision, recall and the area under the precision-recall curve. I try class weights first, and if I resample, I do it inside the training folds only. Then I pick the threshold with the fraud team, based on what a missed fraud costs versus a wrongly blocked customer.
Why is random k-fold cross-validation risky for a sales forecast, and what do you use instead?
Whether you validate models the way they will actually be used.
Random folds let the model learn from the future. Time-based splits train on the past and test on a later period.

Random folds mix dates, so the model trains on next month to predict last month, and lag features leak too. The score looks better than reality. I use a rolling or expanding window: train on data up to a date, test on the weeks after it, then move the cutoff forward. Each test period is one the model has never seen, just like in production.
Your model says a customer has an 80% chance to buy. How do you check whether that number means anything?
Whether you know the difference between ranking well and giving honest probabilities.
Calibration: among cases scored near 0.8, about 80% should buy. Check with a reliability curve; fix with Platt scaling or isotonic regression.

That is a question of calibration. I group held-out cases by predicted score and compare each group's average score with the share that actually bought; near 0.8, about 80% should buy. A reliability plot or the Brier score shows it. Some models are poorly calibrated out of the box, so I recalibrate with Platt scaling or isotonic regression fit on a separate validation set.
A product manager checks the A/B test every morning and wants to stop the day it hits p < 0.05. What is the problem?
Whether you understand how peeking at results inflates false positives.
Repeated looks at a fixed-horizon test push the false positive rate well above 5%. Fix the sample size in advance or use a sequential method.

Each look is another chance for noise to cross the line, so with daily checks the real false positive rate ends up far above 5%. I would agree on the sample size before launch and decide only then. If the team truly needs early answers, I would set up a sequential design, such as alpha spending, where the threshold is adjusted for each planned look.
You tested 20 metrics and one came out significant at 0.05. How do you report it?
How you handle multiple comparisons without fooling yourself or others.
With 20 tests, about one false positive is expected by chance. Correct for it, and lead with the primary metric picked before the test.

If nothing really changed, 20 tests at 5% would still give about one win by chance, so I would not call it a result. I report the primary metric we chose before the test first. For the others I apply a correction such as Benjamini-Hochberg and label any survivor as a lead to test again, not a finding.
Overall conversion went up after a change, but it went down in every region. How can that be?
Whether you recognize Simpson's paradox and know to check the mix.
The mix shifted toward segments with higher base rates. Compare within segments or reweight to a fixed mix before drawing a conclusion.

That is Simpson's paradox. Say traffic shifted toward a region that always converts better: each region dropped a little, but more visitors now sit in the strong one, so the total rises. I would show the change within each region and a total reweighted to the old mix. Then I would ask why the mix moved, since that may be the real story.
Your 50/50 test shows 50,000 users in control and 48,500 in treatment. What do you do?
Whether you catch a broken experiment before reading its results.
Test for sample ratio mismatch with a chi-square test. If it fails, do not trust the results; look for bugs in assignment or logging.

A gap of 1,500 on nearly 100,000 users is far too big for chance; a chi-square test gives a tiny p-value. That is a sample ratio mismatch, so I would not read the metrics yet. I would look for causes such as a redirect that drops some treatment users, a logging bug, or bot filtering that hits one group more. Once it is fixed, I rerun the test.
Marketing launched a campaign in some states only, with no experiment. How would you estimate its effect?
Whether you can estimate a causal effect from observational data and name the assumptions.
A method like difference-in-differences or synthetic control, with its key assumption stated and checked, such as parallel trends before launch.

I would use difference-in-differences: compare the change in sales in launch states with the change in similar states without the campaign, over the same weeks. It rests on parallel trends, so I would check that both groups moved together for months before launch. If no single comparison group fits, I would build a synthetic control from a weighted mix of states.
Your logistic regression gives a coefficient of 0.7 for one feature. What does that number mean?
Whether you can read a logistic model correctly.
It is on the log-odds scale: one unit more multiplies the odds by e^0.7, about 2, with other features held fixed. It does not double the probability.

The coefficient is in log-odds. One unit more of that feature, with the others held fixed, multiplies the odds of the outcome by e to the 0.7, about 2. That is not double the probability: a 10% chance becomes about 18%, and a 50% chance becomes about 67%. Both are a doubling of the odds.
How do a random forest and gradient boosting differ, and when would you pick each?
Your working knowledge of the two most used tree ensembles.
Forest: deep trees in parallel, averaged, cuts variance, little tuning. Boosting: shallow trees in sequence fixing past errors, often stronger but needs tuning.

A random forest grows many deep trees in parallel, each on a bootstrap sample with random subsets of features, and averages them. That mostly cuts variance and works well with little tuning. Gradient boosting adds shallow trees one after another, each fitted to the errors left so far. It often scores higher, but I tune the learning rate and use early stopping, or it overfits.
A stakeholder sees the feature importance chart of your churn model and says the top feature causes churn. How do you respond?
Whether you know the limits of feature importance.
Importance shows what the model uses, not causes. Default tree importance is biased; permutation importance on held-out data is better, and causes need a causal study.

I'd say the chart shows what the model leans on to predict, not what drives churn. Default tree importance also favors features with many unique values and is computed on training data. I'd check permutation importance on held-out data and note that correlated features share credit. To learn what causes churn, we need an experiment or a careful causal study.
Operations gave extra coaching to the 50 worst-performing stores last quarter, and their sales rose 8%. Was it the coaching?
Whether you spot regression to the mean.
Not proven: stores picked for a bad quarter tend to bounce back anyway. A comparison group, ideally random, is needed to measure the coaching.

Not necessarily. Stores picked for one bad quarter partly had bad luck, and bad luck tends not to repeat, so they would likely improve anyway. That is regression to the mean. I'd compare them with similar low stores that were not coached, or next time take the eligible stores and randomly coach half of them.
Your site has little traffic, and the test would need four months to detect the effect the team expects. What are your options?
How you handle an underpowered experiment.
Real levers: a more sensitive metric, variance reduction such as CUPED, a bolder change, a larger minimum effect. And saying so when a test cannot answer.

First I'd check the expected effect is realistic. Then: a metric closer to the change, which moves more; variance reduction like CUPED, which adjusts for each user's behavior before the test; or a bolder change. Halving the effect we must detect needs about four times the sample, so the reverse saves a lot. If nothing works, I say plainly the test cannot answer it.
A redesigned feed shows a strong lift in week one of the test, but the lift shrinks every week. What is going on, and what do you do?
Whether you recognize novelty effects and measure the lasting effect.
Likely novelty. Look at the effect by days since first exposure and for new users; report the level it settles at, and consider a longer holdout.

Likely a novelty effect: people click the new thing because it is new. I'd plot the effect by days since each user's first exposure, and compare users new to the product, who have no old habit, with returning users. If the effect settles at a smaller positive level, that steady level is what I report, and I may keep a small holdout for a few months.
Marketing wants a model to choose who gets a 20% coupon and suggests targeting the customers most likely to buy. What do you say?
Whether you separate predicting an outcome from predicting the effect of an action.
Likely buyers often buy anyway. Target those whose buying changes because of the coupon: randomized data, an uplift model, judged on an uplift curve.

Those people often buy anyway, so the coupon just gives away margin. What we want is who buys because of the coupon. I'd run a test sending the coupon to a random part of customers, then build an uplift model that predicts the difference in buying with and without it, and judge it with an uplift (Qini) curve, not plain accuracy.
You randomize by user, but your metric is click-through rate per page view. How do you compute the confidence interval?
Whether you match the analysis unit to the randomization unit.
Page views from one user are correlated, so a naive interval is too narrow. Use the delta method or a bootstrap that resamples whole users.

Page views from the same user are not independent, so treating each view as its own sample makes the interval too narrow and gives false wins. I treat the metric as total clicks over total views per group and use the delta method, or bootstrap by resampling whole users. Either way, the variance is computed at the unit we randomized.
In a ride-hailing marketplace, a test gives a discount to half the riders. Why might the result mislead, and how would you design it instead?
Your grasp of interference between test groups and the designs that handle it.
Groups share drivers, so treatment takes supply from control and the lift is overstated. Randomize by market or use switchback time blocks.

Riders share the same drivers. Treated riders book more and take drivers from control riders, so control looks worse than it would be and the lift is overstated. I'd randomize whole cities or regions, or use a switchback design, where a market flips between treatment and control in time blocks, and analyze the results by those blocks.
A model scored well offline, but its live performance was far worse from the first week. Where do you look?
How you debug a gap between offline and live results.
Training-serving skew before drift: compare logged live features with offline features for the same cases, and check what data exists at prediction time.

So soon, I'd suspect the pipeline before drift. I log the features the model sees live and compare them with offline values for the same customers and dates. Common causes: a training feature built with data not yet available at prediction time, different handling of empty values, or a unit or time zone mismatch in the live code.

database-administrator.heading: Database administrator questions
qs: What is the difference between RPO and RTO?
Whether you know the two targets that every backup and recovery plan is built around.
RPO is how much data loss is acceptable, RTO is how long downtime is acceptable, and each one drives a different part of the plan.

RPO, the recovery point objective, is how much data we can afford to lose, measured in time. RTO, the recovery time objective, is how long we can be down. An RPO of 15 minutes means changes must be backed up or replicated at least that often. The RTO sets how fast the restore or failover must be, so I time real restores against it.
Explain full, differential and transaction log backups, and how you would combine them.
Your grasp of backup types and the order a restore must follow.
Correct definitions, a realistic schedule, and the right restore sequence: full, latest differential, then logs in order.

In SQL Server terms, a full backup copies the whole database. A differential copies what changed since the last full. A log backup holds every transaction since the last log backup. A common plan is a weekly full, a nightly differential and logs every 15 minutes. To restore, I apply the full, the latest differential, then the logs in order up to the moment I need.
What is the trade-off between synchronous and asynchronous replication?
Whether you understand the balance between data safety and write speed in replication.
Synchronous protects committed data but slows every write; asynchronous is faster but can lose recent changes on failover.

With synchronous replication, the primary waits for the replica to confirm before a commit returns, so a failover loses no committed data, but every write pays the network round trip. Asynchronous commits at once and ships changes after, so it is faster, but a failover can lose the last few seconds. I often use synchronous nearby and asynchronous to a distant region.
What is a deadlock, and how do you reduce them?
Your knowledge of locking and how you work with developers to prevent conflicts.
A clear definition, knowing the database kills one victim, and practical fixes in both the code and the schema.

A deadlock is two transactions each holding a lock the other needs. Neither can move, so the database picks one as the victim and rolls it back. To reduce them, I have code touch tables in the same order, keep transactions short, and add indexes so updates lock fewer rows. The app should also retry the victim, since some deadlocks will still happen.
How do you know your backups will actually restore?
Whether you test recovery or only trust that the backup job ran.
Scheduled test restores, integrity checks, restore times measured against the RTO, alerts on failed jobs, and a protected off-site copy.

A backup is only proven by a restore. I restore the latest backups to a separate server on a schedule, run an integrity check like DBCC CHECKDB, and compare row counts on key tables. I time each restore against our RTO. I also alert on any failed or skipped backup job and keep one copy off site that production accounts cannot delete.
An execution plan shows an estimate of 10 rows, but the actual count is 2 million. What does that tell you?
How well you understand the query optimizer and the statistics it depends on.
Knowing the plan was built on a bad row estimate, and naming likely causes: stale statistics, parameter sniffing, correlated columns.

The optimizer built its plan for 10 rows, so it likely chose a nested loop or an index seek that is terrible for 2 million. First I check whether statistics on those columns are stale and update them. If they are fresh, I look at parameter sniffing, where the plan was built for a rare value, and at correlated columns, which the optimizer treats as independent.
A read replica is 30 minutes behind the primary, and users see old data. What do you check?
How you trace replication lag to a cause while limiting the harm to users.
Splitting the lag into shipping versus applying, checking load on both sides, and routing fresh reads to the primary in the meantime.

First I check whether the lag is in shipping or applying: are changes reaching the replica, or arriving and waiting? Then I look for a big write on the primary, like a bulk update, and for slow disk on the replica. On PostgreSQL, a long report query on the replica can hold back replay. Meanwhile I tell the app team so reads needing fresh data go to the primary.
Someone ran a DELETE without a WHERE clause on a production table 20 minutes ago. What do you do?
How you recover lost data without destroying the good work done since.
No restore over production; a point-in-time restore to a separate copy, then copying the missing rows back and checking them.

I stop anything that could make it worse, like jobs that sync that table. I do not restore over production, because that would wipe 20 minutes of good work. I restore the last backup plus logs to a separate database, stopping just before the delete, which I find by its time in the log. Then I copy the missing rows back and check counts with the data owners.
How would you add an index to a 500-million-row table in production without downtime?
Whether you can change a large live database without blocking the business.
Testing on a copy first, using an online or concurrent build, knowing its limits, and watching locks and replica lag.

I test the change on a restored copy first to see the time and locks. On PostgreSQL I use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which avoids blocking writes, but it cannot run inside a transaction and can leave an invalid index if it fails, so I check afterward. I run it off peak and watch locks and replica lag. Any data backfill goes in small batches.
The primary database is down, and automatic failover did not trigger. Walk me through what you do.
Your judgement in a manual failover, especially avoiding two primaries taking writes.
Confirming the outage, fencing the old primary, stating possible data loss to the business, then promoting and rebuilding the old one.

First I confirm the primary is really down, not just cut off from monitoring. Then I fence it so it cannot take writes if it comes back, because two primaries means split data. I check how far behind the replica was, tell the business what data could be lost, promote it and repoint the apps. The old primary rejoins only after it is rebuilt as a replica.
In a database that uses MVCC, what happens when you update a row, and what does that cost you?
Whether you understand how row versioning works under the hood.
Old row versions stay until no transaction needs them. Cleanup has a real cost, and long-open transactions make it worse.

In PostgreSQL an update writes a new row version and marks the old one dead. Readers keep seeing the old version until they finish, so readers and writers rarely block each other. The cost is cleanup: VACUUM has to reclaim dead rows, and one long-open transaction stops that, so tables and indexes bloat.
What can go wrong at Read Committed that cannot go wrong at Serializable? Give a real example.
Your grasp of isolation levels beyond the textbook definitions.
Names a concrete anomaly, like a non-repeatable read or write skew, and knows Serializable may make the app retry failed transactions.

At Read Committed, two reads in one transaction can return different values because another transaction committed in between. Write skew is worse: two doctors each check that someone else is on call, both go off call, and nobody is left. Serializable prevents that, but the app must be ready to retry transactions the database aborts.
The app team scaled to 200 instances, each with a pool of 20 connections, and the PostgreSQL server is struggling. What do you suggest?
How you handle connection limits and pooling.
Sees that each connection costs a server process and memory, sizes total connections to the server, and knows the limits of a transaction-mode pooler.

That is up to 4,000 connections, and in PostgreSQL each one is a separate server process with its own memory. I would put a connection pooler in front in transaction mode and shrink the app pools. Then a few dozen real connections serve everyone. I would warn the team that session state, like SET commands or advisory locks, does not carry across transactions in that mode.
A stored procedure is fast for most customers but times out for one very large customer, and some days it is the other way round. What is going on?
Whether you recognize a cached plan built for the wrong parameter value.
Identifies parameter sniffing on skewed data and weighs fixes like recompiling, optimizing for a typical value, or forcing a known good plan.

That sounds like parameter sniffing. SQL Server builds the plan for the first value it sees and reuses it. If that was a small customer, the plan suits a few rows and is terrible for the one with millions. I would confirm it in the plan cache or Query Store, then pick a fix: OPTION (RECOMPILE) if the query runs rarely, or forcing a plan that works for both.
On SQL Server, the transaction log has filled the disk. How do you find out why, and what do you avoid doing?
How you diagnose a full log instead of just shrinking it.
Checks log_reuse_wait_desc first, fixes the real cause, such as missing log backups or an open transaction, and does not switch to simple recovery by reflex.

First I query log_reuse_wait_desc in sys.databases; it says what is holding the log. LOG_BACKUP means log backups stopped, ACTIVE_TRANSACTION means something is still open, and replication or an availability group can hold it too. I fix that cause. I do not flip to simple recovery, because that breaks the log chain and point-in-time restore.
A PostgreSQL primary is running out of disk because the WAL directory keeps growing, yet replication looks healthy. What do you suspect?
Whether you know what makes the primary keep old WAL files.
Points to an inactive replication slot or failing WAL archiving, checks pg_replication_slots, and caps how much WAL a slot can hold.

Usually a replication slot whose consumer is gone, such as an old replica. The slot makes the primary keep every WAL file that consumer has not read. I check pg_replication_slots for inactive slots and how much WAL each holds. If the consumer is truly dead, I drop the slot. Then I set max_slot_wal_keep_size so one slot cannot fill the disk again.
Developers want to rename a column that a live application uses. How do you do it without downtime?
How you plan schema changes that stay compatible with running code.
Uses expand and contract: add the new column, write to both, backfill in batches, move reads, then drop the old column in a later release.

I never rename in place, because the running code breaks the moment it happens. First release: add the new column and have the app write to both. Then I backfill old rows in small batches so locks and replication lag stay low. The next release reads from the new column. Once nothing touches the old one, a later release drops it.
What is split brain in a database failover cluster, and how do you prevent it?
Whether you understand the biggest risk of automatic failover.
Two nodes both accepting writes. Prevented with quorum or a witness, and by fencing the old primary before a new one is promoted.

Split brain is when a network break makes two nodes each think they are primary, and both take writes. The data diverges and someone has to reconcile it by hand. I prevent it with quorum, an odd number of voters or a witness, so only one side can win. The old primary must be fenced, shut down or cut off from clients, before the new one is promoted.
A consistency check reports corruption in a production SQL Server database. Walk me through your response.
How you handle corruption without making the data loss worse.
Finds the scope first, avoids repair with data loss as a first move, restores from a clean backup, and checks the storage underneath.

First I read exactly which objects and pages are hit. If it is only a nonclustered index, I drop and recreate it. If it is table data, I restore from the last clean backup and replay log backups, or restore just the damaged pages. REPAIR_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS is a last resort. Then I check the storage logs, because corruption usually comes from below the database.
What is transaction ID wraparound in PostgreSQL, and how do you keep it from taking a database down?
Your depth on PostgreSQL maintenance at a senior level.
Knows IDs are 32-bit and old rows must be frozen by vacuum, monitors age(datfrozenxid), and removes blockers like long transactions or stale slots.

Transaction IDs are 32-bit, so after about two billion transactions they wrap around. Vacuum freezes old rows so they stay visible. If freezing falls too far behind, PostgreSQL stops accepting new writes to protect the data. I alert on age(datfrozenxid) well before that and hunt what blocks freezing: long transactions, forgotten prepared transactions and stale replication slots.

defense.heading: Defense and national security questions
qs: What is the difference between holding a clearance and having access to classified information?
Whether you understand how cleared work is actually controlled.
A clearance is eligibility. Access also needs a need-to-know for that specific information and a signed nondisclosure agreement.

The clearance means the government has found me eligible at a given level, like Secret. It does not let me see everything at that level. I also need a need-to-know for that specific program, and I sign a nondisclosure agreement before I'm read on. If a cleared coworker asks about my program and isn't on it, the answer is no.
What is CUI, and how do you handle it day to day?
Your habits with information that is unclassified but still protected.
CUI is unclassified information the government requires to be safeguarded. It stays on approved company systems and goes only to people with a lawful business need.

Controlled Unclassified Information isn't classified, but a law or government policy says it must be protected, like export-controlled drawings. I keep it on approved company systems, never on a personal phone or personal email. I check the marking before I share a file, and I send it only to people with a lawful business need for it.
Why does it matter which charge number you put your hours on?
Whether you understand the rules for billing work to government contracts.
Hours go to the contract you actually worked on, recorded daily. Moving hours to a contract with budget left is mischarging and can be fraud.

On government contracts the hours I record become costs the government pays for, and auditors check them. So I record time every day, on the charge number for the work I actually did. If my program is out of budget and someone suggests charging another contract, I refuse and tell my manager or the ethics office. That is mischarging, and it can be treated as fraud.
A coworker here on a work visa asks to see the drawings for an ITAR-controlled part. What do you do?
Whether you know that sharing technical data with a foreign person counts as an export.
Under ITAR, releasing controlled technical data to a foreign person, even inside the US, is an export and needs authorization first.

I don't share it yet. Under ITAR, releasing technical data to a foreign person is an export, even if we sit in the same US office. I'd ask our export compliance team whether we hold a license or agreement that covers this person. If not, I tell my coworker kindly that I can't, and that it isn't about trust.
Someone on a networking site offers you a consulting fee to answer questions about your program. What do you do?
Your counterintelligence awareness and whether you report suspicious contacts.
You don't answer or engage further, you keep the messages, and you report the contact to your security officer.

I don't reply with any details, even harmless ones, because small facts add up. I keep the messages, screenshot the profile, and report it to our facility security officer the same day. Fake recruiter profiles are a known way that foreign intelligence services target cleared people. Security decides what happens next, not me.
A buyer found an obsolete chip we need from a broker at half price. What do you say?
Whether you know the risk of counterfeit parts and how to source them safely.
Buy from the original maker or its authorized distributors first. Any other source needs vetting, traceability, testing and approval, because counterfeits fail in the field.

I'd slow down. Brokers outside the authorized channel are the main risk for counterfeit electronics: used or relabeled chips sold as new. First I'd look for stock from the manufacturer or an authorized distributor. If there is none, we use a vetted supplier, get traceability paperwork, test the parts before use, and tell the customer if the contract requires it.
Production wants to move a hole 2 mm because assembly would be easier. Can they just do it?
Whether you respect configuration control on an approved design.
No. The change goes through the engineering change process, the drawing is updated first, and changes to form, fit or function may need customer approval.

Not on the floor. Even a small move can change how the part fits the next assembly or a spare already in the field. I'd write an engineering change request, check what else that hole interfaces with, and update the drawing before anyone cuts metal. If it affects form, fit or function, the customer usually has to approve it, because they control the approved design.
You notice a file with classified markings on an unclassified network share. What do you do?
How you handle a possible classified spill without making it worse.
You don't reopen, copy, forward or delete it. You note where it is and tell the security officer at once, in person or by phone, not by email.

I stop. I don't open it again, forward it, print it or delete it, because each of those can spread it or destroy evidence. I write down the file path and the time, and I call or go see our security officer right away. I don't describe the content in an email. Then I follow their instructions, which may include leaving my computer alone.
A unit fails a vibration test the day before the government witness arrives. How do you handle it?
Your honesty with test results under schedule pressure.
Record the failure, tell the customer, and find the root cause. Never quietly retest until it passes or hide the first result.

I record the failure exactly as it happened and tell my lead and the program office the same day. Then we find out why: the fixture, the setup, or the unit itself. If it's the unit, the witness test moves, and we say so plainly. Rerunning until it passes and showing only the good run would be falsifying a test record, and these units go to people in the field.
The customer's engineer asks you to add a feature that is not in the contract, since you are in there anyway. What do you do?
Whether you know who can change a government contract and how to say no politely.
Only the contracting officer can change the contract. You thank the engineer, log the request and send it to your program manager or contracts team.

I'd say it's a good idea and I'll pass it on, but I can't start it yet. Only the government contracting officer can change what the contract covers; an engineer, even a senior one, can't authorize it. If we did it anyway, we might not get paid and it could cause a dispute later. I write down the request and send it to our program manager and contracts team the same day.
What are the four standard verification methods, and when would you use each?
Whether you know the basic tools for proving that a requirement is met.
Inspection, analysis, demonstration and test, each matched to the kind of requirement, with test kept for what needs measured data.

Inspection is looking or measuring: a label, a dimension, a part number. Analysis is math or modeling, like a thermal model or a reliability prediction. Demonstration shows that a function works without much measurement, like a door that opens. Test measures performance under set conditions, such as output power across temperature. I pick the cheapest method that still gives real proof.
What makes a requirement well written?
Your eye for requirements that can actually be built and verified.
One 'shall' per statement, measurable, unambiguous and traceable to a parent, with a verification method in mind when it is written.

Each statement has one 'shall' and one idea, so it passes or fails on its own. It has a number and units, not words like 'fast' or 'rugged.' It says what, not how, unless the how is truly required. It traces to a parent. While I write it, I ask how I would verify it. If I cannot answer, the requirement is not done.
In the trace matrix you find dozens of subsystem requirements that trace to no parent. What do you do?
How you handle gaps in requirements traceability.
You sort them. True derived requirements get a written rationale, broken links get fixed, and gold plating is removed before it costs money.

First I sort them. Some are real derived requirements, for example a connector rating driven by our own design. Those get a rationale and a link to the design decision. Some lost their link in a tool migration, so I restore it. The rest are nice-to-haves nobody asked for. I raise those with the systems lead, because each one costs design and test time.
What is the difference between qualification testing and acceptance testing?
Whether you understand how a design is proven versus how each unit is screened.
Qualification proves the design with margin on dedicated units. Acceptance screens every production unit at lower levels for workmanship defects.

Qualification proves the design. We test dedicated units at levels above what the product should see in service, to show margin. Those units have used up life, so we normally do not deliver them. Acceptance tests every production unit at lower levels to catch workmanship problems like a bad solder joint, without wearing the unit out.
What should be settled at PDR, and what at CDR?
Your grasp of what each major design review is for.
PDR sets the allocated baseline and shows the design can meet requirements. CDR shows the detail design is ready to build and sets the initial product baseline.

At PDR the requirements are allocated to each item, which sets the allocated baseline, and the preliminary design shows it can meet them with acceptable risk. At CDR the detailed design is mature: drawings largely released, analyses done, test plans ready, so we can start building. CDR sets the initial product baseline. I treat entry criteria as real gates, not a date.
A supplier's datasheet says the unit is 'MIL-STD-810 compliant.' Is that enough for you?
Whether you know environmental test standards must be tailored, not just claimed.
No. MIL-STD-810 is tailored to how the product is used, so you ask which methods, procedures and levels were run and compare them to your own environment.

No. MIL-STD-810 is a set of test methods meant to be tailored to how the product will be used, so 'compliant' alone says little. I ask for the test report: which methods, which procedures, what levels and durations, and which unit configuration. Then I compare that with our own environmental profile. If their vibration levels were lower than ours, I plan a delta test.
Your box fails MIL-STD-461 RE102 radiated emissions at a few frequencies. How do you work it?
How you troubleshoot an electromagnetic interference failure in a structured way.
Identify the source from the frequencies and harmonics, find the coupling path, often a cable, and fix at the source before adding shielding.

RE102 measures the electric field the unit radiates, so I look at where the peaks fall. If they are harmonics of a 25 MHz clock, I know the source. Then I find the path with a near-field probe and a current clamp; often it is common-mode current on a cable. I fix at the source first: layout, filtering, better shield termination. Then I retest the full range.
Explain the difference between a deviation, a waiver and an engineering change proposal.
Whether you know how departures from the approved baseline are formally handled.
A deviation is approved before build, a waiver after a nonconformance is found; both are limited and leave the baseline unchanged. An ECP changes the baseline.

A deviation is permission, before we build, to depart from a requirement for a set number of units or a set time. A waiver is permission to accept units already built that do not conform. Neither changes the design baseline. If the change should be permanent, I write an engineering change proposal, and if it affects form, fit, function or cost, the customer must approve it.
The program manager wants to close a requirement by analysis instead of test to save three weeks. How do you respond?
Your judgement when schedule pressure meets verification rigor.
You weigh whether analysis truly gives proof, note the method is often agreed with the customer, and take the change to them instead of switching quietly.

First I ask if analysis is credible here. A model correlated to earlier test data can be strong; a new design with no correlation is not. Then I check the verification matrix, since the method is often agreed with the customer and changing it needs their approval. I would bring the PM a plan with the risk spelled out and let the customer decide.
Late in development you find a hazard, and the team proposes a warning label as the fix. What do you say?
Whether you apply the MIL-STD-882 order of precedence for reducing hazards.
Labels are near the bottom: first design the hazard out, then reduce it, then add safety devices or warnings. The remaining risk must be formally accepted.

MIL-STD-882 sets an order: eliminate the hazard by design, reduce it by changing the design, add engineered safety features, add warning devices, and only then rely on signs, procedures, training and protective gear. So I ask what design fix is still possible and what it costs. If a label really is the best we can do, the remaining risk is assessed and formally accepted by the right authority.

defi.heading: DeFi and protocol specialist questions
qs: In a constant-product pool, how is the price of a swap set?
Whether you understand the basic pricing math behind automated market makers.
Price comes from the ratio of the reserves, the product of the reserves stays constant, and bigger trades move the price more.

The pool holds two tokens and keeps their quantities multiplied together at a constant: x times y equals k. The price is the ratio of the two reserves. When I buy token A, I add B and remove A, so A gets scarcer and pricier with every unit. That is price impact: a trade that is large next to the pool pays far more than the quoted price. A small fee goes to the pool on top.
What is impermanent loss, and when does it become permanent?
Whether you can explain the main risk of providing liquidity.
LP value falls behind simply holding when prices diverge. It is locked in if you withdraw while prices are apart, and fees may or may not cover it.

If I deposit two tokens and one doubles in price against the other, arbitrage traders rebalance the pool and I end up holding less of the winner. My position is then worth about 5.7% less than if I had just held both. It is called impermanent because it shrinks if prices return, but if I withdraw at the new price it is real. The question is whether trading fees cover it.
On a lending protocol, what is a health factor, and what happens when it drops below 1?
Your grasp of overcollateralized lending and how liquidations work.
Collateral weighted by its liquidation threshold, divided by debt. Below 1, liquidators repay part of the debt and take collateral at a discount.

Borrowing is overcollateralized: I lock more value than I borrow. The health factor is my collateral value times its liquidation threshold, divided by my debt. If prices move and it falls below 1, anyone can repay part of my loan and take some of my collateral plus a bonus. I tell users to keep a wide buffer and to watch the collateral price, not just the debt.
Why do borrowing rates on a lending pool jump sharply when most of the deposits are borrowed?
Whether you understand utilization-based interest rate models.
Rates follow utilization, with a steep slope above a target point so lenders can still withdraw and borrowers are pushed to repay.

Utilization is the share of deposits that is lent out. Most pools raise rates gently up to a target, often called the kink, then steeply above it. If the pool hit 100%, lenders could not withdraw because the cash is out on loan. The steep rate draws in new deposits and makes borrowers repay, which puts liquidity back. I watch that point on any pool I add funds to.
A user's large swap filled at a much worse price than quoted. What likely happened, and how do you prevent it next time?
Whether you know how sandwich attacks and slippage settings affect real users.
Names price impact and sandwiching by bots reading the public mempool, and gives fixes: tighter slippage, private submission, smaller orders.

Two things are likely. The trade was large next to the pool depth, so price impact was high, and a bot saw it in the public mempool, bought just before and sold just after, taking the gap up to the slippage limit. I would check the block for that pattern. Next time: a tight slippage tolerance, a private transaction route, and splitting the order.
A user asks why their wallet wants an unlimited token approval before a swap. What do you tell them?
How you explain approval risk, one of the most common ways users lose funds.
An approval lets a contract move your tokens later and stays open, so approve only what is needed, check the spender and revoke old approvals.

An approval lets the contract move that token from your wallet, not just now but until you change it. Unlimited saves fees on future trades, but if the contract is hacked or the site is fake, the attacker can take the whole balance. I suggest approving only the amount needed, checking the spender address, and revoking old approvals by setting them back to zero.
How can a flash loan be used to attack a protocol that reads prices from one DEX pool?
Whether you understand oracle manipulation and how to defend against it.
Borrow big with no collateral in one transaction, skew a thin pool's spot price, exploit the target, repay. Fix with time-weighted or aggregated oracles.

A flash loan is borrowed and repaid in one transaction, or the whole transaction reverts. The attacker borrows a large sum, swaps it into a thin pool to skew the price, uses that fake price to borrow too much from the target, then repays in the same transaction. The fix: never trust one pool's spot price. Use a time-weighted average or an oracle that aggregates many sources.
A protocol's contracts are upgradeable by an admin key. How do you judge that risk?
How you weigh upgradeability and admin control when assessing a protocol.
Who holds the key, single wallet or multisig, whether a timelock gives users time to exit, and what the admin can change alone.

Upgradeable means a proxy points to logic the admin can swap, so the code reviewed today may not be the code tomorrow. I check who holds the key: one wallet is a red flag, a multisig with known signers is better. I want a timelock so users see changes and can exit first, and I check what the admin can do alone, such as pause, change fees or move funds.
A governance proposal wants to raise the loan-to-value on a volatile, thinly traded token. How do you evaluate it?
Your judgement on collateral risk settings for a lending market.
Looks at liquidity for liquidations, volatility, oracle quality and holder concentration, and offers caps or a smaller step, not just yes or no.

The key question is whether liquidators could sell that collateral in a crash without the price collapsing. I would check how much can be sold on-chain within a few percent of price impact, recent drawdowns, how robust the oracle is, and whether a few wallets hold most of the supply. If it is borderline, I would propose a supply cap and a small step up instead.
You see funds draining from a pool you help run, in what looks like a live exploit. What do you do in the first hour?
How you handle an incident under pressure without making it worse.
Confirms fast, follows the runbook, uses pause powers if they exist, saves evidence, and warns users without exposing the bug.

I confirm it is real from the transactions, then alert the team in our private incident channel and follow the runbook. If we have a pause role, the signers use it to stop further loss. I save transaction hashes and attacker addresses. We tell users to stop depositing, without describing the bug, since copycats read posts too. Root cause comes after the bleeding stops.
What is a liquidation bonus, and what goes wrong if it is set too low or too high?
Whether you understand what makes liquidators act and what it costs borrowers.
Too low and nobody liquidates in a crash. Too high and borrowers lose more, and a liquidation can even leave the position less healthy.

It is the discount a liquidator gets on the collateral they seize when they repay debt. It must cover gas, slippage when they sell, and price moves while they act. Too low and positions sit unliquidated in a crash. Too high and borrowers pay too much, and if the liquidation threshold times one plus the bonus reaches 100%, each liquidation leaves the position worse.
How do you protect a lending protocol from a stale or wrong price feed?
Your grasp of oracle design beyond picking a provider.
Staleness checks against the feed's heartbeat, sanity checks, a second source, and a pause instead of acting on a bad number.

Push feeds update when the price moves past a deviation threshold or when a heartbeat timer runs out. So I read the update time and reject a price older than the heartbeat plus a margin. I also check the price is positive and compare it with a second source. If they disagree too much, new borrowing pauses rather than running on a bad number.
Your dashboard shows a protocol's TVL doubled overnight, but deposits look normal. Where do you look?
How you debug on-chain data before you trust it.
The usual causes in turn: a mispriced thin token, a decimals error, double counting of receipt tokens, then a check of raw balances on-chain.

First the prices: one thin token with a bad or manipulated price can inflate the total. Then decimals: a token with 18 decimals read as if it had 6 looks a trillion times bigger. Then double counting, where a receipt token from one protocol is deposited in another and counted twice. Finally I compare a few raw on-chain balances with the dashboard.
Your indexer writes swaps to a database as each block arrives. How do you handle a chain reorganization?
Whether your on-chain data stays correct when recent blocks are replaced.
Store block hashes, detect a parent hash mismatch, roll back to the last matching block, and use only finalized blocks for anything that moves money.

I save each block's number and hash with the rows from it. When a new block's parent hash does not match what I stored, I walk back to the last block that still matches, delete everything after it and re-index. Reports that move money, like reward payouts, only use blocks the chain has marked finalized, not just the latest head.
In a vault's share math, which way should each calculation round, and why?
Your care with integer math, where small rounding errors can be farmed.
Always in favor of the vault: round down what the user receives, round up what the user must give.

Contract math uses integers, so every division rounds. On deposit and redeem I round down the shares or assets the user gets. On mint and withdraw I round up the assets or shares the user must hand over. If any path rounds toward the user, someone can loop tiny deposits and withdrawals and drain the vault a few wei at a time.
A team wants to accept a fee-on-transfer token and a rebasing token as collateral. What breaks?
Whether you know token behaviors that break standard accounting.
The amount received differs from the amount sent, and rebasing changes balances with no transfer; measure balances or use a wrapped version.

With a fee-on-transfer token, the contract credits the full amount but receives less, so the last people to withdraw find the pool short. I would check the balance before and after each transfer and credit the difference. A rebasing token changes balances with no transfer at all, so stored amounts drift. The usual fix is to accept only a non-rebasing wrapped version.
How do you decide the supply cap for a collateral token on a lending market?
How you turn liquidity analysis into a risk parameter.
Sized so the largest realistic liquidation can be sold on-chain within the liquidation bonus, using depth after a price drop, not calm-day depth.

I estimate how much collateral would need selling after a sharp drop, then measure the slippage of selling that amount through DEX routes. If slippage eats the liquidation bonus, liquidators stop. With concentrated liquidity, depth can vanish once price leaves the active ranges, so I test after a drop. I review the cap as depth changes.
Walk me through the first-depositor attack on a new token vault and how you prevent it.
Your depth in vault security beyond the well-known bugs.
A tiny first deposit, a large direct donation, the next user's shares rounding to zero; fixed with virtual shares, dead shares or a seed deposit.

The attacker deposits 1 wei and gets one share, then sends a large amount straight to the vault without minting. One share is now worth a lot, so the next deposit rounds down to zero shares and the attacker redeems it. Fixes: a virtual offset of shares and assets in the math, burning a few first shares at launch, or a minimum-shares-out check.
For a liquid staking token borrowed against its base asset, would you price it with the market price or the protocol's exchange rate?
Your judgement on correlated-asset risk and oracle choice.
Names the trade-off: the exchange rate avoids liquidations on a brief discount but hides a real depeg; the market price is honest but can cascade.

The exchange rate is smooth, so a short market discount during a withdrawal queue does not liquidate everyone at high LTV. But if the token truly loses value, the protocol keeps lending against a price nobody pays and builds bad debt. I would use it only with caps sized to on-chain exit liquidity and a guard that pauses if the market discount gets deep.
After a crash, some positions on your lending market have more debt than collateral. How should the protocol handle it?
How you handle insolvency honestly without starting a run.
Measure it, stop it growing, cover it from reserves or a backstop where possible, and tell depositors the facts fast.

First I measure the shortfall per asset and stop it growing: freeze new borrowing of the affected asset and set its LTV to zero. Then I cover it in order: protocol reserves, then a backstop fund if one exists, and only then a loss spread across suppliers. I publish the numbers early, because depositors who suspect hidden losses race to withdraw.

delivery-driver.heading: Delivery driver and courier questions
qs: What do you check on the vehicle before you start a route?
Whether you inspect the vehicle as a habit, not only when something feels wrong.
A quick, ordered walk-around: tires, lights, mirrors, brakes, fluids and damage, with problems reported before leaving the lot.

I walk around the van: tires for pressure and cuts, all lights and signals, mirrors, wipers and any new dents, which I photograph. Inside I check brakes, horn, fuel or charge and warning lights. If something is unsafe, like a brake light out, I report it and don't take the van out until it's fixed or swapped.
How do you load your vehicle so the route runs smoothly?
How you organize the cargo area to save time and avoid damage.
Loading in stop order or by zones, heavy items low, fragile items on top, and the load secured so nothing shifts.

I load so the first stops are nearest the door and the last ones deep in the back, grouped by street. Heavy boxes go low and against the walls, fragile ones on top. I strap or brace the load so it doesn't slide on turns. At each stop I can grab the right package in seconds instead of digging.
What makes a good proof-of-delivery photo?
Your care in protecting the package, and yourself, from “not received” claims.
The package clearly visible with the door or house number in the frame, placed out of sight from the street and out of the weather.

The photo shows the package and enough of the door, mat or house number to prove the address. I put the package somewhere hidden from the street and dry, like behind a planter or inside a porch, and follow any delivery note. A blurry photo of a box on concrete proves nothing if the customer calls.
A package needs a signature and nobody answers the door. What do you do?
Whether you follow delivery rules instead of taking shortcuts.
Never signing for the customer or leaving it anyway; leaving a notice and following the company process for a reattempt or pickup.

I knock, ring and wait a reasonable moment, and call or text if the app allows it. If no one comes, I don't leave it and I never sign for them. I scan it as an attempt, leave a notice saying what happens next, like a reattempt or a pickup location, and bring the package back with me.
You pull up to a house and there's a loose dog in the yard. What do you do?
How you handle a common hazard without taking risks.
Staying in the vehicle, not entering a yard with a loose dog, contacting the customer or following policy, and flagging the address.

I stay in the van and honk or call the customer to see if they can secure the dog. If not, I don't go in. I mark the stop as unsafe to attempt with a note about the dog, and add an alert for the address so the next driver knows. If a dog comes at me, I keep the package between us and back away slowly. I never run.
How do you keep a food order safe and in good shape from the restaurant to the door?
Your handling of hot and cold food and of the customer's trust.
Insulated bags, hot and cold kept apart, drinks upright, sealed bags never opened, and going straight to the customer.

I use insulated bags, one for hot and one for cold, and a drink carrier so cups stay upright. I check the order number and that the bag is sealed, and I never open it. I go straight to the customer unless the app has batched orders. Food that spilled or sat too long gets reported, not handed over as if nothing happened.
How do you back up a van safely in a tight spot?
Whether you know the habits that prevent the most common delivery vehicle crashes.
Avoiding backing when possible, getting out to look first, using mirrors and camera, going slowly, and using a spotter when one is available.

First I try not to back at all: I plan to pull through, or back in when I arrive so I can pull forward when I leave. If I must back, I get out and walk around to check for kids, poles and low branches. Then I back slowly using both mirrors and the camera, and stop and look again if I'm unsure.
You're running an hour behind and dispatch is pushing you to finish. How do you handle it?
Whether you keep safety above speed under pressure.
No speeding or phone use while driving; telling dispatch early with a realistic estimate so they can reassign stops or warn customers.

I don't speed, run yellows or text at the wheel to catch up. At my next stop I tell dispatch where I am, how many stops are left and a real finish time. They can move some stops to another driver or tell customers. Then I tighten what I safely can: quicker scans, parking closer, fewer trips back to the van.
Two stops later, you realize you left a package at the wrong address. What do you do?
How you own and fix a mistake.
Going back to retrieve it if possible, delivering it correctly, and reporting honestly to dispatch rather than hiding it.

I tell dispatch right away and go back if it's close. I knock, explain politely, get the package back, then deliver it to the right house and update the scan. If no one is home at the wrong address, I report it with the address and photo so the company can follow up. Hiding it only turns a small error into a lost package claim.
You hit a parked car while making deliveries. It's minor. Walk me through what you do.
Whether you know your legal and company duties after a crash.
Stopping, checking for injuries, finding the owner or leaving contact details, calling police when required, documenting, and reporting to the company at once.

I stop, put on hazards and make sure nobody is hurt. I try to find the owner; if I can't, I leave a note with my name, contact details and what happened where it can be seen, and call police if local rules require it. I photograph both vehicles and the scene, then report it to my supervisor right away. I never just drive off, even for a scratch.
Your routing app gives you a stop order that doesn't make sense to you. When do you follow it and when do you change it?
Whether you can judge a route yourself instead of just following the screen.
Follows the app by default, changes it for time windows, left turns, school zones or closures, and keeps dispatch informed.

I follow it unless I know something it doesn't. I'll move stops for a promised delivery window, a school zone at dismissal or a road closure. I also group stops to cut left turns across traffic. If my change affects promised times, I tell dispatch first.
You're delivering a grocery order that includes beer. What do you check at the door?
Whether you know the rules for handing over age-restricted items.
Checks a valid ID that matches the person, confirms 21 or older and sober, and returns the alcohol per policy if anything fails.

I ask for a valid photo ID, check the photo matches the person and the birth date shows 21 or older. If there's no ID, the person is under 21 or clearly drunk, I don't hand over the alcohol. I deliver the rest of the order and return the beer the way the company says.
Most delivery injuries happen outside the vehicle, not on the road. How do you protect yourself on a 150-stop day?
How you avoid strains, slips and falls over hundreds of repetitive moves.
Concrete habits: three points of contact, no jumping, lifting close to the body, a hand truck for heavy loads, eyes on footing.

I use three points of contact getting in and out and never jump off the cargo floor. I lift with my legs and keep boxes close. Anything heavy or awkward goes on the hand truck. I carry one load I can see over, and I watch steps, ice and wet leaves.
How do you handle your phone and the navigation app while you're driving?
Whether you keep your eyes and hands free while the vehicle is moving.
Sets up the route before moving, keeps the phone mounted, no typing or reading while driving, pulls over to deal with messages.

I load the next stops while parked and mount the phone where I see it without looking down. Once I'm moving I don't type, scroll or read messages. Many states ban handheld use anyway. If dispatch texts, I answer at the next stop or pull over somewhere safe.
It's 98 degrees and your van has no air conditioning in the back. How do you get through the route?
Whether you know the signs of heat illness and act on them.
Steady water, breaks in shade, knows heat exhaustion signs and treats confusion or collapse as heat stroke needing 911.

I start well hydrated and drink water often, not only when thirsty. I rest in shade or the AC cab when I need to. If I feel dizzy, sick or a bad headache, I stop, cool down and call dispatch. Confusion or hot skin is heat stroke, and that means calling 911.
Halfway through your route, the oil pressure warning light comes on. What do you do?
Whether you put the vehicle and safety ahead of finishing the route.
Pulls over safely and soon, shuts off the engine, reports to fleet or dispatch, and does not keep driving to finish.

I signal, pull over somewhere safe and turn off the engine, because low oil pressure can destroy it in minutes. I call dispatch or fleet maintenance and tell them exactly what light came on and where I am. I don't drive on to finish stops; they'll send help or a swap van.
You pick up a box that is wet and smells like chemicals. What do you do?
How you deal with a possible hazardous material leak.
Doesn't touch or sniff further, moves away, ventilates, isolates the package, reports it and does not deliver it.

I put it down carefully, step back and don't open it or touch the wet spot. I open the doors to air out the van and wash my hands if I touched it. I call dispatch to report it and follow their hazmat instructions. That box doesn't get delivered, and if anyone feels sick I call 911.
A customer calls dispatch saying their package never arrived, but your photo shows it on their porch. How do you help?
How you handle a missing-package claim without arguing or covering for yourself.
Gives facts, not blame: photo, time, location. Checks for a wrong address, follows the claim process, no promises outside policy.

I first check that the photo and GPS match their address and not a neighbor's. I give dispatch the time and exact spot I left it. If I'm nearby, I offer to look around the building or nearby doors. I don't accuse anyone of lying; theft happens, and the claims process handles the rest.
If we move you from a cargo van to a box truck, when do federal DOT rules start to apply to you?
Your knowledge of when a delivery vehicle becomes a regulated commercial vehicle.
Knows 10,001 lbs GVWR in interstate commerce brings DOT rules like a medical card and hours of service; a CDL starts at 26,001 lbs.

It goes by the GVWR, the maximum loaded weight on the door sticker, not what I'm carrying. At 10,001 pounds or more in interstate commerce, I need a DOT medical card and must follow hours-of-service and inspection rules. A CDL is needed when the GVWR is 26,001 pounds or more.
If you deliver as an independent contractor in your own car, what do you set up beyond the driving itself?
Whether you understand the insurance and tax side of delivering for pay.
Checks that insurance covers paid delivery, keeps a mileage log and receipts, and sets money aside for quarterly estimated taxes.

I make sure my insurance covers delivery for pay, because many personal policies exclude it, so I add a delivery endorsement. I log every work mile with the date and purpose and keep receipts. Nobody withholds taxes for me, so I set money aside each week and pay estimated taxes every quarter.

demand-generation.heading: Demand generation manager questions
qs: What is the difference between an MQL and an SQL?
Whether you know the basic stages of the lead funnel.
An MQL meets marketing's fit and interest bar; an SQL has been accepted by sales as worth working, using criteria both teams agreed on.

An MQL is a lead marketing judges ready for sales, based on fit, like company size and role, and on behavior, like a demo request or several content visits. It becomes an SQL when sales reviews it and agrees it is worth working. The handoff rules should be written down and agreed by both teams, or the numbers mean nothing.
How do you set up tracking so you know which campaign a lead came from?
Whether you can build the data that every later report depends on.
Consistent UTM tags, hidden form fields that pass them to the CRM, and campaign records set up and tested before launch, not after.

Before launch I write a naming rule for UTM tags, the labels added to links for source, medium and campaign, and I tag every link. Forms carry hidden fields that capture those values and pass them to a campaign record in the CRM. Then I test it: I submit a form myself from each link and check the record shows the right campaign.
When do you gate a piece of content behind a form, and when do you leave it open?
Your judgement on trading lead volume against reach.
Gate high-value, late-stage assets where the contact data is worth the friction; keep early education open to build reach and search traffic.

I gate things a buyer close to a decision would trade an email for: a benchmark report, an ROI calculator, a pricing guide. Blog posts and short guides stay open, because they build search traffic and trust. If I gate everything, I collect names of students and competitors, and sales stops trusting the leads. I also track how many gated leads ever become opportunities.
Walk me through how you would build a lead scoring model.
How you turn fit and behavior data into a rule sales will trust.
Starts from closed-won data, scores fit and engagement separately, adds decay and negative points, then checks the threshold against real conversion.

I start with the last year of closed deals and ask what they had in common: industry, size, job title, and actions like pricing page visits. I score fit and engagement separately, let activity points fade over time, and subtract for students or competitors. Then I back-test: do leads above the threshold convert better than those below? I review it with sales every quarter.
Your webinar had 400 sign-ups and 90 people showed up. What do you do next?
How you get value from a webinar after it ends.
Separate follow-up for attendees and no-shows, a recording sent fast, hot signals passed to sales, and a look at why the show rate was low.

Within a day, attendees get the recording, the slides and one clear next step; anyone who asked a question or stayed to the end goes to sales. The 310 no-shows get the recording too, since many sign up just for that. Then I compare the show rate with past webinars and look at reminder timing, the time slot and how far ahead people registered.
Walk me through working out how many leads you need for $2 million of new pipeline next quarter.
Whether you can plan backward from a revenue goal using funnel rates.
Works back from pipeline to opportunities to SQLs to MQLs using the company's own conversion rates, then checks timing and channel capacity.

I divide by average deal size. At $40,000 that is 50 opportunities. If half of SQLs become opportunities, I need 100 SQLs; if a quarter of MQLs become SQLs, 400 MQLs. I use our own rates, not industry averages, and check timing: leads from late in the quarter may not become pipeline in time. Then I split the 400 across channels by past cost and yield.
Last-touch attribution says paid search drives most deals, and the CEO wants to cut events. How do you respond?
How you read attribution models without being fooled by them.
Explains that last-touch credits only the final click, shows the earlier touches on won deals, and proposes a measured cut instead of a blind one.

Last-touch gives all the credit to the final step, and buyers often search our name right before a demo request because they met us somewhere else first. I would pull won deals and show every touch: how many met us at an event before they searched. I would not defend events blindly either. I would cut the weakest events first and watch branded search and pipeline.
Leads are up 40% this quarter, but pipeline is flat. Where do you look?
How you diagnose a gap between volume and real results.
Checks lead quality by source, conversion at each stage, follow-up speed and routing, before calling the quarter a success.

First I break the leads down by source. Often one channel, like a giveaway or a paid content deal, added cheap names that never convert. Then I check each stage: did MQL to SQL drop, or did sales not follow up? I look at routing and time to first contact too. I would report pipeline, not lead count, and move spend away from the source that inflated the number.
Someone wants to buy a contact list and email it next week. What do you say?
Whether you know the email rules and the risk to deliverability.
Knows CAN-SPAM basics: honest headers, a postal address, a working opt-out. Warns that bought lists hurt sender reputation and may bring in other privacy laws.

In the US, CAN-SPAM does not ban emailing a bought list, but each email needs honest sender and subject lines, our postal address and an unsubscribe we honor within 10 business days. The bigger risk is deliverability: bad addresses and spam traps can get our domain blocked for every email we send. If it has EU contacts, GDPR applies. I would put that money into ways people opt in.
How would you prove that a paid channel brings in pipeline we would not have gotten anyway?
Whether you can measure the real added impact of a channel, not just a correlation.
Proposes a holdout or regional test with a control group, agreed in advance, and judges it on pipeline rather than clicks.

I would run a holdout test. I pick matched regions or a random set of target accounts, turn the channel off for one group and keep it on for the other, long enough to cover our sales cycle. Then I compare pipeline per account between the groups. Any lift is what the channel really adds. I agree the success measure with finance before the test, so nobody argues about it after.
What does every marketing email need to include to follow CAN-SPAM?
Whether you know the basic US law behind every email you send.
Honest headers and subject line, a valid postal address, a clear opt-out honored within 10 business days, and knowing the sender stays responsible.

Accurate from and reply-to lines, a subject line that is not misleading, a note that it is an ad unless people opted in, our valid postal address, and a clear way to unsubscribe. Opt-outs must be honored within 10 business days, and the link has to keep working for at least 30 days after the send. Hiring an agency does not move the responsibility off us.
Why do many teams no longer trust email open rates?
Whether you know how privacy changes broke a common email metric.
Apple Mail Privacy Protection preloads images, so opens are inflated. Clicks, replies and later actions are better signals.

Since 2021, Apple Mail Privacy Protection, for users who turn it on, loads images, including the tracking pixel, whether or not the person reads the email. That makes many opens fake. I still watch opens for sudden drops that hint at deliverability trouble, but I judge emails on clicks, replies, meetings booked and pipeline.
Walk me through building a nurture track for leads who downloaded an ebook but are not ready to talk to sales.
How you move early-stage leads forward without wearing them out.
Clear entry and exit rules, content matched to the problem they showed interest in, a mix of value and soft asks, and a path to sales when behavior shows intent.

Entry is the ebook topic, so the first emails go deeper on that same problem. Over about six weeks I send four or five pieces: a checklist, a customer story, a short video, then an invite to a demo. Anyone who visits pricing or replies leaves the track and goes to sales. Customers and unsubscribes are excluded automatically.
What goes into a lead service-level agreement between marketing and sales?
Whether you can turn the handoff into rules both teams agree to.
The volume and quality marketing commits to, how fast and how often sales follows up, and what happens to leads that are rejected or ignored.

Marketing commits to a number of qualified leads a month that meet an agreed definition. Sales commits to first contact within a set time, often the same business day, and a set number of attempts. Every lead gets an outcome: accepted, rejected with a reason, or recycled. We review the report together monthly, so complaints become data.
What happens to leads that sales rejects or that go cold after a few calls?
How you keep leads from dying quietly in the database.
Required rejection reasons, a recycle status that sends leads back to nurture with scores reset, and using the reasons to fix targeting or scoring.

Rejection needs a reason from a short list: wrong fit, no budget, bad timing, bad data. Bad timing goes back to nurture with the score reset and a date to revisit. Wrong fit shows me where targeting leaks. I review the reasons monthly; once a third of rejects were students, so we changed the form and the ads.
Your email clicks fell by half overnight and you suspect your emails are landing in spam. How do you check and fix it?
Whether you can diagnose deliverability, not just write emails.
Checks authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), complaint and bounce rates and recent list changes, then rebuilds sender reputation slowly with engaged contacts.

First I confirm it with seed tests and the sender reputation dashboards that big mailbox providers offer. Then I check that SPF, DKIM and DMARC, the records that prove the mail is really ours, still pass after any IT change. I look for a recent send to an old or imported list. To recover, I mail only recently engaged contacts and add others back slowly.
Cost per lead on your paid social campaigns doubled in a month with the same budget. How do you find the cause?
How you diagnose a paid channel problem step by step.
Splits price (cost per thousand impressions) from response (click and form conversion), checks ad frequency, creative fatigue and form changes, then tests one fix at a time.

I split cost per lead into its parts: cost per thousand impressions, click rate and form conversion rate. If impression cost rose, it is the auction or a too-narrow audience. If click rate fell and frequency is high, the same people have seen the ad too often, so I rotate creative. If form conversion fell, I check the form and landing page for changes.
A content syndication vendor offers 500 leads at a low cost per lead. How do you judge whether they are worth buying?
Your judgement about cheap lead sources and their real cost.
Judges on pipeline and cost per opportunity, not cost per lead; runs a small filtered test, checks how people opted in, and nurtures before routing to sales.

I start with a small test filtered to our ideal customer and ask how each person opted in and what they saw. Those leads go to nurture first, not straight to sales, because they barely know us. After a full sales cycle I compare cost per opportunity with our other channels. Cheap leads that never become pipeline are the most expensive kind.
Leadership wants to move from counting leads to an account-based approach. What changes in how you measure success?
Whether you can measure demand by account and buying group, not by single leads.
A target account list agreed with sales, then account engagement, buying-group coverage, and opportunities and pipeline from those accounts, over a longer window.

We agree a target account list with sales first. Then I stop asking how many leads and ask how many target accounts are engaged, how many contacts we reach in each buying group, and how many become opportunities. A deal usually involves several people, so three engaged roles beat one keen contact. Reports run by quarter, since these cycles are long.
The CFO asks whether demand generation is worth what it costs. What numbers do you bring, and how do you calculate them?
How you tie marketing spend to revenue in terms finance trusts.
Sourced pipeline and closed revenue, customer acquisition cost and its payback period, with clear definitions and honest limits on attribution.

I bring pipeline and revenue from marketing-sourced deals, with win rates next to sales-sourced ones. Then customer acquisition cost: total sales and marketing spend divided by new customers. Payback is that cost divided by monthly gross profit from a new customer, so the CFO sees months to earn it back. I state the definitions up front and say what attribution cannot prove.

design-systems.heading: Design systems designer questions
qs: What is a design token, and why not just use hex values in components?
Whether you know the basic building block of a modern design system.
A named value stored once and shared by design and code, so one change reaches every product.

A token is a named design decision, like color-text-primary or space-4, stored in one place and exported to design files and code. Components point at the name, not the raw value. If the brand blue changes, we update one token instead of hunting through hundreds of screens, and design and code stay in sync.
How would you structure the color tokens for a product that serves two brands?
How you build token tiers so the system can grow without a rewrite.
