Why would you use consistent hashing instead of hash modulo the number of servers?
Your knowledge of spreading data across nodes.
With modulo, changing the node count moves almost every key. Consistent hashing moves only about one share in N, and virtual nodes even out the load.

With hash mod N, going from 10 to 11 servers changes the home of most keys, so a cache goes cold or a store has to move nearly all its data. With consistent hashing, servers and keys sit on a ring and a new server takes only the keys next to it, roughly one share in N. I give each server many points on the ring so the load spreads evenly.
Why is a node that is slow harder to deal with than one that has crashed?
Whether you understand partial failures and failure detection.
A timeout cannot tell slow from dead. Slow nodes pass simple health checks while hurting latency, so detection must use real latency and accept some false alarms.

A crashed node stops answering and health checks remove it. A slow node, say with a failing disk, still passes a simple ping but makes every request it touches slow. I check health with real work, watch latency per node, and send a backup request to another node when one is slow, accepting that we will sometimes remove a healthy node.
A node holding a lock pauses 30 seconds for garbage collection, its lease expires, and another node takes the lock. What goes wrong, and how do you prevent it?
How you reason about leases, process pauses and two nodes acting as owner.
The old holder wakes up, still believes it owns the lock and writes. Fencing tokens fix it: a rising number that storage checks, rejecting older ones.

The first node wakes up unaware that time passed and writes as if it still holds the lock, so two writers corrupt the data. Checking the lease before writing does not help, since the pause can come right after the check. I have the lock service hand out a number that rises with each grant, send it with every write, and have storage reject any lower number.
An order service must save an order and publish an "order created" event. How do you make sure one never happens without the other?
Your approach to consistency between a database and a message broker.
No dual write. A transactional outbox stores the event in the same database transaction, and a separate process publishes it at least once.

If I save and then publish, a crash in between loses the event; publish first and I may announce an order that never saved. So I write the order and an event row into an outbox table in one transaction. A separate process reads the outbox, publishes, and marks rows as sent. It can publish twice, so consumers skip event IDs they have seen.
What is the difference between linearizability and serializability?
Whether you keep apart two consistency terms that are often mixed up.
Linearizability is about single objects and real-time order. Serializability is about transactions acting as if run one at a time, in some order.

Linearizability says each read or write on an object looks instant and respects real time: once a write finishes, every later read sees it. Serializability says a set of transactions gives the same result as some one-at-a-time order, which need not match real time. Strict serializability is both.
Your service is fine at 70% CPU, but p99 latency triples at 90%. Why?
Whether you understand how queues behave near full capacity.
Waiting time grows sharply, not linearly, as utilization nears 100%. So you keep headroom and shed load before saturation.

Requests arrive in bursts. As utilization nears 100%, the queue is rarely empty, and waits grow roughly with 1/(1 - utilization). Going from 70% to 90% roughly triples that factor. I would plan capacity with headroom, cap queue length, and reject excess work early rather than let every request wait.
A page calls 100 backend servers in parallel, and each is slow on 1% of calls. How often is the page slow, and what do you do?
How you reason about tail latency when one request fans out to many servers.
About 63% of pages hit at least one slow call. Fixes include hedged requests, less fan-out and tighter tails on each server.

The chance all 100 are fast is 0.99 to the power 100, about 37%, so roughly 63% of pages wait on a slow call. I would send a backup request to another replica if the first has not answered by about the 95th percentile, then cancel the loser. I would also cut fan-out where I can. Averages hide this, so I watch p99 per server.
With three replicas, writes to two and reads from two, are reads always up to date?
Whether you know the limits of quorum reads and writes.
R+W>N makes the read and write sets overlap. Sloppy quorums, partly failed writes and concurrent writes can still give stale or inconsistent reads.

The read and write sets overlap in at least one node, so usually yes. But a write that reached only one node before failing can show up on some reads and not others. Concurrent writes need a rule to pick a winner. A sloppy quorum that writes to stand-in nodes breaks the overlap. If I need strict guarantees, I use consensus instead.
Two users edit the same record on different replicas at the same moment. Why is last-write-wins risky, and what are the alternatives?
How you handle concurrent writes in a multi-leader or leaderless system.
Last-write-wins silently drops one write and depends on clocks. Version vectors detect concurrency; the app or a CRDT then merges the writes.

Last-write-wins keeps the write with the later timestamp and throws the other away without telling anyone. Clock skew can even make the older edit win. I would track versions with version vectors so the system knows the writes were concurrent. Then either keep both and let the app merge, or use a CRDT, such as a set or counter whose merges always converge.
In two-phase commit, the coordinator crashes after every participant voted yes. What happens?
Whether you know the blocking weakness of two-phase commit.
Participants are in doubt: they cannot commit or abort alone. They hold locks until the coordinator recovers or a replicated coordinator decides.

Once a participant votes yes, it has promised to commit if told. So it cannot abort on its own, and it cannot commit, because the decision might have been abort. It waits, holding locks, until the coordinator comes back and reads its log. That is why I keep the coordinator's decision in a replicated log, for example a consensus group, and keep transactions short.
In a Raft cluster, why can't the leader just answer reads from its own state?
Whether you know how a consensus system serves reads without returning stale data.
A cut-off old leader may not know it was replaced. It must confirm leadership with a majority before reading, or rely on a lease with bounded clock drift.

A leader cut off from the others can still think it is leader while the majority elects a new one that accepts writes. Its reads would be stale. One fix is to put the read through the log. Another is to note the commit index and get a heartbeat round acknowledged by a majority before answering. Leases skip that round trip but assume clock drift stays within a known bound.
You need to grow a consensus group from three nodes to five. Why not just push the new configuration to every node at once?
Whether you understand safe membership changes in consensus groups.
Nodes switch at different times, so old and new configurations could form two separate majorities. Use joint consensus or change one node at a time.

Nodes would adopt the new config at different moments. For a while, two nodes on the old config could elect a leader with a majority of three. At the same time, three nodes on the new config could elect another with a majority of five. Raft avoids this with joint consensus, which needs majorities of both configs, or by adding one server at a time, so old and new majorities always overlap.
Why does a Raft leader not mark an entry from an earlier term as committed just because a majority has it?
Your depth on the safety rules inside a consensus protocol.
Such an entry can still be overwritten by a later leader. Raft commits by count only entries of the current term, and that commits earlier entries with them.

An entry from an old term can sit on a majority and still be replaced. A node whose log ends in a later term can win an election without that entry, and as new leader it overwrites it. So a leader counts replicas only for entries from its own term. Once one of those is on a majority, every entry before it is committed too. That is why a new leader appends a no-op entry right away.
Walk me through how you would test that a replicated key-value store really is linearizable.
How you design failure testing that finds real bugs, not just happy paths.
Run concurrent clients and inject partitions, crashes, pauses and clock skew. Record every operation, then check the history with a linearizability checker.

I would run several clients doing reads, writes and compare-and-set on a few keys. Each call's start, end and result gets logged, with timeouts marked as unknown. Meanwhile a fault injector cuts the network, kills and pauses nodes and skews clocks. Afterwards a checker searches for a valid one-at-a-time order. I also like deterministic simulation, so a failing run replays exactly.

driver-chauffeur.heading: Driver and chauffeur questions
qs: Walk me through your pre-trip inspection.
Whether you inspect the vehicle as a fixed routine, not a quick glance.
A set order covering tires, lights, brakes, fluids, mirrors and safety gear, with defects written up and not driven on.

I walk around the vehicle the same way every time: tires and lug nuts, lights and signals, mirrors, wipers, leaks underneath. Inside I check the horn, brakes, gauges, seat belts and the emergency kit. Anything wrong goes on the inspection report, and if it affects safety the vehicle stays parked until it is fixed.
How much following distance do you keep, and when do you change it?
Your grasp of space cushions and how conditions change them.
A time-based rule of at least three seconds, more for rain, night, heavy loads or larger vehicles.

I use time, not car lengths. I pick a sign, and when the car ahead passes it I count; I want at least three seconds before I reach it. In rain, fog, at night or in a heavier vehicle I add more, because it takes longer to stop. If someone cuts in, I drop back and rebuild the gap.
You are picking up an executive at the airport and the flight shows a delay. What do you do?
How you plan a pickup and keep the passenger and dispatch informed.
Tracks the flight, adjusts arrival time, agrees on a meeting point, and tells dispatch and the client of changes.

I track the flight number, not the scheduled time, so I arrive ahead of the new landing time. I text the passenger my name, car and where I will meet them. I tell dispatch about the delay so later rides can be moved. If the passenger does not appear, I call, follow our wait policy and log every attempt.
A passenger is late for a meeting and asks you to speed. How do you handle it?
Whether you keep control of safety while staying polite with a client.
A calm, respectful no, plus something useful: a better route, an updated arrival time, or calling ahead.

I would say kindly that I will get them there as fast as I safely and legally can. Then I offer what I can do: check traffic for a faster route, give an honest arrival time and suggest they message the meeting. Most passengers relax once they know the plan. Speeding risks them, me and the license I need to do the job.
You are driving a bus with passengers and come to a railroad crossing. What do you do?
Your knowledge of the federal rule for passenger vehicles at rail crossings.
Stops between 15 and 50 feet from the tracks, looks and listens both ways, then crosses without shifting gears.

I stop no closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail. I turn off the radio and fans, open the window or door to listen, and look both ways. When it is clear and there is room on the far side for the whole bus, I cross in a gear that will not need changing until I am over the tracks.
Your GPS sends your high-roof van toward an underpass with no posted height you can see. What do you do?
Whether you know your vehicle's height and refuse to guess on clearance.
Knows the vehicle height, uses routing set for it, stops short when unsure, and reroutes instead of trying.

I know my van's height, it is on a label on the dash. If I cannot confirm the clearance, I do not go under. I stop somewhere safe, check the route on a map or with dispatch and take another way. Next time I set the GPS to the vehicle's size so it avoids low bridges. A detour costs minutes; a roof strike can hurt people.
Your vehicle starts to hydroplane on a wet highway. What do you do?
Your reaction to a loss of traction, which must be learned before it happens.
Eases off the gas, keeps the wheel steady, avoids hard braking or sharp turns, then slows for conditions.

I take my foot off the gas and hold the wheel straight, steering gently only where I want to go. I do not slam the brakes or jerk the wheel. If I must brake and the vehicle has ABS, I press firmly and steadily and let it work. To prevent it, I slow down in rain, keep cruise control off and watch my tires' tread.
You took a cold medicine that says it may cause drowsiness, and your shift starts in an hour. What do you do?
Whether you treat your own fitness to drive as part of the job.
Does not drive impaired, tells the supervisor early, and knows legal medicine can still make driving unsafe.

I would call my supervisor right away and say I cannot drive safely today. Legal medicine can slow reactions just like being tired, and many employers' rules forbid driving on it. Calling early gives them time to cover my route. Next time I would ask a pharmacist for something that does not cause drowsiness before a work day.
Tell me about a near miss or mistake behind the wheel and what you changed afterward.
Whether you own errors and turn them into a lasting habit.
A real example, told without excuses, and a specific habit that came out of it.

Backing a shuttle at a hotel, I relied on mirrors and tapped a low post I could not see. No one was hurt, and I reported it the same hour. Since then I get out and look before every backing move in a tight spot, and I ask for a spotter when there is one. I also park where I can pull forward to leave when I can.
You have a minor collision in traffic with a client in the back seat. Walk me through the next 30 minutes.
How you handle an incident: safety, the law, the passenger and the report.
Stops, protects the scene, checks for injuries, calls 911 if needed, swaps info, documents, informs dispatch.

I stop, turn on hazards and check that my passenger and the other driver are okay. If anyone is hurt or the road is blocked, I call 911. If it is safe and allowed, I move out of traffic. I exchange license and insurance details, take photos and do not argue about fault. I call dispatch to send another car for my client, then write my report the same day.
How do you give a passenger a smooth ride in city traffic?
Your control of the car beyond simply getting there safely.
Looking far ahead, braking early and gently, and easing off the brake at the stop so the passenger barely feels the car move.

I look well ahead so I see the light change or the car slowing before I need to react. I lift off the gas early, brake gradually, and ease off the pedal just before the car stops so there is no jolt. I take corners slowly and avoid sudden lane changes. If the passenger is reading, they should not notice.
At a busy airport arrivals area, how do you make sure you pick up the right passenger?
Whether you verify identity in a way that protects the client.
The passenger states their name and destination; you do not read them out. A sign shows minimal information, and anything unclear goes to dispatch.

My sign shows only a last name or a code from the booking, never a company name. When someone comes up, I ask them to tell me their full name and where they are going, rather than reading it to them. If anything does not match, I call dispatch before anyone gets in the car. Picking up the wrong person is a safety problem, not just an embarrassment.
Walk me through how you plan a day with an executive who has five stops across the city.
How you prepare routes, timing and backups before the day starts.
Checks addresses, entrances and parking ahead, builds in traffic buffers, knows alternate routes and confirms the schedule with the client's office.

The night before, I confirm the schedule with the assistant and check each address on a map: the exact entrance, where I can wait and where I can park legally. I time each leg for rush hour and add a buffer. I know a second route for the worst leg. In the morning I check traffic and events again, and I arrive at the first pickup early.
You have to back a passenger van into a tight spot behind a hotel. How do you do it?
Your backing habits, where many low-speed crashes happen.
Avoids backing when possible, gets out and looks, backs slowly toward the driver side, and uses a spotter with agreed signals.

First I see if I can pull through instead. If I must back, I get out and walk around: I check behind, overhead and for people. I back toward my driver side when I can, since I see that side best. I go slowly with flashers on. If someone can spot me, we agree on hand signals, and if I lose sight of them, I stop right away.
How do you make a right turn with a bus or long van at a tight city corner?
Whether you understand off-tracking, where the rear wheels cut inside the front wheels.
Keeps the rear close to the curb, goes farther into the intersection before turning, swings wide while finishing, and never swings left first.

The rear wheels follow a tighter path than the front, so I slow down and stay close to the right curb so no car can slip in on my right. I drive farther into the intersection before I turn, then swing wide as I finish, even using part of the next lane if traffic allows. I do not swing left before turning; that opens a gap on my right for a car or bike.
Walk me through securing a passenger who rides in a wheelchair.
Your knowledge of safe wheelchair securement and respectful service.
Four tiedowns on solid frame points, not wheels or armrests, plus a lap and shoulder belt on the person, with the passenger asked how they want help.

I ask the passenger how they prefer to be helped and explain what I am doing. Once the chair faces forward in the station, I set its brakes and attach four straps, two front and two rear, to solid frame points, never to wheels or armrests, and tighten them. Then I fasten the lap belt low across the hips and the shoulder belt on the person. I check it all again before moving.
You are driving a loaded bus down a long, steep grade. How do you control your speed?
Whether you know how to prevent brake fade on a downgrade.
Picks a low gear before the descent, uses the engine or exhaust brake, and brakes in firm, short applications instead of riding the brakes.

I slow down and pick a low gear before I start down, since shifting down mid-grade is hard. I use the engine or exhaust brake if the bus has one. When speed creeps up, I brake firmly enough to feel a clear slowdown, bring it a little below my safe speed, then release. Riding the brakes lightly all the way down overheats them until they fade.
The low air pressure warning comes on while you drive a vehicle with air brakes. What do you do?
How you react to a brake system failure in progress.
Gets safely off the road while service brakes still work, before spring brakes apply on their own, then stops, checks and calls for help.

That warning means I am losing air. I signal, slow down and get to a safe spot off the road right away, while my service brakes still work. If pressure keeps dropping, the spring brakes will apply by themselves, and I do not want that in a travel lane. Once stopped, I set the parking brake, check the gauges, listen for leaks and call maintenance. I do not drive on.
During a ride, you overhear your client discussing a company deal that is not public. What do you do with that information?
Your discretion, which clients trust as much as your driving.
Keeps it to themselves: no repeating, no posting, no acting on it, and no sign they heard. Discretion is part of the job.

Nothing. I do not mention it to the client, my family, other drivers or anyone online, and I would never act on it, like buying or selling a stock. I keep my eyes on the road and do not react. If the car has a privacy partition, I offer to raise it when calls start. What happens in the back seat stays there.
Near the end of a long shift, your client asks you to add a late dinner run, and dispatch says yes. You are worn out. What do you do?
Whether you put fatigue and duty limits ahead of pleasing the client.
Checks hours-of-service limits and their own alertness, tells dispatch early if unsafe, and helps arrange a fresh driver instead of pushing on.

First I check my hours. If my job is under hours-of-service rules and the run would put me over, I cannot take it. If I am within limits but too tired to drive safely, I say so too. I call dispatch right away so they can send a fresh driver, and I tell the client politely that another driver will take them. A tired driver is a risk to everyone in the car.

ecommerce.heading: E-commerce and merchandising questions
qs: How do you calculate conversion rate, and what can that number hide?
Whether you know the core metric of the shop and its limits.
A clear formula with a stated base, plus awareness that a blended average can mislead when the traffic mix changes.

Orders divided by sessions, times 100, for the same period. I always say whether the base is sessions or users, because they give different numbers. A blended rate can hide a lot: if mobile traffic grows and mobile converts lower, the total drops even when nothing broke. So I split it by device, channel, and new versus returning visitors.
What is the difference between margin and markup?
Your grasp of the basic math behind every pricing decision.
Margin divides profit by price, markup divides it by cost, with a worked example and the cost of confusing them.

Both start from price minus cost. Margin divides that by the price; markup divides it by the cost. An item that costs us $40 and sells for $100 has a 60% margin and a 150% markup. Mixing them up is expensive: if someone asks for a 50% margin and you add 50% to cost, you end up at about a 33% margin.
What is sell-through rate, and how do you use it?
Whether you can read inventory performance and act on it in time.
Units sold over units received for a period, compared to plan, used early to drive placement or markdown decisions.

It is units sold divided by units received over a period, usually tracked weekly. If we took in 500 units and sold 200 in four weeks, that is 40%. I compare it to the plan for the season. Slow sell-through early tells me to give the item better placement, fix its page, or plan a markdown before the season ends, not after.
A product page gets plenty of traffic but very few sales. Walk me through what you check.
How you diagnose a product page that attracts visitors but does not sell.
An orderly check: stock and sizes, price, shipping cost, images, reviews, then whether the traffic source matches the product.

First the basics: is it in stock in the common sizes, is the price in line with similar items, and is the shipping cost shown early. Then the images: do they show scale and detail. Then reviews and answers to common questions. Last, where the traffic comes from; an ad promising something the page does not deliver looks like a page problem.
What do you do with the report of site searches that returned zero results?
Whether you treat onsite search data as a source of demand and fixes.
Sorts by volume, fixes wording and tagging gaps, and passes real unmet demand to buying with numbers.

It is a list of what customers want and cannot find. I sort it by volume. Some are wording gaps, like shoppers typing sweatshirt when we call it a crewneck, and I fix those with synonyms. Some are products we carry but tagged poorly. The rest are items we do not sell, and I send those to buying with the search counts as evidence of demand.
Your bestseller will sell out in about ten days and the restock is five weeks away. What do you do?
How you protect customers and spend when a key item runs short.
Confirms the date, stops paying for traffic to an empty page, adjusts placement, captures demand and offers alternatives.

I confirm the restock date with the buyer first. Then I cut paid ads pointing to the item so we do not pay for clicks on an empty page, and move it out of the top homepage spots. When it sells out, I keep the page live with a back-in-stock signup and show the closest alternatives. I would not run any promotion that speeds up the sellout.
How would you set a free shipping threshold?
How you set a pricing lever while keeping an eye on profit.
Starts from how order values are spread and the real shipping cost, tests the change, and judges it on profit, not order value alone.

I look at how orders are spread by value, not just the average, and at our real shipping cost per order. A threshold a little above where many orders cluster nudges people to add one item. I test it against the current setting and judge it on gross profit per visitor, because order value can rise while margin falls if we pay shipping on too many orders.
On a marketplace, another seller lists the same product 15% below your price. Do you match?
Your judgement on price competition when margins and brand rules are at stake.
No automatic match: checks the offer is real, margin after fees, brand price policies, and other ways to compete.

First I check whether the offer is real: in stock, same condition, a seller with a solid rating. Then I work out my margin after marketplace fees and shipping at the lower price. If the brand has a minimum advertised price policy, I follow it. Sometimes I match for a short time; sometimes I hold price, compete on delivery speed, and accept fewer sales on that item.
Conversion rate dropped 30% overnight. What do you do first?
How you work through a sudden drop without guessing.
Rules out tracking first, then site breakage by segment, then traffic mix, and raises the alarm fast if checkout is broken.

First I check the data: did a tracking tag change with last night's release, and do orders in the back end show the same drop. If orders really fell, I split by device, browser and payment method; a checkout broken on one phone type shows up fast. I place a test order myself. If the site works, I look at traffic mix, like a new campaign sending visitors who were never going to buy.
A $99 item has been live at $9.90 for three hours and orders keep coming in. What do you do?
How you contain a costly error and treat customers fairly.
Stops the error everywhere first, sizes the damage, brings options to a manager, tells customers fast, and fixes the process.

I fix the price at once and check that it has reached every channel, including marketplace feeds. Then I count the orders and the cost and bring my manager options: honor all, honor some, or cancel under our terms of sale. If we cancel, customers get a quick apology and a full refund. Afterward I add a rule that flags any price change above a set percentage.
How do you decide the default sort order on a category page?
How you manage the most valuable space in the shop.
A rule that blends sales, margin and stock, checked against data, not a fixed list or one person's taste.

I start from a score that mixes recent sales per view, margin and stock depth, so we don't push items that will sell out in two days. New lines get a boost for a set period so they can earn data. Each week I check clicks and sales by position and adjust the weights.
A shirt comes in six colors and five sizes. How do you set it up on a marketplace?
Your grasp of how listings and variants work.
One parent listing with child variants, each with its own SKU, identifier, price and stock, so traffic and reviews are pooled.

I create one parent listing and 30 child variants, one per color and size. Each child has its own SKU, product identifier, price and stock count, plus images for its color. Shoppers see one page, reviews usually add up in one place, and I can pause one sold-out size without touching the rest.
What is GMROI, and when would you use it instead of margin percentage?
Whether you judge products by the return on the money tied up in stock.
Gross margin dollars divided by average inventory at cost, used to compare items that sell at very different speeds.

GMROI is gross margin dollars for a period divided by average inventory at cost for that period. A candle with a 60% margin that sits for a year can earn less per dollar of stock than a 25% margin item that turns every month. I use it to decide where buying money goes and what to cut.
One dress sells well, but 35% of orders come back. What do you look at?
How you find the cause of returns and weigh them against sales.
Return reasons and reviews first, then fixes to the page; margin judged after returns, not before.

I read the return reasons and the reviews. If most say it runs small, I add a fit note, a measured size chart and a photo on a second model. If they say the color looks different, the images get reshot. Then I check margin after returns, shipping and handling. If it still loses money, I stop buying it.
You have 1,200 winter coats left and six weeks of season. How do you plan the markdowns?
How you clear stock while keeping as much margin as possible.
A sell-through target, a small first cut on the slowest items, weekly checks, deeper steps only when behind, and an exit plan for leftovers.

I set a target, say 90% sold by week six. I start with a modest cut on the slowest colors and sizes, not the whole line, and check sell-through every week. If we fall behind, I take the next step down. What is left at the end goes to an outlet channel or a liquidator rather than sitting in the warehouse for a year.
Finance wants to drop the bottom 20% of SKUs by sales. How do you answer?
Whether you look past one ranking before cutting the range.
Checks what slow items do for the shop: new items still ramping, repeat buyers, baskets they complete, and the cost of holding them.

I agree with the goal and check the list first. Some slow items are new and still ramping. Some are refills or spare parts that bring buyers back, or often sit in baskets with bestsellers. I cut the rest, starting with those holding the most stock at cost, and watch total category sales for a month after.
Several sellers offer the same product on a large marketplace. What decides who gets the main Add to Cart button?
Your knowledge of how marketplaces choose the featured offer.
Knows the formula is not public and names the known factors: total price, delivery speed, stock and seller performance.

Marketplaces don't publish the formula, but the factors are known: price including shipping, delivery speed and fulfillment method, having stock, and seller metrics like late shipments, cancellations and order defects. Being cheapest is not enough. I fix shipping speed and account health before I cut price.
A brand you sell has a minimum advertised price policy, and you want to promote it. What do you do?
Whether you respect supplier pricing rules and still find room to promote.
Reads the brand's actual policy, knows MAP limits the advertised price, and uses what the policy allows, such as gifts or free shipping.

I read the policy itself, since each brand writes its own. MAP limits the price we advertise, and some brands also forbid showing a lower price in the cart. Within the rules I'd use a free gift, free shipping or loyalty points if allowed, or promote other items. Breaking it can mean the brand stops selling to us.
Marketing wants to show 'Was $80, now $40' on a new line that has never sold at $80. What do you say?
Your judgement on reference prices and the rules behind them.
Says no: under the FTC pricing guides a former price must be one really offered in good faith for a reasonable time; offers honest options.

I'd say no. The FTC's guides against deceptive pricing say a 'was' price must be one we actually offered openly and in good faith for a reasonable period, and some states add their own rules. A made-up $80 is a fake discount and a legal risk. We can launch at $40 as the real price, or run an intro offer with a clear end date.
A 25% sitewide sale doubled revenue for a week. How do you decide if it worked?
Whether you measure profit and truly extra sales, not just revenue.
Compares gross profit to a normal-week baseline, counts the margin given away, and checks pull-forward and whether new buyers return.

Revenue is the wrong score. I compare gross profit with a normal week, after the 25% we gave away and the extra shipping and returns. Then I look at the weeks around it: if sales dipped after, some buyers just moved their purchase. I also check how many were new customers and whether they come back at full price.

education.heading: Teaching and education questions
qs: What makes a learning objective well written?
Whether you can write objectives that can actually be assessed.
It names what the learner will do, with an observable verb, under what conditions and to what standard. It avoids “understand” or “know”.

It says what the learner will be able to do, in a verb I can observe. “Understand fractions” is vague. “Add two fractions with unlike denominators and simplify the result” is not. If I cannot picture the task that would prove it, the objective is not done yet, and the assessment will drift.
What do you look for in a good multiple-choice question?
Your skill at writing test items that measure the skill, not test-taking tricks.
One clear stem, one correct answer, and plausible wrong options built from real mistakes. No clues such as a longer correct option.

The stem should pose the whole problem, so a learner could answer before seeing the options. Wrong options should come from real mistakes I have seen, like dropping a minus sign. I keep options similar in length, avoid “all of the above” and double negatives, and check that only one answer can be defended.
How do you build a rubric for a written assignment?
How you make grading consistent and useful to the learner.
Criteria tied to the objectives, level descriptions that are observable, and a test run on sample work before release.

I start from the objectives, usually three to five criteria, like argument, use of evidence and clarity. For each level I describe what the work looks like, not just “good” or “poor”. Then a colleague and I score a few real samples. Where we disagree, the wording is unclear, and I fix it before students see it.
How do you make an online course accessible to learners with disabilities?
Whether you build accessibility in from the start instead of patching it later.
Knows the WCAG guidelines and the basics: captions, transcripts, alt text, contrast, real headings, keyboard use, and testing with a screen reader.

I work to the WCAG guidelines, usually level AA. Videos get accurate captions, not raw auto-captions, plus a transcript. Images get alt text that says what matters, documents use real headings, and I never rely on color alone. Before launch I go through the course using only a keyboard, and again with a screen reader.
A subject matter expert hands you 80 slides and wants a 20-minute module. What do you do?
How you cut content down to what learners need to do.
Starts from what the learner must do after the module, separates need-to-know from nice-to-know, and keeps the expert on side.

I ask the expert what people should do differently after the module and which mistakes cost the most today. Then I sort the slides into need-to-know and nice-to-know. The core becomes practice and examples. The rest goes into a reference guide, so the expert sees nothing was thrown away. I review the draft with them before building.
The course data shows most learners stop in module 3. How do you find out why?
How you use learning platform data to diagnose a problem.
Finds exactly where in the module people stop, checks the item itself, and talks to learners before changing anything.

First I find the exact item where they leave: a long video, a hard quiz, a broken link. I check time on page and quiz attempts for that spot, and test it myself on a phone. Then I ask five or six learners who stopped. Once it was a 25-minute video. Split into short parts with a check after each, completion went up.
You find out a quiz went live with a wrong answer key and 200 learners have taken it. What do you do?
How you handle your own mistake when grades are at stake.
Fix the key, regrade everyone, check what the grade affected, tell learners plainly and quickly, and prevent a repeat.

I fix the key and regrade every attempt, then confirm the gradebook updated, since regrading is not always automatic. I check whether anyone was blocked from the next module or a certificate. Then I send learners a short note on what happened and that grades are fixed. Last, I add a second review of every answer key to our checklist.
How do you design online assessments when learners can look things up or use AI tools?
Whether you can protect assessment integrity without relying only on surveillance.
Tasks that need the learner's own reasoning or context, large question banks for recall, evidence of process, and clear rules on which tools are allowed.

I accept that recall questions are easy to look up, so I keep them low stakes and draw them from a large bank. For graded work I use tasks tied to the learner's own situation, ask for drafts or a short recorded explanation, and say clearly which tools are allowed. If someone can explain their work live, I trust that more than any detector.
A sales team wants to use one district's real student data in a demo for another district. What do you say?
Whether you know student privacy rules bind the people who build education products.
Knows FERPA protects student education records and that a vendor may use them only for the purpose the school authorized. Offers invented data instead.

I say no and offer an alternative. Under FERPA, records a district shares with us are for the service it contracted, not for showing to other customers. Many states add their own student privacy laws on top. I would build a demo account with invented names and realistic scores, so the demo looks just as good and no real student's records are exposed.
Learners rate a course highly, but most fail the final assessment. What do you check?
Your grasp of alignment between objectives, practice and assessment.
Checks that objectives, practice and the final test ask for the same skill at the same level, and that the test items are sound, before blaming learners.

High ratings mean they liked it, not that they learned it. I line up each objective with the activities and the exam items. Often the lessons ask learners to recognize an answer and the exam asks them to produce one. I also run an item analysis: if strong learners miss a question as often as weak ones, the item is the problem. Then I fix the practice, the test, or both.
A narrator reads the exact text that is shown on screen next to a diagram. What would you change and why?
Whether you apply research on how people learn from media.
Names the redundancy effect: narration plus a graphic beats narration, graphic and the same text on screen.

I would cut the on-screen text down to a few labels on the diagram and let the narration carry the words. When people read and listen to the same sentences while looking at a picture, attention is split and they learn less. The exception is captions, which stay available for learners who need them.
What is the difference between SCORM and xAPI, and when would you choose xAPI?
Your grasp of how learning platforms track what learners do.
SCORM reports completion, score and time inside an LMS; xAPI records statements that can come from anywhere and are kept in a learning record store.

SCORM packages a course so a learning management system (LMS) can launch it and record things like completion, score and time spent. xAPI records statements in the form actor, verb, object, such as “Maria completed the safety simulation,” and stores them in a learning record store. I would pick xAPI when learning happens outside the LMS, like in an app, a simulation or on the job.
A client wants every module built in visual, auditory and hands-on versions to match learning styles. How do you respond?
Whether you can push back on a popular myth with evidence and tact.
Knows the matching idea lacks research support and redirects the budget to what works: choosing the format the content needs.

I would say that people do have preferences, but studies that tested matching teaching to a learner's style have not found better results. Three versions would triple the cost for little gain. I would suggest choosing the format the content needs, such as a diagram for a process and practice for a skill, and spending the rest on more practice and feedback.
How would you design a six-week course so that learners still remember it three months later?
How you build lasting memory into a course, not just completion.
Spaced practice and retrieval practice built into the schedule, with feedback, rather than one big review at the end.

I would bring key ideas back several times with growing gaps, for example in week 1, week 2 and week 4, instead of covering each once. Most practice would ask learners to recall from memory, through short low-stakes quizzes, not reread. Each attempt gets quick feedback. After the course, I would send a few spaced recall questions by email to keep it alive.
When do worked examples help learners, and when do they stop helping?
Your depth on how guidance should change as learners gain skill.
Worked examples help novices; for more skilled learners they add load, so guidance should fade. This is the expertise reversal effect.

For beginners, studying a fully solved problem frees their memory to see the steps. As they gain skill, the same examples become extra reading that can slow them down; this is called the expertise reversal effect. So I fade them: a full example, then one with steps missing for the learner to fill in, then problems on their own.
An objective says learners will troubleshoot a network outage, but the final test is 20 multiple-choice recall questions. What is wrong, and how do you fix it?
Whether you see the alignment between objectives, practice and assessment.
The test measures recall, not the skill named. A fix is a scenario or performance task, with practice in the lessons that matches it.

The test only shows that learners can recognize facts. It does not show they can troubleshoot. I would build a scenario: a simulated outage where learners pick what to check, read the results and choose a fix, scored with a checklist. Then I would check the lessons, because if learners never practiced troubleshooting, a fair test needs that practice added first.
Item analysis shows that learners with the highest total scores miss one question more often than low scorers. What do you do?
How you read item statistics and act on them.
Negative discrimination points to a wrong key, an unclear stem or a defensible distractor; review the item before trusting the scores.

A question where strong learners do worse than weak ones has negative discrimination, which usually means something is broken. First I check the key. Then I read the stem and options as a strong learner would: maybe a distractor is also defensible. I would ask an expert to review, fix or drop the item, and rescore if it counted.
Two graders scoring the same essays with your rubric often differ by two levels. How do you fix it?
How you make human scoring consistent and fair.
Calibration with anchor papers, sharper level descriptions, and checking agreement on shared essays before and during grading.

I would look at the essays where they disagree to find which criteria cause it, then rewrite those levels with observable features instead of words like “good” or “strong.” Next, a calibration session: both grade a set of anchor papers, compare, and talk through gaps. During live grading, a share of essays is double-scored so we can catch drift early.
How would you set the passing score for a certification exam?
Whether you can set a cut score you can defend, not just pick a round number.
A standard-setting method such as modified Angoff with an expert panel, built on the minimally competent candidate, then checked against data.

I would not just pick 70%. With a modified Angoff method, a panel of experts first agrees what a minimally competent candidate can do. Each expert estimates, for each item, the share of such candidates who would answer correctly. Those estimates are summed and averaged into a cut score, then reviewed against pilot data and the cost of passing someone who is not ready.
You found an error in a SCORM course that 500 learners are halfway through. How do you publish the fix?
How you change a live course without damaging learners' progress and records.
Tests in a sandbox first, knows replacing a package can reset progress, plans versions, and tells learners what changed.

First I judge how serious the error is. In many LMSs, replacing a package can reset bookmarks or completion, so I test the fix on a copy in a sandbox with test users partway through. If progress would be lost, I let current learners finish the old version with a note correcting the error, and send new enrollments to the fixed version. Then I log what changed and when.

ehs.heading: Environment, health and safety questions
qs: What is the hierarchy of controls, and how do you use it?
Whether you know the basic order for reducing a hazard.
The five levels in the right order, with PPE as the last line of defense, and a real example of going higher.

From most to least effective: eliminate the hazard, substitute something safer, engineer it out, use administrative controls like procedures and job rotation, then PPE. On a noisy grinding line I would look at a quieter process or an enclosure before handing out earplugs, because PPE only works if it is worn right every time.
How do you tell a first aid case from a recordable injury on the OSHA 300 log?
Your working knowledge of OSHA recordkeeping rules.
Knows first aid is a defined list, names what makes a case recordable, and the seven-day deadline to enter it.

First aid is on OSHA's list: bandages, cleaning a wound, cold packs, over-the-counter medicine at normal strength, flushing an eye. Stitches, a prescription, days away or restricted duty make it recordable. If a worker gets four stitches, it goes on the 300 log within seven calendar days, even if he is back at work that afternoon.
A new degreaser arrives at the plant without a safety data sheet. What do you do?
How you apply hazard communication rules in daily work.
No use until the SDS is in hand, then a check of hazards, labels and storage, and training for the users.

It stays sealed and out of use until I have the SDS from the supplier. Then I read the hazard, PPE and storage sections, check the label matches, add it to our chemical inventory and brief the people who will use it. If it is more hazardous than what it replaces, I ask whether we need it at all.
Walk me through locking out a machine for a maintenance job.
Whether you know the lockout/tagout steps well enough to audit them.
Notify, shut down, isolate all energy, personal locks, release stored energy, and verify zero energy before work.

I tell the operators, shut the machine down normally, then isolate every energy source in the written procedure: electrical, air, hydraulic, gravity. Each worker puts on a personal lock and tag. We bleed stored pressure and block parts that could drop. Then we try the start button to verify zero energy and return it to off before work begins.
Before entry into a permit-required confined space, in what order do you test the air, and why?
Your knowledge of confined space entry, where mistakes are often fatal.
Oxygen, then flammables, then toxics, with the reason, testing at several levels, and no rescue entry by the attendant.

Oxygen first, because many combustible gas sensors need enough oxygen to read correctly. Then flammable gases, then toxics like hydrogen sulfide or carbon monoxide. I test at the top, middle and bottom since gases layer, and keep monitoring during the job. The attendant stays outside and never goes in to attempt a rescue.
An investigation of a hand injury comes back with "employee was not careful" as the root cause. What do you do with it?
How you dig past blame to the real cause of an incident.
Rejects carelessness as a root cause and asks why the unsafe act made sense, then fixes the system.

I send it back. Carelessness is where the questions start. Why was his hand near the blade? Was the guard hard to use, was the job behind, had anyone shown him the push stick? In one case like this, operators cleared a jammed infeed by hand every shift. We fixed the jam and the hand injuries on that line stopped.
A production manager wants to run a machine with its guard removed to make a shipment. How do you handle it?
Whether you hold a safety line under pressure while staying useful to operations.
A firm no to running unguarded, an offer to solve the real problem, and calm escalation if needed.

I say no to running unguarded, calmly, and offer help instead. I ask what the guard is slowing down, get maintenance to look at a better guard design, and help find time elsewhere in the schedule. If he still insists, we go to the plant manager together. I would rather explain a late shipment than an amputation.
An employee is admitted to the hospital after a fall at work. What do you owe OSHA, and by when?
Your knowledge of severe injury reporting deadlines.
Inpatient hospitalization within 24 hours, death within 8, the observation-only exception, and recording it too.

If he is admitted as an inpatient for treatment, I report it to OSHA within 24 hours of learning about it; a death is 8 hours, and amputations or loss of an eye are 24 hours. A stay only for observation or tests does not count. I also check our state plan's rules, record it on the 300 log and start the investigation.
A forklift punctures a drum of hydraulic oil near a storm drain. What happens in the first hour?
How you handle an environmental release, not only a safety event.
People safe, source stopped, drain protected first, proper cleanup and disposal, and reporting per the spill plan.

People safe first, then stop the source: upright or plug the drum. Next I cover the drain or berm around it before cleaning the floor, then absorb and bag the oil for proper disposal. If any oil reached the drain or a waterway, I follow our spill plan, which includes calling the National Response Center and the state agency. Then I document everything.
An OSHA compliance officer arrives unannounced at the front gate. Walk me through the visit.
Whether you can manage an inspection professionally and protect the company's record.
Checks credentials, joins the opening conference, escorts throughout, documents the same things, and follows up.

I check credentials, call the plant manager and ask the reason for the visit in the opening conference. I walk with the inspector the whole time, take the same photos and notes, and provide the documents asked for. Employees may speak privately. If we fix a hazard on the spot, I note it. Afterward I track every closing conference item to closure.
How do you calculate TRIR and DART rates, and what do they not tell you?
Whether you know the standard injury rates and their limits.
The 200,000-hour formula done right, and the point that low rates can hide serious risk and underreporting.

TRIR is recordable cases times 200,000, divided by total hours worked; 200,000 is about 100 full-time workers for a year. DART uses only cases with days away, restricted work or a job transfer. Both lag and swing on small numbers, and a low rate says nothing about whether a fatal hazard is waiting, so I pair them with leading measures.
What is a Tier II report, and who receives it?
Your grasp of community right-to-know reporting under EPCRA.
An annual inventory of hazardous chemicals held above set amounts, due March 1, sent to the state, the local emergency planning committee and the fire department.

Under EPCRA section 312, a site that held hazardous chemicals above set amounts at any one time last year reports them by March 1: what, how much and where. It goes to the state commission, the local emergency planning committee and the local fire department. I check the inventory against purchasing records, since firefighters use it to plan a response at our site.
How do you determine the hazardous waste generator status of a site?
Whether you know how RCRA generator categories work in practice.
Counting hazardous waste generated each month, knowing the federal categories, checking stricter state rules and tracking storage time limits.

I count the hazardous waste we generate each calendar month, not what we ship. Federally, 100 kg or less is very small, over 100 and under 1,000 kg is small, and 1,000 kg or more is large; more than 1 kg of acute hazardous waste also makes a large generator. Then I check state rules, which can be stricter, and the storage time limits for our category.
How do you use a risk matrix without letting it mislead you?
How you judge risk beyond a score on a grid.
Treats fatal-potential hazards separately, admits likelihood is often a guess, and uses the score to start a discussion, not end it.

I use it to rank and to talk, not to decide alone. Likelihood is often a guess, so a rare task with fatal potential can score low and get ignored. Any hazard that could kill or maim gets controls regardless of the score. I also score with the people who do the task, since they know how often the odd case really happens.
One full-shift air sample comes back below the OSHA limit. Is the worker safe?
Your judgement in reading exposure monitoring results.
One sample is a snapshot: you look at task variation, worst-case days, similar workers and newer limits than the old OSHA PELs.

Not proven yet. One sample shows one day. I check whether that day was typical, sample more workers in the same group and include the worst-case tasks. Many OSHA PELs date from decades ago, so I also compare against NIOSH and ACGIH limits. If results sit near the limit or vary a lot, I treat the exposure as a problem and reduce it.
A worker who wears a tight-fitting respirator grows a beard and refuses to shave. What are your options?
Whether you know the facial hair rule and can find a workable answer.
No use of a tight-fitting facepiece with hair under the seal, real alternatives such as a loose-fitting PAPR, and religious or medical reasons taken seriously.

OSHA's respiratory standard does not allow a tight-fitting facepiece when facial hair sits under the seal, so he cannot wear it as is. I talk with him first; if the beard is for religious or medical reasons, HR is involved. Options are a loose-fitting powered air-purifying respirator, which needs no fit test, or a task without respirator use. He still needs medical clearance.
An annual audiogram shows a standard threshold shift. What do you do?
Whether you know the hearing conservation steps after a shift.
Written notice to the worker within 21 days, refitting and retraining on protection, a look at the noise source and a correct OSHA 300 log decision.

A shift means an average loss of 10 dB or more at 2,000, 3,000 and 4,000 Hz in either ear versus baseline. I may retest within 30 days to confirm. The worker gets written notice within 21 days, then refitting, retraining and required protection. I check the area's noise. It goes on the 300 log if hearing in that ear is also 25 dB or more above audiometric zero.
A roofing contractor on your site is working at the edge without fall protection. Whose problem is it?
Your grasp of contractor safety and OSHA's multi-employer citation policy.
Stops the work at once, knows the host can be cited as the controlling employer, and fixes the gap in prequalification and oversight.

It is mine too. Under OSHA's multi-employer citation policy, a host who controls the site can be cited along with the contractor who exposed its crew. I stop the work, have their supervisor fix it before anyone goes back up, and write it down. Then I look at why it got through: their safety plan, our prequalification and how often we check contractors at height.
The plant manager wants to pay a bonus for every month with zero recordable injuries. What do you say?
How you push back on a program that can hide injuries.
Explains the reporting risk and OSHA's rule against retaliation for reporting, and offers rewards tied to leading measures instead.

I would say it rewards silence as much as safety. If a crew loses its bonus when someone reports a cut, people stop reporting, and OSHA's recordkeeping rule bars retaliating against workers who report. I would propose rewarding near-miss reports, closed hazard fixes and completed inspections instead, and keep injury rates as something we study, not a prize.
On an ammonia refrigeration system covered by process safety management, maintenance wants to fit a different valve model because the original is backordered. Walk me through it.
Whether you can run management of change on a process safety system.
Not a replacement in kind, so a full management of change: technical review, updated documents, trained people and a pre-startup review where required.

A different model is not a replacement in kind unless it meets the same design specs, so it goes through management of change. Engineering checks pressure rating, material and the effect on relief. We update drawings and procedures, train affected operators and maintenance before startup, and if process safety information changes, do a pre-startup safety review. Only then does it go in.

electrical-engineer.heading: Electrical engineer questions
qs: Why does a decoupling capacitor need to sit close to the chip's power pin?
Whether you understand the physics behind a basic layout rule.
Names trace inductance and fast current bursts, and says the goal is a small current loop.

The chip pulls current in fast bursts, and the trace to the capacitor has inductance that resists fast changes in current. A long path means the rail dips right at the pin. I put a small ceramic cap at the power pin with short vias to the ground plane, so the loop is tiny and the cap feeds each burst locally.
How do you choose between a linear regulator and a switching regulator?
Your grasp of the basic power tradeoff: efficiency against noise.
Knows a linear part turns the voltage drop into heat, does the math, and weighs ripple against efficiency.

A linear regulator turns the drop into heat: roughly input minus output voltage, times the load current. Going from 12 V to 3.3 V at half an amp wastes over 4 W, too much for a small part. A buck converter is far more efficient but adds ripple. For small drops or a quiet analog rail I use an LDO; for big drops, a buck, sometimes with an LDO after it.
How do you size a PCB trace that carries several amps?
Whether you size copper from a method, not by habit.
Starts from current and allowed temperature rise, uses IPC-2152 data, and also checks voltage drop and vias.

I start from the current and the temperature rise I can accept, then use the IPC-2152 charts or a calculator built on them. Copper weight matters, and inner and outer layers are treated differently. On high-current paths I also check voltage drop and use pours and several vias, because one small via can become the hot spot.
You probe a switching node and see large ringing spikes. How do you know they are real?
How you separate a real signal problem from a measurement artifact.
Suspects the long ground lead first, shortens the probe loop, and compares the result.

The long ground clip makes a loop with inductance. On a fast edge it rings with the probe capacitance and picks up magnetic field, so I can see spikes that are not on the board. I swap the clip for the short spring tip and measure right across the node and its local ground. If the ringing shrinks a lot, it was the probe.
Why is it dangerous to clip a standard oscilloscope ground to a circuit powered straight from the wall?
Whether you know a common lab hazard and the safe way around it.
Explains the scope ground is earthed, names differential probes or an isolation transformer, and never defeats the safety ground.

The scope's ground clip is tied to earth through its power cord. If I clip it to a mains-referenced node, I short that node to earth, which can destroy the board or the probe and can hurt someone. I use a high-voltage differential probe, or power the unit through an isolation transformer. I never lift the scope's safety ground to make it float.
Walk me through powering up a brand-new prototype board for the first time.
Your bring-up discipline and how you protect the first boards.
Checks for shorts and orientation before power, limits current, and brings rails up one at a time.

Before power I meter each rail to ground for shorts and check the orientation of diodes, polarized caps and ICs. Then I use a bench supply with a low current limit and watch the current as I raise the voltage. If it hits the limit, I find the hot part with a thermal camera. I confirm each rail before enabling the next stage.
For the switch in a buck converter, how do you trade on-resistance against gate charge?
Your understanding of where losses come from in power electronics.
Splits conduction and switching loss, links gate charge to switching speed and frequency, and checks voltage margin.

Conduction loss is the current squared times on-resistance, scaled by the share of time the switch is on. Switching loss grows with frequency and with how long each transition takes, which depends on gate charge. Lower on-resistance usually means more gate charge. At high frequency, a part with a bit more resistance but less gate charge can run cooler overall.
Your product works on the bench but fails a radiated emissions pre-scan at one frequency. What do you do?
How you trace and fix an emissions failure step by step.
Identifies the frequency source, locates it with a near-field probe, changes one thing at a time and rescans.

First I work out what the frequency is: often a harmonic of a clock or the switching frequency. Then I use a near-field probe to find where it comes from and check whether a cable is acting as the antenna. Fixes go from cheap to costly: a ferrite or slower edges, then a broken return path, then a board change. I rescan after each change.
After a production run, you find two pins swapped on a regulator footprint you created. What do you do?
How you own a costly mistake and stop it from happening again.
Reports fast with facts, offers a rework path, fixes the root cause in the process, not just the part.

I would tell my lead the same day with the facts: which part, how many boards, and whether rework is possible. In a similar case we mounted the part on a small adapter board for the first lot and fixed the footprint in the next revision. I also added a pin-by-pin check against the datasheet to our library review.
A resistor divider scales a 24 V signal into a 3.3 V ADC input. How do you do the worst-case analysis?
Whether you design for every tolerance, not just the typical value.
Lists all error sources, uses true worst case for limits and protection, and checks the highest input against the pin rating.

I list every error: resistor tolerance, drift over temperature, the ADC reference tolerance, and the ADC offset and gain error. I push each to the extreme that hurts most and check two things: accuracy stays in spec, and the highest possible input never drives the pin past its rating. Root-sum-square is fine for typical accuracy, not for the limits.
Why is it a problem to route a fast signal trace across a slot in the ground plane?
Whether you understand where return current actually flows on a board.
Return current at high frequency follows the path under the trace. A slot makes the loop bigger, which radiates and adds crosstalk.

At high frequency the return current flows in the plane right under the trace, because that path has the lowest inductance. A slot forces it to detour around the gap, so the loop gets bigger. That adds inductance, radiates, and couples noise into nearby signals. I route over solid plane, or if a split cannot be avoided, I add a stitching capacitor right at the crossing.
Your output capacitor is a 10 µF, 6.3 V ceramic on a 5 V rail, and the ripple is twice what you calculated. What is going on?
Whether you know how real ceramic capacitors behave under DC voltage.
Names DC bias derating, knows the X7R code covers temperature only, and checks the maker's bias curve before choosing a fix.

That is a common trap. X5R and X7R ceramics lose capacitance as the DC voltage rises, and small packages lose the most. At 5 V that part may keep well under half its value. The X7R code only describes temperature behavior, not voltage. I check the maker's DC bias curve, then choose a larger package, a higher voltage rating, or more capacitors.
How do you lay out a low-value current sense resistor so the reading is accurate?
Your layout habits for precise measurement at high current.
Four-terminal Kelvin sensing: sense traces from the inner pad edges, run as a pair, so solder and copper stay out of the reading.

I use Kelvin, or four-terminal, sensing. The high current uses the main pads, and two thin sense traces leave from the inner edge of each pad and run together as a pair to the amplifier. That keeps solder and copper out of the measurement. Copper resistance changes about 0.4% per °C, so any copper in the sense path adds error that drifts with heat.
How do you estimate a regulator's junction temperature, and why can the datasheet thermal resistance mislead you?
Whether you can do a thermal estimate and know its limits.
Ambient plus power times thermal resistance, plus the warning that the datasheet value comes from a test board. Then measure on the real board.

I estimate the power loss, then junction temperature is ambient plus power times thermal resistance. The trap is that the junction-to-ambient figure comes from a standard JEDEC test board, and my board has different copper and airflow. So I treat it as a rough start, measure the case on the real board with a thermocouple or thermal camera, and use the junction-to-top value to work back.
A buck converter is fine at light load, but at full load the inductor current turns into a sharp spike. What do you suspect?
How you diagnose a magnetic component working past its limits.
Suspects inductor saturation. Compares the worst-case peak current with the hot saturation rating and also considers start-up and fault current.

The inductor is probably saturating. When the core saturates, inductance drops, so the current ramps much faster and peaks far above the design. I compare the peak current, meaning load plus half the ripple at maximum input voltage, with the saturation rating at hot temperature. I also check the current limit, because start-up and shorts can go higher.
Walk me through measuring the stability of a power supply's control loop.
Whether you can verify loop stability by measurement, not just simulation.
Inject a signal into a broken loop and read gain and phase across operating conditions. Then confirm with a load step. A phase margin of about 45° or more is a common target.

I add a small resistor between the output and the feedback divider and inject a signal across it through an isolation transformer. A frequency response analyzer reads gain and phase. I check crossover frequency, phase margin and gain margin over line, load and temperature. Then I confirm with a load step and look for ringing or slow settling.
What rules must a single-cell lithium-ion charger design follow?
Your knowledge of safe battery charging.
CC then CV at the cell's rated voltage, a taper cutoff, precharge, no charging below the low temperature limit, a protection circuit and a thermistor on the cell.

Constant current first, then constant voltage at the cell's rated charge voltage, often 4.2 V, ending when the current tapers to a set fraction. A deeply discharged cell gets a gentle precharge. No charging below the datasheet's low limit, usually 0 °C, because lithium plates on the anode. A protection circuit cuts off at overvoltage, undervoltage and overcurrent.
During an IEC 61000-4-2 ESD test, a zap to the USB connector resets your device. How do you fix the design?
How you design protection against electrostatic discharge at a connector.
A low-capacitance TVS at the connector, ahead of the chip, with a short, wide path to ground. Also checks which line actually caused the reset.

I put a low-capacitance TVS diode right at the connector, so the strike is clamped before it reaches anything else. The path goes connector, then TVS, then chip. The TVS ground needs a short, wide path to the plane and chassis, because inductance there adds voltage. I also find which line caused the reset, often the reset pin, and filter or reroute it.
Your layout designer wants to shrink the gap between primary and secondary on your isolated supply to fit the board. How do you respond?
Your judgement when space pressure meets safety isolation rules.
Says no to a guess, explains creepage and clearance, uses the safety standard's inputs, and offers ways to gain space safely.

I would not just agree. Clearance is the shortest path through air, and creepage is the path along the board surface. The safety standard, such as UL/IEC 62368-1, sets them from working voltage, pollution degree, insulation type and board material. If space is tight, a routed slot can add creepage, or a different transformer or layout can help.
Your hot-swap MOSFET fails short on a few units at plug-in, though its current rating is far above the load. What went wrong?
Whether you understand MOSFET safe operating area in linear mode.
Sees that the FET is in its linear region during inrush, checks SOA for that pulse with heat derating, and fixes the inrush or the part choice.

At plug-in the FET sits in its linear region, holding high voltage and current at once while the output capacitors charge. The DC current rating does not cover that. I check the pulse against the SOA curve, derated for heat, since those curves assume a 25 °C case. Fixes: a slower inrush ramp, less output capacitance, or a FET rated for linear mode.

electrical-technician.heading: Electrical and electronics technician questions
qs: How do you measure voltage and current with a multimeter, and what is the common mistake?
Whether you know basic meter use and the risk of leaving a lead in the amps jack.
Voltage in parallel, current in series with the lead in the amps jack, and moving the lead back afterward.

Voltage is measured across the part, in parallel, with the red lead in the volts jack. For current the meter must be in the path, so I open the circuit and put it in series with the lead in the amps jack. Then I move the lead back right away. Touching a voltage source with the lead still in the amps jack is a short through the meter and can blow its fuse.
What does a good solder joint look like, and what makes you reject one?
Your eye for joint quality on the bench.
Good wetting and a smooth concave fillet, knowing lead-free can look duller, and naming the common defects.

The solder wets both the pad and the lead and flows into a smooth, concave fillet, so I can still see the shape of the lead. Tin-lead joints are bright; lead-free joints can look duller and a bit grainy, which is normal. I reject cold or lumpy joints, solder balled on the pad, bridges, holes, and too little or too much solder.
How do you protect parts from static when you work at the bench?
Whether ESD control is a habit for you.
Grounded strap and mat, a strap check each shift, shielding bags, and knowing static damage can be invisible.

I wear a wrist strap connected to the bench ground point and test it at the start of each shift. Parts stay in shielding bags until they go on the grounded mat. I keep plastic cups and foam off the bench and hold boards by the edges. A discharge I cannot even feel can weaken a part that then fails later in the field.
Which parts on a board must go in a certain direction, and how do you check them?
Your knowledge of polarity markings, including the ones that catch people out.
Names the polarized parts, reads their markings correctly, and knows the tantalum band is the positive side.

Electrolytic and tantalum capacitors, diodes, LEDs, ICs and many connectors. On an aluminum electrolytic the stripe marks negative, but on a tantalum the band marks positive. A diode band is the cathode. ICs have a dot or notch for pin 1 that I match to the silkscreen. A reversed electrolytic can bulge or vent, so I check every polarized part before I solder.
How do you know a crimped terminal is good?
Whether you make crimps that hold, not just crimps that look done.
Right tool and die for the terminal and wire size, correct strip length, visual checks and a pull test.

I use the tool and die the terminal maker lists for that wire size and strip to the length on the spec. After crimping, the conductor shows just past the barrel, no strands stick out, and the insulation grip holds the insulation, not bare wire. I pull test samples, and I do not add solder to a crimp unless the drawing asks for it.
The build calls for 18 AWG wire and the bin only has 20 AWG. Can you use it?
Whether you understand wire gauge and stay away from unapproved substitutions.
Knows a higher AWG number is a thinner wire with less current capacity, and gets a written change instead of swapping.

No, not on my own. A higher AWG number is a thinner wire, so 20 AWG carries less current, drops more voltage over the same run, and can run hot. I would stop that harness, tell my lead, and wait for the right wire or a written change from engineering. Even a thicker wire needs approval, since it may not fit the terminal.
You must replace a part on a lead-free board and your station only has tin-lead solder. What do you do?
How you handle solder alloys and rework rules.
Does not mix alloys, gets the right solder, and adjusts heat, flux and tip for lead-free work.

I get lead-free solder before I start. Mixing alloys gives a joint nobody has qualified, and a board built to be lead-free, for example to meet RoHS rules for export, would no longer comply. Lead-free solder melts hotter, so I set the iron for it, use fresh flux, and keep a separate tip for lead-free work.
A new board pulls far more current than it should on first power-up. Walk me through what you do.
Your method for finding a short without destroying the board.
Current-limited supply, power-off checks first, then locating the hot spot safely; names the usual causes.

I cut power and switch to a bench supply with the current limit set low. With power off I look for solder bridges, reversed parts and wrong values, then measure resistance between the rails. If it is a hard short, I power it at the limit and find the part that heats up with a thermal camera or freeze spray. Often it is a reversed capacitor or a bridge under an IC.
You learn a part went in backwards on 20 boards you built, and some are already in test. What do you do?
How you own a mistake and contain it before it spreads.
Stops, reports at once, holds every affected board, reworks and retests, and fixes the cause.

I stop building and tell my lead right away, with the serial numbers. All 20 boards are tagged and held, including the ones in test, so nobody powers them again. I rework each one per the rework instruction and retest it fully, since the reversed part may have damaged others. Then I find the cause, such as an unclear marking, and fix it.
Why is the ground clip on a scope probe dangerous on a mains-powered circuit, and how do you measure safely?
Whether you know the hidden earth path in a bench scope.
The clip is tied to earth; clipping it to a non-earth point is a short. Uses a differential probe or isolation transformer.

On a normal bench scope the probe ground clip is connected to earth through the power cord. If I clip it to a point that is not at earth, like the primary side of an offline supply, I make a short that can destroy the probe and the board. I use a differential probe, or power the unit through an isolation transformer. I never defeat the scope's ground pin.
On a multi-sheet schematic, how do you follow a signal that runs off one page and onto another?
Whether you can read a full schematic set, not just one page.
Uses net names, off-page connectors and sheet references, then confirms on the board by reference designator and a continuity check.

I find the off-page connector or net label where the line ends. The same net name means the same wire, even with no line drawn. Many drawings print the sheet and zone where it continues. Then I find the parts by reference designator, like R12 or U4, on the assembly drawing and confirm with a continuity check on the board, power off.
How do you check a diode with a meter, and what readings tell you it is bad?
Your basic component testing beyond voltage and resistance.
Diode mode, power off: a forward drop one way and OL the other. Near zero both ways is shorted, OL both ways is open.

I use diode mode with power off. Red on the anode and black on the cathode, a good silicon diode reads roughly 0.5 to 0.7 volts; reversed it shows OL. Near zero both ways means shorted, OL both ways means open. A Schottky reads lower. If the reading looks odd, I lift one leg, since parts in parallel can fool the meter.
A resistor marked 4.7k measures 3.2k in the circuit. Is it bad?
Whether you know why in-circuit readings can mislead you.
Not necessarily: parallel paths only lower a reading. Power off, caps drained, lift a lead before condemning it. A reading well above value does point to a fault.

Not yet. Other parts sit in parallel with it in the circuit, and parallel paths can only pull the reading down. I make sure power is off and the caps are drained, then lift one end and measure it alone. If it reads 4.7k within tolerance, it is fine. A reading well above the marked value is different: that does point to a bad or cracked part.
What is the difference between no-clean and water-soluble flux, and when must you clean the board?
Your knowledge of flux and what residue does to a board.
Water-soluble residue is corrosive and must be washed off soon. No-clean can often stay, but not before coating or when the drawing says to clean.

Water-soluble flux is very active, and its residue is corrosive and can conduct, so the board must be washed soon after soldering, usually with deionized water. No-clean leaves a small, mostly harmless residue, so it often stays. I still clean it when the drawing says so, before conformal coating, or near high-impedance circuits. I never switch flux types without checking the process sheet.
Why does a harness drawing call for some wires to be twisted together?
