Two weeks out, registrations are at 60% of target and you have a food and beverage minimum with the hotel. What do you do?
Your judgement when numbers fall short of a contract commitment.
Tell stakeholders early with the gap in dollars, push what is converting, and move real value into the minimum instead of paying for nothing.

I tell my manager the same day, with the gap in dollars. I push the channels that are converting and check whether late sign-ups are normal for this event. The minimum is a spend figure, so I move value into it: a better reception, coffee for an extra session, meals for staff and speakers. Paying the shortfall for nothing is the worst outcome.
Tell me about an event detail you got wrong and how you fixed it.
Whether you own mistakes and change your process afterward.
A specific error, a quick fix on the day, and a lasting change to a checklist or process.

At a 150-person meetup I gave the caterer a count from early registrations and forgot to update it. We ran out of lunch with 30 people in line. I had sandwiches from a nearby deli within the hour and apologized from the stage. Now my checklist has a final-count date tied to the caterer's deadline, and I recheck registrations that morning.
You have three catering quotes for the same menu. How do you compare them fairly?
Whether you can read past the headline price on food and beverage quotes.
You break each quote into base price, service charge, tax and minimums, then compare the true per-person cost at the same guest count.

I put all three on one sheet at the same guest count. The menu price is only the start. I add the service charge, then tax, and check whether tax applies to the service charge too, since that varies by state. I also check minimums, staffing fees, overtime rules and the guarantee deadline. The cheapest menu price often ends up in the middle.
What do you get from a supplier before they set foot in the venue?
Whether you manage supplier risk on paper, not just on trust.
A signed contract with scope and times, a certificate of insurance that meets the venue's requirements, and load-in details with on-site contacts.

I need a signed agreement listing exactly what they deliver, when, and the cancellation terms. I also need a certificate of insurance with the limits the venue asks for, naming us and the venue as additional insureds when required. Venues often refuse entry without it, so I collect it weeks ahead, along with their load-in time, dock and the site lead's cell number.
How do you make a conference work for attendees with disabilities?
Whether accessibility is built into your planning, not handled after someone complains.
You ask at registration, check physical access on site, and plan captioning, interpreters, seating and stage access ahead of time.

I add a question on the registration form asking what people need, with a named contact. On the site visit I check step-free routes, accessible restrooms, a ramp to the stage and seating with clear sightlines. I book live captioning for main sessions and sign language interpreters when requested, and I send slides early to anyone using a screen reader.
An exhibitor tells you a company called offering cheaper rooms at the show hotel. What do you tell them?
Whether you know the housing scams that target exhibitors.
You recognize a likely housing pirate, point exhibitors to official booking only, and alert all exhibitors and the hotel.

That is very likely a housing pirate, a company posing as official housing. Some take deposits for rooms that do not exist; others book outside our block, which hurts our attrition. I tell them to book only through the link on our official site. Then I email every exhibitor naming our one official housing provider, and I let the hotel know.
Walk me through the emergency plan for a two-day conference at a convention center.
How you prepare for medical calls, evacuations and severe weather before they happen.
You build on the venue's plan with its security team, know exits and AED locations, assign staff roles, and have a fast way to reach attendees.

I start from the venue's emergency plan and meet their security lead. I note exits, assembly points, first aid and AED locations, and who calls 911. Each staff member gets a role. For a medical call, we call 911, send someone to meet responders at the door and clear space. I set up text alerts to attendees and write the stage announcements in advance.
The client wants an open bar at the evening reception. How do you manage the risk?
Whether you understand host liability for alcohol and how to reduce it.
Licensed bartenders who check IDs, limits on service, real food, a bar that closes before the end, and confirmed liquor liability coverage.

I use the venue's or caterer's licensed bartenders, who check IDs and can refuse service. I prefer drink tickets or a timed bar to an unlimited one, serve real food and keep non-alcoholic choices visible. The bar closes 30 to 45 minutes before the end. I confirm liquor liability coverage and share rideshare or shuttle options so no one needs to drive.
When you negotiate a hotel contract, how do you handle the cancellation and force majeure clauses?
How you protect the organization in the clauses that cost the most when things go wrong.
A sliding cancellation scale tied to dates, credit for resold space, and a mutual force majeure clause that lists the events it covers.

For cancellation I want a sliding scale: low damages far out, rising as the date nears, based on the hotel's lost profit rather than full revenue, with credit for rooms and space they resell. Force majeure must be mutual and list what counts, such as severe weather, government orders or outbreaks that stop travel. I add a rebooking option, and our lawyer reviews the final draft.
Three months out, leadership cuts your budget by 25%. How do you decide what goes?
How you protect the event's goal when the money shrinks.
You start from the goal, separate signed from unsigned spend, cut what attendees notice least, and give leadership clear trade-offs.

First I list what is already contracted and what each cancellation would cost, because cutting signed items can save nothing. Then I rank the rest against the goal. If the goal is leads, content and networking stay; I trim décor, swag, a second reception or premium AV. I bring leadership two options with what each one loses, so the decision is theirs and on record.
The venue's final bill is $18,000 over what you expected. How do you handle it?
How you reconcile a master bill and dispute charges with evidence.
A line-by-line check against the contract, signed BEOs and daily bills, disputing in writing only what you can document, and paying the rest on time.

I ask for the itemized master account and go line by line against the contract, the signed BEOs and the daily bills I reviewed on site. Once, $11,000 was a coffee break charged twice and an AV package we had canceled in writing. I sent a written list with copies, paid the undisputed part on time, and the rest was credited within two weeks.
How do you show leadership that a conference was worth what it cost?
Whether you measure events against business goals, not just attendance.
Measures agreed before booking, tracked from registration into the sales system, reported as cost per result next to attendee feedback.

I agree on the measures with leadership before we book anything, say qualified leads, meetings held and sales pipeline from attendees. Registration and badge scans go into our customer database so sales can follow those people for six months. Afterward I report cost per attendee and cost per qualified lead next to survey scores, and I say plainly what did not work.

executive-assistant.heading: Administrative and executive assistant questions
qs: You need a weekly call with people in New York, London and Singapore. How do you pick the time?
Whether you can handle time zones and daylight saving across regions.
Looks for overlapping work hours, rotates the bad slot fairly, and knows the US and Europe change clocks on different dates.

I list each city's working hours in one time zone and look for overlap. With these three cities there is no slot that suits everyone, so I rotate who takes the early or late call. The US and Europe change clocks on different weekends, and Singapore does not change at all. So I check the invite again in March and in the fall.
Walk me through how you prepare your executive for a full day of meetings.
How you prepare meetings so your executive walks in ready.
A short brief for each meeting: who, why, what the other side wants, history and documents, sent ahead with all logistics.

The afternoon before, I send one document for the whole day. For each meeting it lists the time, room or link, who attends and their titles, the purpose, what the other side wants, notes from our last contact, and attachments. I flag anything that needs her decision and leave buffer time between rooms. If a pre-read is missing, I chase it by noon.
Two vice presidents both want the only open hour on your executive's calendar this week. How do you decide?
Your judgment in setting priorities on someone else's calendar.
Uses the executive's stated priorities and deadlines, offers alternatives, and escalates only a real tie, without playing favorites.

I ask each of them what the meeting is for and when the decision is due. If one is tied to a deadline or a priority my executive named this quarter, that one gets the hour. I offer the other a shorter slot, a call during her commute, or the first opening next week. If both are truly urgent, I put the choice to her in one line.
What do you check before booking your executive's first trip to a new country?
Whether you know what can stop a traveler at the border.
Passport validity and blank pages, visa or entry requirements, the State Department travel advisory, and local holidays.

I start with the State Department's page for that country. It lists how long the passport must stay valid, how many blank pages are needed, and whether a visa is required. Some visas take weeks, so I check this before booking anything. I also read the travel advisory, look at local holidays and weekend days, and make sure her phone plan works there.
Your executive lost the receipt for a client dinner. How do you handle the expense report?
Whether you follow expense policy when paperwork is missing.
Tries to get a copy first, then uses the company's missing-receipt process with full details. Never guesses or recreates a receipt.

First I ask the restaurant to email a copy of the itemized bill, and most can. If that fails, I use our missing-receipt form: date, place, amount, guests and business purpose, signed by her, with the card statement line attached. I never recreate a receipt. If the policy limits how often that form can be used, I tell her before I submit.
Your executive's flight is canceled at 9 p.m. and she must be in Chicago for an 8 a.m. meeting. What do you do?
How you solve a travel problem under time pressure.
Works several options at once, protects the meeting, keeps the executive and the hosts informed, and fixes the hotel and car.

I call the airline or our travel agency while I check other airlines and nearby airports online, because the phone line will be slow. If the first morning flight lands too late, I look at a late flight tonight or a drive. Once she is booked, I move the hotel and car, text her the plan, and warn the Chicago host that she may need to start by video.
After a leadership meeting, how do you make sure the action items actually get done?
How you turn a meeting into follow-up that people act on.
Each item has one owner and a due date, the summary goes out fast, and items are tracked in one place and checked before the next meeting.

During the meeting I write down each decision and each task with one owner and a date. I send the summary the same day, while people still remember. The items go into a shared tracker. Two days before the next meeting I check status with each owner and put any overdue item at the top of the agenda, so it gets discussed instead of lost.
A colleague asks you whether the rumored layoffs are true. You know they are. What do you say?
Whether you can keep a confidence without lying or losing trust.
Neither confirms nor denies, does not lie, points to the right channel, and tells the executive the rumor is spreading.

I say I can't talk about anything I see in her calendar or email. I say that to everyone about everything, so it confirms nothing. I don't invent a denial, because that costs trust later. I suggest they take the question to their manager. Then I quietly tell my executive the rumor is out, since the timing of her message may matter.
You emailed a confidential salary file to the wrong distribution list. What do you do?
How you own a mistake that exposes sensitive information.
Acts at once: tries a recall, tells the executive and HR or IT security, asks recipients to delete it, then fixes the cause.

I try to recall the message right away, but I assume it did not work. Within minutes I tell my executive and contact HR or IT security, because they decide the next steps. Then I write to the recipients and ask them to delete it without opening it. Afterward I remove that list from my autocomplete and password-protect files like that one.
Your executive keeps accepting meetings herself and double-booking her week. How do you fix it?
How you agree on working rules with your executive instead of working around her.
Raises it calmly with examples, proposes simple rules and protected time, and holds a regular check-in so the system lasts.

I bring two or three recent examples to our weekly check-in, without blame. I propose one rule: she forwards requests to me or accepts them only as tentative. I block the focus time and travel time she agrees to protect. We review the coming week every Monday in ten minutes. If she still says yes in a hallway, I just ask her to text me.
When you have delegate access to your executive's email, how do you run the inbox day to day?
How you manage an inbox you do not own without overstepping.
A clear sorting system, agreed rules on what you may answer yourself, and a daily summary so nothing important waits unseen.

First we agree on three things: what I may answer in my own name, what I draft for her, and what I never touch. Each day I sort mail into action, waiting and read later. I handle scheduling and routine items myself. At the end of the day I send her a short note listing the five things that need her. I sign as myself unless she tells me otherwise.
You start supporting a new executive on Monday. What do you want to learn in the first two weeks?
Whether you build the working relationship on purpose rather than by guessing.
Specific preferences and priorities gathered in a planned conversation, then checked against what you observe and adjusted.

In the first week I book 45 minutes with her. I ask about her top three goals this quarter and who gets through to her right away. I also ask how she likes to be briefed, when she does her best thinking, and her travel preferences. I write it all down and share it with her. After two weeks I check in and ask what I have gotten wrong.
How do you take minutes for a board or leadership meeting, and what do you leave out?
Your understanding that minutes are a record of decisions, not a transcript.
Attendance, decisions, votes and actions recorded clearly, discussion summarized briefly, and the draft reviewed before it is shared.

I record who attended, whether there was a quorum, each motion and how it was decided, and every action with an owner and a date. Discussion gets a short, neutral summary, not who said what. I leave out side remarks and opinions. The chair or corporate secretary reviews my draft before it goes anywhere, because minutes may be read years later in a dispute.
Your offsite hotel contract has an attrition clause. What does that mean, and how do you protect the budget?
Whether you understand the event contract terms that can cost a company money.
Knows attrition means paying for unfilled rooms below the agreed share of the block, and manages headcount and the cutoff date closely.

It means we promised to fill a block of rooms. If we fill less than the share the contract allows, we pay for part of the empty ones. So I size the block on a realistic headcount, not a hopeful one. I negotiate the allowed drop and a review date, push people to sign up before the cutoff, and release extra rooms in writing while I still can.
An email that looks like it is from your CEO asks you to buy $2,000 in gift cards right now and keep it quiet. What do you do?
Whether you recognize business email fraud and verify through a separate channel.
Does not reply or pay, confirms the request by phone or in person using a known contact, and reports it to IT or security.

Urgency, secrecy and gift cards together are classic signs of a scam. I do not reply to the email or click anything in it. I call the CEO or her assistant on a number I already have, or I walk over. Once it is confirmed fake, I report it to IT security with the original message so they can block it and warn others.
Your executive asks you to submit a dinner with her family as a client dinner. What do you do?
Your integrity when the pressure comes from the person you support.
Declines calmly and privately, explains the risk to both of you, and offers a correct alternative instead of a lecture.

I would not submit it as a client dinner. I would tell her privately that if an audit found it, it would be a problem for both of us. Then I offer a fix. She can pay it herself, or if it went on the corporate card, I mark it personal so she repays it under the card policy. If I say it plainly and without judging, most executives take it well.
How do you decide what reaches your executive and what you handle yourself?
How you filter demands on an executive's time without becoming a wall.
Clear criteria tied to her priorities, a fast route for urgent or sensitive matters, and the rest sent to the right owner.

I ask three questions: does this need her decision, her authority or her relationship? If not, I handle it or send it to the person who owns it, and I tell the sender who that is. Anything touching her top goals, a key client, a legal issue or a person in crisis reaches her the same day. Once a month we review what I filtered so she can correct my calls.
You set a client call in the wrong time zone and the client waited 20 minutes for your executive. What do you do?
How you own a mistake and fix the habit that allowed it.
Apologizes quickly and directly, rebooks on the client's terms, tells the executive first, and changes how invites are set up.

Within minutes I email the client's assistant. I say it was my scheduling error and offer two new times in their time zone. I tell my executive before she hears it from anyone else. Then I fix the cause. Every external invite now shows the time in both zones, and I create the event in the client's zone so the calendar converts it correctly.
The board packet goes out in two days and one department head still has not sent his section. How do you handle it?
How you hold a deadline with senior people you do not manage.
Escalates in steps with a firm time, keeps the rest of the packet moving, and lets the executive decide whether to send it incomplete.

He already has the timeline and two reminders, so now I call instead of emailing. I ask what is blocking him and when I will have it. Meanwhile I finish and proof everything else so only his section is missing. If he will miss the cutoff, I tell my executive that morning and give her options: send it without his section and add it later, or delay a day. She decides, not me.
How would you show your executive where her time actually goes, and what would you do with the result?
Whether you manage a calendar strategically, not just keep it full.
Sorts past weeks of meetings against her stated priorities, shows the gap with numbers, and proposes concrete calendar changes.

I tag the last six weeks of her calendar into four groups: her stated priorities, internal updates, external meetings and admin. Then I show her one page, for example 40% in recurring internal meetings and 10% on her top goal. I propose cutting or shortening five recurring meetings and adding two protected blocks a week for focused work. We check again in a month.

executive-recruiter.heading: Executive and business recruiter questions
qs: What is the difference between a retained and a contingency search?
Whether you know the two main search models and when each one fits.
Retained is paid in stages for an exclusive search; contingency pays only on a hire. Senior or confidential roles usually go retained.

In a retained search the client pays the fee in stages, usually starting at signing, and I run the search exclusively to the end. In contingency, the firm is paid only if its candidate is hired, often while competing with other agencies. For a CFO or a confidential replacement I want retained. For several sales reps, contingency can work.
Walk me through your intake meeting for a CFO search.
How you turn a vague request into a position spec you can search against.
Business context, what the role must deliver early, must-haves versus nice-to-haves, reporting line, full pay and who decides.

I ask why the role is open and what the CFO must deliver in the first year or two, say getting ready to go public or a refinancing. Then must-haves, like public company reporting, versus nice-to-haves. I confirm the reporting line, board exposure, the full pay package and who decides. I write it up as a spec and get sign-off before I call anyone.
What is an off-limits agreement, and how do you work with it?
Whether you respect the rules on recruiting people away from your own clients.
You do not approach a client's employees for the agreed period, you check before every outreach, and you are honest with a candidate you cannot present.

When we take on a client, we agree not to recruit their people, for the length of the search or a set time after. I check our client list before any outreach. If a strong candidate who works at a client calls me, I tell them plainly I cannot present them right now. Breaking that rule would cost the client's trust for every future search.
A candidate for VP of Sales says she hit 140% of quota. How do you check it?
How you verify sales results instead of taking them on trust.
Asking for the detail behind the number: quota in dollars, years, territory, team, trend, and confirming with references who saw the results.

I ask what the quota was in dollars, for which years, how big her team was, and whether the target was lowered midyear. One great year after a territory change means less than three steady ones. Then I ask references who saw the numbers, like her former boss or finance partner, to confirm the range. If details shift between calls, I note it.
You are hiring a general counsel. What do you check that you would not check for other roles?
Whether you know the checks that are specific to legal hires.
Bar admission and good standing, licensing or registration where they will work, public discipline, and possible conflicts from past work.

I confirm the candidate is admitted and in good standing with the state bar, using its public lookup, and whether they must be licensed or registered as in-house counsel in the state where they will work. I check public discipline records. I also ask about past matters that could conflict with the client's business, like litigation against them.
How do you run a search when the person in the job does not know they are being replaced?
How you keep a confidential search confidential.
A blind description, a small circle at the client, confidentiality agreements before names are shared, and a plan agreed in advance for leaks.

I write a blind description that hides the company and anything that gives it away. I name the client only to serious candidates after they sign a confidentiality agreement. Only a few people at the client know, and I agree with the CEO in advance what we say if word gets out. I never post the role publicly.
Your finalist gets a counteroffer from his current employer. What do you do?
How you handle the risk of losing a candidate late in the process.
Raising counteroffers early, reconnecting the candidate to his own reasons for moving, telling the client fast, and no pressure tactics.

I ask about counteroffers in the first call and again before the offer: would money change your mind? When one comes, I go back to the reasons he gave me for looking, which are rarely only pay. I tell the client the same day. If he stays, I accept it; pushing someone into a job they doubt usually fails later.
A client tells you to present only candidates under 45 because the team is young. How do you respond?
Whether you know discrimination law and will push back on an illegal request.
Federal law protects workers 40 and over from age discrimination, and it covers employment agencies too. You refuse, explain, and steer to job-related criteria.

I tell the client I cannot do that: federal age discrimination law protects people 40 and over, and it covers recruiters as well as employers. Then I ask what they really need, maybe comfort with new tools or a pay level, and turn that into criteria we assess for everyone. If they insist, I raise it with my manager and step back.
A candidate would walk away from unvested stock to join. How do you build the offer?
Your grasp of executive pay beyond base salary.
Valuing what is forfeited from documents, then a make-whole offer, such as sign-on cash with a repayment clause and new equity, without distorting base pay.

I ask for the vesting schedules and recent values so we work from documents, not memory. Then I show the client what she gives up: unvested equity and the bonus she would get in March. We usually cover it with sign-on cash, which she repays if she leaves within a set time, plus a new equity grant. Base and bonus stay at market.
An executive you placed is let go after five months. What do you do?
How you handle a failed placement and what you learn from it.
Checking the guarantee in the contract, finding the real cause from both sides, owning your part, and rerunning the search with a better spec.

First I read the guarantee in our agreement; many firms redo the search without a new fee if a hire leaves early. I talk to the client and the executive separately to learn why. Last time the spec said builder, but the CEO wanted someone to fix a crisis. I rewrote the spec, added a case exercise to the interviews, and the replacement stayed.
How do you build the target company list for a search?
Whether you can plan where a leader will come from before you start calling.
Companies chosen for a reason: similar size, model and stage, plus adjacent industries, agreed with the client and checked against off-limits.

I start from the spec: revenue size, business model, stage and region. Then I list direct peers, companies one step bigger, and adjacent industries that face the same problem. I note who the client sees as a no-go, check our off-limits list, and agree the map with the client before I call anyone. For a recent COO search that gave us about 60 companies and 150 names.
How do you open a first call with a sitting executive who is not looking?
How you earn a busy leader's attention while keeping the client confidential.
Short, respectful and honest about the role's shape without naming the client too early; asks for advice and leaves room for a referral.

I say who I am, why I called them in particular, and describe the role in a line or two: size, scope, why it is open. I name the client only once they show interest and agree to keep it private. If it is not for them, I ask who they would hire for it. Many of my best candidates came from those referrals, and the person I called stays a contact.
A CFO candidate's résumé shows great results. How do you tell what she drove from what she inherited?
Your skill at separating a person's impact from the company's momentum.
Asks for the starting point, her own decisions, who else was involved and what changed because of her, then checks the story with references.

I ask what the business looked like the day she arrived, what she changed in her first year, and what she would do differently. I want numbers before and after, and the names of people who worked with her. If she says 'we' for everything and cannot name one decision of her own, I probe further. Then I test the same story with two references.
When do you take a reference the candidate did not give you, and how?
Your judgement on back-channel references and the risk they carry.
Only late in the process, never at the current employer without consent, with discreet sources, and weighing one voice against the whole picture.

Only when a finalist is close to an offer and the stakes are high. I tell the candidate that I check references beyond the list, and I never call anyone at their current company without their OK, because that can cost them their job. I pick people I trust to stay discreet, like former bosses or board members from earlier roles, and I weigh one negative voice against the full picture.
The client wants you to find out what the finalist earns today. How do you handle it?
Whether you know the pay history rules and still get the information the client needs.
Knows many states and cities ban asking about salary history, checks the rules for the location, and asks about expectations and the package needed instead.

Many states and cities now ban employers, and recruiters acting for them, from asking about pay history, so I check the rules for the location first. Instead I ask what package the candidate needs to move: base, bonus, equity and what they would leave behind. That is what the client really needs to build an offer, and it does not anchor pay to an old number.
How do you make sure an offer will be accepted before it goes out?
How you close a candidate before the formal offer, not after.
Tests each part of the offer with the candidate in advance, surfaces family, counteroffer and start date issues, and only lets the client send what will be accepted.

I pre-close. Before the client writes anything, I walk the candidate through the likely numbers and ask: if the offer comes in like this, will you sign? I ask about the spouse, the move, the resignation talk and the start date. If there is a gap, I solve it then. A rejected offer hurts the client and my credibility, so I aim never to send one blind.
Your top candidate for a sales VP role has a non-compete. What do you do?
Whether you spot a legal risk early and route it to the right people.
Gets the actual agreement early, knows enforceability varies by state, and has the client's employment lawyer review it instead of giving legal advice.

I ask for a copy of the agreement early, not after the offer. Rules differ a lot by state: California, for example, voids most non-competes, while other states enforce reasonable ones. I am not the lawyer, so it goes to the client's employment counsel. For a sales leader, the non-solicits on customers and staff often matter more, so I make sure those get read too.
The background check on your finalist turns up a problem and the client wants to pull the offer. Walk me through what has to happen.
Your knowledge of the federal rules for acting on a background report.
Knows the FCRA steps: pre-adverse action notice with the report and a summary of rights, time to respond, then the final notice; plus state and local rules.

If a screening company ran the check, the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act applies. Before deciding, the client sends a pre-adverse action notice with a copy of the report and a summary of rights, then gives the candidate time to respond, since reports can be wrong. Then comes the final adverse action notice. Some states and cities add steps, so I loop in counsel.
A strong candidate fits two searches you are running for different clients. How do you handle it?
Your ethics when your interests and the candidate's choice could pull apart.
Tells the candidate about both, lets the candidate choose, is open with both clients, and never steers based on fee size.

I tell the candidate about both roles and let them decide which to pursue, or both. I tell each client the candidate is in another process, without naming the other client. I do not steer toward the bigger fee or slow one process to help the other. If two offers come, I help them compare honestly. Recruiters who play clients against each other keep neither.
You realize you sent a candidate's résumé to a client before she agreed to that role. What do you do?
How you own a mistake that touches a candidate's privacy and career.
Tells the candidate and the client at once, asks the client to delete it, fixes the process, and does not hide what happened.

I call the candidate first, tell her exactly what was sent and to whom, and apologize. Then I ask the client to delete the file and not act on it, and get that confirmed in writing. If she wants to be considered, we start properly. Then I fix the cause: I now log written consent for each client before any résumé leaves my desk. Candidates forgive a mistake, not a cover-up.

experimentation.heading: Experimentation and causal inference questions
qs: What is a guardrail metric, and why do you set one before a test starts?
Whether you protect the business while chasing a lift on the main metric.
A metric that must not get worse, like errors or refunds, with a limit agreed before launch so a win cannot hide damage.

A guardrail is a metric I do not expect to move but that must not get worse, like page load time, crash rate or refunds. I pick them before launch and agree on a limit with the team. Once the data is in, it is too easy to explain away a bad number when the main metric looks good.
How do you decide how long a test needs to run?
Whether you plan the sample size before launch instead of stopping when the result looks good.
A power calculation from baseline, variance, smallest effect worth detecting and traffic, rounded up to full weeks.

I start from the baseline rate and its variance, the smallest effect worth acting on, the significance level and the power we want, often 80%. That gives the users needed per group. I divide by daily eligible traffic and round up to whole weeks so both weekday and weekend behavior are included.
A stakeholder checks the dashboard daily and wants to stop the test the first day p drops below 0.05. What is wrong with that?
Whether you understand the peeking problem.
Repeated looks inflate the false positive rate. Fix the sample size up front or use a sequential method built for interim looks.

Each look is another chance for noise to cross the line, so checking every day pushes the real false positive rate well above 5%. I agree on the sample size before launch. If the team needs the option to stop early, I use a sequential test designed for repeated looks, with stricter thresholds at each check.
You planned a 50/50 split but got 50,900 users in control and 49,100 in treatment. What do you do?
Whether you catch a sample ratio mismatch before trusting the results.
Test the split with chi-square, hold off on reading results, find the cause in assignment or logging, then rerun.

That is a sample ratio mismatch. A chi-square test on those counts gives a very small p-value, so it is not chance. I would not read the results yet. I look for the cause: a redirect that loses some treatment users, bot filtering that hits one group harder, or a bug in assignment. After the fix I rerun, because the groups may not be comparable.
You randomize by user but report conversion per session. What problem does that create?
Whether you match the analysis to the unit that was randomized.
Sessions from one user are not independent, so naive standard errors are too small. Use user-level metrics, the delta method or a user bootstrap.

Sessions from the same user are correlated, so treating them as independent makes the standard error too small and the result looks more certain than it is. I either analyze at the user level or keep the per-session ratio and compute its variance with the delta method, or by bootstrapping users rather than sessions.
A new feature shows a big lift in week one that shrinks by week three. How do you read it?
Whether you can separate a lasting effect from a novelty effect.
Look at the effect by days since first exposure and by new vs. returning users, decide on the stable level, and consider a long-term holdout.

That pattern often means a novelty effect: existing users click because something looks new. I plot the effect by days since each user first saw it and compare new users, who have no old habit, with returning ones. I decide on the level where the curve flattens, and if the stakes are high I keep a small holdout for a few months.
Your test tracks 20 metrics and one secondary metric is significant at 0.05. Is that a win?
How you handle multiple comparisons.
With 20 metrics about one false positive is expected. Decide on the primary metric named in advance, correct the rest, and retest anything interesting.

Not by itself. With 20 metrics tested at 5%, about one will look significant by chance even if nothing changed. The decision rests on the primary metric we named before launch. For the others I apply a correction such as Benjamini-Hochberg, and if this one still matters I treat it as a hypothesis for a new test.
How can you get a reliable answer from a test faster without adding traffic?
Your knowledge of variance reduction methods.
Use pre-experiment data as a covariate, as in CUPED or regression adjustment, cap extreme values, or pick a more sensitive metric.

I use each user's behavior from before the test, like spend in the prior four weeks, as a covariate. This method, often called CUPED, removes variance the change could not have caused, and because the data comes from before assignment it does not bias the estimate. For revenue I also cap extreme values so a few big buyers do not swamp the signal.
A feature launched in some states first and you could not randomize. How would you estimate its effect?
How you use causal methods when an experiment is not possible.
Difference-in-differences with a check of pre-launch parallel trends, a look for other events, and honest limits on the claim.

I would use difference-in-differences: compare the before-and-after change in launch states with the change in other states over the same period. It rests on parallel trends, so I check that both groups moved together for several months before launch and look for other events in those states. I report it as an estimate with its assumptions, not as proof.
What is an A/A test, and what result would make you distrust your experiment platform?
Whether you validate the system before trusting its results.
Both arms get the same experience; about 5% should come out significant at 0.05, and p-values should spread evenly, so many more signals a bug.

Both groups get the exact same experience, so any difference is noise or a bug. If I run many A/A tests at 0.05, about 5% should come out significant and the p-values should be spread evenly from 0 to 1. If I see 15% significant, or groups of different sizes, I check the assignment, the logging and the variance formula before trusting any real test.
How do you pick the minimum detectable effect, and what happens to the sample size if you halve it?
Your grasp of power analysis as a business choice, not just a formula.
The MDE is the smallest effect worth acting on; sample size grows with one over the effect squared, so halving it needs about four times the users.

I start from the business: the smallest lift that would pay for building and maintaining the change. Then I check if our traffic can detect it at our usual power, often 80%. Required sample scales with one over the effect squared, so going from a 2% to a 1% MDE needs roughly four times the users. If that means a three-month test, we rethink the metric or the design.
Only 8% of users ever open the screen you changed. How do you analyze the test?
Whether you know how to handle dilution with a triggered analysis.
Analyze users who reached the trigger point in both arms, then scale the effect to the whole site; never compare triggered treatment users with all control users.

I log the trigger point in both arms, including control, where users reach the screen but see the old version. Comparing only triggered users removes the noise of the 92% who could not be affected, so the test has far more power. To report the site-wide impact, I dilute: the absolute effect per triggered user times the share triggered gives the effect per user overall.
Treatment raised average order value but lowered conversion. Why is average order value a tricky metric here?
Whether you spot bias from a metric that only counts users who already converted.
AOV is measured only on buyers, and the treatment changed who buys, so the groups are no longer comparable; decide on revenue per randomized user.

Average order value only counts people who bought, and the treatment changed who buys. If it pushed away small-basket shoppers, AOV rises even though no one spent more. The randomized groups are comparable; the buyer subsets are not. I would lead with revenue per user assigned, counting non-buyers as zero, and treat AOV as a description, not the decision metric.
Your revenue metric has a few customers who spend 100 times the median. How do you test it?
How you handle heavy-tailed metrics that drain statistical power.
Cap or winsorize at a percentile set before the test, compare results with and without the cap, and keep raw totals for the business case.

A handful of huge spenders can swing the mean and blow up the variance, so the test barely has power. I would cap values at a high percentile, say the 99.9th, chosen before the test starts and computed on both arms together. I report the capped result for the decision and the uncapped totals alongside it, and if they disagree I check which arm the big spenders landed in.
The test is flat overall, but a product manager found that it wins big for Android users in Texas. What do you say?
Your judgement about subgroup results found after the fact.
Slicing many segments turns up chance winners; treat it as a hypothesis, look for a plausible reason, and confirm it in a new test.

Slicing by device and state means dozens of comparisons, so some will look big by chance alone. I would ask whether there is a real reason Android in Texas would behave differently, like a bug or a payment method used only there. If there is, we run a new test aimed at that segment with the metric set in advance. Until then, it is a lead, not a result.
Engineering wants to ship a cheaper backend and says the test showed no significant difference. Is that enough?
Whether you know that no significant difference is not proof of no harm.
Agree on a margin of acceptable harm in advance and test for non-inferiority: the confidence interval must sit entirely above that margin.

A small test can show no significant difference even when the change hurts. Before testing, I would agree with the team how much loss we accept, say half a percent of conversion. Then the change passes only if the whole confidence interval sits above minus half a percent. If it runs from minus 2% to plus 1%, safety is not shown and we need more data.
You ramped treatment from 5% on Monday to 50% on Friday and pooled all the days. What can go wrong?
Whether you catch the bias a ramp-up creates when the traffic mix shifts over time.
Treatment users come mostly from late days, so day effects mix into the treatment effect; analyze one fixed split or compare within each phase.

Most treatment users entered on Thursday and Friday, while control is spread over the whole week. If Friday users convert differently, that day difference gets credited to the treatment, and the pooled result can even flip sign, which is Simpson's paradox. I would analyze only the days at a fixed split, or estimate within each phase and combine.
In a ride-hailing marketplace, you test a lower price for half the riders. Why can the result be wrong, and how would you fix the design?
Whether you recognize interference between units and know designs that limit it.
Treated and control riders share the same drivers, so one group's gain can come at the other's cost; use switchback or cluster randomization by market.

Riders in both groups compete for the same drivers. If cheaper rides pull more demand, treatment riders take drivers that control riders would have gotten, so the gap looks bigger than a full launch would give. I would use a switchback test, where a whole city flips between versions in blocks of time, or randomize whole regions, accepting less power for less bias.
You can offer a new tool to random users, but only 20% of them turn it on. How do you estimate the effect of actually using it?
Your grasp of intent-to-treat versus the effect on users who comply.
Compare by assignment for the intent-to-treat effect; dividing it by the difference in take-up estimates the effect on adopters, under stated assumptions.

Comparing users who turned it on with those who did not is biased, because keen users self-select. I compare by random assignment: that is the intent-to-treat effect. If control cannot get the tool, dividing that effect by the 20% take-up gives the effect on users who adopt it. That assumes the offer matters only through use, so I check for that.

fabrication-technician.heading: Fabrication technician questions
qs: On a weld symbol, what does it mean when the fillet triangle sits below the reference line?
Whether you can read a weld symbol without guessing.
Below the line means the arrow side; above means the other side. A triangle on both sides means weld both sides.

Below the reference line means I weld on the arrow side, the side of the joint the arrow points to. Above the line means the other side. If the triangle is on both sides, I weld both. Before I strike an arc, I also check the number left of the triangle for the leg size and any length and pitch to the right.
Why do you measure hole locations from one datum instead of from hole to hole?
Whether you understand how small layout errors add up across a part.
Chained measurements stack error. Measuring every feature from one reference edge or line keeps each error separate.

If I lay out six holes each from the last one and I am off a thirty-second each time, the last hole can be off three-sixteenths. If I measure all of them from the same edge or centerline, the one the drawing calls the datum, each hole carries only its own error. I also use one tape for the whole layout.
You have tacked up a rectangular frame. How do you check it is square before welding it out?
Your basic fit-up method before the welds lock in a mistake.
Check side lengths, compare the two diagonals, adjust while only tacked, and check flat too, since square and flat are different.

With the opposite sides already checked to length, I measure both diagonals corner to corner. If they match within tolerance, it is square. If not, I pull the long diagonal in with a clamp while it is only tacked. I check it lies flat with no twist, then recheck after the first few welds because heat can pull it out.
Can you cut stainless plate with an oxy-fuel torch? Why or why not?
Whether you know how each cutting process actually works.
No. Oxy-fuel burns carbon steel in a jet of oxygen; stainless forms an oxide that blocks the reaction. Plasma or a saw is the right tool.

Not cleanly. Oxy-fuel works by heating carbon steel and then burning it in a jet of pure oxygen. The chromium in stainless forms an oxide that melts far hotter than the steel itself, so the cut does not carry through. For stainless I use plasma, a saw, or the laser if the shop has one.
A part keeps cracking on the outside of the bend in the press brake. What do you look at?
How you troubleshoot a forming problem, starting from the material.
Bend radius too tight for the material, bend line running with the grain, and a hard temper; then the tooling and the drawing.

First the inside radius: if the punch is sharper than the minimum radius for that alloy and thickness, the outside stretches too far. Then grain: a bend line parallel to the rolling direction cracks more easily, so I turn the blank in the nest if the drawing allows. Then I check the material cert for temper, since harder tempers need a bigger radius.
Why do you keep separate grinding discs and wire brushes for stainless steel?
Whether you know how stainless gets contaminated in a mixed shop.
Carbon steel particles left on stainless rust and stain it and can start corrosion; dedicated tools and separate storage prevent it.

A brush or disc used on carbon steel leaves tiny iron particles in the stainless surface. They rust within days, leave orange stains, and that spot can start corrosion. So I use tools marked for stainless only, keep stainless off carbon steel racks, and if a part does get contaminated I flag it so it gets cleaned or passivated.
You have to weld galvanized steel. What do you do differently?
Whether you know the hazard of zinc coatings and how to handle it.
Remove the coating at the joint, use local fume extraction or a suitable respirator, and restore corrosion protection afterward.

Burning zinc gives off fumes that can cause metal fume fever, so I grind the coating back from the joint first, which also cuts porosity. I weld with fume extraction at the arc, plus a respirator if the shop's program calls for it, and keep my head out of the plume. After, I touch up the weld with zinc-rich paint so it does not rust.
You find porosity in your MIG welds halfway through a job. How do you track down the cause?
How you diagnose a weld defect step by step instead of turning knobs.
Shielding gas first: cylinder, flow, hoses, drafts, a clogged nozzle; then dirt, oil or coating on the metal. Grind out bad welds and reweld.

I stop and check the gas: is the cylinder near empty, is the flow set right, is a hose leaking, is the nozzle clogged with spatter. Then I look for a fan or open door blowing the shield away. Then the metal: oil, mill scale, paint or moisture. Once I find it, I grind the porous welds back to sound metal and reweld them, never cover them.
You need to weld a long seam on thin sheet without it warping. How do you plan it?
Your ability to control heat distortion before it happens.
Less heat, spread evenly: tight fit-up, close tacks, clamps or a backing bar, skip or back-step welding, and no oversized welds.

I fit it tight so I am not filling gaps, tack it closely, and clamp it to the table or a copper backing bar to pull heat out. I weld short sections spread along the seam, or back-step, instead of one bead end to end. I keep the weld no bigger than the drawing asks, since every extra bit of weld adds shrinkage.
You cut an expensive part a quarter inch short and nobody saw it. What do you do?
Your honesty and judgement when your own mistake costs material.
Tag the part, tell the lead right away, find the cause, and leave any repair to engineering; never quietly weld on a filler piece.

I tag the part so it cannot go into the job and tell my lead right away, with the measurement. Then I find out why: misread dimension, a loose tape hook, or forgetting the kerf. If someone suggests welding in a filler, that is engineering's call, because a hidden splice can fail. Then I recut it and recheck the rest of the batch.
How do you work out the flat length of a part with bends, and where does the K-factor come in?
Whether you can develop a flat pattern instead of cutting long and trimming.
Metal stretches on the outside of a bend and compresses on the inside. The K-factor locates the line that keeps its length, and a test bend confirms it.

In a bend there is a line inside the metal that keeps its length, the neutral axis, and it shifts toward the inside. K-factor is where it sits as a fraction of the thickness, often about 0.3 to 0.5. Bend allowance is the angle in radians times the inside radius plus K times thickness. I bend a test strip on our tooling, measure it and use that number.
What is undercut, what causes it, and how do you repair it?
Your grasp of a common weld defect, its causes and a proper repair.
A groove melted into the base metal at the weld toe and left unfilled. Causes like high amperage, fast travel or a bad gun angle, and a clean, small repair pass.

It's a notch melted into the base metal along the toe of the weld that the filler never filled. The plate is thinner there and stress gathers in it. Usually the amperage is too high, travel is too fast or the gun points too much at one plate. To fix it I clean the area, lay a small stringer bead along the toe at lower heat, and check the result against the acceptance limits.
Why do you TIG weld aluminum on AC but steel on DC electrode negative?
Whether you understand what the current does, not just which setting to pick.
Aluminum oxide melts far hotter than the metal under it, and the electrode-positive half of AC breaks it up. DCEN puts more heat into the work and spares the tungsten.

Aluminum has an oxide skin that melts around 3,700°F, while the aluminum under it melts near 1,200°F. On AC, the electrode-positive half of each cycle cleans that oxide off. Steel has no such skin, so I run DC electrode negative. Most of the heat goes into the work, I get better penetration and the tungsten stays cool. I still brush aluminum with a clean stainless brush first.
When would you switch a MIG job from short-circuit to spray transfer, and what has to change?
Whether you match the transfer mode to the thickness, position and shielding gas.
Spray for thicker metal in flat or horizontal fillet work, with an argon-rich gas and higher settings. Short-circuit for thin metal and out-of-position welds.

Short-circuit runs cool, so it suits thin sheet and vertical or overhead welds. On thick plate in the flat position I'd go to spray for deeper penetration and less spatter. That needs a high-argon mix, like 90 percent argon and 10 percent CO2, not straight CO2, and voltage and wire speed above the transition point. The puddle is big and fluid, so it stays flat or horizontal fillet.
The drawing calls for a 1/4 inch fillet and you have been laying 3/8. The inspector flags it. Why does it matter if it is stronger?
Whether you see weld size as a design value, with costs in metal, time and distortion.
Oversized welds waste wire and time and add heat and distortion. Weld metal grows with the square of the leg, so a 3/8 fillet needs over twice the metal of a 1/4.

Fillet area goes with the square of the leg, so a 3/8 takes about two and a quarter times the metal of a 1/4. That's more wire, more time and more heat, which means more shrinkage and distortion. The engineer sized it for the load. I'd check my welds with a fillet gauge, bring the size back to the print, and ask whether the welds already done need any action.
You see a small crack in the crater at the end of a weld. What do you do, and how do you stop it happening again?
How you handle a crack, the one defect you never weld over.
Grind the crack out completely, confirm it is gone, then reweld. Prevent it by filling the crater before breaking the arc or using a crater-fill setting.

I don't weld over it, because a buried crack can keep growing. I grind it out and confirm it's gone, with a dye test that shows cracks if the part is critical, then reweld. Crater cracks come from stopping too fast, so the thin crater shrinks and tears. I pause or back up a little into the bead before stopping, or use crater fill. On TIG I taper off with the pedal.
You are TIG welding the root on a stainless pipe joint. What do you do about the inside of the pipe, and why?
Whether you know back purging and what happens to a stainless root without it.
Dam and purge the inside with argon before striking an arc and keep it flowing. Without it the root oxidizes into a crusty mess and loses corrosion resistance.

I back purge. I dam both sides of the joint, tape the gap and fill the inside with argon, with a small vent so the air gets pushed out. I give it time, or check with an oxygen meter, before I strike an arc. Without a purge the inside of the root burns black and crusty, called sugaring. That weakens the root and ruins the corrosion resistance the customer paid for.
When do you preheat before welding steel, and how do you check you have reached the temperature?
Your understanding of hydrogen cracking and how preheat helps control it.
Thick sections, higher carbon or alloy steels, and cold parts. The procedure sets the temperature, checked with temperature crayons or a contact thermometer away from the joint.

Preheat slows cooling, so the weld area doesn't harden as much and hydrogen has time to get out, which prevents cracking. Thick plate, higher-carbon or alloy steel and cold parts call for it. I use the temperature on the procedure, heat evenly, and check with a temperature crayon a few inches from the joint, not where the flame just was. I keep it up between passes too.
The shop is out of the 3/16 plate on the drawing, and the foreman says to use 1/4 since it is stronger. What do you do?
Your judgement about changes that need approval from whoever owns the design.
Thicker is not automatically fine: the flat pattern, bend radius, fit, weight and weld procedure can all change. Get the change approved in writing before cutting.

I'd check with whoever owns the drawing before I cut. Heavier plate changes the flat pattern and bend radius, can hit a mating part, adds weight, and may need a different weld or fall outside the procedure. Often it's approved, and then I want it written on the traveler or the drawing, so the inspector and the next shift know why the part doesn't match the print.
A long welded beam has come out bowed. Walk me through how you would straighten it with heat.
Whether you can correct distortion with heat without damaging the steel.
Heated steel that is held in place shrinks as it cools, so you heat wedges on the convex side, stay below red heat, let it air cool and recheck. Some steels need the engineer's limits first.

I find the high side with a string line and mark it. Steel heated while the cold metal around it holds it shrinks when it cools, so I heat wedge shapes on the convex side, wide end at the edge. I stay below a dull red, check with temperature crayons, and let it cool in air, no water. I work a little at a time and recheck. On quenched and tempered steel I'd get the engineer's limits first.

facilities-manager.heading: Facilities manager questions
qs: What is the difference between preventive, predictive and reactive maintenance?
Whether you know the basic maintenance strategies and when each one fits.
Clear definitions, plus the point that run-to-failure is a fair choice for cheap, non-critical items.

Reactive is fixing it when it breaks. Preventive is scheduled work, like changing air handler filters every quarter. Predictive uses condition data, such as vibration or thermal scans, to act before failure. I let a cheap exhaust fan run to failure, but a chiller gets preventive and predictive care because a breakdown costs far more than the upkeep.
You have 40 open work orders and two technicians. How do you decide what gets done first?
How you rank work by risk to life, the building and the business.
A clear order: life safety, then damage to the building, then loss of operations, then comfort and cosmetic work, with requesters told when.

Life safety first: a blocked exit or a dead emergency light. Then anything causing damage, like an active leak. Then things that stop the business, such as a broken loading door. Comfort and cosmetic items come last. I set priority codes in the work order system so the team does not guess, and I give requesters a realistic date instead of letting tickets sit silent.
What do you check before a contractor starts work on your site?
Whether you control the risks contractors bring onto a site.
Insurance certificate on file, scope agreed in writing, permits in place, a site briefing, and hot work or lockout controls where needed.

I make sure we have a current certificate of insurance naming us as additional insured, the scope in writing, and any building permit the job needs. On day one they get a site briefing: exits, alarms, where they can work. If they will weld or cut, they need a hot work permit and a fire watch. If they touch equipment, lockout/tagout is in place before work starts.
A pipe bursts above an office ceiling at 9 p.m. on a Sunday. Walk me through what you do.
How you handle an after-hours emergency, in the right order.
Stop the water, make electrical safe, protect people and assets, then dry quickly, document for insurance and find the cause.

I get the nearest isolation valve closed, through security or in person. If water is near panels or outlets, power to that area is cut before anyone walks in. Then we move equipment and call a restoration company to dry it, since wet materials can grow mold within a day or two. I take photos for the insurer and have a plumber find why the pipe failed.
A sprinkler system has to be shut off for a repair. What do you do before and during the shutdown?
Whether you know how to manage a fire protection impairment safely.
Notify the fire department, insurer and alarm company, keep the outage small and short, post a fire watch, then restore and test.

I treat it as an impairment. I tag the valve, notify the fire department, our insurance carrier and the alarm monitoring company, and tell occupants. I limit the outage to the part being repaired and set up a fire watch while it is down. Hot work in that area stops. When the repair is done, the contractor restores and tests the system, and I tell everyone it is back in service.
You find the monthly emergency generator test logs have gaps for the last three months. What do you do?
How you handle a compliance gap and fix its cause.
Test now, find out why the tests lapsed, fix the process rather than the paper, and never backfill records.

First I get the generator run under load this week to confirm it works, with the results logged honestly. I do not fill in the missing months; a fake log is worse than a gap. Then I find out why it lapsed, often a vendor schedule change or a tech who left. I set the test as a recurring task with a named owner and check the log myself each month.
Leadership wants a 10% cut in energy use with almost no capital budget. Where do you start?
Your practical knowledge of energy savings in existing buildings.
A baseline from utility data first, then fixing schedules, setpoints and broken controls before buying any equipment.

I build a baseline from 12 months of utility bills, adjusted for weather. Then I go after cheap fixes: HVAC schedules that run on empty weekends, systems heating and cooling at the same time, stuck dampers and lights left on in unused areas. I walk the building at night to see what runs. I track monthly use against the baseline to prove the savings.
You are moving 120 people to a new floor over one weekend. Walk me through your plan.
How you plan and run a move without losing a workday.
A seating plan signed off early, movers and IT booked, labeled crates, testing before Monday, and support on the floor Monday morning.

I lock the seating plan with department heads weeks ahead, then book movers and IT for Friday night and Saturday. Each person packs crates labeled with their new desk number. Furniture and network ports are checked before the move. Sunday is for testing phones and computers. On Monday a small team stays on the floor to fix problems fast and keep a punch list.
We are renovating part of a building from the 1970s. What has to happen before anyone opens walls or ceilings?
Whether you know the hazardous material risks in older buildings.
An asbestos survey by an accredited inspector, lead paint checks, and abatement by licensed contractors before demolition starts.

A building from that era may have asbestos in ceiling tiles, pipe insulation, floor tile or joint compound, and lead in paint. Before work starts I get a survey and sampling by an accredited inspector. If anything is found, a licensed abatement contractor removes or encloses it with the required notices and air monitoring. I share the survey with every contractor on the job.
Your budget is cut by 15% mid-year. What do you defer, and what do you refuse to cut?
Your judgement on deferred maintenance and the risk it creates.
Protects life safety, required compliance work and the building envelope; defers cosmetic work; puts the cost of deferral in writing.

I will not cut fire and life safety inspections, required compliance testing, or roof and envelope repairs, because a leak or a failed inspection costs far more later. I would defer painting, carpet and some upgrades, and clean low-traffic areas less often. I list the deferred items in a short memo with the risk and likely cost of waiting a year, so the choice is on record.
What is a facility condition index, and how would you use it?
Whether you can put building condition into numbers that leadership understands.
FCI is deferred maintenance and renewal cost divided by current replacement value. Lower is better, and it shows trends, not single decisions.

It is the cost of the repairs and renewals we have put off, divided by what it would cost to replace the building today. A $2 million backlog on a $20 million building is an FCI of 10%. I use it to compare buildings and track the trend each year, then look at the actual items, because one failing roof matters more than the ratio.
Walk me through how you read a commercial electric bill to find savings.
Whether you understand how utilities charge, not just how much the building uses.
Separates energy (kWh) from demand (kW), knows demand is set by the peak interval, and checks the rate schedule and any power factor charges.

I split the bill into energy, which is total kWh, and demand, which is the highest kW over a short interval in the month, often 15 minutes. On many tariffs demand is a large share. If our peak comes from every rooftop unit starting at 6 a.m., staggering the starts can cut it at no cost. I also check we are on the right rate schedule and look for power factor penalties.
Staff on the third floor complain of stuffiness and afternoon headaches. How do you investigate?
How you handle an indoor air quality complaint with data instead of guesses.
Rules out carbon monoxide first, then measures CO2, temperature and humidity, uses CO2 as a ventilation clue, and checks outside air, schedules and new sources.

If anyone mentions dizziness or nausea near gas equipment or a garage, I check for carbon monoxide first. Then I log CO2, temperature and humidity at desk height for a few days. CO2 rising well above outdoor levels by afternoon points to too little outside air, so I check the outside air damper, schedule and filters. I tell staff what I am testing and when they will hear back.
A contractor will service a chiller that your own team also locks out. Whose lockout procedure applies?
Your grasp of OSHA lockout/tagout rules when two employers work on the same equipment.
Both employers share their energy control procedures before work starts, as OSHA requires, and agree on locks, group lockout and shift changes.

Under OSHA's lockout rule, the contractor and we must tell each other about our energy control procedures before work starts. I meet their lead, agree whose procedure governs the job, and make sure my technicians respect their locks. If both teams work on it, we use group lockout so nobody can restart the chiller until every person has removed their own lock.
A contractor needs to enter a sewage ejector pit on your site. What do you owe them before they go in?
Whether you know a host employer's duties for permit-required confined spaces.
Tells the contractor it is a permit space, shares known hazards and past precautions, coordinates nearby work and debriefs after. The contractor runs its own permit program.

If it is a permit-required confined space, OSHA says I must tell the contractor that, share the hazards we know, like hydrogen sulfide in a sewage pit, and the precautions we have used. They need their own permit program: air testing, ventilation, an attendant and a rescue plan. I coordinate if my staff work nearby, and afterward I ask what they found.
A building sat mostly empty for months. What do you do with the water systems before people return?
Whether you treat stagnant water as a Legionella risk and follow a water management program.
Follows the water management program: flushing, hot water temperatures, disinfectant checks, cooling tower cleaning, and testing when control limits are not met.

Stagnant water lets Legionella grow, so I follow our water management program, built on ASHRAE Standard 188 and the CDC toolkit. We flush every outlet, hot and cold, confirm the water heater holds its set temperature, check disinfectant at the far points, and clean cooling towers and fountains. If control limits are not met, we test and treat before reopening.
How would you write a cleaning contract so you can actually hold the vendor to it?
How you turn a service into terms you can measure and enforce.
Outcome-based specs, joint inspections scored the same way each time, response times, and a fair remedy for repeated misses.

I define results, not just hours: restrooms stocked and clean at set check times, no visible dust on desks, spills handled within a set time. Each month we inspect a random sample of rooms together with the same score sheet. The contract ties a small credit to scores below target and gives them a set period to fix a pattern before we rebid.
On a walk-through you find a contractor welding a railing with no hot work permit. What do you do?
Whether you use stop-work authority and then fix the gap in your permit system.
Stops the work at once, makes the area safe, requires a permit and fire watch before restart, then finds out why the check-in missed it.

I stop the welding right away, politely but firmly. I check for smoldering material, keep someone watching the area, and confirm no detectors or sprinklers were left impaired. No work restarts until a permit is issued with combustibles cleared and a fire watch named. I note it in their file and find out why our contractor check-in did not catch it.
Leadership wants to give up one floor because offices look half empty. How do you test that idea?
How you use occupancy data to support a space decision.
Uses weeks of real occupancy data, plans for peak days rather than averages, and accounts for team needs and lease terms before recommending.

I collect several weeks of badge and occupancy sensor data and look at peak days, not the average, because if everyone comes in on Tuesday, the average hides the crunch. I map which teams need to sit together or need quiet rooms. If peak use fits on the remaining floors with a sensible desk-sharing ratio, I show the lease savings next to the move cost.
You have money for one of three projects: an aging chiller, a leaking roof, or elevator modernization. How do you choose?
Your judgement in ranking capital projects by risk and explaining the trade-off.
A risk-based ranking: safety and code first, then likelihood and cost of failure, stopgap options and lifecycle cost, written up so leaders see what risk they carry.

I score each on chance of failure and what failure would cost: safety, downtime, damage. A leaking roof harms everything below it and gets worse fast, so it often ranks first. For the chiller I check whether a rental unit could cover a failure, and for the elevators whether inspections show safety issues. I put the ranking and the risks we keep in writing.

fellowship-residency.heading: Fellowship and residency questions
qs: What would you want to have finished and in hand when this fellowship ends?
Whether you think of a fixed term in terms of a concrete end product.
A specific deliverable tied to the program's goals, plus a skill you want to build. Not a vague wish to gain experience.

I would want one finished piece the host can use, like a policy brief or a cleaned dataset with a short report, and a talk I gave on it. I would also want to leave able to run a small project on my own, from question to write-up. That is the skill I am weakest at today.
How would you prepare for a weekly meeting with your mentor?
How you use a mentor's limited time.
You bring an agenda, your progress, and specific questions or decisions, and you write down what was agreed.

I send a short note a day ahead: what I did, where I am stuck, and the one or two decisions I need from them. In the meeting I start with the decisions. Afterward I email a three-line summary of what we agreed, so we both have a record and I am not guessing next week.
Your mentor hands you a broad topic, like improving food access in the county. Walk me through how you turn it into a project you can finish in nine months.
Whether you can scope an open question to fit a fixed term.
You narrow it to one question and one user, plan backward from the end date with milestones, and check the scope with the mentor early.

First I ask who will use the result and what decision it should inform. Then I narrow to one question, say, which neighborhoods lack a grocery store within a mile. I plan backward from the end date: draft due at month seven, analysis by month five, data by month three. I show that plan to my mentor in week two, before I commit.
How would you write a one-page memo for a busy official?
Whether you can write for decision makers, a core task in public service placements.
Bottom line first, the ask stated plainly, short evidence, options with tradeoffs, and no jargon.

I put the bottom line and what I need from them in the first two sentences. Then come three short sections: background in a few lines, options with the cost and risk of each, and my recommendation. Sources go in a footnote. I cut every word a non-specialist would trip on. Then I ask a colleague to read it in two minutes and tell me the point.
You join a host office where staff are busy and see fellows as temporary. How do you get the access you need?
How you build trust and earn cooperation in a placement you do not control.
You learn what the office needs, make yourself useful early, respect people's time, and keep your promises.

In the first weeks I meet people one by one and ask what slows their work down. I look for a small task I can finish fast, like cleaning a contact list or summarizing a report, so they see I deliver. When I need data, I ask for exactly what I need, explain how it helps them, and send them the result first.
Your project includes interviewing community members. What do you check before the first interview?
Whether you know the ethics and approval steps for research with people.
You ask whether IRB review applies, plan informed consent and private data storage, and let the IRB decide on exemption, not yourself.

I ask my mentor whether this counts as human subjects research. If so, I submit it to the IRB, the review board that protects participants. I do not decide on my own that it is exempt. I prepare a consent script that says what the study is, that taking part is voluntary, and how answers are used. I plan where notes are stored and remove names before sharing.
How do you make sure your work is still useful after your term ends?
Whether you plan the handoff of a fixed-term project.
You name an owner early, document methods and files, and train whoever will keep the work going.

By the middle of the term I ask who will own the work after me, and I involve that person in reviews. I keep a running read-me file: where the files are, how the analysis runs, what I would do next. In my last month I walk the owner through it and have them run it once while I watch, so gaps show up while I am still there.
Halfway through, your data points the opposite way from what your mentor expected. What do you do?
Your integrity and judgement when results are unwelcome.
You check your own work first, then tell the mentor promptly with the evidence, and report the result honestly either way.

First I check my work: the data source, the cleaning steps, any coding errors. If it holds, I tell my mentor soon, not at the final presentation. I show what I found, how sure I am, and what could explain it. A surprising result is still a result. We may add a check, but we do not drop it because it is unexpected.
In month six you realize the project will not be finished by the end date. What do you do?
How you handle a fixed deadline that will not move.
You raise it early, propose a smaller version that still delivers value, and confirm the new scope in writing.

I tell my mentor that week, with a clear reason, like data that arrived two months late. I come with options: drop one of three sites, or fully answer one question instead of half answering two. Once we pick, I update the timeline and send it to everyone involved, so no one expects the original plan at the end.
A senior official asks you to leave out a finding that makes their program look bad. How do you respond?
Whether you keep findings honest under pressure from someone with more power.
You listen for a valid concern and offer to add context, but you do not hide or change the result, and you bring in your mentor.

I would first ask what worries them. Sometimes a finding needs context, like a small sample or a recent change in the program. I can add that, and their response too. But I would not remove or soften the result itself. I would explain that, and I would bring in my mentor right away so the decision does not rest on a fellow alone.
What is the difference between an output and an outcome?
Whether you can tell activity apart from results when you report on a program.
Outputs are what the program produces; outcomes are the changes that follow. Strong answers report outcomes or say plainly when they cannot be measured yet.

An output is what the program produces: 300 people trained, 12 workshops held. An outcome is the change that follows, like how many trainees had jobs six months later. Officials care about outcomes. So I count outputs to show the work happened, but I report outcomes, or say plainly when we cannot measure them yet.
Why should you write work emails at a public agency as if they could be made public?
Whether you know that government records can be requested by the public.
Emails and drafts at public agencies are often public records under FOIA or state law. Candidates keep writing factual and keep work off personal accounts.

At a public agency, my emails and drafts are usually public records. Under FOIA or the state's public records law, anyone can request them, with some exemptions. So I keep emails factual and leave out jokes or guesses about people. I also never use personal email for work. It can still count as a record, and it is harder to find and keep.
You are placed in a federal agency during an election year. What political activity can you take part in?
Whether you know the Hatch Act and check how it applies to you.
Off duty you can vote and share views. On duty, in the office or on work accounts you stay out of partisan activity, and you never solicit donations. Ask ethics if unsure.
