I look to objective sources first: reversing taxable temporary differences, carrybacks where allowed, and tax planning strategies. What they do not cover usually needs an allowance.
After a reorganization, the CEO reviews results by customer type instead of by region. How does that affect our segment reporting?
Whether you apply the management approach of ASC 280.
Segments follow what the decision maker uses; reassess segments and aggregation, recast prior periods, and revisit goodwill reporting units.

Segments follow how the chief operating decision maker reviews results to allocate resources, so ours likely change. I identify the new operating segments, test aggregation and the 10% thresholds, and recast prior periods unless impracticable. I also update the significant segment expenses we disclose and check whether goodwill reporting units changed, reassigning goodwill if they did.

firmware-engineer.heading: Firmware engineer questions
qs: What does the volatile keyword do in C, and when do you need it?
Whether you know how the compiler treats memory that can change outside your code.
It stops the compiler from caching or removing reads and writes. It is needed for hardware registers and ISR-shared flags, and it is not a lock.

It tells the compiler the value can change behind its back, so every read and write must really happen. I use it for memory-mapped registers and for flags an interrupt sets. It does not make an access atomic, so for shared data I still need a critical section.
Walk me through what happens between power-on and the first line of main().
Your knowledge of startup code and how a program sits in memory.
Reset vector, stack pointer, copying .data, zeroing .bss, clock setup, then main, with real detail for one chip family.

On a Cortex-M the core loads the initial stack pointer from the first word of the vector table and jumps to the reset handler in the second. Startup code copies initialized variables from flash to RAM, zeros the .bss section, usually sets up clocks, then calls main. If .bss is not zeroed, globals start with garbage.
What do you keep in an interrupt handler, and what do you move out of it?
How you write interrupt code that stays fast and safe.
Short handlers: clear the source, grab the data, queue it or set a flag. No blocking calls, long loops or printf.

In the handler I clear the interrupt flag, read data that would otherwise be lost, like a UART byte, put it in a ring buffer and set a flag. Parsing and anything slow runs in the main loop or a task. I never block or call printf in an ISR, because it delays every other interrupt.
A push button gives you several presses for one push. How do you fix it?
Whether you know switch bounce and the usual ways to handle it.
Names contact bounce and debounces in hardware or software, for example by requiring a stable state for a set time.

That is contact bounce: the metal contacts chatter for a few milliseconds. I sample the pin from a timer every few milliseconds and accept a new state only after it reads the same several times in a row, about 20 ms stable. On a new board, an RC filter into a Schmitt trigger input also helps.
When would you use polling, an interrupt or DMA to move data from a peripheral?
Your judgement in trading CPU time, latency and complexity.
Matches the method to the data: polling for simple or rare cases, interrupts for events, DMA for steady streams.

Polling is fine at startup or when the CPU has nothing else to do. Interrupts suit events that arrive at unknown times, like a button or a few UART bytes. For fast ADC sampling or a big SPI transfer I use DMA, so the CPU is not interrupted for every byte, and I take an interrupt only at half or full buffer.
On an 8-bit microcontroller, the main loop reads a 32-bit tick counter that a timer interrupt updates. Sometimes the value is wildly wrong. Why?
Whether you spot a non-atomic access shared between an interrupt and main code.
The read takes several instructions, so the ISR can update the value mid-read. Fix it with a short critical section or a read-until-stable loop.

The CPU reads the four bytes one at a time. If the timer interrupt fires between bytes, I get low bytes from the old value and high bytes from the new one, so the result can jump by 256 or more. I disable interrupts just for the copy and restore them, or read the counter twice until both reads match.
How do you use a watchdog timer, and where do you refresh it?
How you use a watchdog to recover from a hang without hiding real faults.
Refresh only when the whole system is healthy, never from a timer ISR alone, and log the reset cause after a watchdog reset.

The watchdog resets the chip if the code does not refresh it in time. I refresh it in one place, or from a monitor task that checks every other task has checked in. I never kick it from a timer interrupt, because interrupts can keep running while the main code is stuck. At boot I read the reset cause and log watchdog resets.
After a reset in the middle of a transfer, your I2C bus is stuck with SDA held low. What do you do?
Whether you know a common I2C failure and how to recover from it.
A slave is mid-byte waiting for clocks: drive SCL as GPIO up to nine times until SDA is released, then send a STOP.

The slave was sending a byte when the master reset, so it still holds SDA low and waits for clocks. In init I set the pins as GPIO, toggle SCL up to nine times until SDA goes high, create a STOP condition, then give the pins back to the I2C peripheral. If it keeps happening, I check the pull-ups and the reset sequence.
Your Cortex-M device hits a HardFault about once a day in testing. How do you find the cause?
How you debug a crash from the state the processor saves at the fault.
Captures the stacked PC and LR plus fault status registers, maps the address to code, and keeps the data across reset when no debugger is attached.

My fault handler saves the stacked PC and LR plus the CFSR and HFSR into RAM that is not cleared at reset, and logs them on the next boot. The PC usually points at the faulting instruction, which I find with the map file or addr2line. The status bits say if it was a bus error, an undefined instruction or a bad memory access.
How would you design firmware updates in the field so a power cut cannot brick the device?
Your judgement in designing a safe update path.
A small protected bootloader, two image slots, an integrity and signature check before switching, and rollback if the new image fails.

I keep a small bootloader that normal updates never overwrite. The new image goes into a second slot while the old one keeps running. The bootloader checks its CRC and signature, then boots it on a trial basis. If the new firmware does not confirm it is healthy, for example after a watchdog reset, the bootloader rolls back to the old slot.
Why shouldn't you just copy a C struct into a packet you send to another device?
Whether you know how compilers lay out data in memory.
Names padding, byte order and alignment, and serializes field by field in a defined byte order instead.

The compiler may add padding between fields, and the other side may use another byte order or another compiler. A packed struct removes padding but can cause slow or faulting unaligned access. I write explicit serialize and parse functions that put each field into a byte buffer in a defined byte order, and test them against a known packet.
A new SPI sensor returns data that looks like every byte is shifted by one bit. What do you check?
Your grasp of SPI timing and how you debug a bus.
Suspects the clock mode (polarity and phase), confirms with a logic analyzer against the datasheet, then checks chip select and speed.

A one-bit shift usually means the clock mode is wrong. SPI has four modes set by clock polarity, the idle level of the clock, and clock phase, which edge samples the data. I put a logic analyzer on clock, data and chip select, compare with the timing diagram in the sensor datasheet, then check chip select timing and clock speed.
Walk me through your first day with a brand new board fresh from the assembly house.
How you bring up hardware step by step without damaging it.
Power checked before code, then debugger and chip ID, simplest clock first, then one peripheral at a time with logging early.

Before I flash anything, I power the board from a bench supply with a current limit and check every rail and the reset line. Then I connect the debugger, read the chip ID and blink an LED on the internal oscillator. Next I start the external crystal and the PLL, then bring up one peripheral at a time, the debug UART first so I can log.
How do you decide how big each task's stack should be, and how do you catch an overflow?
Whether you size memory from measurement rather than guesswork.
Measures with a fill pattern under worst-case paths, adds margin, and uses hardware so an overflow faults at once.

I fill each stack with a known pattern at startup, run the worst cases, deepest call path, nested interrupts, error paths, then read how much pattern is left. I add a margin, often 25 to 50 percent. I also add a guard: an MPU region below the stack or a stack limit register where the core has one, so an overflow faults at once instead of corrupting data.
What is priority inversion, and how does a real-time operating system deal with it?
Your understanding of scheduling problems in an RTOS.
Explains the three-task case and priority inheritance, and knows to use a mutex, not a plain semaphore, for shared resources.

A low-priority task holds a lock, a high-priority task waits for it, and a medium task that needs nothing preempts the low one, so the high task is stuck behind the medium one. Priority inheritance fixes it: the holder is raised to the waiter's priority until it releases the lock. I use a mutex for shared resources and keep the locked section short.
Your code works with optimization off but breaks at -O2. Apart from a missing volatile, what do you look for?
How you find bugs the optimizer exposes.
Looks for undefined behavior, vanished delay loops and changed stack use, and uses warnings, host tests and disassembly to prove it.

I look for undefined behavior the optimizer now exploits: an uninitialized variable, signed overflow, an out-of-bounds write, or type punning through a pointer that breaks strict aliasing. Busy-wait delay loops can also vanish, and stack use changes. I turn on all warnings, run host tests with sanitizers, and read the disassembly of the suspect function.
Your device should draw a few microamps asleep but draws a few hundred. How do you find the leak?
Your method for low-power debugging.
Trusts the measurement first, then checks pins, clocks and external parts one at a time instead of guessing.

First I check the measurement: a meter range with low burden voltage or a power analyzer, and the debugger unplugged, since debug can keep the chip awake. Then I check every pin, because floating inputs and pull-ups fighting a low line leak current. I make sure peripheral clocks are off and external parts like sensors are in their own sleep mode, then remove them one by one.
On a microcontroller with a data cache, DMA receive buffers sometimes hold old data. Why, and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand cache coherency between the CPU and DMA.
Clean before a DMA send, invalidate before reading after a DMA receive, align buffers to cache lines, or use non-cacheable memory.

The CPU reads its cached copy while the DMA wrote to RAM. After a DMA receive, I invalidate those cache lines before the CPU reads. Before a DMA send, I clean the cache so RAM holds the new data. Buffers are aligned to the cache line, 32 bytes on a Cortex-M7, and sized in whole lines, or I put them in a region the MPU marks non-cacheable.
The hardware team found a board bug and asks you to work around it in firmware to avoid a respin. How do you decide?
Your judgement on trade-offs between hardware and firmware.
Weighs risk, cost and how complete the fix is, documents the workaround, and pushes back with data when it hides a real problem.

If the fix is small, well understood and does not hide a safety or reliability problem, a firmware workaround can ship. I document it, tie it to a board revision check, and log it so the next spin fixes it in hardware. If it costs real power or timing margin, or only works on most units, I push for the respin and bring measurements.
How does a bootloader make sure it only runs firmware your company signed?
Your knowledge of secure boot and its weak points.
Signature checked with a public key in protected memory before jumping, private key never on the device, plus rollback protection.

The build server signs a hash of the image with a private key kept in a protected key store, never on the device. The bootloader sits in memory that cannot be rewritten and holds the public key or its hash. It hashes the image, checks the signature, and only then jumps to it. A version counter in protected memory blocks rollback to old signed images with known flaws.

fleet-manager.heading: Fleet manager questions
qs: What goes into the total cost of ownership of a fleet vehicle?
Whether you look past the purchase price.
Purchase or lease cost, financing, fuel, maintenance, insurance, registration, downtime and resale value, compared per mile or per month.

Everything the vehicle costs from buying it to selling it: the purchase price or lease payments, financing, fuel, maintenance and tires, insurance, registration and taxes, and the cost of downtime. Then I subtract the resale value. I divide by miles driven, so I can compare a van and a pickup on the same basis.
How do you set preventive maintenance intervals for a mixed fleet?
How you plan maintenance so vehicles break down less.
Starts from the maker's schedule, adjusts for how each unit is used, triggers service by miles, engine hours or time, and tracks on-time completion.

I start with the manufacturer's schedule for each model, then look at how it is used. A truck that idles all day on a job site gets serviced by engine hours, not miles. Low-mileage units still get a calendar check. The system flags units coming due, and I track how many services we finish on time each month.
What do you keep in a driver qualification file for a CDL driver?
Your working knowledge of federal driver rules.
The main contents named correctly, and knowing that drug and alcohol testing records are kept secure and separate.

The employment application, the driving record checks from each state where the driver held a license in the past three years, the road test certificate or the CDL accepted in its place, the medical examiner's certificate, the inquiry to previous employers, and the annual driving record review. Drug and alcohol records go in a separate, locked file.
How would you spot fuel card misuse?
How you control fuel spending, often the largest running cost.
Sets card limits, then compares purchases with vehicle data: tank size, fuel type, time, location and miles per gallon.

I set limits on each card: fuel only, a daily gallon cap, and a PIN plus odometer entry. Then I look for exceptions: a fill larger than the tank, premium fuel in a unit that runs on regular, a purchase on a day off, or a station miles from where telematics shows the truck. A sudden drop in miles per gallon on one unit is another flag.
How do you decide when a vehicle should be replaced?
Whether you time replacement on cost data and not on habit.
Tracks cost per mile over the vehicle's life and replaces near the point where rising repairs outweigh falling depreciation, also weighing safety and downtime.

I track each unit's cost per mile. Depreciation falls each year while repairs and downtime rise. Where the total starts climbing is the replacement window. I also look at big repairs coming up and resale value. A truck at 140,000 miles that needs a $6,000 transmission is a candidate to sell before the repair, not after.
When would you lease vehicles instead of buying them?
Your judgement on how to finance a fleet.
It depends on cash, cost of money, mileage, how long units are kept and upfits; compare the total cost both ways over the same term.

Leasing makes sense when the company wants to keep cash for the business, replaces vehicles on a short cycle, or wants a fixed monthly cost. Buying often wins when we keep units a long time or drive high miles, since leases can charge for extra miles and wear. I compare total cost both ways over the same term and bring finance in on the tax side.
Telematics shows one driver with three times the harsh braking events of everyone else. What do you do?
How you use driver data fairly to improve safety.
Checks the data and the route first, then coaches in private with a clear goal and a follow-up date; discipline only if nothing changes.

First I check the data: his route, his vehicle, and whether the sensor is set like the others. If it holds up, I sit down with him privately, show the events and ask what is going on. Often it is following too close in city traffic. We agree on a goal, I check again in two weeks, and I say so when the number drops.
A driver calls you right after a crash. Walk me through what happens next.
Whether you know the steps after an accident, in the right order.
People first and 911 called, then photos and facts, no arguing fault, a DOT post-accident test if the criteria are met, then insurer and records.

First I ask if anyone is hurt and make sure 911 is called. Then I ask for photos, the other driver's details, witnesses and the police report number, and tell him not to argue about fault. For a CDL driver I check at once if the crash meets the DOT post-accident testing criteria, since the time window is short. Then I report it to our insurer and log it.
A safety recall comes in for 40 of your vans and operations wants them all kept on the road. What do you do?
Your judgement when safety and operations pull in different directions.
Reads what the defect is, obeys any do-not-drive warning, schedules repairs in waves with spare units, and records each repair by VIN.

I read the notice first. If the maker says park the vehicles, they are parked and I find rentals. If the risk is lower, I check every VIN, book dealer slots in batches of five or six so routes stay covered, and use spare vans to fill the gaps. I record each repair against its VIN so no van is missed.
You learn a driver has been driving for two months on a suspended license. How do you handle it?
How you handle a serious compliance failure and fix the process behind it.
Takes the driver off the road at once, brings in HR and the insurer, then finds why the check missed it and closes the gap.

He stops driving today, and I bring in HR and our insurer. Then I find out how we missed it. Often it is because records were only pulled once a year. I would move all drivers to continuous record monitoring, which alerts us when a state posts a change, and make it a clear rule that drivers report any suspension to us right away.
A driver's end-of-day inspection report lists a soft brake pedal. What has to happen before that truck runs again?
Whether you know the DVIR rules for defects that affect safety.
The repair is done before dispatch and certified in writing. The next driver reviews and signs the report, and the records are kept for three months.

The truck is held. The shop repairs the brakes, and someone signs on the report that the defect was fixed. Before the next trip, the next driver reviews that report and signs it. We keep the original report and the repair certification for at least three months. No one moves it just for today with a brake complaint.
Operations wants a bigger box truck. Why does the GVWR you spec matter so much?
Whether you know which weight ratings bring new rules for drivers.
From 10,001 lb in interstate use the truck is a CMV under FMCSA rules. From 26,001 lb the driver needs a CDL and joins drug and alcohol testing.

GVWR is the weight rating, not today's weight. From 10,001 pounds in interstate use, the truck is a commercial vehicle: medical cards, driver files, hours rules, annual inspections. From 26,001 pounds the driver needs a Class B CDL and joins drug and alcohol testing. So I size the payload first, because that one choice changes who I can hire.
When do you run Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse queries on CDL drivers, and what kind?
Your grasp of an employer's FMCSA Clearinghouse duties.
A full query with the driver's consent before hire and a query on every driver at least yearly. If a limited query finds a record, a full query within 24 hours.

Before a new CDL driver does any safety-sensitive work, I run a full query, which the driver consents to inside the Clearinghouse. Then every driver gets a query at least once a year; a limited query is fine with a signed general consent. If a limited query shows a record, I run a full query within 24 hours, and the driver stays off the road until it clears.
A driver's ELD fails halfway through a run. What does the driver do, and what do you do?
Whether you know the ELD malfunction rules for drivers and carriers.
The driver notes the failure, tells the carrier within 24 hours and keeps paper logs. The carrier repairs or replaces the unit within eight days.

The driver notes the malfunction, tells us in writing within 24 hours, and switches to paper logs. If the past 7 days can't be shown from the device, the driver rebuilds them on paper. On my side, we must repair or replace the unit within 8 days, or ask FMCSA for more time. I keep the malfunction note with the logs so an inspector sees the full trail.
Maintenance cost per mile jumped 18% this quarter. How do you find out why?
How you take apart a cost number before acting on it.
Checks the miles as well as the dollars, then splits cost by unit, system and vendor to find the real cause.

First I check the miles: if they dropped, cost per mile rises with no new spending. Then I split the dollars by unit and by system using repair codes. Often a few old units or one big engine job explain most of it. I also check labor rates, tire buys, repeat repairs, and warranty work we paid for but should have claimed.
A department asks for five more trucks. How do you decide?
How you use utilization data to approve a request or push back.
Looks at how the current units are really used, tests pooling or rentals for peaks, and buys only for steady demand.

I pull telematics for their current trucks: days used, hours running, miles. Last time a similar request came in, a third of the units sat idle two days a week. We pooled them across two teams and rented for the seasonal peak, and the department got by with one new truck instead of five. If the data shows steady full use, I approve and plan the buy.
Your Vehicle Maintenance BASIC score is climbing toward the intervention line. What do you do?
Whether you understand CSA data and fix the cause, not just the score.
Reads the roadside violations behind the score, fixes the habits that cause them, and challenges wrong records through DataQs.

I pull the inspection reports behind the score and sort the violations. Usually it's lights, tires and brake adjustment, things a good pre-trip catches. I retrain on pre-trips, have the shop check those items at every service, and audit DVIRs. If a violation was recorded wrong, I file a DataQs request. The score follows when roadside inspections come back clean.
How do you run a preventability review after a crash, and what records do you keep?
Whether you judge crashes fairly and keep the accident register right.
One clear standard applied to the facts: could the driver reasonably have avoided it. Plus a three-year register of DOT-recordable crashes.

A small committee looks at the police report, photos, camera video and telematics, and asks one question: did the driver do everything reasonable to avoid it? Not at fault legally is not the same as non-preventable. Crashes with a death, an injury treated away from the scene, or a tow for disabling damage go in the accident register, kept three years.
How would you decide whether to bring maintenance in-house or keep using outside shops?
Your judgement on a large decision about cost and control.
Compares full cost per job and downtime, including technicians, space, tools and waste handling, not just the hourly labor rate.

I'd price the in-house shop fully: technician pay and turnover, the building, diagnostic tools, parts stock, and handling used oil and other waste. Then I compare per job and in days of downtime, since a truck waiting at a vendor costs money too. Often the answer is mixed: in-house for routine service, dealers for warranty work and heavy engine repairs.
Leadership wants electric vans in the fleet next year. How do you evaluate it before committing?
Whether you test a big change against real routes and real costs.
Matches routes to real range in cold weather and under load, checks depot power and charging costs, compares total cost, and pilots first.

I start with telematics: daily miles, idle time and how long vans sit at the depot. Routes well under the van's real range, counting winter and payload, are candidates. Then I check if the site's electrical service can handle chargers and what demand charges add to the power bill. I compare total cost against gas vans and run a small pilot before ordering more.

flight-software.heading: Flight software engineer questions
qs: Why do many flight software teams forbid dynamic memory allocation after startup?
Whether you know why flight code must behave the same way every time.
Fragmentation, allocation failure and unpredictable timing, plus the fix: allocate everything at initialization.

Calling malloc in the middle of a mission can fail when the heap is fragmented, and how long it takes is not predictable. Neither is acceptable in a control loop. I size every buffer and pool at startup, so if memory is short we find out on the ground during initialization, not in orbit.
What does a watchdog timer do, and where in the code do you reset it?
Whether you understand how a system recovers from a hang without a human.
The watchdog resets the processor if not serviced in time; it is serviced only after checking that all critical tasks are alive, not from an interrupt.

It is a hardware counter that resets the processor if the software stops servicing it. I never service it from a timer interrupt, because that keeps running while the main tasks are stuck. A low-priority monitor checks that each critical task has checked in this cycle, and only then resets the watchdog.
In embedded C, what does the volatile keyword do, and what does it not do?
Your grasp of how the compiler treats hardware registers and shared data.
Volatile stops the compiler from caching or removing reads and writes; it does not make an operation atomic or protect data shared between tasks.

It tells the compiler every read and write must really happen, so a status register is read from the hardware each time instead of from a cached copy. It does not make a read-modify-write atomic, and it is not a lock. For data shared between tasks I still need a mutex, disabled interrupts or an atomic operation.
What is priority inversion, and how do you prevent it?
Whether you can reason about real-time scheduling, not just code that works on the bench.
A clear example with three tasks and a shared lock, and a fix: priority inheritance or a priority ceiling, plus short critical sections.

A low-priority task holds a mutex the high-priority task needs. A medium-priority task then preempts the low one, so the high one waits on less important work. I use mutexes with priority inheritance, so the holder is raised to the waiting task's priority, and I keep critical sections short. Then I check worst-case blocking times in the timing analysis.
What is MC/DC coverage, and why is it required for the most critical airborne software?
Your knowledge of the structural coverage asked for at DO-178C Level A.
Each condition in a decision is shown to change the outcome on its own; Level A asks for it because plain branch coverage can miss a condition.

Modified condition/decision coverage means every condition in a decision has been shown to flip the result on its own, with the others held fixed. For 'A and B' that takes three tests: true-true, true-false and false-true. DO-178C asks for it at Level A, where a failure could be catastrophic, because branch coverage alone can leave a condition untested in effect.
How does flight software protect itself against radiation flipping bits in memory?
Whether you know the software side of designing for single event upsets.
Error-correcting memory with scrubbing, checksums on code and tables, redundant copies of critical data, and a way to reload a clean image.

The hardware usually has error-correcting memory, and the software runs a scrubber that reads through it regularly, so a single-bit error gets corrected before a second one lands in the same word. I keep checksums on code and parameter tables, store critical state in more than one copy and compare them, and can reload a clean image from protected storage.
A gyro starts reporting a value outside its physical range in flight. Walk me through what the software should do.
How you design fault detection, isolation and recovery.
No overreaction to one bad sample; a persistence check, isolation of the unit, a switch to a backup or safe mode, and clear telemetry for the ground.

First the reading is rejected, so it never reaches the control law. If it stays bad for a set number of cycles, the fault is declared, the unit is marked failed and the software switches to the redundant gyro or a mode that does not need it. Every step goes into telemetry with a time stamp, so the ground team can see what happened and why.
Code reused from an earlier vehicle converts a 64-bit float to a 16-bit integer and overflows on the new trajectory. What went wrong, and how do you stop it?
Whether you check the assumptions in reused code against the new mission.
Reuse without rechecking ranges is the root cause; the fix is range analysis for the new vehicle, limits before conversion and a defined response.

The code was right for the old flight profile, and nobody rechecked its ranges for the new one. I treat reused code as new for analysis: every input range is traced against the new vehicle's envelope. Before any narrowing conversion I check the range and saturate or flag it, and a fault in a nonessential function must never shut down an essential one.
Two days before launch you find a bug in an error path that only runs if a rare fault occurs. What do you do?
Your judgement about risk when the schedule is tight.
Report it at once with an honest risk assessment; let the review board weigh a late change against a workaround, since every change needs retesting.

I write it up and tell my lead the same day: what triggers it, what happens if it fires and how likely that is. Then I lay out the options: a code change with the regression tests it needs, a procedure the operators can use instead, or flying as is with the risk on record. The board decides; I make sure they decide with the facts.
The vehicle is in orbit and you need to upload a software patch. How do you plan it so a mistake cannot lose the mission?
How you plan an in-flight software change with no chance to touch the hardware.
Testing on a flight-like testbed, a known good image kept untouched, checksum checks before switching, and a fallback if the new image fails to boot.

The patch runs first on our flight-equivalent testbed, including the upload itself and a failed boot. On orbit we write it to a spare memory slot, never over the known good image, and verify the checksum before anything changes. We switch during a ground contact, and if the new image does not come up healthy, the boot logic falls back to the old one.
What does hardware-in-the-loop testing catch that software-in-the-loop testing misses?
Whether you know what each test level can and cannot prove.
Real timing, interrupts, drivers, buses, and the real compiler and processor, plus why software-in-the-loop is still worth running first.

In software-in-the-loop, the flight code runs on a desktop against a simulation, so it is fast and good for logic. In hardware-in-the-loop, the real flight computer runs in real time with real or emulated sensors on its real buses. That catches timing overruns, interrupt problems, driver bugs, byte order mistakes and compiler differences.
How does rate monotonic scheduling assign priorities, and how do you check that a task set is schedulable?
Your grasp of the theory behind fixed-priority real-time scheduling.
Shorter period gets higher priority. The utilization bound is a sufficient test only; response-time analysis gives the exact answer.

The task with the shortest period gets the highest priority. For independent periodic tasks with deadlines equal to periods, total CPU use under n times (2 to the 1/n, minus 1) guarantees every deadline; that bound falls toward about 69%. Above it the set may still work, so I run response-time analysis, which also lets me include blocking and interrupt time.
A unit passes every test but resets after about 49 days of continuous running. What do you suspect?
Whether you recognize a timer rollover and know how to write wrap-safe time code.
A 32-bit millisecond counter wraps at about 49.7 days. Compute elapsed time with unsigned subtraction and test with the counter preset near the wrap.

A 32-bit counter of milliseconds wraps after about 49.7 days, so I suspect code that compares absolute times, like now greater than deadline. I would compute elapsed time as now minus start in unsigned 32-bit math, which stays correct across one wrap. Then I add a test that starts the counter a few seconds before the wrap instead of waiting 49 days.
An interrupt updates a 64-bit timestamp and a task reads it on a 32-bit processor. What can go wrong?
How you reason about atomic access to data shared between interrupts and tasks.
The read takes two loads, so it can be torn. Fix it with a short critical section, a re-read loop or a sequence counter.

The 64-bit read takes two 32-bit loads. If the interrupt fires between them, the task gets the new high half with the old low half, a time that can be far off. I would either disable interrupts for those two loads only, or read high, then low, then high again and retry if the high half changed. Volatile alone does not fix this.
Your attitude controller has an integral term, and the reaction wheels hit their torque limit during a large slew. What happens, and how do you design for it?
Your understanding of control loops working against real actuator limits.
Integrator windup causes a large overshoot after saturation. Fix it with clamping, conditional integration or back-calculation, and test at the limits.

While the wheels are at their limit, the error stays large and the integrator keeps growing. When the vehicle gets close, that stored value drives it far past the target. I stop integrating while the output is saturated, clamp the integrator, and shape the slew so the controller never asks for more torque than the wheels can give. Then I test at full saturation.
Why do you run polarity tests on the integrated vehicle, and how do you do one?
Whether you know that sign errors survive simulation and how to catch them on hardware.
Simulations share the flight code's axis and sign assumptions, and a flipped sign turns feedback positive. Move or command each unit and check the sign in telemetry.

A simulation uses the same axis and sign tables as the flight code, so a wrong sign can pass every sim. On the real vehicle a flipped gyro or thruster turns the control loop into positive feedback. I rotate the vehicle or each sensor in a known direction and check the sign in telemetry, then command each actuator and confirm it moves or fires the expected way.
How do you set the persistence on a fault monitor so it neither trips on noise nor reacts too late?
Your judgement in tuning fault protection between false alarms and missed faults.
Persistence based on real noise data and on how fast the fault becomes harmful, with detection and response time budgeted and tested both ways.

I look at real noise and glitch data to see how many bad samples in a row a healthy unit produces, and I set the count above that, often as M out of N samples. Then I check the other side: how long the fault can last before it hurts the vehicle. Detection plus response must fit inside that, with margin. I test a noisy healthy unit and a true fault.
How would you design the software side of a command that fires a pyrotechnic device?
How you protect an irreversible action against a single error.
Separate arm and fire, checked preconditions, an arm state that times out, hardware inhibits independent of software, and clear telemetry.

Firing cannot be undone, so no single command or single bit flip may do it. I use separate arm and fire commands, check that the vehicle is in the right mode, and let the arm state time out if fire does not follow. The hardware has its own inhibits that software cannot bypass. Every step shows in telemetry, so the ground sees the state before the next step.
How do you show that a task meets its deadline on a processor with caches?
Whether you can argue worst-case timing rather than typical timing.
A measured maximum is not a bound. Combine static timing analysis or worst-case test conditions with cache control, interrupt load and a timing margin.

A measured maximum only shows the worst case we happened to see. With caches, the same code can run much slower after other tasks evict its data. I either use a static timing analysis tool for that processor, or lock or flush caches and measure with worst-case inputs and full interrupt load. I feed the result into response-time analysis and keep a margin.
In orbit, the vehicle drops into safe mode, the team commands it out, and it drops back again. What do you do?
How you lead through an anomaly without making the vehicle less safe.
Stop re-commanding, confirm safe mode is stable, use logs to find the trigger, reproduce it on the testbed, and change only after review.

First I would stop commanding it out. Safe mode is doing its job, so we confirm power, thermal and communication are stable there. Then we pull event logs and telemetry from the seconds before each trip to find which monitor fired and why. We reproduce it on the testbed, agree on a fix such as a corrected parameter, review it, run it on the testbed, and only then uplink.

forward-deployed-engineer.heading: Forward deployed engineer questions
qs: How is the forward deployed engineer role different from a solutions engineer or a consultant?
Whether you understand what the role actually is.
You write and ship production code inside the customer's work, and you carry what you learn back to the product team.

A solutions engineer mostly helps close the sale with demos. A consultant often advises and hands off. I sit with the customer's team, write the code that connects our product to their data and workflow, and own it until people use it. Then I tell our product team what kept breaking, so the next customer needs less custom work.
A customer asks you for a dashboard. How do you find out what they actually need?
Your customer discovery skills.
Asking what decision the dashboard will drive and how they do the work today, before building anything.

I ask what decision they would make differently with it, who makes it and how often. Then I ask them to show me how they do it now, often in a spreadsheet. Once, a dashboard request turned out to be a need for one daily alert about late shipments. We built the alert in two days and skipped the dashboard.
Walk me through your first week on a new customer site.
How you get oriented fast without wasting the customer's time.
Meeting the real users, starting data and system access early, and agreeing on one first problem with a clear way to measure it.

On day one, I make sure access requests are started, since they often take days. Then I sit with the people who do the work, not just the sponsor, and watch how they do it today. By the end of the week I want one narrow problem, a number that shows success, and a rough prototype on real data they can react to.
The data you need sits in an old on-premise database, a vendor API and a few spreadsheets. How do you bring it together?
How you approach data integration in a messy real environment.
Reading without disturbing source systems, matching records across sources, checking totals with the business, and making loads safe to rerun.

I start read-only, ideally from a replica or an export, so I never slow down a system people rely on. I map how records match across sources, like customer IDs formatted differently. I load into a staging area, check row counts and totals with someone who knows the numbers, and make each load safe to rerun without creating duplicates.
The customer wants a tool that answers questions from their internal documents, and you have one week. How do you build the prototype?
Your rapid prototyping with language models on customer data.
Retrieval-augmented generation on a small document set, answers that cite their sources, and a test set of real user questions.

I would use retrieval-augmented generation: split the documents into passages, search for the passages relevant to a question, and give those to the model with the question. Answers show their sources so users can check them. Early on I collect 30 or 40 real questions with known answers, so I can measure whether each change makes it better or worse.
Their security team says no data can leave their network. What are your options?
How you work within a customer's security and compliance limits.
Treating the rule as a requirement, offering options like running inside their environment, and involving security early instead of working around them.

I take it as a design constraint, not an obstacle. Options include deploying our software inside their cloud account or data center, or using models that run in their environment. I would meet the security team early, ask what review they need, and give them a clear diagram of where data goes. I never copy data to my laptop to move faster.
Your prototype impressed the customer, and they want it in production next week. What do you say?
Your judgement about the gap between a demo and a system people depend on.
Being honest about what is missing, like error handling, monitoring and access control, and offering a limited, safe rollout instead of a flat no.

I thank them and say plainly what the demo skips: it runs on a sample, has no login controls, and nobody gets alerted if it fails. I offer a pilot with five users next week while we close those gaps, with a date for wider rollout. That keeps the momentum without putting their operations on something fragile.
A customer asks for a feature only they need. How do you decide whether to build it for them or push for it in the core product?
How you balance one customer's needs against the product as a whole.
Finding the general need behind the request, keeping true one-offs out of shared code, and sending repeated patterns to the product team.

I ask what problem sits under the request, because a one-off ask is often a common need in disguise. If other customers have the same need, I write it up for the product team with examples. If it is really unique, I build it as configuration or a separate extension, not a change to shared code, so it does not make every future upgrade harder.
A week after you ship a report, a finance analyst says your revenue numbers are 8% too high. What do you do?
How you handle your own mistake in front of a customer.
Owning it quickly, warning users, finding the root cause, fixing it, and adding a check so it cannot happen again.

I thank her and tell the report's users right away that the figures are under review. Then I trace it. An overcount like that often comes from a join that duplicates rows, such as orders matched to several address records. I fix it, show her the corrected numbers against her own totals, and add a daily check that compares our totals to the finance system.
The executive who signed the contract wants one thing, and the people who will use the tool want another. How do you handle it?
How you handle conflicting stakeholders inside a customer.
Making the conflict visible with evidence, tying the work to the sponsor's goal, and not quietly choosing a side.

I bring them together with facts. On one project the vice president wanted a forecast, while planners needed cleaner order data, because the forecast would be wrong without it. I showed her forecast errors caused by bad data and proposed two weeks on the data first, then the forecast. She agreed, because it served her goal. I don't quietly build what one side wants.
Two source systems log events in local time and one logs in UTC. How do you join them safely?
Whether you know the time zone traps that break data joins.
Convert to UTC on load, keep the original value and zone, and test the daylight saving change days directly.

I convert every timestamp to UTC when I load it and keep the raw value and its source zone in separate columns. Local time repeats one hour each fall when clocks go back, so I check how each system records that hour. Then I test the join on the March and November change dates, where most of these bugs hide.
What does it mean for a data pipeline to be idempotent, and why does it matter on a customer site?
Your grasp of pipelines that can be rerun without damage.
Running a job twice gives the same result as running it once, so a failed or repeated run never duplicates or loses rows.

It means I can rerun the load for the same day and end up with the same data, not double rows. On site, jobs fail at odd hours and someone reruns them without asking me. So I replace a whole date partition or upsert on a stable key, and I never just append blindly.
You need to match customers across a CRM and a billing system that share no common ID. How do you do it?
How you handle entity resolution when the data does not line up.
Clean the fields, match in tiers from exact to fuzzy, check accuracy on a reviewed sample, and route unclear pairs to a human.

First I put names, addresses, emails and tax IDs into one format. I match exactly on strong fields like email or tax ID, then fuzzy on name plus address. I give a sample of 200 matches to someone in billing to check, tune the thresholds, and send low-confidence pairs to a review list instead of guessing.
How do you know your document question-answering prototype is good enough, beyond the demo looking right?
Whether you can measure an AI tool instead of trusting a few good demos.
A test set of real questions with answers from the customer's experts, scored for correct sources and correct answers, rerun after every change.

I sit with two or three of their experts and collect 50 to 100 real questions, the answers they would accept, and the document each comes from. I score whether the right passage was found and whether the answer is correct and cited. I rerun that set after every prompt or chunking change, so I catch regressions before users do.
Halfway through a project you find the data includes patient health records. What changes?
Whether you stop and handle regulated data the right way.
Pause, tell your lead and the customer's privacy owner, confirm the HIPAA paperwork and access rules, and keep only the data you need.

I stop pulling that data and tell my lead and the customer's compliance contact the same day. If they are covered by HIPAA and this is protected health information, we need a business associate agreement in place before we handle it. Then I limit access, drop fields we do not need, and record what I already touched.
Your nightly pipeline broke because the vendor renamed a field without warning. How do you keep this from hurting you again?
How you design integrations to survive changes upstream.
Fix and backfill first, then add schema checks that fail loudly, alerts to an owner, and a change notice agreement with the source.

I patch the mapping and backfill the missed night first. Then I add a check at the start of the job that compares incoming fields to the expected list and stops with a clear alert instead of loading empty values. I ask the vendor contact for change notices and keep the raw files so I can replay any day.
Two weeks after launch, daily users dropped from 40 to 6. What do you do?
Whether you treat low adoption as your problem to diagnose.
Read the usage data, then watch people work, find where the tool lost to their old way, and fix that before adding features.

I check the logs first: who stopped, and at which step. Then I sit with three people who quit and watch them do the task. Last time it was speed: results took 20 seconds and the old spreadsheet took five. I cached the slow query, told the team, and usage came back over the next two weeks.
A plant manager acted on a wrong answer from your AI assistant. How do you handle it?
How you own a failure in a tool people rely on.
Contain the harm, tell the customer plainly, find the root cause, and add a guard and a test so the same error gets caught.

First I help undo the decision he made, and I tell his lead and mine what happened, without excuses. Then I trace it: which documents were retrieved and why the answer went wrong. I add that case to the test set, make the tool show its sources and say when it is unsure, and tell users what changed.
Your champion at the customer asks you to skip their change approval process to make a deadline. What do you do?
Your judgement when speed and the customer's own controls collide.
You do not bypass controls; you find a faster approved path, such as an expedited review or a smaller first release, and state the trade-off.

I say no to skipping it, kindly, because if something breaks it lands on both of us. Then I ask what the process allows: an expedited review, a smaller release that needs less approval, or a run for one team in a test setup. I offer to write the request myself so it moves fast.
You leave this account in a month. Walk me through how you hand it over.
Whether what you built keeps working after you leave.
Named owners, a runbook, working alerts, and a shadow period where the customer's team runs things while you watch.

I list everything I built and name an owner on their side for each piece. I write a short runbook: how it runs, what each alert means, how to rerun a failed job. For the last two weeks their engineer does the work and I only watch and answer. I also send our product team a note on what others could reuse.

founders-office.heading: Founder’s office and special projects questions
qs: How is a founder's office role different from being the founder's executive assistant?
Whether you understand what the job is and what it is not.
You own outcomes on priority projects, not the calendar. You work with the founder's context but earn authority through results.

An assistant protects the founder's time. I take whole pieces of work off the founder's plate: a launch, a hiring push, a fundraise. I run it end to end, bring decisions back in short form, and then move to the next priority when the quarter changes.
How do you put together a board meeting pre-read?
Your grasp of how a board is kept informed.
It goes out days ahead and is short. It shows numbers against plan, states bad news honestly, and lists the decisions the board is asked to make.

I send it about a week ahead so directors read it before the meeting. It opens with a one-page summary, then key metrics against plan, cash and runway, and what went wrong. The last page lists the decisions we need, so the meeting is spent on discussion, not on reading slides.
Walk me through setting up a data room for a fundraise.
Whether you know what investors look at in due diligence.
Organized documents are ready before the first meeting: corporate records, cap table, financials, contracts, IP and people records, with access tracked.

I build the folders before outreach starts: incorporation and board documents, the cap table, financials and the model, key contracts, IP assignment agreements, and employee and option records. I work with our lawyers to find gaps early, like a missing IP assignment. I also track who opens what, so we can see which investors are serious.
In plain words, what is the difference between raising on a SAFE and raising a priced round?
Your grasp of basic startup financing terms.
A SAFE puts off setting a price and converts into shares later. A priced round sets a valuation and issues shares now.

A SAFE is a simple agreement for future equity. The investor pays now and gets shares later, usually at the next priced round, often with a valuation cap or a discount. A priced round sets a valuation today and issues preferred shares. It comes with more negotiated terms and more legal work.
The founder hands you a project called 'fix churn' and nothing else. What do you do in the first two weeks?
How you turn a vague mandate into a clear plan.
You define the problem with data and with people, agree on a measurable goal and owners, and bring back a plan before doing big work.

In week one I pull the numbers: who leaves, when, and from which plan. I also call ten customers who canceled and talk to support and sales. In week two I bring the founder a one-page brief: the two biggest causes, a target we agree on, who owns each fix, and what I need from the founder.
You are asked to run the search for the company's first head of sales. How do you run it?
Whether you can run a senior hire without wasting the founder's time.
A written scorecard is agreed first. The process is structured, every finalist is assessed the same way, and references are checked with care.

First I write a scorecard with the founder: what this person must achieve in year one and which skills prove it. I screen candidates myself and only send the founder people who fit. Every finalist gets the same interviews and a practical exercise. Before any offer, I check references, including people who managed the candidate.
A department head sees you as the founder's spy and will not share data for your project. How do you handle it?
How you get work done through others without formal authority.
You build trust directly, share credit, and are open about your next steps. You go to the founder only as a last resort.

I meet them one on one and ask what worries them. I show them exactly what I need and why, and I offer to share my findings with them before the founder sees anything. Usually that is enough. If it is not, I tell them I will raise it with the founder, so nothing happens behind their back.
The founder makes a call you think is wrong, and the team asks you what is going on. What do you do?
Your judgement about loyalty, candor and the team.
You disagree with the founder in private and give reasons. Once the decision is made, you explain it to the team without undermining it.

I raise my concern with the founder in private, with evidence, before the decision is final if I can. Once it is decided, I explain the reasons to the team as clearly as I can and do not hint that I disagreed. If new facts show it is not working, I bring them back to the founder quickly.
Tell me about a project you kept alive too long. What did you learn?
Whether you can admit a mistake and stop work that is not paying off.
An honest story with the cost named, and a habit you use now, like setting stop criteria at the start.

I ran a partner program for seven months because we had announced it to the whole company. It brought in two small deals. I should have stopped at month three. Now every project I start has a written goal and a review date. If we miss the goal, I bring the founder a stop-or-change decision, not a status update.
Several people tell you a senior leader is losing their team, and that leader is the founder's close friend. What do you do?
How you handle sensitive people issues close to the founder.
You confirm it is a pattern, protect the people who spoke up, tell the founder plainly, and suggest a fair next step, not a verdict.

First I check that it is a pattern, not one bad week: people leaving, missed goals, what I see in meetings. Then I tell the founder in private, with facts, without naming people who asked to stay anonymous. I suggest a fair next step, like structured feedback or a coach. If any complaint could be a legal matter, I bring in HR.
A board member asks why our ARR does not match revenue on the income statement. How do you explain it?
Whether you know the core SaaS metrics well enough to defend them in the boardroom.
ARR is an annualized snapshot of recurring contracts; revenue is what accounting recognized in the period. One-time fees stay out of ARR.

Revenue is what we recognized in the period under accounting rules, including setup and services fees. ARR is a snapshot: the annual value of the recurring subscriptions live today. They differ because of timing, growth during the year and one-time fees. I would show a short bridge from one to the other and keep the ARR definition written down so it never shifts.
What goes into a good monthly investor update, and what do you leave out?
How you communicate with investors between board meetings.
Short, same format every month, key numbers with context, bad news stated plainly, and specific asks investors can act on.

I keep the same skeleton every month: a three-line summary, the same five metrics against last month and plan, wins, problems, and two or three concrete asks, like an intro to a named buyer. Bad news goes near the top. I leave out detail only the team needs and anything I would not want forwarded.
We are 60 people and growing fast. Design the weekly and monthly operating cadence you would put in place.
Whether you can build a rhythm of meetings and reviews that fits the company's size.
Few meetings, each with a clear purpose: a weekly leadership meeting on one scorecard, monthly reviews, quarterly planning. Meetings that decide nothing get cut.

Weekly: a 60-minute leadership meeting run off one scorecard, where every red metric gets an owner and a date. Monthly: a business review per function and an all-hands. Quarterly: goal setting and a look back. First I would list every recurring meeting, drop the ones with no decision or owner, and check after a month that people actually use the scorecard.
We raise $5 million at a $20 million pre-money valuation, and the investor wants the option pool topped up before the round. Who pays for that pool?
Whether you can do basic round math and spot the option pool shuffle.
Post-money is $25 million, so the investor owns 20%. A pool added pre-money dilutes only existing holders, which lowers the effective pre-money.

Post-money is $25 million, so the new investor owns 5 divided by 25, or 20%. If the pool increase is counted in the pre-money, founders and current holders absorb all of its dilution and the investor's 20% is untouched. So the real price for existing holders is below $20 million. I would size the pool from an actual hiring plan, not a round number, to keep it small.
Explain a 1x non-participating liquidation preference to a new employee who holds options.
Whether you understand the terms that decide who gets paid in a sale.
In a sale the investor takes either their money back or their share as if converted to common, whichever is larger, not both.

If the company is sold, that investor can take back what they put in, once, or convert to common and take their ownership share instead, whichever is more. In a big exit they convert and everyone shares by ownership. In a small exit their money comes out first, so common holders, including your options, may get less or nothing.
Why does the board approve option grants, and why do we care when our last 409A valuation was done?
Whether you understand the equity mechanics behind hiring offers.
The plan gives the board the power to grant, at a strike of at least fair market value. A 409A under 12 months old, with no material event since, supports that price.

The plan gives the board the power to grant options, and the strike must be at least fair market value on the grant date. Set too low, the employee can owe extra tax and penalties under Section 409A. An independent valuation is presumed reasonable for up to 12 months unless something material changes, like a priced round. So I line up grants after a fresh 409A.
You are running a product launch, but marketing, sales and engineering do not report to you. How do you keep it on track?
How you drive work across teams you have no authority over.
A written plan with one owner per workstream, dates and decision rights, a short regular check-in, and early, visible escalation of slips.

First I write a one-page plan: goal, launch date, each workstream with a named owner, and who decides what. The heads agree to it once with the founder in the room, so it carries weight. Then a 20-minute check-in twice a week on a shared tracker. When something slips I go to the owner first, and if it threatens the date I raise it the same day, with options, not blame.
Decisions are piling up waiting for the founder, and teams are stalled. How do you fix that without taking decisions you should not take?
Whether you can widen the founder's reach without overstepping.
Sort which decisions truly need the founder, get explicit delegation for the rest, and prepare the remaining ones so they take minutes, not days.

I list every open decision for a week and sort it with the founder: what only they can decide, what a leader can own, and what I can decide within agreed limits. We write that down and tell the team. For what stays with the founder, I send a short memo with options and a recommendation, and I hold a standing 30-minute decision slot so nothing waits more than a few days.
You sent the monthly investor update, and an hour later you see the cash runway figure is wrong by four months. What do you do?
How you own and correct a mistake in front of investors.
Tell the founder at once, send a short, plain correction the same day, and fix the cause in the process. No hiding or softening.

I tell the founder right away, with the correct number and how the error happened. Then we send a short correction to the same list that day: the right runway, one line on the cause, no drama. Investors forgive a fixed error; they do not forgive finding it themselves. Afterward I add a step where finance signs off on every number before anything goes out.
Two weeks before a raise, the founder wants to count unpaid pilots as ARR in the deck. What do you do?
Your judgement and integrity when there is pressure to make the numbers look better.
You push back in private with the risk spelled out and offer an honest way to show the pilots. You do not ship a misleading number.

I raise it with the founder alone, not in front of the team. Investors check ARR against contracts and bank records in diligence; if pilots show up as recurring revenue, we lose their trust and maybe the round. I suggest showing real ARR and the pilots as a separate line with expected conversion dates. If the founder still insists, I say plainly I cannot put that slide out.

fpga-engineer.heading: FPGA engineer questions
qs: In Verilog, when do you use blocking and when do you use nonblocking assignments?
Whether you know the basic coding rule that keeps simulation and hardware in agreement.
Nonblocking in clocked blocks, blocking in combinational blocks, and an understanding of why mixing them causes simulation races.

In a clocked always block I use nonblocking, <=, so every register updates from the values present at the clock edge, the way real flip-flops behave. In combinational logic I use blocking, =. I never mix both on one signal. That causes races where simulation order changes the result, and the simulation stops matching the hardware.
What makes a synthesis tool infer a latch, and why do you avoid it?
Whether you can spot a common coding mistake in combinational logic.
An output not assigned on every path, the reasons latches are a problem, and a habit that prevents them.

A latch appears when combinational logic does not assign an output on every path. Examples are an if without an else, or a case without a default. The tool must hold the old value, so it builds a latch. Latches are hard to time and are usually a bug. I give every output a default value at the top of the block, and I read the synthesis warnings for inferred latches.
Explain setup and hold time. Which one does a slower clock fix?
Your grasp of the timing basics behind every FPGA design.
Correct definitions, plus the point that a slower clock helps setup but does nothing for hold.

Setup time is how long data must be stable before the clock edge. Hold time is how long it must stay stable after the edge. A setup violation means the path is too slow for the clock period, so a slower clock fixes it. A hold violation means the data changes too soon after the edge. That does not depend on the period, so slowing the clock does not help.
How do you move a signal safely from one clock domain to another?
Whether you handle clock domain crossings for single bits and for buses.
A two-flop synchronizer for one bit, care with short pulses, and a FIFO or handshake for multi-bit data, never per-bit sync.

For one control bit I use a two-flop synchronizer in the receiving domain, which gives a metastable value time to settle. A short pulse from a faster clock can be missed, so I convert it to a toggle first. For a bus I never synchronize each bit separately, because bits can land in different cycles. I use an async FIFO with Gray-coded pointers, or a handshake that holds the data steady.
How do you design the reset, and what does asynchronous assert, synchronous deassert mean?
How you avoid reset problems that only show up on real hardware.
Reset goes active at any time but is released in step with each clock, and only registers that need a reset get one.

The reset can go active at any moment, even with no clock running. Its release is synchronized to each clock domain through a couple of flops. That way no register leaves reset right at a clock edge, which could free some registers a cycle before others. I also reset only what needs it, like state machines and valid flags. Data paths often don't, and that saves routing.
Timing analysis shows negative setup slack on one path at 250 MHz. Walk me through what you do.
How you close timing in a methodical way instead of trying random tool settings.
First check the constraints are right, then find whether logic or routing causes the delay, then fix the design before tuning the tools.

First I confirm the constraints are right: every clock defined, I/O delays correct. Then I see where the delay sits, too many logic levels or long routing. For logic, I add a pipeline register or restructure, like splitting a wide compare. For routing, I look for high fanout and duplicate the driving register. Only then do I try other placement strategies.
Your design passes every simulation but fails on the board. Where do you look?
How you debug the problems simulation cannot show.
Focus on what simulation does not model: constraints, clock crossings, reset and clocks, I/O, then capture real signals on chip.

I start with what simulation doesn't model. I check the timing report for unconstrained paths and undefined clocks. I review clock domain crossings and confirm the logic waits until the clocks are locked before leaving reset. Then I add an on-chip logic analyzer to the failing interface, trigger on the error, and compare the capture with the simulation waveform.
A colleague wants to put a false path on a failing path to close timing before a release. What do you say?
Your judgement on timing exceptions when there is pressure to ship.
A false path only when the path truly never needs to meet timing, documented; otherwise it hides a real failure and the fix belongs in the logic.

I'd ask why the path is false. If it goes through a proper synchronizer, or it's a config register that only changes while the logic is idle, the constraint is right, and we write down why. If it's a normal register-to-register path on one clock, a false path just hides the bug. The build passes and the board fails at random, maybe only when hot. Then we fix the logic or move the date.
For a low-latency trading design, how do you weigh pipeline depth against latency?
Whether you think about latency in real time, not just in clock cycles.
Latency is cycles times clock period, so more stages at a faster clock can win; keep only decision logic on the critical path.

Latency is cycles times the clock period, so I count in nanoseconds, not stages. Each register adds a cycle, but it can let the clock run faster. Ten stages at 400 MHz is 25 ns; eight at 250 MHz is 32 ns. I keep the path from packet in to order out short, run checks in parallel instead of one after another, and move anything not needed for the decision off that path.
Your design will fly on a satellite in an SRAM-based FPGA. How do you deal with radiation?
Whether you know how radiation affects FPGAs and the standard ways to protect a design.
Upsets hit both user logic and configuration memory; scrubbing, triple modular redundancy and ECC, verified with fault injection.

Radiation can flip bits, called single event upsets, in my registers and in the configuration memory that defines the circuit. I use scrubbing, which periodically checks and rewrites the configuration to fix flipped bits. Critical logic gets triple modular redundancy: three copies and a voter. Block RAM gets error-correcting codes, and I test it all by injecting faults on the ground.
When do you use block RAM and when do you use distributed RAM built from LUTs?
Whether you know the memory resources of the fabric and what each costs.
Small, shallow memories go in LUTs; deep ones go in block RAM, with its synchronous read latency planned for.

For a small, shallow memory, like a 32-entry lookup table, I use distributed RAM made from LUTs: it is cheap and can be read without a clock. For anything deep I use block RAM, which comes in fixed-size blocks and has a synchronous read. So I plan one cycle of read latency, or two if I turn on the output register to help timing.
The board designer wants to move a few FPGA pins late in the layout. What do you check before you agree?
Your knowledge of I/O banks, clock pins and pin planning rules.
Bank voltage matches the I/O standard, clocks stay on clock-capable pins, differential pairs stay on true pairs, and the tool's I/O checks are rerun.

All pins in a bank share one supply voltage, so I check the new bank's voltage matches the I/O standard of the signal. Clock inputs must land on clock-capable pins, and differential signals on a true P and N pair. Then I rerun the pin and I/O rule checks in the tool and confirm the interface still meets its speed with the new routing.
A junior engineer divides the clock with a counter and uses the counter's output bit as the clock for a slower block. What is wrong, and what do you suggest?
Whether you know why fabric-generated clocks cause trouble and the safe alternatives.
Logic-made clocks ride general routing with large skew and poor timing analysis; use a clock enable, or a PLL or MMCM with a global buffer.

A clock taken from a flop output runs on general routing, not the global clock network, so its skew is large, and timing analysis is unreliable unless a generated clock is declared. I would keep one clock and make an enable that pulses every Nth cycle. If a truly separate frequency is needed, I use the PLL or MMCM and a global clock buffer.
You build a 64-tap FIR filter with 16-bit signed samples and 18-bit signed coefficients. How wide must the accumulator be, and what do you do at the output?
Your handle on fixed-point bit growth in DSP logic.
Product width is the sum of input widths; summing N terms adds log2(N) bits. Output is rounded and saturated, not just truncated.

Sixteen-bit samples times 18-bit coefficients give a 34-bit full-precision product. Adding 64 products can grow the result by log2 of 64, which is 6 bits, so a 40-bit accumulator can never overflow. That fits in a 48-bit DSP accumulator. At the output I round and saturate to the width the next stage needs instead of just dropping the low bits.
What does the value in a set_input_delay constraint represent, and where do you get the numbers?
Whether you can constrain I/O timing from real board and datasheet data.
It is the time used outside the FPGA after the launching clock edge: upstream clock-to-output plus board delay, with max for setup and min for hold.

It tells the tool how much of the clock period is already used before the data reaches the FPGA pin, measured from the launching clock edge. That is the upstream chip's clock-to-output time plus board trace delay. I take max and min values from the other chip's datasheet and the board trace lengths, and give both: max for the setup check, min for hold.
A path only needs to settle every second cycle because both ends use a clock enable. How do you constrain it, and what is the trap with hold?
Your exact knowledge of multicycle path constraints.
A setup multicycle of 2 on exactly those registers, plus a hold multicycle of 1 to move the hold check back, then a report to confirm.

I set a setup multicycle of 2 from the enabled source registers to the enabled destination registers, nothing wider. The trap is that the tool also moves the hold check one cycle later, which makes hold far too strict. So I add a hold multicycle of 1 to bring it back to the original edge. Then I check the timing report covers exactly the paths I meant.
Your testbench reports 100% code coverage. Are you done?
How you think about verification completeness beyond line coverage.
No: code coverage shows lines ran, not that behavior was right. A functional coverage plan from the spec, plus a scoreboard against a reference model.

No. Code coverage only says each line ran, not that the right thing happened. I write a functional coverage plan from the spec: FIFO full and empty, back-to-back packets, reset in the middle of a transfer. Constrained random stimulus fills it, and a scoreboard checks every output against a reference model, so a line that runs with a wrong result still fails.
A bug shows up on the board, but when you add an embedded logic analyzer to probe it, the bug disappears. What does that tell you?
How you reason about bugs that depend on placement and routing.
A placement-sensitive bug points to timing, unconstrained paths or clock crossings, not logic. Check constraints and CDC reports, and vary placement.

It tells me the bug likely depends on placement, which points to timing or a clock crossing rather than logic. I check that the timing report has no failing or unconstrained paths, run a clock-domain crossing report, and look for inputs without proper I/O constraints. I also build without probes using different placement seeds to see if the failure moves.
Your design is at 88% LUT use and fails timing on many paths where routing delay is most of the total. What do you do?
Your approach to congestion and closure in a nearly full device.
Find the congested region, cut fanout, move logic into hard blocks, trim unused logic, floorplan, and raise a bigger part early if needed.

When routing delay dominates, the wires are the problem, not the logic depth. I open the congestion report to find the hot region, duplicate registers that drive high-fanout nets, move wide muxes or tables into block RAM or DSPs, and remove dead logic. If that fails, I floorplan the worst block and tell the team early that a bigger part may be needed.
On a chip with an embedded processor, how do you decide what goes in the FPGA fabric and what goes in software?
Your judgement on hardware and software partitioning as a senior designer.
Fabric for hard deadlines and high throughput; software for control and rare paths. A small, documented register interface between them.

I put in fabric what needs fixed timing or high throughput: sample-by-sample filtering, packet parsing at line rate, anything with a deadline in nanoseconds. Control, configuration and rare error handling go in software, where changes are cheaper. I keep the register map between them small and documented, because that boundary is what both teams will debug.

fraud-analyst.heading: Fraud analyst questions
qs: What is the difference between first-party and third-party fraud?
Whether you know the basic types of fraud and who the victim is in each.
Third-party fraud is a stranger using someone else's identity or account. First-party fraud is the real customer lying, such as a false dispute.

In third-party fraud a stranger uses someone else's card or identity, so the account holder is a victim too. In first-party fraud the real customer is the fraudster, for example buying something and then claiming the charge was not theirs. They need different handling: the first gets a victim care process, the second does not.
What is synthetic identity fraud, and why is it hard to catch?
Your grasp of a fraud type that looks like a good customer for months.
Real and invented data are mixed into a new person, credit is built slowly, then the accounts are maxed out. No single victim reports it.

A fraudster mixes a real Social Security number, often a child's, with a made-up name and birth date. They pay small accounts on time for months, get higher limits, then max everything out and disappear. No real person notices and complains, so I look for thin credit files and for phones or addresses shared across many applications.
What signs tell you an account has been taken over?
Whether you can read the signs that someone else is inside a real customer's account.
A new device or location, then changes to contact details or password, then money moving out soon after. The sequence matters more than any one signal.

The pattern I watch is a login from a new device or an unusual location, then a password, email or phone change, then a new payee or a large transfer soon after. Any one alone is common. Together, in a short window, they are a strong sign. I would hold the payment and confirm with the customer through the contact details on file before the change.
At 3 a.m. you see hundreds of $1 authorizations on your checkout from different cards, most of them declined. What is happening and what do you do?
How you recognize card testing and respond while it is happening.
Names card testing, slows it fast with limits or challenges, and follows up on the cards that were approved.

That is card testing: someone checking which stolen card numbers still work. I would add velocity limits by IP, device and session, put a challenge such as a CAPTCHA on checkout, and alert the on-call engineer. Then I list the cards that were approved, void those charges and flag the cards, because they will be used for bigger fraud next.
A new-user promotion got 4,000 sign-ups in one day, and you suspect one group made many of them. How do you check?
Whether you can link accounts that pretend to be different people.
Looks for shared devices, cards, addresses and email patterns, and confirms a cluster by hand before acting on it.

I group the sign-ups by what is hard to fake: device fingerprint, payment card, IP range and delivery address, including small variations like 'Apt 2' and 'Unit 2'.
