Emails like jsmith1 and jsmith2 are another clue. When a cluster looks clear, I check a few accounts by hand, then cancel the promo credit for that cluster rather than banning every loose match.
A customer is about to send $9,000 to a 'bank security team' that told her to move her money to a safe account. What do you do?
How you protect a customer who is being scammed and is authorizing the payment herself.
Holds the payment, names the scam plainly and does not accept a coached answer. The customer is the victim here, not the suspect.

That is a known impersonation scam: no real bank asks you to move money to keep it safe. I would hold the payment, contact her directly, ask if someone is on the other line and explain the script calmly. Scammers coach victims to lie to us, so 'yes, it's me' does not end it. I would note everything and escalate if she still insists.
Walk me through how you test a new fraud rule before you turn it on.
Your method for proving a rule works before it touches real customers.
Backtests on past data with known outcomes, counts fraud caught against good customers hit, then runs it silently before going live.

First I backtest it on past transactions where we know the outcome, and count how much fraud it would catch and how many good customers it would hit. Then I run it in shadow mode for a week or two: it scores live traffic but blocks nothing. If the numbers hold, I turn it on, often as a review or extra check first, and watch decline rates daily.
Your new rule cut fraud losses by a third, but the sales team says good customers are being declined. How do you decide what to do?
How you weigh fraud losses against lost good business.
Puts both sides in dollars, including lost sales and customers who leave, then tunes the rule instead of just defending or dropping it.

I would put both sides in money. Fraud saved is easy to count. Then I estimate the good orders declined, using a sample of declined customers who later proved good, and add the value of those who stop buying. If that cost is higher than the savings, I narrow the rule or send borderline cases to review or extra verification instead of a hard decline.
Tell me about a time a rule or decision of yours caused a problem, and how you handled it.
Whether you own mistakes and fix the process, not just the single case.
Admits it fast, limits the harm to customers, and changes how future changes are checked.

I once shipped a rule with a wrong country code, so it flagged every order from a whole region. Declines jumped within an hour. I rolled it back, told my manager and support, and we contacted the 140 customers affected. After that our team added a second reviewer and a quick decline-rate check for every rule change.
If you work at a bank and a customer asks whether you reported them to the government, what do you say?
Whether you know the confidentiality rule for suspicious activity reports.
Never confirms or denies a report; federal law forbids disclosing one. Stays polite and tells compliance the customer asked.

I would not confirm or deny anything. Federal law forbids telling anyone involved, including the customer, that a suspicious activity report was filed or is being considered. I would say I can't discuss internal reviews, help with what I can in general terms, and let our compliance team know the customer asked.
What does 3-D Secure change for a merchant, and what does it not cover?
Your grasp of authentication and of who bears the loss on a fraud chargeback.
Successful issuer authentication generally shifts fraud chargeback liability to the issuer, but it does not cover non-fraud disputes and it adds friction.

With 3-D Secure, the card issuer authenticates the buyer, often silently with device data and sometimes with a one-time code. If the payment is successfully authenticated, liability for a fraud chargeback generally moves to the issuer. It does not help with disputes like item not received, and each challenge costs some sales, so I use it on risky orders, not all.
A customer files a chargeback saying the order never arrived, but tracking shows it was delivered to the billing address. How do you fight it?
How you build a representment case with evidence that fits the claim.
Reads the reason code first, then answers it with matching evidence: proof of delivery, address match, past orders, contact history, in a short clear packet.

First I read the reason code, because the evidence must answer that exact claim. For item not received I send the carrier's proof of delivery, show the address matches the billing address on file, and add earlier undisputed orders from the same address and device. If the customer contacted us, I include our replies. I keep it short so the reviewer gets the point fast.
Your dashboard says fraud last week was the lowest of the year. Why might you not believe it?
Whether you understand that fraud labels arrive late.
Chargebacks and fraud reports come in weeks or months after the purchase, so recent periods look clean. Compare periods at the same age.

Most of our fraud labels come from chargebacks, and cardholders often dispute weeks or months after the charge. So last week has not had time to collect its fraud yet. I compare each week at the same age, say 30 or 60 days after purchase, and watch early signals like customer fraud reports before I call it a good week.
What signs make you think an account at your bank is being used as a money mule?
Whether you can spot accounts that move stolen money for others.
Many unrelated inbound payments sent out quickly, activity out of line with the customer's profile, and device or login links to other accounts.

A new or long-quiet account suddenly gets payments from many unrelated people, then sends nearly all of it out within hours, by wire, payment apps or crypto exchanges. The activity does not fit the profile, like a student account moving thousands a week. Logins shared with other accounts add weight. Some mules are scam victims themselves, so I note that too.
A rule that caught a lot of fraud six months ago now flags almost nothing. What happened, and what do you do?
How you think about fraudsters adapting and about data that quietly breaks.
Considers both that the fraud moved and that the data changed. Checks losses, not just rule hits, and finds where the fraud went.

Two stories fit. Fraudsters may have learned the rule and changed one thing, like the email domain, so the fraud moved rather than stopped. Or a field the rule reads stopped filling after a release. I check losses in that segment, not just hits. If losses held steady, I study recent confirmed fraud to see what changed and target behavior that is harder to fake.
A customer disputes a transfer. Why does it matter whether a fraudster sent it or she sent it herself after being tricked?
Whether you know how US consumer rules treat unauthorized versus scam-induced transfers.
Regulation E covers unauthorized transfers made without the customer's permission. One she made herself, even when deceived, is generally treated as authorized.

Regulation E protects consumers from unauthorized electronic transfers, ones made without their permission, like a thief using a stolen login. If she logged in and sent the money herself because a scammer lied to her, it is generally treated as authorized and the claim is handled differently. So I document who started it, from which device and session, and her account of events.
Your investigation finds 30 accounts that share one device. Do you close them all?
Your judgement before acting on linked accounts.
Not on one link alone. Checks why the device might be shared, looks for more signals, and matches the action to the strength of the evidence.

Not on that link alone. A shared device can be a library computer, a family tablet or a phone repair shop. I look for more: the same cards, similar email patterns, sign-ups minutes apart, the same promo, money flowing to one place. If several line up, I act on the ring and document why. If only the device matches, I add step-up verification instead of closing.
Your company's chargeback ratio is climbing toward the level where card networks put merchants in a monitoring program. What do you do?
How you manage disputes as a business risk, not one case at a time.
Splits disputes by reason code and source, fixes fraud and non-fraud causes separately, and works with payments and support on prevention.

First I split disputes by reason code, product and channel, because fraud and non-fraud disputes need different fixes. For fraud I tighten rules or add 3-D Secure on risky segments. For the rest I look at causes like an unclear billing descriptor, hard-to-cancel subscriptions or slow refunds. Refunding before a dispute is filed also keeps it off the count.
A colleague proposes declining every order shipped to a handful of ZIP codes with high fraud. What is your view?
Whether you see fairness and legal risk in blunt rules, not just loss numbers.
Pushes back: ZIP codes can act as a stand-in for race or national origin and block many good customers. Prefers narrow, behavior-based signals.

I would push back. Blocking whole ZIP codes hits every honest customer there, and location can stand in for race or national origin, which is a real discrimination risk, above all if we extend credit. I would find what the fraud orders share, like a known reshipping address or brand-new accounts, and target that. Then I check decline rates across areas.

fraud-risk.heading: Fraud and risk analyst questions
qs: What is the difference between a false positive and a false negative in fraud rules, and what does each one cost?
Whether you weigh both kinds of error, not only fraud caught.
Both errors defined, with a real cost on each side, and the idea that a rule is judged in dollars on both sides.

A false positive is a good customer we block or delay. It costs the sale, support time and sometimes the customer for good. A false negative is fraud we let through. It costs the goods, the chargeback and the fee. I put a dollar figure on both, because a rule that stops $1,000 of fraud but blocks $20,000 of good orders is a bad rule.
What is friendly fraud, and how do you tell it apart from true third-party fraud?
Whether you know the main dispute types and the data that separates them.
The real cardholder disputes a purchase they made; you compare device, address and history with past good orders.

Friendly fraud is when the real cardholder makes the purchase and then disputes it, saying they never ordered it or it never came. I check whether the device, IP address, shipping address and login history match that customer's past good orders, and whether the item was used or downloaded. A match on all of those points to the cardholder, not a thief.
What signs tell you a checkout is being hit by card testing, and what do you do first?
Whether you recognize a common attack pattern and act on it quickly.
Many small attempts, high declines, shared device or IP; a fast response with limits and a check of cards that got through.

A burst of small authorizations, often a dollar or less, with a high decline rate and many card numbers from one device, IP range or BIN, the first digits that identify the card issuer. I add velocity limits per device and IP, put a challenge such as a CAPTCHA on checkout, block the pattern, and then list the cards that were approved so they can be flagged.
Walk me through how a chargeback works from the merchant's side.
Your grasp of the dispute process and where the merchant can act.
Issuer, network and acquirer in the right order, reason codes and deadlines, and representment with evidence.

The cardholder disputes the charge with their issuing bank. The chargeback moves through the card network to our acquirer, and the money is pulled back, usually with a fee. We get a reason code and a deadline. If we fight it, we send representment: proof of delivery, matching address and device data, customer messages. If the issuer still rules against us, it can go to pre-arbitration or arbitration.
What does an account takeover look like in the data?
Whether you read events as a sequence rather than single flags.
New device or location, then quick changes to contact details or address, then a purchase or payout; the order and timing are the signal.

A login from a new device and place, often after failed attempts, then fast changes: password, email, phone, shipping address, followed by a purchase or payout. Each step alone is normal. The sequence in a short window is the signal. I would hold the transaction and confirm with the customer using the contact details that were on file before the change.
How do you test a new fraud rule before you turn it on?
Your method for launching rules without hurting good customers.
Backtesting on labeled history, a shadow period on live traffic, then a careful launch with monitoring.

I backtest it on several months of labeled data: how many known fraud cases it would have caught, how many good orders it would have hit, and the dollars on each side. Then I run it in shadow mode, scoring live traffic without acting, for a week or two. If the numbers hold, I launch it to a review queue before it ever hard-declines anyone.
A sales manager asks you to whitelist a large customer whose orders keep getting flagged. What do you do?
How you balance revenue pressure against risk.
Find the cause, tune narrowly instead of a full bypass, keep key checks on, and document the exception.

First I look at why the orders flag. If it is a known pattern, like big orders to a new warehouse, I can tune the rule for that account with limits, not a blanket whitelist. A full bypass is exactly what fraudsters exploit when they take over trusted accounts, so I keep account-change and velocity checks on, write down the exception and set a review date.
A rule you launched on Friday doubled declines on good orders over the weekend. What do you do on Monday?
How you own a mistake and fix both the damage and the process.
Stop the harm first, find the cause, recover customers where possible, and change the launch process.

First I roll the rule back or switch it to review-only so the damage stops. Then I pull the declined orders, find the condition that caught good customers, maybe a country list or a new payment method, and work with support to reach the ones we can win back. I write up what happened and add decline-rate alerts to every launch. No more Friday launches.
You suspect an employee is issuing refunds to their own card. How do you investigate?
How you handle an internal case with care for evidence and process.
Quiet data review, refunds matched to original sales, secure records, and HR, legal and security involved before any interview.

I quietly pull the refund logs: who issued each refund, to which card, and whether it matched an original sale. Refunds with no matching purchase, or many going to one card, are the core evidence. I keep everything documented and access-limited, I do not confront the employee myself, and I bring in HR, legal and security before anyone is interviewed.
At a bank, you find activity that may call for a Suspicious Activity Report. What can you tell the customer?
Whether you know the confidentiality rule around SARs.
Never reveal a SAR or anything that shows one exists; routine questions are fine; escalate through compliance.

Nothing about the SAR. Federal law bars disclosing a SAR, or anything that would reveal one exists, to the person involved. I can still ask normal questions about the activity as part of due diligence. I document the facts, escalate to the BSA officer, and let compliance decide on filing. Tipping off the customer can be a crime and can ruin the investigation.
How does 3-D Secure change who pays for a fraud chargeback?
Whether you know how cardholder authentication shifts liability for fraud.
Fraud disputes on authenticated transactions generally become the issuer's loss. The shift does not cover non-receipt or quality disputes.

When a card payment passes 3-D Secure, the cardholder's bank has authenticated the buyer. Fraud-coded chargebacks on that order then generally become the bank's loss, not ours. It does not help with 'item not received' or 'not as described' disputes. It also adds friction at checkout, so I use it on risky orders rather than on everyone.
What is synthetic identity fraud, and why do normal fraud rules often miss it?
Your knowledge of a fraud type that has no victim to report it.
A made-up identity built from real and fake data. It looks like a good customer until a planned bust-out, so you watch for links and fast credit growth.

It is a made-up person built from real and fake pieces, often a real Social Security number paired with a different name and birth date. No true victim reads the statements, so nobody reports it. The identity pays on time for months and grows its limits, then maxes everything out and disappears. I look for thin credit files, numbers or addresses shared across applicants, and fast limit growth.
Last month's fraud losses are the lowest of the year. Why might you not trust that number yet?
Whether you understand that fraud labels arrive late.
Chargebacks come in weeks or months after the sale, so recent months look clean. Compare months at the same age since the sale.

Most fraud chargebacks arrive weeks after the order, and some take months. So the most recent month always looks good at first. I compare each month's loss rate at the same age, for example 30 and 60 days after the sale. I also say clearly that the number is early, before anyone uses it to loosen the rules.
How do you decide where to set the score cutoff for declining orders?
How you turn a risk score into a business decision.
A dollar comparison: expected fraud loss on the order against the margin and customer value lost by declining a good buyer.

I put a dollar cost on both kinds of error. A missed fraud costs the goods, the shipping and the chargeback fee. A wrong decline costs the margin on that order and some chance we lose the customer for good. For each score band I estimate the fraud rate and decline only where expected loss beats expected profit. Bands in between can go to manual review.
You confirm one account is fraudulent. Walk me through how you check whether it is part of a ring.
How you run link analysis without sweeping in innocent customers.
Pivoting on shared device, IP, address, card and email patterns, requiring several links, then acting on the whole cluster at once.

I list what the account touches: device ID, IP addresses, shipping address, cards, phone and email pattern. I search for other accounts sharing any of them and repeat on each new find. A shared office Wi-Fi or dorm address can link honest people, so I want several links together, not one. Then I act on the whole cluster at the same time so the ring cannot shift to accounts I missed.
We get hundreds of chargebacks a month. How do you decide which ones to fight?
Your judgement on the cost of disputing against the chance of winning.
Fight where the evidence fits the reason code and the amount justifies the work; accept the rest and fix the cause upstream.

I sort by reason code and by the evidence we hold. A 'not received' claim with signed proof of delivery is worth fighting. A small order with no proof costs more in staff time than it returns. I track the win rate by reason code. When one type keeps losing, I fix the cause, such as unclear product pages or slow shipping, instead of writing more responses.
Your rules decline the riskiest orders, so you never learn whether they were really fraud. How do you keep learning?
Whether you see the feedback loop that hides how well your rules work.
A small, controlled holdout of would-be declines that go through or to review, giving true labels to measure each rule.

If I only learn from approved orders, my data hides everything the rules stopped, and every new model trains on a biased sample. So I keep a small random holdout: a tiny share of orders that would be declined go through with a low value cap, or go to manual review. It costs a little fraud, but it shows the real fraud rate in that segment and whether each rule still earns its declines.
Fraud dropped after your new rule, then came back three weeks later. What happened, and what do you do?
How you respond when fraudsters adapt to your controls.
They probed and found the rule's edge. Study how the new fraud differs, and move to signals that are hard to see or fake.

Most likely they found the edge of the rule. If I blocked orders over $500, they now place orders at $490. I compare the new fraud to the old pattern: amounts, devices, timing, products. Then I move away from limits they can test, toward signals that are costly to fake, like device history or account age. I also make sure decline messages never tell them which check they failed.
The fraud model's scores jumped overnight, but real fraud did not rise. How do you find the cause?
How you troubleshoot a model problem before it hurts good customers.
Checking your own data and releases first, such as a broken feed or a changed field, while limiting harm to good orders in the meantime.

A sudden overnight shift is usually our own change, not criminals. I check which inputs moved, then ask what shipped: a new checkout release, a vendor feed that went blank, a field that changed format. A missing device ID filled with a default value can push every score up. While I look, I route the affected score band to manual review instead of auto-decline.
Tell me about a fraud call you got wrong and what you changed afterward.
How you own an error and build the lesson into the process.
A specific mistake, its cost in plain numbers, and a lasting change to the process, not just a promise to be more careful.

I once blocked a group of orders sharing one shipping address as a fraud ring. It was a package forwarder used by many honest overseas buyers, and we declined about 40 good orders in two days. I reversed the block, had support contact each customer, and added a check for known forwarders and business addresses to my review steps. Now I learn what an address is before I treat sharing it as a signal.

freight-forwarding.heading: Freight and forwarding operations questions
qs: When would you book a shipment as LCL instead of a full container load?
Whether you know the basic ocean options and how to choose between them.
Explains that LCL shares a container and is priced by volume, while FCL is a whole box, and weighs cost, transit time and handling risk.

LCL means the cargo shares a container with other shippers and we pay by cubic meter. It suits small volumes, but it adds consolidation time and extra handling. Once the volume gets close to what a 20-foot box would cost, I price both, because FCL is often faster, safer and not much more expensive.
An air shipment is one pallet, 120 by 80 by 100 cm, weighing 90 kg. What weight will the airline charge?
Whether you can work out chargeable weight for air freight.
Knows the airline charges the greater of actual and volumetric weight and uses the standard divisor of 6,000 cubic cm per kg.

Airlines charge the greater of actual weight and volumetric weight. Volume is 120 x 80 x 100, so 960,000 cubic centimeters. Divided by 6,000, that is 160 kg. The actual weight is 90 kg, so we pay for 160 kg. I would tell the customer that a lower, stackable pallet could cut the cost.
What is the difference between a house bill of lading and a master bill of lading?
Your grasp of the core shipping documents and who issues them.
Master bill is issued by the ocean carrier to the forwarder; house bill is issued by the forwarder or NVOCC to its own customer.

The master bill is issued by the ocean carrier, usually with us as the shipper and our agent at destination as the consignee. The house bill is the one we issue as the NVOCC, meaning a carrier that does not run ships, to our customer, showing the real shipper and consignee. The cargo is released against the right bill at each level.
A buyer says they bought on FOB terms. What does that mean for who books and who carries the risk?
Whether you understand Incoterms and how they set your role in the shipment.
FOB is for sea freight: the seller loads the goods on board at the named port; risk passes then, and the buyer books and pays the main ocean freight.

Under FOB the seller clears the goods for export and loads them on board at the named port. Risk passes to the buyer once the goods are on board. The buyer books and pays the ocean freight, so we would take the booking from the buyer. FOB is meant for sea freight; for containers handed over at a terminal, FCA usually fits better.
What is an ISF filing and when must it be done for an ocean import into the US?
Your knowledge of US import security filing rules.
The Importer Security Filing, or 10+2, goes to CBP at least 24 hours before cargo is loaded on the vessel at the foreign port.

The ISF, often called 10+2, is a set of data elements the importer must send to US Customs and Border Protection for ocean cargo. It is due at least 24 hours before the container is loaded at the foreign port, not before arrival. Late or wrong filings can bring penalties and holds, so I chase the supplier details as soon as the booking is made.
Explain demurrage and detention, and how you keep a customer from paying them.
How well you know container charges and how you plan to avoid them.
Demurrage is for a container left at the terminal past free time; detention is for keeping the carrier's container outside too long. Planning pickup and return prevents both.

Demurrage is charged when a loaded container sits at the terminal past its free days. Detention is charged when the container is out of the terminal, at the customer, past its free days. I confirm free time when booking, get customs cleared before arrival, book the trucker early and remind the consignee of the return date.
The carrier rolls your customer's container to the next vessel, a week later. What do you do?
How you handle a service failure and keep the customer informed.
Tells the customer fast with facts, looks for a real alternative, and checks knock-on effects like deadlines and documents.

I tell the customer the same day, with the new vessel and arrival date, before they hear it elsewhere. Then I check other sailings or carriers that could beat that date and what they cost. I also check what the delay hits, such as a store launch or a letter of credit date, and update the documents and the delivery booking.
A customer wants to air ship 'electronics' and you learn they contain lithium batteries. What happens next?
Whether you treat dangerous goods by the rules and refuse shortcuts.
Holds the booking, gets the battery details and UN 38.3 test summary, and has trained staff classify, pack and declare under air rules.

Lithium batteries are regulated dangerous goods by air, so I would not book them as general cargo. I hold the booking and ask for the battery type, watt-hours, how they are packed and the UN 38.3 test summary. Then someone with current dangerous goods training classifies and declares them, or we move the cargo by sea if it cannot fly.
A customer complains the final invoice was much higher than your quote. How do you prevent that?
How you build complete quotes and own a pricing mistake.
An all-in quote listing origin, freight, surcharges and destination charges, with clear validity and exclusions, and honesty when a cost was missed.

I quote door to door in clear lines: pickup, origin charges, freight, fuel and other surcharges, destination charges and delivery. I state what is not included, like duties and storage, and how long the rate is valid. If a charge was missed on our side, I say so, and we discuss absorbing part of it instead of just sending the bill.
Cargo arrives with damaged cartons and the consignee wants the carrier to pay in full. What do you advise?
Whether you know the claim steps and the limits of carrier liability.
Note damage on the delivery receipt, take photos, notify the carrier in writing fast, and explain that carrier liability is limited, so insurance matters.

First, write the damage on the delivery receipt before signing and take photos of the cartons and contents. Keep the packaging. Then we send written notice to the carrier quickly, since the notice deadlines are short. I would be honest that carrier liability is limited by law per package or per kilo, so a full payout usually needs cargo insurance.
What is a VGM, who is responsible for it, and how can it be obtained?
Whether you know the container weight rule that can stop a box from being loaded.
The shipper named on the bill of lading owns it, the two allowed weighing methods, and no VGM means no loading.

VGM is the verified gross mass of a packed container, required under the SOLAS convention. The shipper on the bill of lading is responsible. Method 1 weighs the packed container on a calibrated scale. Method 2 adds the weight of all cargo, packing and dunnage to the tare weight on the door. Without it before the carrier's cutoff, the box does not load.
When would you use an original bill of lading, a telex release or a sea waybill?
Your grasp of how cargo release is controlled at destination.
Originals keep control until payment, a telex release surrenders them at origin, and a waybill releases to the named consignee with no paper.

Originals are negotiable. I use them under a letter of credit or when the shipper wants control until the buyer pays: no original, no release. If originals were issued but the buyer paid early, the shipper surrenders them at origin and we telex release. Between related companies or trusted buyers, a sea waybill is simplest: no originals, release to the named consignee.
A customer asks for a CIF quote on an air shipment. What do you tell them?
Whether you match the Incoterm to the mode of transport.
CIF is meant for sea and inland waterway only. CIP fits air, and in Incoterms 2020 it calls for broader insurance cover.

I would suggest CIP instead. In Incoterms 2020, CIF is meant for sea and inland waterway transport, where delivery happens on board a vessel. CIP works for any mode. I would also flag that CIP asks the seller for all-risks level cover, Institute Cargo Clauses (A), while CIF only requires the minimum (C) cover, so the insurance cost may change.
Why might you advise a shipper to sell FCA instead of FOB on a container shipment?
Whether you understand where risk really passes on containerized cargo.
Under FOB the seller carries risk until the box is on board, long after handing it over. FCA moves risk at handover to the carrier.

With FOB, risk passes when the goods are on board the vessel. But the seller hands a container to the carrier at the terminal days earlier and keeps a risk it cannot control. Under FCA, risk passes when the carrier takes the box at the named place. If a letter of credit needs an on-board bill, FCA in Incoterms 2020 lets the buyer have the carrier issue one to the seller.
A new importer has one shipment arriving now and expects monthly shipments after that. Single transaction bond or continuous bond?
How you advise a new importer on customs bonds.
A single bond covers one entry; a continuous bond covers all entries for a year and is sized from duties paid. Plans for setup time.

For monthly imports I would recommend a continuous bond. It covers every entry at every port for a year, so we are not buying a bond per shipment. CBP sizes it from the duties, taxes and fees of the past twelve months, so for a new importer we estimate the first year. Approval takes some days, so this first shipment may need a single transaction bond.
The foreign buyer's forwarder says this export is a routed transaction. Who files the EEI, and what does the US seller still owe?
Your knowledge of who does what in a US export filing.
The buyer's authorized US agent files in AES. The US seller remains the USPPI and must supply accurate data and keep records.

In a routed export, the foreign principal party in interest authorizes a US agent, often its forwarder, to file the EEI in AES. The US seller is still the USPPI. It must give the agent the export data, such as the Schedule B number, value and any license details, and keep its records. I ask to see the buyer's written authorization and a copy of the filed data for the seller.
CBP puts your customer's container on an intensive exam. What happens next, and what do you tell the customer?
How you manage a customs hold you cannot speed up.
Knows the box goes to an exam station at the importer's cost, that timing is up to CBP, and sets cost and time expectations early.

An intensive exam means the container is trucked to a centralized examination station and unloaded for CBP to inspect. The importer pays the drayage, the station fees and any storage or demurrage. I cannot speed CBP up, so I tell the customer right away, give a rough cost range, check free time with the carrier, and have the broker ready with the invoice and packing list.
The shipper calls: the buyer has not paid, do not release the cargo. The container arrives tomorrow. What do you do?
Your judgement on who controls the cargo and what you can actually do.
It depends on the bill: originals give control, a waybill or completed telex release may not. Acts on written instructions from the right party.

First I check how the bill was issued. If we issued originals and the shipper still holds them, nothing is released without one, so the cargo stays put. If it was a sea waybill or a telex release, the named consignee may be entitled to it, so I get the shipper's instruction in writing and escalate before acting. I also confirm the caller is the shipper on the bill.
The vessel carrying your customer's cargo declares general average. Walk me through what happens.
Whether you can guide a customer through a rare but costly event.
All cargo shares the sacrifice. Release needs a GA bond plus an insurer guarantee, or a cash deposit if uninsured.

General average means the ship and all cargo share the cost of a sacrifice made to save the voyage, like salvage or cargo thrown overboard. The average adjuster will not let cargo go until each owner posts security: a GA bond plus a guarantee from the cargo insurer, or a cash deposit if uninsured. I call the customer's insurer at once so the cargo does not sit.
After entry, you learn a product was classified under the wrong HTS code and duty was underpaid. What should happen?
How you handle a compliance mistake with the importer and the broker.
Fix it through the licensed broker: a post summary correction before liquidation, or a prior disclosure. Checks other entries too.

I tell the importer and the licensed customs broker the same day; only a broker can do customs business for the importer. If the entry has not liquidated, the broker can file a post summary correction and pay the duty owed. If it has, or the error repeats across entries, a prior disclosure to CBP may limit penalties. We also fix the code so the next entry is right.

frontend-engineer.heading: Frontend engineer questions
qs: When do you use a button element and when do you use a link?
Whether you know that HTML elements carry meaning for keyboard and screen reader users.
Links go somewhere, buttons do something. A clickable div is not a substitute for either.

A link navigates to a URL, so it belongs in an a tag with an href. A button triggers an action on the page, like opening a menu or submitting a form. Using the right one gives me keyboard support and the correct role for screen readers for free. A div with a click handler gets neither, so I would have to rebuild all of that by hand.
What is layout shift, and what usually causes it?
Your grasp of one of the Core Web Vitals and its everyday causes.
Content that moves after it appears. Usual causes: media without reserved space, late ads or banners, and web fonts swapping in.

It is when visible content moves after the page has drawn it, so someone taps the wrong thing. Google measures it as Cumulative Layout Shift. The usual causes are images without width and height, banners injected above content, and fonts that swap in at a different size. I reserve space with dimensions or aspect-ratio and give late content a fixed slot.
A designer wants light gray body text on a white background, and it fails the contrast check. What do you do?
How you balance a design request against accessibility rules.
Knows the WCAG AA ratio for body text, shows the problem with a tool, and offers a close color that passes instead of just refusing.

WCAG AA asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text. I would run the colors through a contrast checker with the designer, then propose the lightest gray that passes so the look stays close. If the product has accessibility commitments I would mention them, but usually the side-by-side comparison settles it.
A teammate added lazy loading to every image, and now the main content of the page shows up later. Why?
Whether you understand how the browser prioritizes the largest image on the page.
The hero image is often the Largest Contentful Paint element, and lazy loading delays it. Load it eagerly, with high priority.

The big hero image is often what Largest Contentful Paint measures. With lazy loading, the browser waits until layout to know the image is in view, so the download starts late. I would remove lazy loading from images above the fold, add fetchpriority high on the hero, and keep lazy loading only for images further down the page.
Walk me through what a modal dialog must do for keyboard and screen reader users.
Your knowledge of focus management in one of the most common components.
Focus moves in and stays in, Escape closes it, focus returns to the trigger, and the background is inert. Knows the native dialog element.

When it opens, focus moves inside, usually to the heading or the first control. Tab stays within the dialog and the page behind cannot be reached. Escape closes it, and focus goes back to the button that opened it. It also needs an accessible name. The native dialog element opened with showModal handles most of this, so I start there before building my own.
After someone clicks Add to cart, the cart count updates but a screen reader user hears nothing. How do you fix it?
Whether you know how to announce changes that happen without a page load.
A polite live region that is already in the page before its text changes, with a short, clear message, tested with a real screen reader.

I would add a live region, for example an element with role status, which screen readers announce politely when its text changes. It has to be in the page from the start; if I insert it together with the message, many screen readers miss it. Then I set its text to something short like 'Added to cart, 3 items' and test it with an actual screen reader.
After a merge, the JavaScript bundle grew by 200 KB. How do you find out why and fix it?
How you investigate and control what your code ships to the browser.
Compares builds with a bundle analyzer, finds the cause, then trims or splits it. Adds a size budget so it cannot happen silently again.

I run a bundle analyzer on the build before and after the merge and compare. Often it is a whole library imported for one function, or a date library pulling in every locale. I import only the piece needed, swap in a lighter option, or load it with a dynamic import on the screen that uses it. Then I add a size check to CI so the next jump fails the build.
Typing in a search box that filters a list of 5,000 rows feels laggy. How do you approach it?
How you diagnose slow interactions, the kind measured by Interaction to Next Paint.
Profiles first, then cuts the work done per keystroke: render only visible rows, avoid needless re-renders, keep the input itself responsive.

I record a profile in the browser dev tools while typing to see whether time goes to filtering or to rendering. Usually it is rendering thousands of rows, so I virtualize the list and draw only what is visible. I keep the input updating at once and let the list follow a moment later, with a debounce or React's useDeferredValue, and check that nothing unrelated re-renders.
In a server-rendered React app you see a hydration mismatch warning. What causes it, and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand why server and client rendering must agree.
The first client render differs from the server HTML, often due to time, random values, locale or browser-only checks. Match first, update after mount.

Hydration attaches React to HTML the server already sent, so the first client render must produce the same markup. Mismatches come from things like the current time, random IDs, locale formatting, or reading window during render. I make the first render match, use useId for IDs, and move browser-only values into an effect that runs after mount.
Your shared component library needs to change the Button props in a way that breaks existing uses. How do you roll it out?
How you manage change in code that many teams depend on.
Old and new side by side when possible, deprecation warnings, a migration guide or codemod, and removal only in a major version with a date.

First I check whether the new API can live next to the old one. If so, the old props keep working with a warning in development, and I document the migration, ideally with a codemod that rewrites call sites. Removal goes in a major version under semantic versioning, announced ahead. Before picking a date, I search the product code to see how many uses each team has.
How do you respect a user who has asked their system for less motion?
Whether you know the user settings the browser exposes and actually use them.
Names the prefers-reduced-motion media query and removes or softens motion, while keeping content and state changes visible.

The browser exposes that setting through the prefers-reduced-motion media query. When it matches reduce, I turn off parallax, large slides and auto-playing animation, and swap them for a simple fade or an instant change. The information still has to arrive; only the movement goes. I also give carousels a pause control for everyone.
A form uses placeholder text instead of labels to save space. What problems does that cause?
Whether you see the accessibility and usability cost of a common design shortcut.
Several concrete problems: the hint vanishes on typing, often low contrast, unreliable as a name. Plus a fix that keeps a visible label.

The hint disappears as soon as someone types, so people who get distracted lose track of what the field was for, and reviewing a filled form is hard. Default placeholder gray often fails contrast. Assistive tech support for placeholder as a name is uneven. I keep a visible label element tied to the input and use the placeholder only for an example format, if at all.
A teammate made a div clickable and added role="button". What is still missing?
Whether you know that ARIA changes what is announced, not how an element behaves.
Focusability, Enter and Space handling, a disabled state, and above all the advice to use a real button element instead.

The role only changes what a screen reader announces. The div still cannot be reached with Tab, so it needs tabindex="0", and it needs key handlers so Enter and Space activate it, plus a disabled state if it can be disabled. That is a lot of code to copy what a native button gives for free, so I would replace it with a button element and style it.
How do you set caching headers for a site's JavaScript, CSS and HTML files?
Your grasp of HTTP caching and how it fits a build that hashes file names.
Long, immutable caching for files with a content hash in the name; HTML revalidated every time so new deploys reach users.

Build output files get a content hash in the name, like app.3f9a2c.js, so a change always means a new URL. Those I serve with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. The HTML that points to them uses no-cache, which means the browser must check with the server before reuse. A deploy then shows up on the next visit, and unchanged files never download twice.
Our custom web font makes text invisible for a moment, then the layout jumps when it loads. How do you fix both?
Whether you know how web font loading affects what users see and layout stability.
font-display to show fallback text, preloading the key font, and matching fallback metrics so the swap does not move the layout.

Invisible text comes from the browser hiding text while the font downloads, so I set font-display: swap to show a fallback right away. I preload the one or two fonts used above the fold, as woff2 with the crossorigin attribute. To stop the jump, I tune the fallback with size-adjust and related metric overrides in @font-face so it takes up the same space.
In our single-page app, screen reader users say they cannot tell when they move to a new page. Why, and what do you do?
Whether you understand what client-side routing takes away from assistive technology.
No full page load means no announcement and focus left behind; the fix is a title update and a deliberate focus move or announcement.

On a normal page load, the screen reader announces the new title and starts at the top. With client-side routing nothing reloads, so it stays silent and focus stays on the link that was clicked, or drops to the body if that link is gone. On each route change I update document.title and move focus to the main heading, which gets tabindex="-1" so script can focus it.
Lighthouse gives a page a high score, but field data shows poor Interaction to Next Paint. How can both be true, and how do you find the cause?
Whether you know the difference between lab and field data and how INP is measured.
A lab page load has no real interactions, so INP comes from real users; find the slow interaction with attribution and fix the phase that dominates.

A Lighthouse page-load run has nobody clicking, so it cannot measure INP; Total Blocking Time is only a proxy. Field data is real users, often on slow phones. I add attribution to our monitoring to see which element was slow, and whether time went to input delay, processing, or presentation delay. Then I fix that phase, for example by splitting a long event handler.
In an autocomplete, why does focus usually stay in the text box while the user arrows through the options?
Your knowledge of the ARIA combobox pattern and focus management in composite widgets.
Focus stays on the input so typing continues, with aria-activedescendant pointing to the highlighted option; knows when roving tabindex fits instead.

The user must be able to keep typing, so real focus stays on the input. I give each option role="option" and an id, and set aria-activedescendant on the input to the highlighted option's id, which the screen reader announces as if it had focus. The input also has aria-expanded and aria-controls. Roving tabindex, which moves real focus, suits toolbars and grids better.
Teams using our component library keep fighting its CSS with !important. How would you change the library so overrides are easy?
How you design a library's styles so other teams can customize them safely.
Puts library styles in a cascade layer and exposes tokens as custom properties, so normal app CSS wins without specificity wars.

I would wrap the library's styles in a cascade layer with @layer. Normal declarations outside any layer beat layered ones no matter how specific the selectors are, so an app's plain class simply wins. I would keep library selectors low in specificity and expose colors and spacing as CSS custom properties, so most changes are a token, not an override.
Thirty teams build on our component library. How do you keep accessibility from regressing as it grows?
How you build accessibility into a shared library rather than check it at the end.
Accessibility built into components, automated checks in CI, plus manual keyboard and screen reader testing, because tools catch only part of the issues.

I build it into the components. Focus, labels and keyboard support live in the library, so teams get them for free. Automated checks run in CI on every component, but they catch only part of the problems, so each changed component also gets a keyboard and screen reader pass before release. The docs show correct usage with examples.

full-stack-engineer.heading: Full-stack engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between a 401 and a 403 response, and when do you send each?
Whether you use HTTP status codes the way clients expect.
401 means the caller is not authenticated; 403 means they are known but not allowed. Bonus: sometimes 404 hides that a resource exists.

I send 401 when there is no valid login, like a missing or expired token, so the front end knows to send the user to sign in. I send 403 when we know who you are but you lack permission. For private records I may return 404 so a stranger cannot even learn the record exists.
The sign-up form already checks every field in the browser. Why validate again on the server?
Whether you know the browser is not a trusted place.
Anyone can skip the form and call the API directly; client checks are for user comfort, server checks are for correctness and security.

The browser checks are there so people get quick feedback. They protect nothing, because anyone can send a request with a script and skip the form entirely. The server is the only place I control, so it checks types, lengths, formats and permissions on every request, and the database adds constraints as a last line.
How do you stop SQL injection in code that builds queries from user input?
Your grasp of a basic security risk in database code.
Parameterized queries or a query builder that binds values; never glue strings into SQL. Allowlists for things that cannot be parameters, like column names.

I never put user input into the SQL string. I use parameterized queries, so the database gets the query and the values separately and a value can never become code. Column names and sort directions cannot be parameters, so I map them from an allowlist, like sort=price becomes a known column name, and reject anything else.
How should a product store user passwords?
Whether you know safe password storage.
A slow, salted password hash such as Argon2, bcrypt or scrypt. Never plain text, never reversible encryption, never a fast hash like MD5 or plain SHA-256.

I store only a hash made with a slow algorithm built for passwords, like Argon2 or bcrypt, which adds a unique salt per user. At login I hash what was typed and compare. Fast hashes are wrong here because an attacker with a leaked table can try billions of guesses a second. And nobody, including support, should be able to see a password.
The front end calls your API and the browser console shows a CORS error. What is going on and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand how browsers enforce cross-origin rules.
The browser blocks the response because the server did not allow that origin. Fix it on the server with an allowlist, not by turning checks off.

CORS is the browser protecting the user: a page from one origin can only read a response from another origin if that server says so. The same call works from curl, which proves the API is fine. I set Access-Control-Allow-Origin on the server for our real front-end origins, make sure OPTIONS preflight requests are answered, and avoid a wildcard for anything that uses cookies.
A list page is slow and the query filters by customer and sorts by date. How do you decide whether to add an index?
How you reason about indexes and their cost.
Read the query plan first, index for the filter and sort together, and remember every index slows writes and takes space.

First I run EXPLAIN to see if the database scans the whole table. If it does, a composite index on customer_id then created_at lets it find that customer's rows already in date order. Column order matters: the filter column goes first. I check that the table is not write-heavy enough for the extra index to hurt inserts, then compare the plan and timing after.
When would you use cursor pagination instead of page numbers with an offset?
Your understanding of how pagination behaves on large, changing data.
Offset gets slower deep in a list and skips or repeats rows when data changes; a cursor continues from the last row seen using an index.

Offset is fine for small admin tables. But OFFSET 50000 still makes the database walk past 50,000 rows, and if new rows arrive while someone scrolls, they see duplicates. For feeds I return a cursor, like the last created_at and id, and the next query asks for rows before that pair. It stays fast with the right index and never shifts.
Where would you keep a user's login on the web: a token in local storage or a cookie? Why?
Whether you weigh session security choices on the client.
An HttpOnly, Secure cookie with SameSite set keeps the token away from scripts; local storage is readable by any script, so one XSS bug leaks it. Mention CSRF.

I prefer a session cookie marked HttpOnly, so page scripts cannot read it, Secure, so it only travels over HTTPS, and SameSite=Lax, which blocks most cross-site requests. A token in local storage is readable by any script, so one XSS bug hands it to an attacker. Cookies bring CSRF risk, so state-changing requests also need a CSRF token or similar check.
You need to rename a field in an API response, but users have the old front end open in their browsers. How do you ship it?
How you change contracts between front end and back end without breaking live users.
Expand then contract: add the new field alongside the old one, move clients over, watch usage, and remove the old field only when nothing reads it.

I never rename in one step. First the API returns both full_name and the old name. Then I ship the front end that reads full_name. Open tabs and cached apps keep working on the old field. I log or measure who still reads the old one, and after a few weeks with no use, I remove it. Database columns follow the same pattern.
Users type fast in a search box and sometimes see results for an earlier word, not what they typed. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
Whether you spot a race condition between requests and the screen.
Responses arrive out of order and an old one overwrites a newer one. Cancel or ignore stale requests, and debounce to send fewer.

Each keystroke sends a request, and a slow response for "sho" can arrive after the one for "shoes" and overwrite it. I fix it in two ways: wait about 300 milliseconds after typing stops before sending, and cancel the previous request with an AbortController or tag each request with an id and drop any response that is not the latest.
How would you store prices and money amounts in the database and in code?
Whether you know why floating-point numbers are wrong for money.
Integer cents or an exact decimal type, with the currency stored next to the amount, and rounding done once by a stated rule.

I store an integer number of cents, or use an exact decimal column type, never a float. Floats are binary, so 0.1 has no exact value and totals drift by a cent. I keep the currency code beside the amount. I round once, at a defined step, such as when tax is calculated per line, and write that rule down.
A user books a meeting for 9 a.m. their time, six months from now. How do you store it?
How you handle time zones and daylight saving time.
Past events as UTC timestamps; future local-time events as local time plus a zone name, because daylight saving rules can change before the date.

For things that already happened, like when an order was placed, I store a UTC timestamp and convert it on display. A future meeting is different: the user means 9 a.m. where they are. I store the local date and time plus a zone name like America/Chicago, and work out the UTC moment when needed, because daylight saving rules can change before then.
What is the difference between PUT, PATCH and POST, and why does idempotency matter here?
Your grasp of what HTTP methods mean, which clients and proxies rely on.
PUT replaces the resource and is idempotent; POST creates or acts and is not; PATCH changes part of it and is idempotent only if designed that way.

PUT sends the full new version, so sending it twice gives the same result. That is what idempotent means, and it makes a retry safe. POST usually creates something, so two calls can make two records. PATCH sends only the changes: "set name" is safe to repeat, "add 1 to count" is not. I document which is which so clients know when they may retry.
Users can post comments that appear on other people's pages. What could go wrong, and how do you prevent it?
Whether you know cross-site scripting and where escaping must happen.
Escape output for its context, never inject raw HTML, sanitize with an allowlist if rich text is needed, and add a Content Security Policy as a second layer.

The danger is cross-site scripting: a comment holding a script runs in other users' browsers with their session. I let the framework escape text when it renders and never insert user input as raw HTML. If we allow formatting, I sanitize on the server with an allowlist of tags. A Content Security Policy that blocks inline scripts is the backup, not the fix.
We keep the session in a cookie. How do you stop another website from making requests as the logged-in user?
Whether you understand cross-site request forgery and the defences against it.
No data changes on GET, SameSite set on the session cookie, and a CSRF token or origin check on every request that changes data.

The browser can send our cookie even when a form on another site posts to us, so that site acts as the user. I set the cookie HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite=Lax or Strict, never change data on a GET, and require a CSRF token, a random value tied to the session, on every POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE. Checking the Origin header adds a layer.
The sign-up code checks whether the email exists, then inserts the user. Yet the table has duplicate emails. How did that happen?
How you spot a race condition and use the database to close it.
Two requests both passed the check before either inserted; the fix is a unique constraint, with the error caught and turned into a clear message.

Two requests arrived at almost the same moment, maybe from a double click. Both checked, both saw no user, both inserted. Code alone cannot close that gap. I clean up the duplicates, then add a unique index on the normalized email, lowercased and trimmed. I catch the unique violation and return a 409 or a friendly "this email is already registered".
Two support agents edit the same customer record at once, and one agent's changes vanish. How do you fix that?
Whether you can prevent lost updates with optimistic locking.
A version check in the UPDATE, a clear conflict response when it fails, and a way for the user to see the newer data before saving again.

That is a lost update: the last save wins. I add a version column. The form loads version 7, and the save runs UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = 7, setting it to 8. If no row changed, someone saved first, so the API returns 409 Conflict and the screen shows the newer values to merge. Row locks also work, but not while a person sits on a form.
An end-to-end test fails about one run in twenty, and the team keeps re-running the build. What do you do?
How you treat flaky tests and find their real cause.
Treats flakiness as a bug: looks for fixed waits, shared data, test order or the clock, fixes the cause, and quarantines only with an owner and a date.

Re-running teaches people to ignore red builds, so I treat it as a bug. I run the test in a loop and keep logs and screenshots of the failures. Usual causes are a fixed sleep instead of waiting for the element or response, data shared with another test, or a dependence on the clock. If I cannot fix it that day, I quarantine it with an owner and a date.
Should the tests for your data access code use a mocked database or a real one?
Your judgement about what a test can and cannot prove.
A real database of the same engine for queries, constraints and migrations, kept fast with isolated data; mocks only where the database is not under test.

For anything that runs SQL, a real database of the same engine and version, often in a container. A mock only proves I called my own code; it cannot catch a wrong join, a missing constraint or a broken migration. To keep it fast, each test runs in a transaction that rolls back, or gets its own data. Business logic above that layer can use plain unit tests.
After an order is saved, the service sends a confirmation email and publishes an event. Sometimes the email goes out but the order is missing. Why, and how do you redesign it?
Whether you can keep a database write and a message to another system consistent.
Names the dual-write problem and fixes it with an outbox: the message row commits with the order, a worker sends it, and receivers ignore duplicates.

The code sends inside the transaction, then the commit fails, so the email describes an order that never existed. Sending after commit has the opposite gap if the process dies. I write an outbox row in the same transaction as the order. A worker reads unsent rows, sends them and marks them done. It may send twice after a crash, so each message has an ID and receivers skip repeats.

game-artist.heading: Game and concept artist questions
qs: Why does the silhouette of a character matter so much in a game?
Whether you design for how a character reads in play, not only in a close-up painting.
Players often see characters small, fast or in the dark, so the shape alone must say who they are and what they do.

In play, a character is often a few dozen pixels tall and moving. If I fill the shape in solid black, I should still know the class and the threat level. I test that with thumbnails before I add any detail, because detail never saves a weak silhouette.
How do you check that a scene or key art reads clearly before you add color and detail?
Your control of value, the light and dark structure under the color.
Working in a few grouped values first, and checking in grayscale that the focal point has the strongest contrast.

I block the scene in three or four values first: background, middle ground, foreground and the focal point. Then I flip the image to grayscale and mirror it now and then. If the eye doesn't land where the player needs to look, I fix the values before I touch color.
What does a 3D modeler need from your character sheet to build the model without guessing?
Whether your concepts are usable for production, not just nice to look at.
Front, side and back views that line up, scale next to a reference, material callouts and close-ups of tricky parts.

I give an orthographic turnaround, front, side and back, with the proportions lined up across views. I add a height reference, callouts for materials like worn leather or brushed steel, and close-ups of buckles or how armor plates overlap. I also note what is hard surface and what is cloth that will move.
In a PBR workflow, what belongs in the base color map and what should stay out of it?
Your grasp of how physically based materials work in a game engine.
Base color holds the surface color only; lighting, shadows and shine are left out because the engine and other maps handle them.

The base color, or albedo, is the color of the surface without light on it. I keep baked shadows and highlights out, because the engine lights the asset and baked light would look wrong when it moves. Roughness, metalness and ambient occlusion go in their own maps.
What is texel density, and why do you keep it consistent?
Whether you understand a core technical rule of game texturing.
Texture pixels per unit of world space; consistent density keeps assets equally sharp next to each other and spends memory well.

Texel density is how many texture pixels cover one unit of the world, for example per meter. If a crate is sharp and the wall behind it is blurry, the scene looks broken. I set the project's target, check it while I lay out UVs, and only break it on purpose, like giving more to a hero prop the camera gets close to.
The art director needs twenty enemy variations by the end of tomorrow. How do you approach it?
How you produce volume fast without losing quality or consistency.
Quick thumbnails, a clear set of things that vary, an early check-in, then refinement of only the chosen few.

I would not paint twenty finished pieces. I'd agree first on what varies: body shape, weapon, color by rank. Then I do forty fast silhouette thumbnails in an hour or two, show them by midday, and refine the picks. Sharing early keeps me from polishing designs that get cut.
You join a project mid-way and the art bible has a style you would not have chosen. What do you do?
Whether you can serve an established style instead of your own taste.
Studying the art bible and existing assets, matching them closely, and raising concerns with examples through the right channel.

I study the art bible and paint a few studies of existing assets until my work blends in. A game with mixed styles looks worse than one with a style I don't love. If I see a real problem, say characters getting lost against the backgrounds, I bring a side-by-side example to the lead rather than quietly drifting.
Your character looked great in the concept, but in the engine it reads as muddy and noisy. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
How you diagnose the gap between a painting and the real game view.
Checking at the real camera distance and lighting, then simplifying detail and pushing larger shapes and value contrast.

Usually I designed it at close-up size. At the gameplay camera, fine detail turns into noise and similar values merge. I grab screenshots from the real camera in a few lighting setups, then simplify: bigger shape breaks, fewer small details, stronger contrast between main parts. For future concepts I add a small in-game-size view to every sheet.
How do you use photo reference and photobashing without creating legal problems for the studio?
Whether you know the basic rules of using other people's images in commercial work.
Using only own photos, licensed or properly cleared images in final work, and never copying another artist's work.

Reference I only look at can come from anywhere. Anything that ends up in the image itself must be my own photo or come from a source whose license covers commercial use, and I keep a note of the source. I never paint over another artist's work. If I'm unsure about a license, I ask before the piece ships, not after.
Playtesters keep missing the ledges they can climb and the objects they can use. How would you fix that through the art?
How you shape the environment so it guides play, not just looks good.
A consistent visual language for interactive things, kept rare elsewhere, with value and color contrast, then retesting with players.

I'd give interactive things one clear rule, for example worn light-colored edges on every climbable ledge, and keep that look off everything decorative. I'd quiet the background detail around paths so they stand out in value. Then I'd watch new playtests; if people still miss a spot, that spot needs work, not the player.
How do you push depth in an environment painting without relying on detail?
Your command of the depth cues that make a painted space read.
Atmospheric perspective explained correctly: values and colors move toward the atmosphere with distance, plus overlap, size and edge control.

I use atmospheric perspective. As things recede, their values move toward the sky value, contrast drops, edges soften and colors lose saturation. I keep the darkest darks and sharpest edges in the foreground, overlap shapes, and let size shrink with distance. Detail is the last depth cue I add, not the first.
In an eye-level scene with a crowd, how do you keep every figure at the right scale?
Whether you can use the horizon line to place figures correctly.
The horizon is the viewer's eye level, so on flat ground standing adults' eyes sit on it at any distance; other figures are sized against a scale adult.

The horizon line is the camera's eye level. If the camera is at a standing adult's eye height on flat ground, every standing adult's eyes land on the horizon, near or far; only their size changes. For a child or a seated figure, I first sketch a scale adult at that spot and size them against it. On slopes or stairs I find each figure's ground plane first.
How do you use shape language to tell the player who a character is?
How you turn personality and role into readable shapes.
A dominant shape repeated at several scales, the usual readings of round, square and sharp, and a deliberate accent that breaks the rule.

I pick one dominant shape and repeat it at large, medium and small scales. Round shapes read as friendly or soft, squares as stable and strong, triangles and sharp points as fast or dangerous. Then I break it on purpose: a brute built from squares with one jagged weapon tells you he is strong and also a threat.
How do you make a fantasy creature look like it could really move?
Whether your anatomy knowledge holds up beyond human figures.
A real animal skeleton as a base, joints that bend plausibly, mass supported by the legs, and early motion sketches checked with animation.

I start from a real animal skeleton and change it from there. Joints have to bend the way an animator expects, legs have to carry the mass, and the center of gravity sits over the feet. I sketch it walking, turning and attacking before I polish anything, and I show those sketches to an animator early, because bad anatomy shows up in motion first.
The game uses a high isometric camera. How does that change the way you design characters?
How you design for the camera the player will actually see.
Design for the top-down view and small on-screen size: bolder proportions, big color blocks, readable tops, and fine detail moved to portraits.

From that camera the player mostly sees the head, shoulders and silhouette from above, and the character may be only a few dozen pixels tall. I push proportions: bigger heads, hands and weapons, large simple color blocks, and a clear read from the top, like a colored hat or shoulder shape. Fine face detail goes into the portrait art, not the in-game design.
How do you decide how polished a concept needs to be?
Your judgement on time spent versus what the image is for.
Polish matched to the audience and the decision the image supports, and no rendering of designs that are not yet approved.

I ask who the image is for. Exploration for the art director can be rough thumbnails, because the decision is which direction. A callout for a modeler needs clear materials and construction, not dramatic lighting. A pitch image for a publisher needs full polish. Rendering a design nobody has approved yet is the most common way I see concept time wasted.
What is a color script, and how would you use one for a level?
Whether you can plan color and light across a whole experience, not one image.
A sequence of small paintings mapping color and light to emotional beats, used to test contrast between moments before production.

It is a row of small, quick paintings that shows how color and light change across a level or story, beat by beat. I mark the emotional moments first, say a calm village, a tense cave and a boss arena, then give each a palette and light key. Side by side, it shows whether the beats contrast enough before anyone builds the level.
How do you concept an environment that will be built from modular pieces?
How well your concepts fit the way environments are actually produced.
Agreeing the grid and camera with the environment team, designing a kit of snapping pieces plus hero props, and showing how pieces join.

First I ask the environment team for the grid size and the camera. Then I design the space as a kit: walls, corners, doorways, floors and trim that snap on that grid, plus a few unique hero props to hide repetition. I deliver one mood painting and one sheet showing each piece and how they combine, so builders do not have to invent the joins.
Your environment concept was approved, then the blockout shows the doors are too small for the player character. What do you do?
How you own a mistake and fix it from gameplay facts.
Owning it quickly, fixing from the real gameplay measurements, updating the source concept, and adding a habit that prevents a repeat.

I tell the art director and level designer right away that it is my error. The fix starts from gameplay measurements, character height, door width and camera clearance, not from my painting. I paint over a blockout screenshot at the right size and replace the old concept so nobody builds from it. Since then, every concept I make includes a scale figure.
As a lead, how do you give paint-over feedback to a junior artist without taking over their design?
Your ability to direct art and grow other artists at the same time.
The problem named in words and tied to the game, rough options rather than a finished fix, and the junior making the change themselves.

I name the problem in words first, like the focal point competing with the background, and why it matters in the game. If a paint-over helps, I keep it rough and show two options, not one finished answer. Then they make the fix in their own file. On their next piece I check whether the lesson stuck, not just whether this one got fixed.

game-designer.heading: Game designer questions
qs: What is a core loop, and what was the core loop of a game you worked on?
Whether you know the basic unit of game design and can name one from your own work.
A clear definition, then a real loop with an action, a reward and a reason to repeat it.

A core loop is the set of actions the player repeats most, plus the reward that sends them back in. On my last project, a small dungeon game, it was: explore a floor, fight, collect loot, upgrade gear at camp, then go deeper. Every new feature had to feed that loop, or we asked hard questions about it.
How do you teach a new mechanic in a level without a text tutorial?
Your grasp of level design as a teaching tool.
A step-by-step method: safe first contact, practice, a real test, then a twist, with the level itself guiding the player.

I use introduce, practice, test, twist. The player first meets the mechanic where failure is cheap, like a wall jump over a short gap with no pit below. Then a few easy repeats, then a test with real stakes, then a twist that mixes it with something they know. Level shape and lighting point the way, so I rarely need text.
What are sources and sinks in a game economy, and why do they matter?
Whether you understand how in-game currency stays balanced over time.
Sources add currency, sinks remove it; if sources outrun sinks, inflation follows. Bonus for modeling it and watching data after launch.

Sources, or faucets, are where currency enters: quest rewards, drops, daily gifts. Sinks are where it leaves: repairs, upgrades, fees, consumables. If sources outrun sinks, players pile up gold, prices climb and rewards stop meaning anything. I model both per hour of play in a spreadsheet, then watch average balances by player level after launch.
A rare item has a 5% drop chance per kill. How many kills does it take, and how will players feel about it?
Your basic probability and whether you think about how random rewards feel.
The average is 20 kills, but many players need far more. A good answer spots the unlucky tail and offers a fix like a pity timer.

On average it takes 20 kills, but about 36 percent of players will still have nothing after 20, and some will go past 60. That long tail feels unfair. If the item matters, I would add a pity timer that guarantees it after a set number of tries, or raise the odds a little after each miss.
Playtesters find one weapon that beats everything else. What do you do?
How you handle a dominant strategy without breaking what players enjoy.
Finding the cause first, using data not just complaints, small changes tested one at a time, and preferring counters over heavy nerfs.

First I find out why it wins: are the numbers off, or is there no counter to it? I look at pick rate and win rate, not just complaints. If it is numbers, I make small changes one at a time and retest. If it is a design gap, I would rather add a counter than nerf it into the ground, because players chose it for a reason.
Data shows a lot of players quit during level 3. Walk me through how you find out why.
Your method for diagnosing a player problem from data and observation.
Starting from data to find the exact spot, then watching real players, fixing the cause and measuring the result.

I start with data: where exactly they quit, how long they spent, how often they died. Then I watch recordings or run a playtest of that level without helping. Last time, players did not read a door as a door and wandered for ten minutes. We changed the lighting and added a sound cue, and completion went from about 55 to 80 percent.
How do you make a game work for both new players and experts?
How you think about difficulty and challenge for different skill levels.
A fair baseline plus optional depth, lower cost of failure, and testing with both groups, not just the team.

I set a baseline that a new player can finish with some effort, then give experts optional depth: harder side paths, time goals, hidden challenges. Difficulty modes help, but so do things like checkpoints, which make failure cost less without making the game easier. I test with both groups, because the team is always too good at its own game.
The producer wants to cut a feature you designed to save schedule. How do you respond?
Your judgement on scope and whether you can trade off without ego.
Weighing the feature against the core experience, accepting cuts that do not hurt it, and offering a smaller version when it matters.

I ask what the feature costs and what it does for the player. If the core loop works without it, I agree and keep notes so we can add it in an update. If it carries the game, I offer a smaller version. On one project we cut a full crafting tree down to six recipes, which kept the hook and saved about four weeks.
You are asked to add a mechanic that pushes players to spend more money. How do you approach it?
Whether you can design monetization that earns money without tricking players.
Asking about the real goal, offering fair options, and pushing back on manipulative tactics with reasons the business cares about.

I first ask what goal we need to hit, then offer options that earn without tricking players: cosmetics, a fair season pass, prices shown clearly in real money. I push back on fake countdown timers, hidden odds or pay-to-win items. They hurt trust, reviews and long-term revenue, and some bring legal risk. If we sell random items, the odds should be shown.
Tell me about a design change you made that made the game worse. How did you catch it?
How you own a mistake and what process you changed because of it.
A specific change, honest about the cause, a quick fix, and a lasting lesson about testing or data.

On a mobile puzzle game I cut the time limit on later levels by 10 percent because testers said they were too easy. Those testers were veterans. In the soft launch, a small early release, quit rates on those levels doubled. I rolled it back and retested with new players. Now I always ask who the testers are before I trust what they say.
