What is the difference between input randomness and output randomness, and when would you use each?
Whether you know how randomness changes the decisions a player makes.
Input randomness comes before the choice and asks players to adapt; output randomness decides the result after it. Each is tied to the feel the game wants.

Input randomness happens before I decide, like the cards I draw or the map I get. I plan around it, so it creates choices. Output randomness happens after, like a 70% hit roll. It adds tension but can feel unfair when skill loses to a bad roll. In a strategy game I lean on input randomness and keep output rolls small or smoothed.
How would you build a cost curve to balance a set of cards or items?
How you turn balance from gut feel into a model you can test.
A value for each stat or effect, cost checked against total value along a curve, and playtests used to correct the model where it is wrong.

I pick a baseline, say one point of cost buys three points of stats, and price each effect in those points by comparing it to plain items with no special effect. Then I plot every item's value against its cost and look for outliers above or below the line. The model is a starting point; play data tells me where effects like card draw are worth more than I guessed.
How do you guide players through a large level without arrows or a minimap?
Your level design tools for wayfinding.
Landmarks, light, leading lines, sightlines and framing, then tests with fresh players to confirm they go where intended.

I give the level a big landmark visible from most places, so players can orient. Light and color pull the eye toward the main path, and lines in the geometry, like a road or a pipe, lead toward exits. I frame the next goal through a doorway when the player enters a room. Then I watch new testers: if three of five turn the wrong way, the level is wrong, not them.
How do you run a playtest so you do not steer what the players do?
Whether your playtest results can be trusted.
Fresh testers from the target audience, a neutral briefing, no hints, open questions, and observed behavior weighed above stated opinions.

I recruit people who have not seen the game and match the target audience. I give a short neutral briefing, then I stay quiet and take notes, even when they struggle. I ask them to think aloud. Afterward I ask open questions like 'What were you trying to do there?' rather than 'Was the jump too hard?' What they did counts more than what they say they liked.
How do you structure a branching story so the content does not grow out of control?
Whether you can plan narrative scope like a designer, not only a writer.
Paths that split and rejoin, choices tracked as flags that change lines rather than whole paths, and a clear budget for true splits.

Fully independent branches double the content with every choice, so I avoid them. I use a branch-and-bottleneck shape: paths split, then rejoin at key story beats. Choices set flags that change a line of dialogue, a character's attitude, or an ending scene. I save one or two real splits for the choices players remember, and keep a flag chart so testers can check every path.
In your competitive game, one character wins 55% of matches but almost nobody picks it. Is it overpowered?
How you read balance data before acting on it.
Not proven: with a low pick rate, mostly specialists play it. Split win rate by skill and by experience on the character before changing anything.

Not necessarily. If only a few dedicated players use it, the win rate reflects their skill, not the character's power. I would split the data by rank and by how many games each player has on that character. If new players on it still win well above 50%, it is strong. If not, a nerf would punish the experts and leave it unpicked by everyone else.
Your live game's currency is piling up and prices on the player market keep climbing. How do you fix it?
How you repair a live economy without punishing players.
Find which source outgrew the sinks, add sinks players want, trim sources gradually, and tell players what changes and why.

First I find where the money comes from: which sources grew, maybe a farmable quest or more active players. Then I add sinks players want to use, like cosmetics, upgrades or a trade fee, rather than taking money away. I trim the worst source slowly and announce it. Wiping balances breaks trust, so I only consider that for money gained through an exploit.
Players have spent months using an item that is too strong. Do you nerf it or buff everything else?
Your judgement on balance changes in a live game.
Weighs power creep against player loss, usually a targeted nerf to the outlier, with care for what players invested and clear patch notes.

Buffing everything else feels nice but causes power creep: enemies then need buffs too, and the problem grows. Usually I nerf the outlier, but I target the part that breaks the game rather than its whole identity, so it stays fun to use. If people paid for it or earned it slowly, I may offer a refund or reset, and I explain the reason in the patch notes.
Walk me through how you write the spec for a new mechanic.
Whether your documents let a team build the right thing the first time.
Purpose, player-facing rules, edge cases, tuning values kept in data, and what a playtest should show, kept short and up to date.

I start with one sentence on what the mechanic is for and how it should feel. Then the rules from the player's view, with a diagram or mockup. Next, edge cases: what happens if you die mid-dash or dash into a wall. I list every number I want to tune and ask for them in data, not code. I end with what the playtest should show, and I update the page when the design changes.
A week before launch, testers find two systems that combine into a powerful exploit. How do you decide what to do?
How you handle risk and scope when time is short.
Weighs harm to the game, reach, and risk of the fix; picks the smallest safe change, and may keep a harmless exploit as a reward for creativity.

I ask: does it break progression or fairness, how many players will find it, and how risky is a late fix? A broken economy or online advantage must be fixed, ideally with a tuning value, not new code. If it only lets a clever player skip a single-player fight, it may be a reward for creativity, and I would leave it. Either way I log it for the first patch.

game-developer.heading: Game developer questions
qs: Why do we multiply movement by delta time, and what goes wrong if we forget?
Whether you understand frame-rate independence, the first thing every game loop needs.
Delta time is the time since the last frame. Without it, speed depends on frame rate and the game plays differently on every machine.

Delta time is how many seconds passed since the last frame. If I move a character 5 units every frame, it runs twice as fast at 120 fps as at 60. Moving 5 units per second times delta time gives the same speed on any machine. I forgot it once in a game jam and the game was unplayable on a fast laptop.
What is your frame budget at 60 fps, and how do you split it?
Whether you think about performance in milliseconds, not just frames per second.
About 16.7 ms per frame at 60 fps (33.3 ms at 30), shared by gameplay, physics, animation and rendering, with headroom left for spikes.

At 60 fps one frame is about 16.7 milliseconds; at 30 fps it is 33.3. I agree a rough split with the team, for example a few milliseconds for gameplay and physics and most of the rest for rendering. I keep a margin, because a frame that averages 16 ms will still miss when an explosion spawns. I talk in milliseconds because fps numbers do not add up.
The game runs at 40 fps on the target hardware. How do you find out what is slowing it down?
Your method for profiling before you optimize.
Measure first: compare CPU and GPU frame times in a profiler, find the bottleneck, then drill into the slowest systems instead of guessing.

I profile a build close to release settings, not the editor. I compare CPU and GPU frame times. If the GPU is the long one, I drop the render resolution: if the frame rate jumps, I am pixel bound. If the CPU is long, I open the CPU timeline and look for the biggest blocks, like pathfinding or too many draw calls. I fix the largest one and measure again.
The game holds 60 fps but hitches for a moment every few seconds. What do you suspect?
Whether you can read a spike pattern and know the usual causes of hitches.
Spikes, not average cost: garbage collection, asset loading or shader compilation. Find the spike frame in the profiler, then fix the cause, such as per-frame allocations.

A regular hitch smells like garbage collection. I capture the spike frame in the profiler and look at memory allocated per frame. Often it is bullets created and destroyed, or strings built every update. I pool the bullets, cache the strings, and allocations drop to near zero. If it is not memory, I check for loading or shaders compiling the first time they are used.
Why would you run physics on a fixed timestep when rendering runs at a variable rate?
Your grasp of the game loop and of stable, repeatable simulation.
A fixed step keeps physics stable and repeatable. An accumulator runs as many steps as time allows, and rendering interpolates between the last two states.

Physics behaves badly with a changing step: springs explode and jumps reach different heights. So I add each frame's time to an accumulator and run physics in fixed steps, say 1/60 of a second, while the accumulator has enough. Rendering then blends between the last two physics states, so motion looks smooth even when frame rate and physics rate differ.
A fast projectile sometimes passes straight through a thin wall. How do you fix it?
Whether you recognize tunneling and know the standard fixes.
The object jumps past the wall between two physics steps. Use a raycast or sweep along its path, or continuous collision detection, rather than just thickening walls.

That is tunneling: in one physics step the bullet is in front of the wall, in the next it is behind it, so they never overlap. For a bullet I cast a ray from the old position to the new one each step and hit whatever is in between. For bigger fast objects I turn on continuous collision detection for that body only, because it costs more than the default check.
A designer asks for a grappling hook two weeks before a milestone. How do you respond?
How you weigh a design request against scope and schedule.
Neither yes nor no at once: estimate it, offer a quick prototype or smaller version, and make the trade-off visible to whoever owns the schedule.

I ask what problem the hook solves for the player. Then I give an honest estimate: a rough prototype in two days, a polished version with animation and edge cases in maybe three weeks. I suggest the prototype once the milestone build is safe, we playtest it, and the producer decides what it replaces. Saying yes quietly and slipping the milestone helps no one.
In an online shooter, a player swears they hit an enemy on their screen, but the server said miss. What is going on, and what would you do?
Your understanding of latency, server authority and lag compensation.
Each client sees others slightly in the past. The server stays authoritative, and lag compensation rewinds targets to what the shooter saw, within a limit.

The shooter sees the enemy where it was some milliseconds ago, because of latency and interpolation. The server checks the hit against where the enemy is now, so it misses. I keep the server authoritative to stop cheating and add lag compensation: the server stores recent positions and rewinds targets to the time the shooter saw, with a cap on how far back.
A patch you shipped breaks old save files for some players. Walk me through what you do.
How you handle a live mistake and protect player data.
Stop the damage first, keep the broken saves, fix it with a versioned migration, and add old saves to the tests so it cannot happen again.

First I make sure the game does not overwrite the old files, and we tell players not to delete them. I find which field changed, then write a loader that reads the save's version number and converts old formats step by step. We ship a hotfix, and I add saves from every past version to our automated tests so the next change is checked against them.
In a large open world, objects far from the starting point begin to jitter. Why, and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand floating-point precision limits in big game worlds.
32-bit floats lose precision as numbers grow. Keep the play area near the origin by shifting the world, or use double precision for positions.

Positions are usually 32-bit floats, which hold about seven significant digits. Around 10 kilometers from the origin the smallest step is close to a millimeter, so the camera and animation start to shake. I would move the world origin with the player: when they go far enough, shift everything back toward zero. Some engines also offer 64-bit positions for this.
Why do most engines store rotations as quaternions instead of Euler angles?
Whether you understand the math behind rotations, not just the editor fields.
Names gimbal lock and poor interpolation of Euler angles, and knows quaternions slerp smoothly and compose cheaply.

Euler angles are three rotations applied in order. When the middle one lines two axes up, you lose a degree of freedom: that is gimbal lock. They also interpolate badly. A unit quaternion has no gimbal lock, composes cheaply and slerps smoothly. I keep Euler angles in the editor, where people type degrees, and convert to quaternions for runtime math.
Players say jumping feels unfair, yet the code does exactly what the spec says. What would you add?
Your sense of game feel and the small tricks that make controls forgiving.
Knows coyote time and input buffering, explains why they help, and tunes them by playtesting.

Two things. Coyote time: the jump still works for a few frames after the player walks off a ledge, because they pressed it when they saw themselves on the edge. And an input buffer: a jump pressed a few frames before landing fires on landing. I keep both windows short and tune them in playtests until nobody complains about eaten inputs.
How does A* find a path, and what must its heuristic satisfy?
Whether you know pathfinding well enough to choose and tune it.
Cost so far plus estimated cost left; an admissible heuristic never overestimates and gives optimal paths.

A* expands nodes in order of cost so far plus a guess of the cost left. If the guess never overestimates, it is admissible and the path is optimal. On a grid with diagonal moves, Manhattan distance overestimates, so I use octile distance. If speed matters more than a perfect route, I weight the heuristic up on purpose and accept slightly longer paths.
For enemy AI, when would you use a state machine and when a behavior tree?
How you choose an AI architecture for the size of the problem.
A state machine for small, clear behaviors; a behavior tree when transitions explode. Picks what designers can read and tune.

For a guard with patrol, chase and attack, a state machine is clear and easy to debug. Once every state needs exceptions, like fleeing at low health from anywhere, the transitions multiply. Then a behavior tree helps: priorities read top to bottom and branches can be reused. I pick the simplest one the designers can read and tune themselves.
An update loop walks a list of pointers to 10,000 enemy objects and it is slow. Why, and what would you change?
Your grasp of data-oriented design and how the CPU cache affects game code.
Pointer chasing causes cache misses; fix with contiguous arrays of only the needed fields, then measure.

Each enemy sits somewhere random in memory, so most loads miss the cache and the CPU waits on RAM. Memory comes in cache lines, usually 64 bytes, and we use a few bytes of each. I would store the fields this update needs, like position and velocity, in tight contiguous arrays and loop over them in order. Then I profile before and after.
The profiler shows the render thread is the bottleneck, with thousands of draw calls per frame. What do you do?
Whether you can cut CPU rendering cost with the right techniques.
Cull first, then reduce state changes: shared materials, atlases, static batching, GPU instancing, checked step by step.

Each draw call costs CPU time to set state and submit, so thousands of them choke the render thread while the GPU waits. First I cut what gets drawn: frustum and occlusion culling, and LODs. Then I cut state changes: shared materials, texture atlases, static batching for scenery, GPU instancing for repeated meshes like trees. I take a frame capture after each step.
On phones, the frame rate collapses whenever thick smoke fills the screen. What is happening, and how do you fix it?
Whether you can diagnose overdraw and fill-rate limits on mobile GPUs.
Transparent layers shade the same pixel many times; confirm by changing resolution, then reduce overdraw.

Transparent particles cannot hide each other with the depth buffer, so every layer gets shaded and one pixel may be shaded many times. Mobile GPUs run out of fill rate. I confirm by lowering resolution: if frame time drops a lot, I am pixel bound. Then I use fewer particles with denser textures, trim sprite meshes to the visible shape and render particles at lower resolution.
In our co-op game, players are teleporting and giving themselves rare items. What went wrong, and how do you fix it?
How you design network authority so the game resists cheating.
The server trusted client results; clients should send inputs, the server validates, with lag tolerance for honest players.

The server is trusting what the client reports. Clients should send inputs and requests, not results. The server checks them: can this player move that far in that time, did that chest really drop that item. I would move item grants to the server first, since they hurt the economy, then add movement checks with some tolerance for lag so honest players are not snapped back.
You moved animation updates to worker threads, and now the game crashes about once every few hours. How do you approach it?
How you debug rare concurrency bugs and design safe multithreaded code.
Suspects a data race, makes it reproducible, uses tools like a thread sanitizer, and fixes ownership rather than adding random locks.

A rare crash after threading usually means two jobs touch the same data without order. I try to reproduce it faster with stress tests and more threads, run a thread sanitizer build and read the crash dumps for which data was bad. The fix is a clear rule: each job reads last frame's data or writes only its own, with dependencies declared in the job system.
In a lockstep RTS, two machines with the same inputs drift out of sync. What causes this, and how do you prevent it?
Your depth on deterministic simulation, one of the hardest problems in networked games.
Lists float differences, iteration order, unseeded randomness; uses fixed-point or strict math and state checksums.

Lockstep sends only inputs, so every machine must compute the same state bit for bit. Floats can differ across compilers, CPU instructions and math libraries, and fast-math flags make it worse. Hash map order, uninitialized memory and unsynced random seeds also cause it. I use fixed-point math for the simulation, one seeded RNG, and checksum the state each turn.

game-programmer.heading: Game programmer questions
qs: Why do you multiply movement by delta time, and when would you not?
Whether you understand how frame rate affects gameplay code.
Movement must not depend on frame rate. Physics usually runs on a fixed step instead, so its code uses the fixed step, not the render delta.

Delta time is the time since the last frame. If I add speed times delta time each frame, a character covers the same distance per second at 30 or 144 fps. Physics is different: I run it on a fixed timestep, so results stay stable and repeatable whatever the frame rate is.
What is your frame budget at 60 frames per second, and how do you use it?
Your sense of performance as a hard limit, not a nice-to-have.
About 16.7 ms per frame for everything, split between systems and checked in the profiler regularly, not only at the end.

At 60 fps I have about 16.7 milliseconds per frame; at 30 fps about 33.3. Logic, physics, animation, audio and render submission all share it. On our last project each system had a target, physics around 2 ms, and we checked a profile capture on every nightly build, so a regression showed up the day it landed.
Why do engines store rotations as quaternions instead of three angles?
Your grasp of the 3D math behind cameras, animation and movement.
Euler angles can hit gimbal lock and interpolate badly. Quaternions avoid gimbal lock and blend smoothly between two rotations.

With three angles, when two rotation axes line up you lose one degree of freedom. That is gimbal lock, and the camera or bone flips or sticks. Quaternions do not have that problem, they are cheap to combine, and spherical interpolation gives a smooth, even turn between two orientations. I still show angles to designers in the editor because they are easier to read.
A fast projectile sometimes passes straight through a thin wall. What is going on and how do you fix it?
Whether you can spot tunneling and know the standard fixes.
Names tunneling and gives fixes: a sweep or raycast between positions, continuous collision detection, thicker colliders, with their costs.

That is tunneling. In one physics step the bullet is in front of the wall, in the next it is already behind it, so the shapes never overlap. For bullets I cast a ray from the old position to the new one each step. For bigger fast objects I turn on continuous collision detection, but only on those objects, because it costs more.
Players report a short hitch every few seconds, even in an empty room. How do you find the cause?
How you track down a regular stutter with a profiler instead of guessing.
Captures the spike frame, checks for garbage collection or loading, finds per-frame allocations and removes them with reuse or pooling.

A regular hitch that does not depend on what is on screen often means garbage collection. I capture a profile, jump to the spike frame and see what ran. Then I look at memory allocated per frame: string building in an update loop, new lists, temporary arrays. I reuse buffers and pool objects like bullets and effects, then check the allocation counter stays near zero.
The frame rate drops in one area of the level. How do you tell if you are CPU-bound or GPU-bound?
Your method for diagnosing a slow frame before optimizing anything.
Measures first: profiler timings and a quick test like lowering resolution, then targets the side that is actually late.

I first look at the profiler to see whether the CPU is waiting on the GPU or the other way round. A quick test helps: if I drop the render resolution and frame time improves, pixel work on the GPU is the limit. If nothing changes, I look at the CPU side, like too many draw calls, AI or animation updates. I only optimize once I know which side is late.
A designer says the jump feels floaty. What do you change?
Whether you can turn a feel note into concrete code changes and tools for designers.
Knows common game feel techniques and exposes the values as tunables so the designer can iterate without a programmer.

I would ask to play it with them first. Common fixes: stronger gravity on the way down than on the way up, cutting the jump short when the button is released, a few frames of grace to jump after leaving a ledge, and buffering a jump pressed just before landing. I put every value in the editor so the designer can tune it live.
In a large open world, objects far from the start start to jitter. Why, and what do you do?
Your understanding of floating point precision in world coordinates.
Explains that 32-bit floats lose precision as values grow, and fixes it by shifting the world origin or using doubles for positions.

A 32-bit float keeps only about seven significant digits, so the farther from the origin, the bigger the gap between values it can store. Far out, positions snap between those values and things shake. I would move the world origin to stay near the player and shift everything by that offset, or store world positions in doubles and convert to local floats for rendering.
In our online shooter, players complain they got hit after they were already behind cover. Is that a bug, and what do you do?
Your knowledge of network latency handling and the tradeoffs it forces.
Explains server-side lag compensation, why it favors the shooter, and limits it, for example a cap on how far back the server rewinds.

Often it is lag compensation working as designed. The server keeps a short history of hitbox positions, rewinds to what the shooter saw, and checks the hit there. That makes aiming fair, but the target may already be behind cover on his own screen. I would check that the rewind is capped, so very laggy players cannot hit from far in the past, and log real cases to see if anything is off.
The day before a console certification submission, QA finds a rare crash. Do you fix it or ship?
Your judgement on risk when a late fix could cause more harm than the bug.
Weighs how often and how badly it happens against the risk of the fix, decides with QA and production, and plans a patch if it ships.

I would first get a repro rate and a call stack. If it can crash a player during normal play and the fix is small and contained, I make it, have a second programmer review it, and QA retests that area. If the fix touches shared systems, I would raise it with the producer and QA lead, ship with the known issue documented, and put the fix in the first patch.
An enemy should notice the player only inside a 90-degree view cone. How do you test that cheaply?
Whether you use vector math the way engine code does.
Normalize both vectors, take the dot product, and compare it to the cosine of half the cone angle. No angle math every frame.

I take the enemy's forward vector and the vector to the player, normalize both, and take the dot product. That gives the cosine of the angle between them. For a 90-degree cone, half is 45 degrees, so I compare against cos 45, about 0.707, computed once. Above that, the player is inside. Then I do a distance check and a line-of-sight raycast, cheapest test first.
When would you lay out data as a struct of arrays instead of an array of structs?
Your grasp of how memory layout drives CPU performance.
Cache lines: when a hot loop reads only a few fields of many objects, packing those fields together avoids loading bytes it never uses.

The CPU pulls memory in cache lines, typically 64 bytes. If I update positions for 10,000 particles and each struct also holds color, lifetime and flags, most of every line is wasted. With separate arrays for positions and velocities, the loop reads only what it uses, in order, and the prefetcher keeps up. For code that touches every field of one object at a time, array of structs is fine.
Why do many engines avoid general heap allocations during gameplay, and what do they use instead?
Whether you know how engines keep memory cost predictable.
General allocation has unpredictable cost and fragments memory. Pools and per-frame linear allocators make it cheap and bounded.

A general allocator can take a lock, search free lists and fragment memory over a long session. In managed languages it also feeds the garbage collector. So I preallocate. Bullets and effects come from fixed-size pools. Temporary data for one frame goes in a linear allocator: allocating is a pointer bump, and the whole block resets at the end of the frame.
Designers wait on you every time they want to tune a weapon. How would you change that?
How you build tools that let designers work without a programmer.
Move tuning values into data, reload them while the game runs, and validate input so a typo cannot crash the build.

I would move damage, fire rate and spread out of code into data files or editor assets the designers own. Then I add hot reload, so a saved change shows up in the running game within seconds. I check ranges and missing fields on load and show a clear error instead of crashing. I also sit with them for an hour; their real workflow tells me what to build first.
After a patch, players report their old saves will not load. What went wrong, and how do you design saves so it does not happen again?
How you handle a mistake that costs players their progress.
Protect the old files first, then use versioned save formats with ordered migration steps and tests on real saves from every release.

First I make sure the game does not overwrite the old files, so nothing is lost while we fix it. The likely cause is a changed data layout read without a version check. Going forward, every save carries a version number, and the loader runs migrations in order, version 3 to 4 to 5, filling new fields with defaults. Our tests load saves from every shipped version.
A client message says, "I hit player 12 for 80 damage." What is wrong with that design?
Whether you treat the game client as untrusted.
The server decides outcomes. The client sends inputs or intents, and the server checks them against its own state and data.

Anyone can edit packets or memory, so a cheater just sends "I hit everyone for 9,999." The client should send what it did: fired at this time, in this direction, with this weapon. The server checks ammo, fire rate and line of sight, runs its own hit test with lag compensation, and computes damage from its own data. The client only shows the result.
Explain client-side prediction and server reconciliation for player movement.
Whether you understand how movement stays responsive with an authoritative server.
The client moves at once and numbers its inputs; on each server update it resets to the server state and replays the unconfirmed inputs.

If the client waited for the server, every key press would lag by the round trip. So the client applies each input right away and sends it with a sequence number. The server runs the same movement code and replies with the authoritative position and the last input it processed. The client snaps to that state, then replays the inputs not yet confirmed. If the code matches, the fix is invisible.
A 64-player match uses too much server upload bandwidth. How do you bring it down without making the game feel worse?
Your judgement in trading network data against how the game feels.
Measure first, then send less, smaller and less often where players notice least: relevancy, delta compression, quantization, priority by distance.

First I measure which messages cost the most. Then I send each client only what is relevant to it, so players across the map update rarely or not at all. I send changes against the last state the client acknowledged instead of full state, and quantize values, such as positions to centimeters and angles to 16 bits. Nearby enemies keep the full rate, because that is where players notice.
You moved animation updates onto worker threads. Now there is a rare crash, and it runs slower than before. What do you suspect?
How you debug multithreaded engine code.
A data race for the crash; false sharing or jobs too small for the slowdown. Fixed by clear ownership and tools, not by adding sleeps.

For the crash, a data race: two jobs writing the same skeleton, or a job reading a transform the main thread is still changing. I check who owns every write and run a race-detection build. For the speed, false sharing is a classic: per-thread counters packed on one cache line, so cores fight over it. Many tiny jobs also cost more in scheduling than they save.
Our RTS uses deterministic lockstep, and matches between a PC and a console player desync after ten minutes. Where do you look?
Your depth on keeping a simulation identical across machines.
Per-tick state checksums to find the first diverging tick, then floating-point differences, unordered iteration and stray random calls.

First I log a checksum of the game state every tick on both machines and find the first tick that differs. Then the usual suspects: floating-point results that differ by compiler or CPU, such as fused multiply-add or library sin and cos; looping over a container whose order is not fixed; or a random call outside the shared seeded generator. Long term, fixed-point math.

general-counsel.heading: General counsel questions
qs: As general counsel, who is your client?
Whether you know you represent the company, not the CEO or any one officer.
The organization is the client, acting through its board and officers, with clear lines when a person's interests split from the company's.

The company is my client. I take direction from the CEO and the board because they act for it, but I do not represent them personally. If an officer's interests split from the company's, I say so plainly and tell them they may want their own lawyer. That keeps the advice honest and the privilege with the company.
A manager copies you on every email so it will be privileged. Does that work?
Your grasp of when attorney-client privilege actually covers in-house communications.
Privilege covers confidential communications made to get legal advice. Copying a lawyer on business email does not create it, and overuse weakens real claims.

No. Privilege protects confidential communications made to get or give legal advice. Courts look at the main purpose of the message, and they look harder at in-house lawyers, since we also give business advice. A cc on routine email adds nothing. I would show the manager how to send me a direct question, marked as a request for legal advice, and keep the wider thread clean.
Walk me through putting a litigation hold in place.
Whether you can preserve evidence correctly once a dispute is expected.
Acting when litigation is reasonably anticipated, not only when served, and covering people, systems, auto-deletion and follow-up.

The duty starts when we reasonably expect a lawsuit, so a demand letter can trigger it. I identify the people and systems involved, send a written hold in plain language, and have IT suspend auto-delete for those accounts, chats and phones. Each person confirms in writing. I send reminders, add people as facts emerge, and release the hold only when the matter is over.
You are about to interview an employee in an internal investigation. What do you tell them first?
Whether you know the Upjohn warning and why it matters.
You represent the company, not them; the talk is privileged, but the privilege belongs to the company, which may waive it and share what they say.

I tell them I am a lawyer for the company, not for them. What we discuss is privileged, but the privilege belongs to the company, and the company can decide to waive it and share it, including with the government. I ask them to keep the talk confidential and note in my file that I gave the warning. Skipping it can hurt both the privilege and the employee's trust.
How do you decide what to send to outside counsel, and how do you keep the spend under control?
How you run a legal budget and match work to the right lawyers.
Clear criteria for sending work out, plus budgets, staffing rules and regular review of bills against results.

Routine contracts, employment questions and policy work stay in-house. I send out major litigation, deals outside our expertise, and anything needing a specialist or local counsel. Each matter gets a written budget and staffing plan. I read the bills monthly, push back on padded hours, and use fixed fees where work is predictable. Last year that cut our outside spend by about 18%.
The CEO wants to sign a deal this week that you think carries real legal risk. What do you do?
Your judgement in advising on risk while leaving business calls to the business.
Explains the risk in business terms, offers ways to reduce it, and accepts the business decision unless it is illegal, with the advice documented.

I explain the risk in business terms: what could go wrong, how likely it is, what it could cost. Then I bring options, like an indemnity, a cap on liability or a short delay to finish diligence. If the risk is lawful and the CEO accepts it, that is their call, and I put my advice in writing. If the deal would break the law, I say no and take it to the board if needed.
You find evidence the CFO may be booking revenue early to hit targets. What do you do?
Whether you know your duty to report up the ladder when an officer may be breaking the law.
Preserves evidence, does not tip off the officer, reports to the CEO and audit committee, and pushes for an independent investigation.

I preserve the records first and do not tip off the CFO. The professional rules, and for public companies the SEC's attorney conduct rules, require me to report evidence of a material violation up the ladder. Because the CFO is involved, I go to the CEO and the audit committee chair, and recommend the committee hire independent counsel and forensic accountants.
How do you help the board make a big decision that will hold up if a shareholder sues?
Your understanding of directors' fiduciary duties and the business judgment rule.
A careful, informed process: full information in time, conflicts disclosed, independent advice, and minutes that show real deliberation.

Courts generally defer to directors under the business judgment rule if they acted informed, in good faith and without conflicts. So I build the record: materials sent days ahead, expert advisers present, conflicts disclosed and conflicted directors recused. My minutes show the options weighed, not a script. A good process protects directors more than a good outcome does.
IT tells you on a Friday night that customer data may have been stolen. What do you do in the first 48 hours?
How you lead an incident response with legal duties, privilege and deadlines in mind.
Containment with IT, outside counsel directing forensics, mapping state, contract and regulator notice duties, and one voice to the outside.

I convene the response team while IT contains the attack. Outside breach counsel hires the forensic firm to support privilege, though courts do not always protect those reports. We work out whose data was taken: state notice laws differ and customer contracts may set short deadlines. If we are public, I start the SEC materiality analysis. One channel handles all outside statements.
You find the standard severance agreement bars departing employees from contacting any government agency. What do you do?
Whether you can spot and fix a contract term that breaks whistleblower protection rules.
Knows the SEC rule against impeding whistleblowers and other legal limits, fixes the template, and deals with agreements already signed.

I pull the template right away. The SEC bars any action that impedes someone from reporting possible securities violations to it, and it has fined companies for clauses like this. Other agencies and labor law limit such terms too. I add a clear carve-out for reporting to any government agency, and I consider telling past signers in writing that the clause will not be enforced.
Half your advice is business advice. How does that affect privilege, and what do you do about it?
Whether you know how privilege works for an in-house lawyer who wears two hats.
Knows courts ask whether legal advice was the main purpose. Keeps legal advice separate and clearly framed as legal advice.

Courts look at whether a communication was mainly for legal advice. When I weigh in on pricing or strategy as a business person, that is likely not privileged. So I keep legal analysis in separate emails or memos, send them only to the people who need them, and say I am giving legal advice. A label alone does not create privilege, but mixing the two makes it easy to lose.
In a purchase agreement, what is the difference between a deductible basket and a tipping basket?
Your command of the indemnity terms that decide who pays for losses after closing.
Deductible: the buyer recovers only losses above the threshold. Tipping: once losses cross it, recovery goes back to the first dollar.

Both set a level of losses the buyer must reach before it can claim. With a deductible, the seller pays only the amount above that level, so the buyer absorbs the first slice. With a tipping basket, once losses cross the level, the seller pays from the first dollar. As buyer I push for tipping, as seller for a deductible, and I trade that against the cap and how long claims survive.
A key customer wants unlimited liability in our services contract. How do you negotiate the limitation of liability clause?
How you balance real legal risk against getting the deal closed.
A general cap tied to fees, narrow carve-outs for the risks that matter, maybe a higher separate cap for data, and insurance checked.

I start by asking what they actually fear. Usually it is data loss or IP claims. I keep a general cap tied to fees paid, often twelve months, then offer carve-outs for confidentiality breaches, IP indemnity and willful misconduct, plus a separate higher cap for data breaches. I check that our insurance covers what we agree to, so the promise is one we can pay.
What does the board's duty to oversee risk require, and how does it shape what you report to the directors?
Whether you understand directors' oversight duty and how a general counsel supports it.
A reporting system for the company's mission-critical risks that the board actually uses, and red flags acted on and recorded.

Under Delaware law, directors must make a good-faith effort to have a system that brings key risks to them, and they cannot ignore red flags. So I map our mission-critical risks, like product safety or customer data, and make sure each reaches the board or a committee on a set schedule. When a problem surfaces, the minutes show what the board asked and what it ordered done.
How do you decide whether a lawsuit needs a reserve, and how do you answer the auditors' legal letter?
Whether you know the accounting rule for lawsuits and how to protect privilege with auditors.
Accrue when a loss is probable and reasonably estimable, disclose when reasonably possible, and keep the audit letter narrow.

Under the accounting rule for loss contingencies, we record a reserve when a loss is probable and the amount can be reasonably estimated. If a loss is only reasonably possible, we disclose it, with a range if we can. I work that out with the CFO. In the audit letter I give facts and our assessment briefly, without handing over our legal analysis, so privilege is not waived.
At an investor dinner, the CEO tells one analyst that next quarter will beat guidance. What do you do?
Whether you know the selective disclosure rule and act fast enough.
Treats it as unintentional selective disclosure, makes the news public promptly, and fixes the process so it does not happen again.

That is likely material news given to one analyst, which Regulation FD forbids. Since it was unintentional, we must make it public promptly: within 24 hours or by the start of the next day's trading on the NYSE, whichever is later. I would issue a press release or file an 8-K, then tighten who speaks to investors and brief the CEO before each meeting.
A director asks to sell a large block of shares while merger talks are underway, but the trading window is open. What do you say?
Your grip on insider trading rules beyond the trading calendar.
No trading while aware of inside information, open window or not. No new trading plan now. Preclearance once the news is out.

No. An open window does not matter if the director knows about the talks, and talks this far along are likely material. A 10b5-1 plan will not help: it must be adopted while not aware of inside information, and it has a cooling-off period. Once the deal is public or dead, I clear the sale and make sure the Form 4 is filed within two business days.
We signed an acquisition but are waiting on antitrust clearance. Sales wants to start pricing jointly with the target. What do you say?
Whether you know what the parties may and may not do before the merger waiting period ends.
The companies stay independent until clearance: no joint pricing, no control. Planning is fine, with sensitive data kept to a clean team.

Not yet. Until the Hart-Scott-Rodino waiting period ends, we are still competitors, and acting as one company is gun-jumping, which can bring daily penalties. We can plan the integration. Sensitive data like customer prices goes only to a small clean team, often outside advisers, who report back in summary form. Joint pricing waits until closing.
Sales wants to hire a local agent to win a government contract abroad. The agent asks for a large success fee paid offshore. What do you do?
How you spot bribery risk in third parties and act on it.
Names the red flags, pauses until due diligence is done, and requires clear payment terms, audit rights and an anti-bribery clause.

A large success fee, a government buyer and an offshore account are classic red flags under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. We are liable if we ignore signs the agent is paying bribes. I would pause and check who owns the agent, any ties to officials, and what work they actually do. If cleared, we pay a local account in their name against invoices, with audit rights and an anti-bribery clause.
You find a contract your team approved last year with an uncapped indemnity nobody flagged. What do you do?
How you own a mistake and fix both the exposure and the process behind it.
Sizes the exposure, tells the CEO plainly, looks for fixes like insurance or renegotiation, and changes the review so it does not recur.

First I size it: what claims could trigger it and how likely they are. Then I tell the CEO without spin, and finance if it needs disclosure; it was my team's miss. I check whether our insurance responds and look for a chance to renegotiate, for example at renewal. Then I fix the cause: a required checklist for liability terms and a second reviewer on any uncapped promise.

general-manager.heading: General manager questions
qs: What is the difference between gross margin and contribution margin, and when does each matter?
Whether you know the P&L measures you will be judged on.
Gross margin takes out cost of goods sold; contribution margin takes out all variable costs. Contribution is the one for volume and pricing decisions.

Gross margin is revenue minus cost of goods sold, which can include fixed factory costs. Contribution margin is revenue minus only the costs that move with volume, like materials, freight and commissions. When I decide on a price or an extra order, I use contribution, because it shows what each extra sale really adds toward fixed costs and profit.
Your unit made a profit last year but ran short of cash. How can that happen?
Whether you understand that profit and cash are not the same thing.
Names the usual causes: growing receivables, inventory build, capital spending, debt payments. Then says how to fix them.

Profit counts sales when they are earned, not when customers pay. If we grew fast, receivables and inventory soak up cash before it comes back. Capital spending and loan repayments also use cash without hitting profit in full. I would look first at how many days customers take to pay and how many days of stock we hold, then tighten collection and cut slow stock.
Revenue is on plan for the quarter, but operating profit is three points below. Where do you look first?
How you find the cause of a margin gap in the P&L.
A structured walk from plan to actual: price and mix, then volume-driven costs, then fixed costs and one-offs, before acting.

I build a walk from plan to actual, one cause at a time. First price and mix: are we selling more low-margin products or giving bigger discounts? Then variable costs like materials, freight and overtime. Then fixed costs and one-offs. In my last unit the gap was mostly mix: a large low-margin order had replaced smaller profitable ones, so we changed how sales were paid.
A large customer asks for an 8% price cut to renew. How do you decide?
Your judgement on pricing and on what a customer is worth.
Looks at contribution after the cut, the cost of losing the volume, what the customer gives in return, and the effect on other customers' prices.

I check what the cut does to contribution on that account and what happens to our fixed cost coverage if we lose it. I ask what we get back: a longer contract, more volume, faster payment. I also think about precedent, because other customers hear about prices. Often I offer a smaller cut tied to volume levels rather than a flat 8%.
Sales keeps promising delivery dates that operations cannot meet. How do you fix it?
How you settle conflict between your own functional leaders.
Treats it as a process problem: one shared view of capacity, a clear rule for quoting dates and shared goals, not picking a side.

I get both heads in a room with the data: promised dates, actual dates and capacity. Usually sales simply cannot see capacity. We set up a weekly sales and operations meeting, give sales a simple way to check lead times before quoting, and put on-time delivery in both teams' goals. Then neither side wins by blaming the other.
Head office asks you to cut costs by 10% this year, starting now. How do you approach it?
Whether you can cut costs without damaging the business.
Separates waste from spending that drives revenue, protects customer-facing capacity, involves leaders and is honest with staff.

I sort spending into what keeps customers and revenue, what is required, and what is habit. Habit goes first: contractors, travel, unused software, overtime caused by poor planning. I give each leader a target and ask for options ranked by risk. If people must go, I decide once, do it quickly and explain it plainly, rather than cutting in small rounds that wear everyone down.
Your plant manager asks for $2 million for a new production line. How do you evaluate it?
How you judge a capital investment request.
Uses yearly cash flows, payback and net present value at the company's required return, and tests the assumptions behind volume and savings.

I ask for the cash flows year by year: the spend, the savings or extra margin, and running costs. I look at payback and at net present value, which discounts future cash to today at our required return. Then I challenge the inputs, because the math is rarely wrong but the volume forecast often is. I want a downside case and the cost of doing nothing.
At quarter end you learn a sales manager booked revenue on orders the customer had not yet received. What do you do?
Your integrity when the numbers and the rules conflict.
Corrects the books promptly with finance, accepts the miss, and looks at the incentives that caused it, not only the person.

I tell finance the same day and we reverse anything booked before the customer took control of the goods under the contract terms. I would rather miss the quarter and explain it than report wrong numbers. Then I talk to the manager to learn whether pressure from me or the bonus plan drove it, and fix that cause, because a target that invites this is my problem too.
A product line shows a loss once overhead is allocated, but it has a positive contribution margin. Do you drop it?
Whether you understand fixed cost allocation before cutting a product.
Not automatically: dropping it loses its contribution, and the overhead stays unless it truly goes away. Also weighs links to other sales and capacity use.

Not on those numbers alone. If it covers its variable costs, it is helping pay for fixed costs. Drop it and that overhead lands on the other lines, so total profit falls unless the costs actually leave, like a lease we can end or staff we no longer need. I would also check whether customers buy it with other products and whether the capacity could earn more elsewhere.
You take over a unit that has lost money for two years. What do you do in your first 90 days?
How you diagnose a failing unit and start a turnaround.
Secures cash first, finds where money is made and lost by customer and product, assesses the team, and commits to a few clear actions.

First, cash: a 13-week cash forecast so we do not run out while fixing things. Then I split profit by customer, product and site to see where we lose money. I meet key customers and front-line staff, not just managers. By day 60 I know which leaders I keep, and by day 90 I commit to a short plan with three or four actions and monthly numbers to track them.
How do you build an annual budget that is neither padded nor wishful?
How you set targets your team can own and head office can trust.
Bottom-up plans tested against a top-down view and past results, with key assumptions written down and owned.

I ask each manager for a plan built from drivers: volumes, prices, headcount, rates. Finance builds a top-down view from trends and the market. Where the two differ by more than a few points, we argue it out with the assumptions on the table. Every key assumption gets an owner, so in March we know which one broke instead of debating the whole number.
Walk me through how you split a revenue variance into price, volume and mix.
Whether you can explain why revenue moved, not only by how much.
Volume at plan prices and plan mix, mix as the shift between products, price as actual units times the price change. The three add up to the total.

Volume is the change in total units valued at the plan average price. Mix is the effect of selling a different blend of products, each at its plan price. Price is actual units times the difference between actual and plan price. The three add up to the total gap. If volume beat plan but mix is negative, cheaper products drove the growth, and margin will likely suffer.
What is operating leverage, and how does it change the way you plan for a downturn?
Your grasp of how fixed costs make profit swing faster than revenue.
High fixed costs mean a small drop in sales cuts profit by a larger share, so you decide in advance which costs can flex and when.

Operating leverage is how much profit moves when revenue moves. With high fixed costs, a 10% fall in sales can cut operating profit by far more than 10%. So before a downturn I sort costs into fixed, step and variable, and agree triggers: if orders stay below a set level for two months, we freeze hiring, cut overtime and delay planned spend. Decided calmly, ahead of time.
Your cash conversion cycle has grown by 15 days over the year. What drives it, and what do you do?
Whether you manage working capital, not only profit.
Knows the cycle is days of receivables plus days of inventory minus days of payables, and fixes each cause without simply squeezing suppliers.

The cycle is days sales outstanding plus days of inventory minus days payables outstanding. I check which part moved. Often it is receivables, from a few large customers paying late or disputed invoices, or inventory built up for a launch. I fix the cause: billing errors, credit terms, slow-moving stock. Paying suppliers later helps on paper, but it can raise prices and hurt supply.
Your best plant manager tells you a competitor has made her an offer. What do you do?
How you keep key people and weigh retention against fairness to the rest of the team.
Finds out what she really wants, acts within fair pay limits, and knows a counteroffer alone rarely fixes the reason someone started looking.

I thank her for telling me and ask what drew her to the offer: money, scope, location, or something about how we work. If her pay is below market, I raise it on its own merits, not just to match. If it is scope, I can offer a bigger role I had planned anyway. I also check my bench, because if money is the only reason she stays, the question may come back soon.
Finance, HR and IT at your site report to head office, not to you. How do you get things done through them?
How you lead people you do not directly manage.
Shared goals agreed with the functional heads, clear decision rights, and escalation used rarely and openly.

I treat the site finance and HR leads as part of my leadership team: same meetings, and shared targets where possible. I meet their bosses at head office early to agree what the site needs and who decides what. When we disagree, I first try to solve it with the person. If I must escalate, I tell them first and we take it up together.
You have to close a site that employs 150 people. How do you plan it?
Whether you can carry out a hard decision legally and humanely.
Brings in legal counsel early, gives the notice the federal WARN Act and any state law require, plans the customer handover, and treats leavers with respect.

I bring in employment counsel and HR first. The federal WARN Act generally requires 60 days' written notice of a plant closing at covered employers, and some states require more. I plan the customer and supplier handover, decide who we need until the end and offer them a stay bonus, and tell everyone in person, on the same day, before word leaks.
One customer is 35% of your unit's revenue. Is that a problem, and what do you do about it?
How you judge concentration risk without hurting the business that pays the bills.
Sees the risk to profit and bargaining power, protects the account, and grows other customers on purpose rather than walking away from volume.

It is a risk: if they leave or squeeze price, a third of our revenue is in play, and they know it. I would not push them away. I would build the relationship at several levels, not only through one salesperson, and model what losing them would do against our fixed costs. Then I set a target to grow other accounts so their share falls over two or three years.
Head office has bought a smaller competitor and asks you to fold it into your unit. What do you protect, and what do you change first?
Your judgement in integrating a business without destroying what made it worth buying.
Protects customers and key people first, ties the work to the savings and growth the deal promised, and decides fast on whatever creates uncertainty.

First I read the deal case to see what savings and growth we promised and what we paid for. Then I protect revenue: I call the top customers in week one and keep their contacts the same. I name the leadership quickly, since uncertainty is when good people leave. Systems I merge later and carefully; forcing our ordering system on them in month one is a common way to lose orders.

gis.heading: GIS and mapping specialist questions
qs: When would you store data as vector and when as raster?
Whether you know the two basic GIS data models and can pick the right one.
Vector for discrete features with clear edges, raster for continuous surfaces, with a real example of each.

Vector is points, lines and polygons, so I use it for things with clear edges: roads, parcels, fire hydrants. Raster is a grid of cells, each holding a value, so it suits things that change smoothly, like elevation, temperature or satellite imagery. If I need slope or a cost surface, I want a raster. For a street network, I want vector.
What is the difference between a geographic and a projected coordinate system?
Your grasp of coordinates, the base of every measurement you make.
Geographic uses angles on a model of the earth, projected uses flat x and y in linear units; distance and area need a suitable projection or geodesic math.

A geographic system, like WGS 84, gives positions as latitude and longitude in degrees on a model of the earth. A projected system flattens that onto a plane, with x and y in meters or feet. A degree of longitude shrinks as you move toward the poles, so I never buffer or measure in degrees. I project first, or I use geodesic tools.
A planner wants the total acres of wetland in each county of a state. Which projection do you use?
Whether you know that every projection distorts something and choose one for the task.
An equal-area projection fitted to the region, such as Albers, or geodesic area; never Web Mercator for area.

I use an equal-area projection fitted to the region, such as an Albers equal-area conic, or I calculate geodesic area. I would not compute area in Web Mercator: it keeps local shapes but inflates area away from the equator, which is why Greenland looks as big as Africa on web maps. Then I convert to acres and spot-check one county.
Two layers of the same streets do not line up when you overlay them. What do you check?
How you troubleshoot coordinate system and datum problems.
Uses the size of the offset as a clue, checks each layer's defined coordinate system and datum transformation, and fixes the source, not the symptom.

First I look at the size of the shift. Hundreds of meters, or data landing in the wrong place entirely, usually means a layer has the wrong coordinate system defined or none at all. A shift of about a meter points to a datum issue, like NAD83 against WGS 84 with no transformation applied. I fix the definition at the source rather than nudging the data by hand.
A manager wants a county map of crime counts, shaded dark to light. What would you change?
Whether you avoid the classic choropleth mistakes that make a map mislead.
Maps a rate instead of a raw count, chooses class breaks on purpose, and warns about small-area rates and the effect of the chosen units.

Raw counts mostly show where people live, so I would map a rate, like incidents per 10,000 residents. I pick class breaks on purpose and name the method, since quantiles and natural breaks can tell different stories. I would also flag that small counties give unstable rates, and that the pattern can change with the areas you choose.
You geocode 50,000 customer addresses and only 78% match. What do you do?
How you handle messy address data without hiding bad results.
Studies why records failed, cleans and standardizes, reviews low scores and ties, and reports the match rate instead of forcing matches.

I sample the failures to find the pattern: PO boxes, missing ZIP codes, typos, new subdivisions not yet in the reference data. I standardize abbreviations, fix the common errors and rerun. I would not just lower the match score, because that turns misses into wrong points. What still fails I report with the rate, so nobody thinks the map covers every customer.
You merge parcel layers from two counties and find slivers and overlaps along the border. How do you fix them?
Your approach to topology errors and data cleaning.
Runs topology checks to find every error, snaps within a tolerance tied to source accuracy, reviews larger cases by hand and logs changes.

I run topology checks for gaps and overlaps so I see every error, not just the ones I spot. Then I snap edges within a small tolerance, set from the accuracy of the source data, so I do not move real boundaries. Anything bigger I review by hand with the county, since a GIS parcel map is not a legal survey. I keep a log of each change.
A query that finds every store within 2 km of 5 million delivery points runs for hours. How do you speed it up?
Whether you know how spatial indexes and spatial queries work at scale.
Spatial index on both tables, an index-aware distance test instead of computing every distance, and correct units.

First I make sure both tables have a spatial index, like an R-tree, and fresh statistics. Then I write the test as a within-distance check, not distance less than 2,000, because many spatial databases can use the index for the first and must compute every pair for the second. I also check units: in degrees, 2,000 means nothing, so I use a projected system in meters.
Your routing engine sends trucks from an overpass straight onto the highway below, where there is no ramp. What went wrong?
Whether you understand network connectivity, not just line geometry.
Knows that lines crossing on a map are not a junction, and fixes it with grade separation data and connectivity rules, then tests.

Most likely the network was built so every crossing became an intersection, giving the overpass and the highway a shared node. Two lines crossing on a map does not mean you can turn. I would record grade separation with elevation or z-level fields, connect lines only at real junctions, and check one-way and turn restrictions. Then I rerun test routes through known interchanges.
You have GPS traces from delivery vans and need to know which road each van was on. Downtown the points jump around. How do you approach it?
How you deal with noisy location data and real map matching.
Knows why GPS degrades downtown and uses map matching that weighs road connectivity and travel time, not just the nearest road.

Downtown, signals bounce off tall buildings, so points can land a block away. Snapping each point to the nearest road fails at parallel streets and overpasses. I use map matching that scores candidate roads by distance and by whether the drive between them is plausible in the time elapsed, often with a hidden Markov model. Stretches with low confidence I flag, not guess.
Why should you be careful about mapping data by ZIP code?
Whether you know the limits of a common but flawed geography.
ZIP codes are mail routes, not fixed areas. ZCTAs are Census approximations, and results can change with the units you choose.

ZIP codes are USPS delivery routes, not fixed polygons, and they change over time. The Census Bureau builds ZIP Code Tabulation Areas to approximate them, so I use ZCTAs and say so. I also warn that rates can shift just by changing the units. That is the modifiable areal unit problem, so I prefer census tracts when the data allows it.
What is the difference between the US survey foot and the international foot, and when does it matter?
Your grasp of a unit detail that can move coordinates by feet.
They differ by about 2 parts per million, the survey foot is deprecated, and the gap matters on large State Plane coordinates.

The international foot is exactly 0.3048 m. The US survey foot is 1200/3937 m, about 2 parts per million longer. Over a short distance that is nothing. But State Plane coordinates run into the millions of feet, so the wrong foot shifts data by a few feet. The survey foot was deprecated starting in 2023, but older data still uses it, so I read the CRS definition.
A field crew's GPS elevations come out about 30 m lower than the county's elevation model. What is going on?
Whether you can tell ellipsoid height from orthometric height.
GPS gives height above the ellipsoid. Convert it with a geoid model to NAVD 88 before comparing.

GPS gives height above the ellipsoid, a smooth mathematical surface. The county model uses orthometric height in NAVD 88, which is roughly height above sea level. In the lower 48 the geoid sits below the ellipsoid, so ellipsoid heights read lower, often by around 30 m. I convert with the current NGS geoid model, GEOID18, and then compare again.
Your software treats WGS 84 and NAD 83 as the same. When is that a problem?
How well you know datums once accuracy needs drop below a few meters.
They now differ by roughly one to two meters in the US, and the gap grows. Precise work needs an explicit transformation.

For a city web map, a meter does not matter. But NAD 83 is tied to the North American plate and modern WGS 84 is not. They now differ by about one to two meters in the lower 48, and the gap grows each year. For survey-grade or lane-level work I pick an explicit transformation, record the realization and epoch, and never accept a default null shift.
A hospital asks which neighborhoods are within a 15-minute drive. Walk me through how you build that.
Whether you use network analysis instead of straight-line distance.
Travel time on a road network with one-ways and turn rules, stated speed assumptions, and no circle buffers.

A circle buffer would cross rivers that have no bridge, so I build a service area on the road network. I use travel time as the cost, with one-way streets, turn restrictions and realistic speeds, ideally by time of day. Then I overlay the drive-time area on census blocks to count people. I state the speed assumptions so the hospital knows what the edge means.
You have 40 air quality sensors across a city and need a continuous surface. IDW or kriging?
Your judgement on interpolation methods and how they handle uncertainty.
IDW is simple but gives no error estimate. Kriging models spatial correlation and returns prediction error, if the data supports it.

IDW is quick and easy to explain, but its weights ignore how the data actually varies in space, and it gives no error estimate. Kriging fits a semivariogram to the data and returns a prediction plus its standard error. With 40 sensors I would try kriging, check the variogram and cross-validation, and show the error map next to the surface so nobody trusts the gaps.
Your regression of house prices on neighborhood traits looks good, but the residuals cluster on the map. What does that tell you?
Whether you can detect and handle spatial autocorrelation.
Tests residuals with Moran's I, knows OLS errors are no longer independent, and moves to a spatial lag, spatial error or GWR model.

It means the errors are not independent. The standard errors are likely too small, and something spatial is missing. I test the residuals with Moran's I; a significant positive value confirms clustering. Then I look for a missing variable, like school zones, and try a spatial lag or spatial error model, or geographically weighted regression if effects differ by area.
How would you test and report the horizontal accuracy of a new street centerline layer?
Your method for measuring positional accuracy against a named standard.
Independent checkpoints from a more accurate source, RMSE, and a statement under a standard such as NSSDA at 95% confidence.

I pick well-defined points, like intersection centers, spread across the area. I get their positions from a source that is much more accurate, such as survey-grade GPS. NSSDA asks for at least 20 checkpoints. I compute the RMSE of the offsets and report accuracy at 95% confidence, which is 1.7308 times the radial RMSE when x and y errors are similar.
A partner wants our customer locations at the point level to plan their stores. How do you handle it?
How you weigh the value of location data against privacy.
Treats precise points as personal data, asks what decision they need to make, and shares aggregates or masked data under an agreement.

A home location can identify a person even without a name, so I would not send raw points. I would ask what decision they are making. Usually counts by hexagon or census tract, with small counts suppressed, answer the question. If they truly need finer data, it goes through legal review and a data sharing agreement first.
A map release you signed off last week has several one-way streets pointing the wrong way. What do you do?
How you own and contain a data error that has already reached users.
Ships a fast fix, finds the root cause, searches for similar errors, and adds a check so the error cannot pass again.

First I tell my lead and the routing team, and push a hotfix for the known streets. Then I trace the cause, for example a source that digitized lines in the wrong direction, and query the whole release for other edges from that source. Finally I add an automated check, like comparing against GPS traces that show real travel direction, so the next release catches it.

gnc-engineer.heading: Guidance, navigation and control engineer questions
qs: How would you explain the difference between guidance, navigation and control?
Whether you can separate the three jobs in the loop clearly.
Navigation estimates where you are, guidance decides where to go, and control makes the actuators follow that command.

Navigation answers where am I: it fuses sensors into an estimate of position, velocity and attitude. Guidance answers where should I go: it turns the mission and that estimate into a commanded path or acceleration. Control answers how do I get there: it drives the fins, thrusters or motors so the vehicle follows the command.
Why pair an IMU with GPS instead of using either one alone?
Your grasp of sensor strengths and why fusion is needed.
The IMU is fast and self-contained but drifts. GPS has bounded error but is slower and can drop out or be jammed.

An IMU gives high-rate acceleration and rotation with no outside signal, but integrating it lets small biases grow into large position errors over time. GPS has bounded error but updates more slowly and can be blocked or jammed. Together, GPS keeps the IMU drift in check and the IMU carries the solution smoothly through the gaps.
Walk me through how a Kalman filter works, in plain words.
Whether you understand the filter you will tune, not just its equations.
Predict with a model, correct with a measurement, and weight each one by its uncertainty through the process and measurement noise.

It runs two steps. Predict: push the state and its uncertainty forward with a motion model, adding process noise for what the model misses. Update: compare a new measurement with what the filter expected and move the estimate toward it by a gain. If the sensor is precise compared with the state uncertainty, the gain is large and the filter trusts the sensor more.
Why do attitude systems often use quaternions instead of Euler angles?
Your knowledge of attitude representation and its pitfalls.
Euler angles hit gimbal lock. Quaternions avoid that singularity but must be kept unit length, and q and minus q mean the same attitude.

With a yaw-pitch-roll sequence, at plus or minus 90 degrees of pitch two axes line up and you lose a degree of freedom. That is gimbal lock. A quaternion uses four numbers, has no such singularity and is cheap to propagate. The care points: renormalize it so it stays unit length, and remember q and minus q describe the same attitude.
Your rate loop has an integrator and the actuator saturates during a big maneuver. What goes wrong and how do you fix it?
How you handle actuator limits, a common cause of flight problems.
Names integrator windup and the overshoot it causes, and gives an anti-windup method such as clamping or back-calculation.

While the actuator is pinned, the error stays large and the integrator keeps growing. When the vehicle catches up, that stored value drives a big overshoot. I add anti-windup: stop integrating while saturated, or feed back the gap between commanded and actual output to bleed the integrator down. Then I test it in the sim with the real rate and position limits.
Your navigation filter's innovations are consistently larger than the filter predicts. What do you check?
How you debug an estimator using its own health signals.
Data issues first (timing, frames, units, lever arms), then the model and noise tuning, using normalized innovation tests.

First the plumbing: timestamps and latency, sensor frames, units, sign conventions and the lever arm from IMU to antenna. Those cause most of it. Then I normalize the innovations and see if they are biased or just too big. A bias points to a missing state, like a sensor bias. Centered but too big usually means the noise settings are too low.
The vehicle oscillates in its first flight test, though the simulation was stable. How do you approach it?
Whether you know what simulations often leave out.
Pause testing, then use the data: the oscillation frequency points to delay, actuator limits, filter lag or a structural mode.

I pause testing and pull the logs. The oscillation frequency is the first clue. Near a bending mode, the sensor is seeing the structure flex, and a notch filter or a new sensor spot helps. Lower, I look for unmodeled delay, actuator rate limits or filter lag eating phase margin. I add what was missing to the sim and match the flight data before we fly again.
Your Monte Carlo run of 1,000 cases shows 3 failures and the review is Friday. What do you do?
Your judgement on rare failures under schedule pressure.
Treats each failure as real until explained, finds the cause, and reports it honestly instead of calling it 99.7% success.

I don't report 99.7% and move on. I rerun the three seeds, look at which dispersed parameters they share and find the mechanism. If it is a sim bug, I fix it and rerun the full set. If it is a real weakness, like a strong gust with low control authority, I tell the lead what it is, how likely it is and what a fix costs, so the schedule call is made with facts.
Walk me through how you would show that the flight code does what your design model does.
Whether you know the verification steps between a design and flying software.
A stepped chain from model to software, processor and hardware in the loop, with output comparisons and traceable requirements.

I start with model-in-the-loop tests tied to each requirement. Then I run the flight code against the same plant model and inputs, first on a desktop, then on the target processor, comparing outputs to the model within set tolerances. Hardware-in-the-loop adds real sensors, actuators and timing. Any mismatch gets explained, not just covered by a looser tolerance.
What does a pure time delay do to a control loop, and where does it come from in flight software?
Whether you account for the delays that real hardware adds to a loop.
Delay adds phase lag that grows with frequency but leaves gain unchanged, so it erodes phase margin. Sources include sampling, computation, filtering and actuator lag.

A delay of T seconds adds a phase lag of omega times T at frequency omega, with no change in gain, so it eats phase margin near crossover. In flight code it comes from sensor filtering, bus transport, compute time and the zero-order hold, which acts like about half a sample of delay. I budget all of these and put the total in the linear model before I trust a margin.
Explain proportional navigation and where it starts to struggle.
Your knowledge of a classic guidance law and its limits.
The command is proportional to closing speed times line-of-sight rate, with a gain usually of 3 to 5. It is weak against maneuvering targets, seeker noise and acceleration limits.

PN commands lateral acceleration equal to a navigation constant, usually 3 to 5, times closing speed times line-of-sight rate. If the line of sight stops rotating, you are on a collision course. It struggles when the target maneuvers and when seeker noise corrupts the rate. Near the end the commands grow and hit the acceleration limit, and that shows up as miss distance.
Why do most aided inertial systems use an error-state filter rather than estimating the full state directly?
Your grasp of how navigation filters are actually built.
Inertial equations carry the full state while the filter estimates small, nearly linear errors. Attitude error stays a 3-vector, not a constrained quaternion.

The strapdown equations run at high rate and carry the full position, velocity and attitude. The filter only estimates the errors in them, which are small, so linearization holds well. Attitude error is a small three-angle vector, so the covariance avoids the unit-norm constraint of a quaternion. If the filter is slow or faults, the inertial solution keeps running.
In a GPS-aided INS, which states are poorly observable, and what makes them observable?
Whether you know what the measurements can and cannot tell the filter.
Heading is weak without horizontal acceleration, and tilt mixes with horizontal accelerometer bias. Maneuvers or extra sensors separate them, and the covariance shows it.
