In straight, steady flight a heading error barely shows in GPS position or velocity. It only appears when the vehicle accelerates sideways or forward. Level tilt error and horizontal accelerometer bias also look alike when stationary. Turns and speed changes separate them; otherwise I add a magnetometer or dual-antenna heading. I watch those covariance terms to see whether they really shrink.
Tell me about a frame or sign-convention error you caught, or one that got past you.
How you guard against the convention errors behind many GNC bugs.
A specific error, how it was found, and a lasting fix such as clear interface definitions and tests with known rotations.

A vendor star tracker gave quaternions scalar-last and our code assumed scalar-first. In closed-loop simulation it looked like a slow drift, not an obvious bug. I caught it by commanding a known 90-degree rotation on the bench and checking each component. Since then every interface document states order, handedness and frame direction, and every new sensor gets a known-rotation test.
Your filter runs fine in double precision on the desktop, but the covariance loses positive definiteness on the flight computer. What do you do?
How you handle numerical problems in a filter that runs on real hardware.
Recognizes roundoff in the covariance update. Uses the Joseph form, forced symmetry, or a square-root or UD filter, and checks state scaling and precision.

That is roundoff. The standard update subtracts nearly equal numbers and loses symmetry and positive definiteness, and single precision makes it worse. I would switch to the Joseph form of the update and force symmetry. If that is not enough, I would use a square-root or UD-factored filter. I also check state scaling, since mixing meters and micro-g biases makes the matrix badly conditioned.
Your Monte Carlo shows zero failures in 1,000 runs. What can you honestly claim about the probability of success?
Whether you can state what a Monte Carlo result proves and what it does not.
Uses a binomial confidence bound, such as the rule of three, and notes the claim only covers the error sources and ranges that were modeled.

Zero failures does not mean zero risk. With zero failures in n runs, the rule of three gives about 3/n as the 95% upper bound on the failure rate. Here that is about 0.3%, or 99.7% success at 95% confidence. If the requirement is tighter, I need more runs. And it only covers what we dispersed: a missing error source or a range set too narrow is not in that number.
How do flexible bending modes change your autopilot design for a long launch vehicle?
Whether you can design control around structural dynamics, not just a rigid body.
Covers gyro location relative to the mode shape, gain versus phase stabilization, and the phase lag that filters cost the rigid-body loop.

The rate gyro senses bending as well as rigid motion, so where it sits on the mode shape matters. For each mode I either gain-stabilize it, keeping loop gain low there with filters, or phase-stabilize it so the control actually damps it. Notch filters cost phase at the rigid-body crossover, so I trade that. I test with the mode frequencies varied, since they shift as propellant burns.
A week before review, one corner case falls below your phase margin requirement and the program asks you to sign off anyway. What do you do?
Your judgement when schedule pressure meets a stability requirement.
No quiet sign-off. Confirm the case is real, weigh other evidence, offer a fix, and if the shortfall is accepted, record it as a formal waiver by the risk owner.

First I confirm the case is real: right dispersions, right delays. Then I gather other evidence, like disk margin, time response and how often Monte Carlo runs reach that corner. I bring a fix, such as a gain schedule change, and its cost. If the program still accepts the shortfall, it goes in as a written waiver signed by the owner of that risk, not as my quiet sign-off.

go-developer.heading: Go developer questions
qs: How is a goroutine different from an operating system thread?
Whether you understand the basic unit of concurrency in Go.
The Go runtime schedules goroutines onto a smaller set of OS threads. Goroutines start with a small, growable stack, so a program can run very many of them.

The Go runtime schedules a goroutine, not the operating system. It starts with a stack of a few kilobytes that grows as needed, so I can run thousands of them. The runtime spreads goroutines over a smaller set of OS threads. GOMAXPROCS sets how many threads run Go code at the same time, and by default it is based on the available CPUs.
When do you use an unbuffered channel, and when a buffered one?
Whether you know what channels guarantee and how a buffer changes that.
Unbuffered means a handoff that also synchronizes the two sides. A buffer has a clear purpose and a known size, and it is never used to hide a deadlock.

With an unbuffered channel, the sender waits until a receiver takes the value, so the handoff also syncs the two goroutines. With a buffered channel, the sender keeps going until the buffer is full. I start with unbuffered. I add a buffer when I know why I need it, for example a channel of capacity 10 used as a semaphore to cap concurrent calls.
How do you handle and wrap errors in Go?
Your everyday Go error handling style.
Errors are wrapped with %w to add context, and callers check them with errors.Is and errors.As. Each error is handled once, not logged at every layer.

I return errors as values and add context on the way up, with fmt.Errorf("load user %d: %w", id, err). The %w keeps the original error, so a caller can check errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) or use errors.As to get a specific type. I handle each error once: I either log it or return it, never both, so it does not show up five times in the logs.
You append to one slice and another slice changes too. Explain why.
Whether you know how slices share their underlying arrays.
A slice is a pointer, a length and a capacity. Append writes in place when there is room, and the fix is copy, slices.Clone or a full slice expression.

A slice is a pointer to an array plus a length and a capacity. If a has capacity 5 and I take b := a[:2], then append(b, x) has room, so it writes into the same array and overwrites a[2]. When I need an independent slice, I use slices.Clone or copy into a new one. I can also use a[:2:2], which caps the capacity so the next append has to allocate.
How do you use context.Context in a service?
Whether you use context for cancellation and deadlines the way Go code expects.
ctx is the first parameter and is passed down to all I/O, cancel is always deferred, and context values hold only request-scoped data.

Every function that does I/O takes ctx as its first parameter and passes it down. Then, when a client disconnects or a deadline passes, the database and HTTP calls stop too. After context.WithTimeout I defer cancel right away. I do not store a context in a struct. I use context values only for request data like a trace ID, never for optional parameters.
When do you choose a mutex over a channel?
Your judgement in picking the simplest safe concurrency tool.
Channels for passing work or ownership, a mutex for guarding shared state, atomics for simple counters. Clarity about who owns the data is the deciding factor.

When goroutines hand work or ownership to each other, like a pipeline of jobs, I use channels. When they only share some state, like an in-memory cache, a sync.Mutex is simpler and easier to read. For a plain counter, sync/atomic is enough. I pick whatever makes it obvious who owns the data, not whatever looks more like Go.
Two goroutines write to the same map. What happens, and how do you catch this kind of bug?
Whether you know what a data race does in Go and how to detect it.
Concurrent map writes can crash the program with a fatal error that recover cannot catch. The race detector finds races only on code paths the run actually executes.

The runtime can stop the whole program with a fatal error, "concurrent map writes", and recover cannot catch it. I protect the map with a mutex, or use sync.Map for its intended cases, like keys written once and read often. I run tests with -race. It only reports races that happen during the run, so I write tests that really exercise the concurrent paths.
Your function returns a nil *MyError as an error, and the caller's err != nil check is true. Why?
Whether you understand how interface values work and can spot the typed nil trap.
An interface holds a type and a value, so a nil pointer of a concrete type is still a non-nil interface. The fix is to return a literal nil and declare error as the return type.

An interface value holds two things: a type and a value. When I return a nil *MyError as an error, the interface has the type *MyError and a nil pointer, so it is not equal to nil. The fix is to return a plain nil when there is no error, and to declare the return type as error, not *MyError, so a typed nil never slips through.
Memory in your service grows slowly and the goroutine count keeps climbing. How do you find and fix the leak?
How you diagnose and fix a goroutine leak in a running service.
Uses the pprof goroutine profile to see where goroutines are blocked, then gives each goroutine a way to exit, through context, a timeout or a buffered result channel.

I open the goroutine profile from net/http/pprof and look at where most goroutines are parked. Usually it is a send on a channel nobody reads anymore, or a call with no timeout. The fix is to give every goroutine a way out: select on ctx.Done(), or use a buffer of 1 for a result that may be abandoned. Then I add a goroutine count metric with an alert.
Where do you define an interface in Go, and how big should it be?
Whether you design with Go's implicit interfaces rather than against them.
Interfaces belong to the consumer and stay small. They are added when a second implementation or a test needs them, and functions return concrete types.

I define the interface in the package that uses it, with only the methods that code calls, often one or two. Go types satisfy interfaces implicitly, so the producer just returns a concrete struct. That keeps test fakes tiny and lets callers see every method of the real type. I don't create an interface up front for a type with only one implementation.
A service calls a partner API with http.Get and slowly runs out of connections and file descriptors. What would you check?
Whether you know the traps in the net/http client defaults.
Bodies closed and drained, a shared client with a timeout instead of the default one, and connection pool limits sized for the traffic.

First, that every response body is closed, even on error status codes, and read to the end so the connection returns to the pool. Second, http.Get uses the default client, which has no timeout, so a hung partner holds connections forever. I'd build one shared client with a timeout and raise MaxIdleConnsPerHost, which defaults to 2.
When do you reach for generics in Go, and when do you stay with interfaces?
Your judgement about type parameters in real code.
Generics for code that works the same over many types, like containers and slice helpers. Interfaces when behavior differs by type.

I use generics when the code is identical for every type and only the type changes: a set, a cache keyed by any comparable type, a filter over slices. When each type does something different, an interface with methods is clearer. I also avoid generics that make a call site harder to read just to save a few lines of duplication.
Walk me through a graceful shutdown of a Go HTTP service running in Kubernetes.
Whether you can deploy without dropping requests.
Catch SIGTERM, stop taking new traffic, let in-flight requests finish within a deadline, then close dependencies in order.

Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, so I catch it with signal.NotifyContext. I fail the readiness check first and wait a few seconds so the pod leaves the load balancer. Then I call server.Shutdown with a timeout shorter than the pod's grace period: it stops accepting connections and waits for active requests. After that I stop workers, flush queues and close the database pool.
You must fetch 500 items from another service in parallel, at most 20 at a time, and stop at the first error. How do you write it?
How you bound concurrency and handle errors across goroutines.
A bounded pattern such as errgroup with a limit, where the first error cancels the shared context and results are stored without races.

I'd use errgroup.WithContext and SetLimit(20). Each item runs in g.Go, and the call uses the group's context, so when one fails the context is canceled and the rest give up early. Results go into a pre-sized slice by index, so no mutex is needed. g.Wait returns the first error. 500 unbounded goroutines would hammer the other service.
A panic in a goroutine started by an HTTP handler crashed the whole service, but a panic inside a handler did not. Why?
Whether you understand how panic and recover work across goroutines.
recover only works in a deferred call in the same goroutine. net/http recovers handler panics, but not panics in goroutines the handler starts.

The net/http server recovers panics in the goroutine running the handler, logs them and closes that connection. A goroutine I start myself has no such protection, and an unrecovered panic in any goroutine ends the program. Recover only works in a deferred function in the same goroutine. So background goroutines need their own defer with recover and logging, or code that returns errors instead.
You optimized a function and the benchmark says it is 30% faster. How do you know that is real?
Whether you measure performance with the rigour it needs.
Repeated runs compared statistically, work the compiler cannot remove, allocation counts, realistic input, and proof the function matters in production.

I run both versions with -count=10 and compare them with benchstat, which shows whether the change is beyond the noise. I make sure the result is used so the compiler cannot drop the work, and add -benchmem to see allocations. Inputs should look like production data. Then a CPU profile of the real service tells me whether this function mattered at all.
A hot path allocates too much and the garbage collector eats a large share of CPU. How do you cut allocations?
Your skill with Go's memory profiling and escape analysis.
Find allocation sites with a heap profile, see why values escape, then fix them: preallocation, fewer conversions, reuse only where measured.

I take a heap profile with pprof and look at alloc_space to find the hot sites. Then go build -gcflags=-m shows which values escape to the heap and why, for example a pointer returned or a value stored in an interface. Typical fixes: pre-size slices and maps, avoid string and []byte conversions in loops, and reuse buffers with sync.Pool only where a benchmark proves it helps.
Your service runs in a container with a 1 GiB memory limit and gets killed for using too much memory. How do GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT help?
Whether you understand how the Go garbage collector decides when to run.
GOGC sets heap growth between collections relative to the live heap. GOMEMLIMIT is a soft limit that makes the GC work harder near it. Neither fixes a real leak.

With the default GOGC=100, the heap can grow to about twice the live heap before the next collection, so 600 MiB of live data can push toward 1.2 GiB and the container is killed. GOMEMLIMIT, set a bit below the container limit, makes the collector run more often as memory nears it. It is a soft limit: if live data really exceeds it, I must find what holds the memory.
p99 latency is bad, CPU usage looks low, and the container shows heavy CPU throttling. What do you suspect?
Whether you can connect the Go scheduler to container CPU limits.
GOMAXPROCS higher than the CPU quota, so the runtime spends the quota early in each period and gets throttled. Match it to the limit.

I'd check GOMAXPROCS. Go versions before 1.25 set it to the node's CPU count, not the container's limit. On a 32-core node with a 2-CPU limit, up to 32 threads run Go code, use up the quota early in each period, then everything waits, which shows up as tail latency. I'd set GOMAXPROCS to match the limit, or upgrade so the runtime reads the limit itself.

gpu-performance-engineer.heading: GPU and performance engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between a memory-bound and a compute-bound kernel?
Whether you know the first question to ask about any slow kernel.
Uses arithmetic intensity, the work done per byte moved, and compares it with the chip's ratio of peak math speed to memory bandwidth.

A memory-bound kernel spends its time waiting on data. A compute-bound one is limited by the math units. I work out arithmetic intensity, the floating-point operations per byte read or written, and compare it with the chip's peak FLOPs divided by its memory bandwidth. Below that ratio, faster math will not help. I need to move fewer bytes.
What does memory coalescing mean, and how do you get it?
Your grasp of how GPU memory access patterns drive speed.
Neighbouring threads reading neighbouring addresses, and a concrete layout change that makes it happen.

When threads next to each other read addresses next to each other, the hardware combines those reads into a few wide memory transactions. If each thread jumps by a large stride, the same data takes many transactions. I lay out data so the fastest-changing thread index walks the contiguous dimension, for example a structure of arrays instead of an array of structures.
Your kernel has an if-else that depends on each thread's data. Why might that slow it down?
Whether you understand how threads are grouped and executed on a GPU.
Explains that diverging threads in one group run both paths in turn, and offers a fix that is checked against real data.

Threads run in groups called warps, usually 32, that share one instruction stream. If threads in a warp take different branches, the warp runs both paths one after the other with some threads idle. I first check how often threads really disagree. If it is often, I sort or bucket the data so similar items land in the same warp, or rewrite the branch as arithmetic.
A colleague times a GPU function with a CPU timer and reports 0.05 ms. Why might that number be wrong?
Whether you can measure GPU work correctly before trying to speed it up.
Names asynchronous launches, the need to synchronize or use GPU events, warm-up runs, and repeated measurements.

GPU work is launched asynchronously, so the CPU timer may only measure the launch, not the kernel itself. I synchronize the device before stopping the timer, or use GPU events. I also run a few warm-up iterations first, because the first call can include setup and compilation, and I report the median of many runs, not a single one.
Walk me through how you find out why a training step is slower than expected.
How you narrow down a performance problem from the whole system to one kernel.
Starts with a timeline of the whole step to find idle gaps, then profiles only the kernels that take the most total time.

I start with a timeline profile of a few steps after warm-up, not a single kernel. It shows gaps where the GPU sits idle, often waiting on data loading, CPU-side launch overhead or host-to-device copies. If the GPU is busy, I sort kernels by total time and take the top few into a kernel profiler to see if each is limited by memory bandwidth, compute or latency.
Why does fusing several small operations into one kernel often make things faster?
Whether you know where time goes in chains of simple operations.
Fewer trips to GPU memory and fewer launches, with intermediate values kept on chip.

Each separate kernel reads its input from GPU memory and writes its output back, and each launch has overhead. A chain like add bias, then activation, then dropout is mostly memory-bound. Fusing them keeps the intermediate values in registers, so the data crosses memory once instead of three times and there is one launch instead of three.
Is higher occupancy always better? When would you accept lower occupancy?
Your judgement about a common tuning metric that can mislead.
Occupancy helps hide latency but is not the goal; heavy register or shared memory use can win through data reuse. Runtime decides.

Occupancy is how many warps are active on a multiprocessor compared with the maximum. More warps help hide memory latency, but it is a means, not the goal. A matrix-multiply kernel may use many registers and a lot of shared memory per thread block, so fewer blocks fit, yet each thread reuses data more and the kernel runs faster. I judge by measured runtime, not the occupancy number.
When would you train in BF16 instead of FP16, and what changes?
Your understanding of reduced-precision number formats and their risks.
BF16 keeps FP32's exponent range with less precision; FP16 usually needs loss scaling. Master weights and accumulation stay in FP32.

BF16 has the same 8 exponent bits as FP32, so it covers about the same range of values with less precision. FP16 has only 5 exponent bits, so small gradients can underflow to zero and you usually need loss scaling. With BF16 I can often drop loss scaling. In both cases I keep a full-precision copy of the weights and accumulate sums in FP32.
After your optimization, the model's outputs differ from the old version in the fifth decimal place. Is that a bug?
How you tell normal floating-point noise from a real correctness error.
Knows reordering sums changes results, and checks against a higher-precision reference with a sensible tolerance instead of guessing.

Not necessarily. Floating-point addition is not associative, so a new reduction order or atomic adds can change the last bits. I compare against a higher-precision reference, like an FP64 run, using a tolerance that fits the data type, and check that the error does not grow with input size. If it is far outside that tolerance or shows a pattern, I treat it as a bug.
Generating text one token at a time with a large language model leaves the GPU's math units mostly idle. Why, and what would you do?
Whether you can apply performance reasoning to serving AI models.
Each token reads all weights for little math, so it is bandwidth-bound; batching helps until the key-value cache limits memory.

At batch size 1, each new token needs every weight read from memory but does only about two operations per weight, so the step is bound by memory bandwidth. Batching many requests reuses each weight read across them. The limit then becomes the key-value cache, which grows with batch size and sequence length, so I watch cache memory and consider quantized weights to move fewer bytes.
How do you use the roofline model to decide what to optimize in a kernel?
Whether you can place a kernel against the hardware limits before you start tuning it.
Arithmetic intensity measured honestly, compared with the ridge point, and the gap to the right roof used to pick the work.

I compute arithmetic intensity: FLOPs divided by bytes moved from DRAM. Attainable speed is the lower of peak compute and intensity times peak bandwidth. If the kernel sits left of the ridge point, I cut memory traffic. If it sits right, I work on math throughput. If it is far below both roofs, the problem is latency or launch overhead, not either limit.
Your matrix transpose kernel uses a 32 by 32 tile of floats in shared memory and is still slow. What do you suspect?
Your understanding of shared memory banks and how to avoid conflicts.
Names the column read as a 32-way bank conflict and fixes it with padding or a swizzled layout, then confirms it in the profiler.

Shared memory has 32 banks, and consecutive 4-byte words go to consecutive banks. Reading a column of a 32-wide float tile puts all 32 threads of a warp in the same bank, so the reads serialize. I would declare the tile 32 by 33. The extra column shifts each row by one bank. Then I check the bank conflict counters in Nsight Compute to confirm they dropped.
The compiler report shows your kernel spilling registers. Why does that matter, and what do you do?
Whether you know where spilled values go and how to reduce register pressure without making it worse.
Knows local memory lives in device memory, finds the cause, and knows that capping registers can increase spills rather than cure them.

Spilled values go to local memory, which is physically in device memory and only cached in L1 and L2, so a hot loop can turn memory-bound. I check -Xptxas -v for spill loads and stores. Then I look for arrays indexed at runtime, too many live values, or a tight __launch_bounds__ cap forcing it. I shorten live ranges or split the work, and I measure both speed and occupancy afterward.
Nsight Systems shows hundreds of tiny kernels per step with gaps between them, and the GPU is idle half the time. What is going on, and how do you fix it?
How you recognize a step limited by CPU launch overhead rather than GPU work.
Reads the timeline as CPU-bound launching, then uses CUDA Graphs, fusion or a compiler, and knows graphs need fixed shapes and addresses.

Each kernel finishes faster than the CPU can launch the next one, so the GPU waits. First I check the CPU side of the timeline to confirm that. Then I capture the step as a CUDA Graph, which replays all launches with one call. Graphs reuse the same memory addresses and shapes, so dynamic shapes need padding to a few fixed sizes or a recapture per shape.
A matrix multiply with an inner dimension of 4097 runs noticeably slower than one with 4096. Why?
Your knowledge of how GEMM libraries tile work and use tensor cores.
Explains alignment for tensor cores and the extra, mostly empty tile, and suggests padding to a friendly multiple.

Tensor core paths work best when dimensions are aligned, at least a multiple of 8 elements in FP16 and ideally of 64 or more. At 4097 the library may pick a slower kernel, and the extra element still costs a full extra tile of work. I would pad the dimension, for example the vocabulary or hidden size, to a multiple of 64 and benchmark both.
Your histogram kernel uses global atomics and slows down badly on real data. How do you speed it up?
How you handle contention when many threads update the same memory.
Sees that skewed data makes atomics on hot bins serialize, and privatizes counts per block in shared memory before merging.

Real data is skewed, so many threads hit the same few bins and their atomics queue up. I give each block a private histogram in shared memory, where atomics are much cheaper. At the end each block adds its counts to global memory with one atomic per bin. On very skewed data I may also pre-count within a warp so one thread updates the bin for all.
You made a kernel three times faster, but the training step improved by only 2%. What happened, and what do you tell the team?
Whether you measure end-to-end impact before and after optimizing a part.
Uses Amdahl's law, admits the target choice was weak, and redirects effort to where the time actually goes.

The kernel was about 3% of the step, so even making it free would save at most 3%. Three times faster saves about 2%, exactly what Amdahl's law predicts. I would say that plainly, keep the change if it is clean, and show the profile ranked by time so the next work goes to the large items, such as attention or communication.
Why is FlashAttention faster than a plain attention implementation, and does it change the result?
Your grasp of IO-aware algorithm design on GPUs.
Tiling into on-chip memory, online softmax, no full score matrix in HBM, and exact attention apart from floating-point rounding.

Plain attention writes the full sequence-by-sequence score matrix to HBM and reads it back for softmax. FlashAttention loads blocks of Q, K and V into on-chip memory and keeps a running max and sum so softmax is done block by block. The big matrix never touches HBM. It computes exact attention; results differ only by rounding order. The backward pass recomputes scores instead of storing them.
Walk me through estimating how much GPU memory the KV cache needs when serving a language model.
Whether you can size inference memory from the model's shape.
The correct formula with grouped-query heads, a worked number, and what it means for batch size and length.

Per token it is 2 for keys and values, times layers, times KV heads, times head dimension, times bytes per value. With 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head size 128 in FP16, that is 128 KiB per token. A 4,096-token sequence needs 512 MiB, so 32 of them need 16 GiB on top of the weights. That number sets the batch size, or tells me to page or quantize the cache.
Data-parallel training on 8 GPUs gives only 5 times the speed of one GPU. How do you find the cause?
How you diagnose scaling loss across several GPUs.
Checks overlap of gradient all-reduce with backward, bucket sizes, interconnect, per-GPU batch, and stragglers, using a timeline.

I look at a timeline per rank. If the NCCL all-reduce runs after the backward pass instead of overlapping with it, I tune gradient bucket sizes so it starts earlier. I check whether traffic crosses the network instead of NVLink, whether the per-GPU batch got so small that communication dominates, and whether one slow rank, often data loading, makes all the others wait.

graphic-designer.heading: Graphic and brand designer questions
qs: When do you use vector artwork and when do you use raster?
Whether you know the two basic kinds of image files and what each is for.
Vectors for logos, icons and type that must scale; raster for photos and painterly work, made at the size and resolution of the final use.

A logo is always built as vectors, paths defined by math, so it stays sharp on a business card or a billboard. Photos and textured illustrations are raster, a grid of pixels, so I make or buy them big enough for the final output, around 300 pixels per inch at print size. Enlarging a small raster image only makes it blurry.
What is the difference between kerning, tracking and leading?
Your command of basic typography terms.
Kerning is the space between one pair of letters, tracking is even spacing across a range of text, and leading is the space between lines.

Kerning adjusts the space between two specific letters, like a capital A next to a V, which often sit too far apart. Tracking loosens or tightens a whole word or block evenly; I add a little to all-caps labels. Leading is the distance from one baseline to the next. Body text usually needs more of it than a tight headline.
Walk me through how you prepare a brochure file before it goes to the printer.
Whether you can hand off print work that will not come back with problems.
Gets the printer's specs first, then sets bleed and safe margins, the right color mode, sharp images, embedded fonts, a press-ready PDF and a proof.

First I get the printer's specs. I set bleed, usually an eighth of an inch, and keep text inside a safe margin. I convert colors the way the printer asks, CMYK or spot, check that images are sharp at print size, embed the fonts and export a PDF/X file. Then I proof it on paper myself and approve the printer's proof before the run.
How do you specify a brand color so it looks the same on screen, on paper and on a sign?
How you control color across different media.
Separate values for each use: HEX or RGB for screens, CMYK and a spot ink for print, checked by eye on real proofs, not just converted by software.

One color needs several recipes. I pick a spot ink color and check it in both the coated and uncoated swatch books, since the same ink looks duller on uncoated paper. Then I set a CMYK build, plus RGB and HEX for screens. I compare them side by side on proofs and a few screens and adjust by eye. The guidelines list every value.
Before you show a client a new logo, how do you test it?
Whether you check that a mark works in real use, not just on the presentation slide.
Tests it at tiny sizes, in one color, in black, reversed on dark, and in real mockups like a site icon, a social avatar and a sign.

I shrink it to browser icon size and to a quarter inch in print to see if details fill in. I try it in one flat color, in black, and reversed white on dark, since someday it will be embroidered or stamped. Then I put it on real mockups: a profile picture, an invoice, a storefront sign. If it only works big and in full color, it is not done.
The client keeps asking you to make the logo bigger on every ad. How do you respond?
How you handle a common client request without simply giving in or arguing.
Finds the worry behind it, usually recognition, and solves that with hierarchy, placement or a side-by-side test, not a flat yes or no.

Usually the real worry is that people will not know who the ad is from. I ask about that, then show two versions at actual size: one with a bigger logo, and one where the logo sits in a clear spot with more space around it. Seeing them side by side settles most of it. If they still want it bigger, it is their brand, and I make it work.
A client sends you a photo they found online and asks you to use it in an ad. What do you do?
Whether you understand image rights and protect the client from a claim.
Explains that online images are protected by copyright by default, tries to find the owner, and offers a licensed stock or custom alternative.

I explain that a photo online still belongs to someone, and using it in an ad without permission can bring a legal claim. I try a reverse image search to find the owner and ask about a license. If that fails, I find a similar stock photo with a commercial license or suggest a short shoot. I keep every license on file with the project.
The client loves the typeface in your mockups and now wants it on their website and app. What do you check?
Your knowledge of font licensing, which designers often get wrong.
Knows desktop, web and app use are usually separate licenses, reads the foundry's terms, and has the client buy licenses in their own name.

A font license usually covers specific uses. My desktop license lets me make graphics with it, but serving it on a website or embedding it in an app normally needs a web or app license, often priced by traffic or installs. I check the foundry's terms, and the client buys the licenses in their own name so the rights stay with them if we part ways.
Five thousand brochures come back from the printer with a wrong phone number, and the error was in your file. What do you do?
How you own a mistake and fix it under pressure.
Tells the client fast, owns it, offers practical fixes like stickers or a reprint, and changes the proofing process so it does not happen again.

I call the client the same day and say plainly it was my error. Then I give options with costs and dates: correction stickers for the first event, a small reprint, or a full reprint, and I offer to cover my share as our agreement says. Then I add a step: a second person checks every phone number, URL and price against the source before sign-off.
A company with 40 years of history wants a full rebrand. How do you decide what to keep from the old identity?
Your judgement about keeping brand recognition versus making a fresh start.
Research first into what customers recognize and value. Keep the assets that carry recognition, refine how they are drawn, and change only what has a reason.

I start by finding out what people actually recognize. I talk to customers and staff, and look at where the brand shows up: trucks, packaging, signs. If everyone knows the green and the shape of the mark, I keep those and redraw them cleaner rather than throw them away. What gets cut has a reason, like a font that fails on screens.
How do you set up a grid for a multi-page report or magazine layout?
Whether you build layouts on a system instead of placing things by eye.
Margins, columns and gutters chosen from the content and format, plus a baseline grid so text lines up across columns and pages.

I start from the content: text length, image sizes, how many heading levels. Then I set margins, a column count with even gutters, and a baseline grid tied to the body text leading so lines align across columns. A 12-column grid gives me 2, 3 and 4-column options. I break the grid on purpose, never by accident.
For a wordmark, when do you set it in an existing typeface and when do you draw custom lettering?
Your judgement on making a logo ownable, and the limits font licenses can set.
Weighs distinctiveness, budget and timeline, and reads the font license first, since some licenses restrict logo use or changing letter shapes.

An unchanged typeface is fast, but anyone can buy it, so the mark is hard to own. Often I start from a typeface, then redraw key letters and fix the spacing so it becomes ours. Before I alter anything I read the license, because some foundries restrict modifying outlines. If the brand needs real distinction and the budget allows, I draw it from scratch.
Sales teams will build their own decks from your slide template. How do you design it so they cannot easily break it?
Whether you design for non-designers who will use your files every day.
Builds layouts in the slide master with placeholders, sets theme colors and fonts, and tests the template with real users.

I build everything in the slide master: theme colors, theme fonts and named layouts with placeholders for title, text, chart and image. The logo and footer live in the master so nobody drags them around. I use fonts every user has or that embed properly. Then I watch two salespeople make a real deck and fix what trips them up.
A client needs their logo on a 10-foot trade show banner and only has a small JPEG from their website. What do you do?
How you handle poor source files without passing the problem on to the print.
Hunts for the original vector first; if none exists, rebuilds it as vector and gets client approval. Never just enlarges the JPEG.

First I ask who made the logo; the original designer or an old printer often has the vector file. If nobody does, I redraw it as vector, matching the shapes and colors, and identify the typeface if I can. I send a proof next to the old version for sign-off. Enlarging a small JPEG would print blurry and jagged at that size.
What do you put in brand guidelines, and how do you make sure people actually use them?
Whether you can turn an identity into a system others can apply without you.
Covers logo use, color values, type, layout and imagery with do and don't examples, and pairs the document with ready templates and an owner.

Logo versions with clear space and minimum size, color values for print and screen, the type hierarchy, grid rules, photo and illustration style, and do and don't examples. But a PDF alone gets ignored. I ship templates and an organized asset library with it, name someone who answers questions, and update it when teams find real gaps.
Marketing wants a campaign look that breaks several brand rules. How do you decide what to allow?
Your judgement on flexibility versus consistency in a brand system.
Separates the core elements that must stay from the expressive ones that can flex, and ties the call to the campaign's goal and lifespan.

I ask what the campaign must do and how long it runs. Then I sort the rules: logo, core colors and type are what people recognize, so they stay. Layout energy, illustration and accent colors can stretch. If the idea is strong and short-lived, I help it work inside that line. If the same request keeps coming back, the guidelines may need to grow.
How many logo concepts do you present, and how do you present them?
How you guide a client's decision instead of asking them to pick by taste.
A small number of truly distinct directions, each tied to the brief and shown in real use, not on a blank page.

Usually two or three, each a real direction, not variations of one. I restate the brief first, then show each concept small and large, in one color, and on mockups like a sign, an app icon and a business card. I explain how each answers the brief, so the talk is about goals, not favorite colors. I never show one I would not want chosen.
How do you lower the risk that a new logo is too close to an existing trademark?
Whether you know the limits of your role in trademark clearance.
Searches the USPTO database and runs image searches in the client's field early, and says a lawyer should clear the mark before launch.

During concepts I search the USPTO trademark database for similar names and design marks in the client's category, and run reverse image searches on the strongest options. If something looks close, I change or drop it early. But I am clear I am not giving legal advice: before launch, the client's trademark attorney should run a full clearance search.
As a freelancer, a client asks who owns the logo once they pay. What do you tell them?
Your grasp of US copyright basics for commissioned design work.
Knows the freelancer holds the copyright until a signed written transfer, and puts the assignment in the contract.

Under US law I own the copyright in what I create unless I transfer it in a signed written document. A logo from a freelancer usually does not qualify as work made for hire, so my contract includes a written assignment of copyright to the client on full payment. I also tell them that fonts or stock used in the files carry their own licenses.
You are leading a rebrand rollout across signs, vehicles, uniforms, packaging and digital. How do you plan it?
Whether you can run the rollout of a brand, not only design it.
Inventories every touchpoint, sets priorities by visibility and cost, phases out old stock, and checks production quality with each vendor.

I start with an inventory of every place the old brand appears, with owner, quantity and replacement cost. Digital and high-visibility items switch on launch day; costly items like signs and vehicles follow a phased plan timed with normal replacement. I prepare production-ready files, get proofs or samples from each vendor, and track it until the last old item is gone.

graphics-engineer.heading: Graphics and rendering engineer questions
qs: Walk me through what happens to a triangle in the rasterization pipeline, from vertex to pixel.
Whether you know the basic stages of the GPU graphics pipeline and what each one does.
The stages in the right order, with a clear role for the programmable stages and the fixed tests.

Each vertex runs through the vertex shader, which moves it into clip space. The GPU assembles triangles, clips them to the view and rasterizes them into fragments. The fragment shader computes a color. Then depth and stencil tests decide what survives, and blending writes the result to the render target. Tessellation and geometry shaders are optional stages.
Why do we use mipmaps, and what do they cost?
Your grasp of texture sampling and aliasing.
Mipmaps prevent shimmering when a texture is shrunk on screen and help the cache, for about one third more memory.

When a texture is far away, many texels land in one pixel, and sampling only one of them makes it shimmer. Mipmaps are prefiltered copies, each half the size of the last, so the GPU picks the level that matches the size on screen. That also makes texture cache use better. The cost is about one third more memory.
Why does it matter whether you do lighting in linear space or in sRGB?
Whether you handle color spaces correctly, a common source of subtle bugs.
Light math belongs in linear space; color textures are decoded on sampling and output is encoded at the end. Data textures stay linear.

Light adds up linearly, so the math is only right in linear space. Color textures are usually stored in sRGB, so I use sRGB formats and the hardware decodes them when sampled. I light and blend in linear, then encode to sRGB for display. Normal maps and roughness stay linear. If this is wrong, gradients look off and blending looks too dark.
Compare forward and deferred rendering. When would you pick each?
Your knowledge of rendering architectures and their trade-offs.
Deferred makes many lights cheap but costs bandwidth and makes transparency and MSAA hard; forward is the reverse.

Forward shades each object with its lights as it is drawn, so transparency and MSAA are simple, but cost grows with lights. Deferred writes normals, albedo and depth to a G-buffer, then lights each pixel once, so many lights are cheap. The price is memory bandwidth and awkward transparency. With many lights I pick deferred or clustered forward.
How do you render transparent objects correctly alongside opaque ones?
Whether you understand why alpha blending depends on draw order.
Opaque first, then transparent sorted back to front without depth writes, and awareness of where sorting fails.

Alpha blending depends on order. I draw opaque objects first with depth writes on, then transparent ones sorted back to front, depth test on and depth writes off. Sorting per object fails when objects intersect or are very large. If that shows up, I look at order-independent methods such as weighted blended OIT and accept that it is an approximation.
Your shadows show stripy dark patterns on lit surfaces. What is it and how do you fix it?
How you diagnose a classic shadow mapping artifact.
Names shadow acne, fixes it with constant and slope-scaled or normal-offset bias, and knows too much bias causes peter-panning.

That is shadow acne: a surface shadows itself because the shadow map has limited resolution and precision. I add a small constant bias plus a slope-scaled bias, or offset the lookup along the normal. Too much bias makes shadows detach from objects, called peter-panning, so I tune it and improve resolution with cascades instead of just raising the bias.
Distant buildings flicker where two surfaces overlap in a large outdoor scene. How do you fix it?
Your understanding of depth buffer precision.
Explains z-fighting and why precision is uneven, then moves the near plane out and uses reversed-Z with a float depth buffer.

That is z-fighting. A standard depth buffer puts most precision near the camera, so far surfaces get the same depth value. First I push the near plane out as far as gameplay allows, since it matters most. Then I switch to reversed-Z with a 32-bit float depth buffer, which spreads precision far better. For decals on walls I use a small depth offset.
After a new content drop, frame time went from 16 ms to 22 ms. How do you find the cause?
How you use GPU profiling to find a performance regression.
First finds whether CPU or GPU is the limit, then compares frame captures pass by pass and fixes the real cause.

I first check if we are CPU or GPU bound, using GPU timestamp queries against the frame time. If it is the GPU, I take a frame capture before and after and compare each pass. Last time it was new foliage: many alpha-tested layers drawn over the same pixels, called overdraw, doubled the G-buffer pass. Smaller cards and LODs got us back to 16 ms.
A rendering bug shows up on one GPU vendor only. How do you handle it?
How you handle driver differences without blaming the driver too soon.
Assumes your own bug first, uses validation tools, reduces to a minimal repro, and only then reports and works around a driver bug.

I start with validation layers and the debug runtime, because usually it is our bug that other drivers tolerate. Then I cut it down to one draw and one shader. Once it was black pixels on one vendor: an uninitialized shader variable that other compilers happened to zero. If it is truly the driver, I report it with the repro and add a narrow workaround.
On a 90 Hz VR title, the art lead wants a volumetric fog that costs 3 ms. What do you do?
Your judgement on frame budgets and how you work with artists.
Knows the budget is about 11 ms and missed frames cause discomfort, measures headroom, and offers cheaper versions to compare in the headset.

At 90 Hz the whole frame has about 11 ms for both eyes, and missing it causes judder and discomfort, not just a lower number. I measure our headroom first. If there is no room, I offer cheaper versions: fog at lower resolution with upsampling, fewer steps, reuse across frames. Then we compare them side by side in the headset and decide together.
Why do you transform normals with the inverse transpose of the model matrix instead of the model matrix itself?
Whether you understand the math behind lighting, not just the formula.
Non-uniform scale breaks perpendicularity; the inverse transpose of the upper 3x3 fixes it, and you renormalize afterwards.

A normal must stay perpendicular to the surface. Rotation and uniform scale keep that, but non-uniform scale tilts the normal the wrong way. The inverse transpose of the upper 3x3 keeps it perpendicular. It can change the length, so I renormalize in the shader. For rotation-only matrices the two are the same, so I skip the extra work.
Foliage textures show dark halos around the leaf edges, worse in the distance. What is going on?
How you diagnose a classic texture filtering artifact.
Filtering mixes the color of fully transparent texels into the edge; premultiplied alpha or color dilation fixes it.

The transparent texels around the leaves are probably black. Bilinear filtering and mipmapping average them with the edge, so the edge goes dark, and smaller mips average more. I would store the texture with premultiplied alpha, or dilate the leaf color out into the transparent area at import, and generate the mips after that.
In a microfacet specular BRDF, what do the D, F and G terms each do?
Your grasp of physically based shading beyond copying a shader.
D is the distribution of microfacet normals, F the Fresnel reflectance, G the shadowing and masking, each with a common model named.

D says how many microfacets face the half vector, so it sets the shape and width of the highlight; GGX is the usual choice. F is Fresnel: reflectance rising toward grazing angles, often with Schlick's approximation. G covers microfacets shadowing and masking each other, usually a Smith form. The product is divided by 4 times N·L times N·V.
A dense mesh with tiny triangles is slow even though it covers few pixels. Why?
Whether you know how GPUs really shade pixels.
Pixels are shaded in 2x2 quads for derivatives, so tiny triangles waste lanes, plus vertex and setup cost. LODs fix it.

GPUs shade pixels in 2x2 quads so they can compute derivatives for mip selection. A triangle that covers one pixel still runs four shader invocations, three of them as helper lanes. Triangle setup and vertex work add up too. I would check quad efficiency in a profiler, then add LODs so triangles stay several pixels wide.
When is an if statement in a pixel shader expensive, and when is it fine?
How you reason about divergence on SIMD hardware.
Lanes in a wave run in lockstep; a branch costs both paths only when lanes disagree. Coherent or uniform branches are cheap.

Threads run in groups, called warps or waves, that share one instruction stream. If every lane takes the same side, the GPU skips the other side and the branch is cheap. If lanes split, the wave runs both paths with some lanes masked off. So a branch on a material ID that changes per pixel can hurt, while a branch on a constant usually does not.
A profiler says your compute shader has low occupancy. Do you always try to raise it?
Your judgement with GPU metrics instead of chasing one number.
Occupancy hides memory latency, but it is a means. Check whether the shader is latency bound before trading registers for it.

Not always. Occupancy is how many waves can be resident on a core at once, limited by registers, shared memory and group size. More waves help hide memory latency. If the shader is bound by math or bandwidth, more occupancy may change nothing. I check stall reasons first; if it waits on memory, I cut register use and measure again.
Your temporal anti-aliasing leaves ghost trails behind a moving character. How do you track it down?
How you debug a temporal technique with several failure points.
Check motion vectors first, then history rejection: neighborhood clamping and disocclusion handling.

First I view the motion vector buffer. Ghosting often means an object writes no motion, like a skinned mesh missing last frame's pose, or particles. If the vectors are right, I look at history rejection: clamping history to the min and max of the current 3x3 neighborhood, and dropping history where the reprojected depth does not match.
Players report a hitch the first time each new effect appears on screen. What do you suspect and what do you do?
Whether you know modern API pipeline costs and how to ship around them.
Pipeline state compiled at first draw; fix by collecting and precompiling pipelines, caching them, and cutting permutations.

On DX12 or Vulkan, creating a pipeline state object compiles shaders for the GPU, which can take many milliseconds. If that happens at first draw, the frame hitches. I confirm it in a capture, record the pipelines used in play tests, create them at load or on background threads, keep a pipeline cache on disk, and cut shader permutations.
In a big open world, meshes wobble and jitter far from the map's origin. Why, and what is your fix?
Your understanding of floating point precision in rendering.
32-bit floats lose precision at large values; render relative to the camera or rebase the origin, with big positions in doubles on the CPU.

A 32-bit float has about 7 significant digits, so tens of kilometers from the origin the step between values reaches millimeters, and vertex math rounds visibly. I keep world positions in doubles on the CPU, subtract the camera position there, and send camera-relative matrices to the GPU. Some engines also shift the world origin as the player moves.
A Vulkan or DX12 frame shows random flickering in one pass, and it vanishes when you capture it. How do you approach it?
How you handle a GPU synchronization bug, one of the hardest to see.
Suspect a missing or wrong barrier; use validation and sync validation, force serialization to confirm, then fix the dependency.

Flicker that hides under a capture smells like a race: a pass reads a texture before the earlier write finishes, or a layout transition is wrong. I turn on the validation layer with synchronization validation, or GPU-based validation on DX12. To confirm, I add a full barrier around the pass; if the flicker stops, I find the exact dependency and fix it.

grocery-associate.heading: Grocery store associate questions
qs: What does it mean to face or block a shelf, and why do stores do it?
Whether you know the basic shelf work that keeps a grocery aisle shoppable.
Pulling products to the front edge, labels out and lined up, so the shelf looks full and customers find items fast.

Facing means pulling each item to the front of the shelf with the label turned out. Blocking is lining them up in neat rows. The shelf looks full, customers find what they want faster, and I can spot what is running low and needs to come from the back.
How do you rotate stock when you fill the dairy case?
Whether you use first in, first out so older stock sells before newer stock.
Older dates move to the front, new stock goes behind, and anything out of date or damaged is pulled while filling.

I pull the product already on the shelf forward, then put the new cases behind it. That way the earliest dates sell first. While I do it, I check dates and packages, and I pull anything expired, swollen or leaking instead of leaving it for a customer to find.
You find a few yogurts past their date at the back of the shelf. What do you do?
How you handle out-of-date product and what it tells you about the shelf.
Pull them, record them as the store requires, and check the rest of the section since one miss usually means poor rotation.

I pull them right away and log them the way the store tracks spoiled or out-of-date items. Then I check the rest of that product and the ones around it, because if a few old cups were hiding in back, the shelf probably was not rotated. I would mention it to whoever stocks that case.
A jar of pasta sauce has broken and spread across the aisle. Walk me through what you do.
How you deal with a slip hazard and broken glass safely and quickly.
Guard the spot first, call for help, set out wet floor signs, pick up glass without bare hands, then clean and dry the floor.

I stay by the spill or ask someone to watch it so nobody walks through. I put out wet floor signs and call for the cleanup supplies. I pick up the glass with a dustpan and broom, never bare hands, and put it in a safe container. Then I mop, dry the floor and check nearby products for splashes.
A customer says the shelf tag shows $2.99 but the item rang up at $3.49. What do you do?
How you fix a pricing error for the customer and for the store.
Check the tag, follow the store price policy for the customer, then fix or report the tag so it does not happen again.

I go look at the tag with the customer or ask a coworker to check it. If the tag is wrong, I follow store policy, which usually means giving the shelf price, and I get a manager if I need an override. Then I pull the wrong tag and tell the person who handles pricing so the next customer is not overcharged.
A customer at the deli asks whether a salad has nuts in it, and the label is not clear. What do you tell them?
Whether you avoid guessing when a customer may have a food allergy.
Never guess; check the ingredient list or recipe, ask a lead, and if it cannot be confirmed, say so plainly.

I tell them I do not want to guess about an allergy. I check the ingredient label and the recipe or product sheet, and I ask the deli lead. If I still cannot confirm it, I say we cannot promise it is nut free. I also mention that things prepared in the same area can touch shared tools.
The cooler for milk reads 48°F and the jugs feel warm. What do you do?
Whether you know cold foods must stay at 41°F or below and act on a failing cooler.
Report it to a manager at once, move product to a working cooler if told, and let the manager decide what can still be sold.

Milk should be held at 41°F or colder, so 48 is a problem. I tell my manager right away and stop filling that case. If they say so, I move the product to the walk-in or another working cooler. I note the time and reading, and the manager decides what is safe to sell. I would not just hope it cools down.
A man buys a case of beer, and you see a young-looking friend hand him money for it before he comes to the register. What do you do?
Your judgement on alcohol sales when the real buyer may be underage.
Recognizes a possible third-party sale, asks for ID from everyone in the group or refuses, stays calm and gets a manager if needed.

That looks like an adult buying for someone who may be under 21, so I would not just ring it up. I would ask both of them for ID. If the friend cannot show he is 21, I politely refuse the sale and call a manager if they argue. Losing one sale is much better than a fine or the store losing its license.
Walk me through cleaning a deli slicer safely.
Whether you know the safe steps for the most dangerous tool at the counter.
Unplugged, blade set to zero, cut-resistant glove, parts taken off and washed, rinsed, sanitized, never reaching across the blade.

First I turn it off and unplug it, and set the thickness dial to zero so the blade edge is covered. I put on a cut-resistant glove. I remove the carriage and guards, then wash, rinse and sanitize them. I wipe the blade from the center outward, never across the edge. I let parts air dry and put it back together before plugging it in.
What is the difference between a sell-by, a use-by and a best-if-used-by date?
Whether you know what date labels mean and which one matters most.
Most dates are about quality, not safety. Store policy decides when items come off the shelf, and infant formula is never sold past its date.

Sell-by tells the store how long to display the item. Best-if-used-by is when quality is best. Use-by is the last day the maker recommends for peak quality. Except for infant formula, federal law does not require these dates, so I follow our pull policy for each department. Formula past its date always comes off the shelf.
Why do you keep bananas and apples away from lettuce in the back cooler?
Your knowledge of how produce ripens and spoils.
Some fruits give off ethylene gas, which speeds ripening and spoils sensitive items like leafy greens.

Apples, bananas and tomatoes give off ethylene, a gas that makes produce ripen. Leafy greens, broccoli and cucumbers are sensitive to it and turn yellow or spotted faster. So I keep them in separate areas of the cooler, and I put ripe bananas out first instead of letting them sit next to the greens.
What is shrink, and what can you do about it in your own section?
Whether you see the business side of stocking and rotation.
Shrink is product lost to spoilage, damage, theft or errors. A good answer names daily habits that cut it.

Shrink is stock the store paid for but never sold: spoiled, damaged, stolen or lost to paperwork mistakes. In my section I rotate first in, first out, handle cases so they don't get crushed, and log every markdown and throwaway. If the same item keeps going bad, I tell my manager so we can cut the order.
A truck arrives with dairy and frozen product. What do you check before you sign for it?
How you protect the cold chain when product comes in the door.
Counts against the invoice, damage, temperatures and signs of thawing, with problems noted before signing.

I count cases against the invoice and look for crushed or leaking boxes. I take the temperature of a few dairy items; they should meet our cold standard, usually 41°F or below. Frozen should be hard, with no soft spots, big ice crystals or stains that show it thawed and refroze. I note anything wrong before I sign, then get it all cold fast.
You are stocking ice cream and a manager calls you to the front for ten minutes. What do you do with the pallet?
Whether you protect frozen product when you are pulled away.
The product goes back into the freezer first, even if it costs time, and frozen work is done in small batches.

I roll the pallet back into the freezer before I go, even if it takes two minutes. Ice cream that softens and refreezes gets icy and can't be sold the same way. That's also why I bring out only what I can stock in one go. If I truly can't leave it, I tell the manager and ask someone else to cover the front.
Walk me through checking an ID for a wine sale.
Whether you check ID fully and the same way every time.
Photo, birth date math, expiration and signs of tampering, with no sale when in doubt.

I take the ID out of the wallet and hold it. I match the photo to the face, then do the math on the birth date against today. I check the expiration date and feel the card for peeling or raised edges. A vertical license usually means the person was under 21 when it was issued, so I look closely, though they may be 21 now. If I'm not sure, I don't sell.
A customer pays with SNAP EBT for groceries, a hot rotisserie chicken and a six-pack of beer. How does that work at the register?
Your knowledge of what SNAP benefits can and cannot buy.
SNAP cannot pay for alcohol or hot prepared food. The customer pays for those another way, and you handle it quietly.

SNAP covers the groceries, but not beer or food sold hot to eat right away, like the hot chicken. The register usually splits eligible items for me. I tell the customer quietly that those two items need another form of payment. If they'd rather skip them, I void them. A cold chicken from the case would be eligible, so I can mention that.
During a temperature check, the rotisserie chickens in the hot case read 128°F. What do you do?
How you handle a food safety problem at the deli counter.
Stop sales, find out how long the food has been below 135°F, reheat or discard by the deli's rule, then fix the cause.

Hot food must stay at 135°F or above, so I pull the chickens from sale right away. I check the log for the last good reading. Under our deli's rule, if that was less than two hours ago they can be reheated to 165°F; if nobody knows, they get thrown out. Then I check the case setting, tell my lead and log what I did.
A recall notice comes in for a brand of bagged spinach with certain lot codes. Walk me through it.
Whether you can carry out a recall completely and fast.
Product pulled from every place it could be, lot codes matched, held apart as do not sell, and the manager told.

I read the notice for the exact product, sizes and lot codes. Then I check the shelf, the back cooler, any end displays and the deli or salad bar if they use it. Matching bags go into a marked bin that says do not sell, away from other stock. I tell my manager so the register can block the item, and I record how many I pulled.
How would you decide how much bread to order for a holiday weekend?
Your judgement in ordering, where too much and too little both cost money.
Sales history, the weekly ad, the weather and stock on hand, weighed against how fast bread goes stale.

I start with what we sold the same weekend last year and over the last few weeks. I check the ad, since a sale on burgers sells buns. I count what's on the shelf and in back, and look at the forecast: a sunny weekend means cookouts. Bread goes stale fast, so I'd rather sell out late Sunday than throw out a full rack on Monday.

group-product-manager.heading: Group and principal product manager questions
qs: How is your job different from the job of a senior product manager?
Whether you understand the shift from owning a product to owning a group and its direction.
The work moves from shipping features to setting strategy, shaping how teams are split, and growing other PMs, while staying close enough to the product to judge quality.

A senior PM owns one problem space and ships against it. In my role I own the strategy across several teams, decide where the boundaries between them sit, and coach the PMs who run them. I still read specs and talk to customers, but my output is mostly better decisions by other people, not my own roadmap.
What goes into a product strategy for an area like yours?
Your grasp of what a strategy contains beyond a list of features.
A clear diagnosis of the market and customer, a few choices about where to play and what not to do, and how progress will be measured.

I start with who the customer is and what problem is worth solving, backed by data and research. Then I name two or three bets, and just as clearly what we will not do this year. Each bet gets a measurable outcome and the main risks. If a team cannot use it to say no to a request, it is not a strategy yet.
How do you choose a north star metric for your group, and what sits under it?
Whether you can connect team work to one outcome the business cares about.
A metric that reflects value delivered to customers, broken into input metrics each team can actually move, with guardrails against gaming it.

I look for the moment a customer gets real value, for example weekly active teams that complete a core task, not raw sign-ups. Under it I set input metrics each team owns, like activation rate or time to first success. I add guardrails such as retention and support tickets, so a team cannot push its number up by hurting the experience.
How do you split your group's capacity between new features, improving what exists, and technical debt?
How you think about investment across a portfolio rather than one backlog.
An explicit allocation agreed with engineering leads, tied to strategy and product health, and revisited when conditions change.

I agree a rough split with my engineering partners each quarter, say 50% new bets, 30% core improvements, 20% platform and debt. The numbers move with the situation: after an outage streak, reliability gets more. Writing the split down stops every request from being argued one by one, and it lets teams protect debt work when a deadline gets loud.
Two PMs in your group both claim the same customer problem, and their roadmaps now overlap. What do you do?
How you handle ownership conflicts and team boundaries.
You fix the structure, not just the argument: one clear owner, a written boundary, and a plan for the work already in flight.

First I hear each side alone, then together, focused on the customer problem, not who is right. Usually the overlap means my team boundaries are unclear, which is my fault. I pick one owner, write down who owns what, and decide which in-flight work continues. The other PM gets a clear, worthwhile scope so it does not feel like a loss.
A PM on your team shows you a roadmap that is just a list of features with dates. How do you coach them?
How you develop product thinking in other PMs.
Questions that lead them to outcomes and evidence, rather than rewriting the roadmap for them.

I ask what each item is meant to change for the customer and how we would know. Then I ask which one they would cut if they lost half their engineers. That usually shows which items carry the bet. I have them rewrite it as problems and outcomes, with features as current guesses, and I review the second version with them rather than fixing it myself.
Walk me through how you would hire a product manager for your group.
Whether you can run a fair, structured hiring process for product roles.
Defined criteria before interviews, structured questions with each interviewer covering one area, and a decision based on evidence against the criteria.

I write down what this role needs before I see a resume, for example strong discovery skills and working well with a skeptical engineering team. Each interviewer covers one area with the same questions for every candidate, including a product case. Feedback is written before the debrief so people do not anchor on each other. Then we decide against the criteria, not on gut feel.
Your launch depends on another group, and they just moved your work down their list. What do you do?
How you get results through teams you have no authority over.
Understanding their priorities first, making the shared impact visible, offering trade-offs, and escalating openly only if needed.

I meet their lead to understand what pushed us down; often they have a good reason. I show the impact in their terms, like revenue or customers blocked, and offer options: we lend an engineer, cut scope, or shift our date. If we still disagree, we take it up together to our shared manager with both views written down, so it is a decision, not a fight.
Leadership asks you to commit to dates for every item on next year's roadmap. How do you respond?
How you balance predictability for the business against honest uncertainty.
Firm commitments where the work is understood, ranges or outcome goals where it is not, and a clear cadence for updating.

I would not refuse, and I would not fake precision. Work we understand well gets a date. Work further out gets a quarter or an outcome, like cutting churn in a segment, with a note on what we must learn first. I promise a monthly update on what changed. Leaders usually want to plan around us, and honest confidence levels help them more than dates we will miss.
How would you decide to shut down a product that some customers still use?
Your judgement on retiring products and handling the impact on customers.
A decision based on cost, strategic fit and who depends on it, followed by a respectful migration plan with notice and a path for key customers.

I look at usage, revenue, the engineering and support cost, and whether it fits our strategy. I talk to the heaviest users to learn what they would lose. If we shut it down, customers get clear notice, a migration path or alternative, and a firm end date. I brief sales and support first, so no customer hears it from a surprised account manager.
How do you size an opportunity before it goes into your group's strategy?
Whether you can put a number on a bet and show how you got it.
A bottom-up estimate from real customer counts and plausible adoption, checked against a top-down view, with the key assumptions named.

I build it bottom-up: how many accounts have the problem, what share might adopt in the first year, and what each is worth. Then I check it top-down against the total market so it is not absurd. I write down the three assumptions that move the number most, because those are what discovery should test first.
A PM shows you interview notes where most customers said they would pay for a new feature. What do you look at?
Whether you can tell weak discovery evidence from strong evidence.
Knows that stated intent is weak evidence. Looks for past behavior, current workarounds and spending, and how the questions were asked.

First, how the question was asked. “Would you pay for this?” invites a polite yes. I look for what people already do: workarounds they built, tools they pay for, time they spend on the problem today. Then I ask the PM to test real commitment, like a pilot sign-up or a letter of intent, before we plan engineering around it.
How do you divide a large product area among the PMs in your group?
How you design ownership so teams can move without constant coordination.
Clear lines by customer journey, user type or platform layer, with the trade-offs of each named and an owner for the seams between them.

I prefer to split by customer outcome, like onboarding, daily use and billing, so each PM owns a metric end to end. Splitting by technical layer makes every feature need three teams. Whatever the split, I name an owner for each handoff point and revisit the map yearly, since the product changes under it.
How do you decide whether to build, buy, or partner for a capability your group needs?
How you weigh cost, control and focus on a strategic choice.
Builds what sets the product apart; buys or partners for the rest, counting the full cost of ownership and the risk of depending on a vendor.

I ask if this is why customers choose us. If it is, we build and own it. If it is needed but not a differentiator, like payments or search, I compare buying against the true cost of building: the first version plus years of upkeep. I also check the vendor's data terms and what leaving them would take, since switching later is expensive.
When should a capability become a shared platform instead of being built inside each product team?
Your judgement on platform investment and what it costs.
A platform when several teams need the same thing and duplication costs more than coordination, not before the need is proven.

When two or three teams are building the same thing and the copies are drifting apart, a platform pays off. Before that, I let one product team build it well and learn what users really need. A platform built too early guesses at needs, slows every team that depends on it, and is hard to change once others build on it.
An experiment raises sign-up conversion by 6%, but the new users churn faster in their first month. What do you recommend?
Whether you read a result against guardrail metrics, not only the headline number.
Does not ship on the top-line win. Looks at the full funnel and value per user, and finds out why the new users leave.

I would not ship yet. More sign-ups from users who leave fast can lower revenue and add support cost. I would compare retained users and value per visitor across both groups, not just sign-ups. Then I would look at who the extra users are: if the change pulled in people the product does not serve, we fix the targeting, not the button.
Sales promised a large prospect a feature by next quarter to close the deal, without asking you. What do you do?
How you handle a commitment you did not make without damaging the deal or the roadmap.
Gets the facts, judges the request on its merits, gives sales an honest answer quickly, and fixes the process so it does not repeat.

First I find out exactly what was promised and whether it is in the contract. Then I judge it like any request: does it fit our strategy and help other customers? If yes, we may pull it forward and say what drops. If not, I join a call to offer what we can do. Afterward I agree with the sales lead that no dates go out for unbuilt features without product sign-off.
Halfway through a quarter, you see that one team's main project no longer fits the strategy. Do you stop it?
Whether you can cut work in progress and treat the team well when you do.
Ignores sunk cost, weighs the remaining cost against the value left, decides quickly, and explains the reason to the team.

I look only at what is left: the remaining cost against the value we would still get. Time already spent does not count. If finishing is cheap and useful, we finish small. If not, I stop it, tell the team myself with the reason, save what we learned, and give them a clear next problem. Leaving a team on work I know is wrong wastes their time and trust.
How do you make performance ratings fair across the PMs in your group?
How you judge PM performance on evidence rather than visibility or charm.
Clear expectations by level, evidence of outcomes and behavior, comparison across managers, and checks for bias toward the most visible people.

I write down what each level is expected to do, then rate against that with examples: outcomes, quality of decisions, how they work with engineering and design. In calibration I ask for evidence behind every rating and watch for the usual traps, like rewarding whoever presented to executives most or whoever had the easiest product area.
The CEO wants your group to go after a new market, and your research says demand is weak. How do you handle it?
How you push back on senior leadership with evidence, then commit.
Shares the evidence privately and early, proposes a cheap test that could change either side's mind, and fully commits once the call is made.

I would ask what the CEO sees that I may not, then show my evidence one to one, not in a big meeting. I would propose a small, time-boxed test, like a pilot with five prospects and a clear bar for success, so the data decides. If the CEO still says go, I commit fully and track the signals we agreed on, so we can change course fast if needed.

growth-engineer.heading: Growth engineer questions
qs: How do you make sure a user sees the same variant of an experiment on every visit?
Whether you know how experiment assignment works under the hood.
Assignment is deterministic from a stable ID and salted per experiment, with a plan for logged-out users.

I hash the user ID together with the experiment key and map the result to a bucket, say 0 to 99. The same input always gives the same bucket, so no lookup table is needed. The experiment key keeps tests independent of each other. For logged-out visitors I use an anonymous ID in a first-party cookie and link it to the account at sign-up.
You are adding tracking to a new sign-up flow. What events do you send, and from where?
How you build data that people can trust when they make decisions.
One event per real step, a written schema, and key conversions sent from the server, since browser events get blocked or lost.

I send one event per step: form viewed, submitted, email verified, first key action. Names and properties go in a shared tracking plan so analysts know what each one means. The account-created event fires from the server after the database write, because ad blockers drop browser events. Before launch I compare event counts to the users table.
A new sign-up page raises sign-ups by 10%. Before shipping it, what else do you look at?
Whether you look past the top of the funnel.
