Guardrail and downstream metrics such as activation, retention, revenue and fake accounts, so the win is not just lower-quality sign-ups.

I check what those extra users do next. If the page removed a step, we may have gained people who never activate. So I compare activation rate, week-one retention, paid conversion and spam accounts per variant. If sign-ups rise 10% but activated users stay flat, we did not grow; we added empty accounts.
Your manager checks the test dashboard daily and wants to stop the test the day it hits significance. What do you say?
Whether you understand the peeking problem.
Repeated looks at a fixed-sample test inflate false positives; set the sample size in advance or use a method built for early checks.

Each look is another chance for noise to cross the line, so stopping at the first green day gives far more false wins than the 5% we think we accept. I would agree the sample size and duration before launch, in full weeks. If we truly need the option to stop early, we use a sequential test designed for repeated looks.
A 50/50 test shows 51,200 users in one arm and 48,800 in the other. What do you do?
Whether you can spot a broken experiment before reading its results.
Calls it a sample ratio mismatch, refuses to trust the metrics, and looks for the cause in assignment, redirects or logging.

With 100,000 users, a gap that size is far too big to be chance, so it is a sample ratio mismatch. I would not read any metric yet. I check whether one variant loads slower and loses users before the exposure event fires, whether bots are filtered unevenly, and whether both arms log exposure at the same point. Fix it, then restart.
You are building a referral program that gives both people a credit. How do you keep it from being gamed?
Whether you design incentives with abuse in mind.
Rewards only after a real qualifying action, flags self-referrals, caps rewards, and keeps a manual review path.

I pay the credit only after the new user does something costly to fake, like a first paid order past the refund window. I flag referrals that share a device, card or address with the referrer, cap rewards per account per month, and send outliers to review. Each week I compare the cost per referred customer with what those customers are worth.
Marketing wants to email everyone who signed up in the last three years to win them back. What do you check first?
Whether you protect sender reputation and follow email rules.
Honors unsubscribes and suppressions, includes a working opt-out, and starts with engaged users so old addresses do not hurt deliverability.

First, anyone who unsubscribed or bounced stays off the list, and the email carries a working unsubscribe link and our postal address, as US law requires for marketing email. Then deliverability: old lists hold dead addresses and spam traps. I would start with users active in recent months, raise volume over several days and watch bounce and complaint rates.
Why would you keep a small group of users out of all growth changes for a whole quarter?
Whether you know why individual test wins rarely add up.
A long-term holdout measures the combined real effect, since single lifts overlap, fade, or were partly false positives.

If we ship ten tests that each won 3%, the product rarely grows 30%. Wins overlap, some fade, and some were false positives. A holdout of a few percent that sees none of the changes shows what the whole program really added. The cost is that those users miss improvements, so I keep it small and time-limited.
You want to test a bigger referral reward. Why might a normal user-level A/B test give a wrong answer?
Whether you see when users in a test affect each other.
Spots interference: treated users reach or influence control users, so arms are not independent. Suggests randomizing by larger units.

Referrals connect users, so the arms leak into each other. A treated user invites a friend who lands in control, or control users hear about the bigger reward. That breaks the assumption that one user's outcome does not depend on another's. I would randomize by region or time period, or put invited users in their inviter's arm, and accept less precision.
Before a test starts, how do you decide how long it needs to run?
Whether you plan the sample size before launch instead of waiting for a good-looking result.
Uses the baseline rate, the smallest effect worth detecting, the significance level and power, then rounds up to full weeks.

I start with the baseline conversion rate, the smallest lift worth shipping, a 5% significance level and 80% power. A power calculator turns that into users per arm, and our daily traffic turns it into days. I round up to whole weeks so weekday and weekend users are both in, and I write the end date down before launch.
Sign-up conversion fell this month overall, yet it rose in every channel. How is that possible?
Whether you recognize a mix shift, also called Simpson's paradox.
Explains that traffic moved toward a lower-converting channel, and checks the mix before blaming the product.

The weights changed. If a new paid campaign sent lots of traffic that converts at 2% while organic converts at 8%, each channel can improve and the blended rate still drops. I would show conversion by channel next to each channel's share of traffic, so nobody spends a week hunting for a bug in the sign-up form.
How would you choose an activation metric for a new product?
How you link an early user action to long-term retention.
Looks for an early action within a time window that predicts retention, then tests whether pushing users toward it actually moves retention.

I list early actions, like creating a first project or inviting a teammate within seven days, and compare day-30 retention for users who did each one and users who did not. I pick one that predicts retention well, that a fair share of users reach, and that we can measure quickly. Then I treat it as a hypothesis and test whether nudging users toward it really lifts retention.
Users who finish the onboarding checklist retain twice as well. The PM wants to make the checklist mandatory. What do you say?
Whether you separate correlation from cause before forcing users through a step.
Points out that motivated users self-select into finishing, and proposes an experiment with retention as the goal and drop-off as a guardrail.

Users who finish it may simply be the ones who were already keen. Forcing it could add friction and lose people early. I would test it: one group gets the mandatory checklist, one keeps it optional, and we compare day-30 retention, not checklist completion. I would also watch how many people abandon during onboarding.
Your client-side experiment shows the old page for a split second before the new one appears. Why does it matter, and how do you fix it?
Your grasp of how the way an experiment is delivered can bias its results.
Knows flicker can change behavior and slow the page, and prefers server-side or edge assignment, or hiding content until the variant is applied.

Users see the control first, which can confuse them and slows the page, so the variant is measured with a handicap. The cleanest fix is assigning the variant on the server or at the edge, so the page arrives already right. If it must stay client-side, I hide the affected area until the variant loads, with a short timeout so the page never stays blank.
We randomize by user, but the analyst computes click-through rate per page view and treats every view as independent. What is wrong?
Whether you match the statistics to the unit that was randomized.
Explains that views from one user are correlated, so errors look too small; fixes it with per-user metrics, the delta method or a user-level bootstrap.

One heavy user can produce hundreds of views that behave alike, so they are not independent. Treating them as separate data points makes the standard error too small and produces false winners. I would analyze a per-user metric, or keep the ratio and compute its variance with the delta method or a bootstrap that resamples users, not views.
A test tracks 20 metrics and one of them is significant at p < 0.05. The team wants to call it a win. What do you do?
How you handle many comparisons in one test.
Notes that about one false positive in 20 is expected by chance, and relies on the primary metric chosen in advance or corrects for many tests.

With 20 metrics and no real effect, we would expect about one to cross 0.05 by luck. So I go back to the primary metric we named before launch. If that did not move, the test did not win. The odd metric becomes a hypothesis for a new test, or I apply a correction like Benjamini-Hochberg if we really need to read all 20.
Our product gets few sign-ups, and tests take two months to finish. What can you do besides waiting?
Your toolkit for getting answers when traffic is low.
Names real levers: bolder changes, a more sensitive metric closer to the change, and variance reduction with pre-experiment data such as CUPED.

First, test bigger changes; small tweaks need huge samples. Second, use a metric closer to the change, like step completion, while keeping sign-up as a guardrail. Third, for users we already know, CUPED adjusts each result using that user's pre-experiment behavior, which can cut the sample needed. And some questions are better answered with user research than a test.
Last year our team shipped tests whose lifts add up to 15%, but the main metric grew only 3%. Explain the gap.
Whether you understand why measured wins overstate real impact.
Names the winner's curse, false positives, fading novelty and overlapping changes, and suggests a long-term holdout to measure the combined effect.

Winning tests are picked because they look good, so their measured lift is biased upward; that is the winner's curse. Some wins were false positives, some were novelty that faded, and changes aimed at the same users overlap instead of adding up. Outside forces move the metric too. I would report shrunk estimates and keep a holdout to measure the combined effect directly.

growth-manager.heading: Growth manager questions
qs: What is activation, and how would you define it for a product?
Whether you know the step between signup and real use, and how to find it in data.
Activation is the first moment a user gets real value. It is found by comparing users who stayed with those who left, then tested, not guessed.

Activation is the moment a new user first gets the value the product promises. For a team chat app it might be sending messages with two coworkers in the first week. I find it by comparing users still active at day 30 with those who left, then I test whether pushing people toward that action actually lifts retention.
You have 40 experiment ideas and room for three this month. How do you pick?
How you prioritize a test backlog with limited traffic and time.
A simple scoring method such as ICE, tied to the target metric, plus a check that the test can reach a clear result with the traffic available.

I score each idea on impact, confidence and ease, often called ICE. Impact is measured against the metric we are trying to move, and confidence comes from data or past tests, not gut. Then I check traffic: a test on a page with 500 visits a week may never reach a clear result, so a bigger-reach idea can win even with a lower score.
What makes a good North Star metric, and what makes a bad one?
Whether you can choose one number that tracks real customer value.
It reflects value delivered and leads to revenue. A bad one is easy to inflate without helping anyone, like downloads or page views.

It is the one number that best captures the value customers get and that drives revenue over time. For a meal kit company, weekly orders delivered beats signups. A bad one is easy to inflate without helping anyone, like page views or app downloads. I pair it with a few input metrics the team can move week to week.
Walk me through how you read a cohort retention chart.
Your ability to read retention data and judge product health from it.
Rows are start cohorts, columns are time since start. A flattening curve means lasting value; newer cohorts sitting higher means changes are working.

Each row is a group of users who started in the same week, and each column shows what share are still active after one, two, three weeks. I look for the curve to flatten, which means a core group found lasting value. If newer cohorts sit higher, recent changes are working. If curves never flatten, more acquisition just fills a leaky bucket.
How do you calculate CAC payback, and why use gross margin instead of revenue?
Whether you know the unit economics that decide how fast you can spend to grow.
CAC divided by monthly gross margin per customer. Revenue alone ignores the cost of serving the customer and makes payback look shorter than it is.

I take customer acquisition cost, sales and marketing spend for the period divided by new customers, and divide it by the monthly gross margin each customer brings. If CAC is $300 and a customer pays $50 a month at 80% margin, that is $40 a month, so payback is about 7.5 months. Revenue alone hides the cost of serving them.
Your A/B test hits significance on day 3 of a planned 14-day run. Do you ship it?
Whether you know the peeking problem and other traps of stopping a test early.
No. Stopping on the first significant result inflates false positives, and three days miss weekly cycles and novelty effects.

No. I set sample size and duration before the test, and stopping on the first significant result pushes the false positive rate well above the 5% we planned for. Day 3 also misses weekly patterns, since weekend users behave differently, and early lifts often come from novelty. I let it run the full two weeks unless a guardrail like refunds breaks.
A shorter signup form raised signups 20%, but revenue did not move. What do you look at?
How you judge a win on a top-of-funnel metric against what the business needs.
Following the extra users down the funnel against control, checking intent and quality, and judging future tests on a metric closer to revenue.

I would follow the new signups down the funnel, activation, trial to paid and early retention, against the control group. Often a shorter form lets in people with less intent, so the extra signups never pay. I also check the test split was clean. Then I keep what helped real buyers and judge the next test on paid conversion, not signups.
What is a viral coefficient, and why is it rarely the whole story?
Your grasp of referral loops and how they add to growth.
K equals invites per user times the invite conversion rate. Above 1 is rare; below 1 still amplifies other channels, and loop speed matters.

It is how many new users each user brings in: invites sent per user times the share of invites that convert. If each user sends 4 invites and 10% sign up, K is 0.4. Above 1 the base grows on its own, which is rare. Below 1 referrals still multiply paid acquisition, and a loop that turns in two days beats one that takes a month.
Overall conversion fell this month, but conversion went up in every channel. How is that possible?
Whether you catch a mix shift before calling the funnel broken.
A change in traffic mix toward a weaker channel lowers the blended rate even when each channel improves. Break it out before reacting.

That is a mix shift, sometimes called Simpson's paradox. If a low-converting channel, say a new display campaign, grew from 10% to 40% of traffic, the blended rate drops even though each channel improved. I would break conversion out by channel and by new versus returning users, and report the blended number with the mix next to it.
Retargeting ads show the best return in your dashboard. How do you find out if they really drive sales?
How you test incrementality instead of trusting attributed credit.
Retargeting reaches people likely to buy anyway. A randomized holdout shows the true lift, which is often far below the attributed number.

Retargeting reaches people who already visited, many of whom would buy anyway, so last-click credit flatters it. I would randomly hold out 10 to 20% of the audience from the ads and compare purchase rates. In one test like that the dashboard claimed $8 per dollar spent, the holdout showed about $1.50, and we cut that spend in half.
How do you work out how long an A/B test needs to run before you start it?
Whether you plan sample size from power and effect size instead of guessing.
Baseline rate, smallest effect worth detecting, power and significance set the sample size. Traffic sets the days, rounded up to full weeks.

I start with the baseline, say 4% conversion, and the smallest lift worth acting on, say 10% relative. At 80% power and 5% significance that is roughly 38,000 visitors per arm. With 6,000 visitors a day split in two, that is about two weeks. I run full weeks so weekday and weekend users are both in.
Monthly active users are flat. How do you break that number down to find out why?
Whether you use growth accounting to see the flows behind a flat total.
Splits users into new, retained, resurrected and churned. A flat total can hide heavy churn covered by heavy acquisition.

I split this month's actives into new, retained from last month, and resurrected, and I count churned users who were active last month but not now. The quick ratio, new plus resurrected divided by churned, shows the health. Flat with a ratio near 1 and big inflows means we are filling a leaky bucket, so I look at retention first.
You are testing a new onboarding flow. What guardrail metrics do you set, and why?
How you protect the business from a test that wins on one number and hurts others.
Names metrics that must not get worse, such as retention, support tickets, refunds or page speed, with limits written down before launch.

The primary metric is activation, say finishing setup on day one. Guardrails are week-four retention, support tickets per new user, unsubscribe rate and page load time, each with a limit I write down before launch. If activation rises but tickets jump, I don't ship. We may just be pushing people through steps they don't understand.
Paid social has a $40 blended CAC and our target is $60. The CEO wants to triple the spend. What do you say?
Whether you know the next customer usually costs more than the average one.
Separates average from marginal CAC and proposes raising spend in steps while tracking the cost of the extra customers.

The $40 is an average over the cheapest audiences we have already reached. New dollars go to colder audiences, so extra customers cost more. I'd raise spend in steps, maybe 30% at a time, and compute marginal CAC: added spend divided by added customers. We stop scaling when that number reaches $60, not when the average does.
What does net revenue retention above 100% mean, and how is it calculated?
Your grasp of revenue retention in a subscription business.
Same starting customers only: starting revenue plus expansion, minus downgrades and churn, divided by starting revenue. New customers are left out.

Take revenue from the customers we had a year ago. Add what they expanded, subtract downgrades and what churned, and divide by the starting revenue. New customers don't count. Above 100% means the existing base grows on its own despite churn. I also check gross retention, which ignores expansion, to see the churn hiding underneath.
Your test was set to split 50/50, but after a week it shows 52% versus 48% on 200,000 users. What do you do?
Whether you spot a sample ratio mismatch and distrust the results until it is explained.
Treats it as a bug, not noise: a chi-square test shows it is far from chance, so results are not read until the cause is found.

On 200,000 users, a 4,000-user gap per arm is far outside chance; a chi-square test gives a tiny p-value. That is a sample ratio mismatch, so I don't read the results. I look for causes: a redirect that loses users in one arm, bot filtering, a variant that fails before it logs, or assignment that changed mid-test. I fix it and restart.
A team shows you an LTV to CAC ratio of 5 to 1. What makes you doubt it?
How you test a flattering unit-economics number before you trust it.
Asks about margin, churn taken from young cohorts, CAC blended with free users, and costs left out of CAC.

First, is LTV on gross margin or on revenue? Second, the churn rate: if it comes from cohorts only three months old, margin divided by churn can promise years nobody has seen. Third, is CAC blended with free organic users, and does it include salaries and tools? Fix those and 5 to 1 often turns into 2 to 1.
Your test tracked 20 metrics. The main one is flat, but one secondary metric moved with a p-value of 0.03. What do you report?
Whether you understand the multiple comparisons problem.
Knows that with 20 metrics at a 5% cutoff, about one false positive is expected even with no real change. Treats the move as a lead for a new test.

With 20 metrics at a 5% cutoff, I'd expect about one to cross the line by chance even if nothing changed. So I report the main result as flat. The secondary move is a hypothesis, not a finding. A Bonferroni correction here would need p below 0.05 divided by 20, or I rerun a test with that metric as the primary.
You want to test a rider discount in a two-sided marketplace. Why might a normal user-level A/B test give the wrong answer?
Whether you see when test and control groups affect each other.
Explains interference: both groups share the same drivers, so the test group takes supply from control. Suggests region-level or switchback tests.

Riders in both groups compete for the same drivers. If the discount brings more test rides, control riders wait longer and ride less, so the gap looks bigger than the real effect at full launch. I'd randomize by city or region, or run a switchback test that turns the discount on and off for the whole market in time blocks.
Last year's winning tests added up to a 30% lift in conversion, but real conversion rose 5%. Explain the gap.
Whether you understand why test wins rarely add up in the real numbers.
Names the winner's curse, novelty effects, overlapping wins and a changed traffic mix, and proposes a long-term holdout to measure the true total.

Several things. The tests we ship are partly the ones that got lucky, so their measured lift is inflated; that is the winner's curse. Some wins fade once novelty wears off. Wins overlap: two tests fixing the same drop-off do not add up. Traffic mix also changed. Next year I'd keep a small holdout that sees none of the changes, to measure the real combined effect.

growth-marketing.heading: Growth and performance marketing questions
qs: How do CAC, LTV and payback period fit together?
Whether you know the unit economics that decide how much you can spend.
Clear definitions, LTV based on margin rather than revenue, and payback as the cash check that LTV alone hides.

CAC is what we spend to win one paying customer: all acquisition costs divided by new customers. LTV is the gross margin a customer brings over their life, not the revenue. Payback is how many months of margin it takes to earn the CAC back. A good LTV to CAC ratio means little if payback takes three years and we run out of cash first.
How do you set up UTM tags, and what usually goes wrong?
Whether your tracking is clean enough to trust.
A fixed naming rule for source, medium and campaign, and awareness of case errors, typos and tags on internal links.

I keep a shared sheet with the allowed values for source, medium and campaign, all lowercase, and build every link from it. The common breaks are “Facebook” and “facebook” showing as two sources, someone inventing a new medium, and UTM tags on internal site links, which overwrite the real source of the visit. I audit the source report every month.
Our email open rates jumped a few years ago and never came back down. Why might that be, and what do you measure instead?
Whether you know how privacy changes affect email metrics.
Some mail apps preload images for privacy, which inflates opens; emails are judged on clicks, conversions and revenue.

Since 2021, a major mail app has loaded email images in the background for privacy, so many emails count as opened whether or not anyone read them. That makes opens unreliable for subject line tests and list cleaning. I judge emails on clicks, conversions and unsubscribes, and I define engaged subscribers by clicks or site visits, not opens.
Walk me through the email sequence you would build for someone who just started a 14-day free trial.
How you plan lifecycle email around what the user does, not a calendar.
Emails triggered by behavior that push the one action tied to paying, with separate paths for active and stuck users.

First I find the action that best predicts paying, say inviting a teammate. Day 0 is a welcome with one step to take. Users who do it get tips for the next feature; those who do not get a nudge on day 2 and a short how-to on day 5. Near the end comes a reminder of what they built and the plan price. I measure trial-to-paid, not opens.
You find out a promo email went to people who unsubscribed last week. What do you do?
How you handle a compliance mistake and fix its cause.
Stops further sends, owns the mistake, knows CAN-SPAM requires opt-outs to be honored within 10 business days, and fixes the gap.

I pause any scheduled sends to that segment and tell my manager right away. Under CAN-SPAM, opt-outs must be honored within 10 business days, so this can be a legal issue, not just an annoyance. I confirm those people are suppressed now, find the cause, often a list import that skipped the suppression list, and add a check before every send.
Our emails started landing in spam folders. How do you work out why?
Your knowledge of email deliverability and sender reputation.
Checks authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), complaint rates, domain reputation and recent changes to lists or volume.

First I check authentication: SPF, DKIM and DMARC, the records that prove mail really comes from our domain, must all pass. Then complaint rates and reputation in the mailbox providers' sender dashboards. Then recent changes: a new list import, a sudden jump in volume, or mailing people who have not engaged in a year.
Your cost per acquisition on paid social doubled overnight. Where do you look first?
How you troubleshoot a sudden performance drop in a sensible order.
Rules out broken tracking and site problems before blaming the auction, and checks what changed on your own side.

I check whether sales really dropped or just stopped being tracked: compare the platform to our backend and test the pixel and checkout. Then the landing page: is it up, fast, and is the offer still live? Then our own changes, like a new audience or big edits. Only then the auction: rising cost per thousand impressions or a holiday spike.
A campaign has a great cost per acquisition, so the team wants to multiply its budget by five tomorrow. What do you advise?
Whether you understand diminishing returns when scaling paid spend.
Expects cost per customer to rise as spend reaches less likely buyers; scales in steps and watches the cost of the added customers.

That number is an average from the cheapest buyers the platform could find. More spend reaches people less likely to convert, so the extra customers cost more. A big jump can also send the campaign back into the platform's learning phase. I would raise budget in steps every few days, track the cost of the added customers, and stop where it crosses our target.
The CFO wants to cut branded search ads because people searching our name would find us anyway. How do you answer?
Whether you can tell credited results from results the ads truly caused.
Grants the point may be partly true, checks competitor bidding, and proposes a regional pause test before deciding.

She may be right; brand ads get credit for many sales that would happen anyway. But if competitors bid on our name, pausing can hand them those clicks. I would pause brand ads in a set of matched regions for a few weeks and compare total search sales, paid plus organic, with regions still running. The difference is what the ads really add.
Each ad platform reports its own conversions, and together they claim 40% more sales than we actually had. How do you decide where budget goes?
How you handle attribution overlap and make budget calls on imperfect data.
Explains double counting across platforms, treats the backend as the truth, and uses blended CAC plus holdout tests to split budget.

Each platform counts any sale it touched within its own window, including ad views, so one customer can be claimed three times. I treat our backend as the total and watch blended CAC: all spend divided by all new customers. To split budget, I run holdout tests on the biggest channels and use the results to discount each platform's reported numbers.
A partner offers to send a promo for our product to their email list. What has to be true before you say yes?
Whether you know the US email law that applies even when someone else hits send.
CAN-SPAM basics stated correctly, plus the point that we can be held responsible for a send that promotes us.

Under CAN-SPAM, the company whose product is promoted can be held responsible, not just the sender. So I check for an honest from line and subject, clear notice that it is an ad, a valid postal address and a working opt-out honored within 10 business days. I also ask how they built the list, because a bad list hurts our brand too.
A paid social ad that worked for two months now gets fewer clicks each week. How do you tell if it is creative fatigue?
How you read ad delivery data before changing anything.
Looks at frequency and click rate over time, rules out other causes, and has a plan to refresh creative.

I chart frequency, the average number of times each person saw the ad, next to click rate and cost per result. If frequency climbs while clicks fall and the audience has not changed, it is fatigue. Then I launch new concepts, not just new colors, and widen the audience. If frequency is flat, I look at auction costs or tracking instead.
Site conversion rate fell this quarter, yet it went up in every single channel. How is that possible?
Whether you can spot a change in traffic mix behind a blended number.
Explains mix shift: more traffic from a low-converting source pulls the average down even when every part improves.

The mix changed. Say we scaled display ads, which convert at 0.5%, while search converts at 4%. Each channel improved a bit, but display grew from 10% to 40% of visits, so the blended rate dropped. I would report conversion by channel and track volume and cost per customer, not the blended rate alone.
Your test is set to split users 50/50, but after 100,000 users you have 52,000 in one arm and 48,000 in the other. What do you do?
Whether you catch a broken experiment before reading its results.
Calls it a sample ratio mismatch, knows it is far beyond chance at this size, and finds the cause before trusting any result.

That gap is far too big to be chance at this size, so I treat it as a sample ratio mismatch and do not read the results. Common causes are a redirect that loses users in one arm, bots, caching, or assignment happening after a filter. I find and fix the bug, then restart the test, because the users who went missing are rarely random.
The team checks the test dashboard every morning and wants to stop as soon as it shows significance. What is the problem?
Whether you know how repeated peeking breaks a standard test.
Explains that stopping at the first significant look inflates false positives, and offers a fixed horizon or a sequential method.

A standard test assumes one look at a sample size set in advance. If you check daily and stop at the first p below 0.05, random swings will cross that line far more often than 5% of the time. I would fix the sample size from a power calculation and wait, or use a sequential testing method built for checking along the way.
Someone tested 20 subject lines against the control, and one won with p = 0.04. Do we roll it out?
How you handle many comparisons at once.
Notes that one false winner is expected by chance among 20, and confirms with a correction or a retest.

Not yet. With 20 comparisons at the 5% level, we expect about one false winner even if nothing works; the chance of at least one is about 64%. I would apply a correction such as Bonferroni, which here means p below 0.0025, or rerun the winner alone against control. If it wins again, we ship it.
A new signup page raised trial starts by 15%, but paid conversions from those trials fell. Which result wins?
Whether you choose a success metric that tracks real value, not the nearest number.
Picks the metric closest to revenue as primary, reads the signup lift as lower-quality volume, and sets guardrails next time.

Paid conversions win, because that is where the money is. The page probably pulled in people with lower intent. I would compare revenue per visitor across both arms, and if it is flat or down, I would not ship. Next time I would make revenue the main metric and track signup rate and refunds as guardrails.
How would you prove our lifecycle emails bring in revenue that would not have come anyway?
Whether you can measure incremental impact instead of counting clicks.
A randomized holdout that gets no marketing emails, compared on revenue per user over a set period.

I would randomly hold out about 10% of eligible users from all marketing emails, while they still get receipts and password resets. After a set period, say 90 days, I compare revenue per user between the two groups. The difference is what email adds. Revenue credited to clicks overstates it, because many of those buyers were coming back anyway.
Walk me through a geo test to measure what a paid channel really adds.
Your ability to design an incrementality test when you cannot randomize individual users.
Matched regions, random assignment, a pre-period check, a long enough run, and a comparison against a predicted baseline.

I pick regions whose sales moved together in the past year and randomly assign some to change spend, for example turning the channel off. Before launch I check that control regions predict test regions well. I run it long enough to cover the buying cycle, then compare actual sales in test regions with what the controls predicted. The gap is the lift.
Our marketing mix model says paid social returns half of what our lift test showed. Which do you trust?
How you reconcile two measurement methods that disagree.
Knows the lift test is causal but narrow and the model is broad but correlational, and uses tests to calibrate the model.

For that channel at that spend level, I trust the lift test more, because it was randomized. A mix model learns from patterns over time and can confuse channels whose spend rises together. But first I check both measured the same thing: time window, spend level, and the same sales outcome. Then I use the test result to calibrate the model, and retest as spend changes.

growth-product-manager.heading: Growth product manager questions
qs: What does activation mean in a growth funnel, and how would you pick an activation metric?
Whether you understand the step between signing up and getting real value from the product.
Activation is the first moment of real value. The metric is an early action that predicts long-term retention, and you test that link before trusting it.

Activation is when a new user first gets the core value, not just creates an account. I look at which early actions retained users took that churned users did not, like inviting a teammate in week one. Then I run a test that pushes that action and check that retention moves too, so I know it is a cause and not just a sign of keen users.
What is the difference between a funnel and a growth loop?
Whether you think about growth as a system that feeds itself, not only as a set of steps.
A funnel turns outside traffic into users in a straight line. A loop uses what users do to bring in the next users, so growth compounds.

A funnel is linear: traffic comes in from ads or search, and each step loses some people. A loop feeds itself. For example, users publish public pages, those pages rank in search, new visitors sign up and publish more pages. I map both, but I look hardest for loops because each turn adds new input without new spend.
How do you read a retention curve, and what shape worries you?
Whether you can judge product health from cohort retention data.
A curve that flattens shows a core group that stays. A curve that keeps sliding toward zero means growth spending is filling a leaking bucket.

I plot the share of each signup cohort still active by week since signup. I want it to drop early and then flatten, because a flat tail means some users found lasting value. If it keeps falling toward zero, I fix retention before buying more traffic. I also compare cohorts: newer curves sitting higher means our changes are working.
A test raised signups by 8% but paid conversion fell. What do you do?
How you use guardrail metrics and look past the first step of the funnel.
Do not ship on the top-line win. Check the downstream metric that pays the bills, find why quality dropped, and judge on revenue per visitor.

I would not ship it yet. More signups that pay less often may mean we pulled in people with weak intent, for example by hiding the price. I compare paid users and revenue per visitor across both groups. If revenue is flat or down, the win is not real. I would set paid conversion as a guardrail metric before the next test, so the trade-off is agreed up front.
Your traffic is low and a test would need four months to reach significance. What do you do?
How you keep learning when classic A/B testing is too slow.
Test bolder changes, use a higher-volume metric nearer the change, and add research. Ship small reversible changes with monitoring rather than wait.

Small tweaks are not worth testing at that volume, so I test bigger changes that could move the metric a lot. I measure a step closer to the change, like trial starts instead of paid plans. I add user interviews and session recordings. For low-risk changes that are easy to undo, I ship and watch the trend, and I say clearly that this is weaker evidence.
A test you are running for 14 days looks like a big win after day 3. The head of marketing wants to stop it and ship. What do you say?
Whether you understand peeking, novelty effects and weekly cycles.
Stopping a fixed-length test at the first good result raises false positives. Early lifts often shrink, and full weeks are needed to cover weekday patterns.

I would explain that checking daily and stopping at the first win makes false wins much more likely. Early lifts also shrink once the novelty wears off, and three days miss the weekend pattern. I would keep the planned length. If speed matters often, I would switch to a sequential testing method built to allow early looks, and agree on that before the test starts.
You are testing a new trial length, but paid conversion only shows up after 60 days. How do you run the test?
How you handle tests whose true outcome comes late.
Pick a leading indicator that past data ties to paying, decide the rules in advance, and still confirm with the late revenue result.

I would find an early signal that predicted paying in past cohorts, such as using the key feature three times in the trial. I would read that first, but keep a cohort from each group and check real paid conversion and refunds at 60 days before calling it final. Trial length also changes when people pay, so I compare at the same days after signup.
Your 50/50 test shows 52,000 users in one group and 48,000 in the other. What do you do?
Whether you spot a sample ratio mismatch and know it makes results untrustworthy.
A gap that size is far beyond chance, so assignment or logging is broken. Do not read the results until the cause is found and fixed.

With 100,000 users, a 52/48 split is far too big to be chance; a chi-square test on the counts would confirm it. Something is wrong: a redirect losing users in one group, bots, a crash, or events not logged. I would pause any decision, find the cause with engineering, fix it and rerun. A biased split can make a loser look like a winner.
The finance team asks you to make cancelling harder to cut churn. How do you respond?
Your judgement on growth tactics that hurt trust or break consumer rules.
Refuse to hide or block cancellation. Offer honest save options like pause or downgrade, learn why people leave, and involve legal on subscription rules.

I would say no to hiding the button or adding hoops. It leads to chargebacks, bad reviews and legal risk, since US consumer protection laws on auto-renewing subscriptions expect cancelling to be simple; legal should review the flow. Instead I would add a short reason question and honest offers like pausing or a cheaper plan, then fix the top reasons people leave.
When would you choose a free trial over a freemium plan, and what is a reverse trial?
Your grasp of the main models for turning free users into paying ones.
Ties the choice to how fast users see value and the cost of serving free users, and defines a reverse trial correctly.

A trial fits when the value shows up within days and serving free users is costly. Freemium fits when free users spread the product or cost little to serve. A reverse trial gives new users the full paid plan for a set time, then drops them to the free plan instead of locking them out. They feel what they lose but stay in the product.
Which guardrail metrics would you set on an onboarding experiment, and why?
Whether you protect the business from a test that wins its own metric and hurts something else.
Names guardrails tied to real harm, such as retention, paid conversion, support load or speed, and agrees in advance what drop stops the test.

The primary metric might be activation within 7 days. Guardrails would be day-30 retention, paid conversion, support tickets per new user and load time of the new screens. Before launch I agree with the team how much of a drop in each one blocks shipping, so nobody argues about it after the results come in.
How do you pick the minimum detectable effect before you start a test?
How you size a test from business value, not from hope.
Starts from the smallest lift worth shipping, then uses the baseline rate and traffic to check the test can detect it in a reasonable time.

I ask what the smallest lift is that pays for building and maintaining the change. Then I put the baseline conversion rate, that lift, our traffic and the usual 80% power into a sample size calculator. If the answer is ten weeks, I either test a bolder change or pick a metric that moves more often and still predicts revenue.
Users who invite a teammate in their first week retain twice as well. Do you make inviting a required onboarding step?
Whether you can tell a sign of engaged users from a cause of retention.
Treats the link as a hypothesis, tests a nudge to invite, and judges it on retention rather than on invite count.

Not right away. Teams that were already serious may both invite and stay, so the invite could just be a sign. I would test an invite prompt against no prompt and measure 30-day retention, not invites. If invites rise and retention does not, the invite was a symptom, and forcing it would only add friction and lose some signups.
A redesigned home screen lifts engagement 12% in week one, but the lift shrinks every week. How do you read that?
Whether you spot a novelty effect and know how to measure the lasting effect.
Names the novelty effect, splits new and existing users, and runs long enough to see where the lift settles.

It looks like a novelty effect: existing users click on what is new, then fall back to old habits. I would split results into new users, who have no old habit, and existing users, and plot the lift by week since first exposure. If new users show a steady lift, the design may be better. If both groups fade toward zero, I would not ship it on an engagement claim.
How would you test a price increase on your main paid plan?
How you run a pricing test without hurting trust or reading the wrong metric.
Tests on new visitors only, judges revenue per visitor and early churn rather than conversion alone, and plans for existing customers.

I would show the new price only to new visitors, keep it the same for each person across visits, and leave current customers on their price. The main metric is revenue per visitor, not conversion, since a higher price can lose buyers and still earn more. I also watch refunds and month-two churn, because a price that converts can still cancel faster.
A test lost overall but won clearly on Android. A stakeholder wants to ship it to Android only. What do you do?
Whether you resist picking a winning segment after the fact.
Treats a segment found afterwards as a new hypothesis, looks for a real reason, and confirms it with a new test before shipping.

If we slice results enough ways, some segment will win by chance. So first I ask whether there is a real reason, like a layout that suits small screens. If there is, I run a new test on Android only, with that as the planned hypothesis. If it wins again, we ship it there. If we cannot explain it, I treat it as noise.
You are testing a bigger referral reward, but people in the test group invite friends who land in the control group. What is the problem, and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand interference between test groups in social or referral features.
Explains the groups are no longer independent so the gap is biased, and credits referred users to the inviter's group or randomizes by cluster.

The control group gains users because of the treatment, so the two groups are no longer separate and the measured gap is off. I would credit every referred user to the group of the person who invited them and judge the test on new paid users per inviter. If spillover is large, I would randomize by team or by region instead of by user.
Your team shipped six winning tests this quarter, each with a 3 to 5% lift, but revenue barely moved. What could explain it?
How you reason about why test wins do not add up in the business.
Names real causes: false positives, overstated winners, local metrics that shift users rather than add them, and overlap; proposes a holdout.

Usually several things at once. Some wins were likely false positives, and the winners we pick tend to overstate their true lift. Several tests moved one funnel step, so users may just have dropped off at the next step instead. Lifts on the same users also do not simply add up. I would keep a holdout group that sees none of the changes to measure the real combined effect.
Would you keep a long-term holdout group, and what does it cost you?
Your judgement on measuring the lasting effect of a growth program against its costs.
Describes a small group kept off all changes for months, and weighs lost revenue, code upkeep and user fairness against a true long-term read.

Yes, for a program of many changes I would keep about 5% of new users on the old experience for a quarter or two. It is the only clean read on whether our changes add up and last. The costs are real: those users get a worse product, the old code must be maintained, and support needs to know why some users see something different.

hardware-engineer.heading: Hardware engineer questions
qs: Why do we put small decoupling capacitors right next to the power pins of a chip?
Whether you understand power delivery on a board, not just the rule of thumb.
Chips draw fast current bursts; the cap supplies them locally. Placement and loop inductance matter more than the value.

Every chip pulls current in fast bursts when it switches. The path back to the main supply has inductance, so the voltage at the pin dips. A small ceramic cap at the pin supplies that burst. I place it as close as I can, with short, wide connections and a via straight to ground, because the loop inductance matters more than the value printed on the cap.
Why does an I2C bus need pull-up resistors, and how do you pick their value?
Your grasp of a common interface and the trade-off behind a simple part choice.
Open-drain lines can only pull low. Too large a value gives slow rising edges; too small exceeds the sink current the devices allow.

I2C lines are open-drain: devices can only pull a line low, so a resistor pulls it high. Too large a value and the bus capacitance makes the rising edge too slow for the bus speed. Too small and the devices must sink more current than their spec allows. I estimate bus capacitance, check rise time against the spec for the mode, then confirm on the scope.
A linear regulator takes 12 V down to 3.3 V at 300 mA. Is that a problem?
Whether you check power dissipation and temperature before trusting a part.
Power is the voltage drop times the current, about 2.6 W here. Junction temperature is ambient plus power times thermal resistance, checked against the limit.

A linear regulator burns the difference: 8.7 V times 0.3 A is about 2.6 W. I multiply that by the package's junction-to-ambient thermal resistance, add the worst-case ambient, and compare with the maximum junction temperature. In a small package that fails. I would use a buck converter, or a part and copper area that can actually shed the heat.
Why shouldn't a fast signal trace cross a split in the ground plane?
Your understanding of return current, which drives most layout decisions.
High-frequency return current flows in the plane right under the trace. A split forces a detour, a large loop that radiates and breaks impedance.

At high frequency, the return current flows in the plane directly under the trace, because that path has the lowest inductance. A split forces it to detour around the gap. That makes a big loop, which radiates and picks up noise, and the impedance jumps. If a signal has to change reference, I put a stitching via or capacitor right next to the crossing.
You see heavy ringing on a fast clock edge on the scope. What do you check?
Whether you can tell a real signal problem from a measurement problem.
The probe setup first, especially a long ground lead. Then trace length, termination and impedance mismatch.

First I suspect my measurement. A long ground clip on the probe forms a loop that rings by itself, so I switch to a short ground spring at the test point and check the probe bandwidth. If the ringing stays, I look at the trace: its length against the edge rate, missing series termination, impedance mismatch. A small series resistor near the driver often fixes it.
What is the difference between a setup time violation and a hold time violation, and how do you fix each?
Your timing knowledge for digital and chip design.
Setup is too slow a path; fix with less logic, pipelining or a slower clock. Hold is data arriving too early; add delay, since clock speed does not help.

Setup time is how long data must be stable before the clock edge; hold time is how long after. A setup violation means the path is too slow, so I cut logic between flops, add a pipeline stage, or relax the clock. A hold violation means data arrives too soon. Slowing the clock does not help, so I add delay on that path. That makes hold the more dangerous one.
Prototype boards arrive and you find a footprint error you made. What do you do?
How you own a mistake and keep the project moving.
Report it fast, find a rework so testing continues, and fix the root cause in the library, not only this board.

I tell the lead the same day and log it, so nobody builds more. Then I see what the boards can still do: if two pins are swapped, I can cut traces and add wires, or put the part on an adapter, so testing goes on. I fix the footprint in the library, not just this design, and recheck the other parts made from the same source before the next spin.
The board works, but a pre-compliance emissions scan shows a peak over the limit at 150 MHz. How do you approach it?
How you find and fix an EMC problem methodically.
Trace the peak to a source, often a clock harmonic, locate it with a near-field probe, then fix from cheapest to costliest.

First I look for the source: 150 MHz could be the 6th harmonic of a 25 MHz clock or the 3rd of a 50 MHz one. I sweep the board and cables with a near-field probe to see where it is strongest; cables are often the antenna. Then I try fixes from cheap to costly: slower edges with series resistors, a ferrite on the cable, better shield grounding, then layout changes.
A regulator on your board has a 40-week lead time and purchasing found a "drop-in" replacement. What do you check before approving it?
Your judgement on part substitutions and the risk they hide.
Pin-compatible is not equivalent: compare datasheets in detail, test real boards with the new part, and document it as an approved alternate.

Pin-compatible does not mean the same. I compare the datasheets line by line: pinout, enable logic, switching frequency, stability with my output capacitors, soft start, thermal pad. Then I build a few boards with it and repeat the key tests: load steps, ripple, startup, temperature. Only then do I add it to the bill of materials as an approved alternate.
How do you choose the load capacitors for a crystal?
Whether you know the math behind a part many people copy from a reference design.
The series formula with stray capacitance included, and a check of the real frequency on the board.

The crystal datasheet gives a load capacitance, say 12 pF. The two caps act in series, plus pin and board stray, often a few pF. So CL = C1×C2/(C1+C2) + Cstray; with 3 pF of stray, that gives 18 pF each. Then I measure the frequency on the prototype through a buffered clock output, because a probe on the crystal pin changes what I am measuring.
How do you measure the output ripple of a switching regulator with a scope?
Your lab technique on a measurement that is easy to get wrong.
No long ground clip, a short ground at the output capacitor, the right bandwidth limit, and awareness of probe noise.

I take off the long ground clip, because its loop picks up switching noise and shows spikes that are not on the rail. I use a spring ground tip right across the output capacitor, AC coupling, and the 20 MHz bandwidth limit if the spec is defined that way. For millivolt ripple I prefer a 1x probe or a rail probe, since a 10x probe raises the noise floor.
A schematic shows a 10 µF, 6.3 V, X5R capacitor in an 0402 case on a 5 V rail. What concerns you?
Whether you know that ceramic capacitors lose capacitance under DC voltage.
DC bias derating of Class II ceramics, a check of the maker's curve, and the knock-on effect on the regulator.

Class II ceramics like X5R lose capacitance under DC bias, and small cases with low voltage ratings lose the most. At 5 V on a 6.3 V part in 0402, the real value can be a small fraction of 10 µF. I check the maker's DC bias curve, usually move to a larger case or a higher rating, and then recheck the regulator's stability with the real value.
How do you estimate the junction temperature of a part, and why should you not trust the first number?
Your thermal basics and whether you know the limits of datasheet figures.
Tj = Ta + P × θJA, with the caveat that θJA comes from a standard test board, then a better method on the real board.

First pass is Tj = Ta + P × θJA. At 1 W, 40 °C/W and 50 °C ambient, that is about 90 °C. But θJA is measured on a standard JEDEC test board, and my copper, airflow and neighbors change it a lot. On the prototype I measure the top of the case and use ψJT from the datasheet: Tj is about Tcase + ψJT × P. For tight margins I run a thermal simulation.
Walk me through the first power-up of a new prototype board.
How you bring up a board without destroying it.
Checks for shorts before power, a current-limited supply, rails one at a time, then clocks, resets and debug.

Before power, I measure resistance from each rail to ground and compare it with an unpowered good board if I have one. Then I use a bench supply with a low current limit and watch the current as it comes up. I check each rail and the power sequence, look for hot parts with a thermal camera, then check clocks and reset, connect the debugger, and only then load firmware.
How do you protect a USB connector from ESD, and where does the protection go?
Whether you place protection so the strike goes to ground before it reaches the chip.
A low-capacitance TVS right at the connector, a short path to ground, and clamping checked against the chip.

I put a low-capacitance TVS diode array right at the connector, first on the line, with a short, wide path to ground through several vias. The strike should go to ground at the edge of the board, not through the chip. On the data pair the diode capacitance must be low enough not to hurt the signal, and I compare the clamping voltage with what the chip can take.
Your regulator output is set by a resistor divider. How do you prove it stays within the ±3% the load needs?
Whether you do a real tolerance analysis instead of using nominal values.
Each error source at its worst corner: reference, resistors, drift, load regulation, ripple, and a fix if it does not fit.

Vout = Vref × (1 + R1/R2). I take the reference tolerance over temperature from the datasheet, add resistor tolerance and drift, and compute the extremes with each at its worst. Then I add load regulation, ripple and transient dips. If the worst case does not fit, I move to 0.1% resistors or a tighter regulator rather than hope the parts land near nominal.
How do you pass a multi-bit counter value from one clock domain to another?
Whether you know why a two-flop synchronizer on each bit is not enough for a bus.
Bits can be caught mid-change; Gray code for counters, an async FIFO or handshake for data, and proper constraints.

If I synchronize each bit on its own, the receiver can catch a mix of old and new bits, because they settle at different times. For a counter I convert it to Gray code, so only one bit changes per step, then synchronize. For general data I use an asynchronous FIFO or a handshake, where a synchronized flag says the data is stable. I also constrain those paths for the timing tool.
How do you decide how much decoupling the core rail of a large FPGA needs?
Whether you design the power network to a target instead of copying a capacitor count.
Target impedance from allowed ripple and current step, held across frequency, verified by simulation and measurement.

I start from target impedance: allowed ripple divided by the current step. For a 1.0 V rail with 3% ripple and a 3 A step, that is 10 milliohms. The path from regulator through bulk caps, ceramics and planes should stay under that up to the frequency where the package and die capacitance take over. I simulate with the vendor's tool, then check the rail under load in the lab.
The launch date is fixed, and the first production run would need two rework wires on every board. Do you ship it?
Your judgement when schedule and reliability pull in opposite directions.
No reflex answer: weigh the risk of the specific fix, get agreement in writing, and have the respin already moving.

Not without a plan. I check whether the wires can be reliable: glued down, inspected, covered by the production test, and allowed by the customer and any certification. If the risk is low and the decision is written down, a short run with documented rework can be fine, with the corrected board already ordered. If the wire is on a fast signal or a safety circuit, I say no and explain why.

hardware-program-manager.heading: Hardware program manager questions
qs: What is the difference between EVT, DVT and PVT builds?
Whether you know the stages a hardware product goes through before mass production.
Each build has a clear purpose: does the design work, does it meet every spec on production tools, can the line build it at rate.

EVT, engineering validation, checks that the design works, often with soft tooling and some hand fixes. DVT, design validation, uses production-intent parts and tools to prove the design meets all specs and passes reliability and certification tests. PVT, production validation, runs on the real line at speed to prove the process, the yield and the test stations.
What do you check in a build readiness review before a pilot build at the factory?
How you keep a costly build from starting without what it needs.
A concrete list: parts and their revisions, tooling, fixtures, test software, work instructions, open issues, and a clear go or no-go.

I confirm every line of the bill of materials is on hand or arriving before its station needs it, at the right revision. I check tool and fixture status, test station software, work instructions and the unit count per configuration. Open issues from the last build get an owner or a known workaround. Then we call go or no-go out loud, with the factory in the room.
A key chip has a 40-week lead time and your design is not frozen yet. How do you handle it?
Whether you manage supply risk before it turns into a schedule problem.
Flags the part early, orders or forecasts in time, weighs the cost of an early buy against a slip, and looks for a second source.

I get engineering to commit to that part now, even if the rest of the design still moves, and place a purchase order or a firm forecast with the supplier. If finance worries about the liability, I show the cost of the buy next to the cost of a 40-week slip. In parallel I ask whether a pin-compatible second source exists.
The first shots from a new injection mold show sink marks and one dimension out of tolerance. What happens next?
Your grasp of tooling and how fixes move through the toolmaker.
Measure everything, separate what process tuning can fix from what needs steel or design changes, and plan the next tool trial into the schedule.

I get a full dimensional report on the parts, not just the one flagged. Sink marks often come from thick walls; process changes like longer pack time may reduce them, or the wall may need to be made thinner. For the dimension, if the tool was cut steel safe, the toolmaker removes steel to bring it in. I book the next trial and decide which build those parts will feed.
Engineering wants a design change after tooling is cut, two weeks before DVT. How do you decide?
Your judgement on change control when every change costs time and money.
Asks what problem the change fixes and what it costs in tooling, parts and retesting, then decides through a formal change process.

I ask what breaks if we do not change it: a safety or spec failure is different from a nice-to-have. Then I get the full cost: tool rework, scrapped parts, new lead times and which tests must be redone. If it must happen, it goes through an engineering change order so suppliers, the factory and the BOM all move together. If it can wait, it goes into a later revision.
A supplier sends an end-of-life notice for a part in your product. What do you do?
How you handle supply changes during the life of a product.
Checks the last-time-buy date and quantity against the forecast, and starts qualifying a replacement well before the stock runs out.

I find the last order date and work out how much stock we need until a replacement is qualified, plus a buffer for repairs. Purchasing places the last-time buy. Engineering picks an alternate part, and I plan the validation, any retesting and the change order so the switch happens before the stock we bought is gone.
First-pass yield at PVT is 82% and the target for mass production is 95%. Walk me through what you do.
How you drive a yield problem to its root cause with the factory.
A Pareto of failures, the biggest ones first, design, part and process causes kept apart, and fixes tracked with data every day.

I get the failure data by station and failure mode and sort it into a Pareto chart. Usually two or three modes cause most of the loss. For each, we decide if it is design, a supplier part or the process, and we check the test station itself for false failures. Each fix has an owner and a date, and I review yield daily until it holds at target.
When do you plan regulatory testing, such as FCC emissions testing and safety certification, and why?
Whether you build compliance into the schedule instead of finding problems at the end.
Early pre-scans to find problems, formal tests on production-intent units, and margin in the plan for a failed test and a retest.

I book a pre-scan at a lab around EVT to catch emissions problems while the board can still change. Formal testing runs on DVT units with production-intent parts, because results must match what we ship. I book lab time early, since slots fill up, and keep a few weeks of margin for a fail, a fix and a retest. Any later change gets reviewed for whether it needs retesting.
The factory says a supplier delay will push the pilot build back two weeks, and the launch date is fixed. What do you do?
How you handle a schedule slip and the choices you give leadership.
Confirms the facts, finds real recovery options with their cost and risk, and tells stakeholders early with a recommendation.

First I check the delay myself with the supplier and ask for a recovery date with evidence. Then I look at options: faster shipping, a partial build with the parts we have, overlapping some tests, or another approved source. I take leadership two or three options with cost and risk for each, plus my recommendation, the same week. Bad news only gets worse with time.
Three weeks after launch, returns show a power button failing in the field. How do you run the response?
How you lead containment and root cause when the product is already with customers.
Contain first, find the root cause from returned units, fix design or process through change control, and verify the fix before closing.

First, containment: I check by date code and lot whether units in the warehouse and on the line are affected, and hold suspect stock. We pull returned units for failure analysis and compare them with good ones. Once we know the cause, design, part or process, we fix it with a change order and confirm the fix on new builds. Support and leadership get the failure rate every week.
What is a first article inspection, and when do you require one?
Whether you know how a new part is proven against its drawing before production.
Every characteristic on the drawing measured on early parts from the production process, repeated when the tool, process, material or site changes.

It is a full check of the first parts made by the real production process: every dimension, note and material call-out on the drawing, recorded in a report. I require it for each new part and again whenever the tool, the process, the material or the supplier site changes. Parts without a passed first article do not go into a build.
How does change control work once the factory is building your product?
Your grasp of the engineering change order process and what a change touches.
A formal request, an impact review across cost, stock, tooling and certification, a clear start point, and a decision on old inventory.

Every change goes in as a change request. Before approval we review cost, tooling, stock on hand and on order, test results, and whether certifications are affected. The board approves it with an effective date or serial number. Then the BOM is updated, the factory confirms it, and we decide what happens to old parts: use as is, rework or scrap.
What does a Cpk of 1.33 tell you, and when do you trust the number?
Whether you can read a process capability figure and know its limits.
Cpk 1.33 puts the mean at least four standard deviations from the nearest spec limit, and it only means something for a stable process.

Cpk compares the spread of a process to the spec limits and accounts for how centered it is. At 1.33 the average sits at least four standard deviations from the nearest limit, a common target for key dimensions. I trust it only if the process is stable on a control chart and the parts, often 30 or more, come from the production tool.
How do you decide how many units to build at EVT and who gets them?
How you plan a prototype build around what each team really needs to learn.
A build matrix from each team's test plan, configurations listed, spares included, and a cost and lead-time check before the number is fixed.

I ask each team for its test plan and the units it needs: electrical, mechanical, firmware, reliability, a pre-scan for emissions. I put that in a build matrix by configuration, add about ten percent spares for failures, and check it against part lead times and cost. Last time asks came to 160 units; we cut to 120 by sharing units between tests.
How do you use takt time when you plan the ramp with the factory?
Your ability to turn demand into a line plan the factory can run.
Takt is available time divided by demand; every station must beat it, and the slowest station sets real output.

Takt time is available production time divided by the units we need. Two shifts with 20 working hours is 72,000 seconds; for 3,000 units a day, takt is 24 seconds, or 150 units an hour. Then I compare each station's cycle time to 24 seconds. The slowest one is the bottleneck, so we balance work or add a second fixture there before we ramp.
In the DVT drop test, one unit out of 30 cracks. The mechanical lead calls it an outlier. What do you do?
How you treat a single test failure when people want to move on.
No dismissing it before failure analysis; check the unit, the setup and the part history, then retest with a larger sample.

One crack is a signal until failure analysis says otherwise. I send the unit to the lab and check the drop orientation, the height, and the part's mold cavity and date. If the crack starts at a thin wall or sharp corner, it is a design issue. I rerun with more units on that orientation and keep the DVT exit item open until we know the cause.
You find out the factory has been using a different capacitor than the approved one, without telling you. How do you handle it?
How you handle an unapproved part substitution and contain the risk.
Contain first, find the affected lots, assess the part, then fix the process so no change happens without approval.

First I stop the substitute from being used and find which lots and serial numbers have it. Engineering compares the datasheets and we test affected units. If the part is acceptable, we approve it formally through a deviation and add it to the approved vendor list. Then I go back to the contract: no part change without written approval, and I audit their records.
Who should own the production tooling, and what do you put in the agreement?
Your commercial sense about tooling paid for by your company.
If you pay for the tool, the contract says you own it, it is tagged, maintained, insured and can be moved, with a stated tool life.

If we pay for the tool, we should own it, and the agreement says so in writing. The tool is tagged as ours, the supplier maintains it for a stated shot life and insures it, and we can move it to another supplier with notice. I also ask for the steel type, the cavity count and photos at handoff, so a dispute or a move later is not a fight.
How do you decide whether a program is ready to exit DVT?
Your judgement on gate decisions with open issues still on the list.
Exit criteria agreed before the build, open issues ranked by severity, and a conditional exit only with owners and dates.

We agree the exit criteria before the build: all design verification tests run, results reviewed, no open issue that could cause safety problems or a field failure. On exit day I bring the open list ranked by severity. Minor items can go to PVT with an owner and a date. If a serious one is still open, I recommend we hold, and I show leadership what that costs.
Leadership wants to save six weeks by merging DVT and PVT into one build. What do you tell them?
How you push back on schedule pressure with risk, cost and options.
The real risk in plain terms, what each build proves, and options that save time without skipping what must be learned.

I explain what we would lose: DVT proves the design, PVT proves the factory can build it at rate. Merge them and a design fix forces a tool change during the line ramp. I offer options: start PVT line setup during DVT, use production tools early, or run a small DVT-2 only on the risky parts. Then I show the time and risk of each so they can choose.

harness-engineer.heading: Wire harness engineer and technician questions
qs: What is a formboard, and why do harness shops use one?
Whether you know how harnesses are actually built on the shop floor.
A full-scale layout board that fixes branch lengths and positions, so every harness comes out the same.

It is a board with the harness drawing printed at full scale, with pegs or fixtures at each branch point and connector. The builder lays wires along the paths, so lengths, breakout points and tape locations match the drawing every time. It also lets a new builder work from the board instead of measuring each wire.
How do you choose the wire gauge for a circuit?
Your grasp of the electrical sizing behind every harness.
Current and inrush, voltage drop over the real run length, temperature and bundle derating, then the fuse. Not just a chart lookup.

I start with the steady current and any inrush. Then I check voltage drop over the actual run length, since a long run at 12 V can need a bigger wire than the current alone suggests. I derate for ambient temperature and for how many loaded wires share the bundle. Finally I make sure the fuse protects that wire.
What does the fuse in a circuit actually protect?
Whether you understand circuit protection the way a harness designer must.
The wire. The fuse must open before the wire overheats, so it sits above the load but below what the wire can safely carry.

Mainly the wire, not the device. If a wire chafes and shorts to ground, the fuse has to open before the insulation melts. So I pick a fuse above the normal load and inrush but below what the wire can safely carry in that bundle and temperature. If someone upsizes a fuse, the wire has to be upsized too.
How do you tell a good crimp from a bad one?
Whether you know the measurable checks behind crimp quality.
Visual checks, crimp height to the terminal maker's spec, pull test, cross-sections on new setups, with IPC/WHMA-A-620 as the acceptance reference.

Visually I want strands just visible past the wire crimp, a small bellmouth (a slight flare where the wire enters), no strands outside the barrel, and the insulation grip on insulation, not bare wire. Then I measure crimp height against the terminal maker's spec and run a pull test. For new setups I also cut a cross-section. IPC/WHMA-A-620 is our acceptance reference.
A builder wants to add solder to a crimped terminal to make it stronger. What do you tell them?
Whether you know why more is not always better in a joint.
Not unless the drawing calls for it: solder wicks up the strands and makes a stiff point that breaks under vibration.

I would say no, unless the drawing calls for it. A good crimp already forms a tight, cold-welded joint. Solder wicks up the strands past the barrel and leaves a stiff spot right where the wire flexes, so under vibration the strands break there. If they doubt the crimp, the fix is checking crimp height and the tooling.
What do you do with unused cavities in a sealed connector?
Your attention to the details that keep water out of a harness.
Fill them with the cavity plugs the connector maker specifies, and match each wire seal to the insulation diameter.

They get the cavity plugs, sometimes called seal plugs, that the connector maker specifies. An open cavity lets water and dirt straight in, and the connector's sealing rating is gone. I also check that each wire seal matches the insulation diameter, because a thin-wall wire in a seal sized for thicker insulation will leak.
Why are CAN bus wires twisted, and how would you check the termination on a harness?
Whether you know how data lines differ from power wiring.
Twisting cancels picked-up noise. High-speed CAN has a 120-ohm resistor at each end, so about 60 ohms across the pair with power off.

The two wires carry opposite signals, and twisting makes outside noise hit both equally, so the receiver cancels it; it also cuts what the pair radiates. A high-speed CAN bus has a 120-ohm resistor at each end. With power off I measure across CAN high and low and expect about 60 ohms. Around 120 means one end is missing; very low means an extra resistor or a short.
Walk me through how you route a harness through an engine bay or machine frame.
How you protect a harness from the environment it lives in.
Away from heat, edges and moving parts, grommets through panels, regular clipping, bend radius respected, service slack and water kept out of connectors.

I keep it away from exhaust and hot surfaces, or add heat shielding, and away from belts, pulleys and anything that moves. Every pass through sheet metal gets a grommet, and I clip at intervals so it cannot rub or sag. I respect the cable's minimum bend radius, leave slack for movement and service, and route connectors so water drips away instead of running in.
Pull tests on one terminal start failing halfway through a shift. What do you do?
How you contain a quality problem before you solve it.
Stop the station, quarantine parts since the last good check, find what changed, verify the fix before restarting.

First I stop that crimp station and tag everything made since the last passing check, because those parts are suspect. Then I look for what changed: a new wire reel, a worn or chipped applicator (the crimp die set), strip length, or a setup adjustment. Once fixed, I verify with crimp height and pull tests before restarting, and the tagged parts get inspected or scrapped.
Late in the program, the customer wants two more circuits on a harness already in production. How do you handle it?
Your judgement in managing a design change without breaking production.
A formal change: spare cavities, wire and fuse sizing, fit, then drawing, BOM, formboard and test program updated together with a planned cut-in.

I treat it as a formal engineering change, not a quick note. I check whether the connectors have spare cavities or must change, size the new wires and protection, and see if the bundle still fits its clips and grommets. Then the drawing revision, bill of materials, formboard and tester program change together, and we agree a cut-in date and what happens to stock already built.
What changes when a harness is built to IPC/WHMA-A-620 Class 3 instead of Class 2?
Whether you know how the standard's product classes set the acceptance bar.
Class 3 is for high-performance or harsh-environment products that must work every time. Criteria are tighter, and some conditions acceptable in Class 2 become defects.

Class 2 is dedicated service: long life is expected, but a failure is not critical. Class 3 is for high-performance or harsh-environment products that must work every time. Some conditions that are acceptable in Class 2 are defects in Class 3, so inspection is stricter. The class must come from the drawing or the contract. We never pick it at the bench.
In SAE J1128 wire, when would you pick TXL, GXL or SXL?
Your knowledge of the common automotive primary wire types.
