Agrees instead of arguing, tests one specific weak spot, and leaves a dated next step if there is no pain today.

I agree first, because most people who say that are not in pain today. Then I ask one specific question about a known weak spot, like what happens to their renewals when the person who set up the system leaves. If nothing lands, I ask if I can check back after their next planning cycle and log the date. I do not try to argue them into a problem.
Your only contact on a large deal leaves the company two weeks before the close date. What do you do?
How you rescue a single-threaded deal and what you change afterward.
Finds the new owner fast, re-sells the business case, adjusts the forecast honestly, and builds more contacts next time.

I find out who inherits the project, through my contact if I can still reach them. Then I contact the economic buyer and others I met, recap the business case in writing, and offer the new owner a short call. I move the deal out of commit until that person confirms the timeline. On future deals I want at least three contacts before I send a proposal.
On the last day of the quarter, a buyer says they will sign today if you take 20% off. What do you do?
Your judgement on discounting under deadline pressure.
Trades rather than gives: asks for something in return, stays within approval limits, and protects future pricing.

I do not give a discount for nothing. I ask what they can offer in return: a longer term, payment upfront, more seats, or a case study. Anything past my approval limit goes to my manager before I say yes. If they only want a lower number, I hold, because a discount given once becomes their starting point at renewal.
Your manager wants a deal you think is 50/50 moved to commit. How do you handle it?
Whether you keep the forecast honest when there is pressure to inflate it.
Lays out the facts, names what would make it commit, and asks for help instead of just agreeing.

I show what is confirmed and what is not: legal has not started and the signer has not joined a call. I say I will call it commit the day those are done, and ask what help could get them done this week. A forecast is only useful if it is honest. A missed commit hurts the team's plan more than a smaller number that holds.
A deal you had in commit slips on the last day of the quarter. Walk me through what you do.
How you own a forecast miss and learn from it.
Tells the manager right away, gives the reason and a new buyer-confirmed date, then fixes the gap in the process.

I tell my manager the same day, not at the next forecast call. I give the reason in one line, the new date the buyer confirmed, and what I will do to protect it. Then I look back: often I missed a step, like a vendor setup form that takes procurement three weeks. I add that step to every close plan so it shows up early next time.

instructional-designer.heading: Instructional designer questions
qs: What makes a learning objective a good one?
Whether you write objectives that can be observed and measured.
An observable action verb, the conditions and a standard of performance, with no vague verbs like know or understand.

I use the parts of a classic objective: what the learner will do, under what conditions, and to what standard. 'Understand the return policy' can't be checked. 'Given a receipt, process a return in the system with no errors' can. I avoid know and understand because I can't watch them happen, and I draft the assessment item right after the objective.
How do ADDIE and SAM differ, and when would you pick each?
Your grasp of the main design models and when each fits.
ADDIE as a phased process suited to stable content; SAM as rapid, iterative prototyping suited to unclear needs.

ADDIE runs in phases: analysis, design, development, implementation, evaluation. It fits stable content and compliance work where sign-offs matter. SAM, the Successive Approximation Model, builds rough prototypes early and revises them in short cycles with learners and stakeholders. I pick SAM when requirements are fuzzy, because people react better to a draft than to a document.
What is cognitive load, and how does it shape the way you build a screen?
Whether you apply how memory works to the way a screen is built.
Cutting extra load: less decoration, chunked steps, no full script on screen with narration, worked examples before practice.

Working memory holds little at once, so I cut what doesn't serve the objective: stock photos, extra text, background music. I break a process into short steps, each beside its graphic. With narration, I don't also put the full script on screen; reading and hearing the same words competes for attention. For hard content I show worked examples before practice.
What do you check to make an e-learning module accessible?
Whether accessibility is built into your work, not added at the end.
A named standard, concrete checks like captions, alt text, keyboard use and contrast, and testing with real tools.

I aim for at least the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1, level AA. That means captions, transcripts for audio, alt text on meaningful images, keyboard-only navigation, a sensible screen reader order, and text contrast of at least 4.5 to 1. I never use color alone to mark right and wrong. Then I test it myself with a keyboard and a screen reader.
What is the difference between SCORM and xAPI, and when does it matter?
Your knowledge of how courses report data to a learning system.
SCORM for packaging and basic tracking inside an LMS; xAPI for richer statements, sent to a record store, even outside the LMS.

SCORM is the older standard for packaging a course so a learning management system (LMS) can launch it and record completion, score and time. xAPI sends simple statements, like 'Ana completed the forklift simulation', to a learning record store, and can track activity outside the LMS, like a mobile app or a job checklist. If the client only needs completions, SCORM is simpler.
Your objective says learners will troubleshoot a jammed printer, but the quiz is ten recall questions about printer parts. What do you change?
Whether you align assessments with the level of the objective.
Spotting the gap between recall and application, and replacing items with scenarios or a simulation of the real task.

The quiz tests a lower level than the objective. Naming parts is recall; troubleshooting is applying a process to a new case. I'd replace it with scenarios: here are the symptoms and the error code, what do you check first? Better still, a simulation where a wrong step has a visible result. Scored that way, a pass means they can actually do the task.
A subject matter expert sends you 200 slides and says all of it must be in the course. What do you do?
How you cut content down to what learners need while keeping the expert on side.
Separating need-to-know from reference material, moving reference to job aids, and showing the expert where everything went.

I thank them, then ask what people get wrong on the job and what those mistakes cost. That gives me the need-to-know. Reference material like specs and edge cases goes into a job aid or a searchable page, not the course. I show the expert a short outline mapped to objectives, so they see their content isn't lost, just placed where learners will use it.
Sales staff are not using the new customer system, and their manager asks for a training course. What do you ask before you agree?
Whether you check that training is the right fix before building it.
A quick analysis: is it a skill gap or a cause like process, tools, incentives or follow-up that training cannot fix.

I'd find out whether it's a skill problem at all. Can they do it if they have to? If yes, training won't fix it. The cause may be that the system adds steps, managers still ask for spreadsheets, or nobody checks. I'd ask to watch two reps work and look at usage data. Training fits only the part that's a real gap in knowledge or skill.
A stakeholder wants a 60-minute course in two weeks. Your honest estimate is six weeks. What do you do?
How you handle scope and deadlines without cutting quality silently.
Offering a smaller version that fits, phasing the rest, and putting the trade-offs in writing so the stakeholder decides.

I'd show what fits in two weeks instead of just saying no. Usually that's the core: a short module on the two or three things people must do on day one, plus a job aid. The rest can follow in a second release. I'd put the trade-off in writing: what's in, what's out, and what risk that leaves, so the stakeholder decides with eyes open.
After launch, 70% of learners miss the same quiz question. How do you find out why?
How you diagnose a problem in an assessment or in the course behind it.
Checking the item first, then which wrong answer was chosen, then whether the content taught it, and asking learners.

First I check the item itself: is the key right, is the wording ambiguous, are two answers defensible? Then I see which wrong option they chose. If most picked the same one, that points to a specific misconception, maybe one the course reinforced. I compare the item to the content to confirm we taught it, and I ask a few learners to talk through their answer.
How do you use Gagné's nine events when you build a module?
Whether you know a classic sequencing model and use it with judgement.
Names the events correctly and treats them as a checklist for gaps, not a rigid script for every screen.

I use them to check a draft. Gain attention, state the objective, recall prior knowledge, present content, guide, have learners practice, give feedback, assess, then support transfer to the job. Weak modules usually skip practice and feedback, so I look there first. A short module may cover several events on one screen.
A manager tells you her team are visual learners and asks you to design for that. How do you respond?
Whether you know the research on learning styles and can explain it tactfully.
Research has not shown that matching teaching to a stated style improves learning. Choose media for the content, and say so without lecturing.

I agree visuals will help, because most people learn better from words plus a relevant picture than from words alone. But studies have not found that sorting people by style and teaching to it improves results. So I pick the format by the task: a diagram for a process, hands-on practice for a skill. I keep it about her goal, not about proving her wrong.
How do you write the wrong answers in a multiple-choice question?
Your craft in writing assessment items that measure understanding, not test-taking skill.
Distractors come from real mistakes, are plausible and parallel to the correct answer, and avoid giveaways like all of the above.

I ask the expert what new people actually get wrong and turn those errors into distractors. Each option is about the same length and grammar as the correct one, so length does not give it away. I avoid 'all of the above', negative stems and trick wording. If nobody picks a distractor in the pilot, it does no work and I replace it.
When do you recommend a job aid instead of a course?
Whether you can tell when training is not the right answer.
When the task is rare, has many steps, can be looked up during the work, and a short pause to check is safe.

If the task happens twice a year, has twelve steps and people can stop to check a sheet, a checklist beats a course they will forget. I keep training for things that must be done from memory, fast or under pressure, like an emergency procedure. Often the answer is both: short practice plus the job aid they use on the job.
How do you design a branching scenario so it teaches and does not just test?
How you build realistic practice with consequences that teach.
Choices based on real decisions, consequences shown before the explanation, and a way to recover or replay.

I start from the decisions people really get wrong and write options that are all tempting. When a learner picks one, I show what happens next, like the customer getting angrier, before any explanation. A weak choice can still be recovered later. At the end I debrief the key moments and let them replay. I keep a few decision points so the branches stay manageable.
The business wants one full-day workshop and nothing after. How do you still build in spacing and retrieval practice?
Whether you apply learning science within real business limits.
Knows that spaced, effortful recall beats one block of content, and proposes light follow-ups that cost little time.

Inside the day I mix topics and open each block with a quick recall of the one before, without notes. Then I propose three five-minute follow-ups: a scenario question by email after two days, one after a week, one after a month. I also ask managers to run one practice in a team meeting. It costs little, and people forget much less than after a single day.
Walk me through the item analysis you run after piloting a certification exam.
Your skill with the data that shows whether each test item works.
Checks difficulty and discrimination per item and how often each distractor is picked, then sends flagged items to expert review.

For each item I check difficulty, the share who got it right, and discrimination: do high scorers get it right more often than low scorers? If low scorers do better, that is a red flag, often a wrong key or unclear wording. I also check that every distractor gets picked. Flagged items go to expert review before they count toward anyone's score.
How would you set the passing score for a certification test?
Whether you can defend a cut score instead of picking a round number.
Uses a standard-setting method such as Angoff, built around a minimally competent person, and documents how the score was set.

I avoid a default like 80%. I use a method such as Angoff: a panel of experts pictures a person who is just competent enough, estimates for each item the chance that person gets it right, and we average those estimates into a cut score. We discuss outliers, check pilot results, and document the process so the score can be defended if challenged.
Two senior experts review your module and give opposite feedback on the same procedure. What do you do?
How you resolve content conflicts without guessing or taking sides.
Brings both together with the source document, gets one written decision from the content owner, and logs it.

I do not pick a side or blend the two. I put both comments side by side and ask them to meet with me for twenty minutes, with the procedure document open. Often one is describing an older version. If they still disagree, the named content owner decides and I record the decision in the review log, so it does not reopen at the next review.
Learners average 95% on the final assessment, yet errors on the job have not dropped. What is your diagnosis?
How you diagnose a gap between test scores and job performance.
Suspects the test measures recall rather than the task, and checks the work setting: tools, feedback, manager support and incentives.

First I suspect the test: a high score on recall questions says little about doing the task under real conditions. I would compare the items to the actual errors. Then I look outside the course: maybe the live screen differs from our demo, nobody gets feedback on errors, or speed is rewarded over accuracy. I watch a few people work before I change any training.

insurance.heading: Insurance questions
qs: What is the difference between an occurrence policy and a claims-made policy?
Whether you know the two main liability coverage triggers.
Occurrence follows the date of the event; claims-made follows the date the claim is made, with a retroactive date and possible tail coverage.

An occurrence policy responds to injury or damage that happens during the policy period, even if the claim comes years later. A claims-made policy responds to claims first made while it is in force, for events after the retroactive date. If a claims-made policy ends, the client may need tail coverage, which is an extended reporting period.
Explain actual cash value and replacement cost to a homeowner.
Whether you can explain a basic valuation term in plain words.
Replacement cost pays to replace with like kind and quality; actual cash value takes off depreciation, with the method set by the policy and state law.

Replacement cost pays what it takes to repair or replace the item with like kind and quality today. Actual cash value is often figured as replacement cost minus depreciation, though the exact method depends on the policy and state law. On a 12-year-old roof the gap can be large, so I make sure the client knows which one they bought.
What does a combined ratio tell you?
Your grasp of the main measure of underwriting results.
Losses plus expenses as a share of premium; under 100% is an underwriting profit, before investment income.

It adds losses and loss adjustment expenses to underwriting expenses, each as a share of premium. Under 100% means we made money on underwriting before investment income. At 104% we paid out $1.04 for every dollar of premium. I look at the loss part and the expense part separately, because they have different fixes.
Our insured was rear-ended by another driver. How does subrogation work on this claim?
Whether you know how the insurer recovers what it paid from the party at fault.
Pay the insured under their own coverage, then recover from the at-fault party or carrier, protect the evidence, and pursue the deductible too.

We pay our insured under their collision coverage, minus the deductible, so they are not left waiting. Then we pursue the at-fault driver's carrier to recover what we paid. I keep the photos, police report and statements. I tell the insured we will also try to recover their deductible, and if the carriers disagree, it can go to inter-company arbitration.
A building worth $500,000 has an 80% coinsurance clause, $300,000 of coverage, a $1,000 deductible and a $100,000 loss. What do we pay?
Whether you can apply the coinsurance clause correctly.
Required is $400,000; carried is three quarters of that, so the payment is $75,000 minus the deductible: $74,000, with the math explained.

With an 80% clause they should carry $400,000. They carry $300,000, which is three quarters of that. So on a $100,000 loss we pay three quarters, $75,000, minus the $1,000 deductible: $74,000. Before I send it, I confirm the building value is right and explain the math to the insured and the agent in writing.
You start handling a liability claim but are not sure the policy covers it. What do you do?
How you protect coverage positions while still treating the insured fairly.
Keep investigating, send a timely reservation of rights letter citing the wording at issue, and do not let delay waive the insurer's defenses.

I keep investigating and, if we defend, I send a reservation of rights letter. It says we are handling the claim but may later deny coverage, and it quotes the policy wording in question. That protects us from waiving defenses and tells the insured early, so they can involve their own lawyer. Waiting too long can cost the insurer the right to deny.
After binding a policy, you notice you rated the building with the wrong construction class. What do you do?
How you own and fix an underwriting mistake.
Report it promptly, correct it by endorsement under policy and state rules, tell the agent plainly, and change the process that let it through.

I tell my manager the same day; I don't wait for an audit to find it. We correct the class by endorsement and work out the premium change under the policy terms and state rules. I tell the agent plainly what happened. Then I look at why: if I misread the inspection report, I add a check to my routine so it does not happen again.
A claim turns on a word in the policy that can be read two ways. How do you handle it?
Your judgement when policy wording is unclear.
Read the whole policy first; if truly ambiguous, know courts usually read it against the insurer, so get coverage counsel rather than deny on your own reading.

First I read the whole policy: definitions, endorsements, exclusions. Many words that look unclear are defined. If it truly reads two ways, I know courts usually construe that against the insurer who wrote it, so I don't deny on my preferred reading. I take it to coverage counsel and flag the wording so the next edition is clearer.
After a fire, you learn the insured left a prior fire off the application. What now?
How you handle possible misrepresentation without acting rashly.
No reflex denial: check if the question was clear and the fact material, document, meet response deadlines, and involve counsel since rules vary by state.

I don't deny on the spot. I check whether the application asked clearly, and whether underwriting would have declined or priced it differently had they known; materiality is what counts in most states. I document everything, keep the insured updated within required time frames, and bring in counsel before any rescission, because the rules vary by state.
A commercial account's losses jumped last year and the broker wants a flat renewal. How do you price it?
How you weigh loss history, credibility and terms in a pricing decision.
Look past one year, separate one large loss from a trend, weigh credibility and open claims, and use terms like deductibles, not just rate.

I look at five years, not one. One large fire is different from a rise in small claims. I weigh how credible the account's own history is for its size, estimate where open claims will finally settle, and adjust for changes in exposure. Then I might offer flat rate with a higher deductible and a safety plan, instead of only raising the price or walking away.
What is the difference between a physical hazard, a moral hazard and a morale hazard?
Whether you can name what drives a risk beyond the building itself.
Clear definitions with an example each, and a sense that moral and morale hazard are judged from the insured, not the property.

Physical hazard is a tangible condition, like old wiring or a fryer with no hood system. Moral hazard is dishonesty, like an owner in deep debt with an overinsured building. Morale hazard is carelessness because insurance will pay, like leaving the shop unlocked. I read the last two from loss history, finances and how the owner talks about past losses.
How is the duty to defend different from the duty to indemnify?
Your grasp of what a liability insurer owes once a suit is filed.
The duty to defend is broader and set by the allegations. Indemnity depends on the facts proven.

Indemnity means paying a judgment or settlement for a covered loss, and it turns on the real facts. The duty to defend is broader: if the complaint alleges anything potentially covered, we generally defend. In a standard general liability policy, defense costs sit outside the limit, so even a weak suit can cost a lot.
A subcontractor needs the general contractor added as additional insured on a primary and noncontributory basis. What does that mean, and what do you check?
Whether you understand contract-driven endorsements in commercial liability.
The GC can claim under the sub's policy, which pays first and does not seek a share from the GC's own insurer. The underwriter checks the contract and prices the exposure.

Additional insured status lets the general contractor claim under the sub's policy for liability arising from the sub's work. Primary and noncontributory means our policy pays first and does not ask the GC's own insurer to share. I read the contract, confirm we attach the right endorsements, including completed operations if required, and price the added exposure.
How do you set a case reserve on a bodily injury claim, and what is stair-stepping?
How you reserve: on what you know, at the likely final cost.
A reserve set at the likely final cost from the facts in hand, changed in full when facts change, not raised in small steps that hide the true cost.

I set the reserve at what I expect the claim to cost in the end: medical bills, lost wages, a range for pain and suffering, and likely defense cost, adjusted for liability. Stair-stepping is raising it a little each month instead of facing the real number. It hides the cost from pricing and management, so when I learn something, I move the reserve once, fully.
After a hurricane, a home has roof damage from wind and four feet of water from storm surge. How do you adjust it under a homeowners policy?
Whether you can separate covered and excluded causes on one loss.
Wind is covered and flood is excluded under the standard form. The damage is split by evidence, with the policy's causation wording read closely.

Wind damage is covered. Storm surge is flood, which the standard homeowners form excludes, so that part goes to a flood policy if they have one. I read the causation wording, document water lines and roof damage, and bring in an engineer if the split is unclear. I also check the hurricane deductible and explain the split to the homeowner in writing.
Several fraud indicators show up on a theft claim. What do you do, and what do you not do?
How you handle suspected fraud while still treating the insured fairly.
Document the indicators, refer to the special investigations unit, and keep handling the claim on time and in good faith, without accusing anyone.

A brand-new policy, receipts that look altered and a story that keeps changing are red flags, not proof. I document them and refer the file to the special investigations unit. I do not accuse the insured or stall, because claim-handling deadlines still apply. Many states also require insurers to report suspected fraud, and SIU handles that.
A small account has three years of clean loss history. How much weight do you give its own experience?
Your use of credibility when an account's record is thin.
Blend the account's experience with the manual rate by a credibility weight that grows with volume. A few quiet years on a small risk can be luck.

I use credibility. The rate is a blend: Z times the account's own experience, plus one minus Z times the manual rate. Z grows with the number of claims and the exposure. A small account with three clean years has low credibility, because a quiet stretch happens easily by chance. So I give a modest credit, not the full drop the broker asks for.
Walk me through building a rate indication from historical losses.
Whether you know the steps that turn past losses into a future rate.
Develop losses to ultimate, trend them to the future policy period, bring premium to current rate level, and compare with the target loss ratio.

I take losses by accident year and use development factors from loss triangles to estimate their ultimate cost. I trend them from the old average accident date to the new period's, for inflation and frequency. I restate past premium at current rates, add expected loss adjustment expense, and compare with our permissible loss ratio to get the indicated change.
A risk needs a $15 million limit, but your net line and treaty support $10 million. How do you handle it?
How you work within reinsurance capacity.
No writing beyond capacity. Check the treaty's exclusions, then buy facultative cover, share the risk, or offer a lower limit.

I cannot write past what our net line and treaty support. First I check the treaty wording, since some classes are excluded anyway. Then the options are facultative reinsurance for the extra $5 million, another carrier taking a share or an excess layer, or offering $10 million and letting the broker place the rest. I build the cost of any facultative cover into the price.
A claimant's lawyer sends a time-limited demand for the policy limit on a serious injury claim. How do you handle it?
Your judgement on a demand that can expose the insurer to a bad faith claim.
Meet the deadline, weigh the insured's exposure as much as the insurer's, request missing records in writing, and keep the insured and defense counsel informed.

I calendar the deadline the day it arrives and read the exact terms. If liability is clear and damages likely exceed the limit, an unreasonable refusal could leave us owing a judgment above the limit. If records are missing, I ask for them in writing before the deadline. I tell the insured, involve defense counsel and my manager, and answer in writing on time.

intellectual-property.heading: Intellectual property and patent specialist questions
qs: What does a provisional patent application do, and what does it not do?
Whether you know the basic filing tools and their limits.
It sets an early US filing date and starts a 12-month clock. It is never examined and never becomes a patent by itself.

It gives us a US filing date and lets us say patent pending. It is not examined, it needs no formal claims, and it expires after 12 months. To keep that date we must file a nonprovisional, and usually foreign applications, within the year. And the date only covers what the provisional actually describes, so a thin one protects little.
A client wants to register QUICK CLEAN for a home cleaning service. What do you tell them?
Your grasp of how strong or weak a trademark is.
Spots a descriptive mark, explains the likely refusal and the options, and steers the client toward a more distinctive name.

The name describes the service, so the examiner will likely refuse it on the Principal Register as merely descriptive. We could try the Supplemental Register, or wait until we can prove customers see it as a brand, but that is slow and weak. I would suggest a coined or unrelated word, or a suggestive one, which is easier to register and to enforce.
What is the difference between a patentability search and a freedom-to-operate search?
Whether you can match the search to the business question.
Patentability asks if we can get a patent. Freedom to operate asks if our product infringes someone else's live claims where we sell.

A patentability search looks at all prior art, any age, any country, including papers and products, to see if our invention is new and not obvious. A freedom-to-operate search looks only at patents still in force where we make or sell, and reads their claims against our product. Owning a patent does not mean we are free to sell; those are separate answers.
An engineer presented the invention at a conference two months ago and nothing has been filed. What now?
Whether you know how public disclosure affects patent rights in the US and abroad.
Knows the US one-year grace period for the inventor's own disclosure, and that most other countries require absolute novelty.

In the US, the inventor's own disclosure gives us one year from the talk to file, so we file fast, ideally within weeks. Abroad it is worse: Europe and many other countries require absolute novelty, so those rights are probably lost. I would get the slides and any recording, check exactly what was shown, and set a rule that talks get cleared before they go out.
Which deadlines keep a US trademark registration and a US utility patent alive after they are granted?
Your command of post-grant deadlines, the core of IP docketing.
Section 8 and 9 filings for marks, maintenance fees at 3.5, 7.5 and 11.5 years for patents, and grace periods only as a fallback.

For a mark, a Section 8 declaration of use is due between the fifth and sixth year after registration, then Sections 8 and 9 together between the ninth and tenth year and every ten years after. For a utility patent, maintenance fees fall due 3.5, 7.5 and 11.5 years after grant. Each has a six-month grace period with a surcharge, but I docket the real due date, never the grace date.
Someone is using our client's product photos on their own shop page. Walk me through a DMCA takedown.
How you handle a common online copyright problem by the book.
Checks ownership and fair use first, knows what the notice must contain, and knows the counter-notice path.

I confirm we own the photos, save dated screenshots and consider fair use. Then I send the host's designated agent a signed notice naming our work, the copies and their links, our contact details, a good-faith statement that the use is not authorized, and a statement that the notice is accurate and, under penalty of perjury, that we may act. After a counter-notice, we must sue fast or the photos go back up.
A client found a competitor copying its software code, but never registered the copyright. What do you do first?
Whether you know when registration matters for enforcement.
Registers now, since a US work needs a registration decision before suit, and explains that late registration limits statutory damages and fees.

Copyright exists without registration, but for a US work we cannot sue until the Copyright Office registers or refuses it. So I file now, with special handling if suit is close; it costs more but is much faster. I also warn the client that since the copying began before registration, statutory damages and attorney fees are likely out, so we will need proof of real losses or the copier's profits.
While drafting, an inventor mentions a competitor's paper that is close to the invention and asks you to leave it out. What do you do?
Your understanding of the duty of candor to the patent office.
Cites it in an information disclosure statement, explains why, and knows that hiding it can make the patent unenforceable.

I say no, kindly but clearly. Everyone substantively involved in the application has a duty to disclose information they know is material, so the paper goes into an information disclosure statement. I explain that hiding it on purpose can make the whole patent unenforceable later, while citing it just means we draft claims that are clearly different. Then I ask what else they have read.
The client wants a cease-and-desist letter sent today to a company using a similar name. What do you check before it goes out?
Judgement before taking an action that can backfire.
Checks own rights, priority, evidence and the risk of the target suing first for a declaratory judgment, and keeps the tone measured.

I check that we own the mark and used it first, how close the names and the goods really are, and that our evidence is saved. I also look at who they are: a firm demand can let them sue us first for a declaratory judgment in a court they choose, and a bullying letter can go viral. If our case is solid, I send a firm, factual letter; if not, a softer one or none.
You find that a response deadline on the docket passed last week and nothing was filed. What do you do?
How you own a mistake when a client's rights are at stake.
Reports it right away, checks extension and revival options and their time limits, and fixes the process that let it happen.

I tell my supervising attorney the same hour, with the dates in hand. Then we check options: many patent deadlines can still be extended for a fee, and an application abandoned by mistake can often be revived by petition, but those have their own time limits. We tell the client honestly and file. Then I find why the docket failed, like a missing reminder, and fix it.
A startup filed an intent-to-use trademark application and got a notice of allowance, but its product launch has slipped. Walk me through their options.
Whether you know the intent-to-use timeline after allowance.
A statement of use within six months, extensions in six-month steps up to three years in total, and no registration until real use is shown.

They have six months from the notice of allowance to file a statement of use. If the launch slips, they can ask for six-month extensions, up to five, so three years in total. Each request restates their bona fide intent to use the mark, and from the second one on they must show ongoing efforts. Until they prove real use in commerce, nothing registers.
The examiner refused the specimen for a clothing mark because it is a magazine ad. How do you fix it?
Whether you know what counts as proof of use for goods and what counts for services.
Ads do not show use for goods. A label, a tag or a web page where the item can be bought does, and the substitute must be verified.

For goods, advertising is not use. For services it can be. I would ask the client for a photo of a hang tag or label, or a web page showing the mark next to the shirt with a price and a way to order. The substitute must have been in use by the filing date, with a signed declaration. If they have nothing yet, we can amend the basis to intent-to-use.
Explain the difference between a continuation, a divisional and a continuation-in-part.
Your command of how a patent family is built.
Same disclosure versus new matter, divisionals following a restriction, and filing while the parent is still pending.

All three must be filed while the parent is still pending. A continuation keeps the same disclosure and goes after new claims. A divisional does the same for claims split off by a restriction requirement. A continuation-in-part adds new matter, and claims that rely on it only get the new filing date. The term still runs from the earliest non-provisional date claimed.
You get a restriction requirement splitting the claims into a method group and a device group. How do you decide what to elect?
How you weigh business value when the USPTO forces a choice.
Elect what competitors would actually infringe, decide whether to traverse, and plan a divisional for the rest.

I ask which claims a competitor would actually practice and which we could prove. Device claims are often easier to enforce, because you can buy the product and look inside. If the groups really overlap, I elect with traverse to keep the argument on record. The other group is not lost: it can go into a divisional while this application is still pending.
An office action refuses your client's mark under Section 2(d) based on one prior registration. What options do you lay out?
Whether you see more than one way past a likelihood-of-confusion refusal.
Arguments on the marks and the goods, a narrower description, a consent agreement, and a check on whether the cited mark is still in use.

First I compare the marks and goods the way the examiner will: sight, sound, meaning, and whether buyers meet both in the same channels. Then I list the options: argue the differences, narrow our description of goods, ask the owner for a consent agreement, or check whether they still use the mark. If they stopped, a cancellation for abandonment may clear the way.
A product director wants to be named as an inventor because she funded and managed the project. How do you handle it?
Whether you know inventorship is a legal test and not a reward.
Inventorship turns on contributing to the conception of at least one claim. Funding or managing is not enough, and errors must be corrected.

I explain that inventorship is not a credit line. A person is an inventor only if they helped conceive what at least one claim covers. I would interview her and the engineers, claim by claim. If she contributed an idea that is claimed, she goes on the list. If not, she stays off, because a wrong inventor list can put the patent's validity at risk.
A US client filed a utility application ten months ago and now wants protection in Europe and Japan. What do you tell them?
Your grasp of priority deadlines and foreign filing rules.
The 12-month Paris priority window, the PCT as a way to delay national costs, Europe's strict novelty rule, and the foreign filing license.

They have two months left in the 12-month Paris Convention window. A PCT application filed now keeps both countries open and pushes national costs to about 30 months from the US date. Europe has no general grace period, so any disclosure before our filing date could hurt there. I also confirm the filing receipt shows a foreign filing license.
The examiner rejects your software claims as an abstract idea under Section 101. How do you respond?
Whether you can work through the patent-eligibility test, not just argue against it.
The two-step test, a specific technical improvement or practical application, and amendments backed by the specification.

I follow the examiner's own framework. Is the claim really directed to an abstract idea, like organizing data? If so, does it apply that idea in a practical way, for example making the computer run faster or use less memory? I look for that improvement in the specification, amend the claims to recite how it is achieved, and often ask for an interview first.
A client is sure a competitor's new product infringes its patent. Walk me through what you check before recommending a suit.
How you test an infringement claim before the client spends money on it.
A claim chart where every element is met, limits from the file history, validity, marking, and the damages window.

I build a claim chart: every element of a claim must be in the product, literally or as an equivalent. I read the file history, because what we gave up to get allowance we usually cannot claim back as an equivalent. I check prior art, since they will attack validity. Then damages: whether the client marked its products, and the six-year look-back limit.
Our client was just served with a patent infringement complaint. When does an inter partes review make sense, and what is the deadline?
Whether you know when to fight a patent at the patent office instead of only in court.
Only patents and printed publications as prior art, a lower proof standard than in court, the one-year bar from service, and estoppel.

Inter partes review lets us challenge the patent at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board on novelty or obviousness, using only patents and printed publications. The burden is a preponderance of the evidence, lower than clear and convincing in court. The petition must be filed within one year of service. Grounds we raised, or reasonably could have, are barred later, so we use our best art.

intern.heading: Intern and new grad questions
qs: Someone shows you a new task once, quickly. How do you make sure you can do it alone next time?
How you learn a process after seeing it only once.
Notes in your own words, doing it once while they watch, and a written checklist you test and keep.

I write the steps as they go, in my own words, and note where the files live and who approves what. Then I ask to do the next one while they watch. That evening I turn my notes into a short checklist. The next time, I follow it exactly and fix any step that was wrong.
Your manager gives you a one-line assignment and is in meetings all afternoon. What do you do?
How you handle vague instructions without stalling.
You write down how you understand the task, start on the clear parts, and check your guesses early instead of carrying them to the end.

I write two or three lines on what I think is wanted: the goal, the format, the deadline. I send that as a short message so she can correct me between meetings, and I start on the parts that do not depend on her answer. If a teammate knows the project, I ask them. I would rather show a rough draft at 3 p.m. than a polished wrong one at 5.
How do you decide whether to ask a question or keep trying on your own?
Your judgement about other people's time and your own.
A time limit set in advance, a real search first, and questions grouped together and asked along with what you already tried.

I give myself a set time, often 20 or 30 minutes, to search my notes, the documents and past work. If I am still stuck, I ask, and I say what I tried so the answer is quick. Small questions I save and ask together once a day. Anything that could cause harm, like sending something outside the team, I ask about before I act, not after.
You will miss a deadline by one day. Tell me the message you send your supervisor.
Whether you can write a short, clear message that carries bad news.
An early warning, the fact first, the reason in one line, a new date, and an offer of what can still be delivered on time.

Subject: Market summary, one day late. Hi Dana, the summary will be ready Thursday at noon, not Wednesday. Two data sources disagree and I am checking which one is right. The first two sections are done, and I can send them today if that helps. I would send this as soon as I knew, not on the due date.
Tell me about a group project where one person was not doing their part. What did you do?
How you deal with a teammate problem directly and fairly.
A private, direct talk first, a clear split of tasks with dates, and going to the instructor or lead only if that fails.

In a class project, one teammate missed two meetings and his section was empty. I called him instead of complaining in the group chat. He was working extra shifts. We moved him to the slides, which he could do at night, and set a Sunday check-in. He delivered. If he had not, I would have told the professor the facts, without blame.
A supervisor returns your draft covered in edits. How do you react, and what do you do next?
Whether you take written feedback well and learn from it.
No defensiveness, asking about any edit you do not understand, and spotting the pattern so the same edit is not needed twice.

I read every edit before replying, and I say thanks, because a marked-up draft means someone spent time on me. If I do not understand an edit, I ask why. Then I look for the pattern. Last year most of my edits were long sentences with the main point buried at the end. Now I put the conclusion first and cut each draft hard before I send it.
A big internship deliverable is due the same week as your final exams. How do you handle it?
How you manage school and work without surprising anyone.
Seeing the clash weeks ahead, telling the supervisor early, and offering a plan, such as finishing early or working fewer hours that week.

I put both calendars side by side at the start of the term, so I would see the clash weeks ahead. I would tell my supervisor then, not that week, and offer a plan: finish most of it the week before, work fewer hours during exams, and stay reachable for questions. Then I stick to the plan, so the next request is easy to trust.
On the shared drive you find a spreadsheet with everyone's salaries, which you should not be able to see. What do you do?
Your discretion with confidential information.
Close it, do not copy or share it, and tell your supervisor or IT quietly so the access can be fixed.

I close it and do not open it again, copy it or mention it to the other interns. Then I tell my supervisor privately, or the IT team, that the file seems open to more people than it should be, and where it is, so they can fix the permissions. I would rather report it than hope nobody else finds it.
You notice an error in a report your supervisor already sent to a client. What do you do?
Whether you raise a senior person's mistake in the right way.
Checking you are right, then telling the supervisor privately and quickly, with the evidence and a corrected figure, never going around them.

First I double-check, because I may be missing context. If the error holds, I go to my supervisor alone and soon, not in a team meeting. I would say: I think the total on page 4 should be $18,200, not $21,800, and here is the source. I would have the fix ready. Whether and how to tell the client is their call, not mine.
Your internship ends in two weeks and your project will not be finished. Walk me through how you hand it off.
Whether you leave work that someone else can pick up.
A written handoff with status, files, open issues and contacts, a walk-through with the new owner, and small pieces finished fully.

I agree with my supervisor on who takes over and what I should finish versus leave in good order. Then I write a short handoff document: what is done, what is not, where every file is, open questions and who to ask. I walk the new owner through it in person while I can still answer. A half-done part with clear notes beats a rushed one called done.
You need 20 minutes with a senior person in another department whom you have never met. Write me the email.
Whether you can write a short, polite request that is easy for a busy person to say yes to.
A clear subject line, who you are in one line, a specific reason, a small ask, and flexible times. No long life story.

Subject: 20 minutes on how your team forecasts demand? Hi Ms. Lee, I am the summer intern on the pricing team. My project uses your forecasts, and I want to make sure I read them correctly. Could I have 20 minutes next week? I am free Tuesday or Thursday afternoon, or any time that suits you. Thank you, Sam.
You took notes in a team meeting. What does the version you send afterward look like?
Whether you know that useful notes are about decisions and next steps, not a transcript.
Decisions first, then action items with an owner and a date, then open questions. Sent the same day, short enough to read on a phone.

I send it the same day. At the top: what we decided, in two or three lines. Then a list of action items, each with one name and a due date. Then open questions. I leave out who said what. If I was unsure about an owner or a date, I mark it and ask the group to correct me.
Your manager asks you for a weekly update. What goes in it?
How you report progress so a manager can act without asking follow-up questions.
Done, next, and blocked, with the blockers and any risk to deadlines stated plainly at the top.

Three short parts. What I finished this week, with links. What I plan next week. Where I am stuck or need a decision, and by when. If a deadline is at risk, that goes in the first line, not the last. I keep it under half a page so it actually gets read.
A vice president has five minutes to read a 30-page report you worked on. Walk me through how you summarize it.
Whether you can lead with what matters to a senior reader and cut the rest.
Bottom line first, then the two or three facts behind it, then what you need from them. Details stay in the report with page references.

I start with one sentence: the main finding and what it means for her. Then three bullets with the key numbers, each pointing to the page with details. Then the decision or action we need from her, if any. I write it, then cut it by a third, and ask my manager to read it as if she had no context.
Two people on the team give you tasks due the same day, and each says theirs is urgent. What do you do?
How you handle conflicting priorities without guessing or quietly letting one person down.
You do not pick alone: you tell both, ask your manager to set the order if needed, and confirm the new timing in writing.

I tell each of them about the other request and give a realistic time for both. If they cannot agree, I ask my manager to decide, since that is their call, not mine. Then I send a short note to both with the agreed order and dates, so nobody is surprised at five o'clock.
You are working remotely, your task is done, and no one has contacted you in three days. What do you do?
Whether you take initiative to stay visible and useful when the structure is loose.
You report the finished work, propose next tasks, and set up regular check-ins instead of waiting.

I send my manager a note: here is what I finished, here are two things I could take on next, which do you prefer? I also ask for a standing 15-minute check-in each week. Meanwhile I review open tickets or documentation I could improve, so I am not idle while I wait for an answer.
Your review says you should be more proactive. What do you do with that feedback?
How you turn vague feedback into specific changes.
You ask for an example and what proactive would have looked like, then agree on visible actions and check back later.

I thank them and ask for one recent example where I should have acted differently. Usually it means raising problems earlier or offering a next step instead of waiting. I would pick two concrete habits, like flagging risks in my weekly update, and ask in a month whether they see a difference.
You want to use an AI chatbot to speed up a draft that includes internal company data. How do you decide whether you can?
Your judgment about confidential information and company rules on new tools.
You check the company policy and approved tools before pasting anything in, and you verify every output yourself.

First I check our policy or ask my manager which tools are approved. Many public tools may keep what you type, so I would not paste client names, financials or anything internal into one that is not approved. If it is allowed, I treat the output as a rough draft and check every fact and number myself.
Your analysis shows the opposite of what your manager expects. How do you bring it to them?
Whether you can deliver an unwelcome result honestly and carefully.
You double-check the work first, then present the result with the method and its limits, early and privately, not in a group meeting.

First I recheck my data and steps, and ask a peer to look at it. Then I go to my manager one on one before any meeting. I say what I found, how I got it, and what could make it wrong. I do not soften the result, but I ask what I might be missing. Better they hear it from me early than from a client later.
Near the end of your internship, how do you raise the question of a full-time offer?
How you advocate for yourself with timing and professionalism.
You ask directly, at a good moment, with your results in hand, and ask how decisions are made and when.

I ask for a short meeting a few weeks before the end, not on the last day. I say I have enjoyed the work and would like to return full time, then summarize what I delivered. I ask how return offers are decided and the timeline. If the answer is not yet, I ask what would make me a stronger candidate.

internal-communications.heading: Internal communications manager questions
qs: How do you decide which channel a message goes on?
How you match the message to the channel and the audience.
The channel is chosen by urgency, sensitivity and who must act. News that changes someone's job is said in person first.

I ask three things: how urgent is it, how sensitive is it, and does anyone need to act? A policy reminder fits the newsletter. An outage needs chat and email now. Anything that changes someone's job is said live, by their manager or a leader. Only then is it written down, so people can reread it.
How do you know if your internal communications are working?
Whether you measure understanding and action, not only opens.
Open and click rates as a start, plus short surveys, the behavior that changed, and what managers hear back.

Open rates tell me who saw a message, not who understood it. So I pair them with a quick two-question survey, for example: 'Do you know what this change means for your team?' I also track the action we wanted, like enrollment numbers, and ask a few managers what questions came up. If people keep asking the same thing, the message failed.
Walk me through how you plan an all-hands meeting.
Your process for a large live event, from agenda to follow-up.
A clear purpose, a tight agenda, rehearsed speakers, real Q&A, access for remote and shift staff, and a recap afterward.

I start with the one or two things every employee should leave knowing. Then I build a short agenda, brief each speaker and run a tech rehearsal. I collect questions ahead, including anonymous ones, and keep time for live ones. Remote and shift staff get a recording with captions. Within a day I send a recap and answer the questions we missed.
Your CEO drafts a message full of jargon. How do you fix it without offending them?
How you edit a senior leader's words while keeping their voice.
Edits tied to the reader, shown side by side, with the leader's voice and intent kept.

I don't call it bad writing. I say, 'A warehouse lead will read this on a phone; here is how it lands for them.' I rewrite the key paragraph in plain words, keep the phrases that sound like them, and show both versions. Most leaders pick the clear one once they see it. I also ask what they want people to do after reading, and put that near the top.
How do you reach frontline employees who don't have a company email or sit at a desk?
Whether you can reach deskless workers, not only office staff.
Several channels that fit the shift: huddles, supervisors, screens, posters, an app or opt-in texts, timed to when people are on site.

I start with how they actually spend their shift. Short pre-shift huddles led by supervisors work best, so I give supervisors a one-page talking guide. I add break-room screens and posters for reminders, and a mobile app or opt-in texts for urgent news. I check reach by asking a few people on each shift what they heard, not by counting messages sent.
Walk me through how you would announce a reorganization.
Your sense of sequence: who hears what, in what order, and when.
Leaders aligned, managers briefed, affected people told privately first, then the company the same day, with an FAQ and follow-up.

First I get leaders to agree on the why and the core message. Managers are briefed shortly before, with talking points and an FAQ. People whose roles change hear it from their manager in private. The company announcement goes out the same day as those talks, so rumors have no gap. Then I keep a place open for questions and update the FAQ for the next two weeks.
News of a change leaks on the company chat before your planned announcement. What do you do?
How you respond when you lose control of the timing.
Quick agreement with leadership on what can be confirmed, an earlier announcement or holding note, and no guessing in public.

I tell the sponsor right away and ask what we can confirm. Silence lets the rumor become the story. Usually we move the announcement up and send a short holding note: 'You may have seen talk about this. Here is what we can say now; full details come at 3 p.m.' Finding the source can wait. My job is accurate information now.
Leadership wants to say 'there are no plans for layoffs,' but you know cost cuts are being discussed. What do you do?
Your judgement when a message could later prove false.
You push back on promises that may not hold, offer honest wording instead, and protect trust in leadership.

I'd tell them that if layoffs happen in three months, that line will be quoted back and nothing they say after will be trusted. I'd propose something true: 'We are reviewing costs. No decisions have been made, and if anything affects jobs, you will hear it from us first.' Then I'd make sure we can keep that promise. If they insist, I'd raise it with HR and legal.
You send the company newsletter and find it has the wrong deadline for benefits enrollment. How do you handle it?
How you own and correct a mistake that could cost employees.
A fast, plain correction through the same channels, a check with HR on who was affected, and a fix to the review process.

I'd confirm the right date with HR, then send a short correction within the hour through every channel the original used: 'Correction: enrollment closes on the 15th, not the 22nd.' No long apology, just the fact made easy to find. I'd fix the intranet copy and ask HR whether anyone acted on the wrong date. Then I'd add a fact-check step with the owner of each item.
An employee posts a sharp criticism of a new pay policy under the CEO's intranet post, and an executive asks you to delete it. What do you do?
Whether you balance leadership's wishes, open dialogue and the legal limits on removing posts.
No quick deletion: check the posting rules and with HR or legal, since talk about pay and conditions can be protected, and answer the substance.

I wouldn't delete it on the spot. Talk among employees about pay and working conditions can be protected by federal labor law, even without a union, so I'd check with HR or legal first. Unless it breaks a clear rule, like a threat or someone's private data, I'd leave it up and ask the policy owner to reply with facts. A calm public answer builds more trust than a deleted post.
What do you put in a manager toolkit for a big change?
Whether you can equip managers to explain a message, not just forward it.
The core message and the reason, an honest FAQ, what is not decided yet, the timing, and a way for managers to send questions back.

A one-page summary with the three points that matter, the reason for the change and the timeline. Then an FAQ written from the employee's side, including 'Will my job change?', a line on what is not decided yet, and a form where managers log questions they could not answer. Managers get it a day before staff, with a 30-minute briefing.
Your newsletter open rate jumped from 38% to 65% in one month with no change in content. What happened?
Whether you know the limits of email metrics.
Suspects the measurement before claiming success: privacy features and security scanners can register opens nobody made. Checks clicks and other signals.

I would not celebrate yet. Some mail apps now preload images to protect privacy, so the tracking pixel fires and the email counts as opened even if nobody read it. Corporate security scanners can do the same. I would check clicks, intranet visits from newsletter links and a quick pulse question, and report those instead of opens.
How do you make an all-hands accessible to everyone who attends?
Whether accessibility is built into your planning, not added on request.
Live captions, readable slides described aloud, a recording with a corrected transcript, and a clear way to ask for accommodations in advance.

Live captions on the stream, with a person checking names and terms. Speakers describe charts out loud instead of saying 'as you can see.' Slides use large text and strong contrast. The recording goes out within a day with a corrected transcript, and the invite says who to contact for an interpreter or other accommodation, early enough to arrange it.
Five teams each want the lead story in Monday's newsletter. How do you decide?
How you protect a channel and say no to senior requesters.
An agreed rule based on how many people it affects and whether they must act; the rest get a shorter slot or another channel, with the reason given.

I use the rule we agreed with leadership: the lead goes to what affects the most people and needs action by a date. If benefits enrollment closes Friday, that leads. A product win becomes a two-line item with a link; a team event goes to that team's channel. I tell each requester why and when their item runs, so the rule makes the call, not my mood.
Tell me about a message that landed badly. What did you change afterward?
Whether you own mistakes and turn them into a better process.
A specific failure, how it was spotted, the quick fix, and a lasting change such as testing drafts with a few employees first.

We announced a new hybrid policy as 'more flexibility,' but for warehouse staff it changed nothing and some office teams got more days in. The chat filled with sarcasm within an hour. We sent a plain follow-up by group showing what changed for each. Since then I test big drafts with five or six employees from different roles before anything goes out.
Walk me through the communication sequence on the day of a layoff.
Whether you can sequence a layoff so affected people are treated with dignity.
Affected people hear first, privately and from a person; the all-staff note follows quickly; legal checks notice rules such as the WARN Act; managers are briefed.

Before the day, legal confirms notice duties and HR has packets ready. Affected people hear first, in a private meeting with their manager and HR, never through an email or a badge that stops working. Within an hour the CEO tells all staff what happened, why, which teams are affected and what support leavers get. Managers meet their remaining teams the same day.
A serious injury happens at one of your sites. What do you do in the first hour?
How you communicate in a crisis when the facts are incomplete.
Works with safety, HR and legal, sends a short note with confirmed facts only, protects the person and family, and sets a time for the next update.

I join the response call with safety, HR and legal and write down only what is confirmed. Within the hour, staff at that site get a short note: there was an incident, the area is closed, support is available, next update by 3 p.m. I do not name the injured person until HR has spoken with the family and they agree. Then I keep the promised update time, even with little news.
We are buying a smaller company. The deal is signed but not closed. What do you tell the employees we are acquiring?
Whether you know what can and cannot be said between signing and closing.
Honest answers on job, pay, manager and benefits, no promises on undecided points, and the two firms treated as separate until the deal closes.

Their questions are personal: my job, my pay, my boss, my benefits. I answer what is decided, say plainly what is not and when they will know. Until closing we are still two separate companies, so we do not give them instructions or start integrating, and legal reviews every message. Their own leaders tell them first, then we hold a joint Q&A.
We are a public company and will announce a major restructuring with our earnings. When do employees hear?
Whether you can sequence internal news around public disclosure.
Plans with legal and investor relations so staff hear at or just after the public release, keeps early knowledge to a short insider list, and assumes leaks.

News that could move the stock goes out publicly first or at the same moment, so employees never hold information the market lacks. I plan with legal and investor relations: the press release goes out, and the internal note lands minutes later. The few people who help draft it are on the insider list. I write the internal note as if it will be screenshotted, because it will.
Employees at one site start a union drive, and leadership wants talking points for managers. How do you approach it?
Whether you know the legal limits on employer speech during union organizing.
Brings in labor counsel first and trains managers on the limits: no threats, interrogation, promises or surveillance, often called TIPS.

I would not draft anything before labor counsel is involved. Under federal labor law, managers cannot threaten employees, question them about union activity, promise benefits to sway them or watch who goes to meetings. I build talking points from facts counsel approves, train managers on those limits, and tell them to send questions they cannot answer to HR instead of improvising.

internal-controls.heading: SOX and internal controls specialist questions
qs: What is the difference between SOX Section 302 and Section 404?
Whether you know what the law asks of management and of the external auditor.
302 is the CEO and CFO certification of each quarterly and annual report. 404 is the yearly assessment of internal control, with auditor attestation for larger filers.

Section 302 makes the CEO and CFO certify each 10-Q and 10-K, including that they evaluated disclosure controls. Section 404(a) requires management's annual assessment of internal control over financial reporting as of year-end. 404(b) adds the external auditor's attestation, which applies to accelerated and large accelerated filers.
What is the difference between design effectiveness and operating effectiveness, and how do you test each?
Your grasp of the two basic questions behind every control test.
Design asks if the control, done as written, would address the risk. Operation asks if it was done that way all period. A walkthrough for one, sample testing for the other.

Design is whether the control, performed as written, addresses the risk: right person, right precision, right timing. I test it with a walkthrough: I follow one transaction end to end and look at the real evidence. Operating effectiveness is whether it ran that way across the period, so I pull a sample over the year and inspect or reperform each one.
Give me a segregation-of-duties conflict in purchase-to-pay. What if the team is too small to split it?
Whether you can spot conflicting duties and design around them in a small team.
A clear conflict, such as vendor setup plus payment release, and a compensating control, like an independent review of changes, when duties cannot be split.

If one person can add a vendor and also release payments, they can pay a fake vendor. In a three-person team I may not split it, so I add a compensating control: the controller reviews a system report of every vendor master change each month, ties it to support and signs it. Access logs show who changed what, so the review has real data.
What are IT general controls, and what happens to your automated controls if they fail?
Your understanding of how IT controls support the rest of the control set.
Access, change management and IT operations, plus the link: if ITGCs fail, you cannot rely on automated controls and system reports without extra work.

ITGCs cover who can get into systems, how program and setting changes are approved and tested, and how jobs and backups run. Automated controls rely on them. If change management failed, I cannot assume the invoice matching setting stayed the same all year, so I test it at more points or lean on manual controls.
A reviewer relies on a system report to perform a control. How do you get comfort on that report?
Whether you test the data a control uses, not just the sign-off.
Testing the report's completeness and accuracy: how it is produced, its parameters, whether it can be edited, and tying it back to source data.

That report is information produced by the entity, so I test that it is complete and accurate. I look at how it is run: standard or custom, which parameters were used, and whether anyone can edit it. Then I tie totals to the general ledger and trace a few items both ways, from report to source and from source to report.
Payroll is outsourced. How do you use the provider's SOC 1 report?
Your handling of controls that sit at a service organization.
A Type 2 report, period coverage, exceptions, the user controls you must run yourself, a bridge letter for any gap, and any subservice providers left out.

I want a Type 2 report, because it tests operation over a period, not just design. I check the period against our fiscal year and get a bridge letter for any gap. I read the opinion and the exceptions, then map the complementary user entity controls, the ones we must perform ourselves, to our own tested controls. I also note subservice providers the report leaves out.
You are testing invoice approvals and one of your 25 samples has no approval. What do you do?
How you treat an exception without hiding it or overreacting.
No swapping the sample. Find the cause, see if it is isolated, extend testing only if the method allows, and judge the severity.

I do not replace the sample. First I confirm with the owner that the approval is really missing, not filed elsewhere. Then I find why: a new clerk, a system bypass, a rush. If our method allows, I extend the sample to see if it is isolated. Either way I log the deviation, check whether the invoice itself was valid, and assess the deficiency.
A controller signs a monthly variance review, but there are no notes or thresholds. Does the control pass?
Your judgement on review controls, where a signature alone proves little.
A signature is not evidence of review. You need a set threshold, what was investigated, and how differences were resolved.

Not as it stands. A signature shows someone saw the file, not what they checked. I would ask what threshold triggers a follow-up, which variances crossed it and what was found. If the controller can show the questions and answers, I can document that. Going forward I would agree on a written threshold and a place to record explanations.
How do you decide whether a deficiency is a material weakness?
Whether you can weigh severity the way the standards define it.
A reasonable possibility that a material misstatement is not prevented or detected in time, weighing size, likelihood, other controls and combined deficiencies.

I ask two things: could this failure lead to a misstatement, and how big could it get. It is a material weakness if there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement would not be prevented or detected on time. I look at the account's size, what else would catch the error, and whether other deficiencies in the area add up. An actual error is not required.
A key control failed in the third quarter. The owner fixed it and wants it closed. What do you need first?
Your grasp of what makes remediation count before the year-end assessment date.
The new control must operate long enough and be tested as effective before year-end. A fix in place is not enough.

The assessment is as of fiscal year-end, so the fix only counts if the improved control has run enough times and we have tested it before then. I would agree on the new design, document it, let it operate, then test a fresh sample from after the fix date. For a quarterly control fixed late in the year, there may not be enough runs to test, and I would say that early.
Walk me through how you run a walkthrough.
Whether you can follow one transaction end to end and confirm the controls really exist.
One real transaction traced from start to the ledger, with inquiry backed by inspection or observation, and any gap between the narrative and practice noted.

I pick one real transaction, say a purchase order, and follow it from request to the general ledger using the actual documents and system screens. At each control I ask the person who does it, then look at the evidence or watch it done. If what I see differs from the narrative, I update the narrative or flag a design gap.
How do you decide which accounts and locations are in scope for SOX?
Your grasp of the top-down, risk-based approach to scoping.
Start from the financial statements: accounts with a reasonable possibility of material misstatement, judged on size and risk, then locations by risk, not by habit.

I start at the financial statements, not the control list. An account is significant if there is a reasonable possibility of a material misstatement, so I look at size, volume, complexity, judgment and fraud risk. Then I map relevant assertions and locations. A small unit with complex revenue terms can be in scope while a larger, simple one is not.
How do you choose a sample size for a control test?
Whether you tie testing effort to how often a control runs and how much risk it covers.
Size driven by control frequency and risk, with automated controls handled differently and effective IT general controls as the condition.

I start from how often the control runs. Our methodology uses a table, for example one instance for an annual control and two for a quarterly one, with larger samples for daily ones. I go higher when the risk is high or the control is complex. For an automated control I can test one instance, as long as the IT general controls over that system are effective.
A key reconciliation lives in a spreadsheet. How do you control it?
How you handle spreadsheet risk inside a key control.
Locked formulas, restricted access, version control, inputs tied to source, and a review that checks the logic, not just the totals.

I treat the file as part of the control. It sits in a restricted folder, formulas are locked, and changes to logic are logged and reviewed. Inputs are tied back to the system report each month. The reviewer checks that totals agree to source and looks at any changed formula. Without that, a broken formula can pass a sign-off for months.
How do you test controls over manual journal entries?
Whether you address management override, a core fraud risk.
A complete population pulled from the system, approval by someone other than the preparer, and attention to unusual entries such as post-close or senior-level postings.

First I get the full population of manual entries from the system and prove it is complete, for example by tying it to general ledger activity. Then I sample and check that someone other than the preparer approved each entry, with support attached. I also look at who can post at all, and at entries made after close or by senior people.
You tested a control through September. What do you do for the rest of the year?
Your understanding that the assessment of internal control is as of year-end.
Roll-forward work sized to risk: ask about changes, and test more where the control is risky, changed, or showed issues at interim.

Our assessment is as of year-end, so interim results alone are not enough. I ask the owner whether the control, the people or the system changed, and I look at events since September. For a low-risk control with clean results, inquiry plus a small extra sample may do. For a high-risk one, or one that changed, I test the fourth quarter again.
A control owner says a later review compensates for a control that failed. How do you decide whether it does?
How you judge whether a compensating control really covers the same risk.
Same risk and assertion, precise enough to catch a material misstatement, and tested itself; it can lower severity but does not erase the failure.

I check three things. Does the review cover the same risk and assertion? Is it precise enough, with thresholds low enough, to catch an error that could matter? And has it been tested and shown to work? If yes, it can lower the severity of the deficiency. The original failure is still a deficiency and still gets fixed and reported.
The company goes live on a new ERP in October, and the year ends in December. What changes in your plan?
Whether you can plan controls work around a system change late in the year.
Data conversion controls, IT general controls and access roles on the new system, time for new controls to operate before year-end, and a plan for the old system's months.

I want controls over data conversion, so balances and open items move completely and accurately, with evidence. The new system needs IT general controls and access roles that respect segregation of duties from day one. New controls must run long enough before year-end to test enough instances. I also agree with the external auditor how the old system's months are covered.
We have over 600 key controls. How would you cut that number without adding risk?
Your ability to rationalize a control set from risks rather than habit.
Map each control to a risk and assertion, keep the ones that cover it at the right precision, mark duplicates non-key, and agree changes with the external auditor.

I map every key control to the risk and assertion it covers. Where three controls cover one risk, I keep the most precise and reliable one, often automated or preventive, and mark the others non-key. They still run; we just stop testing them for SOX. I agree the changes with the external auditor before the year starts, so nobody is surprised.
The external auditor wants to rely on our testing. What will they look at, and how do you make that work?
Whether you know how an external auditor uses the work of others.
Competence and objectivity of the testers, documentation good enough to reperform, and less reliance in high-risk areas; scope and timing agreed up front.

Under PCAOB standards they judge the competence and objectivity of whoever tested, and the higher the risk, the more they do themselves. So I keep testers independent of control owners, agree the controls and timing with them early, and document each test so someone could reperform it from my file: population, sample, evidence and conclusion.

inventory-specialist.heading: Inventory specialist questions
