qs: What is the difference between cycle counting and a full physical inventory?
Whether you know the two main ways to count stock and when each one is used.
A full count checks everything at once, usually with work stopped. Cycle counts cover small parts on a schedule and catch errors sooner.

A full physical inventory counts every item at one time, usually with receiving and shipping stopped, often once a year. Cycle counting means counting a few locations or items every day, so the whole building gets covered over the year. It finds errors sooner, and the business keeps running while we count.
Why would you hand a counter a blank sheet instead of one showing the system quantity?
Whether you understand blind counts and why they matter.
Counters who see the expected number tend to find it. A blind count gives an honest number to compare against the record.

That is a blind count. If the sheet says 48, people tend to count until they reach 48 and stop looking. With no number shown, they count what is really there. The system then compares it, and any location off by more than our tolerance gets a recount by a different person.
How would you decide which items get counted most often?
How you use ABC analysis to spend counting time where it matters most.
Ranks items by value or movement, counts the high-impact A items most often, and adds extra counts where problems show up.

I would sort items by yearly value or by how often they move. The top group, the A items, are few but carry most of the value, so I count them often, maybe monthly. B items get counted less, C items a few times a year. I also add a count when a location had a recent error or a picker reported a short.
A picker reports a bin empty, but the system shows 12 on hand. What do you do?
How you handle phantom stock so orders do not get stuck.
A quick search of likely spots, a count, a fix to the record so the system stops sending pickers there, then a look for the cause.

I go see the bin myself and check the locations around it, the overflow and any staging area. If I find the stock, I put it back and fix the location. If not, I count and adjust so the system stops promising stock that is not there and purchasing knows to reorder. Then I trace the history to see if a receipt went to the wrong bin.
What does it mean when an item shows a negative quantity on hand, and how do you fix it?
Your understanding of how transactions post and what a negative balance says about the process.
Something left the system before it arrived in it, often an unposted receipt or a unit mix-up. You fix the root transaction, not just the number.

You cannot have less than zero on a shelf, so a negative means a transaction is missing or wrong. Most often stock was shipped before its receipt was posted, or cases and single units got mixed up. I find that receipt or error and correct it. Just adjusting up to zero hides the problem, and it comes back.
The system says 50 units in a bin and you count 40. Walk me through what you check before adjusting.
How you research a variance instead of simply overwriting the record.
Recounts, then checks open transactions, nearby and overflow locations, unit of measure and item history before any adjustment.

First I recount, ideally with a second person. Then I look for timing: picks taken but not confirmed, or a putaway not posted. I check nearby bins and overflow for mislocated stock, and whether someone counted cases where the system tracks single units. I read the item history. Only if nothing explains it do I adjust, with a reason code.
How do you set up the cutoff for a full physical inventory?
Whether you can keep counts and paperwork in sync during a wall-to-wall count.
Posts all completed movements, records the last receiving and shipping documents, and keeps late arrivals apart from counted stock.

Before the count I post every receipt and shipment that has physically happened. I note the last receiving document and last bill of lading before the freeze. Goods arriving during the count go to a marked area and are not counted. Orders staged but not shipped count as on hand. Afterward I check against those documents so nothing is counted twice or missed.
Our shrink went up this quarter. Where would you look for the causes?
How you separate the sources of loss: theft, damage, vendor and paperwork errors.
Breaks shrink down by item, area and reason, tests paperwork errors first, and brings in security only when the data points to theft.

I break the losses down by item, location and adjustment reason. A lot of shrink is paperwork: receipts keyed wrong, vendor shortages missed at the dock, returns not posted. I check for damage thrown out without a write-off. If losses cluster on small, high-value items in one area, I bring that data to my manager and security instead of guessing who it is.
You find that an adjustment you posted last week moved 200 units to the wrong item. What do you do?
How you own and fix your own error in the records.
Reports it quickly, reverses it with a clear note, and checks what else the error touched, such as orders or reorders.

I tell my supervisor right away, then post correcting adjustments on both items with a note pointing to the original. I check whether orders were promised against stock that was not real, or whether purchasing skipped a reorder because of it. Then I find out why it happened. If the two items look alike, I ask for a second check on adjustments that large.
Before an audit, a manager asks you to adjust a few items so the system matches the shelves, without researching them. How do you respond?
Your integrity with records and how you push back respectfully.
Will not post unsupported adjustments to hide variances, and offers a fast research plan with proper approval instead.

I would say I understand the time pressure, but adjusting without research hides the real problem, and auditors review adjustments too. I would offer to count and research those items today, starting with the highest values. Whatever still cannot be explained, we post with honest reason codes and the approval our policy requires.
The packing slip says 100 units, but you count 95 on the pallet. What do you receive into the system?
How you handle a short shipment at the receiving dock.
Receives what is physically there, notes the shortage before signing, and tells purchasing so the company does not pay for 100.

I receive 95, because the system should show what we actually have. I recount once, write the shortage on the delivery receipt before signing, and photograph the pallet if it looks tampered with. Then I flag it to purchasing so we are billed for 95 or the vendor ships the rest. We should never pay for 100 units we did not get.
Freight sits on the dock overnight before it is put away. Why does that matter for inventory accuracy?
Whether you understand where stock lives in the system between receiving and put-away.
Knows received stock counts as on hand but is not in its bin, which can trigger false shortages and wrong adjustments, and closes that gap.

Once received, the system counts it as on hand, but in a dock or staging location, not the bin. Pickers can be sent to an empty bin, and a counter may see the shelf short and adjust it wrongly. I push to put away the same shift, keep anything left in a labeled staging location, and check open put-away tasks before any count.
During a count you find cartons that are crushed and leaking. How do you handle them in the system?
How you keep damaged stock from being picked or counted as good.
Moves it to a hold or damage location with a reason code so it cannot be picked, then routes it to the right disposition.

I count it as found, then move it in the system to a damage or hold location that cannot be picked, with a damage reason code, and tag it on the floor too. Then whoever owns disposition decides: return to vendor, carrier claim if it arrived damaged, or write-off. If it is leaking a chemical, I check the safety data sheet and follow our spill procedure before touching it.
One SKU keeps showing variances in multiples of 12. What does that suggest to you?
Whether you spot a unit of measure problem from the pattern of the numbers.
Names a case versus each mix-up and checks how the item is set up, received and picked before adjusting.

It points to a unit of measure problem: a case of 12 is being scanned or keyed as one each, or the reverse. I would check the item's unit of measure setup and conversion, then look at receipts and picks around the variance to see which step treats cases as eaches. Fixing the setup stops it; adjusting alone hides it until the next count.
We handle lot-coded food products. How does that change how you count and rotate stock?
Whether you can run lot control and rotation by expiration date.
Counts by lot and expiration, not just SKU, and rotates first expired, first out, so recalls and expirations can be traced.

Each lot is its own record, so I count by SKU, lot and expiration date, not just the total. We pick first expired, first out, so I watch that newer lots are not put away in front of older ones. If a recall comes, clean lot records let us find and hold every case of that lot fast. A lot mix-up is a real error even when the total is right.
How do you measure inventory record accuracy, and why is net dollar variance not enough?
Your grasp of how accuracy is measured and how overs and shorts can hide each other.
Scores each location or SKU as a hit or miss within tolerance, and knows overs and shorts net out, so net dollars can look perfect while records are wrong.

I score each location counted as a hit if the system matches the shelf within our tolerance; accuracy is hits divided by locations counted. Net dollar variance matters to finance, but a bin 50 dollars over and another 50 dollars short nets to zero while both records are wrong, and pickers still walk to empty bins. So I report hit rate, net and gross variance.
How does an inventory adjustment show up on the company's financial statements?
Whether you see the money side of every count variance.
A shortage lowers the inventory asset and is expensed, usually to cost of goods sold or a shrink account, so it cuts profit; an overage does the reverse.

Inventory is an asset on the balance sheet, valued at cost. When I adjust down, that value comes off the asset and goes to an expense, usually a shrink line within cost of goods sold, so profit drops by the cost of the units. An overage does the reverse. That is why I research before adjusting: a wrong adjustment misstates profit, not just a bin.
The same SKU fails its cycle count three months in a row. How do you find the root cause?
How you dig past the adjustment to the process that keeps breaking.
Reviews every transaction between counts, checks look-alikes, extra locations, unit of measure and substitutions, then fixes the step and verifies.

I pull every transaction since the last clean count: receipts, picks, moves, returns and adjustments. Then I check the usual suspects: a look-alike SKU next door, a second location nobody counts, a wrong unit of measure, or pickers substituting. Once I found returns going back to the shelf unscanned. We fixed that step and the item counted clean after.
Who should approve inventory adjustments, and why shouldn't the person who counted post them alone?
Your understanding of controls that protect inventory from errors and theft.
Separation of duties: counting, approving and posting are split, with dollar thresholds that need a manager, and every adjustment documented.

Counting, approving and posting should not all sit with one person, because whoever can both count and adjust can hide a loss, by mistake or on purpose. Small variances can go to a lead, and anything above a dollar threshold set by finance needs a manager. Every adjustment carries a reason code and the recount evidence, so an auditor can follow it.
Your shrink data points to losses on one shift, and one name keeps coming up. What do you do?
How you handle suspected theft without accusing anyone or spoiling an investigation.
Keeps it confidential, documents facts, and hands it to the manager, loss prevention or HR instead of confronting the person.

I do not confront anyone or talk about it on the floor. A pattern is not proof; it could be a training gap or a faulty scanner. I document what I have: dates, SKUs, transactions and counts, and take it to my manager and loss prevention or HR. They decide next steps, like reviewing cameras. My job is clean facts, not a verdict.

investigations.heading: Investigations specialist questions
qs: What is the fraud triangle, and how do you use it in a case?
Whether you know the basic model of why people commit fraud.
Pressure, opportunity and rationalization, with the point that controls mainly reduce opportunity.

It says fraud usually needs three things: a pressure, like debt or a sales target; an opportunity, like weak controls; and a rationalization, like “I’ll pay it back.” In a case I use it to look for motive and access, but I treat it as a guide for my questions, not as proof. Opportunity is the part a company can fix, so my recommendations focus there.
An anonymous tip says a buyer is “getting kickbacks” and gives nothing else. Do you open an investigation?
How you decide whether there is enough basis, called predication, to start a case.
A quiet preliminary check first, then a decision based on whether facts give reasonable grounds. No confronting anyone on a bare tip.

Not a full one yet. First I check what I can quietly: the buyer’s vendors, price changes, sole-source awards, any vendor added without bids. If I find something that would make a trained person reasonably believe fraud may have occurred, that is predication and I open the case. If nothing turns up, I document what I checked and close it, without tipping off the buyer.
What is chain of custody, and how do you keep it?
Whether your evidence would hold up if the case goes to court or arbitration.
A written record of who held each item, when and why, from collection on, with items sealed, labeled and stored under control.

It is the unbroken record of who had a piece of evidence from the moment I collected it. I label each item with a number, the date and where I found it, seal it, and log every handoff with a signature. Originals stay locked up; we work from copies. If there is a gap in the log, the other side can argue the item was changed.
You are reviewing accounts payable data for a fake vendor. What do you look for?
Your knowledge of the red flags of fictitious vendor schemes.
Concrete tests: matches to employee data, missing vendor details, invoice patterns, amounts just under approval limits, and who set the vendor up.

I match vendor addresses, phone numbers and bank accounts against employee records. I flag vendors with only a P.O. box, no tax ID, or consecutive invoice numbers, a sign we may be their only customer. I look for round amounts and payments just under an approval limit. Then I check who created the vendor and who approves its invoices; one person doing both is a problem.
A manager wants to log in to the suspect’s laptop right now to see what is there. What do you say?
Whether you protect digital evidence before anyone touches it.
Stop the browsing, secure the device, and have a trained examiner make a forensic copy so the original is not altered.

I ask him not to. Logging in and opening files changes dates and other data, and the other side can then say the evidence was altered. I secure the laptop as it is, record who had it, and have a trained examiner make a forensic copy with a write blocker and hash values that prove the copy matches. We review the copy. I also ask IT to preserve email and server logs.
In what order do you interview people in a case, and why?
How you plan interviews so the facts are known before the key conversation.
Neutral witnesses and record keepers first, then people closer to the matter, the subject last, once the facts are known.

I start with people who can explain the process and the records but are not involved, then witnesses closer to the events, then anyone who may have helped. The subject comes last. By then I know the documents and the story, so I can tell when an answer does not fit. Going to the subject first warns them and gives them time to line up a story.
An employee you are interviewing asks you to keep what they say confidential. How do you answer?
Whether you make only the promises you can keep.
No promise of full secrecy: sharing on a need-to-know basis, clarity on who you work for, and a clear word that retaliation is not allowed.

I tell them the truth: I share what they say only with people who need it for the case, but I cannot promise it stays secret, since it may be needed for a decision or a legal process. If lawyers run the case, they explain they represent the company, not the employee. I also say retaliation for helping an investigation is not tolerated, and how to report it.
The subject admits taking the money during your interview. Is the case done?
Whether you back up an admission with independent evidence.
No: get a signed written statement, then match the admission to the records, because confessions are often partial or wrong.

No. I ask them to put the admission in a written statement in their own words, signed, saying it was given voluntarily. Then I check it against the records: the amounts, the dates and the method. People often admit less than they took, or cover for someone else. The report rests on the documents; the admission supports them.
A colleague’s draft report says “Mr. Lee stole $40,000.” What do you change?
How you write findings without deciding guilt yourself.
Replace the conclusion of guilt with facts and their sources. Guilt is for management, lawyers or a court, and the label invites a legal challenge.

I would rewrite it to state what the evidence shows: for example, that 14 payments totaling $40,000 went to an account in Mr. Lee’s name, with the bank records attached. Whether that is theft is a legal conclusion for management, lawyers or a court. The report sticks to facts, cites the source of each one, and leaves out opinions on guilt.
Halfway through a case, the evidence points to the executive your team reports to. What do you do?
Your independence and how you escalate when your own chain of command is conflicted.
Escalate around the conflict as policy sets out, usually to the general counsel or audit committee, secure the evidence, and keep the circle small.

I stop reporting progress through that executive. I follow the escalation path in our policy, usually the general counsel or the audit committee chair, and bring the documents, not a theory. I make sure the evidence is stored where the executive cannot reach it, and I limit who knows. Then the board or outside counsel decides who runs the case from there.
What is a lapping scheme, and how would you spot one in receivables?
Whether you know a classic receivables fraud and the traces it leaves.
Explains the rolling cover-up with later payments and names concrete signs: late postings, mismatched remittances, customer complaints.

The clerk steals Customer A's payment, then posts Customer B's payment to A's account, and so on. I compare remittance advices and deposit slips to what was posted, look for payments that keep getting posted days late, and confirm balances directly with customers. A clerk who never takes vacation is a warning sign too.
When is Benford's law useful in a fraud review, and when is it not?
Whether you use data tests with a clear view of their limits.
Knows the expected first-digit pattern and which data fits it, and treats a deviation as a lead, not proof.

In many natural data sets the first digit is 1 about 30% of the time and 9 under 5%. It works on things like invoice amounts that span several orders of magnitude. It fails on assigned numbers, capped amounts or small sets. A spike only tells me where to look; I still pull the documents behind it.
What is an Upjohn warning, and when do you give it?
Your grasp of privilege in interviews run under counsel.
Says counsel represents the company, not the employee, and the company owns and may waive the privilege. Given at the start, then documented.

When I interview for counsel, the employee is told at the start that the lawyers represent the company, not them. The talk is privileged, but the privilege belongs to the company, which may waive it and share what they say, including with the government. I note in my memo that the warning was given and understood.
Do you record your interviews? Why or why not?
Whether you know consent rules for recording and follow policy and counsel.
Knows federal law is one-party consent but some states, like California and Florida, require everyone's consent; checks policy and counsel first.

Only if policy and counsel allow it, and I always tell the person and get consent on the record. Federal law needs one party's consent, but states like California and Florida require all parties. For calls across state lines I follow the strictest rule. Otherwise I interview in pairs, with one person taking careful notes.
A union employee asks for a steward before your interview starts. What do you do?
Whether you know Weingarten rights and handle the request correctly.
Knows the right exists when discipline could follow; stops and either brings in a steward or ends the interview. Never pushes on.

If the employee reasonably believes the interview could lead to discipline, they have a right to a union representative once they ask. So I stop. I either wait for the steward or end the interview and decide next steps with HR. The steward can advise and ask questions but cannot answer for the employee or block the interview.
The suspect has no bank records missing, but lives far beyond their salary. How do you show unexplained income?
Your command of indirect methods of proving income.
Describes the net worth method correctly and the need to rule out legitimate sources like gifts, loans or inheritance.

I use the net worth method. I measure assets minus debts at the start and end of the period. The increase, plus living expenses, minus known income, is the unexplained amount. Then I check for innocent sources, such as an inheritance, a loan or a spouse's pay, before I put any figure in a report.
When does a legal hold need to go out, and what does it cover?
Whether you protect evidence early enough and broadly enough.
Ties the hold to when litigation is reasonably anticipated, covers all custodians and data types, and stops automatic deletion.

As soon as litigation or a government inquiry is reasonably anticipated, not when the lawsuit lands. With counsel I list custodians and sources: email, chat, shared drives, phones used for work, paper files. IT must suspend auto-delete and mailbox purges for those people. I track who acknowledged the hold and reissue it if the scope grows.
You work at a bank. A customer you investigated asks if the bank reported them to the government. What do you say?
Whether you know SAR confidentiality and avoid tipping off.
Neither confirms nor denies; knows disclosing a SAR or its existence is prohibited by federal law; escalates to BSA compliance.

I would not confirm or deny anything. Federal law bars disclosing a Suspicious Activity Report or any information that would reveal one exists. I would say I cannot discuss internal reviews, keep my tone normal so I hint at nothing, and tell our BSA officer about the question right away.
Late in an interview the subject says, “If I pay it all back, can we forget this?” How do you respond?
How you handle an offer without making promises or threats.
Makes no promise or threat, says the decision is not theirs, keeps the person talking about the facts and records the offer.

I say I cannot promise anything, because what happens next is not my decision. I never threaten charges to get money back, which can be illegal. I note the offer word for word, then ask what amount they mean and how they arrived at it. That figure often leads to a fuller admission.
The employee who reported the fraud is suddenly put on a performance plan by the manager you are investigating. What do you do?
How you protect a reporter and the case when retaliation is possible.
Escalates at once to counsel and HR, documents the timeline, seeks a pause on the action and keeps the reporter's identity protected.

I take it to counsel and HR that day and ask that the plan be paused until someone independent reviews it. I set out the timeline: the report date, past reviews, then the plan. Retaliation can break federal and state law and can sink the case. I do not tell the manager anything that reveals who reported.

investment.heading: Investment and corporate development questions
qs: Walk me through a discounted cash flow valuation.
Whether you know the core valuation method and its moving parts.
Unlevered free cash flow, a discount rate that matches it, a terminal value, and a sense of which inputs drive the answer.

I project unlevered free cash flow for five to ten years: after-tax operating profit plus depreciation, minus capex and the increase in working capital. I discount it at the WACC and add a terminal value from a perpetuity growth rate or an exit multiple. That gives enterprise value. Then I check how much of it is terminal value, since that is often most of the answer.
How do you get from enterprise value to equity value per share?
Your grasp of the bridge between what the business is worth and what shareholders own.
Subtract debt and debt-like items, add cash, and divide by fully diluted shares, not basic shares.

I start from enterprise value, subtract debt, preferred stock and noncontrolling interest, and add cash. I also look for debt-like items such as unfunded pensions or deferred purchase payments. Then I divide by diluted shares, counting in-the-money options with the treasury stock method.
Two companies in the same industry trade at 8x and 14x EBITDA. Why might that be?
Whether you can read a valuation multiple instead of just applying it.
Growth, margins, capital needs, risk and quality of revenue explain the gap; the cheaper one is not automatically the better buy.

I would look at growth first, then margins and how much capex each needs, since EBITDA ignores capex. Recurring revenue, customer concentration and leverage matter too. If the 14x company grows twice as fast and turns more of its EBITDA into cash, the gap may be fair. Cheap can just mean a worse business.
What drives returns in a leveraged buyout?
Your understanding of how a financial sponsor makes money on a deal.
EBITDA growth, debt paydown and change in the multiple, with a view on which one is safest to count on.

Three things: growing EBITDA, paying down debt with the company's own cash flow, and selling at a higher multiple than we paid. I like deals where the first two carry the return. Multiple expansion depends on the market at exit, so I usually model the exit at the entry multiple or lower and see if the deal still works.
When is an all-stock acquisition accretive to earnings per share?
Whether you can reason about accretion and dilution without opening a model.
Compare the acquirer's P/E with the P/E paid for the target; and know that accretion alone does not mean the deal creates value.

Before synergies and deal costs, it is accretive if the acquirer's P/E is higher than the P/E we pay for the target, premium included. Our shares buy more earnings than they carry. But accretion is not value creation: a deal can lift EPS and still overpay, so I also look at the return on the price we pay.
What do you look for in a quality of earnings report?
Your due diligence judgement on whether reported earnings are real and repeatable.
Testing every add-back, revenue recognition, one-off items and cash conversion, not taking adjusted EBITDA at face value.

I go through every adjustment to EBITDA and ask if it is truly one-off. A real one-time lawsuit cost can be fair; restructuring that happens every year is not. I check revenue recognition, customer churn, and whether EBITDA turns into cash. If adjusted EBITDA is far above reported EBITDA, each add-back needs proof.
In diligence you learn the target's largest customer is 35% of revenue and its contract renews in six months. What do you do?
How you handle a serious risk found in the middle of a deal.
Size the risk, verify it directly, and protect against it through price or deal structure, not just note it in the memo.

First I size it: what happens to EBITDA and the debt plan if that customer leaves or pushes the price down. I ask for the contract, the renewal history, and a customer call with the seller's consent. Then I bring options to the team: a lower price, an earnout tied to renewal, part of the price held back, or walking away if the risk is too big.
Management's plan shows revenue flat for three years, then growing 25% a year. How do you treat it in your model?
Your judgement with optimistic projections from a seller.
Ask what drives the turn, build your own base case, and price the deal on that, with the seller's plan shown as upside.

I ask what changes in year four: a new product, a new market, a price increase, and what evidence exists today. Then I build our own base case from the history and the sales pipeline, and show management's case as an upside. We pay for what we believe, and if the deal only works on the hockey stick, I say so in the memo.
The night before the investment committee, you find an error in your model that lowers the return from 22% to 17%. What do you do?
Your integrity and how you handle your own mistake under a deadline.
Fix it, tell the deal lead at once, and send corrected numbers with a clear note, even if it hurts the deal.

I fix it, check that nothing else depends on the same mistake, and call the deal lead that night instead of waiting. I send updated pages showing what changed and why. A 17% return may or may not clear our hurdle, but the committee must decide on true numbers. Then I add a check to my model so the same error cannot slip through again.
When can IRR and the multiple of money tell different stories about the same deal?
Whether you understand how time changes the way returns are read.
IRR rewards speed, while the multiple shows how much money was made. A quick, small gain can show a high IRR on a low multiple.

IRR depends on time and the multiple does not. If we double our money in two years, IRR is about 41%. If it takes seven years, it is about 10%, at the same 2.0x. A quick exit or an early dividend recap can push IRR up while the multiple stays modest, so I always show both and ask which one matters most to our investors.
How do you get a discount rate for a private target that has no traded stock?
Your grasp of cost of capital when market data is missing.
Peer betas unlevered, then relevered at the target's capital structure, plus open judgement on size and risk, cross-checked against what buyers expect to earn.

I take betas from listed peers, unlever each one to remove the effect of their debt, and use the median. I relever it at the target's expected debt-to-equity and tax rate and run it through CAPM. For a small private company I often add a size or company-specific premium and say so openly. Then I check the result against returns buyers of similar businesses expect.
Walk me through a sell-side auction process, from first contact to close.
Whether you know the stages of a deal and what each document does.
The steps in order, which bids are binding and which are not, and why the seller keeps buyers competing until exclusivity is granted.

We send a short anonymous teaser, then the confidential information memorandum to buyers who sign an NDA. First-round bids are non-binding indications of interest. A shortlist gets management meetings and the data room, then submits final bids with a markup of the purchase agreement. The seller grants exclusivity to one buyer, we sign, and we close after approvals and financing.
How does a net working capital peg work in a purchase agreement?
Whether you know how the price really moves between signing and closing.
Both sides agree a normal level of working capital, and the price adjusts dollar for dollar if working capital at closing is above or below it.

Buyer and seller agree on the working capital the business normally needs, often a trailing twelve-month average to smooth out seasons. At closing we compare actual working capital to that peg. If it is $2 million short, the price drops $2 million; if it is over, the seller gets more. It stops a seller from collecting receivables and delaying payments to suppliers just before close.
Why would a buyer prefer an asset purchase to a stock purchase, and why might the seller resist?
Your understanding of how deal structure changes taxes and risk.
The buyer gets a stepped-up tax basis and can leave liabilities behind, while a C corporation seller can face two layers of tax.

In an asset deal the buyer's tax basis equals the price paid, so it can depreciate the assets and amortize goodwill for tax over 15 years, and it picks which liabilities to take. A C corporation seller pays tax on the gain, then its owners pay again when cash is paid out, so it prefers a stock sale. For an S corporation or a subsidiary, a 338(h)(10) election can bridge the gap.
How much of the expected synergies should we pay the seller?
How disciplined you are about paying for value the buyer itself has to create.
Only a share of synergies net of costs and risk. Cost synergies count for more than revenue ones, and integration costs and timing are included.

As little as the competition allows, because we carry the risk of delivering them. I value synergies net of one-time integration costs, phased in over two or three years, and I cut revenue synergies hard because they rarely arrive on time. If we only win by paying away most of that value, the deal works for the seller's owners, not ours.
The seller wants $300 million and we think the business is worth $250 million. When would you offer an earn-out, and what can go wrong?
Whether you can bridge a price gap without creating a dispute later.
An earn-out suits a gap caused by uncertain future results. The risks are fights over the metric, the accounting and how the buyer runs the business.

If the gap comes from growth the seller believes in and we doubt, I would pay $250 million at close and up to $50 million more if revenue hits set targets. Disputes come later: how the metric is measured, whether we starved the business, or merged it so results cannot be tracked. So I keep one simple metric, tight definitions, a short period and clear rules on how we run it.
A limited partner asks why our fund shows a 25% IRR while it has returned little cash so far. How do you answer?
How you explain fund performance honestly to an investor.
Separating cash returned from paper value with DPI and TVPI, and being open about what lifts early IRR, such as a subscription credit line.

I would say the IRR rests mostly on unrealized valuations. That is why DPI, cash returned divided by cash paid in, is still low, while TVPI, which adds the remaining value, is higher. I would also say our credit line let us call investors' money later, which raises early IRR. Then I would show how the valuations were set and when we expect exits to turn them into cash.
In the final round, the deal lead wants to bid above the walk-away price you set in the model. What do you do?
Your judgement and backbone when the pressure to win a deal builds.
Asking what facts have changed. If none, stating plainly what the higher price assumes and letting the committee decide with that in view.

I would ask what new information justifies it. If diligence found something real, I update the model and the walk-away price moves. If it is only fear of losing, I show what the higher price requires, for example margins reaching 18% when they have never passed 14%, and put that in the committee memo. Losing a deal costs less than overpaying for one.
A year after an acquisition you championed, the business is 20% below plan. What do you do?
How you own a deal that is going wrong and act on it.
Diagnose fast, tell leadership early, fix what can be fixed, and flag accounting effects such as a possible goodwill impairment test.

First I split the gap: market, execution or a wrong assumption in my model. I tell leadership early, not at year end. Then a plan with owners and dates, whether that means fixing pricing or replacing a leader. I warn finance, since a lasting shortfall can call for an interim goodwill impairment test, and I write down what we missed so the next model learns from it.

investment-banking.heading: Investment banking analyst questions
qs: What is the difference between enterprise value and equity value?
Whether you know the basic valuation bridge every model and pitch book uses.
Equity value belongs to shareholders; enterprise value covers all capital providers, with the correct items added and subtracted.

Equity value is what the shares are worth: share price times diluted shares outstanding. Enterprise value is the value of the operating business to everyone who funds it. To get there I start from equity value, add debt, preferred stock and noncontrolling interest, and subtract cash. That is why I pair EV with EBITDA and equity value with net income.
Why do bankers compare companies on EV/EBITDA rather than only on P/E?
Whether you match each multiple to the right measure of value.
EBITDA is before interest, so it pairs with EV and removes the effect of capital structure; P/E is distorted by debt levels and taxes.

EBITDA is earned before interest is paid, so it belongs to both lenders and shareholders, and enterprise value matches it. P/E sits below interest and taxes, so two companies with the same business but different debt can show very different P/Es. EV/EBITDA lets me compare how the businesses perform, whatever way they are financed.
Walk me through a DCF.
Your command of the core intrinsic valuation method.
Unlevered free cash flow, a terminal value, discounting at WACC, then the bridge from enterprise value to a value per share.

I project unlevered free cash flow for five to ten years: EBIT less taxes, plus depreciation and amortization, minus capex and the increase in working capital. I add a terminal value using a perpetual growth rate or an exit multiple, discount it all back at WACC to get enterprise value, then subtract net debt and divide by diluted shares.
How do you choose the companies for a set of trading comps?
How you judge which peers are truly comparable.
Filters on business model, size, growth and margins, checked against filings, with outliers flagged rather than hidden in the average.

I start with the same industry and business model, then filter by size, growth, margins and geography. I read the 10-Ks instead of trusting a database label. I would rather show six real peers than fifteen loose ones, and I flag outliers, say a company with a one-time gain, so the median is not skewed.
Why do precedent transaction multiples usually come out higher than trading comps?
Whether you understand what a buyer pays for in an acquisition.
A control premium and expected synergies are in the deal price; market conditions at the time of each deal also matter.

A buyer taking over the whole company pays for control and often for synergies it expects, so the price carries a premium over where the stock traded. Trading comps reflect small stakes changing hands every day. I also check deal dates, because multiples from a hot market several years ago may not fit today.
In an all-stock deal, how can you tell quickly whether it will be accretive or dilutive?
Your grasp of merger math and its limits.
Compare the buyer's P/E with the P/E paid for the target, then say what the shortcut ignores and confirm in the full model.

I compare P/Es. If the buyer's P/E is higher than the P/E it pays for the target, it buys earnings more cheaply than its own stock is valued, so EPS should rise. If it is lower, the deal is dilutive. That ignores synergies, fees and amortization of new intangibles, so I confirm it in the pro forma model.
Walk me through a simple LBO.
Whether you understand how a financial sponsor makes its return.
Purchase price and sources and uses, debt paid down from cash flow, an exit, and IRR, with the drivers of return named.

A sponsor buys the company with mostly debt and some equity. I set the price and the sources and uses, project cash flow, use it to pay down debt, then assume an exit after about five years at a chosen multiple. Equity at exit versus equity put in gives the IRR and the money multiple. Returns come from EBITDA growth, debt paydown and any rise in the multiple.
A friend asks you over drinks whether the company you are working on is about to be sold. What do you do?
Whether you handle confidential deal information the way the law and your firm require.
No confirming or denying; knowing it is material nonpublic information, that tipping is illegal, and when to involve compliance.

I do not confirm or deny anything, not even with a joke. What I know is material nonpublic information; passing it on, or trading on it, can break insider trading law for both of us. I change the subject, and if he keeps pressing I tell compliance. I also use deal code names and never discuss work in public places.
Your VP and your MD give you conflicting comments on the same page. How do you handle it?
How you manage competing instructions without wasting time or going around anyone.
Raise the conflict early with the direct supervisor, suggest a solution, and avoid silently picking one version.

I go to the VP first, since that is my direct line, and show both markups side by side. I might suggest a version that meets both points, or ask whether the VP wants to raise it with the MD. Meanwhile I keep both drafts saved so we can switch quickly. What I avoid is guessing and having the page redone at midnight.
It is 1 a.m., the pitch book goes to the client at 8, and you find the comps page uses an old share count. What do you do?
How you handle your own error under deadline pressure.
Fix it at the source, trace every page it flows into, and tell the deal team right away instead of quietly editing.

I pull the share count from the latest 10-Q and fix it in the model, not just on the page. Then I trace everything that links to it: multiples, the football field, the summary. I message my associate with what changed and why, and ask for a second check. I would rather flag it at 1 a.m. than have the client find it at 9.
How do you get from basic shares to the fully diluted share count you use in a valuation?
Whether you can turn equity value into a per-share figure without share-count errors.
The treasury stock method for in-the-money options, unvested RSUs added, and convertibles counted only when converting is worth it.

I start with the latest basic shares, usually from the cover of the most recent 10-Q or 10-K. For in-the-money options I use the treasury stock method: add the new shares, then subtract the shares bought back with the exercise proceeds at today's price. I add unvested RSUs. I count convertibles as shares only if converting is worth more than holding the bond.
When do you discount cash flows at the WACC, and when at the cost of equity?
Whether you match each cash flow with the right discount rate.
Unlevered free cash flow goes with WACC and gives enterprise value; levered free cash flow goes with cost of equity and gives equity value.

It depends on whose cash flow it is. Unlevered free cash flow is before interest, so it belongs to lenders and shareholders; I discount it at the WACC and get enterprise value. Levered free cash flow is after interest and debt repayment, so it belongs to shareholders only; I discount it at the cost of equity and get equity value. Mixing the two is a classic error.
How is goodwill created in an acquisition, and what happens to it afterward under US GAAP?
Your grasp of purchase accounting in M&A models.
Price minus fair value of identifiable net assets; for public companies goodwill is not amortized but tested for impairment at least yearly.

The buyer restates the target's assets and liabilities at fair value, including identified intangibles such as customer relationships. Whatever part of the price is left over becomes goodwill. For a public company, goodwill is not amortized; it is tested for impairment at least once a year, and a write-down hits the income statement. Most of the new intangibles, by contrast, are amortized.
Walk me through a typical two-round sell-side auction.
Whether you know the steps of a sale process and what the analyst produces at each one.
Teaser, NDAs, CIM, first-round indications, management meetings and data room, draft purchase agreement, final bids, then negotiation to signing.

We build a buyer list and a teaser, then sign NDAs and send the confidential information memorandum. Buyers submit non-binding indications of interest with a price range. We pick a short list for management presentations and data room access, send a draft purchase agreement, and ask for final bids with a markup. Then we negotiate with the best bidder through signing.
A buyer offers $500 million on a cash-free, debt-free basis with a normalized working capital target. What does that mean for the seller's proceeds?
Whether you can go from a headline price to what the seller actually receives.
The price is an enterprise value: debt is repaid, cash is credited, and the price moves if closing working capital differs from the target.

The $500 million buys the business without its cash or debt. At closing the seller's debt is repaid out of the price and the seller is credited for its cash, so the equity proceeds are about $500 million minus debt plus cash, before fees. If working capital at closing is above the agreed target, the price usually goes up by the difference; if it is below, the price goes down.
Your three-statement model does not balance. How do you find the error?
How you debug a model with a method instead of guessing.
Find the first period that breaks, check every balance sheet line flows through the cash flow statement with the right sign, and never plug.

First I look at how the gap behaves. If it is the same in every year, the problem is in the opening balance sheet. If it starts in one year and grows, I focus on that year. I check that each balance sheet change runs through the cash flow statement with the right sign, and that cash on the balance sheet links to the cash flow statement. I never plug the difference.
Your DCF's terminal value is 80% of enterprise value. Is that a problem, and how do you check it?
Your judgement on the assumption that drives most of a DCF.
A high share is common; the real test is cross-checking the implied growth rate or implied exit multiple against long-run growth and comps.

On its own it is common, especially for a growing company. What I check is whether the terminal assumption is sane. If I used an exit multiple, I back out the implied perpetuity growth rate. If I used perpetuity growth, I back out the implied EV/EBITDA multiple. Growth above long-run economic growth, or a multiple far above today's comps, means the number is doing too much work.
In diligence, the target's adjusted EBITDA is 30% above reported EBITDA because of add-backs. How do you test them?
Whether you can challenge management's numbers before a buyer does.
Each add-back backed by documents and tested for being truly one-time; recurring 'one-time' costs and unrealized savings called out.

I list every add-back with its amount and ask for support: invoices, contracts, board minutes. Then I ask whether it really will not come back. Restructuring costs that appear every year are a cost of doing business. Projected savings that have not happened yet I show on a separate line. I tell the deal team which add-backs a buyer's diligence team will likely reject.
Your MD asks you to raise the growth assumptions so the DCF supports the price the client wants. What do you do?
How you keep a valuation defensible under pressure from a senior banker.
Ask for the basis, change inputs only with support and a source, and show what growth the target price needs so seniors decide with open eyes.

I would ask what the higher growth is based on. If there is a real reason, like a new signed contract, I update the model and note the source. If not, I would show the MD a sensitivity table: the growth needed to reach that price, next to the company's history and the comps. The valuation has to hold up when buyers test it, and the bank's name is on it.
After the model went to the client, you find an error that changes the valuation range. What do you do?
How you own a mistake that has already left the building.
Size the impact, tell your VP right away with a corrected file, let seniors send a clear correction, then add a check so it cannot recur.

I fix it in a copy first so I know the true impact, say the range drops by $1.50 a share. Then I tell my VP within the hour: what went wrong, the size of it, and the corrected file. The senior bankers decide how to tell the client, usually a short note with the revised page. Afterward I add a check to the model so the same error cannot slip through again.

ios-developer.heading: iOS developer questions
qs: When do you use a struct and when a class in Swift?
Whether you understand value and reference types, the base of Swift.
Structs are copied and classes are shared by reference. Default to structs and use a class when shared identity or inheritance is needed.

A struct is a value type. When I pass it around, each holder gets its own copy, so a change in one place doesn't surprise another. A class is a reference type, so everyone points at the same object. I default to structs for models and use a class when I need shared identity, inheritance, or Objective-C APIs.
Your crash reports show “Unexpectedly found nil while unwrapping an Optional value.” What does that mean and how do you fix it?
How you handle optionals, a common source of Swift crashes.
Finding the force unwrap and handling the nil case on purpose, not hiding it with a silent default value.

Somewhere the code used ! on a value that was nil, either a force unwrap or an implicitly unwrapped optional. I find the line from the symbolicated stack trace, then ask why it can be nil. Usually I replace it with guard let or if let and handle the missing case clearly, like showing an error state. A silent default can hide the real bug.
The app crashes the moment a user taps “Scan receipt” to open the camera, and the console mentions privacy. What is wrong?
Your knowledge of iOS privacy permissions and Info.plist.
The missing usage description key, plus asking for permission at the right moment and handling a denial.

The app is missing the camera usage description in Info.plist, the NSCameraUsageDescription key. iOS terminates an app that accesses the camera without it. I add a clear sentence on why we need the camera, ask for access only when the user taps the button, and show a path to Settings if they said no before.
Where do you store a user's login token on the device, and why?
Whether you protect sensitive data on the device.
In the Keychain, not UserDefaults or a plain file, with an access level that fits when the app needs the token.

In the Keychain. UserDefaults is a plain property list in the app's container and is not meant for secrets. The Keychain encrypts items and lets me choose when they can be read, for example after the first unlock if a background refresh needs the token. On logout I delete the item.
Scrolling a list of photos stutters. How do you find and fix the cause?
How you keep the main thread free and measure performance.
Measuring with Instruments first, then moving heavy work like image decoding and resizing off the main thread and caching the results.

I profile on a real device with Instruments, starting with the Time Profiler, to see what blocks the main thread. Often it is full-size images decoded while scrolling. I resize them to the cell size in a background task, cache the result, and only set the image on the main thread. Then I profile again to confirm the fix.
Memory grows every time a user opens and closes a detail screen. What do you suspect, and how do you prove it?
Your grasp of ARC and retain cycles.
A retain cycle, confirmed with the Memory Graph Debugger or Instruments, and broken with a weak or unowned reference.

I suspect a retain cycle: the view controller holds a closure that captures self strongly, so neither is ever freed. I open and close the screen a few times, then use Xcode's Memory Graph Debugger to see the leftover instances and what holds them. The fix is usually [weak self] in the closure or a weak delegate. A log in deinit confirms it.
Your app is mostly UIKit. Would you build a new settings screen in SwiftUI? How do you decide?
Your judgement in mixing SwiftUI and UIKit in a real app.
Weighing the minimum iOS version, team skills and screen complexity, and knowing the two frameworks can live together.

Probably yes. Forms and lists are where SwiftUI saves the most code. I'd check that our minimum iOS version supports the SwiftUI features I need and that the team can maintain it. I'd host it in a UIHostingController so it fits our UIKit navigation. For a complex custom screen with heavy gestures, I might stay in UIKit.
A user fills in a long form, switches to another app to look up a number, and comes back to an empty form. What happened?
Whether you understand the app lifecycle and that iOS can end a suspended app.
Knowing the system can terminate a suspended app with no warning, and saving the draft when the app leaves the foreground.

In the background the app was suspended, and iOS then terminated it to free memory. The app gets no callback for that, so I can't wait for one. I save the draft when the scene moves to the background, or as the user types, and restore it on the next launch. I test it by backgrounding the app and stopping it from Xcode.
A user leaves a screen while its network request is still loading. What should happen, and how do you make sure it does?
How you use Swift concurrency and cancellation.
Cancelling the work tied to the screen, knowing cancellation is cooperative, and never updating a screen that is gone.

The request should be canceled so we don't waste data or update a screen that's gone. In SwiftUI I start it in the .task modifier, which cancels the task when the view disappears. In UIKit I keep the Task and cancel it when the screen goes away. Cancellation is cooperative, so long loops check Task.isCancelled, and I don't show an error alert for a cancel.
A release you shipped crashes on launch for some users. What do you do in the first hours?
How you handle a bad release when the App Store has no rollback.
Pausing the rollout, shipping a fix fast with expedited review, and using remote flags, knowing users who already updated can't be rolled back.

I check the crash reports to see who is affected, for example one iOS version. If we used a phased release, I pause it so fewer automatic updates go out. There is no rollback for people who already updated, so I fix the cause, test it, and submit with a request for expedited review. If a remote flag can turn off the broken feature, I do that first.
What is the difference between a universal link and a custom URL scheme, and which would you use for links in emails?
Whether you know how iOS hands a web link to an app and what breaks when it fails.
Universal links need the Associated Domains entitlement and a file on the website; they fall back to the web if the app is missing.

A custom scheme like myapp:// can be claimed by any app, and if our app is not installed the link just fails. A universal link is a normal https link. The app lists the domain in its Associated Domains entitlement, and the site serves an apple-app-site-association file that names the paths. If the app is missing, the link opens the website. For emails I use universal links.
Xcode shows a purple runtime warning that a UI property is changed from a background thread. Why does it matter, and how do you fix it properly?
Whether you understand the main thread rule and fix it at the source, not line by line.
UI code is not thread-safe, so bugs are random. A lasting fix lets the compiler enforce it, for example with @MainActor on the view model.

UIKit and SwiftUI expect UI changes on the main thread. Off it, you get glitches or rare crashes that are hard to reproduce. Wrapping the line in DispatchQueue.main.async works once, but I'd rather mark the view model @MainActor. Then the compiler flags every wrong call, and the network code returns to the main actor with await.
A crash report shows only memory addresses instead of function names. What is missing, and how do you prevent it next release?
Your understanding of symbolication and of a release process that keeps crash reports readable.
The dSYM for that exact build is missing; it must match the binary's UUID. Uploading dSYMs automatically from CI prevents it.

The report is not symbolicated: the crash tool has no dSYM file for that exact build. A dSYM only works for the binary with the same UUID, so one from another build will not help. I'd find the right one in the archive in Xcode Organizer and upload it. Then I'd add a CI step that uploads the dSYMs for every release build automatically.
How would you roll out a release with a risky change to millions of users?
How you limit the damage of a bad release before it reaches everyone.
Phased release plus a remote flag, metrics watched daily. Knowing phased release covers only automatic updates; people can still update by hand.

I put the risky part behind a remote feature flag, off by default, and turn on phased release in App Store Connect. That gives automatic updates to a growing share of users over seven days. Users can still update by hand, so I also watch the flag. Each day I check crash-free sessions and key metrics. If something looks wrong, I pause the rollout or switch the flag off without a new build.
A user records a large video and leaves the app while it uploads. How do you make sure the upload finishes?
Whether you know how iOS lets transfers continue after the app is suspended.
A background URLSession with an upload from a file, and handling the relaunch. Knowing a force-quit by the user cancels the transfer.

A normal request stops soon after the app is suspended. I'd use a URLSession with a background configuration and an upload task from a file, since background sessions upload from files, not from data in memory. The system keeps the transfer going, even if it terminates our app, and relaunches the app in the background to report the result through the session delegate.
Product wants to refresh content every hour with silent push notifications. What do you tell them?
Whether you know the limits iOS puts on background work and can say no with a better plan.
Silent pushes are low priority, can be throttled, and do not reach an app the user force-quit. Use them as a hint, plus refresh on foreground.

Silent pushes are treated as low priority. The system may delay or drop them, and it does not deliver them to an app the user force-quit. Apple also advises sending only a few per hour. So I'd treat them as a hint, not a schedule. I'd add a background app refresh task and always refresh when the app comes to the foreground, so the data is fresh when the user looks.
You add a field to a Core Data entity, and testers crash on launch after updating the app. What went wrong?
How you handle data that already lives on users' phones when the model changes.
The model was likely edited in place, so the old store will not load. A new model version, lightweight migration, and an upgrade test with real data.

Most likely the model was edited in place, so the store on disk no longer matches and loading fails. I'd restore the old model as a version and add a new model version with the change. Lightweight migration handles simple changes like a new optional field, or a required one with a default. Then I test the upgrade from the shipped version with real data, not a fresh install.
Crash reports show the code 0x8badf00d, mostly on older devices at launch. What does it mean and what do you do?
Whether you recognize a watchdog termination and know where to look.
The system killed the app for blocking the main thread too long. Find the blocking work in the main thread stack, move or defer it, measure on old devices.

That is the watchdog: the system killed the app because the main thread was blocked too long, here during launch. I read the main thread's stack in the report. Often it is a synchronous network call, a big file read or database setup. I move that work off the main thread or defer it until after the first screen, then measure launch in Instruments on an old device.
Inside an actor, a method checks a cache, awaits a download, then saves to the cache. Logs show two downloads of the same image. Why?
Your depth in Swift concurrency, especially actor reentrancy.
Actors are reentrant: other calls run at each await. Store the in-flight Task before awaiting, and re-check state after every await.

Actors are reentrant. At each await, the actor can run other calls. Both calls checked the cache, found nothing, and both started a download. I'd store the in-flight Task in a dictionary before the await, so a second caller awaits the same task instead of starting a new one. And after any await I re-check state rather than assume it did not change.

it-manager.heading: IT manager questions
qs: What does a good laptop lifecycle look like, from purchase to disposal?
Whether you know the full life of an asset, not just the help desk part.
Standard models tracked in an inventory, encrypted from day one, refreshed on a plan, and wiped with proof before disposal.

We buy a few standard models, log each one by serial number and owner, and ship it with disk encryption and device management already on. We plan a refresh every three to four years so costs are predictable. At the end I wipe it, keep the wipe record or the recycler's certificate, and remove it from the inventory and the licenses.
Walk me through what happens when an employee leaves the company.
How you close access quickly and keep the company's data.
One checklist, run on time: accounts, sessions, MFA, shared passwords, devices, licenses, and data handed to the manager.

HR tells us the date ahead, and on the last day we disable the account in the identity system, which cuts most apps at once. We sign out active sessions, remove MFA devices and change any shared passwords they knew. Mailbox and files go to the manager, the laptop comes back and is wiped, and the licenses are freed. A checklist means nothing depends on memory.
What is the 3-2-1 backup rule, and is it enough?
Your grasp of backups as a recovery plan, not a setting.
Three copies, on two kinds of storage, one off site; plus a copy ransomware cannot change and restores that are actually tested.

Three copies of the data, on two different types of storage, with one copy off site. Today I also want one copy that ransomware cannot alter, either offline or immutable. And a backup is only proven when you restore from it, so I schedule test restores and time them against what the business says it can tolerate.
What is the difference between RPO and RTO, and who decides them?
Whether you can turn recovery into business terms.
RPO is how much data you can lose, RTO how long you can be down; business owners choose them and IT shows what each costs.

RPO, recovery point objective, is how much data we can afford to lose, measured in time: nightly backups mean up to a day. RTO, recovery time objective, is how long a system can be down before it really hurts. I don't pick them alone. I ask each department head, show what each target costs, and they choose.
How do you keep software license costs under control?
Whether you manage licenses as spending, not just as tickets.
One inventory, regular usage reviews, seats reclaimed at offboarding, and renewal dates tracked well before notice periods.

I keep one list of every subscription with its owner, seat count and renewal date. Every quarter I compare seats to actual logins and reclaim the unused ones. Renewals go on a calendar months ahead, because many contracts auto-renew if you miss the notice window. Card spending on software gets reviewed so tools bought outside IT come to light.
An employee calls: they typed their password into a fake login page an hour ago. What do you do?
How you respond to a compromised account in the first hour.
Reset and revoke at once, then look for what the attacker did: sign-ins, mailbox rules, MFA changes, mail sent.

I thank them for calling fast, then reset the password, sign out all sessions and check MFA methods for anything new. I review sign-in logs for odd locations and the mailbox for forwarding or delete rules attackers like to add. If mail went out from it, we warn the recipients. Then I block the fake site and warn staff, without naming the person.
Your CEO wants local admin rights on their laptop. How do you handle it?
Your judgement when security meets seniority.
A respectful no to permanent admin rights, a real fix for the need behind the request, and a written exception if leadership insists.

I ask what they are trying to do; usually it is one app they can't install. I fix that today. Then I explain that executives are the top phishing target, and admin rights let malware install itself. If they still insist, I offer a separate admin account used only when needed, and I write the risk down so the decision is theirs, on paper.
A critical security patch comes out on a Friday afternoon for a system everyone uses. What do you do?
How you weigh the risk of an attack against the risk of a bad patch.
Check exposure and active exploitation, test on a small group, roll out with a rollback plan, or apply a workaround if it can wait.

I check whether we are exposed and whether the flaw is being exploited in the wild. If it is and the system faces the internet, I patch this weekend: a test group first, then everyone, with a rollback ready and someone on call. If it can wait, I apply the vendor's workaround now and patch in our normal window. Either way, users hear what to expect.
A change your team pushed took down the network for the whole office. How do you handle it, during and after?
How you own a mistake your team caused.
Service restored first, updates on a steady rhythm, then a blameless review that changes the process rather than blaming a person.

I roll back first and investigate second; getting people working matters more than knowing why. I post updates every 30 minutes, even when nothing has changed. Afterwards we run a blameless review: what we changed, why testing missed it, and what stops it next time. Last time that meant a pilot group and a written rollback step for every network change.
Walk me through how you build next year's IT budget.
Whether you can plan and defend IT spending.
Start from what is already committed, add projects with business cases, separate one-time from recurring costs, and keep a contingency.

I start with what is committed: subscriptions, support contracts, and laptops due for refresh from the inventory. That is the cost to run. Then I list projects, each tied to a business goal with a cost and an owner. I separate one-time from recurring costs, add a small contingency, and walk finance through the trade-offs instead of handing over one total.
What does SCIM add when you connect a new SaaS app to single sign-on?
Whether you know how accounts are created and removed automatically, not just how people log in.
SSO controls the login. SCIM creates, updates and removes the account itself, so leavers lose access without manual cleanup.

SSO only controls how people sign in. SCIM is an open standard that lets the identity provider create, update and deactivate accounts in the app. Without it, a leaver can keep a live account, an API token or a local password after we disable them centrally. For any app holding company data, I ask for SSO and SCIM in the contract.
Which kinds of multi-factor authentication would you roll out, and which would you retire?
Your grasp of how strong each MFA method is against real attacks.
Ranks methods correctly: security keys and passkeys resist phishing, push needs number matching, and SMS is the weakest.

I aim for phishing-resistant methods, meaning FIDO2 security keys or passkeys, starting with admins and finance. Authenticator push is acceptable with number matching turned on, so people cannot just tap approve on a flood of prompts. I retire SMS codes where I can, because SIM swaps and fake login pages can capture them.
An employee moves from finance to sales. What happens to their access?
Whether you handle internal moves, where access piles up quietly.
Access follows the new role: old rights removed, new ones granted through role groups, with reviews to catch leftovers.

Movers are where privilege creep happens: people keep the old access and add the new. I tie access to role-based groups, so the HR change removes the finance groups and adds the sales ones. Anything granted by hand gets a short grace period for handover, then goes. Quarterly access reviews catch what the process misses.
How would you keep guest Wi-Fi and office printers apart from staff laptops on the network?
Your practical knowledge of network segmentation.
Separate VLANs with firewall rules between them. Guests get internet only; devices accept only the ports they need.

Each group gets its own VLAN. Guest Wi-Fi goes to the internet only, with client isolation so guests cannot see each other. Printers sit on their own VLAN, and the firewall lets staff laptops reach them only on printing ports. Nothing on the device VLAN can start a connection to laptops, so one hacked printer does not reach the rest of the office.
Staff want work email on their personal phones. How do you set that up?
How you protect company data on devices you do not own while respecting privacy.
Protects the work data, not the whole phone: work profile or app policies, conditional access, and selective wipe only.

I would not fully manage a personal phone. On Android I use a work profile; on iPhone, user enrollment or app protection policies. Company apps get a PIN, no copying data out, and conditional access blocks phones that are not compliant. If the phone is lost or the person leaves, I wipe only company data. I also write down plainly what IT can and cannot see.
You find a department has paid for a SaaS tool on a company card for two years, and it holds customer data. What do you do?
How you handle shadow IT without breaking trust or ignoring the risk.
Learns why it happened, checks the data risk first, then brings the tool under IT control or migrates it, without blame.

First I talk to the team: they bought it because we did not meet a need. Then I check the risk: who has accounts, whether former staff still log in, the vendor's security terms, and where the data sits. If it passes, it moves to a proper contract with SSO. If not, we plan a migration together. Then I fix intake so asking IT is faster than using a card.
How do you decide whether to keep a server room or move those workloads to the cloud?
Whether you compare the true total cost and risk, not just the monthly bill.
Full cost of ownership both ways, including power, cooling, refresh and staff time, plus egress fees, latency and skills.

I compare total cost over five years. On premises that means hardware refresh, power, cooling, licenses, support contracts and the hours my team spends patching. In the cloud it means compute, storage, backup and data egress fees. Then the non-money items: latency for local apps, compliance needs and our cloud skills. Often the answer is mixed, workload by workload.
A software vendor sends notice of a license audit. Walk me through your response.
How you protect the company during a vendor audit.
Reads the audit clause, involves legal and procurement, runs its own count first, and controls what data is shared.

I do not reply right away. I bring in legal and procurement, read the audit clause in our contract, and agree on scope, timing and confidentiality in writing. Meanwhile my team counts our installs against our entitlements, so we find gaps first. One person handles all contact, and we review any script the vendor wants to run before it touches our systems.
You find a service account with domain admin rights that three systems use and no one owns. What do you do?
How you reduce a privileged-account risk without breaking production.
Maps usage from logs first, assigns an owner, then replaces it with least-privilege accounts and rotated passwords.

I do not just disable it; something would break. I check logon logs to see where and how it is used, and name an owner. Then each system gets its own account with only the rights it needs, using group managed service accounts where possible so Active Directory rotates the password. Once nothing uses the old account, I disable it, watch for errors, then delete it.
At 9 a.m. a laptop shows signs of ransomware. What are your first moves?
Whether you can lead the first hour of a security incident in the right order.
Isolates without powering off, contains accounts, protects backups, follows the plan and calls legal and the insurer early.

I cut the laptop off the network but leave it on, so evidence in memory survives. I disable the user's account and sessions and check other machines for the same signs. I confirm our offline backups are untouched. Then I follow the incident plan: call legal, leadership and our cyber insurer early, since many policies require their response firm.

it-project-manager.heading: IT project manager questions
qs: What goes into a cutover plan for a system go-live?
Whether you have actually planned and run a go-live weekend.
A step-by-step runbook with owners, checkpoints, a rollback trigger and the communications around it.

A step-by-step runbook: each task with an owner, start time, duration and the check that proves it worked. It covers freezing the old system, data loads, smoke tests, a go/no-go checkpoint, the point after which rollback is no longer practical, and who tells users what and when. We rehearse it at least once in a test environment and time it.
What is the difference between system testing and user acceptance testing, and who signs off UAT?
Your grasp of the test stages on an IT project.
System testing proves it works as built; UAT proves it supports the real business process. The business owner signs UAT, not IT.

System testing is done by the delivery team against the requirements: does each function and integration work. UAT is done by real users running their actual processes, like closing a month or onboarding a hire, with realistic data. The business process owner signs it off, because they accept the risk of using it. If IT signs its own UAT, nobody has really accepted it.
How do you choose between a big-bang go-live, a phased rollout and a parallel run?
How you match the rollout approach to risk, cost and the business.
Trade-offs named for each: big bang is fast but risky, phased limits exposure, parallel is safest but doubles user work.

Big bang switches everyone at once; it is cheapest, but a failure hits everyone. Phased goes by site, region or module, so early waves teach us before the rest. A parallel run keeps both systems live and compares results; it suits things like payroll, but staff enter data twice, so I keep it short. I pick based on how bad a failure would be and how easily we can recover.
Walk me through how you plan a data migration from a legacy system.
Whether you treat data migration as its own workstream, not a single task.
Profiling and cleanup early, mapping signed off by data owners, several trial loads, and reconciliation with agreed counts and totals.

I start by profiling the old data to find duplicates, gaps and odd formats, and give cleanup to the business owners early. Then field mapping, signed off by the data owners. We run two or three trial loads into test, each timed and reconciled: record counts, control totals like open balances, and spot checks by users. The final load uses the same scripts we rehearsed.
What is hypercare, and how do you decide when it ends?
Whether you plan for the weeks after go-live, not just launch day.
A defined period of extra support with exit criteria agreed in advance, then a clean handover to the support team.

Hypercare is the period right after go-live when the project team stays on hand with faster response and daily ticket triage. I agree the exit criteria before go-live: for example, no open critical tickets, ticket volume near normal for two weeks, and the support team trained with runbooks. Then I formally hand over to operations so the project can close.
The tech lead wants to switch off the old system the week after go-live. What do you check first?
Whether you think about everything still depending on the old system.
Data retention and legal holds, hidden integrations and reports, access to history, and contract terms, before anything is shut down.

First, records retention: what data must be kept, for how long, and whether any is under a legal hold. Then dependencies: scheduled jobs, reports or other systems still reading from it, which I confirm from access logs. Then how users will look up history, and the license or hosting contract terms. I would usually make it read-only first and switch it off later.
Your go-live date lands inside the company's year-end change freeze. What do you do?
How you work with IT change control instead of around it.
Raising it early, bringing options with their risks, and following the change approval process; never pushing a change through quietly.

I raise it as soon as I spot it, not in the last week. I take options to the sponsor: go live before the freeze with a tighter plan, move after it, or request an exception through the change advisory board with a clear rollback plan. Freezes exist because finance and operations cannot absorb risk then, so the answer is usually to move the date.
The vendor tells you their integration API will be three weeks late. How do you respond?
How you handle a dependency you do not control.
Impact on the critical path first, then options like resequencing or building against a mock, and a prompt update to the sponsor.

First I check whether the API is on the critical path; if other testing can continue, the real slip may be smaller. I ask the team whether we can build against a mock of the API so our side is ready. I ask the vendor for a firm date in writing and check the contract. Then I give the sponsor the new forecast and options that week, not at the next status meeting.
Two days before go-live, UAT finds that some invoices calculate tax wrong. Do you go live?
Your judgement on a go/no-go decision under deadline pressure.
Sizing the impact first, checking the agreed go/no-go criteria and workarounds, and letting the business owner decide on the facts.

I find out how many invoices are affected and whether a fix can be tested in two days. Wrong tax on customer invoices is a financial and compliance risk, so unless there is a reliable workaround, like holding those invoices for manual review, I recommend no-go.
