The business owner decides against the criteria we agreed earlier, and I record the decision and why.
Midway through a weekend cutover, reconciliation shows 3% of customer records did not load. What do you do?
How you lead when a cutover goes wrong in real time.
Pausing to diagnose within a time box, using the rollback trigger agreed in the plan, and updating stakeholders on a set schedule.

I pause further steps and get the data lead to find the cause, with a time box. If it is a known, fixable reason, like a date format the load rejected, we fix it, reload and reconcile again. If we cannot explain it before our planned rollback deadline, we roll back as the runbook says. Meanwhile I send updates on a fixed schedule to the sponsor and support leads.
What is the critical path, and why do you care about float on the other tasks?
Whether you understand what really drives the end date of a schedule.
The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks, with zero float. Tasks with little float are watched too, since they can become critical.

The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks. It sets the earliest date we can finish, and any slip on it moves go-live. Float is how long a task can slip before it delays the end date. I watch near-critical tasks with only a few days of float, because one late vendor delivery can make them the new critical path.
The team has never done this kind of work and cannot give you one estimate. How do you estimate it?
How you build an estimate under uncertainty and show the range honestly.
A method such as three-point estimating, with assumptions written down and a range given instead of a single false number.

I ask for three numbers: optimistic, most likely and pessimistic. Say 4, 6 and 14 days. The weighted average (O + 4M + P) / 6 gives 7 days. The wide spread tells me the risk is high, so I report a range, write down the assumptions, and plan a short spike to learn more before I commit the date.
What is the difference between contingency reserve and management reserve?
Your grasp of how a budget handles known and unknown risk.
Contingency covers identified risks and sits in the cost baseline; management reserve covers unforeseen work and sits outside it, released by management.

Contingency reserve is money or time set aside for risks we have identified, like a data cleanup that may run long. It is part of the cost baseline and I can draw on it under the plan. Management reserve covers the unknowns. It sits outside the baseline, and using it needs approval from the sponsor or leadership.
Halfway through, your cost performance index is 0.85 and your schedule performance index is 0.9. What does that tell you, and what do you do?
Whether you can read earned value numbers and turn them into a forecast and action.
Correct reading of both indexes, a forecast of the final cost, and a look at the causes before reporting with options.

CPI of 0.85 means we get 85 cents of planned work for each dollar spent. SPI of 0.9 means we have done 90% of the work planned by now. If the trend holds, a $1M budget ends near $1.18M, which is budget divided by CPI. I find the tasks driving the overrun, then bring the sponsor a forecast and options, not just the numbers.
Who sits in your go/no-go meeting, and how do you set the criteria?
How you make the go-live decision clear, owned and not driven by pressure on the day.
Criteria agreed in writing well before the meeting, each with an owner, and one named decision-maker, usually the business sponsor.

I agree the criteria weeks ahead: no open critical defects, UAT signed off, data reconciliation within the agreed tolerance, support team trained, rollback tested. Each has an owner who reports red or green. The business sponsor makes the call. Agreeing it early stops people from moving the bar on the night because the date feels fixed.
Six weeks before go-live, the sponsor asks to add a new report that a VP wants. How do you handle it?
How you protect the baseline without saying no to the business by reflex.
The request goes through change control with its impact on time, cost and risk shown, and the sponsor decides with clear options.

I thank them and log it as a change request. The team sizes it, and I show the impact: say eight days of build and test, plus risk to the UAT window. I give options: add it and move the date, swap out lower-value scope, or deliver it in a release after go-live. The sponsor picks, and I update the plan and log the decision.
Every workstream reports green, but your gut says the project is in trouble. What do you do?
Whether you can find the real status behind optimistic reporting.
Looking at evidence such as burn-down, defect trends and missed handoffs, talking to the people doing the work, and making red safe to report.

I stop reading the colors and look at evidence: tasks finished versus planned, defect open and close rates, and dependencies that slipped. I talk to the engineers, not just the leads. If a green turns out amber, I thank whoever raised it. People hide problems when red gets punished, so I make an early red feel like a good thing.
When would you choose a fixed-price contract with a vendor, and when time and materials?
Your judgement on vendor contracts and where the risk sits.
Fixed price when scope is clear and stable; time and materials when it is not, with caps and close tracking. Knows fixed price brings change orders.

Fixed price fits when scope is well defined, like installing a known product to a clear spec. The vendor carries the overrun risk, but every change becomes a change order, often at a premium. Time and materials fits discovery work where scope will move. Then the risk is ours, so I set a not-to-exceed cap and review hours against deliverables every week.
You inherit a project that is four months late and the team is worn out. What do you do in your first month?
How you recover a troubled project with honesty and a credible new plan.
Listening first, finding the true status, cutting or resequencing scope, and resetting a believable baseline with the sponsor instead of promising to catch up.

First two weeks, I listen: one-on-ones with the team, the sponsor and key users, and I find what is really done. Then I rebuild the plan from the remaining work, not the old date. I bring the sponsor a reset baseline with scope options. I also stop extra weekend work unless it is critical, because a tired team makes the defects that cause more delay.
Tell me about a project decision you would make differently today.
Whether you learn from mistakes and own them.
A real, specific mistake, owned without blaming others, with the cost and a concrete change in how the candidate works now.

On an ERP rollout I let the vendor run integration testing alone to save time. We found two interface failures in UAT, which cost us three weeks. Now I insist on joint integration testing with our own test cases, and I put entry criteria for UAT in the plan so a phase cannot start until the one before it has really finished.

it-support.heading: IT support questions
qs: A laptop shows an IP address starting with 169.254. What does that tell you?
Whether you know basic network addressing on a client device.
The device got no answer from DHCP and gave itself a link-local address, so the fault lies between the laptop and the DHCP server.

It means the laptop asked for an address, got no answer from the DHCP server, and gave itself a link-local one. With that address it cannot reach the gateway. I would check the cable or Wi-Fi connection and renew the lease. Then I would see whether other devices on the same port or network have the same problem.
A user calls and says the internet is down. Walk me through your first five minutes.
How you narrow down a vague complaint step by step.
Scope comes first: one user or many. Then you work up from the physical link to the IP address, the gateway, DNS and the specific site.

First I ask what exactly fails and whether coworkers have the same issue. If many do, it is an outage and I escalate. If it is one person, I check Wi-Fi or cable, then the IP address, then ping the gateway, then try a site by name and by IP. Each step tells me which layer broke, and I note it in the ticket as I go.
A user can reach a server by its IP address but not by its name. Where do you look?
Whether you can tell a name resolution problem from a connection problem.
It points to DNS. Check which DNS servers the device uses, test with nslookup, clear the local cache, and look for a wrong or stale record.

If the IP works, the network path is fine, so it is almost always DNS. I run nslookup on the name to see what answer comes back and from which server. If the device points at the wrong DNS server, say from a home router or VPN setting, I fix that. If the record itself is wrong or old, I flush the cache and tell whoever manages DNS.
What do you write in a ticket before you close it?
Your documentation habits, and whether others can use your notes later.
The cause, what was done, and how the fix was confirmed with the user. Repeat issues get turned into a knowledge base article.

I write what the user reported, the cause I found, the exact steps I took, and how I confirmed the fix, ideally with the user. If it is the third time I have seen the same issue, I write or update a knowledge base article and link it. That way the next tech can fix it in two minutes instead of twenty.
A user asks for local admin rights so they can install software themselves. How do you respond?
Whether you apply least privilege without blocking people's work.
Find out what they need and offer the approved route, such as a one-time install, the software catalog or a temporary approved elevation. Avoid permanent admin rights.

I ask what they want to install and why. Often it is one tool, so I install it for them or add it to our self-service catalog after it is checked. Permanent admin rights make malware and accidental changes much easier, so I do not hand those out. If their role truly needs it, there is an approval process with their manager and security.
Someone calls saying they are a vice president traveling abroad, locked out, and needs a password reset right now. What do you do?
How you hold to identity verification under pressure.
The approved verification applies to everyone, such as a callback to the number on file or a self-service reset with MFA. Urgency plus rank is a red flag.

I stay polite but use the same verification as for anyone. I call back the number on file, not the one they are calling from, or have them use self-service reset with their MFA. Urgency plus a big title is a classic social engineering pattern. If I cannot verify, I do not reset, and I log the call and tell security.
An employee leaves the company today. Walk me through the offboarding on the IT side.
Whether you know the steps that close access cleanly and keep the data.
Disable rather than delete, end active sessions, remove group and shared access, collect devices, and keep the mailbox and files as policy says.

At the agreed time I disable the account and sign out all sessions, so phone apps and webmail stop too. I remove groups, shared mailbox access and admin roles, and change shared passwords they knew. I collect the laptop and badge, pass the mailbox and files to the manager per policy, and free the licenses. I do not delete the account right away.
A user tells you their company laptop was stolen from their car. What do you do?
How you contain the risk from a lost or stolen device.
Confirm the disk is encrypted, lock or wipe it remotely, reset the password and end sessions, and report it as a security incident.

First I check in our device management tool that the disk is encrypted, and I send a remote lock or wipe. I reset the user's password and sign out their sessions, since saved logins may be on it. I ask what data was on it, file the security incident report, and suggest they file a police report. Then I get them a replacement so they can work.
A user clicked a link in an email and typed in their password. They tell you an hour later. What do you do?
Your response to an account that is likely compromised.
Reset the password, end sessions, check for new MFA methods and mailbox rules the attacker added, and hand off to security. Thank the user for reporting.

I thank them for telling me, then reset the password and sign out all sessions. I check whether new MFA methods or devices were added, and look for mailbox rules that forward or delete mail, which attackers often set up. I review the sign-in log for odd locations, send it all to security, and check who else got the same email.
You pushed a settings change to all laptops and it broke the VPN for a hundred people. What now?
How you own a mistake and limit the damage.
Roll back first, tell users and the team plainly, then find the cause and use a small pilot group before wide changes.

I roll the change back first and confirm on a couple of machines that the VPN works again. I send a short note to users and my lead: what broke, that it is fixed, and what to do if it is not. Then I find out why my testing missed it. From then on, changes go to a small pilot group for a day before everyone gets them.
What is the difference between a security group and a distribution group in Active Directory?
Whether you know the basic building blocks of account administration.
Security groups grant access to resources; distribution groups are only email lists. Mentions that a security group can also be mail-enabled.

A security group can be given permissions on a shared folder, a printer or an app. A distribution group is only an email list and cannot grant access to anything. A security group can also be mail-enabled, so I use that when a team needs both. I name groups by purpose, so the next person knows what removing someone does.
A user's account locks out every morning, even right after you reset it. How do you find the cause?
How you trace a repeating problem to its source instead of fixing the symptom.
Uses the domain controller logs to find the source device, knows the usual stale-credential causes, and fixes the source before resetting.

I check the domain controller security log for event 4740, which names the computer the bad attempts came from. Usually it is a phone still syncing mail with the old password, a mapped drive with saved credentials, or a task running as the user. I clear the stale password there, then reset once. Resetting without that just restarts the cycle.
A laptop shows the error that the trust relationship between this workstation and the primary domain failed. What does it mean and how do you fix it?
Your understanding of how domain-joined computers authenticate.
Explains that the computer account password is out of sync with the domain, names a common cause, and repairs the secure channel or rejoins.

The laptop's computer account password no longer matches what the domain has, often after it was restored from an old image or snapshot. I sign in with a local admin account, run Test-ComputerSecureChannel with the Repair switch and domain admin credentials, and reboot. If that fails, I remove it from the domain and rejoin it.
A user's laptop boots to a BitLocker recovery screen. Why did it happen and what do you do?
Whether you know disk encryption well enough to unlock a device safely.
Names likely triggers, verifies the caller before giving a key, finds the key by its ID, and rotates the key afterwards.

Something changed in what the TPM checks at boot: a BIOS update, a changed boot order or Secure Boot setting. I confirm who the caller is, ask for the key ID shown on screen, and read them the 48-digit recovery key from where we store keys. Then I find the trigger and rotate that key, since it was just read out loud.
Around noon, new devices on the office Wi-Fi cannot get online, but people who connected in the morning are fine. What is your theory?
How you reason from a pattern of symptoms to a network cause.
Suspects DHCP scope exhaustion, confirms it in the lease table, and gives both a quick fix and a lasting one.

It sounds like the DHCP scope is full: every address is leased, so new devices get nothing while existing leases keep working. I check the lease table to confirm and see who holds the addresses; phones and guests are usual culprits. Short term I clear stale leases or shorten lease time. The real fix is a bigger scope or a separate guest network.
A vice president's printer and a whole team's shared drive break at the same time. You are alone. Which comes first?
Your judgement in setting ticket priority under pressure.
Prioritizes by impact and urgency rather than title, gives the VP a workaround and a time, and stays open to new facts.

The shared drive comes first: a whole team is stopped, and the VP can print elsewhere today. I tell the VP directly, give a time and point to the nearest working printer. Priority comes from how many people are affected and how badly, not title. If the VP must print a board document in an hour, that changes urgency and I say so.
How do you set up access for a new hire so it is right on day one and stays right?
How you build onboarding that is fast, repeatable and follows least privilege.
Role-based access instead of copying a coworker, approval before the start date, device ready in advance, and regular access reviews.

I build access from the role, not by copying a coworker's account, because copying spreads old permissions. Each role has a set of groups, licenses and a device profile, approved by the manager before day one. The laptop is enrolled and tested before the start date. Extra access needs its own approved ticket, and access is reviewed on a schedule.
How do you roll out monthly Windows updates to the whole company without breaking everyone at once?
Your approach to patching at scale while managing risk.
Staged rings starting with IT and a pilot group, monitoring between rings, ability to pause, and faster handling of actively exploited flaws.

I use rings. Microsoft releases security updates on the second Tuesday of the month. They go first to IT machines, then a pilot group from several departments, then everyone, a few days apart. Between rings I watch failed installs and help desk calls, and I can pause. Fixes for actively exploited flaws move faster, with that risk said openly.
A user says their phone keeps showing sign-in approval prompts they did not start. What do you do?
Whether you recognize an account compromise in progress and contain it.
Treats it as a stolen password, has the user deny prompts, resets and revokes sessions, checks logs and attacker changes, and reports it.

Prompts they did not start mean someone likely has their password. I tell them to deny every prompt, then reset the password, revoke active sessions and check sign-in logs for where attempts came from and whether any worked. I look for new MFA methods or mail forwarding rules an attacker added, and report it to security. Number matching makes blind approval harder.
You discover that a shared folder with salary data has been readable by every employee for months. What do you do?
How you handle a sensitive mistake openly instead of quietly fixing it.
Records the current state, closes access at once, escalates to manager and security, checks access logs, and finds the root cause.

I save the current permission list, then remove the broad access right away, so the change is on record. I tell my manager and security, because months of exposure may be a privacy matter that is not mine to judge alone. If auditing was on, logs show who opened the files. Then I find how it happened, like a group added by mistake, so it does not repeat.

java-developer.heading: Java developer questions
qs: What is the contract between equals and hashCode, and what breaks if you ignore it?
Whether you know the rule that every hash-based collection in Java relies on.
Equal objects must return equal hash codes. Breaking that makes HashMap and HashSet miss keys or hold duplicates.

If two objects are equal by equals, they must return the same hashCode. If I override equals and forget hashCode, a HashSet can hold two equal customers, and a HashMap lookup misses a key that is there. I also keep mutable fields out of both methods, because changing a key after it is in a map makes it unfindable.
Why shouldn't you use double for money, and what traps does BigDecimal have?
Your care with money, the core of most bank and payment code in Java.
Binary floating point cannot hold 0.1 exactly. With BigDecimal: build from strings, set rounding when dividing, and compare with compareTo.

A double stores binary fractions, so 0.1 plus 0.2 is not exactly 0.3, and those errors add up over many transactions. I use BigDecimal, created from a String or valueOf, never new BigDecimal(0.1). I set the scale and RoundingMode when dividing, and I compare with compareTo, because equals treats 2.0 and 2.00 as different.
When do you use a checked exception and when an unchecked one?
Whether you handle errors with a clear rule instead of habit.
Checked for conditions the caller can recover from, unchecked for programming errors. Wrap with the cause kept, and never swallow an exception.

Checked exceptions are for things the caller can act on, like a file that may be missing. Programming errors, like a null argument, are unchecked. In service code I often wrap low-level checked exceptions in a domain exception and keep the original as the cause. What I never do is catch Exception and leave the block empty, because the failure then disappears.
Two threads increment a shared int counter and the total comes out too low. Why, and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand race conditions and the basic Java concurrency tools.
count++ is read, add, write, so it is not atomic. Fix with AtomicInteger, LongAdder or a lock; volatile alone does not help.

count++ is three steps: read, add one, write back. Two threads can read the same value and both write the same result, so one increment is lost. Marking the field volatile does not fix it; it only makes writes visible. I would use AtomicInteger, LongAdder if many threads update it often, or a synchronized block if the counter changes together with other state.
A Spring method marked @Transactional throws an error, but the data is still saved. What could be wrong?
Whether you know how Spring transactions really work behind the annotation.
Names the usual causes: a call from the same class that skips the proxy, a checked exception, or an exception caught inside the method.

First I check how it was called. Spring wraps the bean in a proxy, so a call from another method in the same class skips the transaction. Next, by default Spring rolls back only on unchecked exceptions and errors, so a checked exception commits unless rollbackFor says otherwise. Last, a try-catch inside the method may swallow the error before Spring sees it.
Java has a garbage collector. How can a Java service still leak memory?
Your understanding of how memory is kept alive in the JVM and how to find a leak.
Objects stay reachable by mistake: growing static maps, unbounded caches, ThreadLocals on pooled threads. Found with a heap dump and retained sizes.

The collector frees only objects nothing points to. A static map that only grows, a cache with no size limit, or a ThreadLocal never removed on a pooled thread keeps objects alive. To find it I take a heap dump, for example with jcmd GC.heap_dump, and look in an analyzer for the objects holding the most retained memory and what references them.
A service stops answering requests, but its CPU use is near zero. What do you do?
How you diagnose a hung JVM instead of restarting it blindly.
Takes several thread dumps before restarting and looks for deadlocks, threads blocked on one lock, or workers stuck waiting on a pool or a remote call.

Before restarting I take two or three thread dumps a few seconds apart with jstack or jcmd Thread.print. Low CPU means threads are waiting, not working. I look for a reported deadlock, many threads blocked on the same lock, or every request thread waiting for a database connection or a remote call with no timeout. Then I restart, with the dumps saved.
When would you use virtual threads, and when would they not help?
Whether you know modern Java concurrency and its limits.
Useful for many concurrent tasks that block on I/O. No gain for CPU-heavy work; do not pool them, and still limit access to scarce resources.

Virtual threads, final since Java 21, are cheap, so I can run one per request even with thousands waiting on I/O. They help when threads mostly wait on the network or a database. They do not make CPU-heavy work faster. I create one per task instead of pooling them, and since the database pool is still fixed, I limit concurrent calls with the pool or a semaphore.
Walk me through moving a service from Java 8 to Java 21.
Your experience with real version upgrades and what breaks in them.
Updates build tools and libraries first, handles removed Java EE modules and blocked JDK internals, tests fully, and rolls out gradually.

First I update build plugins and libraries, since old versions often fail on new JDKs. Java 11 removed modules like JAXB, so I add them as dependencies. Since Java 17, most JDK internals are blocked by default, which breaks some old libraries. If we also move to Spring Boot 3, javax packages become jakarta. Then full tests and a canary release with metrics compared.
Response times spike every few minutes and you suspect garbage collection. How do you confirm it and what do you change?
How you tune JVM performance from evidence rather than by guessing at flags.
Proves it with GC logs matched to the spikes, then reduces allocation or fixes heap size before trying a low-pause collector under real load.

I turn on GC logging with -Xlog:gc* and line up pause times with the latency spikes. If they match, I check whether the heap is too small or the code allocates heavily, for example large temporary lists per request. Cutting that allocation often fixes it. If pauses are still too long, I test a low-pause collector such as ZGC under real load before rolling it out.
A loop over an ArrayList removes some items and throws ConcurrentModificationException, though only one thread runs. Why?
Whether you know how Java collections guard against changes made during iteration.
The for-each loop's iterator is fail-fast. Removal must go through the iterator itself or through removeIf.

The for-each loop uses an iterator, and calling list.remove behind its back changes the list's modification count. On the next step the iterator notices and throws. No second thread is needed. I would use removeIf with a condition, or call remove on the iterator itself, which keeps its count in step.
Can you use a Java record as a JPA entity? Where do records fit well?
Whether you know what records are and the limits that come with them.
No: entities need a no-arg constructor and a non-final, mutable class. Records suit DTOs, query results and value objects.

No. A record is final, its fields are final, and it has no no-argument constructor. JPA needs to create the entity empty, set its fields and often subclass it for lazy proxies. I use records for API request and response objects, read-only query projections and small value types like a money amount, where equals and hashCode come for free.
What does volatile guarantee, and what does it not?
Your grasp of the Java memory model beyond just using synchronized.
Visibility and ordering through happens-before, but no atomic read-modify-write. Knows where a volatile flag is enough.

A write to a volatile field is seen by any thread that reads it afterwards, and writes made before it become visible too. It does not make count++ atomic, since that is a read, an add and a write. I use volatile for a stop flag or a reference published once, as in double-checked locking, and AtomicLong or a lock when several threads update one value.
Under load, a Spring service sometimes returns another user's data or garbled dates. Review finds a field set inside a method. What is wrong?
Whether you know Spring beans are shared singletons and what that means for state.
Default singleton scope means one instance serves all threads at once. Per-request state belongs in local variables or immutable objects.

By default a Spring bean is a singleton, so one instance handles every request thread at the same time. A field written per request gets overwritten by another thread mid-call. A shared SimpleDateFormat has the same problem, since it is not thread-safe. I move the state into local variables or parameters and use DateTimeFormatter, which is immutable and safe to share.
After a service method returns an entity, the API layer reads its lazy list of items and gets an error. Why, and how do you fix it properly?
How well you understand the JPA persistence context and where loading can happen.
The persistence context closed with the transaction. Load what is needed inside it, with a fetch join, entity graph or DTO, not by making everything eager.

The lazy list is a proxy that needs an open persistence context, and that closed when the transactional method ended. I load what the endpoint needs inside the transaction: a fetch join or an entity graph for that query, or better, map to a DTO there. I avoid making the relation eager, which loads it everywhere, and I avoid keeping the session open for the whole web request.
You keep the current user in a ThreadLocal. A tester sees another customer's name on about one request in fifty. What happened?
Whether you understand how ThreadLocal behaves on pooled threads.
Pool threads are reused, so a value not removed leaks into the next request. Clear it in a finally block at the point where it is set.

Server threads come from a pool and are reused. If one request sets the ThreadLocal and an error path skips the cleanup, the next request on that thread can read the old user. I set the value in the entry filter and call remove() in a finally block there, and I add a test that runs two requests in a row on a one-thread pool.
A job scheduled with scheduleAtFixedRate ran for weeks, then silently stopped. Nothing is in the logs. What is your first suspicion?
Whether you know how executors treat exceptions thrown by tasks.
One run threw, which suppresses all later runs, and nobody read the future. Wrap the task body in try/catch with logging.

The Javadoc says that if one run throws, later runs are suppressed. The exception is stored in the returned future, and since nobody calls get on it, it is never printed. I wrap the whole task body in a try/catch that logs the error so the schedule keeps going, and I add a metric for the last successful run so an alert fires if it stalls.
The team calls other services with CompletableFuture.supplyAsync, and under load everything slows, even parallel streams elsewhere. Why?
Whether you know where async tasks run by default and why blocking there hurts.
Without an executor they run on the shared common ForkJoinPool, sized to the CPU count. Blocking I/O there starves all work sharing it.

Without an executor argument, supplyAsync runs on ForkJoinPool.commonPool, which by default has one thread fewer than the CPU cores. Parallel streams use that same pool. Blocking HTTP calls hold those few threads, so all other work waits. I pass a dedicated executor sized for the I/O, with timeouts on the calls, or run the blocking calls on virtual threads.
Your service in a container with a 2 GB limit is killed with exit code 137, yet there is no OutOfMemoryError and the heap looks fine. Walk me through it.
How you reason about JVM memory beyond the heap when running in containers.
Exit 137 means the kernel killed it for going over the limit. Heap, metaspace, thread stacks, code cache and direct buffers must all fit, so the heap needs headroom.

Code 137 means the process got a kill signal, here from the kernel's out-of-memory killer, not from the JVM. The process uses more than heap: metaspace, a stack per thread, the JIT code cache and direct buffers. I turn on Native Memory Tracking and read it with jcmd, then size the heap with MaxRAMPercentage to leave room, and look for growing threads or buffers.
A teammate wants to accept serialized Java objects from a partner over HTTP to save time. What do you say?
Whether you know the security risk of Java deserialization and the safer alternatives.
Reading untrusted bytes with ObjectInputStream can run code through library classes. Use plain DTOs over JSON, and strict filters if native serialization stays.

I would say no. ObjectInputStream creates whatever classes the bytes name, and chains of ordinary library classes on our classpath can be abused to run code during that step. I would agree a JSON format mapped to simple DTOs, without letting the input pick types. If native serialization truly cannot go, I add a deserialization filter that allows only a short list of classes.

junior-software-engineer.heading: Junior software engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between a unit test and an integration test?
Whether you know the basic kinds of tests and what each is for.
Unit tests check one small piece alone and run fast. Integration tests check that pieces work together. Both have a place.

A unit test checks one function or class on its own. Outside things like the database are replaced by fakes, so it runs in milliseconds and points right at the failure. An integration test runs real parts together, say my code and a test database, and catches problems in the wiring. I write many unit tests and fewer integration tests.
You pushed a bad commit to a shared branch. How do you undo it in Git?
Whether you can use Git safely when other people share the history.
Uses git revert, which adds a new commit that undoes the change. Avoids rewriting shared history with reset and a force-push.

I would run git revert on that commit. It makes a new commit that undoes the change, so nobody else's history breaks. Git reset moves the branch back and rewrites history. That is fine on my own local branch, but on a shared one it needs a force-push that can wipe out teammates' work. I would also tell the team in chat what happened.
How do you find your way around a large codebase you have never seen?
How you learn unfamiliar code without trying to read all of it.
Starts from one real path through the code, runs it, uses tests and the debugger, and saves questions for a mentor.

I don't try to read it all. I get it running locally, then pick one feature, like login, and follow a request from the entry point to the database with a debugger and breakpoints. Tests show me how pieces are meant to be used, and git blame shows why a line changed. I keep a list of questions and take them to my mentor in one batch.
Walk me through how you fix a bug from a ticket.
Your method for fixing a bug so that it stays fixed.
Reproduce first, find the cause rather than the symptom, add a test that fails before the fix, then check nothing else broke.

First I reproduce it with the exact steps and data from the ticket. Then I narrow down where it goes wrong, with logs or a debugger, until I understand the cause, not just where it shows. I write a test that fails because of the bug, fix the code until it passes, run the full test suite, and note the cause in the pull request.
What makes a pull request easy to review?
Whether you make your work easy for teammates to check.
Small and focused, a clear note on what changed and why, how it was tested, and no unrelated changes mixed in.

It does one thing. If I fixed a bug and also renamed files, those go in two pull requests. The description says what changed, why, and how I tested it, with a screenshot if the screen changed. I read my own diff before asking anyone, to catch debug prints and leftover comments. Then a reviewer can finish it in fifteen minutes instead of putting it off.
You have been stuck on a problem for two hours. When and how do you ask for help?
Your judgement between working things out alone and wasting time.
A time limit set in advance, and a question that shows what was tried, what was expected and what actually happened.

I set a limit before I start, often about an hour without progress, shorter if the task is urgent. At two hours I am past it, so I ask. I write the question so it is quick to answer: what I am trying to do, what I expected, what actually happens, and the three things I already tried. Often writing that out shows me the answer before I send it.
A senior engineer asks for a change in code review that you think is wrong. What do you do?
How you take feedback and disagree with respect.
Asks for the reason first, gives one concrete argument, then accepts the reviewer's or the team's decision without a fight.

First I ask why, because they often know something about the system that I don't. If I still disagree, I reply once with a concrete reason, for example that their version calls the database inside a loop. If we still differ, I suggest a short call. If they still prefer their way, I make the change and move on. One review is not worth a fight.
Your tests pass on your laptop but fail in the CI pipeline. How do you track it down?
How you debug a difference between two environments.
Reads the actual failure log, looks for differences in versions, settings, time zone, test order or timing, and reproduces it locally first.

CI is the server that runs our tests on every push, starting from a clean machine. I read the full failure log first. Then I look for what differs from my laptop: a library version, a missing environment variable, a different time zone, or tests running in another order. I try to reproduce it locally, for example in the same container image, before changing any code.
You estimated a task at two days. It is the end of day three and you are halfway. What do you do?
Whether you raise a slipping deadline early and honestly.
Tells the lead now, with the reason and a new estimate, and offers options like cutting scope or getting help instead of quietly working late.

I should have said something on day two, so I say it now. I tell my lead where I am, what took longer, for example code I didn't know other features shared, and a new honest estimate. Then I offer options: ship the main part first and the rest later, or pair with someone who knows that code. Staying silent only makes the surprise bigger.
You notice you pushed an API key to a public repository an hour ago. What do you do?
How you handle a security mistake, and in what order.
Treats the key as stolen: revokes and replaces it first, tells the team, checks usage logs, and only then cleans the code and history.

I assume it is already compromised, because bots scan public repositories for keys within minutes. First I revoke the key and create a new one, then I tell my lead and our security contact. We check the provider's logs for use we don't recognize. After that I move the key into a secret store and clean the history. Deleting the commit alone does not make it safe.
What is the difference between authentication and authorization, and which HTTP status codes go with each?
Whether you know two security basics that people often mix up.
Authentication is who you are; authorization is what you may do. 401 is for a missing or bad login, 403 is for a known user without permission.

Authentication checks who you are, for example with a password or a token. Authorization checks what you are allowed to do once we know who you are. If the request has no valid login, I return 401, even though its name says Unauthorized. If the user is logged in but may not touch that resource, I return 403 Forbidden.
Why does 0.1 + 0.2 not equal 0.3 in most languages, and how would you store prices?
Whether you understand floating point well enough to keep money correct.
Binary floating point cannot hold 0.1 exactly, so small errors add up. Money goes in integer cents or a decimal type.

Most languages use binary floating point, and 0.1 has no exact binary form, just as 1/3 has no exact decimal form. The tiny rounding errors show up when you add. For prices I store whole cents as an integer, or use a decimal type in the database and the code. I round only at clearly defined steps, like when tax is calculated.
How fast is looking up a key in a hash map, and when can it be slow?
Your grasp of the data structure you will use most often.
Constant time on average. Much slower when many keys collide, plus the occasional cost of resizing. For tiny collections a list can be just as fast.

On average a lookup is O(1): the key is hashed to a bucket and found almost directly. If many keys land in the same bucket, it can slow toward O(n), for example with a poor hash function or input crafted by an attacker. Resizing the table also costs time now and then, and for a handful of items a plain list can be just as fast.
A teammate builds a SQL query by pasting the user's search text into the string. What is the risk and what do you suggest?
Whether you spot SQL injection and know the real fix.
Names SQL injection and fixes it with parameterized queries, not hand-made escaping. Adds a database user with only the rights it needs as a second layer.

That is SQL injection: someone can type text that ends our query and adds their own, for example to read or delete data. The fix is a parameterized query, where the SQL and the values are sent separately, so the input is always treated as data. I would not rely on cleaning the string by hand. I would also check that the app's database user has only the rights it needs.
How do you store dates and times in an app with users in several time zones?
Whether you avoid the time zone bugs that hit almost every product.
Past moments in UTC, converted for display. Future local events also keep the time zone name, because offsets and daylight saving rules change.

For past events, like when an order was placed, I store the moment in UTC and convert to the user's zone only for display. For a future local event, like a 9 a.m. meeting in Chicago, I also store the zone name, America/Chicago, not a fixed offset like -06:00. The offset changes with daylight saving time, and the rules themselves can change before the date.
Two requests read a stock count of 1, both see the item is available, and both sell it. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
Whether you can recognize a race condition and fix it in the right place.
Names the read-then-write race. Makes the check and the change one atomic step, like a conditional update or a row lock, and notes app locks fail across servers.

It is a race condition: each request read the count, checked it, then wrote, and they overlapped in between. I would make the check and the change one step in the database, for example UPDATE stock SET count = count - 1 WHERE id = ? AND count > 0, then confirm one row changed. A lock inside the app would not help once we run on several servers.
When would you rebase your branch and when would you merge, and what is the one rule you never break?
Whether you use Git safely on a team, not only alone.
Rebase your own local work for a clean history, merge shared work. Never rewrite commits that others have already pulled.

I rebase my own feature branch on the latest main before a pull request, so my commits sit on top and the history stays straight. I merge when a branch is shared and the history should stay as it happened. The rule: I never rebase or force-push commits others have already pulled, because that rewrites history under them. On my own pushed branch I use --force-with-lease.
You need to fix a bug in an old function with no tests, and you would love to clean it up. How do you go about it?
How you change risky code without breaking what already works.
Pins down current behavior with tests first, makes the smallest fix, and puts any cleanup in a separate pull request.

First I write tests that capture what the function does today, including odd cases, and one test that fails because of the bug. Then I make the smallest fix that turns that test green. The cleanup goes in a separate pull request, so a reviewer sees the fix alone and we can roll back either one. If old behavior looks wrong elsewhere, I ask before changing it.
A service's memory grows for days until someone restarts it. How can that happen in a garbage-collected language, and how would you find it?
Whether you can debug a problem that builds up slowly in production.
Knows the collector frees only unreachable objects, so leaks are forgotten references. Compares heap snapshots over time to find what grows.

The garbage collector only frees objects that nothing points to. So a leak is usually something still holding references: a cache or map with no size limit, event listeners added and never removed, or a static list that keeps growing. I would take two heap snapshots a few hours apart, compare which object types grew, then follow what keeps them alive.
A test fails about one run in twenty, and the team wants CI to retry failed tests automatically. What do you say?
Your judgement on flaky tests, a team habit that can hide real bugs.
Accepts quarantining that one test with a ticket, but warns that blanket retries hide real bugs. Looks for the cause: timing, test order, shared state.

A retry turns the build green, but the flakiness may be a real bug, like a race condition users will hit too. I would quarantine this one test with a ticket and an owner instead of retrying everything. Then I would look for the usual causes: fixed sleeps instead of waiting for a condition, tests that depend on run order or shared data, and real clocks or random values.

kernel-engineer.heading: Kernel and operating systems engineer questions
qs: What happens when a user program makes a system call on x86-64 Linux?
Your grasp of the boundary between user space and the kernel.
The register convention, the switch to kernel mode, the handler lookup, careful copying of user data, and the return path with an error code.

The C library puts the call number in rax and the arguments in other registers, then runs the syscall instruction. The CPU switches to kernel mode, and the entry code saves registers and calls the handler from the syscall table. The handler checks its arguments and copies user memory with copy_from_user. The result comes back in rax; a negative value becomes errno in libc.
What is a page fault, and is it always a bug?
Whether you understand virtual memory as the kernel sees it.
Most faults are normal: demand paging, copy-on-write, swap-in. Only an access with no valid mapping or the wrong permissions ends in a signal or an oops.

No, most are normal. The CPU faults when a page is not mapped or the access breaks its permissions. The kernel looks up the memory area. If it is valid, it allocates a page, reads it from a file or swap, or copies it for copy-on-write, then retries the instruction. If no valid area covers the address, the process gets SIGSEGV; in kernel code it can be an oops.
Your interrupt handler needs to update a list that process code also uses. Which lock do you use, and how?
Whether you know what may and may not sleep in the kernel.
A spinlock, not a mutex, because interrupt context cannot sleep; process context disables local interrupts while holding it to avoid a self-deadlock.

A spinlock, because a handler cannot sleep, so a mutex is out. In process context I take it with spin_lock_irqsave. Otherwise the interrupt could fire on the same CPU while the lock is held and spin forever. I keep the critical section short and never call anything that can sleep inside it, such as a GFP_KERNEL allocation.
Your driver's interrupt handler takes too long and hurts latency. How do you restructure it?
How you split urgent work from work that can wait.
Acknowledge the device and save the minimum in the hard handler, then move the rest to a threaded IRQ or a workqueue, chosen by whether it must sleep.

The hard handler should only check that the interrupt is ours, acknowledge the device, and save what is needed. The rest moves out. I usually use request_threaded_irq, so the heavy part runs in a kernel thread that can sleep and be scheduled. If the work is batched or not tied to the interrupt, a workqueue fits. Then I measure latency before and after.
How does a hypervisor run a guest kernel that believes it owns the hardware?
Your understanding of virtualization at the CPU and memory level.
Hardware support such as VT-x or AMD-V, exits on sensitive operations, second-level page tables, and paravirtual devices to cut the number of exits.

With VT-x or AMD-V the guest runs directly on the CPU in a guest mode. Sensitive operations, like some I/O or control register writes, cause a VM exit; the hypervisor handles or emulates them and resumes the guest. Second-level page tables (EPT on Intel, NPT on AMD) map guest memory to host memory in hardware. For devices, virtio queues avoid an exit per register access.
A customer sends you a kernel oops log. Walk me through how you read it.
Whether you can turn a crash report into a source line and a likely cause.
Start with the first oops, read the faulting address, instruction pointer and taint flags, then map function plus offset to source using the exact build.

I read the first oops only; later ones are often fallout. A faulting address near zero suggests a NULL pointer. I note the kernel version and taint flags, since an out-of-tree module changes the picture. I take the function plus offset from the instruction pointer and map it to a source line with faddr2line and the matching vmlinux. Then I read that code against the call trace.
Your driver writes a DMA descriptor, then writes the device's doorbell register, but the device sometimes reads stale data. Why, and how do you fix it?
Your knowledge of memory ordering and DMA between the CPU and a device.
Stores can be reordered or sit in caches. Use the DMA API, a dma_wmb() before handing over ownership, and an ordered writel() for the doorbell.

The CPU or compiler can reorder the stores, and on some platforms the data is still in a cache the device cannot see. I allocate descriptors with dma_alloc_coherent, fill the fields, then call dma_wmb() before setting the ownership bit. For the doorbell I use writel(), which is ordered after earlier memory writes; writel_relaxed() is not.
A fuzzer reports a use-after-free in code you merged last month. What do you do?
How you own and fix a mistake in low-level code.
Reproduce it with memory checking on, fix the real lifetime bug instead of masking it, and mark the fix so it reaches stable kernels.

I reproduce it on a build with KASAN, the kernel's memory error checker, which shows where the object was freed and where it was used later. In my case a timer could still run after the device was removed. I fixed the order: stop the timer, then free. I added a Fixes: tag pointing to my commit, copied the stable list, and added a test that removes the device under load.
Explain RCU and when you would use it instead of a reader-writer lock.
Your depth in kernel concurrency.
Readers take no lock and never wait; writers publish a new copy and free the old one only after a grace period. It suits read-mostly data.

Readers enter rcu_read_lock, follow pointers with rcu_dereference, and must not sleep. A writer makes a new copy, publishes it with rcu_assign_pointer, then waits for a grace period with synchronize_rcu or call_rcu before freeing the old one. So reads are nearly free. I use it for read-mostly data like routing tables; with frequent writes, a plain lock is simpler.
Why is a 4 KB array on the stack a problem in kernel code but not in a user program?
Whether you know the limits the kernel puts on code that user space does not have.
Kernel stacks are small, fixed and do not grow, so an overflow crashes or corrupts memory. Large buffers belong on the heap or in a preallocated buffer.

Each thread's kernel stack is small and fixed, 16 KB on x86-64, and it does not grow on demand like a user stack. Deep call chains through filesystem, block layer and driver all share it. A 4 KB array takes a quarter of it. I allocate with kmalloc or use a preallocated buffer, and I watch the compiler's frame size warnings.
What is atomic context, and what goes wrong if you call a function that may sleep inside it?
Whether you know where the kernel forbids sleeping and how to stay out of trouble.
Interrupt handlers, held spinlocks and disabled preemption are atomic. Sleeping there can deadlock. Use non-sleeping calls or defer the work.

Atomic context is code that must not be scheduled away: an interrupt handler, code holding a spinlock, or code with preemption off. If it sleeps, say a GFP_KERNEL kmalloc or a mutex_lock, the CPU can switch away with a spinlock held and the system can deadlock. I use GFP_ATOMIC or move the work to a workqueue, and I test with CONFIG_DEBUG_ATOMIC_SLEEP on.
What does Linux do when memory runs out, and why can malloc succeed and the process still die later?
Your grasp of overcommit and the OOM killer.
Explains that pages are given on first touch, the OOM killer picks a victim by score, and cgroup limits trigger the same inside a group.

By default Linux overcommits: malloc reserves address space, and real pages come only on first touch. If reclaim and swap cannot free enough, the OOM killer picks a process by its oom_score, mostly memory use, adjusted by oom_score_adj, and kills it. A cgroup memory limit does the same inside that group. vm.overcommit_memory=2 makes allocations fail up front instead.
What is priority inversion, and how does the Linux kernel deal with it?
Whether you understand a classic scheduling hazard and its standard fix.
A clear three-task example and priority inheritance as the fix, with rt_mutex and PI futexes named as the Linux mechanisms.

A low-priority task holds a lock a high-priority task needs, and a medium-priority task keeps the low one off the CPU, so the high one waits on the medium one. The fix is priority inheritance: the lock holder runs at the waiter's priority until it releases. In Linux, rt_mutex does this, and user space gets it through PI futexes, like a pthread mutex set to PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT.
Lockdep reports a possible circular locking dependency, but nobody has ever seen the machine hang. What do you do?
How you treat a deadlock warning that has not bitten anyone yet.
Treats it as real, reads both paths, and fixes the lock order. Annotations only for a true false positive, never just to silence it.

Lockdep records the order in which lock classes are taken, so it flags A then B on one path and B then A on another even if they never raced. I read both stack traces, find the two paths and choose one order to document and keep. If that fails, I drop one lock before taking the other. I only annotate it for a true false positive, like same-class locks nested by design.
A program that maps and unmaps memory often runs much slower on a 128-core machine than on 8 cores. What might be going on?
Whether you can connect a scaling problem to TLB coherence across CPUs.
Names TLB shootdowns and the inter-processor interrupts they need, shows how to confirm it, and suggests reducing unmaps.

Likely TLB shootdowns. When a mapping is removed, every CPU that may have it cached in its TLB must flush it, so the kernel sends inter-processor interrupts and waits for answers. With threads spread over many cores, each munmap stalls on many of them. I'd check the TLB shootdown count in /proc/interrupts and profile with perf, then suggest reusing mappings or batching unmaps.
A memory-heavy workload runs 20 percent slower in a VM than on bare metal, while CPU-bound code is near native. Where do you look?
Your understanding of what hardware virtualization costs for memory access.
Explains the two-level page walk on a TLB miss with nested paging, and fixes like huge pages on both levels and NUMA placement.

With hardware nested paging, a TLB miss in the guest walks the guest page tables, and each step also needs a walk of the host tables, so a miss costs several times more than on bare metal. I'd measure TLB misses with perf, back guest memory with huge pages on the host and use them in the guest. I'd also check that the vCPUs and the VM's memory sit on the same NUMA node.
The machine hard-locks under load: no oops, no response, the screen just freezes. How do you get information?
How you debug a hang when the normal tools cannot run.
Gets output off the box, uses the lockup detectors and kdump to capture state, and knows what SysRq can still do.

First I get messages off the box with a serial console or netconsole, since the screen may never update. I enable the lockup detectors set to panic; the hard lockup detector uses an NMI, which arrives even with interrupts off, so it prints the stuck CPU's backtrace. With kdump set up, the panic saves a vmcore I open in crash. If the keyboard still works, SysRq can dump task stacks.
After a kernel upgrade, a customer's database throughput drops 15 percent. Walk me through finding the cause.
Your method for tracking a performance regression to one change.
Reproduces with a controlled setup, compares configs and profiles, then bisects with a scripted, repeatable benchmark.

First I reproduce it on the same hardware, and I diff the two kernel configs, since a changed default can be the cause by itself. Then I compare perf profiles of old and new kernels to see where the time moved. If that does not point at one change, I run git bisect between the versions with a scripted benchmark, so each step is a clean build, a boot and a pass or fail by threshold.
Your patch fixes a real bug, but it changes a behavior that a widely used program depends on. What do you do?
Whether you know the kernel's rule on user space compatibility and can work within it.
Knows a change that breaks working programs is a regression to avoid or revert, and finds a fix that keeps the old visible behavior.

In Linux the rule is that we do not break user space: if an existing program stops working after a kernel change, that is a regression, even if it relied on odd behavior. So I'd keep the old behavior where the program sees it and fix the bug behind it, or offer the new behavior through a new flag. Internal kernel APIs are different: they can change if I update every in-tree caller.

key-account-manager.heading: Key account manager questions
qs: How is a key account manager different from an account executive?
Whether you understand what the role is for.
KAM means long-term ownership of a few large customers and growth over years, not winning a deal and handing the customer on.

An account executive is usually measured on winning new deals and then hands the customer on. As a key account manager I own a few large customers over years. I know their plans, coordinate our service, product and finance people around them, and grow revenue through renewals, new products and new divisions.
What goes into a strategic account plan?
Your grasp of the core working document of the role.
Customer goals, who decides, current spend and share of wallet, gaps, risks, and objectives with owners and dates, reviewed regularly.

Mine fits on a few pages. It covers the customer's goals for the year, a chart of who decides what, what they buy from us and from competitors, gaps where we could help, risks to the account, and three or four objectives with actions, owners and dates. I review it with my manager each quarter and share a short version with the customer.
How do you map the stakeholders in a large account?
Whether you avoid depending on a single contact.
Everyone who touches the decision, rated on influence and attitude, with a plan to build links beyond one person.

I list everyone who touches the decision: the person who signs, the users, technical evaluators, procurement and anyone who prefers a competitor. For each I note influence, how they see us and how often we talk. If all my contact runs through one person, that is a risk, so I set a goal to build real links with at least two more senior people.
How do you find growth in an account that already buys from you and says it is happy?
How you grow an account beyond what it already buys.
A method: map what they buy against divisions and needs, find the gaps, and lead with a business problem rather than a product.

I map each division and site against what we sell and mark where they buy from someone else or nothing at all. Then I ask my contact for an introduction to a division with a problem we have solved elsewhere. At one account only one site used us; a pilot at a second site, backed by results from the first, doubled the account in a year.
How do you run a quarterly business review that the customer actually wants to attend?
Your ability to make a review useful to the customer, not a sales pitch.
Agenda agreed with the customer, results in their terms, honest about problems, a forward look, and clear follow-up actions.

I agree the agenda with my contact two weeks ahead so it covers their priorities. I open with results against the goals we set last time, in their numbers, then issues and what we fixed, then what is coming in their business and ideas for it. Slides stay short and half the time is discussion. I send actions with owners within two days.
How can you tell an account is at risk before the customer tells you?
Whether you watch for early warning signs and act on them.
Concrete signals like falling usage, fewer senior contacts or reorganizations, and early, direct action when they appear.

I watch usage or order volumes, how fast they reply, whether senior people still come to meetings, late payments and new names from procurement. A reorganization or a new executive is a signal too. When two of these move at once I call my sponsor, ask directly what has changed and bring our leadership in early, while there is time to fix it.
Your main contact at your biggest account just left the company. What do you do in the first two weeks?
How you protect a relationship when your champion leaves.
Quick contact with the successor, a clear summary of value delivered, checking other relationships, and staying in touch with the person who left.

I call my contact to thank them and ask who takes over and who else I should know. Then I meet the successor quickly with a short summary of what we deliver and the value so far, and ask what they want to change. I check how strong my other relationships are. I also stay in touch with the person who left; they may buy from us at their new company.
Procurement at a key account demands a 10% price cut at renewal or they will put the contract out to tender. How do you respond?
How you negotiate with professional buyers without giving value away.
No free discount: understand the pressure, involve the business users, and trade any price move for something of value, within a limit set in advance.

I do not cut 10% for nothing. First I find out whether the tender is real or a target, and I remind my business contacts what a switch would cost them in time and risk. If price must move, I trade: a lower unit price for a longer term, more volume or a smaller scope. I know my walk-away point before the meeting, agreed with my manager.
A key account asks for a custom product change or contract term your company does not normally give. How do you decide?
Your judgement in balancing one big customer against your own company's interest.
Weighing cost, precedent and lifetime value with the internal teams, and a fast, honest answer to the customer either way.

I check three things: what it costs us to deliver, whether it sets a precedent other customers will ask for, and what the account is worth over the next few years. I take that to the people who would build it and to finance. If the answer is no, I tell the customer quickly, explain why and offer what we can do instead.
Your company made a delivery mistake that hurt a key account. Walk me through how you handled it with the customer and inside your own company.
How you handle a failure on both sides: owning it with the customer and driving the fix internally.
Fast, honest contact without blaming colleagues, a recovery plan you pushed through internally, and a written cause and fix.

A shipment to a customer's main plant arrived a week late and stopped one of their lines. I called my contact the same day, said what went wrong without blaming the warehouse, and gave a recovery date. Internally I got operations to rush the next orders and held a weekly check until it was stable. I sent the cause and fix in writing within ten days. They renewed.
When you take over a key account, which contract terms do you check first?
Whether you know where the money, the dates and the risks sit in a customer contract.
Term, notice period and auto-renewal first, then pricing changes, service levels, termination rights and any special promises, with dates tracked.

I read the contract before I meet anyone. First the end date, the notice period and whether it renews on its own, because a missed notice window can cost us the renewal. Then pricing and any yearly increase, service levels with penalties, termination rights, and any promise that no one gets a better price. I put the key dates in the CRM with alerts.
How do you estimate your share of wallet when the customer will not tell you their total spend?
How you size the real opportunity in an account from indirect evidence.
A rough total built from outside data and benchmarks, then checked with people inside the account, site by site or line by line.

I build it from the outside in. I look at their revenue, number of sites or users, and what similar customers spend per unit, which gives a rough total. Then I check it with people inside: operations staff often say which other suppliers they use and for what. If our share is 30% at one site and 80% at another, the gap shows me where to look.
What is net revenue retention, and why does it matter in this job?
Your grasp of the main number used to judge a book of existing accounts.
The right definition: same customers only, expansion added, downgrades and losses subtracted, new customers left out.

It is the revenue we get now from the customers we had a year ago, divided by what those same customers paid us then. Expansion counts, downgrades and lost customers come off, and new customers are left out. Above 100% means the base grows on its own. For me it is the clearest score: it shows whether my accounts grow or quietly shrink.
How do you bring your own executives into a key account without losing your place as the owner?
How you use senior people in your company as a tool, not a crutch.
Peer-level meetings with a clear purpose, a full briefing beforehand, and the account manager running the follow-up.

I match levels: our VP meets their VP, with a clear reason, like a strategy review or a problem that needs a senior promise. I brief our executive on the account plan, the ask and what not to offer. I attend and send the follow-up myself. The customer sees our executive backing my plan, not going around me.
Your champion at a key account loves your proposal but cannot sign it. How do you test whether it has real backing?
Whether you can tell a friendly contact from a real path to the person who approves the spend.
Asking the champion for a small, costly action, like access to the budget owner, and adjusting the forecast if it never comes.

I ask the champion to do something that costs them a little: get me thirty minutes with the person who owns the budget, or explain how their company approved the last purchase this size. If they can, I learn who signs and what they care about. If they keep stalling, I mark the deal as unconfirmed in my forecast and look for a second route in.
Walk me through how you prepare for the renewal of your largest contract.
Your preparation for a high-stakes negotiation with an existing customer.
Starts months early: proven value, open issues, decision makers, both sides' best alternatives, and internal limits agreed before talks start.

I start months ahead. I list what the customer got from us in numbers, what still bothers them, and who decides. Then I write down our walk-away point, what we can give and what we want back, and an honest view of their alternatives: switching cost, a rival's likely price, the risk of changing. I agree the limits with my manager and finance before the first meeting.
A key account offers a bigger volume commitment in exchange for a lower price. How do you structure it?
Whether you trade concessions and protect your company if the promised volume does not come.
Price tied to volume actually bought, through tiers or a year-end rebate, plus something firm in return for every concession.

I tie the price to what they actually buy, not what they promise. Tiered pricing, or a rebate paid at year end on real orders, protects us if their forecast was optimistic. For the better rate I also ask for something firm: a longer term, preferred supplier status, or a case study. Every give gets a get, and it goes into the contract.
Your biggest account grew 20% this year, but its margin keeps falling. What do you do?
How you judge account profitability, not just revenue.
Finding the cost to serve, then going to the customer with numbers and choices instead of a flat price rise.

I find out where the cost goes: rush orders, custom packaging, a support team answering every small request, payment terms that slipped. Then I show the customer the numbers and offer choices: keep the extra service and pay for it, or change how they order and keep the price. Often a service they value little costs us a lot, and both sides can drop it.
Before a renewal decision, the buyer at a key account asks if you can get his team tickets to a big game. What do you do?
Your judgement on gifts and entertainment when a buying decision is open.
Checking both companies' policies, declining during a live decision, and knowing rules are stricter for government buyers.

I check two rule books, ours and theirs. Many large companies forbid staff from taking gifts while a purchase is open, and ours needs approval above a set value. During a live renewal I would decline politely and suggest something together after the decision. If the buyer were a public official the rules are stricter still. I do not want a renewal won on tickets.
You discover your company has underbilled your key account for eight months. How do you handle it?
How you handle a costly mistake that touches both revenue and trust.
Facts confirmed with finance, manager told at once, contract checked, customer told before any invoice, with fair options to settle.

First I confirm the amount and cause with finance and tell my manager the same day. Then I read what the contract allows. I call my contact before any invoice goes out, explain what went wrong and own it as our error. I offer options agreed with finance, like spreading the catch-up over several months or waiving part. A surprise bill for eight months would cost more trust than it is worth.

kubernetes-engineer.heading: Container and Kubernetes engineer questions
qs: When would you use a Deployment, a StatefulSet or a DaemonSet?
Whether you know the basic workload types and pick the right one for the job.
Deployment for interchangeable copies, StatefulSet for stable identity and storage, DaemonSet for one pod per node.

A Deployment runs copies that are all the same, like a web API. A StatefulSet gives each pod a stable name and its own disk, so I use it for things like databases or queues. A DaemonSet puts one pod on every node, or on a chosen set of nodes, which fits log collectors and monitoring agents.
What is the difference between a liveness probe and a readiness probe, and what is a common mistake with them?
Your grasp of how Kubernetes decides to restart a container or send it traffic.
Liveness failure restarts the container; readiness failure only takes the pod out of traffic. Names a real mistake, like a liveness check that depends on the database.

If liveness fails, the kubelet restarts the container. If readiness fails, the pod stays up but is removed from the Service, so it gets no traffic. A classic mistake is a liveness check that calls the database: when the database blips, every pod restarts at once and a small problem becomes an outage.
Why is deploying an image with the tag latest a bad idea?
Whether you know how image tags affect what really runs and whether you can roll back.
You cannot tell which version is running, nodes may run different builds, and rollback is unreliable. Use immutable version tags or image digests.

latest is just a label that moves, so two nodes can pull different builds under the same name, and the manifest does not tell me what is running. Rolling back to latest does nothing useful. I tag each build with a version or the commit ID, or pin the digest, so every deploy is traceable and repeatable.
What are resource requests and limits, and what happens when a container goes over its memory limit versus its CPU limit?
Your understanding of scheduling and of how CPU and memory limits behave differently.
Requests guide scheduling; limits cap use. Over the memory limit the container is OOMKilled; over the CPU limit it is throttled, not killed.

The scheduler places pods based on requests, the amount reserved for them. Limits are the ceiling. If a container goes over its memory limit, it gets killed and shows OOMKilled. If it hits its CPU limit, it is slowed down, or throttled, but keeps running. So memory limits need real headroom.
A pod has been stuck in Pending for ten minutes. What do you check?
How you troubleshoot a scheduling problem in order.
Starts with kubectl describe and the events, then checks resources, taints, node selectors or affinity, and unbound volume claims.

I run kubectl describe pod and read the events, since the scheduler usually says why. Common causes: no node has enough free CPU or memory for the requests, a taint the pod does not tolerate, a node selector or affinity no node matches, or a PersistentVolumeClaim that is not bound. Then I fix the cause, not just add nodes.
A new release goes into CrashLoopBackOff. Walk me through finding the cause.
Your method for debugging a container that keeps crashing.
Reads logs from the previous run, checks exit code and last state, rules out OOM, bad config and a probe killing the app.

First kubectl logs with --previous, because the current container may have no output yet. Then kubectl describe for the exit code and last state: OOMKilled points to memory, exit code 1 usually means the app failed, often a missing env var or secret. I also check whether a liveness probe is killing a slow start. If users are hit, I roll back first.
How does a request from the internet reach a pod in the cluster?
Whether you understand Services, Ingress and how traffic is routed inside the cluster.
A load balancer or Ingress takes the request, a Service picks pods by label, and kube-proxy or the network plugin routes it to a ready pod.

Usually a cloud load balancer sends traffic to an Ingress controller, which routes by host name and path to a Service. The Service finds its pods through label selectors and keeps a list of ready endpoints. kube-proxy, or the network plugin, programs each node so traffic to the Service address lands on one of those pods.
A developer asks you for cluster-admin so they can debug their service. What do you do?
Your judgement on access control and least privilege with RBAC.
Says no to cluster-wide admin but solves the need: a namespaced Role and RoleBinding with only the rights required, ideally time-limited.

I ask what they actually need. Usually it is reading pods, logs and events in their own namespace, maybe exec. I give that with a Role and RoleBinding in that namespace, often starting from the built-in view role. cluster-admin can read every secret and delete anything, so it stays with a very small group.
How do you upgrade a production cluster to a new Kubernetes version without an outage?
How you plan a risky change: version order, API removals and moving workloads safely.
Checks removed APIs first, upgrades control plane before nodes one minor version at a time, and drains nodes gradually with PodDisruptionBudgets in place.

I read the release notes for removed APIs and fix any manifests using them. I try it on a staging cluster. Then I upgrade the control plane first, one minor version at a time, and the nodes after. I cordon and drain nodes a few at a time; drain respects PodDisruptionBudgets, so each service keeps enough pods running.
During every deploy, a few requests fail with 502 errors for a few seconds. What is going on, and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand pod shutdown and why traffic can still reach a pod that is stopping.
Knows endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen at the same time, so pods must keep serving briefly, finish requests, and have readiness probes for new pods.

When a pod is deleted, it gets SIGTERM at about the same time it is removed from the endpoints, and the load balancer learns late. If the app exits at once, requests still arriving fail. I add a short preStop sleep, make the app finish open requests on SIGTERM, set a long enough grace period, and make sure new pods have a readiness probe.
What are the three QoS classes, and which pods does the kubelet evict first when a node runs low on memory?
Whether you know how requests and limits decide who is evicted under memory pressure.
Guaranteed, Burstable and BestEffort defined correctly, with eviction tied to usage above requests and to priority, not to the class name alone.

Guaranteed means every container has CPU and memory requests equal to its limits. BestEffort means no requests or limits at all. Everything else is Burstable. Under memory pressure the kubelet first evicts pods using more than they requested, ranked by priority and by how far over they are. BestEffort pods go early because any use is over a request of zero.
An autoscaler targets 70% CPU, but the service never scales out even under heavy load. What do you look at?
How well you understand the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler's math and what it depends on.
Utilization is measured against the CPU request. The answer checks the metrics pipeline, the HPA status and maxReplicas, and knows the replica formula.

First I run kubectl describe hpa. If the metric shows unknown, metrics-server or the metrics API is broken. Then the requests: utilization is usage divided by the CPU request, so with no request it cannot be computed, and with a huge request 70% is never reached. I also check maxReplicas. The formula is current replicas times current over target, rounded up.
You apply a default-deny NetworkPolicy to a namespace and every service breaks, even the ones you allowed. What did you probably miss?
Your grasp of how network policies select traffic, including egress.
Names DNS egress to the cluster DNS pods on port 53, UDP and TCP, and knows policies only work if the network plugin enforces them.

Usually DNS. If the default deny covers egress, pods cannot reach CoreDNS, so every name lookup fails and it looks like everything broke. I add an egress rule to the DNS pods in kube-system on port 53, UDP and TCP. I also confirm our network plugin enforces policies at all. Some do not, and then the rules silently do nothing.
A node drain during maintenance hangs and never finishes. How can a PodDisruptionBudget cause that, and what do you do?
