Whether you understand how disruption budgets interact with planned maintenance.
Eviction respects the budget. The answer spots a budget that allows zero disruptions and fixes the cause with the owner instead of force-deleting pods.

Drain uses the eviction API, which refuses any eviction that would break a PDB. If a team set minAvailable to 2 with only 2 replicas, or some pods are unhealthy, no eviction is ever allowed. I run kubectl get pdb and look for zero allowed disruptions. Then I talk to the owner: add a replica or change the budget. I do not delete their pods by hand to get around it.
A node goes NotReady. What happens to its pods, and why might a StatefulSet pod not come back on its own?
Your knowledge of node failure handling and StatefulSet identity guarantees.
Pods are evicted after a toleration period, five minutes by default. A StatefulSet will not start a second copy until the old pod is confirmed gone.

Pods get default tolerations for not-ready and unreachable of 300 seconds. After that they are marked for deletion and controllers create replacements, so a Deployment just starts new pods elsewhere. A StatefulSet keeps one pod per identity, so it waits until the old pod is really gone. If the node is dead, I confirm it is powered off, then delete the node object or force-delete the pod.
The cluster autoscaler adds nodes without trouble but never removes them, and the bill keeps growing. What do you check?
Whether you know what keeps the cluster autoscaler from scaling down.
Scale-down is based on requests, not real usage. Names the usual blockers: PDBs, pods with no controller, local storage, and the safe-to-evict annotation.

Scale-down looks at requested resources, not actual use, so an idle node whose pods request a lot still looks busy. Then I look for pods that block removal: pods not owned by a controller, pods using local storage depending on our settings, PDBs that allow no disruption, and the annotation that marks a pod not safe to evict. The autoscaler's logs and status name the blocking pod.
Calls from pods to an outside API are slow, and CoreDNS is very busy. How can the ndots setting cause that?
Your depth in cluster DNS and how pod name resolution works.
Names with fewer than five dots try every search domain first. Fixes: a trailing dot, a lower ndots in dnsConfig, or a node-local DNS cache.

Pods get ndots:5 by default. A name like api.example.com has only two dots, so the resolver first tries it with each search domain, the namespace, svc and cluster suffixes, before the real name. That is several wasted lookups, often doubled for IPv4 and IPv6. I use a trailing dot on full names, set a lower ndots in the pod's dnsConfig, or add NodeLocal DNSCache.
What is stored in etcd, and how would you back it up and restore it on a self-managed cluster?
Whether you can protect and recover the cluster's state, not just its workloads.
etcd holds all cluster state, including Secrets. Snapshots are kept off the cluster, protected like passwords, and the restore has actually been tested.

etcd holds every cluster object, including Secrets, which are only base64 encoded unless encryption at rest is turned on. I take regular snapshots with etcdctl, copy them off the cluster and protect them like passwords. To restore, I stop the API servers, restore the snapshot into a new data directory and point etcd at it. I rehearse that in a test cluster; an untested backup is a hope.
Two teams want to share one production cluster. What do you put in place so one team cannot hurt the other?
Your judgement in designing tenant isolation inside a shared cluster.
Layered controls: namespaces with scoped RBAC, quotas and default limits, network policies, Pod Security Admission, and knowing when separate clusters are better.

Each team gets its own namespaces and RBAC roles scoped to them, never cluster-wide. ResourceQuota caps their total CPU, memory and object counts, and LimitRange sets default requests. I add default-deny network policies and Pod Security Admission at the restricted level to block privileged pods. If they need strict compliance separation, I give them separate clusters.

lab-technician.heading: Research associate and lab technician questions
qs: You need 50 mL of 1X buffer from a 10X stock. How do you make it?
Whether you can do basic lab math quickly and correctly.
C1V1 = C2V2 done right: 5 mL of stock brought up to 50 mL, mixed and labeled.

I use C1V1 equals C2V2. 10X times V1 equals 1X times 50 mL, so V1 is 5 mL. I measure 5 mL of stock, bring it up to 50 mL with purified water in a graduated cylinder or volumetric flask, mix it well, and label it with the contents, date and my initials.
What is the difference between a biosafety cabinet and a chemical fume hood?
Whether you know which piece of safety equipment protects what.
A fume hood protects the user from vapors; a Class II cabinet protects user, sample and room from particles, and HEPA filters do not stop vapors.

A fume hood pulls air away from me and out of the building, so it protects me from chemical vapors but does nothing for the sample. A Class II biosafety cabinet uses HEPA-filtered airflow to protect me, the sample and the room from microbes and particles. HEPA filters do not trap vapors, so I do not use volatile chemicals in a cabinet that recirculates air.
How do you know a pipette is still accurate between service visits?
Your habit of checking instruments instead of trusting them.
A gravimetric check with water on a calibrated balance, corrected for temperature, and taking the pipette out of use if it fails.

I do a quick gravimetric check. I pipette purified water onto a calibrated analytical balance several times at the volume I use, note the water temperature, and convert mass to volume with the water density at that temperature. If the average is off or the readings scatter beyond our tolerance, I tag the pipette out of use and send it for service.
The centrifuge starts to shake and get loud as it speeds up. What do you do?
How you react to an equipment hazard in the moment.
Stop the run, wait for the rotor to stop before opening, find the imbalance, and treat a broken tube as a spill.

I press stop and step back, and I do not open the lid until the rotor has fully stopped. Then I check the balance: tubes of equal mass opposite each other, the right adapters, nothing cracked. If a tube with biological material broke, I keep the lid closed for the time our biosafety rules set so aerosols settle, then clean up as a spill.
Your PCR no-template control shows a band. What does that tell you, and what do you do?
Whether you understand what controls are for and act on them.
The run is not trustworthy, so no results go out; fresh reagents, a clean area, a rerun, and a search for the source if it repeats.

It means something is contaminated, usually a reagent, the water or the work area, so I cannot trust any positive in that run. I do not report the samples. I use fresh aliquots of water and master mix, clean the bench and pipettes, and rerun. If it comes back, I test reagents one at a time to find the source and keep pre-PCR and post-PCR work in separate areas.
How do you spot contamination in a cell culture, and what kind can you not see?
Your hands-on knowledge of cell culture and its hidden risks.
Cloudy or yellow medium, fungal threads or yeast under the microscope, plus routine testing for mycoplasma, which you cannot see.

Bacteria often make the medium cloudy and turn it yellow fast as the pH drops. Fungi show as threads or fuzzy clumps, and yeast as small round budding cells under the microscope. Mycoplasma is the one I cannot see: the medium stays clear. So we test on a schedule with a PCR kit, and I discard and decontaminate anything positive instead of trying to rescue it.
Someone knocks over a 1-liter bottle of solvent on the open bench. Walk me through what you do.
How you handle a chemical spill safely and in the right order.
People first, then the SDS, ignition sources off if flammable, and cleanup only if small and trained; otherwise leave and call safety staff.

I warn people nearby and check if anyone was splashed; they go straight to the eyewash or safety shower. I check the SDS and shut off ignition sources if it is flammable. If the spill is small and I am trained for it, I use the spill kit with the right gloves and goggles. If it is large, toxic or I am unsure, I leave, close the door and call environmental health and safety.
The -80 freezer alarm goes off at 6 p.m. and the display reads -55. What do you do?
Your judgement when samples that took months to collect are at risk.
A quick check for a simple cause, samples moved by priority to backup or dry ice, the right people told, and times and temperatures logged.

First I check for a simple cause like a door not fully closed. If it keeps warming, I move samples to the backup freezer, irreplaceable ones first, or onto dry ice if there is no space, with insulated gloves and good ventilation. I tell the lab manager, call for service, and log times and temperatures so we know which samples may be affected.
A new lot of a key antibody arrives. What do you do before using it on real samples?
Whether you know that reagent lots can differ and how to check.
A side-by-side test with the old lot on the same controls, a documented comparison, and lot numbers recorded on every run.

I run it side by side with the old lot on the same control samples, same protocol, same day. If signal and background match within what we accept, I record the lot number and the comparison and switch over. If they differ, I keep the old lot for ongoing work, tell the lead, and we decide whether to titrate the new one again. Every run notes which lot it used.
Your supervisor asks you to leave out one replicate that looks wrong before the data goes into a paper. What do you do?
Your handling of data integrity under pressure from someone senior.
No silent deletion: excluding data needs a documented reason or a set rule, and the raw data always stays.

I would ask what the reason is. If there is a real one, like a failed control or a pipetting error I noted at the bench, we exclude it and document why. If it only looks inconvenient, I would say I am not comfortable dropping it, offer to repeat the experiment, and keep the raw data either way. Leaving out data without cause is falsification.
When would you use reverse pipetting instead of forward pipetting?
Whether you know how to pipette liquids that a standard technique handles poorly.
Names viscous, foaming or volatile liquids and describes the technique correctly: aspirate to the second stop, dispense to the first.

I use it for viscous liquids like glycerol, for solutions that foam, like detergents, and for volatile solvents. I press to the second stop to draw up a little extra, then dispense only to the first stop. The leftover stays in the tip and I discard it. That gives me a more accurate volume than blowing out.
Why do we aliquot reagents and samples instead of using them straight from the main tube?
Your understanding of how handling damages materials over time.
Freeze-thaw cycles degrade proteins, enzymes and nucleic acids, and every opening risks contamination. Aliquots protect the stock and make problems traceable.

Each freeze-thaw cycle can degrade proteins and enzymes, and every time a tube is opened it can get contaminated. So when a new antibody or sample comes in, I split it into single-use aliquots, label each with name, date and concentration, and thaw only what I need. If one aliquot goes bad, the rest of the stock is still good.
The autoclave tape on a load turned dark. Does that prove the load is sterile?
Whether you know the difference between an exposure indicator and proof of sterilization.
No: tape only shows the surface saw heat and steam. Sterilization is checked with biological indicators placed inside the load, on the schedule the lab sets.

No. The tape only tells me the outside of the package was exposed to heat and steam. It says nothing about the middle of a dense load. To verify the cycle, we use biological indicators with Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores, placed where steam reaches last, then incubated. No growth means the cycle worked.
How do you decide where a new chemical goes on the shelves?
Your knowledge of safe chemical storage by compatibility.
Storage by hazard class, not alphabetical order, using the SDS. Flammables in a flammable cabinet, oxidizers away from flammables, acids apart from bases.

I read the safety data sheet first, section 7 covers storage. Then I store by hazard class, never alphabetically. Flammables go in the flammable cabinet, oxidizers away from flammables and organics, acids apart from bases, and nitric acid apart from organic acids like acetic acid. I log it in the inventory with the date it was received.
In an ELISA, several samples read above your highest standard. What do you do?
How you handle results outside the range the assay can measure.
Does not extrapolate past the curve. Dilutes the samples in assay diluent, reruns them, and multiplies by the dilution factor.

I don't report a number from beyond the top of the curve, because the fit is not reliable there. I dilute those samples in the same assay diluent, for example 1:10, and rerun them so they land in the middle of the curve. Then I multiply by the dilution factor and note the dilution in the record.
Your qPCR standard curve has a slope of about -3.9 and the melt curve shows two peaks. What does that tell you?
Whether you can read qPCR quality checks and not just the Ct values.
A slope of -3.32 means 100% efficiency; -3.9 is near 80%, too low. A second, lower melt peak often means primer dimers or a non-specific product.

A perfect doubling each cycle gives a slope near -3.32. At -3.9 the efficiency is around 80%, below the 90 to 110% most labs accept. The extra melt peak, often at a lower temperature, suggests primer dimers or a second product. I would check primer design, try a higher annealing temperature and run a gel before trusting the data.
You find a tube in a freezer box with a smudged label you can't read. What do you do?
Your judgement on sample identity and traceability.
Never guesses identity from position or memory. Isolates the tube, checks inventory and the freezer map, asks the owner, and documents it.

I don't guess, even if its spot in the box suggests what it is. I set it aside in a marked bag, check the freezer map and inventory, and ask whoever owns that box. If nobody can confirm its identity with records, it cannot be used as that sample. I write down what happened and tell my supervisor.
The daily check weight on the analytical balance reads out of tolerance. Walk me through what you do.
How you treat an instrument check failure and its effect on past data.
Stops using it, rules out simple causes, rechecks, tags it out if it still fails, and looks at work done since the last good check.

I stop weighing on it. I check that it is level, clean the pan, close the draft shield and let it warm up, then recheck with the certified weight. If it still fails, I tag it out of service and call for service. Then I look at what was weighed since the last passing check and tell my supervisor, since that data may need review.
You find a wrong number in an entry you made in the notebook yesterday. How do you correct it?
Whether you know data integrity rules for correcting records.
A single line through the error so it stays readable, the correct value, initials, date and reason. No erasing, no white-out, no backdating.

I draw one line through the wrong value so it can still be read, write the correct one next to it, and add my initials, today's date and a short reason, like transcription error. I never erase or use white-out. Records should stay attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original and accurate, and that includes the correction.
An assay that worked for months now gives weak signal in every run. How do you find the cause?
How you troubleshoot in a structured way instead of changing everything at once.
Checks controls and what changed recently: lots, expiry, instrument, people. Tests one variable at a time with side-by-side comparisons.

First I look at the controls: if the positive control is also weak, the problem is the method, not the samples. Then I list what changed, such as reagent lots, expiry dates, storage, a plate reader setting. I test one thing at a time, for example old lot against new lot side by side. Changing everything at once fixes the run but hides the cause.

launch-operations.heading: Launch and test operations questions
qs: What is the difference between a hold, a recycle and a scrub?
Whether you know the basic language of a countdown.
Clear, correct definitions, and an understanding that each choice has different follow-on work for the team.

A hold stops the countdown clock so we can check or fix something, then pick up again. A recycle sends the count back to an earlier point, often to redo steps like propellant conditioning. A scrub ends the attempt for that window. We safe the vehicle, drain if needed and plan a new try.
What is a redline, and what happens when one is crossed?
Your understanding of how limits drive decisions in a count.
A limit set in advance with a response already written: a hold, safing or abort. The candidate calls it exactly as written and does not debate it live.

A redline is a limit on a measurement, like a tank pressure or a temperature, set by engineering. The response is written in advance: a hold, a safing action or an abort. Late in the count the automated sequencer watches most of them because people are too slow. My job is to know my redlines cold and call them on the net exactly as written.
Walk me through what you check before and during liquid oxygen loading.
Whether you understand the main hazards of cryogenic propellant.
Area clear, oxygen-clean hardware, a slow chilldown, and limits watched. Grease and oil kept away from oxygen.

Before loading I confirm the area is cleared, the oxygen-clean lines and seals are verified, and the vent paths are open. We chill the lines and tank slowly so the liquid does not flash to gas and surge. I watch pressure, level and temperatures against limits. Nothing oily goes near, because oil can ignite in rich oxygen.
Why do you do a closeout inspection before closing a compartment, and what do you look for?
How you prevent foreign objects and loose ends from flying.
Tool and part counts, no debris, connectors mated, fasteners torqued and marked, and a second person who verifies.

Once a panel is closed, nobody sees inside again before flight. I count tools and hardware against the kit list and look for debris, tape and caps left on fittings. I check that connectors are mated and locked, fasteners carry torque stripes, and lines are clamped. Then a second person inspects and we photograph the compartment before it is closed.
What precautions do you take when working near ordnance such as pyrotechnic initiators?
Your safety habits with explosive devices.
Treats every device as live. Grounding, safe and arm in safe, shorting plugs, radio controls, minimum people and two-person verification.

I treat every initiator as live. Before handling, I ground myself and the hardware. I check that the safe and arm device is in safe and the shorting plugs stay installed until the procedure says otherwise. We follow the radio and transmitter controls for the area, keep only the people the procedure needs, and make connections in the written order with a second person verifying.
You are working in a compartment during a nitrogen purge and your oxygen monitor alarms. What do you do?
How you react to an oxygen-deficient atmosphere.
Leave at once, warn others, report it, and never go back in unprotected to rescue someone. Re-entry only after the air is tested.

I get out to fresh air right away and tell the people with me to do the same. I call the test conductor or safety so the area is closed and the purge is checked. If someone is down inside, I do not go in without supplied air. I call the rescue team, because many people who die in these spaces were trying to rescue someone. Nobody goes back in until the air is tested and cleared.
An engine shuts down on its own right after ignition, with the vehicle still on the pad. What happens next?
Whether you know how to handle a pad abort.
Nobody approaches. Remote safing per procedure, data watched for fire or rising pressure, and the pad reopened only by the safety lead.

Nobody goes near. The vehicle is still loaded and pressurized, and something made it shut down. We follow the abort safing procedure from the control room: safe the engine, vent or offload as written, and watch the data for fire, leaks or rising pressure. Teams go back only when the safety lead clears the pad. Meanwhile I save the data and my log notes.
A recovered booster or capsule is brought in. How do you approach it?
Your understanding of the hazards in recovered hardware.
Assumes it is hazardous: leftover propellant, charged pressure bottles, unfired ordnance. Safes it step by step and records its condition.

I treat it as unsafe until it is proven safe. There may be leftover propellant, pressure bottles still charged and ordnance that did not fire. We approach from upwind, check for vapors with detectors and look for damage before touching anything. First we vent pressure, safe the ordnance per procedure and cap the open lines. Then we secure it for transport and photograph everything for the engineers.
After a compartment is closed, you notice a wrench is missing from your kit. What do you do?
How you own a mistake that could put a flight at risk.
Stops and reports at once, searches, and accepts reopening the compartment. Hiding it is never an option.

I stop and report it right away, before anyone signs the next step. We search my work area and the vehicle with a light and a mirror, and recount the kit. If the wrench is not found, the compartment gets reopened and inspected, even if that costs a day. A loose wrench in flight can short a harness or jam a valve.
Late in the count, a reading is still within limits but has been drifting, and the window is closing. What do you say?
Your judgement when schedule pressure meets an unexplained trend.
Speaks up with facts on the net and asks for an explanation. Recommends a hold if nobody can explain it, and does not let the window decide.

Within limits is not the same as understood. I would call it out on the net with the value and the trend, and ask engineering whether there is a known reason. If nobody can explain it before the next hold point, I would recommend we hold or scrub. A missed window costs a day. Flying with a problem we cannot explain can cost the vehicle.
During a go/no-go poll, what exactly are you answering for when you say "go"?
Whether you understand what a poll response commits you to.
Go means your own system is ready and you have no open concern. Any doubt means no-go or a request to hold, never a quiet go.

I am saying my system is configured, in limits and ready for the next phase, and that I have nothing open. I answer only for my station, not for anyone else's. If I am unsure, or a reading is still settling, I say no-go or ask for a hold. Saying go to keep the count moving is how small problems get carried into flight.
Why do cryogenic loads start with a slow fill before going to fast fill?
Your grasp of the physics behind the loading sequence.
Warm lines and tanks flash the cryogen to gas, causing pressure surges, thermal stress and geysering. Chilling down slowly first avoids that.

When liquid oxygen hits warm pipe and tank walls, it boils off violently. That gives pressure spikes, big thermal stress on joints and seals, and geysering in long vertical lines. A slow fill chills everything down until liquid can collect. Then we go to fast fill, and later to topping, which replaces what keeps boiling off until launch.
Why are propellant tanks pressurized before and during flight?
Whether you know what ullage pressure does for the engine and the structure.
It keeps pump inlet pressure high enough to stop cavitation and stiffens thin tank walls to carry flight loads. Pressure-fed engines rely on it to move propellant.

Ullage pressure is the gas pressure above the liquid. It keeps the pressure at the turbopump inlet above the propellant's vapor pressure, so the pump does not cavitate. It also stiffens thin-walled tanks so they can carry loads during flight. On a pressure-fed engine, that same pressure is what pushes propellant into the chamber.
How is working with hypergolic propellants different from working with cryogens?
Your knowledge of toxic propellant hazards and controls.
It names the toxicity, ignition on contact, full suits with supplied air, vapor monitoring, and strict separation of fuel and oxidizer work.

Cryogens mainly bring cold burns, asphyxiation and fire risk. Hydrazine fuels and nitrogen tetroxide ignite on contact with each other and are toxic. Oxidizer vapor can cause lung damage that shows up hours later. So we load in fully enclosed suits with supplied air and monitor vapor. Fuel and oxidizer operations are never run at the same time. Spill kits and decontamination are set up first.
Weather is green on the ground, but a launch weather criterion is red. Why would you still hold?
Whether you understand why weather launch commit criteria exist, especially lightning.
A rocket and its plume can trigger lightning in clouds that would not strike on their own. The rules are written for the flight path, not just for the pad.

A rocket and its exhaust plume act like a long conductor and can trigger lightning in electrified clouds that would not strike on their own. Apollo 12 was hit twice right after liftoff. The rules look at anvil and cumulus clouds, field mill readings and upper-level winds along the flight path. Clear skies over the pad do not clear the flight path, so we hold.
Walk me through how you verify instrumentation before a static fire.
How you make sure the test data will be trustworthy before you spend hardware on it.
End-to-end checks from sensor to recorded value, calibration, correct channel mapping, and redline channels confirmed live.

I check calibration dates and ranges against the test plan. Then I run end-to-end checks. I stimulate each sensor, for example by applying known pressure or running a shunt calibration on load cells and strain gauges, and confirm the right channel reads it with the right sign. I check zero readings with no load and confirm sample rates. Last, I confirm every redline is wired to a live, verified channel.
During hydrogen fast fill, a sensor near the ground umbilical starts reading hydrogen. Walk me through your response.
How you handle a live leak on a loaded vehicle.
Call it on the net and follow the leak procedure. Watch the concentration trend and safe the system remotely. Nobody walks out to look.

I call it on the net with the sensor and reading, and we follow the leak procedure, usually stopping the fill. I watch whether the concentration rises against the procedure's limit, knowing hydrogen's lower flammability limit is about four percent in air. If it climbs, we safe and drain remotely. Hydrogen fire is nearly invisible in daylight, so we use thermal cameras, never a person.
A senior manager wants to waive a launch constraint to make the window, and you think the rationale is weak. What do you do?
Your judgement and backbone when schedule pressure meets a safety constraint.
State the concern on the record, with data, through the proper channel. Ask for documented rationale. Accept a properly approved decision but never stay silent.

I say clearly, on the net or in the review, what the constraint protects against and why I think the rationale does not cover it, with data if I have it. I ask what evidence shows the risk is acceptable and that it be written down. If the approving authority still signs it, that is their call, but my dissent is on the record. Missing a window costs a day; flying a known risk can cost the vehicle.
A test article fails on the stand. How do you run the first days of the investigation?
How you preserve evidence and find root cause instead of the first plausible story.
Secure the site and the data, impound the hardware, build a timeline, and use a fault tree. Separate root cause from proximate cause before any fix.

First, safe the stand and keep everyone out until hazards are cleared. Then impound the hardware and data, and photograph everything before anything moves. I build a timeline from the high-speed data and video, and start a fault tree covering every possible cause. We close branches only with evidence or tests. We do not fix anything until we know the root cause, not just the part that broke first.

legal-counsel.heading: Legal counsel questions
qs: What is the difference between an indemnity and a limitation of liability clause?
Whether you know the two clauses that decide who pays when a deal goes wrong.
An indemnity shifts specific losses, often third-party claims, to one party; a cap limits total damages. You see how carve-outs connect the two.

An indemnity is a promise to cover certain losses, usually claims brought by third parties, such as an IP infringement suit. A limitation of liability caps what one side can recover from the other, often at fees paid in the last 12 months. The key is the carve-outs: I check whether indemnities sit inside or outside the cap, because that decides the real exposure.
A vendor sends its own 20-page form for a software subscription. Walk me through your first read.
How you triage a third-party contract under time pressure.
A clear order: the terms that carry real risk first, a short list of must-haves versus nice-to-haves, and no line-by-line rewrite of boilerplate.

First I ask the business what the deal is worth and what data the vendor will touch. Then I read the cap, the indemnities, data security and breach notice, IP ownership, term, auto-renewal and termination rights, and governing law. I mark three or four must-haves and let minor points go, so the deal closes this week instead of next month.
As in-house counsel, who is your client?
Whether you understand that you represent the company, not the people who call you.
The organization, as ABA Model Rule 1.13 says, and knowing when to give an employee an Upjohn warning.

The company is my client, acting through its authorized people. Most days that makes no difference, but it matters when interests split. If I interview an employee in an investigation, I give an Upjohn warning: I represent the company, not them, the talk is privileged, and the company alone decides whether to waive that privilege.
When is an email to you not privileged, even though you are the company's lawyer?
Your grasp of attorney-client privilege as it applies to in-house lawyers.
Privilege covers confidential requests for legal advice, not business advice; copying a lawyer does not protect an email, and sharing it widely can waive it.

Privilege protects confidential communications made to get legal advice. Many courts look at the primary purpose, and in-house lawyers also give business input, so a pricing discussion with me on copy is not protected. Sharing it with outsiders can waive it too. I tell teams to ask me a legal question directly and keep my answer within the people who need it.
Our purchase order and the supplier's order acknowledgment have conflicting terms. Whose terms govern?
Whether you know the battle of the forms under the Uniform Commercial Code.
For goods, UCC 2-207 rather than the mirror-image rule; conflicting terms often knocked out for UCC defaults; a signed master agreement as the fix.

For goods, UCC 2-207 applies, not the old rule that an acceptance must mirror the offer exactly. Between merchants, an added term joins the deal unless the offer limited acceptance to its terms, the term materially alters the deal, or someone objects. For conflicting terms, many courts knock out both and use UCC defaults. The fix is a signed master agreement that overrides any form.
You learn a salesperson promised a customer, by email, a refund right that is not in the contract. What do you do?
How you handle side promises that can change a signed deal.
Getting the facts, judging whether the email could bind the company, involving finance, and fixing the process rather than blaming.

I get the full email thread and the contract first. Even with a clause requiring signed amendments, a written promise from someone who looked authorized can start a dispute, and it can change how finance books the revenue. I tell finance, decide with the sales lead whether to honor, paper or walk it back, and then tighten who may promise terms.
A former distributor's lawyer sends a letter threatening to sue. What happens in the first 48 hours?
Whether you know when the duty to preserve evidence starts and how to act on it.
A litigation hold once suit is reasonably anticipated, auto-deletion stopped, insurers notified on time, and outside counsel chosen if needed.

A credible threat means litigation is reasonably anticipated, so the duty to preserve starts now. I send a written hold to the people involved and to IT, suspend auto-deletion of their email and chat, and track who has confirmed. I check our insurance policies for notice deadlines, pull the contract, and decide whether to bring in outside litigation counsel.
When would you push for arbitration in a commercial contract, and when would you prefer court?
Your judgement on dispute resolution clauses, not just a default preference.
Weighing privacy, cost, appeal rights and enforcement abroad against the deal at hand, with no one-size answer.

Arbitration fits when we want privacy, an arbitrator who knows the industry, or a foreign counterparty, because awards are easier to enforce abroad under the New York Convention. Court fits when we want a right to appeal, since arbitration awards are very hard to overturn. For small contracts, arbitration fees can exceed what is at stake, so court may be the better choice.
Tell me about a contract issue you missed and what you changed afterward.
Whether you own mistakes and turn them into a better process.
A real miss, told plainly, with the cost, the fix for that deal, and a lasting change such as a checklist or a tracking system.

I once approved a vendor form without catching that it auto-renewed for three years with a 90-day notice window. We missed the window and were locked in at a 12% higher price. I negotiated a partial credit, then set up a contract database that flags notice dates 120 days ahead. No renewal has slipped since.
An employee tells you a senior manager may be inflating sales numbers. How do you handle it?
How you handle a serious internal report when your duty runs to the company.
Taking it seriously, preserving evidence, protecting the reporter from retaliation, reporting up the chain, and independent counsel when leaders are involved.

I thank the employee, take notes, and make clear there will be no retaliation, which federal law also protects at public companies. I preserve the relevant records quietly. Because a senior manager is involved, I report it up to the general counsel and, if needed, the audit committee, and recommend outside counsel run an independent investigation. I do not tip off the manager.
An NDA from a large partner includes a residuals clause. What is it, and would you accept it?
Whether you spot a clause that quietly weakens a confidentiality agreement.
Explains that it lets the other side use what its people remember, and limits or rejects it based on what we will disclose.

A residuals clause lets the receiving side use ideas and know-how its people keep in unaided memory, without looking at the documents. If we are sharing source code or a roadmap, I strike it. If we must keep it, I exclude patents and trade secrets, limit it to general skills, and bar anyone from memorizing on purpose.
What is the difference between best efforts and commercially reasonable efforts, and how do you draft around it?
Your grasp of efforts clauses, where courts do not agree on the meaning.
Admits US courts read these terms inconsistently and fixes the problem by defining the obligation in the contract.

Many lawyers treat best efforts as the highest bar, possibly requiring spending against your own interest. But US courts have not applied a consistent ranking, and some read the terms almost the same. So I do not rely on the label. I write what the duty means: named actions, a budget, a timeline, and what the party need not do.
The business wants a $5,000-per-day late fee in a supply contract. Will a court enforce it?
Whether you know the line between liquidated damages and an unenforceable penalty.
Explains the test: a reasonable estimate of likely harm where damages are hard to prove, not a punishment, and builds a record of the estimate.

Only if it is liquidated damages, not a penalty. Courts ask whether the amount was a reasonable forecast of the harm, judged at signing or in light of actual loss, and whether actual damages would be hard to prove. I would ask operations what a day of delay really costs us, keep that analysis on file, and not set the fee far above that figure.
A customer asks for a mutual waiver of consequential damages. What do you carve out, and why?
How you protect the company inside a standard damages waiver.
Knows lost profits can be direct or consequential depending on the facts, and carves out confidentiality, data security, indemnity and willful misconduct.

Consequential damages are losses that flow from special circumstances, like a customer's lost business from downtime. I accept a mutual waiver but carve out breach of confidentiality and data security, indemnity for third-party claims, and willful misconduct. I also check whether lost profits are named, because courts sometimes treat them as direct damages.
Legal cannot review every contract. How do you decide what the business may sign without you?
How you scale the legal function without losing control of risk.
Templates and a playbook, clear thresholds by value and type of risk, a written signing-authority policy, and regular spot checks.

I set up templates and a playbook for routine deals, with fallback positions sales can accept on their own. Anything above a dollar threshold, with uncapped liability, personal data, exclusivity or changes to our paper comes to legal. A signing-authority policy says who can sign what, and I audit a sample each quarter to see if the rules hold.
We are buying a smaller company. What do you look for in its customer contracts?
Whether you can find the contracts a deal could break.
Anti-assignment and change-of-control clauses, required consents, and exclusivity or most-favored-customer terms that could bind the buyer after closing.

First, clauses that need consent to assign or let the customer terminate on a change of control. Whether a merger or stock sale counts as an assignment depends on the wording and the governing law, so I read each one. I also flag exclusivity, most-favored-customer pricing and non-competes that could bind us later, and list the consents we need before closing.
We are hiring a sales leader from a direct competitor. What do you check before the offer goes out?
Your handling of restrictive covenants and trade secret risk in hiring.
Reviews the candidate's agreements under the right state law, separates non-compete from non-solicit and confidentiality, and keeps the old employer's data out.

I ask for every agreement the candidate signed. Non-compete enforceability depends heavily on state law; California, for example, voids most of them. Non-solicitation and confidentiality duties often survive even where a non-compete fails. I tell the candidate in writing to bring no files or customer lists from the old job, and to confirm it, since misuse could bring a trade secret claim against us.
A marketing vendor will handle our customers' personal data. What must the contract say?
Whether you can turn privacy law into concrete contract terms.
Use limited to our purpose, security duties, breach notice, control of subcontractors, deletion at the end, and the terms the CCPA requires for service providers.

The vendor may use the data only to serve us, not for its own purposes, and may not sell or share it. It must keep reasonable security, tell us quickly of any breach, flow the same terms to subcontractors, help us answer consumer requests, and return or delete the data at the end. The CCPA requires these limits in the contract itself, so I use our data addendum.
A sales VP mentions he and a competitor discussed next year's pricing at a trade show dinner. What do you do?
How you respond to possible antitrust exposure, where speed matters most.
Sees possible per se Sherman Act liability, stops the contact, preserves records, investigates under privilege and weighs DOJ leniency early.

Agreeing on prices with a competitor can be a per se violation of Section 1 of the Sherman Act, which is a crime. I tell him to have no further pricing contact, preserve his messages, and I interview him under privilege with outside antitrust counsel. If there was an agreement, I brief leadership fast, because the DOJ leniency program favors the first company to report.
You are interviewing an employee in an internal investigation. What do you tell them before the first question?
Whether you know the Upjohn warning and why you give it.
You represent the company, not them; the talk is privileged but the company owns the privilege and may waive it; they should keep it confidential.

I give an Upjohn warning and note that I gave it. I say I am the company's lawyer, not theirs. The conversation is privileged, but the privilege belongs to the company, which can waive it and share what they say, including with the government. I ask them to keep it confidential. If their interests seem to conflict with the company's, they may want their own lawyer.

lending.heading: Lending and mortgage questions
qs: What are the five Cs of credit, and which one do you weigh most?
Whether you know the basic framework for judging a borrower.
All five named correctly, with capacity to repay put first, since collateral is a fallback and not a source of payment.

Character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions. I weigh capacity most: can the borrower's steady cash flow cover the payment? Collateral matters, but it is the way out if things go wrong, not the plan. A loan that only works if we take the house or the equipment is a bad loan.
How do you calculate a borrower's debt-to-income ratio for a mortgage?
Your grasp of the core affordability measure and what goes into it.
Gross monthly income as the base, the full new housing payment plus recurring debts on top, and everyday living costs left out.

I add the new housing payment, meaning principal, interest, property taxes, homeowners insurance, any HOA dues and mortgage insurance, to the monthly debts on the credit report and other obligations like child support. I divide that by gross monthly income. Utilities and groceries are not counted. Housing payment alone over income is the front-end ratio.
What is loan-to-value, and why does it change the terms a borrower gets?
Whether you understand how equity protects the lender.
The correct formula, the lower-of-value-or-price rule on purchases, and the link between thin equity, pricing and mortgage insurance.

It is the loan amount divided by the property value; on a purchase I use the lower of the appraised value and the price. A $320,000 loan on a $400,000 home is 80% LTV. The higher it goes, the less equity protects us if prices fall, so pricing gets worse, and a conventional loan above 80% usually needs mortgage insurance.
A small business shows a debt service coverage ratio of 1.10. What does that tell you?
Whether you can read cash-flow coverage on a business loan.
The ratio explained as cash flow over debt payments, with 1.10 seen as a thin cushion that needs a closer look, not an automatic yes.

It is the cash available for debt, often net operating income, divided by the year's principal and interest payments. At 1.10 the business covers its payments with only 10% to spare. A small drop in sales or a rate rise wipes that out, so I look at trends, the owner's outside income and whether a smaller amount or longer term makes it safer.
When do the Loan Estimate and the Closing Disclosure have to reach the borrower?
Your knowledge of the federal mortgage disclosure timeline.
Loan Estimate within three business days of application; Closing Disclosure received at least three business days before closing.

The Loan Estimate goes out within three business days after we have an application, which under the rule means six items: name, income, Social Security number, property address, estimated value and loan amount. The borrower must receive the Closing Disclosure at least three business days before consummation, so I plan the closing date backward from that.
The bank statements show an $18,000 deposit two months ago with no explanation. What do you do?
How you verify where a borrower's funds come from.
The deposit is sourced, not ignored: a written explanation and paper trail, and a proper gift letter and transfer record if it came from family.

I ask the borrower for a written explanation and documents that trace it, like a sale receipt or a statement from the account it came from. If it was a gift from a parent, I need a signed gift letter saying no repayment is expected and proof of the transfer. If it cannot be sourced, I leave it out of the funds to close.
The appraisal comes in $15,000 under the purchase price, and the agent asks you to call the appraiser and get it raised. How do you handle it?
Whether you respect appraisal independence while still helping the deal.
No pressure on the appraiser; real errors raised through a formal reconsideration of value, and the borrower's options explained plainly.

I will not contact the appraiser to push for a number; that breaks appraisal independence rules. If the agent has better comparable sales or sees a factual error, I send it through our formal reconsideration of value process. Otherwise the options are a lower price, a bigger down payment to keep the LTV, or walking away if the contract allows it.
You have to decline a loan application. What do you owe the applicant?
Your knowledge of adverse action rules under fair lending and credit reporting law.
A timely written notice with specific, real reasons, the ECOA notice, and credit report disclosures when a report was used.

Under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act I send a written notice within 30 days of the completed application, with the specific principal reasons, such as debt too high for income, not a vague 'did not meet our standards'. It includes the ECOA notice. If a credit report played a part, I add the bureau, the score and the right to a free report and to dispute.
A commercial borrower's annual statements show it fell below the coverage ratio its loan agreement requires. What do you do?
How you handle early warning signs in a loan you look after.
Fast contact, the cause understood, the risk rating updated, and a documented decision on waiver, amendment or tighter terms.

First I confirm the math, then I call the borrower to learn why: a one-time cost or a real decline. I ask for interim numbers and a plan. I update the risk rating and write it up for credit. If it is temporary, a waiver with a fee or tighter reporting may fit; if not, we discuss more collateral, a guarantee or a paydown.
A homeowner calls to say he lost his job and will miss next month's payment. Walk me through how you help him.
Whether you know loss mitigation options and the servicing rules that protect borrowers.
Options like forbearance, a repayment plan or modification, a complete application gathered, and awareness of federal limits on early foreclosure.

I thank him for calling early and explain the options: forbearance, a repayment plan, or a loan modification once income returns. I send a list of what a complete application needs and follow up on gaps. Federal servicing rules generally bar a first foreclosure filing until a loan is over 120 days delinquent, and a complete application gets reviewed first.
A borrower put 10% down on a conventional loan and pays private mortgage insurance. When can it come off?
Whether you know the Homeowners Protection Act rules for removing private mortgage insurance.
Borrower can request it at 80% of original value and it ends automatically at 78% on the original schedule, if the loan is current. FHA insurance follows its own rules.

She can ask in writing to cancel once the balance reaches 80% of the original value, meaning the lower of the price or the appraisal at closing, if she is current with a good payment record. The lender can ask for proof the value has not dropped. If she does nothing, it ends automatically when the scheduled balance reaches 78%. FHA premiums follow their own rules.
Explain a 5/1 adjustable-rate mortgage with 2/1/5 caps to a first-time buyer.
Whether you can explain how an adjustable rate really moves, in words a borrower understands.
The fixed period, the reset frequency, what each cap limits, index plus margin, and showing the worst-case payment.

The rate is fixed for five years, then it resets once a year. At the first reset it can move at most 2 points, after that at most 1 point per reset, and never more than 5 points above the starting rate. The new rate is an index plus a fixed margin. I would show her the payment at the highest possible rate, so she knows the worst case before she signs.
A self-employed borrower's net income fell from $92,000 to $71,000 last year. How do you work out qualifying income?
How you handle self-employed income when the trend is going the wrong way.
Uses tax returns, adds back noncash items, does not average a falling income, and checks whether the decline has stopped before using it at all.

I work from the tax returns, usually two years, and add back noncash expenses like depreciation. With income falling, I do not average the two years. At most I use the lower, recent figure, and only if a year-to-date profit and loss shows the decline has stopped. If it is still sliding, I may not be able to count the income at all.
Fees went up between the Loan Estimate and closing. Which increases are allowed, and what happens if you went over the limit?
Your working knowledge of the TRID fee tolerance rules.
Zero tolerance for lender charges and transfer taxes, 10% total for recording fees and lender-list services, no limit for prepaids and shopped services; refund within 60 days.

Our own charges, like origination fees, and transfer taxes cannot go up at all unless there is a valid changed circumstance. Recording fees and services picked from our provider list can rise, but that group's total cannot grow more than 10%. Prepaid interest, insurance and services the borrower found on his own have no limit. If we went over, we refund the difference within 60 days of closing.
What does the ability-to-repay rule require, and what does a Qualified Mortgage add?
Whether you understand the federal rule behind every home loan decision you make.
A good-faith decision on verified records across the required factors, the risky features a QM excludes, and the legal presumption that QM status gives the lender.

I must make a good-faith decision, on verified records, that the borrower can repay: income or assets, job, the new payment, other debts, DTI or residual income, and credit history. A Qualified Mortgage adds limits: no interest-only period, no negative amortization, no term over 30 years, capped points and fees. In return the lender gets a presumption that it met the rule.
A colleague asks a married applicant whether she plans to have children soon, to check she can keep working. What do you do?
Whether you know fair lending rules well enough to act on them in the moment.
Knows Regulation B bars questions about plans to have or raise children, stops it calmly, keeps it out of the file and tells compliance.

I would step in politely and move the meeting on, then talk to my colleague privately. Regulation B forbids asking about plans to have or raise children, and nothing like that can be used in the decision. I would make sure it did not go into the file and tell compliance, because the bank needs to know if this has happened on other applications too.
A manufacturer wants a 10-year loan on equipment that will last about five years. How do you structure it?
How you match the loan structure to the asset and the source of repayment.
Amortization matched to useful life, and a high payment treated as a warning about the purchase, solved with equity or collateral, not a longer term.

I would match the amortization to the useful life, so five years or less. If the loan outlasts the machine, the borrower keeps paying for something that no longer earns money, and our collateral is worth little. If the five-year payment is too heavy, that tells me the purchase may not pay for itself. I would look at a larger down payment or extra collateral, not a longer term.
The business covers its debt, but the owner who guarantees it also owns two rental properties with their own loans. How do you look at the whole picture?
Whether you can run a global cash flow across a business and its guarantor.
Combines business, personal and rental cash flow against all debt, avoids counting the same dollar twice, and sees how one weak part can sink the rest.

I build a global cash flow: the business cash flow, the owner's other income and the rentals' net income, set against every debt payment, including his home mortgage and an allowance for living costs. I make sure a distribution is not counted both in the business and in his personal income. A strong business can be dragged down by a rental that loses money every month.
Your review says a long-time client's loan should go on the watch list, and the relationship manager asks you to wait one more quarter. What do you do?
Your judgement when a correct risk rating meets pressure from the business side.
Listens for facts the numbers miss, but rates the risk as it is today, documents it, and agrees a plan with the relationship manager.

I would listen, because he may know something the numbers do not, like a signed new contract. But the rating has to show the risk today. If the facts support it, I downgrade, write down why, and agree a plan with him: monthly reporting and a meeting with the client. A late downgrade hides risk from our loss allowance and from the examiners.
After closing, a quality control review finds you counted overtime income that did not have enough history. The loan is yours. What do you do?
How you own a mistake and limit its damage to the borrower and the bank.
Owns the error at once, recalculates to see the real impact, lets the bank handle investor exposure, and fixes the process, not just the file.

I would tell my manager and QC straight away that it was my error. Then I would recalculate DTI without the overtime and see whether the loan still qualifies. If it does, we document that. If not, the bank decides how to handle the investor and any repurchase risk. Then I would find why I missed it, for example a missing income history step in my checklist, and fix that.

life-sciences.heading: Life sciences and lab questions
qs: You are about to use a chemical you have never handled. Where do you look first, and what do you look for?
Whether you check the hazards before you open a bottle.
The Safety Data Sheet, especially the sections on hazards, handling, storage and protective equipment, plus the lab's own written procedures.

I read the Safety Data Sheet first. Section 2 tells me the hazards, Section 7 covers handling and storage, and Section 8 covers exposure controls and protective equipment. I check whether it must go in the fume hood, what it reacts badly with, and how its waste is collected. If our lab has a written procedure for it, I follow that too.
What is the difference between a biological replicate and a technical replicate?
Your grasp of what an n actually counts.
Biological replicates are independent samples that capture real variation. Technical replicates measure the same sample again and only show measurement noise.

A biological replicate is an independent sample, like cells from a separate culture or a different animal. A technical replicate is the same sample measured again, like three wells loaded from one tube. Technical replicates tell me how precise the assay is. Only biological replicates tell me whether the effect is real, so they are what I count as n.
You need 100 mL of 70% ethanol and the stock is 95%. How do you make it?
Whether you can do a routine dilution correctly at the bench.
Uses C1V1 = C2V2, gets about 73.7 mL of stock, and brings it to volume with water instead of adding a fixed amount.

I use C1V1 = C2V2: 95% times V1 equals 70% times 100 mL, so V1 is about 73.7 mL. I measure that in a graduated cylinder and add water up to the 100 mL mark. I do not just add 26.3 mL of water, because ethanol and water shrink a little when mixed. Then I label it with the contents, the date and my initials.
If you left tomorrow, could someone repeat last week's experiment from your notebook? What would they find there?
Your record keeping as a scientist, so that work can be repeated by someone else.
Date, aim, exact protocol with any changes, reagent lot numbers, instrument settings, where the raw data files are, and what went wrong.

Yes. Each entry has the date, the question I was testing and the protocol, with every change from the standard version written in. I note reagent lot numbers, cell passage numbers and instrument settings, plus the path to the raw data files. I also write what failed or looked odd that day, because that is usually what the next person needs most.
Walk me through how you would design an experiment to test whether a new compound slows the growth of a cell line.
How you build an experiment that can actually answer its question.
A clear question, a vehicle control, a positive control, a dose range, independent replicates, analysis planned ahead, and randomization where possible.

I start with one clear question and one main readout, such as cell counts at 72 hours. I include a vehicle control with the same amount of solvent, a positive control known to slow growth, and several doses. I plan at least three independent experiments, decide the analysis before I see data, and randomize plate positions so edge effects do not line up with treatment.
You knock over a flask of a BSL-2 bacterial culture on the bench. What do you do?
Whether you handle a biohazard spill safely and in the right order.
Warn others, protect yourself, cover with absorbent material, disinfect for the full contact time in the lab's spill plan, discard as biohazard, and report it.

I tell people nearby and keep them back. With gloves, lab coat and eye protection on, I cover the spill with paper towels and pour on the disinfectant our spill plan names, working from the edges in. I leave it for the full contact time, pick up any broken glass with tongs, put everything in biohazard waste, wipe again, and report the spill to my supervisor.
Your qPCR no-template control shows a signal. What does that tell you, and what do you do next?
How you troubleshoot a failed control instead of ignoring it.
A signal with no template means contamination or primer-dimers. Check the melt curve, replace reagents, clean up and rerun before trusting the plate.

A no-template control has no DNA, so a signal means contamination or primers binding to each other. With a dye-based mix, I check the melt curve: a peak at a lower temperature than the product points to primer-dimers. If it matches the product, I assume contamination, throw out the working aliquots, clean the area and rerun. I do not report that plate.
How do you make sure the cell line you are working with is really what the label says?
Whether you know the checks that keep cell-based data trustworthy.
Trusted sources, identity checks such as STR profiling for human lines, regular mycoplasma testing, and low, recorded passage numbers.

I get lines from a trusted repository or a known lab, not an unlabeled tube from a freezer box. For human lines we confirm identity with STR profiling, which compares short DNA repeat patterns to a reference profile. I test for mycoplasma on a regular schedule, since it does not cloud the medium. I also track passage numbers and go back to early frozen stocks.
A colleague compared four treatment groups by running a t-test on every pair. What is the problem, and what would you suggest?
Your judgement on the basic statistics behind lab results.
Many tests raise the chance of a false positive. Use ANOVA with a post-hoc test or correct for multiple comparisons, with n as independent replicates.

Four groups means six pairwise tests, and each one carries its own chance of a false positive, so the overall chance of at least one fluke goes up. I would suggest a one-way ANOVA followed by a post-hoc test such as Tukey's, or a correction for multiple comparisons. I would also check that n counts independent experiments, not wells.
Your PI wants to drop one replicate that spoils a nice result, with no clear technical reason. How do you handle it?
Your integrity with data when there is pressure to get a clean result.
Data are not dropped because they are inconvenient. Exclusion needs a rule set in advance or a documented technical failure, and it must be reported.

I would first look for a real cause in my notebook, like a failed control or a pipetting error I wrote down. If there is none, I would say calmly that we cannot remove it just because it disagrees. I would offer options: show all the data, run more independent replicates, and set exclusion rules before the next round. Removing it quietly could count as falsifying data.
In a figure, when do you show the standard deviation and when the standard error of the mean?
Whether you know what each error bar tells the reader.
SD shows the spread of the data; SEM shows how precisely the mean is known and shrinks as n grows. Always say which one and give n.

I use the standard deviation when I want to show how variable the samples are. The standard error is the SD divided by the square root of n, so it shows how precisely I know the mean and gets smaller with more samples. Whichever I use, the legend says which bar it is and what n is, because small SEM bars can make noisy data look tidy.
An old protocol says to spin at 13,000 rpm. Why is that not enough information, and what do you do?
Whether you understand centrifugal force rather than just rotor speed.
The force depends on the rotor radius as well as the speed. Convert to relative centrifugal force (x g) for the rotor you actually use.

Rpm is only speed. The force on the sample also depends on the radius of the rotor, so 13,000 rpm gives a different g-force in a different rotor. I find out which rotor they used and work out the g-force with RCF = 1.118 x 10^-5 x radius in cm x rpm squared. Then I set my centrifuge to that g. I write my own protocols in x g for this reason.
Your RNA kit waste contains guanidine salts. Can you add bleach to it before disposal?
Whether you know a chemical incompatibility that is common in molecular biology labs.
No. Bleach mixed with guanidine salts can release toxic gas. The waste goes to labeled chemical waste, following the SDS and the institution's rules.

No. The lysis and wash buffers in many RNA and DNA kits contain guanidine thiocyanate or guanidine hydrochloride, and mixing them with bleach can give off toxic gas. That waste goes in a labeled chemical waste container, never into a bleach bucket. If the samples were infectious, I follow the kit's SDS and our safety office's instructions for handling that waste.
Your treatment seems to change the level of GAPDH, the loading control on your Western blot. What do you do?
How you handle a control that is no longer a control.
Housekeeping proteins can be regulated. Switch to total protein staining, or to a control shown to stay stable under this treatment.

If GAPDH moves with the treatment, I cannot use it to normalize, because it is part of the effect. Treatments that affect metabolism often change it. I would check equal loading with a total protein stain on the membrane, such as Ponceau S, or test other controls and keep one that stays flat across my conditions. Then I re-quantify from the raw images.
How do you convince yourself that an antibody really detects your protein?
Your standard for trusting a reagent you did not make.
Testing in your own system with a knockout or knockdown control and the expected band size, and ideally confirming with a second, independent method.

The datasheet is a starting point, not proof. I run the antibody on cells where the protein is knocked out or knocked down, and the signal should disappear. On a blot I check that the band is at the expected size. Where I can, I confirm with a second method, such as another antibody to a different part of the protein. I record the catalog and lot number too.
You plan to use the delta-delta Ct method for qPCR. What do you check about your primers first?
Whether you know the assumption behind the most common qPCR calculation.
Delta-delta Ct assumes target and reference both amplify near 100% efficiency. Check with a dilution standard curve and a single melt-curve peak.

Delta-delta Ct assumes the product doubles every cycle for both the target and the reference gene. I run a serial dilution and plot Ct against log input. A slope near minus 3.32 means about 100% efficiency; I want both primer pairs roughly in the 90 to 110% range and close to each other. A single melt-curve peak tells me there is one product, not primer dimers.
How do you decide how many samples or animals an experiment needs?
Whether you plan sample size before you start, not after.
A power analysis using the smallest effect worth detecting, an estimate of variability, the significance level and the power you want.

I do a power analysis before starting. I need the smallest difference that would matter, an estimate of the variability from pilot data or earlier work, the significance level, usually 0.05, and the power, often 80%. That gives the n. For animal work the numbers also go in the protocol, because the animal care committee expects us to justify them and use no more animals than needed.
Your RNA-seq comparison gives 2,000 genes with p below 0.05 out of 20,000 tested. What do you make of that?
Whether you understand multiple testing in large datasets.
About 1,000 would pass by chance even with no real change. Use false discovery rate correction, such as Benjamini-Hochberg, and check fold changes.

With 20,000 tests, even if no gene had changed, about 5%, so roughly 1,000 genes, would fall below 0.05 by chance. A large part of that list could be noise. I would use adjusted p-values that control the false discovery rate, like the Benjamini-Hochberg method most RNA-seq tools report, and look at fold change too. Then I would confirm key genes in new samples.
What changes can you make to a blot or microscope image before it goes into a figure, and what can you not do?
Your grasp of the image integrity rules that journals and funders enforce.
Brightness and contrast applied to the whole image, and equally to images being compared. No erasing, cloning or hidden splicing. Raw files kept.

I can adjust brightness and contrast if I apply it to the whole image and treat the images I compare the same way. I cannot erase, clone or add anything. If I join lanes from different parts of a gel, I show a clear dividing line and say so in the legend. I keep the raw, uncropped files, because journals often ask for them.
You cannot reproduce a key result from a published paper your project builds on. How do you work through it?
How you troubleshoot methodically and judge when a result may not hold.
Rules out problems on your own side first, matches conditions closely, contacts the authors, and reports the outcome honestly instead of forcing it.

First I rule out my own side: positive controls, reagent lots, cell line identity and passage number. Then I compare every condition with the methods and supplements and note what is missing. If it still fails, my PI and I write to the authors for details or materials. If it never works, we say so and adjust the project, rather than tweak until it fits.

lifecycle-marketing.heading: Lifecycle and CRM marketing manager questions
qs: What lifecycle stages would you map for a subscription app, and what is the goal at each?
Whether you think in customer stages rather than single campaigns.
Clear stages from signup to win-back, each tied to one behavior to drive, not just a message to send.

I would map new signup, activated, habitual, at risk, lapsed and churned. Each stage has one goal. For new users it is reaching the first key action, for habitual users it is an upgrade or referral, for at-risk users it is getting a session back. I define each stage by behavior in the data, so a person moves between stages automatically.
Why are email open rates less reliable than they used to be, and what do you track instead?
Your grasp of how privacy changes weakened a classic metric.
Knows that some mail apps preload images, which inflates opens, and judges results on clicks, conversions and lift.

Some mail apps now download images, including the tracking pixel, as soon as the email arrives, so many opens are machine opens. I treat opens as a rough trend at best. I judge campaigns on clicks, conversions and revenue per recipient, and I avoid triggers built on opens, because they include people who never saw the email.
Walk me through how you would build an onboarding series for new signups.
How you design a behavior-triggered flow, not a fixed calendar of sends.
Starts from the action that predicts retention, uses triggers and exit rules, and measures against a holdout.

First I find the action that best predicts who stays, say setting up a first project within three days. Message one welcomes and points to that action. Later messages fire only if the person has not done it yet, and anyone who completes it exits to the next stage. I mix email with in-app tips and keep a small holdout to measure the series.
What is a holdout group, and how do you set one up for an automated flow?
Whether you can measure true lift instead of just taking credit.
A random share kept from the message, compared on the outcome that matters, with enough size and time to read it.

A holdout is a random slice of eligible customers who do not get the message. I assign it at random when people enter the flow, often 5 to 10 percent, and keep it fixed. Then I compare conversion or retention between the two groups over the same window. The difference is the lift the flow caused, not just the sales it happened to be near.
What must every marketing email include to comply with CAN-SPAM?
Your knowledge of the federal rules for commercial email.
Honest headers and subject, ad identification, a physical postal address, a clear opt-out honored promptly, and responsibility for vendors.

The From line and subject must not mislead, the email must be identifiable as an ad, and it needs a valid physical postal address. It needs a clear way to opt out, honored within 10 business days, with no fee and no extra hoops. If a vendor sends on our behalf, we are still responsible for what goes out.
Your emails suddenly start landing in spam at one big mailbox provider. What do you check?
How you diagnose a deliverability problem step by step.
Authentication, complaint rate, recent list or volume changes, and a plan to rebuild reputation with engaged users first.

I check that SPF, DKIM and DMARC, the records that prove we may send for our domain, still pass. Then the provider's sender data for complaints and reputation. Next, what changed: a send to old addresses, a new list source, a volume spike. I pause risky segments, mail only recently engaged people for a while, then add the rest back slowly.
How do you decide when to stop emailing an inactive subscriber?
Your judgement in balancing list size against sender reputation.
A defined sunset rule based on real engagement, a last re-permission attempt, then suppression from regular sends.

I set a sunset rule, for example no click, visit or purchase in 180 days. Those people get a short re-engagement series asking if they still want to hear from us. If they do not respond, I suppress them from regular sends. A smaller list that engages protects inbox placement for everyone, and the inactive part was not buying anyway.
Three teams want to email the same customers this week. How do you handle it?
How you manage frequency and priority across a shared audience.
A frequency cap, a clear priority order by value and urgency, and one shared calendar, with transactional messages outside the cap.

We keep a weekly cap per person, say three marketing messages, and a priority order: triggered messages tied to the customer's own action beat broad promos. I put all three requests on the shared calendar, show the overlap, and suggest merging two into one email. Receipts and password resets sit outside the cap because they are not marketing.
An abandoned-cart email went to 20,000 people who had already bought. What do you do?
How you own and recover from an automation error.
Stop the flow, find who got it and why, follow up only if needed, fix the root cause and add a safeguard.

I pause the flow first. Then I confirm who got it and why; often the purchase event arrived late or the exit rule checked the wrong field. A wrong reminder to a buyer is mostly confusing, so I send no apology unless support sees complaints. I fix the rule, add a purchase check right before send, and write up what happened for the team.
Your win-back campaign shows strong attributed revenue, but the holdout shows almost no lift. What do you tell leadership?
Whether you report incremental impact honestly when it hurts your own numbers.
Explains that attributed revenue includes people who would have returned anyway, and proposes tests to find real lift.

I would say most of those buyers were coming back anyway, and the email got credit for sales it did not cause. The discount may even cost margin on people who would have paid full price. I would show both numbers side by side, then test a smaller offer, different timing, or targeting only people unlikely to return on their own.
What is RFM segmentation, and how would you use it?
Whether you know a basic segmentation model and can turn it into action.
The three parts defined correctly, a simple scoring method, and a different treatment for each key segment.

RFM ranks customers on recency, how long since they last bought; frequency, how often they buy; and monetary, how much they spend. I score each from 1 to 5 by quintile. Top scorers get early access, not discounts. Customers with high frequency but falling recency are my at-risk group, and that is where a timely nudge pays most.
Explain SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and how they work together.
Your grasp of the email authentication that inbox providers now expect from bulk senders.
Each one defined correctly, with DMARC tying the checks to the visible From domain and setting a policy on failure.

SPF is a DNS record listing the servers allowed to send for our domain. DKIM adds a signature to each message that the receiver checks against a public key in our DNS, so it proves the mail was not altered. DMARC ties both to the visible From domain, tells receivers to do nothing, quarantine or reject on failure, and sends us reports.
The orders team wants to add a promo block to the order confirmation email. What do you think about?
Whether you know how CAN-SPAM separates transactional from commercial email.
The primary purpose test: subject line and opening must stay transactional, or the email becomes commercial with all its rules.

Under CAN-SPAM the primary purpose decides the rules. If the subject line and the top of the email are about the order, it stays transactional and a short promo lower down is fine. If the promo leads, it counts as commercial and needs an unsubscribe link and must respect opt-outs. So the receipt comes first and the offer stays small and below it.
When and how do you ask app users for push permission?
How you protect a permission you usually get only one clean chance at.
Not on first launch; a pre-prompt at a moment of value, because a declined system prompt is hard to reverse on iOS and Android 13+.

Not at first launch. On iOS the system prompt shows once, and if they decline they must go into Settings to turn it on. So I wait for a moment of value, like after they save a first item, and show our own screen first saying what we will send. Only a yes there triggers the system prompt. Android 13 and later also asks at runtime, so the same logic applies.
We want to add SMS to the abandoned-cart flow. What has to be in place first?
Whether you know the consent and timing rules for marketing texts in the US.
Express written consent with clear disclosure, working STOP opt-out, carrier registration and federal and state quiet hours.

Express written consent for marketing texts, collected with a clear disclosure of what we send, how often, that rates may apply, and that consent is not a condition of purchase. STOP must unsubscribe at once. I register our brand and use case with the carriers for business texting, and send only between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. recipient time, tighter where state law asks.
You have 8,000 lapsed customers and want to test two win-back offers. How do you plan the test?
How you size and run a test on a small segment without fooling yourself.
A metric and baseline set first, an honest view of the smallest lift the sample can detect, a fixed end date and no early stopping.

First I set the metric, purchase within 14 days, and check the baseline, say 3%. With 4,000 per arm I can only detect a large change, about 3% to 4.1%, so I tell the team up front. I fix the sample and end date before sending and do not stop early because one side looks ahead. If the gap is smaller, I report that the test did not show a winner.
Your win-back flow leads with 20% off, and repeat buyers now wait for the coupon. How do you fix it?
Your judgement on discount dependency and margin, not just conversion.
Lead without a discount, escalate offers only for non-responders, cap offers per customer and judge on margin, not redemptions.

I test a no-discount first step: a reminder of what is new or what they liked. Only people who do not respond get an offer at a later step. I cap how often one customer can receive a win-back offer, say once a year, and I judge the flow on margin and on repeat purchases made without a code, not on coupon redemptions.
A triggered browse-abandon flow sent three times its normal volume overnight. Walk me through what you do.
How you handle a live automation fault, from stopping harm to preventing a repeat.
Pause first, find the root cause in the trigger data, assess who was affected and add monitoring so it is caught fast next time.

First I pause the flow. Then I compare trigger events with the day before: often an app release renamed an event or fired it twice. I check the frequency cap and re-entry rule too.
