Once fixed, I find who got duplicates and watch complaints and unsubscribes on those sends. Then I add an alert on daily volume so we catch it within an hour next time.
Data science gives you a churn score for every subscriber. Who do you target with a save offer?
Whether you target the people a message can change, not just the riskiest ones.
Understands that highest risk is not highest lift; tests across score bands with a holdout and targets where the lift actually is.

Not simply the highest scores. Some of them will leave whatever we send, and the lowest scores will stay anyway. I want people whose behavior a message can change. So I run the offer with a random holdout in each score band, see where the real lift is, and target those bands. Often it is the middle, and we stop paying discounts to people who would stay.
The CFO asks what the whole CRM program is worth. How do you answer?
How you prove the value of a full program with evidence finance will trust.
A long-running global holdout compared on revenue and retention, scaled to the base, with the cost of holding out stated openly.

With a global holdout: a small random share of customers, say 5%, who get no marketing messages, only transactional ones. After six to twelve months I compare revenue and retention per customer between the two groups. The gap, times the customer base, is the program's value. I also show what the holdout costs us, so finance sees the trade-off.

litigation.heading: Litigation questions
qs: When does the duty to preserve evidence start, and what goes into a litigation hold?
Whether you know when preservation starts and how to make a hold work in practice.
Preservation starts when litigation is reasonably anticipated, not at service. The hold names custodians, data and dates, and stops auto-deletion.

The duty starts when we reasonably anticipate a suit. That can be a demand letter or a serious incident, well before a complaint arrives. My hold names the people, the data types and the date range. It tells IT to suspend auto-delete and asks for written acknowledgment. I refresh it every few months and make sure it covers departing employees' laptops and phones.
A new complaint lands on your desk. Walk me through your first two weeks.
How you run an early case assessment before costs start to build.
Deadline and hold first. Then facts, insurance, likely exposure and defense cost, ending in a recommendation the business can act on.

Day one, I calendar the response deadline and send the hold. Then I check for insurance and indemnity and give notice, since late notice can cost coverage. I talk to the key people, pull the contract or file, and pick counsel. By week two I send a short memo: what happened, a range of outcomes, a defense budget and whether to explore early settlement.
You are interviewing an employee about the facts behind a claim. What do you tell them before you start?
Whether you know who you represent and how to protect privilege in internal interviews.
An Upjohn warning: you represent the company, not them. The talk is privileged, but the company owns that privilege and may waive it.

I tell them I am a lawyer for the company, not for them personally. What we discuss is protected by the company's attorney-client privilege, but the company controls it and can choose to share it, including with the government. I ask them to keep it confidential. If they want their own lawyer, I pause. I note in my file that I gave the warning.
How do you keep an outside firm's bill in line with the value of the case?
How you manage outside counsel spending without hurting the defense.
A phase budget agreed up front, clear staffing rules, monthly invoice review, and early talks when work drifts from the plan.

I ask for a budget by phase: pleadings, discovery, motions, trial. Our billing guidelines set who staffs the case and what we won't pay for, like four lawyers at one deposition. I read every invoice monthly against the budget. If a phase runs 20% over, we talk before the next bill. Spend should track exposure; a $200,000 claim does not get a $500,000 defense.
What does Federal Rule of Evidence 408 protect in settlement talks, and where are its limits?
Your grasp of how settlement communications can and cannot be used later.
Offers and statements in compromise talks can't be used to prove or disprove the claim or its amount. They can be used for other purposes, and facts don't become secret.

It keeps offers, and statements made while negotiating, out of evidence when used to prove liability or the amount of the claim, or to impeach with a prior inconsistent statement. It does not shield a document just because we mention it in talks, and a court can admit statements for other purposes, like showing a witness's bias. State courts have their own versions, so I check them.
Finance asks whether to book a reserve for a pending case. How do you answer?
Whether you can turn a case assessment into the accounting rule finance applies.
Under ASC 450, accrue when a loss is probable and reasonably estimable; disclose when reasonably possible. The advice stays privileged and is updated as the case moves.

I give my view on likelihood and range, and finance applies ASC 450. If a loss is probable and we can estimate it, they accrue it; if we only have a range with no best number, they book the low end. If a loss is reasonably possible, it goes into the disclosures. I put my analysis in a privileged memo and revisit it after each major ruling or mediation.
When would you make a Rule 68 offer of judgment in federal court?
Whether you know a cost-shifting tool and when it actually adds pressure.
It's a defense tool: if the plaintiff rejects it and does no better at judgment, they pay costs after the offer. It bites most where a statute makes fees part of costs.

I use it when a plaintiff is overvaluing the case. It must be served at least 14 days before trial. If they reject it and the judgment is not more favorable, they pay the costs incurred after the offer. Ordinary costs are small, so it matters most under statutes that treat attorney fees as costs. I word the offer carefully on fees and costs so we don't pay more than I meant.
At mediation, the plaintiff's last number is just above your settlement authority. What do you do?
Your judgment on settlement authority, timing and when to walk away.
Not exceeding authority, but having the decision-maker reachable, a reasoned case for more, and willingness to end the day without a deal.

I never go past my authority. Before the session I make sure the person who can raise it is reachable by phone. I call with numbers: our defense cost to trial, the odds and range at verdict, and what the gap buys us. If they approve, we close today. If not, I ask the mediator for a mediator's proposal or keep talks open; the gap often closes within a week.
After the hold went out, you learn a manager deleted emails about the dispute. What do you do?
How you handle a spoliation problem honestly while limiting the damage.
Stop further loss, try to restore from other sources, involve outside counsel, and be candid. Hiding it is the real risk under Rule 37(e).

First I make sure it stops: I talk to the manager and have IT lock the account. Then we try to recover the emails from the server, backups and recipients' inboxes. If they're fully restored, the harm is small. If not, outside counsel and I decide how to disclose it. Under Rule 37(e), the harshest sanctions need intent to deprive, so a quick, honest fix matters.
You discover a privileged memo went out in a document production. What do you do?
How you handle a privilege mistake fast enough to keep the protection.
A prompt clawback notice under the protective order or Rule 26(b)(5)(B), fixing the review gap, and relying on FRE 502 or a 502(d) order.

Counsel sends a clawback notice that day under our protective order and Rule 26(b)(5)(B). The other side must return, sequester or destroy it and can't use it until the claim is resolved. Under Rule 502(b), we keep privilege if the disclosure was inadvertent, our review was reasonable and we acted fast. Then I find why review missed it. I also ask for a 502(d) order early.
What limits the scope of discovery in federal court today, and how do you use that in a dispute with the other side?
Whether you know the proportionality standard and can use it in practice.
Rule 26(b)(1): discovery must be relevant to a claim or defense and proportional to the needs of the case, argued with real cost and burden figures.

Rule 26(b)(1) allows discovery that is relevant to a claim or defense and proportional to the needs of the case. The factors include the amount in controversy, who has access to the information, and whether the burden outweighs the benefit. I argue it with numbers, such as custodians, data volume and review cost. I offer a phased plan instead of a flat no.
We are sued in state court by a plaintiff from another state. What do you weigh in deciding whether to remove, and how fast must you move?
Your grasp of removal rules and forum strategy.
Knows the 30-day deadline, complete diversity, the amount in controversy and the forum-defendant rule, then weighs the court itself, not just the label.

The notice of removal is due within 30 days after we are served, so the decision is fast. For diversity, I check three things: complete diversity, an amount in controversy over $75,000, and the forum-defendant rule. That rule means we cannot remove on diversity if we are a citizen of the state where we were sued. Then I weigh the judges, the jury pool and federal procedure.
When would you advise against filing a motion to dismiss, even if it has a fair chance of winning?
Whether you weigh motion practice against cost and what it teaches the other side.
Sees that a first Rule 12(b)(6) win often comes with leave to amend, so the motion may only educate the plaintiff and add cost.

After a first dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6), courts usually give leave to amend. If the flaw is easy to fix, the motion just teaches the plaintiff to plead a better complaint, and we pay for two rounds. I file when the motion can end a claim for good, such as a time bar or a claim the law does not recognize, or when it narrows discovery in a way that matters.
We received a Rule 30(b)(6) notice with 40 topics. How do you handle it and prepare the witness?
Your practical command of corporate depositions.
Confers on the topics as the rule requires, and prepares each designee on what the company knows, not only on what the witness personally knows.

First I confer with the other side, as the rule now requires, to narrow vague or overlapping topics, and I put objections in writing. I may split the topics among designees. Each one must be prepared on what is reasonably available to the company, not just on personal knowledge. An unprepared designee can limit what we may prove later or lead to sanctions.
A new lawsuit may be covered by one of our insurance policies. What do you do, and what can go wrong?
Whether you protect insurance coverage from day one.
Gives prompt notice under every policy that might respond, reads any reservation of rights, and respects the consent-to-settle terms.

I send notice right away under every policy that might respond, current and older ones, because late notice can cost us coverage. If the carrier defends under a reservation of rights, I read exactly what it reserves. I check whether state law lets us pick independent counsel. And I remember that policies usually bar settling without the insurer's consent.
Walk me through how you put a settlement value on a case early on.
How you turn a case into numbers the business can decide on.
Probability of each outcome times its cost, plus defense fees and business effects, updated as the case develops.

I map the main outcomes with outside counsel: we win on a motion, or we lose at trial with low or high damages. I give each a rough probability, and probability times amount gives an expected loss. I add what it costs to get there, in fees and in employee time, plus any effect on other cases or customers. I update the numbers after key rulings and depositions.
We have agreed on a number. What other terms in the settlement agreement do you care about?
Whether you know a settlement is more than the payment.
Release scope and parties, no admission, dismissal with prejudice, payment timing, and confidentiality and waiver terms the law will actually enforce.

I want a release that covers all related claims, signed by everyone who could bring them. I want no admission of liability, dismissal with prejudice, and payment due only after signed papers. I check confidentiality terms against legal limits, such as employees' right to talk to government agencies. For age claims, the release must give the federal review and revocation periods.
Our consumer contracts have an arbitration clause with a class waiver. Thousands of individual arbitration demands arrive at once. How do you respond?
How you handle mass arbitration and the risk built into your own contract terms.
Knows class waivers are generally enforceable, sees that company-paid fees create pressure, and pairs a near-term plan with a redrafted clause.

Class waivers are generally enforceable under the Federal Arbitration Act, but here the cost runs our way: in consumer cases the company usually pays most of the fees, case by case. I check that each claimant is a real customer bound by the clause. I use the provider's mass-filing procedures and model a global settlement against the fees. Then we redraft the clause, for example with batching terms.
After serving your expert's report, you learn one of its damage calculations is wrong. What do you do?
Your candor and how you fix a mistake under the disclosure rules.
Corrects it promptly with a supplemental report under Rule 26(e), ideally before the expert's deposition, instead of waiting to be caught.

Rule 26(e) requires us to supplement an expert report that turns out to be incorrect, and the duty runs at least until pretrial disclosures are due. I have the expert confirm the error and check what else it touches. Then I serve a corrected report quickly, ideally before the deposition. Fixing it ourselves costs a little credibility; having it found on cross costs far more.
A putative class action is filed against us. What are the class certification requirements, and where do you usually focus the defense?
Your depth on class actions, where the certification ruling often decides the case.
Names the Rule 23(a) and 23(b)(3) requirements and builds discovery and experts to show that individual issues predominate.

Under Rule 23(a), the plaintiff must show numerosity, commonality, typicality and adequacy. For a damages class under 23(b)(3), common questions must also predominate, and a class action must be superior. I usually fight on predominance: if reliance, injury or damages vary from person to person, one class trial cannot answer them. I build our discovery and expert work to show that variation.

llm-researcher.heading: LLM researcher questions
qs: In plain words, what does self-attention do inside a transformer?
Whether you understand the core building block of the models you train.
Each token weighs other tokens by relevance, using queries, keys and values, and the cost grows with the square of the sequence length.

Each token asks a question, its query, and compares it with a key from every token it is allowed to see. The scores become weights, and the token takes a weighted mix of their values. That is how "it" can pull meaning from the noun it refers to. The catch is cost: comparing every pair grows with the square of the sequence length.
Why does the tokenizer matter, and what can go wrong with it?
Your grasp of a design choice that is made early and is hard to change later.
Explains subword methods like byte-pair encoding and their real effects: sequence length, cost per language, and quirks with numbers and code.

Most models use subword tokens built by merging frequent byte pairs. The tokenizer decides how many tokens a text costs, so a language it saw little of gets split into many pieces: slower, pricier, and less fits in the context. Odd number splits can hurt arithmetic. Changing it after training means retraining the embeddings at least.
Walk me through the stages that turn a raw pretrained model into a chat assistant.
Whether you know what each training stage adds and what it cannot fix.
Pretraining gives knowledge, supervised fine-tuning gives the format, preference tuning shapes behavior; later stages rarely add new knowledge.

Pretraining on a large corpus teaches next-token prediction and most of what the model knows. Supervised fine-tuning on prompt and answer pairs teaches it to follow instructions. Preference tuning, such as reinforcement learning from human feedback, uses answers ranked by people to push it toward the better ones. Missing facts are a pretraining problem.
You have a fixed compute budget for pretraining. How do you decide the model size and the number of training tokens?
Whether you can use scaling laws to plan a run instead of guessing.
Fits loss on small runs, picks the compute-optimal size, then adjusts for serving cost, which often favors a smaller model trained longer.

Training compute is roughly six times parameters times tokens, so size and data trade against each other. I would train a ladder of small models, fit how loss falls with size and data, and read off the compute-optimal point. If the model will serve heavy traffic, a smaller model trained on more tokens is cheaper to run for nearly the same quality.
How do you pick hyperparameters like the learning rate for a run too expensive to repeat?
How you get reliable settings without wasting the compute of a full run.
Sweeps on small proxy models, a parametrization that lets settings transfer across sizes, warmup and decay, and a short pilot at full size.

I sweep the learning rate on small proxy models and check how the best value shifts as width grows. A parametrization like muP is built so the best rate stays nearly the same across widths, which makes the transfer safer. I use warmup and a decay schedule, then run the full-size model briefly to check loss and gradient norms before committing.
Halfway through a large pretraining run, the loss spikes and does not come back down. What do you do?
How you diagnose a costly training failure under pressure.
Pauses the run, rolls back to a checkpoint, looks at data, learning rate and numeric causes, and changes one thing at a time.

First I pause the run so it stops burning compute. I check the batches just before the spike for corrupt or repeated data, and look at gradient norms and any overflow in the logs. Then I restart from a checkpoint before the spike, usually skipping those batches or lowering the learning rate a little. I change one thing so I know what fixed it.
How do you make sure a benchmark score is not inflated because test questions leaked into the training data?
Whether you protect the honesty of your evaluation numbers.
Searches training data for overlap with test items, compares clean and suspect subsets, and keeps fresh or reworded held-out sets.

I search the training corpus for long n-gram overlaps with each test item, meaning matching runs of words, and split the benchmark into clean and suspect parts. If the model does much better on the suspect part, the headline number is inflated. I also keep a private test set written after the data cutoff and try reworded questions to see if the score holds.
After preference tuning, the model's answers keep getting longer and the reward keeps rising. What is going on?
Whether you can spot a model gaming its reward instead of getting better.
Names reward hacking, checks whether the reward model favors length, and fixes it with length control, a KL penalty and human checks.

Most likely the reward model learned that longer looks better, and the model is exploiting that rather than improving. I would plot reward against length and have people compare answers of similar length. Fixes: a length penalty, a stronger KL penalty that keeps the model close to its starting point, and reward data where the shorter answer wins.
A new checkpoint beats the old one on every benchmark, but users in a blind test prefer the old one. What do you do?
Your judgement when offline metrics and real user preference disagree.
Trusts the user signal, reads real outputs to find the cause, and extends the evaluation suite so it measures what users care about.

I trust the blind test more, since benchmarks are only a proxy. I read a sample of the lost comparisons by hand and tag the reasons: tone, refusals, verbosity, formatting. Often the new model got stiffer or refuses more. I would not ship it, and I would add evals for what we found so the next checkpoint is tested for it.
Tell me about a result you believed that turned out not to hold. What changed in how you work?
Whether you are honest about errors and run experiments that can be trusted.
A specific story, the real cause such as seed noise or a bug, and a lasting habit like several seeds or rerunning baselines.

I once reported that a data filter raised a small model's reasoning score by two points. A teammate reran it with three more seeds and the gap vanished: the spread between seeds alone was about two points. Since then I run at least three seeds for small ablations, report the spread, and rerun the baseline in the same code instead of copying old numbers.
What is the KV cache, and why does it limit long-context serving?
Whether you understand what drives inference memory and cost.
Keys and values stored per layer for past tokens, memory that grows with context length and batch size, and ways to shrink it such as grouped-query attention.

When the model generates a token, it reuses the keys and values it already computed for earlier tokens instead of recomputing them. That store sits in GPU memory for every layer and grows with context length times batch size. At long context it, not the weights, often caps how many users fit on a GPU. Grouped-query attention shares key and value heads across query heads to cut it.
Why do most large runs train in bf16 rather than fp16?
Your grasp of numeric precision and its effect on training stability.
bf16 keeps the exponent range of fp32 with fewer mantissa bits, so overflow and underflow are rare and loss scaling is usually not needed.

bf16 uses the same 8 exponent bits as fp32, so it covers the same range of magnitudes; it just keeps less precision. fp16 has a much narrower range, so small gradients underflow to zero unless you use loss scaling. I still keep master weights and optimizer states in fp32 and watch softmax and norms, where low precision bites first.
Roughly how much GPU memory does it take to train a 7-billion-parameter model with Adam, and how do you make it fit?
Whether you can estimate training memory and know the tools to split it.
About 16 bytes per parameter for weights, gradients and Adam states in mixed precision, plus activations; then sharding, parallelism and activation checkpointing.

With mixed precision and Adam, a common estimate is 16 bytes per parameter: bf16 weights and gradients, plus fp32 master weights and two Adam moments. That is about 112 GB before activations, too much for one GPU. I shard states across GPUs with ZeRO or FSDP, add tensor or pipeline parallelism if needed, and use activation checkpointing to trade compute for memory.
How does DPO differ from RLHF with PPO, and when would you pick each?
Your depth on preference-tuning methods beyond the names.
DPO trains directly on preference pairs with no separate reward model or sampling loop; PPO costs more but learns from fresh samples scored by a reward model.

DPO turns preference pairs into a loss: push up the chosen answer over the rejected one, relative to a frozen reference model. It needs no reward model and no sampling, so it is cheap and stable. PPO scores fresh samples with a reward model: costlier, but it learns from the model's current outputs. I start with DPO and go online when it stalls.
Why do you deduplicate pretraining data, and how do you do it at web scale?
Whether you know how data quality shapes a pretrained model.
Duplicates waste compute, raise memorization and skew the mix; exact hashing plus near-duplicate detection such as MinHash with locality-sensitive hashing.

Repeated documents waste tokens, make the model more likely to memorize and regurgitate text, and quietly overweight whatever got copied most. I remove exact duplicates with hashes, then near duplicates with MinHash and locality-sensitive hashing over word n-grams, so I never compare all pairs. I also read samples by hand, because boilerplate like cookie banners slips through.
Checkpoint B scores one point higher than checkpoint A on a 500-question benchmark. Is B better?
How you reason about noise in evaluation numbers.
Not on that alone: the standard error at that size is around two points, so you need a paired comparison, more evals or repeated runs.

Not proven. With 500 questions and accuracy near 70%, the standard error is about two points, so one point is inside the noise. I would compare the two question by question, since a paired test is more sensitive, check variance across seeds and sampling settings, and look at other evals. If the decision matters, I want a bigger or more targeted test.
You use a strong model as a judge to compare answers. What biases do you guard against?
Whether you can use LLM-as-judge evaluation without fooling yourself.
Position, length and self-preference bias, handled by swapping order, controlling for length and checking agreement with human labels.

Judges tend to favor one slot, longer answers, and answers in their own style. I run each pair in both orders and count a win only if it holds both ways, report length next to win rates, and avoid using the same model family as judge and contestant. Before I trust it, I check its agreement with a few hundred human-labeled pairs.
A fine-tuned model looked great in your evals but gives odd, rambling answers once deployed. Where do you look first?
How you debug a gap between training and serving.
The prompt format: chat template, special tokens, system prompt and stop tokens, compared token by token between training and serving.

I first suspect the prompt format. I dump the exact token IDs the server sends and compare them with a training example: chat template, role markers, special tokens. If the end-of-turn token is not set as a stop token, the model just keeps going. Then I check sampling settings like temperature, and that the right checkpoint and tokenizer are loaded.
After fine-tuning on a large medical dataset, the model's general reasoning and instruction following got worse. How do you fix it?
Whether you can handle forgetting when adapting a model to a domain.
Measure it on held-out general evals, then mix general data back in, lower the learning rate or train fewer steps, or use adapters like LoRA.

That is catastrophic forgetting: the update pulled weights away from what general skills relied on. I track general evals during training, not just at the end. Then I mix general and instruction data back in, lower the learning rate, and stop earlier. Training a LoRA adapter instead of all weights also limits drift, though it may learn the domain less fully.
A data-mix change helps clearly at 1B parameters. How do you decide whether to bet a 70B run on it?
Your judgement on whether small-scale results transfer to large scale.
Test at several scales to see if the gain holds or shrinks, check downstream evals and not just loss, and size the bet to its cost.

One scale is not a trend. I run the change at three or four sizes with matched, compute-optimal settings and plot the gain against compute. If it holds or grows, good sign; if it shrinks with scale, a bigger model may learn it anyway. I check downstream evals, not only loss, and if the evidence is mixed I test it in a mid-size run first.

localization.heading: Localization and translation questions
qs: What is the difference between internationalization and localization?
Whether you know where engineering work ends and language work begins.
Internationalization makes the product ready for any locale; localization adapts it to one market. A clear example of each is a plus.

Internationalization is the engineering groundwork: strings moved out of the code, Unicode everywhere, dates and currency formatted by locale, layouts that can grow. Localization is the work done per market: translating, adapting images, units and examples. If internationalization is skipped, every new language turns into a code change.
What is a fuzzy match in a translation memory, and how do you treat one?
Your grasp of the core tool of the trade and how carefully you reuse past work.
A similar but not identical segment with a percentage score, always checked for what changed, never accepted blindly.

A fuzzy match is a stored segment that is similar to the new source text but not identical, say 85 percent. I never accept it as is. I compare the two sources, find what changed, often a number, a negation or a product name, and fix the target. Even a 100 percent match gets a look for context, since the same English can need a different translation.
A developer sends you "You have", "new messages" and "in your inbox" as three separate strings to translate. What do you say?
Whether you spot string concatenation and fix it at the source.
Ask for one full string with a named placeholder, because word order and plural forms differ by language.

I ask for one string, like "You have {count} new messages in your inbox", with a named placeholder and a plural rule. In pieces, a translator cannot move the number where Japanese or Turkish needs it, and Russian changes the noun ending depending on the number. Fixing the code once is cheaper than a workaround in every language.
Why is a "one item, many items" setup not enough for plurals?
Your knowledge of how plural rules differ across languages.
Knows languages have different numbers of plural forms, cites the CLDR rules, and makes sure the code uses a plural-aware format.

English has two forms, but many languages have more. The Unicode CLDR rules give Polish and Russian separate forms for one, few and many, and Arabic has six categories, including zero and two. Japanese has only one. So I make sure the code uses a plural-aware format, such as ICU MessageFormat, and each language gets exactly the forms its rules call for.
What is pseudo-localization, and when do you run it?
Whether you test a product for localization problems before paying for translation.
Fake translated text with accents, padding and brackets, run early to catch hardcoded strings, truncation and encoding bugs.

Pseudo-localization swaps the English for fake text like [Śëţţîñĝš ~~~~]: accented letters, extra length and brackets. I run it on builds before translation starts. Plain English left on screen means text written in the code, not the string file. A missing bracket means truncation. Broken accents mean an encoding bug. All caught before any translation is paid for.
In German, the label on a key button is cut off. How do you fix it?
How you solve text expansion without hurting the translation or the design.
Looks for a shorter correct term with the linguist first, then pushes for a layout that can grow, instead of truncating.

First I look at the screen with the German linguist: is there a shorter term users would know? Often there is. If not, I ask design to let the button widen or wrap, since German often runs about a third longer than English and short labels can double. I also log it as a design issue, so new screens get room built in from the start.
We are launching in Arabic. What changes beyond the translated text?
Your experience with right-to-left languages and what goes into adapting a layout for them.
Mirrored layout with known exceptions, mixed-direction text handled, font support checked, and real screens tested by a native speaker.

The whole layout runs right to left: navigation, alignment, progress bars and back arrows flip. Some things must not flip, like logos, phone numbers and code. Mixed text, such as an English brand name inside an Arabic sentence, needs careful testing. I check the font joins Arabic letters correctly, and a native speaker tests real screens, not just files.
An in-country reviewer keeps changing approved glossary terms. How do you handle it?
Your judgement when quality feedback conflicts with agreed terminology.
Separates real errors from preference, settles terms once with the market in the glossary, and keeps translator and reviewer aligned.

I sort the changes first: real errors get fixed, preference edits get noted. Then I meet the reviewer with the translator and the glossary. If the market has a good reason, say users really call it something else, we update the termbase and old content on a plan. If not, the approved term stays, and I explain why so the edits stop.
A release went out where the French app shows "{0}" instead of the user's name. What do you do?
How you handle a shipped bug and stop it from happening again.
Fixes it fast, checks every language for the same fault, and adds an automatic placeholder check to the workflow.

I find the string and fix it. Often the placeholder was altered, like {0} turned into { 0 }. I get a hotfix or remote string update out, then search all languages for the same fault. To stop it coming back, I turn on the placeholder check in our translation tool and add a build test that fails when placeholders differ from the source.
Marketing wants machine translation for everything to cut costs. How do you decide where it fits?
Your judgement in matching the translation method to the risk and value of the content.
Decides by content type and risk, explains post-editing and transcreation, and tests on a sample before promising savings.

I sort content by risk and visibility. Help articles can go through machine translation with post-editing, where a linguist corrects the output. Taglines need transcreation, a rewrite for the market. Legal and safety text gets full human translation and review. I pilot first: measure editing time and quality on a sample before promising savings.
What do the tags pt-BR, es-419 and zh-Hant tell you, and why does it matter which one we ship?
Whether you know how locales are named and why a language alone is not enough.
Language, region and script parts explained correctly, with a real reason the choice changes the product.

They are BCP 47 language tags. pt-BR is Portuguese as used in Brazil, es-419 is Spanish for Latin America, and zh-Hant is Chinese in Traditional characters. Brazilian and European Portuguese differ in vocabulary and forms of address, so the wrong one feels foreign. The tag also drives date, number and currency formats, so it must match the market we target.
How do you decide between formal and informal address, like du or Sie in German, and where do you record the decision?
How you turn tone decisions into rules a whole team can follow.
A choice based on brand, audience and market norms, written into the style guide with examples and checked the same way everywhere.

I look at the brand voice, the audience and what users in that market expect. A consumer app for young people in Germany often uses du; banking or business software usually keeps Sie. Once we pick, it goes into the style guide with example sentences, and the QA checklist flags any mix. Switching later means touching every string, so I settle it before the first batch.
What fields do you put in a termbase entry, and how do you handle terms we must never use?
Your grasp of terminology management beyond a two-column word list.
Definition, context, part of speech, status, and approved and forbidden variants per language, kept in a shared format that tools can check.

Each entry has the source term, a short definition, an example sentence, part of speech, the product area and a status such as approved or deprecated. Per language I add the approved term and any forbidden variants, so the automatic QA check can flag them. I keep it in our translation tool and export it as TBX, the standard exchange format, so every vendor loads the same list.
A developer formats dates and prices by hand with string templates. Why is that a problem, and what do you suggest?
Whether you know locale formats come from shared locale data, not from translators.
Concrete examples of format differences and a fix that uses locale-aware formatting APIs backed by CLDR data, not translated patterns.

Formats differ more than people think. 03/04/2025 is March 4 in the US and 3 April in the UK, and Germany writes 1.234,56 where the US writes 1,234.56. Hand-built templates get these wrong or make translators edit code. I ask the team to use the platform's locale-aware formatters, which draw on CLDR data, and pass the raw date or number into the string.
In Polish and Russian, 'Anna liked your photo' needs a different verb ending than 'Jan liked your photo'. How do you build that string?
Whether you can handle grammatical gender with message formats instead of code hacks.
A select on a gender value, for example in ICU MessageFormat, a neutral fallback when gender is unknown, and no word endings glued on in code.

If the product knows the user's grammatical gender, I pass it as a variable and use an ICU MessageFormat select: one branch for female, one for male, and the required 'other' branch. Translators fill in each branch. When gender is unknown, 'other' uses neutral wording, such as a noun phrase instead of a past-tense verb. I never let code add endings to words.
We plan one Chinese version to serve both mainland China and Taiwan. What do you advise?
How you weigh real market differences against cost when scoping a launch.
Knowing that converting the script is not localizing: vocabulary and conventions differ, so Taiwan needs its own version reviewed by a local linguist.

Mainland China uses Simplified characters and Taiwan uses Traditional, so one file cannot serve both. Automatic conversion is not enough: many everyday tech words differ, such as the terms for software and network. I would budget zh-Hans and zh-Hant-TW as separate targets. We can start Taiwan from a converted base, but only with a full review by a Taiwan linguist.
A vendor's batch fails your quality review, and they dispute most of the errors. How do you settle it?
How you run linguistic quality review so scores are fair and hold up when challenged.
An error typology and severity scale agreed up front, item-by-item review against the style guide and termbase, and preferences not counted as errors.

First I check the review itself. We score with an MQM-style model: error category, severity and a pass threshold agreed in the contract. I go through the disputed items one by one against the source, the style guide and the termbase. Edits with no rule behind them are preferences and come off the score. Real errors stay. If the reviewer logged many preferences, that is feedback for them too.
Right after our Turkish launch, some users cannot log in, and all of them have the letter i in their email. What do you suspect?
Whether you know the classic locale bugs that live in code, not in the translation.
Spotting the Turkish dotted and dotless i case-mapping issue and asking for locale-independent case handling on identifiers.

The Turkish i. Turkish has a dotted i and a dotless ı, so under a Turkish locale, 'i' uppercases to 'İ' and 'I' lowercases to 'ı'. If the code changes the case of emails using the device or server locale, the strings stop matching. Identifiers like emails and keys need locale-independent case conversion. I would also add Turkish to our test matrix for good.
Two days before release, product rewrites 40 source strings that are already translated into 12 languages. How do you handle it?
How you protect both quality and the date when the source changes after translation.
Triage by meaning and visibility, a rush batch for what matters, a clear trade-off for the rest, and a process fix afterward.

I first split real meaning changes from polish. Polish can wait for the next release, since the old translation still says the right thing. Meaning changes on visible screens go out as a rush batch with screenshots to our regular linguists, with review time planned. Anything we cannot cover safely, I take to the product owner as a clear trade-off. Then we agree on a string freeze date.
We have budget for three new languages next year. How would you choose them?
Whether you can tie localization to business results, the core of a senior role.
Data on traffic, revenue, sign-ups and support, weighed against cost, legal needs and readiness, with metrics to judge results after launch.

I start with data: traffic and sign-ups by country, revenue we already earn from non-English users, support tickets in other languages and sales requests. Then cost and risk: word count, language complexity, local-language legal rules, and whether we can support users there. I pick the top three by expected return and set metrics, like conversion per locale, to review after six months.

logistics-coordinator.heading: Logistics coordinator questions
qs: When do you book a full truckload instead of LTL?
Whether you know the two main ways to ship freight by truck and what drives the choice.
Explains that LTL shares a trailer and goes through terminals, while FTL is dedicated, and compares cost, transit time and handling risk.

LTL means our pallets share a trailer with other shippers' freight. It is cheaper for a few pallets, but it moves through terminals, which adds handling and days. Full truckload is a dedicated trailer that goes door to door. I look at pallet count, weight, fragility and urgency. On larger loads I quote both, plus volume LTL, and pick the best total cost.
What goes on a bill of lading, and why does it matter if it is wrong?
Your knowledge of the core shipping document.
Knows the BOL is the carrier's receipt and the contract for the move, and links errors to rebills, wrong equipment or claim problems.

The bill of lading is the carrier's receipt for the freight and the contract for the move. It lists shipper, consignee, piece count, weight, freight class, special services like liftgate, and who pays. If the weight or class is wrong, the carrier can reweigh or reclass and rebill us. If a service is missing, the driver may show up without the right equipment.
A carrier invoice comes in 30% higher than the quote. What do you do?
How you audit freight bills and handle extra charges.
Checks line by line for reweigh, reclass and accessorials, asks for proof, disputes with documents, and fixes the root cause if the error was ours.

I compare the invoice line by line with the quote. Usually it is a reweigh or reclass, or an extra charge like liftgate, residential delivery or driver detention. I ask the carrier for the inspection certificate or the detention time stamps. If our BOL was right, I dispute with the paperwork. If our data was wrong, I fix the item record so it does not happen again.
A customer calls: the pallet arrived with crushed cartons. Walk me through what happens next.
Whether you know how to protect a freight damage claim.
Notes damage specifically on the delivery receipt, keeps photos and goods, notifies the carrier, and files a documented claim in writing inside the deadline.

First I ask whether the damage was written on the delivery receipt, and how. It should say exactly what was wrong, like "2 cartons crushed," not just "subject to inspection." I ask for photos and tell them to keep the goods and packaging. Then I file a written claim with the BOL, signed delivery receipt, invoice and photos, well within the deadline.
A shipment has shown no tracking update for a day, and it is due at the customer tomorrow morning. What do you do?
How you handle a shipment that may be late before it becomes a problem.
Gets a real location from dispatch, warns the customer early with options, and records the cause for carrier performance.

I call the carrier's dispatch and ask where the driver actually is, not what the portal says. If it will miss, I tell the customer today with a new ETA and their options, such as expediting or sending a partial from stock. Waiting until the delivery window passes is the worst choice. I also log the cause so it shows up when we review that carrier.
How do you check a carrier you have never used before you give it a load?
Whether you can spot fraud and risk when you onboard a carrier.
Checks FMCSA authority and safety record, gets insurance proof straight from the agent, and knows the warning signs of double brokering.

I look up the USDOT and MC numbers in the FMCSA database. I check that the operating authority is active, how long it has had it, and its safety record. I get the insurance certificate sent directly from the insurance agent. A brand-new authority, contact details that don't match the record, or a rate far below market make me slow down. That is how double brokering and cargo theft usually start.
One overseas supplier quotes EXW, another quotes FOB Shanghai. What is the difference for us?
Your understanding of Incoterms and who carries cost and risk.
Knows EXW puts nearly all cost and risk on the buyer from the seller's door, while under FOB risk passes when goods are on board the vessel.

Under EXW, the supplier only makes the goods available at its own site. We arrange and pay for pickup, export clearance and everything after that, and the risk is ours from that point. Under FOB Shanghai, the supplier clears export and loads the goods onto the vessel we booked, and risk passes to us once they are on board. So the two prices are not directly comparable.
A carrier is 15% cheaper than our regular one but has a weaker on-time record. How do you decide?
Your judgement on total cost versus the freight rate.
Weighs late fees, customer penalties and service risk against the rate, and matches the carrier to the lane or customer, not just the price.

The lowest rate is not always the lowest cost. If a carrier misses appointments, we pay for redeliveries, overtime at the dock and sometimes customer fines. I compare on-time performance, claims and how often they accept our loads. I might give the cheaper carrier flexible freight and keep the reliable one for customers with tight delivery windows.
Sales asks you to ship a pallet of aerosol cans tomorrow, mixed in with a normal order. What do you do?
Whether you recognize hazardous materials and know who may prepare the paperwork.
Treats aerosols as possible hazmat, checks the SDS, and makes sure only a person with current DOT hazmat training prepares the shipment.

Aerosols are usually regulated as hazardous materials, though some may ship under limited quantity rules. I would not just add them to a normal order. I check the safety data sheet, where section 14 gives transport information, and confirm how it ships. Only someone with current DOT hazmat training can prepare the papers and markings. If no one trained is available, the pallet waits and I tell sales why.
Tell me about a shipping mistake you made and what you changed afterward.
How you own an error and stop it from happening again.
Names a real mistake, says what it cost, shows the quick fix, and describes a process change rather than just promising to be careful.

I once booked an LTL delivery to a grocery distribution center without making an appointment. The driver was turned away, and we paid a redelivery fee and a day of storage. I called the receiver, got the next slot and told our customer the new date. Afterward I added an "appointment required" field to our booking sheet, and I now check receiving rules for every new consignee.
What decides the freight class of an LTL shipment, and what happens if we get it wrong?
Whether you understand how LTL pricing is built.
Names density, stowability, handling and liability, and knows the carrier can inspect, reclass and rebill, often with a fee.

Class comes from the NMFC, based on density, stowability, handling and liability. For most items density matters most, so I need accurate weight and dimensions. If we declare too low a class, the carrier can inspect, reclass and rebill us, often with a fee. I measure the pallet and keep each item's NMFC number on file.
Our contract rates did not change, but our freight spend per load went up this month. What would you look at?
How you read a freight bill beyond the base rate.
Checks the fuel surcharge tied to the weekly diesel index first, then accessorials, reweighs and the mix of loads.

First the fuel surcharge. Most carriers tie it to the weekly national diesel price the government publishes, so it moves even when the base rate is fixed. Then I sort the accessorials: liftgates, detention, reweigh and reclass charges. Last I check the mix, for example more short or rush loads. That shows which part we can actually control.
A customer wants a pallet delivered to a small shop with no loading dock. What do you set up before booking?
Whether you plan for delivery conditions before they turn into extra charges.
Asks about the site, books liftgate and any limited-access or appointment service up front, and puts a contact on the paperwork.

I ask the customer about the site: is there a dock or forklift, any narrow street or height limit, and who receives. With no dock, I book a liftgate delivery and, if needed, an appointment or limited access. I put a contact name and phone on the bill of lading. Added later, those services usually cost more, and the driver may leave without delivering.
You are booking a truckload of frozen food. What instructions do you give the carrier and the warehouse?
Your knowledge of temperature-controlled shipping.
Set point in Fahrenheit, continuous mode, a pre-cooled trailer, product loaded already at temperature, and records kept.

I put the set point in Fahrenheit, for example 0 °F, and continuous mode on the rate confirmation and the bill of lading. The trailer must be pre-cooled, and the product must already be frozen: a reefer holds temperature, it does not pull it down. The warehouse records product temperature at loading, and I ask for the unit's temperature download if there is a claim.
A customer wants a 900-mile load picked up at 4 p.m. and delivered by 8 a.m. the next day. Can one driver do it?
Whether you know driver hours-of-service rules and plan transit time around them.
No: a solo driver may drive at most 11 hours within a 14-hour window after 10 hours off, so this needs a team or a new schedule.

No. A solo property-carrying driver can drive at most 11 hours, within a 14-hour window, after 10 hours off duty. 900 miles is about 16 to 18 hours of driving. So I either book a team, which costs more, or offer the realistic options: an earlier pickup or delivery a day later. I would not push a carrier to promise it.
A customer wants full coverage on a $40,000 LTL shipment of electronics. What do you tell them?
Whether you understand carrier liability limits and how to cover high-value freight.
LTL carriers usually cap liability per pound in their tariff, so you offer excess declared value or third-party cargo insurance.

Carrier liability in LTL is usually capped per pound in the carrier's tariff, and electronics are light for their value, so a total loss might pay back only part of it. I check the limit for that carrier, then quote two options: declaring excess value with the carrier for a fee, or a third-party cargo insurance policy. The customer chooses, in writing, before pickup.
An import container sits at the port because the customs release is late. What is the difference between demurrage and detention, and what do you do?
Your grasp of container charges and how fast they add up.
Demurrage is for the box staying in the terminal past free time; detention is for keeping it outside too long. Then acts on the release and dates.

Demurrage is charged while the full container stays at the terminal after the free days. Detention, or per diem, is charged when we keep the carrier's container outside the terminal too long before returning it empty. I call the customs broker to find what holds the entry, check the last free day, and book a trucker and dock slot so we pull it and return it fast.
The driver at your dock is from a different company than the carrier you booked. What do you do?
Whether you can spot possible double brokering or cargo theft and stop it.
Does not load until the booked carrier confirms, using contact details from its official record, not from the driver's paperwork.

I hold the load. I call the carrier we booked, using the phone number from its FMCSA registration record, not the one on the paperwork or email. If they say they gave the load to someone else, that is double brokering and against our agreement. If they never heard of it, the driver may be a thief. Either way, nothing leaves until I have confirmation in writing.
In peak season your primary carrier starts rejecting a third of the loads you tender. How do you keep freight moving?
How you manage capacity and cost when the market turns tight.
Moves down the routing guide, uses spot with an agreed budget, finds out why the carrier rejects, and plans earlier for next peak.

Short term, I go down the routing guide to our backup carriers and use the spot market up to a cost ceiling my manager approves. I call the primary to learn why: rates below market, a lane they dislike, or slow loading at our docks. For next peak I share forecasts earlier, fix dock delays and rebid the hardest lanes. I report the extra cost per load each week.
A big retail customer has started fining us for loads that arrive early or late. How would you get the fines down?
How you dig into a recurring problem with data instead of blaming the carrier.
Pulls each fine, sorts by cause, fixes appointments, transit plans and carrier choice, and disputes fines with proof.

I pull every fine and sort it by cause: missed appointment, early arrival, short shipment, carrier late, or our loading late. Usually a few lanes or one dock cause most of it. Then I fix those: book appointments earlier, plan realistic transit times, change a weak carrier. Where we were on time, I dispute the fine with tracking timestamps and the gate check-in.

machine-learning-engineer.heading: Machine learning engineer questions
qs: What is data leakage, and how have you caught it in a project?
Whether you can spot training information that the model will not have at prediction time.
A clear definition, a real example such as a feature computed after the event, and a habit of distrusting scores that look too good.

Leakage is when the model trains on information it will not have when it makes a real prediction. On a churn model I got an AUC of 0.97, which was too good. One feature, days since last login, was computed after the cancel date. I rebuilt the features as of the prediction date and the score dropped to 0.81, which was honest.
When would you serve predictions in batch, and when online?
Your sense of how serving choices follow from what the product needs.
Batch when inputs are known ahead and a slightly stale answer is fine; online when the prediction depends on the request itself. Mentions cost and latency.

If we can score every user overnight and the answer stays useful for a day, like a weekly email recommendation, batch is cheaper and simpler: write scores to a table and look them up. If the prediction depends on what the user just did, like fraud on a card swipe, it has to be online, with a response time limit and a service that stays up.
Your data is a history of transactions over time. How do you split it for training and testing?
Whether you avoid random splits that let the model see the future.
Train on the past and test on a later period, ideally over several rolling windows, and keep the same customer from leaking across sets when it matters.

I split by time: train on January to September, validate on October, test on November. A random split lets the model learn from later rows to predict earlier ones, so the score looks better than it will be live. I check several rolling windows for stability, and leave a gap between train and test if labels take time to arrive.
Another team uses your model's scores as probabilities. How do you check they can trust them?
Your grasp of calibration, not just ranking quality.
Compares predicted probabilities with observed rates in bins, and fixes gaps with Platt scaling or isotonic regression fit on held-out data.

A good AUC only says the model ranks cases well. I group predictions, for example all cases scored around 0.3, and check that about 30% of them are actually positive. A reliability plot shows this at a glance. If it is off, I fit Platt scaling or isotonic regression on a held-out set, not the training data, and check again on a separate test set.
A teammate cannot reproduce your training result from last month. How do you prevent that from happening?
How you make experiments repeatable.
Versioned code, data and environment, recorded config and seeds, and honesty that some GPU operations are not fully deterministic.

I log every run with the commit hash, the exact dataset snapshot, the config, the random seeds and the library versions, usually inside a container image. Then anyone can rerun it. I also say upfront that some GPU operations are nondeterministic, so we expect small differences unless we turn on deterministic settings, which can be slower.
Your training loss turns into NaN halfway through a run. Walk me through how you debug it.
How you work through a common training failure step by step.
Looks at gradients, learning rate, bad inputs, unsafe math like log of zero, and mixed precision; reproduces the failure on the batch that caused it.

I plot the gradient norm: a spike right before the NaN points to exploding gradients, so I lower the learning rate or add gradient clipping. Then I check that batch for bad inputs like infinite values, and the code for log of zero or division by zero. With mixed precision I check loss scaling. I rerun on that batch to confirm the fix.
What is training-serving skew, and how do you guard against it?
Whether you know why a model that tested well can behave worse once it is live.
Features computed differently in training and in serving; fixes include one shared feature definition and logging live features to compare with training data.

It is when the features the model sees live differ from the ones it trained on. A classic case: training computed average spend in SQL over 30 days, while the service computed it in Python over 7. I keep one shared feature definition for both paths, log features at serving time, and compare their distributions with the training data.
Your new model beats the old one offline, but the A/B test shows no lift. What do you look at?
How you investigate a gap between offline evaluation and live results.
Checks the experiment setup, skew, whether the offline metric matches the business goal, and bias from data collected under the old model.

First I check the test itself: traffic split, logging, enough users. Then skew: are live features the same as offline? Then the metric: better log loss may not move clicks. Also, offline data was collected under the old model, so it only shows results for items that model chose to show. I slice results by segment before concluding.
Your new model is 3% better overall but clearly worse for new users. The product manager wants to ship it Friday. What do you do?
Your judgement when an overall gain hides a loss for one group.
Brings the slice numbers into the decision, weighs how much that group matters, and offers options instead of blocking or shipping quietly.

I show the product manager the slice: new users are where we win or lose people, so a drop there may cost more than the 3% gain elsewhere. Options: ship to existing users and keep the old model for new ones, or fix it first with more new-user data. If we ship anyway, I set an alert on that group. The call is shared, made with the numbers in view.
Your fraud dataset has one positive in a thousand. How do you train and evaluate on it?
How you work with a rare positive class without fooling yourself.
Keeps the test set at the true rate, uses precision-recall measures, and knows resampling or class weights shift the scores.

I keep validation and test at the real 1-in-1,000 rate, so results mean something. For training I try class weights or downsampling negatives. Downsampling shifts the scores, so I recalibrate before anyone uses them. I report precision and recall at the threshold the review team can handle, plus PR-AUC, because 99.9% accuracy is what doing nothing gets.
What is the difference between data drift and concept drift, and how does each show up in monitoring?
Whether you can tell why a live model is getting worse.
Data drift is a change in the inputs; concept drift is a change in how inputs relate to the label. Only labels reveal the second.

Data drift means the inputs change, like more mobile traffic than in training. I catch it by comparing live feature distributions to training ones, for example with a population stability index. Concept drift means the same inputs now lead to a different outcome, say fraudsters change tactics. Input checks can miss it; I need delayed labels and tracked performance to see it.
You ran 300 hyperparameter trials and picked the best on the validation set. How much do you trust that score?
Whether you know that heavy tuning overfits the validation set.
The best of many trials is biased upward; a test set used once at the end, or nested cross-validation, gives the honest number.

Not fully. Picking the top of 300 noisy scores favors the lucky ones, so the winner's validation score is too high. I report a test set that played no part in tuning, used once at the end. With small data I would use nested cross-validation. I also check whether the top ten configs are close; if they are, I pick the simplest.
Your annotators disagree on 25% of examples. What do you do before training?
How you judge label quality before blaming the model.
Measures agreement properly, finds out why people disagree, fixes the guidelines, and decides how to treat truly ambiguous cases.

I measure agreement with a chance-corrected statistic, like Cohen's kappa for two raters, then read a sample of the disagreements. Often the guideline is vague on a few cases, so I rewrite it with examples and relabel. Truly ambiguous items I keep as soft labels or leave out of the test set. Label noise also caps what any model can score, so it sets realistic targets.
Fine-tuning a large model, you hit out-of-memory errors on the GPU. What are your options, and what does each cost?
Your practical grip on GPU memory during training.
Knows what uses memory (weights, gradients, optimizer state, activations) and matches each fix to it with its trade-off.

Memory goes to weights, gradients, optimizer state and activations. Mixed precision cuts memory, usually with little loss in quality. Gradient checkpointing recomputes activations, saving memory for extra compute. Gradient accumulation keeps the effective batch with smaller micro-batches. Adapter methods like LoRA train a few small added weights, so optimizer state shrinks a lot.
Your model meets accuracy targets, but p99 latency is 400 ms against a 100 ms budget. Walk me through what you try.
How you trade speed against quality when serving a model.
Profiles first to find where the time goes, tries the cheapest fixes, and measures quality loss for every change.

First I profile: often the time is in feature fetching or preprocessing, not the model. Then cheap fixes: cache frequent requests, batch on the server, use a runtime optimized for our hardware. If the model itself is slow, I try quantization or distilling it into a smaller model. After each step I check accuracy on the same test set and p99, not just the average.
You move training from one GPU to eight with data parallelism. What changes in your setup?
Whether you understand what scaling out does to optimization.
The effective batch grows eightfold, so learning rate and warmup need retuning; data sharding, seeds and metrics across workers need care.

Each GPU gets its own slice of the batch, so the effective batch is eight times larger. I raise the learning rate, often starting near linear scaling with a warmup, then tune it, because that rule breaks down at large batches. I make sure each worker sees different data, set seeds per worker, and combine metrics across all workers, not just one.
Tell me about a model that failed after launch. What did you change in how you work?
Whether you own a failure and turn it into a lasting fix.
A specific failure, a clear cause, and a process change that would catch it next time, not just a patch.

A churn model I shipped dropped sharply after two weeks. An upstream team had changed a field from days to hours, and nothing checked it. I fixed the feature, then added schema and range checks on inputs that block a training run or alert us at serving time. Since then I treat agreements with upstream data owners as part of the model.
Your recommender is retrained on clicks from what it showed. What goes wrong over time, and how do you fix it?
Whether you see the feedback loop a model creates with its own data.
Names exposure and position bias and the narrowing to what was already shown; fixes include exploration traffic and logging how items were chosen.

The model only learns from items it chose to show, and top slots get clicks partly because they are on top. Over time it narrows to what it already likes. I keep a small slice of exploration traffic, log the position and the chance each item had of being shown, and use those to correct training, for example with inverse propensity weighting.
We are adding an LLM feature that drafts support replies. How would you evaluate it before and after launch?
How you evaluate a model whose output has no single right answer.
A fixed test set from real cases, a clear rubric, automated judges checked against human ratings, and live signals after launch.

Before launch I build a test set of real tickets, including hard and risky ones, and a rubric: correct, safe, follows policy, right tone. People grade a sample; an LLM judge grades the rest, but only after I check it agrees with the people. I rerun the set on every prompt or model change. After launch I track how much agents edit drafts, escalations and customer ratings.

machinist.heading: Machinist questions
qs: A diameter on the drawing reads 0.750 +0.000/-0.001. What size do you aim for, and why?
Whether you read tolerances correctly and plan for real-world variation.
Knows the limits are 0.749 to 0.750 and aims near the middle, leaving room for tool wear and measurement error.

The part is good anywhere from 0.749 to 0.750. I aim for about 0.7495, the middle of the band. If I sit right on 0.750, a bit of tool wear or a slightly warm part can push me out. In the middle I have room to adjust the wear offset before I make scrap.
How do you work out spindle speed and feed rate for an end mill?
Your grasp of the basic cutting math every machinist uses.
Uses RPM from surface speed and diameter, feed from RPM times chip load times flutes, then adjusts by sound, chips and machine limits.

RPM is surface feet per minute times 3.82, divided by tool diameter in inches. For a half-inch carbide end mill in aluminum at 800 SFM, that is about 6,100 RPM. Feed in inches per minute is RPM times chip load per tooth times the number of flutes. Then I check the machine's limits and listen to the cut and look at the chips.
When do you climb mill and when do you conventional mill?
Whether you understand cutter direction, finish and machine backlash.
Climb on rigid CNC machines for better finish and tool life; conventional on manual machines with backlash or through hard scale.

On a CNC with ball screws I climb mill by default. The chip goes from thick to thin, so I get a better finish and less tool wear. On a manual mill with backlash in the leadscrew, climb milling can pull the table into the cutter, so I go conventional. I also go conventional through hard scale on castings so the tool does not start each cut on the crust.
You need to tap a blind hole in steel. How do you set it up?
Your practical knowledge of tapping and chip control.
Right tap drill, enough drill depth below the thread, a spiral flute tap to pull chips out, and care not to bottom out.

I check the tap drill size on a chart and drill deeper than the full thread so chips have room and the tap does not bottom out. For a blind hole I use a spiral flute tap, which pulls chips up and out. A spiral point tap pushes chips ahead, which is for through holes. I use tapping fluid and rigid tapping or a tension holder.
Walk me through setting work and tool offsets on a CNC mill for a new job.
How you establish where the part and tools are before cutting.
Sets X, Y, Z zero to match the drawing's datums, measures each tool length, and double-checks values before running.

I indicate the vise so it is square, then find X and Y zero with an edge finder or probe at the corner the program uses, and store it in G54. I touch off each tool on a setter or gauge block for tool length. Then I jog to zero with the first tool and check the screen reads what I expect before I run anything.
How do you prove out a new CNC program before running production?
Whether you protect the machine, the tooling and the first part.
Dry run or single block with rapids turned down, watches distance-to-go, then a full first article inspection before running more.

I check the program in the simulator first. At the machine I turn rapids down to 25 percent, run single block, and keep a hand on feed hold. On the first moves toward the part I compare distance-to-go with what is left in real space. After the first part I measure every dimension on the drawing before I let it run.
Your boring bar starts to chatter halfway through a job. What do you try?
How you troubleshoot vibration in a cut.
Checks rigidity first: shorter stickout, solid clamping. Then changes RPM, feed or depth, and checks the insert edge.

First I stop and look at the insert; a worn edge chatters. Then rigidity: I shorten the stickout as much as the bore depth allows and make sure the bar is clamped tight. If it still sings, I change RPM to get off the resonance and try a little more feed, which often settles it. Smaller nose radius helps too.
A hole is called out with a position tolerance of 0.010 at MMC. The hole measures larger than its minimum size. What does that mean for you?
Your working knowledge of GD&T and bonus tolerance.
For a hole, MMC is the smallest size; as the hole grows, the position tolerance grows by the same amount.

For a hole, maximum material condition is the smallest allowed size. Say the hole is 0.250 +0.005/-0.000 and measures 0.253. It is 0.003 away from MMC, so I get 0.003 of bonus. The position can be off by up to 0.013 diameter, not 0.010. That can save a part that looks out on the CMM report at first glance.
A thin-walled aluminum part measures fine in the vise but warps after you unclamp it. How do you fix that?
How you handle distortion from clamping and internal stress.
Lighter clamping, soft jaws or fixtures, rough first, release and re-clamp, then light finish passes.

Two causes: the vise squeezes it, or cutting releases stress in the material. I rough all sides first and leave about 0.020. Then I loosen the vise, let the part relax, and re-clamp lightly in soft jaws cut to its shape. I finish with light passes and sharp tools so I add little heat and pressure.
You crash a tool into a fixture on a CNC. What do you do next?
Your honesty and judgement after a mistake on expensive equipment.
Stops, reports it right away, finds the cause, and checks the spindle and setup before running again.

I hit emergency stop, then tell my lead right away, even if it looks minor. I figure out why: wrong offset, wrong tool number, or a program error. Before cutting again I check spindle runout with an indicator and recheck the fixture and offsets. Hiding a crash can mean bad parts or a damaged spindle later, which costs far more.
Why does the order of datums in a feature control frame matter when you set up a part?
Whether you can turn a datum reference frame into a real setup.
The primary datum gets at least three points of contact, the secondary two, the tertiary one. That order sets how the part sits in the fixture and in inspection.

The order tells me how to locate the part. The primary datum sits on at least three points, the secondary touches two, the tertiary one. Real surfaces are never perfect, so if I swap the order the part rocks differently and my holes land somewhere else. I build the fixture and the inspection setup in the order the frame lists.
You finish a 10-inch aluminum part, measure it right off the machine, and it is on size. Is it good?
Whether you account for heat when you measure close tolerances.
Parts are judged at 68°F. Aluminum grows about twice as much as steel per degree, so a warm part that measures on size can shrink under size.

Not yet. Aluminum grows about 13 millionths of an inch per inch for each degree Fahrenheit. If the part is 15 degrees warm, 10 inches is about 0.002 longer than it will be at 68 degrees, the standard measuring temperature. I let it soak next to my gauge, or I learn the difference from a cooled part and cut to that.
The last machinist kept burning drills on a 304 stainless job. What would you change?
Your knowledge of how stainless steel behaves under the tool.
Knowing that 304 work hardens: keep the tool cutting with a steady feed, no dwelling or rubbing, sharp tools, a rigid setup and good coolant.

304 work hardens, so every time a drill rubs instead of cutting, the next layer gets harder and the drill burns. I keep the feed up and steady, never let it dwell at the bottom, and use a sharp drill with good coolant. If a hole is already glazed, I cut under the hard skin with a fresh tool instead of pushing harder.
The print calls for a 32 Ra finish on a turned diameter and you are getting about 63. What do you change?
How you find the cause of a surface finish problem instead of guessing.
Feed and nose radius set the theoretical finish; then worn edges, built-up edge and chatter. One change at a time, measured each time.

Both numbers are microinches, so I need about half the roughness. The peak to valley height goes with feed squared over eight times the nose radius, so a lower feed per rev or a bigger nose radius helps most. A wiper insert can let me keep the feed. If the cut looks torn, I check for a worn or built-up edge and raise the speed. One change at a time, then I check with the roughness tester.
How do you cut soft jaws to hold a thin-walled ring on a lathe without squeezing it out of round?
Your workholding skill on parts that distort easily.
Bore the jaws while loaded on a plug at the pressure you will run, to the part's size, so they wrap the diameter; then use the lowest pressure that holds safely.

I clamp a plug in the back of the jaws so they are loaded the way they will be in the cut, at the same chuck pressure. Then I bore the jaws to the part's diameter so they touch almost all the way around, not on three narrow lines. For the finish pass I drop the pressure as low as still holds the part safely and take light cuts.
A pin is turned exactly to its maximum diameter but is slightly bent. The drawing gives only a size tolerance. Is it good?
Your grasp of Rule #1, the envelope rule in ASME Y14.5.
No. Under Rule #1, a feature at its maximum material size must have perfect form, so a bent pin at max size is rejected.

No. Rule #1 says that when only size is given, the size limits also control form. At maximum size the pin must be perfectly straight, so it would not pass through a perfect gauge ring of that size. If the pin were 0.001 under max, it could be bent up to 0.001. A straightness callout on the axis, or the independency symbol, would change that.
Your bore reads on size all the way around with a two-point gauge, but the mating pin will not go in. What could be going on?
Whether you know the limits of your measuring tools.
Knowing that a three-lobed bore can read the same width in every direction with two points, and checking it with a plug gauge or a CMM.

A thin part held in a three-jaw chuck can spring into three lobes when it is released. A three-lobed shape measures the same width every way you turn a two-point gauge, yet the largest pin that fits is smaller. I would try a go plug gauge and ask for a CMM check with many points. The fix is in the holding: soft jaws, lighter pressure or a different clamp.
Halfway through a run you find the last 30 parts are out because of an offset you entered wrong. What do you do?
Your honesty and control when your own error has reached parts.
Stop, tag and separate parts back to the last verified good one, tell the lead and quality at once, then fix both the cause and the check that missed it.

I stop the machine, then tag and separate every part back to the last one I measured good, not just the 30 I think are bad. I tell my lead and quality right away, before anything ships. Rework is their call. Then I fix why my check missed it, for example measuring that feature on the next part after any offset change.
Four holes are dimensioned in a chain from an edge, each ±0.005. Assembly says the last hole is off, but your parts meet print. How do you handle it?
Whether you understand tolerance stack-up and can raise it with engineering.
Chained tolerances add, up to ±0.020 at the last hole. Program every hole from one zero and suggest baseline or position dimensions to engineering.

Each ±0.005 adds up, so the last hole can legally sit 0.020 from where assembly expects it. In my program I already place every hole from one zero, so my errors do not pile up. But I would show engineering the stack and suggest dimensioning all holes from a datum edge, or using a position tolerance. Until the print changes, the parts meet it.

maintenance-technician.heading: Maintenance technician questions
qs: What is the difference between preventive and corrective maintenance, and why does it matter?
Whether you understand the basic logic of keeping equipment running.
Preventive is scheduled work before failure, corrective fixes what broke; planned work costs less than downtime.

Preventive maintenance is scheduled work done before something fails: changing filters, greasing bearings, checking belts. Corrective is fixing what already broke. Preventive costs less because I choose the time. A breakdown picks its own time, often on a busy Saturday, and we lose sales or product while we wait for parts.
What do you check on a routine maintenance visit to a rooftop HVAC unit?
Your hands-on knowledge of the most common building equipment.
A clear checklist: filters, belts, condensate drain, coils, electrical connections, motors, and notes kept for the next visit.

I check or change the filters, look at belt tension and wear, and clear the condensate drain and pan so water does not back up. I check the coils for dirt, tighten electrical connections with the power locked out, and listen to motors and bearings. On gas units I look at the burners and flue. I write down readings so the next visit can compare.
