Walk me through locking out a machine before you work on it.
Whether you follow lockout/tagout in the right order, every time.
Notify, shut down, isolate every energy source, apply your own lock and tag, release stored energy, verify zero energy.

I tell the people who use the machine, then shut it down the normal way. I isolate every energy source at the disconnect or valve, put my own lock and tag on it, and bleed off stored energy like air pressure or springs. Then I try to start it to prove it is dead, and set the controls back to off. Only my key comes off my lock.
Water is dripping from the ceiling onto the sales floor during business hours. How do you set up?
How you keep customers and yourself safe while working in an open building.
Barricade and contain first, check for water near electrical fixtures, then trace the source, which may not be directly above.

First I block the area with cones and wet floor signs and put a bucket or tarp down to catch water. If I need a ladder, I set a barrier so nobody walks under me. Before I open the ceiling I check whether water is near light fixtures; if it is, I shut off that circuit. Then I trace the leak, which is often several feet away from the drip.
The walk-in cooler reads 45°F and is still rising. What do you do?
Your troubleshooting order and your awareness of food safety.
Protect the food and tell the manager right away, then check the simple causes: door, iced coil, fans, dirty condenser.

I tell the manager right away and note the time, and we move product to another cooler, because cold food has to stay at 41°F or below. Then I check the simple things first: is the door closing and sealing, is the evaporator coil iced over, are the fans running, is the condenser coil clogged with dust. If it is a refrigerant problem, I call a certified tech.
You have three work orders: water leaking onto the floor, a dock door that will not close, and a flickering light in the office. Which comes first?
How you rank work by risk to people, property and the business.
Safety and damage first, then security and operations, comfort last, with the reason said out loud and the requester told.

The leak first: it is a slip hazard and it is damaging the building. Next the dock door, because an open door is a security and temperature problem and blocks deliveries. The flickering light can wait. I would tell the office I have it on my list and when I expect to get to it, so they are not left guessing.
A motor keeps tripping its breaker, and someone suggests putting in a bigger breaker. What do you say?
Whether you fix the cause instead of defeating a safety device.
A firm no, because the breaker protects the wiring, plus a real diagnosis: amp draw, voltage, bearings and load.

No. The breaker is sized to protect the wire, and a bigger one can let that wire overheat. I lock out the motor and check whether the bearings or the load are binding. Then I measure the amp draw against the full-load amps on the nameplate and check the voltage on each leg. The fix is whatever is making it pull too much current.
The relief valve on a water heater is dripping. How do you handle it?
Your plumbing knowledge and respect for a critical safety valve.
Never plug or cap it; check temperature and pressure, including thermal expansion, before replacing the valve.

A dripping relief valve is a warning, so I never plug or cap it. I check the temperature setting and the water pressure. In a closed system, where a check valve stops water flowing back to the street, a failed expansion tank often causes it. If temperature and pressure are normal, the valve itself may be worn, and I replace it.
Your manager asks you to add a new electrical circuit for a display. You are not a licensed electrician. What do you do?
Whether you know the limits of your license and can say no the right way.
Explains that the work needs a licensed electrician and often a permit, and offers real help instead of a flat refusal.

I explain that in most places a new circuit needs a licensed electrician and often a permit, and that unlicensed work can fail inspection and cause insurance trouble. Then I offer what I can do: get two quotes, clear the area, and be there with the contractor. If I am pushed to do it anyway, I politely say no and put it in an email.
Tell me about a repair that failed again soon after you finished it. What did you learn?
How you own a mistake and whether you look for root causes.
An honest story, a second look that found the real cause, and a habit that changed afterward.

I replaced a burned-out fan motor in a walk-in cooler, and the new one failed three weeks later. I had fixed the symptom. The second time I checked the supply voltage and found a loose connection that was starving the motor. Now, before I close a work order, I ask why the part failed, not just whether the new one runs.
How do you test a run capacitor on a condenser unit, and how do you know it is bad?
Whether you can test a common failure part safely instead of guessing.
Power off and verified dead, capacitor discharged, then a capacitance reading compared to the rated value and tolerance on the label.

I shut the disconnect, verify zero volts with my meter, and discharge the capacitor with an insulated resistor tool. Then I pull the wires and read it in capacitance mode. If the reading in microfarads falls outside the tolerance printed on the label, or it is bulged or leaking, I replace it with the same rating.
There is a sewer smell near a floor drain in the back room. What do you check first?
Your plumbing basics and whether you start with the simple, likely cause.
A dry trap first, since an unused drain loses its water seal. Then the trap primer, vents and nearby fixture seals.

Most of the time the trap has dried out, so sewer gas comes straight up. I pour water in to restore the seal. If it keeps drying out, I check whether the trap primer works or the drain needs one. If the smell stays, I look at the vent and the wax rings on nearby toilets.
When do you check refrigerant charge by superheat, and when by subcooling?
Whether you understand how the metering device changes the way you judge charge.
Superheat for a fixed orifice like a piston or cap tube; subcooling for a TXV system, read against the maker's target. EPA 608 certification to do the work.

On a fixed orifice, like a piston or capillary tube, I charge by superheat. On a TXV system the valve holds superheat steady, so I use subcooling and compare it to the manufacturer's target. Either way I am EPA 608 certified, because you need that to open a system or buy refrigerant.
A reach-in freezer's evaporator coil is a solid block of ice. What could cause it?
How you think through the defrost system rather than just melting the ice and leaving.
Lists the defrost heater, timer or control, termination switch, evaporator fan, door gaskets and drain line, and fixes the cause after defrosting.

I move the product to another freezer and defrost the coil. Then I find the cause: a failed defrost heater, a bad timer or control, a bad termination switch, an evaporator fan that stopped, or a torn gasket letting in humid air. I also check that the drain line is clear, or the water just refreezes.
A three-phase motor is running hot and humming. What do you check?
Your electrical troubleshooting on three-phase equipment.
Voltage on all three legs and amps against nameplate, looking for a lost phase or imbalance, then connections and starter contacts with the power locked out.

I measure voltage between all three legs and amps on each leg, and compare amps to the nameplate full load rating. A missing phase or a large imbalance points to a blown fuse, a burned contact or a loose lug. A small voltage imbalance causes a much bigger current imbalance, so I do not ignore it. Then I lock out and check connections.
A GFCI outlet in the kitchen keeps tripping and the cook asks you to swap it for a regular outlet. What do you do?
Whether you find the fault instead of removing a safety device the code requires.
Refuses the swap. Isolates the cause by testing loads one at a time and checks for moisture and wiring faults.

No. Code requires GFCI protection in commercial kitchens, and the trip means current is leaking somewhere. I unplug everything and reset. If it holds, I plug things in one at a time. Often an older appliance with a heating element is the culprit. If it trips with nothing plugged in, I check for water in boxes and wiring faults.
A unit has needed refrigerant twice this month, and the manager says to just keep topping it off. How do you respond?
How you handle pressure to take a shortcut that breaks rules and wastes money.
Explains that the leak must be found and fixed, that venting is illegal, and that larger systems have federal leak repair rules.

I explain that refrigerant does not get used up, so it is leaking out, and each charge is money gone. Knowingly releasing refrigerant is prohibited, and bigger systems have federal leak repair and record rules. I find the leak with a detector or bubbles, repair it, pressure test with nitrogen, pull a vacuum and recharge.
A sprinkler pipe is leaking and part of the system has to be shut down. What has to happen before and after?
Whether you know a fire protection shutdown is a controlled impairment, not just a closed valve.
Notify the manager, monitoring company, fire department and insurer as required, tag it, use a licensed contractor and fire watch, then restore and notify.

A shut sprinkler is an impairment, so I tell the manager and we notify the alarm monitoring company, the fire department and the insurer as our procedures require. I tag the closed valve. A licensed sprinkler contractor does the repair, and we set up a fire watch if it runs long. After, we reopen, check for alarm and notify everyone.
A rooftop unit fails a few times a week but always runs fine when you get there. How do you track it down?
How you solve an intermittent fault without swapping parts at random.
Gathers when and how it happens, logs data, checks connections and heat-related faults, and changes parts only on evidence.

I ask staff exactly when it happens: time, weather, what they heard. I check the control board for stored fault codes and put a data logger on temps and voltage. Then I look for loose or burned connections, a contactor with pitted points, or a part that fails only when hot. I replace a part only when the data points to it.
You are asked to build a preventive maintenance schedule for a new site. How do you decide what gets checked and how often?
Your ability to plan maintenance by risk and data, the work of a senior technician.
Starts from equipment criticality and manufacturer guidance, then adjusts intervals using failure history from work orders.

I list every asset and rank it by what happens if it fails: a walk-in cooler outranks an office fan. I start intervals from the manufacturer's manuals. Then I use work order history. If filters are always dirty at 90 days, I go to 60. If cheap items are not critical, I may run them to failure. I review the schedule every quarter.

manufacturing.heading: Manufacturing and quality questions
qs: What is the difference between control limits and specification limits?
Whether you know the basic idea behind statistical process control.
Spec limits come from the customer or drawing. Control limits come from the process data. The two answer different questions.

Spec limits come from the drawing or the customer. They say what a good part is. Control limits come from the process itself, usually three standard deviations either side of the average on the chart. A process can be in control and still make bad parts if its spread is wider than the spec.
How do you calculate takt time, and what do you do if one station runs slower than it?
Your grasp of line balancing when a design moves into volume production.
The right formula, a worked number, and fixing the bottleneck by removing waste before adding people or machines.

Takt time is available production time divided by customer demand. With 450 minutes a shift and 900 parts needed, that is 27,000 seconds over 900, or 30 seconds a part. If one station takes 38 seconds, it is the bottleneck. I remove waste there first, then shift work to stations with slack, and only then add a fixture or staff.
What is the difference between Cp and Cpk, and what does it tell you when they differ a lot?
Whether you can read a capability study and act on it.
Cp is potential based on spread only. Cpk also counts centering. A big gap means the process is off center, not too variable.

Cp compares the spec width to six standard deviations of the process. It says what the process could do if centered. Cpk uses the distance from the average to the nearer spec limit, divided by three standard deviations. If Cp is 1.6 and Cpk is 0.9, the spread is fine but the process sits off center, so I recenter it first.
Why would you run a gauge R&R study before you trust a control chart?
Whether you check the measurement system before blaming the process.
Knows repeatability versus reproducibility and that a noisy gauge makes the chart show gauge noise, not the process.

In a gauge R&R, several operators measure the same parts several times. Repeatability is the variation when one person measures the same part again. Reproducibility is the difference between people. If the gauge uses up most of the tolerance, the chart shows gauge noise. A common guideline calls under 10% of tolerance good and over 30% not acceptable.
A changeover on our press takes 90 minutes. How would you cut it?
Your practical use of lean methods on the shop floor.
A SMED approach: observe, split internal from external steps, move steps outside the stop, then simplify what remains.

I would film one changeover and list every step. Then I sort steps into internal, which need the press stopped, and external, which can happen while it runs, like staging the next die and tools. I convert internal steps to external where I can, and shorten the rest with quick clamps and fixed locating pins instead of adjusting by eye.
Every point on the chart is inside the control limits, but the last nine are all above the centerline. What do you do?
Whether you recognize a non-random pattern and investigate it the right way.
Sees a likely shift under common run rules, looks for what changed, and does not just tweak the machine.

Nine in a row on one side is a run that the common rule sets flag as a shift, even inside the limits. By chance alone it is unlikely. I would check what changed when the run started: a new material lot, a tool change, another shift, a gauge. I fix that cause, or recalculate the limits if the change was intended.
An operator adjusts the machine after every part, based on the last measurement. Is that a problem?
Whether you understand common-cause variation and the cost of tampering.
Explains that adjusting a stable process for random noise widens the spread, and gives a clear rule for when to adjust.

Yes. If the process is stable, each part's deviation is mostly random noise. Adjusting for noise adds new error on top, so the spread gets wider, not narrower. Deming called this tampering. I would show the operator the control chart and agree on a rule: adjust only when the chart signals a real change, not after each part.
Our corrective action for a recurring defect was to retrain the operator. Three months later the defect is back. What went wrong?
How you handle a root cause analysis that stopped too early.
Sees retraining as a weak fix, goes back to the process, and aims for error-proofing that does not rely on memory.

Retraining is rarely a root cause. If a skilled operator can make the mistake, the process allows it. I would go to the floor, watch how the error happens, and keep asking why the process lets it through. Then I aim for error-proofing: a fixture that only takes the part one way, or a sensor that stops the cycle when a step is missed.
It is the last day of the month and a lot just failed sampling inspection by a small margin. Production wants to ship it. What do you do?
Your judgement when schedule pressure meets a quality decision.
Keeps the lot on hold, studies the failure, and offers proper options: sorting, approved rework, or a written customer deviation.

I keep the lot tagged and on hold, then look at the failures: which feature, how far out, does it affect fit or function. The honest options are to sort 100% and ship the good parts, rework under an approved procedure, or ask the customer for a written deviation. A late shipment costs money; shipping suspect parts costs trust.
A customer reports cracked brackets from three different lots. Walk me through your first week.
How you run a structured root cause and corrective action process under real pressure.
Containment first, a cross-functional team, facts before theories, causes tested, and the fix verified and written into the control plan.

Day one is containment: I hold stock here and in transit and help sort what the customer has. I pull in production, design and quality. I gather facts: which lots, where cracks start, what the lots share. A fishbone lists causes, and I test the likely ones, like a new steel supplier. I close it only when the fix is verified and the control plan updated.
You track the share of defective units in daily lots that range from 200 to 900 pieces. Which control chart do you use, and why?
Whether you can match the chart to the type of data.
A p chart, because the data are pass/fail proportions and the limits must adjust to each day's sample size.

A p chart. Each unit is good or bad, so it is attribute data, and the lot size changes every day. The p chart plots the fraction defective, and its limits widen on small days and tighten on big ones, because they depend on the square root of the sample size. An np chart only works when the sample size stays the same.
Walk me through how you calculate OEE, and what you look at first when it is low.
Whether you know the three parts of OEE and use them to find the loss.
Availability times performance times quality, each defined correctly, then a drill-down to the biggest specific loss.

OEE is availability times performance times quality. Availability is run time over planned production time. Performance is ideal cycle time times total count, divided by run time. Quality is good parts over total parts. If OEE is low, I find which factor drags it down, then the top few losses inside it, like one long changeover or a frequent minor stop.
A bracket can be installed upside down, and it has happened twice this quarter. What fixes do you consider, and in what order?
How you rank mistake-proofing options from strongest to weakest.
Make the error impossible first, through design or fixture; detection that stops the line next; signs and training last.

First I ask design whether we can make the part symmetric, so either way is right, or add a tab so it only fits one way. If not, a fixture pin that blocks the wrong orientation. Next, a sensor that checks orientation and stops the line before the next step. A photo in the work instruction helps, but on its own it relies on people never slipping.
In our PFMEA, two failure modes both have an RPN of 120. How do you decide which to work on first?
Whether you understand the limits of the risk priority number.
RPN hides risk, so severity comes first. Knows the AIAG-VDA action priority method and prefers cutting occurrence over adding inspection.

I look at the three ratings, not the product. A severity 10 with low occurrence can be a safety issue, while a severity 3 is a nuisance, and both can reach 120. The AIAG-VDA FMEA handbook replaced RPN with action priority for that reason: severity first, then occurrence, then detection. And I would rather lower occurrence than add another check.
Why does a good 8D report need more than one root cause?
Whether you look at why the defect escaped, not only why it was made.
One cause for why the defect occurred, one for why it was not caught, and ideally the system gap that allowed both.

The occurrence cause explains why the part was made wrong, for example a worn locating pin. The escape cause explains why our checks let it through, for example a gauge that never checked that feature. I also ask what in our system allowed both, like a PFMEA that missed the failure mode. Fixing only the first leaves the door open for the next defect.
Our order lead time is six weeks, but the actual work on a part takes about three hours. Where do you start?
Whether you see lead time as a queue problem, not a machine speed problem.
Maps the value stream, sees that waiting in inventory makes the lead time, and cuts work in process and batch sizes instead of speeding up machines.

Almost all of those six weeks is parts waiting. By Little's Law, lead time equals work in process divided by throughput, so with the same output, half the work in process means half the lead time. I would walk the value stream, count inventory between steps, and go after the biggest piles: large batches, long changeovers, and orders released before the line can take them.
On a four-cavity mold, each subgroup on our X-bar and R chart takes one part from each cavity. The X-bar chart hugs the centerline. What is happening?
Your grasp of rational subgrouping and what it does to control limits.
Cavity-to-cavity differences inflate the ranges, which widens the X-bar limits, so the chart cannot detect real shifts. Subgroup by cavity instead.

The range in each subgroup includes the fixed difference between cavities, not only short-term noise. X-bar limits are built from the average range, so they come out too wide and the points look calm. The chart would miss a real shift. I would chart each cavity separately, or use a group chart, and treat the cavity differences as their own problem.
Purchasing found a cheaper resin supplier. Lab tests show the parts measure the same. Can we switch next month?
Whether you respect change control and customer approval before changing a proven process.
Not on dimensions alone: trial runs, capability, updated PFMEA and control plan, and customer notice and approval where the contract or PPAP requires it.

Not on that evidence alone. A few parts with the same dimensions say nothing about strength over time or how the material runs at volume. I would run a trial lot, check capability and key properties, and update the PFMEA and control plan. In automotive, a new material source needs customer notification and usually a new PPAP approval before we ship.
Flatness data are skewed and can never go below zero. Your software reports a Cpk of 0.9. Do you trust it?
Whether you know when the standard capability formula does not apply.
Standard Cpk assumes normal data. Checks stability first, uses only the upper spec, and fits a suitable distribution or transform before reporting.

Not yet. The usual Cpk assumes a symmetric bell curve, and flatness is bounded at zero with a long right tail. First I confirm the process is stable on a control chart. Flatness has only an upper limit, so only the upper index counts. Then I fit a distribution like Weibull or lognormal, or transform the data, and estimate the share of parts beyond the limit from that fit.
Five process settings might drive weak welds, and each test run costs a day. How would you design the experiment?
How you plan an efficient experiment and protect it from hidden noise.
A screening fractional factorial with randomized runs and center points, the measurement checked first, then confirmation runs at the chosen settings.

A full factorial at two levels is 32 runs. A half fraction is 16 and still separates main effects and two-factor interactions, since it is resolution five. I would check the pull test gauge first, randomize the run order so drift does not pose as an effect, add center points to spot curvature, then confirm the best settings with a few runs before changing the process.

manufacturing-engineer.heading: Manufacturing engineer questions
qs: What is takt time, and how do you use it when you lay out a line?
Whether you can tie the line design to customer demand.
Available time divided by demand, used to size stations and balance work, and never confused with cycle time.

Takt time is the available production time divided by the units the customer needs in that time. With 450 minutes a shift and 900 units, takt is 30 seconds. I split the work so no station's cycle time goes over 30 seconds, and I move tasks or add a station when one does. Cycle time is what we actually take; takt is the pace we must hit.
A process has a Cp of 1.6 but a Cpk of 0.9. What does that tell you, and what do you do?
Your grasp of process capability beyond the formula.
The spread is fine but the process is off center, so re-centering is the fix, not a new machine.

Cp only compares the spread to the tolerance width, so 1.6 says the process is tight enough. Cpk also looks at where the mean sits, and 0.9 says it has drifted toward one limit. I first check the process is stable on a control chart, then re-center it, for example with a tool offset, and recheck Cpk on a fresh sample.
Operators keep installing a bracket backwards at one station. How do you fix it?
Whether you fix the process instead of blaming the operator.
Contain what was already built, then mistake-proof so the error cannot happen or is caught at once.

First I contain: check everything built since the last good audit. Retraining alone will not hold. I look for mistake-proofing, meaning a design where the error cannot happen, like a locating pin in the fixture that only fits one way, or a sensor that stops the cycle if the bracket is flipped. If possible, I ask design to make the part asymmetric.
Your line is 15% short of the output you need. Where do you start?
How you find and work on the real constraint.
Find the bottleneck with data first, since gains elsewhere do not raise output. Cheap fixes come before buying equipment.

I find the bottleneck first, by timing each station and watching where work piles up in front of one station and starves the ones after it. Speeding up any other station adds nothing. At the bottleneck I keep it running through breaks, move tasks to stations with spare time, and cut its downtime. A second machine is the last option, not the first.
OEE on a cell dropped from 72% to 61% in a month. How do you dig into it?
Whether you can break a summary metric into causes you can act on.
Split OEE into availability, performance and quality, find which one moved, then check the data against the floor.

OEE is availability times performance times quality, so I split the drop into those three first. If availability fell, I sort the downtime log by reason and minutes. If performance fell, I look for slow cycles and short stops nobody logs. If quality fell, I go to the scrap tags. Then I watch the cell for a shift to check the data matches reality.
Walk me through how you build a process FMEA for a new assembly step.
Your method for finding risks before a process goes live.
A mixed team goes step by step through failure modes, effects and causes, rates them, acts on the worst, and feeds the control plan.

I bring in an operator, quality and maintenance, and go step by step through the process flow. For each step we list how it could fail, the effect on the customer, and the cause, then rate severity, occurrence and detection. High-severity items get action first, even if they seem unlikely. The controls we choose go into the control plan and work instructions.
A new gauge starts rejecting parts that the old one passed. How do you tell whether the parts or the gauge are wrong?
Whether you check the measurement system before trusting the data.
Measure the same parts on both gauges and a reference, check calibration and fixturing, and run a gauge R&R study.

I take a set of parts, including some rejects, and measure them on the old gauge, the new one and a reference like the CMM, the coordinate measuring machine. I check both calibrations and the fixturing. Then I run a gauge R&R, where several operators measure the same parts several times, to see how much variation comes from the gauge itself.
You found a way to cut cycle time by changing a weld setting on a released part. What happens before it goes into production?
Whether you follow change control instead of just changing the machine.
A documented change, a trial with test data, updated FMEA, control plan and instructions, sign-off, and customer approval where required.

I write it up through our change process; I do not just adjust the machine. I run a trial lot and test the welds, for example with destructive pull tests, against the current setting. If the results hold, I update the PFMEA, control plan and work instructions, get quality to sign off, and check whether the customer must approve the change first, as many do.
Final inspection finds a lot with one dimension slightly out of spec, and it is due to ship tomorrow. What do you do?
Your judgement when schedule pressure meets a quality problem.
Quarantine, check other lots, find the cause, and let the formal review decide. Shipping as is usually needs the customer's approval.

I put the lot on hold and tag it so nobody ships it by mistake. I check whether earlier lots are affected and find the cause on the line. Then the material review board decides: rework, scrap, or use as is. Use as is goes to the customer as a deviation request; we do not decide it alone. I warn the customer early that the shipment may be late.
Explain the 3-2-1 principle when you design a fixture.
Your grasp of how a fixture locates a part the same way every time.
Six locating points fix six degrees of freedom on three datum planes, and clamps push the part toward the locators.

Three points on the primary datum plane, two on the secondary and one on the tertiary locate the part in all six degrees of freedom without over-constraining it. I put the locators on the same datums the drawing uses and spread them as far apart as the part allows. I aim the clamps toward the locators so the clamping force cannot push the part off them.
A changeover takes 90 minutes. How would you cut it using SMED?
Whether you can run a setup reduction, not just name the method.
Film a real changeover, separate internal from external steps, move external work outside the stop, then shorten what is left.

I would video a real changeover and list every step with its time. Then I sort them: internal steps need the machine stopped, external ones can be done while it runs. Staging the next die, tools and material is external, so that moves out first. Then I shorten internal steps with preset stops or quick clamps instead of bolts, and write the new method as standard work.
Total work content is 300 seconds and takt is 55 seconds. Walk me through balancing the line.
How you balance a line with real numbers and real constraints.
Minimum stations rounded up, tasks assigned in precedence order without passing takt, and balance efficiency checked.

300 divided by 55 is 5.45, so the theoretical minimum is six stations. I list every task with its time and what must come before it, then fill each station in that order without passing takt, keeping a small margin for variation. If the slowest station ends at 52 seconds, balance efficiency is 300 over 6 times 52, about 96%.
When do you use a worst-case tolerance stack, and when a statistical one?
Whether you know what each stack-up method assumes and what it risks.
Worst case guarantees every assembly fits. Root sum square assumes independent, centered, capable parts and accepts a small chance of no fit.

Worst case adds every tolerance at its limit, so every assembly fits, but it pushes me to tight, costly tolerances. Root sum square takes the square root of the sum of the squared tolerances, which gives a smaller total. It is only fair when the parts vary independently, run centered with good capability and the stack has several parts. For a safety-critical fit or a short stack I use worst case.
A root cause report on your desk says the cause was operator error. What do you do with it?
How you push a root cause past blame to the process.
Treat it as a starting point: ask why the process allowed the error, and fix that with a real control.

I send it back, politely. Operator error tells me where it happened, not why. I would go to the station, watch the job and ask why the mistake was possible: an unclear work instruction, poor lighting, a part that fits both ways, or a new person without training. The corrective action has to change the process, ideally with error-proofing, not just retrain and hope.
How do you decide a new line is ready for full production?
Your judgement on launch readiness beyond the first good part.
Evidence at rate: a run at takt with the real crew, capable key characteristics, sound gauges, a working control plan and trained people.

One good part proves little. I want a run at full rate with production operators, normal material and a real shift length. Key characteristics need capability studies that meet the customer's target, the gauges need passing measurement studies, and the control plan with its reaction plans must be in use. I also check scrap, downtime and spares for critical tooling.
Design releases a part with a tolerance your process cannot hold. How do you handle it?
How you work with design engineering using data instead of opinion.
Bring capability data, ask what function needs the tolerance, offer options with costs, and never quietly build to a looser limit.

I show the data first: our capability on that feature and the scrap rate the tolerance would mean. Then I ask the designer what the tolerance does for the function. Sometimes it can open up. Sometimes it really matters and we need a different process, an extra operation or a better fixture. Until a revised drawing is released, we build to the current one and contain.
A kaizen cut cycle time by 20%, and six months later the cell is back where it started. What went wrong, and what do you do?
Whether you know how improvements are kept, not just made.
Find why it slipped, then lock it in with standard work, visual controls, regular audits and ownership by the cell's own team.

Usually the change lived with the event team, not with the shift. I would watch the cell, compare it with the standard work and ask operators what got in the way. Often a tool was moved, a new person was never trained or a supply problem forced a workaround. I rebuild the standard with them, add visual controls and supervisor audits, and track the metric every week.
You want a $400,000 robotic cell to replace two manual stations. How do you build the case?
How you justify capital spending with full costs and honest risks.
All costs and real savings over the cell's life, payback or net present value, and the risks: volume changes, uptime and support skills.

I start with the problem it solves: labor, quality, ergonomics or capacity. Then I list all costs: equipment, integration, guarding, installation, training, spares, maintenance and lost output during startup. Savings must be real, like labor on every shift or scrap cost. I show payback and net present value under a few volume scenarios, and what happens if uptime is lower than the vendor claims.

marketing-analyst.heading: Marketing analyst questions
qs: What is the difference between ROAS and ROI?
Whether you know the two money metrics the job is judged on.
ROAS compares revenue to ad spend; ROI compares profit to all costs. You know a good ROAS can still lose money.

ROAS is revenue from the ads divided by ad spend, so $40,000 from $10,000 is a ROAS of 4. ROI looks at profit: revenue minus product costs, ad spend and other costs, divided by what we invested. With thin margins a ROAS of 4 can still lose money, so I ask for the margin before I call a campaign a winner.
What are UTM parameters, and what usually goes wrong with them?
Whether you know how traffic gets tagged and how tracking breaks in practice.
Tags on a link that tell analytics the source, medium and campaign; the common failures are messy naming and tags on internal links.

They are tags added to a link, like utm_source, utm_medium and utm_campaign, so analytics knows where a visit came from. The usual problems are messy naming, like “Email” and “email” showing as two rows, and tags on internal site links, which overwrite the real source. I keep one shared naming sheet and a link builder so everyone tags the same way.
How do you calculate customer acquisition cost and lifetime value?
Your grasp of the unit economics behind every budget decision.
CAC from total acquisition cost over new customers; LTV built on gross margin and retention, not revenue alone, plus a look at payback time.

CAC is total sales and marketing cost for a period divided by the new customers won in that period. LTV is average revenue per customer times gross margin times how long customers stay, often estimated from churn. A common rule of thumb is LTV around three times CAC, but I also watch payback: how many months of margin it takes to earn the CAC back.
What is wrong with last-click attribution?
Whether you understand how the credit model shapes which channels look good.
It gives all credit to the final touch, which flatters bottom-funnel channels and hides the ones that created demand.

Last click gives all the credit to the final touch before the sale. That flatters brand search, retargeting and email, which often catch people who had already decided, and it starves the video or social ads that made them aware in the first place. I use it as one view, never the only one, and check the big channels with holdout tests.
The ad platform reports 500 conversions last month and our analytics shows 320. Why, and which do you report?
How you handle numbers from sources that never agree.
Knows the real causes: view-through credit, different windows, platforms overlapping, tracking loss. Uses the order system as the anchor.

Neither is simply wrong. Ad platforms count view-through conversions and use their own attribution windows, and each platform claims the same sale, so their totals exceed real orders. Analytics loses some visits to ad blockers and consent choices. I compare both with the order database, which is the truth for sales, and report one agreed source.
Our brand search campaign shows a ROAS of 12. A manager wants to put more money into it. What do you say?
Your judgement on a number that looks great but may not be real.
Questions whether brand clicks are new sales at all, proposes a test to find out, and weighs competitors bidding on the brand name.

Not on that number alone. Many people searching our name would find us anyway through the free listing, so much of that ROAS is credit, not new sales. I would pause brand ads in a few test regions for several weeks and compare total orders with similar regions. If competitors bid on our name, the paid ad may still be worth keeping to protect those clicks.
A channel returns $5 for every $1 we spend. Should we double the budget on it?
Whether you think in marginal returns, not averages.
Explains diminishing returns: the average does not tell you what the next dollar earns. Scales in steps and watches the return on added spend.

Not yet. A ROAS of 5 is an average over spend we already made, and the next dollar usually earns less because we reach less interested people. I would raise spend in steps, say 20% at a time, and watch the return on the added spend only. When the extra dollars stop paying back above our target, that is where I stop.
You find out a report you sent last month counted some conversions twice. What do you do?
How you own a data mistake and stop it from happening again.
Tells the people affected quickly with the size of the error, finds the root cause, fixes it and adds a check.

I tell my manager and everyone who saw the report the same day, with what was wrong and how big the error was. In one case the purchase tag fired again when buyers reloaded the thank-you page, so conversions looked about 15% higher. I counted each order ID once, reissued the numbers and added a weekly check against the order system.
How would you prove a campaign actually caused new sales and did not just take credit for them?
Whether you can design an incrementality test.
A holdout or geo test with a comparable control group, run long enough, measuring lift and cost per incremental sale.

I would run a holdout. For example, split comparable regions, run the campaign in half and keep the other half dark for four to six weeks, then compare the change in sales. The gap is the lift the campaign caused. Where a platform supports it, I use a user-level holdout instead. Cost divided by the extra sales gives the true cost per incremental sale.
When would you use a marketing mix model instead of attribution?
Your knowledge of the measurement methods and their limits.
MMM uses aggregate data over time, covers offline media and privacy limits, needs long history; attribution is faster but sees only tracked paths.

Mix modeling uses weekly data on spend by channel, sales, price, season and promotions, and uses regression to estimate what each channel adds. It needs no user tracking, so it covers TV and survives privacy limits, but it needs a couple of years of data. Attribution is faster and more detailed but only sees tracked clicks. I use the model for the yearly budget split and check it with lift tests.
Should conversion rate be calculated per session or per user?
Whether you know a rate means nothing until its denominator is defined.
Picks the denominator to fit the decision, knows a "user" is really a browser or device, and keeps the definition fixed across reports.

It depends on the question. Per session suits a quick impulse buy. Per user suits a purchase people research over several visits; otherwise repeat visits make the rate look worse. Either way, a user in analytics is usually a browser on a device, not a person. I write the definition on the report and never switch it midstream.
Walk me through what you decide before an A/B test starts.
How you plan a test so its result can be trusted.
One primary metric, the smallest effect worth detecting, a sample size and run time fixed in advance, and full weekly cycles.

I write down the hypothesis and one primary metric, plus a guardrail like refund rate. We agree on the smallest lift worth acting on, then I use the baseline rate to calculate sample size and run time. I round up to full weeks so weekday and weekend buyers are both in. If traffic cannot reach that size, we test something bolder or skip it.
We optimized paid social and cost per lead fell 30%, but sales says the leads got worse. How do you check?
Whether you judge campaigns by what reaches revenue, not by the cheapest top-of-funnel number.
Follows leads through the CRM to qualified rate, pipeline and closed revenue per dollar, and moves optimization to a deeper signal.

I join the leads to the CRM by campaign and compare before and after: share that sales qualified, meetings held, pipeline and closed revenue per dollar spent. Often the platform found people who fill forms easily, not buyers. If so, I send qualified-lead events back to the platform as the goal to optimize, even if cost per lead goes up.
Site conversion rose from 3.0% to 3.4%, yet it fell on both mobile and desktop. How is that possible?
Whether you spot a mix shift before you report a win.
Explains that traffic moved toward the higher-converting segment, so the total rose while each part fell, and reports segments next to the total.

The traffic mix changed. Say desktop converts at 5% and mobile at 2%, and this month a much bigger share of visits came from desktop. Both rates can dip while the blended rate rises. That is Simpson's paradox. I would report each segment, find what moved the mix, such as an email sent mostly to desktop users, and not credit the site for the total.
Four days into a planned two-week test, the new page is significant at p = 0.03 and the director wants to ship it. What do you say?
How you handle pressure to stop a test early.
Explains that checking repeatedly and stopping at the first significant result raises false positives, and holds to the plan unless a sequential method was set up.

If we stop the first time it crosses 0.05, our real false-positive rate is well above 5%, because we gave chance many tries. Four days also miss a full weekly cycle. I would run the planned two weeks. If the team often needs early reads, I would set up a sequential test, which is designed to be checked while it runs.
A test set to split traffic 50/50 has 50,000 users in A and 47,000 in B. What do you do?
Whether you check that a test ran correctly before reading its result.
Recognizes a sample ratio mismatch, confirms it with a chi-square test, and finds the cause before trusting any lift.

With 97,000 users, a gap that size is far too big to be chance; a chi-square test confirms it. It is called a sample ratio mismatch, and it means something drops users from one arm: a redirect that loses tracking, a slower page, bot filtering. I would not read the result. I would find the cause, fix it and rerun the test.
The team tested 20 headlines against the control and one won at p = 0.04. Do we roll it out?
Whether you understand that many comparisons produce chance winners.
Knows that 20 comparisons at 0.05 make a false winner likely, adjusts the threshold or retests the winner alone.

Not yet. With 20 comparisons at a 5% threshold, there is about a 64% chance at least one looks like a winner by luck alone. A p of 0.04 does not survive a Bonferroni correction, which here needs about 0.0025. I would run that headline alone against the control as a fresh test, sized for the lift we saw.
When cash is tight, would you show the CFO the LTV to CAC ratio or the payback period?
Your grasp of unit economics the way finance sees them.
Payback, built on gross margin not revenue, because it shows how long cash is tied up; LTV to CAC can look healthy while cash runs out.

Payback period first. It is the months of gross margin a customer needs to repay what we spent to acquire them. A 4 to 1 LTV to CAC ratio can still mean waiting years for the money, and LTV rests on guesses about retention. I would show payback by channel, on gross margin, since some channels pay back in months and others take years.
After Apple's App Tracking Transparency, our app campaigns report far fewer conversions while installs and sales hold steady. How do you adjust?
Whether you can keep measuring when user-level tracking is lost.
Sees a measurement loss, not a performance drop, and leans on aggregate data, first-party data and holdout tests rather than cutting spend.

Since iOS 14.5, apps must ask permission before tracking people across other companies' apps and sites, and many say no. The platforms see fewer conversions; the business did not change. I would not cut spend on that signal. I would compare spend with total installs and revenue over time, use Apple's aggregated attribution data, and run regional holdouts.
A TV campaign launched the same week as a price cut, and sales rose 18%. Leadership asks how much came from TV. What do you answer?
How you give an honest answer when two changes overlap.
Says the data cannot fully separate them, uses what can (regions without TV, timing, branded search), gives a range, and asks to stagger launches next time.

I would say plainly that launching both together blurs the answer. Then I use what we have. If TV aired only in some markets, I compare those with markets that got only the price cut, and I check whether branded search jumped on air dates. I give a range, not one number, and ask that next time we stagger launches or keep some markets dark.

marketing-coordinator.heading: Marketing coordinator questions
qs: What is a content calendar, and what do you put in one?
Whether you know the basic planning tool a marketing team runs on.
Dates, channels, owners, status and deadlines for drafts and approvals, not just publish dates.

It is a shared schedule of everything we plan to publish. For each item I list the date and time, the channel, the topic, who writes it, who approves it, and its status. I also add the draft and approval deadlines, because a post usually goes wrong at the approval step, not the publish step.
What is a UTM parameter, and why would you add one to a link?
Your grasp of how campaign results are tracked.
Tags added to a URL so analytics can show which source, medium and campaign brought the visitor.

It is a tag added to the end of a link, like source, medium and campaign. When someone clicks, the analytics tool records where they came from. If the spring email and the Instagram post both link to the same page, UTMs let me tell which one drove the sign-ups. I keep names lowercase and consistent so reports do not split.
After an email send, which numbers do you look at, and which one do you trust least?
Whether you can read email results with some judgement.
Clicks, conversions, unsubscribes and bounces; open rate trusted least because privacy features inflate it.

I look at click rate, conversions, unsubscribes and bounces. I trust open rate least. Some email apps, like Apple Mail with its privacy setting on, load images automatically, so an email can count as opened when nobody read it. I use opens to compare subject lines loosely, and clicks to judge the email.
Walk me through what you check before a marketing email goes out.
Your attention to detail and basic email rules.
Test send, links, personalization, the right list, plus an unsubscribe link and postal address, as CAN-SPAM requires.

I send a test to myself and a teammate and open it on a phone and a laptop. I click every link, check the discount code, and check that the first-name field has a fallback so nobody gets Hi blank. I confirm the audience list and send time. Last, I make sure the unsubscribe link works and our physical postal address is in the footer, which the law requires.
A local creator will post about our product in exchange for free items. What needs to happen first?
Whether you know the disclosure rules for paid or gifted posts.
The FTC expects a clear, visible disclosure of the connection, even when payment is only free product.

Free product counts as a material connection, so the FTC expects the post to say so clearly. I would put it in writing: the creator adds something like #ad or Gifted by us at the start of the caption or says it in the video, not buried in hashtags. I would also check their posts after they go live and keep a record.
You find a great photo on Google Images for our Friday post. Can we use it?
Your understanding of image rights.
No by default: images are usually copyrighted. Use owned, licensed or properly credited free-license images.

Not unless we know we have the right. Most images online are copyrighted even with no notice on them. I would use our own photos, our paid stock library within its license terms, or ask the owner for written permission. Being findable on Google does not mean free to use, and a takedown or invoice later costs more than a stock photo.
Walk me through planning a customer event for 50 people, six weeks out.
How you organize an event from start to finish.
Budget and goal first, then venue, invitations, RSVPs, vendors and a run of show, with a timeline backwards from the date.

I confirm the goal and budget, then book the venue and catering in week one, since those fill up. Invitations go out about four weeks ahead with an RSVP date. I keep one sheet with vendors, costs and contacts. The week before, I write a run of show: who does what, minute by minute. Afterward, I send a thank-you email and report attendance against the goal.
The designer tells you Thursday's launch banner will be two days late. What do you do?
How you handle a slipping deadline that affects others.
Learn why, look for options, tell the owner early with choices, and update the schedule.

I ask what is holding it up; sometimes it is waiting on copy or feedback I can chase. If it is truly late, I look at options: launch with a simpler version, or move the post and email. Then I tell my manager that day with those choices, not on Thursday morning, and update the calendar and anyone else waiting on it.
Two managers each want their project done first by Friday, and you cannot do both. How do you handle it?
Your judgement when priorities conflict.
Not choosing silently: make the conflict visible and let the person who sets priorities decide.

I would not quietly pick one. I would write down what each task needs and how long it takes, then bring both to my direct manager, or to both managers together, and ask which comes first. While they decide, I would start on any shared piece. Then I tell both people what was agreed and when each will be done.
A promo email went to 8,000 subscribers with the wrong discount code. What do you do in the first hour?
How you handle a public mistake under time pressure.
Stop further sends, tell the manager, fix it at the source if possible, then a short correction, and a check to prevent repeats.

First I pause any scheduled resends and tell my manager right away. Then I check whether we can make the wrong code work at checkout, which fixes it for everyone who already clicked. If not, we send a short correction with the right code and a brief apology. I also tell customer service so they can help callers. Later I add a code test to our pre-send checklist.
What is the difference between reach and impressions?
Whether you read basic social media numbers correctly.
Reach counts unique accounts that saw the content. Impressions count every time it was shown, so impressions are equal to or higher than reach.

Reach is how many different accounts saw the post. Impressions count every time it appeared on a screen, so one person scrolling past it three times is one reach and three impressions. If impressions climb much faster than reach, the same people keep seeing it, and we may need new audiences rather than more posts.
A flyer looks bright on screen but dull when it comes back from the printer. What happened?
Your grasp of the print basics behind campaign materials.
Screens use RGB light and printers use CMYK ink. Some bright screen colors cannot be printed, so files are set up in CMYK and checked on a printed proof.

Screens mix red, green and blue light, while printers use cyan, magenta, yellow and black ink. Some bright RGB colors fall outside what ink can reproduce, so they print flatter. Next time I would ask the designer for a CMYK print-ready PDF with bleed, which is extra image past the cut line, and approve a printed proof before the full run.
What is the difference between a hard bounce and a soft bounce, and what do you do about each?
Whether you keep an email list clean.
Hard bounces are permanent and get suppressed at once. Soft bounces are temporary, but repeated ones are treated as hard to protect sender reputation.

A hard bounce is a permanent failure, like a misspelled or closed address, so I suppress it right away. A soft bounce is temporary, like a full inbox or a server that is down, and the platform usually retries. If an address soft bounces on several sends in a row, I treat it as a hard bounce, because mailing dead addresses hurts our sender reputation.
How do you make an email or a social post accessible to someone using a screen reader?
Whether accessibility is part of your routine, not an afterthought.
Useful alt text, no key message trapped in an image, good contrast, camel-case hashtags, captions and descriptive links.

I write alt text that says what the image shows and why it matters, not a file name. I never put the main message only inside an image, and I keep text contrast high. Hashtags go in camel case, like #SpringSale, so screen readers say the words. Videos get captions, and links say where they go instead of “click here.”
How would you set up a subject line test so the result actually means something?
How you run a fair email test and read it honestly.
One variable, random groups, a winning metric chosen in advance, caution about inflated opens, and calling a tie when the gap is small.

I change only the subject line and keep the content, sender and send time the same. The platform splits a random part of the list into two groups, and I pick the winning metric before sending. I lean on clicks, because Apple Mail Privacy Protection inflates open rates. If the groups are small or the gap is tiny, I call it a tie instead of crowning a winner.
A venue sends the contract for our client dinner. What do you look for before it goes to signature?
Whether you spot the clauses in an event contract that cost money.
Food and beverage minimum, attrition, cancellation terms, service charges and tax, AV and insurance, plus knowing who is allowed to sign.

I check the food and beverage minimum, the attrition clause that charges us if fewer guests come, and the cancellation dates and fees. I look at whether service charge and tax sit on top of the quoted price, what AV costs extra, and whether they need our insurance certificate. Then I send my manager a short summary of the risks, since signing is not my call.
My manager wants to buy a list of 20,000 emails to grow fast. What do you tell him?
Your judgement when a quick win puts the email program at risk.
Explains the risks plainly: complaints, bounces, spam traps, platform bans. Then offers a better way to grow the list.

I would explain the risk calmly. Those people never asked to hear from us, so complaints and bounces go up, and bought lists often hide spam traps that can get our domain filtered. Most email platforms ban purchased lists in their terms and can suspend the account. I would propose growing the list through a sign-up offer or an event instead.
A customer replies “take me off your list” to our newsletter, and a sales rep still wants to email him offers. What do you do?
Whether you know and apply the opt-out rules for commercial email.
Honors the request across all marketing email within the CAN-SPAM deadline of 10 business days, and explains to the rep what is still allowed.

Even though he did not click the link, I treat his request as an opt-out and suppress him everywhere we send marketing from. Under CAN-SPAM, opt-outs must be honored within 10 business days. I would tell the rep that order and account emails can continue, but no promotional messages unless the customer opts back in himself.
A tragic news event breaks while we have upbeat posts scheduled for the next three days. What do you do?
How you protect the brand when the news changes fast.
Pauses everything first, tells the manager, reviews each item before restarting, and has a plan ready for next time.

I pause the whole queue first, on every platform plus any scheduled emails, because a cheerful post next to bad news reads as tone-deaf. Then I tell my manager what is paused and when each item was due. We review the posts together and restart only when the team agrees the tone fits. Afterward I write a short checklist so the next pause takes minutes.
Our webinar campaign got 120 sign-ups against a goal of 200. How do you write the recap?
Whether you can report a miss honestly and turn it into next steps.
Leads with the gap, breaks results down by channel against past campaigns, and ends with specific changes backed by data.

I lead with the number and the gap, with no spin. Then I break sign-ups down by channel and compare each to past campaigns, so we see where it fell short: maybe email held steady and paid social underdelivered. I list what worked, what I would change, and one or two tests for next time, with the data behind each point.

marketing-manager.heading: Marketing manager questions
qs: What are CAC and LTV, and how do you use them together?
Whether you know the two numbers that say if growth pays for itself.
Clear definitions, and the point that what you can spend to win a customer depends on what that customer is worth over time.

CAC is customer acquisition cost: total sales and marketing spend divided by new customers won. LTV is lifetime value: the gross profit a customer brings over the whole relationship. If LTV is not comfortably above CAC, each new customer loses money. I also watch how many months it takes to earn back CAC, since cash can run out long before a lifetime ends.
Walk me through what goes into a campaign brief.
How you set up a campaign before anyone starts making anything.
One goal with a number, a defined audience, one main message, channels, budget, dates and the metric that will judge success.

I start with the business goal and a number, like 400 demo requests in eight weeks. Then the audience, the problem we solve for them, and the one message they should remember. Then channels, budget, deadlines, who approves, and the metric we will judge it by. If a brief runs past two pages, it is usually hiding a decision nobody made.
What do you set up before a campaign goes live so you can measure it?
Whether your results can be trusted before the first dollar is spent.
Consistent UTM tags, conversion tracking tested end to end, and a baseline written down to compare against.

I agree a naming scheme for UTM tags, the small labels added to links that tell analytics which source, medium and campaign a visit came from. I fire a test conversion myself and confirm it shows up in analytics and the CRM. And I write down the baseline: leads and sales in the four weeks before, so we can see the real change.
Your email open rate jumped 20 points overnight. What do you check?
Whether you question a number that looks too good.
Knowing that privacy features and security scanners can register opens automatically, and judging email by clicks and conversions instead.

First, I would not celebrate. Some mail apps now preload images for privacy, which logs an open whether or not anyone read the email, and corporate security scanners do the same. I would split opens by mail client, check whether clicks and conversions moved too, and from then on report email results on clicks and revenue.
Our emails started landing in spam. Where do you look?
How you diagnose an email deliverability problem.
Sender authentication, list quality, bounce and complaint rates, and any recent change in volume or content.

First, authentication: the SPF, DKIM and DMARC records that prove to inbox providers the mail really comes from us. Then list hygiene: old addresses, bounces, a bought list someone slipped in. Then spam complaints and any sudden jump in volume. I would pause the least engaged segment and mail only recent clickers and buyers while our reputation recovers.
A creator we pay posted about our product without saying it was paid. What do you do?
Whether you know the FTC rules on paid endorsements.
Get a clear disclosure added fast, since the brand can be held responsible too, then build disclosure rules and monitoring into every deal.

I would ask the creator to edit the post today with a clear disclosure, like #ad or “paid partnership,” placed where people will see it, not buried in a pile of hashtags. FTC guidance says a paid relationship must be disclosed, and brands are expected to instruct and monitor the people they pay. Then I add the rule to our contracts and check posts before payment.
Our ad platforms together claim 650 sales last month, but we only had 400. How do you explain that?
Whether you understand attribution and how each platform counts credit.
Each platform claims any sale it touched, so credit overlaps; the fix is one source of truth, one model, and tests of what is truly incremental.

Each platform claims a sale if its ad was seen or clicked within its own window, so a buyer who saw a social ad and later clicked a search ad is counted twice. I would treat our own order system as the truth, use one attribution model across channels, and run a holdout test, pausing a channel in some regions, to see what it really adds.
Leads are up 40% this quarter but pipeline is flat. Your boss wants to open the report with the 40%. What do you do?
Your honesty in reporting and whether you measure what the business cares about.
Show both numbers, explain the gap, and steer the team toward pipeline and revenue rather than lead volume.

I would put both numbers on the first slide. More leads with flat pipeline usually means lower quality, maybe from an easy content offer or loose targeting. I would bring a breakdown by source showing which leads became sales meetings, and a plan to move spend there. A flattering number gets found out at the next review anyway.
An email with the wrong discount code just went to 200,000 customers. Walk me through the next hour.
How you handle a costly mistake under pressure.
Stop further sends, decide quickly with finance whether to honor it, send one clear correction, and fix the step that let it through.

First I stop any scheduled resends and check whether the code works and what it could cost. With finance and support, I decide fast whether to honor it; a short window often costs less than angry customers. Then one short, honest correction, a script for support, and from now on a second person checks every code before a send.
Our target is $2 million in new revenue next year. Walk me through how you turn that into a marketing plan.
How you build a plan backward from a revenue goal.
Works back through deal size and conversion rates to leads and budget, then checks the result against sales capacity and past data.

I divide $2 million by the average first-year deal, say $10,000, so we need 200 customers. If 20% of opportunities close, that is 1,000 opportunities. If 10% of leads become opportunities, that is 10,000 leads. Then I price those leads by channel from last year's cost per lead, and I check that sales can handle that volume before I ask for budget.
What does US law require in every marketing email we send?
Whether you know the CAN-SPAM basics that apply to every commercial email.
Honest sender details and subject line, a valid postal address, an ad label unless the person opted in, and a working opt-out honored within 10 business days.

Under CAN-SPAM, the from line and subject must not mislead, and the email needs our valid physical postal address. Unless the person opted in, it must clearly say it is an ad. It needs a clear opt-out that works for at least 30 days after sending, and we honor opt-outs within 10 business days. If an agency sends it for us, we are still responsible.
Paid search brings customers at a $40 cost per acquisition, and our ceiling is $60. The CFO says double the spend. What do you say?
Whether you know that the average cost and the cost of the next dollar are different.
Explains diminishing returns: the extra customers cost more than the average, so scale in steps and watch the cost of the added customers.

The $40 is an average. The cheapest searches are already bought, so new dollars go to higher bids and weaker keywords. If doubling spend from $20,000 to $40,000 adds 300 customers instead of 500, those extra customers cost about $67, above our ceiling. I'd raise spend in steps of about 20% and track the cost of the added customers, not the blended number.
We spend $15,000 a month bidding on our own brand name. Is that money well spent?
How you question spend that may be buying sales you would get anyway.
No automatic yes or no: competitors bidding on the name matter, and pausing brand ads in some regions shows the real lift.

Brand ads look great because people searching our name were already looking for us, and many would click the free listing instead. But if competitors bid on our name, the ad protects those clicks. I'd pause brand ads in a few matched regions for four weeks and compare total sales from brand searches, paid plus free, against regions that kept the ads.
How would you prove our retargeting ads cause sales rather than just follow them?
Whether you can measure the sales an ad creates, not just the sales it gets credit for.
A random holdout group that sees no ads; the real effect is the gap in buying rate between the two groups, and cost is judged against that gap.

Retargeting reaches people who already visited, so many would buy anyway. I'd randomly hold out about 10% of the audience from the ads and run long enough for a solid sample. If 4% of the group that saw ads buys and 3.6% of the holdout buys, only 0.4 points come from the ads, and I'd judge the cost against that, not the full 4%.
Your team checks A/B tests daily and stops each one the first day it shows a significant result. What is wrong with that?
Whether you understand how stopping early produces false winners.
Each extra look raises the chance of a false winner; fix sample size and run time in advance, or use a method built for checking early.

Every look is another chance for random noise to cross the line, so stopping at the first significant day crowns many winners that are not real. I'd set the sample size before the test, based on the smallest lift we care about, run full weeks to cover weekday swings, and call it only at the end. If we must look early, we use a sequential method designed for that.
Product wants the headline “Twice as fast as any competitor.” What do you need before it runs?
Whether you know a claim needs proof before it runs, not after.
Knows the FTC expects a reasonable basis for objective claims before the ad runs, and that the proof must match the exact wording.

The FTC expects us to have a reasonable basis for an objective claim before it runs. “Any competitor” means we tested against every real competitor, on fair settings, recently, and won by at least double. We usually can't prove that, so I'd narrow it to what we tested, like “twice as fast as the two leading tools in our test,” and keep the test records on file.
Someone suggests sending a $10 gift card to customers who leave a five-star review. What do you say?
Whether you know the FTC rules on rewarded reviews.
No: the FTC rule on consumer reviews bans rewards that depend on a positive review. Offer the same reward for any honest review instead.

I'd stop it. The FTC rule on consumer reviews bans rewards that depend on the review being positive, and breaking it can bring civil penalties. If we want more reviews, we ask every recent buyer and offer the same reward for any honest review, good or bad, and we make the reward clear. We also show negative reviews instead of hiding them.
When would you use a marketing mix model instead of multi-touch attribution?
Whether you know the main measurement methods and where each one fails.
Attribution follows tracked clicks and misses what it can't track; a mix model uses spend and sales over time and covers offline. Both are checked with tests.

Multi-touch attribution splits credit across tracked clicks and views. It is fast and detailed for digital, but blind to TV, word of mouth and users hidden by privacy settings. A mix model uses two or more years of weekly spend and sales to estimate each channel's effect, offline included. I'd use the model for yearly budget splits and check it against holdout tests.

marketing-operations.heading: Marketing operations manager questions
qs: In lead scoring, what is the difference between fit and engagement, and why keep them apart?
Whether you understand how a scoring model is built.
Fit is who the lead is and engagement is what they do. Kept apart, a busy student does not look like a ready buyer.

Fit scores who the person is: job title, company size, industry, region. Engagement scores what they do: demo requests, pricing page visits, webinars. I keep two scores because a student who downloads everything can pile up points while a VP who asked for a demo once looks cold. Engagement points should also decay over time.
How do you keep UTM tracking clean when many people on the team build their own links?
How you protect the data that every campaign report depends on.
A fixed naming convention, a shared link builder, and regular checks for stray values, since tools treat 'Email' and 'email' as different.

I publish one convention: lowercase only, a fixed list of sources and mediums, campaign names with a date. People build links in a shared builder that only offers those values. Most analytics tools are case sensitive, so 'LinkedIn' and 'linkedin' split into two rows. Once a month I pull the source and medium list and fix anything off it.
What does CAN-SPAM require of a commercial email we send?
Your knowledge of the US law that governs marketing email.
Honest headers and subject lines, a physical postal address, a working opt-out honored within 10 business days, and responsibility even when a vendor sends.

The from line and subject cannot mislead. Each email needs a valid physical postal address and a clear way to opt out that keeps working for at least 30 days after sending. We must honor opt-outs within 10 business days, with no fee and no demand for more than an email address. If an agency sends for us, we are still responsible.
Open rates jumped after Apple Mail Privacy Protection came in. How do you treat opens now?
Whether you know which email metrics still mean something.
Opens are inflated by machine opens, so you rely on clicks and conversions and keep opens out of scoring and test decisions.

Mail Privacy Protection loads images on Apple's servers, so many emails register as opened whether anyone read them or not. I still watch opens as a rough health signal, but I took open points out of lead scoring, judge tests on clicks and conversions, and build re-engagement lists from clicks or site visits instead of opens.
Explain SPF, DKIM and DMARC as you would to a marketing director.
Your grasp of email authentication, the base of deliverability.
SPF lists who may send, DKIM signs the message, DMARC ties them to the from address, sets what happens on failure and sends reports.

SPF is a list in our domain's DNS of servers allowed to send as us. DKIM adds a digital signature proving the message came from our domain and was not changed. DMARC checks that these line up with the visible from address, tells inboxes to deliver, quarantine or reject mail that fails, and sends us reports. Without them, more of our mail lands in spam.
Clicks on the newsletter fell by half overnight and one big mailbox provider seems to send it to spam. What do you do first?
How you diagnose a deliverability problem under time pressure.
Hold big sends, check authentication, complaints and recent changes, then send only to engaged contacts and ramp volume back slowly.

I hold the next big send. I confirm SPF, DKIM and DMARC still pass, since a DNS change can break them, and check the provider's sender dashboard for complaints and reputation. Then I ask what changed: a list import, a new link domain, a bigger send. While it recovers I mail only people who clicked recently and raise volume step by step.
Reps say the MQLs you pass are not ready to buy. How do you find out whether the scoring model is the problem?
Whether you test a scoring model against outcomes instead of opinions.
Follow past leads to their outcomes, compare scores of won deals and rejected leads, and reset the threshold with sales.

I pull two quarters of MQLs and follow each to its outcome: rejected with a reason, opportunity, won. If won deals and rejected leads score about the same, the model is not separating them. Often one action, like a content download, is overweighted. I reweight, test the new model on past data, and agree the threshold with the sales lead before switching.
A workflow you built overwrote the lead source field on 20,000 records. What do you do?
How you own and recover from a data mistake.
Stop the workflow, find the scope, restore from history or backup, tell the people whose reports were affected, and add a safeguard.

I turn the workflow off so it stops spreading. I find exactly which records changed and when, using field history or the last export, and restore the original values. I tell the sales ops and reporting owners which dashboards were wrong for which dates. Then I add a rule that lead source is only set when blank, and I test workflows on a small list first.
The CFO asks which channel drove last quarter's pipeline. How do you answer?
Your judgement about attribution models and their limits.
More than one model, what each one favors, and honesty that attribution shows association, not proof of cause.

I show first touch, last touch and a multi-touch view side by side. First touch favors channels that find people, like paid social; last touch favors ones that close, like branded search. Where they agree I am confident, and where they differ I say so. For a causal answer on a big channel, I would propose a holdout test: pause it in some regions and compare.
Walk me through your first 60 days auditing a marketing tech stack you inherited.
How you take stock of tools, data and processes before changing them.
Inventory tools, owners and costs, map and test data flows, find broken syncs and unused licenses, then rank fixes with stakeholders.

First I list every tool, its owner, cost and renewal date. Then I map how data moves from forms to the email platform, the CRM and reports, and test each sync with a fake lead. I check field definitions, duplicates and old workflows nobody remembers. By day 60 I share a ranked list of what is broken, what is wasted and what to fix first, and agree the order with sales.
What is the difference between a hard bounce and a soft bounce, and how should each be handled?
Your grasp of list hygiene and how it protects sender reputation.
Hard bounces are permanent and suppressed right away. Soft bounces are temporary and suppressed only after repeated failures.

A hard bounce is a permanent failure, like an address that does not exist. I suppress it at once, because mailing dead addresses hurts our reputation with mailbox providers. A soft bounce is temporary, like a full mailbox or a server that is down. Most platforms retry, and I suppress an address only after several soft bounces in a row. I also check the exact rule our platform applies.
How do you define lifecycle stages so that funnel reports can be trusted?
Whether you can build a funnel that counts the same way every month.
One written entry rule per stage, a date stamp when a record enters it, and stages that only move forward, with recycling as its own path.

Each stage gets one written entry rule agreed with sales, such as a score over the threshold plus a business email. When a record enters a stage, a workflow stamps the date in its own field and never overwrites it. Records do not move backward. A lost deal sends the person to a recycled status. That way conversion rates and time between stages stay honest.
The marketing platform and the CRM both store job title and lead status. How do you decide which system wins when they disagree?
How you design the data sync between marketing and sales systems.
A named owner and sync direction for each field, written down, so blank or stale values never overwrite good data.

I keep a field map. Each field gets one system of record: sales owns lead status and owner in the CRM, marketing owns source and score. For shared fields like job title, I let the newest non-blank value win, so an empty form field never wipes good data. The map lives in a shared document, and any new field or sync change goes through review first.
Walk me through how you test a multi-step nurture before you turn it on.
Whether you catch errors before contacts do.
