For a sentinel event we finish the analysis and action plan within 45 business days, then check the fixes work.
A vendor offers an algorithm that predicts length of stay to drive post-acute denials for our Medicare Advantage members. Would you use it?
Your judgement on automated tools in coverage decisions.
Only as support. Decisions must rest on the member's own circumstances and Medicare coverage criteria, with a physician reviewing denials.

Only as a flag for review, never as the decision. CMS rules say Medicare Advantage plans must base medical necessity decisions on the member's own circumstances and Medicare coverage criteria, not on an algorithm's prediction alone. I would test it for accuracy and bias, have a physician review every denial, and audit how often its flags end in overturned decisions.

mental-health.heading: Mental health and therapy questions
qs: Walk me through the first session with a new client.
How you run an intake assessment and set up the work.
Consent and the limits of confidentiality first, then history, symptoms, a risk screen and the client's own goals.

I start with consent: how sessions work, fees, and the limits of confidentiality, like serious risk of harm and child abuse reporting. Then I ask what brings them in now, symptom history, past treatment, health, substance use, sleep and support. I always screen for suicide risk. I end by agreeing on what they want to be different.
How would you explain CBT to a client who has never had therapy?
Whether you can explain your main method in plain words.
The link between thoughts, feelings and actions, a practical tone, and the fact that the client practices between sessions.

I'd say how we read a situation shapes how we feel and what we do. If you think a friend's silence means she's angry, you feel hurt and avoid her. We'll learn to catch those thoughts, test them against the facts, and try new actions. It's practical, usually time-limited, and includes short practice between sessions.
How do you use measures like the PHQ-9 or GAD-7 in your work?
Whether you use measurement to guide treatment, not just to fill in a form.
Given at intake and regularly after, scores reviewed with the client and used to adjust the plan. A screener alone is not a diagnosis.

I give them at intake and then every few sessions, and I go over the scores with the client. If the PHQ-9 isn't dropping after several weeks, I rethink the plan. They are screeners, not diagnoses. I always read item 9, the question about thoughts of death or self-harm, right away and follow up in that same session.
A client says, “I just want to feel less anxious.” How do you turn that into a treatment goal?
How you write a treatment plan with goals you can measure.
A specific, measurable goal tied to daily life, in the client's words, with a timeframe and a way to track progress.

I ask what she would do if anxiety weren't in the way. Say she'd drive on the highway again. The goal becomes: drive a 15-minute highway route alone, with anxiety under 4 out of 10, within 12 weeks. The steps are learning calming skills and working through a graded exposure list. We also track her GAD-7 score monthly.
What goes into a good progress note?
Your clinical documentation and whether it would hold up to an audit or a records request.
A standard format like SOAP or DAP, linked to the treatment plan, factual, with risk noted and a clear plan for next time.

I use DAP. Data is what the client reported and what I observed, plus any scores. Assessment is my clinical read and progress toward the plan's goals. Plan is homework and next steps. I note any risk screen and what I did about it. I keep it factual, write it the same day, and remember the client may read it.
What do you check at the start of every video session?
Whether you know how to run telehealth safely and legally.
The client's current location and an emergency contact, a private space, a backup plan, and a license valid where the client is.

I confirm where the client is right now: in a crisis I need to send local help, and I must be licensed for the state they are in. I check they're alone and can talk freely, and I have a phone number in case video drops. I use a HIPAA-compliant platform. If they're driving or at work, we reschedule or adjust.
Your client with panic attacks keeps texting you for reassurance between sessions. What do you do?
How you apply CBT when the client's way of coping is part of the problem.
Seeing reassurance as a safety behavior that keeps anxiety going, setting a kind boundary, and building exposure into the plan.

Reassurance calms panic for a minute but teaches her she can't cope alone, so the fear stays. I'd raise it in session without blame, explain that, and agree on clear rules for contact. Then we'd practice sitting with uncertainty and do interoceptive exposure, like spinning in a chair to bring on dizziness, so she learns the sensations are safe.
A former client sends you a friend request on social media. What do you do?
Your judgement on boundaries and dual relationships.
Not accepting, protecting the client's privacy, and explaining the policy kindly, ideally one already set out at intake.

I don't accept, and I don't reply on the platform, since even a reply could show we're connected. My consent form says I don't connect with current or former clients online, so if it comes up I point back to that. If they return to therapy, I'd talk about it openly: it protects their privacy and our work, it's not a rejection.
On a video session, a client says she has been thinking she'd be better off dead. Walk me through what you do.
How you assess suicide risk and act on it.
Asking directly about plan, intent, means and history, building a safety plan, acting on the level of risk, consulting and documenting.

I stay calm and ask directly if she is thinking of killing herself. Asking does not plant the idea. Then plan, intent, access to means, past attempts and reasons to live. If risk is lower, we write a safety plan together and put means out of reach. If she has intent and means, I keep her on the call and get emergency help to her location. Then I consult and document.
Your client has had 10 sessions of CBT for depression and her scores have not moved. What do you do?
How you handle treatment that is not working.
Reviewing it openly with the client, rechecking diagnosis, alliance and barriers, getting consultation, and changing course or referring.

I'd show her the scores and ask what she thinks is getting in the way. Then I recheck: is the diagnosis right, could it be bipolar or a medical issue, is she drinking, is homework happening, does she trust me? I'd take it to consultation. Options include behavioral activation, a referral for a medication evaluation, or a different therapist or level of care.
How do you tell generalized anxiety disorder apart from ordinary worry?
Your grasp of the diagnostic criteria, not just the label.
Worry that is excessive, hard to control and present more days than not for six months, with physical symptoms and real impairment.

Everyone worries. For GAD under DSM-5-TR, the worry is excessive, hard to control, and present more days than not for at least six months. In adults, at least three symptoms come with it, like restlessness, fatigue, poor sleep or muscle tension, and it causes real distress or impairment. I also rule out substances, medical causes and other disorders that explain it better.
Why does behavioral activation work for depression, and how do you start it?
Whether you understand the model behind a core depression treatment.
Withdrawal cuts off reward and keeps mood low. You start with monitoring, then schedule small, specific activities tied to what the client values.

Depression makes people pull back, which removes the things that lift mood, so mood drops further. I start with a week of activity and mood monitoring. Then we schedule small, specific activities, picked from what matters to the client, and act before motivation arrives instead of waiting for it. We review what happened, not just whether it got done.
Walk me through how you build a case formulation for a new client.
How you turn an assessment into a working explanation that guides treatment.
Links triggers, thoughts, feelings and behaviors into a cycle that keeps the problem going, shared with the client and revised as you learn.

I start with the current problem and map one recent episode: the trigger, the thought, the feeling, the body response and what the client did. Then I ask what keeps it going, like avoidance, and what made them vulnerable in the first place. I draw it out with the client, check it fits, and use it to pick targets. It is a hypothesis, so I revise it.
In exposure work for social anxiety, why do you pay attention to safety behaviors?
Your understanding of what makes exposure work or fail.
Safety behaviors stop the client learning that the feared outcome is unlikely or bearable. You name them and drop them during exposures.

Things like rehearsing sentences, avoiding eye contact or holding a drink to hide shaking feel protective, but the client then credits them for getting through. The fear never gets tested. I list them with the client, explain this, and we drop them during exposures, then compare what they predicted with what really happened.
Why do you ask about past manic or hypomanic episodes before you treat depression?
Whether you screen for bipolar disorder before treating a depressed client.
A depressive episode can be part of bipolar disorder, which changes the plan. You screen for it and coordinate with a prescriber when signs appear.

Many people with bipolar disorder first come in depressed, and they rarely mention the highs unless asked. I ask about times of needing much less sleep, racing thoughts, unusual energy or risky spending, and I check family history. If I see signs, I coordinate with the prescriber, because antidepressants alone can be risky in bipolar disorder.
Your client has started arriving late and answering in one word. What do you do?
How you notice and repair a strain in the therapeutic relationship.
Raising it openly and without blame, inviting criticism, owning your part and adjusting the work together.

I would name it gently: 'I have noticed things feel different lately, and I wonder if something in our work is not sitting right.' Then I listen without defending. Often it is pace, like pushing homework too fast. I own my part, we agree on a change, and I check back the next week. A repaired rupture often makes the relationship stronger.
A client you see online says she will spend the next two months at her parents' home in another state. What do you do?
Whether you know telehealth licensure follows where the client is located.
Practice rules generally depend on where the client is during the session. You check that state's rules and any compact before continuing, and plan for gaps.

In general I need to be allowed to practice in the state where the client is during the session, not where I sit. So before she leaves I check that state's rules, any temporary practice allowance, and whether an interstate compact covers my license. If I cannot see her there, we plan a pause, a local referral and an emergency contact near her.
An adult client tells you her partner hits her 8-year-old son. Walk me through what you do.
Your handling of mandatory reporting while keeping the client engaged.
Knows this must be reported under state law, reports promptly, tells the client when it is safe to, and keeps safety planning going.

Child abuse is something I must report under state law, and I explained that limit of confidentiality at intake. I get enough detail to report, then tell her I will be calling child protective services and why, unless telling her would put her or the child in more danger. I make the report promptly, document it, and we work on a safety plan for both of them.
A client says he is so angry at his former boss that he could kill him. How do you handle it?
Your violence risk assessment and your grasp of duty-to-warn rules.
Assesses intent, plan, means and history; knows the duty to warn or protect differs by state; consults and documents each step.

I take it seriously without overreacting. I ask whether he means it, whether he has a plan, access to weapons, or a history of violence. Most statements like this are anger, not intent. If the risk is real, I follow my state's duty-to-warn or protect law, which differs by state, consult my supervisor, and document what I assessed and why I acted.
An insurance reviewer asks for your psychotherapy notes on a client. How do you respond?
Whether you know how HIPAA treats psychotherapy notes compared with the rest of the record.
Separately kept psychotherapy notes need the client's specific authorization, and a plan cannot require it for payment. Share only the minimum necessary.

Under HIPAA, notes I keep separately about session content are psychotherapy notes, and releasing them needs the client's specific authorization. A health plan cannot make that a condition of paying. I offer what the review needs from the record: dates, diagnosis, treatment plan, symptoms and progress, limited to the minimum necessary, and I tell the client what was shared.

merchant-support.heading: Merchant and partner support questions
qs: How is supporting a merchant different from supporting a shopper?
Whether you understand that a merchant's problem is a problem for their whole business.
Time is money for them, one issue can hit many orders, and the relationship is long term, so you fix the cause and follow up.

A shopper usually has one order at stake. A restaurant with stuck orders loses sales every minute and has angry customers of its own. So I move faster, look at the whole account instead of one ticket, and follow up, because I will talk to the same owner again next month.
A restaurant owner says this week's payout is smaller than expected. Walk me through how you check it.
How you read a payout statement and explain a gap.
You rebuild it line by line: gross sales, commission, fees, refunds, adjustments and the pay period dates.

I open the statement for that period and rebuild it with the owner: gross sales, minus our commission and processing fees, minus refunds charged back to the store, plus any adjustments. Most gaps are a refund or orders that fall into the next pay period. If the math still does not match, I open a case with the payments team and give a date.
A restaurant's order tablet stops receiving orders in the middle of the dinner rush. What do you do first?
Whether you act fast to stop lost orders during an outage.
Protect open orders first, pause the store if needed, check the simple causes, and see whether other stores are hit too.

First I check whether orders are coming in and failing, so customers are not waiting on food no one is making. I can read them the open orders or pause the store if they want. Then the basics: Wi-Fi, power, app version, logging out and back in. If several stores report the same thing, I flag a possible outage instead of fixing them one by one.
A caller says they own a shop and wants to change the bank account for payouts right now. How do you handle it?
Whether you protect a merchant's money from fraud by verifying identity.
No change without the platform's verification process; a pushy, urgent caller is a warning sign, not a reason to skip steps.

Bank changes are a favorite target for fraud, so I follow our verification process every time: confirm the caller is an authorized owner the way our policy requires, and send the change through the secure flow, not over the phone. If they rush me, I stay polite and still skip nothing. A real owner would rather wait an hour than lose a week of payouts.
A driver writes that their account was deactivated and they need to work tonight. What do you say?
How you handle a partner's income with honesty about what you can and cannot change.
Empathy, the reason as far as policy allows, the appeal path and timeline, and no false promise.

I say I understand this is their income and I will check the account right away. I tell them what I am allowed to share about the reason, explain how the appeal works and what to send, like photos or trip details, and when they should hear back. I do not promise it will be reversed tonight, because I cannot decide that and false hope makes it worse.
A seller asks which tax form they will get from us and whether they owe tax on it. How do you answer?
Whether you stay inside your role on tax and legal questions.
You give the facts the platform owns, which form, when and where to find it, and send tax questions to a tax professional.

I tell them which form our platform sends, when it goes out, and where to download it in their account. I also check that the tax details on file are correct. Whether they owe tax and how much is tax advice, so I say that plainly and suggest a tax professional. A guess from me could cost them real money.
A merchant got a chargeback notice and asks what it means and what they can do.
Your grasp of card disputes and how a merchant can respond.
A chargeback is a buyer disputing a charge with their bank; the merchant can send evidence before a deadline, and you help them build it.

I explain that the buyer asked their card issuer to reverse the payment, so the money is usually taken back while the bank decides. The merchant can often respond with evidence, like delivery proof, tracking, receipts or messages with the buyer, and there is a deadline. I tell them the date, which evidence fits the buyer's stated reason, and how to submit it.
A restaurant asks you for a customer's phone number so they can follow up on a complaint. What do you do?
Whether you protect customer data while still helping the merchant.
You do not share personal data beyond what policy allows, and you offer a channel that meets the merchant's goal.

I would not give out the customer's phone number; it is personal data and our policy limits who sees it. I ask what the restaurant wants to do, maybe apologize or offer a credit, and use the tools we have, like a message through the platform. The owner gets to fix it and the customer's privacy stays safe.
One of our largest merchants says they will leave the platform unless you waive their fees. How do you handle it?
How you keep a valuable partner without making promises you cannot keep.
You listen for the real problem, stay within your authority, and bring in the account manager or the team that owns pricing.

I would not waive fees I am not allowed to waive, and I would not just say no either. I ask what is behind it: falling margins, a fee they did not expect, a competitor's offer. I fix what I can, like a wrong charge, and pass the rest to the account manager with the numbers and the owner's deadline. Then I tell the owner who will call and when.
Within an hour, several merchants in one city report a missing payout. What do you do?
Whether you spot a wider incident and escalate it instead of answering ticket by ticket.
You link the tickets, escalate early with evidence, give merchants one honest message, and update them on time.

Several similar tickets from one city in an hour is a pattern, not bad luck. I tag and link them, check what they share, such as the bank, the pay date or the app version, and escalate to the payments team with examples. Meanwhile every merchant gets the same honest message: we know, we are on it, next update by a set time. Then I keep that promise.
Walk me through what a new restaurant needs set up before it can take its first order.
Whether you know the full onboarding path, not just one step of it.
Verification, bank and tax details, menu, hours and prep times, the tablet or POS link, and a test order before going live.

First the business is verified: legal name, tax ID and the owner's identity. Then the bank details for payouts. Then the menu with prices and add-ons, opening hours and prep times. Then the tablet or POS connection, meaning the restaurant's own order system. Last, I run a test order end to end, so the first real customer is not the test.
A merchant's payout shows as sent three days ago, but it is not in their bank. How do you work it?
How you trace money after it has left the platform.
Counts business days and bank holidays, checks the bank details on file, and gives the trace number so the bank can find the deposit.

I check the send date against business days, since ACH bank transfers do not settle on weekends or federal bank holidays. I confirm the account and routing numbers on file match theirs. If all is right, I give them the trace number so their bank can find the deposit, and I open a trace with our payments team if the bank still cannot.
Onboarding fails because the business name does not match the tax ID. What do you tell the merchant?
Whether you know why tax ID matching matters and how a merchant fixes it.
The name must match IRS records exactly. Use the legal name from the IRS EIN letter, not the trade name on the sign.

Often they typed the name on the sign, not the legal name tied to their EIN, the federal tax ID. I ask them to check the IRS letter they got when the EIN was issued, or request a 147C confirmation letter from the IRS, and enter the name exactly as shown. Customers can still see their trade name on the store page.
A new merchant is angry that part of each payout is held in a reserve. How do you explain it?
Whether you can explain a risk control without it sounding like an accusation.
What a reserve is, why it exists and when the money comes back, without promising a release you cannot approve.

I say a reserve is a share of each payout we hold for a set time and then release, to cover refunds and chargebacks that can arrive weeks after a sale. It is common for new accounts with no history. I show them the release schedule on their account and say risk reviews it as their history builds. I do not promise an early release I cannot approve.
A merchant wants to fight an 'item not received' chargeback on a delivered order. What evidence do you help them gather?
Your working knowledge of how card disputes are won.
Proof tied to that exact order: address, delivery time, GPS or photo, customer messages, all sent before the deadline.

I pull the order record: the delivery address, the time it was marked delivered, the driver's GPS trail and any drop-off photo. I add messages with the customer and whether they ordered again later. I write a short summary linking each item to the claim and make sure it goes in well before the deadline, since no reply in time means the merchant loses.
A merchant refunded a customer directly after the customer had already filed a chargeback. What happens now?
Whether you spot the double-refund risk and know the fix.
The customer could be paid twice. The merchant answers the dispute with proof of the refund instead of paying again.

The customer could get the money back twice, once from the refund and once from the chargeback. I tell the merchant not to send anything more, and to answer the dispute with proof the refund was issued, with date and amount. That is a recognized defense. Then I explain that once a dispute is open, refunds should not go around it.
A shop owner says they got login codes they did not request, and now the email on their account has changed. What do you do?
How you contain an account takeover before you restore access.
Contain first: lock the account and freeze payout and bank changes, verify the real owner, then review what was changed.

I treat it as a takeover. I lock the account and freeze payouts and bank changes right away, and send it to our security team. Before restoring access I verify the owner with details already on file, not ones given on this call. Then we check what changed: bank account, menu, prices, users. Last, a new password and two-step login.
Engineering closed your escalation as 'working as intended', but merchants keep writing in about it. What do you do?
How you push back on another team with evidence, not frustration.
Counts the contacts and their cost, takes it to the product owner as a design problem, and gives agents one clear answer meanwhile.

If it works as designed, then the design is causing the contacts. I tag the tickets for two weeks and bring numbers: how many merchants, handle time, any lost orders. I take that to the product owner, not back to the same queue. Meanwhile I write one clear reply template and a help article, so agents agree and merchants know the workaround.
A new merchant shows a spike in orders from fresh accounts using a few cards, and asks for an early payout. What do you do?
Whether you recognize possible fraud and stay within your role.
No accusation and no early release. Flags the pattern to the risk team with evidence and gives the merchant a neutral answer.

That pattern can mean stolen cards, or a merchant ordering from itself to cash out. Deciding that is not my call, and neither is releasing money early. I send the order IDs and what I saw to risk, and tell the merchant early payouts are not available on their account right now. I do not accuse them; I may be wrong, and risk has the tools to check.
Payout questions are our top contact reason. How would you cut them by a third?
How you turn ticket data into fewer contacts, the work expected of a senior person.
Splits the reason into sub-reasons with data, fixes the biggest ones at the source, and measures contacts per merchant, not raw volume.

I would split payout contacts into sub-reasons from a sample of tickets: timing, deductions, holds, bank errors. Usually two or three cover most of them. For each, I ask what the merchant could not see, and work with product on a clearer payout statement or status page. I track contacts per thousand active merchants, so growth does not hide progress.

mid-market-account-executive.heading: Mid-market account executive questions
qs: How is selling to a 300-person company different from selling to a 20-person one or a 10,000-person one?
Whether you understand the segment you would be selling into.
More people than small business, less process than enterprise, cycles of weeks to a few months, and many deals run at once.

Compared with a small business, more people are involved: a department head, finance, often IT for security. Compared with enterprise, there is less procurement and legal, so a deal can close in one to three months. That means I carry more deals at once, so I qualify fast and keep each one moving with a clear next step.
How do you prepare a demo for a mid-market prospect?
Whether you show what matters to this buyer instead of the whole product.
A demo built from discovery: it opens on their problem, shows the few workflows they named, and ends with an agreed next step.

I only demo after discovery. I start by repeating the problem they told me, in their words, and check it is still right. Then I show the two or three workflows that solve it, with their kind of data, and skip features they did not ask about. I leave time for questions and end by agreeing who sees it next and when.
What is a mutual action plan, and when do you bring it in?
How you keep a deal on a timeline both sides have agreed to.
A shared list of steps, owners and dates, built back from the buyer's go-live date, introduced once the buyer sees value.

It is a short shared document: the steps both sides need to reach a signed contract and a start date, who owns each one, and by when. I build it backward from the date they want to be live. I bring it up after a good demo, when they agree the problem is worth solving. If they will not commit to any dates, that tells me the deal is not real yet.
Your contact wants to be the only person you talk to. How do you reach the rest of the buying group?
Whether you can multi-thread a deal without going around your contact.
Getting the contact's help to bring others in, framed as helping them succeed, and treating a single-threaded deal as higher risk.

I ask for help, not permission to go around them. I say: deals like this usually need finance and IT to sign off, and it goes faster if I answer their questions early so you are not stuck relaying them. I offer to prep them for that meeting. If they still refuse, I mark the deal as single-threaded and higher risk in my forecast.
You have 35 open opportunities and one week. How do you decide where to spend your time?
How you prioritize a full mid-market pipeline.
Ranking by size, stage and whether there is a real dated next step, and closing out stale deals instead of carrying them.

First I look at which deals have a dated next step with the buyer; those get my prep time. Then I rank by size and how close they are to a decision. Deals with no reply in weeks get a direct note asking if the project is still on; if not, I close them out. A clean pipeline of 20 beats a hopeful one of 35.
How do you decide which deals go in your commit for the quarter, and what happens when one slips?
Whether your manager can trust your forecast.
Commit means the decision, the signer and the paper process are confirmed, not just enthusiasm; slips are reported early with a reason.

A deal goes in commit only when the economic buyer has said yes, we know who signs, and I have walked through their legal and purchasing steps with my contact. An excited champion puts it in best case, not commit. If a commit deal starts to slip, I tell my manager the day I know, with the reason and a new date.
The CFO says they will sign by Friday if you take 25% off. What do you do?
How you handle a discount request as a trade, not a giveaway.
No instant yes: you find what drives the ask, trade any discount for something of value, and stay within your approval rules.

I would not say yes on the call. I would ask what is behind it: budget, a competing quote, or a test. If there is room, I trade rather than give: a longer term, payment upfront, or a reference, and I get any discount approved first. Cutting 25% to close three weeks early often costs more than waiting.
Their legal team sends back heavy redlines and a security questionnaire the week the deal should close. How do you keep it on track?
How you manage the paper process without losing the deal or misleading your forecast.
Bringing in your own legal and security teams at once, finding which points truly matter, and resetting dates openly.

I send the redlines to our legal team and the questionnaire to our security team the same day and ask for a review date. Then I call my contact to learn which changes they truly need and which are standard asks. I update the close date in the CRM and tell my manager. Next time I ask about legal and security steps in the first weeks.
Your champion leaves the company two weeks before the deal should close. What do you do?
How you recover a deal when your inside seller is gone.
Fast contact with the other stakeholders, a recheck of the problem and the buyer, and an honest move of the deal out of commit.

I reach out the same day to the others I have met, ideally the economic buyer, and ask who owns the project now. I set a short call to recap the problem, the value and the plan, and check it is still a priority. I move the deal out of commit until I have a new champion. I also stay in touch with the old one; they may buy again at their new company.
How do you tell a real champion from a friendly contact?
Whether you test your champion instead of assuming you have one.
A champion has power and sells for you when you are not in the room. You test that with real asks, not feelings.

A friendly contact gives me information. A champion has influence and spends it for me. I test with a real ask: set up a meeting with the VP, share the approval steps, or present our case internally. If they do it, they are a champion. If they keep saying it looks great but nothing moves, they are a coach, and I keep looking.
How much pipeline coverage do you need for next quarter, and how do you work it out?
Whether you base coverage on your own numbers rather than a rule of thumb.
Coverage comes from your own win rate and cycle length. A 3x rule means little if your win rate is 20%.

I start from my win rate on qualified opportunities. If I close about 25% of what I qualify, I need about four times my number in qualified pipeline. Then I check cycle length: if deals take 90 days, next quarter's pipeline must exist now. So with a $300,000 quota and a 25% win rate, I want about $1.2 million qualified early.
Walk me through how you build a business case with a prospect.
How you tie your price to the customer's own numbers.
The numbers come from the buyer and are checked by them, so the champion can take the case to the budget owner.

I ask for their numbers, not mine: hours spent on the task, how many people, error rates, what a delay costs. Say six analysts spend ten hours a week on manual reports. I build a one-page case with them, cost today versus cost with us, and let my champion correct it. Modest figures they own carry more weight with a CFO than big ones I made up.
The prospect uses a competitor and their contract auto-renews in eight months. When do you start, and what do you ask first?
Whether you understand renewal timing and notice periods.
The key date is the notice deadline, not the renewal date. You work back from it, leaving time for evaluation and approvals.

I start now. The first thing I ask is the notice period. Many contracts require written notice 30 to 90 days before renewal, so the real deadline may be five or six months away. I work backward from that date: evaluation, security review, legal, signature. If they miss notice, they are locked in another year, so that date goes into our plan.
A prospect asks for a free 60-day pilot before they commit. How do you respond?
How you protect the deal from a pilot that never ends.
A pilot with written success criteria, a set end date, a named decision maker and commercial terms agreed before it starts.

I am open to proving value, but not to an open trial. I ask what result would make them buy, and we write it down: for example, cut ticket handling time by 20%. We agree on a shorter time if we can, who decides at the end, and the price and contract if it succeeds. If they will not agree to that, they are not ready to buy, and I learned it cheaply.
A prospect loved the demo, then stopped answering for three weeks. What do you do?
How you re-engage without chasing or begging.
A short, useful message tied to their pain, another contact path, and a willingness to close the deal out if it is dead.

First I check myself: did we set a next step with a date? Usually not. Then I send one short note tied to their problem, not 'just checking in.' Something like, 'You said month-end close takes eight days. Is that still a priority this quarter, or should I close the file?' I also reach another person I met. A clear no beats a deal I keep forecasting.
Procurement comes in late and asks for net 90 payment terms and a three-year price lock. How do you handle it?
Whether you trade concessions instead of giving them away.
Each ask has a cost. You check with finance or the deal desk and trade it for something of value, like a longer commitment.

I don't say yes or no on the call. I find out why: is net 90 their standard policy or a test? Then I check with our deal desk, because terms affect our cash. I trade: a three-year price lock in exchange for a three-year commitment, and net 60 instead of 90 if they sign this month. Every give has a get, written into the same proposal.
In a deal review, your manager says your biggest deal is 'happy ears.' How do you respond?
Whether you can back a forecast with evidence, not enthusiasm.
Facts that came from the buyer: a met economic buyer, a confirmed process and budget. And admitting gaps instead of defending them.

I would lay out what the buyer has done, not what they said. Have I met the person who signs? Do I know their approval steps and who reviews the contract? Is the budget confirmed? Did they keep the dates in our plan? If two of those are missing, my manager is right, and I say what I will do this week to fill the gaps or move the deal out of commit.
After closing, you realize the customer believes a feature is coming that is not on the roadmap. What do you do?
Your honesty when a misunderstanding could cost the account.
Raising it fast with your team and the customer, owning your part, and offering a real path before the gap blows up later.

I raise it right away, before implementation starts. I tell my manager and customer success first, then call the customer. I say what I said, what I should have said, and what is true: the feature is not planned. Then I bring options, like a workaround or a call with a product manager. Hearing it from me now hurts less than finding out at renewal.

mission-operations.heading: Mission operations and flight controller questions
qs: What is the difference between a real-time command and a stored, time-tagged command, and when do you use each?
Whether you know the basic ways a spacecraft is commanded.
Real-time commands run when they are received during a pass. Stored ones run later by onboard time, so you check timing, order and the onboard clock.

A real-time command executes as soon as the spacecraft receives it, so I use it when I want to watch the result during the pass. A time-tagged command waits in an onboard queue and runs at a set time, often when we have no contact, like imaging over the ocean. For those I check the onboard clock, the order and that nothing in the queue conflicts.
Walk me through how you prepare for a ground station pass.
How you plan a contact so its few minutes are not wasted.
You check the schedule, station and link, review the command plan and procedures, and know the priorities and go/no-go points before the pass starts.

I confirm the pass time and station, and that the antenna and link are set up. I review the command plan against the procedures and the latest health data, and I list what must be downlinked. Before acquisition of signal I know the priorities in order, so if the pass is short or the link drops, the most important commands and data go first.
What do yellow and red limits on a telemetry point mean, and what do you do when one trips?
Your understanding of telemetry limits and how you respond when one is crossed.
Yellow is a caution to watch and report; red calls for action, usually by a written contingency procedure. First you confirm the reading is real.

A yellow limit is a caution: the value is off-nominal but not yet harmful, so I watch the trend and tell the lead. A red limit means a level that can damage the spacecraft or the mission. I first check the reading against related sensors to rule out a bad sensor, then follow the contingency procedure for that point. I do not improvise on a red limit.
You send a command and see no acknowledgment in telemetry. What do you do?
Whether you avoid resending a command blindly.
You find out whether the command arrived before sending it again, by checking counters and telemetry, because a repeat can do harm.

I do not just send it again. I check the uplink status and the onboard command counter, then the telemetry the command should change. It may have run and the report has not come down yet. If it is a toggle, a second send could undo it. If I confirm it was not received, I resend by the procedure and log both attempts.
The spacecraft has gone into safe mode and you see it at the start of a pass. Walk me through your first steps.
How you respond calmly when the spacecraft has protected itself.
Confirm power, attitude and link are stable, stop planned commands, gather the data, and do not rush recovery before the cause is known.

First I confirm it is stable: in its safe attitude, battery charging, link good. I hold the planned command load and tell the flight director. Then I dump the event log and the telemetry around the trigger. Recovery waits until we know the cause, because returning to normal mode on an unknown fault can send it straight back to safe mode, or make things worse.
Why does the battery matter so much in eclipse, and what do you watch?
Your grasp of power as a limit on what you can command.
In Earth's shadow the spacecraft runs on battery alone; you track charge and depth of discharge and plan loads so it recharges in sunlight.

In most low Earth orbits the spacecraft crosses Earth's shadow once per orbit, and then it runs only on the battery. I watch state of charge, voltage and temperature, and how deep each discharge goes, since deep cycles age the battery faster. Before a power-hungry activity, I check it fits the power budget so the battery is full again before the next eclipse.
The reaction wheels are close to their speed limit. What does that mean and what do you do?
Whether you understand momentum management on a wheel-controlled spacecraft.
Wheels absorb small outside torques and speed up over time; a momentum dump with magnetic torquers or thrusters unloads them before they saturate.

Small torques from drag, solar pressure or gravity build up, and the wheels spin faster to hold attitude. At their limit they cannot control it anymore. So we unload momentum: magnetic torquers push against Earth's field, or thrusters fire, while the wheels slow down. I track wheel speeds and schedule dumps so they do not clash with imaging or a pass.
You get a warning that another object may pass very close to your satellite in 36 hours. How do you handle it?
How you handle a collision risk and the decision to maneuver.
Follow updated predictions and collision probability, plan a maneuver early with flight dynamics, screen the new orbit, and decide by the mission's threshold.

I pull the latest conjunction data and look at miss distance, collision probability and how uncertain the orbits are. With flight dynamics I plan a maneuver early while new tracking keeps coming in. We check the new orbit does not create another close approach. If the risk stays above our threshold at the decision time, we execute; if it drops, we stand down and log why.
During a pass, a scientist asks you to send a command that is not in the approved plan. What do you do?
Your judgement when someone pushes for a change outside the approved plan.
No unreviewed commands on a live pass: send it through the flight director and the change process, and offer the soonest safe slot.

I would not send it on the spot, even if it looks harmless. A command outside the plan has not been checked against power, attitude or the other activities. I tell the flight director, write up the request, and see if it can be reviewed and added to the next pass. Usually the scientist gets it within a day, and safely.
Mid-pass, you realize you uplinked a command with a wrong parameter. What do you do?
How you own and contain a mistake on a live spacecraft.
Say it at once, assess the effect with the team, correct it by a reviewed command, then report it and fix the process.

I say it on the voice loop right away; speed matters more than pride. With the flight director we check what the wrong value does and whether waiting for the next pass is too late. Then we correct it with a reviewed command. Afterward I write the anomaly report, and we look at why the check missed it, for example by adding a range check in the command tool.
Why does pass planning depend on fresh orbit data, and what goes wrong if it is old?
Whether you understand where pass times and antenna pointing come from.
Predictions come from the orbit solution. Drag and maneuvers make old data drift, which causes late acquisition or a missed pass.

Rise and set times and antenna pointing angles are predicted from our latest orbit solution. In low orbit, drag changes the orbit every day, and a maneuver changes it at once. With old data the antenna points behind the satellite, and we acquire late or not at all. I check the age of the orbit file before every planning cycle and after every burn.
How do you use long-term trending to catch a problem before any limit trips?
How you find slow degradation that real-time limits miss.
Comparing values over weeks under the same conditions, like orbit phase or season, and raising a drift early with the data to back it.

Limits only tell me when something is already out of range. I plot key points over weeks, like battery end-of-discharge voltage, wheel friction and heater on-time, and compare like with like: same eclipse length, same mode. Once a heater was on a little longer each week. We raised it with engineering months before any limit would have tripped.
What makes a command hazardous, and what extra controls do you put around it?
Whether you know which commands can harm the mission and how they are guarded.
Commands that cannot be undone or can damage hardware get arm-then-execute steps, a second person's check and approval in the plan.

A hazardous command cannot be undone or can damage the spacecraft: firing a pyro device, turning off a receiver, disabling fault protection. These usually need an arm command before the execute. A second operator checks the parameters against the approved procedure, and I confirm the spacecraft state matches what the procedure expects before I send.
What has to be in a shift handover in a control room?
How you pass on the state of the spacecraft without losing anything.
Current mode and health, open anomalies, the stored command load on board, upcoming passes and temporary constraints, both written and spoken.

I give the spacecraft mode and anything off nominal, every open anomaly and who owns it, what stored commands are on board and when the load runs out, the next passes and what each must do, and temporary constraints like a heater left off. It goes in the log first, then we talk it through, and the incoming controller asks questions before taking the console.
After you uplink a stored command load, how do you know it is correct on board?
Whether you verify a load instead of assuming the uplink worked.
A checksum or memory dump compared with the ground file, the command count and time span checked, and no gap or overlap with the previous load.

Uplink success only means the frames were accepted. I compare the onboard checksum with the one computed on the ground, or dump the load and compare it. I check the number of commands, the first and last execution times, and that the new load starts cleanly where the old one ends, with no gap and no overlap. Only then do I enable it.
Why does spacecraft clock correlation matter for time-tagged commands?
Your understanding of onboard time and how it ties to ground time.
The onboard clock drifts from UTC. Correlation converts planned UTC times to onboard time, and a stale correlation shifts every timed event.

On many spacecraft, time-tagged commands run on a free-running onboard clock, not on UTC. That clock drifts, so we keep measuring its offset and drift rate and use them to convert planned UTC times into onboard time. If the correlation is stale, an imaging command or a burn can fire off target. I check the correlation age before building every load.
Forecasters warn of a strong solar storm. What does it change for a satellite in low orbit, and how do you prepare?
Whether you know how space weather affects daily operations.
The upper atmosphere heats and drag rises, so predictions age fast, and energetic particles can flip bits. More orbit updates, closer watch, no risky activities.

The storm heats the upper atmosphere, so drag rises and our pass predictions and close-approach screenings go stale much faster. I ask for more frequent orbit updates and widen acquisition margins. Energetic particles can flip bits in electronics, so I watch error counters and unexpected resets, and I would postpone a software upload or a planned maneuver until it calms down.
You have one short pass, and both a recovery activity and an urgent science downlink want it. How do you decide?
Your judgement between spacecraft health and mission data.
Health first when waiting adds risk; checking whether both fit, saying the trade openly and finding more contact time.

First I check whether both fit: a short recovery step plus the most urgent files may share the pass. If not, spacecraft health wins when waiting adds risk, like a power or thermal problem. If the spacecraft is stable and the recovery can wait an orbit, the data may go first. I tell both leads the decision and the reason, and I request extra time on another station.
You lose the signal halfway through a pass, with no warning. How do you tell a ground problem from a spacecraft problem?
How you isolate a fault across the ground side and the space side.
Checking ground equipment, pointing and other users of the station first, then the last telemetry and any timed event, before assuming the worst.

I check the ground first because it is quicker: antenna tracking, receiver lock, station status, and whether other missions on that station lost signal too. Then I study our last frames. Was a timed command due, like a mode change or transmitter switch? Was there a drop in power or attitude? If the ground is clean, I book the next station and plan recovery steps before we acquire.
An onboard fault-protection response keeps tripping and safing the spacecraft. Engineering wants to disable it to save science time. How do you evaluate that?
Your judgement on risk when changing onboard protection.
Finding why it trips first; preferring a tuned threshold or persistence over disabling, with review, simulator testing and a ground watch in its place.

First I want the cause: a real fault, a noisy sensor, or a threshold set too tight. Disabling removes protection for the day the fault is real, so I prefer adjusting the threshold or the persistence, meaning how many bad samples in a row trigger it. Any change goes through review, is tested on the simulator, gets a ground limit to watch instead, and has a date to revisit.

mlops.heading: ML infrastructure and MLOps questions
qs: What is the difference between batch inference and online serving, and when would you pick each?
Whether you know the two basic ways a model is served and their trade-offs.
Batch scores many records on a schedule; online answers each request live. The choice follows how fresh predictions must be, with cost and simplicity in mind.

Batch inference scores a large set of records on a schedule, like every night, and writes results to a table that apps read later. Online serving answers one request at a time behind an API, so latency matters. I pick batch when predictions can be a few hours old, since it is cheaper and simpler, and online when the answer depends on what the user just did.
What is training-serving skew, and how do you prevent it?
Whether you know a common way models fail quietly in production.
Features computed differently in training and serving. Prevent it with one shared feature definition and by checking served features against training data.

It is when the model gets features computed one way in training and another way in production, so it does worse live than offline. A common cause is two code paths, like a SQL job for training and hand-written serving code. I make both use one shared feature definition, log the features served live, and compare their distributions to the training data.
What do you record so a training run can be reproduced months later?
How you think about versioning data, code and environment together.
Code commit, data snapshot, container image with pinned libraries, config and seeds, plus honesty that some GPU operations are not deterministic.

I record the code commit, a snapshot or version of the exact data, the container image with pinned library versions, the config and the random seeds, and store them with the model. Even then, some GPU operations are not deterministic, so I either turn on deterministic mode and accept slower runs, or agree that results within a small tolerance count as reproduced.
Explain dynamic batching in a model server and what it trades off.
Your understanding of how serving throughput and latency interact on a GPU.
Requests are held briefly and run together, raising GPU throughput at the cost of a small added wait, tuned with a max batch size and max delay.

The server holds incoming requests for a few milliseconds and runs them through the GPU together. A GPU often takes only a little longer for 16 inputs than for one, so throughput rises a lot. The cost is that each request waits a bit. I set a maximum batch size and a maximum wait, then tune both under load against our latency target.
A training job runs out of GPU memory. What do you try, and in what order?
Whether you know the standard ways to fit a model into limited GPU memory.
Find the cause first, then mixed precision, smaller batch with gradient accumulation, activation checkpointing, and sharding the model only if needed.

First I watch memory over steps to see if it is a leak or just too big. Then I try mixed precision, which stores many values in 16 bits; a smaller batch with gradient accumulation so the effective batch size stays the same; and activation checkpointing, which recomputes some values instead of storing them. If it still does not fit, I shard the model across GPUs.
GPU utilization sits around 30% during training. How do you find the bottleneck?
How you diagnose an expensive, underused GPU.
Profile before guessing. Most often the input pipeline starves the GPU; also check batch size and communication between nodes.

I profile a few hundred steps to see where time goes. Most often the GPU waits on data: slow reads from network storage, image decoding on too few CPU workers, or no prefetching. Fixes are more loader workers, prefetching, a packed file format and caching data on local disk. If data is fine, I check for a batch too small to fill the GPU or slow sync between nodes.
We want to train on cheaper preemptible instances that can be taken away at any time. How do you design for that?
Whether you can make long training jobs survive interruption.
Frequent checkpoints to durable storage with full training state, handling the shutdown notice, and automatic resume from the latest checkpoint.

I save checkpoints to durable storage, not the node's disk, often enough that losing one interval is cheap, say every 20 to 30 minutes. Each holds weights, optimizer state, learning-rate schedule, step count and data loader position. The job catches the shutdown notice and writes a last checkpoint if it can, and the scheduler restarts it from the latest one.
What is the difference between a shadow deployment and a canary release for a new model?
Your grasp of safe rollout patterns for models.
Shadow mirrors traffic with outputs logged but not used; canary serves a small share of real users. Both need clear rollback limits.

In a shadow deployment the new model gets a copy of live traffic, but its answers are only logged, never shown, so users are not at risk. It tests load and lets me compare outputs. A canary sends a small share, say 5%, of real users to the new model. I shadow first, then canary to measure real impact, with automatic rollback if errors or a key metric cross a set limit.
Three teams share 64 GPUs and each says its work is urgent. How do you set up scheduling?
Your judgement on fair, efficient sharing of a GPU cluster.
Guaranteed quotas with preemptible borrowing, priority for production work, gang scheduling for distributed jobs, and usage data shared openly.

Each team gets a guaranteed quota and can borrow idle GPUs, but borrowed jobs can be preempted when the owner needs them back. Production retraining outranks experiments. Distributed jobs are gang-scheduled, so all their GPUs start together or not at all; otherwise half-started jobs hold GPUs and block each other. I publish weekly usage per team so quota talks use data.
A new model version went out, the business metric dropped, but every infrastructure dashboard is green. What do you do?
How you handle a production incident where the system looks healthy but the model is wrong.
Roll back first, then compare versions on the same inputs, look for pipeline causes, and add a check that would have caught it.

I roll back to the previous model first, because rollback is cheap and the loss is real. Then I run both versions on the same inputs. The cause is often outside the weights: a changed preprocessing step, a feature that is null in production, or the wrong model file. Once it was a tokenizer version mismatch. After that I added a fixed test set both versions must pass before any rollout.
When does plain data parallel training stop being enough, and what do you move to?
Whether you know how large models are split across GPUs, and why.
Data parallel copies the whole model to every GPU. Once weights, gradients and optimizer state do not fit, you shard them or split the layers.

Data parallel puts a full copy of the model on every GPU and splits the batch; an all-reduce averages the gradients each step. It stops working when weights, gradients and optimizer state no longer fit on one GPU. Then I shard them across GPUs with FSDP or ZeRO, or split the layers themselves with tensor or pipeline parallelism.
What is the practical difference between training in fp16 and in bf16?
Your grasp of number formats and why mixed precision can fail.
bf16 keeps the fp32 exponent range, so it rarely needs loss scaling. fp16 has a narrower range, so small gradients underflow without a loss scaler.

Both use 16 bits. bf16 keeps the 8-bit exponent of fp32 and gives up precision, so it covers the same range. fp16 has a 5-bit exponent, so small gradients can underflow to zero and you need loss scaling. On hardware that supports bf16 I use it and usually drop the scaler. Master weights and some sums still stay in fp32.
We moved a job from 8 GPUs to 4 and doubled gradient accumulation. Is the training the same?
Whether you know what changes and what stays the same when you resize a training job.
The global batch stays the same, so the optimizer math is close. Per-batch effects like batch norm change, steps take about twice as long, and schedules must count optimizer steps.

The global batch is per-GPU batch times GPUs times accumulation steps, so it stays the same and the updates are nearly equivalent. It is not identical: batch norm statistics are computed per micro-batch, and data order may shift. Each optimizer step takes about twice as long. I also check that the learning rate schedule and logging count optimizer steps, not micro-batches.
We have twenty small models, each using a fraction of a GPU, and each one has its own full GPU on Kubernetes. How do you pack them?
Your knowledge of GPU sharing options and their isolation limits.
Knows Kubernetes allocates whole GPUs by default. Compares serving several models in one process, MIG slices with memory isolation, and time-slicing without it.

By default a pod requests nvidia.com/gpu as a whole number, so each model locks a full card. First I would serve several models from one server process on a shared GPU. If they must stay separate, MIG on A100 or H100 cards gives slices with their own memory. Time-slicing is simpler, but there is no memory isolation, so one leaky model can starve the others.
Our GPU inference service autoscales on CPU usage and still misses its latency target at peak. What would you change?
How you pick scaling signals for GPU serving and handle slow startup.
Scale on load the model actually feels, such as queue depth or in-flight requests, tuned by a load test. Plan for slow cold starts with warm capacity.

CPU is a weak signal because the GPU does the work, and GPU utilization can look high even with spare capacity. I would scale on in-flight requests or queue depth per replica, with a target taken from a load test at our latency goal. A new replica can take minutes to pull the image and load weights, so I keep a warm minimum, scale up early and scale down slowly.
Why does the cost of serving a large language model depend so much on context length?
Whether you understand the memory behavior of LLM inference.
Explains the KV cache growing with tokens and concurrent requests, decode being limited by memory bandwidth, and techniques like paged KV cache and continuous batching.

For every token in context, each layer stores its keys and values, the KV cache, so memory grows with context length times the number of requests in flight. That caps how many users fit on one GPU. Decoding makes one token per step and is limited by memory bandwidth, not compute. Paged KV cache and continuous batching help pack more requests into the same memory.
Finance asks us to cut inference cost by quantizing our main model to 8-bit. How do you decide?
Your judgement in trading model quality against cost with evidence.
Measures quality on the team's own eval set and key slices, measures real speed on the target hardware, then rolls out gradually.

I would quantize a copy and run it on our own eval set, looking at slices like rare classes or long inputs, not just the average. Then I measure latency and throughput on the hardware we actually run, because the gains depend on kernel support. If quality holds, I run it in shadow, then a small canary, and report cost per thousand requests next to the quality numbers.
Offline metrics look great, but online the model is weak. You find the training set joined each event to the latest feature values. What went wrong, and how do you fix it?
Whether you recognize leakage from time and know point-in-time joins.
Names the leakage: features from after the event. The fix is an as-of join on timestamps, allowing for ingestion delay, then retraining and re-evaluating.

The model saw feature values from after each event, so it learned from the future. That inflates offline scores. I would rebuild the training set with a point-in-time join: for each label, take the latest feature value with a timestamp at or before the event, minus the delay before that value is really available in production. Then retrain, re-evaluate and add a test that catches future timestamps.
A 32-node training job freezes. GPUs show high utilization, but no steps are logged. What do you do?
How you debug a hang in distributed training.
Suspects a collective waiting on one rank, gets stack traces from every rank, checks the network and hardware logs, and sets timeouts so hangs fail loudly.

That pattern usually means a collective like all-reduce is spinning while one rank never arrives. I would dump stack traces from every rank with py-spy and find the rank in a different place. Then I check that node's kernel logs for GPU errors and its network link, and rerun with NCCL_DEBUG=INFO. I also look for code where ranks take different paths, and set a collective timeout.
Day three of a two-week training run, the loss spikes and then goes to NaN. Walk me through what you do.
How you protect an expensive run and find the cause of instability.
Stops wasting compute, finds the step, checks data, gradient norms and learning rate, then restarts from a clean checkpoint with a targeted fix.

First I stop the job so we stop paying for NaN steps. I find the step where gradient norms started climbing and inspect the batches just before it for corrupt or extreme data. I check the learning rate schedule and gradient clipping. Then I restart from the last checkpoint before the spike, skipping the bad batches or lowering the peak learning rate, and watch gradient norms closely.

mobile-engineer.heading: Mobile engineer questions
qs: Where do you store a user's login token on the phone, and why there?
Whether you know the secure storage each platform provides.
Keychain on iOS, a key in the Android Keystore on Android, never plain preferences or a text file.

On iOS I put it in the Keychain, which the system encrypts and keeps apart from normal app files. On Android I encrypt it with a key held in the Android Keystore, so the key cannot simply be copied out. I never put tokens in UserDefaults or plain SharedPreferences, because those are easy to read on a rooted or jailbroken phone or from an unencrypted backup.
What makes an app freeze or show an "App not responding" message, and how do you prevent it?
Whether you understand the main thread and keep slow work off it.
Slow work blocks the main thread; move it to background threads and come back to the main thread only to update the screen.

The screen is drawn on the main thread, so a network call, a big file read or heavy JSON parsing there freezes everything. On Android, if input gets no response for about five seconds, the user sees an ANR dialog. I run that work with coroutines or Swift async/await off the main thread, then update the UI on the main thread. On Android I turn on StrictMode in debug builds to catch disk access on the main thread.
In Swift, a screen is closed but its memory is never freed. What is a likely cause, and how do you fix it?
Your grasp of memory management on iOS.
A retain cycle, often a closure capturing self strongly; break it with a weak or unowned reference and confirm with the memory tools.

Most often it is a retain cycle: the view controller holds a closure, and the closure captures self strongly, so neither can be released. I capture [weak self] in the closure, or unowned when I am sure self lives longer. To find it I use the Xcode Memory Graph Debugger or the Leaks tool in Instruments, then check that the screen is freed after I close it.
Your crash reports show only memory addresses or names like a.b.c instead of real function names. Why, and how do you fix it?
Whether you know symbolication and deobfuscation for release builds.
Release builds strip or shrink symbols; upload the dSYM files for iOS and the R8 mapping file for Android for every release.

Release builds do not carry readable names. On iOS the names live in dSYM files, so I make sure the build uploads them for every version to the crash tool. On Android, R8 shrinks and renames code, so I upload the mapping file from each release build. I also archive both per version, because a mapping from another build will translate the trace wrongly.
When do you ask the user for permission to send push notifications?
How you balance product goals against platform rules for permissions.
Ask in context, after showing the value, because a refusal is hard to undo on iOS and on recent Android versions.

Not at first launch. I ask when it makes sense, for example after the user orders and wants delivery updates, often with a short screen that explains why first. On iOS the system prompt appears only once; after a no, the user has to change it in Settings. Android 13 and later also needs a runtime permission, and after repeated refusals the system stops showing the prompt.
The backend team wants to rename a field in an API the app uses. What do you tell them?
Whether you know that old app versions stay in use for a long time.
Old versions keep calling the API for months; add the new field, keep the old one until usage drops, and have a minimum version check.

Users do not all update, so versions from many months ago will still call this API. I would ask them to add the new field alongside the old one, ship the app that reads the new one, and watch version adoption. They remove the old field only when the versions using it are a tiny share, or after we force an update through a minimum supported version check.
You need to change the local database schema in the next release. How do you ship it safely?
Whether you protect user data during local storage migrations.
Write migrations that work from every older schema, test real upgrades, and avoid destructive fallbacks that wipe data.

Users can jump from any old version straight to the new one, so I write a migration for each step and test upgrading from every schema we have shipped, using a database file saved from that version. I never rely on a destructive fallback that drops tables, because that silently deletes unsynced data. If the migration is risky, I add logging so a failure shows up in monitoring and does not crash at launch.
The release branch is cut tomorrow and your feature is only half done. What do you do?
How you work with release trains and feature flags.
Do not hold the train or rush; ship the code behind a flag turned off, or leave it for the next release.

I would not ask to delay the release or rush the last part. If the code is merged and stable, I keep it behind a feature flag that is off by default and make sure it is not reachable. Then I finish it and turn it on later, maybe for a small group first. If the half-done work could affect other screens, I keep it out of the branch and ship it in the next train.
On Android, a user fills in a long form, switches to the camera, and comes back to an empty form. What happened?
Whether you understand process death and how Android restores a screen.
Names process death, knows a ViewModel alone does not survive it, and saves small state with SavedStateHandle or saved instance state.

While the camera was open, the system likely killed our process to free memory. When the user came back, Android rebuilt the screen, but the ViewModel was new and empty. I would keep the form input in SavedStateHandle, or save a draft to disk if it is large. To reproduce it, I put the app in the background and run adb shell am kill with the package name.
The app must keep uploading photos after the user leaves it. How do you do that on iOS and on Android?
Your knowledge of background execution limits on both platforms.
Knows the OS decides when background work runs: a background URLSession on iOS, WorkManager on Android, with no promise of exact timing.

On iOS I use a background URLSession, so the system carries on the transfer even if the app is suspended or ended by the system. On Android I enqueue a WorkManager job with a network constraint, so it survives restarts and battery saving. In both I keep the queue on disk and show the user what is still pending, because the timing is up to the OS.
Links to your website should open the app, but on some phones they open the browser. Where do you look?
Whether you know how universal links and Android App Links are verified.
Checks the association files on the domain, the app entitlement or intent filter, and the signing certificate fingerprint.

First the server: apple-app-site-association and assetlinks.json under /.well-known/, served over HTTPS with no redirects. Then the app: the associated domains entitlement on iOS, the intent filter with autoVerify on Android. A common Android cause is a fingerprint in assetlinks.json from the debug key instead of the Play app signing key.
Cold start time has doubled over the past year. How do you bring it back down?
How you measure and reduce app launch time.
Measures first on a real low-end device, then moves work off the launch path: lazy setup, no disk or network on the main thread before the first screen.

I measure on a cheap real device with a release build and find what runs before the first frame. Usually it is SDKs set up eagerly, heavy dependency setup, or disk reads on the main thread. I defer what the first screen does not need. On Android I add a Baseline Profile, which precompiles startup code. Then a launch-time check in CI keeps it from creeping back.
How do you decide when to drop support for an older iOS or Android version?
Your judgement in weighing users lost against engineering cost.
Uses the app's own analytics, not global numbers, and weighs the share of users and revenue against the APIs and testing time gained.

I look at our own analytics: the share of active users and of revenue on that version, and the trend. Then what we gain: newer APIs, workarounds we can delete, devices we stop testing. If the share is small and the cost is real, we drop it, warn users ahead of time, and keep the backend working with the last supported build for a while.
Day two of a staged rollout, crashes jump on one Android version. Walk me through what you do.
How you run a release when a rollout goes wrong.
Halts the rollout first, knows a shipped build cannot be pulled back from users, and fixes forward with a new version or a remote flag.

I halt the rollout in the Play Console so no new users get the build. People who already have it keep it; there is no recalling a binary. I read the crash stacks and see which devices it hits. If the crash sits behind a feature flag, I switch it off remotely. Otherwise I ship a hotfix with a higher version code and roll it out slowly again.
Two years from now, today's build will still be on some phones. How do you design for that?
Whether you plan for app versions you can no longer change.
Backward-compatible APIs, a server-driven minimum version check, and remote flags to turn off broken features.

I assume every release lives for years. The app sends its version with each request, so the backend can answer each one correctly. At launch it reads a minimum supported version from a config endpoint and, below it, shows an update screen. Risky features sit behind remote flags. That check must ship early, because you cannot add it to builds already out.
A user edits the same note offline on two devices, then both sync. How do you resolve the conflict?
How you design sync for edits made offline.
A clear conflict rule agreed with product, versions on records, safe retries, and no silent loss of the user's work.

Each record carries a version from the server. A write sends the version it was based on; if the server has moved on, it is a conflict. For notes I avoid plain last write wins, since it silently drops text. I merge field by field where I can, otherwise keep both copies and let the user choose. Queued writes carry a unique ID so a retry never makes a duplicate.
The security team asks you to add certificate pinning. What do you tell them?
Your judgement on a security control that can break every installed app.
Explains the risk of locking users out when certificates change, and if pinning, pins public keys with a backup and a rotation plan.

Pinning blocks some interception attacks, but if our certificate changes and no pin matches, every installed copy stops reaching the server until users update. If we do it, I pin the public key rather than the certificate, add a backup key kept offline, and agree a rotation plan with whoever owns the certificates. I would also ask which threat it covers that normal TLS does not.
On a shared tablet, the second user who logs in briefly sees the first user's data. How do you fix it?
How you handle a data leak between accounts on one device.
Treats it as a privacy incident, clears every per-user store on logout, and scopes caches to the account so old data cannot appear.

I treat it as a privacy bug and fix it first. On logout I cancel requests in flight, delete the token, wipe the local database, image and HTTP caches, and unregister the push token. Then I key caches by user ID, so even a store I missed cannot show another account. I add a test: log in as A, log out, log in as B, and check nothing of A remains.

motion-designer.heading: Motion designer and animator questions
qs: What is the difference between timing and spacing in animation?
Whether you know the two basic tools that decide how a move feels.
Timing is how many frames a move takes; spacing is how far the object travels between those frames, which creates the ease.

Timing is how long an action lasts, counted in frames. Spacing is how the positions are spread across those frames. Two moves can both last 12 frames, but if the drawings bunch up near the end, the object slows into place. Close spacing reads as slow, wide spacing as fast.
How do you use the graph editor to make a move feel natural?
How you shape motion beyond default keyframe easing.
Reads the speed or value curve, avoids flat linear moves, and adjusts handles so speed builds and settles smoothly without sudden spikes.

I set the key poses first, then open the speed curve. A linear move shows a flat line and looks mechanical, so I pull the handles to get a gentle rise and a long settle. I look for sharp peaks or kinks, because those show up as a jolt on screen. Then I play it back at full speed, not scrubbing.
When would you animate on twos instead of on ones?
Your understanding of frame rate as a style choice, not just a technical setting.
Knows twos means a new pose every second frame, and when that suits the style or saves time versus when smooth ones are needed.

On twos means a new pose every two frames, so 12 poses a second in a 24 fps project. It gives a hand-made, snappy feel and halves the drawing work for character pieces. I switch to ones for very fast actions, smooth camera moves or UI motion, where the stepping would look like stutter.
Walk me through how you build a basic walk cycle.
Whether you know character animation fundamentals, not only moving shapes.
Names the key poses, the rise and fall of the body, and opposite arm swing, and treats the cycle as two steps that loop cleanly.

I start with the contact pose, heel touching down, then the down pose where the body is lowest as weight lands. Next the passing pose as the back leg swings through, then the up pose where the body is highest. Then I mirror it for the other leg. Arms swing opposite to the legs, and I check the last frame flows into the first so the loop does not hitch.
An editor asks for your animated title with a transparent background. What do you send them?
Your knowledge of delivery formats and alpha channels.
Exports in a format that carries an alpha channel and avoids a standard H.264 MP4, which does not; confirms what their software accepts.

A standard H.264 MP4 cannot hold transparency, so I would not send that. I export an image sequence such as PNG with alpha, or a mastering video codec that supports an alpha channel. I ask the editor which one their system handles best, then send a short test clip before the full delivery.
You designed a screen transition for an app. How do you hand it off so it ships the way you made it?
How you turn a motion idea into specs a developer can build.
Gives exact duration, delay and easing values plus a reference video, and keeps UI motion short and purposeful.

I send a reference video and a spec for each element: duration in milliseconds, delay, and the easing written as curve values the developer can paste in. Elements entering usually decelerate into place, elements leaving speed up as they go. I keep it short so it never makes the user wait, then review the build on a real phone.
The director wants motion on every element and the piece now feels busy. What do you do?
Your judgement about hierarchy and where the viewer should look.
Directs attention to one thing at a time, staggers or holds secondary elements, and shows the director an alternative rather than just arguing.

The eye can follow only one main action at a time. I would pick the key message for each beat and let that move first, then let secondary elements settle with small, quiet moves or hold still. I would make a short version side by side with the original so the director can see the difference instead of hearing my opinion.
A client wants 40 versions of an ad in different sizes and languages. How do you set up the project?
How you build files that survive late changes and many outputs.
A master template with shared assets, central controls for text and color, clear naming, and a batch render plan.
