I build one master animation with the logo, colors and text driven from a single control layer, so a change happens once. Each size gets its own layout that references the master. Text sits in boxes that adjust to longer languages, and I test the longest one first. Files follow a naming system so I can queue all 40 renders and check them fast.
Your final render will take nine hours and the deadline is tomorrow morning. What do you do?
How you solve a technical problem under time pressure.
Finds what is slow, pre-renders heavy parts, renders to an image sequence that survives crashes, and warns the client early if needed.

I render a few frames to see which section is slow, often blur, motion blur or a heavy 3D layer. I pre-render that part once and swap it in. I output an image sequence, so a crash means restarting from the last frame, not from zero. If it still will not fit, I tell the producer tonight, not at 8 a.m.
You delivered a vertical ad and the client says the call to action is hidden once it runs. What happened and how do you fix it?
How you own a delivery mistake and prevent it next time.
Recognises safe areas and platform interface overlays, fixes and redelivers fast, and adds a check to the process.

The platform puts its own buttons and caption over the edges of vertical video, and my text sat under them. I would own it, move key text and the logo inside the safe area and redeliver the same day. Since then I keep an overlay guide of the platform interface on every vertical project and check exports with it on.
A logo reveal you inherited feels stiff, even though the easing is fine. What do you change?
Whether you know the principles that make motion feel alive beyond easing curves.
Overlap, follow-through and offset timing named and applied, so parts no longer start and stop together.

Stiff usually means every part starts and stops on the same frame. I offset the pieces by a few frames, let lighter parts drag behind and settle after the main shape stops, and add a small anticipation before the big move. Then I watch it at full speed, not frame by frame.
When do you move from storyboards to an animatic, and what does the animatic settle?
How you plan timing before you spend days on final animation.
The animatic locks timing against voiceover and music, so changes happen when they are cheap.

Once the boards are approved, I cut them to the scratch voiceover and the music. The animatic settles shot length, pacing and where cuts land on the beat. If a shot needs eight seconds of talk and I planned four, I find out now, before I animate it, not after.
In a kinetic type piece, how do you decide how long each word or line stays on screen?
Your sense of readability in animated text.
Hold time judged by reading, with the text still while it is read and the eye guided to where the next line appears.

Text has to be read, so it needs to sit still long enough. My rule of thumb is to read the line aloud twice at a normal pace while it holds. I keep the move in short, put the next line where the eye already is, and have someone who has never seen it read it cold.
What is the difference between IK and FK in a character rig, and when do you use each?
Your rigging knowledge and how it shapes the way you animate.
FK rotates joints from parent to child; IK places the end and solves the chain. IK for planted limbs, FK for swinging arcs.

With FK, I rotate the shoulder, then the elbow, then the wrist, so arcs come out naturally. With IK, I move the hand or foot and the solver bends the joints. I use IK when a foot is planted or a hand is on a table, and FK for a free arm swing. Good rigs let me switch between them.
A fast whip pan in your piece looks choppy, like a strobe. What do you check?
How you diagnose a motion problem that is about spacing and blur, not timing.
Spacing between frames and motion blur checked, with blur matching a real camera and smear frames if needed.

Choppy fast moves mean the object jumps a long way between frames with nothing in between. I turn on motion blur, often with a 180-degree shutter to match live footage, and check the spacing on the fastest frames. For very fast moves in 2D, I may draw a smear or stretch frame.
How do you build a seamless loop, and what usually breaks it?
Whether you can make a loop with no hitch at the join.
Matching start and end state without rendering the duplicate frame, and checking the loop at the join.

The last frame must lead into the first, not repeat it. I put the end key at the comp duration so it matches frame zero, and that frame falls just outside the render. In After Effects, loopOut("cycle") helps on repeating keys. A doubled frame or an ease at the join is what usually causes the hitch.
The footage is at 23.976 fps and the client asks for a 30 fps comp. What do you do?
Your grasp of frame rates and what happens when they are mixed.
Matches the comp to the footage, explains judder, and confirms whether the client means 29.97 before converting.

If I drop 23.976 footage into a 30 comp, frames repeat in a pattern and motion judders. I ask what they really need, since 30 often means 29.97. I animate at the footage rate, and if delivery truly must be 29.97, I plan a proper conversion at the end and show them a test first.
The client says the colors in your MP4 look washed out on their laptop. How do you handle it?
Your color management and how you troubleshoot a problem that may not be in your file.
Checks the export's color tagging and the viewer, compares several players, and reviews on the target platform.

First I check that the export is tagged Rec. 709, the usual standard for video. Some players read that tag differently, so the same file can look lighter in one app than another. I open it in a few players and in a browser, and if it runs on social, I upload a private test. Then I show the client which view to trust.
A client sends you a font and a music track to use in a broadcast ad. What do you check first?
Whether you protect the client and yourself on licensing.
Confirms the font and music licenses cover video and broadcast use, and flags gaps before production.

A font file in hand does not mean a license for video. I ask who bought it and whether the license covers video and broadcast. Same for the music: personal or web-only stock licenses often exclude TV. I raise it in writing early, because swapping a font or track after approval costs everyone.
Your character's knee snaps or pops when the leg straightens in a walk. What is happening and how do you fix it?
How you solve a common IK rig problem at senior level.
Knows the knee pop comes from the IK chain nearing full extension, and fixes it in the pose or with soft IK.

That is the classic knee pop. As an IK leg nears full reach, the solver turns the knee very fast over a frame or two. I keep the hip low enough that the leg never quite locks, or use a soft IK or stretch setting if the rig has one. Then I check the hip's arc in the graph editor.

network-engineer.heading: Network engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between a switch and a router?
Whether you know the basic layers a network engineer works with every day.
Switches forward frames by MAC address inside one network; routers forward packets by IP address between networks.

A switch works at layer 2. It learns which MAC address sits on which port and forwards frames inside one local network. A router works at layer 3. It looks at the destination IP address, checks its routing table and sends the packet to another network. A layer 3 switch can do both.
What does a VLAN do, and what is a trunk port?
Your grasp of how one physical switch is split into separate networks.
A VLAN is its own broadcast domain; a trunk carries several VLANs on one link using 802.1Q tags. Traffic between VLANs needs routing.

A VLAN splits a switch into separate broadcast domains, so voice, guests and staff stay apart. An access port belongs to one VLAN. A trunk carries many VLANs between switches by adding an 802.1Q tag with the VLAN number to each frame. To get from one VLAN to another, traffic has to go through a router or a layer 3 switch.
Walk me through what happens when a laptop pings a server on a different subnet.
Whether you understand ARP, the default gateway and how a router forwards a packet.
The host sees the target is off its subnet, ARPs for the gateway, and the router looks up the route, lowers the TTL and builds a new frame.

The laptop compares the server's IP with its own subnet mask and sees it is remote. It sends the packet to its default gateway, using ARP first if it does not know the gateway's MAC address. The router removes the frame, lowers the TTL, finds the route, ARPs for the next hop and sends a new frame. The reply comes back the same way.
What would you monitor on a network, and where does the data come from?
How you see problems before users report them.
Interface use, errors and discards, device health, logs and flow data, plus tests that measure what users feel.

I poll devices with SNMP for interface use, errors, discards, CPU and memory. I send syslog to one place so I can match events across devices. Flow records show who talks to whom when a link fills up. I also run small tests from a few sites, like ping and DNS checks, to see latency and loss the way users see them.
When would you use OSPF and when would you use BGP?
Your knowledge of interior and exterior routing and why each exists.
OSPF inside one organization for fast, automatic convergence; BGP between autonomous systems, such as to ISPs, where policy matters.

OSPF is a link-state protocol for inside one network. Routers share the topology and pick the lowest-cost path, and it converges fast. BGP connects separate autonomous systems, like our network and two internet providers. It is built for policy: I can choose which provider carries traffic in and out, not just the shortest path.
Someone plugs both ends of a cable into the same switch and the floor goes down. What happened, and how do you stop it next time?
Whether you understand switching loops and spanning tree.
A layer 2 loop causes a broadcast storm because frames have no TTL. Spanning tree, BPDU guard and storm control prevent it.

That made a loop. Ethernet frames have no TTL, so broadcasts circle forever and swamp every switch. Spanning tree should block the extra path, so I check it is running on every switch. On user ports I turn on BPDU guard, which shuts a port that hears another switch, and storm control to cap broadcast traffic.
Users say Wi-Fi keeps dropping in one big conference room during meetings. How do you work on it?
How you troubleshoot wireless problems with real data, not guesses.
Survey first: channel overlap, number of clients per access point, signal levels. On 2.4 GHz in the US only channels 1, 6 and 11 avoid overlap.

I go there during a meeting and check how many clients each access point has and what signal they see. Often nearby APs share a channel. On 2.4 GHz I only use 1, 6 and 11, which do not overlap in the US. I push clients to 5 GHz, use narrower channels in dense rooms, and add an AP if one is carrying sixty laptops.
A vendor asks for a firewall rule allowing any traffic from their network to our servers. What do you do?
Your judgement about least privilege and security requests.
You find out what they really need and allow only those sources, hosts and ports, with an owner, a ticket and an end date.

I would not open everything. I ask what the vendor needs to reach and why. Usually it is one or two servers on a few ports. I allow only their source addresses to those hosts and ports, log the rule, tie it to a ticket with an owner and set a review date. Since the firewall is stateful, replies come back without extra rules.
You change a config on a remote router and lose access to it. How do you recover, and how do you avoid it?
How you handle your own mistakes and make changes safely.
Calm recovery through out-of-band access, then habits: timed automatic rollback, saved backups, a tested plan and a change window.

First I tell the team and use out-of-band access, like a console server or a cellular modem, to undo the change. If there is none, I get local hands. Now I always save a backup and set a timed rollback that restores the old config unless I confirm the change worked. I test the plan in the lab and do it in a change window.
After a new site-to-site VPN goes up, small web pages load but large file transfers hang. What do you suspect?
Whether you can find a classic MTU problem that simple ping tests miss.
Tunnel overhead lowers the usable MTU; if ICMP is blocked, path MTU discovery fails. Test with don't-fragment pings and clamp TCP MSS.

I suspect MTU. The tunnel adds headers, so full 1,500-byte packets no longer fit. Normally the router sends an ICMP message saying the packet is too big, but if a firewall blocks it, big packets just vanish. I test with pings of growing size with don't-fragment set, then allow those ICMP messages and clamp TCP MSS on the tunnel.
A switch port shows CRC errors climbing steadily. Where do you look first?
Whether you read interface counters and start at the physical layer.
Starts with the physical path into that port: cable, optic, clean fiber, light levels, and a speed or duplex mismatch on copper.

CRC errors mean frames arrive damaged, so I suspect the physical path into that port. I check the patch cable and jacks. On fiber I read the optic's light levels and clean the connectors. On copper I confirm both ends agree on speed and duplex. Then I clear the counters and watch whether they still climb.
We bonded four 10-gig links into one port channel, yet one big backup job never goes faster than 10 gig. Why?
Whether you know how link aggregation spreads traffic.
Explains per-flow hashing that keeps packets in order, so one flow rides one member link; more flows or a faster link help, not more members.

A port channel does not split one flow across links. The switch hashes fields like source and destination addresses and ports, and every packet of a flow takes the same member so nothing arrives out of order. One backup stream is one flow, so it gets one 10-gig link. Parallel streams or a faster link would help.
Graphs show the uplink at 30% use, but the interface keeps counting output drops. Is the link fine?
How you read monitoring data that can hide short bursts.
Knows that averages over minutes hide millisecond bursts that overflow buffers, and gets finer data before deciding.

No. A five-minute average can sit at 30% while traffic spikes past line rate for a few milliseconds and overflows the buffer. That is a microburst. I would pull counters at a much shorter interval or use streaming telemetry, find which hosts burst, and then look at buffer settings, QoS or a faster uplink.
Two OSPF routers see each other but stay stuck in EXSTART or EXCHANGE. What do you check?
Your working knowledge of how OSPF neighbors form.
Names an interface MTU mismatch as the usual cause and a duplicate router ID as another, and fixes the cause instead of hiding it.

In those states the routers trade database descriptions, and the classic cause is an MTU mismatch: the side with the smaller MTU rejects the bigger packets. I compare the interface MTU on both ends and fix it, rather than telling OSPF to ignore MTU. I also check that the two routers do not share a router ID.
A new eBGP peering with a provider sits in the Active state. What does that tell you, and what do you check?
Whether you can troubleshoot a BGP session that will not come up.
Knows Active means the session is not getting established, and checks reachability, addresses, AS numbers, TCP port 179, passwords and update source.

Active means my router keeps trying to open the session and it is not completing; it does not mean things work. I ping the peer, confirm the neighbor IP and remote AS on both sides, and check that nothing blocks TCP port 179. If we peer from a loopback I check the update source and multihop setting, and I compare the MD5 password with the provider.
Voice calls sound choppy when the WAN link is busy. How do you set up QoS for them?
Whether you can apply QoS end to end, not just turn it on.
Marks voice at a trusted edge, gives it a capped priority queue, applies the policy wherever congestion can occur, and knows QoS only acts under congestion.

I mark voice as Expedited Forwarding, DSCP 46, at the phone or access switch and trust markings only from there. On the WAN edge I put EF in a priority queue with a bandwidth cap so it cannot starve other traffic. The policy must match on every hop that can congest. Over the public internet my markings will not be honored.
After adding a second firewall at a new edge, some connections fail while others work. Routing looks fine. What do you suspect?
Whether you understand how stateful firewalls interact with routing.
Spots asymmetric routing: replies hit a firewall that never saw the session start and get dropped. Fixes path symmetry or shares state.

I suspect asymmetric routing. A stateful firewall only passes return traffic for sessions it saw start. If the SYN leaves through one firewall and the reply comes back through the other, the second has no session and drops it. I would trace a failing flow both ways, then make the paths symmetric or run the pair as a cluster that shares state.
We have two internet providers and want most inbound traffic on the cheaper one. How do you influence that?
Your grasp of what you can and cannot control in BGP.
Separates outbound control (local preference) from inbound, and uses prepending, provider communities or more specific prefixes, with no promise of exact results.

Outbound is easy with local preference. Inbound is decided by other networks, so I can only nudge it. I would prepend our AS on the expensive link, or use the provider's documented communities to lower our preference inside their network. More specific prefixes on the cheap link also work, but most networks filter IPv4 routes longer than a /24. Then I measure and adjust.
We are turning on IPv6. A colleague wants to block all ICMPv6 at the firewall, like we did with ICMP for IPv4. What do you say?
Whether you know what IPv6 depends on that IPv4 did not.
Explains that IPv6 needs ICMPv6 for neighbor discovery and Packet Too Big messages, and filters by message type instead of blocking all.

I would push back. IPv6 uses ICMPv6 for neighbor discovery, which replaces ARP, so the firewall's own interfaces need it. Routers also do not fragment IPv6 packets, so hosts rely on Packet Too Big messages to find the path MTU; block them and transfers hang. I would allow the needed types, following RFC 4890, and filter the rest.
Two routers redistribute between OSPF and another routing protocol, and some routes start looping. How did it happen, and how do you fix it?
How you handle mutual redistribution at more than one point.
Explains routes fed back into the domain they came from, and fixes it with tags and filters at each point while checking administrative distance.

With two redistribution points, a route from domain A enters B at one router, and the second router sends it back into A as an external route. Depending on administrative distance and metrics, a router can prefer that copy and traffic loops. I tag routes as they are redistributed, deny routes carrying the other domain's tag at each point, then verify the paths.

nlp-engineer.heading: NLP and speech engineer questions
qs: What is word error rate, and how do you compute it?
Your grasp of the core metric for speech recognition.
Substitutions, deletions and insertions divided by the reference word count, found by alignment, and knowing the score can go above 100%.

I align the system output to the human reference transcript using edit distance. Then I count substitutions, deletions and insertions. WER is that sum divided by the number of words in the reference. Because insertions count, a very bad output can score above 100%. I also report it per speaker group, not only as one average.
Why do modern language models use subword tokens instead of whole words?
Whether you understand how text becomes model input.
Explains that subwords avoid unknown words and keep the vocabulary small, and names a real cost, such as uneven token counts across languages.

A whole-word vocabulary either grows huge or maps every new word to “unknown”. Byte-pair encoding starts from characters and keeps merging the most frequent adjacent pairs. Common words stay whole, and rare ones split into known pieces like “un”, “break”, “able”. The catch is that some languages get split into many more tokens, which costs context length and money.
What does self-attention do, and why did it replace recurrent networks for most language tasks?
Your understanding of the transformer, the base of current language and speech models.
Each token mixes in information from all others with learned weights; training runs in parallel; cost grows with the square of length.

Each token builds its representation as a weighted mix of all the other tokens. The weights come from how relevant each token is to it. An RNN passes information step by step. Attention links distant words directly, and training runs in parallel over the sequence. The price is that cost grows with the square of the sequence length, which hurts on long documents.
Your WER jumped after a model update, but listeners say the transcripts read better. What do you check first?
Whether you know how text normalization can distort speech metrics.
Looks at the actual errors and normalizes output and reference the same way before trusting the score: numbers, case, punctuation, contractions.

I would read the errors themselves. Often the new model writes “25” where the reference says “twenty five”, or it adds capitals and punctuation. Each of those counts as an error. I would run one normalizer on both sides, covering numbers, case, punctuation and “don't” versus “do not”, and then recompute. If the gap disappears, the model was fine and the scoring was not.
A team reports a higher BLEU score for their new translation model. What would you want to see before shipping it?
How you judge translation quality beyond one automatic number.
Knows BLEU counts n-gram overlap with reference translations and misses meaning. Asks for human review and targeted checks on names, numbers and negation.

BLEU measures how many word sequences match one or a few reference translations, with a penalty for short output. A correct paraphrase can score low, and a fluent error, like a dropped “not”, can score high. I would want human ratings on a sample, a learned metric alongside, and spot checks on names, numbers, dates and negation.
Your speech model does well on the test set but badly on recorded phone calls. What is likely going on?
Whether you can diagnose a mismatch between training audio and real audio.
Suspects narrowband telephone audio against wideband training data. Measures on real calls, then adapts with matched or simulated phone audio.

First I check the audio. Phone calls are often sampled at 8 kHz and lose most sound above about 3.4 kHz, while many models train on 16 kHz audio. Upsampling does not bring that back. I would measure WER on a labeled sample of real calls. Then I would fine-tune on call audio, or on training audio downsampled to phone quality with added noise and codec effects.
How do you set the detection threshold for a wake word on a smart speaker?
How you balance two kinds of errors in a voice product.
Frames it as false accepts against false rejects, measured on long real-world audio and varied voices, with the product team choosing the point.

I plot false rejects, when a user says the word and nothing happens, against false accepts per hour of background audio like TV and conversation. Then I pick a point with the product team. Waking at random erodes trust and raises privacy worries. Missing the word annoys people. I test across voices, accents and distances, not only clean recordings.
Your text classifier scored 97% offline and 80% in production. You find many near-duplicate texts in the data. What happened?
Whether you can spot data leakage in a language dataset.
Sees duplicates crossing the train-test split. Deduplicates, splits by source so related texts stay together, and re-measures before blaming drift.

Copies or templated variants of the same message were probably in both training and test, so the test rewarded memory, not generalization. I would deduplicate with a similarity check on normalized text. Then I would split by source, for example by customer or by thread, so related texts stay on one side. The honest offline number becomes the baseline.
A support chatbot built on document retrieval gives confident answers that are not in your documents. How do you fix it?
How you debug a retrieval-based chat system step by step.
Separates retrieval failure from generation failure, measures each on real questions, and adds grounding, citations and a way to say “I don't know”.

I split the problem. On a set of real questions, I check whether the right passage was retrieved at all. If not, I fix chunking or the search, maybe adding keyword search. If it was retrieved and the model still invented things, I tell it to answer only from the passages, cite them, and say it doesn't know otherwise. I track the rate on a fixed test set.
The product team wants to keep every voice transcript to improve the model. What do you raise?
Your judgement on privacy when working with speech and text data.
Raises consent, collecting only what is needed, redaction of personal data, retention limits and access control, with legal and privacy staff involved early.

Transcripts hold names, addresses, card numbers and health details. I would ask what users agreed to, and bring in legal and privacy early, since recording consent rules differ by state. Then I would redact sensitive details before storage, keep only the sample we need, set a deletion date and limit access. Redaction models miss things, so I would audit them too.
What does perplexity measure, and when can't you compare two models by it?
Whether you understand the most common language model metric and its limits.
Perplexity is the exponent of the average negative log-likelihood per token. It is comparable only on the same test text with the same tokenizer.

Perplexity is the exponent of the average negative log-likelihood the model gives each token of a test text. Lower means the model is less surprised. It depends on the tokenizer: a model with bigger tokens predicts fewer, harder units. So I compare only on the same text and tokenization, or switch to bits per byte, which does not depend on the tokenizer.
How is diarization error rate computed, and what can it hide?
Your grasp of how speaker diarization is scored.
Missed speech plus false alarm plus speaker confusion, over total reference speech time. It is time-weighted and sensitive to scoring settings.

DER adds three durations: speech we missed, non-speech we labeled as speech, and speech given to the wrong speaker. Then it divides by total reference speech time. It is time-weighted, so a speaker who says yes twice barely counts. A forgiveness collar around boundaries and whether overlapped speech is scored can move it a lot, so I always report those settings.
For live captioning, would you choose a CTC model, a transducer, or an attention encoder-decoder, and why?
How you match a speech model design to a streaming product.
Knows CTC predicts tokens independently, transducers stream with a built-in model of past tokens, and full attention decoders usually wait for the whole input.

I would lean to a transducer. CTC streams well but predicts each frame's token independently, so it leans on an external language model. An attention decoder usually needs the whole utterance before it writes, which hurts latency. A transducer adds a prediction network over past tokens and emits as audio arrives. I would limit encoder lookahead to keep delay within budget.
Why can beam search suit translation but give dull text in a chat assistant?
Whether you know how decoding choices shape generated text.
Most likely sequences fit tasks with few right answers. Open-ended text needs sampling, with temperature and top-p explained correctly.

Translation has a narrow set of right outputs, so searching for the most likely sequence works. In open-ended text the most likely sequence tends to be generic or repetitive. For chat I use sampling with a temperature and top-p, which draws only from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to a chosen share, such as 0.9.
Your ASR test WER is far better than what customers see, and the test set was split at random by utterance. What went wrong?
Whether you can spot leakage that is specific to speech data.
Same speakers and sessions in train and test inflate the score. The fix is a split by speaker, and by session or device where possible.

A random split by utterance puts the same speakers, and often the same sessions and microphones, in both train and test. The model partly learned those voices, so the score is too optimistic. I would re-split by speaker, and by session or device where I can, so no speaker appears in two sets, then rerun the evaluation before touching the model.
Your encoder-decoder transcription model writes full sentences during long silences in meetings. How do you deal with it?
How you handle hallucination in sequence-to-sequence speech models.
Knows these models can invent text on non-speech, and gates input with voice activity detection plus checks on confidence and repetition.

These models are trained to produce text, so on silence or noise the decoder can invent fluent sentences or repeat a phrase. I would run voice activity detection first and pass only speech. Then I would drop segments with a high no-speech score, low average log-probability or heavy repetition, and add noise clips with empty targets to the fine-tuning data.
You have 40 hours of transcribed speech for a new language. How do you build a usable recognizer?
Your approach to low-resource speech recognition.
Fine-tunes a multilingual pretrained model, augments the audio, settles text normalization early and holds out unseen speakers.

I would fine-tune a model pretrained with self-supervision on many languages rather than train from scratch. I would stretch the data with speed perturbation and SpecAugment, which masks bands of time and frequency. I would set text normalization rules with a native speaker early, hold out whole speakers for testing, and add a language model trained on cheaper text.
You use one LLM to grade another's answers. How do you know the grades can be trusted?
Whether you know the weak points of automatic judging with language models.
Names judge biases such as answer order, length and self-preference, and measures agreement with human labels before relying on it.

Judge models have known biases: they can favor an answer by its position, prefer longer answers, and like outputs that resemble their own. I would have people label a few hundred items and measure agreement with the judge. For pairwise grading I score both orders and count only consistent wins, and I recheck whenever the judge model or prompt changes.
Our LLM service is fast at low load but runs out of GPU memory with long prompts and many users. Why, and what do you do?
Your understanding of what drives memory when serving language models.
Points to the key-value cache growing with context length and concurrent requests, and names fixes like paged allocation, cache quantization or caps.

During generation the model stores keys and values for every earlier token in every layer, so memory grows with context length times concurrent requests. I would admit requests by memory, not by count, use paged cache allocation to cut waste, and try quantizing the cache. Models with grouped-query attention share keys and values across heads, so their cache is smaller.
A new model jumps ten points on a public benchmark. How do you check it is not contamination?
How you judge whether a benchmark gain is real or memorized.
Looks for test items in the training data and tests on fresh or rewritten items, instead of trusting one score.

First I search the training data for long n-gram overlaps with the test items and score the overlapping and clean subsets separately. I check whether the benchmark was public before the data cutoff. Then I test on items written after the cutoff or on paraphrased versions. If the gain shrinks a lot there, the model memorized the test rather than learned the skill.

nurse-practitioner.heading: Nurse practitioner questions
qs: How does practice authority for nurse practitioners differ from state to state?
Whether you know the legal framework you work in.
Names full, reduced and restricted practice, and checks the state board's rules instead of guessing.

States fall into three broad groups. With full practice, I can evaluate, diagnose and prescribe on my own license. Reduced practice requires a collaborative agreement with a physician for at least one area, often prescribing. Restricted practice requires supervision. Before I work in a state I read its board of nursing rules, because details like controlled substance prescribing differ.
On a video visit, what makes you stop and send the patient to be seen in person?
How you judge the limits of telehealth.
Concrete red flags, plus the cases where a needed exam or test cannot be done on camera.

Red flags mean the ER or 911 right away: chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of stroke, a sudden worst-ever headache. Short of an emergency, I convert when I need to touch, listen or test: an ear I must look into, lungs I need to hear, a belly that could be surgical. I tell the patient where to go and how soon, and I document why.
A patient has had sinus congestion for four days and asks for an antibiotic. What do you do?
Your antibiotic stewardship and how you say no without losing the patient.
Knows the signs that point to bacterial sinusitis, offers real symptom relief, and sets a clear point to call back.

At four days most sinus infections are viral, so an antibiotic adds side effects without helping. I look for signs of bacteria: symptoms past ten days without improvement, a severe start with high fever and thick discharge, or getting better then worse. If none fit, I suggest saline rinses, a nasal steroid and pain relief, and say when to call back.
A patient's blood pressure is high at one office visit. How do you confirm hypertension?
Whether you diagnose from good measurements, not from a single reading.
Correct measuring technique, repeat readings, and confirmation outside the office before labeling the patient.

One reading is not a diagnosis. I recheck after five minutes seated, back supported, feet flat, arm at heart level, with the right cuff size. If it stays high and nothing is urgent, I confirm with readings outside the office, home monitoring or an ambulatory monitor, to rule out white coat hypertension. Then we talk about treatment.
Your video patient mentions they are on vacation in another state. Does that change anything?
Whether you know telehealth licensing follows the patient's location.
Knows the license that counts is generally for the state where the patient is, and handles it without leaving them stranded.

Yes. Licensure is generally based on where the patient is during the visit, not where I am. If I am not licensed there, I should not diagnose or prescribe. I confirm location at the start of every visit. If the problem is urgent I direct them to local care or 911; otherwise we reschedule for when they are home or with a clinician licensed in that state.
Before you prescribe a controlled substance, what do you check?
Your safe prescribing habits for drugs that can be misused.
Checks the state prescription monitoring program, registrations, risk factors and interactions, and documents the reason.

I check the state prescription drug monitoring program for other prescribers, early fills, or opioids overlapping with benzodiazepines; many states require this. I review substance use history, other sedating drugs and sleep apnea. I confirm my DEA and any state registration cover that schedule, prescribe the smallest amount that works, and set a follow-up.
A 79-year-old comes in on twelve medications and has had two falls. Walk me through your review.
How you handle polypharmacy and deprescribing in older adults.
A full medication review, a check against the Beers Criteria, focus on fall-risk drugs, and changes made one at a time.

I ask them to bring every bottle, including over-the-counter pills and supplements. I check each drug for a current reason and against the Beers Criteria, looking hard at sedatives, anticholinergics like diphenhydramine, and blood pressure drugs that cause dizziness. I check orthostatic vitals, stop or taper one drug at a time, and follow up within weeks.
A patient on warfarin needs an antibiotic for a urinary tract infection. What are you thinking about?
Whether you catch a serious drug interaction before it happens.
Knows some antibiotics, like trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, can raise the INR, chooses carefully and plans an INR check.

Warfarin interacts with many antibiotics, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a big one: it can raise the INR fast and cause bleeding. I check kidney function, allergies and any culture, and pick an option with less interaction when I can. Either way I arrange an INR check within a few days, tell whoever manages the warfarin, and teach the patient the bleeding signs.
A patient with two weeks of low back pain asks for an MRI and something strong for the pain. How do you respond?
How you follow the evidence when a patient wants something else.
Screens for red flags, explains why early imaging and opioids rarely help, and offers a plan the patient can accept.

First I screen for red flags: numbness in the groin, bladder or bowel changes, fever, cancer history, worsening weakness. Without them, an early MRI rarely changes care and often shows findings that worry people for no reason. Most back pain improves within weeks, so I suggest heat, staying active, an anti-inflammatory if safe, and physical therapy, and book a recheck.
A lab result you ordered comes back critical at 6 p.m., and the patient does not answer the phone. What do you do?
Whether you own the results you order until the loop is closed.
Acts the same evening, tries every contact route, escalates under clinic policy, and documents each attempt.

A result I ordered is mine until it is handled. I call again, try the alternate number and emergency contact, and send a portal message. If the value is dangerous, like a very high potassium, and I still cannot reach them, I follow our policy, which can mean asking police for a welfare check. I document every attempt with the time and tell the on-call clinician.
Walk me through a diabetic foot exam.
Whether you can do a core chronic disease exam the way the guidelines expect.
Inspection, pulses, and sensation testing with a 10-gram monofilament plus one other test, done at least once a year.

I do it at least once a year, more often if risk is high. I look at the skin, nails, calluses, deformities and between the toes, and I check pedal pulses. For neuropathy I use a 10-gram monofilament plus one more test, like vibration with a 128-Hz tuning fork or pinprick. I also look at their shoes and teach daily self-checks.
How do you choose the level of an office visit when you code it?
Your grasp of how outpatient visits are coded and billed.
Office visit level is set by medical decision making or by total time on the date of the visit, and the note must support it.

I pick the level either by medical decision making, meaning the problems addressed, the data reviewed and the risk of the treatment, or by my total time on that date, including charting and calls. I use whichever fits better and document it. History and exam still go in the note, but they no longer set the level.
A patient twisted an ankle yesterday and booked a video visit. How do you decide if they need an X-ray?
How you adapt a hands-on exam to video with a proven decision rule.
Uses the Ottawa ankle rules: bone tenderness at set points, or not being able to take four steps, means an X-ray.

I use the Ottawa ankle rules. On camera, I have them press along the back edge and tip of each ankle bone, the base of the fifth metatarsal and the navicular on top of the midfoot. Then I ask them to walk four steps. Tenderness at any of those spots, or not managing four steps, means an X-ray. If all are negative, I treat it as a sprain.
A routine TSH comes back at 7 with a normal free T4. What do you do?
Whether you avoid treating one mildly abnormal lab value.
Repeats the test, checks antibodies and symptoms, and decides on treatment from the trend, the level and the patient's situation.

That is subclinical hypothyroidism if it holds. I repeat TSH and free T4 in 6 to 12 weeks, since TSH can rise after an illness, and check TPO antibodies, which predict progression. I ask about symptoms, biotin use and pregnancy plans. At this level most adults are watched; treatment is usually considered at a TSH of 10 or more, or sooner in pregnancy.
A 32-year-old woman with hypertension is doing well on lisinopril. What else do you need to talk about?
Whether you think about pregnancy when prescribing to patients who could become pregnant.
ACE inhibitors can harm a fetus, so you discuss pregnancy plans and contraception and plan a switch to a pregnancy-safe drug.

ACE inhibitors carry a boxed warning for fetal toxicity. I ask about pregnancy plans and birth control and document the talk. If she may become pregnant, we plan a switch ahead of time to a drug used in pregnancy, such as labetalol or nifedipine. If she becomes pregnant while on it, she stops it and calls me right away.
A 55-year-old has a 10-year heart risk of 9% and does not want a statin. How do you handle it?
How you use risk tools and shared decision making in prevention.
Treats intermediate risk as a conversation: looks for risk enhancers and uses a coronary calcium score if the choice is still unclear.

At 9% he is in the intermediate range of the ACC/AHA guideline, so a statin is reasonable but it is a shared decision. I look for risk enhancers like early heart disease in the family, high Lp(a) or chronic kidney disease. If he is still unsure, a coronary calcium score helps: a score of zero in a nonsmoker often lets us wait and recheck later.
A patient with type 2 diabetes and heart failure has an A1c above goal on metformin. What do you add, and why?
Whether you choose diabetes drugs by the patient's heart and kidney disease, not only by A1c.
An SGLT2 inhibitor, because it lowers heart failure hospitalizations; protecting the heart drives the choice, apart from A1c.

With heart failure I add an SGLT2 inhibitor. These drugs cut hospital stays for heart failure, and the ADA standards recommend them for that reason, apart from A1c. I check kidney function, warn about genital yeast infections, and teach sick-day rules: hold it when not eating or before surgery because of rare ketoacidosis. I avoid pioglitazone, which can worsen heart failure.
On a video visit, a patient's depression screen shows thoughts of self-harm. What do you do next?
How you assess suicide risk safely when the patient is not in the room.
Asks directly about plan, intent and means, knows where the patient is, and matches the response to the risk with a safety plan and close follow-up.

I ask directly about thoughts of suicide, a plan, intent, past attempts and access to guns or pills, often using the Columbia scale. I confirm their exact location, which I record at the start of every video visit. If risk is imminent, I keep them on the call while emergency services go. If not, we make a safety plan, limit means, give them 988 and set close follow-up.
A 70-year-old has a new headache, jaw pain when chewing and some blurred vision. What is your plan?
Whether you recognize an emergency hiding behind a common complaint.
Suspects giant cell arteritis, sends the patient for same-day evaluation, and knows steroids should not wait for a biopsy.

A new headache after 50 with jaw pain on chewing and vision changes is giant cell arteritis until proven otherwise, and it can cause permanent blindness. I send the patient for same-day evaluation, usually the emergency department, and call the physician there. ESR and CRP get drawn, high-dose steroids start right away, and the biopsy or ultrasound can still be done afterward.
Reviewing a chart, you find a lung nodule on a CT from eight months ago that nobody followed up. What do you do?
How you handle a missed result: the patient, the disclosure and the fix to the system.
Contacts the patient, discloses honestly, arranges follow-up by guideline, and reports it so the tracking gap gets closed.

I call the patient, explain plainly that the finding was not followed up and that I am sorry, and order the follow-up the Fleischner Society lung nodule guidelines call for by size and risk, often a repeat CT. I document the call, tell my lead and file a safety report. Then I push for a tracking list so incidental findings cannot slip again.

nursing.heading: Nursing questions
qs: Walk me through the nursing process.
Whether you know the framework behind every care plan.
All five steps in order, and the point that evaluation feeds back into a new assessment.

It is assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation and evaluation. I gather data, name the nursing problem, like risk for falls, set a goal the patient can reach, carry out the interventions, then check whether the goal was met. If it was not, I reassess and change the plan. It is a loop, not a checklist.
How do you check that a patient really understood what you taught?
How you make patient education stick.
Teach-back: the patient explains or shows it in their own words, and you reteach the gaps instead of asking 'Any questions?'.

I use teach-back. After explaining a new inhaler, I say, 'I want to be sure I explained it well. Can you show me how you will use it at home?' If a step is missing, I teach that part again in simpler words and ask once more. Asking 'Do you understand?' almost always gets a yes, so it tells me nothing.
In a video visit you cannot touch the patient. How do you assess them?
Whether you can assess by telehealth and know its limits.
Using what you can see and hear, home devices and the patient's own hands, with clear triggers for in-person or emergency care.

I watch their breathing, color, alertness and whether they can finish a sentence. I ask them to read their home blood pressure cuff or pulse oximeter on camera, and to press on their shin so I can see any swelling. If I see red flags, like chest pain or struggling to breathe, I have them call 911 and stay on the line until help arrives.
A patient refuses a medication you are due to give. What do you do?
How you balance a patient's right to refuse with their safety.
Respect the refusal, find out why, explain the risk, inform the provider and document. Never hide or force a medication.

First I ask why. Often it is a side effect, a cost worry, or not knowing what the pill is for. I explain what it does and what may happen if they skip it, without pressure. If they still say no, that is their right. I do not give it, I let the provider know, and I chart the refusal, the reason and what I taught. If I doubt they can make decisions, I raise that too.
What can you delegate to a nursing assistant, and what must you keep?
Your grasp of delegation and of the RN's responsibility for it.
Routine tasks on stable patients can go; assessment, care planning and judgment stay with the RN, who stays accountable. Exact rules vary by state.

I can delegate routine tasks with predictable results, like vital signs on a stable patient, bathing or helping someone walk, if that assistant is trained for it. I keep assessment, care planning, teaching and anything needing judgment. I give clear directions, say what to report back right away, and follow up, because I am still accountable for the outcome.
Your patient's blood pressure is dropping and you call the provider. What do you say?
Whether you can report a concern clearly and get action.
A structured report such as SBAR that ends with a specific request, plus a read-back of any new order.

I use SBAR. Situation: Mr. Lee in room 12 has a pressure of 86 over 50, down from 120 over 70 four hours ago. Background: day two after bowel surgery. Assessment: heart rate 112, he is pale and his urine output has dropped; I am worried about bleeding or fluid loss. Recommendation: please come see him; do you want labs and fluids? I read back any order.
A confused patient at high fall risk keeps trying to get up alone. What do you do?
How you prevent falls without jumping to restraints.
Finding the reason, such as toileting, pain or delirium, using rounding, a low bed and alarms, and treating restraints as a last resort with an order.

I look for why. Often they need the bathroom, are in pain or are newly confused, so I take them to the toilet on a schedule and report the confusion. I keep the bed low and locked, the call light in reach, nonslip socks on and the bed alarm set. I may move them closer to the station or ask for a sitter. Restraints need an order and are a last resort.
What early signs make you think of sepsis?
Whether you recognize sepsis before the patient crashes.
Suspected infection plus changes such as fast breathing, high heart rate, new confusion, low blood pressure or low urine output, and acting fast.

Any patient with a known or possible infection who starts breathing faster, has a racing heart, a fever or a low temperature, new confusion, falling blood pressure or less urine. New confusion in an older patient is easy to miss. I do not wait for every sign: I follow our sepsis screening protocol and call the provider or rapid response team right away, because delay costs lives.
After you give an opioid for pain, what do you watch for, and when?
Whether you know how to monitor opioids safely.
Reassessing pain and sedation when the drug peaks, knowing that rising sleepiness usually comes before slowed breathing.

I reassess pain and sedation when the drug should peak, sooner for IV than by mouth, at the times our policy sets. Rising sleepiness usually comes before slowed breathing, so I check how easily they wake and stay awake, plus breathing rate, depth and oxygen. If they drift off mid-sentence, I hold further doses, stay with them and call the provider.
You get an order for a dose that looks far too high. What do you do?
Whether you will question an order instead of just following it.
Hold the dose, verify with references and the pharmacist, clarify with the prescriber, and go up the chain of command if it is not resolved.

I hold it. I check it against a drug reference, the patient's weight and kidney function, and I ask the pharmacist. Then I call the prescriber, say exactly what worries me and ask them to confirm or change it. If it still looks unsafe, I go to my charge nurse and up the chain of command. I am accountable for what I give, not just for following orders.
What is the difference between a nursing diagnosis and a medical diagnosis?
Whether you understand what nursing adds to the medical plan.
The medical diagnosis names the disease. The nursing diagnosis names the patient's response that the nurse can act on, and it drives nursing interventions.

A medical diagnosis names the disease, like pneumonia. A nursing diagnosis names the patient's response that I can act on, like impaired gas exchange or risk for falls. It drives my interventions: positioning, breathing exercises, safe mobility. Two patients with the same pneumonia can have very different nursing diagnoses.
What is your role when a patient signs a consent form for surgery?
Whether you know who obtains informed consent and where the nurse's part ends.
The provider explains and obtains consent. The nurse witnesses the signature, checks capacity and understanding, and stops if the patient is unsure.

The surgeon explains the procedure, risks and alternatives and obtains consent. My part is to witness the signature and check that the patient is alert, not sedated, and understands. If the patient says she is not sure what they will do, I do not have her sign. I call the surgeon back to explain again, and I document it.
A patient's adult son offers to interpret because his mother speaks little English. What do you do?
Whether you use qualified interpreters for teaching and assessment.
A qualified medical interpreter, by phone or video if needed. Family and especially children are not used, except in an emergency.

I thank the son and call a qualified medical interpreter, by phone or video if no one is on site. Family members may leave out bad news or medical words, and patients may not speak freely in front of them. Children should not interpret except in an emergency. I note the interpreter's ID in the chart and speak to the patient, not to the interpreter.
Your patient is NPO for a procedure and has scheduled insulin due this morning. What do you do?
How you handle an order that no longer fits the patient's situation.
Neither giving it blindly nor skipping it alone: check glucose, call the provider for a clear order, and watch for low blood sugar.

I do not just give it or skip it. I check the blood glucose and the orders, then call the provider. Long-acting insulin is often given at a reduced dose and mealtime insulin held, but that is the provider's decision. I tell the procedure team, check glucose per protocol, and watch for signs of low blood sugar like sweating, shakiness or confusion.
Fifteen minutes into a blood transfusion, your patient has chills, a fever and back pain. Walk me through what you do.
Your response to a possible transfusion reaction, in the right order.
Stop the transfusion first, keep IV access with saline through new tubing, assess, notify the provider and blood bank, and return the bag per policy.

I stop the transfusion right away and stay with the patient. I keep the IV open with normal saline through new tubing, so the blood left in the line does not go in. I check vital signs and breathing, call the provider and the blood bank, and follow their orders. I send the bag and tubing back as policy says, and document the times, symptoms and actions.
A patient with heart failure goes home tomorrow. What do you teach, and how?
Your discharge teaching for a condition where self-care at home prevents readmission.
Daily weights done the same way, the weight gain that means calling, low-salt diet, each medicine, warning symptoms, and a set follow-up visit.

I teach weighing every morning after urinating, before breakfast, on the same scale, and writing it down. I explain the gain that means calling the clinic, using the number the provider set. We go over low-salt choices, each medicine and why, and warning signs like swelling or breathlessness lying flat. I book the follow-up visit before discharge and have him show me the plan back.
You find a patient on blood thinners on the floor next to her bed. Nobody saw her fall. What do you do?
How you assess after an unwitnessed fall and why the anticoagulant changes the plan.
Assess before moving her, assume a possible head injury, call the provider promptly even if she looks fine, then neuro checks and reporting.

I stay with her, call for help, and check airway, breathing, vital signs and a neuro check before anyone moves her. I look for head injury and hip pain. Because she takes a blood thinner, I call the provider right away even if she looks fine, since bleeding in the head can show up hours later. I expect imaging and frequent neuro checks, then report the fall per policy and review why it happened.
What risks do you see in copy-forward and alerts in the electronic health record?
Whether you use the EHR critically instead of trusting it.
Copied text can carry findings that are no longer true under your name. Alerts must be read, and alerts that fire too often should be reported.

Copy-forward saves time but can carry old findings into today's note: a wound that has healed, a drain that was removed. That is false documentation with my name on it, so I chart only what I assessed this shift. I read alerts instead of clicking through. If one fires too often for no reason, I report it so it gets fixed rather than ignored by everyone.
You get your assignment and believe it is not safe for the patients. What do you do?
Your judgement when staffing and patient safety conflict.
Raise it early with specifics, ask for changes, do not abandon accepted patients, and document the concern through the facility's process.

I raise it with the charge nurse before taking report, with specifics: two fresh post-op patients and an insulin drip. I ask for a change or for help. If nothing changes, I take the assignment, because leaving patients once I have accepted them would be abandonment, and I file my concern through the facility's process. Then I set priorities and ask for help early.
You suspect a colleague is working impaired. What do you do?
Whether you put patient safety ahead of loyalty and act through the right channel.
Report promptly to the charge nurse or manager with facts, not rumor. Do not ignore it or handle it alone.

Patient safety comes first, so I do not ignore it or confront her alone in the hallway. I tell the charge nurse or manager right away with what I saw: slurred speech, late doses, gaps in how controlled drugs were wasted. They can remove her from patient care. Many states have programs that help nurses recover, so reporting is also how she gets help.

observability-engineer.heading: Observability engineer questions
qs: What are logs, metrics and traces, and when would you reach for each?
Whether you know the three main signals and what each one is good at.
Metrics for trends and alerts, logs for the detail of single events, traces for following one request across services.

Metrics are numbers over time. They are cheap to store and good for dashboards and alerts. Logs record single events with the detail of what happened. Traces follow one request through every service it touches and show where the time went. I alert on metrics, use traces to find the slow hop, then read the logs to see why.
What are the RED and USE methods, and where does each fit?
Whether you have a system for choosing what to measure.
RED for services that answer requests, USE for resources like CPU, disks and pools; both keep dashboards focused.

RED is rate, errors and duration: how many requests come in, how many fail, how long they take. I use it for every service that answers requests. USE is utilization, saturation and errors, for resources such as CPU, memory, disks and connection pools. A new service gets RED panels on day one, and its main resources get USE panels.
A developer writes plain text log lines like 'checkout failed for user'. What would you ask them to change?
Whether you know what makes logs searchable and useful across services.
Structured fields, a trace or request ID on every line, sensible levels, and no personal data or secrets.

I would ask for structured logs, one JSON object per line, with fields like order ID, error code and duration, so we can filter and count. Every line should carry the trace ID passed in from the caller, so we can join it with other services. And no card numbers, passwords or tokens in any message, ever.
Why is average latency a poor number to alert on, and what do you use instead?
Your grasp of latency distributions and percentiles.
Averages hide the slow tail; use percentiles built from histograms, and know that percentiles cannot simply be averaged.

An average can look fine while one request in a hundred takes eight seconds. I watch p50, p95 and p99, where p99 is the time 99% of requests beat. I record latency as histograms, because bucket counts can be added up across servers and the percentile computed from the total. Averaging each server's p99 gives a number that means nothing.
A developer wants to add customer ID as a label on a request metric. What do you say?
Whether you understand cardinality and what it costs a metrics system.
Each unique label value creates a new time series; unbounded IDs belong in logs or traces, not metric labels.

Each distinct combination of label values is its own time series. With half a million customers, that one label could add half a million series per endpoint, slow every query and raise the bill. I would keep labels bounded, like endpoint, status class and region, and put the customer ID on the trace and in the logs, where we can still search by it.
How would you set an SLO for a checkout service, and what does the error budget do?
Whether you can turn the user experience into a target the team can act on.
A measure taken close to the user, a target below 100% agreed with the business, and a budget that guides release pace.

First the SLI, the measure of good service: the share of checkout requests that succeed within, say, 800 milliseconds, measured at the load balancer. Then a target from past data, maybe 99.9% over 30 days. The 0.1% left over is the error budget, about 43 minutes if it were all downtime. If we burn it early, we slow releases and fix reliability first.
The on-call team gets about 200 pages a week and ignores most of them. What do you do?
How you handle alert fatigue without hiding real problems.
Review each alert's value, page only on user-facing symptoms, turn the rest into tickets or delete them, and track page volume.

I pull a month of pages and mark each one: did someone act, and did users feel it? Pages nobody acted on get deleted or become tickets. Cause alerts like high CPU give way to symptom alerts tied to the SLO, using burn rate, how fast we spend the error budget: a fast burn pages, a slow burn opens a ticket. Then I report pages per week so it does not creep back.
Every dashboard is green, but customers say the app is failing. How can that happen, and how do you close the gap?
Whether you can find blind spots in what is being measured.
Seeing that monitoring may sit behind the point of failure, and adding checks from the user's side: edge, synthetic and client data.

Usually we measure only what reached our servers. If DNS, a certificate, the content delivery network or a mobile release breaks, failed requests never show up in our metrics. Once a bad config cut off one region and our error rate went down. I add synthetic checks from outside, edge and client-side error rates, and an alert when traffic drops below normal.
When would you choose head-based sampling for traces, and when tail-based?
Your knowledge of trace sampling and its trade-offs.
Head sampling is cheap but blind to the outcome; tail sampling keeps errors and slow traces but must hold whole traces before deciding.

Head sampling decides at the start of a request, say keep 5%, and passes that choice downstream. It is simple and cheap, but it drops most errors because it cannot know the outcome yet. Tail sampling waits until the trace is done, so I can keep every error and every slow request. The cost: collectors must hold whole traces in memory, and every span of a trace must reach the same one.
Your monitoring system itself goes down at 3 a.m. How would anyone find out?
Whether you plan for the failure of the observability stack itself.
Monitoring from outside the stack, such as an always-firing heartbeat alert that pages someone when it stops arriving.

If the alerting system is down, it cannot page about itself. I set up a heartbeat: an alert that always fires and goes to an outside service, which pages us if it stops hearing it for a few minutes. I also watch collection failures and ingestion lag, and run the monitoring in a different failure domain from the systems it watches.
In Prometheus, when would you use a histogram rather than a summary?
Whether you know which latency data can be combined across many servers.
Summaries compute quantiles inside each process and cannot be combined; histograms can be summed across instances, with accuracy set by the buckets.

Almost always a histogram. A summary works out the 99th percentile inside each process, and you cannot average percentiles from twenty pods into a true fleet number. A histogram exports bucket counts, which add up across pods, and histogram_quantile estimates the percentile. I put a bucket boundary at the SLO threshold, say 300 milliseconds, so the share of requests under it is exact.
Why do you apply rate() before sum() on a counter, and not the other way round?
Your grasp of how counters and counter resets work.
rate() detects resets in each series; summing raw counters first hides a restart and produces false drops or spikes.

A counter only goes up until the process restarts, then it drops to zero. rate() spots that drop in each series and treats it as a reset. If I sum the raw counters of ten pods first, one restart looks like the total falling, and the rate of that total is wrong. So it is sum(rate(...)), never a rate of a sum. Recording rules keep that order consistent.
A nightly batch job runs for ninety seconds. How do you get its metrics into Prometheus?
Whether you know the limits of pull-based metrics.
A Pushgateway fits a service-level batch job, used with its caveats known: pushed values never expire on their own, so it is not for long-running services.

Prometheus scrapes on an interval, so a short job may finish before it is ever scraped. At the end of the job I push a few results to a Pushgateway: last success timestamp, records processed, duration. Then I alert if the last success is older than about 26 hours. Pushed values stay until deleted, so I do not use it for per-instance metrics of long-running services.
Your error-rate alert pages someone at 4 a.m. because 2 of 5 requests failed. What is wrong with the alert?
How you handle alerts on services with low or uneven traffic.
Ratios are noisy at low volume; add a minimum request count, a longer window or budget-based alerting so a handful of failures does not page.

At 4 a.m. a 40% error rate from five requests says almost nothing; at noon the same rule is fine. I would add a floor, for example only fire when the window holds at least a few hundred requests, and move to burn-rate alerting with longer windows. If those few night users truly matter, a synthetic check gives a steady signal instead.
Walk me through multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting on an SLO.
Whether you can alert on an SLO without paging too late or too often.
Burn rate is how fast the budget is spent; fast burns page, slow burns open tickets, and a short window confirms the problem is still happening.

Burn rate 1 means we spend the whole error budget exactly by the end of the SLO window. With a 30-day window, a burn rate of 14.4 held for one hour uses 2% of the budget, so that pages. A rate near 1 over three days opens a ticket. Each alert also checks a short window, like 5 minutes, so it stops firing soon after the problem is fixed.
Traces stop at the message queue: the producer span and the consumer span end up in two separate traces. How do you fix it?
Your understanding of trace context propagation across asynchronous hops.
Inject the trace context into message headers on publish and extract it on consume; for batch consumers, use span links rather than a single parent.

HTTP calls carry the W3C traceparent header through instrumentation, but the queue client was not instrumented, so the context was lost. I make the producer inject the context into the message headers and the consumer extract it before starting its span. When one consumer handles a batch of 50 messages from different traces, I start one span with links to each, since a span has only one parent.
You run tail-based sampling and scale the collector from one instance to four. Sampled traces come out broken. Why?
Whether you understand what tail sampling needs from the telemetry pipeline.
Tail sampling must see every span of a trace in one place; route spans by trace ID through a load-balancing tier in front of the samplers.

Tail sampling decides after the trace is complete, so one collector must hold all spans of that trace. With four instances behind a plain round-robin balancer, spans of one trace land on different instances, and each decides on a fragment. I add a first tier with a load-balancing exporter keyed on trace ID, so every span of a trace reaches the same sampler.
The logging bill doubled in a quarter and finance wants it cut by 40%. How do you approach it?
How you cut telemetry cost without leaving teams blind.
Measure volume by source first, then cut the biggest waste: noisy debug logs, duplicates, long hot retention, and logs that should be metrics.

First I break volume down by service and log type; a handful of sources usually make most of the bill. Last time, three services logging every health check made a quarter of it. I drop or sample debug and success logs, turn per-request counts into metrics, and move older logs to cheap storage. Error logs stay whole, and I agree each cut with the owning team.
You discover that a service has been writing customer emails and full card numbers into the logs for two weeks. What do you do?
Your judgement when sensitive data leaks into telemetry.
Bring in security at once, stop the flow, find and purge every copy including archives and exports, and add checks so it cannot recur.

I tell the security team right away, because card numbers in logs are a compliance problem and they own decisions on disclosure. Meanwhile we stop the leak: a redaction rule in the pipeline today, a code fix after. Then we find every copy, in the log store, archives and exports to other tools, and delete it with a record. Last, an automated check that flags card-like patterns.
You have to bring fifty product teams onto one observability standard. How do you get them to adopt it?
How you drive adoption across teams you have no authority over.
Make the right way the easy way: shared libraries and defaults, a short minimum standard, early wins with a few teams, and coverage tracked in the open.

I would not start with a policy document. I would ship a shared library and service template that give structured logs, RED metrics and tracing with no extra work, then pilot with two or three teams that have real pain. Their before-and-after numbers sell it. Then I publish a short minimum standard, track coverage per team, and add it to the production readiness review.

office-manager.heading: Office manager questions
qs: How do you decide when to reorder office supplies and how much to order?
Whether you run supplies with a system instead of reacting when something runs out.
A reorder point based on actual use and delivery time, a simple tracking method, and fewer rush orders.

I track how fast we use each core item, like paper, toner and coffee, and how long delivery takes. I set a reorder point that covers that lead time plus a small buffer. I check stock on a fixed day each week and order in one batch. Rush orders get noted so I can adjust the levels.
What does a good visitor check-in process look like?
How you balance a warm welcome with knowing who is in the building.
Greeting, sign-in, host notified, a visitor badge, escort where needed, sign-out, and a log that is kept private.

The visitor is greeted, signs in with name, company and host, and gets a dated badge. I notify the host, who comes to collect them. Visitors are not left to wander. At sign-out the badge comes back. The log is not left open for the next guest to read, and it doubles as our headcount if we ever have to evacuate.
Walk me through how you prepare for a new hire's first day.
Your planning across IT, HR and the space so a new person feels expected.
Work starts days ahead: desk, equipment and accounts arranged with IT, badge and keys ready, and a planned first morning.

About a week out I confirm the start date with HR and the manager. I ask IT for the laptop and accounts, and I set up the desk, chair and badge. On day one I meet them at the door, give a short tour, show the restrooms, kitchen and exits, and hand them to their manager with a lunch plan, so nobody is sitting alone waiting for a password.
An employee's last day is today. What is on your offboarding checklist?
Whether you close access and recover company property without fuss.
Badge and building access shut off on time, keys and equipment returned, IT told in advance, and the person treated with respect.

I agree the timing with HR so access is cut at the right moment, not weeks later. I collect the badge, keys, parking pass, laptop and any company card, and I check them against what was issued. IT turns off accounts and I ask building management to deactivate the fob. I remove the person from desk charts and lists, and I thank them on the way out.
The heat stops working on a cold Monday morning. What do you do?
How you handle a facilities problem: who to call, what to tell staff, and what to do meanwhile.
A ticket with building management or the vendor right away, a clear note to staff with the next update time, and a sensible plan B.

I call building management and put in a written ticket, and I ask for an arrival time. Then I message staff: the heat is out, it has been reported, the next update is at ten. I check with leadership about letting people work from home. I do not bring in space heaters unless building rules allow them, since they can be a fire risk. I log the outage for the landlord.
How would you plan a holiday party for 60 people on a fixed budget?
Your event planning: budget, headcount, logistics and inclusion.
Budget split by line with a reserve, an RSVP count, dietary and accessibility needs, a clear alcohol plan, and a time that works for most staff.

I start from the budget and keep about ten percent in reserve. I send an RSVP with a dietary question and pick a date and time that works for parents and remote staff too. Food gets the biggest share. If there is alcohol, I set limits and offer good non-alcoholic choices. I book the venue early, check access for anyone who needs it, and track every cost in one sheet.
Two teams have booked the big conference room for client meetings at the same time. How do you sort it out?
Your judgement when two fair claims collide, and how you prevent a repeat.
Facts first, a quick fair call or an alternative space, both teams told directly, and a fix to the booking system.

I check the booking system to see who booked first and whether it was a glitch. Then I call both organizers and look for a way out: another room, a nearby meeting space, or shifting one meeting by an hour. If neither can move, the first booking stands and I help the other team find a space. Afterwards I look at why the system allowed it.
You discover the copier lease auto-renewed for three more years at a higher rate. What do you do?
How you handle a contract mistake and how you stop it happening again.
Read the contract, talk to the vendor about options, tell your manager honestly, and set up a contract calendar with notice dates.

First I read the lease for the renewal terms and any exit or downgrade clause. I tell my manager what happened and what it costs. Then I call the vendor: we are a steady customer, and I ask for the old rate, a smaller machine or a shorter term. Afterwards I build a contract list with every renewal and notice date and set reminders well ahead of each one.
How do you get an office ready for an emergency evacuation?
Whether you treat emergency preparedness as a plan people have practiced, not a sign on the wall.
Posted routes and an assembly point, floor wardens with backups, a way to account for everyone including visitors, help planned for those who need it, and drills.

I work from the building's emergency plan and make sure exits and the assembly point are posted and known. Each area gets a floor warden and a backup. At the meeting point we account for staff from the in-office list and visitors from the sign-in log. I ask privately who would need help on stairs and plan that with them. We practice with drills, use the stairs, never the elevators, and fix what was slow.
Walk me through how you would plan moving a 60-person office to a new floor.
Your ability to run a large project with many vendors, a hard date and minimal downtime.
A timeline worked back from the move date, early IT and vendor booking, a seating plan, labeled crates, a weekend move, and a team on hand on day one.

I start from the move date and work back. I book movers and IT early, since network and phones take the longest. I build a seating plan with managers and give each person a numbered label and crates. Most packing happens Thursday, the move over the weekend, and IT tests desks on Sunday. Monday morning I walk the floor with IT to fix problems, and a week later I collect a punch list.
What is a three-way match, and why do you do one before a vendor gets paid?
Whether you control spending with a basic accounts payable check.
Names the three documents (purchase order, receiving record, invoice) and holds payment when they do not agree.

Before I approve an invoice, I compare three documents: the purchase order, the receiving record or packing slip, and the invoice. Item, quantity and price have to agree. If we ordered 20 chairs and the invoice bills 22 at a higher price, I hold payment and ask the vendor for a corrected invoice.
How do you keep the office first aid kits and AED ready to use?
Whether you treat emergency equipment as something to check on a schedule, not once.
A regular logged check, attention to pad and battery expiry dates, restocking after use, and staff knowing where things are.

I do a monthly check and log it. On the AED I look at the status light and the expiry dates on the pads and battery, and I order replacements before they run out. I restock first aid kits after every use and check dates on what is inside. I also keep the list of trained responders current and make sure people know where the AED hangs.
Our cleaning vendor keeps skipping the restrooms on Fridays. How do you fix it without just switching vendors?
How you manage a vendor's performance against the contract.
Checks the written scope, documents the misses, escalates to the account manager, and uses the contract terms only if it continues.

First I read the scope of work to confirm Friday restroom service is in it. Then I log each miss with dates and photos and meet the account manager, not only the night crew. We agree on a fix and a checklist the crew signs off. If misses continue, I follow the contract's notice terms and start collecting quotes.
An employee asks you for a standing desk because of a back problem. How do you handle it?
Whether you spot a possible disability accommodation request and route it correctly.
Brings in HR so the ADA interactive process is followed, keeps medical details private, and helps carry out what is agreed.

Once someone ties a request to a health condition, I treat it as a possible accommodation request and bring in HR the same day so it is handled and documented properly. I do not ask about the diagnosis myself, and I keep it private. Once HR agrees on a solution, I source the desk or converter and set it up quickly.
Someone without a badge follows an employee through the secure door. What do you do?
How you handle tailgating politely while keeping the office secure.
