A friendly approach, an escort to sign in, and no physical confrontation; security or 911 if there is a threat.

I walk up in a friendly way and ask who they are here to see. Most are visitors who did not know the rule, so I take them to the front desk to sign in, get a badge and meet their host. If someone refuses or acts strangely, I do not block them physically. I keep them in sight and call building security, or 911 if there is a threat.
What are CAM charges in a commercial lease, and what do you check at the year-end reconciliation?
Your understanding of the lease costs that sit on top of base rent.
Defines CAM as the tenant's share of common area costs, and checks the share, exclusions and caps against the lease.

CAM charges are our share of the building's common area costs, like lobby cleaning, landscaping and shared repairs. We usually pay a monthly estimate, then the landlord reconciles to actual costs once a year. I check our percentage share matches the lease, that excluded items were not billed, and any cap. If something looks off, I ask for the backup.
The landlord has not fixed a roof leak after two phone calls. What do you do next?
How you escalate a facilities problem with a landlord while protecting the office.
Written notice the way the lease requires, documentation, immediate protection of people and equipment, and escalation inside the company.

I stop relying on calls. I send written notice in the form and to the address the lease's notice clause requires, with dates, photos and the damage so far. Meanwhile I move desks, put out buckets and cover equipment. I log every contact. If nothing happens, I bring in leadership and whoever manages the lease, since our options depend on its terms.
You find that you paid the same vendor invoice twice last month. How do you handle it?
How you own a mistake and close the gap that caused it.
Tells finance and the manager right away, recovers the money in writing, and adds a check so it cannot recur.

I tell my manager and finance the same day rather than fix it quietly. I send the vendor both payment records and ask in writing for a refund or a credit on the next invoice. Then I find the cause. Once it was an invoice sent by email and by mail, entered twice. I added a check for duplicate invoice numbers before anything is approved.
Most staff come in only two or three days a week. How would you decide whether we need all this space?
Whether you use real occupancy data to make space decisions.
Badge, booking and headcount data, attention to peak days rather than averages, and lease limits checked before any change.

I gather a few weeks of data: badge swipes, desk and room bookings, and a quick headcount at peak hours. Peak days matter more than the average, since everyone may come on Tuesday. If peak use is around 60% of desks, we could consolidate, try desk sharing, or sublease if the lease allows. I share the findings with staff before moving anyone.
Leadership wants a 15% cut in the office budget. Where do you look first, and how do you present it?
Your judgement on cost cuts that save money without hurting the people the office serves.
Starts from a full list of spend and contracts, takes low-impact savings first, and gives leadership options with trade-offs.

I list every line, contract and renewal date first. Then I look for savings people will not feel: unused subscriptions, duplicate vendors, rebidding supplies and cleaning, fewer printers. Coffee and events affect morale, so I would trim those, not drop them. I would bring leadership options with the savings and the effect on staff, so they make the call.

operations-analyst.heading: Operations analyst and associate questions
qs: Walk me through how you map a process you have never seen before.
How you learn a process as it really runs, not as it is written.
Observing and talking to the people who do the work, noting steps, triggers, waits and handoffs, then checking the map with the team.

I start by walking it with the people who do it, not from the written procedure. I note each step, who does it, what triggers it, and how long it waits between steps. I draw it as a simple swimlane, one lane per role, then check it with the team. The handoffs between lanes are usually where the delays and errors are.
What does Little's Law tell you about a work queue?
Whether you can link backlog, throughput and waiting time with a simple rule.
Average work in progress equals throughput times average time in the system, applied to averages in a fairly stable process.

On average, the work in the system equals throughput times the time each item spends there. If we have 200 open cases and close 50 a day, a case waits about four days. So to cut wait time I either close more per day or let fewer cases pile up. It holds for averages in a fairly stable system, not for one bad day.
Our average ticket resolution time is two days, yet customers keep complaining about slow service. What would you look at?
Whether you look past an average to the spread and the segments behind it.
Median and high percentiles, split by type or channel, to find the slice that waits far longer than the average shows.

An average hides the tail. I would look at the median and the 90th percentile, and split by ticket type and channel. Often most tickets close the same day while a slice waits a week, maybe one category that needs a second team. Fixing that slice changes what customers feel more than shaving the average.
A weekly report shows volume dropped 30% overnight. What do you do before telling anyone?
Your habit of checking the data before raising an alarm.
Checking the pipeline, filters, field changes and source outages, then spot-checking raw data, and bringing facts either way.

I treat it as a data problem until proven otherwise. I check whether the job ran fully, whether a filter or field name changed, and whether the source system had an outage. Then I spot-check a few days against the raw system. If the drop is real, I bring the numbers and what I checked, so the conversation starts from facts.
The same error keeps coming back in a process. How do you find the root cause?
How you move from symptoms to a cause you can fix.
Counting errors to see where they cluster, asking why with the people involved, and fixing the process rather than blaming people.

First I count: which error types, which steps, which shifts. A Pareto chart usually shows a few causes making most of the errors. Then I ask why it happens, several times, with the people on that step. Once, wrong addresses traced back to a form field that allowed free text. We changed the field, not the people, and errors fell by more than half.
How do you decide whether a manual task is worth automating?
Your judgement on the cost and benefit of automation.
Frequency, time and error cost weighed against build and upkeep, plus a stable process; sometimes removing the step is better.

I estimate how often the task runs, minutes each time, and the cost of an error, then compare that with build time and upkeep. A 10-minute daily task is about 40 hours a year. I also check the process is stable; automating a step that changes every month just moves the work. And sometimes the better fix is removing the step.
A metric got worse this week and your manager wants an explanation. How do you tell a real change from normal variation?
Whether you can separate a signal from noise before anyone reacts.
Looking at the metric over many periods, using control limits or a clear baseline, and saying plainly when a dip is just noise.

I look at the metric over time, not two points. With 20 or more past periods I can draw a control chart: an average line and limits about three standard deviations out. A point outside the limits, or a long run on one side of the average, says something changed. A single dip inside the limits is usually noise, and I say that before anyone reacts.
A manager wants a new KPI that you think will push people toward the wrong behavior. What do you do?
How you push back on a metric with evidence and respect.
Naming the likely side effect with an example, proposing a balancing measure, and testing it, while respecting the final decision.

I would say what behavior I expect it to drive, with an example. Calls per hour alone rewards short calls, so customers call back and total work goes up. I would suggest pairing it with a balancing measure, such as repeat contacts within seven days, and testing both for a month. If the manager still wants it, I track it and report the side effect honestly.
An automation you built failed silently for a week before anyone noticed. How do you handle it?
How you own a mistake, repair the damage and stop it happening again.
Telling people quickly, fixing the backlog and checking it, then adding monitoring so a failure cannot go unnoticed again.

I tell my manager and the affected team right away, with what failed and since when. Then I fix the backlog: in one case a nightly import had stopped, so I reran the missed days and checked totals against the source. After that I added an alert that emails me when a run fails or loads zero rows. The silent failure was the real bug, not the import.
What is takt time, and how is it different from cycle time?
Whether you know the basic pacing measures of process work.
Takt is set by customer demand, cycle time by the process. Any step slower than takt cannot keep up.

Takt time is the pace demand sets: available working time divided by the units customers need in that time. With 450 minutes and 150 orders, takt is 3 minutes per order. Cycle time is how long a step actually takes per unit. If any step's cycle time is longer than takt, we fall behind unless we add capacity or change that step.
A manager wants the team at 100% utilization. Why might that make service worse?
Whether you understand how queues behave when work arrives unevenly.
Wait time rises steeply, not in a straight line, as utilization nears full. Slack is what absorbs spikes.

Work never arrives evenly. A team with no slack builds a queue every time a spike hits and has no spare time to clear it. Wait time climbs sharply as utilization gets close to 100%. I would show our queue and wait-time data, then suggest a target that leaves buffer, based on what our own numbers show, and test it for a few weeks.
Step two got 40% faster, but daily output did not change. Why?
Your grasp of bottlenecks and where throughput is really set.
Output is limited by the constraint. Improving another step only moves work faster into the queue in front of it.

Output is set by the slowest step, the bottleneck. If step two was not the bottleneck, speeding it up just feeds work faster into the pile in front of the real one. I would look at where work piles up and which step has the lowest capacity, focus effort there, and make sure that step never sits idle waiting for input.
Finance and your dashboard show different numbers for last month's on-time rate. How do you reconcile them?
How you trace a data disagreement to its source.
Compare definitions, filters, dates and refresh times, trace sample records, then agree one written definition.

I put both definitions side by side: what counts as on time, which orders are in or out, cancellations, which date is used, time zone, and when each report refreshed. Then I trace a few orders that are counted differently. It is usually a definition gap, so I agree one written definition with finance and note it on both reports.
Volume is forecast to grow 25% next quarter. How do you estimate the staff needed?
Your method for capacity planning.
Workload from volume and handle time, adjusted for shrinkage, with a queueing model where service levels matter.

I start with workload: forecast volume times average handle time gives hours of work. I divide by productive hours per person after shrinkage, meaning breaks, training, meetings and absence. If customers wait in a queue with a service target, I use a queueing model like Erlang C, because simple workload math understaffs peaks. I plan by hour or day, not monthly totals.
The error rate went down at every site, but the company total went up. How is that possible?
Whether you can spot a mix effect behind an average.
Volume shifted toward a higher-error site. The candidate names the mix effect and splits mix from performance.

The mix changed. If more volume moved to the site with the highest error rate, the overall rate can rise even though each site improved. This is called Simpson's paradox. I would show each site's rate with its volume, and split the total change into the part from mix and the part from performance, so nobody blames teams that actually got better.
You changed a process at one site. How do you show the change, and not something else, moved the numbers?
How you measure the effect of a change fairly.
A baseline, a comparison site over the same period, the difference in change, and a guardrail metric.

Before the change I take a baseline over several weeks to know normal variation. I compare the pilot site with a similar site that did not change, over the same weeks, so seasonality and volume swings hit both. I look at the difference in improvement between them. I also watch a guardrail like error rate, so speed did not come at the cost of quality.
The process you are automating has dozens of exceptions. How do you decide what the automation handles?
Your judgement on automation scope.
Automate the common paths found in real data, route the rest to people with a reason, and track the exception queue.

I count past cases by type over a few months. Usually a few standard paths cover most of the volume. I automate those and send everything else to a human queue with the reason attached, instead of coding every rare case. I track that queue, and if one exception type keeps growing, I add it later or fix its cause upstream.
Six months after a process improvement, how do you make sure the team has not drifted back?
How you make a change last after the project ends.
A written procedure with an owner, a reviewed metric with a trigger, system design that blocks the old way, and planned check-ins.

I plan for it at launch. The new steps go into a written procedure with one owner. The key metric goes on a chart the team reviews weekly, with a clear trigger for action. Where I can, I build the step into the system so the old way is hard to do. At 30, 90 and 180 days I check the numbers and watch the work, because drift usually starts with workarounds.
Your analysis shows a delay comes from another department, and its manager disputes your data. What do you do?
How you handle a finding that crosses team lines.
Talks privately first, shows the method and real cases, listens for missing context, and frames a shared fix.

I go to that manager one on one before any wider meeting. I show the data, how I pulled it, and a few real cases they can check, and I ask what I might be missing. Sometimes they know something the data does not show. If the finding holds, I frame it as a handoff problem we share and propose a fix we measure together.

operations-manager.heading: Operations manager questions
qs: What is the difference between a leading and a lagging indicator in operations?
Whether you manage with numbers that warn you early, not only ones that report the past.
A clear definition with a real example of each, and why you need both.

A lagging indicator tells me what already happened, like on-time delivery last month or cost per order. A leading indicator moves first, like the backlog at noon, open positions or machine downtime this week. I watch the leading ones daily so I can act before the lagging number goes bad, and I use the lagging ones to confirm the result.
How do you find the bottleneck in a process, and why does it matter?
Your grasp of how flow and capacity work.
The slowest step sets the output of the whole process; time saved at other steps does not add output.

I walk the process and look where work piles up and where people downstream sit waiting. Then I check each step's capacity against demand. The slowest step sets the output of the whole process, so an hour saved there is an hour for the whole operation. An hour saved elsewhere often just makes a bigger pile in front of the bottleneck.
The same shipping error keeps coming back every few weeks. Walk me through how you get to the root cause.
How you solve a problem for good instead of patching it.
Facts first, asking why until you reach a cause in the process, a fix that is tried out, and a check that it held.

I pull the recent cases and look for what they share: shift, product, station, person. Then I keep asking why until I reach something in the process, not just “someone was careless.” Say two items have look-alike labels. I change the label or the bin layout, try it on one shift, and track the error rate for a month to make sure it stays down.
Two suppliers quote the same part, and one is 6% cheaper. How do you decide?
Whether you look at total cost, not just the price on the quote.
Total cost of ownership: quality, lead time, reliability, freight, payment terms and the cost of switching.

I compare total cost, not unit price. I look at defect rates, on-time history, lead time, minimum order size, freight, payment terms and what it costs to approve a new supplier. If the cheaper one ships late twice a year and we pay for rush freight and overtime, the 6% is gone. I would also ask for references and start with a trial order.
Cost per unit rose 8% last month. Walk me through how you find out why.
How you break a cost number down before you act on it.
Separating volume from rates, usage and product mix, and checking fixed costs spread over fewer units, before blaming anyone.

First I check volume. If we made fewer units, fixed costs like rent and salaried staff spread over less, and unit cost rises even if nobody spent more. Then I split the rest into rates and usage: did labor hours, overtime, scrap or material prices go up? I also check whether the product mix shifted. Only then do I sit down with the team on a fix.
One key component comes from a single supplier. What do you do about that?
How you weigh supply risk against cost and effort.
Sizing the exposure first, then choosing a fitting response: a second source, safety stock, or contract terms and closer watching.

I first ask how long we could run if they stopped shipping, and how long it would take to approve someone else. If the answer is days against months, that is a real exposure. Options are a second source, extra safety stock, or a contract with notice terms. I pick based on cost and how critical the part is, and I keep an eye on the supplier's health.
Our on-time shipping rate is 98%, but customers say their orders arrive late. How do you explain that?
Whether you question a metric when it does not match what customers experience.
Checking what the number really measures, finding the gap, and adding a measure that matches what the customer sees.

Most likely we measure the wrong thing. On-time shipping may count when the box leaves our dock against our own date, not when it reaches the customer against the date we promised. Carrier delays, split shipments or promise dates changed by staff would all hide there. I would trace a sample of orders end to end, then add a delivered-on-time measure.
One supervisor hits every target, but his team's turnover is twice the site average. What do you do?
How you judge a manager on how results are reached, not only on the results.
Gathering facts first, a direct private talk with clear expectations, and treating turnover as part of performance.

Turnover is a cost, so his numbers are not as good as they look. I would read exit interview notes, talk to a few people on his team, and look at overtime and absences. Then I meet him alone, share what I found, and make retention one of his goals with a date to review it. If what I hear points to mistreatment, I bring in HR right away.
You rolled out a new process, and three months later the teams have slipped back to the old way. How do you handle it?
Whether you know how to make a change stick.
Finding out why people went back before enforcing anything, then written standard steps, an owner and regular checks.

First I ask why. Often the new way is slower in some case we did not plan for, or new hires were trained by someone who never used it. I fix that problem, write the steps as a short standard with photos, and give each area an owner. Then I check it on the floor every week for a while, and less often once it holds.
You are asked to cut operating costs by 10% without hurting service. Where do you start?
Your judgement on cutting costs without damaging the operation.
A map of where the money goes, waste and outside spend before people, and service measures watched during the cuts.

I start with a breakdown of where the money goes, because the biggest lines decide the plan. I look at waste first: overtime caused by poor scheduling, rework, rush freight, unused contracts and supplier prices nobody has rebid in years. Cutting staff is the last lever. I set the service numbers I will not let drop and review them weekly while we cut.
What is Little's Law, and how would you use it on the floor?
Whether you know the basic math that links work in progress, throughput and lead time.
Work in progress equals throughput times lead time, applied to a real decision like cutting queues to shorten lead time.

Average work in progress equals average throughput times average lead time. If a line finishes 50 orders a day and 400 sit in process, lead time is about 8 days. If I want 4 days without adding capacity, I have to cut work in progress to about 200, usually by limiting what we release to the floor.
How do you calculate inventory turns, and what does a falling number tell you?
Your grasp of how inventory ties up cash.
Cost of goods sold divided by average inventory, and a falling number treated as a question to dig into, not a verdict.

Turns are cost of goods sold for the period divided by average inventory at cost. If turns fall from 8 to 6, stock is sitting longer and tying up cash. I look item by item: often a few slow movers or one overbuy explain most of it. Then I fix the reorder points or work down the excess.
Why is it a bad idea to plan a team or a machine at 100% utilization?
Whether you understand how queues behave when capacity is tight.
As utilization nears 100%, waiting time climbs steeply because normal variation has no slack to absorb it.

Work never arrives evenly. With some slack, a busy hour gets absorbed. Near full load, every small spike becomes a queue that never clears, and wait times grow much faster than the load. I plan people below their full available time and protect the bottleneck so it never sits idle waiting for work.
Tomorrow's forecast is 12,000 units. Walk me through how you set the headcount for the shift.
How you turn a demand forecast into a staffing plan.
Volume divided by a measured rate gives labor hours, then adjustments for breaks, absence and the mix of work.

If our measured pick rate is 120 units per labor hour, 12,000 units is 100 hours. On 8-hour shifts with about 7 productive hours after breaks, that is 15 people. I add one or two for typical absence and check the mix: bulky orders lower the rate, so I plan more. At midday I compare actual against plan.
Your team has run heavy overtime for three months. How do you decide between more overtime and hiring?
Your judgement on labor cost, fatigue and whether the extra demand will last.
Compares the true cost of each option, counts fatigue and errors, and asks whether the extra volume is permanent.

Federal law requires at least time and a half for nonexempt staff after 40 hours in a workweek, and some states, like California, add daily overtime. Hiring adds wages, benefits and training time. If the volume looks permanent, I hire. If it is seasonal, I use temps or capped overtime. I also watch errors and injuries, which rise with fatigue.
Your labor cost is 10% over budget, but volume was 15% over plan. How do you report that?
Whether you can separate volume effects from efficiency in a budget review.
Flexes the budget to actual volume first, then shows whether cost per unit got better or worse.

A fixed budget makes us look bad for doing more work. I flex it: if labor was planned at $2.00 a unit, 15% more units earns 15% more labor budget. Spending only 10% more means cost per unit fell, by about 4%. I report both: volume drove the spend, and we got more efficient. If it had gone the other way, I would say so just as plainly.
You want $400,000 for a conveyor system. How do you build the case for the finance team?
How you build a capital request that finance will trust.
Measured savings, all costs including maintenance and install downtime, a payback period and a view that counts the time value of money.

I start from measured numbers: labor hours the conveyor removes at loaded wage rates, plus fewer errors. Say that is $160,000 a year, minus $20,000 maintenance: payback is under three years. Finance will also want net present value, which discounts future savings at the company's required return. I add the risks: install downtime, ramp-up and a drop in volume.
An employee is admitted to the hospital after an accident on your site. What happens in the next 24 hours?
Whether you know OSHA reporting duties and how to handle a serious incident.
Care for the person first, secure the scene, report the in-patient hospitalization to OSHA within 24 hours, then investigate.

First the person gets care, and someone keeps in touch with the family. I secure the area and stop that task until we know the cause. A work-related in-patient hospitalization must be reported to OSHA within 24 hours; a death, within 8. Then I collect statements and photos while memories are fresh and record the case on our OSHA injury log.
You take over a site that has missed its targets for a year. What do you do in your first 90 days?
How you diagnose before you change things in a new role.
Listening and data before decisions, a few quick fixes that build trust, then a plan with clear owners.

The first month I listen and measure: I walk every process, work some shifts, and check whether the numbers are even right. By day 45 I pick two or three fixes the team already knows are needed and get them done fast. By day 90 I share a plan with targets, owners and dates, and I tell my boss honestly which problems will take longer.
We need to close the night shift and let 60 people go. What do you plan before anyone is told?
Whether you handle a reduction in force legally, fairly and with care for the people.
Involves HR and legal on WARN and state notice rules, uses fair written criteria, and plans the message, the day and the work transfer.

I bring in HR and legal first: the federal WARN Act can require 60 days' written notice, and some states have their own rules. We set fair, written selection criteria and check them for bias. I plan who tells each person, face to face, with severance and benefits details ready, and how the day shift absorbs the work so customers are not hurt.

optics.heading: Optics and photonics questions
qs: What is the difference between f-number and numerical aperture?
Whether you know the two basic ways to describe how much light an optical system collects.
F-number as focal length over entrance pupil diameter, NA as index times the sine of the cone half-angle, and the rough link between them.

F-number is focal length divided by entrance pupil diameter, so it is common for camera lenses. Numerical aperture is the refractive index times the sine of the half-angle of the light cone, common for microscopes and fibers. For a lens focusing light from far away, F-number is roughly one over two times NA, so f/2 is about NA 0.25.
Name the main monochromatic aberrations. How would you reduce spherical aberration in a single lens?
Your grasp of the aberrations every lens design starts from.
The five Seidel aberrations named correctly, and real fixes: lens bending, splitting power, higher-index glass, an asphere or a smaller aperture.

Spherical aberration, coma, astigmatism, field curvature and distortion. For a single lens I would first bend it to the best shape, which for a collimated input is close to plano-convex with the curved side facing the incoming beam. If that is not enough, I would split the power over two lenses, use higher-index glass, or make one surface aspheric.
What does an MTF curve tell you, and how would you measure it on a camera module?
Whether you can connect image sharpness to a number you can test.
Contrast transfer versus spatial frequency, read at frequencies tied to the sensor, at center and corners, plus a real method such as slanted-edge.

MTF shows how much of an object's contrast survives the system at each spatial frequency, usually in line pairs per millimeter. I read it at frequencies tied to the pixel pitch, such as half the Nyquist frequency, at the center and the corners. On a camera module I would use a slanted-edge target, a tilted dark-to-light edge that gives MTF from a single image.
An interferometer report gives a peak-to-valley and an RMS wavefront error. Which do you trust more, and what counts as diffraction-limited?
Your reading of interferometer results and the usual pass criteria.
PV is driven by one bad spot or noise; RMS describes the whole aperture. The Maréchal criterion: about 1/14 wave RMS, Strehl ratio near 0.8.

Peak-to-valley is just the two extreme points, so one dust spot or a noisy pixel can inflate it. RMS averages over the whole aperture and predicts image quality better. A common rule is the Maréchal criterion: about one-fourteenth of a wave RMS, a Strehl ratio near 0.8, is called diffraction-limited. I still check the spec, since some customers write PV limits.
Walk me through aligning a laser beam down a rail using two steering mirrors.
Whether you have actually aligned a beam by hand on a bench.
Two irises at beam height; upstream mirror centers the beam on the near iris, downstream mirror on the far iris; repeat until both stay centered, then lock.

I set two irises at the same height, one near and one far along the rail, and work at low power. I adjust the upstream mirror to center the beam on the near iris, then the second mirror to center it on the far iris. Each change disturbs the other, so I repeat until both stay centered. Then I lock the mounts and check again, since tightening can shift the beam.
You need a smaller focused spot from a laser. What can you change?
Your working knowledge of how Gaussian beams focus.
Spot size grows with wavelength, focal length and M squared, and shrinks with a larger input beam; a smaller spot also means a shorter depth of focus.

The focused spot is roughly proportional to wavelength times focal length divided by the input beam size, times the beam quality factor, M squared. So I can expand the beam before the lens, use a shorter focal length, or use a shorter wavelength or a cleaner beam. A smaller spot also gives a shorter depth of focus, and the lens must stay free of aberration at the larger aperture.
The tolerance analysis says one lens needs a centering tolerance the shop says will triple its cost. What do you do?
Your judgement in trading performance against cost and manufacturability.
Confirm the result with compensators and realistic tolerances, look at desensitizing the design or active alignment, and bring options with cost and yield to the team.

First I check the number is real: I rerun the Monte Carlo with focus as a compensator and the shop's standard tolerances to see the yield. If yield is too low, I look at desensitizing the design, for example spreading the power so that surface matters less, or centering that lens actively at assembly. Then I bring each option's yield and cost to the team.
A lens designed and tested in the lab will fly on a satellite. What could move its focus in orbit, and how do you plan for it?
Whether you design for the environment the optics will really work in.
Vacuum removes the air index and shifts focus; temperature changes glass index and housing length. Design for vacuum, athermalize, and verify in thermal vacuum testing.

Two things. In vacuum the index around the lens drops from about 1.0003 to exactly 1, which shifts focus, so I design for vacuum and set focus on the ground with a calculated offset. Temperature changes both the glass index and the housing length, so I pick glass and housing materials whose effects cancel, and I confirm it in a thermal vacuum test before launch.
How does a single-layer anti-reflection coating work, and what is its limit on ordinary crown glass?
Whether you understand thin-film interference well enough to use it, not just to order coatings.
Two reflections half a wave apart cancel; perfect cancellation needs an index near the square root of the glass index, so one layer leaves some loss.

A layer a quarter wave thick makes two reflections, one from each face, half a wave apart, so they cancel. Full cancellation needs an index of about the square root of the glass index, near 1.23 for crown glass. Magnesium fluoride is about 1.38, so one layer brings roughly 4% per surface down to about 1.3%, at one wavelength. For broadband or lower loss I go multilayer.
Why does an achromatic doublet pair a crown glass with a flint glass, and what color error is still left?
Your grasp of chromatic correction and glass choice.
Low- and high-dispersion glasses of opposite power cancel color at two wavelengths; secondary spectrum remains and needs anomalous partial dispersion glass.

Crown has a high Abbe number, so low dispersion; flint has a low one. A positive crown with a weaker negative flint brings two wavelengths, often blue and red, to one focus while keeping net positive power. Secondary spectrum remains: other colors still focus slightly apart. To cut it I use glasses with anomalous partial dispersion, which gives an apochromat.
A client wants all the light from a large LED pushed into a small, low-NA fiber. What do you tell them?
Whether you know etendue limits and can explain them to a client.
Etendue cannot be reduced by passive optics, so the coupling limit is set by numbers, followed by real options.

Etendue, roughly source area times solid angle, cannot shrink in a passive optical system. The fiber accepts its core area times its NA cone. If the LED's etendue is larger, no lens fixes it; the extra light is lost. I would compute both numbers, show the best possible coupling, and offer options: a larger core, a higher NA fiber, or a smaller, brighter source.
Why would you specify an object-space telecentric lens for a measuring system, and what does it cost you?
Your knowledge of stop placement and its effect on measurement.
Chief rays parallel to the axis keep magnification steady with depth; the price is a front lens as large as the field and a fixed working distance.

With the aperture stop at the back focal point of the front group, chief rays on the object side run parallel to the axis. So magnification barely changes if the part shifts in depth, and a measured edge stays put. The cost: the front lens must be at least as wide as the field, so the lens is large, heavy and expensive, and it works at one set distance.
A camera has 3-micron pixels. How do you decide what resolution the lens needs?
How you match a lens to a sensor.
Nyquist from pixel pitch, MTF checked at Nyquist and half Nyquist across the field, and awareness of aliasing.

Sensor Nyquist is one over twice the pitch: 1 / 0.006 mm, about 167 line pairs per millimeter. I check lens MTF at Nyquist and at half Nyquist, about 83, across the field, since specs often sit at half Nyquist. A lens much sharper than Nyquist can cause aliasing and moire without a low-pass filter; a much softer one wastes the pixels.
How do you measure M-squared on a laser, and what mistake do people often make?
Your hands-on beam characterization and knowledge of the standard method.
Second-moment widths at many planes through a focus, per ISO 11146, fitted to a hyperbola; single-plane or noisy-background errors named.

I focus the beam with a lens and measure second-moment widths at many planes through the waist, as ISO 11146 describes: at least ten points, about half within one Rayleigh range and half beyond two. Then I fit the hyperbola. The usual mistakes are measuring at only one or two planes, or poor background subtraction on the camera, which inflates the widths.
Coupling into a single-mode fiber is stuck at 40%. How do you find what is wrong?
How you debug a coupling problem step by step.
Mode field match first, then offset, angle and focus one at a time, then beam quality, fiber end and back reflection.

First I check mode match: the focused spot should match the fiber's mode field diameter, not its core, and the cone should fit its NA. Then I walk lateral offset, angle and focus one at a time on a power meter. I also check beam quality, a clean fiber end, and back reflection. A well-matched Gaussian beam reaches well over 80%, so 40% means a real error.
The interferometer shows astigmatism on a flat. How do you tell if it comes from the part, the mount or the test?
Whether you separate part error from test error before you blame the shop.
Rotate the part and see whether the error follows it, test mount stress, and check against the reference calibration.

I rotate the part 90 degrees in the mount and measure again. If the astigmatism turns with the part, it belongs to the part. If it stays fixed, it comes from the reference or the setup. If it changes when I loosen the mount, it is mount stress, so I support the part on three points and repeat. I also compare with the reference flat's calibration.
Images from a new camera show a faint ghost of bright lights. How do you track it down?
How you find and fix stray light in a real system.
Ghost analysis of surface pairs in the model, tested against the real ghost's motion and color, then targeted fixes.

In the design software I trace every pair of surfaces that can reflect twice and come back to focus near the sensor. Then I move a point source across the field and watch how the ghost moves and its color, and match it to a path. The IR filter and sensor cover glass are common culprits. Fixes are better coatings, tilting a flat filter, or changing a curvature.
On a high-power laser line, the focus moves as power rises over the first minutes. What is happening, and what do you do?
Your understanding of thermal effects in laser optics.
Thermal lensing from absorption, index change with temperature and expansion; check contamination first, then materials, coatings and cooling.

Most likely thermal lensing: an optic absorbs a little light, heats in the center, and its index changes with temperature while the glass swells, so it acts as a weak lens. I check for a dirty or damaged surface first. Then materials: fused silica absorbs little and expands little. Fixes are cleaner optics, low-absorption coatings, better cooling, or a focus compensator.

paralegal.heading: Paralegal and legal operations questions
qs: What tasks must a paralegal leave to the attorney?
Whether you know where your work ends and the practice of law begins.
No legal advice, no setting fees, no taking on clients, nothing signed or argued as a lawyer. Your work is done under attorney supervision.

I don't give legal advice, quote fees, accept a client or appear for one in court. I can draft, research and talk to clients about facts and scheduling, but an attorney reviews my work and signs what goes out. If a client asks me 'should I sign this?', I say I'll get the attorney to answer.
What personal information do you redact before filing a document in federal court?
Your knowledge of the privacy rules for public court filings.
The Rule 5.2 list: last four digits of Social Security, taxpayer ID and account numbers, birth year only, minors' initials. Exhibits are checked too.

Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 5.2, I leave only the last four digits of Social Security, taxpayer ID and financial account numbers, the birth year, and a minor's initials. I check the exhibits too, and I use true redaction so the text is removed from the file, not just covered by a black box.
A signed vendor contract lands on your desk. What do you record in the contract system?
How you turn a signed contract into dates and duties someone will act on.
Parties, dates, renewal and notice terms, termination rights and key obligations, with reminders set well before any notice deadline.

I save the fully signed copy and log the parties, effective date, term, and whether it renews on its own. The notice period matters most: if we must give 60 days' notice to cancel, I set a reminder at 90 days for the business owner. I also note payment terms, termination rights, governing law, and any assignment or change-of-control clause.
How do you count a court deadline that is stated in days?
Whether you count court deadlines the way the rules do.
Find the governing rules, skip the trigger day, count every calendar day, roll a weekend or holiday end date forward, and have the result double-checked.

First I check which rules apply: federal, state, local, and the judge's own orders. Under the federal rules I skip the trigger day, count every day including weekends and holidays, and if the last day is a weekend or legal holiday, it moves to the next day that is not. Then a second person checks it and it goes on the firm calendar with reminders.
Before a case goes into a brief, how do you make sure it is still good law?
Your research habits beyond finding a case that sounds right.
Running a citator, reading the negative treatment, checking whether the court is binding, and reading the full opinion, not just a summary.

I run it through a citator to see if it was reversed, overruled or questioned, and I read the cases that treat it badly rather than trusting the flag. I check that the court is binding in our jurisdiction or note that it is only persuasive. And I read the opinion itself, so the quote and pin cite match what the court actually held.
The company expects to be sued. What is a litigation hold, and what is your part in it?
Whether you know the duty to preserve evidence and how to carry it out.
Preservation starts when litigation is reasonably anticipated. Notices go to custodians, auto-deletion is paused, and acknowledgments are tracked.

Once a lawsuit is reasonably expected, we must keep relevant documents and data. I help list the custodians, send the hold notice the attorney approves, and work with IT to stop automatic deletion of their email and files. I track who has acknowledged it, follow up with those who haven't, send reminders, and log the release when the matter ends.
What goes into a privilege log, and what must stay out of it?
Your grasp of privilege in document review.
Enough for the other side to assess the claim: date, author, recipients, privilege type, general subject. Never the privileged advice itself.

For each withheld document I list the date, author, all recipients, the privilege claimed, like attorney-client or work product, and a short description such as 'email requesting legal advice on lease terms.' The description must not reveal what the advice was. I also flag any outside third party on the email, since that can break the privilege.
The final brief reaches you 30 minutes before the filing deadline, and the court's e-filing system rejects the PDF. What do you do?
How you handle a filing problem against the clock.
Tell the attorney at once, fix the likely cause, document any system failure, and follow the court's rules for technical failures.

I tell the attorney right away and read the error. Often the file is too large or not text-searchable, so I split the exhibits into separate attachments as the local rules allow, or re-save the PDF. If the court's system itself is down, I take timed screenshots and we follow the court's technical-failure rules. Afterward I push for earlier internal deadlines.
You realize a privileged email went out in yesterday's document production. What do you do?
Whether you own a mistake fast and know how it can be fixed.
Telling the attorney immediately, without hiding it. The attorney can then try to claw it back under the protective order or the rules, and speed matters.

I tell the supervising attorney within the hour, with the document's production number and how it slipped through. The attorney decides on a clawback notice, which the protective order or the federal rules allow, and acting fast matters. I don't contact the other side myself. Then I find the gap, like a missed search term, and recheck the rest of the set.
Contract requests reach the legal team by email, chat and hallway talk. How would you fix the intake?
How you design a legal operations process people will actually use.
One front door, a short form with the facts lawyers need, routing by type and risk, templates for routine deals, and simple metrics.

I would set up one intake form that asks the deal type, counterparty, value and deadline, and route by type: an NDA on our template goes to self-service, a high-value deal goes to an attorney. I'd remind people politely that hallway requests go through the form. After a month I'd report volume and turnaround so we can see where the delays are.
Opposing counsel sends back our contract draft with their changes marked. How do you review it?
Whether you trust a counterparty's markup or verify it yourself.
Running your own comparison against the last version you sent, because unmarked changes happen, then checking each change against the playbook.

I never rely only on their markup. I run a compare between the last version we sent and their draft, so any unmarked edit shows up. Then I list each change, note which ones match our playbook fallbacks and which need the attorney, and save the file with a clear name and date so we never negotiate from the wrong draft.
A software contract renews automatically for one-year terms unless either side gives notice 90 days before the term ends. What do you calendar?
Whether you track the notice deadline, not just the end date.
The last day to give notice as the key date, with early reminders to the business owner, plus a note on how notice must be given.

The date that matters is the last day to give notice, 90 days before the term ends, not the end date itself. I set a reminder about 30 days before that, asking the contract owner to decide: renew or cancel. I also record the notice clause: who receives it and whether email counts or it must go in writing by courier, so a valid notice goes out in time.
A new matter comes in. What names do you run through the conflicts check?
Your grasp of how conflicts of interest are caught before work starts.
Not only the client and the opponent: affiliates, officers, co-parties and key individuals, with every hit sent to an attorney to resolve.

I run the client and its parent and subsidiaries, the adverse parties and their affiliates, co-parties, and people named in the intake, such as officers or key witnesses. I check name variants and former names. I do not decide whether a hit is a real conflict; I send the report to the responsible attorney and keep a record that the check was cleared before any work started.
What does a document production contain besides the documents themselves?
Your knowledge of how electronic productions are put together.
Bates numbers and confidentiality labels, extracted text, load files carrying the metadata, and a cover letter and log of what was produced.

Each page gets a unique Bates number and any confidentiality label the protective order requires. With the images go extracted text and load files: a data file with fields like custodian, date and Bates range, and an image cross-reference file that tells the review tool where each page sits. I add a cover letter with the Bates range and log what went out and when.
Opposing counsel proposes a list of search terms for our email collection. How do you help the attorney respond?
Whether you can test search terms with data instead of guessing.
A hit report with unique hits and family counts, a sample review of noisy terms, and tested narrower alternatives the attorney can propose.

I run the terms in the review tool and build a hit report: hits per term, unique hits, and the total with families included. A term like "deal" pulling 40,000 documents is a flag. I review a sample of its hits; if most are newsletters, I suggest a narrower version, such as a proximity search, and rerun it so the attorney can negotiate with real numbers.
A process server hands a third-party subpoena for records to our receptionist. What happens next?
How you handle incoming legal papers whose deadlines start running on arrival.
Logging the date and manner of receipt, routing it to the attorney the same day, calendaring objection and compliance dates, and preserving the records.

I log when and how it arrived and send a scan to the responsible attorney the same day. Under the federal rules, written objections to a document subpoena are due before the earlier of the compliance date or 14 days after service, so I calendar both; a state subpoena follows that state's rules. I also flag the records it covers so nothing is deleted while we respond.
We are buying a company and you are reviewing its contracts in the data room. What clauses do you flag?
Whether you know which contract terms can affect a deal.
Anti-assignment and change-of-control clauses first, then exclusivity, non-competes, most-favored pricing, termination rights and uncapped liability.

First, anti-assignment and change-of-control clauses, because they decide whether a contract survives the deal or needs consent. Then exclusivity and non-compete terms that could bind the buyer, most-favored-customer pricing, termination for convenience and uncapped indemnities. I log each hit in a tracker with the clause text, page, and whether consent or notice is needed.
An attorney asks you, as a notary, to notarize a client's signature on a document the client signed yesterday and dropped off. What do you do?
Your integrity when a senior person asks for a shortcut.
A polite no with a fix: the signer must appear before the notary, so you arrange a meeting or a remote notarization where the state allows it.

I would say no, politely. The signer has to appear before me and prove who they are; certifying a signature I never saw acknowledged is a false notarization that can cost my commission and taint the document. I would offer a fix: the client comes in and acknowledges the signature in front of me, or we use remote online notarization if our state allows it.
You discover that a response deadline was docketed a week late, and the real deadline is tomorrow. What do you do?
How you own a serious mistake and limit the damage.
Telling the attorney at once, supporting the response or an extension request, then rechecking related entries and fixing the process.

I tell the responsible attorney right away, in person or by phone, not in a quiet email. Then I help with whatever they choose: drafting the response, or preparing an extension request or a stipulation with opposing counsel. Once the deadline is handled, I recheck every date I entered from the same order and propose a second-person check on court deadlines.

partner-manager.heading: Partner manager questions
qs: What is the difference between a reseller, a referral partner and a technology partner?
Whether you know the basic partner types and how each one makes money.
Clear lines on who owns the customer contract, who sells, and how each partner is paid or adds value.

A reseller buys from us or sells our product on its own paper, so it owns the customer contract and earns a margin. A referral partner only introduces the customer; we sell and pay a fee. A technology partner builds an integration with our product; it may sell nothing, but customers who use the integration tend to stay longer.
What is deal registration, and why does it matter?
Your grasp of a core channel tool and the rules behind it.
Explains protection for the partner who found the deal, early pipeline visibility, and why fast, written rules keep partners using it.

The partner logs an opportunity with us early. If we approve it, that partner gets protection, often a better discount, and others should not take the deal for a set period. It rewards the partner who found it and gives me early sight of pipeline. I keep approvals fast and the rules written, or partners stop registering.
How do you measure whether a partner program is working?
Whether you track the numbers that show real partner impact.
Separates sourced from influenced revenue and adds measures like active partners, win rate and time to first deal.

I separate partner-sourced revenue, where the partner brought the deal, from partner-influenced, where they helped close or deliver it. I also watch active partners, win rate and deal size versus direct, time to first deal for new partners, and retention of customers using integrations. A count of signed partners alone tells me little.
A reseller also carries a competitor’s product. How do you get their sellers to sell ours?
How you win mindshare inside a partner’s sales team.
Makes the product easy and worth selling: simple pitch, fast support, fair margin, and help winning the first deals.

Sellers sell what is easy and pays. I make ours easy: a short pitch, a clear customer profile, a demo they can run, and a named contact who answers fast. I check that their margin is competitive. Then I help them win their first deals, because one closed deal together does more than any training session.
A partner signed six months ago and has brought in zero deals. What do you do?
How you handle an inactive partner without wasting time or giving up too early.
Finds the cause first, agrees on a short plan with named accounts, then lowers the tier if nothing moves.

First I find out why. I talk to the partner owner and two of their sellers: do they know who to target, is the margin worth it, did training happen? Then we agree on a 90-day plan with a few named target accounts and a joint call each month. If nothing moves after that, I move them to a lower tier and spend my time elsewhere.
A partner asks for marketing funds to run an event. How do you decide?
Your judgement in spending partner marketing money.
Ties funds to a written plan with expected results and the partner’s own share, pays against proof, and tracks the pipeline after.

I ask what the event should produce: how many target accounts attend, how many meetings, how much pipeline, and what the partner puts in itself. I tie the funds to that plan and pay against proof, like the attendee list and invoices. Afterward I track which deals came from it, and that decides the next request.
Our direct sales rep and a partner both claim the same customer. How do you handle it?
How you resolve channel conflict fairly and keep both sides working.
Checks the facts, applies the written rules of engagement, escalates fast when rules are silent, and fixes the gap afterward.

I check the facts: who registered the deal, when, and who has really been working the customer. I apply the rules of engagement as written, not who argues louder. If the rules do not cover it, I bring in the sales leader and decide fast; often the best answer is working it together. Then I fix the gap in the rules.
You learn a reseller has been promising customers features our product does not have. What do you do?
How you protect customers and the brand while keeping the partnership workable.
Gets the facts, raises it with partner leadership, corrects it with affected customers, retrains, and escalates under the agreement if repeated.

I get the facts first: which customers, what was said, in writing if possible. Then I call the partner owner, not just the seller, and explain the risk to both of us. We correct it with each affected customer, often with our sales engineer on the call. I retrain their team, and if it happens again I escalate under the partner agreement.
Walk me through the joint business plan you would build with a top partner.
Whether you can plan growth with a partner as a shared commitment.
Shared targets, concrete actions with owners on both sides, and a regular review that changes what is not working.

I start with shared goals for the year: revenue, new customers and certified staff. Then the actions that get there: target accounts we work together, two campaigns, training dates, and who owns each step on both sides. We review it every quarter against the numbers. If only my name is on the actions, it is not a joint plan.
What should a new partner be able to do by the end of onboarding, and how do you know they got there?
How you define partner onboarding by results, not by courses completed.
Clear milestones such as certified sellers, a technical contact and a first registered deal, with time to first deal tracked.

By day 90 I want at least two certified sellers, a technical contact who can run a demo alone, and one registered deal in the pipeline. Finished courses tell me little. I track time to first registered deal and time to first closed deal. If a partner passes 60 days with no registered deal, I set up a pipeline session with their sales lead.
How would you design partner tiers, and what should move a partner up or down?
Your grasp of how tier programs reward the behavior the company needs.
Tiers tied to a mix of revenue, certifications and customer results, benefits partners value, and a regular review that can also move partners down.

I'd use three tiers based on trailing 12-month revenue, number of certified people and customer retention, so one big deal can't buy a tier. Higher tiers get a better discount, shared leads and a named contact. We review once a year. Partners below the bar get a warning and a grace period, then move down, or the tiers stop meaning anything.
What is the difference between a front-end discount and a back-end rebate, and when would you use each?
Whether you understand reseller margin tools and the behavior each one drives.
A front-end discount comes off list price when the order is placed; a back-end rebate is paid later for hitting goals. Each steers partners differently.

A front-end discount is taken off the list price when the partner places the order, so it is their everyday margin. A back-end rebate is paid after the period if they hit goals, like growth or new customers. I keep the front-end discount high enough that selling us is worth it, and use rebates to reward what we want more of, such as new logos rather than renewals.
How do you separate partner-sourced from partner-influenced revenue, and why does it matter to leadership?
How you attribute revenue honestly and avoid counting the same deal twice.
Written definitions agreed with sales operations: sourced means the partner brought the deal, influenced means they helped one we already had.

Sourced means the partner brought us an opportunity we did not know about, usually shown by an approved deal registration. Influenced means they helped move a deal we already had, for example with a joint call or a customer reference. I agree these rules with sales operations before the year starts. If they blur, the channel looks bigger than it is and money goes to the wrong partners.
Our direct reps see partners as competition and won't bring them into deals. How do you change that?
Whether you can get direct sales to co-sell with partners instead of fighting them.
Fixing the incentives first, usually by making rep pay the same with or without a partner, then proving value with wins other reps can see.

First I check the pay plan. If a rep earns less when a partner is on the deal, no speech will fix it, so I push for comp neutrality, meaning the rep is paid the same either way. Then I pick two or three reps, find deals where a partner adds real value, like local implementation, and share those wins in the sales meeting. Reps copy what their peers get paid for.
At quarter end a reseller orders three times its usual volume, but its sales to customers are flat. What do you do?
How you spot channel stuffing and protect the company from inflated numbers.
Comparing orders to us with the partner's sales to customers, telling finance, and not pushing partners to take stock they cannot sell.

Orders to us jumping while their sales to customers stay flat means stock is piling up at the partner. I ask them why, check whether anyone on our side offered extra discounts or return rights to pull the order in, and tell finance, because return rights and side deals can change how revenue is booked. A big quarter followed by returns and an empty next quarter helps nobody.
A strong reseller asks for exclusive rights to a region in return for a big revenue commitment. How do you respond?
Your judgement on exclusivity, market coverage and who holds the leverage.
Weighing the risk of losing coverage; if granted at all, a narrow scope, firm targets and a clear exit, with legal writing the terms.

I'd rarely give full exclusivity, because if that partner stalls we lose the whole region. If the commitment is real, I'd offer something narrower: one industry, for 12 months, tied to revenue and certification targets, ending automatically if they miss. Legal writes the terms. Often a higher tier and first look at leads earns the same commitment without locking us in.
We changed our API and a technology partner's integration broke for shared customers. You hear about it from a customer. What do you do?
How you handle a technical partner problem that hurts joint customers.
Fix first with both engineering teams, one agreed message to customers, then a process so partners hear about changes before release.

First I get engineers from both companies on a call the same day and agree who tells affected customers what, so they don't hear two stories. Our support team gets a short note too. Once it's fixed, I push for a partner change policy: advance notice of breaking API changes, a test environment and a named technical contact. A partner should never learn about our release from their customers.
We want to sign a reseller in a new country to sell to government agencies there. What checks do you run first?
Whether you know the compliance risk that comes with partners, including bribery through third parties.
Due diligence on ownership and ties to officials, anti-bribery contract terms, and knowing US law can hold the company liable for a partner's bribes.

Under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, a US company can be liable for bribes a partner pays if it knew or ignored the warning signs. So with compliance I check who owns the reseller and any links to government officials. I watch for red flags like unusually high margin requests or payments to a third party. The contract includes anti-bribery terms and audit rights.
Leadership asks whether to keep investing in the channel or move that money to direct sales. How do you build the case?
How you prove the economics of a partner program to senior leadership.
Comparing full cost of sale, win rate, cycle and retention by route, counting discounts and program costs, and being honest where the channel loses.

I'd compare both routes on the same terms: cost to win a dollar of revenue, counting partner discounts, marketing funds and my team's cost; win rate; sales cycle; and retention after two years. Partners often win where we have no reps or customers need local services. If some segments are cheaper direct, I'd say so and move partner money to where partners clearly earn it.

partner-marketing.heading: Partner marketing manager questions
qs: What is the difference between MDF and co-op funds?
Whether you know the two main ways vendors fund partner marketing.
MDF is allocated by the vendor for approved activities. Co-op is earned by the partner from its sales. Both are usually paid against proof of performance.

MDF is money we set aside and give to chosen partners for specific, pre-approved activities, usually based on a plan and how strategic they are. Co-op is earned: a partner builds up a share of what it sells and spends it on marketing within our rules. Both usually need proof of performance, like invoices and results, before we reimburse.
How do you tell partner-sourced pipeline from partner-influenced pipeline?
Your grasp of how partner results are counted and reported.
Sourced means the partner brought the deal; influenced means the partner helped on a deal someone else owned. Rules are agreed upfront and nobody double counts.

Sourced means the partner found the opportunity and brought it to us, usually shown by an approved deal registration. Influenced means our sales team owned it but the partner helped, for example with a reference or a joint demo. I report them separately and agree the rules with sales operations before the quarter starts, so nobody counts the same deal twice.
What goes into a campaign-in-a-box for resellers?
Whether you can build marketing that small partners will actually launch.
Targeting guidance, ready and editable assets, a landing page, a follow-up path for leads, and a check on who actually used it.

I include a short brief on who to target and why, ready emails and social posts with editable fields, a co-brandable landing page, a call script, and a simple way to register leads. I keep it to what a two-person reseller can launch in an afternoon. Then I track who used it and call the partners who downloaded it but never launched.
Walk me through building a joint marketing plan with a new strategic partner.
How you turn a partnership into a shared, measurable plan.
Shared target customers and goals, a few plays with named owners on both sides, agreed budget split and tracking, and a regular review rhythm.

I start with shared goals: which customers we both want and what pipeline number we both sign up to. Then we pick two or three plays, name an owner on each side, agree the budget split and how we track leads. We review monthly against the plan and hold a proper quarterly review with a sponsor from each company in the room.
You run a joint webinar with a partner. Who gets the registrant list, and what do you set up first?
Whether you handle shared lead data properly and plan the follow-up.
Lead sharing is agreed in writing and disclosed on the registration form, both sides honor opt-outs, and follow-up is split so buyers are not hit twice.

Before we promote it, we agree in writing who gets the list and how fast each side follows up. The registration form says plainly that details go to both named companies, with a link to each privacy policy. Both sides honor unsubscribes, and we split follow-up by account or territory so a buyer does not get two calls on the same day.
A partner asks for MDF to host a golf day for customers. What do you ask before you say yes?
Your judgement on whether a funding request will produce business.
Who attends, the cost per guest, the follow-up plan, the pipeline expected, and what proof will be submitted to claim the funds.

I ask who is on the guest list and whether they are real buying prospects or just friends of the account team. Then the cost per guest, which of our products the follow-up will push, and what pipeline they expect within a quarter. If it holds up, I approve it with proof required: attendee list, invoices and the deals registered afterward.
Your product is now listed on a cloud marketplace. How do you drive sales through it?
Your understanding of marketplaces as a sales channel.
Knows why buyers use marketplaces, such as simpler buying and existing cloud spend, and works with both internal sales and the marketplace's partner team.

A listing alone sells little. I tell our sales team why buyers like it: the purchase goes on their existing cloud bill, it can skip a new vendor setup, and for some buyers it counts toward a spend commitment they already have. I make private offers easy to request, add a marketplace buy option to our campaigns, and work with the marketplace's partner team on joint selling.
A reseller runs ads with an old version of your logo and a 'cheapest on the market' claim you cannot back up. What do you do?
How you protect the brand without damaging the partner relationship.
Treats the unsupported claim as the urgent risk, acts the same day, gives the right assets, and adds a check so it does not recur.

The price claim is the bigger problem, because an unsupported claim can be false advertising and it carries our name. I call the partner that day, ask them to pause the ad, and send the current logo pack and approved claims. If the ad used our funds, it is not reimbursed as it stands. Then I add a quick approval step for co-branded ads.
Your direct sales rep and a reseller both claim a deal that came from a joint event. How do you settle it?
How you handle channel conflict fairly and keep partner trust.
Uses the written rules of engagement and deal registration, not opinions, decides quickly, and closes the gap in the rules afterward.

I go to the written rules first. If the partner registered the deal and it was approved before our rep logged the opportunity, the partner keeps it. If the rules do not cover the case, I bring the sales and channel leaders together quickly, we decide once, and I write the gap into the rules. Partners stop bringing deals the moment they think we take them.
Last year's MDF produced a lot of leads but very little pipeline. How do you redesign the program?
How you tie partner funding to results that matter to the business.
Finds where it broke first, then funds fewer partners, pays against pipeline rather than lead counts, and requires a real follow-up plan.

First I find where it broke: poor-fit leads, or good leads nobody called. I pull a sample and check. Then I fund fewer partners, tie the next payment to registered opportunities instead of lead counts, and require a follow-up plan with named sales staff. Partners who turned funds into pipeline get more; the rest get training before more money.
How do you decide which partners get the most marketing investment?
Whether you can segment a partner base instead of treating every partner the same.
Partners tiered by current results and real potential, with a different level of support per tier and regular reviews.

I score partners on two things: what they sell with us today and what they could sell, based on their customer base and skilled staff. The top tier gets a named marketing contact, planned joint campaigns and proposal-based funds. The middle tier gets campaign kits and some funds. The long tail gets self-serve content. I review the tiers every six months.
What proof of performance do you require before you pay an MDF claim?
Your control over partner funds and the paperwork behind them.
Proof the approved activity ran, with real costs and results, submitted within the program's claim window.

I want proof the activity ran as approved: the third-party invoice and evidence of the work, like screenshots of the ads, a copy of the email with send counts, or the event attendee list. For anything meant to create leads, the leads must be in our system. Claims must come in within the window set in the program guide, or they are not paid.
How do you measure whether your partner enablement program actually works?
Whether you measure enablement by partner behavior and pipeline, not by attendance.
Metrics that run from training to action to pipeline, compared against partners who did not take part.

I don't stop at attendance. I track time from onboarding to a partner's first campaign, how many partners use the campaign kits, and certifications earned. Then I compare pipeline per enabled partner with partners who skipped the program. If people finish training but never launch a campaign, I fix that gap before I build more training.
You pass marketing leads to partners and most of them are never followed up. What do you do?
How you run lead passing as a process with rules and feedback.
Finds the cause first, then sets acceptance deadlines, a return path for leads, and sends more leads to partners who follow up.

First I find out why. Often the leads are too early, go to the wrong person, or arrive with no context. I set a rule: the partner accepts or rejects a lead within a few days, with a reason, or it comes back to us or goes to another partner. I add notes on what the lead did, and I send more leads to partners who prove they follow up.
A reseller wants to email its own customer list about a joint offer with your logo on it. What do you check first?
Your grasp of US email marketing rules when two brands share a message.
CAN-SPAM basics covered, and a clear agreement on who is the sender and who handles opt-outs.

I check the email meets CAN-SPAM: a truthful from line and subject, a clear notice that it is an ad, a valid physical postal address, and a working opt-out honored within 10 business days. Since both brands appear, we agree in writing which company is the designated sender and handles opt-outs. I also ask how the list was built and approve the copy and logo use.
A partner is bidding on your brand name in paid search and pushing up your own cost per click. How do you handle it?
How you manage marketing conflict with a partner without damaging the relationship.
Checks the agreement, talks to the partner with data, and moves their spend toward demand that is new to both companies.

I check our partner agreement and brand rules first; many programs ban bidding on our brand terms or allow it only with approval. I call the partner, show the auction data, and ask them to add our brand as a negative keyword. If it continues, the agreement gives us remedies, but I'd rather move their budget to non-brand terms where they bring us new buyers.
A partner has a large accrued fund balance that expires in six weeks and sends you a rushed plan to spend it all. What do you do?
Your judgement when spending pressure conflicts with good use of funds.
Approves only the parts that fit the target and can be measured, holds to the expiry rule, and prevents the same rush next year.

I would not approve spend just to use it up. I go through the plan with the partner and keep the parts that reach our target customers and can be measured, like a campaign to their installed base. Weak items I decline and I explain that unused funds expire as the program guide says. Then I set quarterly check-ins so the balance doesn't pile up again.
An invoice attached to an MDF claim looks like it has been edited. How do you handle it?
How you handle possible fraud fairly and through the right people.
Holds payment, verifies with the source before accusing, and escalates to finance and channel leaders under the program's audit terms.

I hold the payment and don't accuse anyone yet. I ask the partner for the original from the vendor, or contact the vendor to confirm the amount and date. If it was altered, I bring in finance and the channel lead, follow the audit terms in the program agreement, and review that partner's earlier claims. It's a contract and trust issue, not one I settle alone.
How would you show leadership that MDF drives revenue partners would not have generated anyway?
Whether you can prove the incremental effect of partner funds, not just report activity.
A comparison against a fair baseline, measured in pipeline and closed revenue, with an honest read if there is no difference.

I compare like with like. I group partners of similar size and region and compare funded with unfunded ones over a few quarters, or look at a partner's results before and after funding. I measure pipeline and closed revenue, not leads. If funded and unfunded partners grow at the same rate, the money is paying for marketing they would have done anyway.
Your largest partner just announced a partnership with your main competitor. How do you change your joint marketing?
How you adjust strategy and investment when a key partner becomes a shared one.
Talks to the partner before reacting, shifts funds to plays where you clearly win, and ties investment to pipeline for your product.

I don't cut them off the same day. I meet the partner's leaders to learn how they will position both products and where we still win. Then I move our funds to joint plays where we are the clear choice, like our strongest use case, and tie MDF to pipeline on our product. I also limit early roadmap details until we see how the new deal plays out.

payments-engineer.heading: Payments engineer questions
qs: Why should you never store money amounts as floating-point numbers?
Whether you know the most basic rule of handling money in code.
Floats cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly. Use integer minor units or a decimal type, and keep the currency code with every amount.

Binary floats cannot hold 0.1 exactly, so 0.1 plus 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004, and those errors add up across millions of rows. I store integer minor units, like cents, with a currency code. Not every currency has two decimals: the Japanese yen has none, so I read the exponent per currency.
What is the difference between authorization, capture and settlement on a card payment?
Your grasp of how a card payment actually moves through the system.
Authorization checks the card and places a hold. Capture asks for the money. Settlement is when funds actually move to the merchant's bank. Unused authorizations expire.

Authorization asks the issuing bank to approve the charge and hold the funds, but no money moves. Capture tells the processor to collect that amount. Settlement is when the networks and banks actually move the money, usually in batches. Shops that ship goods often authorize at checkout and capture at shipping, and they have to capture before the hold expires.
Explain double-entry bookkeeping as you would build it into a ledger service.
Whether you can design a ledger that stays correct to the cent.
Every transaction is a set of entries that sum to zero across accounts. Entries are append-only, and balances are derived from the entries.

Every money movement is recorded as at least two entries: a debit to one account and a credit to another, and they must sum to zero. A $50 payment debits the customer receivable and credits merchant payable. I enforce the zero sum in the same database transaction, never edit entries, and compute balances from them. If the books do not sum to zero, I know something broke.
How do you keep card numbers out of your own systems as much as possible?
Your understanding of PCI DSS scope and how to shrink it.
Hosted fields or a processor's page so card data goes straight to the processor, tokens stored instead of numbers, and never storing the CVV after authorization.

I use the processor's hosted fields or payment page, so the card number goes from the browser straight to them and we only get a token back. That keeps most of our servers out of PCI scope. We store the token, the last four digits and the expiry if needed. The security code is never stored after authorization, not even encrypted; PCI DSS forbids it.
A $100 refund has to be split evenly across three sellers. How do you do it?
How you handle rounding so the parts always add up to the whole.
Work in cents, give the leftover cent to one party by a fixed, documented rule, and assert the parts sum to the total.

In cents that is 10,000 split three ways: 3,333 each leaves one cent.
