I write only what I saw or heard, and I mark statements from others as theirs, with quotes where I can. No guesses, no opinions like “he looked guilty.” Then I note who was called and what footage exists.
A senior manager walks up without a badge and says, “You know me, just let me in.” What do you do?
Whether you apply the access rules the same way to everyone.
Polite, firm and by the book: verify identity, issue a temporary badge per policy, log it, and call a supervisor rather than make exceptions.

I greet them by name and say I still have to follow the badge policy. I check their ID against the employee list, issue a temporary badge and log the time and reason. It takes two minutes. Most managers respect it. If someone pushes back, I call my supervisor rather than make an exception on my own.
The fire alarm goes off on your shift. What do you do?
Whether you know your role in the site's emergency plan.
Check the panel for the location, call it in per the plan, move people out by the stairs, meet the fire department, and leave the reset to them.

I read the fire panel to see which zone and device went off, and make sure 911 and my dispatch are called as the plan says. I radio the location, help move people to the stairs and the assembly point, and keep them away from elevators. I meet the fire department at the main entrance with the panel information and keys. I do not reset the alarm; that is the fire department's call.
A person runs out of the store past you with unpaid merchandise. What do you do?
Whether you know the limits of your authority and put safety over property.
Following company policy and state law, which often means observe and report, not chase; getting a good description and calling it in.

I follow the site's policy, and the retail posts I have worked were observe and report. So I do not chase into the parking lot. I note the description, clothing, direction, any vehicle and plate, and the time, and I call it in and contact police if the policy says to. Then I save the footage and write the report. Merchandise is not worth anyone getting hurt.
On camera, you see someone in a restricted area after hours. Walk me through your response.
How you use CCTV and the radio together without putting yourself at risk.
Keeping eyes on the person, calling for backup and police per post orders, guiding responders by radio, and not walking in alone.

I keep the person on camera and follow them from view to view. I radio my supervisor or the patrol officer with the location, a description and whether I can see a weapon or tools, and call police if the post orders say so. I guide responders as the person moves. I note the times and camera numbers so the footage can be saved, then write it up.
Police ask you for video of an incident. How do you hand it over so it holds up as evidence?
Whether you understand chain of custody for video evidence.
Exporting unedited footage in the recorder's original format, noting any camera clock offset, and logging every handoff with signatures.

I export the clips without editing them, in the system's original format with its player, and keep a copy. I check the camera clock against real time and write down any difference. I fill out a chain of custody form: what was exported, by whom, when, and who received it, with a signature. I also lock that time period on the recorder so it is not overwritten.
You answer the phone and the caller says there is a bomb in the building. What do you do?
Whether you stay calm and gather the details responders will need.
Keeping the caller talking, writing exact words and details on a bomb threat checklist, then notifying police and following the site plan.

I stay calm and keep the caller on the line as long as I can. I use the bomb threat checklist by the phone, write the exact words, and ask where the bomb is and when it will go off. I note the voice, accent, background noise and the time. Then I call 911 and my supervisor, and the site's plan decides on search or evacuation. I do not touch any suspicious item.
After you submit a report, you realize you wrote the wrong time for a key event. How do you fix it?
Your honesty and how you correct a record without damaging it.
Owning the error quickly and correcting it openly, with a supplemental report or a dated correction, never by erasing the original.

I tell my supervisor the same day. I do not change or delete the original report. I write a supplemental report that says which time was wrong, what the right time is and how I know, for example the camera timestamp. In a paper log I would draw one line through the error, write the correction and initial it. An honest correction keeps the report credible; a hidden edit ruins it.
What does “observe and report” mean on a post, and when would you step in physically?
Whether you know the limits of your role and authority.
You watch, document and call the right people. Physical action only where post orders and state law allow it, mainly to protect life.

It means my job is to be a trained witness: see it, record it, call police or my supervisor. I am not a police officer, and on most posts I may not chase or hold anyone. I would step in physically only to protect someone from immediate harm. Even then I follow post orders and the law of that state, and I report every detail.
Why should patrol routes and times vary, and how do you do it without missing areas?
How you plan patrols that cannot be predicted but still cover everything.
Predictable rounds let people time around you. Vary order and timing, but still hit and log every checkpoint, with more visits to high-risk spots.

If I walk the loading dock every hour on the hour, anyone watching knows when it is empty. I change my start point, my direction and the gaps between rounds, and sometimes I double back. Every checkpoint still gets scanned in the guard tour system each shift. High-risk spots, like exterior doors and the dock, get more visits than a quiet hallway.
What goes into a good pass-down at shift change?
Whether you hand over a post so nothing falls through the gap.
Open issues, equipment status, people and keys still out, and anything unusual. It is written in the log and also said face to face.

I tell the next officer what is still open: a door that will not latch, a camera that is down, a contractor still on site with a temporary badge, keys signed out. I mention anyone we were watching and any call I am waiting on. It all goes in the pass-down log too, and we check the key box and radio together before I leave.
An employee tells you they lost their access card last night. What do you do?
How you close a security gap fast.
Disable the card at once, check its recent use, log the loss, and reissue only after verifying identity.

First I deactivate the card in the access control system right away, not at the end of my shift. Then I pull its activity since they last remember having it, to see if anyone used it after it went missing. I log the loss and check their ID against the employee record before I issue a new card. If the card opened sensitive areas, I tell my supervisor.
Someone collapses in the lobby and is not responding. Walk me through your first minutes.
Your response to a medical emergency before help arrives.
Have someone call 911 and fetch the AED, start CPR if the person is not breathing normally, and guide responders in.

I check if they respond and are breathing normally. If not, I point at one person to call 911 and another to bring the AED, and I start chest compressions. When the AED arrives I turn it on and follow its voice prompts. I radio the control room to hold an elevator and send someone to meet the medics at the door. Afterward I write the report with exact times.
A man in the lobby is shouting and refuses to leave. How do you handle it?
How you de-escalate and when you hand off to police.
Calm voice, safe distance, a clear request to leave, then police if he refuses or threatens anyone. No grabbing to move him out.

I keep a safe distance, stand at an angle instead of toe to toe, and keep my own exit clear. I speak slowly and ask what he needs. If he has to go, I tell him plainly that he is being asked to leave the property. If he refuses or threatens anyone, I call police with a description and keep staff and visitors away until they arrive.
You are asked to review camera coverage at a store entrance. What do you look for?
Your understanding of what makes CCTV useful, not just present.
Whether each camera can identify a face, copes with backlight, shows the correct time and keeps footage as long as policy requires.

I ask what each camera is for: seeing that someone came in, or identifying who it was. At the door I want a view at face height, close enough to recognize a person, not a wide shot of the parking lot. Glass doors cause glare in daylight, so I check daytime footage. I also check that the clock is correct and that footage is kept as long as our policy says.
A door-forced alarm goes off ten times a night and staff say it is always false. What do you do?
How you handle nuisance alarms without ignoring a real one.
Check and log every alarm, find the cause and get it fixed. Never bypass an alarm without documented approval.

I still check every one, by camera or in person, because the night it is real will look exactly the same. I log each alarm with the time and the cause. If the pattern shows a weak door closer or staff propping the door, I send that to my supervisor and facilities with the log attached. I never bypass the alarm on my own; only an approved, documented bypass with an end time.
What is your role if there is an active shooter in the building?
Whether you know current active-threat guidance and your part in it.
Run, Hide, Fight for yourself and others, clear information to 911, lockdown if that is the plan, and a safe approach to arriving police.

The guidance is Run, Hide, Fight. I get people out if there is a safe way, or lock and barricade if not. If I can stay safe in the control room, I give 911 the location, description and number of attackers from the cameras, and start the lockdown if that is our plan. When police arrive I keep my hands empty and visible and follow their commands, since they do not know who I am.
Your supervisor asks you to leave a detail out of an incident report because it makes the site look bad. What do you do?
Your integrity when there is pressure to change a record.
You keep the report factual and complete, explain why calmly, and escalate if the pressure continues.

I would say I cannot leave out something I saw, because the report may end up with police, an insurer or a court, and a missing fact hurts us more later. I can make sure it is written neutrally, facts only, no opinions. If they still pushed, I would take it to the next level of management or the company's ethics line, and keep my own note of the request.

physician.heading: Physician questions
qs: Walk me through how you build a differential diagnosis for a new complaint.
Your clinical reasoning when the cause is not yet known.
A structured approach: history first, then causes ranked by likelihood and by danger, so the can't-miss ones are ruled out early.

I start with a careful history, because it gives most of the diagnosis, then a focused exam. I list causes by how likely they are and, separately, by how dangerous. For chest pain I think of heart attack, pulmonary embolism and aortic dissection first, even if reflux is most likely. Then I pick tests that will change what I do.
A patient with three days of low back pain and no warning signs asks for an MRI. What do you do?
Whether you order tests by evidence and can say no kindly.
Checks for red flags, explains that early imaging does not help without them, and gives a clear plan and signs that should bring the patient back.

I ask about red flags: fever, a cancer history, weight loss, leg weakness, numbness in the groin, or bladder and bowel changes. If there are none, I explain that most episodes improve within weeks and an early MRI often shows findings that don't explain the pain. I give a plan for staying active and controlling pain, and tell them exactly what should bring them back sooner.
Your patient speaks little English and her teenage son offers to translate. How do you proceed?
Whether you communicate safely across a language barrier.
Uses a qualified medical interpreter, in person, by phone or by video. Family, and minors above all, are not used for clinical content.

I thank the son but call a qualified interpreter, by phone or video if no one is on site. Family may leave things out or soften bad news, and a teenager should not carry his mother's diagnosis. I speak to the patient, not the interpreter, use short sentences, and ask her to repeat back the plan. I note the interpreter's ID in the chart.
What has to be in place before a patient's consent to a procedure is valid?
Your understanding of informed consent beyond the signed form.
Capacity, enough information (nature, risks, benefits, alternatives including doing nothing) and a free choice. The form only records the talk.

The patient must have capacity to decide, and the choice must be voluntary. I explain what the procedure is, why I recommend it, the common and the serious risks, the expected benefit, and the alternatives, including doing nothing. I check understanding by asking them to explain it back. The signature documents that conversation; it does not replace it.
How do you assess whether a patient has decision-making capacity?
Whether you can judge capacity yourself, one decision at a time.
The four abilities: understand, appreciate, reason and state a choice. Capacity is specific to the decision and can change; disagreeing is not lacking it.

I check four things. Can the patient tell back the facts in their own words? Do they see how those facts apply to them? Can they weigh the options and give reasons? Can they state a clear choice? Capacity is for one decision at one time, so a delirious patient may regain it. And refusing my advice is not, on its own, a sign of incapacity.
A patient with chest pain wants to leave against medical advice. What do you do?
How you balance a patient's right to refuse with keeping them safe.
Assesses capacity, learns the reason, explains the risk plainly, offers the next-best option and documents. The door stays open.

First I sit down and ask why. Often it is a pet at home or a worry about cost, and a social worker can help. If he has capacity, I say plainly that this could be a heart attack. If he still leaves, I offer whatever partial treatment and follow-up I can, give clear return signs, and document the talk. He should never feel he can't come back.
A test you ordered for a disease you thought very unlikely comes back positive. How do you read it?
Whether you interpret results with pretest probability in mind.
Knows that when the chance of disease is low, even a good test gives many false positives; reassesses and confirms before labeling the patient.

The meaning of a positive depends on how likely the disease was before the test. When that chance is very low, many positives are false, even with a good test. I recheck the history and exam and confirm with a more specific test before I treat or put the diagnosis in the chart. It also reminds me to order tests only when I have a clear question.
How do you make sure no test result falls through the cracks after a patient leaves?
How you close the loop on results that come back after discharge.
A named owner for every pending result, the patient told what to expect, a way to reach them, and abnormal results acted on and documented.

At discharge I list pending tests in the summary and name who will follow them, usually me. I tell the patient which results are pending and confirm a working phone number. When an abnormal result comes in, I call the patient, arrange the next step, tell their primary care doctor and note it in the chart. If I can't reach them, I keep trying and record each attempt.
Walk me through how you tell a patient they have a serious diagnosis, such as cancer.
Your skill with the hardest conversations in the work.
A structured approach: private setting, find out what they know, give a warning, say it plainly, respond to emotion, agree on next steps.

I find a private room, sit down and hand my pager to a colleague if I can. I ask what they already know and how much detail they want. I give a short warning, then say it plainly: the biopsy shows cancer. Then I stop and let them react. I name the emotion I see, and before we end we agree on the next step and when we will talk again.
You smell alcohol on a colleague who is about to see patients. What do you do?
Whether you put patient safety first while treating a colleague fairly.
Acts at once to keep the colleague away from patients, privately and with respect, then reports through the proper channel so help can start.

Patients come first, so it can't wait. I speak to the colleague privately, say what I noticed, and ask them not to see patients now. I tell the person in charge, such as the department chief, so care is covered and the right process starts. Most states have a physician health program that offers confidential help. Staying silent protects no one, including the colleague.
A drug cuts heart attacks by 50% in a trial. What else do you need to know before you tell a patient that?
Whether you can turn trial results into numbers that matter to one patient.
Absolute risk and number needed to treat, not just relative risk, plus harms and whether the trial patients match yours.

I need the baseline risk. If heart attacks fell from 2% to 1% over five years, that is a 50% relative drop but only a 1% absolute drop, so we treat 100 people for five years to prevent one. Then I weigh side effects and cost, and check whether the trial patients look like mine.
An 82-year-old comes in on eleven medications from four prescribers. How do you approach it?
How you handle polypharmacy and deprescribing in older adults.
A full list including over-the-counter drugs, a check against the Beers Criteria, one change at a time, and the patient's own goals.

I ask her to bring every bottle, including supplements and sleep aids. For each drug I ask what it is for, whether it is still needed, and whether it is on the Beers Criteria list of drugs risky in older adults. I look hard at sedatives and duplicates. I stop or taper one at a time, tell the other prescribers, and follow up to see what changed.
A patient's blood pressure stays high on three drugs. Walk me through your next steps.
Your approach to resistant hypertension before adding a fourth drug.
Confirm the reading and adherence first, look for things raising pressure such as NSAIDs, then screen for secondary causes such as primary aldosteronism and sleep apnea.

First I make sure it is real: right cuff size, proper technique, and home or ambulatory readings to rule out white coat effect. Then I check that the patient takes the pills, and ask about NSAIDs, decongestants, alcohol and salt. I make sure one drug is a diuretic at a good dose. If it is still high, I screen for primary aldosteronism and sleep apnea before adding spironolactone.
Your patient with type 2 diabetes also has heart failure, and her A1C is at goal on metformin. Would you add anything?
Whether you choose diabetes drugs for organ protection, not only for blood sugar.
Yes: an SGLT2 inhibitor for its heart failure benefit whatever the A1C, with attention to volume, genital infections and ketoacidosis risk.

Yes. Current diabetes guidelines recommend an SGLT2 inhibitor in heart failure to lower the risk of hospitalization, whether or not the A1C is at goal. I check kidney function, review her diuretic dose since it adds fluid loss, warn her about genital yeast infections, and tell her to hold it when she is sick and not eating, because of the risk of ketoacidosis.
A patient from your clinic calls from another state while on vacation and wants a video visit. Can you do it?
Whether you know the licensing rules that apply to telehealth.
The visit is generally regulated where the patient is located, so you need a license there or a state exception; otherwise you direct them to local care.

Telehealth is usually practiced where the patient is sitting, not where I am. If I am not licensed in that state, I check whether it has an exception for existing patients. If not, I do not do the visit. I help her find urgent care there, and if it sounds serious I tell her to go to the emergency room. Then we pick up when she is back.
A CT for kidney stones shows a 7 mm solid lung nodule in a 58-year-old smoker. What do you do with it?
How you manage an incidental finding so it gets the right follow-up.
Uses Fleischner Society guidance by size and risk, tells the patient, orders follow-up with a tracking system, and addresses smoking.

I tell the patient, even though it was not why we did the scan. For a single solid nodule of 6 to 8 mm in a high-risk patient, Fleischner Society guidance is a repeat CT in 6 to 12 months, then again at 18 to 24 months if it is stable. I order it, put it on a tracking list, and talk about quitting smoking.
Routine labs show a potassium of 6.5 in a patient who feels well. The lab calls you at 5 p.m. What do you do?
How you handle a dangerous lab value that may or may not be real.
Acts the same day: asks about hemolysis, reviews drugs and kidney function, and gets an ECG and a repeat level now, sending to the emergency room if needed.

I ask the lab if the sample was hemolyzed, which can falsely raise potassium. Then I call the patient. I look at his kidney function and drugs such as ACE inhibitors, spironolactone or potassium supplements. With a value that high I do not wait until morning: he needs an ECG and a repeat level tonight, usually in the emergency room, where they can treat it if it is real.
A new patient on long-term opioids from a doctor who retired asks you to continue them. How do you handle it?
Your judgement in prescribing controlled drugs safely without abandoning the patient.
Neither refusing nor rubber-stamping: verify the history, check the state monitoring program, avoid abrupt stops, offer naloxone, and agree on a plan.

I do not stop them suddenly; that risks withdrawal and a turn to street drugs. I get the old records, check the state prescription drug monitoring program, and ask about pain and daily function. We sign a treatment agreement and I prescribe naloxone. Then we decide together to keep the dose, taper slowly, or add other treatments.
A patient has a first seizure and plans to drive home. What do you tell him, and do you report it?
Whether you know your duty on driving safety and that the rules depend on the state.
Clear advice not to drive, documented, and knowing that state law sets the seizure-free period and whether a physician must report.

I tell him not to drive until he is cleared, and I write down that I said it. He needs a ride home today. The seizure-free period before driving, and who reports, are set by state law. In most states the patient must report himself; a few require the physician to report. I check the rule for my state, follow it, and explain it to him.
An elderly patient with advanced dementia has pneumonia and no advance directive. Her children disagree about a breathing tube. How do you proceed?
How you lead a goals-of-care decision when the patient cannot speak and the family is split.
Finds the legal surrogate under state law, steers to what the patient would have wanted, gives a clear recommendation, and uses ethics or palliative care if stuck.

I find the legal decision-maker; with no health care proxy, state law sets the order, and adult children often decide together. I meet them as a group and ask what their mother valued, not what they want. I give an honest picture of what a breathing tube would mean for her, and a recommendation. If they stay split, I call palliative care or the ethics committee.

platform-engineer.heading: Platform engineer questions
qs: What is a golden path, and why would a platform team build one?
Whether you understand the core idea behind an internal platform.
A supported, easy default way to build and ship, with good practice built in, that teams choose because it saves them work.

A golden path is the standard, supported way to create and run a service: a template, a pipeline, logging and alerts already wired in. Teams can leave it, but they should not want to. It lets a new service reach production in a day, not a month, and security and reliability come built in instead of being added later.
How do you know whether your platform is actually helping the teams that use it?
Whether you treat the platform as a product with users.
Measures adoption and developer outcomes such as lead time and deploy frequency, and talks to users, not just uptime.

I treat the other teams as customers. I track how many services use the platform, how long it takes a new service to reach production, and deploy frequency and change failure rate. Each quarter I also sit with a few teams and watch them ship. If people build workarounds, that tells me more than any dashboard does.
In Kubernetes, what is the difference between resource requests and limits?
Your grasp of how shared clusters schedule and constrain workloads.
Requests drive scheduling; limits cap use. Going over a CPU limit means throttling; going over a memory limit gets the container killed.

A request is what the scheduler reserves when it picks a node, so it decides where the pod fits. A limit is the ceiling. If a container hits its CPU limit it gets throttled and runs slower. If it goes over its memory limit it is killed, which shows up as OOMKilled. So memory limits need to be set from real usage, with some headroom.
Several teams share one cluster. How do you stop one team from hurting the others?
How you design multi-tenancy and isolation on shared infrastructure.
Separate namespaces, access control, resource quotas, default limits and network policies, plus a clear rule for workloads that need their own cluster.

Each team gets its own namespace, and role-based access lets them change only their own. Resource quotas cap what a namespace can use, and default requests and limits catch pods that set none. Pods can talk to each other freely by default, so I add network policies to block traffic between teams. Anything with strict compliance needs gets its own cluster.
Someone changed a setting by hand in the cloud console, and now your infrastructure code wants to undo it. What do you do?
How you handle drift between code and real infrastructure.
Does not blindly apply. Finds out why it changed, then either puts the change into code or reverts it, and closes the gap that allowed it.

I do not just apply the plan, because the change might be an incident fix holding production up. I find who made it and why. If it should stay, I add it to the code so the plan shows no changes. If not, we revert it at a planned time. Then I look at why hand edits were possible, for example by making console access read-only for most people.
A team wants to skip the standard deploy pipeline and use their own tool. How do you respond?
Your judgement in balancing team freedom with a supported standard.
Asks what need the platform is not meeting, sets clear minimum requirements for going off path, and feeds the gap back into the roadmap.

First I ask what is missing, because a team leaving the golden path is feedback. Often it is one feature we can add. If they still need their own tool, that is fine on a few conditions: it meets our security and audit rules, it sends the same logs and metrics, and they own its support. I add their need to our roadmap so the next team does not leave.
You must make a breaking change to a shared module that forty teams use. How do you roll it out?
How you change shared infrastructure without breaking its users.
Versioned releases, old and new supported side by side, a migration guide or tooling, a clear deadline, and tracking who has moved.

I release it as a new major version so nobody gets it by surprise, and keep the old version working for a set period, say one quarter. I write a short migration guide and, where I can, a script that makes the change for them. I track which teams have moved, help the slow ones directly, and only remove the old version once usage is near zero.
Walk me through upgrading your production Kubernetes clusters to a newer version.
Whether you can plan a risky platform upgrade that touches every team.
Checks for removed APIs, upgrades one minor version at a time, test clusters first, control plane before nodes, drains nodes carefully.

I read the release notes and scan every team's manifests for APIs the new version removes, then help teams fix them first. I upgrade one minor version at a time, test clusters before production. The control plane goes first, then node pools, draining nodes a few at a time so disruption budgets are respected. I announce the window and watch error rates after each step.
You pushed a new base build image and now every team's CI builds are failing. What do you do?
How you own and recover from a mistake that blocks many teams.
Rolls back first, tells people fast, finds the cause after, and changes the release process so one push cannot break everyone.

I roll back to the previous image right away, then post in the shared channel that builds are failing because of my change and should recover once teams rerun them. Once things are green I find the cause. Then I fix the process: new images go to a few volunteer teams first, and teams can pin a version instead of always pulling the latest one.
How do you let teams create their own infrastructure without letting them build something unsafe or very expensive?
How you design self-service with guardrails instead of ticket queues.
Templates with safe defaults, policy checked automatically in the pipeline and at deploy time, quotas and budget alerts, and clear error messages.

Teams pick from templates that already have encryption, tagging and sensible sizes. Rules are written as code and checked in the pipeline and again when resources are created, so a public storage bucket or an untagged database is rejected with a message saying how to fix it. Each team gets a budget with alerts. Teams move fast, and nobody waits on a ticket for normal requests.
In Kubernetes, what is the difference between a liveness probe and a readiness probe?
Whether you know how Kubernetes decides to restart a pod or stop sending it traffic.
Liveness failure restarts the container; readiness failure only removes the pod from traffic. Bonus for warning against liveness checks that call dependencies.

If the liveness probe fails, the kubelet restarts the container. If the readiness probe fails, the pod is taken out of the Service endpoints, so it gets no traffic but keeps running. I never make liveness depend on a database: if the database blips, every pod restarts at once and a small problem becomes an outage.
How do you make sure the image running in production is exactly the one your pipeline built and tested?
Your grasp of software supply chain basics for container images.
Deploy by digest, not by a tag that can be moved, and add signing plus an admission check so unsigned images are refused.

Tags can be moved, so a tag like v1.4 can point to a different image tomorrow. I deploy by the image digest, which is a hash of the content. The pipeline signs the image after tests pass, and an admission policy in the cluster rejects any image without a valid signature from our build system. We also store a parts list of each image so we can find affected services fast.
Our main CI pipeline takes 40 minutes and developers hate it. Where do you start?
How you find and fix the real bottleneck in a slow build.
Measure each step first, then fix the biggest: caching dependencies and image layers, running tests in parallel, and only building what changed.

First I pull timing for every step over the last few hundred runs, because guessing wastes weeks. The big wins are usually caching: in the Dockerfile I copy the dependency files and install them before copying the source, so that layer is reused when only code changes. Then I split tests across parallel runners and skip jobs for parts of the repo that did not change.
Why do teams store infrastructure state remotely with locking, and what goes wrong without it?
Whether you understand how infrastructure as code tools track what they manage.
State maps code to real resources; shared remote state with a lock stops two runs from clobbering each other. Notes that state can hold secrets, so access is limited.

The state file is the tool's record of which real resources match which code. If it lives on one laptop, nobody else sees the current truth. Without a lock, two people can apply at once and overwrite each other's changes or corrupt the state. I keep it in a remote backend with locking and versioning, and limit who can read it, because state often holds secrets in plain text.
How would you set an SLO for the CI system itself, and what would you do with the error budget?
How you apply reliability targets to an internal platform, not only to customer services.
A measure developers actually feel, a realistic target, and a budget that decides when to slow platform changes and fix reliability instead.

I pick what developers feel: the share of pipeline runs that finish without a platform-caused failure, and the share that start within two minutes. Say we target 99.5% over 30 days; the other 0.5% is the error budget. If we burn it early, we pause risky platform changes and spend the time on reliability. If we never touch it, the target may be stricter than anyone needs.
Every time a service deploys, a handful of requests fail with 502 errors. What is likely going on?
Whether you know how pod shutdown and traffic removal interact during a rolling update.
Pods get SIGTERM while traffic is still routed to them. Fix with graceful shutdown in the app, a short preStop delay, and a grace period long enough for both.

When a pod is terminated, Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and starts removing it from the endpoints at the same time. Those run in parallel, so the load balancer can still route to a pod that already stopped. I add a short preStop sleep so traffic drains first, make the app finish in-flight requests on SIGTERM, and make sure the grace period covers both.
Your CI system deploys to the cloud using a long-lived access key stored as a secret. How would you replace it?
Your knowledge of short-lived, identity-based credentials for automation.
Federated identity through OIDC: the cloud trusts tokens from the CI system and issues short-lived credentials scoped to one repo and branch.

I would set up OIDC federation. The CI system issues a signed token for each job that says which repo and branch it came from. The cloud account trusts that issuer and swaps the token for credentials that expire in minutes or hours, tied to a role that only allows that repo's deploy from the main branch. Then I revoke the old key, so there is nothing left to leak or rotate.
A node drain for maintenance has been stuck for an hour. What is the likely cause, and what do you do?
Whether you understand how drains, evictions and PodDisruptionBudgets work together.
A disruption budget that allows zero evictions blocks the drain. Find it, work with the owning team, and do not force it blindly.

Drain uses the eviction API, which respects PodDisruptionBudgets. A common cause is a budget that can never be met, like minAvailable of 1 on a single-replica service, so every eviction is refused. I find the blocking budget, talk to the owning team, and scale them to two replicas first. Long term, I add a policy check that flags budgets which allow zero disruptions.
You review an infrastructure plan and see it will destroy and recreate a production database. What do you do, and how do you stop it from happening again?
How you handle a dangerous change and build guardrails against the next one.
Stop, find why a replacement is triggered, fix it without data loss. Then add layered protection: deletion protection, destroy blocks in code, and plan checks.

I stop the apply and read why the plan wants a replacement. Often a field changed that cannot be updated in place. I fix the code or move the state instead. Then I add layers: deletion protection on the database itself, a setting in the code that blocks destroy, and a pipeline check that fails any plan deleting a stateful resource without a second approval.
Leadership asks whether we should build our own internal developer portal or adopt an existing one. How do you decide?
Your judgement on build versus buy, including the long-term cost of owning software.
Starts from the problem teams have, counts years of upkeep, and builds only what is truly unique to the company.

I start with the problem: are developers lost finding services, owners and docs, or blocked creating new ones? Then I compare total cost over three years, not just the first build. A homegrown portal needs a team forever. I would usually adopt an existing open-source or paid option for the catalog, and build only the plugins tied to our own workflows, after a short pilot with two teams.

policy.heading: Policy and government affairs questions
qs: Walk me through how a federal agency rule goes from proposal to final.
Whether you know the notice-and-comment process that most of the regulatory work runs on.
The proposed rule, the public comment period, the agency's duty to answer significant comments, and the final rule with a delayed effective date.

The agency publishes a proposed rule in the Federal Register with a comment period, and anyone can comment in the public docket. The agency must consider significant comments and explain its response in the preamble of the final rule. The final rule is also published and usually takes effect at least 30 days later. Before a proposal, I watch the agency's regulatory agenda.
What makes a comment letter actually change an agency's final rule?
Your understanding of what agencies weigh in written submissions.
Agencies do not count votes; evidence, legal arguments tied to the statute, and workable alternatives do. It also builds the record for any later challenge.

Agencies do not count votes, so a thousand form letters weigh less than one solid comment. What moves them is cost or feasibility data, a legal argument tied to the statute, and a workable alternative with exact proposed text. I write it so a staffer can lift a paragraph into the final rule, and so our points are in the record if a court reviews it.
We track dozens of bills and rules. How do you decide which ones get your time?
How you set priorities across a large policy portfolio.
A simple screen of business impact against the real chance the measure moves, reviewed often, with low-priority items still watched.

I score each item on two things: how much it would cost or help the business, and how likely it is to move this session. A bill with a sponsor on the committee and a hearing scheduled ranks above a messaging bill. High impact and high likelihood get active work, the rest get a watch list. I review the list every two weeks, because a quiet bill can jump onto a must-pass vehicle.
You have a first meeting with a congressional staffer on our issue. How do you prepare, and what do you leave behind?
How you run a meeting with legislative staff.
Research on the member and the district, a short clear ask, local impact, and a one-page leave-behind; then follow-up on what was promised.

I read the member's committee seats, past votes and statements, and find our employees or sites in the district. I go in with one clear ask, explained in under five minutes, and local numbers. I leave a one-page summary with my contact details. Within a day I send a thank-you and anything I promised, and I log the meeting for our disclosure records.
What disclosure and ethics rules do you check before lobbying, federally or in a new state?
Whether you know the compliance rules that govern your own work.
Lobbying Disclosure Act registration and reports, House and Senate gift rules, and each state's own lobbying law, with counsel involved.

Federally, I check whether our activity crosses the Lobbying Disclosure Act thresholds, that we are registered, and that quarterly activity and semiannual contribution reports are right. I check House and Senate gift rules before any meal or event. In a new state I read its lobbying law, since registration triggers and gift limits differ, and some states cover procurement contacts.
Our trade association is about to take a position that hurts us. What do you do?
How you handle a conflict inside a coalition you belong to.
Raise it early through the right channel with a concrete alternative, accept that you may lose, and keep the option to speak separately.

I raise it early in the working group, not after the vote, with data on how it hits us and alternative wording. I look for other members with the same problem. If we still lose, I ask the association to stay silent on that point or I tell leadership we may file our own comments. I keep it professional, because we need that coalition on the next ten issues.
You gave a legislative staffer a figure that turned out to be wrong. What do you do?
How you handle a mistake that touches your credibility with government.
Correct it quickly, in writing, before it is used, with the right number and its source. Credibility outweighs a weaker argument.

I call the staffer the same day and follow up in writing with the corrected figure and where it comes from. I do not wait to see if anyone notices. Then I find how the error happened, usually a stale internal number, and add a second check. Staff trust is the whole job; a weaker number told honestly is better than a strong one that falls apart in a hearing.
How would you build a coalition with groups that disagree with us on other issues?
Your skill at coalition building around a narrow shared interest.
A tightly defined shared goal, clear ground rules on what the coalition speaks to, and credit shared with partners.

I define the one outcome we share, say a fix to a single rule, and keep the coalition's voice to that. I agree ground rules up front: who signs letters, who speaks to press, and what is out of scope. Groups we fight elsewhere often bring credibility we lack, like a consumer group. I share credit and never surprise a partner with a public move.
A bill that hurts us has just passed committee. Leadership wants it stopped. How do you approach the next steps?
Your judgement on strategy once a bill gains momentum.
A realistic read of the odds, more than one path (floor, the other chamber, amendments, the rule that follows), and honest advice to leadership.

First I tell leadership the odds honestly; a bill out of committee is not law, but it has momentum. I would work three paths at once: floor votes and amendments to fix the worst sections, the other chamber's committee, and the agency that would write the rules. Often the best realistic win is a narrower amendment, and I would say so rather than promise a kill.
The CEO asks you to send a company check to a federal candidate who supports our bill. What do you do?
Whether you know the basic campaign finance limits on corporate money.
Corporate treasury money cannot go to federal candidates; personal giving and a company PAC funded voluntarily are the options, and state law differs.

I would stop the check before it goes out. A corporation cannot contribute from its treasury to a federal candidate. The CEO can give personally within the legal limit. If we have a PAC, it can give from voluntary contributions by eligible employees. For state races I would check that state's law, since some allow corporate giving, and I would bring in counsel.
What is the difference between an authorization bill and an appropriations bill, and why would we care about both?
Whether you understand how Congress creates, funds and shapes the programs we deal with.
Authorization creates or changes a program; appropriations fund it. A spending bill can carry a limit that blocks an agency action.

An authorizing bill creates or changes a program and its rules, through the committee that oversees the agency. An appropriations bill provides the money, usually for one fiscal year. We care about both because a spending bill can include a line saying no funds may be used to carry out a certain rule, which can stall it even if the underlying law never changes.
The Supreme Court overruled Chevron in 2024. How does that change the way you work on a rulemaking?
Whether you follow how courts now read agency power and adjust your strategy to it.
Courts now decide for themselves what a statute means, so arguments tied to the statutory text and a solid record matter more.

In Loper Bright, the Court said judges must use their own judgment on what a statute means instead of deferring to a reasonable agency reading. So in our comments I tie each point to the statute's text and build a record a court can use later. Drafting also matters more, so I push for precise language when a bill is being written.
What does OIRA do, and when would you ask for a meeting there?
Your knowledge of White House review of significant rules and how to use it well.
OIRA, inside OMB, reviews significant rules before proposal and before final. Outside parties can request meetings, which are listed publicly.

OIRA is the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs inside OMB. Under Executive Order 12866 it reviews significant rules, including the agency's cost analysis, before the proposal and again before the final rule. While a rule is under review I can request a meeting, which is listed publicly with attendees. I would bring new cost data, not a repeat of our comment letter.
You met agency staff on an open rulemaking two weeks ago, and you just realized nobody filed the ex parte summary the agency requires. What do you do?
How you handle a procedural slip that could hurt our standing in the public record.
File a complete, accurate summary now, tell counsel and the agency contact, and fix the process that let it slip.

I would write the summary today, covering who attended, what we argued and any handouts, and file it in the docket with a short note that it is late. I would tell our counsel and email the agency contact so they hear it from us first. Then I would add a step to our checklist: one named person files every summary within the agency's deadline.
The agency's economic analysis badly underestimates our compliance costs. How do you challenge it?
Whether you can contest an agency's numbers with evidence it has to answer.
Specific, sourced data and a clear critique of the agency's method, filed in the record, not just a claim that costs are higher.

I would find exactly where the gap is: wrong unit costs, missing tasks, or too few affected firms. Then I would give replacement figures with the method behind them, ideally from a member survey or an outside economist, and show how they change the agency's own totals. If small businesses are hit, I would also challenge the Regulatory Flexibility Act analysis.
Our coalition includes direct competitors. What rules do you set for those meetings?
Whether you know where joint advocacy stops and antitrust risk starts.
Joint petitioning of government is generally protected, but talk about prices, customers or markets is not. Agenda, counsel and minutes.

Working together to petition the government is generally protected under the Noerr-Pennington doctrine. That protection does not cover side talk about prices, wages, customers or who sells where. So every meeting has a written agenda that antitrust counsel reviews, someone keeps minutes, and if talk drifts to business terms I stop it and note that in the minutes.
Our CEO will testify before a House committee next month. How do you prepare?
How you prepare an executive for a hearing, including the rules that apply to witnesses.
Written testimony by the committee's deadline, the House disclosure form, hard mock questioning, and no claim that cannot be backed up.

I would get the committee's deadline for written testimony and complete the House Truth in Testimony form, which asks about federal grants, contracts and foreign government payments related to the topic. We would run two mock hearings with hard questions from both parties. False statements to Congress are a crime, so if she is unsure of a fact, she offers to follow up in writing.
Five states have passed different versions of a law on our product. Do we push for a federal standard?
Your judgement on federal preemption, a trade-off with real risks on both sides.
Knows a federal floor still lets states go further, insists on clear preemption language, and weighs the risk of a stricter federal law.

Only if we can get the right bill. A federal law that only sets a floor still lets states go further, so we could end up with six rules instead of five. I would want express preemption language, a standard we can live with, and support from both parties. If Congress would only pass a tougher bill, working state by state toward model language may be safer.
An agency just finalized a rule we oppose, and a new Congress is coming in. Is the Congressional Review Act a real option?
Whether you know how Congress can undo a final rule and when that path is realistic.
A joint resolution of disapproval with fast Senate procedures, signed by the President. The agency then cannot reissue a substantially similar rule.

It can be. Congress passes a joint resolution of disapproval; in the Senate it moves under fast rules and cannot be filibustered. The President must sign it, so it mostly works after a change of administration. Rules issued late in a session can fall into a lookback window for the new Congress. If it passes, the agency cannot reissue a substantially similar rule without a new law.
We want to hire a senior official who just left the agency we lobby. What do you check before she starts?
Whether you know the post-employment limits on former federal officials and plan her work around them.
Federal post-employment law, any ethics pledge she signed, and a written review by ethics counsel, then work that keeps her clear.

I would get any ethics advice her agency gave her and have our counsel review federal post-employment law. Among other limits, senior officials face a one-year ban on contacting their former agency to influence it for someone else, and a lifetime bar on specific-party matters she worked on personally. A pledge may add more. Until cleared, she advises us internally only.

power-electronics.heading: Power electronics engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between a buck and a boost converter?
Whether you know the basic converter topologies well enough to explain them quickly.
Buck steps voltage down, boost steps it up, with the ideal duty-cycle relations and where the inductor sits in each.

A buck steps the voltage down: in continuous conduction the output is about the duty cycle times the input. A boost steps it up: the output is the input divided by one minus the duty cycle. In a buck the inductor is on the output, so output current is smooth. In a boost it is on the input, so input current is smooth and output current is pulsed.
Why would you use a synchronous rectifier instead of a diode in a low-voltage buck converter?
Your grasp of conduction losses and the trade-off that comes with them.
A MOSFET's on-resistance loss beats a diode's fixed drop at low voltage, at the cost of a second driver and careful dead time.

A diode drops around half a volt, so at 10 A that can be close to 5 W when it conducts most of the period. A MOSFET with a few milliohms of on-resistance loses far less. The cost is a second gate driver and dead time: both switches must be off briefly so they never conduct together, and during that gap the body diode carries the current.
Where do switching losses come from in a hard-switched MOSFET, and how do you reduce them?
Whether you understand the physics behind the loss budget.
Voltage and current overlap during edges, output capacitance energy at turn-on, gate drive loss, all scaling with frequency, plus real ways to cut them.

During each edge the switch briefly has voltage across it and current through it, and that overlap turns into heat. At hard turn-on, the energy stored in the output capacitance is also dumped into the channel. All of it scales with frequency. I cut it with a stronger gate drive, a better device, soft switching like zero-voltage switching, or a lower frequency if the magnetics allow.
Walk me through how you choose the inductor for a buck converter.
Your method for sizing magnetics, not just picking a part number from a catalog.
A ripple target sets the inductance, peak current sets the saturation rating, and copper and core loss set the temperature rise.

I pick a ripple current, often 20 to 40 percent of full load, and solve L = (Vin - Vout) x D / (ripple x fsw) at the highest input voltage, where ripple is worst. Then I check that saturation current is above load current plus half the ripple, with margin when hot. Last, I estimate copper and core loss to confirm it stays within its temperature rating.
On a buck converter layout, which loop do you route first, and why?
Whether you know where parasitic inductance does the most damage on a board.
The hot loop of input capacitor and both switches, kept small with a ground plane right under it to limit ringing, spikes and EMI.

The hot loop: input capacitor, high-side switch, low-side switch and back. Its current jumps on every edge, so any inductance in it causes ringing, voltage spikes on the switches and EMI. I place a small ceramic capacitor right at the switches, keep the loop tight, and return it on a solid ground plane on the next layer so the fields cancel.
How do you measure ringing on a switch node, and what can go wrong with the probe?
Your bench skill and whether your measurements can be trusted.
A short ground connection, enough bandwidth, and differential or isolated probes for floating nodes, never a scope with its ground lifted.

I take off the long ground clip and use a short spring ground at the tip, because a few inches of lead adds inductance that creates ringing that is not really there. The probe and scope need enough bandwidth for the edge. For a floating node like a high-side gate, I use a differential or isolated probe, never a scope with its ground lifted, which can put line voltage on the case.
For a new design, how do you choose between silicon, silicon carbide and gallium nitride switches?
Your judgement in matching device technology to voltage, frequency and cost.
A choice driven by voltage class, switching frequency, thermal needs and cost, with awareness that each needs a different gate drive.

I start from voltage, frequency and cost. For a 48-volt server converter, silicon MOSFETs are cheap and proven, and GaN pays off if I need high frequency and small size. For an 800-volt EV system, SiC is the usual pick: it blocks high voltage with low loss and handles heat well. GaN parts today mostly sit at 650 volts and below. Then I check the gate drive each one needs.
How do you know your control loop is stable, and what margins do you aim for?
Whether you verify stability by measurement rather than trusting a simulation.
A measured loop gain with clear phase and gain margin targets, crossover well below switching frequency, confirmed by a load step test.

I measure the loop gain with a network analyzer, injecting a small signal across a resistor in the feedback path. I look for at least 45 degrees of phase margin and around 10 dB of gain margin, with crossover well below the switching frequency, often a tenth to a fifth of it. Then I run a load step: a clean recovery with little ringing confirms the numbers.
Your prototype keeps killing the low-side MOSFET when the high-side turns on. How do you find the cause?
How you debug a destructive failure methodically instead of swapping parts.
Measure first: gate voltage for false turn-on, drain peak against rating, dead time. Then fix the root cause, not the symptom.

I run at low input voltage with a current-limited supply and watch the low-side gate during the high-side edge. The fast voltage rise can pull that gate up through the Miller capacitance and cause shoot-through. I also check the drain peak against the rating and the dead time. Fixes include a stiffer gate pull-down, a negative off voltage, a slower edge or a snubber.
You add an EMI input filter and the converter starts oscillating. What is going on?
Your understanding of how a filter and a regulated converter interact as one system.
A regulated converter acts as a negative input resistance; the filter's output impedance must stay well below it, usually with damping added.

A regulated converter draws constant power, so when its input voltage rises its current falls: it behaves like a negative resistance. If the filter's output impedance peak comes close to the converter's input impedance, the pair becomes unstable. I compare the two impedances, keep the filter's well below, and add damping, for example a resistor and capacitor across the filter capacitor.
Why does peak current-mode control need slope compensation, and how much do you add?
Whether you understand the main instability of current-mode control.
Names subharmonic oscillation above 50% duty in continuous conduction, and adds a ramp of at least half the inductor down-slope without overdoing it.

In peak current mode with continuous conduction, an error in inductor current grows cycle by cycle once duty passes 50 percent. That shows up as subharmonic oscillation: alternating wide and narrow pulses. I add a ramp to the sensed current of at least half the inductor's down-slope, and not far more, since too much ramp makes it behave like voltage mode.
Why is a boost converter in continuous conduction harder to compensate than a buck?
Your grasp of the right-half-plane zero and where it limits bandwidth.
Explains the right-half-plane zero physically, knows it is lowest at full load and minimum input, and keeps crossover well below it there.

A boost has a right-half-plane zero. When the loop raises duty to deliver more power, the diode conducts for less time, so the output first dips before the inductor current catches up. It adds gain but phase lag. It sits lowest at full load and minimum input voltage, so I set crossover at a fifth to a third of it at that corner.
Conducted emissions fail at the low end of the band. How do you tell whether it is common mode or differential mode?
Whether you diagnose EMI before you add filter parts.
Separates the two modes with a current probe or a noise separator, then applies the fix that matches each mode.

I clamp a current probe around line and neutral together: differential current cancels, so what remains is common mode. Around one wire I see both. A noise separator on the LISN outputs does the same. Differential mode gets X capacitors and series inductance; common mode gets a common-mode choke, Y capacitors and less switch-node capacitance to the heatsink.
Your flyback shows a big drain spike at turn-off. How do you design the clamp?
Your handling of leakage energy and the trade-off in clamp voltage.
Ties the spike to leakage inductance, sets clamp voltage between reflected voltage and switch rating, and reduces leakage at the source.

The spike is leakage inductance energy that cannot reach the secondary. The clamp voltage must sit well above the reflected output voltage, or the clamp eats main power. A higher clamp resets faster and wastes less, so I pick the highest that keeps about 20 percent margin on the switch at max input. Then I cut leakage by interleaving windings.
A full-bridge converter runs fine for a while, then the primary current starts spiking. What do you suspect?
Whether you recognize flux walking in a transformer and know the cures.
Identifies volt-second imbalance building a DC offset to saturation, and fixes it with a blocking capacitor or current-mode control.

Probably flux walking. If the two half-cycles do not apply exactly equal volt-seconds, from slightly different switch drops or timing, a DC offset builds in the core until it saturates. I would confirm uneven current peaks with a probe on the primary. In voltage mode I add a DC blocking capacitor in series with the primary; peak current mode also corrects it cycle by cycle.
You added copper layers to a high-frequency transformer and winding loss went up. Why?
Your understanding of proximity effect in magnetics.
Explains proximity effect across layers, uses MMF and Dowell-type analysis, and cures it with interleaving, optimum thickness or Litz wire.

Proximity effect. The field from neighboring layers drives eddy currents, so each extra layer carries more circulating current and AC resistance climbs, as Dowell's method predicts. I sketch the MMF across the window: interleaving primary and secondary halves its peak. Then I pick layer thickness near the optimum, or Litz wire with strands thinner than the skin depth.
A customer wants ten-year life from a supply sealed in a hot enclosure. How do you handle the electrolytic capacitors?
How you make a lifetime claim you can defend.
Bases life on measured core temperature from ripple heating and real ambient, and changes parts or layout when the margin is not there.

Electrolytic life is set by core temperature; as a rule of thumb from capacitor makers, it roughly doubles for every 10 °C cooler. I measure ripple current at line and switching frequency, compute ESR heating, and measure case temperature in the real enclosure at max ambient. Short of ten years with margin, I use higher-rated, paralleled, polymer or film parts.
A product in production starts showing MOSFET failures in the field at a few hundred parts per million. How do you run the investigation?
How you lead a field failure from data to root cause and fix.
Collects returns and data, uses failure analysis to read the damage, tests the least-covered corners, and verifies the fix before release.

I collect returns with serial and date codes and send failed switches for analysis to see whether damage looks like overvoltage, overcurrent or heat. Then I test corners we covered least: hot startup, output short, surge, brownout. In a similar case it was avalanche during short-circuit shutdown at high line; a softer turn-off fixed it, proven before release.

power-plant-operator.heading: Power plant operations questions
qs: What do you cover when you hand over a shift?
Whether you pass on the plant state so nothing is lost between crews.
Unit status, abnormal conditions, equipment out of service and clearances, open work, and a walk of the boards together.

I go through each unit's load and status, any alarms that are in and why, equipment out of service and the clearances hung, and work still open. We look at the boards and logs together, and I don't leave until my relief says they have the shift. If something is unusual, I say it out loud, not just write it in the log.
Walk me through the steam cycle of a fossil plant in plain words.
Your grasp of how the main parts of the plant work together.
A clear loop: pump, boiler, turbine, condenser, back to the pump, plus why the condenser vacuum matters.

Feedwater pumps push water into the boiler, where the heat from the fuel turns it into high-pressure steam. The steam spins the turbine, which turns the generator. Leaving the turbine, the steam goes to the condenser, where cooling water turns it back into water under vacuum. That vacuum lets the turbine get more work out of the steam. The water is then heated and pumped back to the boiler.
Why is drum level watched so closely on a drum boiler, both high and low?
Your understanding of one of the main boiler protections.
Low level can starve and overheat tubes; high level carries water into the steam and toward the turbine. Both are protected by alarms and trips.

Low level means the waterwall tubes can run short of water and overheat, which can rupture them. High level lets water carry over with the steam, which can damage the superheater and send water into the turbine. I watch level, steam flow and feedwater flow together, and I remember that level swells for a moment when pressure drops fast, so I don't overcorrect.
Walk me through hanging a clearance on a pump so a mechanic can open it.
Whether you can isolate equipment so others can work on it safely.
Stop the pump, lock out the motor, close and tag discharge then suction, bleed to zero, verify, and get an independent check.

I stop the pump, rack out or lock the breaker, and try a local start to prove it's dead. I close and tag the discharge, then the suction, plus any seal or cooling lines. I open vents and drains and confirm zero pressure and a safe temperature. A second operator checks every tag against the clearance sheet before I release it to maintenance.
What has to match before you close the generator breaker onto the grid?
Your knowledge of synchronizing, a task where a mistake can damage the generator.
Phase sequence, voltage, frequency and phase angle, with the synchroscope turning slowly in the fast direction and the breaker closed just before 12 o'clock.

Phase rotation has to be right, which is proven at commissioning. Then I match voltage to the bus, and set the generator slightly faster than the grid so it picks up load instead of motoring. I watch the synchroscope turn slowly clockwise and close just before 12 o'clock to allow for breaker closing time, with the sync check relay as a backstop.
Grid frequency drops suddenly after another plant trips. What does your unit do, and what do you do?
Whether you understand how your unit supports the grid.
The governor raises output automatically through droop; the operator watches limits, doesn't fight the response, and follows dispatch.

The governor sees the speed drop and opens the control valves to pick up load in proportion to the drop, before anyone touches a thing. I watch steam pressure, temperatures and the boiler, which has to catch up, and keep us inside limits. I don't pull it back to the old setpoint on my own; I follow the dispatcher as the grid recovers.
Condenser vacuum is slowly getting worse on your unit. How do you work it out?
How you troubleshoot a common problem before it trips the unit.
Checks the usual causes in a sensible order: cooling water, air removal, gland seal, air leaks, and reduces load if it keeps falling.

First I confirm it on a second indication. Then circulating water: pumps, flow, inlet temperature, fouled screens. Next the air removal, the ejectors or vacuum pumps, and gland seal steam pressure. If those look fine, I suspect an air leak and have someone check flanges and valves under vacuum. If it keeps falling, I reduce load before it reaches the trip.
Tell me about an operating mistake you made, or nearly made, and what changed afterward.
Whether you own errors and fix the cause, not just the moment.
An honest story, reported quickly, with a lesson that changed a procedure, a label or a habit.

During a lineup I opened a drain on the wrong heater; the two valves looked alike and sat side by side. A level alarm came in within a minute and I closed it. I reported it to my supervisor that shift. We relabeled both valves, and now I touch the tag and read it aloud before I turn any valve.
Turbine bearing vibration is climbing toward the trip setpoint and dispatch wants you to hold full load for the evening peak. What do you do?
Whether you put the equipment and the people ahead of the schedule.
Follows the alarm procedure, reduces load if needed, tells dispatch early, and never bypasses the protection.

I follow the alarm response: which bearing, the trend, oil temperature and pressure, and any change in steam temperatures. If it keeps rising, I reduce load as the procedure says and call dispatch right away so they can find the megawatts elsewhere. I won't block the trip to make the peak; a damaged turbine is out for months.
The unit trips with no warning. Walk me through your first few minutes.
How you take control after a trip and bring the unit to a safe state.
Verify the trip is complete, protect the turbine and boiler, check auxiliaries and power, then find the cause before any restart.

I confirm the stop valves are closed, the generator breaker is open and speed is falling. I check that station power transferred, the lube oil pumps are running, and later that the turbine reaches turning gear. I verify the fuel is off and the boiler is safe, call dispatch and my supervisor, and read the first-out alarm. No restart until we know why.
Why does a steam turbine stay on turning gear after shutdown, and what does that mean for a restart?
Whether you understand rotor bow and why it matters.
A hot rotor left still bends as it cools unevenly. Turning gear keeps it straight, and you confirm eccentricity is normal before rolling.

A hot rotor that stops cools unevenly: the top stays hotter and the shaft bows. Turning gear keeps it rolling slowly so it cools evenly. Before rolling with steam I check that eccentricity is back within limits and that lube oil, and lift oil if fitted, are normal. If the rotor sat still, I follow the procedure for extended turning time, not my own guess.
You are putting a cold steam line in service. How do you do it, and why?
Whether you know how to avoid water hammer and thermal shock.
Drains open first, a slow warm-up through a bypass or cracked valve, and condensate cleared before full flow.

Cold pipe condenses steam. Slugs of that water pushed by steam cause water hammer, which can break hangers or the pipe. I open the drains and traps, crack the warm-up or bypass valve, and let the line heat slowly while the drains clear. I watch for banging and pipe movement. I only open fully once the drains blow dry steam and the line is near steam temperature.
On a substation clearance, why does the breaker open before the disconnects, and when do the grounds go on?
Your switching order and the reason behind each step.
Disconnects are not built to break load: open the breaker, verify it, open the disconnects, test for absence of voltage, then ground.

Most disconnects are not rated to interrupt load current, so opening one under load draws an arc. I open the breaker and confirm it by indication and a zero current reading. Then I open the disconnects and check the blades visually. I test for absence of voltage with a detector I have proven works, and only then apply grounds. Grounds come off last, after everyone is clear.
Why does a boiler purge before light-off, and what do you do after a flame failure on the last burner?
Whether you respect the risk of a furnace explosion.
The purge clears fuel that may have built up. After a flame-out the fuel is shut off and the furnace purged again before any relight, never a quick retry.

Unburned fuel or gas in a furnace is an explosion waiting for a spark. The purge moves a set volume of air through at a minimum airflow and proves the fuel valves are shut before ignition is allowed. If I lose the last flame, the master fuel trip shuts the fuel off. I do not try to relight into it: I find the cause and run a full purge first.
Why is a hydrogen-cooled generator purged with carbon dioxide instead of going straight from air to hydrogen?
Your knowledge of the hydrogen hazard on the generator.
Hydrogen and air burn over a wide range of mixes. CO2 as a middle step keeps them from meeting, confirmed by purity readings.

Hydrogen burns in air from about 4% to 75%, so going straight from air to hydrogen would pass through that range inside the generator. We push the air out with CO2 until purity analysis confirms it, then admit hydrogen and push the CO2 out. Going back to air for maintenance is the same in reverse. Seal oil stays in service while there is gas pressure in the casing.
Why is a hot start ramped differently from a cold start?
Whether you understand thermal stress in thick metal parts.
Steam temperature is matched to metal temperature. A gap either way stresses rotors, casings and drums, so ramp rates follow the start curves.

Thick parts like the turbine rotor, steam chests and the drum heat from the surface in. A big gap between steam and metal temperature cracks them over time. On a cold start I ramp slowly. On a hot start the metal is already hot, so I need hot steam before I admit it; cold steam on a hot rotor is just as bad. I follow the start curves and watch metal temperatures and differential expansion.
Cation conductivity at the condensate pump discharge starts climbing. What are you thinking, and what do you do?
How you respond to an upset in cycle chemistry.
Suspects a condenser tube leak, gets chemistry to confirm, follows the plant's action levels, and isolates waterbox halves to find the leak.

Most often that is cooling water leaking into the condenser through a tube, bringing in chlorides and other salts. I call chemistry to confirm with a grab sample and check sodium. Then I follow our action levels, which may mean cutting load. If the condenser is split, I isolate one waterbox half at a time to see which side clears. Running long on contaminated water damages the boiler and turbine.
A DC ground alarm comes in on the station battery system. Why does it matter, and how do you find the ground?
Your understanding of DC control power and careful troubleshooting.
One ground on an ungrounded DC system does no harm alone, but a second can cause a false trip or block one. Search methodically, knowing what each circuit feeds.

Our DC system is ungrounded, so one ground does not trip anything. A second ground can energize a trip coil or keep a breaker from tripping when it should. I check the ground detector for which pole is grounded, then follow the procedure to open branch circuits briefly, one at a time. Before I open any, I know what it feeds, so I do not drop protection or the emergency oil pump on a running unit.
At night the transmission operator asks your generator to absorb more reactive power. What limits how far you can go?
Whether you can run the generator within its capability curve.
Underexcited operation is limited by stator end heating, stability and the minimum excitation limiter. Auxiliary bus voltage also drops.

Absorbing VARs means running underexcited. On that side the capability curve is limited by heating at the ends of the stator core and by stability, since a weaker field holds the rotor less firmly to the grid. The minimum excitation limiter stops us before that. I also watch terminal and auxiliary bus voltage, because motors do not like low voltage. I go as far as the curve allows and tell them where we stop.
A maintenance supervisor asks you to crack a tagged valve for two minutes to fill a line, saying the crew is on break. What do you do?
How you protect a clearance when someone pushes for a shortcut.
No operating a tagged device. The clearance is changed or released through the formal process, with every holder signed off.

I do not crack it under the tag. Whatever I am told, I cannot see whether anyone has the system open. If the fill is needed, we use the plant's process: every worker on the clearance signs off or the clearance is formally modified, I walk down the boundary, and then I operate the valve. It costs twenty minutes. Afterward I tell my shift supervisor what was asked.

power-systems.heading: Power systems engineer questions
qs: Why do power engineers work in per-unit, and how do you pick the bases?
Whether you have the basic tool of system studies in hand.
One base MVA for the whole system, base kV set by transformer ratios in each zone, and the payoff: transformers drop out and errors stand out.

I pick one base MVA for the whole system and a base kV for each voltage zone, following the transformer ratios. Base impedance is kV squared over MVA. A transformer then has the same impedance on both sides, and values land near 1, so a bus at 0.6 per unit or an impedance ten times too large jumps out at once.
In a load flow study, what are the slack, PV and PQ buses?
Your grasp of how a load flow model is set up.
What is fixed and what is solved at each bus type, and that a generator hitting its reactive limit stops holding voltage.

The slack bus holds voltage magnitude and angle fixed and picks up whatever power is left over, including losses. A PV bus is usually a generator: real power and voltage are set, reactive power and angle are solved. A PQ bus is a load: real and reactive power are set, voltage is solved. If a generator hits its reactive limit, the program treats it as PQ.
Customers at the end of a long rural feeder report low voltage at peak load. What do you look at?
How you work a common distribution problem in order, from data to fix.
Confirm with measurements first, then try the cheaper fixes (regulator settings, capacitors, load transfer) before new conductor.

First I confirm it: meter data or a recorder at the end of the line, compared with ANSI C84.1 Range A. Then I run the feeder model at peak. Options in rough cost order: adjust the substation regulator or line drop compensation, add switched capacitors to cut reactive current, add a line regulator midway, move load to another feeder, and last, bigger conductor.
Walk me through an arc flash study for an industrial plant.
Whether you know the steps and the standards behind an arc flash label.
Data, short circuit, coordination for clearing times, IEEE 1584 for incident energy, NFPA 70E for labels, and minimum fault cases checked too.

I build the model from the one-line, utility fault data, cables, transformers and every protective device. I run short circuit, then coordination to get clearing times. Incident energy comes from IEEE 1584. I run both maximum and minimum source cases, since lower current can trip slower and release more energy. The results go on labels and in the safe work program under NFPA 70E.
What drives the design of a substation ground grid?
Whether you know how a grid keeps people safe during a ground fault, following IEEE 80.
Touch and step voltage limits set by clearing time and surface layer, soil resistivity measured on site, and the share of fault current that enters the grid.

The goal is keeping touch and step voltages under IEEE 80 limits during a ground fault. Those limits depend on fault clearing time and the surface layer, like crushed rock. I need measured soil resistivity, usually from a Wenner four-pin test, and the part of the fault current that enters the earth. If the grid fails, I add conductors, tighten spacing, add rods or extend the rock.
A 50 MW solar plant will connect near one of your substations. What changes for protection?
Whether you understand how inverter-based sources behave in a fault.
Inverters give limited fault current set by their controls, so overcurrent, directional or distance elements may not respond as expected; studies must use the real model.

An inverter gives fault current set by its controls, often little more than its rating, unlike a spinning generator. Overcurrent relays may barely see a fault, and directional or distance elements may misread it. I would get the maker's fault model, re-run the studies, and check ride-through rules under IEEE 2800 or 1547.
To save money, a client wants one substation transformer instead of two. How do you respond?
