How you weigh cost against reliability and put the risk in front of the client.
No flat refusal: show what a transformer failure means in outage time and cost, offer middle options, and let the client decide in writing.

I would show what one transformer means: if it fails, the site is out until a replacement arrives, and large units can take many months. I would put a cost on that outage next to the cost of the second unit. Then I would offer middle options, like a tie to another feeder or a pad and connections for a mobile substation. It is their call, but I document the decision.
A plant adding many variable frequency drives asks if it will meet IEEE 519. How do you answer?
Your knowledge of harmonic limits and where they apply.
Limits apply at the point of common coupling, current limits depend on the short-circuit to load current ratio, and capacitor banks can cause resonance.

IEEE 519 limits apply at the point of common coupling with the utility, not at each drive. Current limits depend on the ratio of short-circuit current to load current. I would model the drive harmonics, check current and voltage distortion, and look for resonance with capacitor banks. Fixes include line reactors, multipulse drives or active filters.
After energizing a new feeder, you find the relay settings used the wrong current transformer ratio. What do you do?
How you own a mistake that leaves equipment less protected than it should be.
Report it at once, assess and cover the risk, correct and verify the settings, then check the rest of the job and fix the process.

This happened to me: the relay was set for 600:5 but the CT was wired on the 1200:5 tap, so the relay saw half the real current. I told the operations lead that day, confirmed the backup protection covered the feeder, and issued corrected settings. Then I checked every relay in that package and added an in-service load check to our commissioning steps.
Which sequence networks do you use for a line-to-line fault versus a single line-to-ground fault?
Your command of symmetrical components, the math behind every fault study.
Line-to-ground puts the positive, negative and zero networks in series; line-to-line puts positive and negative in parallel, with no zero sequence.

For a bolted single line-to-ground fault, I connect the positive, negative and zero sequence networks in series. The fault current is then three times the prefault voltage over the sum of the three impedances. For a line-to-line fault I use only positive and negative, in parallel. With no path to ground there is no zero sequence current.
Why can a ground fault at a substation bus be larger than a three-phase fault at the same bus?
Whether you understand what zero sequence impedance does to fault duty.
Ground fault current is higher when zero sequence impedance is below positive, as near a solidly grounded wye winding, so both must be checked.

Bolted ground fault current is 3V over Z1 plus Z2 plus Z0, while three-phase is V over Z1. With Z1 equal to Z2, the ground fault is larger whenever Z0 is smaller than Z1. Near a delta-wye transformer with a solidly grounded wye, the transformer gives a low zero sequence path. So I always compute both and check equipment duty against the larger.
Why is zone 1 of a distance relay usually set short of the remote end of the line?
Whether you know why instantaneous protection must underreach.
Errors in line data, CTs, VTs and the relay could make it trip instantly for faults past the line, so zone 2 with a delay or a pilot scheme covers the rest.

Zone 1 trips with no intentional delay, so it must never see a fault past the remote bus. Errors in line impedance data, CTs, VTs and the relay add up, so I set it around 80 to 90 percent of the line. Zone 2 reaches past the remote end with a time delay. For high-speed tripping over the whole line, I add a communication scheme such as permissive overreaching transfer trip.
How does a transformer differential relay avoid tripping on magnetizing inrush?
Your grasp of transformer protection beyond the basic differential principle.
Inrush is rich in second harmonic, so the relay restrains or blocks on it, while an unrestrained high-set element still trips fast for heavy internal faults.

On energizing, inrush flows in one winding only, so the differential sees it as an internal fault. Inrush is rich in second harmonic, so the relay restrains or blocks when that harmonic is above a set percentage. I keep an unrestrained high-set element so a severe internal fault still trips at once. Fifth harmonic restraint covers overexcitation.
A pad-mounted transformer fed by a long underground cable shows wild overvoltages when the crew switches it with single-phase cutouts. What is happening?
Whether you recognize ferroresonance and know how to prevent it.
Ferroresonance between cable capacitance and the transformer's magnetizing reactance with a phase open; fix it with three-phase switching, load, or less cable.

That is ferroresonance. With one or two phases open, the open phase is fed through the cable capacitance, which can resonate with the transformer's nonlinear magnetizing reactance. Light load and an ungrounded primary, like delta, make it worse. I would switch with a three-phase gang-operated device, keep some load on, or switch near the transformer so less cable is in the circuit.
The utility upgrades its transformer, and your updated short-circuit study shows several feeder breakers are now overdutied. What do you do?
How you handle a hidden hazard that appears after a change outside your control.
Verify the data, warn the owner in writing at once, set interim measures, then choose a lasting fix such as higher-rated breakers or added impedance.

First I confirm the new utility fault data and X/R ratio, since breaker duty depends on both. If it holds, I tell the owner in writing right away: an overdutied breaker can fail violently when it interrupts. Interim steps may mean changing the switching setup and keeping people away. Lasting fixes are higher-rated breakers, current-limiting reactors or fuses, or more source impedance.
A low-impedance bus differential relay tripped for a fault outside its zone. What do you suspect, and what do you check?
How you troubleshoot a protection misoperation from evidence.
CT saturation on the faulted feeder from high current and DC offset; check event records, CT class, burden, polarity and ratio settings.

My first suspect is CT saturation on the faulted feeder. That CT carries the whole fault current, often with a large DC offset, and if it saturates the relay sees a false difference. I pull the event record to see the waveforms, then check CT class, burden, polarity and ratio settings. Fixes include a higher class CT, less lead burden, or better saturation detection settings.
Your study shows very high incident energy at a plant's main switchgear. The owner asks what can bring it down. What do you offer?
Your judgement in turning an arc flash result into practical mitigation.
Faster clearing as the main lever, the line-side limit, and that NEC 240.87 requires an energy-reducing method on breakers that can be set to 1200 A or more.

Incident energy grows with clearing time, so I look for faster tripping. Options are a maintenance mode switch, zone-selective interlocking, bus differential, or an arc flash relay that trips on light and current. The main breaker's line side is cleared only by the upstream device, often the utility's, so I check that too. Remote racking and switching keep people farther away.
What is the short-circuit ratio at a point of interconnection, and why does a low value worry you for a large inverter-based plant?
Whether you understand weak-grid risks of solar, wind and battery plants.
Short-circuit MVA at the point divided by plant MW; a weak grid can make inverter controls unstable, which calls for EMT studies and possible grid support.

It is the short-circuit MVA at the point of interconnection divided by the plant's MW rating. Below about 3, the grid is usually called weak. Inverter controls, such as the phase-locked loop that tracks grid voltage, can then oscillate. Phasor studies may miss this, so I ask for an electromagnetic transient study with vendor models, and consider a synchronous condenser.
A developer's interconnection study assigns network upgrades the project cannot afford. What options would you walk them through?
How you weigh technical and commercial trade-offs in grid interconnection.
Find the cost drivers, then real options: resize, move the point of interconnection, energy-only service, storage or limits, with timing set by withdrawal rules.

First I find which constraints drive the cost; often one line or breaker is most of the bill. Then the options: cut the MW size, move to a stronger point of interconnection, request energy-only service, which often needs fewer upgrades, or add storage and output limits. Under cluster studies, withdrawal costs grow at each stage, so we decide early.

pricing.heading: Pricing and economics questions
qs: What is the difference between markup and margin?
Whether you have the basic pricing arithmetic right.
Markup is profit over cost, margin is profit over price, shown with a quick example and why mixing them up costs money.

Markup is profit divided by cost. Margin is profit divided by price. If an item costs $60 and sells for $80, the $20 profit is a 33% markup but only a 25% margin. I always label which one I mean, because a quote built on the wrong one quietly gives away the profit we planned.
An elasticity estimate comes back at -1.5. What does that tell you?
Your grasp of price elasticity and what it means for revenue.
A 1% price rise cuts volume by about 1.5%, so demand is elastic and revenue falls with a price increase, with the note that revenue is not profit.

For small changes, a 1% price increase cuts units sold by about 1.5%. Volume moves more than price, so demand is elastic and raising price would lower revenue. But revenue is not profit. Before I recommend a cut, I check margins, because selling more units at a thin margin can still lose money.
When would you use cost-plus pricing, and when value-based pricing?
Whether you know the main pricing approaches and their limits.
Cost-plus is simple and fits commodity or contract work; value-based ties price to what the customer gains and needs evidence of that value.

Cost-plus adds a set markup to cost. It is quick and easy to defend, so it fits commodity goods or contracts that require it. But it ignores what the customer will pay. Value-based pricing starts from the benefit to the customer, like time or money saved, and prices below that. It earns more but needs real customer research.
We sell at a 40% gross margin and want to cut price 10%. How much more volume do we need to keep the same gross profit?
Whether you can run the break-even math on a price change.
About 33% more units, worked out per unit, plus the point that most people wrongly guess 10%.

Take a $100 item: cost is $60 and gross profit is $40. After a 10% cut the price is $90 and profit per unit drops to $30. To keep the same total profit I need 40 divided by 30, about 1.33 times the volume, so roughly 33% more units. People often guess 10%, which is why so many price cuts lose money.
How do you gather competitor pricing, and where are the limits?
Your competitor research methods and your sense of the legal lines.
Public and customer-facing sources only. Never discuss or exchange prices with competitors, which creates antitrust risk.

I use public price lists and websites, quotes any customer could get, third-party market data, and win-loss notes from our sales team. The hard line: I never talk to a competitor about prices or plans, and I do not use confidential documents a new hire brought from a rival. Sharing price information between competitors can break antitrust law.
What is a price waterfall, and what do you look for in one?
Whether you can trace where list price leaks away before it reaches the bank.
Steps from list price down to pocket price: discounts, rebates, payment terms, freight. Look for leakage that is large, uneven or not tied to volume.

It starts at list price and subtracts each give-away: invoice discounts, volume rebates, early-payment terms, free freight, co-op money. What is left is the pocket price we actually keep. I compare it across customers. Last time I found small accounts getting bigger rebates than large ones, which no one had decided on purpose.
Our main competitor just cut prices 15%. Sales wants us to match by Friday. What do you do?
Your judgement under pressure when a price war could start.
Gathers facts before reacting, checks which customers are at risk, weighs targeted responses against a blanket match.

First I check what was cut: all products or a few, list or net price, and for how long. Then I ask sales which deals are actually at risk. Matching across the board costs margin on customers who were never going to leave. Usually I suggest a targeted answer, like help on specific competitive deals, and review the data again in a few weeks.
You estimated elasticity from two years of sales history and got a positive number: higher prices, more sales. What went wrong?
Whether you spot confounding in observational price data.
Prices moved with demand, such as seasons or promotions, so the estimate is biased; control for those drivers or use test data.

Most likely prices went up when demand was already strong, like peak season, so the model credits price for what demand did. Promotions with ads and displays muddy it too. I would add controls for season, promotion, ads and distribution, and look for clean price changes. If none exist, I would push for a small controlled test instead of trusting history.
Leadership wants a 6% increase across all customers next quarter. How do you model it and roll it out?
How you turn a price decision into a plan with numbers and risks.
Segments by sensitivity and contract terms, models churn scenarios, suggests exceptions, prepares sales and tracks results after launch.

I split customers by size, contract terms and past reaction to increases, then model low, mid and high churn for each group. I check how much notice contracts require. If a few large accounts look risky, I propose a smaller step for them. Sales gets talking points before customers hear. After launch I track churn and extra discounting monthly against the model.
How do you estimate willingness to pay for a product that is not on the market yet?
Whether you know the research methods and their weak spots.
Names methods such as Van Westendorp, Gabor-Granger or conjoint, and knows that what people say they would pay runs higher than what they actually pay.

For a first range I use Van Westendorp: four questions on when the price feels too cheap, a bargain, expensive and too expensive. To pick a point I prefer conjoint, which makes people trade price against features. People overstate what they would pay, so I treat survey results as a ceiling and confirm with a live test after launch.
Should our fixed costs affect the price we set?
Your grasp of which costs matter for a pricing decision.
The profit-maximizing price depends on demand and variable cost. Fixed costs decide whether the product is worth selling at all.

Not the price point itself. Rent and salaries are the same whatever we charge, so the best price is set by how demand responds and by the variable cost per unit. Fixed costs matter one level up: if the best contribution we can earn cannot cover them over time, the question is whether to keep the product, not how to raise its price.
How would you build a good-better-best lineup for one of our products?
How you design tiers that move customers up instead of down.
Tiers built on what each segment values, with clear fences between them and a top tier that makes the middle look sensible.

I start from research on which features different segments value. The must-haves for price-sensitive buyers go in Good, and what heavier users need goes in Better. Fences, such as user limits or support levels, stop big customers from buying down. I watch the mix after launch: if almost everyone takes Good, the gap to Better is too wide.
A 20%-off promotion doubled unit sales for the week. Was it a success?
Whether you measure true incremental profit, not just the sales spike.
Compares gross profit with a baseline and nets out pull-forward, cannibalization and the discount given to people who would have bought anyway.

We do not know yet. I would compare gross profit, not units, with a baseline for that week. Then I check the following weeks for a dip from customers who bought early, and nearby products for lost sales. At a 40% margin, a 20% discount halves the profit per unit, so doubling units only breaks even before those losses. It likely lost money.
Our price increase last year barely changed volume in the first quarter. Can we say demand is inelastic?
Whether you know that customer reaction can lag a price change.
Explains that contracts, renewal cycles, switching costs and slow competitor moves delay the response, and checks later cohorts before concluding.

Not from one quarter. Many customers were on contracts or annual plans and had not faced the new price yet, and switching takes time. I would look at renewals since the increase, win rates on new deals and churn by cohort. Long-run elasticity is usually larger than short-run, so the full effect may still be coming.
Walk me through how you would design a price test for an online subscription.
How you set up a test that gives a trustworthy and fair answer.
Random assignment, sample size fixed in advance, one consistent price per visitor, and a read on retention and revenue, not just sign-ups.

I randomize new visitors into two or three price groups and keep each visitor on the same price on every visit. I fix the sample size and length before starting, so we do not stop when the numbers look good. The main metric is revenue per visitor after at least one renewal, since a higher price can lift sign-up revenue and then lose more at renewal. Legal reviews the setup first.
We plan to launch a cheaper version of our flagship. How do you tell whether it adds profit?
How you account for cannibalization in a launch case.
Counts profit from new buyers minus the margin lost on customers who trade down, and estimates each group with research or a test.

Every buyer of the new version is either new to us or a flagship customer trading down. Say it earns $30 a unit and the flagship $80. A new buyer adds $30; a switcher costs us $50. So if more than three in eight buyers are switchers, we lose money. I would estimate that share with a conjoint study or a limited test, and use fences to keep it low.
Average discounts crept from 12% to 19% over two years. How do you bring them back without losing deals?
How you fix discount leakage in a sales team.
Uses deal data to find where discounts do not win deals, then sets clear bands, approval levels and a give-get rule, with sales leadership on board.

First I look at win rates against discount size by segment and rep. Often deals at 25% close no more often than at 15%. With sales leadership, I set discount bands by deal size, require approval above them, and ask for something in return, such as a longer term. Paying reps partly on margin, not only revenue, keeps discounts from creeping back.
We want to give our largest distributor a lower price than its smaller rivals get. What do you check first?
Your knowledge of price discrimination law in business-to-business sales.
Knows the Robinson-Patman Act covers goods sold to competing buyers, and its main defenses: real cost savings and meeting a competitor's price in good faith.

Whether the Robinson-Patman Act applies. It covers sales of goods of like grade and quality to buyers who compete with each other, where the price gap can harm competition. The main defenses are real cost savings, such as shipping full truckloads, or meeting a competitor's lower price in good faith. I would document the cost case and take it to legal before quoting.
A sales rep heard from a competitor's rep at a trade show that they will raise prices in March. What do you do?
Whether you know the antitrust line on competitor information.
Does not use the tip or reply to it, reports it to legal, and knows that agreeing on prices with a competitor is illegal under the Sherman Act.

I would not put it in any model, and I would ask the rep not to respond. Then I report it to our legal team, who decide how to document it. Agreeing on prices with a competitor is illegal under the Sherman Act, and even swapping future price plans can look like an agreement. Public price announcements and our own customer data are fine to use.

privacy.heading: Privacy questions
qs: What is the difference between a controller and a processor, and what are the CCPA equivalents?
Whether you know the basic roles that decide who carries which duties.
The controller decides why and how data is processed; the processor acts on its instructions. The CCPA terms are business and service provider or contractor.

The controller decides the purpose and the means, so it owns the duties to people, like notices and requests. The processor handles data only on the controller's documented instructions, under a contract. Under the CCPA the matching terms are business and service provider, or contractor. A processor that starts using data for its own purposes becomes a controller for that use.
Why not just rely on consent for everything under GDPR?
Your grasp of the six lawful bases and when each one fits.
Consent must be freely given and can be withdrawn at any time. Contract, legal obligation or legitimate interests often fit better.

GDPR gives six bases: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task and legitimate interests. Consent has to be free, specific and as easy to withdraw as to give. If we would process the data anyway, say for payroll, asking for consent misleads people. I pick the basis that truly fits before processing starts and record why.
Walk me through how you would build a data map for a company that has none.
How you find out what personal data exists and where it goes.
Start from systems and business processes, interview owners, record data, purpose, basis, recipients, transfers and retention, and keep it current.

I start with a list of systems from IT and procurement, then interview each team owner about their processes. For each one I record what data, whose, why, the lawful basis, who receives it, where it is stored, any transfers abroad and how long we keep it. That becomes our record of processing. I tie updates to procurement and project intake so it does not go stale.
When does GDPR require a data protection impact assessment, and what goes into one?
Whether you know the triggers and the content of a DPIA.
Required when processing is likely to be high risk, like large-scale sensitive data or systematic monitoring. It covers purpose, necessity, risks and measures.

It is required before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to people. Examples are profiling with significant effects, large-scale health data and wide monitoring of public areas. It describes the processing, tests necessity and proportionality, weighs risks to people and sets measures to reduce them. If high risk remains, we consult the regulator first.
A customer emails support asking for "all the data you have on me." Walk me through what happens.
How you run a data subject access request from intake to reply.
Log it, verify identity in proportion to the risk, search all systems, remove other people's data, and reply within the legal deadline.

Support logs it the same day and sends it to us. I verify identity in proportion to the risk, often by matching account details. Then I search every system on the data map, not just the CRM, and review the results to remove other people's data. Under GDPR the reply is due within one month, extendable in complex cases; under the CCPA, 45 days.
Our website receives a Global Privacy Control signal from a California visitor. What must we do?
Whether you know the CCPA opt-out rights for selling and sharing data.
Treat it as a valid request to opt out of sale and sharing for that browser, and for the account if known, with no extra steps from the visitor.

Under the CCPA regulations, an opt-out preference signal like GPC counts as a request to opt out of the sale and sharing of personal information. Sharing here means cross-context behavioral advertising. So that browser must not fire ad pixels that sell or share data, and if the visitor is logged in, I apply it to the account too. We cannot make them fill out a form to make it count.
Marketing picked a new email vendor that stores data in the US. What do you check before EU customer data goes there?
How you review a processor and an international data transfer.
A processor contract with the required terms, a security review, and a valid transfer tool such as Data Privacy Framework certification or standard contractual clauses.

First, a data processing agreement with the Article 28 terms: act only on our instructions, security, sub-processor approval, help with requests and deletion at the end. I review their security controls. For the transfer, I check whether they are certified under the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework; if not, we sign standard contractual clauses and do a transfer impact assessment.
The product team wants to use years of customer support chats to train an AI model. How do you approach it?
Your judgement on reusing personal data for a new purpose.
Checks whether the new purpose is compatible, the lawful basis, what notices said, sensitive content and minimization, often through a DPIA.

Those chats were collected to solve tickets, so training a model is a new purpose. I would check whether it is compatible with the original one, what basis applies, and what our privacy notice told people. Chats often hold health or payment details, so I would push for filtering and de-identification first. Likely a DPIA, and a clear way for people to object.
A customer asks us to delete their data, but legal has a litigation hold on their account. What do you do?
How you handle a conflict between a privacy right and another legal duty.
Erasure has exceptions, including legal claims. Keep only what the hold covers, delete the rest, and tell the person what is kept and why.

The right to erasure is not absolute. GDPR allows keeping data needed for legal claims, and the CCPA has similar exceptions. I confirm with legal exactly what the hold covers, delete or restrict everything else, and lock the held data from other use. Then I tell the customer what we deleted, what we kept, the reason, and that we will delete it when the hold ends.
An employee emailed a spreadsheet of 2,000 customers' names and account numbers to the wrong outside address. Walk me through your first 72 hours.
How you contain and assess a breach and decide who must be notified.
Contain first, assess risk and who is affected, notify the regulator within 72 hours where GDPR requires it, check each US state law, and document everything.

First, contain: try to recall the email, ask the recipient to delete it and confirm in writing. Then assess what was exposed and where the people live. Under GDPR, the regulator must hear within 72 hours of us becoming aware unless risk is unlikely. US state laws differ in triggers and timing, so I check each state with counsel. Every step goes into the breach log.
What is the difference between pseudonymized and anonymized data under GDPR, and why does it matter?
Whether you know when data falls outside the scope of GDPR.
Pseudonymized data is still personal data. Only data that can no longer reasonably identify anyone falls outside GDPR.

Pseudonymized data has the names swapped for codes, but someone holding the key could link it back, so GDPR still applies in full. Anonymized data cannot reasonably be tied to a person by anyone, using means likely to be used, so it falls outside the law. Many teams call hashed emails anonymous. They are not, because the same email always gives the same hash.
Walk me through a legitimate interests assessment.
Your grasp of the test behind one of the most used lawful bases.
The three parts, written down: a real and lawful purpose, necessity, and a balance against the person's interests and expectations.

I run three tests and write them down. Purpose: what interest do we have, and is it lawful and specific? Necessity: do we need this data for it, or is there a less intrusive way? Balance: would the person expect this use, how sensitive is the data, and what safeguards, like an easy opt-out, tip it our way? If the balance fails, we need another basis or we stop.
What must a GDPR contract with a processor contain?
Whether you know Article 28 well enough to review a vendor's contract.
The core terms: documented instructions, confidentiality, security, sub-processor approval, help with rights and breaches, deletion or return, audits.

Article 28 sets the list. The vendor acts only on our documented instructions, binds its staff to confidentiality, keeps appropriate security, and uses sub-processors only with our authorization and the same terms. It helps us with rights requests, breaches and impact assessments, deletes or returns data at the end, and gives us the information and audits to prove all of it.
Under the CCPA, what is the difference between selling and sharing personal information, and how does a vendor avoid being either?
Whether you understand the California rules behind the ad tech opt-out.
Sharing means disclosure for cross-context behavioral advertising, paid or not. A vendor under a proper service provider contract is neither.

Selling is disclosing personal information to a third party for money or other valuable consideration. Sharing, added by the CPRA, is disclosing it for cross-context behavioral advertising, paid or not. Both give the consumer an opt-out. A vendor that only works for our business purpose, under a contract with the terms the law requires, is a service provider, and that is neither.
How does the treatment of sensitive data differ between California and states like Virginia or Colorado?
Whether you can work across the patchwork of US state privacy laws.
California gives a right to limit the use of sensitive data. Virginia and Colorado require opt-in consent before processing it.

Virginia and Colorado are opt-in: we need the person's consent before we process sensitive data such as health or biometric data. California is mostly opt-out: consumers can tell us to limit sensitive data to the uses needed to provide the service. For a national product I usually design to the opt-in standard, so one flow works everywhere.
How would you build a data retention schedule from scratch?
How you turn storage limitation into rules that systems actually follow.
Start from the data map, set periods by legal minimum and business need, name an owner, and make deletion automatic and checked.

I start from the data map, one row per data set. For each I note any law that sets a minimum period, like tax records, and the real business need. The period covers the legal minimum and no more than we need. Each row gets an owner and a trigger, like account closure. Then engineering makes deletion run automatically, and we check that it did.
How do you verify the identity of someone making a data request without collecting more data than you need?
Whether you can stop imposters without blocking genuine requests.
Match against data already held, scale the checks to the risk of the request, and ask for more only when there is real doubt.

I match what the person gives us against data we already hold, and I scale it to the risk. A logged-in user deleting an account needs little more. Someone asking for copies of sensitive data needs stronger matching; California's rules set a higher bar for specific pieces of information. Under GDPR we ask for more only if we have reasonable doubts, and we don't ask for ID documents by default.
You learn that marketing has been using purchase history for a purpose the privacy notice never mentioned. What do you do?
How you handle a live compliance gap without simply shutting the business down.
Find the facts, test purpose compatibility and lawful basis, pause if needed, fix the notice, and record what was decided and why.

First I find out what is being done, since when, and on whose data. Then I check whether the new use is compatible with the original purpose: the link between them, what customers would expect, and the safeguards. If it is not, it needs its own lawful basis, often consent, and we pause it. Either way I update the notice before going further and write up the decision.
HR in our German office wants software that tracks employees' screen activity. How do you respond?
Your judgement on employee monitoring, where consent rarely works.
Consent is weak because of the power imbalance. Proportionality, a DPIA, clear notice and the works council's role decide it.

I ask what problem they want solved, because screen tracking is very intrusive. Employee consent is rarely valid, since staff cannot freely say no to their employer. We would need another basis, a DPIA and clear notice. If the office has a works council, it has a say over monitoring tools, so it must be involved. Usually I steer HR to something narrower, like access logs on sensitive systems.
You join a company with no data map, few vendor contracts and a product launch in three weeks. What do you fix first, and what do you leave?
How you set priorities for a privacy program by real risk.
The launch and the riskiest data first, contracts with key vendors next, a dated plan for the rest, and leadership told in writing what stays open.

I review the launch first, since it is the newest and most visible risk: what data, which vendors, what notice. Then I list vendors that hold sensitive or large volumes of data and get processor terms signed with those. The full data map and policies go on a 90-day plan. I tell leadership in writing what risk remains open and who accepted it, so nothing is hidden.

procurement.heading: Procurement questions
qs: What is the difference between an RFI, an RFQ and an RFP?
Whether you know which sourcing tool fits which purchase.
RFI to learn the market, RFQ when the spec is fixed and price decides, RFP when the solution itself is part of the choice.

An RFI, request for information, is for learning who is out there and what they can do. An RFQ, request for quotation, is for a clear spec, like 200 laptops of a set model, where price and delivery decide. An RFP, request for proposal, is for when suppliers propose how to meet the need, like a new IT service, and I score more than price.
What is a three-way match, and why does it matter?
Your grasp of the control that stops paying for goods that were not ordered or received.
PO, receiving record and invoice must agree on item, quantity and price before payment; mismatches are held and resolved.

Before an invoice is paid, it is matched against the purchase order and the receiving report. Item, quantity and price must agree within the set tolerance. If we ordered 500 units at $4, received 480, and were billed for 500 at $4.20, the invoice is held until the supplier corrects it or someone with authority approves the difference.
Two suppliers quote the same machine part, and one is 10% cheaper. How do you decide?
Whether you look at total cost of ownership, not just unit price.
Compares quality, lead time, freight, minimum order, payment terms and the cost of failures, and puts numbers on each.

I build a total cost view. The cheaper one may ship from overseas with a 12-week lead time, a large minimum order and freight on top, so we hold more stock and tie up cash. I also check defect rates and terms. If the lower price disappears once I add freight, holding cost and a 2% scrap rate, I choose the other supplier and show the math.
What is the difference between sole source and single source?
Your precision on a term that changes the risk and the paperwork.
Sole source: only one supplier exists. Single source: others exist but you chose one. The second is a choice you can revisit; the first needs a justification.

Sole source means only one supplier can provide it, for example because it holds the patent. Single source means others could, but we buy from one on purpose, maybe for price or quality. Single source is a choice I can revisit. Sole source needs a written justification and a closer watch on that supplier's risk.
One quote says EXW and another says DDP. What changes for us?
Whether you know how Incoterms shift cost and risk between buyer and seller.
EXW puts nearly all transport, clearance, duties and risk on the buyer; DDP puts them on the seller up to the named destination.

Under EXW, Ex Works, the seller makes the goods available at its premises, and we handle loading, freight, export and import clearance, duties and the risk in transit. Under DDP, Delivered Duty Paid, the seller carries cost and risk to our named place, import duties included. So I compare them only after adding freight, insurance and duties to the EXW price.
Walk me through how you prepare for a negotiation with a key supplier.
How you build leverage before you sit down at the table.
Knows the spend, the market and the supplier's position, sets a target and a walk-away point, and plans trade-offs in advance.

I pull our history with them: volume, price trend, on-time rate, quality issues. I check market prices and get alternative quotes, which tells me my walk-away option if we cannot agree. Then I set a target and a limit, and list what I can give, like a longer contract or a better forecast, for what I want, like price or payment terms.
A supplier announces a 12% price increase, citing raw material costs. What do you do?
How you push back on a price increase with facts rather than a flat refusal.
Asks for evidence, checks the material's share of the price against a market index, counters with a fair figure and lines up alternatives.

I ask for the cost breakdown. If steel is 40% of the part price and steel rose 10%, that supports about 4%, not 12%. I check a published index for that material, counter on that basis, and propose index-linked pricing so the price can come down too. Meanwhile I ask two other suppliers to quote in case we cannot agree.
An engineer has already promised a supplier the order and wants a PO today. How do you handle it?
Your judgement when a colleague skips the buying process.
Respects the urgency but keeps the policy: checks approval limits, gets quotes or a documented justification, and explains why without blocking.

I ask why this supplier and why today. If the amount is under our limit for competitive quotes, I can move fast. If not, I get two quick quotes or a written justification signed by the right approver. I explain that this protects the engineer too. Then I ask to be brought in before anyone talks price with a supplier next time.
You find a software contract auto-renewed for three years at a higher rate because no one gave notice. What do you do?
How you handle a contract mistake and stop it from happening again.
Reads the actual terms, asks the vendor for a fix, reports the miss honestly, and sets up notice-date alerts for every contract.

First I read the contract: the notice window, the renewal term and any cap on price increases. Then I call the vendor; many will agree to a shorter term or the old rate to keep a customer, especially if we can add users. I tell my manager plainly what happened. Then I put every contract's notice date in a tracker with alerts 90 and 30 days ahead.
Your only supplier for a critical component is paying its own vendors late, and lead times are slipping. What do you do?
How you manage supply risk before it turns into a shortage.
Acts early: sizes the exposure, talks to the supplier, builds buffer stock, starts qualifying a second source and informs management and finance.

I size our exposure: weeks of stock on hand and which products stop without the part. I talk openly with the supplier's leadership. I add buffer stock where I can, start qualifying a second source with engineering now, since approval can take months, and check whether we own the tooling so we could move it. My manager and finance hear about it this week.
How do you segment your spend, and how does that change how you buy?
Whether you treat categories differently instead of running one playbook for everything.
A clear model, such as the Kraljic matrix of profit impact against supply risk, with a different tactic for each group.

I sort purchases by profit impact and supply risk. Leverage items, like packaging, I bid out hard. Strategic items, high on both, get long-term partnerships and joint planning. Bottleneck items, low spend but hard to get, I protect with safety stock or a second source. Routine items go to catalogs or purchasing cards to cut the cost of the process itself.
A supplier offers terms of 2/10 net 30. Should we take the discount?
Whether you can price payment terms as money, not just as a habit.
The math: 2% for paying 20 days early is roughly 37% a year, so it is usually worth it if AP can pay on time.

It means 2% off if we pay within 10 days, otherwise full price at day 30. Paying 20 days early to save 2% works out to about 37% a year, since 2/98 times 365/20 is roughly 0.37. That beats almost any return on our cash, so I would take it unless we must borrow at a higher rate. I would also check that AP can approve invoices inside 10 days.
Finance says your reported savings never show up in the budget. How do you measure savings?
Your credibility with finance and how you define a saving.
Separating cost reduction from cost avoidance, agreeing the baseline with finance in advance, and counting savings only when volume flows.

Cost reduction is a lower price than we paid before for the same thing, and it shows in the budget. Cost avoidance is an increase we stopped, like a 9% ask held to 3%; it is real, but spend does not drop. I report the two separately, agree the baseline method with finance up front, and count savings only as the volume is actually bought.
During an open RFP, a bidding supplier offers you tickets to a big game. What do you do?
Your ethics and how you protect a fair award.
Declining during the sourcing event, following the code of conduct, disclosing it, and escalating if a team member already accepted.

I decline politely, whatever the value, because during an open bid it looks like influence even if it is not. I tell the supplier our policy, record the offer as our code of conduct requires and let my manager know. If someone on the evaluation team already accepted, I raise it with compliance so we can decide whether the award still holds up.
A spend analysis shows 40% of indirect spend is going around your contracts. How do you fix it?
How you handle off-contract spending without just issuing a stricter rule.
Finding the cause first, making the contracted path the easy one, then policy and tracking by department.

First I find out why. Often the contract is hard to use, items are missing from the catalog, or people do not know it exists. I fix the easy path first: catalogs inside our buying system with the preferred suppliers. Then policy, such as no invoice paid without a PO, with an emergency exception. I track compliance by department monthly and share it with budget owners.
How would you build a should-cost model for a machined part?
Whether you can judge a price from what the part really costs to make.
Breaking cost into material, machine time, labor, overhead, scrap, freight and margin, then using gaps to start a fact-based talk.

I split the part into material, machine time, labor, overhead, scrap, freight and margin. Material is weight times a published price for the alloy; machine time is cycle time times a regional hourly rate. If my model says $14 and the quote is $19, I do not accuse. I ask the supplier to walk me through where our numbers differ. Often it is cycle time or scrap, and that is where we can work together.
Walk me through how you would write an index-based price adjustment clause.
Your skill at turning commodity risk into fair, clear contract terms.
Indexing only the material share, a named public index, base period, review schedule, a threshold band, and adjustments both up and down.

I tie only the material share of the price to the index. If steel is 40% of a $50 part, $20 moves with a named public index, such as a government producer price index, and $30 stays fixed. I set the base month, review quarterly, add a band so small moves change nothing, and make it work both ways so we get decreases too.
A software vendor wants to cap its total liability at the fees paid in the last 12 months. How do you respond?
Whether you know which risks a liability cap should not cover.
Accepting a cap for ordinary breaches but pushing for carve-outs or a higher cap for data, confidentiality, IP indemnity and gross negligence.

A cap at 12 months of fees can be fine for ordinary breaches. I push for carve-outs: breach of confidentiality, the vendor's indemnity for IP infringement, and gross negligence or willful misconduct. If they hold customer data, I often ask for a separate, higher cap for data breaches and check that their cyber insurance supports it. Legal signs off on the final wording.
Our PO has our terms, and the supplier's order acknowledgment has different ones. Which terms govern?
Your grasp of the battle of the forms and how to avoid relying on it.
Knowing the UCC rule does not let either form win automatically, and fixing it with a master agreement and legal input.

Neither form wins automatically. For goods, the UCC battle-of-the-forms rule says the acknowledgment can still form a contract, and added terms that materially change it, like a new liability cap, usually do not become part of it. But the result depends on the facts and the state, so I would not rely on it. I object in writing, involve legal, and put a master agreement in place that governs.
We want a second source for a critical part without hurting supply. How do you run the switch?
How you qualify a new supplier while keeping the incumbent cooperative.
A qualification plan with engineering, first article and pilot lots, a gradual volume shift, and honest early talk with the incumbent.

I start with a qualification plan engineering agrees to: drawings, specs and critical features. The new supplier makes a first article, we inspect every dimension, then run a pilot lot through our line. Only after it passes do I shift volume, maybe 20% first, while the incumbent keeps supplying. I tell the incumbent early, because surprising them is how you lose priority mid-switch.

procurement-operations.heading: Procurement operations specialist questions
qs: What is the difference between a purchase requisition and a purchase order?
Whether you know the basic documents of the buying process.
A requisition is an internal request for approval. A PO is the official order sent to the supplier, which becomes a contract once accepted.

A requisition is an internal request: someone in the company says what they need, how many and roughly what it costs, and it goes for approval. Once it is approved, I turn it into a purchase order. That is the official document sent to the supplier with price, quantity, terms and delivery date. When the supplier accepts it, it is a contract.
Walk me through a three-way match.
Whether you understand the control that protects every payment.
The PO, the receiving record and the invoice are compared on item, quantity and price before payment, and any exceptions are held.

Before an invoice is paid, I compare three documents: the purchase order, the receiving record that shows what actually arrived, and the supplier's invoice. Item, quantity and price must agree within our tolerance. If we ordered 100, received 90 and were billed for 100, the invoice is held until the shortage is resolved or credited.
When would you set up a blanket purchase order instead of single POs?
Your judgement in choosing the right order type.
For repeated buys from one supplier, with a set period, agreed prices and a dollar cap, and with spend tracked against it.

I use one when we buy the same things from one supplier again and again, like janitorial supplies or monthly gas cylinders. One blanket PO with a set period, agreed prices and a total dollar limit replaces dozens of small POs. Each release draws down the balance. I watch that balance so we renew or re-approve before it runs out, not after.
An invoice comes in 8% higher than the PO price. What do you do?
How you handle a price variance without paying blindly or stalling the supplier.
You check the tolerance and the cause, then get either a revised and re-approved PO or a corrected invoice, and you record why.

First I check our tolerance rule. 8% is usually outside it, so the invoice is held. Then I look for the cause: a freight charge, a price increase we never agreed to, or a wrong unit. If the increase is valid, the buyer revises the PO and it is re-approved. If not, I ask the supplier for a corrected invoice. Either way, I note the reason in the system.
A manager bought equipment without a PO and now sends you the invoice to pay. How do you handle it?
Whether you can enforce policy and still keep the supplier paid.
You follow the after-the-fact process, never backdate a PO, explain the rule kindly and escalate repeat cases.

The supplier delivered in good faith, so I do not leave them unpaid. I follow our after-the-fact process: the manager submits a requisition marked as a confirming order, it goes through normal approval, and I never backdate the PO. Then I explain why the rule exists and show how to order next time. If the same person keeps doing it, I report the pattern to my manager.
Someone sends three $4,000 requests to the same supplier on the same day, and anything over $10,000 needs director approval. What do you do?
Whether you spot split purchases made to get around approval limits.
You recognize the split, hold the requests, ask the requester, and route the total through the correct approval level.

Three requests to one supplier on one day that add up to $12,000 looks like a split order. I hold them and ask the requester whether it is really one purchase. Often it is impatience, not bad intent. If it is one need, I combine the three into one requisition and send it to the director. If it keeps happening, I flag it to my manager.
A supplier emails asking you to update their bank account before the next payment. What do you do?
Whether you know how payment-change fraud works and how to stop it.
You never act on the email alone. You verify by calling a known contact at a number already on file, and a second person checks the change.

I treat it as possible fraud until it is proven real, because fake bank change requests are a common scam. I do not reply to the email or call any number in it. I call our contact at the number we already have on file and confirm the request. The change needs their signed form, and a second person reviews it in the vendor file before the next payment goes out.
What do you collect and check before you set up a new supplier in the system?
Your grasp of vendor master data and the controls around it.
Legal name and tax ID from a W-9, address, remit-to and bank details, insurance where needed, and a search for duplicate records.

I get a signed W-9 so the legal name and tax ID are right for 1099 reporting. I also collect the address, the remit-to address and the bank details on our form. For service work on our site, I ask for a certificate of insurance. Before any of that, I search the vendor file for duplicates, since two records for one supplier is how double payments happen.
A supplier confirms only 60 of the 100 units on a PO, and the rest is backordered for six weeks. How do you handle it in the system?
How you manage a partial order so records, receiving and the requester stay aligned.
You update the PO lines and dates, tell the requester, and decide whether to wait or cut the balance and source it elsewhere.

I update the PO with the confirmed date for each part, so receiving expects 60 now and 40 later. I tell the requester right away and ask if six weeks works. If it does not, I reduce the PO to 60 with a change order, close the balance, and buy the 40 from another approved supplier. That way we never wait on, or pay for, units that will not come.
Your approver is out and your manager tells you to just approve your own PO in the system. What do you do?
Whether you protect segregation of duties under pressure.
You decline politely, explain the control, and offer a proper fast path: the delegated approver or the next level up.

I would not approve my own request, even if the system let me. The person who creates a PO should not be the one who approves it. That separation is what catches errors and stops fraud. I would check who is set as the delegate for the absent approver, or route it one level up, and tell my manager how quickly I can get it approved that way.
A supplier offers terms of 2/10 net 30. What does that mean, and is it usually worth taking?
Whether you understand payment terms and what an early payment discount is worth.
Reads the terms correctly and knows that skipping the discount is expensive, so it is usually worth taking when cash allows.

It means we can take 2% off if we pay within 10 days; otherwise the full amount is due in 30. Giving up 2% to keep the cash 20 more days works out to roughly 37% a year, so it is usually worth taking. My part is getting those invoices matched and approved fast enough to hit day 10.
Which purchases would you set to a two-way match instead of a three-way match, and why?
Whether you can fit the control to the risk of the purchase.
Two-way (PO and invoice) for low-risk items with nothing to count, like subscriptions; three-way where goods arrive and quantities matter.

A two-way match checks the invoice against the PO only. I use it for low-risk, recurring items with no delivery to count, like a software subscription or a fixed monthly service fee. Anything physical, or priced by quantity, gets a three-way match so we pay only for what was received. I set the rule by category, not case by case.
How do you handle receiving on a services PO, where nothing shows up at the dock?
How you confirm that services were delivered before they are paid.
The person who saw the work confirms it in the system, against hours or milestones, before the invoice is released.

I set the PO up by amount or by milestone instead of units. The person who saw the work, usually the requester, enters the receipt for what was done, like 40 hours or phase one complete. The invoice is matched to that confirmation. If a contractor bills more hours than were confirmed, the invoice holds until the owner checks the timesheet.
At month end, finance asks for the list of goods received but not invoiced. What is it, and how do you help?
Whether you understand how purchasing data feeds the books at close.
Knows these are accrued as a liability so costs land in the right month, and cleans wrong or stale receipts so the accrual is accurate.

Those are items received in the system with no supplier invoice yet. Finance accrues them as a liability so the expense lands in the right month. I run the report and chase the oldest lines first: some are wrong receipts, some are invoices stuck in someone's inbox. Cleaning those keeps the accrual from being overstated.
A new contractor will not send a W-9 but wants the PO issued today. What do you do?
Whether you know the tax side of onboarding and hold the line on it.
No setup without a taxpayer ID, and knows that paying a reportable payee without one means backup withholding.

I explain that we need the W-9 for the taxpayer ID we report payments under. If we paid a contractor without a valid one, we would have to withhold part of each payment as backup withholding and send it to the IRS. Most suppliers send the form quickly once they hear that. The PO waits until the vendor record is complete.
One invoice charges sales tax on a purchase we are exempt from. Another has no tax on an item that is taxable. How do you handle each?
Your grasp of sales and use tax as it shows up on invoices.
Sends the exemption certificate and asks for a corrected invoice; flags untaxed taxable items so the company accrues use tax.

For the first, I check the supplier has our exemption certificate. If not, I send it and ask for a corrected invoice; I do not just short-pay the tax line. For the second, when a seller does not charge tax on a taxable item, the buyer generally owes use tax to the state. I route it to whoever accrues use tax so it gets reported.
Your spend report shows 30% of spend coded as miscellaneous. How do you fix it?
How you make spend data reliable enough to act on.
Cleans the history starting with the biggest suppliers, and fixes the cause so new spend comes in coded correctly.

I sort the miscellaneous spend by supplier. A few dozen suppliers usually make up most of it, so I map those to real categories and recode the history. Then I fix the cause: category becomes a required field, vague options come off the list, and the category defaults from the supplier record. I track the share monthly until it is small.
How would you set the price and quantity tolerances for invoice matching?
Your judgement in balancing control against invoices stuck on hold.
Uses hold data, pairs a percentage with a dollar cap, keeps quantity tighter, and never lets a large overcharge pass automatically.

I start with the data: how many invoices go on hold, and for how much. Then I pair a small percentage with a dollar cap, so rounding differences pass but a big invoice cannot go through thousands over. Quantity I keep tighter, because paying for units we never got is a pure loss. I review holds each quarter and adjust.
A requester keeps choosing one supplier, and you learn his brother-in-law owns it. What do you do?
How you handle a possible conflict of interest without accusing anyone.
Gathers facts, reports through the proper channel under the conflict-of-interest policy, and does not act or accuse alone.

I do not confront him or block orders on my own. I note the facts: how much spend went to that supplier, whether quotes were taken, how its prices compare. Then I raise it with my manager or compliance under our conflict-of-interest policy. Often the fix is a written disclosure and a different person approving that supplier's orders.
You find that requesters enter receipts before goods arrive so invoices get paid faster. How do you deal with it?
Whether you see why a false receipt breaks the match and how you would change the habit.
Knows a receipt is the proof of delivery; sizes the problem, finds why people do it, and changes the process, not just sends a reminder.

A receipt is our proof we got the goods, so an early one makes the three-way match meaningless. I compare receipt dates to delivery dates to size the problem, then ask why. Often suppliers chase late payments and requesters want peace. I fix the payment delay, explain that receipts are a control, and move receiving to the dock where we can.

producer.heading: Producer (games and media) questions
qs: What is the producer's job on a team, and what is it not?
Whether you understand where the producer role starts and stops.
Owns schedule, budget, risks and communication, and clears blockers. Does not make the creative calls that the director or leads own.

I own the plan: the schedule, the budget, the risk list and who needs to know what. I clear blockers so people can do their work. I don't decide how the level plays or how the episode is cut; the director and leads own that. My job is to make sure they can make those calls in time and know what each one costs.
What is a vertical slice, and why would you schedule one early?
Your grasp of a standard game production milestone.
A small part of the game at near-final quality across all disciplines, used to prove the pipeline and estimate the rest.

It is a short piece of the game, say one level or ten minutes of play, built to close to final quality in art, audio, design and code. I want it early because it shows whether the pipeline works and how long one finished minute really takes. That number makes the rest of the schedule far more honest, and it gives the publisher something real to judge.
How do you track whether a project is on budget week to week?
How you watch spending before it becomes a problem.
Compares actual spend and burn rate to plan, ties cost to progress, and flags the gap early with a forecast.

I keep a sheet with planned spend per month by department and update actuals weekly from timesheets and invoices. The key number is burn rate, how fast we spend, against progress: if we have spent 40% of the budget but finished 30% of the deliverables, that gap is the warning. I flag it to the director with a forecast to the end, not just the overage so far.
Marketing wants a popular song in our trailer. What has to happen before we can use it?
Whether you know the basics of music clearance for media.
Two rights: a sync license for the composition, usually from the publisher, and a master use license for the recording, usually from the label.

A recorded song has two sets of rights. The composition is usually controlled by a music publisher, so we need a sync license from them. The recording is usually owned by the label, so we need a master use license too. Each must cover our media, territories and term. If the master costs too much, we can license only the composition and have a cover recorded.
An artist tells you a task you estimated at five days will take ten. What do you do?
How you handle a bad estimate without blaming anyone or ignoring it.
Asks why, checks the impact on dependent work, picks between moving, simplifying or adding help, and updates the plan.

First I ask what changed: unclear specs, a tool problem or a harder task than we thought. Then I check what depends on it. If nothing downstream waits on it, I move it and update the schedule. If it blocks animation, I talk to the lead about a simpler version or moving another artist onto it. I also note the miss so similar tasks get better estimates next time.
Two leads both need the same engineer this sprint. How do you decide?
Your judgement when people compete for the same resource.
Decides by milestone priority and the critical path, gets the leads to agree, and escalates only when they can't.

I look at which task is on the critical path for the next milestone, meaning the chain of work where any delay moves the date. That one usually wins. I bring both leads together with that picture rather than deciding in private. If the priorities really tie, I take it to the director with a recommendation. The lead who waits gets a firm date for when the engineer is free.
An outsourced art vendor sends a batch that is late and below the quality bar. How do you handle it?
How you manage outside partners and protect quality.
Specific written feedback against the agreed spec, a fix plan with dates, and a backup plan if the vendor can't recover.

I review the batch with our art lead and write down exactly what misses the spec, with examples of what passes. Then I call the vendor, go through it, and agree on a fix date per asset. I check the contract for review rounds so we know what is included. Meanwhile I plan for the worst case: which assets our own team could take if the second batch also fails.
Tell me about a time a date slipped. How did you tell the people above you?
How you deliver bad news early and own it.
Told them as soon as the risk was clear, with the cause, the impact and options to choose from, not just an apology.

On a ten-episode podcast series, our host fell ill and we lost two recording weeks. The same day I knew, I emailed the executive producer with what happened, which episodes moved, and two options: push the launch two weeks, or launch on time and release the last two episodes late. They chose to launch on time. Since then I report risks when they appear, not when they land.
Midway through production, the client asks for a new feature but won't change the budget or date. What do you do?
How you handle scope creep and keep agreements intact.
Estimates the cost, shows the tradeoff in writing, and lets the client choose what gives. Never absorbs it silently.

I get the request in writing and estimate the work and its risk with the leads. Then I go back with clear options: add it and drop something of similar size, add it in a later update, or add it with more time or money. I don't absorb it quietly, because the team pays for it in crunch and the client gets a weaker product. Whatever they choose goes into a signed change order.
What is the critical path in a production schedule, and why do you watch it so closely?
Whether you understand how task dependencies set the real ship date.
The longest chain of dependent tasks, with no slack, and the awareness that a different chain can become critical when it slips.

It is the longest chain of dependent tasks from start to finish, and it sets the earliest possible end date. Tasks on it have no float, meaning no slack, so a day lost there moves the ship date. I map the dependencies, find that chain and watch it most closely. I recheck it often, because when another chain slips it can become the new critical path.
On a video or show budget, what is above the line and what is below the line?
Your grasp of how media budgets are structured and why the split matters.
Creative talent and rights versus crew, gear, locations and post, and why the two behave differently as the schedule moves.

Above the line covers the creative people and rights locked before shooting: writers, director, producers, lead talent and story rights. Below the line is what makes it happen: crew, gear, locations, catering, editing and the sound mix. I track them apart because above-the-line costs are mostly fixed by deals, while below-the-line costs move with shoot days and scope.
How do you build and run a risk register for a project?
Whether you manage risk as a regular practice, not a one-time list.
Each risk has likelihood, impact, an owner, a mitigation and a trigger, and the register is reviewed often with the top risks escalated.

Each risk gets a line: what could happen, how likely it is, how bad it would be, an owner, a mitigation and a trigger that tells us it is becoming a real issue. For example, if we have one network engineer, cross-training is the mitigation. I review it weekly with the leads, close what has passed, and bring the top few to stakeholders rather than all forty.
A publisher pays us on milestones. How do you write the acceptance criteria for one?
How you protect cash flow with clear, testable deliverables.
Criteria anyone can test, plus agreed delivery format, review window and what happens on rejection.

Each deliverable has to be testable, not a feeling. Instead of “combat is fun,” I write “three enemy types playable in level two, at the target frame rate on minimum spec, with no known crash bugs.” I also agree how the build is delivered, how many days the publisher has to review it, and what happens if they reject it, so payment does not stall on a vague word.
How do you plan for console platform certification in a game schedule?
Whether you know certification can block a release and plan for it early.
Knows each platform tests against its own requirements, failures mean resubmission, and builds in pre-checks, booked slots and resubmission time.

Each platform holder tests the build against its own technical requirements, and a failure means fixing and resubmitting, which can cost weeks. I have the team read the current requirements in pre-production, run our own pre-check pass, book submission slots early, and leave room for at least one resubmission before the release date.
Before you sign a new outsourcing vendor, what do you make sure is in the contract?
Your sense of the terms that protect scope, quality, money and ownership.
Deliverables, revision rounds, payment tied to accepted work, confidentiality, and a written assignment of rights, with legal reviewing the wording.

Clear deliverables and specs, a review process with a set number of revision rounds, payments tied to accepted work, confidentiality, and ownership. I want a written assignment of all rights to us, not just a “work for hire” label, because that label alone does not always hold for outside contractors. Legal reviews the wording; I make sure the scope is right.
The team's velocity has dropped three sprints in a row. How do you figure out why?
How you diagnose a slowdown before reacting to it.
Checks the data first, then where work stalls, then talks to people, and fixes the biggest cause before judging again.

First I check the numbers are honest: did estimate sizes change, or were people pulled onto support work? Then I look at where tickets stall, like waiting on review or blocked by another team. I also talk to the leads and a few people one to one, because burnout or unclear direction rarely shows in a chart. Then I fix the biggest cause and watch the next two sprints.
Tell me about a schedule you built that turned out badly wrong. What do you do differently now?
Whether you own your estimating mistakes and changed your method.
A specific cause, honest about the impact, and a concrete change in how estimates are made and checked.

On a 12-episode podcast season I set edit time per episode from our pilot, which had one guest. Later episodes had three, and edits took nearly twice as long. We slipped two weeks. Now I estimate from a range of real samples, not the best case, add time for review and fixes, and recheck the estimates after the first few episodes are done.
We have to cut about 20 percent of scope to make the date. Walk me through how you decide what goes.
Your judgement in cutting scope while protecting the core product and commitments.
Starts from the core experience and promises made, weighs cost left against value and risk with leads, and records and communicates every cut.

I start from the core: what the player must feel in the first hour, and what we promised the publisher and marketing. With the leads I list features by cost left, risk and value, and cut high-cost, low-value items first, watching for hidden dependencies. I check what was shown publicly, write down each cut and why, and tell the team clearly so nobody keeps working on dead features.
Leadership wants mandatory overtime for six weeks to hit a milestone. What do you tell them?
How you push back on crunch with facts and offer real options.
Explains the cost of crunch, offers cuts or date options from the critical path, and if extra hours remain, keeps them short, capped and legally paid.

I would push back on mandatory crunch: long stretches raise bug rates and burn people out, and the lost time usually comes back later. I show what is on the critical path and offer cuts or a date move. If some short, voluntary extra hours still make sense, I cap them, make sure hourly staff get the overtime pay the law requires, and give time back afterward.

product-analyst.heading: Product analyst questions
qs: How would you build a funnel for our sign-up flow, and what do you look at first?
Whether you can turn a user flow into steps you can measure.
Clear steps counted as unique users within a time window. The biggest drop is split by device or source before blaming the design.

A funnel counts how many users reach each step in order, for example: landed on the sign-up page, entered an email, verified it, finished the profile. I count unique users, set a window like seven days, and find the biggest drop. Then I split it by device and source, because a drop on only one platform usually means a bug, not a design problem.
What does the DAU/MAU ratio tell you, and when can it mislead?
Your grasp of a common engagement metric and its limits.
It measures habit: the share of monthly users active on a typical day. It fits poorly for rarely needed products and can rise when casual users leave.

It is the share of monthly users who show up on an average day, so it measures habit. At 50%, a typical user comes about 15 days a month. It misleads for products people need only now and then, like a tax app. It can also rise just because casual users left: the ratio looks better while the user base shrinks.
Engineering is about to build a new feature. How do you make sure we can measure it after launch?
Whether you plan event tracking before release instead of after.
A tracking plan built from the team's questions: each event named and defined, with its properties. It is agreed with engineers and tested in a build before release.

I start from the questions the team wants answered, then list each event: its name, exactly when it fires, and its properties, like plan type or screen. I agree on a naming rule with the engineer, such as object_action. Then I check the events in a test build before release. Without that, the first weeks of data are often unusable.
You plot a retention curve for a new app. What are you looking for?
How you read retention beyond a single day-30 number.
Whether the curve flattens, which shows a core of lasting users. Newer cohorts should flatten higher if the product is improving.

I want to know if it flattens. A curve that drops fast and then levels off at, say, 25% means a core group finds lasting value. One that keeps sliding toward zero means people try it and leave. I compare curves by sign-up month to see whether newer groups level off higher, which tells us our changes are working.
What is a guardrail metric? Give an example.
Whether you protect the product from wins that cause hidden harm.
A metric the test is not meant to move but must not hurt. The acceptable limit is agreed before launch.

A guardrail is a metric we do not try to move but must not hurt. If a test sends more notifications, the goal might be sessions, and the guardrails would be unsubscribes, uninstalls and support tickets. Before launch we agree how big a drop in a guardrail would stop the release, so nobody argues about it after seeing a win.
After an app release, the count of one event doubled overnight. What do you do?
How you handle a tracking problem that looks like user behavior.
Suspect the data first. Tie the jump to the release and app version, check whether users and sessions moved too, then warn people and fix it with engineering.

First I suspect tracking, not users. I check whether the jump lines up with the release and app version, and whether users and sessions moved too. If only the event count doubled on the new version, it probably fires twice, for example on screen load and on tap. I warn the team, flag the affected dashboards, and work with engineering to fix it and mark the bad days.
A new design wins big in its first week, but the lift shrinks every day after. What is going on, and what do you do?
Whether you recognize a novelty effect and know how to test for it.
Names the novelty effect, plots the lift by day and compares new with returning users. Waits for the effect to settle before deciding.

It may be a novelty effect: regular users click the new thing because it is new, and the effect fades. I would plot the lift by day and split it by new versus returning users. New users have no old habit, so their result is closer to the lasting effect. If the lift keeps shrinking, I would run the test longer before calling it.
Your test was set to split users 50/50, but with 200,000 users you see 52% versus 48%. What do you do?
Whether you spot a sample ratio mismatch and refuse to trust the results.
Sees that a gap this size is not chance at this sample, calls it a sample ratio mismatch, and finds the cause before reading any results.

With 200,000 users, a 52/48 split is far too uneven to be chance. A chi-square test would give a tiny p-value. That is a sample ratio mismatch, and it means something is broken: a redirect that loses users, a bot filter, or logging that fails in one version. I would not read the results until I find the cause, because the groups may no longer be comparable.
A test showed no overall effect, but the PM found one segment out of twelve with a significant lift and wants to ship for it. What do you say?
How you handle slicing results after the fact.
Explains that many segments make a false positive likely. Treats the segment as a lead to test again, not as a result.

With twelve segments tested at the 0.05 level, the chance that at least one looks significant by luck alone is close to half. So one winning segment is a lead, not a result. I would ask whether we predicted it before the test and correct for the number of comparisons. If it still looks real, I would run a new test aimed at that segment.
A feature was launched to everyone without a test, and the PM asks what it did. How do you estimate the impact?
Whether you can estimate impact without a randomized test, and say how sure you are.
Looks for a natural comparison, such as a staggered rollout, and uses difference-in-differences with its parallel-trends check. States that the evidence is weaker than a test.

I would look for a natural comparison. If the feature rolled out country by country, I compare the change in launched countries with the change in countries not yet launched over the same weeks. That is difference-in-differences. It relies on both groups trending alike before launch, which I check. I also say plainly that this is weaker evidence than a randomized test.
How would you define an active user for a product like ours?
Whether you tie a core metric to real value instead of to any logged event.
An action that reflects the product's value, a time window that fits how often people need it, and a check that it predicts retention.

I would not count app opens or logins, since a push notification can inflate those. For a budgeting app I might count a user who reviewed or categorized a transaction in the past 7 days. I pick the window from how often people naturally need the product. Then I check that this definition predicts next month's retention better than the alternatives.
A PM checks the test every morning and wants to stop the day it hits p below 0.05. What do you say?
Whether you understand how peeking at results inflates false positives.
Repeated looks at a fixed threshold push the false positive rate well above 5%. Fix the sample size up front or use a method built for early looks.

Every look is another chance for noise to cross the line, so checking daily and stopping at the first p below 0.05 gives far more than a 5% false positive rate. I would agree on the sample size before launch and read the result once. If the team needs the option to stop early, I would use a sequential method that adjusts the threshold for each look.
We randomize by user, but the metric is click-through rate per page view. What can go wrong with the standard analysis?
Whether you match the statistics to the unit of randomization.
Page views from one user are not independent, so a plain test on views understates the variance. Use the delta method or a bootstrap by user.
