A user who views 200 pages counts 200 times, and those views are correlated. Treating them as independent makes the standard error too small and the p-value look too good. I keep the ratio as total clicks over total views per group, but compute the variance with the delta method or a bootstrap that resamples whole users. Otherwise we ship false wins.
Only 3,000 users a week reach the screen we want to test, and the test would need six months. What are your options?
How you plan an experiment when traffic is too low.
Honest trade-offs: a bolder change, a more sensitive metric, variance reduction with pre-test data, or a decision made without a test.

First I check the smallest effect we care about; a bolder design may have a bigger effect and need far fewer users. I can use a metric closer to the change, like completion of that screen, and reduce noise by adjusting for each user's behavior before the test. If it still takes months, I would suggest shipping with before-and-after monitoring and user interviews.
We want to test a new search ranking in a two-sided marketplace. Why might a normal user-level A/B test give the wrong answer?
Whether you spot interference between the test groups.
Treated and control users compete for the same supply, so the groups affect each other. Randomize by market or by time blocks instead.

If the new ranking steers buyers to the best-priced listings, treated users may book items control users would have booked. The test then shows a gain partly taken from control, which shrinks at full launch. I would randomize by city, or run a switchback test that turns the ranking on and off in a market in time blocks, and accept a wider confidence interval.
A test raised checkout conversion by 4%, but the 30-day refund rate also went up. How do you decide?
How you weigh a win against a cost that shows up later.
Check the refund rise is real, find which orders drive it, and put both effects in one unit like net revenue or margin.

First I check whether the refund increase is significant and which kinds of orders drive it. Then I put both in one unit: extra orders times margin, minus refunded orders, return shipping and support cost. If buyers who later regret the purchase are the cause, I would keep the faster flow but fix what misleads them, like unclear sizing, and test again.
How would you measure the combined effect of everything the team shipped this year?
Whether you know why test wins do not simply add up, and how to measure the total.
Summing individual lifts overstates the total. A long-term holdout group kept on the old experience shows the real cumulative effect.

Adding up each test's lift usually overstates the total: some winners were false positives, effects overlap, and some fade. I would keep a small holdout, a few percent of users, who do not get new launches for the year. Comparing them with everyone else gives the cumulative effect. Those users miss improvements, so I keep the group small and time-limited.
Tell me about an analysis you got wrong after people had already acted on it.
How you own and fix your mistakes.
You found it, told the people affected quickly, corrected the decision if needed, and changed your process.

I reported a 9% lift in trial starts, and the team expanded the feature. A week later I found my query counted users who restarted a trial twice. The real lift was about 3%. I told the PM that day and sent a corrected note to everyone who saw the first one. We still kept the feature. Since then, I check row counts against a second source before sharing results.
A VP wants to ship a redesign even though the test showed a small drop in conversion. How do you handle it?
How you push back with data while respecting who makes the call.
State the cost with its uncertainty, separate data from belief, propose a way to limit the risk, then accept the decision.

I would show the drop with its confidence interval and turn it into expected lost orders per month, so the cost is concrete. Then I ask what the VP expects the redesign to win, like brand or long-term retention, and how we would see it. If they still ship, I suggest keeping a holdout and agreeing now on a number that would trigger a rollback.

product-designer.heading: Product designer questions
qs: What is the difference between a wireframe, a mockup and a prototype, and when do you use each?
Whether you choose the right level of detail for the question you are trying to answer.
Clear definitions tied to purpose: structure first, visuals next, interaction last, with fidelity matched to what needs testing.

A wireframe shows structure and priority with no styling. I use it to agree on layout fast. A mockup adds real visuals, type and color for visual review. A prototype is clickable, so people can try a flow. I keep fidelity as low as the question allows, because rough work invites honest feedback.
Beyond the main path, which states do you design for a typical screen?
Whether you think past the ideal screen to what users really see.
Names empty, loading, error, partial and success states, plus edge cases like long text or no permission.

I design the empty state for first use, loading, errors with a clear way to recover, partial data, and success. I also test long names, huge numbers and a user without permission. Engineers will hit all of these anyway, so I would rather decide them than leave them to guesswork.
How would you design the interaction for deleting a project?
Your judgement on preventing and recovering from costly user errors.
Matches friction to the damage: undo for recoverable actions, a specific confirmation for permanent ones, never a vague "Are you sure?".

First I ask if it can be undone. If yes, I delete at once and show an undo option, which is less annoying than a dialog. If it is permanent, I use a confirmation that names the project and what will be lost, with a clear "Delete project" button instead of "OK". For big losses I may ask the user to type the name.
A signup form has high drop-off. How would you approach redesigning it?
Your practical knowledge of form design and how you find the real cause.
Looks at where people quit first, then cuts fields, uses visible labels, sensible validation and autofill.

I would check analytics to see which field people abandon on. Then I would remove anything we do not need yet, keep one column, use labels that stay visible instead of placeholder text only, and validate when a user leaves a field rather than on every keystroke. I would support autofill and explain why we ask for sensitive data.
How do you run a usability test without leading the participant?
Whether you can get honest behavior instead of polite answers.
Task-based scenarios without interface words, think-aloud, neutral prompts, no rescuing, and watching behavior over opinions.

I give a goal, like "You want to change your delivery address," never "Click Settings." I ask them to think aloud and reply to questions with "What would you expect?" If they struggle I stay quiet longer than feels comfortable. I trust what they do more than what they say they like.
A team asks you to add a new button style to the design system for one screen. How do you decide?
How you balance consistency of a design system with real product needs.
Asks what problem the variant solves, checks existing components first, and adds only reusable, documented patterns.

I ask what the current buttons fail to do. Often an existing variant or a layout change solves it. If the need is real and likely to come up again, I add it properly, with states, usage rules and code parity. If it is a true one-off, I keep it local so the system does not fill up with exceptions.
In testing, three of five users fail a task, and a stakeholder says they just were not tech-savvy. What do you do?
How you defend findings with evidence without turning it into a fight.
Checks recruiting honestly, then shows clips and the pattern, and frames it as risk to the business.

First I check whether we recruited the right people; if not, that is a fair point. If they match our users, I show short clips of each failure at the same step. Three people stuck in one place is a pattern. I frame it as support tickets and lost signups, and propose a quick fix we can retest.
The product manager wants to ship in two weeks with no time for research. What do you do?
Your judgement on fitting research to real deadlines.
Finds fast, cheap evidence, names the riskiest assumption, and plans to learn after launch with metrics.

I would not block the launch. I would pull existing data and support tickets, then run quick tests with three or four people on a rough prototype, which fits in two or three days. I focus on the riskiest assumption. We agree on metrics to watch after launch and a date to review them.
The business asks for a cancellation flow that makes it hard for users to quit. How do you respond?
Whether you can push back on manipulative design with good arguments.
Refuses dark patterns, explains trust and legal risk, and offers honest retention options instead.

I would explain that hiding the cancel path is a dark pattern. It angers users, drives chargebacks and complaints, and regulators like the FTC have acted against deceptive design. I would offer honest options: ask why they are leaving, offer a pause or cheaper plan once, then let them cancel in a few clear steps.
After your checkout redesign launches, conversion drops 8%. Walk me through what you do.
How you investigate a problem with your own work calmly and with data.
Verifies the data, segments to find where and for whom it dropped, looks at sessions, and rolls back if needed.

First I confirm the drop is real: tracking changes and seasonal effects can fake one. Then I split by step, device and new versus returning users. If mobile users quit at payment, I watch session recordings there. If the loss is costly, I push to roll back or run the old and new versions side by side while we fix it.
An action sometimes takes several seconds to complete. How do you design the feedback the user sees?
How you design for waiting and perceived speed.
Feedback scaled to the wait: instant acknowledgment, a spinner or skeleton for short waits, real progress and a way to keep working for long ones.

Classic response-time research gives rough limits: about 0.1 second feels instant, about 1 second keeps the flow of thought, and near 10 seconds attention drifts. So the button reacts at once and disables to stop double taps. Past a second I show a skeleton or spinner. For long jobs I show real progress, let people keep working, and notify them when it is done.
A VP says your five-person usability study is not statistically significant. How do you respond?
Whether you know what qualitative research can and cannot prove.
Agrees it is not a statistic: small tests find problems and explain why; measuring how often something happens needs a larger quantitative study.

I agree, and that was never the goal. Five sessions are for finding problems and understanding why they happen. A problem that trips several people is real, even if we cannot say it hits 40% of users. If we need a rate, like task success to compare two designs, I would plan a quantitative test or an A/B test with a sample sized for that question.
How would you design a data table with eight columns for a phone screen?
How you adapt dense information to a small screen.
Starts from what users do with the table on a phone, then picks a pattern: priority columns, cards, or a frozen first column with sideways scroll.

First I ask what people do with it on mobile: scan, compare or act on one row. For scanning I keep the two or three columns that matter and move the rest to a detail view. For comparing I freeze the first column and let the rest scroll sideways, with a visible cue. For acting on rows I turn each row into a card with the key fields and actions.
You have twelve interview transcripts and one week. Walk me through how you get from them to design decisions.
How you turn raw research into findings a team can act on.
A clear path from notes to patterns to insights, with evidence kept attached and each finding tied to a specific design decision.

I pull observations into notes, one fact or quote each, tagged by participant. Then I cluster them in an affinity map and look for patterns across people, not one loud voice. Each insight gets a count and two supporting quotes. Last, I write what it means for the design, like which step to cut, and review it with the PM and the engineering lead.
When is it right to break a platform convention, like the standard back gesture or tab bar?
Your judgement on consistency versus invention.
Conventions are the default because users already know them; breaking one needs a clear gain, shown in testing, that outweighs the cost of relearning.

Rarely. People bring habits from every other app, so a custom back behavior costs them before it helps. I would only break a convention if the standard pattern fails a key task and testing shows the new one works better. Even then I keep the system gestures working, because users will try them anyway and should not get stuck.
How would you set success metrics for a feature before it launches?
Whether you can tie design work to measurable outcomes.
Goals first, then signals and metrics, with a baseline captured before launch and a guardrail metric so one win does not hide a loss elsewhere.

I use the HEART framework: happiness, engagement, adoption, retention and task success. For the parts that matter I write a goal, the signal that shows it, and a metric. For a bulk edit tool that might be adoption among active admins and time to edit 50 items. I capture a baseline before launch and add a guardrail, like error rate or support tickets.
You need to retire a component used in 60 places across four product teams. How do you do it?
How you manage change in a design system without breaking other teams' work.
A planned deprecation: usage audited, replacement and reason documented, a migration guide and timeline agreed, and hands-on help, not a sudden removal.

First I check where it is used and why, since some uses may reveal a need the replacement misses. Then I mark it deprecated in the design library and in code, with a note pointing to the replacement and a migration guide. I agree a timeline with each team, pair on the hardest screens, track usage down to zero, and only then delete it.
Tell me about a design decision you got wrong after it shipped. How did you find out, and what did you change?
Whether you own mistakes and learn from evidence.
A real, specific mistake, how data or users revealed it, the fix, and a change in process so it does not happen again.

I hid filters behind an icon to clean up a search page. Two weeks after launch, filter use fell by about half and support got questions about missing options. I owned it in our review, we moved the top three filters back into view, and use recovered. Since then I test any removal of visible controls with real tasks before it ships.

product-engineer.heading: Product engineer questions
qs: How do you run a customer interview so you learn what they really need?
Whether you can get real needs out of users instead of opinions about your idea.
Asks about past behavior and real cases, avoids leading questions and pitching, and listens more than talks.

I ask about the last time they hit the problem: what they were doing, what they tried, what it cost them. I do not show my idea first or ask "would you use this?", because people say yes to be polite. I take notes on their exact words and look for the same pain across several people.
A large customer asks for a specific feature. What do you do before writing any code?
How you turn a feature request into the underlying problem.
Digs into the job behind the request, checks if other users share it, and considers simpler solutions before committing.

I ask what they are trying to get done and what they do today without the feature. Often the request is one solution to a wider problem. Then I check usage data and support tickets to see if other customers have the same pain. Only then do I decide whether to build what they asked, something simpler, or nothing.
How do you decide what goes into the first version of a feature?
Your ability to cut scope while keeping the version useful.
Starts from the one problem to solve and the question to answer, ships the smallest version that tests it, and lists what was cut.

I write down the one problem we are solving and what we need to learn. Anything that does not help with those waits. For a recent export feature we shipped CSV only, no scheduling, no custom columns. I wrote the cut items in the ticket so the team knew they were postponed, not forgotten.
When do you build a throwaway prototype instead of production code?
Whether you match the effort to the uncertainty.
Prototypes when the main risk is whether users want it or understand it; clear about throwing the prototype away, not shipping it.

When the big unknown is whether people want it or can use it, I prototype: a clickable mockup or a hacky version behind a flag for five users. It skips tests and edge cases on purpose. I tell everyone up front it gets rewritten, so nobody ships the hack because it happened to work.
How do you choose the metrics for an A/B test?
Whether you can define success before the test starts.
One primary metric tied to the goal, chosen in advance, plus guardrail metrics that must not get worse.

I pick one primary metric that the change should move, like the share of new users who finish setup, and I write it down before launch. Then I add guardrails such as page load time, error rate and cancellations. If I track twenty metrics and pick the winner afterwards, one will look good by chance.
How do you release a new feature to users safely?
Your practice with feature flags and gradual rollouts.
Ships behind a flag, rolls out in steps while watching errors and key metrics, and can turn it off without a deploy.

I put the feature behind a flag and turn it on for the team first, then a small share of users, then more in steps. At each step I check errors, latency and the metric we care about. If something looks wrong I switch the flag off, no redeploy needed. Once it is fully out, I remove the flag so old code does not pile up.
The product manager checks the A/B test every day and wants to stop it the first day it shows a significant result. What do you say?
Whether you understand the risk of peeking at test results.
Explains that repeated checks raise the false positive rate; fix the sample size in advance or use a method built for checking early.

Each time we look and could stop, we get another chance for random noise to look like a win. Checking daily and stopping at the first good day makes false wins much more likely. I would set the sample size before launch from the smallest lift we care about, run for full weeks, or use a sequential test designed for early looks.
Your test was set to split users 50/50, but with 200,000 users it shows 52% and 48%. What do you do?
Whether you spot a sample ratio mismatch and know not to trust the result.
Recognizes the gap is too large to be chance at that size, pauses the analysis, and looks for an assignment or logging bug.

With that many users, a 52/48 split is very unlikely by chance; a chi-square test would confirm it. It usually means a bug: one variant crashes before it logs, a redirect loses users, or bots land in one group. I would not read the results until I find the cause, because the groups are no longer comparable.
Your A/B test raised sign-ups by 6%, but support tickets went up too. Do you ship it?
How you weigh a win on one metric against a cost on another.
Does not ship on the primary metric alone; finds why tickets rose, estimates the net effect, and fixes the cause before deciding.

Not yet. I would read the new tickets to see what confuses people. If the new flow hides a step, the extra sign-ups may churn later or cost more in support than they bring. I would fix the confusing part, rerun the test, and also check whether the new users stay as long as the old ones.
Three months after you shipped a feature, very few people use it. What do you do?
How you handle a feature that did not work and whether you can let it go.
Checks whether users find it or it misses the need, talks to users, and is willing to improve it or remove it.

First I check whether people even see it, using the funnel from the entry point. Then I talk to a few users who tried it once and stopped. If it is a discovery problem I fix the entry point. If it solves the wrong problem, I propose removing it, because every unused feature still costs us in bugs, tests and support.
Users who turn on our reminders feature retain twice as well as those who don't. Can we say the feature causes it?
Whether you can tell correlation from cause in product data.
No: users who opt in were likely more engaged already. Names a way to test cause, such as a randomized experiment or a holdout.

Not yet. People who bother to turn on reminders were probably more committed to begin with, so they would retain better anyway. I'd compare similar users before they opted in. If the decision matters, I'd run a test that offers reminders to a random half of new users. Only that random split tells us what the feature itself does.
Walk me through what you set up to measure a feature before it ships.
How you plan measurement as part of building, not after.
Events tied to a clear question, a baseline captured beforehand, a check that tracking fires correctly, and a query ready on day one.

I write down the questions first: who sees it, who tries it, who comes back. Each becomes one event with clear properties, like plan type and platform. I check that the events fire in staging and once in production, because broken tracking is common. I also record the current baseline, so a week after launch I compare against real numbers, not memory.
When would you use a fake door test, and how do you keep it fair to users?
Your judgement on cheap ways to test demand before building.
Used to measure interest before building. Kept short and small, honest with users who click, and never misleading about something they pay for.

If we're unsure anyone wants a feature, I add the button or menu item before building it and count clicks. Whoever clicks sees a short note: this is coming, do you want to hear when it's ready? I show it to a small share of users for a week or two, never on paid features people would think they bought, then remove it. It's a signal of interest, not proof of use.
Your test assigns variants by browser cookie, and many users log in on both phone and laptop. Why is that a problem, and what would you do?
Whether you understand how the unit of randomization affects results.
One person can see both versions, which blurs the effect. Assign by user ID where possible, and analyze at the same unit you randomized on.

The same person may get version A on the phone and B on the laptop. They see an inconsistent product, and their behavior counts in both groups, which blurs the difference. For logged-in features I'd assign by user ID so a person always gets one version. For logged-out pages a cookie may be the only option; then I accept some noise and analyze per cookie, the unit I split on.
A redesigned page lifted clicks 8% in the first week of a test. What makes you cautious?
Whether you know about novelty effects and short-term bias in tests.
New things draw clicks from curiosity. Look at the lift day by day, compare new and returning users, and run full weeks before deciding.

Returning users often click something just because it's new, and that fades. I'd plot the daily lift: if it shrinks every day, it's probably novelty. I'd also look at new users, who have no old version to compare with. And I'd run at least two full weeks so weekday and weekend behavior are both covered before deciding.
The power calculation says your test needs four months of traffic. What are your options?
How you work when an experiment is too slow to be useful.
Knows the trade-offs: a bolder change, a metric closer to the change, variance reduction, or shipping without a test when the risk is low.

First I ask if the hoped-for effect is realistic. Detecting half the lift needs about four times the users, so a bolder change can cut the time a lot. I can also measure a metric nearer the change, like form completion instead of revenue, or reduce noise using each user's data from before the test. If the change is low risk and easy to undo, I may ship it behind a flag and watch.
The test is flat overall, but the analyst found a 12% lift for Android users. Do you ship to Android?
Whether you resist chasing segments found after the fact.
Slicing many segments will find chance winners. Treat it as a new hypothesis, look for a real reason, and confirm with a test planned for that segment.

Not on that alone. If you slice results ten ways, one slice will look good by chance. I'd ask whether there's a real reason, say the old screen was broken on Android, and check whether other segments went down. If the story holds, I run a new test on Android only, with that lift as the planned metric. If it holds again, we ship.
You want to test a lower delivery fee in a marketplace with a limited number of couriers. Why can a normal user-level A/B test mislead you here?
Whether you spot interference between test groups that share resources.
Groups share couriers, so the test group's extra orders take supply from control and the gain looks bigger. Randomize by city or by time block instead.

The two groups compete for the same couriers. If the cheaper fee brings more orders, those orders take couriers away from the control group, whose deliveries get slower. The test then looks better than a full launch would. I'd randomize by city or region, or switch the whole market between versions in time blocks, and accept that fewer units means wider error bars.
Leadership asks whether the twenty features your team shipped this year added up to real growth. How would you answer?
How you measure the combined, long-term effect of many changes.
Individual test wins do not simply add up. A long-running holdout group kept on the old experience gives an honest combined measure.

Adding up the lifts from twenty tests overstates it: some wins were noise, some fade, and features overlap. Going forward, I'd keep a small holdout of users who stay on the old experience for a quarter or more. Comparing them with everyone else shows the real combined effect. For this year, I'd be honest that we only have per-test estimates.
A feature costs a lot to maintain and only 3% of users touch it. How do you decide whether to remove it, and how do you do it?
Your judgement when removing something people rely on.
Finds out who the 3% are and what they lose, then removes in steps: notice, workaround or export, gradual turn-off, and watching support and churn.

3% can matter if they're our biggest accounts. I'd look at who uses it and talk to a few of them to learn what job it does. If we still remove it, I announce a date, offer a workaround or export, hide it from new users first, then turn it off behind a flag so we can bring it back. I watch support tickets and cancellations for those users afterward.

product-manager.heading: Product manager questions
qs: What makes a good customer interview question, and what makes a bad one?
Whether you can learn from users without leading them to the answer you want.
Asks about real past behavior and its cost, not opinions on future features or yes/no questions that invite polite agreement.

A bad one is “Would you use an export to Excel?” People say yes to be kind. A good one is “Tell me about the last time you needed this data outside our app. What did you do?” I ask about real events, what they tried and what it cost them. Then I stay quiet and let them talk.
What goes into a spec you hand to engineering?
Your ability to write a document a team can actually build from.
The problem, who has it, the goal and metric, scope and non-goals, flows and edge cases, open questions. The what and why, with the how left to engineers.

I start with the problem, who has it and the evidence. Then the goal and the metric we expect to move, what is in scope and what is explicitly out, and the main user flows with edge cases like empty states and errors. I end with open questions. I leave the technical design to engineers and keep the doc updated as we decide things.
Walk me through how you would score a backlog with a framework like RICE.
Whether you know a common prioritization method and where it stops being useful.
Reach times impact times confidence, divided by effort; treated as a way to compare and discuss, not as the final answer.

RICE stands for reach, impact, confidence and effort. I estimate how many users a change touches in a quarter, impact on a small scale, my confidence as a percentage, and effort in person-weeks. The score is reach times impact times confidence, divided by effort. It helps compare similar items, but the inputs are guesses, so I check the top of the list against our strategy.
How do you choose the main metric for a product, and what keeps it honest?
Your grasp of a primary metric and the guardrail metrics that protect it.
A metric tied to the value users get, paired with guardrails that catch gains made at the user's expense.

I pick a number that rises only when users get real value. For a meal-planning app, that might be weekly users who planned at least three meals. Then I add guardrails: unsubscribe rate, support tickets and page load time. If the main metric goes up while a guardrail gets worse, we may be pushing people rather than helping them.
Sales wants a firm date on the roadmap for a feature a big prospect needs. How do you respond?
How you handle roadmap commitments under commercial pressure.
Learns the prospect's real need, commits only to what the team is confident about, and is honest about uncertainty instead of inventing a date.

First I ask sales to set up a call so I hear the prospect's actual problem; often a smaller change or a workaround solves it. If it fits our plan, I give a date only once engineering has scoped it, and I share a range for anything further out. I would rather lose a promise today than break one in six months.
Your A/B test hit statistical significance on day three of a planned two-week run. Do you stop it?
Whether you understand the risk of peeking at test results.
No: checking often and stopping at the first significant result inflates false positives. Run to the planned sample and full weeks unless the test was designed for early stopping.

No. If you check a test every day and stop the first time it looks significant, you raise the chance of a false win a lot. Early results also miss weekly patterns, since weekend users behave differently. I let it run the full two weeks to the planned sample size. If we need early stopping, we design for it up front with a sequential method.
The team will miss the launch date by three weeks. What are your options?
How you trade scope, time and quality when a plan slips.
Raises it early, lays out cutting scope or moving the date, and makes the trade explicit; does not quietly cut testing or quality.

I tell stakeholders as soon as I know, not the week before. Then I lay out options. We can cut scope to the core flow that solves the main problem and ship the rest later, or keep the scope and move the date. Adding people this late rarely helps. What I will not do is skip testing to hit the date, because a broken launch costs more than a late one.
A senior executive asks you to add their idea to this quarter's roadmap, but it does not fit the strategy. What do you do?
How you push back upward without damaging the relationship.
Takes the idea seriously, finds the problem behind it, shows the trade-off in plain terms and lets the decision be made openly.

I ask what problem they want solved, because the goal is often good even if the feature is not. Then I show where it would land against our current priorities and what we would have to drop to fit it in. If they still want it, that is a valid call, but it is made openly, and I tell the team what moved and why.
Weekly active users dropped 8% the week after your release. Walk me through how you investigate.
How you diagnose a metric drop before jumping to a cause.
Rules out tracking errors first, then segments by platform, app version, region and user group, checks outside causes, then ties it to the change.

First I check the data itself: did tracking break, did an event get renamed? Then I segment the drop by platform, app version, region and new versus existing users. If it sits only on the new version, the release is the likely cause. I also check outside factors like a holiday or an outage. Once I find it, I decide with engineering whether to roll back or fix forward.
How would you decide whether to retire a feature that a small group of customers relies on?
Your judgement on removing things, not only adding them.
Weighs the ongoing cost against value to those users, talks to them, and retires with notice, a migration path and a clear date.

I measure what the feature costs us: bugs, support time, how much it slows other work. Then I look at who uses it and talk to some of them. If the cost wins, I announce it with plenty of notice, offer an export or alternative, and give a firm date. In one case, 3% of accounts used an old report, and a simple export covered nearly all of them.
What is the difference between an outcome roadmap and a feature roadmap, and when would you use each?
Whether you plan around results for users or around a list of features.
Outcomes as the default, with features shown as current bets; firm feature dates only where a real commitment needs one.

A feature roadmap lists what we will ship and when. An outcome roadmap lists the problems we will move, like cutting setup time in half, with our best current ideas under each. I lead with outcomes because the team can change the solution as we learn. I add firm feature dates only where a contract or a launch partner depends on them.
How would you size the opportunity for a new product line before asking for a team?
Your ability to turn a market into a number you can defend.
A bottom-up estimate from real customer counts and prices, with total, serviceable and obtainable market kept apart and assumptions stated.

I build it bottom up: how many companies fit the profile, what share we can reach with our channels, and what they would pay per year. That gives the total, serviceable and obtainable market, kept separate. I write every assumption next to the number and test the weakest one, often price, with five or six customer calls before I ask for headcount.
What is a guardrail metric, and how do you pick them for an experiment?
Whether you protect the rest of the product while chasing one number.
Metrics that must not get worse, chosen with a harm threshold before the test, such as load time, cancellations or support tickets.

A guardrail is a metric we are not trying to move but must not hurt. If I test a bigger upgrade prompt, the goal is upgrades, and the guardrails are cancellations, refunds, page load time and support tickets. I set them and the threshold for harm before launch, so a win on upgrades that raises refunds is not called a win after the fact.
How do you read a retention curve to judge product-market fit?
Whether you can tell real fit from early growth.
Cohort curves that flatten above zero show a core group that stays; curves that keep falling show a leak that more growth will not fix.

I plot retention by signup cohort: the share still active in week one, week two, and on. If the curve keeps sliding toward zero, we are filling a leaky bucket and more marketing only hides it. If it flattens, say at 25% from week eight, a group keeps getting value. Then I study who they are and point the product and sales at more people like them.
How would you test whether users want a feature before the team builds it?
Whether you can get evidence of demand cheaply.
Cheap tests of behavior, not opinion, like a fake door or a manual pilot, with a pass mark set in advance and users told honestly.

I want behavior, not answers to 'would you use this?' One way is a fake door: a button for the feature, and when people click, an honest note that it is coming and an offer to join a pilot. I set the pass mark first, say 4% of visitors clicking. For bigger bets I run the service by hand for ten customers before writing code.
Your experiment was set to a 50/50 split, but the data shows 53% of users in control. What does that tell you?
Whether you spot a broken experiment before reading its results.
A sample ratio mismatch: assignment or logging is broken, so no result can be trusted until the cause is found and fixed.

That is a sample ratio mismatch. With tens of thousands of users, a quick chi-square test shows it is not chance. Maybe the variant crashes on some browsers, or a redirect drops users before they are logged. I would not read the lift at all. I would check the split by platform and day with engineering, fix the cause and rerun the test.
A test tracked 20 metrics, and one moved with a p-value below 0.05. The team wants to ship. What do you say?
Your grasp of false positives when many metrics are read at once.
With 20 metrics, about one false positive at 0.05 is expected by chance; treat it as a lead to retest, not a result.

If none of the 20 truly changed, we would still expect about one to cross 0.05 by luck. So one hit out of 20 is what noise looks like. Unless that metric was the primary metric we named before the test, I treat it as a hypothesis: correct for the number of comparisons, or run a new test with it as the main metric.
Your test is flat overall, but new users improved and existing users got worse. How do you decide?
How you read results that differ between groups of users.
Asks whether the split was planned or found after the fact, confirms it, then weighs each group's long-term value rather than the average.

First I ask if we planned to compare new and existing users. If we found it by slicing afterward, it may be noise, so I confirm with a test aimed at those groups. If it holds, the flat average hides two real effects. Existing users carry most revenue, so I would not ship to them; I might ship only to new users and watch their retention.
Should we build, buy or partner for a capability like payments or search? Walk me through how you decide.
Your judgement on where the team's limited time should go.
Build only what sets the product apart; buy or partner for common needs, weighing total cost, lock-in, data and compliance.

I ask if this is why customers choose us. If not, building it means maintaining it forever, so I lean to buy or partner. I compare total cost over three years: license, integration, upkeep and the cost to switch later. For payments I also weigh the card security standard, PCI DSS; a good provider takes much of that work off our plate.
Another team's onboarding change lifted signups 10% but cut activation of your feature. Both teams hit their own goals. How do you handle it?
How you resolve a clash between team metrics for the good of the company.
Works it out with the other PM first, judges by the shared goal above both, like retained users, and escalates only with a joint proposal.

I would check the data with the other PM first, not their manager: is the drop real, and which users does it hit? Then we look at the goal both serve, say users still active after 30 days. If the extra signups do not stay, the change is a net loss. We take one joint proposal to leadership, like keeping the faster signup but restoring my setup step for users who need it.

product-marketing.heading: Product marketing manager questions
qs: What is the difference between positioning and messaging?
Whether you know the two building blocks of the job and which one comes first.
Positioning is the strategic choice of who the product is for and why it wins. Messaging is the words built on top of it, so positioning comes first.

Positioning is the decision: which customer, which problem, what we compare against and why we win. It is internal and rarely changes. Messaging is how we say that to a given audience, in headlines, pitches and web pages. If the messaging shifts every quarter, usually the positioning was never agreed.
Where does your job end and the product manager's job begin?
Whether you understand the split of roles you will work in every day.
The PM owns what gets built and why. The PMM owns how it is positioned, launched and sold, and brings market insight back to the PM.

The product manager owns the roadmap: what we build and in what order. I own how the market hears about it: positioning, launch, pricing pages and sales tools. The overlap is customer insight. I bring win/loss findings and competitor moves to roadmap reviews, and the PM tells me early what is coming so I can plan the launch.
Walk me through how you would position a new product from scratch.
Your method for positioning, not just your instinct.
Starts from the best current customers and their real alternatives, then names the unique value, the target segment and the category, and tests it.

I start with the customers who love the product most and ask what they would use if we did not exist. That list is the real competition. Then I note what we do that those options cannot, what value that brings, and which customers care most. Last, I pick the category frame that makes that value obvious and test it on sales calls before writing copy.
What goes into a good competitive battlecard, and how do you keep it current?
Whether you can turn competitor research into something a rep can use in the middle of a call.
Short, honest content: where we win and lose, questions that expose weak spots, objection answers and proof. Plus an owner, a review cycle and input from the field.

One page per competitor: when we win, when we lose, questions that expose their weak spots, answers to their top three objections against us, and a customer story. I admit where they are stronger, or reps stop trusting it. I review each card monthly against win/loss notes, and reps post what they hear in a shared channel so updates come from real deals.
How do you run a win/loss analysis?
How you find the real reasons deals are won and lost.
Interviews with buyers, not only CRM fields, done by someone neutral soon after the decision, with patterns shared with product and sales.

CRM loss reasons mostly say price, so I interview the buyers themselves, won and lost, within a few weeks of the decision. I or a neutral third party ask, not the rep, so people speak openly. I ask how they decided, who else they looked at and what almost changed their mind. Each quarter I share the patterns with product and sales, with quotes.
How do you decide how big a launch should be?
Whether you tier launches by impact instead of treating every release the same way.
A tiering rule based on customer impact, revenue and competitive weight, agreed with product, so the effort and noise match the release.

Three tiers, agreed with product. Tier one is a new product or a new market: full launch, press, sales training. Tier two is a big feature for current customers: email, blog, demo update. Tier three is an improvement: release notes and an in-app note. I score each release on customer impact, revenue and competitive value, so the loudest voice does not set the tier.
Sales says nobody uses the pitch deck you built. What do you do?
How you handle sales materials that are not landing.
Curiosity before defending: check usage, sit in on calls, rebuild with the best reps, and retire what nobody uses.

First I find out why. I check the usage data, sit in on a few calls and ask the top reps what they show instead. Often they built their own slides because ours were too long or led with features. I rebuild it with two of those reps, cut it to the slides that move a deal, and they present it at the next team meeting. Reps trust a peer more than marketing.
An executive wants the launch page to say we are the fastest product on the market. How do you handle it?
Whether you know a claim must be backed up before it goes public.
Knows US ad claims must be truthful and backed by evidence before they run; gets the test data and legal review, or narrows the claim to what can be proven.

I ask what the claim rests on. In the US, an objective claim like “fastest” needs evidence before it runs, and a comparison with rivals must be fair. If we have a recent, repeatable benchmark, I note the test conditions and have legal review it. If not, I write what we can prove, such as “loads reports in under two seconds”, which often persuades better anyway.
Two weeks before launch, engineering says the date will slip a month. Press briefings and a customer webinar are booked. What do you do?
How you handle a launch problem without losing trust.
Gets the facts and a firm new date, decides what moves and what goes ahead, and tells press, customers and sales early and plainly.

First I confirm what is slipping: the whole product or one feature. If the core works, I may keep the date and launch a smaller story. If not, I get a date engineering will commit to, call the journalists myself, move the webinar with a short honest note, and brief sales so nobody promises the old date. Telling people early costs far less than a late surprise.
A main competitor launches a copy of your key feature at a lower price. Sales wants a discount and an attack page. What do you recommend?
Your judgement when a competitor move puts pressure on your positioning.
No panic: measures the real impact in deals, sharpens the differences that remain, and avoids a price war or attack copy not backed by evidence.

I would not react on day one. I get a demo of their version, check where it really matches ours, and track how often it shows up in deals over the next few weeks. Usually a copy covers the headline but not the depth, so I update the battlecard and messaging around what is still unique. A price cut is a leadership decision made with data, not a reflex.
What is the difference between an ideal customer profile and a buyer persona?
Whether you know who you target at the account level and at the person level.
The ICP describes the company that fits; personas describe the people in its buying group, each with different worries.

The ideal customer profile describes the account: industry, size, tools they already run, the trigger that makes them buy. Personas describe the people inside it, like the IT director who signs and the team lead who uses it daily. One deal can involve four personas, and each needs a different reason to say yes.
How do you size the market for a new product, and why build the number bottom-up?
Your grasp of market sizing and whether your numbers survive a finance leader's questions.
Clear TAM, SAM and SOM definitions, and a count of real buyers times a realistic price instead of a percentage of a big report figure.

TAM is all the demand for this kind of solution, SAM is the part our product, channels and regions can actually serve, and SOM is what we can realistically win soon. I count companies that match our profile, times a likely price, times a win rate we have actually seen. A top-down “1% of a huge market” figure falls apart at the first question.
How do you run a customer interview so you learn why they bought, not what they think you want to hear?
How you get honest buying insight without leading the customer.
Asks about real past events in order: the trigger, the options tried, the moment of choice. Avoids hypothetical and yes/no questions.

I ask them to tell the story: what was happening the week they started looking, what they tried first, who else got involved, what almost stopped them. I ask what they did, never “would you use this?” I stay quiet after each answer. The words they use for the problem often end up in our messaging.
How would you decide which features go into which pricing tier?
Your judgement on packaging, where positioning meets revenue.
Tiers built around distinct segments and what they value, with clear reasons to upgrade, checked against usage data and sales input.

I start from segments, not features. Each tier should fit one type of buyer, so I group features by who values them. What every user needs goes in the entry tier; what only larger teams need, like admin controls or single sign-on, becomes a reason to upgrade. I check it against usage data and deal notes, and make sure a buyer can pick a tier in a minute.
How do you know your sales enablement is actually working?
Whether you measure enablement by sales results, not by the amount of content produced.
Leading signs like content use and pitch practice, tied to results like win rate, deal size and new-rep ramp time, compared before and after.

Counting decks shipped tells me nothing. I look at whether reps use the material, whether they can deliver the pitch in a practice call, and then at results: win rate against the competitor we trained on, time for a new rep to close a first deal, deal size. If usage is high and win rate is flat, the content is wrong, not the reps.
A sales rep suggests signing up for a competitor's free trial under a fake name to capture their screens. What do you say?
Your ethics and judgement in gathering competitive intelligence.
A clear no with the reasons: misrepresentation, broken terms of use, legal and reputation risk. Then lawful sources that give the same insight.

I say no. Lying about who we are likely breaks the trial's terms, and misrepresentation can count as an improper means under trade secret law. It would also look terrible if it came out. We can get most of the same picture from public demos, help docs, review sites and win/loss calls with buyers who evaluated both products.
A case study you published says a customer cut costs by 40%. Their marketing team calls: they never approved that number. What do you do?
How you handle an error that touches a customer relationship and a public claim.
A fast correction everywhere the number appears, owning the mistake, and a fixed approval step so it does not happen again.

I thank them, apologize, and take the number down that day: the web page, the PDF, the sales deck and any ads. I ask what figure, if any, they are comfortable with and get it in writing. Then I tell sales to stop using the old version. Afterward I add a rule: no customer metric goes live without written approval of the exact final text.
We are moving from small businesses to enterprise buyers. What changes in your messaging and materials?
Whether you understand how enterprise buying differs and what product marketing must build for it.
A larger buying committee, risk and proof over speed, security and integration content, a business case for finance, and references of similar size.

Small businesses often buy on ease and price, with one person deciding. Enterprises buy through a committee: a sponsor, IT, security, procurement, legal. So I add proof of scale, security documents, integration detail, a return on investment model for finance, and references of similar size. The message shifts from “start today” to “low risk, proven, fits what you run.”
What signs tell you a product needs to be repositioned, and how do you decide?
Your senior judgement on when positioning, not the product or the sales team, is the real problem.
Evidence like longer sales cycles, unexpected competitors, growing discounts, or top customers using it differently, checked with data before changing anything.

Warning signs: deals take longer, we lose to tools we never saw as rivals, discounts grow, or prospects ask “so what is it?” The strongest signal is when our happiest customers describe the product differently than we do. I check win/loss notes and how the best accounts use it, then test the new framing on live deals before rewriting the website.
The CEO wants the launch message to speak to every segment, since the product works for all of them. How do you push back?
How you defend focus with a senior leader using evidence instead of opinion.
Explains the cost of a broad message, proposes a lead segment backed by data, and still serves other segments with tailored secondary material.

I agree the product fits many buyers, then show why one message for everyone lands with no one. I bring data: which segment wins fastest, at the best price, with the shortest cycle. I propose leading with that segment and giving the others their own pages and sales talk tracks. I offer a review after one quarter, so it is a test, not a lost argument.

product-operations.heading: Product operations questions
qs: What does product operations own that a product manager does not?
Whether you understand where the role starts and stops.
Clear ownership of the systems around the product: launches, tooling, feedback flow and shared data. Product decisions stay with the PM.

The PM decides what to build and why. I own the machinery that helps PMs do that well: the launch process, the feedback pipeline from support and sales, the tools and templates, and the shared metrics. If a PM spends Friday cleaning a spreadsheet of customer requests, that is a gap I should close.
What is a staged rollout, and when would you push for one?
Your grasp of how to release changes with limited risk.
Release to a small share of users first, check agreed metrics, and widen only if they hold, with a way to switch the feature off.

We release behind a feature flag, which is a switch that turns the feature on for chosen users. We start with about 5% of users, then 25%, then everyone. Before each step we check error rates, support tickets and the metric we agreed on. I push for it when a change touches billing, data or a workflow people use daily.
Walk me through how you plan a launch for a mid-size feature.
How you structure launch work across several teams.
A fixed timeline with a named owner per team, a readiness review, a go or no-go call, and a plan for day one monitoring and support.

Six weeks out I hold a kickoff with product, engineering, support, marketing and sales. Each team gets a named owner and due dates in one tracker. Two weeks out we review docs, training and the rollout plan. A week out we make the go or no-go call against agreed criteria. On launch day someone watches tickets and dashboards, and we hold a review two weeks later.
How do you turn hundreds of support tickets into something a product team can act on?
Your method for analyzing customer feedback at scale.
A consistent tagging scheme, counts tied to accounts or revenue, and a short summary with real quotes instead of a raw export.

First, a short tag list everyone applies the same way: product area, problem type and severity. Each month I count tickets by tag, add how many accounts and how much revenue sit behind each theme, and pull three real quotes. The PM gets one page: the top five themes, what changed since last month, and links to the tickets.
How do you train support agents on a feature before it ships?
Whether you prepare the front line in a way that works on launch day.
Early hands-on access, a short written guide with known limits and escalation paths, and saved replies ready before launch.

Agents get the feature in a test account about two weeks out. I run a 30 minute session where they click through it, not a slide deck. They get a one-page cheat sheet: what it does, who has it, known limits and when to escalate to engineering. Saved replies are ready before launch, and I read the first week of tickets to see what we missed.
How do you close the loop with customers and support once requested work ships?
Whether feedback handling goes all the way back to the people who raised it.
Requests stay linked to tickets and accounts, so the right people hear when it ships, and support knows before customers do.

Every request is linked to the ticket and the account it came from. When the feature ships, I pull that list and hand it to support and account managers with a short note they can send. Support hears first, so nobody is caught off guard. It also shows customers that writing in works, which keeps good feedback coming.
A team asks for a new roadmap tool. How do you decide?
How you handle tool requests without piling up tools nobody maintains.
Starts from the problem, checks what current tools already do, counts the full cost including migration, and pilots before buying.

I ask what problem they hit with the current setup. Often it is a missing view or a messy template that I can fix in a day. If the gap is real, I compare two or three options on license, setup and the cost of moving data, then run a four-week pilot with one team. We roll out only if that team keeps using it without being chased.
Two days before launch, support says the help articles are not ready. What do you do?
Your judgement on a go or no-go call when one piece is missing.
Weighs customer impact, looks for a smaller fix or a smaller audience, and brings options to the owner quickly instead of slipping by default.

I ask what is missing and how many customers will hit it. If the feature is simple, I write a short interim article with the PM and we ship. If customers cannot use it without help, I suggest launching to a small group first or moving the date a few days. Either way, the PM gets the options that same day, not on launch morning.
Tell me about a process you designed that people did not follow.
Whether you learn from low adoption instead of blaming the users.
Owns the design mistake, asks users why, simplifies, and measures adoption after the change.

I built a launch intake form with 22 fields. After a month, only two of eight PMs used it. When I asked, they said it took an hour and half the fields did not apply. I cut it to eight required fields, pre-filled the rest from the ticket, and sat with each PM for their first one. Seven of eight used it the next quarter.
The day after a launch, support tickets triple. Walk me through your first few hours.
How you sort out a launch problem under pressure.
Quickly splits the spike by cause, separates bugs from confusion, uses the flag or pause when needed, and keeps support and leaders updated.

In the first hour I tag the new tickets: bug, confusion or unrelated. If a bug hits many users, I bring the numbers to engineering and the PM and ask whether to pause the rollout. If it is confusion, I fix the article, update saved replies and send agents a short note. I post an update every couple of hours until volume settles.
How do you tier launches, and what actually changes between tiers?
Whether you match launch effort to the size and risk of the change.
Clear criteria like customer impact, revenue and risk, with concrete differences in comms, training and review for each tier.

I use three tiers. Tier 1 is a new product or a pricing change: press, sales enablement, full support training and an exec go/no-go. Tier 2 is a notable feature: blog post, help articles and a support briefing. Tier 3 is a small fix: release notes only. The tier is set early, by impact and risk, not by how proud the team is.
How do you design a tagging taxonomy for customer feedback that still works a year later?
How you keep feedback data consistent as the product and the team change.
A short list tied to owned product areas, clear definitions, a regular review, and a check on how consistently people tag.

I keep the top level small and mapped to product areas that have an owner, with a one-line definition and an example for each tag. Agents pick from a list, never free text. Every quarter I merge dead tags and split ones that grew too big. I also have two people tag the same 50 tickets. If they disagree a lot, the definitions need work.
Engineering has 400 feature flags and nobody knows which are still needed. What process would you set up?
Whether you treat flag cleanup as part of launch work, not an afterthought.
An owner and removal date for every flag at creation, removal as a ticket in the launch plan, and a regular review of stale flags.

Going forward, every flag gets an owner and an expected removal date when it is created. Removing it is a ticket in the launch plan, done once the rollout has sat at 100% for an agreed period. For the backlog, I'd list flags not changed in 90 days, send each to its team and track removals weekly. Old flags hide dead code and make bugs harder to trace.
Most of your feedback comes through the account managers of your largest customers. What bias does that create, and how do you correct for it?
Whether you can spot whose voice is missing from the feedback data.
Names the skew toward big, vocal accounts and adds other sources, like usage data, self-serve users and churn reasons, before weighting.

It overweights large accounts and whatever their account managers think is worth passing on. Small and self-serve customers barely show up, and churned ones never do. I'd add in-app feedback, churn survey reasons and tickets from smaller plans, then report requests by segment and by number of accounts, not only by revenue, so the team sees both views.
Sales wants call recordings stored in the shared feedback repository. What do you check first?
Your care with consent and personal data when you collect customer feedback.
Recording consent under state law, what customers agreed to, access limits, retention and removing personal data, checked with legal.

First, consent. Some states require every party on a call to agree to the recording, so I'd confirm with legal how calls are disclosed. Then what our contracts and privacy policy let us do with them. If that is fine, I'd limit access, set a retention period, and share short clips or transcripts with personal details removed rather than full recordings open to everyone.
What goes into your go/no-go decision, and how do you set rollback criteria?
How you make a launch call on evidence agreed before the pressure of launch day.
Written readiness criteria per function, one named decision-maker, and rollback triggers with thresholds set in advance.

A short checklist each function signs off: engineering on quality and monitoring, support on articles and training, legal or security where needed. One person makes the call. Before launch we write down rollback triggers, like an error rate above an agreed level or a spike in one ticket tag, and who can turn the flag off. Deciding that early stops arguments on launch day.
You support six product teams. Which processes do you make standard, and where do you let teams work their own way?
Your judgement on where consistency matters and where it only adds overhead.
Standardizes what other functions depend on, like the launch calendar, tiers, feedback tags and release notes, and leaves internal rituals to teams.

I standardize what crosses team lines: the launch calendar, tier definitions, feedback tags and the release note format, because sales, support and leadership read those across all teams. How a team runs standups, writes specs or plans sprints is up to them. If one team's way works better, I'd rather copy it into the standard than force it out.
A launch slipped three weeks because nobody flagged that it needed a security review. How do you fix the process without adding red tape?
How you fix a process gap at its cause without slowing every team down.
A blameless look at why it was missed, then a trigger built into an existing step, like intake questions, instead of a new approval for everyone.

I'd first find out why it was missed: did the team not know the rule, or was it hard to see? Usually it's the second. I'd add two or three questions to the launch intake form, like whether it touches customer data or login, that route to security automatically. Teams that answer no lose nothing. Teams that answer yes find out in week one, not week six.
Walk me through retiring a feature that 5% of customers still use.
How you plan a deprecation so customers are not surprised and support is not flooded.
Usage data to find who is affected, a contract check, a timeline with several notices, a migration path, and support ready before the first notice.

I'd pull usage to see exactly which accounts use it and how much, and check contracts for any promised notice. Then a timeline: a first notice with the reason and the alternative, reminders, an in-app banner, and direct outreach to heavy users. Support gets a FAQ and a ticket tag before the first email. I'd watch that tag and move the date if migration stalls.
A new executive asks what product ops has actually delivered. How do you answer with evidence?
Whether you can measure your own function's impact, not only its activity.
Outcomes with before-and-after numbers, like time to launch, post-launch ticket spikes or hours saved, plus honesty about what is hard to attribute.

I'd skip activity counts and show outcomes. For example, time from code complete to launch went from five weeks to three after we set up tiers, ticket spikes after launches fell because support was trained earlier, and teams spend fewer hours on status reports. I'd say plainly which numbers are clean comparisons and which other changes also helped.

production-planner.heading: Production planner questions
qs: What is the difference between the master production schedule and MRP?
Whether you know the two core planning tools and how they connect.
The MPS sets which finished goods are built, how many and when; MRP turns that into dated part needs using the BOM, stock and lead times.

The master production schedule says which finished products we build, how many, and in which week. MRP takes that plan, explodes it through the bill of materials, subtracts stock on hand and open orders, and offsets by lead time. The result tells us which parts to buy or make, and when.
What is a bill of materials, and what happens when it is wrong?
Your grasp of the data that every plan depends on.
A clear definition, the real effect of a bad BOM (shortages or excess), and fixing it at the source with engineering.

It is the list of every part and quantity that goes into one unit, often in levels. Once a gasket was listed at one per unit when the unit used two, so MRP ordered half of what we needed and the line stopped mid-order. I got engineering to correct the BOM in the system instead of patching it in a spreadsheet.
How do you set safety stock for a part?
Whether you size buffers on risk rather than habit.
Based on demand swings, lead time length and reliability, and the cost of running out, then reviewed on a schedule.

I look at how much demand moves, how long the supplier lead time is and how much it varies, and how bad a stockout would be. A steady part from a reliable local supplier needs little. A single-source import with lumpy demand needs more. I review it every quarter so it does not stay padded after the risk is gone.
What is a frozen zone in a schedule, and why do plants use one?
Your understanding of schedule stability and the cost of late changes.
The near-term window that does not change without approval, because material and labor are committed and changes there are costly.

It is the next week or two of the schedule, where we do not change anything without sign-off. Material is staged, people are assigned and the line is set up, so a change there means overtime, extra changeovers and expediting. Further out, changes are cheap, so that is where I want sales to bring new requests.
How do you find the bottleneck in a plant, and how do you plan around it?
Whether you plan to the constraint instead of to every machine equally.
Compares load to capacity by work center, notes where work piles up, and protects the constraint with buffers and priority.

I compare the load against capacity for each work center, and I walk the floor: the bottleneck is usually where work-in-process piles up and the machine never waits. Then I schedule it first, keep a small buffer of parts in front of it, cover breaks so it keeps running, and only feed it work we need. An hour lost there is an hour lost for the whole plant.
How do you sequence jobs on a line with long changeovers?
How you balance setup time against due dates.
Groups similar setups to cut changeovers, follows rules like allergen-free before allergen runs, and still checks every due date.

I group jobs with similar setups: light colors before dark, one size family at a time, and in food plants allergen-free products before allergen ones, then a full cleanup. On a paint line, going light to dark cut our flushes from six a day to three. But I check due dates first; a perfect sequence that makes an order late is not a good plan.
MRP tells you to order 5,000 of a part that the floor uses about 1,000 of a month. What do you check?
Whether you question system output before acting on it.
Checks the inputs (demand, BOM, unit of measure, on-hand, lot rules, open orders) and fixes the root data, not just this order.

I do not place it until I know why. I check whether a big order or forecast hit the master schedule, then the BOM quantity and unit of measure, since boxes versus single pieces is a common mistake. Then on-hand accuracy, minimum order rules, and receipts not yet entered. Once I find the cause, I fix the data so it does not happen again.
Your capacity plan shows a key line loaded at 120% next month. What do you do?
How you solve an overload with real options and trade-offs.
Verifies the routing data, then lays out options like overtime, shifting work, building ahead or moving dates, with costs for each.

First I check that the routing times behind the load are right; a wrong cycle time can make an overload look worse than it is. If it is real, I list options: overtime or a Saturday shift, moving some work to another line, building ahead this month at an inventory cost, or moving low-priority dates. I bring those with costs to the operations manager.
Sales wants you to fit a rush order for a big customer into next week. Walk me through how you decide.
Your judgement when one customer's gain may be another's delay.
Checks material and capacity, shows what would move and what it costs, and lets the right person decide rather than quietly bumping orders.

I check if the material is on hand or can arrive in time, and whether the bottleneck has room. Then I give sales clear options: we can ship it Friday if another order slips three days, or with Saturday overtime at a known cost. Someone with authority chooses which customer waits. I never quietly bump an order and let a customer find out late.
Tell me about a time your schedule failed. What went wrong and what did you change?
Whether you own planning mistakes and build a fix into your process.
An honest example, the real cause, and a lasting change to how you plan, not just a one-time recovery.

I planned a week around a new die the toolmaker said would arrive Monday. It came Thursday, and I had no backup, so two shifts sat on other filler work. Now any job that depends on new tooling needs a confirmed ship date before I schedule it, and I keep a ready backup job with material staged. We have not lost a shift to tooling since.
When would you use lot-for-lot instead of a fixed order quantity or EOQ?
Whether you know the main lot-sizing rules and their trade-offs.
Lot-for-lot keeps stock low for expensive or lumpy items. Fixed or economic quantities fit cheap, steady parts where each order or setup has a real cost.

Lot-for-lot orders exactly the net requirement for each period, so I use it for expensive parts, custom parts and anything with lumpy demand. For cheap, steady parts where each order or setup has a real cost, a fixed quantity or EOQ makes sense: EOQ balances ordering cost against holding cost. Then I round to supplier minimums and pack sizes.
What is the difference between rough-cut capacity planning and capacity requirements planning?
Your grasp of the capacity check at each level of the plan.
Rough-cut tests the master schedule against key resources using load profiles. CRP uses MRP orders and routings to show detailed load by work center.

Rough-cut checks the master schedule against a few critical resources, using a load profile per product, like hours per unit on the bottleneck. It is fast and catches an impossible plan early. CRP comes after MRP: it takes planned and released orders, applies routings, and shows load by work center by period. It is more detailed, but only as good as the routings.
What is pegging, and when do you use it?
Whether you can trace a component need back to the order that drives it.
Pegging links a requirement to the parent and customer orders behind it. You use it to see which orders a shortage or late purchase order really hurts.

Pegging shows where a component requirement comes from: which parent orders, and up to which customer order or forecast. When a buyer says a part will be two weeks late, I peg it up. If it only covers forecast, I can shift things quietly. If it hits a firm order for a key customer, I escalate and look for substitutes or a partial build.
Which parts would you take off MRP and run on kanban, and how would you size the loops?
How you choose between push and pull planning for a part.
Kanban for steady, repeat parts with short, reliable replenishment. Loop size from demand over replenishment time plus a buffer, divided by container size.

Kanban fits parts with steady daily use and short, reliable replenishment, like fasteners or common subassemblies. Lumpy or custom items stay on MRP. To size a loop: daily demand times replenishment lead time in days, plus a safety margin, divided by the container quantity, rounded up. I recheck the card count when demand shifts, not once a year.
How does planning change between make-to-stock, assemble-to-order and make-to-order products?
Whether you know where the master schedule sits for each strategy.
Make-to-stock schedules end items to forecast. Assemble-to-order schedules modules, often with planning bills, and final assembly runs to orders. Make-to-order waits for the order.

For make-to-stock I master-schedule finished goods against forecast and a stock target. For assemble-to-order I master-schedule the modules, often with a planning bill that splits the family forecast by option percentages, and final assembly is scheduled when the order arrives. For make-to-order the order drives most of it, so I may stock only long-lead raw material.
Demand is seasonal with a summer peak. Would you level production or chase demand?
Your judgement on production strategy at the sales and operations planning level.
Weighs carrying cost, space and shelf life against overtime, hiring and capacity limits. Often lands on a hybrid with a planned build-ahead.

Level means a steady rate and building stock before the peak. Chase means changing output with overtime, temps or extra shifts. I price both: carrying cost, storage space and obsolescence risk against overtime premiums, training temps and quality dips. Usually I propose a hybrid: a steady base rate, a build-ahead starting in spring, and overtime for the top weeks.
MRP gives you 400 reschedule messages every morning. How do you deal with that?
How you control system nervousness instead of chasing every message.
Filters by tolerance and impact, fixes root causes like bad lead times or noisy lot sizing, and uses firm planned orders and time fences.

I do not act on all 400. I set tolerances so small date moves are ignored, and I sort by impact: shortages against firm orders first. Then I look for causes: wrong lead times, stale open orders, lot-for-lot on noisy parts, or a master schedule that changes daily. Firm planned orders and an agreed time fence calm most of the rest.
Engineering releases a change that replaces a component. How do you plan the cutover?
Whether you can manage an engineering change without stranding old stock or stopping the line.
Asks if the change must cut in now or can use run-out, sets the effectivity date, adjusts open orders, and plans old stock to zero or to scrap with a cost.

First I ask whether it is a safety or fit issue that must cut in now, or whether we may use up the old part. If run-out is allowed, I count on-hand and open orders of the old part, cancel what I can, and set the effectivity date when old stock reaches zero. If it must cut in, I set the date, quarantine old stock and get a cost for scrap or rework.
A component short for two weeks goes into two products, one high-margin and one for your largest customer. How do you allocate it?
How you make an allocation call with clear rules and the right people involved.
Pegs firm orders and dates, checks contracts and penalties, brings options with numbers, and gets sales and leadership to decide.

I peg the demand to see which orders are firm and when they ship. Then I check contracts, penalties and stock already at the customer. I bring sales and the plant manager two or three options, like covering the big customer's firm orders and splitting the rest, with revenue and late orders for each. They decide, and I write down the rule for next time.
Schedule adherence is at 60% and supervisors run their own priorities. How do you fix it?
Whether you can find why a schedule is not trusted and rebuild that trust.
Looks at the plan side first, like overloading or missing material, makes the schedule doable, then measures adherence openly with the floor.

I would first ask why. Usually the schedule is not doable: it is loaded past real capacity, or material is missing when the job starts, so supervisors skip ahead. I would load to demonstrated rates, release only jobs with material on hand, and hold a short daily meeting with supervisors. Then I track adherence by line and review misses together, without blame.

production-supervisor.heading: Production supervisor and plant manager questions
qs: What is OEE, and how do you calculate it?
Whether you know the basic measure of how well a line uses its time.
The three factors multiplied together, each defined correctly, and a word on why the split matters more than the total.

OEE is availability times performance times quality. Availability is run time over planned time. Performance is actual output against the ideal cycle rate. Quality is good parts over total parts. A line running 90% of planned time at 90% speed with 98% good parts has an OEE of about 79%. The useful part is seeing which loss is biggest.
Walk me through how you start a shift.
How you take over a line and get a crew aligned in the first hour.
A face-to-face handover, a short crew huddle with numbers, plan and safety, then time on the floor early.

I get the handover from the outgoing supervisor at the line, not by text: what ran, what is down, open quality holds, safety issues. Then I hold a ten-minute huddle with the crew: yesterday's numbers, today's plan, staffing moves, one safety point. After that I walk the lines, because problems are cheapest to fix early in the shift.
What is takt time, and how do you use it on the floor?
Your grasp of pacing production to customer demand.
Available time divided by demand, a worked example, and using it to spot stations that cannot keep pace.
