Takt time is available production time divided by customer demand. With 450 minutes of run time and 900 units ordered, takt is 30 seconds a unit. If any station's cycle time is over 30 seconds, that station sets our pace and we miss demand. That is where I rebalance the work or add help.
Two hours into the shift, the line is 15% behind plan. What do you do?
How you find and fix a shortfall while the shift can still recover.
Going to the line, finding the bottleneck and its cause, protecting it, and warning the manager early with a real number.

I go to the line, not the report. I look for the bottleneck: work piling up before a station and the next one starved. Then I find why: a breakdown, a missing person, late material, a reject loop. I fix what I can, keep the bottleneck running through breaks, and tell my manager early with a realistic end-of-shift number.
You find an operator running a machine with the guard bypassed. What do you do?
Whether you act on a serious hazard at once and also fix the reason behind it.
Stop the machine now, no restart until the guard is restored, then find out why and remove the cause, with documentation.

I stop the machine right away, safely, and it does not run again until the guard is back and checked. Then I ask why, calmly. Often it is to clear jams faster, so the real fix is lockout for jam clearing and maintenance looking at the jams. I document it and follow our policy, but the bigger job is removing the reason to bypass.
Quality tells you a dimension has been out of spec for an unknown time on a running line. Walk me through your response.
How you contain a defect before it spreads or ships.
Stop making it, segregate back to the last known good check, sort with quality, fix the cause, restart on first-piece approval.

First I stop that operation so we make no more. Then I contain: tag and segregate everything back to the last check known to be good, including parts already in the warehouse. Quality and I agree a sort plan while maintenance finds the cause. We restart only after first-piece approval, and quality handles any customer notice.
A machine jams several times a shift, and maintenance just resets it each time. How do you get to the root cause?
Whether you replace quick fixes with data and real problem solving.
Logging each event with its conditions, asking why with the team, and a fix that is proven by the numbers afterward.

Resetting is a patch, so I start logging every jam: time, product, operator, material lot. Then the team and I ask why at the machine until we reach something we can fix. Once the jams tracked one supplier's carton lot that was slightly oversize. We added an incoming check, and jams fell from about eight a shift to one.
One of your best operators has been late four times this month. How do you handle it?
How you deal with a people problem fairly without losing a good worker.
A private, prompt talk with facts, listening for the cause, consistent use of policy, and notes kept.

I talk to him privately, soon, not at the huddle. I state the facts, ask what is going on and listen. If there is a fixable cause, like a childcare change, I look at what our policy allows. I am also clear the attendance rules apply to everyone, and I document the talk so it stays fair and consistent across the crew.
It is the last day of the month, you are short on an order, and someone suggests shipping parts just outside tolerance. What do you do?
Your judgement when output targets and quality pull against each other.
No shipping out-of-spec parts without a formal approved deviation, early honesty about the shortfall, and real recovery options.

I do not ship them. Only quality, and the customer where required, can approve a deviation, in writing. I tell my manager the real shortfall right away, look at overtime or a partial shipment, and let sales talk to the customer about a date. A late order hurts one month; a field failure can cost the customer.
You take over a plant with high scrap and low morale. What do you do in your first 90 days?
How you lead change across a whole operation, not just one shift.
Listening and data first, a few visible wins with the floor, a simple daily routine, and follow-through that builds trust.

The first month I listen: I walk every shift, talk to operators and read the scrap and injury data. Then I pick two or three problems, like the top scrap causes, and fix them with the people on the floor. I set a short daily meeting on safety, quality and output. Morale usually follows when people see their ideas used and old problems stay fixed.
When does a workplace injury become OSHA recordable, and how is that different from first aid?
Your working knowledge of OSHA injury recordkeeping.
Days away, restricted duty, treatment beyond first aid, loss of consciousness or a significant diagnosis makes it recordable. The record is honest, never steered.

It is recordable if it causes days away, restricted work or a job transfer, medical treatment beyond first aid, loss of consciousness, or a significant diagnosed injury. Cleaning a cut, a bandage or Steri-Strips are first aid; stitches are medical treatment. I never push a clinic toward first aid to protect a number. A hidden injury hides the hazard too.
Walk me through how you would cut a changeover from 90 minutes to under 30.
Whether you can apply SMED, the quick changeover method, on a real machine.
Time the current changeover, split internal from external steps, move work outside the stop, simplify the rest, and lock it in as standard work.

First I video one changeover and list every step with its time. Then I separate internal steps, which need the machine stopped, from external ones like fetching tools or preheating dies, which can happen while it runs. I move all I can outside the stop, then shorten the rest: quick clamps, preset tooling, two people in parallel. The new method becomes the written standard.
The plant wants to buy a faster machine for a station that is not the bottleneck. What do you say?
Whether you understand constraints and where real capacity comes from.
Output is set by the bottleneck; speeding up another station adds inventory, not shipments. Money and attention go to the constraint first.

I would ask what problem it solves. The plant can only ship what the bottleneck makes, so a faster machine upstream just builds a bigger pile in front of it. I would first keep the bottleneck running through breaks and changeovers, make sure it never works on a part that gets scrapped later, and offload work from it. If we still need capacity, we buy it there.
A customer asks for a Cpk of 1.33 on a critical dimension. What does that mean, and how would you get there?
Your grasp of process capability and how to improve it.
Cpk compares the distance from the mean to the nearest spec limit with three standard deviations. You raise it by centering the process and cutting variation.

Cpk takes the distance from the process average to the nearer spec limit and divides it by three standard deviations. At 1.33 that nearest limit sits four standard deviations away. First I confirm the process is stable and the gauge is reliable, because a poor measurement system shows up as variation. Then I center the average and attack the biggest sources of variation.
An engineer wants to change a temperature setting mid-run to fix a defect, with no paperwork. How do you handle it?
How you balance a quick fix against change control and traceability.
No undocumented process changes. A trial is fine as a recorded, approved deviation with quality involved and the affected parts identified.

I want the defect fixed too, so I do not just say no. We write it up as a temporary deviation: what changes, the limits, who approved it, with quality signing off. We tag and hold the parts made during the trial so they can be traced. If it works, it goes through the normal change process and the setup sheet is updated, so the next shift runs the same process.
Day shift and night shift keep blaming each other for problems left at shift change. How do you fix it?
How you build accountability across shifts.
A structured face-to-face handover, shared metrics for both shifts, and a manager who gathers facts on both shifts instead of taking sides.

I would set a fixed handover: ten minutes, face to face at the line, with one written sheet covering safety issues, machine status, quality holds and open work. Both leads sign it. Both shifts go on the same board so it is one team's numbers. Then I would work a few nights myself. Blame often comes from people who never see each other's conditions.
Tell me about a 5S or kaizen improvement you led that slipped back within a few months. What went wrong?
Whether you learn from improvements that did not stick.
Honest ownership of the cause, often no owner, no standard and no audit, plus a concrete change in how gains are sustained.

We redid a cell in one week, and three months later the shadow boards were half empty. I had run it as an event and moved on. The operators had not designed it, and nobody checked it. Next time the cell team led the layout, each area got an owner, and leaders did a five-minute weekly audit with scores posted. That cell held for over a year.
One of your supervisors hits every output target, but his crew has the highest turnover in the plant. What do you do?
How you judge and coach leaders on more than output.
Gets facts from exit data and the floor, talks to him directly, sets clear expectations with follow-up, and treats turnover as a real cost.

First I look at facts: exit interviews, transfer requests, overtime and safety records for his crew. I spend time on his line. Then I tell him plainly that numbers built by burning people out are not results; every person we lose costs hiring and training time. We agree on specific behaviors, I check in weekly, and retention becomes part of his review.
An operator on your shift loses part of a finger in a press. Walk me through the first 24 hours.
How you lead through a serious injury, including OSHA reporting duties.
Care first, secure the scene, report the amputation to OSHA within 24 hours, investigate the root cause, and check similar machines.

Care first: first aid, call 911, and someone stays with him. Any severed part goes in a clean bag kept cool, not directly on ice. I lock out the press and keep the scene untouched. An amputation must be reported to OSHA within 24 hours, so I make sure that happens. Then we interview witnesses, find why the guarding failed, and check every similar press before it runs.

production-worker.heading: Production worker and machine operator questions
qs: The drawing says 1.250 inches, plus or minus 0.005. Your part measures 1.257. Is it good?
Whether you can read a tolerance and make the call on a part.
The right range, 1.245 to 1.255, a clear reject, and a second measurement before tagging the part.

No. Plus or minus 0.005 means anything from 1.245 to 1.255 is good, so 1.257 is 0.002 over. I would measure it again to rule out my own error, then tag it as reject, set it aside and check the parts made just before it.
How do you use a go/no-go gauge on a hole?
Your hands-on knowledge of a basic inspection tool.
The go end must enter and the no-go end must not; the gauge is checked for a current calibration label and never forced.

The go end has to slide into the hole and the no-go end must not go in. If both go in, the hole is too big; if the go end won't enter, it's too small. I never force it, I keep the gauge clean, and I check the calibration sticker is current before I use it.
What does 5S mean on a shop floor?
Whether you know the basic workplace organization method most plants use.
The five steps named and explained in practical terms, with the point that it makes problems visible.

Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardize and Sustain. You remove what you don't need, give every tool a marked place, keep the area clean, make it the same way every shift, and keep doing it. At my last station, a shadow board showed right away when a gauge was missing.
What is takt time, and why should an operator care about it?
Your understanding of line pace and how your station fits into it.
Takt is available time divided by customer demand; a station slower than takt holds up the whole line.

Takt time is the available production time divided by the number of units needed. If we have 450 minutes and need 900 parts, that's one part every 30 seconds. If my station takes 35 seconds, the line can't keep up, so I tell the lead instead of rushing and making scrap.
Walk me through what you do when you take over a machine at the start of a shift.
How you start work with the right information and a machine you have checked.
Talks to the outgoing operator, reads the log and job paperwork, checks guards, fluids and gauges, and verifies the first parts.

I talk to the operator going off: what's running, any problems, any parts on hold. I read the shift log and the job traveler. Then I walk the machine: guards in place, air and oil levels, no leaks, gauges calibrated. I check the first few parts before I settle into the rhythm.
What is a first-piece inspection, and when do you do one?
Whether you know to prove a setup before running production.
After every setup, changeover or major adjustment, the first part is checked against the drawing and signed off before the run continues.

After a setup, a changeover, a tool change or a big adjustment, I run one part and stop. I check every critical dimension and feature against the drawing and get it signed off by quality or the lead. Only then do I run the batch. It costs ten minutes and can save a whole lot of scrap.
A part jams inside your machine. Walk me through clearing it.
Whether you lock out a machine before reaching into it.
Machine stopped, own lock and tag on every energy source, stored energy released, zero energy tested, then the jam cleared and reported if it repeats.

I stop the machine and tell the people nearby. I shut off and lock every energy source with my own lock and tag, bleed the air, and block anything that could drop. Then I press start to prove it won't run. Only then do I reach in. If it keeps jamming, I report it so maintenance finds the cause.
Halfway through a run, you find a part that is out of spec. What do you do?
How you contain a quality problem before it spreads.
Stops the run, isolates suspect parts back to the last good check, tags them, and tells the lead or quality before restarting.

I stop the machine first. Then I go back to the last part I know was good and set aside everything made since, in a red tagged bin, so nothing gets mixed in. I tell my lead and quality, and we find the cause before I restart. Last time it was a worn insert, and we caught 40 parts, not 400.
You see a coworker taping down a guard interlock so the machine runs faster. What do you do?
Your judgement when safety and output pull in different directions.
Speaks up right away, does not run the machine bypassed, and reports it so the real problem behind the shortcut gets fixed.

I'd tell him to stop and pull the tape, calmly, right then. An interlock is there so the machine can't move when a hand is inside. If he refused, I'd go to the lead at once. Usually the shortcut means the guard is slowing the job, so I'd also ask that someone look at why, so nobody feels the need to bypass it.
Your lead says to keep shipping parts that are just out of tolerance because the truck leaves at 3. What do you do?
How you handle pressure to pass bad parts.
Does not pass nonconforming parts on their own say-so; points to the quality process, such as a deviation approved by quality, and offers ways to save the shipment.

I'd say I can't pass parts I know are out, but I want to help make the truck. Quality or the customer can approve a deviation if the part still works; that is their call, in writing. Meanwhile I'd sort the good parts from the bad and see if we can fix the setup and run more good ones before 3.
Why is hitting the emergency stop not the same as locking out a machine?
Whether you know the difference between stopping a machine and isolating its energy.
The E-stop only stops motion through the controls; lockout cuts the energy at the source, under your own lock, and you prove it is dead.

The E-stop stops motion through the control circuit, but the power is still there. Someone can reset it, a fault can restart it, and air or hydraulic pressure stays in the lines. Lockout means I shut off the energy at the disconnect or valve, put my own lock and tag on it, and then try to start the machine to prove it will not run.
The calibration sticker on your micrometer expired last week. Can you still use it?
Whether you trust only measuring tools that are in calibration.
No. Pull the tool, get a calibrated one, and tell quality so they can decide on parts measured after the due date.

No. Once the sticker is past due, I cannot prove the readings are right. I set it aside with a tag and take it to the crib or quality for calibration. I switch to a calibrated mic, and I tell quality which lots I checked with the old one since the due date, so they can decide whether to recheck them.
An assembly calls for six bolts torqued in a star pattern. Why the pattern, and how do you use the torque wrench?
Your skill with torque and why the order of tightening matters.
The pattern clamps the part evenly. Tighten in steps, pull smoothly to the click, use a calibrated wrench, and store it at its lowest setting.

Going across in a star pulls the parts together evenly, so a flange or cover does not tilt or leak. I snug all bolts first, then go around in two or three steps up to the final value. I pull slowly and stop at the click, never past it. I check the calibration date and turn a click wrench back to its lowest setting when I put it away.
What is the difference between internal and external work in a changeover?
Whether you know how to cut machine downtime during a changeover.
Internal work needs the machine stopped; external work can be done while it runs. Move as much as possible to external.

Internal work can only happen with the machine stopped, like swapping the die. External work can be done while the last job is still running: staging the next tooling, pulling the program, getting gauges and material ready. On one changeover I just prepared everything on a cart before the run ended, and we cut the stop by about 20 minutes.
Your control chart shows the last several points climbing steadily toward the upper control limit, but every part is still in spec. What do you do?
How you read a process trend before it makes bad parts.
A steady trend means the process is changing, even inside spec. React now: find the cause, adjust per procedure, and tell the lead.

Control limits show what the process normally does; spec limits show what the customer accepts. A steady climb means something is changing, like tool wear, heat or a new lot of material. I would not wait for a bad part. I would check the likely causes, make an adjustment if my procedure allows it, note it on the chart and tell my lead.
On a CNC lathe, the outside diameter grows a little every hour. What is likely happening, and how do you correct it?
Your grasp of tool wear and how an operator makes offset adjustments.
The insert is wearing, so the cut gets shallower and the diameter grows. Adjust the wear offset in small steps, check the next part, and change the insert at its limit.

Most likely the insert is wearing, so it cuts a little less and the diameter grows. I would measure, then change the wear offset by a small amount, not the geometry offset, and check the next part. If the drift is fast or the finish gets rough, I change the insert. I also note it, so the team can plan insert changes before parts drift.
You have locked out the electrical disconnect on a press that has an air-powered clamp. Is it safe to reach in?
Whether you know to control every energy source, including stored energy.
Not yet. Lock the air valve too, bleed the pressure to zero, block parts that could drop, then test that nothing moves.

Not yet. The air is a second energy source. I close and lock the air supply valve, open the dump to bleed the lines and check that the gauge reads zero. If the ram or anything else could drop by gravity, I put in a block. Then I try the controls to make sure nothing moves. Only after that do I put my hands in.
You find two different lots of the same component mixed in one bin at your station. What do you do?
How you protect traceability when material gets mixed up.
Stop using the bin, tag it on hold, tell the lead or quality, and help work out which lot went into which finished units.

I stop pulling from that bin. Our records link each finished unit to the lot inside it, and now we cannot say which lot is in which unit. I tag the bin on hold, tell my lead and quality, and write down what I have built since I started on it. I would not guess by how the parts look; quality decides whether to sort, scrap or trace the units.
You come in and find another person's lock on a machine you need, and that person has gone home. What do you do?
Whether you respect lockout rules when they slow you down.
Never remove or cut it yourself. The supervisor follows the written removal procedure: confirm they are gone, try to reach them, and make sure they know first.

I do not touch it. That lock means someone's safety, or a job left half done. I tell my supervisor. Under our written procedure, the supervisor confirms the person is not in the building, tries to reach them, checks the machine is safe to run, and makes sure they are told before they start their next shift. Until then, I work on something else.
The same defect comes back after every changeover, and each shift just fixes it and moves on. How would you get to the root cause?
How you turn a repeated fix into a lasting solution.
Collect data across changeovers, ask why until you reach a cause you can control, then lock in the fix with standard work or error-proofing and check it holds.

I would start by writing down every time it happens: which shift, which setup, what was adjusted. Then I ask why, again and again. In one case the cause was a locator pin that could go in two ways. We made it fit only one way and added a check to the setup sheet. I would watch the next ten changeovers to prove the defect is gone.

professional-services.heading: Professional services consultant questions
qs: What is the difference between configuring a product and customizing it?
Whether you know the basic choice behind every implementation.
Configuration uses built-in settings and survives upgrades. Customization adds code or scripts that someone must own and retest.

Configuring means using the settings the product already offers: fields, workflows, roles, rules. Customizing means writing code or scripts to make it do something it does not do out of the box. I configure first, because it is supported and survives upgrades. Custom code needs an owner, documentation and retesting at every release.
Walk me through how you run a discovery session with a new customer.
How you gather requirements before building anything.
Prepared questions, the right people in the room, the current process mapped, and a written summary the customer confirms.

I send a short agenda and ask for the people who do the work, not only the sponsor. They walk me through the current process step by step, including the workarounds. I ask what success looks like in numbers. Within two days I send a written summary of requirements and open questions, and I ask them to confirm it before we design anything.
How does working on a fixed-fee project differ from time and materials?
Your understanding of how services work is sold and billed.
Fixed fee puts the cost of overruns on the provider, so scope control matters more. Time and materials bills actual hours, so tracking and early warnings matter.

On time and materials the customer pays for the hours we work, so I log time accurately and warn them early if the estimate is slipping. On fixed fee the price is set, so every hour over the plan is our cost. There I am stricter about scope: anything not in the statement of work goes through a change request before I start it.
What do you need from the customer before you start building an integration with their system?
Whether you know what an integration depends on before any code is written.
A technical owner, documentation, test credentials, and an agreed data flow: direction, frequency, and which system is the source of truth.

I need a technical contact on their side, API documentation, and credentials for a test environment, not production. We agree which system owns each piece of data, which direction it flows and how often it syncs. I also ask about rate limits, firewall rules and who gets the alert when a sync fails. Missing any of these usually costs weeks later.
Halfway through, the customer asks for a report that is not in the statement of work. What do you do?
How you handle scope creep without damaging the relationship.
No silent yes: acknowledge the need, size it, raise a change request, and let the customer choose.

I say it sounds useful and that it is outside what we agreed, so I want to size it properly. I estimate the hours, note the effect on the timeline, and send it through our change request process with my project manager. The customer then decides: add it now, swap it for something else, or park it until after go-live. I do not build it quietly.
How do you plan a data migration from a customer's old system?
Your method for moving data safely and accurately.
Field mapping, cleanup owned by the customer, test loads, reconciliation of counts and totals, and a clear cutover plan.

First I map every old field to a new one and agree with the customer what is not coming over. They own cleaning duplicates and bad records; I give them reports to find them. I run at least one test load into a sandbox and reconcile record counts and key totals with them. Then we set a cutover window, freeze changes in the old system and do the final load.
An integration you built works most of the time but drops records every few days. How do you find the cause?
How you troubleshoot an intermittent integration failure.
Logs and patterns first, then common causes like expired tokens, rate limits, timeouts and bad data, plus recovery of the missed records.

I pull the logs for the failed runs and look for a pattern: same time of day, same record type, same error code. Common causes are an expired auth token, hitting the API rate limit in a busy batch, a timeout, or a value the other system rejects. Once the cause is fixed, I replay the dropped records and add an alert so failures are seen the same day.
You are 40% through the budgeted hours but only 20% through the work. What do you do?
How you manage a project budget and raise overruns early.
Find out why, tell the project manager now with numbers, and come with options: change request, rescope or a reset plan.

First I find out why: a bad estimate, extra requests we absorbed, or the customer being slow with data. Then I tell my project manager right away, with numbers. If extra requests are the cause, they become change requests. If our estimate was wrong, we decide internally how to recover and reset the plan with the customer. Hiding it only makes the gap bigger.
Go-live is in a week and the customer's team has barely started user acceptance testing. What do you do?
Your judgement when a launch date is at risk.
Raise the risk in writing early, propose a focused test plan, and let the sponsor decide on the date with the facts.

I tell the sponsor that day, in writing, what has and has not been tested. I propose a short plan: the ten processes the business cannot run without, with named testers and a daily check-in. If those are not signed off by a set date, I recommend moving go-live. The decision is theirs, but they make it with the facts.
The customer insists on custom code you think will break at the next product upgrade. How do you handle it?
Your judgement in pushing back on a risky design while still serving the customer.
Explain the risk in business terms, offer a supported alternative, and if they still insist, document the decision and its upkeep cost.

I explain the risk plainly: every release, someone will need to retest and maybe rewrite this, and that is an ongoing cost. Then I show what the product can do out of the box, often most of what they want. If they still want the custom version, I build it with documentation and tests, and I record in writing that they accepted the upkeep. It is their call.
The customer's admin wants to connect the integration with his own login. Why might you push back?
Whether you know how integrations fail when they depend on one person's account.
A dedicated integration account with only the permissions it needs, so it survives staff changes and its actions stay traceable.

If the integration runs under his account, it stops the day he leaves, changes his password or loses his access. Every change it makes also shows his name in the audit log. I ask for a dedicated integration user with only the rights the sync needs, and I write down who owns its credentials.
What goes into a statement of work so that it still protects both sides six months later?
How you write scope that settles arguments instead of starting them.
Countable deliverables, written assumptions, explicit out-of-scope items, customer duties, acceptance criteria and a change process.

I list each deliverable in countable terms, like three integrations and up to 20 reports, not "reporting setup". I write the assumptions, what is out of scope, and what the customer must provide and by when. Each deliverable gets an acceptance test, and there is a change request process so new asks have a path.
What does it mean for an integration to be idempotent, and why do you care?
Your grasp of how integrations behave when the same message arrives twice.
Processing a message twice leaves the same result as once, done with unique external IDs and upserts so retries do not create duplicates.

It means that if the same record arrives twice, the end state is the same as if it arrived once. Networks fail and systems retry, so duplicates will happen. I key records on a unique external ID and use upsert, meaning update if it exists and insert if not, so a retried order does not become two orders.
How do you prove to a customer that a data migration is complete and correct?
Whether you validate a migration with evidence, not a feeling.
Counts and totals reconciled between source and target, rejected rows logged, records spot-checked by users, and sign-off before cutover.

I reconcile record counts per object, plus control totals like the sum of open invoice balances, between the old system and the new one. Every rejected row is logged with a reason. Then the customer's own users check a sample of records they know well, including odd cases, and sign off on each mock run before the real one.
The customer's nightly sync started failing with HTTP 429 errors after their data volume doubled. What do you do?
How you handle API rate limits in a live integration.
Knows 429 means too many requests; retries with backoff, honors Retry-After, batches calls and syncs only what changed.

429 means "too many requests": we are hitting the API's rate limit. First I make failed calls retry with exponential backoff, waiting longer each time, and respect the Retry-After header if the API sends one. Then I cut the volume: bulk endpoints where they exist, and syncing only records changed since the last run instead of everything.
A customer emails you a spreadsheet with employees' Social Security numbers for the migration. What do you do?
Whether you protect sensitive data even when the customer is careless with it.
Stops the spread, follows the company's data handling policy, moves to an approved secure channel and asks if the field is needed at all.

I don't forward it or save it to my laptop. I tell our security contact, follow our policy for removing it from email, and ask the customer to resend through our approved secure transfer. I also ask whether the new system needs the full numbers. If not, we leave them out, because data we never hold cannot leak.
The customer wants the new product set up to copy their old process step for step. How do you respond?
How you balance what the customer asks for with what the product does well.
Asks why each step exists, runs a fit-gap review, shows the standard way where it meets the need, and keeps custom work for real requirements.

I walk the old process with them and ask why each step exists. Some steps guard against a real risk; others were workarounds for the old system. Where the product's standard flow meets the need, I demo it, since standard setups cost less to maintain and survive upgrades. Real gaps go on a list with costs so they decide with numbers.
How do you estimate a project type your team has never delivered before?
Your estimating method when there is no history to copy.
Breaks work into small pieces, gives ranges not one number, writes assumptions down and proposes discovery or contingency for unknowns.

I break it into tasks small enough to estimate, a few days each at most, and give a low and a high figure for each. I borrow from the closest past project and note where it differs. Every assumption goes in writing. If the unknowns are big, I propose a paid discovery phase first, then a firm estimate once we have seen their systems.
Walk me through the cutover plan for a go-live weekend.
Whether you can run a go-live with a planned way back if it fails.
A rehearsed, timed runbook with owners, a data freeze, final load and checks, agreed go/no-go criteria and a rollback point set in advance.

We rehearse it at least once. The runbook lists every step, its owner and its time. Friday evening users stop entering data in the old system, we take a backup, run the final load and reconcile. At a set hour the sponsor and I check agreed go/no-go criteria. If we miss them, we roll back to the old system, kept ready, and pick a new date.
Midway through, the customer's executive sponsor leaves and the new one questions the whole scope. What do you do?
How you protect a project when the person who backed it is gone.
Meets the new sponsor fast, learns their goals, shows what was agreed and delivered, and turns real changes into a formal change request.

I ask for a meeting in the first week and mostly listen: what does she need this project to deliver? Then I show the signed scope, what is done and what remains, tied to business goals. Where her priorities differ, we write a change request with cost and timeline instead of drifting. I also tell my own leadership, since the account may be at risk.

program-manager.heading: Program and project manager questions
qs: What is the difference between a project and a program?
Whether you know the basic terms of the trade.
A project delivers a defined output and then ends. A program groups related projects to reach a benefit none of them reaches alone.

A project is a temporary effort with a set scope, like building a new billing page. A program is a group of related projects managed together because the value comes from them combined, like moving all customers to a new billing system. In a program I spend more time on the links between projects and on whether the business result actually shows up.
What is the critical path, and why do you watch it?
Your grasp of how schedules actually work.
The longest chain of dependent tasks sets the earliest finish date. A slip on it moves the end date, and the path itself can shift.

It is the longest chain of dependent tasks from start to finish, so it sets the earliest date we can finish. Tasks on it usually have no float, meaning any slip moves the end date. I check it every week, because when a task off the path slips far enough, it can become the new critical path without anyone noticing.
How do you set up a RACI, and where does it usually go wrong?
Whether you can make ownership clear across many teams.
Exactly one Accountable person per deliverable, named Responsible people, and a short Consulted list so decisions do not stall.

RACI stands for Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed. I list the main deliverables and decisions, then name exactly one Accountable person for each. It goes wrong when two people are Accountable, so no one really is, or when everyone is Consulted and a decision needs ten sign-offs. I review it with the leads before kickoff so they agree to it in the room.
How is your status update for executives different from the one for the working team?
How you tailor stakeholder updates to the audience.
Executives get overall status, the key risks and the decisions needed from them. The team gets tasks, owners, dates and blockers.

For executives I keep it to one page: overall status with a reason, the top three risks, and any decision I need from them by a set date. For the team I go into tasks, owners, dependencies and blockers for the next two weeks. If an executive has to read three paragraphs to find out whether we are on track, I wrote it wrong.
Walk me through how you build the first schedule for a program that spans five teams.
Your method for turning a goal into a plan many teams can commit to.
Break the work down, get estimates from the people doing it, map the hand-offs between teams, add buffer, then baseline it.

I start with the end goal and major milestones, then break the work into deliverables each team owns. Each team estimates its own work; I do not guess for them. Then I map the hand-offs between teams, because that is where programs slip. I find the critical path, add buffer at integration points, review it with all leads, and only then set the baseline.
Your CPI is 0.85 and your SPI is 1.05. What does that tell you?
Whether you can read earned value numbers and act on them.
Over budget but slightly ahead of schedule, which often means money is buying speed. Find the cause and update the final cost forecast.

CPI is earned value divided by actual cost, so 0.85 means we get about 85 cents' worth of planned work for each dollar spent. SPI is earned value divided by planned value, so 1.05 means we are a bit ahead of schedule. Together that often means we are buying speed with overtime or extra contractors. I would find the cause and update the final cost forecast before the sponsor asks.
Two projects in your program need the same engineer in the same sprint. How do you decide?
How you resolve resource conflicts using program priorities, not who asks loudest.
Check which work is on the critical path and tied to the main goal, show the impact of each option, and escalate if it is not your call.

First I check whether both truly need that person, or whether someone else could cover one task after a short handover. If not, I look at which task is on the critical path and which serves the program's top goal. I write the impact of each choice in dates and agree it with both leads. If we cannot agree, I take both options to the sponsor with my recommendation.
Every team reports green, but integration is three weeks away and nothing has been tested together. What do you do?
Whether you look past status colors to the real risk.
Treats green without evidence as a risk, asks for proof, tests the riskiest connection early, and changes the program status honestly.

Green from each team only means each team's own part looks on track. Nobody owns the gaps between them. I would ask each lead for evidence, like a demo or interface tests, and set up an early end-to-end test of the riskiest connection this week. If that shows problems, I mark the program amber or red and say why, even if every team is still green.
Leadership wants the launch pulled in by a month. What options do you lay out?
Your knowledge of schedule compression and what it costs.
Crashing, fast-tracking and cutting scope, each with its cost and risk, plus an honest view of what date is realistic.

There are three main levers. Crashing means adding people or money to critical path tasks, but new people slow a team down at first. Fast-tracking means doing in parallel tasks we planned in sequence, which adds rework risk. Cutting scope means launching with less. I show each with its cost, risk and a realistic date, and say plainly if a month is not possible.
Tell me about a cross-team dependency you missed. How did you catch it and what changed?
How you own a planning mistake and fix the process behind it.
Honest ownership, a fast fix worked out with the affected teams, and a change to how dependencies get found next time.

On a data migration program, I missed that the reporting team needed the database structure frozen two weeks before cutover. Their lead raised it six weeks out. I met both teams that day, moved the freeze up and used part of our buffer. Since then I run a dependency session where each team states what it needs from the others and by when, and I track it in a shared log.
What is the difference between total float and free float?
Whether you read a schedule beyond the critical path.
Total float protects the end date; free float protects the next task. Using one task's float can eat a successor's room.

Total float is how long a task can slip before it moves the project finish date. Free float is how long it can slip before it delays the early start of the very next task. A task can have ten days of total float and zero free float. If it slips, the next team loses its start date even though launch is still safe, so I tell that team early.
A team lead gives you one number for a risky piece of work. How do you turn it into something you can plan with?
How you handle uncertainty in estimates.
Asks for a range (optimistic, most likely, pessimistic) and plans to a likely figure, not the best case, with the worst case shown as a risk.

I ask for three numbers: best case, most likely and worst case. Say 10, 15 and 32 days. A PERT estimate weights the middle: (10 + 4×15 + 32) / 6, about 17 days. I plan to that, show the 32 as the risk, and ask what would push us toward it. That answer usually becomes a new entry in the risk register.
You are hiring a vendor for part of the program. When would you choose a fixed-price contract, and when time and materials?
Your grasp of who carries cost risk in a contract.
Fixed price when scope is clear, since the seller carries overrun risk. Time and materials when scope is unclear, with a cap and close tracking.

Fixed price works when I can write a tight scope, like migrating a known set of reports. The vendor carries the overrun risk, but every change becomes a change order, so a vague scope gets expensive. If we are still discovering the work, time and materials is more honest, but the cost risk is ours. I set a not-to-exceed cap and review hours every week.
When is it right to rebaseline a schedule, and when is it not?
Whether you keep the baseline honest as a measure of performance.
Rebaseline after an approved change to scope, budget or date, never just to make variance disappear. Keep the old baseline for the record.

I rebaseline when the sponsor approves a real change, like a new market added to scope or a funded date move. I do not rebaseline just because we are late; that hides the problem and makes our variance numbers meaningless. When I do it, I keep the original baseline on file and note in the change log what moved and who approved it.
Four of your teams run two-week sprints, and one hardware vendor works to a fixed waterfall plan. How do you plan across them?
How you connect teams that plan in different ways.
Ties everyone to shared dated milestones and written interface agreements, and plans sprint work around the vendor's fixed delivery dates.

I do not force one method on everyone. I put the vendor's fixed dates, like prototype boards arriving in a given week, in as hard milestones. The sprint teams plan so their software is ready to test when the boards land. We agree the interfaces in writing early. At each sprint review I check the vendor's latest dates and adjust the sprint plans if they slip.
We are halfway through the budget. How do you forecast what the program will cost at the end?
Whether you can forecast cost from earned value, not just report what was spent.
Uses estimate at completion, picks the formula that fits the cause of the variance, and checks it against a bottom-up re-estimate.

I start from estimate at completion. If the overrun so far was a one-off, like a rush fee, EAC is actual cost plus the remaining planned work: AC + (BAC − EV). If it reflects how we really work, I use BAC divided by CPI. Then I ask each lead to re-estimate what is left and compare. A big gap between the two numbers tells me where to dig.
How do you decide when to escalate a problem, and what does your escalation say?
Your judgement on timing and your ability to get a clear decision from leaders.
Escalates when the fix is beyond the team's authority and waiting would cost a milestone, and brings options, a recommendation and a decision date.

I escalate when the fix is outside what the teams can decide and waiting would cost a milestone. Before I go up, I tell the people involved so nobody is surprised. The note is short: the problem, its impact on date and cost, two or three options with my recommendation, and the date we need a decision. Leaders should be choosing, not investigating.
You reported a workstream as green last month, and now you learn it was red the whole time. What do you do?
How you own a reporting mistake and fix its cause.
Corrects the record fast and plainly, takes ownership, and changes how status is gathered so it rests on evidence, not feelings.

I correct it in the next update, not next quarter: what I reported, what is true, and the impact. I own it, because the report had my name on it. Then I find out why. Usually green meant we feel fine. I would switch that workstream to evidence, like test results and finished milestones, and ask the lead for their top risk every week.
You inherit a program that is already red. What do you do in your first 30 days?
How you take control of a troubled program and reset it.
Listens and gathers facts before changing much, rebuilds the real critical path and top risks, then agrees a realistic reset plan with the sponsor.

The first two weeks I listen: one-on-ones with each lead and the sponsor, and a look at what has actually been delivered, not what the plan says. Then I rebuild the critical path and the top five risks from facts. By day 30 I bring the sponsor a reset plan with a realistic date, what we cut or fund to hit it, and how we will report from now on.

programmer.heading: Programmer questions
qs: Why shouldn't you compare two floating-point numbers with ==?
Whether you understand how computers store decimal numbers.
Most decimals have no exact binary form, so you compare within a tolerance that fits the scale of the values.

Most decimals, like 0.1, have no exact binary form, so 0.1 + 0.2 comes out as 0.30000000000000004 in double precision. Two values that should match can differ in the last bits. I compare with a tolerance that fits the size of the numbers, often a relative one. For money I use whole cents or a decimal type instead.
A game must run at 60 frames per second. How much time do you have per frame, and what do you do when you go over?
Whether you think in time budgets, not just in correct results.
About 16.7 milliseconds for everything. Measure with a profiler on the target hardware before changing code, then fix the biggest cost first.

One second divided by 60 is about 16.7 milliseconds, shared by game logic, physics, animation and rendering. When we go over, I profile on the target hardware, not my desktop, and find what really takes the time. Often one system does work every frame that could run less often or be spread over several frames.
What is a race condition, and how do you prevent one?
Your grasp of code that runs on several threads at once.
Shared data whose result depends on timing. Prevent it with locks or atomic operations, or better, by not sharing the data at all.

Two threads both read a counter as 10, both add one, both write 11, so one increment is lost. The result depends on timing, which is why it shows up rarely. I guard the data with a mutex, use an atomic operation for a simple counter, or better, design so each thread owns its data and passes messages.
What is undefined behavior in C or C++? Give an example.
Your knowledge of the rules of the language you write in.
The standard sets no requirement for what happens, and the compiler may assume it never occurs. Examples: signed overflow, out-of-bounds access, use after free.

It is code the language standard gives no meaning to, so anything can happen, and the optimizer may assume it never occurs. Examples are signed integer overflow, reading past the end of an array and using memory after it is freed. I catch it with strict compiler warnings, runtime sanitizers in test builds and careful review.
A bug shows up in the release build but never in the debug build. What do you suspect?
How you reason about what optimization and build settings change.
Uninitialized variables, undefined behavior the optimizer exploits, races hidden by debug timing, and real work placed inside asserts.

First, an uninitialized variable: debug builds often fill memory with a set pattern, release builds leave whatever was there. Second, undefined behavior the optimizer now takes advantage of. Third, a race that slower timing hid. Fourth, real work written inside an assert, which release removes. I build release with debug symbols to narrow it down.
You must change a 20-year-old function that has no tests and that nobody understands. Walk me through it.
How you change old code without breaking what depends on it.
Record current behavior with tests first, make the smallest change, and keep cleanup separate from the fix.

I first write tests that record what the function does today, odd parts included, using real inputs where I can. They tell me if I break something. Then I make the smallest change that does the job, in its own commit, and leave cleanup for later. If a strange branch looks wrong, I ask before touching it: someone may rely on it.
Why do many games run physics on a fixed time step instead of each frame's time?
Whether you know how a game loop keeps the simulation stable.
Variable steps make physics unstable and frame-rate dependent. A fixed step with an accumulator gives repeatable results, and rendering blends between states.

If physics uses each frame's time, a slow frame means a big step: objects pass through walls, springs blow up, and the game acts differently on fast and slow machines. I add frame time to an accumulator and run physics in fixed steps, like 1/60 of a second, as many as fit. Rendering blends the last two states so motion stays smooth.
What should code inside an interrupt handler do, and what should it never do?
Your knowledge of embedded and real-time code.
Short work only: read the data, set a flag, return. No blocking, printing or allocation, and safe access to data shared with the main code.

It should be as short as possible: read the register, put the value in a buffer, set a flag and return. The main loop does the real work. It must never wait on a lock, print or allocate memory. Shared variables are marked volatile, but volatile does not make access atomic, so for multi-byte values I briefly disable interrupts or use atomic operations.
Your loop updates 100,000 game objects and is slow, though the math is simple. What do you look at?
Whether you understand how memory and the CPU cache shape speed.
Memory access, not math: scattered objects cause cache misses. Pack the fields the loop needs into arrays and walk them in order, then measure.

With simple math, the time usually goes to waiting on memory. If each object is a separate allocation reached through a pointer, many reads miss the cache. I would store the fields the loop uses, like position and velocity, in packed arrays and walk them in order, so each cache line the CPU loads is full of useful data. Then I measure again.
A customer's machine is down, and your manager wants a fix to the motion control code sent today without testing it on a real machine. What do you do?
Your judgement when deadline pressure meets safety in code that moves real equipment.
No untested motion code goes out. You offer the fastest safe path, explain the risk plainly, and look for a safe stopgap.

I would not send untested code that moves an axis; one wrong sign or unit can crash the spindle into the part or hurt someone. I would tell my manager that plainly and offer the fastest safe path: test today on our own machine or simulator at reduced speed, then install it with the customer's operator present. Meanwhile I look for a safe workaround.
Why shouldn't money be stored in a float or a double?
Whether you know how binary floating point treats decimal values.
Most decimal fractions cannot be stored exactly in binary. Use integer cents or a decimal type, and round once, by an agreed rule.

Binary floating point cannot store most decimal fractions exactly. 0.1 is kept as a value very close to 0.1. Add up thousands of prices and the cents drift. I store whole cents in an integer, or use a decimal type, and round once, at a fixed point, with a rule the business has agreed to.
A feature worked three months ago and is broken now, with 400 commits in between. How do you find the commit that broke it?
Whether you search for a regression methodically instead of guessing.
A binary search through history, such as git bisect, automated with a script where possible, then a careful read of the guilty change.

I use git bisect. I mark one commit I know is good and the current bad one, and Git checks out the middle. I test it and mark it good or bad, and each test halves the range, so 400 commits take about nine tests. If I can script the check, git bisect run does it without me. Then I read that commit's diff closely.
What does the volatile keyword do in C, and what does it not do?
Your grasp of a keyword that embedded and systems code depends on and often misuses.
It forces every access to really happen, which suits hardware registers and interrupt flags. It does not give atomicity or ordering between threads.

It tells the compiler that every read and write of the variable must really happen, so it cannot keep the value in a register or drop a write. I use it for memory-mapped hardware registers and for flags set in an interrupt. It does not make an operation atomic, and it does not order memory between threads. For that I use atomics or a lock.
A controller starts misbehaving after about 49 days of running without a restart. What do you suspect?
Whether you spot a timer wraparound and know how to write code that survives it.
A 32-bit millisecond counter wraps after about 49.7 days. The fix is unsigned subtraction for elapsed time, tested by presetting the counter.

A 32-bit millisecond counter. 2 to the 32 milliseconds is about 49.7 days, and then it wraps to zero. A check like 'now greater than start plus timeout' breaks at the wrap. I compute elapsed time as unsigned now minus start and compare that to the timeout, which stays correct across a wrap. To test it, I start the counter just before the wrap point.
Why do many teams forbid heap allocation inside a game frame or a control loop?
How you think about timing that must be predictable, not only fast on average.
Allocation time is unpredictable and the heap fragments over long runs. Preallocate with pools or arenas, and check that the loop really allocates nothing.

malloc or new can take an unpredictable time. It may search free lists, take a lock or ask the operating system for memory. Over hours the heap also fragments. In a loop with a hard deadline, that means a missed frame or a missed cycle. So I allocate up front: fixed pools, an arena reset every frame, ring buffers. Then I add a counter or hook to prove the loop allocates nothing.
How should firmware feed a hardware watchdog, and what is the common mistake?
Whether you use a watchdog so it really catches a hung system.
Feed it only when the whole system is shown to be healthy, not from a timer interrupt, and make sure a reset leaves the machine safe.

The watchdog resets the chip if nobody feeds it in time, so feeding it should prove the system is healthy. The classic mistake is feeding it from a timer interrupt. That interrupt keeps firing while the main loop is stuck, so the reset never comes. I feed it from the main loop, only after each task has checked in. On a machine I also make sure the outputs go to a safe state on reset.
Two threads each hold one lock and wait for the other's. How do you fix it and keep it from coming back?
How you resolve a deadlock and prevent the whole class of bug.
One fixed order for taking locks, short locked sections, no unknown code called under a lock, and stack traces to find the stuck pair.

That is a deadlock. The main fix is one fixed order for taking locks: every thread takes A before B. I keep locked sections short and never call unknown code while holding a lock. In C++ I can take both locks in one call with std::scoped_lock, which avoids deadlock. To find such a bug, I look at the stacks of the stuck threads in a debugger or a dump.
On a real-time system, a high-priority task misses deadlines while it waits on a mutex held by a low-priority task. What is going on?
Whether you know priority inversion and the standard fix for it.
Names priority inversion and explains the medium-priority task. Fixes it with a priority-inheritance mutex and short critical sections.

Priority inversion. The low task holds the mutex. A medium task that needs nothing from it preempts the low task, so the low task cannot finish and release the lock. The high task ends up waiting on the medium one. The fix is a mutex with priority inheritance, which most RTOSes offer: the holder runs at the waiter's priority until it releases. I also keep critical sections short.
Your team wants to rewrite a 15-year-old system from scratch because the code is ugly. How do you weigh that?
Your judgement about risk when replacing old working code.
Old code holds fixes no spec lists. Prefer gradual replacement with tests that pin down current behavior, and keep a full rewrite for a dead platform.

Ugly code often holds years of bug fixes and customer cases that no spec lists. A rewrite has to match all of them while the old system keeps changing. I usually replace it piece by piece behind a stable interface, with tests that record what the old code does today, and move work over part by part. I back a full rewrite only when the platform itself is dead.
A patch you shipped is corrupting some users' saved data. What do you do in the first day?
How you own a serious mistake and limit the damage before fixing it.
Stop the spread first, tell support, find the cause and who is hit, repair data where possible, then add a test and an honest review.

First I stop the damage: pull or pause the patch, and give support clear words for users. Then I find the cause and which files are affected, and write a fix that repairs damaged data where it can, using backups if we keep them. Afterwards I add a test that loads old files through every version, and I write up plainly how the bug got past me.

project-manager.heading: Project manager questions
qs: What is the critical path, and what does float tell you?
Your grasp of the basic tool for scheduling.
The longest chain of dependent tasks sets the end date; float is how long a task can slip without moving that date.

The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks from start to finish, so it sets the earliest end date. Tasks on it usually have zero float. Float is how many days a task can slip before it delays the project. I watch critical tasks closely and use the float on other tasks to smooth out who works when.
How do you estimate a task the team has never done before?
How you build an estimate when there is no history to lean on.
Ranges instead of a single guess, input from the people doing the work, and assumptions written down.

I ask the people who will do it for three numbers: best case, most likely and worst case. A common weighting is best plus four times most likely plus worst, divided by six. For 4, 6 and 14 days that gives 7 days. I write the assumptions next to the number and re-estimate once the first piece of work is done.
What is the difference between a contingency reserve and a management reserve?
Whether you know how money for risk is set aside and controlled.
Contingency covers identified risks and sits in the cost baseline; management reserve covers unforeseen work, sits outside the baseline and is released by management.

Contingency reserve is money for risks we have named, like a vendor price rise, and it is part of the cost baseline I manage. Management reserve is for problems nobody foresaw. It sits outside the baseline, and using it takes approval from management and a change to the baseline. I never quietly spend either one to hide an overrun.
When would you choose a fixed-price contract with a supplier, and when time and materials?
How you match the contract type to how well the work is defined.
Fixed price when scope is clear and stable, since the supplier carries cost risk; time and materials when scope is uncertain, with a cap and close tracking.

Fixed price fits clear, stable work, like installing 200 workstations to a spec. The supplier carries the cost risk, but every change becomes a priced change order. Time and materials fits work we cannot define yet, like early discovery. Then the buyer carries the risk, so I add a not-to-exceed cap and review hours every week.
Your report shows a cost performance index of 0.85 and a schedule performance index of 1.05. What does that tell you?
Whether you can read earned value numbers and act on them.
Over budget for the work done and slightly ahead of schedule; then finding out why, for example overtime buying speed.

CPI is earned value divided by actual cost, so 0.85 means we get about 85 cents of planned work for each dollar spent. SPI is earned value divided by planned value, so 1.05 means we are a little ahead. Together they often mean we are buying speed with overtime or extra people. I would check that, and ask whether we need the speed at all.
A key supplier tells you their delivery will be three weeks late. What do you do in the first 48 hours?
How you coordinate suppliers when a delivery slips.
Confirm the facts and the impact on the critical path, look for options, check the contract, and tell the sponsor with a plan.

First I get the facts in writing: what is late, why, and how firm the new date is. Then I check whether the item is on the critical path or has float. I look for options: a partial shipment, a second source, or resequencing work around it. I check what the contract says about delays, then tell the sponsor the impact and my recommendation.
Two of your projects need the same database specialist in the same week. How do you decide?
Your judgement when shared resources clash.
Compare the impact on each schedule and on the business, and let the person who owns priorities decide; no quiet favors.

I check where her work sits in each schedule. If one task has two weeks of float and the other is on the critical path, the answer is often clear. If both are critical, I put the cost of each delay side by side and take it to the person who sets priorities across projects. Then I confirm the decision in writing to both teams.
Your team leads report green every week, but the milestones keep sliding. How do you handle it?
Whether your status reports tell the truth.
Status tied to evidence like finished deliverables and forecast dates, and making it safe to report amber early.

Green outside and red inside usually means status is based on effort, not results. I change the rule: a task is green only if its deliverable is done or its forecast date still holds. I ask leads for the forecast date, not a color. And I thank the first person who reports amber, so people learn that early bad news helps.
After the budget is approved, you find your estimate left out a cost worth 8% of the total. What do you do?
How you own a mistake in your own numbers.
Telling the sponsor quickly with the corrected figure and options, not hiding it in contingency without saying so.

I confirm the number, then tell the sponsor the same week, before it shows up as a variance. I say plainly that it was my miss, give the corrected total and a few options: use part of the contingency and accept the risk that brings, trim scope, or raise the budget through change control. Then I add that item to my estimating checklist.
What is the 100% rule in a work breakdown structure?
Whether you know how scope is broken down so that nothing is missed or added.
The WBS holds all of the scope, including project management work, and nothing outside it. The child elements at each level add up to exactly their parent.

The WBS has to contain 100% of the work in scope, including things like project management and testing, and nothing that is out of scope. At every level, the child elements add up to exactly the parent. If a task or cost shows up that maps to no WBS element, then either the scope is wrong or someone is doing unapproved work.
What is the difference between crashing and fast-tracking a schedule, and what does each cost you?
Your grasp of the two standard ways to compress a schedule and their trade-offs.
Crashing adds resources to critical path work and costs money. Fast-tracking overlaps work that was planned in sequence and adds rework risk. Both only help on the critical path.

Crashing means adding people, overtime or equipment to critical path tasks, so it costs money. I pick the tasks with the lowest cost per day saved. Fast-tracking means overlapping tasks planned one after another, like starting the build before design is signed off. It costs little upfront but raises the risk of rework. Shortening work off the critical path saves nothing.
What is the difference between resource leveling and resource smoothing?
Whether you understand how fixing overloaded people can move the end date.
Leveling removes overallocation even if that changes the critical path and the end date. Smoothing works only within float, so the end date holds but some overloads may remain.

Both deal with people booked over their capacity. Leveling moves tasks until nobody is overloaded, and that can push the end date and change the critical path. Smoothing only moves tasks within their float, so the end date stays fixed, but it may not remove every overload. I tell the sponsor which one I used, because only one of them protects the date.
Halfway through, how do you forecast what the project will cost at completion?
How you turn earned value data into an honest forecast.
You pick the formula by asking whether past cost performance will continue. You also check the result against a bottom-up re-estimate of the remaining work.

First I ask whether the overrun so far is typical. If it is, I divide the budget at completion by the CPI. If it came from a one-off, like a single bad invoice, I use actual cost plus the remaining budgeted work: AC plus BAC minus EV. Then the team re-estimates what is left, bottom-up, and I compare. If the numbers disagree a lot, I find out why before I report.
How do you set up the payment schedule in a supplier contract?
Whether you use payment terms to protect the project, not just to pay bills.
Payments are tied to accepted deliverables with clear acceptance criteria. Some money is held back until final acceptance, and nothing is paid ahead of real progress.

I tie each payment to a deliverable we can inspect, with acceptance criteria written into the contract, not to dates or hours. On larger contracts I hold back a share of each payment, called retainage, until final acceptance. I also make sure early payments do not run ahead of the value delivered. That way, if the supplier fails, we have not prepaid for work we never got.
When is it right to rebaseline a project, and when is it not?
Your judgement on keeping the baseline an honest yardstick.
You rebaseline after approved scope changes, or when the old plan no longer means anything, always with sponsor approval. Never just to make variances disappear.

I rebaseline when an approved change alters the scope, or when the plan is so far off that measuring against it tells us nothing. It goes through change control and the sponsor signs it. I never rebaseline just to turn a red report green. I keep the original baseline on file too, so anyone can see how far we moved from the first commitment and why.
You learn a vice president asked a developer directly for a feature, and it is half built. What do you do?
How you handle scope that slipped around change control without starting a fight.
You pause the work calmly, size the impact and take it through change control to a decision. You fix the channel with the executive instead of blaming the developer.

I ask the developer to pause, without blame, and find out what was asked and what is done. I size the impact on schedule, cost and testing. Then I see the vice president, say the feature may well be worth it, and bring a short change request: approve and fund it, defer it, or drop it. We also agree that future asks come through me, so the team is not caught in the middle.
Four parallel paths feed one integration date, and each has an 80% chance of finishing on time. How confident are you in that date?
Whether you understand merge bias and schedule risk where paths converge.
You see that the joint chance is far lower, about 41% if the paths are independent. You respond with buffers, earlier integration or a Monte Carlo simulation.

Not very. Integration starts on time only if all four paths finish on time. If they are independent, that is 0.8 to the fourth power, about 41%. This is called merge bias, and a single-path view hides it. I would show the sponsor that number, add a buffer before integration, integrate pieces early where we can, and run a Monte Carlo simulation to get a realistic date range.
The sponsor wants to cut the testing phase in half to hit the launch date. How do you respond?
How you push back on a risky shortcut with facts and still leave the decision to the sponsor.
You make the risk concrete and offer alternatives, such as cutting scope or a phased launch. The decision and the accepted risk go on record.

I would not just say no. I show what half the testing leaves untested and what failures in those areas would cost after launch. Then I offer options: launch with fewer features, fully tested, test the riskiest areas first, or move the date a little. If the sponsor still chooses the cut, I record the decision and the accepted risk in writing and plan extra support for the launch.
You are 70% through the budget and the business case no longer holds. What do you recommend?
Whether you can judge a project on its future value, not on money already spent.
You ignore sunk cost and compare remaining cost with remaining benefit. You bring the sponsor a clear recommendation, including stopping, with a clean close-out plan.

The 70% already spent is gone, so it should not drive the choice. I compare the cost to finish with the benefit we would still get, and look for a smaller version worth saving. If nothing is worth it, I recommend stopping. Stopping well matters: close supplier contracts under their termination terms, keep what is reusable, and record why, so the call is not seen as failure.

proposal-manager.heading: Proposal and capture manager questions
qs: What is the difference between capture management and proposal management?
Whether you know where a contract is really won or lost.
Capture shapes the deal before the RFP: customer, competitors, partners, price. The proposal turns that strategy into a compliant, scorable document.

Capture starts months before the request for proposal, or RFP. It means learning the customer's problem, sizing up competitors, picking partners and estimating the price likely to win. Proposal management starts when the RFP is released: schedule, outline, writers, reviews, submission. If capture was skipped, the proposal team writes blind, and it shows.
Walk me through how you build a compliance matrix.
Your grasp of how a federal solicitation is structured.
Every requirement from Sections L, M and C traced to a place in the outline and an owner, so nothing is missed and evaluators find each item.

I read Section L for the instructions, Section M for the evaluation criteria and Section C, the statement of work, line by line. Each requirement gets a row: its RFP reference, where we answer it in our outline, and who writes it. I update it with every amendment, and the final check before submission is against this matrix, not memory.
What happens at a pink team review and at a red team review?
Whether you run reviews with a purpose, not as calendar events.
Pink checks the approach and outline early; red scores a near-final draft as an evaluator would. Knowing that names vary by company is a plus.

Names vary between companies, but in my teams pink team reviews storyboards or an early draft: are we answering the right question with the right solution? Red team reads a near-final draft against Section M and scores it the way the government will, listing strengths and weaknesses. I give reviewers the RFP and the scoring criteria, not just the draft.
What is a discriminator, and how is it different from a feature?
Whether you can write win themes that earn points, not just sound good.
A discriminator is something the customer values that competitors cannot easily claim, backed by proof and tied to a benefit.

A feature is something we have, like a help desk staffed around the clock. It becomes a discriminator only if the customer cares, rivals cannot say the same, and we can prove it. So I write: we cut the ticket backlog by 40% on a similar contract, with the data in our past performance. Without proof it is just a claim evaluators skip.
How do you make a bid or no-bid decision?
Your judgement about where to spend limited bid money and people.
Clear criteria: customer knowledge, eligibility, competition, ability to perform, price, cost to bid. And the nerve to recommend not bidding.

I score it against set questions. Did we know the customer before the RFP? Do we meet every mandatory requirement, including set-aside status? Who is the incumbent and are they doing well? Can we price to win and still make money? If we first heard of it when the RFP posted and the incumbent is strong, I usually recommend passing and saving the team for a better shot.
Section L asks for one structure, and Section M scores the factors in a different order. How do you organize the volume?
How you handle conflicting instructions without losing points.
Ask the contracting officer during the question period. If nothing changes, follow L's structure and make each M factor easy to find.

First I submit a question to the contracting officer during the Q&A window, because the answer may come as an amendment. If nothing changes, I follow Section L's structure, since that is the instruction, and I map every Section M factor in headings and a cross-reference table so an evaluator can find each one in seconds.
After the RFP is out, a program manager wants to call a friend at the agency to ask what they really want. What do you say?
Whether you know the rules on contact with the customer during a competition.
Once the solicitation is released, questions go to the contracting officer through official channels. Side contacts put the bid at risk.

I would stop that call. Once the RFP is released, questions go to the contracting officer named in it, usually in writing, so every bidder gets the same answer. A side conversation can raise procurement integrity concerns and hurt us in the competition. If he has a real question, I help him word it and we submit it officially.
Two days before the deadline, the technical volume is eight pages over the limit. What do you do?
How you cut under pressure while keeping what scores.
Check the format rules, cut what does not answer Section M, use tables to save space, and never break font or margin rules to fit.

Many RFPs say pages over the limit will not be read, so cutting is not optional. I check the format rules first: font, margins, what counts toward the limit. Then I cut anything not tied to a Section M factor, merge repeated content, and turn dense paragraphs into a table. I never shrink fonts or margins below what the RFP allows; that can cost more than the pages.
A solution architect writes that we will cut processing time in half, and no one can back it up. What do you do?
Whether you protect the company from promises it cannot keep.
No unsupported claims: proposal content can become part of the contract, and evaluators discount unproven ones. Replace it with what you can prove.

I take it out or ask for the evidence. What we write can be made part of the contract, and evaluators tend to discount claims with no proof anyway. I ask the architect what we have actually achieved, maybe 30% faster on a similar system last year, and write that with the source. A smaller true number scores better than a big one we may have to defend later.
We lost a bid we expected to win. What do you do in the next two weeks?
How you learn from a loss and use the rules to get feedback.
Request a debriefing in writing right away, since the window is short, then compare the findings with your own reviews and feed lessons into the next capture.

I request a debriefing in writing the day we get the notice, because the window is only a few days and missing it can cost us the right to one. I prepare questions about our weaknesses and ratings. Then I run a lessons-learned session with capture, pricing and writers, compare the findings with our red team scores, and update our templates.
Beyond Sections L and M, which parts of an RFP in the Uniform Contract Format do you read closely, and why?
Whether you read the whole solicitation, not just the instructions and evaluation factors.
Names B for line items and pricing, C for the work, H for special requirements, J for attachments and K for certifications, with a reason for each.

Section B lists the contract line items and how they are priced, which shapes our pricing. C is the actual work, so the solution traces back to it. H hides special requirements like clearances or key personnel rules. J lists attachments, often the real statement of work. K has the reps and certs someone must sign.
How does your writing change when an RFP is lowest price technically acceptable instead of best value tradeoff?
Whether you understand how the source selection method changes what is worth writing.
Under LPTA you write to be clearly acceptable and push on price; under a tradeoff you sell strengths worth paying more for.

Under LPTA the government rates each proposal acceptable or unacceptable, then picks the lowest price among the acceptable ones. Extra features earn no credit, so I write tight, fully compliant answers with no gaps and push the team on cost. Under a tradeoff, strengths can justify a higher price, so I make each benefit easy for evaluators to note as a strength.
