If nobody fits, I move just that one session and tell the candidate right away with new options. Every invite shows the time in the candidate's own zone to avoid a second mistake.
We are posting a remote job open to people anywhere in the US. What do you check before it goes live?
Whether you know that posting rules differ by state and city.
Pay transparency laws in several states and cities, some covering remote roles; a good-faith range agreed with compensation, and legal review when unsure.

Several states and some cities now require a pay range in the job posting, and some of those laws cover remote jobs that could be done from there. So I get a good-faith range from compensation, include it in the ad, and add a benefits summary where a law asks for one. If we truly cannot hire in a state, I say so in the posting. When I am unsure about a rule, I check with legal.
Half the hiring managers never update candidate stages in the ATS, so the pipeline reports are wrong. How do you fix it?
How you get busy people to use the system without nagging forever.
Find why they skip it, make it easier (mobile, email links, recruiter owns moves), show managers what they lose, and report on stale candidates.

I would ask a few managers why they skip it; often it is too many clicks. Then I make it easier: feedback links from email, fewer required fields, and recruiters move stages after debriefs. I add a weekly list of candidates stuck over seven days by team. When managers see their own open roles look slow because of stale data, most start updating.
A former candidate posts a harsh review of our interview process on a public review site. How do you respond?
Your judgement in protecting the employer brand without making things worse.
Check the facts first, reply calmly and briefly without candidate details, offer a private channel, and fix the real problem if one exists.

First I look up what happened: stages, dates, how long they waited for news. Then a short public reply: thank them, say we take it seriously, and invite them to contact us directly. I never share details of their application. If the facts show we went silent for three weeks, I fix that step in the process, because the next review will say the same thing.
A background check comes back with a record, and the hiring manager wants the offer pulled today. What do you tell them?
Whether you know the required adverse action steps under federal law.
Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, a pre-adverse action notice with the report and summary of rights comes first, then time to respond, then the final notice.

I would ask them to wait. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act we first send a pre-adverse action notice with a copy of the report and the summary of rights, and give the person a reasonable time to dispute or explain. Only after that can a final adverse action notice go out. Some states and cities add their own fair chance steps, so I would bring in HR or legal before deciding.
We are moving to a new ATS in four months. How would you plan the migration, and what usually goes wrong?
How you plan a system change that touches data, integrations and people.
Map and clean data first, decide what to migrate, test integrations, run a pilot, train users, and keep open reqs moving during cutover.

I start by mapping every field, stage and integration in the old system, and decide what we migrate versus archive. I clean duplicates before moving them, not after. Common failures are broken job board feeds, lost interview history and missing records we must keep, so I test those in a sandbox. Then a pilot with one team, training, and a cutover date with no new reqs opened that week.
Finance and the head of talent each pulled time to fill from the same ATS and got 38 days and 52 days. How do you sort it out?
How you handle metric definitions and trust in recruiting data.
Finds the definition gap first, agrees on one written definition, then fixes the reporting so it cannot drift again.

I rebuild both numbers side by side. The gap is usually a definition: one starts at approval and one at posting, one ends at accepted offer and one at start date, or one leaves out canceled reqs. I agree on one definition with both of them, write it in a metrics glossary, and make a single saved report the source everyone uses.
How would you tell whether our employer brand work is actually working?
Whether you measure brand by hiring results, not just likes and views.
Links brand to hiring outcomes: applicant quality from brand channels, offer acceptance, candidate survey answers, and why people say they applied.

Followers and views are a start, not the goal. I track how many applicants from the careers site and brand content reach final interviews, our offer acceptance rate, and answers to a short post-interview survey. I also ask at offer stage: why did you apply? If the brand works, those answers start to repeat our message.
Offer acceptance fell from 85% to 65% this quarter. How do you find out why?
How you diagnose a funnel problem with both data and conversations.
Splits the drop by team, level, location and recruiter, reads decline reasons, and talks to people who said no before proposing a fix.

First I split the declines by department, level, location and recruiter to see if the drop is broad or in one pocket. Then I read the decline reasons and call a few people who said no. In a similar case it was one team: offers took nine days after the final round, and candidates took other jobs. We cut offer approvals to two days.
A recruiter wants to bulk-delete candidate records older than six months to clean up the ATS. What do you check first?
Whether you know that applicant records have legal retention rules.
Knows federal law sets a minimum retention period, that legal holds override any cleanup, and that state privacy laws may also apply.

I would stop the delete. Federal rules require keeping applications and hiring records for at least one year, longer for some federal contractors, and nothing can go while a charge or lawsuit is pending. I check our retention policy with legal, any legal holds and state privacy rules, then set up an automated purge that follows the policy.
An offer letter went out at a salary above the approved range, and the candidate accepted. What do you do now, and what do you change?
How you handle a control failure without blaming anyone and without hiding it.
Escalates the facts quickly, does not retract the offer on their own, and fixes the approval step that let it through.

I tell the recruiting lead and the compensation partner the same day, with the facts. Whether we honor it is their call with legal; pulling an accepted offer hurts trust, so it is often honored. Then I find the gap. In one case the salary field stayed editable after approval. I locked it so any change sends the offer back for approval.
An automated workflow just sent rejection emails to 300 candidates, including some in final rounds. Walk me through the next hour.
How you contain and repair a mass mistake in a recruiting system.
Stops the workflow, pulls an exact list, reaches active candidates personally first, and finds the root cause before turning automation back on.

I switch off the workflow so it cannot fire again. I pull everyone who got the email and their real status. Active candidates get a call or a personal note from their recruiter within the hour. Others sent it by mistake get a short, honest correction. Then I trace the trigger, fix it, test it in a sandbox and only then turn it back on.
Leadership plans 120 hires in the next six months. How do you work out how many recruiters and interviewers we need?
Your ability to turn a hiring plan into capacity using funnel math.
Works backward from hires through our own conversion rates to interview hours and recruiter load, and names the bottleneck.

I work backward from our funnel. If one hire takes about four final interviews, eight phone screens and 40 applicants, 120 hires means about 480 finals. At five interviewer hours each, that is 2,400 hours, which I split by team. For recruiters I use our past hires per recruiter per quarter by role type, since senior roles take more time than high-volume ones.
A new skills test passes 60% of white applicants and 40% of Black applicants. How do you look at that?
Whether you know how adverse impact is assessed and what to do when you see it.
Applies the four-fifths rule from the federal Uniform Guidelines correctly, knows it is a rule of thumb, and brings in legal before keeping or changing the test.

Under the four-fifths rule, I compare selection rates: 40 divided by 60 is about 67%, below 80%, which signals possible adverse impact. It is a rule of thumb, so with small numbers I also want a statistical test. I bring it to legal, confirm the test is tied to the job, and look for an alternative that measures the same skill with less impact.
A vendor pitches an AI tool that ranks resumes. What do you ask before we buy it?
How you weigh automation against fairness, legal risk and candidate trust.
Asks for independent bias audit results, how scores are made, and who stays accountable, and knows places like New York City regulate these tools.

I ask what data it was trained on, what it scores, and whether we can see why someone ranked low. I want adverse impact results from an independent audit; New York City requires a bias audit no more than a year old and notice to candidates. We stay responsible for its decisions, so a recruiter still reviews them, and I would pilot it beside our current process first.

regional-sales-director.heading: Regional sales director questions
qs: How would you design territories for a region you are taking over?
How you balance opportunity and workload when you divide a region among reps.
Territories built on data, such as account potential, current business and workload, so each rep has a fair shot at quota.

I start with the account list, not the map. I score accounts by potential, using size, industry fit and current spend, then add travel time and existing relationships. I aim for territories with similar opportunity, not similar account counts. Before I finalize, I check them with my managers, who know where the real buying power sits.
What is pipeline coverage, and how do you decide how much your region needs?
Whether you understand pipeline math instead of repeating a rule of thumb.
Coverage tied to your own win rate and sales cycle, not a fixed 3x quoted from habit, plus a check on deal stage and timing.

Coverage is open pipeline divided by the quota still to close in the period. The right ratio comes from our win rate: if we close about one in four qualified deals by value, we need roughly 4x. I also check stages and close dates, because a pipeline full of early deals dated for the last week is weaker than the ratio says.
Walk me through how you run a weekly forecast call with your managers.
How you inspect a forecast instead of just collecting numbers.
Clear forecast categories, inspection of the biggest deals, and calls based on evidence such as dated next steps and buyer actions.

Each manager gives commit, the deals they would bet on, then best case and what changed since last week. We go through the five largest commit deals: who signs, what is next, is it on the buyer's calendar, is procurement involved yet. If a deal has no dated next step from the customer, it moves out of commit. I submit my own number, not the sum of theirs.
How do you split a regional quota among your managers and reps?
Whether you set quotas that are fair, reachable and still add up to the regional number.
Quota tied to territory potential and history, a cushion above the target to cover misses, and reduced quotas while new reps ramp.

I start with the regional number and add some cushion, often a few percent, because not every rep will hit. Then I split it by territory potential and past performance, not evenly. Reps still ramping get a reduced quota for their first quarters. I share the method with managers before the numbers, so the debate is about inputs, not about who complained loudest.
How do you tell if a new rep is ramping on track before their first full quarter ends?
Whether you watch leading indicators instead of waiting for missed revenue.
Early activity and pipeline milestones checked against a ramp plan, with coaching started as soon as one slips.

Revenue comes too late to tell me much. I set milestones with the manager: product certification by week four, a set number of first meetings by week six, and a target amount of qualified pipeline by day ninety. If a rep misses one, the manager joins their calls that week. Most ramp problems show up first as a thin calendar.
One of your managers has a large deal in commit, and you do not believe it. What do you do?
How you challenge a forecast without undermining the manager.
Asking for evidence, joining a customer call if needed, and making your own forecast call while coaching the manager.

I ask the manager the questions I would ask the buyer: who signs, is the budget approved, what happens next and when. If the answers are vague, I ask to join the next customer call. I do not overrule them in front of the team. In my own forecast I carry the deal at the level I believe, and I tell the manager why, so they learn to inspect the same way.
Halfway through the quarter, your region is tracking to about 80% of plan. What do you do?
How you respond to a likely miss: early, honest and with a specific plan.
Finding exactly where the gap is, telling leadership early, and putting effort on deals that can truly close this quarter.

First I find where the gap is: one team, one segment, or deals that slipped. Then I tell my VP the likely number and the plan, not just the bad news. We pull forward deals that are truly ready, managers focus on the top twenty deals, and I join the biggest meetings. I avoid deep discounts that just steal from next quarter.
On the last day of the quarter, a rep asks you to approve a 30% discount to close a large deal. How do you decide?
Your judgement on discounting, margin and the habits a quarter-end deal teaches buyers.
Weighing margin and precedent, and trading discount for value such as a longer term or prepayment, within approval rules.

I ask why the buyer needs it and what we get back. A discount in exchange for a longer term, prepayment or a reference can make sense. A discount just to close today teaches the customer to wait for the last day every year. I check the margin and our approval rules, and if it is above my authority, I take it up with a clear recommendation.
Two of your reps both claim credit for the same account. How do you settle it?
Whether you apply rules of engagement fairly and keep the team working together.
A fast decision based on the written rules and the CRM record, and a fix to the rule if it caused the dispute.

I go to our rules of engagement and the CRM history: who owns the account by territory, who logged the opportunity first, and who did the work. I decide within days, because an open dispute poisons both reps. If the rules were unclear, I may split the credit this time and then fix the rule in writing so it does not happen again.
Your top-producing manager hits the number every quarter, but their team has the highest turnover in the region. What do you do?
Whether you look past revenue to the health of a team and act on what you find.
Treating attrition as a real cost, finding the cause from data and conversations, and coaching the manager with clear expectations.

Hitting the number with constant turnover is expensive: each lost rep means months of hiring and ramp. I look at exit interviews, one-on-one talks with their reps and how long people stay. If the cause is the manager's style, I tell them directly that retention is now part of how I judge them, set a specific goal, and coach them on it.
How do you work out how many reps you need to hit next year's number?
Whether you can turn a revenue target into a hiring and capacity plan.
Working backward from the target using real attainment, not 100%, and allowing for ramp time and attrition.

I work backward. Say the target is $24M and a ramped rep carries a $1.2M quota. Reps rarely all hit 100%, so I use our real average attainment, say 80%, or about $960K per rep. That is 25 ramped-rep equivalents. Then I add for new-hire ramp time and expected attrition, and I hire early enough that people are productive when the number needs them.
What is the difference between bookings, billings and revenue, and which one do you forecast?
Your grasp of how a signed deal turns into money the company reports.
Clear definitions, knowing a signed deal is not yet recognized revenue, and awareness of what finance needs from sales.

Bookings are the value of contracts signed in the period. Billings are what we invoice. Revenue is what accounting recognizes as we deliver, under the ASC 606 rules, so a three-year deal signed today books now but becomes revenue over time. I forecast bookings with my team, and I flag terms like billing frequency and start dates, because finance plans revenue and cash from them.
Walk me through the account plan you would build for your largest customer.
How you manage a key account for growth and protection, not just the next deal.
Starts from the customer's business, maps several relationships at several levels, finds whitespace, and is reviewed on a set rhythm.

I start with how the customer makes money and what their priorities are this year. Then I map who decides, who influences and who uses us, so we have relationships at several levels, not one champion. I list the whitespace: divisions or products they have not bought yet. We review the plan with the account team each quarter and pair one of our executives with one of theirs.
Your biggest account tells you they plan to move to a competitor at renewal in 90 days. What do you do?
How you respond when a key account is at risk.
Listens before pitching, finds the real cause, brings a concrete fix, and updates the forecast and leadership at once.

First I get a call with the decision maker, ideally with our executive sponsor, and ask what drove it without pitching. Often the real cause is a service failure or a champion who left. If we can fix it, I bring a plan with owners and dates. I also tell my manager and finance right away, because the forecast changes today, not in 90 days.
Your region's win rate dropped from 25% to 18% over two quarters. How do you find out why?
Whether you diagnose a sales problem with data before acting on a guess.
Splits the drop by rep, segment, competitor, source and stage, checks whether the pipeline mix changed, then hears from lost buyers.

I split the drop before guessing. Is it every rep or a few, one segment, one competitor, one lead source? At which stage are we losing? Sometimes the mix changed: more early, weaker leads entering the pipeline lowers win rate without anyone selling worse. Then I listen to several lost-deal calls and talk to a few buyers who said no.
How would you use the comp plan to win more new customers without hurting renewals?
Your judgement in using pay to steer behavior without side effects.
A simple plan with few measures, renewals still rewarded, no hard earnings caps, and the plan modeled on past deals before launch.

I would pay a higher rate on new-logo bookings, or a modest new-logo bonus, while still paying enough on renewals that nobody neglects them. I keep it to two or three measures so reps know what pays. I avoid hard caps, which make top reps stop selling or push deals out. Before launch I run last year's deals through the plan to see who would earn what.
One of your managers forecasts low every quarter and then beats the number by 20%. Why is that a problem, and what do you do?
Whether you value forecast accuracy, not just beating the number.
Sees that sandbagging costs the business real decisions, looks for the cause, and makes accuracy part of how the manager is judged.

A miss on the low side hurts too: finance holds back hiring or spending we could have made. I would look at their calls against results over several quarters, then ask why. Often they were punished for a miss once. I would tell them accuracy is part of how I judge them, and review their commit deal by deal with them for a few weeks.
Your reps say marketing's leads are bad, and marketing says sales does not follow up. How do you settle it?
How you fix a conflict with another team using shared rules and data.
Written shared definitions and follow-up times, both sides measured, and a regular joint review instead of blame.

I would get both leaders to agree in writing on what a qualified lead is and how fast sales must follow up, say within one business day. Then we track both sides: lead quality by how many become real opportunities, and follow-up speed by rep. Within a month the data shows the gap. Usually it is some of each, and a weekly joint review keeps it from turning into blame again.
Mid-year, you have to move several strong accounts from one rep to another. How do you handle it?
How you change territories without losing deals, trust or the rep.
Tells the rep first with the reason, settles credit on open deals in writing, adjusts quota, and plans a warm customer handoff.

I tell the rep in person before any announcement, with the reason. For deals they had moved well along, I agree a clear credit split in writing so nothing stalls. Their quota is adjusted to the new territory. Then I plan the handoff with each customer: a joint call where the old rep introduces the new one, not an email from someone they have never met.
The CRO asks you to raise your region's number by 15% mid-year with no new headcount. How do you respond?
Whether you can push back on a target with facts and still offer a way forward.
No reflex yes or no: returns with the math, specific levers, a split between commit and upside, and what the rest would require.

I would not say yes or no in the room. I would come back with the math: what our pipeline and win rates can produce, and which levers could close the gap, like expansion in key accounts or moving reps to higher-yield segments. I would show what I can commit to, what is upside, and what the rest would take. Agreeing to a number I cannot back hurts everyone at year end.

regulatory-affairs.heading: Regulatory affairs specialist questions
qs: What is the difference between a 510(k), a De Novo and a PMA?
Whether you know the main US routes to market for a medical device.
A 510(k) shows substantial equivalence to a predicate. De Novo is for new low-to-moderate risk devices with no predicate. PMA is for most Class III devices.

A 510(k) shows the device is substantially equivalent to a legally marketed predicate. A De Novo is for a new device of low to moderate risk with no predicate; if granted, it creates a new classification others can use. A PMA is for most Class III devices and must show reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness, usually with clinical data.
We have a new device and nobody is sure how it is classified. How do you find out?
How you work out the class and the pathway of a product.
Searching FDA databases for similar devices and product codes, reading the classification regulation, and using a 513(g) request when it is still unclear.

I start with the intended use and how the device works. Then I search FDA's product classification database and the 510(k) database for similar devices and their product codes, and read the regulation they fall under. If it is still unclear, I can file a 513(g) request, which asks FDA in writing for its view on the class and requirements.
How do you prepare for a Pre-Submission meeting with FDA?
Whether you can get useful feedback from a regulator before you file.
A focused package with specific questions FDA can answer yes or no, using the meeting for open points, and documenting what was agreed.

I send a short package: device description, intended use, the test plan and a few specific questions, like 'Does FDA agree this bench test protocol is enough?' Vague questions get vague answers. FDA usually sends written feedback before the meeting, so we spend the meeting on what is still open, and I draft the minutes afterward.
An FDA inspection ends with a Form 483. What happens next?
Your grasp of inspection follow-up and what is at stake.
A 483 lists observations, not a final decision. A written answer within 15 business days with root cause, fixes and evidence lowers the risk of a warning letter.

A 483 lists what the investigator observed; it is not a final agency decision. I aim to respond in writing within 15 business days, because FDA can consider that response before deciding on a warning letter. For each item: the root cause, the fix, how we check it works, and dates. Every commitment must be one we will actually meet.
Marketing wants a brochure to say our device also helps with a use it was not cleared for. What do you say?
How you handle claims that go beyond the cleared labeling.
A clear no to promoting an uncleared use, a reason the team can accept, and options: wording within the clearance, or a path to add the new use.

I say we cannot promote a use FDA has not cleared; that can make the device misbranded and lead to a warning letter. Then I offer options: claims that fit our cleared indication, backed by data we have, or a plan to add the new use, which may need a new 510(k) and data. I give the cost and timeline so they can choose.
Engineering changed a material in a cleared device. Do we need a new 510(k)?
Whether you can make and document a change assessment.
Asking whether the change could significantly affect safety or effectiveness, using FDA's change guidance and test data, and documenting the decision either way.

It depends on whether the change could significantly affect safety or effectiveness. For a material that touches the patient, I look at biocompatibility and performance data and work through FDA's guidance on changes to an existing device. If a new 510(k) is needed, we file before we ship. If not, I write a memo to file with the reasoning and evidence.
A complaint says our device failed during a procedure. How do you decide whether it must be reported to FDA?
Your knowledge of the medical device reporting rules.
Applying the MDR criteria: a death or serious injury the device may have caused or contributed to, or a malfunction likely to do so if it recurred, on time.

Under the MDR rule, we report if the information reasonably suggests the device may have caused or contributed to a death or serious injury, or malfunctioned in a way likely to cause one if it happened again. The usual deadline is 30 calendar days from when we become aware. When in doubt, I report, and I document the decision either way.
FDA sent an additional information request on our 510(k), and engineering disagrees with one item. How do you handle it?
How you deal with a reviewer's request under a deadline.
Understanding what the reviewer needs, answering every item fully, disagreeing only with data, and never missing the response deadline.

First I make sure we understand the concern; I may ask for a short call with the reviewer. The file is on hold, and if we miss the response deadline it is treated as withdrawn, so I plan backward from that date. For the item we dispute, I show with test data or a recognized standard why it is covered. Arguing without evidence just costs a review cycle.
After filing, you find a test result in the submission was reported wrong. What do you do?
Your honesty and your process when your own filing has an error.
Confirming the error, telling FDA promptly with a correction, and fixing the cause, never hoping nobody notices.

I confirm the error with the lab and find out how big it is. Then I tell my manager and send FDA a correction promptly, with the right data and a plain explanation, as an amendment if the file is still under review. Then I fix the cause, for example a second check of data tables against the test reports. Trust with a reviewer is hard to rebuild.
The reviewer asks for a clinical study you believe the device does not need. How do you push back?
How you push back on a regulator without hurting the relationship.
Using the least burdensome principle with evidence, such as bench, animal or published data, that answers the reviewer's actual question.

I first ask what question the study is meant to answer. Then I show how other evidence answers it: bench tests to a recognized standard, published data, or the predicate's history. FDA must consider the least burdensome way to get the needed information, so I can cite that, politely. If they still disagree, I ask what would satisfy them and weigh the cost with the team.
How do you choose a predicate device when several could work?
Whether you pick a predicate on strategy, not just on the first match you find.
Same intended use, closest technology, a legally marketed device and a clean safety record. No taking intended use from one predicate and technology from another.

I list every legally marketed candidate, then compare intended use first, then technology and test methods. I prefer a recent clearance with modern testing and no design-related recalls. I can cite reference devices for specific features, but one primary predicate must carry both the intended use and the core technology.
What is the difference between intended use and indications for use, and why does it matter in a 510(k)?
Your grasp of the terms that decide substantial equivalence.
Intended use is the general purpose; indications name the condition and patients. Reworded indications may still fit; a new disease or patient group often does not.

Intended use is the general purpose, like cutting soft tissue. Indications for use say which condition and which patients, like soft tissue cutting in adult general surgery. We need the same intended use as the predicate, so I write indications carefully: adding children or a new disease can turn into a new intended use.
When would you file a Special 510(k) instead of a Traditional one?
Whether you choose the faster pathway only when it truly fits.
For a change to the company's own cleared device, tested with well-established methods and reviewable in summary form; otherwise Traditional.

A Special 510(k) fits a change to our own cleared device when the change can be checked with well-established methods and the results reviewed in summary or risk analysis form. FDA aims to finish those in 30 days. If the change needs new test methods or a full data review, I file Traditional rather than risk a conversion that costs us time.
We want to run a clinical study of an investigational device. How do you decide whether we need an IDE approved by FDA?
Your knowledge of significant risk versus nonsignificant risk studies.
Check the exemptions, then judge risk: significant risk needs an FDA-approved IDE; nonsignificant risk goes to the IRB under abbreviated rules. FDA settles doubt.

First I check whether the study is exempt under Part 812. If not, I judge risk: if the device presents a potential for serious risk to subjects, for example some implants or life-supporting devices, we need an FDA-approved IDE before enrolling. A nonsignificant risk study goes to the IRB, which can disagree. If in doubt, I ask FDA for a risk determination.
Our next device connects to the internet. What does that change in the premarket submission?
Whether you know the cyber device requirements of section 524B.
Names the 524B items: a postmarket vulnerability plan, secure design and update processes, and a software bill of materials, planned from early design.

If it has software and can reach the internet, it is likely a cyber device under section 524B. The submission then needs a plan to find and fix vulnerabilities after launch, including coordinated disclosure, proof of secure design and a way to ship patches, and a software bill of materials, open-source parts included. I raise this at design start, not at filing.
Units with a wrong expiration date on the label have already shipped. Walk me through the decision on a correction or removal.
How you handle a field action and the Part 806 reporting duty.
Assess the health risk, decide the action, report to FDA within 10 working days if it reduces a risk to health, and document the reasoning either way.

First I get a health hazard evaluation: could an expired product, maybe no longer sterile, reach a patient? If we remove units to reduce that risk, Part 806 requires a report to FDA within 10 working days of starting. FDA then classifies the recall. If we find no risk to health, we still keep a written record of why we did not report.
FDA published a draft guidance that would add testing for our main product line. What do you do?
How you shape new rules instead of only reacting to them.
An impact assessment, a specific comment to the docket backed by data, work with industry peers, and a plan in case the guidance is finalized.

I estimate the impact: which products, which tests, what cost and time. Then I submit a comment to the docket on regulations.gov within the comment period, with data and a workable alternative, and share it with our trade association. Guidance is not binding, so I note where another approach meets the regulation. Meanwhile I plan as if it becomes final.
Our algorithm will be retrained after launch. How would you use a Predetermined Change Control Plan?
Whether you can build future changes into today's submission.
Explains the PCCP parts: planned modifications, the protocol to make and validate them, and an impact assessment. Changes outside the plan still need a submission.

A PCCP is authorized under section 515C and is reviewed with the marketing submission. I would describe the exact planned changes, such as retraining on new data, the protocol for data management, testing and acceptance criteria, and an impact assessment. Once authorized, changes made within the plan need no new submission. Anything outside it, like a new indication, still does.
Our quality system was built for the old Part 820. What do you change for the QMSR?
Whether you can lead the move to the new Quality Management System Regulation.
Knows the QMSR applies from February 2, 2026, incorporates ISO 13485:2016, and opens management review and audit reports to FDA inspection.

The QMSR applies from February 2, 2026 and incorporates ISO 13485:2016 by reference, so I run a gap check against the standard plus the US rules FDA kept, like UDI and complaint links to MDR. A big change: management review, internal audit and supplier audit reports are no longer shielded from inspectors, so I make sure they are complete.

reinforcement-learning.heading: Reinforcement learning researcher questions
qs: What is the difference between on-policy and off-policy reinforcement learning?
Whether you know the core split in how RL methods use their data.
On-policy learns from data the current policy just generated; off-policy can learn from data collected by another policy, such as a replay buffer.

On-policy methods, like PPO, update the policy using samples it just produced, so old data goes stale after each update. Off-policy methods, like DQN with a replay buffer, can learn from data gathered by an older or different policy. Off-policy reuses data better; on-policy is usually more stable and simpler to tune.
Why do policy gradient methods subtract a baseline, and what is an advantage?
Your grasp of why variance is the usual problem in policy gradients.
A baseline that does not depend on the action keeps the gradient unbiased but cuts its variance; the advantage is how much better an action did than expected.

Raw returns are noisy, so the gradient jumps around. Subtracting a baseline, often a learned value estimate, does not change the expected gradient as long as it does not depend on the action, but it lowers variance a lot. The advantage is return minus that baseline: positive means the action did better than the policy usually does from that state.
Walk me through how a model is trained with reinforcement learning from human feedback.
Whether you know the standard post-training pipeline end to end.
Supervised fine-tuning, a reward model trained on human preference pairs, then RL against that reward with a penalty for drifting from the starting model.

First we fine-tune the base model on good example answers. Then people compare pairs of responses, and we train a reward model to score the preferred one higher. Last, we optimize the policy with an RL method such as PPO to raise that score, with a KL penalty, a cost for drifting from the fine-tuned model, so it does not wander into odd text.
Why keep a KL penalty against the reference model, and how do you pick its strength?
How you weigh gaining reward against keeping the model sound.
The reward model is only trustworthy near the data it saw; the KL term limits drift. Strength is tuned by watching reward, KL and real quality together.

The reward model was trained on outputs like the reference model's, so far from them its scores mean little. The KL term keeps the policy where the reward is trustworthy and keeps the text fluent. I sweep a few values and plot reward against KL; too weak and the model games the reward, too strong and nothing changes. Held-out and human evals pick the point.
How does DPO differ from PPO-based RLHF, and when would you choose each?
Whether you know the main options for preference training and their costs.
DPO trains directly on preference pairs with a simple loss, no separate reward model or sampling loop; PPO costs more but learns from fresh samples.

DPO turns the preference objective into a classification-style loss on chosen and rejected pairs, using the reference model, so no reward model or online generation is needed. It is cheap and stable. PPO samples new responses during training, so it can go beyond a fixed dataset and use any reward. I often start with DPO and move to online RL when it plateaus.
Explain how GRPO estimates advantages without a value network.
Your knowledge of the methods used in current language-model RL.
It samples a group of answers per prompt and scores each against the group's mean reward, often scaled by the standard deviation, so no critic is needed.

For each prompt the model writes several answers, say eight. Each one's advantage is its reward minus the group mean, usually divided by the group's standard deviation. Answers better than their siblings get pushed up, worse ones down, with no value model to train. The catch: if all eight get the same reward, every advantage is zero and that prompt teaches nothing.
Annotators disagree on about a third of your preference pairs. How do you handle that?
Your judgement about noisy human labels.
Separates real ambiguity from unclear guidelines or weak raters, measures agreement, and fixes the process instead of just throwing data away.

First I check where they disagree. If it is close pairs where both answers are fine, that is real noise, and I may drop ties or give them lower weight. If it clusters on one topic or one rater, the guidelines are unclear or a rater needs retraining. I measure agreement per batch and add gold questions with known answers to catch problems early.
Your reward keeps climbing but people say the answers are getting worse. What is happening and what do you do?
How you recognize and handle reward hacking.
Names it as reward over-optimization, reads samples to find the exploit, rolls back to a good checkpoint and fixes the reward or the penalty.

The policy is exploiting flaws in the reward model, often by getting longer, more flattering or more confident. I read high-reward samples to find the pattern, check length against reward, and go back to the last checkpoint humans preferred. Then I fix the cause: more preference data on that failure, a length control, a stronger KL penalty, or earlier stopping.
How would you train with rewards you can verify, like math answers or code tests, and what can go wrong?
Whether you know the strengths and traps of verifiable rewards.
Checks answers automatically instead of with a learned judge, but guards against weak tests, format tricks and prompts that are too easy or too hard.

I sample several answers per problem and give 1 if the final answer matches or all tests pass, else 0. There is no reward model to fool, but the checker can be fooled: code may special-case visible tests, or a loose parser may accept a bad answer. I use hidden tests, a strict parser, and drop prompts the model always or never solves.
Halfway through a PPO run, KL to the reference spikes and the output turns into repeated tokens. How do you debug it?
How you diagnose an unstable training run.
Stops the run, checks which logged metrics moved first, reads samples, and looks at learning rate, clipping, entropy and data before changing anything.

I stop it and roll back to the last healthy checkpoint. Then I look at what moved first: entropy dropping, clip fraction rising, or gradient norm jumping. I read samples just before the spike and check that batch for bad prompts or a reward bug. Usual fixes are a lower learning rate, fewer epochs per batch or a stronger KL term, one change at a time.
How is a reward model trained on pairwise preferences, and what does its score actually mean?
Whether you know the loss behind a reward model and what its numbers can and cannot tell you.
Names the Bradley-Terry loss, which pushes the chosen score above the rejected one. Only differences matter, so an absolute score means nothing alone.

I put a scalar head on a language model and minimize minus log sigmoid of the chosen score minus the rejected score. That is the Bradley-Terry model. Adding a constant to every score changes nothing, so a 3.2 means nothing alone. I compare scores within a prompt, and I often normalize rewards before RL so the scale stays stable.
What does the lambda in generalized advantage estimation control?
Your grasp of how advantage estimates trade bias against variance.
Lambda blends one-step TD errors (low variance, biased by the value model) with full returns (unbiased, noisy).

GAE is a weighted sum of TD errors, the one-step surprise against the value estimate. At lambda 0 it is just that one step: low variance, but biased if the value model is wrong. At 1 it is the full return minus the value baseline: unbiased but noisy. With one reward at the end of a response, many teams set lambda near 1 because the value model is weak early on.
What does the clipping in PPO's objective do, and what does it not guarantee?
Whether you understand PPO's trust region well enough to debug it.
Clipping removes the incentive to push the probability ratio past 1 plus or minus epsilon in the favored direction; it does not hard-bound the policy change or the KL.

The loss takes the minimum of the ratio times the advantage and the clipped ratio times the advantage. Once the ratio leaves the band in the direction the advantage favors, that token's gradient goes to zero. It is not a hard limit: with many epochs the policy can still drift far. So I watch the clip fraction and approximate KL, and cut epochs or learning rate if they climb.
You use a strong model as a judge to compare your model with the baseline. What biases do you guard against?
How you keep automatic evaluation honest.
Names position, length and self-preference bias, and checks the judge against human labels before trusting it.

Judges often favor one position, longer answers, and text in their own style. I run every pair in both orders and count a win only if it holds both ways, report a length-controlled win rate, and avoid pitting the judge's own model family as a contestant. Before trusting it, I check its agreement with a few hundred human labels on our tasks.
After RLHF your answers are 60% longer and win rates went up. How do you find out whether the model really got better?
Whether you can separate real quality from length bias in rewards and evaluation.
Treats length as a confounder: measures reward against length, compares at matched length, and fixes the data or reward if the gain is only length.

First I plot reward model score against length on held-out answers; a strong slope means the reward pays for length. Then I compare answers of similar length, or use a length-controlled win rate. If the gain vanishes, I balance length in the preference pairs, add a length term to the reward, or retrain the reward model with pairs where the shorter answer wins.
During DPO training, the log-probability of the chosen answers goes down, not up. Is that a bug?
Your knowledge of what DPO optimizes and its known failure modes.
Not necessarily: DPO widens the margin, and both sides can fall. It matters if quality drops; then lower the step size, raise beta or add a likelihood term on chosen answers.

Not by itself. DPO's loss only cares about the gap between chosen and rejected, relative to the reference model. Both can drop as long as rejected drops faster, and probability mass can move to answers in neither set. I check samples and evals. If quality falls, I lower the learning rate, raise beta, or add a log-likelihood term on the chosen answers.
In your GRPO run on math, most prompts give either all correct or all wrong answers across the group. Why does that hurt, and what do you change?
Whether you see how group-relative advantages lose signal and how to fix the prompt mix.
Equal rewards in a group give zero advantage, so those prompts teach nothing. Filter or resample toward prompts the policy solves only some of the time.

The advantage is each reward minus the group mean, so if all eight samples score the same, every advantage is zero and the prompt adds no learning signal. It just dilutes the batch. I would filter those prompts out and refill the batch, and build a curriculum from pass rates measured on the current policy, keeping prompts it solves sometimes but not always.
When would you use a process reward model instead of an outcome reward, and what does it cost you?
Your judgement on credit assignment in long reasoning tasks.
Process rewards give denser credit per step but need costly step labels and can be gamed; outcome rewards are cheap and harder to fool when answers can be checked.

If answers can be checked, I start with outcome rewards: cheap, and hard to game if the checker is sound. A process reward model scores each step, so it helps when chains are long and a final pass or fail says little about where it went wrong. The cost is step labels, which are expensive, and a new target to hack, like steps that look careful but are not.
After RL, pass@1 on your benchmark rose 12 points. How would you tell whether the model learned something new or just samples its best answers more often?
Whether you can read what RL changed rather than just the headline number.
Compares pass@k curves of the base and RL models out to large k, and looks at which problems newly become solvable.

I compute pass@k for the base and the RL model from 1 up to a large k, like 256. If the base model catches up at high k, RL mostly moved probability onto answers it could already find. If the RL model solves problems the base never solved in any sample, that is new reach. I also check the benchmark for overlap with the training prompts.
Your new reward model gives a 1.5-point gain over the old one, from one run each. The team wants to ship it. What do you say?
How you judge a result when RL runs are noisy.
Asks for the seed-to-seed spread before claiming a gain; reruns with several seeds, reports confidence intervals and checks other metrics did not get worse.

One run each tells us little: RL runs can differ by a point or more just from the seed. I would rerun both setups with three to five seeds and report the mean with a confidence interval, plus the eval's own sampling error. If the gain holds above that spread and no safety or length metric got worse, I support shipping.

renewals.heading: Renewals manager questions
qs: How far ahead of the end date do you start working a renewal, and what do you do first?
How you plan a renewal so nothing is decided at the last minute.
A start months ahead, set by account size and risk, and the contract read before the first call.

For a typical account I start about 120 days out, earlier for large or shaky ones. First I read the contract: end date, notice period, auto-renew terms and any price clause. Then I check usage and open tickets, and I call the main contact to hear how the year went before price ever comes up.
Which signs tell you an account may not renew?
Whether you spot churn risk early from real signals.
Concrete signals from usage, people and behavior, checked on a regular schedule, not a gut feeling.

Falling logins or seat use, a champion who left, a new executive or a budget freeze, emails that go unanswered, and repeat escalations to support. Questions about exporting data are a loud one. I review my accounts every week, and two signals together put an account on my at-risk list with a plan.
When do you bring up an upsell, and when do you hold back?
Your judgement on selling more without hurting the renewal.
Upsell when the customer gets value and has a clear need; fix problems first and never tie them together.

I raise it when the data shows a need: they are at their seat limit or a team keeps asking for a feature in a higher plan. If they have open problems or low use, I hold back and secure the renewal first. Pushing more product on an unhappy customer turns a safe renewal into a risky one.
We are raising prices 8% this year. How do you tell a customer?
How you deliver a price increase so the customer still renews.
Early notice that respects the contract's terms, a plain reason, the value they got, and options to choose from.

I tell them early, well before the notice date in their contract, and in writing after a call. I say the number plainly, give the reason, and show what they got this year, like hours saved or new features. Then I offer options, for example locking the price with a two-year term. No surprise on an invoice.
A customer asks for 20% off to renew. How do you handle it?
Whether you protect revenue while keeping the customer.
Find the real reason first, and trade instead of giving: any discount gets something back, within approval limits.

I ask what is behind it: budget cut, a competitor quote, or low use. Low use I fix with a right-sized plan, not a discount. If a concession fits, I trade it: a smaller discount for a two-year term or signing a month early. Anything past my limit goes to my manager with the reasons written down.
Your champion at a large account just left, 90 days before renewal. What do you do?
How you rebuild a relationship under time pressure.
Quick contact with the new owner and other users, value shown again from scratch, and the risk flagged in the forecast.

I flag the account as at risk that day. I ask the departing champion, if reachable, who takes over, and I reach out to the new owner and two or three daily users. I book a short review of the results they got this year, since the new person never saw them. I also make sure their admin training is current.
A contract auto-renewed, and the customer says they meant to cancel. What do you do?
Your judgement when the contract is on your side but the customer is upset.
Facts checked first, no hiding behind the clause, finance or legal brought in, and a fair outcome sought.

I check the contract terms and whether our renewal notice went out on time and to the right person. Then I listen to why they want to leave. If we missed a step, I own it and work with finance on a fix. If we did everything right, I still look for a fair middle path, like a shorter term or fewer seats, with my manager's approval.
Walk me through how you forecast your renewals for the quarter.
Whether your forecast rests on evidence your manager can trust.
Categories tied to clear proof, like a verbal yes or paperwork in procurement, updated weekly and honest about risk.

I sort every renewal into commit, likely and at risk. Commit means a verbal yes and paperwork moving through their procurement. Likely means good usage and engagement but no yes yet. At risk means two or more warning signs. I update it weekly, and I would rather call an account at risk and save it than surprise my manager.
Tell me about a renewal you lost. What would you do differently?
Whether you learn from churn instead of blaming the customer.
An honest account of the real cause, your own part in it, and a change you made to your process afterward.

I lost a 40-seat account because I worked only with one manager. Their finance head cut the tool in a budget review I never knew about. Now I map at least three contacts per account, including the budget owner, and I send a short value summary each quarter that the champion can forward upward.
What is the difference between gross and net revenue retention, and why watch both?
Whether you know the core retention metrics and what each one hides.
Gross excludes expansion and cannot pass 100%; net includes it. Strong net can hide a weak base, so gross shows whether the base is sound.

Gross retention is the revenue we kept from the customers we started with, after churn and downgrades, with no credit for upsells, so it can never pass 100%. Net retention adds expansion back in. Net can look healthy while gross slips, which means upsells are hiding a leak. I watch gross to see if the base itself is sound.
What does co-terming mean, and when would you push for it?
Your grasp of contract mechanics that affect renewal risk.
Aligning all subscriptions to one end date, usually by prorating add-ons. Fewer renewal dates mean fewer churn points and less procurement work.

Co-terming means lining up all of a customer's subscriptions to one end date, usually by prorating an add-on to the main contract's term. I push for it when an account has three orders renewing in three different months. Each date is another chance to churn and another procurement cycle for them. One date is simpler for both sides.
A customer wants to cut 40% of their seats at renewal. How do you respond?
How you handle a downsell without losing the account or the relationship.
Finds the reason first, checks usage, and accepts right-sizing when it is fair, while trading for term or a growth plan.

First I ask why: layoffs, low adoption or an overlapping tool. Then I check usage. If only 55% of seats are active, I would rather right-size now and keep their trust than force a renewal that churns next year. I might trade the smaller count for a longer term or a price lock, and agree on a plan to grow back as adoption rises.
How do you decide between offering a multi-year deal and a one-year renewal?
Your judgement on term length, price and risk.
Multi-year suits stable, well-used accounts that want price certainty; trade a cap or small discount for term, and avoid locking in a shaky account.

Multi-year fits when the product is deeply used and the customer wants budget certainty. I offer a price cap or a modest discount for the longer commitment, often billed yearly so their cash is not hit at once. I avoid it for a shaky account, where a long lock-in only delays an unhappy exit, or when it would freeze a price far below our list.
Two weeks before the end date, the customer's procurement team sends a long list of contract changes. What do you do?
How you manage a late legal and procurement cycle without letting service lapse.
Brings in legal fast, gets all changes at once, sorts them by what needs approval, and uses a written short extension if time runs out.

I bring in our legal team the same day and ask procurement for their full list at once, not piece by piece. I sort the changes: what we can accept, what needs approval, what is a firm no. If we cannot finish in time, I propose a short written extension on current terms so service does not stop. And I note to start legal earlier with this account next year.
A customer says a competitor quoted them half our price. How do you handle it?
How you defend value in a competitive renewal without giving away margin.
Looks at what the quote includes, shows switching costs, asks whether price is the real issue, and only concedes in exchange for something.

I ask what the quote includes, because half price often means fewer features, lower support or a first-year teaser rate. I lay out the real cost of switching: migration, retraining, lost history. I also check if price is the true reason or a cover for an unhappy team. If I do move on price, I ask for something back, like a longer term or a reference.
The contract ended yesterday, and the customer's purchase order is still stuck in their system. Do you cut off access?
Your judgement on lapsed contracts, policy and the customer relationship.
No surprise shutoffs. Follows company policy, gets approval for a short documented grace period when renewal is confirmed, and escalates before any cutoff.

Not if they have confirmed in writing that they are renewing and the delay is their paperwork. I follow our policy, get approval for a short grace period, and put the new date in an email to the buyer. If there is no written commitment and no reply, I go to my manager before any shutoff, and the customer gets clear warning first, never a surprise.
Walk me through how you prepare a business review with a customer's executive before a large renewal.
Whether you can prove value to a senior buyer in their own terms.
Starts from the customer's stated goals, uses numbers they confirm, admits problems honestly, and ends with a plan that sets up the renewal.

I start from the goals they named when they bought, then pull numbers tied to them: hours saved, tickets cut, adoption by team. I ask their admin to confirm the figures so they are not just ours. I keep it to a few slides, name one or two problems honestly, and end with next year's plan. That sets up the renewal without a hard sell.
Sales promised a feature that has not shipped, and the customer will not renew without it. What do you do?
How you handle a broken promise you did not make.
Finds out exactly what was promised, tells the truth on timing, looks for workarounds, offers fair concessions, and never invents a new date.

First I find out exactly what was promised and check the real date with product. Then I tell the customer the truth, even if it slipped. I ask what they need the feature for, since a workaround may cover it. If the miss is ours, a credit or shorter term is fair, but I do not promise a date I cannot control. Then I raise it with sales leadership.
You inherit a book of 300 accounts with no renewal process. What do you set up in your first 90 days?
Whether you can build a renewals operation, not just work deals.
One clean list with end dates and notice periods, tiering by value and risk, coverage matched to tier, and a regular risk review and forecast.

First month, I get every account into one list with end date, value, notice period and owner, because missed notice dates are the easiest loss to avoid. Then I tier by value and risk: big accounts get a person and a 120-day start, small ones get an automated email series. By day 90 I want a weekly risk review with customer success and a forecast I can defend.

research-analyst.heading: Research analyst questions
qs: What is the difference between market cap and fully diluted valuation, and when does the gap matter?
Whether you know the supply figures that drive a token's valuation.
Market cap uses circulating supply and FDV uses maximum or total supply. A wide gap means future supply that can weigh on price.

Market cap is price times the tokens circulating today. FDV is price times the maximum supply, or total supply if there is no cap. If only 15% of tokens circulate, FDV can be several times market cap. The rest will reach the market through unlocks and emissions, and that future selling is the first thing I check.
What does TVL measure, and why can it mislead?
Whether you can read the most quoted DeFi metric with care.
TVL is the dollar value of assets deposited in a protocol. It moves with token prices and can be inflated by double counting and looped deposits.

TVL is the dollar value of assets locked in a protocol's contracts. It can rise just because ETH went up, with no new deposits. The same asset can be counted twice, for example a liquid staking token deposited again in a lending market, and borrowers can loop deposits. I look at TVL in native units and at who the largest depositors are.
A dashboard shows a protocol made $40 million in fees last year. Is that its revenue?
Whether you separate what users pay from what the protocol keeps.
Fees are what users pay. Revenue is the share the protocol or token holders keep after paying liquidity providers or lenders.

Usually not. Fees are everything users paid. On a DEX most of that goes to liquidity providers, and on a lending market most interest goes to lenders. Revenue is the slice kept by the treasury or token holders, which can be small. I check the contracts and fee settings, not just the dashboard label, because tools define these terms differently.
A chain reports two million daily active addresses. What does that tell you about users?
How you avoid treating wallet counts as people.
Addresses are not users. One person or bot can run many, so you filter by value, behavior and repeat activity.

Less than it sounds. One person can hold dozens of addresses, and bots or airdrop farmers can create thousands for almost nothing on a cheap chain. I filter out dust-sized transfers, check how many addresses come back over 30 days, and look at fees paid. Two million addresses paying fractions of a cent is a different story from 50,000 paying real money.
How do you check the trading volume a crypto exchange reports?
Whether you know which crypto data is self-reported and how to test it.
Centralized exchange volume is self-reported. You compare it with order book depth, spreads, on-chain flows and peers instead of trusting the headline.

On a centralized exchange trades happen off-chain, so the volume is whatever the exchange reports. I compare it with order book depth near the price, spreads, the deposit and withdrawal flows I can see on-chain, and peers of similar size. Huge volume on a thin order book is a red flag for wash trading. DEX volume I can rebuild from on-chain swaps.
Walk me through how you assess a large token unlock coming next month.
How you size future supply and judge who is likely to sell.
Size against circulating supply and daily volume, who receives the tokens, their cost basis, past behavior and any further vesting.

First the size: the unlock as a share of circulating supply and as days of average trading volume. Then who gets it. Early investors with a low cost basis are more likely to sell than a team still vesting. I read the vesting contract, watch whether recipient wallets move tokens to exchanges, and check price around past unlocks. I write it as a range, not a call.
How do you run an interview with a protocol founder so you get more than the pitch?
Your interview skill with a source who wants good coverage.
Prepare from on-chain data first, ask specific and checkable questions, ask about failures and rivals, and verify claims afterward.

I do the data work first so I can ask specifics: why deposits fell 30% in March, who the five largest wallets are. I ask what went wrong last year and which competitor worries them. I avoid questions that invite a slogan. Any claim, like a partnership or a user count, stays marked unverified until I check it on-chain or with the other party.
You suspect most of a protocol's growth is airdrop farming. How would you show it?
How you test a hunch with on-chain evidence.
Cluster wallets by funding source and behavior, compare activity around reward snapshots, check retention, and state the limits.

I look for clusters: many wallets funded from one source, making the same transactions minutes apart, often in round amounts. Then I compare activity before and after any announced snapshot or points change. If usage drops sharply when rewards end and few wallets return within 30 days, that supports farming. I show the method, the share I flagged, and what I could not rule out.
A protocol offers to pay your firm for a research report on it. How do you handle that?
Your judgement on independence and disclosure.
Payment and holdings disclosed in the report, no client control over conclusions, and compliance involved early.

Paid research can be fine if readers know. I want it in writing that the client sees the draft only to correct facts, not to change conclusions. The report states who paid, plus any tokens I or the firm hold. I bring in compliance early, because rules on paid promotion may apply. If they push to soften findings, we walk away.
After publishing, you find a number in your report was wrong and it changes one conclusion. What do you do?
How you own a mistake that readers may already have acted on.
Tell your lead at once, publish a dated, visible correction stating the impact, and fix the process that let it through.

I tell my lead the same day, with the correct figure and what it changes. We put a dated correction at the top of the report with the old and new number and the effect on the conclusion, and send it to everyone who got it. Then I find the cause. Last time a query counted bridged tokens twice, so I added a check against a second data source.
A protocol advertises a 20% staking yield. How do you work out how much of it is real?
Whether you separate yield paid from fees from yield paid in newly minted tokens.
Splitting yield by source and comparing it with supply inflation, so the answer is in share of the network, not just token count.

First I split it by source: fees users pay versus new tokens minted. Then I compare it with supply growth. If supply grows 18% a year and I earn 20%, my share of the network rises only about 2%. Most of the yield just offsets dilution. The part paid from fees is the part that would survive if emissions stopped.
The top ten wallets hold 70% of a token. What do you check before you call it concentrated?
How you read onchain holder data instead of taking a raw list at face value.
Labelling wallets first: exchanges, contracts, treasury and vesting are not single owners, and linked wallets may be one owner.

I label each wallet. An exchange wallet holds coins for many customers. Staking, bridge, liquidity pool and vesting contracts are not investors either. Then I look the other way: wallets funded from the same source may be one owner. After that I check the vesting schedule, because locked team tokens matter later, when they unlock.
Two analytics providers disagree by 30% on a DEX's monthly volume. How do you find out which is right?
Whether you can reconcile data sources by checking definitions before blaming either one.
Comparing definitions line by line, then rebuilding a sample from raw onchain data.

Usually both are right about something different. I list what each counts: which chains and contract versions, whether a swap routed through two pools counts twice, how they price thin tokens, whether they filter wash trading, and where the day cuts off. Then I query one day of raw swap events myself and see which definition my number matches.
A colleague backtested a strategy on today's top 20 tokens by market cap and it beat the market easily. What is wrong with it?
Whether you spot survivorship and look-ahead bias in a crypto backtest.
Naming that the list was picked with knowledge of the future, and rebuilding the universe as it stood on each past date, dead tokens included.

The basket was chosen using today's ranking, so it only holds the tokens that survived and grew. Many tokens in the top 20 a few years ago have since collapsed or been delisted. I would rebuild the top 20 as it was on each rebalance date, keep the dead tokens in with their real losses, and add trading costs. The edge usually shrinks a lot.
What is MEV, and how would you estimate what sandwich attacks cost a DEX's users?
Your grasp of transaction ordering and how you turn it into a measurable number.
A correct definition of maximal extractable value, the sandwich mechanics, and a method that finds the pattern in block data.

MEV is profit from choosing which transactions go in a block and in what order. In a sandwich, a bot buys just before a user's swap and sells right after, so the user gets a worse price within their slippage limit. I look for one address trading the same pool just before and after a victim in the same block, then compare the victim's fill with the price before the bot's trade.
A protocol says it is fully governed by token holders. How do you test that claim?
Whether you check onchain who can actually change the contracts, not what the docs say.
Checking upgrade and admin keys, timelocks and real voting power, and whether passed votes actually execute.

I start onchain: who holds the upgrade and admin rights, and can a small multisig change contracts without a vote? Is there a timelock that gives users time to exit? Then I look at voters, not holders: turnout, how many addresses decide a typical vote, and how much power sits with the team and early investors. Last, I check that passed proposals were actually executed.
How do you assess the risk of a cross-chain bridge before a client moves funds through it?
Your understanding of bridge trust models, where many of the largest crypto hacks happened.
Asking who can approve a withdrawal, how keys are held, who can upgrade it, and how much value sits in one contract.

The core question is who can sign off on a message from the other chain. If it is a multisig of a few keys, the bridge is only as safe as those keys; several large bridge hacks came from stolen validator keys. Designs that verify proofs of the other chain's state remove much of that trust. Then I check upgrade keys, timelocks, audits, rate limits and how much value is locked.
A lending protocol accepts a small-cap token as collateral. How do you judge its oracle risk?
Whether you see how price manipulation turns into bad debt for a lender.
Linking the price source and market depth to borrow limits, and naming manipulation and bad debt as the failure.

If the price comes from a thin DEX pool, an attacker can push it up, often with a flash loan, borrow against the inflated collateral and leave the protocol with bad debt. I check where the price comes from, whether it is a time-weighted average or spot, how much it costs to move the market 20%, and whether supply and borrow caps keep the possible loss below that cost.
How do you judge how much of Ethereum's security a rollup really inherits?
Your depth on layer 2 design: proofs, data availability, sequencing and upgrade control.
Covering whether proofs are live, where data is posted, whether users can force inclusion, and whether they can exit before an upgrade.

I ask four things. Are fraud or validity proofs live, and can anyone submit them? Is transaction data posted to Ethereum, or kept off-chain? If the sequencer censors me, can I force a transaction through Ethereum? And can a multisig upgrade the contracts faster than users can withdraw? A rollup that fails the last test is trusting its key holders.
Your head of research is publicly bullish on a protocol, and your data points the other way. How do you write the report?
How you keep your findings honest under pressure from inside the firm.
Taking it to the senior first with the evidence, keeping the conclusion the data supports, and stating what would change it.

I would not soften it quietly. I take the data to them before drafting, show the method, and ask what I might be missing; sometimes they know something I do not. If the data still holds, the report says what it shows, gives the bull case fairly, and names the signs that would prove me wrong. Our readers pay for the analysis, not for agreement.

research-scientist.heading: Research scientist questions
qs: Why should the test set be used only once, at the end of a project?
Whether you keep evaluation honest.
Tuning on test makes the score too optimistic. Choices are made on a validation split, and the test set is run once.

Every choice I make while looking at a split leaks some of that split into the model. If I pick learning rates or checkpoints on test, the score no longer estimates performance on new data. So I tune on validation, freeze the setup, then run test once. If a benchmark has no validation split, I carve one out of the training data.
What makes a baseline fair?
Whether your comparisons would survive a skeptical reviewer.
Same data, a similar tuning budget and compute, a strong recent version, and rerunning it when setups differ instead of copying numbers.

The baseline gets the same data, the same preprocessing and roughly the same tuning effort as my method. I pick the strongest recent version, not an easy one. If my setup differs from the original paper, I rerun the baseline myself rather than copy its reported number. Then any gap comes from the idea, not from extra care.
Your method beats the baseline by half a point on a single run. Is that a result?
How you treat noise from random seeds.
Not yet. Several seeds for both methods, the mean with spread or a confidence interval, and a check that the gap is larger than seed-to-seed noise.

Not yet. On many benchmarks, changing only the random seed moves the score by half a point. I would run five or more seeds for both methods and report the mean and standard deviation. If the gap stays clear of the spread, I believe it. If the ranges overlap heavily, I call it inconclusive and do not claim a win.
Walk me through how you would design ablations for a method with three new parts.
Your ability to show which part of a method does the work.
Remove each part from the full method, and add each to the baseline, with everything else held fixed. Interactions get checked and all seeds reported.

I start from the full method and remove one part at a time, holding data, compute and tuning fixed. Then I add each part alone to the baseline. If removing part A hurts only when B is present, they interact, and I test that pair directly. Each row gets several seeds, so the table shows real effects and not noise.
How do you write a paper so another lab can reproduce your results?
Your scientific writing for reproducibility.
Full hyperparameters, data versions and preprocessing, seeds, compute used, released code where possible, and honest limitations.

I add a table with every hyperparameter, including the ones we never tuned. I name the exact data version, the splits and the preprocessing steps. I state how many seeds we ran and the compute each run took. When I can, I release code and configs. I also write a limitations section, so readers know where the method failed.
Your training loss turns into NaN after 20,000 steps. What do you do?
How you debug a failed training run step by step.
Reload a checkpoint from before the failure, find the batch and layer where it starts, and check usual causes: learning rate, overflow, log of zero.

I reload the last good checkpoint and replay with gradient norms logged per layer. Often the norm spikes a few steps before the NaN. Then I check the usual causes: learning rate too high, a log or division by zero, or overflow in 16-bit math. Fixes might be gradient clipping, a lower learning rate or a numerical guard. I also look at that exact batch.
You suspect test questions from a benchmark are in your pretraining data. What do you do?
Whether you handle data contamination with honesty.
Measure the overlap, report scores on clean and overlapping subsets, and disclose it in the paper instead of hiding it.

I search the pretraining corpus for long word sequences that match each test item, and I flag the hits. Then I report the score on the full set and on the clean subset only. If the clean score drops a lot, the headline number is inflated and I say so. Either way, I describe the check and its limits in the paper.
You have a fixed compute budget for one large training run. How do you choose its settings?
Your judgement in planning expensive experiments.
Small-scale sweeps across sizes, a fitted trend to extrapolate, and checks that key settings transfer. Evals and checkpoints are planned before launch.

I spend a small share of the budget on runs at several smaller sizes. I fit how loss changes with model size and data, then extrapolate to choose the big run's size and token count. I confirm the learning rate trend holds across sizes. Before launch I set regular checkpoints and evals, so a problem shows up early, not at the end.
A reviewer says your gain comes from extra parameters, not from your idea. How do you respond?
How you handle criticism with evidence instead of argument.
Treat it as a fair question: run a baseline with matched parameters, report the result either way, and adjust the claim if needed.

It is a fair point, so I answer with an experiment. I would widen or deepen the baseline until its parameter count matches ours, tune it the same way, and run several seeds. If our gain holds, I add that table to the paper. If it shrinks, I say so in the rebuttal and narrow the claim to what the data support.
After your paper is accepted, you find a bug that inflates the main result. What do you do?
Your integrity when a published result turns out wrong.
Tell coauthors at once, rerun with the fix, contact the venue about a correction, and post a corrected version with a clear note.

I tell my coauthors the same day and fix the bug. We rerun the affected experiments and see what still holds. Then we contact the program chairs about correcting the camera-ready version, post a new preprint with a note saying what changed, and update the code. If others built on our number, I tell them directly. A smaller true result beats a large wrong one.
Why does a transformer scale attention scores by the square root of the key dimension?
Whether you understand why a standard design choice exists.
Dot products grow with dimension. Without scaling, the softmax saturates and gradients become tiny.

Say query and key entries are independent with unit variance. Their dot product then has variance equal to the key dimension d. Large scores push the softmax toward one-hot outputs, where gradients are close to zero. Dividing by the square root of d brings the variance back to about one, so training stays stable.
Your model scores well during training but much worse in evaluation, and it uses batch norm. Where do you look first?
How you debug a mismatch between training and evaluation behavior.
Mode switching and running statistics. Evaluation uses stored averages, so the wrong mode or stale statistics break results.

In training, batch norm normalizes with the current batch's statistics. In eval it uses running averages collected during training. I check that the model is really switched to eval mode and that the running stats were built on data like the test data. Then I compare outputs in both modes on the same batch to see where they split.
Why do many teams train in bfloat16 instead of float16?
Your grasp of number formats in mixed-precision training.
bfloat16 keeps float32's exponent range, so gradients rarely underflow and loss scaling is usually not needed. It gives up precision instead.
