Float16 has 5 exponent bits, so small gradients can underflow to zero and you need loss scaling. Bfloat16 has 8 exponent bits, the same range as float32, but only 7 mantissa bits. It rarely overflows or underflows, at the cost of precision. I still usually keep master weights and optimizer states in float32.
Is weight decay the same as L2 regularization when you use Adam?
Whether you know an optimizer detail that changes results.
No. With Adam the L2 gradient is rescaled per parameter. AdamW decouples the decay and applies it directly to the weights.

With plain SGD they are equivalent, up to how you set the coefficient. With Adam, an L2 term is added to the gradient and then divided by the adaptive denominator, so weights with a large gradient history are decayed less. AdamW applies the decay directly to the weights, separate from the adaptive step, so its setting behaves more predictably.
A colleague says gradient accumulation over 8 micro-batches is identical to one batch 8 times larger. Is that right?
How carefully you reason about training equivalences.
Mostly, if the loss is scaled correctly. Batch norm statistics and averaging over sequences of uneven length break the equivalence.

For the gradient, it is close if each micro-batch loss is scaled so the sum equals the large-batch mean. There are two traps. Batch norm sees only the micro-batch, so its statistics differ. With variable-length sequences, averaging per micro-batch weights tokens differently than one average over all tokens, so I normalize by the total token count.
You plan to use a language model as a judge to compare two systems. What can go wrong, and how do you guard against it?
Your awareness of bias in automatic evaluation.
Known biases such as position, length and self-preference, handled with controls and a check against human ratings.

Model judges are known to favor the answer shown first, longer answers, and outputs from their own model family. I run each pair in both orders, control or report length, and avoid a judge from the same family as either system. Then people rate a random sample, and I report how often the judge agrees with them before I trust it.
Your method leads on a popular benchmark, but on a new test set collected the same way the gain disappears. What do you conclude?
How you read a result that does not transfer.
You suspect overfitting to the benchmark through repeated design choices, and check the new set's match and size before deciding.

My first suspicion is that many design choices were made by looking at that benchmark, so the gain fits its quirks. I check that the new set really matches: same sources, labeling and difficulty. I also check that it is large enough to detect the old gain. If it holds up, I report that the gain does not transfer instead of quietly dropping the new set.
You compare your method with four others on twelve datasets and win on five. How do you report it?
Your handling of many comparisons at once.
You account for multiple comparisons, report every dataset with its variance, and claim no more than the evidence supports.

With dozens of comparisons, some wins appear by chance. I report every dataset with the mean and spread over seeds, not only the wins. For the overall claim I use a test across datasets, such as a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, or I correct per-dataset tests for multiple comparisons. Then I say where the method helps and where it does not.
A week before the deadline, a preprint appears with an idea very close to yours. What do you do?
Your judgement and integrity under competition.
You read it closely, cite it, state honestly what differs, and check the venue's rule on concurrent work.

I read it carefully and list what overlaps and what does not. I cite it and say plainly how our work differs, for example in method, setting or results. I check the venue's policy, since most treat very recent papers as concurrent work. If the overlap is large, I agree with coauthors on adding a comparison or reframing. I do not hide it.
Three months into a project, the results are flat. How do you decide whether to stop, pivot or push on?
How you make hard calls on research direction.
First rule out a bug. Then find the smallest test that could still change the picture, and set a deadline for it.

First I rule out a bug: does the method beat a trivial baseline on a toy problem where it should clearly win? Then I ask what we learned and whether one cheap experiment could change our view. If yes, I run it with a fixed end date. If not, I write up the negative findings for the team and move the time to the most promising variant.

retail.heading: Retail and store questions
qs: What does FIFO mean when you stock shelves, and why do stores use it?
Whether you know the basic rule of stock rotation.
First in, first out: older stock moves to the front so it sells before newer stock, which cuts waste from expired or dated goods.

It means first in, first out. When I put out new stock, I pull the older items forward and put the new ones behind them, so the oldest product sells first. In a grocery aisle it stops things from expiring on the shelf. In clothing it keeps older styles from sitting in the back until they need a markdown.
What does it mean to face or zone a section, and when do you do it?
Your grasp of everyday floor upkeep and visual merchandising.
Pulling products to the front edge, labels out, in the right spot on the planogram, done all through the shift and not only at close.

Facing means pulling each product to the front of the shelf with the label turned out, so the shelf looks full and neat. Zoning is the bigger pass: putting strays back where they belong and matching the planogram, which is the map of where each item goes. I do quick passes in slow moments and a full zone before close.
Walk me through what you check when you open the store.
Whether you know the routine that has to be done before the first customer walks in.
A set order: entry secured, lights and systems on, tills counted, floor safe and stocked, signs right, doors opened on time.

If the store requires two people to open, I wait for my partner and we lock the door behind us. I turn on lights and systems and count the opening till against the set amount. Then I walk the floor: no spills, exits clear, displays full. I check that sale signs match this week's prices, then unlock right on time.
A shelf tag shows a lower price than what scans at the register. What do you do?
How you handle a price error fairly for the customer and the store.
Checking the tag quickly, following the store's price policy, usually honoring the lower price, and getting the tag fixed.

I have a coworker check the tag so the line keeps moving. If the tag matches the item and is still current, I give the customer the shelf price, with an override or a manager if needed. Then I make sure the wrong tag gets fixed or pulled so the next customer does not run into the same problem.
You spot a spill in an aisle while you are helping a customer. What do you do?
Whether you put safety first without dropping the customer.
Guarding the spill right away, getting a sign up or a cleanup, then going back to the customer. A slip can cause a real injury.

I tell the customer, "Excuse me one second, I need to block this so nobody slips." I stand by the spill or put a wet floor sign over it and call a coworker on the radio. If no one can come, I clean it myself. Then I go back to the customer, thank them for waiting and finish helping them.
A delivery arrives during your shift. How do you check it in?
Your understanding of receiving and why it matters for stock counts.
Counting cartons against the paperwork before signing, noting damage or shortages on the driver's copy, then checking contents against the packing slip.

Before I sign, I count the cartons against the delivery paperwork and look for crushed or wet boxes. Anything short or damaged gets written on the driver's copy, because after I sign it clean a claim is harder. Then I open the cartons, check items and quantities against the packing slip, and tell my manager about any difference.
A customer's card is declined and there is a line behind them. How do you handle it?
How you protect a customer's dignity while keeping the line moving.
Saying it quietly and neutrally, offering to retry or use another payment, and never guessing the reason out loud.

I keep my voice low and say, "It's not going through. Would you like to try again or use another card?" I don't say "declined" loudly or guess why; it could be a chip problem or a bank hold. If they need a minute, I suspend the sale if our system allows it, help the next person, and pick it back up when they're ready.
A customer buying an age-restricted item gets annoyed when you ask for ID. What do you do?
Whether you follow the law and store policy under pressure.
Polite and firm: no valid ID, no sale. In many states the clerk, not just the store, can be fined for selling to a minor.

I stay friendly and say, "Our policy is to check ID for everyone who looks under a certain age. It's nothing personal." If they can't show a valid ID, I can't finish that part of the sale, and I say so calmly. Selling to a minor can mean a fine for me and the store, so I don't bend. If they get loud, I call my manager.
The system says we have six of an item, but the shelf looks empty. What do you do?
Your understanding of how inventory records drift and why that matters.
Searching the likely spots first, then reporting so the record is corrected. A false count can stop automatic reordering.

First I look where it could be: backroom overstock, a second display, the returns cart, the wrong shelf. If I truly find none, I tell my manager or make the count correction our process allows. If the system keeps showing six, it may never reorder, and the shelf stays empty while customers leave without buying.
You think a customer is hiding items in their bag. What do you do?
Whether you know the safe way to deal with suspected theft.
Offering service instead of accusing, never chasing or touching anyone, and telling the manager or loss prevention what you saw.

I don't accuse anyone, because I could be wrong. I walk over and offer help, like "Can I get you a basket or a fitting room?" That often stops it. I quietly tell my manager or loss prevention what I saw and what the person is wearing. I never block, chase or grab someone; most stores forbid it because people get hurt over merchandise.
What does shrink mean in a store, and where does it come from?
Whether you know the main ways a store loses stock and money.
Shrink is the gap between recorded and actual stock. Causes include theft by outsiders and staff, paperwork or scanning errors, damage and vendor mistakes.

Shrink is the stock the system says we have but we cannot find or sell. Shoplifting is part of it, but so is employee theft, wrong counts, items rung up wrong, damaged goods not written off, and vendors shorting a delivery. Many of those I can help prevent just by scanning and counting carefully.
You are setting a shelf from a planogram, and the product does not fit the space it shows. What do you do?
Your understanding of planograms and how you handle a gap between the plan and the shelf.
Knows a planogram is the store's shelf map, checks own work first, does not improvise freely, and reports the problem so it can be fixed.

A planogram is the diagram that shows where each item goes and how many facings it gets. First I check that I read it right and the shelf heights match. If it still does not fit, I set it as close as I can, note what changed, and tell my manager, because other stores may have the same problem and the plan may need fixing.
Your drawer is $20 over at the end of your shift. Is that good news?
Whether you treat an overage as an error, not a gift.
Says an overage is still a mistake, often a customer shortchanged or a wrong ring. Reports it honestly and never pockets it or covers it up.

No. Over means something went wrong, maybe I gave a customer too little change or rang a sale wrong. I count again, write down the overage, and tell my manager. I do not take it or hide it. Then I think back on the shift, like a large bill I broke in a rush, so I can find the cause and slow down at that step.
A customer keeps asking you to swap bills back and forth while you are making their change. What do you do?
Whether you can spot a quick-change scam and stay in control of the drawer.
Recognizes the pattern, finishes one transaction at a time, closes the drawer before any new exchange, and calls a manager if it continues.

That sounds like a quick-change scam, where someone confuses the cashier until they hand over extra money. I would finish the first sale and close the drawer. If they want a different exchange, I treat it as a separate step, counting out loud. If they keep pushing, I politely call a manager over and do not let my drawer leave my control.
Walk me through how you would build an endcap display that actually sells.
Your sense of visual merchandising beyond keeping shelves tidy.
A clear theme, best sellers at eye level, enough stock to look full, clear price signs, and a check of the sales afterward.

I pick one clear idea, like a weekend grilling set, so shoppers get it in a few seconds. The best seller or highest margin item goes at eye level. I keep it full and neat, use clear price signs, and leave easy access so people can grab without knocking things over. After a week I look at the sales and change what is not moving.
What is a store's conversion rate, and what can you do on the floor to raise it?
Whether you link your daily actions to the numbers a store tracks.
Conversion is the share of visitors who buy. Greeting, quick help, stocked shelves and short lines raise it.

Conversion rate is the number of sales divided by the number of people who came in. If 200 people walk in and 50 buy, that is 25%. I can raise it by greeting people, offering help without hovering, knowing where things are, keeping sizes on the floor, and calling for backup before the line makes someone put things down and leave.
Walk me through how you close the store at night.
How you handle the security and money steps of closing.
A walk-through for anyone left inside, locked doors, money counted out of sight, an alarm set and not leaving alone, following the store's checklist.

I follow the store's closing checklist. Near close I announce it, then check fitting rooms, restrooms and back areas so no one is left inside. I lock the doors, count the drawers in the office, not at the front, and put the money in the safe. I recover the floor for the morning, set the alarm, and leave with a coworker, never alone.
You get a notice that a product we sell has been recalled. What do you do?
Whether you act fast and fully on a safety recall.
Pulls every unit from the shelves and the back room, keeps it apart from sellable stock, stops it from being sold, and follows the recall instructions.

I pull it right away, from the shelf, the back stock, displays and returns, and check the lot or model numbers the notice lists. I put it in a marked area away from sellable stock and ask my manager to block it at the register so it cannot be sold. Then I follow the notice on returns and what to tell customers who bring it back.
A parent runs up to you and says their child is missing in the store. What do you do?
How you act in a real emergency on the floor.
Gets a description, alerts all staff with the store's code, watches the exits, starts a search, and calls police fast if the child is not found.

I get the child's name, age, and what they are wearing, and I keep the parent with me. I alert the team using the store's missing child code so staff stop work, search, and watch every exit. No child leaves with anyone until we check. If the child is not found within minutes, as the procedure says, we call police. A store's work can wait.
You are the key holder, and an hour before close your only coworker goes home sick. What do you do?
Your judgement on safety and responsibility when you are alone in charge.
Calls the manager right away, does not close alone if policy forbids it, asks for help or another plan, and puts safety ahead of finishing tasks.

I call my manager right away instead of waiting until close. Many stores do not allow one person to close alone, and I would not count money or lock up alone without approval. I would ask if someone can come in or if the manager wants to come. Until then I keep the front covered and do only the tasks I can do safely from the floor.

retail-sales-associate.heading: Retail sales associate questions
qs: What does it mean to face or zone a shelf, and why does it matter?
Whether you know the basic floor tasks of the job.
Pulling products forward with labels out and items behind the right tag, so shoppers find things and real gaps show.

Facing means pulling each product to the front edge of the shelf with the label turned out. Zoning is doing that for a whole section and putting strays back behind their own price tag. It makes the shelf look full, helps people find things fast, and shows me the real gaps I should report for restock.
How do you approach a customer who is just browsing?
How you open a sale without crowding the shopper.
A quick, friendly greeting, an open question tied to what they are looking at, and room to browse.

I greet them within a few seconds of seeing them, then give them a moment. If they stop at something, I ask an open question like, “Is this for you or a gift?” instead of “Can I help you?”, which almost always gets a “no.” If they want space, I tell them my name and where I will be.
What do you do with go-backs, the items customers leave in the wrong place?
Whether you know how stock gets back to the shelf and what needs to move first.
Clearing them often, handling cold or frozen items first by store policy, and putting each item back behind its own tag.

I keep a go-back bin at the register and clear it every hour or when it fills. Anything cold or frozen goes first, and if I don't know how long it sat out, I ask a manager whether it can still be sold. Everything else goes back behind its own price tag, not just on any shelf nearby.
A customer says the shelf tag showed a lower price than what rang up. What do you do?
How you handle a price mistake fairly and fix its cause.
Checking the tag quickly, following store policy on the price, and getting the tag or system fixed so it does not happen again.

I ask where they saw it, or send a coworker to check, so the line keeps moving. If the tag matches that item, I follow our policy, which at most stores means giving the posted price, with a manager override if needed. Then I tell the manager so the tag or the system gets fixed before the next customer.
A customer asks which of two products is better, and you do not know. What do you say?
Your honesty and how you find product facts fast.
Admitting you are not sure, asking about their needs, and checking labels, a coworker or the store system instead of guessing.

I say I want to give them a real answer, not a guess. I ask what they will use it for, then compare the two labels with them or check the product info in our system. If a coworker knows that department, I bring them in. Afterward I read up on both so I can answer it myself next time.
A regular customer brings a coupon that expired yesterday. Do you take it?
Your judgement between store rules and keeping a good customer.
Knowing an expired coupon is not yours to accept alone, and asking a manager instead of giving a flat no.

Not on my own. A manufacturer coupon that has expired usually won't be paid back to the store, so it is not my call. I tell the customer I can't override it myself, but I ask my manager, who can sometimes honor it or give a store discount. Either way, the customer gets a real answer quickly.
Someone buying an age-restricted product has no ID but says they are clearly old enough. What do you do?
Whether you follow ID rules even under pressure.
No valid ID, no sale, said politely, and the store's ID policy applied every time, however old the person looks.

I say I'm sorry, but I need a valid photo ID for this item, no matter how old someone looks. That is our rule, and selling to a minor can bring fines for the store and sometimes for the clerk. I don't argue. I offer to hold the item or ring up the rest of the order, and if they push hard, I call my manager.
A customer hands you a $100 bill that feels wrong. What do you do?
Whether you know how to check a bill and stay safe and polite.
Checking security features like the watermark and security thread, not relying only on a pen, and calling a manager without accusing anyone.

I hold it to the light for the portrait watermark and the security thread, and tilt it to see the color-shifting 100 in the corner. Real bills also have raised print you can feel. If it still seems off, I calmly say a manager needs to approve it and keep it out of my drawer. I don't accuse anyone or put myself at risk; the manager follows our policy.
You think a customer just put something in their bag without paying. What do you do?
Whether you handle a suspected theft safely and within store rules.
No chasing, touching or accusing; attentive service as a deterrent, and a quiet report to a manager or loss prevention.

I don't accuse, block or follow anyone out; that isn't my job and it isn't safe. I go over and offer help, like, “Can I get you a basket for those?” Often that is enough. Then I quietly tell my manager or loss prevention what I saw, what the person looks like and where they are, and let them handle it under our policy.
What is stock rotation, and how do you do it when you restock a shelf?
Whether you know how to keep older stock selling first.
First in, first out: older or shorter-dated product goes to the front, new stock goes behind it, and dates are checked along the way.

Rotation means older stock sells first. When I fill a shelf, I pull what is already there forward, put the new cases behind it and check dates as I go. Anything past its date or close to it goes to my manager, not back on the shelf. It matters most for food and anything that expires, but I rotate everything so nothing sits for months.
What is a planogram, and what do you do when the product you have will not fit the space it shows?
Your understanding of how a shelf is planned, and when to ask before changing it.
A planogram is the diagram of where each item goes and how many facings it gets. You follow it and report a problem instead of quietly rearranging.

A planogram is the map for a shelf or fixture: which item goes where, at what height and with how many facings, meaning how many units show across the front. If the stock will not fit, I put the extra in backstock with a label. I do not cram it onto another shelf. Then I tell my lead, because the plan may be out of date or we got the wrong pack size.
What is conversion rate in a store, and what can you do on the floor to raise it?
Whether you understand how store results are measured and your part in them.
It is the share of visitors who buy: sales divided by traffic. Floor habits like greeting people, staying available and keeping sizes full move it.

Conversion is the number of sales divided by the number of people who came in. If 200 people walked in and 50 bought, that is 25%. On the floor I raise it by greeting people quickly, checking back with browsers, knowing what is in stock and keeping shelves full. A customer who cannot find their size or cannot find help leaves without buying.
A delivery arrives and needs to be worked, but the floor is getting busy and you are the only one out there. How do you split your time?
How you balance tasks and customers when you cannot do both at once.
Customers come first. Cold items are put away at once, the rest is worked in short bursts near the floor, and the lead hears early if it will not get done.

Anything cold or frozen goes into the cooler right away, since it cannot sit out. After that, customers come first, because a lost sale is gone and freight can wait an hour. I put out sale items and empty-shelf items first, working near the front where I can see people. If I see I will not finish, I tell my lead early so they can send help or change the plan.
A customer slips on a spill in your aisle. Walk me through what you do.
How you put safety first and follow store procedure after an accident.
Check on the person, get a manager, guard and clean the spill, and leave the report and any talk of fault to the manager.

First I ask if they are hurt and tell them not to rush getting up. I call a manager, and if they seem badly hurt, I ask someone to call 911. I keep others away from the spill with a sign or by standing there, then clean it. I do not argue or say whose fault it was. I tell the manager exactly what I saw so it goes into the incident report.
A customer returns an opened item that does not work. After the refund, what happens to the product?
Whether you know a returned defective item cannot go straight back on the shelf.
It is tagged as defective, set aside and logged, then sent back to the vendor or written off by store policy. It is never put back on the shelf.

It never goes back on the shelf. I tag it as defective, write down the reason and put it in the returns area. From there it follows store policy: some items go back to the vendor for credit, others are written off as damaged. Logging it matters, because the system has to know that unit is no longer stock we can sell.
You hear that a product your store sells has been recalled. What do you do?
Whether you act fast and thoroughly when a product is pulled for safety.
Tell the manager, pull every unit, including backstock and displays, keep them apart and labeled, and answer customers from the notice, not from guesses.

I tell my manager right away and follow the recall notice exactly, matching lot numbers or dates if it lists them. I pull every unit from the shelf, endcaps, backstock and the returns area, mark them do not sell and keep them apart. If a customer asks, I tell them what the notice says and how the store handles returns for it, without guessing about the risk.
An older customer is buying $1,500 in gift cards while someone on the phone tells them what to do. What do you do?
Whether you can spot a common scam and step in kindly.
Ask gently what the cards are for, explain that real agencies and businesses do not demand gift card payment, and bring in a manager.

I would ask in a friendly way what the cards are for. If it is to pay a fine, the IRS, a utility bill or a relative in trouble, I explain that this is how scams work: real agencies and businesses do not ask for payment in gift cards. I call my manager and suggest they hang up and call the agency or family member directly. Most people are grateful someone asked.
A customer pays, then keeps changing their mind, asking for different bills and offering to swap money back and forth. What is happening and what do you do?
Whether you can spot a quick-change scam at the register.
You recognize a quick-change attempt, finish one transaction at a time with the drawer closed, and call a manager if it continues.

That is often a quick-change scam: the goal is to confuse me until I hand back more than I got. I slow down. I finish the first sale and close the drawer before anything else. If they want to swap bills, I take their money first, count it, then give mine. I never mix my drawer money and theirs on the counter, and if they keep pushing, I call a manager.
You find out the sale signs you hung yesterday show a lower price than the register charges, and customers have been buying all day. What do you do?
How you own a mistake and limit the harm to customers and the store.
Fix the signs now, tell the manager at once with the details, and let the store decide how to make it right. No hiding the mistake.

I pull or fix the signs first so nobody else is misled. Then I tell my manager what happened, which items and since when, even though it was my mistake. Some states have price accuracy rules, so the store may need to refund the difference to customers who come back. From then on, I check each sign against the register price before I hang it, not after.

revenue-accountant.heading: Revenue accountant questions
qs: A customer pays $12,000 up front for a one-year subscription starting January 1. How do you book it?
Whether you can turn a common contract into correct entries.
Cash and a contract liability (deferred revenue) at the start, then about $1,000 of revenue a month as the service is delivered.

When we collect, I debit cash and credit deferred revenue, which is a contract liability, for $12,000. Each month I move $1,000 from deferred revenue to revenue, because the customer gets the service evenly over the year. At March 31, $9,000 is still deferred on the balance sheet.
How do you decide whether implementation services are a separate performance obligation from the software subscription?
Your grasp of the distinct test, the core judgement in step two.
Both parts of the test: the customer can benefit from it alone or with readily available resources, and it is separately identifiable in the contract.

I ask two questions. Can the customer benefit from the setup alone or with resources it could get elsewhere, for example, do other firms offer it? And is it separate in the contract, or does it significantly customize the software into one combined output? If third parties do standard setups, it is usually distinct. If our team heavily modifies the code, I combine them.
When is revenue recognized over time rather than at a point in time?
Whether you know the three criteria for recognizing revenue over time.
Any one of three: the customer consumes the benefit as you perform, the customer controls the asset as it is built, or no alternative use plus an enforceable right to payment.

Over time applies if one of three things is true. The customer receives and uses the benefit as we perform, like a cleaning service. Our work creates or improves an asset the customer controls. Or the item has no alternative use to us and we have an enforceable right to payment for work done to date. If none apply, it is a point in time, when control passes.
Our marketplace sells a third party's products. How do you decide whether to report revenue gross or net?
How you apply the principal versus agent test, which changes reported revenue.
Focus on control of the good before transfer, supported by indicators: fulfillment responsibility, inventory risk and pricing discretion.

The key question is whether we control the product before the customer gets it. I look at who is primarily responsible for delivering what was promised, who carries inventory risk, and who sets the price. If the seller ships, sets prices and handles returns, we are an agent and record only our commission, net. If we do those things, we report the full sale, gross.
A contract gives the customer a rebate if it buys more than 10,000 units this year. How does that affect revenue each quarter?
Whether you estimate variable consideration and apply the constraint.
Estimate the rebate by expected value or most likely amount, include only what is probable not to reverse significantly, and update each period.

The rebate makes the price variable, so I estimate it from the first sale instead of waiting for year end. The outcome is yes or no, so I use the most likely amount. If order trends make 10,000 units likely, I record revenue net of the rebate. I include only what will probably not reverse significantly, and I adjust revenue in the quarter the estimate changes.
Midway through a two-year service contract, the customer adds a new module at a deep discount. How do you account for the change?
How you handle contract modifications, one of the trickiest areas of the standard.
The three outcomes: separate contract if distinct and at standalone price; otherwise prospective if remaining services are distinct; cumulative catch-up if not.

First I check whether the module is distinct and priced at its standalone selling price. It is well below what similar customers pay, so it is not a separate contract. Next, are the remaining services distinct from what we already delivered? Monthly service usually is, so I treat it as a new contract: the unrecognized price plus the new fee, spread over what remains.
How do you account for sales commissions paid on a three-year contract?
Whether you know the rules for costs of obtaining a contract, which revenue teams often own.
Capitalize incremental costs expected to be recovered and amortize them over the benefit period; mention the one-year practical expedient.

A commission is an incremental cost of obtaining the contract: we pay it only because the deal was signed. If we expect to recover it, I capitalize it and amortize it over the period the customer gets the services, which can include expected renewals. If that period is one year or less, we can expense it right away under the practical expedient.
On the last day of the quarter, sales asks you to book a large deal. The customer signs two days later, and an email promises a free extra year of support. What do you do?
Your judgement under pressure and how you protect the integrity of reported revenue.
No revenue until a contract exists under company practice; the side promise is part of the deal and must be accounted for; escalate rather than bend.

If our normal practice is a signed contract, there was no contract at quarter end, so the deal goes in the next quarter. The email matters too: free support is a promise to the customer, so it is a performance obligation that gets part of the price. I would explain this to sales, document it and tell my controller, because side promises are a control issue.
What is the difference between a contract asset, a receivable and a contract liability?
Whether you can keep the three balance sheet lines of ASC 606 apart.
A receivable is an unconditional right to cash, a contract asset depends on more performance, and a contract liability is consideration received or due before delivery.

A receivable means only time stands between us and the cash. A contract asset means we earned revenue but still have to do something else, like finish a milestone, before we can bill. A contract liability, often called deferred revenue, means the customer paid, or owes unconditionally, before we delivered.
We sell equipment with a standard one-year warranty and an optional extended warranty. How do you treat each?
Whether you can tell an assurance warranty from a service warranty.
The standard warranty is a cost accrual, not a performance obligation. The extended warranty sold separately is a service recognized over the period it covers.

The standard warranty only promises the product works as specified, so it is an assurance warranty: I accrue the expected repair cost when the sale is recorded. The extended warranty is sold separately, so it is a distinct service. I defer its price and recognize it over the period it covers.
A bundle has no observable standalone price for one of its parts. How do you estimate it?
Your command of standalone selling price methods and when the residual approach is allowed.
Uses observable data first, names adjusted market assessment and expected cost plus margin, and limits the residual approach to highly variable or uncertain prices.

I start with observable data: our own standalone sales, then competitor pricing adjusted for our position, which is the adjusted market assessment. If that is thin, I use expected cost plus a reasonable margin. The residual approach is allowed only when the price is highly variable or uncertain, and I document why we chose it.
Customers can return products within 60 days for a full refund. How does that change the entry at the point of sale?
How you handle a right of return as variable consideration.
Revenue only for goods not expected back, a refund liability for the rest, and an asset for goods to be recovered, net of recovery costs.

Say we ship $100,000 and history says 5% comes back. I record $95,000 of revenue and a $5,000 refund liability. I record an asset for the right to recover the goods at their former cost less expected recovery costs and any loss in value, and cost of sales only for what stays sold. I true up the estimate each period.
A new customer signs, but you doubt it will pay. It sends a first payment anyway. Can you book revenue?
Whether you know the collectibility test in step one and what to do when it fails.
No contract exists under ASC 606 until collection is probable; cash received sits as a liability until one of the specific events allows revenue.

If collection of substantially all the consideration is not probable, step one fails: there is no contract under ASC 606 yet. I hold the cash as a liability. It becomes revenue only if, say, the contract is terminated and the payment is nonrefundable, or we have stopped transferring, owe nothing more, and the payment is nonrefundable. I reassess each period.
A one-year contract lets the customer renew next year at 40% off list price. Does that discount affect this year's revenue?
Whether you spot a material right hidden in a renewal option.
A discount the customer would not get without this contract is a material right: a separate obligation that takes part of the price until used or expired.

If 40% off is more than new customers normally get, it is a material right. I treat the option as its own performance obligation and allocate part of this year's price to it, based on the discount and the likelihood of renewal. That amount stays deferred and is recognized when the renewal year is delivered or the option lapses.
A customer pays for equipment but asks us to keep it in our warehouse for three months. Can we recognize revenue now?
Your knowledge of the bill-and-hold criteria.
Only if control has passed: a substantive reason, goods set apart as the customer's, ready to ship, and not usable for other customers.

Only if the customer has control. I check four things: the customer asked for the arrangement for a real reason, such as no space at its site; the units are tagged and stored apart as theirs; they are ready to ship; and we cannot use them or send them to anyone else. I also ask whether storage is a separate service that needs some of the price.
We license software for three years and, separately, let a retailer use our brand name for three years. Do both follow the same revenue pattern?
Whether you know functional versus symbolic intellectual property.
Software with standalone function is recognized at a point in time once the term starts; a brand license is symbolic and recognized over the term.

No. Software that works on its own is functional IP, so the license fee is recognized when the customer can use it and the license period has begun. A brand is symbolic IP: its value depends on our ongoing activities, so the fee is recognized over the three years. If the brand fee is a percentage of sales, I recognize it as those sales happen.
A customer pays the full price of a three-year service up front at a large discount. Is there a financing component?
How you assess a significant financing component and the one-year practical expedient.
Notes the one-year expedient does not apply, weighs why the discount exists, and if significant, accrues interest expense that increases revenue.

The gap runs past one year, so the practical expedient does not apply. If the discount mostly reflects the time value of money, the customer is lending to us. I accrue interest expense on the contract liability, which grows it, so total revenue ends above the cash received. If prepayment has another real purpose, like securing scarce capacity, there may be no financing component.
Auditors ask how you know there are no side agreements that change contract terms. What controls do you point to?
How you build revenue controls that catch terms outside the signed contract.
Several layers: sales certifications, legal review of nonstandard terms, contract-to-system checks, and a look back at credits and free goods.

I point to layers. Sales leaders sign a quarterly certification that no side terms exist. Legal must approve any nonstandard terms. We match each booked deal to the signed contract and the order in the billing system. After quarter end, I review credits, concessions and free services to see if they trace back to a promise we missed. And I test that each control actually ran.

rf-engineer.heading: RF and wireless engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between dBm, dBi and dBc?
Whether you use the basic units of RF work correctly.
dBm is absolute power against 1 mW, dBi is antenna gain against an isotropic radiator, and dBc is a level relative to the carrier.

dBm is power relative to one milliwatt, so 0 dBm is 1 mW and +30 dBm is 1 W. dBi is antenna gain compared with an ideal antenna that radiates equally in all directions; a half-wave dipole is about 2.15 dBi. dBc tells how far below the carrier something sits, like a harmonic at -40 dBc.
An antenna shows a return loss of 10 dB. What does that mean in practice?
Your feel for what matching numbers mean.
About 10% of the power reflects and about 90% is accepted, a VSWR near 1.9. A good match alone does not prove the antenna radiates well.

About 10 percent of the power comes back and roughly 90 percent goes into the antenna, which is a VSWR of about 1.9. For many small devices that is an acceptable target. But a good match only means the power is accepted. A lossy antenna, or even a resistor, can match well, so I also want the radiation efficiency measured.
Why do most RF systems use 50 ohms?
Whether you know the reasoning behind a standard you use every day.
A compromise for air coax: about 77 ohms gives the lowest loss and about 30 ohms the most power handling. Today it is mainly a standard for compatibility.

It is a historical compromise. For air-filled coax, the impedance with the lowest loss is around 77 ohms and the one that handles the most power is around 30 ohms. Fifty sits between them. Cable TV and video picked 75 ohms because low loss mattered more than power. Today 50 ohms is mostly a standard so parts work together.
Walk me through a link budget for a point-to-point link.
Whether you can size a radio link from start to finish.
Transmit power plus antenna gains, minus path and other losses, compared with receiver sensitivity; what is left is the fade margin.

I start with transmit power in dBm, add both antenna gains and subtract cable and connector losses. Then free-space path loss, which grows 20 dB per decade of distance and of frequency, plus extra for rain, trees or anything blocking the clear zone around the line of sight. I compare the received level with the receiver sensitivity at the needed data rate. What is left is my fade margin.
In a receiver, should the filter go before or after the low-noise amplifier?
Whether you understand how noise figure adds up in a receiver chain.
The first stage sets most of the noise figure and loss before the amplifier adds dB for dB, so a filter goes first only when strong signals demand it.

The first stage dominates the noise figure, and any passive loss before the low-noise amplifier adds straight to it: a 1.5 dB filter in front costs about 1.5 dB. So I prefer the amplifier first. If a strong nearby transmitter could overload it, I put a low-loss filter in front and accept that penalty.
Two strong signals at 100 and 101 MHz reach your receiver. Where do the worst distortion products land, and why do they matter?
Your understanding of linearity and intermodulation.
Third-order products at 99 and 102 MHz, too close to filter out. They grow 3 dB per 1 dB of input, which is why the third-order intercept matters.

The third-order products land at 2f1 minus f2 and 2f2 minus f1, so 99 and 102 MHz. They sit right next to the wanted band, so a filter cannot remove them. They rise 3 dB for every 1 dB of input. That is why I check the third-order intercept point of the amplifier and mixer against the strongest signals the receiver will see.
Your network analyzer measurement of a filter is 2 dB off from the simulation. What do you check first?
How you separate a measurement error from a design error.
The setup first: calibration, reference plane, cables, connectors, fixture. Only then the model or the board.

First the setup. I check that the calibration is current, covers the right frequency range, and puts the reference plane at the filter, not at the end of the cable. Then I measure a known load to confirm the cal, watch for cable movement and connector torque, and remove the effect of the fixture traces. If the setup is clean, I compare the board stackup and material values with the model.
The antenna met spec on the test board but is badly detuned in the finished product. What happened, and what do you do?
Whether you know how a real product changes an antenna.
Names likely causes like the plastic housing, nearby metal, battery, ground size or the user's hand, then measures in the real product and re-tunes the match.

The enclosure plastic, the battery, a display, cables and a different ground plane size all shift the resonance, usually downward. I measure the antenna inside the real housing, with a hand or head model if the product is handheld. Then I re-tune the matching network. If the shift is large, I change the antenna length or clearance and push for that change early in the next build.
Your product fails a pre-scan for radiated emissions a week before the certification lab date. What do you do?
How you handle a compliance problem under schedule pressure.
Finds the source with near-field probes, fixes the cause rather than hiding it, rescans, and warns the team early if the date is at risk.

First I find which frequency fails and whether it is a harmonic of the transmitter, a clock or a switching regulator. With near-field probes I locate the source. Then I fix the cause: a harmonic filter, better grounding, a shield can or a slower clock edge. I rescan and tell the project lead early if the lab date is at risk. Going to the lab with a known fail wastes the slot.
The product manager wants to cut the fade margin from 15 dB to 5 dB so you can use a cheaper amplifier. How do you respond?
Your judgement when cost pushes against reliability.
Explains what the margin buys in outages the customer will notice, offers other ways to save, and puts the trade-off in writing.

I translate the margin into what the customer will see. Losing 10 dB means the link drops far more often during rain or signal fading. I show the expected outage time for both cases, then offer other savings: a higher-gain antenna, shorter cable runs or a lower data rate. If we still cut the margin, the decision and the expected outage go in writing.
How are an antenna's gain, directivity and efficiency related?
Whether you keep the basic antenna terms straight.
Gain equals directivity times radiation efficiency. Directivity describes only the pattern shape, while gain also counts losses.

Directivity is how much the pattern concentrates power compared to an isotropic antenna, with no losses counted. Efficiency is the share of accepted power that actually radiates. Gain is directivity times efficiency. So a small antenna can have decent directivity and still poor gain, because much of the power heats the ground plane and the matching parts.
A customer uses a linearly polarized antenna to receive a circularly polarized satellite signal. What loss should they expect?
Your grasp of polarization mismatch in a real installation.
About 3 dB, regardless of how the linear antenna is rotated. Cross-polarized linear antennas or opposite-hand circular antennas lose far more.

In theory about 3 dB, whatever the rotation of the linear antenna, because it picks up only one of the two field components. That is much better than two cross-polarized linear antennas, which can lose 20 dB or more. If margin is tight, I would use a circular antenna of the same hand as the satellite, because the opposite hand also rejects strongly.
You can mount the LNA at the antenna, or in the equipment room after 3 dB of cable. What does that change?
Whether you apply noise figure cascading to a real choice.
Loss before the LNA adds directly to system noise figure. After a high-gain LNA, the Friis formula makes the cable's effect small.

A passive loss at room temperature has a noise figure equal to its loss, so 3 dB of cable ahead of the LNA adds 3 dB to the system noise figure. With the LNA at the antenna, the Friis formula divides the cable's noise contribution by the LNA gain. With 20 dB of gain, the cable barely shows. That is why tower-mounted amplifiers exist.
Your radar needs twice the detection range. What does that cost in transmit power, all else equal?
Your understanding of the radar range equation and its trade-offs.
Echo power falls with range to the fourth power, so twice the range needs 16 times the power (12 dB). Antenna gain counts twice.

Echo power falls with the fourth power of range, because the signal spreads on the way out and again on the way back. Twice the range means 16 times the power, or 12 dB. That is a lot to get from the transmitter alone. So I also look at antenna gain, which counts twice in a monostatic radar, longer integration time and lower receiver noise.
You see a spur on the spectrum analyzer that might come from the analyzer itself. How do you tell?
Whether you can separate real signals from test equipment artifacts.
Add input attenuation. A real signal keeps its displayed level, while a product made in the analyzer's mixer moves.

I add 10 dB of input attenuation. If the spur is real, its displayed level stays the same, because the analyzer corrects for the attenuator. If the displayed level drops or the spur vanishes, the analyzer's own mixer was overdriven and made it. I can also put a filter ahead of the input to knock down the strong signal and see if the spur goes with it.
A layout engineer routes an RF trace across a split in the ground plane. Why do you send it back?
Your understanding of return current paths on a circuit board.
At RF, return current flows under the trace. A split forces a detour that changes impedance, radiates and couples noise.

At RF, the return current flows in the plane directly under the trace. A split forces it to detour around the gap, which makes a loop. The impedance jumps, the line radiates and noise couples into other circuits. I ask for an unbroken reference plane under every RF trace and ground vias stitched along it. If a crossing truly cannot be avoided, a capacitor should bridge the split right at the trace.
Your amplifier oscillates on the bench at a frequency far outside the band it was designed for. How do you track it down?
How you debug stability problems in an RF amplifier.
Check stability wherever the device has gain, not just in band, using K and delta or mu. Then fix it with resistive loading, decoupling or lower source inductance.

First I check stability across every frequency where the transistor has gain, not only the design band. Out of band is where these usually hide. I want K above 1 with delta below 1, or mu above 1. Common fixes are resistive loading at low frequency, better bias decoupling, or more ground vias at the source to cut inductance. Then I retest with open and shorted loads.
Your new OFDM signal needs the power amplifier backed off several dB. How do you weigh linearity against efficiency?
Your judgement when signal quality and power use pull in opposite directions.
High peak-to-average ratio causes clipping near compression, which hurts EVM and adjacent channel leakage. Weigh backoff against predistortion and crest factor reduction.

OFDM has a high peak-to-average ratio. Running the PA near compression clips the peaks, which raises error vector magnitude and spreads energy into neighboring channels. Backing off fixes that, but it wastes power as heat. I would compare crest factor reduction, digital predistortion and a different PA design. I pick using the EVM and adjacent channel limits plus the battery and thermal budget.
A customer wants to put a higher-gain antenna on our FCC-certified radio module. What do you tell them?
Your knowledge of how certification limits changes to a radio design.
The grant covers the antennas listed. Equal or lower gain of the same type is generally fine. Higher gain needs a permissive change with new data, or new certification.

Not as it stands. The grant covers the antennas tested with the module. Another antenna of the same type with equal or lower gain is generally allowed. Higher gain can push radiated power and emissions past what was tested. The path is a Class II permissive change with new test data, often with power turned down to stay within limits. Until then, they ship with a listed antenna.

risk-manager.heading: Risk manager questions
qs: What is the difference between inherent risk and residual risk?
Whether you know the basic language of a risk assessment.
Inherent risk is before controls, residual is after, and residual is what you compare to the risk appetite.

Inherent risk is the exposure before any controls, for example the chance a clerk pays a fake vendor. Residual risk is what is left after controls such as dual approval and calling the vendor back on a known number. We judge whether the residual risk fits our appetite. If it does not, we add controls, transfer the risk or stop the activity.
Explain the three lines of defense and where a risk manager sits.
Your grasp of who owns risk and who oversees it.
The business owns and runs the risk, risk and compliance challenge it, and internal audit gives independent assurance. The risk manager is second line.

The first line is the business: it takes the risk and runs the daily controls. The second line, risk management and compliance, sets the framework and limits and challenges the first line. The third line is internal audit, which tells the board independently whether both work. I sit in the second line, so I advise and challenge, but I do not own business decisions.
How do you estimate the expected loss on a loan or a customer credit line?
Whether you know the building blocks of credit risk.
Probability of default times loss given default times exposure at default, with a worked example and the link to unexpected loss.

Expected loss is probability of default times loss given default times exposure at default. If a borrower has a 2% chance of default in a year, we lose 40% of what is owed after recoveries, and we expect $5 million drawn at default, the expected loss is $40,000. That is priced in or reserved. Capital is there for unexpected loss, the swings around that average.
Explain Value at Risk in plain words, and tell me where it falls short.
Whether you can explain the main market risk number and its limits.
A correct one-line definition plus its blind spots: says nothing about the size of the tail loss and leans on past data.

A one-day 99% VaR of $2 million means that on about 99 days out of 100 we expect to lose less than $2 million, if the model and recent history hold. It says nothing about how bad the other day can be, and it can understate risk just before a crisis. So I pair it with expected shortfall, the average loss in that worst tail, and with stress tests.
The board says it will accept a certain loss in a bad year. How do you turn that into limits a desk can follow?
How you translate risk appetite into working limits.
A cascade from board appetite to business and desk limits, with a buffer, daily measurable metrics, early warnings and named owners.

Say the board accepts losing no more than 5% of annual earnings in a severe year. I turn that into stress loss and VaR limits by business, keeping part unallocated as a buffer. Then desks get limits they can watch daily, such as position size and how much they lose per move in rates. Each limit has an early warning level, an owner and an escalation path.
How would you assess the risk of our main cloud provider going down for a full day?
Your approach to operational risk, not just market and credit risk.
Maps dependent processes, puts a cost on downtime, compares tested recovery time with what the business can tolerate, and closes gaps.

I map which processes depend on it, such as payments and customer logins, and estimate the cost per hour of each being down: lost sales, penalties, overtime. Then I compare how fast we actually recover in tests with how long the business can tolerate. Gaps lead to actions like failover to a second region, manual workarounds or stronger contract terms.
You arrive in the morning and see a trader breached a limit overnight. What do you do?
How you handle a limit breach step by step.
Confirm it is real, size it, escalate per policy the same day, agree a documented fix with a deadline, then look at root cause.

First I confirm it is real and not a data error, then I find the size, the cause and whether it is still open. I escalate to the desk head and my manager that morning, as the policy says, and we agree in writing to cut the position or approve a temporary excess with a deadline. Then I log it and ask whether the limit or the process needs to change.
A 99% one-day VaR model had 9 exceptions in the last 250 trading days. What do you make of it?
Whether you can read a backtest and react to a failing model.
Knows about 2 or 3 are expected, so the model understates risk; checks data first, finds the cause, and adds caution until fixed.

At 99% we expect about 2 or 3 days where the loss beats VaR, so 9 means the model understates risk. I first check the data, for example fees or new trades mixed into the profit and loss. Then I look at where the misses cluster: often the history misses a recent jump in volatility or a product is modeled poorly. Until it is fixed I flag it and add a buffer or tighten limits.
The head of sales wants a deal that would put 30% of our receivables on one customer, against a 15% limit. What do you do?
Your judgement when the business pushes against a limit.
Shows the impact in money, offers ways to make the deal fit, and routes any exception to the right approver with a written view.

I would not just say no. I would show what a default by that customer would do to our cash and earnings, and suggest ways to fit the limit: credit insurance, a letter of credit from their bank, payment upfront or a smaller first order. If he still wants it, the exception goes to whoever the policy names, often the CFO or risk committee, with my view in writing.
Tell me about a time a control you relied on did not work.
How you own a failure and fix the cause, not just the symptom.
A specific failure, quick containment, a fix to the root cause, and a lasting change in how you test controls.

We had a monthly review of access to the payments system, always signed off. When I tested it, the report behind it left out contractor accounts, so three former contractors still had access. We removed them that day and fixed the report. I added a check that the number of accounts reviewed matches the system. Now I test the data behind a control, not just the sign-off.
How do you design a key risk indicator that warns you before a loss, not after?
Whether you know the difference between leading and lagging risk indicators.
A measure tied to a cause of loss, with thresholds agreed in advance and an owner who must act when one is crossed.

I start from a loss we fear, say failed payments, and ask what rises first. Staff turnover in the payments team, manual overrides per week and the backlog of unreconciled items all move before money is lost. I set green, amber and red thresholds with the owner, and red means a named action, not just a chart.
An employee sent a payment twice, and the bank returned the money the next day. No loss. Do you record it?
How you treat near misses in operational risk.
Yes: a near miss shows a control gap as clearly as a loss. Log it, find the root cause and fix the control.

Yes. We were lucky, and the control still failed. I log it as a near miss with the amount at risk, then ask why the system allowed a duplicate. Often it is a missing check on amount, payee and date. If staff see that reporting a near miss leads to a fix and not to blame, they keep reporting.
What is the difference between funding liquidity risk and market liquidity risk, and how can one cause the other?
Your grasp of liquidity risk and how it can spiral in a crisis.
Funding liquidity is meeting cash needs; market liquidity is selling assets without moving the price. Forced sales and rising margin calls link the two.

Funding liquidity risk is not having cash to pay what is due, for example when lenders stop rolling our short-term debt. Market liquidity risk is not being able to sell an asset near its fair value. They feed each other: we lose funding, we must sell, prices drop, our collateral is worth less, lenders ask for more margin, and we must sell again.
What is wrong-way risk, and where would you look for it in our book?
Whether you can spot exposures that grow just as the counterparty gets weaker.
Exposure that rises as the counterparty's credit quality falls, such as collateral in the borrower's own shares or protection bought from a firm hit by the same event.

It is when what they owe us goes up at the moment they are least able to pay. Classic cases: a loan secured by the borrower's own shares, or buying default protection on a bank from another bank in the same country. I look at collateral linked to the counterparty and at trades that pay us in the same stress that hurts them, then ask for more margin or cap them.
An airline hedged its jet fuel with crude oil futures. Fuel costs rose and the hedge did not cover it. What went wrong?
Whether you understand basis risk in hedging.
Basis risk: the hedge and the exposure are different prices that can move apart. A strong answer measures that gap before calling something a hedge.

Crude and jet fuel usually move together, but not always. If refining margins widen, jet fuel can rise much more than crude, and the futures gain only part of the extra cost. That gap is basis risk. Before approving a proxy hedge, I would check how far the two prices drifted apart in past stress periods and report the leftover risk, not treat the hedge as perfect.
Why is a VaR limit alone not enough for an options desk, and what limits would you add?
Your knowledge of non-linear risk and the sensitivity limits that control it.
Option values do not move in a straight line with the market, so VaR can miss risk. Add limits on delta, gamma and vega, plus stress losses on large moves.

Option values do not move in a straight line with the underlying, and a short options book can look calm until a big move. So besides VaR I cap delta, the exposure to price; gamma, how fast delta changes; and vega, the exposure to volatility. I also limit the loss under large price shocks combined with a jump in volatility.
Walk me through how you would run a reverse stress test.
Whether you can work back from failure to the scenarios that would cause it.
Start from the outcome that breaks the business, such as capital or cash running out, and find the plausible combinations of events that lead there.

I start from the end point: the loss or cash outflow at which we breach our capital minimum or cannot pay our bills. Then I work back to find which mixes of events get us there, like a large client default during a funding squeeze. If that path looks more likely than we assumed, that is the finding, and we change limits, buffers or plans before it happens.
Your stress test shows that diversification across desks cuts the total loss by 40%. Do you trust that number?
How you challenge correlation assumptions in a stress test.
Correlations measured in calm markets tend to rise in a crisis. A good answer reruns the test with stressed correlations and shows the board both figures.

Not without testing it. That 40% comes from correlations measured mostly in normal markets, and in a crisis many assets fall together, so the benefit shrinks. I would rerun it with correlations from past crises and with a case of no diversification at all. Then the board sees the range and does not count on an offset that may vanish when it is needed.
A business line built a new pricing model and wants to use it next week. What has to happen first?
Your knowledge of model risk management and independent validation.
Independent validation and approval before use, as the US bank model risk guidance SR 11-7 expects: sound theory, testing, known limits and ongoing monitoring.

It goes into the model inventory and gets validated by people who did not build it. They check the theory and data, test outputs against market prices, and list known weaknesses. Any early use needs formal approval, tight limits and a reserve for model error. That is what the bank model risk guidance known as SR 11-7 expects.
The head of a business line says your stress scenario is unrealistic and asks you to soften it before the board meeting. What do you do?
Your independence and how you handle pressure from the business.
Weigh the argument on evidence, change the scenario only for a real flaw, and if you still disagree, show both views to the board instead of quietly giving in.

I ask what exactly is unrealistic and look at the evidence. If he shows a real flaw, I fix it and record why. If the result just looks bad, I keep it, and I can add his view as an alternative case so the board sees both. If the pressure continues, I raise it with the chief risk officer. A risk number the business can edit is not worth showing.

robot-operator.heading: Robot operator questions
qs: What makes a teleoperated demonstration useful as training data?
Whether you understand what the robot learns from your demonstrations.
Smooth, deliberate, complete motions done the same way each time, with success clear and the cameras seeing what matters.

The model copies what I do, so I move smoothly and with purpose, with no hesitating or wandering. I finish the task fully, keep the gripper and object in camera view, and use one consistent strategy unless the team asks for variety. A fast but jerky demo is worse than a slower, clean one.
Walk me through the checks you do before you start a collection session.
Your setup routine before any data is recorded.
Clear workspace, stop button tested, cameras checked, recording confirmed with a short test episode, and the task sheet reread.

I clear loose items from the cell and make sure nobody is inside the robot's reach. I test the emergency stop, home the arms, and check every camera feed is live, in focus and not bumped. Then I record one short test episode and play it back to confirm all streams saved and line up in time. Last, I reread the task sheet for the day.
Halfway through an episode the object slips out of the gripper. Do you recover or restart?
How you follow the collection protocol when a demonstration goes wrong.
Follows the protocol, knows recovery data can be valuable if labeled, and never saves a messy episode as a clean one.

It depends on what the team asked for. Some projects want recoveries, because a robot that has seen a re-grasp can fix its own slips. If so, I recover calmly and tag the episode as a recovery. If the protocol says clean demos only, I stop, mark the episode failed, reset the scene and start again.
You notice the robot lags behind your hand more than usual. What do you do?
Whether you spot control problems and stop before they spoil data or cause a collision.
Pauses collection, checks the network and computer load, reports it, and does not keep recording with delayed control.

I stop recording and move the arm slowly to a safe position. Lag makes me overshoot, and the data then shows corrections that are not part of the task. I check the network link and whether another program is loading the computer. If I cannot fix it quickly, I report it and flag the episodes recorded just before.
When do you hit the emergency stop, and what happens after you do?
Your judgement on stopping and your routine for restarting safely.
Stops without hesitation when people, the robot or the setup are at risk; then inspects, reports and restarts only once the cause is known.

Anytime someone enters the robot's reach, the arm moves in a way I did not command, or it is about to hit something hard. I do not wait to be sure. After, I make sure everyone is clear, look for damage to the gripper, cables and fixtures, write down what happened and tell the lead. We restart only once we know why it happened.
During an evaluation run, the learned policy drives the arm toward the table edge. How do you handle it?
How you supervise a robot running on its own learned behavior rather than on your hands.
Hand on the stop, a stop rule agreed in advance, early intervention, and the failure logged as useful information.

When the robot runs on its own, I keep my hand on the stop and agree beforehand on when to step in, for example if it leaves the work area. If it heads for the edge, I stop it; I do not gamble on it correcting itself. Then I log the episode with the time and what the arm was doing, because failures like that are what the researchers need to see.
How do you keep your demonstrations consistent over a long shift?
Whether you manage fatigue and drift in your own motions.
Takes regular breaks, watches own success rate and episode times, and flags it when quality drops.

Fatigue shows up in the data before I feel it: longer episodes and more small corrections. I take short breaks on a schedule, stretch my arms and look away from the screen. Every hour I glance at my success rate and average episode time. If they slip, I tell the lead and switch to resets or labeling for a while.
What information do you record with each episode, and why does it matter?
Your understanding of logging and labeling as part of the data itself.
Task, success or failure, operator, setup and anything odd; knows a mislabeled episode can mislead training.

At minimum: the task and its variant, success or failure, my operator ID, the robot and camera setup, and any oddity such as dropped frames or a re-grasp. Researchers filter the data by these tags. If I mark a failed episode as a success, the model learns from a mistake and nobody can find it later.
You find out the wrist camera was loose for the last two hours of recording. What do you do?
How you own a mistake that affects data already collected.
Reports it at once, finds the affected episodes, flags rather than deletes them, fixes the mount and adds a check.

I stop and tell the lead right away, even though it means lost work. I play back episodes to find when the view started to shift, then flag every episode from that point instead of deleting them, so the team can decide. I tighten the mount, recheck the camera, and add a quick camera view check to my hourly routine.
The research team wants more variety in the data. How do you add it without ruining the task?
Whether you can balance variety in the data with a consistent, clear task.
Varies the scene in planned, recorded ways such as positions, objects and lighting, while the goal and success rule stay fixed.

I vary what the robot sees, not what counts as success. I move objects across a grid of positions, swap in similar objects, change the lighting and add clutter, a few changes at a time, and note each one with the episode. The goal stays the same, so the model learns the task and not one table layout.
What is the difference between leader-follower teleoperation and controlling the arm with a VR controller?
Whether you understand how your input becomes robot motion in each setup.
Leader-follower maps joint to joint; VR maps hand pose to gripper pose through inverse kinematics, so the elbow is not directly under your control.

With leader-follower I move a small copy of the arm, and each robot joint follows the matching joint, so the posture is always what I set. With a VR controller the system tracks my hand and solves inverse kinematics for the joints. I control where the gripper goes, and the elbow can end up somewhere I did not expect.
What is a singularity, and how does it show up when you teleoperate?
Your grasp of the arm's kinematics and how it affects safe, smooth control.
Joint axes line up and the arm loses a direction of motion; near it, small hand moves demand very fast joint moves. You plan around it.

It is a pose where two or more joint axes line up and the arm can no longer move in some direction. Near it, a small hand motion can demand very fast joint motion, so the wrist may whip or the controller may stop. I learn where they sit for each task, keep the wrist bent on approaches, and slow down if the arm starts to feel jumpy.
The gripper jammed on a part. Is pressing the emergency stop enough before you reach into the cell?
Whether you know the difference between an emergency stop and lockout/tagout.
No. Servicing needs the site's lockout/tagout procedure, including stored energy like air pressure and gravity on the arm, and a check that it will not start.

No. The e-stop is for emergencies, and a reset or someone else can bring motion back. For a jam I follow the cell's lockout/tagout procedure: power isolated under my own lock, air bled from the gripper lines, and the arm supported if an axis could drop. Then I try to start it to confirm it is dead before I reach in.
The arm is sold as a collaborative robot. Does that mean you can work right next to it without extra precautions?
Whether you know that safety comes from a risk assessment of the whole setup, not a label.
Collaborative describes the application. The tool, the parts, speeds and body exposure still need a risk assessment, and measures follow from it.

No. Collaborative describes the application, not just the arm. The same arm holding a knife is not safe to stand beside. Standards such as ISO 10218 still call for a risk assessment of the whole cell: tool, parts, speeds, and where my head and hands can be. Then the measures fit the result, like force limits, lower speed or a scanner that slows the arm when I come close.
Why does it matter that camera frames and joint readings are recorded in sync, and how do you check it?
How well you understand what the model learns from and how timing errors corrupt it.
The model pairs each observation with an action; a time offset shifts every label. You check rates, drops and sync before collecting, and stop if they are off.

The model learns which action follows which image, step by step. If a camera frame is 100 milliseconds older than the joint reading, every label is shifted and the policy learns to react late. Before a session I check the logged rates and dropped frames. If one stream stutters, I stop and fix it rather than collect hours of misaligned data.
Why can it hurt the policy if you sometimes solve a task one way and sometimes another way?
Whether you understand how inconsistent demonstrations affect learning.
A simple model can average two strategies into one that fails. You agree on one strategy, or balance both on purpose and label them.

If half my demos go around the cup on the left and half on the right, a simple model trained to predict one average action can learn to go straight through the middle and hit the cup. Some newer policy types handle several strategies better, but they still need enough examples of each. So I ask which strategy the team wants, or we balance both on purpose and log which one each episode used.
The team asks you to record recovery demonstrations. Why do they want them, and how do you avoid teaching the robot the mistake?
Whether you understand distribution shift and can build data that fixes it.
Clean-only data leaves the policy lost once it drifts. You start from a bad state and show the fix, without recording yourself causing the error.

A policy trained only on clean runs drifts into states it never saw and does not know how to get out. So I start from a bad state, like the block half out of the gripper or the arm off target, and show the correction. I set up the bad state with recording paused, or mark that segment, so the model learns to fix the error, not cause it.
You have to teleoperate a peg-in-hole insertion with no force feedback. How do you avoid jamming or damaging parts?
How you handle contact-rich tasks when you cannot feel the force.
Slow approach, alignment from more than one view, force or current readings watched as a substitute for touch, backing off instead of pushing harder.

I slow right down before contact and align by eye from two camera views. I keep the force or motor current readout on screen and treat a jump as my sense of touch. I wiggle slightly and back off rather than push harder. If the cell has a compliant or force-limited mode for contact, I make sure it is on, and I flag any episode where force spiked.
How do you run an evaluation so that two policies are compared fairly?
Your rigor in testing, so results are not biased by the setup or by you.
Success rule fixed in advance, same start positions, mixed order, blind if possible, every failure logged with its type and no quiet reruns.

We write the success rule before any run, for example cup upright inside the marked zone within 60 seconds. Both policies get the same start positions, in mixed order so lighting or battery drift does not favor one. Where possible I do not know which policy is running. I log every failure type, not just pass or fail, and any rerun is noted with the reason.
A new batch of data trains a worse policy than the old one, and nothing looks broken. How do you find out why?
How you investigate a data problem methodically instead of guessing.
Compare batches: metadata and hardware first, then episode statistics by operator, then watch samples side by side. Report findings with episode IDs.

I compare the batches step by step. First the metadata: robot, gripper, camera serials, software version, calibration date. Then numbers like episode length, speed, idle time and success rate per operator. Then I watch random episodes side by side. Often it is small, like a camera bumped a few degrees or a new operator who pauses a lot, and I report it with episode IDs.

robotics.heading: Robotics and autonomy questions
qs: What is the difference between open-loop and closed-loop control, and when is open loop good enough?
Whether you understand why robots need feedback.
Open loop trusts the command, closed loop measures and corrects; open loop only fits known, steady loads.

Open loop sends a command and trusts it, like running a motor for two seconds and assuming the arm moved 90 degrees. Closed loop measures the result with a sensor, such as an encoder, and corrects the error. Open loop is fine for a stepper motor with a light, known load. Anything with changing loads or disturbances needs feedback.
Explain what each term of a PID controller does and what can go wrong with it.
Your grasp of the most common controller in the field.
P, I and D explained by effect, with the real failure of each: offset or overshoot, integral windup, noise.

P pushes in proportion to the current error, so it reacts fast but can leave a steady offset or overshoot if set too high. I adds up past error and removes that offset, but it winds up when the motor saturates, so I clamp it. D reacts to how fast the error changes and damps overshoot, but it amplifies sensor noise, so I filter it.
