Compare lidar, cameras and radar for an outdoor robot. What is each good and bad at?
Whether you know the strengths and limits of the main sensors.
Honest tradeoffs for each sensor, and the conclusion that they cover each other's gaps.

Lidar gives direct, accurate range and works in the dark, but heavy rain, fog and very dark or shiny surfaces hurt it. A camera gives color and texture, so it reads signs and lanes, but one camera gives no direct depth and struggles in glare or low light. Radar measures speed directly and sees through weather, with low resolution. That is why cars carry all three.
Why would you fuse an IMU with GPS instead of using either one alone, and how would you do it?
Your understanding of sensor fusion and state estimation.
The IMU drifts, GPS is slow and noisy; a Kalman filter combines them weighted by uncertainty.

An IMU is fast and smooth, but integrating it drifts within seconds. GPS does not drift, yet it is slow, noisy and drops out near tall buildings. A Kalman filter predicts the state from the IMU, then corrects it each time a GPS fix arrives, weighting each source by its uncertainty. I tune the noise values from logged data, not by guessing.
When would you plan a path with A* and when with a sampling planner like RRT?
Whether you can pick a motion planner to fit the problem.
A* for low-dimensional grids where shortest paths matter; sampling planners for high-dimensional spaces like arms.

For a warehouse robot on a 2D grid I use A*: with a heuristic that never overestimates the remaining cost, it finds the shortest path on that grid. For a seven-joint arm a grid is far too large, so I use a sampling planner like RRT. It finds a path fast but not the shortest, so I smooth it. RRT* moves toward the best path if given more time.
Your arm misses every grasp by the same 2 centimeters. Where do you look?
How you trace a systematic error through coordinate frames and calibration.
A constant offset means calibration or frames, not noise; you check the camera-to-robot transform, units and tool point.

A constant offset points to calibration, not noise. I check the camera-to-robot transform first: I touch the tool tip to a few known marks and compare with what the camera reports. Then I check frame conventions, like a flipped axis or millimeters read as meters, and the tool center point setting. If the offset changes with arm speed, I look at timestamps instead.
After the team added a heavier gripper, the arm started to oscillate when it stops at a target. How do you fix it?
How you debug a control problem with data instead of guessing gains.
Links the change in load to the tuning, measures the response, and checks the fix across the whole range of loads.

A heavier payload changes the inertia, so gains tuned for the light gripper may no longer fit. I log a step response to see the oscillation frequency and check that the motor is not hitting its limits. Then I retune or add feedforward based on the new mass, and test with both the light and heavy load so the fix works across the range.
A grasping policy succeeds 95% of the time in simulation and 40% on the real robot. What do you do?
How you close the gap between simulation and hardware.
Finds what the simulator models wrong, measures the real values, and makes the policy robust instead of tuning to one setup.

First I check what the simulator gets wrong: friction, motor delay, sensor noise and lighting are the usual gaps. I measure the real values, for example motor delay from a logged step, and put them in the model. Then I randomize those values in training so the policy cannot depend on one exact number, and test on hardware in small steps.
Your delivery robot's main lidar stops sending data while it is moving. What should the robot do?
Your judgement on failure handling and safe degraded behavior.
The failure is detected by design, the robot slows and stops safely, and it does not resume until the sensor is healthy.

I design for it before it happens. A watchdog flags the sensor when data stops for longer than a set timeout. The robot then slows, uses the remaining sensors only for what they can cover, and comes to a safe stop if the gap lasts. It logs the event and does not return to full speed until the sensor is healthy and checked.
Your 500 Hz control loop runs on the same computer as perception and sometimes misses its deadline. How do you fix it?
Whether you understand real-time constraints in a robot's software.
Measures jitter first, isolates the fast loop by priority or hardware, removes blocking work, and fails safe on a miss.

I measure first: loop period and jitter over hours, not seconds. Then I separate the work. The control loop runs at high priority on a real-time kernel or on a microcontroller, and heavy perception runs elsewhere and passes results through a buffer. I keep memory allocation and blocking calls out of the loop, and the controller fails safe if a deadline is missed.
Why do many robotics systems store orientation as quaternions instead of Euler angles?
Whether you understand rotation representations beyond the textbook.
Gimbal lock and smooth interpolation, plus the practical traps: keeping unit length, and that q and -q are the same rotation.

Euler angles hit gimbal lock: at certain angles, like 90 degrees of pitch, two axes line up and you lose a degree of freedom. Quaternions avoid that, combine cheaply and interpolate smoothly. The traps are drift from unit length, so I renormalize, and the fact that q and -q mean the same rotation, which breaks naive comparisons.
Why can't a differential-drive robot follow any path a planner draws, and how does that change your planner?
Your grasp of non-holonomic constraints and what they mean for planning.
It cannot move sideways, so paths must respect heading and turning limits, through a kinematically feasible planner or a smoothing step.

A differential-drive base cannot slide sideways; its motion is tied to its heading. A grid path with sharp corners forces it to stop and spin in place. A car-like robot is worse, with a minimum turning radius. So I plan in x, y and heading, for example with hybrid A* or a state lattice, or connect poses with Dubins curves, or Reeds-Shepp curves when reversing is allowed.
When would you pick a Kalman filter, an extended Kalman filter or a particle filter for localization?
Whether you match the estimator to the problem instead of using one by habit.
Kalman for linear Gaussian systems, EKF for nonlinear ones with a single-peak belief, particle filter when the robot may be in several places, at higher cost.

A plain Kalman filter is optimal when motion and measurements are linear with Gaussian noise. Most robots are nonlinear, so an EKF linearizes around the current estimate; it works well while the belief has a single peak. When the robot could be in several places at once, like at startup in a known map, a particle filter holds many hypotheses, at a higher compute cost.
Obstacles in your lidar map look smeared or doubled only while the robot is turning. What is going on?
Whether you think of timing and motion distortion, not just sensor noise.
Time sync errors between lidar and odometry, and motion distortion within a scan; fixed with a shared clock, correct timestamps and deskewing.

If it only happens when turning, I suspect time. A spinning lidar takes a scan over up to about 100 milliseconds at a common 10 Hz rate while the robot rotates, so each point needs correcting with the pose at its own timestamp. I also check that lidar and odometry share a clock and that the transform lookup uses the scan time, not the time the message arrived.
What happens when a 6-axis arm moves near a singularity, and how do you handle it in a straight-line tool move?
Your understanding of manipulator kinematics where it matters in practice.
The arm loses a direction of motion, so small tool moves demand huge joint speeds; handled with path checks, damped solutions or a joint-space move.

At a singularity, like the wrist case where two wrist axes line up, the arm loses a direction of motion. Near it, a slow straight-line tool move can ask for very high joint speeds. I check planned paths for how close they get, use a damped inverse kinematics solution so speeds stay bounded, and move in joint space when the exact tool path does not matter.
Your warehouse robots sometimes localize confidently in the wrong aisle. How do you approach it?
How you handle look-alike places in a repetitive environment.
Sees that identical aisles fool scan matching; adds distinct cues, rejects implausible jumps, and lets the robot stop when it is unsure.

Identical racks make scans from different aisles look the same, so the filter can lock onto the wrong one. I would replay logs to see where it jumps. Fixes include unique markers at aisle ends, using wheel odometry to reject big jumps, and keeping more hypotheses alive. The robot should also slow and stop when its match score drops instead of trusting a bad pose.
When is model predictive control worth its cost over a well-tuned PID?
Your judgement on control design beyond the basics.
MPC when limits and coupled inputs matter and you have a decent model and the compute; PID when a loop is simple and fast.

MPC predicts over a short horizon and solves an optimization every cycle, so it can respect limits like steering angle, acceleration and lane bounds directly. That helps path tracking on a car at speed. It costs a good model, compute time and a solver that must finish every cycle. For a single motor speed loop, PID is simpler, faster and easier to verify.
Walk me through how you would validate a new motion planner before it goes to the whole fleet.
How you take a change from code to the field without surprising anyone.
Layers: scenario tests in simulation, log replay against a baseline, a small real pilot, then a staged rollout with a fast rollback.

First, scenario tests in simulation, including every edge case that broke us before. Then I replay recorded logs and compare with the current planner on agreed metrics: near misses, stops, travel time, smoothness. Next a few robots in a controlled area, then a small share of the fleet with monitoring and quick rollback. Each step has pass criteria written before we start.
Operations wants the mobile robots to drive 30% faster to hit throughput. The safety laser scanner fields were set for the old speed. What do you say?
Whether you protect the safety function under schedule pressure.
Faster means longer stopping distance, so protective fields are recalculated, stops tested with real loads and the change revalidated first.

I would agree to study it, not to just change a parameter. Stopping distance grows with speed, and the braking part grows roughly with its square, so the protective fields must be recalculated from measured stopping times and distances. Then we update the field sets, test stops at the new speed with real loads, and update the risk assessment before any robot runs faster.
A software update you approved made a robot bump a rack at a customer site. No one was hurt. Walk me through the next two days.
How you own a field incident and stop it from happening again.
Contain first, save the data, find the root cause and the test gap that let it through, and tell the customer plainly.

First I roll the update back across the fleet, or restrict the robots if rollback is not safe, and make sure the recorded sensor logs are saved. Then I replay the event to find the cause and ask why our tests missed it. The customer gets a plain account and a date for the fix. The fix includes a new regression test built from this exact scenario.

rust-developer.heading: Rust developer questions
qs: What rules does the borrow checker enforce?
Whether you know the core of Rust's memory model.
Many shared references or one mutable one, never both at once, and no reference outliving the value it points to.

At any moment a value can have many shared references or exactly one mutable reference, not both. A reference can never outlive the value it points to. Each value has one owner, and when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped. That is how Rust stops data races and dangling pointers at compile time, with no garbage collector.
When do you return a Result, and when is it fine to panic?
How you handle errors in code other people depend on.
Result for failures a caller can expect and handle. Panic only for bugs and broken invariants, or in quick tools and tests.

If the failure can happen in normal use, like a missing file or a network error, I return a Result and let the caller decide, often passing it up with the question-mark operator. A panic means a bug: something I believed was always true is false. In a library I avoid unwrap. If I must use it, I use expect with a message that says why it cannot fail.
When would you use a generic type parameter, and when a trait object like Box<dyn Trait>?
Your grasp of static and dynamic dispatch and what each costs.
Generics are compiled per type: fast and inlinable, but more code. Trait objects use a method table: one copy, mixed types together, a small cost per call.

Generics get compiled into a separate copy for each concrete type, so calls can be inlined and are fast, but binary size and compile time grow. A trait object holds a pointer to the data and a table of methods, so one function serves every type and I can keep different types in one Vec. I default to generics on hot paths and use dyn for plugins or mixed collections.
Explain Rc versus Arc, and RefCell versus Mutex.
Whether you know how Rust shares data and why some types cannot cross threads.
Rc and RefCell are for one thread; Arc and Mutex work across threads. Mentions Send and Sync, and that RefCell checks borrows at run time.

Rc counts owners without atomic operations, so it is cheap but cannot go to another thread; Arc uses atomic counts and can be shared across threads. RefCell lets me mutate through a shared reference by checking borrow rules at run time, and it panics if I break them. It is not Sync. Across threads I use Mutex or RwLock instead. The compiler refuses the wrong choice, which catches it early.
A teammate silences every borrow checker error by adding .clone(). What do you do?
Your judgement on when a quick fix is fine and when it hides a design problem.
No blanket rule: cheap clones are fine, but clones of large data on hot paths point to an ownership design worth fixing, explained kindly.

First I look at what is being cloned and where. Cloning a small struct at startup costs nothing and keeps the code simple. Cloning a large Vec inside a loop that runs on every request is a real cost. There I would sit with them and look at ownership: maybe the function should borrow, take ownership, or the data should live in an Arc. I explain the why, not just reject the change.
Can safe Rust leak memory? Give an example.
Whether you know what Rust's safety promise covers and what it does not.
Yes, leaks are not unsafe. Rc or Arc cycles, mem::forget and Box::leak all leak; a Weak reference breaks the cycle.

Yes. Rust promises memory safety, not freedom from leaks. The classic case is two Rc values pointing at each other, like a parent and child in a tree: the counts never reach zero, so nothing is dropped. I fix it by making the back link a Weak reference. Box::leak and mem::forget also leak on purpose, and both are safe functions.
What happens if you call a blocking function, like a large file read from the standard library, inside an async task?
Whether you understand how an async runtime schedules work.
The task holds a worker thread, so other tasks stall. Fix with the runtime's pool for blocking work, an async API, or a dedicated thread.

Async tasks only give up the thread at an .await. A blocking call never yields, so it ties up one of the runtime's worker threads and every task queued behind it waits; with few threads, latency jumps across the service. I move that work to the runtime's pool meant for blocking calls, or use an async version of the API. Long CPU-heavy loops get the same treatment.
Your code holds a standard library MutexGuard across an .await and will not compile when you spawn it. Why, and how do you fix it?
How you reason about Send, futures and locks together.
The std guard is not Send, so the future is not Send. Holding a lock while suspended also risks deadlock. Drop the guard before awaiting.

A future stores everything that stays alive across an .await. The std MutexGuard is not Send, so the whole future is not Send, and a multi-threaded runtime needs Send to spawn it. Even where it compiles, holding a lock while suspended can stall other tasks or deadlock. I copy out what I need and drop the guard in a small scope before the await, and use an async mutex only if I must hold it.
What does unsafe let you do, and how do you review an unsafe block?
Whether you treat unsafe code with the care it needs.
Knows unsafe unlocks a few operations but keeps the borrow checker on. Wants small blocks, written safety reasoning, a safe wrapper and tests.

It unlocks a few extra operations: dereferencing raw pointers, calling unsafe functions like C code, using mutable statics, implementing unsafe traits and reading unions. The borrow checker still runs on everything else. In review I want the block small, a SAFETY comment saying why each rule holds, a safe wrapper around it, and tests run under an undefined-behavior checker.
Your Rust rewrite runs slower than the old C++ version. Walk me through how you find out why.
How you approach performance with measurement instead of guesses.
Confirm a release build first, then profile on real input. Common causes: allocation or cloning in hot loops, unbuffered I/O, the default hasher.

First I check it was built with --release, since debug builds can be many times slower. Then I profile on real input instead of guessing. Usual suspects: allocating or cloning in a hot loop, unbuffered reads and writes on a File, and a HashMap using the default attack-resistant hasher where a faster one fits. I fix one thing, measure again, and keep a benchmark so it does not regress.
A colleague writes let _ = state.lock(); to hold a mutex for the rest of the function. What is wrong with that?
Whether you know exactly when Rust drops a value.
The plain underscore binds nothing, so the guard drops at once. A named binding like _guard keeps the lock until the end of the scope.

The plain underscore does not bind the value, so the lock result and its guard are dropped at the end of that statement. The lock is released right away, and the code after it runs unprotected. I would write let _guard = state.lock().unwrap(); or, better, keep the guard in a named variable and use it to reach the data, so the protection is visible.
A spawn function requires T: 'static. Does that mean the value has to live for the whole program?
Whether you read lifetime bounds correctly.
No. The type must hold no borrowed references that could expire. Owned data like a String qualifies and can still be dropped at any time.

No. The bound says the type contains no borrows that could expire, so the task can safely outlive the function that started it. A String or a Vec<u8> is 'static because it owns its data, and it is still freed when the task drops it. If I need to share a local value, I move ownership in, or wrap it in an Arc and move a clone.
What do Send and Sync mean, and can you name a type that is Send but not Sync?
Your grasp of the traits that make Rust's thread safety work.
Send: a value can move to another thread. Sync: a shared reference to it can be used from several threads. Cell is Send but not Sync.

Send means a value can be moved to another thread. Sync means a shared reference to it can be used from several threads at once; formally, T is Sync when &T is Send. Cell<i32> is Send but not Sync: moving it is fine, but two threads calling set through shared references would race, because Cell has no locking. Rc is neither, since its count is not atomic.
You maintain a library with a public error enum. Is adding a new variant a breaking change, and how do you plan for it?
Whether you think about semantic versioning for code other people compile against.
Yes: callers' exhaustive matches stop compiling. Marking the enum #[non_exhaustive] from the first release forces a wildcard arm and makes new variants minor.

Yes. Any downstream match that lists every variant without a wildcard would fail to compile, so under semver it needs a major version. For enums I expect to grow, I add #[non_exhaustive] from the first release. Code outside my crate must then include a _ arm, and a new variant is a minor release. Adding the attribute later is itself breaking, so it belongs in the first design.
In a latency-sensitive order path, how do you keep heap allocations out of the hot loop?
How you control memory behavior where microseconds matter.
Measure first, then preallocate and reuse buffers, avoid hidden allocations, and prove it with an allocation-counting test.

First I confirm allocations show up in the profile. Then I size buffers at startup with with_capacity and reuse them by calling clear instead of building new ones. I watch for hidden allocations: format!, to_string, collect, and new boxed closures. In tests I install a counting global allocator and assert that the hot loop allocates zero times.
Two threads each update their own atomic counter, yet adding the second thread made both slower. What is likely happening?
Whether you understand how CPU caches affect concurrent code.
False sharing: both counters sit on one cache line, so the cores keep taking it from each other. Separate lines or per-thread counters fix it.

The counters are probably next to each other in memory, on the same cache line, which is usually 64 bytes on x86-64. Every write by one core invalidates that line in the other core's cache, so they fight over it without sharing any data. I would align each counter to its own line with #[repr(align(64))], or give each thread a local counter and merge at the end.
One thread writes data and then sets an AtomicBool flag; another waits for the flag and reads the data. Which memory orderings do you use, and why not Relaxed?
Your understanding of memory ordering with atomics.
Release on the store and Acquire on the load, so the data is visible once the flag is seen. Relaxed makes only the flag itself atomic.

The writer stores the flag with Release and the reader loads it with Acquire. When the reader sees true, everything the writer did before that store is visible to it. With Relaxed, the flag is still atomic, but the compiler and CPU may reorder other memory around it, so the reader could see the flag set and stale data. It might pass tests on x86 and fail on ARM.
You expose a Rust function to a C program. What rules do you follow for strings, memory and panics?
Whether you can cross a language boundary without undefined behavior.
Only C-compatible types, memory freed by the side that allocated it, and no panic allowed to unwind into C.

The exported function is extern "C" and takes only C-compatible types. Strings cross as *const c_char: I read input with CStr and hand strings out with CString::into_raw, plus a matching free function that calls CString::from_raw, because C's free must not release Rust memory. I wrap the body in catch_unwind and return an error code instead of letting a panic reach C.
Why does Future::poll take Pin<&mut Self>?
Your understanding of how async Rust works under the hood.
Async code compiles to state machines that may borrow from their own fields. Pin promises the future stays put, so those internal references stay valid.

An async fn becomes a state machine that stores its local variables between awaits. If one local borrows another across an .await, the struct points into itself, and moving it would leave a dangling pointer. Pin guarantees that once the future is pinned it stays at the same address until it is dropped. Types with no self-references implement Unpin, and for them Pin changes nothing.
In an async select loop over a channel and a socket read, messages sometimes go missing. What do you suspect, and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand cancellation in async Rust.
A branch that is not cancel-safe: when another branch wins, the losing future is dropped and any partial progress inside it is lost.

When one branch of the select finishes, the other futures are dropped, which cancels them. If the socket read had already pulled part of a message into its own internal buffer, that data is lost with it. I check each branch's documentation for cancel safety, keep buffers in the loop's state instead of inside the future, or create the future once, pin it, and keep polling the same one.

sales-coordinator.heading: Sales coordinator and deal desk questions
qs: What is the difference between a quote, a contract and a sales order?
Whether you know the documents of a deal and what each one does.
A quote is an offer, the contract is the signed agreement, and the order is the internal record that triggers delivery and billing.

A quote is our offer: products, prices and how long the price holds. The contract is what both sides sign, and it sets the legal terms. The sales order is our internal record built from the signed deal. It tells fulfillment what to deliver and finance what to bill. If the three don't match, something goes wrong downstream.
How would you explain the difference between ARR and total contract value?
Your grasp of the deal numbers that sales and finance report on.
ARR is the yearly value of recurring subscription revenue. TCV is everything in the contract over its full term, one-time fees included.

ARR is annual recurring revenue: the subscription value of one year, without setup or training fees. TCV is the total the customer commits to over the whole term, one-time fees included. A three-year deal at $40,000 a year plus a $5,000 setup fee is $40,000 ARR and $125,000 TCV.
Walk me through how you check a quote before it goes to the customer.
How careful you are with the document the customer will hold you to.
A set routine: right legal entity, products and quantities, prices against the price book, approvals on record, terms and expiry date.

I open the opportunity next to the quote. I check the customer's legal name and billing address, then each product and quantity against what the rep wrote. Prices must match the price book or have an approved discount on record. Then payment terms, start date and expiry date. Last, I check the total against the rep's number. Five minutes catches most errors.
A customer's purchase order doesn't match the signed quote. What do you do?
Whether you stop an order that would bill the wrong amount.
Holding the booking, finding which document is wrong, and getting the PO or the quote corrected in writing before the order is entered.

I don't book it as is. I compare line by line to find the gap; last time the PO had 50 licenses and the quote had 55. I tell the rep and ask the customer's buyer for a revised PO, or we reissue the quote if ours was wrong. I note it on the opportunity so finance knows why the booking waited a day.
During forecast review, a third of open deals have close dates already in the past. How do you deal with it?
How you keep CRM data honest enough to forecast from.
Getting the reps to fix their own deals rather than guessing for them, and setting up a report so stale dates show up every week.

I pull a list by rep and send it before the next review, asking each one to update the date or close the deal as lost. I don't change dates myself, because I don't know the deal. Then I set up a weekly report of past-due close dates for the sales manager, so it stays a five-minute task instead of a big cleanup.
A rep needs a 25% discount approved today, and the approver for that level is on vacation. What do you do?
Whether you respect the approval rules when a deal is under pressure.
Using the named backup or the next level up, and never putting the discount on a quote before it is approved.

I check the approval matrix for a delegate; most companies name a backup for each level. If there isn't one, I go one level up and send a short deal summary so they can decide fast. What I won't do is put the discount on the quote and get approval later. If it can't be approved today, the rep tells the customer the quote comes tomorrow.
A rep offers 30% off year one and list price in year two. List is $100,000 a year. What is the real discount on the deal?
Your deal math and whether you can show what a discount really costs.
Total paid against total list: $170,000 versus $200,000 is 15% off over the term, and year two is about a 43% price jump for the customer.

Over two years the customer pays $70,000 plus $100,000, so $170,000 against $200,000 at list. That is 15% off the contract. I'd also flag the renewal risk: going from $70,000 to $100,000 is about a 43% jump in year two, and the customer will notice. A flat 15% each year costs us the same and is easier to renew.
A customer sends back the contract asking for net 90 payment terms and uncapped liability. How do you handle it?
Whether you know which changes you can accept and which belong to finance or legal.
Spotting non-standard terms, sending payment terms to finance and liability to legal, and tracking both so the deal does not stall.

Neither is mine to accept. Net 90 means we wait three months for the cash, so finance has to approve it. Uncapped liability means unlimited risk, so legal reviews it. I send each to its owner with the deal size and close date, tell the rep what's pending, and log it in the CRM. Legal often offers a cap tied to fees paid instead.
On the last day of the quarter, a rep asks you to book a deal the customer will only sign tomorrow. What do you say?
Your integrity when there is pressure to make the numbers.
A clear no with the reason, booking only on signature, and real help getting the signature in time.

No. A deal is booked when it is signed, not before. Booking it early would put revenue in the wrong quarter, and auditors compare signature dates with booking dates. I'd help in other ways: have the contract ready for e-signature tonight and help the rep reach the customer's signer. If it lands tomorrow, it counts next quarter.
You find that a quote you prepared had the wrong price and the customer has already signed. What do you do?
How you own a mistake that costs money and touches the customer.
Telling the manager and rep right away with the numbers, letting the company decide to honor or amend, and fixing the step that let it through.

I tell my manager and the rep the same day, with the numbers: what we quoted, what it should have been, and the gap. I don't contact the customer myself; the company decides whether to honor the signed price or ask for an amendment. Then I find how it slipped through, for example a skipped price book check, and add that check to my routine.
A customer on an annual plan wants to add 10 seats halfway through the term. How do you quote it?
Whether you understand co-terming and proration on subscription add-ons.
You co-term to the existing end date and prorate for the time left. The add-on uses the customer's contracted rate unless an approval says otherwise.

I co-term the seats so they end with the main subscription. If seats are $1,200 a year and six months are left, each seat is $600 for this term, so $6,000 for ten. I use the customer's contracted per-seat rate, not list, unless the contract says otherwise. The renewal quote then shows all seats at the full annual price.
A customer returns a signed quote that expired two weeks ago, and our list prices went up since. What do you do?
How you handle expired pricing without losing the deal or quietly giving away margin.
You don't book it as is. You flag it to the rep and either reissue at current prices or get the old price formally approved on a new quote.

I don't book it, because the offer had lapsed when they signed. I tell the rep the same day and lay out two options: a new quote at current prices, or an approval to honor the old price with a fresh expiry date. If the delay was ours we often honor it, but it goes through approval and gets reissued so the record is clean.
The signed order form names a customer entity that doesn't match their legal name or the billing account in the CRM. Why does it matter, and what do you do?
Whether you know who is actually bound by the contract and who gets billed.
The contract binds the entity it names. A wrong name causes billing, tax and collection trouble, so you confirm the exact legal name and fix it before booking.

The contract binds whatever entity is named. If it names the parent but the buyer is a subsidiary, we may invoice the wrong party or apply the wrong sales tax. I ask the rep to confirm the exact legal name and address with the customer, often from their W-9. Then I fix it by amendment or a re-signed form, and match the CRM account before I book.
A rep offers 12 months at $120,000 plus three free months up front. What is the effective discount, and what do you flag?
Whether you can see a discount hidden in the term instead of the price.
Fifteen months for $120,000 is $8,000 a month against $10,000, a 20% effective discount. The renewal date and renewal price also need attention.

The customer gets 15 months of service for $120,000, so $8,000 a month instead of $10,000. That is a 20% discount even though the price line shows none, so it needs approval at the 20% level. I also flag that the renewal date moves out three months. The renewal must be quoted at the full $10,000 a month, not at the blended rate.
You find the same customer under three account records in the CRM, each with open opportunities. How do you clean it up?
How you fix CRM data without breaking reports, ownership or history.
You check owners and open deals first and pick the master record by a clear rule. You merge so history follows, then stop the duplicates at the source.

First I check who owns each record and whether any open deals overlap, and I talk to those reps before touching anything. I pick the master by rule: the one tied to the signed contract and billing. I use the CRM's merge function so contacts, activities and deals move with it. Then I add a duplicate rule on email domain so it doesn't happen again.
The customer's purchase order arrives with their own preprinted terms on the back. Which terms apply, and what do you check?
Whether you know how a PO's own terms interact with the signed agreement.
If the signed agreement says PO terms don't apply, it controls. You check that clause, match the PO to the quote, and send real conflicts to legal.

If our signed agreement says preprinted PO terms have no effect, the PO is just their billing paperwork. I confirm that clause exists, then match the PO to the quote: entity, amounts, dates and products. If there's no such clause, or the PO says its terms override ours, I don't decide alone. I send it to legal before we accept or book.
You notice a rep sent the same customer two quotes a week apart, each just under the discount level that needs VP approval. What do you do?
Your judgement when someone works around the approval rules.
You treat the quotes as one deal for approval. You raise it with the rep first and escalate only if it repeats; the aim is control, not blame.

I'd treat it as one deal: same customer, same need, close timing. Combined, it needs VP approval, so I hold booking and tell the rep that plainly. It may be innocent, like a second team's budget. If it's a pattern, I tell the sales manager. I'd also suggest the approval rule look at a customer's total over a period, not each quote alone.
A rep wants to email the customer a promise of a free cancellation right that isn't in the contract. How do you respond?
Whether you know why every commercial term has to live in the contract.
No side deals. An off-contract promise can bind the company, change how revenue is recognized and hide risk. Put it in the contract through approval, or drop it.

I'd stop it. An email promise can still bind us, and finance has to account for any term that changes what the customer owes. A hidden cancellation right can change how the deal's revenue is booked. If the customer needs it, we write it into the order form, get the approvals it requires, and finance sees it. If it can't be approved, the rep says no.
Walk me through how you would design a deal approval matrix from scratch.
How you balance control with deal speed when setting approval rules.
Tiers tied to what really creates risk: discount, deal size, payment terms, price locks and legal changes. Each approver has a named backup and a turnaround time.

I'd start from what costs money or adds risk: discount depth, deal size, payment terms beyond standard, multi-year price locks and changes to legal terms. Each gets tiers, with low risk approved by the sales manager and the rest by finance, legal or a VP. Every approver has a backup and a response time, say one business day. I review it each quarter.
Leadership says average selling price has dropped for three quarters. How would you find where discount is leaking?
Whether you can turn deal data into a clear finding on pricing.
You compare list to net price across rep, segment, product and timing, and count non-price giveaways too. You bring the finding with a proposed fix.

I'd pull every closed deal with list price, net price and approvals, then split the gap by rep, region, deal size, product and quarter end. I'd count hidden giveaways too: free months, extra seats, longer payment terms. Usually a few reps or end-of-quarter deals drive most of it. I'd show that with examples and propose a fix, like approval for non-price concessions.

sales-development.heading: Sales development representative questions
qs: Where does your job end and the account executive's job begin?
Whether you understand the SDR role and the handoff to the person who closes the deal.
You open and qualify, then hand over a clean meeting with notes. You do not quote prices or try to close.

My job is to start the conversation, check there is a real fit and book a meeting the AE wants to take. Before the meeting I log who the prospect is, the problem they named and who else is involved, so the AE does not ask the same questions twice. Pricing, demos and the deal itself belong to the AE.
Which numbers would you track to know if your outreach is working?
Whether you look past activity counts to the steps that actually lead to meetings.
A funnel from activity to meetings held, with the conversion rate at each step, used to find the weak step.

I track dials, connects, conversations and meetings booked. On email I watch the reply rate, not just opens. The number that matters most is meetings held and accepted by the AE. If I connect a lot but book little, my talk track needs work. If I book but people do not show up, my qualifying or confirming is weak.
Walk me through the first 30 seconds of a cold call.
How you open a call so the prospect keeps listening.
Name and company, an honest reason for the call tied to their role, then a question. No long pitch.

I say who I am and admit it is a cold call, because honesty buys me a few seconds. Then one line on why I called them: teams their size often lose hours on manual reporting. Then a question, like how they handle that today. If they talk, I listen and dig in. If not, I ask for 15 minutes later in the week.
What makes a cold email get a reply?
Your grasp of how a first email is written and why most get ignored.
Short, about the reader, one specific reason for reaching out, and one easy ask.

Keep it short and make it about them, not us. Open with something specific: a new job posting, an expansion, a problem their role usually has. Then one sentence on how we help, with a real result. End with a small ask, like “worth a short call next week?” A plain subject line usually beats a clever one.
A prospect picks up and says, “Just send me an email.” What do you do?
How you handle the most common brush-off without being pushy.
Agree, ask one question so the email is relevant, and set a follow-up in the CRM.

I say sure, and ask what would make the email worth opening: is this something they are working on now, or not on the radar at all? That question often starts a real conversation. If not, I send a short email within the hour that uses what they told me, and I set a follow-up call in the CRM for two days later.
An assistant answers and asks, “What is this regarding?” How do you respond?
Whether you work with a gatekeeper honestly instead of trying to trick your way past.
A short, true reason, respect for the assistant, and a request for their help. Never pretending to know the boss.

I tell the truth in one sentence: I am calling about how their team handles scheduling and want to see if it is a priority. Assistants know who owns what, so I ask who handles that area and when is a good time to reach them. I never claim to be a friend or to be returning a call. That burns the whole account.
How would you build a sequence of touches for a new list of prospects?
Whether you can plan follow-up across channels instead of sending one email and giving up.
Several touches over a few weeks across phone, email and LinkedIn, each adding something new, with a clear end point.

I would plan eight to ten touches over about three weeks, mixing calls, emails and a LinkedIn connection request. Each touch adds something: a short customer story, a question, a useful article, never just “bumping this up.” The last email closes the loop politely. Then I compare reply rates by step and rewrite the weak ones.
A prospect replies, “Stop emailing me.” What do you do, and what does the law require?
Whether you know the basic rules for commercial email and respect an opt-out.
Stop all outreach, mark the contact do-not-contact, and know that CAN-SPAM requires a working opt-out that is honored.

I stop the sequence right away and mark the contact do-not-contact in the CRM, so no teammate emails them either. Under the federal CAN-SPAM Act, commercial email needs an honest subject line, our postal address and a way to opt out, and opt-outs must be honored within 10 business days. I do it the same day and send nothing more.
An account executive tells you a third of your meetings are no-shows. How do you fix it?
How you take feedback and improve the quality of the meetings you book.
Look at which meetings fail, tighten qualifying, confirm the value of the meeting, and remind the prospect before it.

First I check which meetings failed: same lead source, same job title, booked weeks out? Often it is meetings I pushed that the prospect never really wanted. I would ask one more qualifying question, send the invite while still on the call, confirm the day before with a note on what we will cover, and book within a week when I can.
A sequence just went to 300 prospects with “Hi {FirstName}” in the greeting. What do you do?
How you handle a visible mistake quickly and honestly.
Pause the sequence, tell your manager, find the cause, fix the data and test before sending again.

I pause the sequence at once so the next steps do not go out broken, and I tell my manager before anyone asks. The cause is usually contacts with an empty first-name field. I fix or remove those records and send a test to myself. In the next touch I may open with one human line owning the mistake. Some people reply to that.
How do you handle an inbound lead differently from an outbound prospect?
Whether you know that intent and timing change how you work a lead.
Inbound gets a fast reply built on what the person already did; outbound needs a reason to care first. Both still get qualified.

An inbound lead raised a hand, so speed matters most. I try to call within minutes and open with what they downloaded or asked about. An outbound prospect never asked to hear from me, so I lead with the specific reason I picked them. In both cases I still check fit before I book anything.
What do you say in a voicemail, and when do you leave one?
How you use voicemail as one touch in a sequence, not as the whole pitch.
Short, one clear reason for calling, name and number said slowly, and a link to the email that follows.

I keep it under 30 seconds: my name, my company, one line on why I am calling them in particular, and my number said twice, slowly. Then I say I will send a short email on the same topic, so the voicemail and the email point at each other. I do not leave one on every attempt, usually just the first and the last.
What goes into your handoff note when you pass a booked meeting to an account executive?
Whether your meetings arrive ready for the account executive to use.
Who the person is, why they took the meeting in their own words, what was confirmed and what is still open.

I write their name and role, the problem they described in their own words, and how they came to us. Then what I confirmed, like team size, current tool, timeline and who else decides, and what I could not confirm, like budget. The account executive should walk in without making the prospect repeat anything.
A prospect says, “We already use one of your competitors and we are happy.” What do you say?
How you handle the most common brush-off without arguing or running down a competitor.
Accepting it, asking one real question about where the current tool falls short, and never criticizing the competitor.

I say, “That makes sense, most teams we talk to already have something in place.” Then one question: “When you renew, what is the one thing you wish it did better?” If there is nothing, I ask if I can check back near renewal and log the date in the CRM. Criticizing their tool only makes them defend their own choice.
A contact tells you, “I am not the right person for this.” How do you use that?
Whether you turn a wrong contact into a referral instead of a dead end.
Asking who owns the decision, getting permission to use their name, and updating the CRM so the record is right.

I thank them and ask, “Who would own a decision like this on your side?” If they give a name, I ask if I can mention we spoke. My next email opens with “Dana on your team suggested I reach out,” which gets read. In the CRM I update the first contact's role so nobody calls them about this again.
You are handed 200 named accounts on your first day. How do you decide which to work first?
How you set priorities when you cannot give every account the same effort.
Tiers built on fit with current customers and on timing signals, with deep research saved for the top tier.

I sort first by fit with our best customers: industry, size, the tools they use. Then I look for timing signals, like a new leader in the buying role, a funding round, or job posts for the team we serve. The top 20 or so get researched, personal outreach. The middle gets a lighter sequence. The rest I check monthly for new signals.
Your call connect rate has dropped by half over a month. What do you look at?
How you diagnose a calling problem before simply dialing more.
Checking data quality, how the caller ID shows up, and call timing, one change at a time.

First the data: are these direct dials and mobiles, or main lines that go to a phone menu? Then the caller ID: I call my own cell to see whether our number shows as possible spam. Then timing: I compare connects by hour on my own list. I change one thing at a time so I know what actually fixed it.
Your email replies fell off and your bounce rate went up. What do you check before you send anything else?
Whether you understand email deliverability, not just the wording of the message.
Pausing sends, cleaning the list, and checking domain authentication such as SPF, DKIM and DMARC before blaming the copy.

I pause the sequence, since more sending makes it worse. Bounces mean bad addresses, so I run the list through verification and remove invalid ones. I ask our ops person whether SPF, DKIM and DMARC are set up; those records prove our mail really comes from us. I also confirm the unsubscribe works and lower daily volume per inbox.
You realize you just emailed three people at an account where an account executive has an open deal. What do you do?
How you respect account ownership and repair a mistake inside your own team.
Stopping all touches, telling the account executive right away, letting them lead, and fixing the step you skipped.

I stop all touches to that account and message the account executive right away with exactly what I sent and to whom. They decide if anything should be said to the prospect. Then I find the cause: I skipped checking open opportunities in the CRM before loading the list. Now I filter out accounts with open deals before any sequence starts.
It is the last week of the month and you are two meetings short. A prospect will take a meeting but clearly has no need. Do you book it?
Your judgement when your own number and the team's interest pull apart.
Refusing to book a meeting you know is empty, being open with the manager, and putting the effort into real prospects.

I would not book it. A meeting with no need wastes an hour of the account executive's time, and if it never turns into an opportunity it hurts my numbers anyway. I would tell my manager I am two short and show my plan: a call block on my warmest accounts and follow-ups to recent replies. Missing by two beats a calendar nobody trusts.

sales-enablement.heading: Sales enablement manager questions
qs: What is the difference between sales enablement and sales training?
Whether you understand the scope of the role beyond running classes.
Training is one part; enablement also covers content, tools, coaching and onboarding, tied to how reps actually sell.

Training teaches a skill at one point in time. Enablement is everything a rep needs to sell well, all the time: onboarding, playbooks, the content they send buyers, coaching with their managers, and tools that are easy to use. I judge my work by what changes in the deals, not by how many sessions I ran.
How would you build a 90-day onboarding plan for new account executives?
How you structure ramp-up so new reps sell sooner.
Clear stages with milestones, practice before live calls, managers involved, and a measure like time to first closed deal.

Weeks one and two cover the product, buyer personas and our sales process, with a short quiz each week. Weeks three to six are shadowing, role-plays graded against a rubric, and a pitch certification before they run calls alone. After that come live deals with weekly manager coaching. I track time to first meeting booked and time to first closed deal for each group.
What goes into a good sales playbook?
Your grasp of content reps will actually use in a deal.
Built around buyer situations and stages, with questions, talk tracks, objections and proof, short enough to use during a call.

I organize it by buyer and deal stage, not by product feature. For each stage: the goal, the questions to ask, short talk tracks, common objections with answers, and the proof to send, like a customer story. I write it with top reps, keep each section to a page, and give it an owner and a review date so it does not go stale.
How do you decide what to train reps on next?
Whether you base your plans on evidence rather than on requests alone.
Uses data and listening: where deals stall, call reviews, win-loss notes and manager input, then ranks gaps by impact.

I look at where deals stall in the CRM, for example many deals dying between demo and proposal. Then I listen to recorded calls from that stage and ask managers what they see. If reps skip discovery before the demo, that is the topic. I rank gaps by how much revenue they touch and how much training can actually fix them.
A major product launches in three weeks. How do you get the sales team ready?
How you plan and run a launch under a tight deadline.
Agrees the message with product marketing, keeps training short and role-based, checks readiness, and keeps supporting after launch.

First I agree with product marketing on who the product is for, the problem it solves and how it differs from alternatives. Then a short live session, a one-page brief, a demo script and an objection list. Reps record a two-minute pitch that managers review before launch day. After launch I collect the questions buyers ask and update the materials.
How do you measure whether a training program worked?
Whether you measure behavior and results, not only satisfaction.
Goes past survey scores: tests knowledge, checks behavior on real calls, then compares business metrics with a baseline.

I use the four Kirkpatrick levels. Did reps find it useful. Did they learn it, shown by a quiz or a graded role-play. Do they use it, which I check in real calls or CRM fields a month later. And did the numbers move, like conversion at the targeted stage compared with before. The first level is the easiest to get and tells me the least.
Three months after launch, most reps still are not using the new pitch deck. What do you do?
How you handle low adoption without blaming the reps.
Finds out why before pushing harder: checks usage data, asks reps, fixes the deck or access, and gets managers to reinforce it.

I check the usage data, then talk to five reps, including two top performers. Often the deck is too long, hard to find, or does not fit the buyers they meet. I fix what they point to, cut it down, and ask a respected rep to show how she uses it. Then managers ask to see it in deal reviews, so using it becomes routine.
A sales VP asks you for a training because win rates dropped. How do you respond?
Your judgement on whether a problem can actually be solved by training.
Diagnoses first: not every drop is a skills gap. It could be pricing, lead quality, a new competitor or territory changes.

I say yes to looking into it, not yet to the training. I check whether the drop is across all reps or a few, which deal types, and what loss reasons say. If a new competitor is winning on price, a class will not fix it, and I bring that to the VP with the data. If reps lose at the same skill step, training plus coaching is the answer.
Tell me about an enablement program that did not work. What did you change?
Whether you own your mistakes and learn from the data.
A real failure, a clear reason found, and a specific change that was measured afterward.

I ran a full-day negotiation workshop. Reps rated it highly, but a month later call reviews showed almost no change in how they handled discounts. The problem was no follow-up. I rebuilt it as short weekly sessions, each followed by a role-play with their manager. The next quarter, the average discount on that team's closed deals fell from 18% to 13%.
How do you show leadership that enablement drove revenue when so many other things affect it?
How you prove impact honestly when cause and effect are hard to separate.
Uses baselines, comparison groups and leading indicators, and is clear about what the data can and cannot prove.

I avoid claiming all the revenue. I set a baseline before a program starts and, where I can, roll it out to one team first and compare it with a similar team over the same period. I track leading measures like ramp time and stage conversion. When I report, I say what the data shows and what it does not, so leaders trust the numbers I do claim.
What is the difference between a talk track and a script, and when would you use each?
Whether you know how to give reps words they will actually use.
A talk track gives points and order for the rep to say naturally; exact wording is kept only where it must be, like approved legal or pricing language.

A script is word for word. A talk track gives the points to hit, the order, and a few proof points, and the rep says it in their own words. I use talk tracks for discovery and demos, where the rep must react to the buyer. I keep exact wording only where it matters, like a required disclosure or a pricing statement legal has approved.
What goes on a good competitive battlecard, and how do you keep it accurate?
Your grasp of competitive content and the care it needs.
Short, usable content with sourced, dated claims, since a false statement about a competitor hurts credibility and can create legal risk.

One page: where we win, where they win, the traps they set, three questions that expose their weak spots, and short answers to their common claims. Every claim has a source and a date, like a public pricing page or a win-loss interview. I review cards each quarter and after any competitor launch, and I leave out anything we cannot prove.
Walk me through how you coach a rep using one of their recorded calls.
How you turn a call review into a change in behavior.
One focus, the rep reflects first, practice of that exact moment, and a follow-up on the next calls.

I listen first and pick one moment, not ten. In the session I ask the rep what they would change before I say anything. Then we work on one skill, say asking a second question after the buyer names a problem, and role-play that moment twice. I write down the one behavior and listen for it on their next two calls.
Your team wants to start using call recordings for coaching. What do you check first?
Whether you know that recording calls has legal and privacy rules.
Consent rules differ by state, so you involve legal, make sure recording is announced, and limit access and retention.

Federal law allows recording with one party's consent, but some states require every party on the call to agree, and calls cross state lines. So I confirm with legal that our tool announces the recording and that reps get consent at the start. I also check who can access recordings and how long we keep them, since calls hold customer data.
How do you certify that a rep can actually deliver a new pitch, not just pass a quiz?
How you test skill rather than memory.
A rubric tied to the playbook, a live or recorded performance scored by the manager, and a retry with specific feedback.

I write a short rubric from the playbook: does the rep open with the customer's problem, ask at least two discovery questions, and handle the top objection. Reps record a pitch or role-play live with their manager, who scores it. Anyone below the bar gets specific feedback and tries again within a week.
How do you get frontline sales managers to reinforce what you train?
Whether you know managers decide if training sticks.
Managers are trained before reps and given simple tools to coach the skill in their regular meetings.

Managers decide what happens after training, so I train them first, a week before reps. I give them a short coaching guide: what good looks like, two questions to ask in one-on-ones, and one call to review together. I ask them to bring examples to pipeline meetings, and I show their VP which teams are using it.
Your top rep says your training is a waste of their time. What do you do?
How you handle pushback from people who outsell the program.
Curiosity instead of defense: learn what the rep does, use it in the program, and offer a test-out instead of forcing a beginner session.

I ask what they do instead, because a top rep often has a better way. If it works, I record it and build it into the training, with their name on it. I would not force them through a beginner session, but I might ask them to test out or co-lead a role-play. Most top reps want respect more than an excuse.
The content library has 900 assets and reps say they cannot find anything. What do you do?
How you run content governance, not just content creation.
Use data to cut, give every asset an owner and review date, and organize by deal stage so reps find things when they need them.

First I pull usage data; usually a small share of assets does most of the work. I archive anything unused for six months or out of date, after a quick check with owners. Each remaining asset gets an owner, a review date and a tag by deal stage. New content comes in only with an owner attached.
You find that a battlecard you published had a wrong claim about a competitor, and reps have used it on calls. How do you handle it?
How you own and repair a mistake that reached customers.
Fast removal, a clear correction to reps, telling leaders and legal, fixing it in open deals, and a new check so it does not recur.

I pull the card the same day and send reps a short note: what was wrong, what is true, and what to say if a buyer brings it up. I tell sales leaders and legal, since a false claim about a competitor can be a legal risk. Then we find the open deals that heard it so reps can correct it. Last, I add a source check before any claim is published.

sales-engineer.heading: Sales engineer questions
qs: What do you need to learn in technical discovery before you build a demo?
Whether you know what discovery is for in this role.
The business problem, the current setup and where it breaks, who decides and how they will judge success, not just a list of features.

I want the problem in their words, what they use today and where it breaks, which systems we must connect to, who signs off technically and what a win looks like for them. If I only learn which features they asked about, I end up demoing everything and proving nothing.
How do you tailor a standard demo for a specific customer?
How you turn a generic product tour into a story about the buyer.
Lead with their biggest pain, use data and terms that look like theirs, show the few workflows that matter and cut the rest.

I start from the two or three pains I heard in discovery and open with the one that hurts most. I load sample data that looks like theirs, use their job titles and words, and show the outcome first, then how we get there. Features they did not ask about stay out unless they ask. Twenty strong minutes beat sixty tired ones.
A prospect asks a technical question in a demo and you do not know the answer. What do you do?
Your honesty under pressure in front of a buyer.
Say you do not know, write the question down, commit to a time for the answer and follow up in writing. No guessing.

I say I am not certain and I will not guess, because a wrong answer can come back later as a promise. I write the exact question down, ask a short follow-up to understand the context, and give a day for the answer. Then I check with product or engineering and send it in writing, copying the account executive.
Your demo environment crashes in the middle of a live presentation. Walk me through how you handle it.
How you recover from a failure without losing the room.
Stay calm, name it briefly, switch to a prepared backup, keep the conversation useful and follow up with the part they missed.

I say plainly that the environment has dropped and move to my backup: a second instance or a short recording of the same flow, which I keep ready for every call. If neither works, I sketch the workflow on a whiteboard and use the time for their questions. Afterward I book a short session to show the missed part live, and I find out why it failed.
How do you set success criteria for a proof of concept?
Whether you can scope a proof of concept so it ends in a clear decision.
A few measurable tests agreed in writing with the decision maker before work starts, plus dates, owners on both sides and the next step if it passes.

Before we start I write down three to five tests with the customer, each with a pass mark they agree to, like loading their own data and producing a given report within a set time. We fix the dates, who does what on both sides, and what happens if it passes, such as a purchase decision. The person who signs off reviews the plan, not only the engineer who tests.
When would you push back on a customer's request for a proof of concept?
Your judgement about where scarce technical time is worth spending.
When the deal is not qualified, there are no criteria, or a cheaper step would answer the doubt; you offer that alternative instead of a flat no.

A proof of concept costs weeks of my time and theirs, so I push back when there is no budget, no decision date or no agreed criteria, or when it is really a free trial with no buyer behind it. Often a tailored demo, a reference call or a sandbox answers the doubt. If they still need one, I tie it to a written plan and a decision at the end.
Halfway through a proof of concept, the customer keeps adding new requirements. How do you handle it?
How you control scope creep without damaging the relationship.
Go back to the agreed criteria, separate what changes the decision from what can wait, and reset time or scope openly with the sponsor.

I bring out the written success criteria and ask which new items would change the buying decision. Those I discuss with the sponsor: we add them and move the end date, or swap out a lower priority test. The rest go on a list for after purchase. I keep the account executive informed so a two week trial does not drift into two months.
The account executive promised a prospect a feature the product does not have. What do you do?
Whether you protect the customer's trust and your working relationship at the same time.
Raise it privately with the account executive first, then correct it with the customer plainly, sharing a workaround and only confirmed roadmap facts.

I talk to the account executive privately first, so we correct it together and not in front of the customer. Then we tell the prospect plainly what the product does today, show the closest workaround, and mention a roadmap date only if product management has confirmed it. Losing a deal now is cheaper than a customer who finds out after signing.
How do you handle a security questionnaire or a request for proposal with hundreds of technical questions?
Your process for accurate, consistent written answers at volume.
Reuse approved answers, route certification and legal items to their owners, never claim more than is true, and track the deadline.

I start from our library of approved answers and update anything that has changed. Questions about certifications, data handling or contract terms go to the security or legal owner, because a wrong yes can turn into a contract promise. I mark partial items as partial with a short explanation, and I keep a tracker so nothing misses the deadline.
Tell me about a deal where you won the technical evaluation but still lost. What did you learn?
Whether you understand that the technical win is only one part of the sale.
An honest story with a clear reason outside the technology, such as budget, champion or timing, and a real change in how you work since.

We passed every test in a proof of concept for a mid-size logistics company, then lost on price to a tool their finance team already used. I had worked only with the engineers and never met the person who controlled the budget. Now I ask in discovery who approves the spend, and I make sure that person sees the business case, not just the IT team.
How do you open a demo, and what do you show first?
Whether you build a demo around the buyer's problem instead of a tour of the product menu.
A short recap of the pain found in discovery, then the result the buyer cares about first, before any setup or feature tour.

I spend two minutes replaying what I heard in discovery and ask if it is still right. Then I show the outcome first, for example the finished dashboard their operations manager wants, and only then how we get there. If I start with login screens and settings, I lose the room before the part that matters.
How do you split the work with the account executive on a deal?
How you work as one half of a selling team.
Clear roles agreed early: the AE owns the commercial process, the SE owns the technical win, and both work from one shared account plan.

Before the first call we agree who leads what. The AE runs the relationship, pricing and contracts. I own technical discovery, the demo and the proof of concept. We debrief for ten minutes after every meeting and keep one shared plan, so the customer never hears two different stories from us.
A director likes the feature but asks why it is worth the money. How do you answer?
Whether you can turn a technical feature into business value.
Ties the feature to a problem the customer named, uses the customer's own figures, and lets them check the math.

I go back to what they told me in discovery. Say their team spends 30 hours a week fixing failed data loads. If our automatic retries and alerts cut that in half, that is 15 engineer hours a week back. I write the math with their numbers and ask them to correct it. A number they built with me is one they will repeat to their CFO.
Your demo audience is the CIO and three hands-on engineers. How do you run it?
How you serve very different audiences in the same room.
Leads with the outcome for the executive, saves deep detail for a follow-up session, and keeps both groups engaged.

I open with the business problem and the end result, because the CIO may leave after twenty minutes. I tell the engineers I will hold their deep questions for a technical session later that week, and I write each one down where they can see it. Before the CIO leaves, I ask what would have to be true for this to move forward.
The prospect wants to load real customer records with personal data into the proof of concept. What do you do?
Whether you protect data and the deal at the same time.
Prefers masked or sample data; if real data is truly needed, involves security and legal on both sides and settles storage and deletion first.

First I ask whether masked or sample data would prove the same thing, because it usually does. If they truly need real records, I bring in our security team and theirs, confirm the agreements, where the data will live and how it is deleted when the trial ends. I never accept a spreadsheet by email just to keep the trial moving.
The prospect is also evaluating a competitor. How do you position against them?
How you compete without bad-mouthing a rival.
Focuses on the buyer's criteria, suggests tests that show your strengths, and makes no claims about the rival that cannot be backed up.

I never trash the other vendor; it makes us look nervous, and the buyer may like them. I find the criteria where we are strong, such as audit logging, and suggest they test it in both products with the same scenario. If they ask me about the rival directly, I only say what is public and current, and I suggest they ask the rival to show it.
A prospect says they will sign only if a feature on our roadmap ships next quarter. What do you say?
Whether you can talk about the future without making promises the company cannot keep.
No dates promised alone: the roadmap is called a plan that can change, product management is brought in, and the deal rests on what exists today.

I tell them honestly that a roadmap is a plan, not a commitment, and dates can move. I ask what they need the feature for, because a current workaround often covers it. If it is a real blocker, I bring in our product manager and the AE, and any commitment goes through proper approval, not my word in a meeting.
After a demo you realize you told the prospect something wrong about the product. What do you do?
Your honesty when a mistake could cost the deal.
Corrects it fast and in writing, tells the AE first, gives the true answer with an option, and does not hope nobody notices.

I tell the AE first, then email the prospect within a day: last week I said single sign-on with their system works out of the box; in fact it needs a configuration step, and here is how it works. A correction I make costs a little. One their engineers find during the trial costs us trust in everything else I said.
A senior architect at the prospect seems set on proving our product fails. How do you handle it?
How you turn a hostile technical evaluator into a fair one.
Treats the objections as real, invites the architect to shape the test plan, admits real limits, and does not argue in front of the group.

I ask for a one-on-one and find out what went wrong for them before, because there is usually a story. Then I ask them to write the hardest test cases and we run them together. Where we have a real limit, I say so and show the workaround. A skeptic who signs off becomes the strongest voice in the room.
If you joined us, how would you measure whether our presales team is doing well?
Whether you think about the presales function as a whole, not just your own deals.
Uses a few outcome measures like technical win rate and proof-of-concept conversion, and knows activity counts alone can mislead.

I would track the technical win rate, how many proofs of concept turn into closed deals, and how long the technical phase takes. I would also ask new customers whether what we showed matched what they got after go-live. Demo counts alone tell me little; a team can run many demos and still lose deals it should have qualified out.

sales-manager.heading: Sales manager questions
qs: What do you look for when hiring a salesperson, and how do you test for it in the interview?
How you hire reps on evidence rather than on charm.
A mock call or role play, specific proof of past results, and a test of coachability: give feedback and see if they adjust.

I ask for numbers: quota, attainment, deal size, and how they found their deals. Then we do a short mock discovery call. Halfway through I give one piece of feedback and run it again. If they use it, I can coach them. A smooth talker who ignores the feedback is a risk.
Walk me through how you coach a rep after listening to one of their recorded calls.
Your coaching method, as opposed to just giving opinions.
The rep reviews the call first, the manager picks one or two behaviors, and they practise the change before the next call.

I ask the rep to listen first and tell me what went well and what they would change. Then I pick one thing, say, they pitched before asking about the buyer's problem. We role-play that part twice, and I listen to their next call to see if it stuck. One fix at a time works better than ten notes.
How do you run a weekly deal review with your team?
Whether you inspect deals or just collect status updates.
The same questions on every deal: buyer, pain, decision process, next step with a date. Deals without those facts get flagged.

Each rep brings their top deals. For each one I ask: who signs, what problem we solve for them, how they decide, and what the next step is with a date on the calendar. If the answer is "they will get back to me", the deal goes back to an earlier stage. It takes 45 minutes and it stops surprises.
How much pipeline do you need going into a quarter, and how do you work out that number?
Whether you understand pipeline coverage beyond a rule of thumb.
Coverage is derived from the team's own win rate and slippage, not a fixed 3x copied from a blog.

I start from our history. If we win about a quarter of qualified pipeline by value, I need about four times the quota in pipeline, plus a bit for deals that slip. I check it by stage too: early-stage pipeline converts less, so a big number made of first meetings is not the same as real coverage.
How do you build a revenue forecast you are willing to stand behind?
Your forecasting method and its discipline.
A bottom-up call by deal with clear category rules, checked against history and a top-down view, adjusted for each rep's track record.

I put each deal in commit, best case or pipeline using written rules: commit means the buyer confirmed the timeline and the signer. I add it up, then compare with what our weighted pipeline and past quarters suggest. I also know which reps are optimistic and which sandbag. If the numbers disagree, I dig in before I submit.
You have six reps and one region to split. How do you draw the territories?
How you plan territories so they are fair and workable.
Balance by revenue potential and workload, not just account count or map size, while keeping existing customer relationships where possible.

I score accounts by potential: company size, industry fit, and what we already sell them. Then I build six groups of about equal potential and check travel time and current relationships. I do not move a rep off an account they are about to close. I share the logic with the team so nobody thinks the split was personal.
How do you set a quota for a new rep who starts in the middle of the year?
Whether you plan for ramp time instead of setting new people up to fail.
A ramped quota based on how long new reps really take to reach full productivity, prorated for the months left.

I look at how long our past hires took to close at full pace, say five or six months. The new rep gets a low target the first months that rises step by step, and the annual number is prorated. I also give activity goals early, like meetings booked, because results lag. My own team forecast counts them as ramping, not full.
Your best rep asks for a 30% discount to close a deal before quarter end. How do you decide?
Your judgement on discounting and its long-term cost.
Find out why the buyer needs it, trade the discount for something of value, and think of the precedent for this customer and the team.

First I ask what the buyer actually said. Often the issue is budget timing, not price. If we discount, I want something back: a longer contract, payment up front, or a reference. I keep it within what I can approve and explain it. If every quarter ends with big discounts, buyers learn to wait, and that hurts every future deal.
A deal in a rep's commit has slipped for the third quarter in a row. What do you do?
How you handle a stuck deal and protect the forecast.
Take it out of commit, requalify it with the rep, and test whether the buyer is real, possibly by joining a call.

I take it out of commit now; it has not earned its place. Then I sit with the rep and go through what changed each time. If nobody can name the signer or a reason to buy this quarter, it goes back to an early stage. I may join a call with the buyer myself. Sometimes the right move is to stop spending time on it.
Two of your reps claim the same account and the commission on a new deal. How do you settle it?
How you handle conflict between reps fairly and fast.
Decide quickly from the written rules of engagement and CRM records, explain the decision, and fix the rule if it was unclear.

I check the territory rules and the account history: who owned it, who sourced the opportunity, what was logged and when. I decide within a day and tell both reps the reason face to face. If the rule was vague, I may split this one and rewrite the rule for everyone. A slow decision costs more trust than either answer.
What is the difference between a commit deal and a best-case deal in your forecast?
Whether you use forecast categories with clear rules instead of gut feel.
Clear entry rules for each category, tied to buyer actions, and the rep accountable when a commit deal slips.

A commit deal is one I would bet my own number on: the buyer has confirmed the budget, the signer, and the date, and the paperwork is moving. Best case means we can win it this quarter, but one thing is still open, like legal review or a final approval. I hold reps to the rule, so a commit deal that slips is a conversation, not a shrug.
How can you tell whether a rep is sandbagging?
How you spot reps who hide deals to look safe or to push revenue into a later period.
Looks at patterns over several quarters and at deal evidence, then fixes it with clear rules rather than blame.
