I look for a pattern: a rep who forecasts low every quarter and then lands well above it, or deals that appear late in the CRM already near signature. I ask what the buyer has done so far. If it keeps happening, I explain that a forecast that is too low hurts hiring and planning as much as one that is too high, and I check their calls against the CRM each week.
Next year your team's target goes up by 40%. How do you work out how many reps you need to hire?
Your capacity planning: ramp time, real attainment and attrition, not just quota divided by heads.
Uses actual productivity per rep, adjusts for ramp and turnover, and times hiring so new reps produce in the year.

I start from what a ramped rep actually closes, not the quota. Say our reps average about $900K on a $1.1M quota. New hires take around six months to ramp, so a rep hired in March gives maybe half of that this year. I add the one or two reps we usually lose each year, then hire early and keep some buffer so I am not one resignation away from missing.
Our team's win rate fell from 25% to 18% over two quarters. How would you find out why?
How you diagnose a drop with data before you jump to a fix.
Breaks the number down by stage, rep, segment, source and competitor, then confirms with lost-deal calls.

First I check that the definition did not change, such as a rule for when a deal gets created. Then I split losses by stage, rep, deal size, lead source and competitor. If most losses happen late against one competitor, that is a pricing or product story. If they happen early, it is qualification. I also call five lost buyers myself, because CRM loss reasons are often vague.
The company launches a new product and wants your reps to sell it. How do you use the comp plan to make that happen?
Whether you understand how commission design changes what reps actually do.
Simple plan, a meaningful but limited incentive, a time limit, and enablement so reps can actually sell the product.

I keep the plan simple, because a plan nobody can calculate changes nothing. I might add a bonus or a higher rate for the new product for two quarters, sized so it matters without pulling reps off the core number. Money alone will not do it, so I pair it with training and a few early wins we share with the team. Then I watch whether reps are pushing it into deals where it does not fit.
You find out a rep promised a customer a feature that is not on the roadmap, and the deal just closed. What do you do?
How you protect the customer relationship and the company when a rep oversells.
Tells the customer the truth fast, works with product and the account team on a remedy, and coaches the rep.

I get the facts from the rep, then talk to product about what is realistic. Then the rep and I call the customer together, before they find out on their own, and say plainly what we can and cannot deliver, with any workaround or remedy we can offer. With the rep, I am clear that a deal won on a false promise usually becomes churn, and I review their next few proposals.
Your top rep, who carries 40% of the team's number, resigns two weeks before quarter end. What do you do?
How you keep deals and accounts safe during a sudden departure.
Moves fast on open deals and customer contact, follows company policy on the exit, and resets the forecast honestly.

I ask for a full handover the same day: every open deal, its status and the main contacts. I follow HR policy on access and on how long they stay. I personally call the buyers in the large deals to introduce myself and the new owner. Then I tell my manager which deals are at risk and adjust the forecast now, not on the last day of the quarter.
Your VP asks you to raise your forecast by 10% before next week's board meeting. What do you say?
Whether you keep your forecast honest under pressure from above.
Does not inflate the number, but offers a clear upside case with the deals and conditions behind it.

I would say my committed number stays where it is, because a forecast changed for a meeting stops meaning anything. Then I offer the upside: these three deals, worth this much, could close if specific things happen, and here is what we are doing to make them happen. That gives the VP a range to present with real reasons behind it.
A rep wants a customer to sign this quarter and offers a side letter that lets them cancel later. How do you handle it?
Whether you know why undisclosed side agreements are a serious risk to booking revenue correctly.
Stops it, explains that every term must go through the contract and finance, and treats a repeat as a conduct issue.

I stop it. Any term that changes a deal, like a right to cancel, has to be in the contract and seen by finance, because it can change how and when revenue is recorded. A hidden side letter can make our reported numbers wrong. I tell the rep to sell the deal on its real terms, and if the customer needs an out clause, it goes through legal openly. If it happens again, I involve HR.
You take over a team that has missed its forecast four quarters in a row. Walk me through your first 90 days.
How you diagnose and rebuild a team's forecast accuracy and results in a structured way.
Learns before changing, fixes pipeline truth and qualification first, sets clear rules, and makes people decisions on evidence.

In the first month I listen: one-on-ones with every rep, ride-alongs on calls, and a review of every deal over a set size. Usually the pipeline is too optimistic, so in month two I clean it, agree on stage rules and set a weekly forecast call. By month three I make people decisions based on what I have seen, and I give my manager a number I can defend, even if it is lower.

sales-operations.heading: Sales and revenue operations questions
qs: What forecast categories do you use, and what does each one mean?
Whether you know the basic language of a sales forecast and why it must be defined.
Clear categories like commit, best case and pipeline, each with written entry rules that every rep applies the same way.

I use pipeline, best case, commit and closed. Commit means the rep would bet on it this period: a confirmed buyer, agreed terms and a signing date. Best case is likely but has a gap, like legal not started. Pipeline is everything else open. The labels only work if everyone uses the same definitions, so I write them down with clear exit criteria.
What is pipeline coverage, and how do you decide how much is enough?
Whether you can calculate coverage and tie the target ratio to real win rates.
Open pipeline divided by the remaining target, with the needed ratio derived from the team's own win rate, not a borrowed rule of thumb.

Coverage is open pipeline closing in the period divided by what is left of the target. The ratio we need comes from our own history: if we win about one in three qualified dollars, we need roughly three times the gap. I also look at it by stage, because coverage made of early-stage deals dated for next week is not real coverage.
Explain how accelerators and decelerators work in a commission plan.
Your grasp of commission mechanics and the behavior they drive.
Accurate definitions plus the reason behind them: reward overperformance, pay less for weak results, and avoid caps that make reps hold deals.

An accelerator raises the rate once a rep passes quota, say from 10% to 15% on bookings above 100%. A decelerator pays a lower rate below a threshold, so a rep at 40% earns less per dollar than one at 90%. I avoid hard caps where I can, because a cap tells top reps to push deals into the next period.
How would you design territories for a team of twelve reps?
How you balance opportunity and workload when splitting a market.
Territories balanced on potential and workload, built from account data, tested against history, with input from sales leaders before launch.

I start with account data: industry, company size and current spend, to score the potential of each account. Then I group accounts so each rep has similar potential and a workload one person can cover, not just the same number of names. I test the split against last year's bookings and review it with the managers before we announce it.
Reps keep leaving old close dates and wrong stages in the CRM. How do you fix it?
How you improve data quality without just nagging people.
A mix of system rules, clear stage definitions, manager follow-up and making the cost of bad data visible to reps.

First I make the stage rules clear: what must be true to enter each stage. Then I add checks, like flagging any deal with a close date in the past. I send managers a weekly list of stale deals to review in one-on-ones. Last, I show reps that the forecast and their territory reviews use this data, so clean data helps them.
A rep says their commission statement is wrong and they are upset. What do you do?
How you handle a pay dispute fairly and keep trust in the plan.
Listen, check the deal against the written plan and crediting rules, explain the result in writing, and fix real errors fast.

I thank them for flagging it and ask which deals they think are off. I check each one against the signed plan and our crediting rules: booking date, split, product type. If we made a mistake, I correct it on the next payroll and tell them when. If the statement is right, I walk them through the math in writing so they can see it.
How do you set quotas for next year?
Your method for quotas that are both ambitious and reachable.
Top-down company target checked against a bottom-up capacity model with ramp time, attrition and territory potential.

I start with the company bookings target, then build a capacity model from the bottom: number of reps, their ramp time if new, expected turnover and the potential in each territory. If the two numbers do not meet, I show leaders the gap before quotas go out. A plan where most reps miss quota usually means the quotas were wrong.
We missed last quarter's forecast by 20%. How would you find out why?
How you diagnose forecast error instead of blaming one cause.
Trace what was in commit at each point, where deals slipped or were lost, and whether the miss was judgement, data, or process.

I would take snapshots of the forecast from each week and compare them with what closed. For each commit deal that missed, I check: did it slip, shrink or get lost, and why? Then I look for patterns by rep, segment and stage. Often it is a few big deals called too early, which tells us to tighten what counts as commit.
Your top rep wants to keep a large account that moves to another territory in a realignment. How do you handle it?
Your judgement when fairness, the plan and a key person's pay collide.
Hold to the design rule, but offer a fair transition such as a short split credit, decided with leadership and applied the same way to everyone.

I would not make a one-off exception, because others would ask too. But I understand the loss. I would propose a rule for all reps: if a deal is already far along, the original rep keeps credit or shares it for that deal only. I take that to the sales leader, agree it, and then explain it to the rep before the change is announced.
The new commission plan is causing heavy discounting at quarter end. What would you change?
Whether you can trace a behavior back to the plan design and fix it without new side effects.
Confirm with data, then tie pay to what the company values, like discount level or margin, and check the fix will not create a new problem.

I would first confirm it: compare discount rates by week and by rep before and after the plan. If pay is based only on bookings, discounting is the easy path. I might pay a lower rate on deals above a set discount level and require approval for deep discounts. I would model past deals under the new rules before changing anything.
How do you calculate win rate, and what choices change the number?
Whether you define a core metric precisely before you report it.
Names the denominator, count versus dollar value, the time window and the stage where deals start counting.

I divide closed-won by all closed deals, won plus lost, for opportunities that passed qualification. By count it shows how often we win. By dollars, a few big deals can swing it. I fix the window by close date and print the definition on the dashboard, so nobody compares two versions of the same number.
What is the difference between bookings, billings, revenue and ARR?
Your grasp of the numbers that sales and finance each care about.
Bookings are signed value, billings are what is invoiced, revenue is what is earned under accounting rules, and ARR is the yearly value of recurring contracts.

Say a customer signs three years at $120,000 a year, billed yearly. Bookings could be $120,000 or $360,000 depending on our policy, so I always state which. Billings are $120,000 when we invoice. Revenue is recognized as we deliver, about $10,000 a month. ARR is $120,000 and leaves out one-time services fees.
How do you calculate net revenue retention, and how is it different from gross retention?
Whether you can compute a key recurring-revenue metric correctly.
Starts from a fixed customer group a year ago, adds expansion, subtracts contraction and churn, and excludes new customers. Gross retention ignores expansion.

I take recurring revenue from the customers we had twelve months ago, add their upsells, subtract downgrades and churn, and divide by the starting figure. New customers stay out. If we start at $1 million, gain $150,000 and lose $80,000, NRR is 107%. Gross retention leaves out the gains, so it can never go above 100%.
Walk me through how you decide how many reps to hire to hit next year's number.
How you turn a revenue target into a realistic hiring plan.
Uses actual productivity rather than quota, and accounts for ramp time, attrition and hiring lead time.

I start with the target minus what current reps and other channels will bring. Then I use real output, not quota: if ramped reps average 80% of an $800,000 quota, each brings about $640,000. New hires produce less while they ramp, often six months or more, and some reps will leave. So I hire earlier than the first math suggests and recheck every quarter.
We are changing our opportunity stages. How do you keep historical reporting usable?
How you manage a process change without breaking trend data.
Maps old stages to new ones, keeps the old values, snapshots the pipeline and flags the break in comparisons.

Before the switch I map each old stage to a new one and note where the fit is loose. I keep the old stage in its own field and snapshot the pipeline the day before. For a couple of quarters I flag conversion rates and cycle times as a break in the series. Then I train reps on the exit criteria for each stage, not just the new names.
A deal involved a rep, a solutions engineer and a partner. How do you handle credit?
Your judgement on crediting rules when several people touch a deal.
Separates quota credit from payout, allows planned double credit for overlay roles and settles disputes with rules written in advance.

The rep gets full credit. The solutions engineer is an overlay role, so they often get credit too, on their own quota. That is fine if finance has budgeted the double payout. For the partner I follow rules set before the deal, like who registered it first. Those rules live in the plan document, not in emails written after the deal closes.
How does the revenue accounting standard affect the way commissions are recorded?
Whether you understand where commission plans touch accounting.
Under ASC 606 and ASC 340-40, incremental commissions are capitalized and expensed over the benefit period, with an option to expense at once if that is a year or less.

Commissions paid only because a contract was signed are a cost of getting it. Under ASC 340-40, part of the ASC 606 change, they are recorded as an asset and expensed over the period the contract benefits, which can include expected renewals. If that period is a year or less, a company may expense them at once. I keep payouts tied to each deal so finance can do this.
A rep was paid commission on a deal that canceled three months later. How should clawbacks work?
How you design plan rules that are fair and hold up.
Written terms on what triggers a clawback and for how long, applied the same way to everyone, with legal or HR checking state wage rules.

The plan should say in advance what triggers a clawback, like cancellation or nonpayment within a set window, and how it is recovered, usually against future commissions. Some states, California among them, require commission plans in writing with a signed copy given to the rep, and wage deductions have limits, so legal reviews it. Then we apply it the same way to every rep.
Your CRO asks you to raise the forecast going to the board because the team will find the deals. What do you do?
Your integrity when the data and leadership disagree.
Keeps the forecast call honest, shows which deals the higher number needs, and offers any extra as clearly labeled upside.

I would not change the call itself. I would show the CRO the commit and best case side by side, the deals that would have to close for the higher number, and how deals like them have converted before. If they still want to show more, it goes in as a labeled upside. A board that gets surprised once starts doubting every number after.
You find a calculation error that overpaid twenty reps for two quarters. What do you do?
How you own a costly mistake and fix it properly.
Fixes the error, sizes it per rep, tells leadership and finance fast, and lets HR and legal decide on recovery before reps are told.

First I fix the formula so the next run is right and work out the amount per rep. I tell my manager and finance that day. HR and legal decide whether and how to recover it, since wage rules vary by state. Each rep hears it from their manager with their own numbers, never as a surprise deduction. Then I add a check that would have caught it.

sales-representative.heading: Sales representative questions
qs: What is the difference between a feature and a benefit? Give me an example from something you sold.
Whether you sell outcomes rather than reading out a spec sheet.
A clear split: the feature is what the product has, the benefit is what it changes for this buyer, tied to a real example.

A feature is what the product has; a benefit is what it does for the buyer. When I sold scheduling software, automatic text reminders were the feature. The benefit for a dental office was fewer no-shows, so fewer empty chairs and more billed hours. I lead with the benefit and use the feature as the proof.
How do you ask for the close? Tell me the words you actually use.
Whether you ask for the business directly instead of waiting for the buyer to offer.
A plain, direct ask after confirming value, then silence, and a clear next step whatever the answer.

First I check we agree: 'You said the main goal is cutting setup time, and the trial showed that. Is there anything we haven't covered?' If not, I ask: 'Shall we get the order in so you start on the first of the month?' Then I stop talking. If they hesitate, I ask what is holding them back.
On a cold call, the receptionist asks what this is about. How do you get through to the decision maker?
How you treat gatekeepers and reach the right person without tricks.
Respect and honesty: a short, clear reason, asking for help, and using the gatekeeper as a source of information.

I tell the truth in one sentence: 'I work with clinics on billing errors and wanted to see if Dr. Lee is the right person for that.' I ask for help, not permission, and get the right name and the best time to call. I never pretend to be returning a call. Gatekeepers remember, and they often have a say in the decision.
A prospect says, 'Just send me some information.' What do you do?
Whether you can tell a brush-off from real interest and keep the conversation going.
Agree, then ask a question that narrows what to send, and book the follow-up before hanging up.

I say yes, then ask: 'So I send something useful and not a stack of brochures, what matters most to you right now, cost or speed?' The answer tells me if there is interest. If there is, I send one page on that point and set a 15-minute call for later that week. If they won't answer anything, it was a polite no, and I note it and move on.
A buyer tells you, 'We're happy with our current supplier.' How do you respond?
How you handle the status quo, the most common objection in sales.
No knocking the competitor; curiosity about what could be better, and a low-risk way in such as a second source or a small trial.

I take it at face value: 'Good, that's hard to find. What do you like most about them?' Then: 'If you could change one thing, what would it be?' There is usually something, like lead times. I don't attack the competitor. I offer to be the backup on one product line, so they can compare us at low risk.
A prospect asks if your product does something it doesn't. What do you say?
Your honesty when the truth may cost you the deal.
A straight no, then how much the need matters, a workaround if a real one exists, and no roadmap promises you can't keep.

I say no, plainly. Then I ask how they would use it and how often, because sometimes it is a must-have and sometimes a nice-to-have. If there is a real workaround, I show it. I don't hint that it is coming soon unless the product team has committed to it. Overselling wins a deal and loses the account at renewal.
The demo went great, then the prospect stopped answering. What do you do?
How you follow up on a stalled deal without pestering or giving up.
A few spaced touches that add value, a different channel or contact, and a polite closing message that often gets a reply.

I look back at what we agreed as the next step; often there wasn't a firm one, which is on me. Then I send something useful, like a short case study tied to their goal, and try a call. After two or three tries over two weeks I send a short note: 'Should I close your file for now?' That gets a reply more often than anything.
Your contact loves the product but can't sign. How do you get the deal through?
Whether you understand that deals are bought by a group, not by one fan.
Mapping who decides and who can block, helping the champion sell inside, and reaching the budget holder with them, not around them.

I ask my contact: 'Who else has to say yes, and what will each of them worry about?' Finance cares about cost, IT about security. I give my champion a one-page business case in their own numbers and offer to join the meeting with the budget holder. I don't go over their head; that loses me the person who wants us.
You can discount up to 10%. The buyer wants 15% to sign today. What do you do?
How you negotiate within your authority and trade concessions instead of giving them away.
No promise beyond your authority; ask for something in return, like volume, a longer term or prepayment, and take that trade to your manager.

I don't say yes to 15%, and I don't jump straight to 10 either. I ask what the extra 5% is about. Then I trade: 'If you sign for two years, or prepay the year, I can take that to my manager.' Every discount gets something back. If my manager says no, I offer what I can and explain why, honestly.
You promised a delivery date, then learn operations can't meet it. What do you do?
How you own a mistake with a customer and fix it with your own team.
Tell the customer early, with the new date and options, work with operations rather than blame them, and change how you promise dates.

I call the customer the same day, before they find out on their own. I say I gave a date without checking, give the real date, and offer what I can: a partial shipment or faster freight if operations agrees. I don't blame the warehouse. Afterward I confirm stock and lead times with operations before I quote any date.
A prospect asks for the price in the first two minutes of the call. How do you handle it?
Whether you can respect a direct question without losing the chance to learn what the buyer needs.
You answer honestly with a range or starting point, then earn the right to ask questions. You do not dodge or play games.

I give a straight answer: "Most customers your size land between 400 and 900 dollars a month." Then I say the exact number depends on a few things and ask two or three quick questions. People relax once they hear a real number, and the questions feel fair instead of evasive.
What rules do you follow before you call consumers at home or on their cell phones?
Your knowledge of the basic US telemarketing rules for calling consumers.
Check the National Do Not Call Registry and the company list, call only between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. local time, honor opt-outs, no robocalls without written consent.

I make sure the list is checked against the National Do Not Call Registry and our own internal list. I call only between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. in the person's time zone. If someone says not to call again, I log it right away. I never use recorded messages or autodialed calls to consumers without their prior written consent, and I ask compliance when I'm unsure.
Your average deal is $5,000, you close 20% of qualified opportunities, and your quota is $100,000 a quarter. How much pipeline do you need?
Whether you can turn a quota into daily activity with simple pipeline math.
$500,000 in qualified pipeline, about 100 opportunities, then working back to how many meetings and calls that takes.

I need 20 deals to hit $100,000. At a 20% close rate that means about 100 qualified opportunities, or $500,000 in pipeline, five times quota. Then I work backward: if one in four first meetings becomes qualified, I need around 400 meetings across the quarter, so I check my call-to-meeting rate and set weekly targets from that.
Late in a deal, a competitor comes in 25% cheaper. What do you do?
How you defend value against a lower price without panicking or bashing the competitor.
You find out what is really being compared, go back to the buyer's own goals and costs, and only then decide whether to move on price.

First I ask what exactly they quoted, because lower prices often leave out setup, support or features the buyer said they needed. Then I go back to the problem we agreed on and the cost of getting it wrong. I don't run the competitor down. If the gap is real and the buyer still values us, I look at terms, not just price.
How do you decide whether a deal goes into your forecast as committed?
Your honesty and rigor in forecasting.
Commit only with buyer-confirmed evidence: decision maker engaged, budget approved, close date tied to a buyer event, paperwork steps known.

A deal goes into commit only when the buyer has confirmed it, not when I feel good about it. I need the person who signs to be involved, budget approved, a date the buyer gave me for a reason of their own, and the legal and purchasing steps mapped. If one of those is missing, it stays in best case, even if my manager wants a bigger number.
You notice that a quote you sent last week is priced too low by mistake. The customer is ready to sign. What do you do?
How you handle your own mistake when fixing it may cost you the deal.
You tell your manager first, then the customer, quickly and plainly, with a fair way forward. You do not let them sign a wrong quote.

I'd tell my manager the same day and agree what we can offer. Then I'd call the customer before they sign, not email: "I made an error on the quote, and I want to fix it before you sign." I'd explain the correct price and what we can do to be fair. Losing trust over a hidden error would cost more than this one deal.
You just closed a deal, and another rep says the account was theirs. How do you handle it?
How you handle a territory or credit dispute with a colleague.
You check the CRM record and the rules of engagement, talk to the rep directly, and let the manager decide without a fight.

I'd look at the CRM history and our territory rules first, so I'm talking about facts. Then I'd speak to the rep directly and calmly, and if we still disagree, we take it to our manager together. I'd rather lose a split commission than the trust of someone I work with every day. The customer never hears about it.
A buyer hints that a personal gift or favor would help get the contract signed. What do you do?
Your ethics when a deal depends on something improper.
A clear no, kept polite, then you report it to your manager or compliance and follow company policy, even if the deal is lost.

I'd say no, politely and clearly: "I can't do anything like that, but I can make sure you get the best terms we offer." Then I'd tell my manager and follow our compliance policy. A deal built on a personal payment can hurt both companies and my own career. If we lose the deal over it, that's the right loss.
Your biggest deal of the quarter slips to next quarter two days before the close date. Walk me through what you do.
How you recover a slipped deal and manage the impact on your number.
Find the real reason fast, tell your manager the same day, build a new dated plan with the buyer, and cover the gap with other deals.

First I call my contact and ask what changed and who is involved now. I tell my manager the same day, not at the end of the quarter, so the forecast is honest. Then I agree a written plan with the buyer: each step, owner and date to signature. In parallel I push my next two best deals to help close the gap.

salesforce.heading: Salesforce specialist questions
qs: What is the difference between a profile, a role and a permission set?
Whether you know how Salesforce decides what a user can do and what they can see.
Profiles and permission sets grant what a user can do. Roles shape which records a user sees through the role hierarchy.

A profile is the base every user has: which objects, fields and apps they can use. A permission set adds rights on top for some users, without making a new profile. A role sits in the role hierarchy and controls record visibility: a manager can see records owned by people below them. I keep profiles lean and grant extra access with permission sets.
When would you use a master-detail relationship instead of a lookup?
Your grasp of the data model and what each relationship type changes.
Master-detail ties the child to the parent: the parent is required, deletes cascade, sharing is inherited and roll-up summaries work. A lookup is looser.

I use master-detail when the child cannot exist alone, like invoice lines on an invoice. The child then takes its sharing from the parent, is deleted with it, and I can build roll-up summary fields such as a total on the parent. If the child should survive without a parent or needs its own owner, I use a lookup.
Walk me through a validation rule that stops reps from marking an opportunity Closed Lost without a loss reason.
Whether you can write formula logic and know the rule blocks the save when it is true.
A formula that returns true for the bad case, a clear error message on the right field, and a test before release.

Say Loss Reason is a text field. The formula is AND(ISPICKVAL(StageName, "Closed Lost"), ISBLANK(Loss_Reason__c)). When it is true, the save is blocked. I show the error on the Loss Reason field with a message that says what to fill in, then test it in a sandbox as a rep before it goes live.
A team hands you a spreadsheet of 200,000 contacts to load. Which tool do you use and how do you prepare?
Whether you can load data cleanly without creating duplicates or orphan records.
Picks Data Loader for a large load, cleans and deduplicates first, links records to parents by ID, and tests a small batch.

At that size I use Data Loader; the Import Wizard suits smaller loads of standard objects. First I clean the file: trim spaces, fix formats and check it against existing contacts so I do not create duplicates. I link each contact to its account by ID or an external ID, load 50 rows as a test, check them, then run the rest and keep the success and error files.
A sales rep says she cannot see an account her colleague can see. How do you find out why?
How you troubleshoot record access step by step.
Checks object permissions first, then org-wide defaults, ownership, role hierarchy and sharing rules, using the record's sharing tools.

First I check that her profile or permission sets give read access to accounts. If they do, the issue is record sharing. I look at the org-wide default for accounts, the record owner, and where both reps sit in the role hierarchy. The Sharing Hierarchy button on the record shows who has access and why. If a sharing rule should cover her and does not, I fix the rule, not just this one record.
How do you choose between a validation rule, a flow and Apex code for a new requirement?
Whether you pick the simplest tool that does the job well.
Clicks before code: validation rules to block bad data, Flow for most automation, Apex only for logic or volume that Flow handles badly.

If the need is to stop bad data, a validation rule is enough. If records must be created or updated, I build a record-triggered flow; Salesforce is ending support for workflow rules and Process Builder in favor of Flow. I use Apex when the logic is complex or must run over large volumes efficiently, and Apex needs test classes before it can be deployed.
Walk me through how you move a change from a sandbox to production.
Whether you build outside production and deploy with a plan.
Build and test in a sandbox, deploy with change sets or the CLI, validate first, meet Apex test coverage, and tell users.

I build in a developer sandbox, then test as real users in a sandbox with realistic data. I package the components in a change set or deploy with the Salesforce CLI. I run a validation-only deploy first, which also runs the Apex tests; production needs at least 75% code coverage. I deploy at a quiet hour and tell users what changed.
The sales VP asks you to make fifteen new fields required on the opportunity. How do you respond?
Your judgement in balancing a request against user adoption and data quality.
Asks what each field is for, requires fields only when they matter, often by stage, and keeps the page short so reps keep using it.

I ask what decision each field feeds. Often only a few matter, and only at certain stages. I would require those with validation rules by stage, not on every save, and show the rest only when they matter using conditional visibility on the record page. Fifteen required fields at creation means reps type junk to get past them, and the VP's reports get worse.
A flow that loops over related records works in testing but fails with a limit error when 500 records are loaded at once. What is likely wrong?
Whether you understand governor limits and bulk-safe design.
Names queries or updates inside a loop hitting per-transaction limits, and fixes it with one query before the loop and one update after.

Most likely there is a Get Records or Update Records element inside the loop. Salesforce caps how many queries and updates one transaction can run, and a bulk load puts many records into one transaction. I query once before the loop, change values in a collection inside it, and save with one Update Records at the end. Then I test with a few hundred records in a sandbox.
You ran a mass update that wrote the wrong values into a field on 3,000 accounts. What do you do?
How you handle your own mistake on live data.
Stops, tells people quickly, restores from a backup taken before the update, and checks what automation the update set off.

I stop any further loads and tell my manager and the account owners right away. Before every mass update I export the records with their IDs, so I restore the old values from that file with Data Loader. Then I check what the update triggered, like flows or emails to customers, and clean that up too. Afterwards I add a peer check before large updates.
Which sandbox type would you use for user acceptance testing with realistic data, and why?
Whether you know what each sandbox type copies and when each one fits.
Developer sandboxes copy metadata only. Partial Copy brings a sample of data through a template. Full copies all data and costs more, so it is saved for UAT and final checks.

Developer and Developer Pro sandboxes copy setup but no records, so they suit building. For UAT I want real-looking data, so I use a Partial Copy with a sandbox template that picks accounts, contacts and opportunities. If testers need the full volume, like a big reporting check, I use the Full sandbox and plan its refresh ahead with the team.
When do you build a before-save record-triggered flow instead of an after-save one?
Your grasp of how Flow runs and what each trigger timing can and cannot do.
Before-save updates fields on the triggering record quickly with no extra save. After-save is needed for related records, emails or actions.

If I only need to set fields on the record being saved, like filling a region from the billing state, I use a before-save flow. It runs before the record is written, so it is fast and costs no extra update. If I need to create a task, update the parent account or send an email, that has to be after-save.
Today every rep can see every opportunity. Management wants reps to see only their own, with managers seeing their team's. What do you change?
Whether you know how org-wide defaults, the role hierarchy and sharing rules work together.
Set the opportunity default to Private, rely on the role hierarchy for managers, open exceptions with sharing rules, and check View All permissions.

I set the organization-wide default for opportunities to Private. Managers then see their team's deals through the role hierarchy, which always grants access upward on standard objects. Sharing rules can only open access, so I add them for groups like finance. I also check that no profile or permission set grants View All or View All Data by mistake.
Sales ops wants a list of accounts that have had no new opportunity in the last 12 months. How do you build it?
Your reporting skills beyond a basic filter.
An accounts report with a cross filter for accounts without opportunities, plus a subfilter on the opportunity's created date.

I start an Accounts report and add a cross filter: Accounts without Opportunities. Inside that cross filter I add a subfilter, Created Date equals last 12 months. That returns accounts with no opportunity created in that window. I add owner and last activity as columns and save it in a shared folder so ops can schedule it.
A dashboard shared with all reps shows deal amounts from other regions they are not supposed to see. What happened?
Whether you understand that a dashboard shows data as its running user sees it.
The dashboard runs as a user with wide access. Fix it with a dynamic dashboard or a running user whose access matches the audience.

A dashboard shows data as its running user sees it, not as the viewer does. Someone likely set a VP or an admin as running user, so every rep sees that person's data. I would switch it to run as the logged-in user, a dynamic dashboard, or make region versions with a fitting running user, then check the folder sharing.
Reps keep creating duplicate accounts and contacts. How do you set up Salesforce to stop that, and what about the duplicates already there?
How you use duplicate management and handle the cleanup that rules alone do not cover.
Matching rules define a duplicate; duplicate rules alert or block on create and edit. Existing duplicates need a separate cleanup and merge.

I start with matching rules that define a match, such as same email for contacts, and fuzzy name plus city for accounts. Then duplicate rules decide what happens: I usually alert first and report on it, then block once the rule proves accurate. Rules only check new saves, so I run reports on existing duplicates and merge them with the owners' agreement.
A senior rep is leaving on Friday. Walk me through what you do with her user record and her data.
How you offboard a user without losing data, access or automation.
Freeze to block login right away, reassign records and open work, check automation and defaults that name her, then deactivate. Users cannot be deleted.

On her last day I freeze the user so she cannot log in at once. Then I transfer her accounts and open opportunities to the new owner her manager names, with the Mass Transfer tool or Data Loader. I check queues, flows, email alerts and default owner settings that name her, then deactivate. Salesforce does not let you delete users, and deactivating frees the license.
Security asks you to make sure staff can only log in from the office network. Is adding the office IP to the trusted IP ranges enough?
Whether you know the difference between org trusted IP ranges and profile login IP ranges.
No. Org trusted IP ranges only skip the identity check. Profile login IP ranges are what deny logins from outside.

No. Trusted IP ranges in Network Access only mean users inside that range skip the identity verification challenge; outside, they are asked to verify but can still get in. To block logins from elsewhere I set login IP ranges on the profiles. I would test with one profile first and keep an admin profile without the restriction so we cannot lock ourselves out.
Two record-triggered flows on Opportunity both update the same field, and the result changes from save to save. How do you sort it out?
How you diagnose automation that collides on one object.
Find every automation on the object, check the order they run in, then set a trigger order or merge them so one owner controls the field.

I open Flow Trigger Explorer for Opportunity to see every record-triggered flow, its timing and trigger order. I also check for Apex triggers and older workflow rules. If two flows set the same field, I merge the logic into one flow or set an explicit trigger order so the final value is predictable. Then I write down which automation owns that field.
Our org has 40 profiles, many nearly the same. How would you move us to a cleaner access model?
Your judgement on a large access redesign done safely.
Few minimal profiles, access granted through permission sets and groups, built from real job needs, and rolled out in stages with testing.

I would export what each profile grants and group users by what they actually do. Then I build a few minimal profiles and move access into permission sets bundled into permission set groups per job, using muting permission sets for exceptions. I test each group in a sandbox with real users, move one team at a time, and only then retire the old profiles.

sap.heading: SAP consultant questions
qs: What is the difference between configuration and custom development in SAP?
Whether you know when the standard system is enough and when code is needed.
Configuration sets standard behavior through customizing. Code comes last and is kept out of standard objects so upgrades stay safe.

Configuration means setting up standard SAP through customizing in SPRO, like company codes or tolerance limits. Development means ABAP code, such as an enhancement or a custom report. I try configuration first, then a process change, and only then code. When I do write code, I use released extension points so an upgrade does not break it.
Walk me through the procure-to-pay process in SAP.
Your grasp of the core purchasing flow and where finance enters it.
The steps in order, the role of the GR/IR clearing account, and the three-way match between order, receipt and invoice.

A purchase requisition becomes a purchase order. When goods arrive, the warehouse posts a goods receipt in MIGO, which credits the GR/IR clearing account. Accounts payable posts the vendor invoice in MIRO, which debits GR/IR and credits the vendor. SAP checks that order, receipt and invoice match. Then the payment run in F110 pays the vendor.
How does a change move from development to production in an SAP landscape?
Whether you work within the transport system and change control.
Change built in development, recorded on a transport request, tested in QA, imported to production in order after sign-off.

I make the change in the development client and save it to a transport request. Customizing and code changes go in separate requests. Once released, it is imported into QA, where key users test it. After sign-off, Basis imports it to production in the agreed order. Production is locked against direct changes, so the transport is the only path and the record of what changed.
What changed for finance when companies moved from ECC to S/4HANA?
Your knowledge of the current SAP finance model.
The Universal Journal, cost elements as GL accounts, and business partners replacing separate customer and vendor masters.

The biggest change is the Universal Journal, table ACDOCA, which holds finance and controlling line items in one place, so FI and CO agree by design. Cost elements are now GL accounts. Customers and vendors are kept as business partners. Many old totals tables became views, so reports read line items directly and some reconciliation steps went away.
A user says they cannot post because the posting period is not open. What do you check?
How you troubleshoot a common month-end error.
Knowing finance and materials periods are separate, checking which one blocks, and not opening periods without finance approval.

First I read the exact message, because finance and materials periods are separate. Finance periods are kept by period variant in OB52; the materials period moves forward in MMPV. Then I check the posting date, since the user often picked the wrong month. If a period truly needs opening, the controller approves it, because it affects the close.
An invoice was posted but is blocked for payment. How do you find out why and get it released?
Whether you know invoice verification and fix the cause, not the symptom.
Reading the block reason, linking it to tolerances or a missing receipt, and releasing it properly instead of loosening tolerances.

I display the invoice in MIR4 to see the block reason. Often price or quantity differs from the order or receipt beyond the tolerance set in configuration. If the goods receipt has since been posted, MRBR can release it automatically. Otherwise the buyer confirms the price and AP releases it in MRBR. I would not widen tolerances just to clear one invoice.
The finance lead asks you to make a quick configuration change directly in production. What do you do?
Your judgement under pressure from the business.
A polite no with the reason, and a fast, controlled alternative such as an emergency change with approval.

I say no and explain why: a change made only in production is not in development or QA, so nobody tested it and the next transport can overwrite it. If it is urgent, I use the emergency change process: build it in development, test it fast in QA, and import it with approval. I give a realistic time, often the same day.
How do you run a fit-to-standard workshop?
How you steer the business toward standard processes in a new implementation.
Demo of the standard process on real data, each step rated fit or gap, and gaps questioned before anyone writes code.

Before the session I set up the standard process in a sandbox with their sample data. I demo it end to end and let key users try it. For each step we mark it as fits, fits with configuration, or gap. For each gap I ask what business result it protects, because often a report or a small process change solves it. I log every decision with an owner.
How do you plan the migration of master data and open items into a new S/4HANA system?
Your method for moving data safely and proving it arrived correctly.
Agreed scope, cleansing at the source, several mock loads, and finance reconciling totals before go-live.

First we agree what moves: usually master data, open items and balances, not years of closed documents. We clean data in the old system. Then we run at least two mock loads into a test system, and finance reconciles each one: record counts, totals by account, open payables and receivables. Cutover follows a timed plan with sign-off after each step.
You imported a transport to production and goods receipts started failing. What do you do?
How you handle your own mistake in a live system.
Telling people fast, knowing transports cannot simply be undone, a tested correcting transport, and checking the damaged postings.

I tell the support lead and the warehouse right away so users stop and report. A transport cannot simply be rolled back, so I use the transport log and version history to find what changed. I build a correcting transport in development, test it quickly in QA and import it. Then I check which receipts failed or posted wrongly and why our test missed it.
A company has two legal entities that buy from the same suppliers through one central buying team. How would you set up the organizational structure?
Whether you can map a real business onto SAP's organizational units.
Two company codes, one purchasing organization not tied to a single company code and assigned to the plants of both, with a reason for each choice.

Each legal entity gets its own company code, because that is where balance sheets and tax are reported. I would create one purchasing organization, leave it unassigned to any company code, and assign it to the plants of both. Buyers negotiate once, and each purchase order still posts to the right company code through its plant.
In S/4HANA, why can't you simply create a vendor with XK01 anymore, and what does that mean for a system conversion?
Your grasp of the Business Partner model in S/4HANA.
The business partner is the single entry point for suppliers and customers, linked to vendor records by customer/vendor integration, which must be done before converting.

In S/4HANA the business partner is the one place to create suppliers and customers; the old vendor transactions send you to transaction BP. Vendor data still exists underneath, linked by customer/vendor integration, or CVI. For a conversion, every vendor must become a business partner in ECC first, so I plan time to clean duplicates and align number ranges.
What is the difference between standard price and moving average price on a material, and when would you choose each?
Your understanding of how inventory is valued and where differences go.
Price control S values stock at a fixed price and sends differences to a price difference account; V lets the price follow receipts. The choice is tied to costing needs.

With standard price, price control S, stock is valued at a fixed price, and any gap between that price and the PO or invoice goes to a price difference account. With moving average, price control V, the price is recalculated with each receipt. I use standard for manufactured goods where controlling wants stable costs and variance reports, and moving average for many purchased goods.
A goods receipt for a new material posted to the wrong inventory G/L account. How do you trace the cause?
Whether you know how automatic account determination works for goods movements.
Valuation class in the material master, then transaction key BSX in OBYC; fix master data and correct past postings with finance.

The account comes from automatic account determination. I check the valuation class in the material's accounting view, then the BSX entry in OBYC, the key for inventory postings, for that chart of accounts. Usually the material got the wrong valuation class. Changing it is often blocked while stock exists, so I plan the correction with finance and fix the data for new materials.
Finance says the GR/IR clearing account balance keeps growing every month. How do you investigate it?
How you handle a common reconciliation problem between purchasing and accounts payable.
Open items aged and grouped by cause, root causes fixed with buyers, and only truly closed items cleared, for example with MR11, plus a regular review.

GR/IR holds goods received but not invoiced, and invoices not yet matched to receipts. I list open items by purchase order and age them. Old items are usually POs that will never be invoiced, quantity or price gaps, or receipts posted twice. I fix each cause with the buyers, clear the truly closed items with MR11 once they agree, and set up a monthly review.
A large purchase order went to the supplier without approval, even though you have a release strategy. What could cause that?
Whether you know how classification-based release strategies behave when nothing matches.
A PO that matches no release strategy needs no release. Checks the characteristics and values, finds the gap, and makes sure every case is covered.

In SAP, a purchase order that matches no release strategy needs no approval, so it goes straight through. I check the release class and its characteristics, usually net value, plant and document type. A common cause is a new plant or document type that was never added to the values. I fix the values, test edge cases, and check that every combination falls under a strategy.
Why would a company turn on document splitting, and what do you warn them about?
Your depth in S/4HANA general ledger design.
It gives full balance sheets by profit center or segment, zero balancing keeps each one balanced, and the decision belongs before go-live.

Document splitting copies characteristics such as profit center or segment onto every line, including payables and tax, so you can produce a balance sheet per segment. With zero balancing, SAP adds clearing lines so each segment balances. I warn them to decide before go-live, since adding it later is a migration project, and if the field is mandatory, bad master data stops postings.
How do you prove to finance that the migrated balances are right before they sign off on go-live?
How you make data migration verifiable rather than trusted on faith.
Agreed reconciliation reports, trial balance and subledgers compared with legacy, migration offset account at zero, every difference explained, written sign-off.

I agree the reconciliation reports with finance before the first mock load. After each load I compare the trial balance by account and company code with legacy, open items by vendor and customer, and stock quantity and value by plant. The migration offset account must net to zero. Every difference gets an owner and a reason, and finance signs a file, not a verbal OK.
A month after go-live, a third of purchase orders are created after the invoice arrives. What do you do?
How you handle a process problem after go-live, not just a system one.
Data first to find who and why, targeted training, a better tool for recurring spend, and a policy agreed with finance.

First I find out why. I pull POs dated after their invoice and group them by buyer, plant and material group. Often it is a few teams who were never trained, or spend like services or utilities that fits a normal PO badly. I retrain those teams, set up a framework order for recurring costs, and agree with the controller that AP sends back invoices with no PO.
A plant manager insists the standard goods receipt screen will not work for them and wants a custom one. How do you handle it?
Your judgement on custom development versus keeping a clean, upgradable system.
Understands the real problem first, tries standard options, prefers extensions over modifications, and makes the long-term cost visible to the decision makers.

I watch the receiving process on the floor before I argue. Often the issue is too many fields or slow entry, which a standard Fiori app or field defaults can solve. If there is a real gap, I prefer an extension through released interfaces over modifying SAP code, and I show the cost of retesting it at every upgrade so the business owner decides with the full picture.

scrum-master.heading: Scrum master and delivery manager questions
qs: What is the difference between the Definition of Done and acceptance criteria?
Whether you know the basic quality rules a Scrum team works by.
Done is one shared quality standard for every item. Acceptance criteria are specific to one story. A story needs both.

The Definition of Done applies to every backlog item, for example: code reviewed, tested, merged and documented. Acceptance criteria belong to one story and say what that feature must do, like 'a user can reset a password by email.' A story is finished only when it meets its own criteria and the Definition of Done.
Walk me through how you get a team ready for sprint planning.
How you prepare the meeting that shapes the whole sprint.
Refined top items, known capacity and a proposed Sprint Goal, so planning is about choices, not first reads.

In the week before, I make sure we have held refinement so the top items are small, clear and estimated. I collect capacity: holidays, on-call duty, training days. I ask the Product Owner to bring a proposed Sprint Goal. In planning, the developers decide how much they can take. I keep time and make sure we leave with a goal and a plan for the first days.
Your daily scrum has turned into each person reporting status to you. How do you fix it?
Whether you know who the daily scrum is for.
It belongs to the developers and is about progress toward the Sprint Goal. The scrum master steps back so they talk to each other.

First I stop being the center. I stand to the side, and some days I skip it on purpose. I ask the team to walk the board from the right, finishing work first, and to talk about the Sprint Goal, not their own tasks. Long problems go to a short follow-up after the 15 minutes, with only the people who are needed.
How do you run a retrospective that leads to real change, not just complaints?
How you turn reflection into actions the team actually takes.
Checks last time's actions, uses facts from the sprint, and ends with one or two small actions that each have an owner.

I open by reviewing the actions from last time: did we do them, and did they help? I bring a few facts, like carry-over or bugs found late, so we do not argue from memory. We pick one or two improvements small enough to finish in a sprint, each with an owner, and often add them to the Sprint Backlog. I change the format so it does not go stale.
Stories keep rolling over from sprint to sprint. How do you find out why?
How you diagnose a delivery problem instead of guessing.
Looks at the data: story size, work in progress, unplanned work, waits on others. Then tests one fix at a time.

I look at the last few sprints. Often stories are too big, so I check how many we split in refinement. I check how much was started at once: ten items in progress for five people means little gets finished. I measure unplanned work and waits on other teams. Then the team picks one change, like a work-in-progress limit, and we watch whether carry-over drops.
Mid-sprint, a director asks a developer directly to drop everything for an urgent request. What do you do?
Whether you protect the sprint while still respecting real business needs.
Routes the request to the Product Owner, who decides. Any change in scope is agreed openly, not slipped in quietly.

I thank the director and bring the request to the Product Owner the same day, since they own the backlog. If it truly cannot wait, the Product Owner and developers agree what comes out to make room, and we say so openly. If it makes the Sprint Goal pointless, only the Product Owner can cancel the sprint. What I avoid is a developer quietly doing both.
A blocker sits with another team that keeps putting it off. How do you get it removed?
How you remove blockers that sit outside your own team.
Talks to the other team first, makes the cost visible, escalates with facts if needed, and plans around the wait.

I go to their scrum master or lead and ask what is in their way; often they lack details or have their own deadline. I show the cost: three stories and a release date depend on it. If it still stalls, I bring both product owners together to set priority. Meanwhile we work on what does not depend on it, and we flag such dependencies earlier in refinement.
Your manager wants to compare velocity between teams to see who works harder. How do you respond?
Whether you understand what velocity can and cannot measure.
Explains that story points are relative to each team, so comparing them means little and invites inflation. Offers better measures.

I explain that each team sizes points against its own past work, so one team's 40 is not another team's 20. If points become a score, they inflate and stop helping anyone plan. I offer what the manager really wants to know: cycle time, how often we release, defects found after release and whether we meet Sprint Goals. Velocity stays a planning tool inside the team.
On the last day of the sprint, a story is almost done but its testing is not finished. The Product Owner wants it in the release. What happens?
Whether you hold the Definition of Done under pressure.
An item that is not Done cannot be released; it returns to the Product Backlog. You explain the risk and look for the cause.

In Scrum, an item that does not meet the Definition of Done is not released or shown as done; it goes back to the Product Backlog. I explain to the Product Owner that untested code is a risk our users would carry. Next sprint it is usually first in line. In the retro we ask why testing came last, and often the fix is to test as we build.
Your Product Owner is rarely available, and the team keeps guessing what to build. What do you do?
How you handle a gap in a role you do not own.
Raises it with the Product Owner, sets fixed time for questions and refinement, escalates if needed, and does not take over the role.

I talk to the Product Owner first and find out why; often they cover too many teams. We agree on fixed slots: refinement twice a week and a daily time for questions. I help them write clearer items and a Product Goal. If nothing changes, I raise it with whoever assigned the role. I do not start setting priorities myself, because that only hides the problem.
In Scrum, each artifact comes with a commitment. What are they, and why do they matter?
Whether you know the current Scrum framework beyond the meeting names.
Product Backlog to Product Goal, Sprint Backlog to Sprint Goal, Increment to Definition of Done, and what each gives the team.

The Product Backlog commits to the Product Goal, the long-term target for the product. The Sprint Backlog commits to the Sprint Goal, the one objective for the sprint. The Increment commits to the Definition of Done, the quality bar work must meet to count as done. Together they give focus and make progress something you can check.
On a cumulative flow diagram, the band for work in testing keeps getting wider. What does that tell you?
Whether you can read flow data and act on it.
A queue is building in testing; you look for the cause and limit work in progress instead of starting more.

Work is entering testing faster than it leaves, so a queue is forming there and cycle time will rise even if everyone looks busy. I would check whether testers are short, stories are too big or the test environment is down. Then I would get the team to cap work in progress so developers help finish testing before they start new items.
When would you suggest a team move from Scrum to Kanban?
Whether you choose a method to fit the work, not out of habit.
When most work is unplanned and cannot wait for the next sprint, with WIP limits and the habit of improving kept.

When most of the work arrives daily and cannot wait two weeks, like a support or platform team. Their sprint plans break every few days. Kanban with work-in-progress limits and a target such as most tickets closed within five days fits better. I would keep regular reviews and retrospectives so the team still improves.
Your team wants to switch from two-week to four-week sprints because big stories do not fit. How do you respond?
How you find the real problem behind a request.
Knows a month is the limit, but treats it as a story-size problem and tries splitting before changing length.

Four weeks is allowed, since Scrum caps a sprint at one month, but it hides the real issue: the stories are too big. Longer sprints mean slower feedback and more at risk each sprint. I would run a splitting session with the Product Owner, cutting stories into thin slices that each deliver something testable, and try that for two sprints first.
In estimation, the team always goes with whatever the senior developer says. How do you handle it?
How you protect honest team input without embarrassing anyone.
Names the anchoring problem, uses simultaneous estimates, draws out quiet people and speaks privately to the senior person.

That is anchoring. I would use planning poker so everyone shows a card at the same time, then ask the highest and lowest to explain, starting with the quieter person. I would also talk privately with the senior developer and ask them to speak last. Most are glad to help newer people think for themselves.
Leadership asks you for a firm date for a release that is 300 story points away. How do you answer?
How you forecast honestly from team data.
A range based on past velocity, stated assumptions, updated each sprint, and scope offered as the lever if a date is fixed.

I give a range, not one date. If the team's last eight sprints ran between 30 and 45 points, 300 points is about 7 to 10 sprints, before any new scope. I show that range, the assumptions behind it, and update it every sprint. If they need a fixed date, we talk about which scope can move.
You learn the team has been marking stories done without the required tests to keep velocity up. What do you do?
Whether you hold the quality line and fix the cause, not just the symptom.
Undone work does not count or ship; raise it openly without blame, return items to the backlog, and address the pressure behind it.

Those items are not done, so they cannot be released or counted. I would raise it with the team right away, without blame, and ask why. With the Product Owner, the items go back to the Product Backlog. Then I deal with the source, often a manager watching velocity, and show what hidden undone work will cost later.
Three Scrum teams work on one product and keep breaking each other's code at integration. What would you change?
Your knowledge of how Scrum works across several teams on one product.
One Product Backlog, one Product Owner, one shared Definition of Done, plus continuous integration and early dependency work.

Teams on one product should share one Product Backlog, one Product Owner and one Definition of Done, so I check that first. Then I push for integrating every day, not at sprint end, with automated tests every team must pass. A short cross-team refinement spots dependencies early, and one integrated Increment each sprint makes breakage visible fast.
A release you coordinated caused a production outage. How do you lead the follow-up?
How you turn a failure into lasting fixes without blame.
Restore service first, then a prompt blameless review with a timeline, a few owned fixes tracked to done, and open reporting.

Once service is back, I set a blameless review within a few days while memories are fresh. We build a timeline and ask how the process let the failure through, not who caused it. We pick a few fixes with owners, like a missing check in the deploy pipeline or a slow rollback, track them in the backlog, and I share the write-up with stakeholders.

search-engineer.heading: Search and recommendations engineer questions
qs: What is an inverted index, and why does search need one?
Whether you know the basic data structure behind text search.
A map from each term to the documents that contain it, so a query reads short lists instead of scanning every document.

It works like the index at the back of a book. For every term, it stores a postings list: the documents that contain it, often with counts and positions. A query for two words reads two lists and intersects them, instead of scanning millions of documents. The positions let me answer phrase queries too.
How does BM25 decide that one document matches a query better than another?
Your understanding of the classic lexical scoring function.
Term frequency with diminishing returns, rare terms weigh more, and length normalization so long documents do not win by size.

It adds up a score for each query term. A term counts more the more often it appears in the document, but with diminishing returns, so the tenth mention adds little. Terms that are rare across the collection weigh more than common ones. It also adjusts for document length, so a long page does not win just because it mentions everything.
Users search for “sneakers” and get no results, but you sell hundreds of running shoes. How do you fix it?
How you handle the gap between the words users type and the words in the catalog.
Starts from the query logs, uses synonyms, stemming or meaning-based retrieval, and checks the fix does not hurt precision.

First I pull the zero-result queries from the logs to see how big the gap is. For a known gap, a synonym rule linking sneakers, trainers and running shoes is quick. For the long tail, I would add vector retrieval that matches by meaning. Then I check precision, because broad synonyms can flood results with wrong items.
How do you measure whether a new ranking is better before it reaches users?
Your knowledge of offline ranking metrics.
Names a position-aware metric like NDCG or MRR on labeled queries, and knows an offline gain still needs an online test.

I build a test set of real queries with relevance labels, from human raters or from past clicks and purchases. Then I compute NDCG, which rewards putting the most relevant items near the top, and MRR when there is one right answer. I compare both rankings on the same set, read the queries that got worse, and only then run an A/B test.
Your click data says the first result is the best one almost every time. Why might that be wrong?
Whether you understand position bias in click data.
Users click the top slot partly because it is on top; you correct for that before training a model on clicks.

People click what they see first, so top slots get clicks even when lower results are better. Trained on raw clicks, a model learns to copy the old ranking. I would estimate the bias with small randomized position swaps, then weight clicks by how likely each position was to be seen. Interleaving tests also compare rankings more fairly.
A new product was added today and no one has clicked on it yet. How does your recommender handle it?
How you handle the cold start problem.
Uses content features like title, category and price, plus a little controlled exploration so new items can earn data.

A model trained only on clicks cannot place an item with no history. So I use content: title, category, brand, price and text or image embeddings, to find similar items that do have history. I also keep a small share of slots for showing new items, so they collect clicks. Once there is enough data, behavior signals take over.
Why do most search and recommendation systems retrieve candidates first and rank them in a second step?
Your grasp of the two-stage architecture and its speed and recall trade-offs.
Cheap retrieval narrows millions of items to hundreds; a heavier model reranks only those, inside the latency budget.

Scoring millions of items with a heavy model on every request is too slow. So a cheap stage, like BM25 or a nearest neighbor search on embeddings, pulls a few hundred candidates fast. A richer model then ranks only those. The catch: if retrieval misses a good item, the ranker never sees it, so I measure the recall of each stage separately.
Your new model beat the old one on every offline metric, but the A/B test shows no change. What do you do?
How you reason when offline and online results disagree.
Checks the experiment and the data pipeline first, then looks for gaps between offline labels and what users value, without forcing a launch.

First I check the experiment: is traffic split correctly, is the new model really serving, is the test big enough to detect the lift we expected. Then I look for a mismatch, like labels built from old clicks that reward copying the old ranking, or features that arrive late in production. I would not ship on offline numbers alone.
Your “you may also like” list shows the same bestsellers to everyone. Is that a problem, and what would you do?
Your judgement about popularity bias and feedback loops.
Sees the feedback loop, weighs short-term clicks against discovery, and proposes measured fixes like diversity rules.

It can be. Bestsellers get shown, so they get clicked, so the model shows them more, and the rest of the catalog never gets a chance. I would measure catalog coverage and how personal the lists are. Then I would try a popularity penalty or a diversity rule, like at most two items per category, and check engagement over weeks, not days.
The business team wants to push high-margin items higher in search. How do you handle it?
How you balance revenue goals against relevance and user trust.
Neither refuses nor blindly complies: boosts only among relevant results, tests long-term effects, and labels paid placements.

I would not add a flat boost, because irrelevant items on top cost us searches and trust. I would boost only among items that already pass a relevance threshold, and test it on revenue per search and repeat visits, not margin alone. If a supplier pays for the spot, it is an ad, and it has to be clearly labeled as sponsored.
When would you report MRR instead of NDCG for a search system?
Whether you pick a ranking metric that fits what the user is actually looking for.
MRR when there is one right answer; NDCG when several results are useful at different grades, with a discount by position.

MRR averages one over the rank of the first relevant result, so it fits queries with one right answer, like an order number or a known product. NDCG uses graded labels and discounts each gain by position, so it fits browse queries where several results help and some help more than others.
Your spell checker changes the model number “XR500” into a different word. How do you fix it without turning spelling correction off?
How you handle query understanding for tokens that are not ordinary words.
Protect catalog terms, treat letter-digit tokens differently, correct only when confident, and replay real queries to test.

I would build a protected vocabulary from the catalog: brands, model numbers, SKUs. Tokens that mix letters and digits skip correction unless they match nothing and a close catalog term exists. I would also index model numbers with and without separators so “XR-500” and “XR500” both match, then replay a sample of logged queries to check nothing else broke.
You run BM25 and a vector search side by side. How do you merge the two result lists?
Whether you know why raw scores from different retrievers cannot simply be added.
The scores live on different scales; use rank-based fusion such as reciprocal rank fusion, or a reranker, checked on judged queries.

BM25 scores are unbounded and vary by query, while cosine similarity sits in a narrow range, so adding them lets one side dominate. I would start with reciprocal rank fusion: each document gets the sum of one divided by a constant plus its rank in each list. It works without tuning. Later, a reranker that sees both signals as features usually does better.
After the catalog doubled, your vector search returns worse neighbors at the same latency. What do you look at?
Your grasp of approximate nearest neighbor search and its trade-offs.
Measure recall against exact search first, then tune query-time search depth or graph settings, and check deletes and filters.

First I measure it: compare the index against exact brute-force search on a few thousand queries to get recall at 10. With HNSW, raising ef_search, the candidate list size at query time, buys recall for latency. If that is not enough, I rebuild with a larger M, more links per node, which costs memory. I also check whether deleted items or strict filters cut off good neighbors.
Explain the difference between pointwise, pairwise and listwise learning to rank.
Whether you understand what a ranking model is actually trained to optimize.
Pointwise scores items one by one, pairwise learns which of two is better, listwise optimizes the order of the whole list.

Pointwise treats each query and document alone, like predicting click probability. Pairwise learns which of two documents should rank higher, which is closer to the real task. Listwise looks at the whole ranked list. LambdaMART sits between the last two: it learns from pairs but weights each swap by how much it would change NDCG, so mistakes at the top count more.
When would you use interleaving instead of a regular A/B test for a ranking change?
Whether you know a more sensitive way to compare rankers, and its limits.
Interleaving finds user preference with far less traffic but does not measure revenue or retention, so winners still get an A/B test.

In interleaving, each user sees one list mixed from both rankers, and each click is credited to the ranker that supplied the item. Since every user compares both, it finds a winner with much less traffic. I use it to screen many candidate rankers fast. It shows which list users prefer, not what happens to revenue, so the winner still goes through an A/B test.
Your 50/50 A/B test on two million users ended with 50.8% in control and 49.2% in treatment. What do you do?
Whether you catch a broken experiment before trusting its results.
Names it a sample ratio mismatch, confirms it with a test, refuses to read the metrics, and finds the cause before rerunning.

At that size, a gap of about 32,000 users is far beyond chance; a chi-square test would confirm it. It is a sample ratio mismatch: something dropped users unevenly, so I would not trust any metric. Usual causes are the new ranking timing out for some users, bot filtering that treats the arms differently, or logging that fails in one arm. I find it, fix it and rerun.
A new feature lifts offline AUC a lot. Then you find it counts purchases up to the end of the day. What went wrong, and how do you prevent it?
Whether you spot label leakage and know how to build features that are correct in time.
The feature saw the future. Build training data with values known at impression time, and ideally train on features logged at serving.

The feature includes the purchase we are trying to predict, so the model learned to read the answer. Online that data does not exist yet, so the lift would vanish. I would rebuild training data with point-in-time joins, using only values known at the moment of the impression. Better, log features as the server computed them and train on those logs, which also catches training and serving skew.
Your recommender is retrained every day on clicks from its own recommendations. What risk does that create, and how do you manage it?
Whether you see how a model shapes the data it later learns from.
A feedback loop narrows what gets shown. Keep some exploration, log how likely each item was to be shown, and keep a holdout.

Items the model never shows never get clicks, so it grows sure of a narrow set and new or niche items cannot break in. I would reserve a small share of slots for exploration and log the probability each item had of being shown, so training can reweight by it. A small holdout served by a random or older policy gives clean data to check whether the loop is drifting.
