You train a two-tower retrieval model with in-batch negatives and it under-retrieves popular items. Why, and how do you fix it?
Your depth on how negative sampling biases a retrieval model.
Popular items show up as negatives far more often, so they get over-penalized; apply logQ correction or add uniform negatives.

With in-batch negatives, the other items in the batch act as negatives, and popular items appear in many more batches, so the model learns to push them down. The usual fix is logQ correction: during training, subtract the log of each item's sampling probability from its score. I estimate that probability from item frequency and also mix in some negatives drawn uniformly from the catalog.

security-analyst.heading: Security analyst and incident response questions
qs: What is the difference between an event, an alert and an incident?
Whether you use the basic terms of the work precisely.
Events are anything logged, alerts are events a rule flagged, incidents are confirmed or likely harm that needs a response.

An event is anything a system records, like a logon. An alert is an event or pattern that a rule flagged as worth a look. An incident is when we confirm, or strongly suspect, that something is actually threatening our systems or data. Most alerts I close never become incidents, and that is normal.
Which Windows event IDs do you check first when looking at logon activity?
Your hands-on knowledge of the Windows Security log.
4624 and 4625 for success and failure, the logon type, and related IDs such as 4672 and 4688, with a clear idea of what each one tells you.

4624 is a successful logon and 4625 a failed one. I always read the logon type: 10 means Remote Desktop, 3 means a network logon such as a file share. 4672 shows special privileges were assigned at logon, so an admin session. If process creation auditing is on, 4688 tells me what ran after the logon.
How would you tell password spraying apart from a brute-force attack in the logs?
Whether you can turn an attack pattern into something a detection rule can find.
Brute force is many tries on one account. Spraying is a few common passwords across many accounts, so the rule must count distinct users per source.

Brute force hammers one account, so I look for many failures on a single user. Spraying tries one or two common passwords across hundreds of accounts to stay under the lockout limit. For that I count distinct usernames with failed logons from one source IP in a time window, and I check whether any of those accounts then had a success.
An alert shows PowerShell running with an encoded command on a finance laptop. How do you triage it?
How you work through a common alert step by step.
Decode the command, check the parent process, the user and the network activity, then decide on isolation based on what it actually does.

First I decode it: the -EncodedCommand value is Base64 of UTF-16 text. Then I check the parent process. Word or Outlook launching PowerShell is a bad sign; a management tool may be normal. I look at what it connected to and what files it wrote. If it downloads code from an unknown site, I isolate the laptop through the endpoint agent and open an incident.
One of your detection rules fires 300 times a day and almost all are false positives. What do you do?
How you tune detections without creating blind spots.
Find why it is noisy and narrow it with specific, documented exceptions. Never just turn it off or let analysts get used to ignoring it.

I group the hits to see what drives the noise; often one backup job or admin script causes most of it. I add a narrow exception for that exact host, account and command line, write down why, and set a date to review it. Then I test the rule against a known bad sample to make sure it still fires. Disabling it would just hide the next real attack.
A user reports they clicked a phishing link and typed in their password. What do you do in the first hour?
Whether you know the full set of steps after stolen credentials, not just a password reset.
Reset the password and revoke sessions, check sign-ins and MFA changes, look for mailbox rules, and find and remove the email from other inboxes.

I reset the password and revoke active sessions, since a reset alone may not end a session the attacker already has. I check sign-in logs for logons from new places and whether a new MFA device was added. I look for inbox forwarding or delete rules, a common trick. Then I search all mailboxes for the same email, remove it, and block the sender and link.
How would you look for malware beaconing in proxy or DNS logs?
Your ability to hunt for threats that no rule has caught yet.
Regular connection timing, rare destinations and steady request sizes, then checking against what is normal before calling it malicious.

Malware often calls home at steady intervals, say every 60 seconds with a little random variation. I group connections by host and destination and look for very regular gaps, similar byte counts and domains few other machines visit. Software updaters do this too, so I check the domain's age and the process making the calls before I raise it.
Why shouldn't you just power off a machine you think is compromised?
Whether you protect evidence while containing a threat.
Memory holds evidence that is lost at shutdown. Isolate from the network instead, capture the most volatile data first, and hash what you collect.

Memory holds running processes, network connections and sometimes code that never touches the disk, and a shutdown wipes it. I cut the machine off the network, usually through the endpoint agent, then capture memory before the disk image. I hash each file I collect and log who handled it, so we can show later it was not changed.
Tell me about an alert you closed as a false positive that turned out to be real. What did you change?
How you own a mistake and fix the process behind it.
Honest about the miss, quick to reopen and escalate, and a concrete fix such as a better rule, a checklist step or a second review.

I closed a login alert from a new country because the user often traveled. Two days later the same account sent internal phishing. I reopened it, escalated, and we contained it that afternoon. I had assumed instead of checked. Now I confirm travel with the user or manager, and we added device details to that alert so the next analyst sees more.
The IT manager wants to wipe and rebuild an infected server right now to get the business running. What do you say?
Your judgement when speed and investigation pull in different directions.
A fast path that preserves evidence first and finds how the attacker got in, so the rebuilt server is not breached again the same way.

I would say I want it back up too, but if we rebuild before we know how they got in, they can use the same door again tonight. I ask for an hour or two to capture memory and a disk image and check for other infected hosts. Meanwhile we keep it isolated, restore from a backup we have checked is clean, and close the entry point.
What is the order of volatility, and how does it change what you collect first?
Whether you collect evidence in an order that does not destroy it.
Most volatile first: memory, network connections and running processes before disk, then logs and backups.

It ranks evidence by how fast it disappears. Memory, running processes and open network connections go first, because a reboot or even time loses them. Then disk, then remote logs and backups, which last longer. So on a live host I capture memory before I image the disk, and I write down every command I run, since each one changes the system a little.
Why is a list of bad file hashes a weak detection on its own?
Your grasp of which indicators actually cost an attacker effort.
Hashes are trivial to change. Detections built on behavior and techniques hold up much longer.

Changing one byte gives a new hash, so the attacker loses nothing. IPs and domains are cheap to swap too. I use hashes for quick scoping, but my lasting rules target behavior: say, Office spawning a script host, or a new service created over the network. That is the top of the Pyramid of Pain, where the attacker has to change how they work.
Walk me through how you test a new detection rule before you put it in production.
How you build rules that fire on the real thing and stay quiet otherwise.
Simulate the technique, run the rule over past data to count noise, write a runbook, then review after it goes live.

First I confirm the log source records the fields I need. I simulate the technique in a lab, using tests mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, and check the rule fires. Then I run it over 30 days of past data to see how often it would have fired and why. I write a short runbook for the analyst who gets the alert, and I review the rule after two weeks live.
What traces does PsExec-style lateral movement leave on the target machine?
Your knowledge of how remote execution shows up in Windows logs.
A network logon, admin share access and a new service install, seen together on the target within seconds.

On the target I expect a network logon, type 3, event 4624, then access to the ADMIN$ share, then a new service being installed: event 7045 in the System log, or 4697 in Security if that auditing is on. One of these alone is normal admin work. All three within seconds from a workstation that is not an admin jump box is worth a look.
How would you detect Kerberoasting?
Whether you know how attacks on Active Directory service accounts look in the logs.
Service ticket requests (event 4769) with weak RC4 encryption, many services from one account, and strong service account passwords.

The attacker requests service tickets and cracks them offline. On domain controllers I watch event 4769 for tickets with encryption type 0x17, which is RC4, and for one account asking for tickets to many services at once. A decoy service account nobody uses makes a clean alert. Long random service account passwords make cracking fail.
A developer's cloud access key was pushed to a public code repository an hour ago. What do you do?
How you contain a leaked credential and scope what was done with it.
Disable the key first, then review the audit logs for its use and remove any persistence the attacker created.

I deactivate the key right away; bots scan public repos within minutes, so I assume it was used. Then I search the cloud audit logs, CloudTrail on AWS, for every call made with that key: new users, new keys, changed policies, new instances. Anything created I remove. Finally I purge it from the repo history and add secret scanning before push.
On a Windows host, how can you tell a file's timestamps were faked?
Your depth in file system forensics when building a timeline.
Compare NTFS $STANDARD_INFORMATION and $FILE_NAME times, and check against other sources such as the USN journal or prefetch.

NTFS keeps two sets of times for a file. Common timestomping tools change the $STANDARD_INFORMATION set, which is what Explorer shows, but the $FILE_NAME set is harder to change. If $SI says 2019 and $FN says last Tuesday, that is a red flag. I also check the USN journal and prefetch, and zeroed fractions of a second in the times are another hint.
You find that logs from two domain controllers stopped reaching the SIEM two weeks ago. What do you do?
How you handle a gap in visibility, including your own team's miss.
Fix the feed, recover the missing logs from the source if they still exist, hunt the gap, and add log-source health alerts.

First I restore the feed and check whether the controllers still hold the missing events locally; if they rolled over, I note the gap. I pull what exists and run our key detections over those two weeks by hand. Then I report it plainly as a blind spot, and add an alert when any critical source goes quiet for more than an hour.
You suspect the attacker can read your company email. How does that change how you run the response?
Your judgement about operational security during an incident.
Move response talk to an out-of-band channel, keep the circle small, and avoid tipping off the attacker before containment.

I move the team to a channel the attacker cannot reach, such as phone calls and a chat workspace set up outside our domain, with accounts not tied to our directory. I keep the circle small and stop discussing the case in tickets or email. I also avoid early moves the attacker would notice, like resetting one admin password, until we can act everywhere at once.
We've cleaned the hosts we found. How do you decide the attacker is really out of a domain where they had admin rights?
Whether you can plan a full eviction rather than chase single machines.
Scope fully first, then evict all at once: remove persistence, reset privileged and service credentials, reset krbtgt twice, then watch closely.

With domain admin, I assume any credential could be stolen, including the krbtgt account that signs Kerberos tickets. So we scope first, then act in one window: remove every persistence point we found, reset admin and service passwords, and reset krbtgt twice, waiting for replication and ticket lifetime between resets. Then we watch for weeks for any reuse of old access.

security-architect.heading: Security architect questions
qs: What does zero trust mean to you, beyond the buzzword?
Whether you understand the model itself and not just the label.
No trust is granted from network location alone. Every request is checked on identity, device and context, and access is kept narrow.

It means being inside the network earns you nothing by itself. Each request is checked on who the user is, the state of the device and what is being asked for. Access is granted per app, not to a whole subnet. It is a direction you move toward over years, through identity, device health and segmentation, not one product you buy.
In the cloud shared responsibility model, what stays with us?
Whether you know where the provider's job ends and the company's begins.
The provider secures the underlying infrastructure. The customer owns identities, configuration and data, and the split shifts between IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.

The provider runs the data centers, the hardware and the base platform. We own who gets access, how services are configured, and our data. On plain virtual machines we also patch the operating system; with SaaS we mostly own users and settings. Most cloud breaches I have studied were customer-side mistakes, like a storage bucket left public.
Walk me through how you threat model a new service.
Your method for finding design risks before anything is built.
Draw data flows and trust boundaries, list threats with a framework like STRIDE, rank them, and turn them into design changes.

I sit with the team and draw the data flow: users, services, data stores, and where data crosses a trust boundary. At each boundary I go through STRIDE: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege. We rank what we find by likelihood and impact, and each real threat becomes a ticket or a design change.
Which MFA methods would you allow for admin accounts, and why?
Whether you know which second factors actually stop phishing.
Phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2 security keys or passkeys, because SMS codes and simple push prompts can be phished or approved by mistake.

For admins I want phishing-resistant MFA: FIDO2 security keys or passkeys. They are tied to the real site's domain, so a fake login page gets nothing usable. SMS codes can be stolen through SIM swaps, and push prompts invite fatigue attacks where a tired user taps approve. Those are not acceptable for privileged accounts.
How would you segment a flat network where everything can talk to everything?
How you plan a big structural change without breaking the business.
Map real traffic first, build zones by function and sensitivity, default-deny between them, and roll out in monitored stages.

First I learn what really talks to what from flow logs, since diagrams are often wrong. Then I group systems into zones, such as user devices, servers, payments and management, with the tightest rules around the most sensitive. I run new rules in log-only mode, fix what would break, then switch to default deny. Ransomware on one laptop then cannot reach the database servers.
How should we encrypt sensitive data at rest, and where should the keys live?
Your grasp of key management, which matters more than the cipher itself.
Keys held in a key management service or HSM, apart from the data, using envelope encryption, rotation and tightly controlled, logged key use.

I would use envelope encryption: each data set is encrypted with a data key, and that data key is encrypted by a master key held in a key management service or hardware security module. The master key never leaves it. Key use is limited by role and logged, so a stolen copy of the files alone is useless.
A developer pushed a cloud access key to a public repository an hour ago. What do you do?
Whether you act in the right order when a secret leaks.
Revoke and rotate the key first, since deleting the commit is not enough. Then check logs for any use of the key and fix the cause.

First I have the key disabled and replaced, right now. Bots scan public repos within minutes, and deleting the commit does not remove it from history. Then I check the audit logs for any use of that key. Last, I fix the cause: secret scanning in the pipeline and short-lived credentials that expire on their own.
A critical legacy system cannot be patched or replaced this year. How do you protect it?
How you reduce risk when the ideal fix is not available.
Compensating controls: isolate it, allow only needed connections, add monitoring, and document the risk with an owner and a review date.

I put it in its own segment and allow only the few connections it really needs, with admin access through a jump host. I remove internet access, add logging and alerts around it, and harden what can still be changed. Then a business owner signs the documented risk with a review date, so the exception does not quietly become permanent.
The business wants to launch next week, and your review found a serious design gap. What do you do?
How you weigh security risk against business needs without simply blocking.
Explain the risk in business terms, offer options with mitigations, and have an accountable owner accept any remaining risk in writing.

I explain the gap plainly: what an attacker could do and what it would cost us. Then I offer options, for example launch with the feature behind login and a rate limit, and fix the root issue within thirty days. If they go ahead, a named business owner accepts the risk in writing with a fix date. My job is to make the risk clear, not to own every decision.
How should our services authenticate to each other instead of using shared passwords?
Your design for machine identity, a common weak point in modern systems.
Each workload gets its own identity with short-lived, automatically issued credentials, such as mutual TLS or platform tokens, and no long-lived secrets in code.

Each service gets its own identity and short-lived credentials issued automatically. That can be mutual TLS, where both sides present certificates that rotate often, or tokens the cloud platform issues to the workload. Each call is checked against a policy of which service may call which. No passwords sit in config files, and a stolen credential expires quickly.
What is the difference between OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, and why does it matter for design?
Whether you know which protocol proves identity and which grants access.
OAuth delegates access with access tokens; OIDC adds an ID token that says who signed in. Treating an access token as proof of login is a known flaw.

OAuth 2.0 lets an app act for a user with an access token. It says what the app may do, not who the user is. OpenID Connect sits on top and adds an ID token, a signed JWT about the sign-in. If a team logs users in by accepting any access token, a token issued to another app could be replayed into ours. For login I want OIDC, with the audience checked.
Which logs must exist before an incident happens, and where would you keep them?
Whether your design makes a later investigation possible.
Identity, cloud control plane, endpoint, DNS and network logs, sent to a separate place attackers cannot edit, kept long enough to look back.

Sign-ins and admin changes from the identity provider, cloud audit logs for every account, endpoint detection data, DNS queries and firewall or flow logs. They go to a separate logging account that production admins cannot touch, with write-once storage. Retention follows our policy and legal needs, and I test that they actually arrive.
How would you structure cloud accounts for a company with 40 product teams?
How you use account boundaries to limit how far one breach can spread.
Separate accounts by workload and environment, guardrails set at the organization level, and central accounts for logging and security tools.

One account per workload and environment, so a breach in test does not reach production. Accounts sit in an organization with policies at the top that nobody inside can override, like blocking log deletion or unused regions. Logging and security tooling get their own accounts. People sign in through our identity provider and assume roles; nobody gets long-lived user keys.
How would you control outbound traffic from our production cloud network?
Whether you treat outbound traffic as a control against data theft and attacker remote control.
Default deny, one known path out through a proxy or firewall with an allowlist, private endpoints for cloud services, and logged DNS.

Most workloads should not reach the open internet at all. I would deny outbound by default, send what is needed through one egress point with a domain allowlist, and reach cloud services over private endpoints. DNS goes through a resolver we log. Then a stolen server cannot easily call home or upload data, and when something tries, we see it.
How do you keep the CI/CD pipeline from becoming the way into production?
Whether you see the build system as a high-value target that needs its own design.
Short-lived credentials instead of stored keys, reviewed changes, pinned dependencies, and signed artifacts checked at deploy.

The pipeline gets short-lived cloud credentials through federation, so no long-lived keys sit in its settings. Changes to main need a review, and only protected branches can deploy to production. Third-party build steps are pinned to exact commits. We sign what we build and the deploy step checks the signature, so an artifact from anywhere else cannot ship.
How would you design break-glass accounts for our identity provider and cloud?
How you plan for the day normal sign-in fails without leaving a back door.
At least two emergency accounts with phishing-resistant sign-in, independent of normal dependencies, alerting on every use and tested on a schedule.

I would keep two cloud-only emergency accounts that do not depend on our federation or one person's phone. Each uses a hardware security key kept in a separate safe. They are excluded from policies that could lock everyone out, but any sign-in pages the security team at once. We test them every quarter and rotate anything that was used.
A team wants a SaaS tool that needs read access to every mailbox in our tenant. How do you decide?
Your judgement on third-party access that bypasses the network entirely.
Asking if a narrower scope works, reviewing the vendor, requiring admin consent, and planning how the access is monitored and revoked.

First, what does the tool really need? Often it works with a few shared mailboxes, and the platform can limit an app to those. Then I review the vendor: its audit report, where data is stored, how it protects our tokens. Users cannot grant this themselves; an admin approves it. I log the app's activity and name an owner who reviews it each year.
We use phishing-resistant MFA, yet an attacker replayed a stolen session cookie. How should the design limit that?
Whether you know MFA protects the sign-in, not the session that follows it.
Short or device-bound sessions, access tied to managed devices, fast revocation, fresh sign-in for sensitive actions, and catching the malware.

MFA happened before the theft, so the cookie carries it. I would shorten admin sessions, require a managed device, and bind tokens to the device where supported. Signs of theft, like a new country, should end the session fast. Sensitive actions ask for a fresh sign-in. Endpoint detection should catch the malware that steals cookies.
We just acquired a company with its own identity provider and an unknown network. How do you connect them?
How you balance a fast integration against importing someone else's risk.
Assess before connecting, give access per application instead of network to network, and bring identities onto one controlled path.

I would not join the networks on day one. First a quick assessment: who their admins are, what is exposed to the internet, any signs of past compromise. Their staff reach our apps through federation, app by app, with MFA. Their admin credentials get reset. Only after that do we plan a full merge, step by step.
Tell me about a security design of yours that turned out wrong. What did you change?
Whether you can own a design mistake and learn from it.
A specific flaw, how it was found, the fix, and how it changed the way you design since.

I once built segmentation around subnets, and the firewall rules grew to over 900 lines nobody understood. A review found a broad rule added during an outage and never removed. We moved to rules by workload identity and tags, with an owner and an expiry date on each exception. Now every design I write says how its rules will stay small.

security-compliance.heading: Security compliance (GRC) questions
qs: What is the difference between a SOC 2 Type I and a Type II report?
Whether you know the basic shape of the audit you would be running.
Type I tests control design on one date. Type II tests design and operation over a period, so it needs evidence across months.

A Type I says the controls were designed properly on a single date. A Type II says they were designed properly and actually worked over a period, often six to twelve months. Most customers want the Type II, so a company often gets a Type I first and then runs its first observation period.
SOC 2 has five Trust Services Criteria. How do you decide which ones go in scope?
How you scope an audit to what customers actually need.
Security is always in. The others are added when customer commitments or the product call for them, not for show.

Security is required; its controls are called the common criteria. Then I look at what we promise customers. If contracts include uptime commitments, Availability makes sense. If we hold their confidential data, Confidentiality. Processing Integrity and Privacy fit fewer companies. Every extra criterion adds controls and evidence, so I add one only when a customer need backs it.
What is the difference between a policy, a standard and a procedure?
Your skill at writing documents people can follow and auditors can test.
Policy says what and why, the standard sets the measurable rule, the procedure gives the steps. Keeping them apart keeps policies short and stable.

A policy states the rule and who owns it, for example: access follows least privilege. A standard makes it measurable: access is reviewed every quarter. A procedure is the steps: export the user list, send it to managers, record the changes. I keep policies short so they rarely need new approval, and put details that change into standards and procedures.
Walk me through how you run a risk assessment.
Whether your risk assessment drives decisions or just fills a spreadsheet.
Assets and threats, likelihood and impact, a treatment and an owner for each risk, and a review on a set schedule.

I start with the assets that matter: customer data, production systems, key vendors. With system owners I list threats and rate likelihood and impact to get inherent risk. Then I map existing controls, rate residual risk, and pick a treatment: reduce, transfer, avoid or accept. Every risk gets an owner, and accepted risks get a leadership sign-off. I rerun it at least yearly.
The auditor asks for evidence of your quarterly user access reviews. What do you hand over?
Your sense of what makes evidence complete and believable to an auditor.
A system-generated user list, proof of who reviewed it and when, and tickets showing the requested removals were actually made.

For each quarter: the user list pulled straight from the system, with the date and source visible, so it is complete. The reviewer's dated sign-off. And the tickets for every change they asked for, showing the access was really removed. A spreadsheet someone typed by hand, with no trail back to the system, usually gets questioned.
A prospect asks for our SOC 2 report, but the period ended five months ago. What do you send?
Whether you know how SOC 2 reports are shared and kept current.
The report under NDA, since a SOC 2 is meant for specified users, plus a bridge letter covering the gap since the period ended.

A SOC 2 is meant for specified users, so I share it under an NDA. Because the period ended months ago, I add a bridge letter: a statement from our management that there have been no material changes to the controls since then, and when the next report is due. If they only want a public summary and we have a SOC 3, that can go out freely.
Sales wants to tell a big prospect we are 'SOC 2 certified' while our first audit is still underway. How do you handle it?
How you protect the company from claims it cannot back up.
No overclaiming: SOC 2 is an auditor's attestation report, not a certification. Then an accurate line sales can still use to close.

I would stop that wording. SOC 2 is not a certification, it is an auditor's report, and we do not have one yet. A false claim could cost the deal or breach a contract. I would give sales an accurate line: our Type II observation period is underway with an independent CPA firm, and we expect the report in the fall. I would also offer a call with me.
Mid-audit, you find two quarterly access reviews were never done. An engineer offers to do them now and date them back. What do you do?
Your integrity when the audit result is on the line.
Refuse backdating, tell the auditor, fix the control and write a management response. An honest exception beats a falsified record.

I would say no right away. Backdated evidence is falsified evidence, and if the auditor finds it, the whole report is in doubt. I would tell the auditor about the gap, run a review now with today's date, remove any access that should not be there, and fix the cause, such as a missing owner or reminder. The exception goes in the report with our management response.
We run on a large public cloud provider. How does that show up in our SOC 2?
Whether you understand subservice organizations and shared responsibility.
The provider is a subservice organization, usually carved out. You review its own SOC 2 and cover your side of the shared controls yourself.

The provider is a subservice organization. Most reports use the carve-out method: its controls are left out, and our report lists the ones we rely on it for, such as data center physical security. Each year I review the provider's own SOC 2 and its exceptions, and make sure our side, like access and configuration, is covered by our own controls.
Leadership now wants ISO 27001 on top of SOC 2. How do you avoid doing everything twice?
How you build one control program that serves several frameworks.
One control set mapped to both, plus the ISO-only pieces: a defined ISMS scope, the Statement of Applicability, internal audit and management review.

I keep one set of controls and map each to both the SOC 2 criteria and ISO 27001's Annex A, so one piece of evidence serves both audits. Then I add what ISO needs that SOC 2 does not: a written scope for the management system, a Statement of Applicability explaining which controls apply and why, an internal audit, and a management review.
In ISO 27001, what is the Statement of Applicability, and what makes one hold up in an audit?
Whether you know the document that links risk treatment to the Annex A controls.
It lists each Annex A control, whether it applies, why, and its status, and every choice traces back to the risk treatment plan.

It lists every Annex A control, says whether we apply it, gives the reason for including or excluding it, and shows whether it is implemented. Auditors push hardest on exclusions, so each needs a real reason, like 'we develop no software in-house.' I also make sure every control in it traces back to a risk in our treatment plan.
Write me a change management control, out loud, that an auditor could actually test.
Whether you can write controls that are specific and leave evidence behind.
Names who does what, when, and what record is left, with the check enforced by the system rather than promised.

Every change to production code goes through a pull request that someone other than the author must approve before merge. Branch protection on the main branch enforces this. Only two admins can bypass it, and every bypass is logged and reviewed monthly. The evidence is the list of merges for the period, and the auditor can sample any merge and see the approver.
You are reviewing a key vendor's SOC 2 Type II report. What do you actually read?
How you do vendor due diligence beyond filing the PDF.
Scope, period, the opinion, exceptions, carved-out subservice organizations, and the controls the vendor expects you to run yourself.

First the scope and period: does it cover the service we buy, and is it recent. Then the opinion, to see if it is qualified. Then the exceptions and the vendor's responses. I note which subservice organizations are carved out, and I list the complementary user entity controls, the ones the vendor says we must run, and confirm we run them.
The auditor picks samples from a list you exported. How do you show that list is complete?
Whether you understand completeness and accuracy of the populations you give an auditor.
The list comes from the source system, the export is reproducible, and it is reconciled against a second source.

I pull it straight from the system of record, not from a spreadsheet someone keeps. I save the query, or record the export with the date range and filters on screen. Then I reconcile it: new hires in the HR system should match new accounts in the identity system. If a list cannot be reproduced, the auditor cannot rely on any sample drawn from it.
Our compliance automation dashboard shows every control green. Why wouldn't you rely on that alone?
Whether you know what automated monitoring can and cannot prove.
Tools only test what they are connected to; they miss unconnected systems and controls that need human judgement.

A tool only tests what it is connected to. If someone opens a new cloud account, or a test checks that a review ticket exists but not that anyone looked, it stays green. So I spot-check: I compare the tool's asset list to billing and the identity provider, and I open a few reviews to see real decisions, like access actually removed.
A security questionnaire asks, 'Is all customer data encrypted at rest?' One legacy database is not. How do you answer?
Your honesty and judgement when an answer is only partly true.
No false yes. A qualified answer with the scope, the compensating controls and a fix date, and the gap logged as a risk.

I would not answer a plain yes, because questionnaire answers often end up in contracts. I would write: yes for all production systems except one legacy database, which sits on a private network with restricted access and is scheduled for encryption by the end of next quarter. Then I make sure that gap is in the risk register with an owner.
An engineering team cannot fix a high risk before the audit and asks for an exception. What does a good exception look like?
How you run risk acceptance so it stays a decision, not a hiding place.
Written, approved at the right level, with an owner, compensating controls and an expiry date that forces a review.

It names the risk, the control we are not meeting, and why. It lists what we do in the meantime, such as extra monitoring. The person who owns the business risk signs it, not the engineer asking, and for a high risk that means an executive. It has an end date, and when it expires it comes back for review instead of renewing quietly.
An engineering lead suggests leaving the messy legacy billing system out of SOC 2 scope so we pass. When is that fine, and when is it not?
Whether you scope by what customers rely on, not by what passes easily.
Scope follows the service customers buy and the data it touches; dropping a system they rely on makes the report misleading.

It is fine if the system does not support the service the report describes and does not touch customer data in scope. If customer data flows through it, leaving it out makes the report misleading, and the auditor may push back anyway. Then I keep it in, fix what we can, and accept that a few exceptions beat a report nobody trusts.
The auditor tells you one control had exceptions in testing. Walk me through what happens next.
Whether you know how exceptions affect a SOC 2 report and how to respond.
Knows an exception does not automatically mean a qualified opinion; finds root cause, checks other controls on the same risk, writes a factual response.

First I confirm the facts: how many samples failed, out of how many, and why. Then the root cause: a one-off slip or a broken process. An exception is listed in the report, but it does not automatically mean a qualified opinion. I check whether another control covers the same risk, fix the process, and write a short, factual management response for the report.
We had a real security incident in the middle of the audit period. How does that change the SOC 2, and what do you do?
Your judgement on disclosure and on how an incident reaches the report.
Tells the auditor early, knows significant incidents may need to be described in the report, and shows the response followed the plan.

I tell the auditor early. Management signs a representation letter at the end saying we disclosed what we know, and surprises hurt trust. Incidents that caused a significant failure to meet our commitments must be described in the report, so we judge that together. Either way, I collect evidence that our response followed the plan: ticket, timeline, root cause and fixes.

security-engineer.heading: Security engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between cross-site scripting and cross-site request forgery?
Whether you know two classic web flaws well enough to tell them apart.
XSS runs attacker script in the victim's page; CSRF makes the browser send a request the user did not mean. Each has its own fix.

In cross-site scripting, attacker input ends up running as script in another user's browser, so it can read the page and act as that user. The fix is output encoding for each context plus a content security policy. In CSRF, another site makes the user's browser send a request with their cookies. The fix is anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies.
A developer asks how to store user passwords. What do you tell them?
Whether you know current password storage practice.
A slow, salted hash built for passwords, such as Argon2id or bcrypt. Never plain text, reversible encryption, or a fast hash alone.

Never store the password itself or encrypt it so it can be decrypted. Use a password hashing function made to be slow, such as Argon2id or bcrypt, with a unique salt per user, which the library handles. A fast hash like SHA-256 alone is wrong because attackers can try billions of guesses a second. Tune the cost so login stays quick but cracking stays expensive.
How do you stop SQL injection, and why is escaping input not enough?
Your grasp of the root cause of injection and the reliable fix.
Parameterized queries keep data apart from code. Escaping is easy to get wrong, and raw queries inside ORM code still need checking.

Injection happens when user input is glued into the query text, so the database reads it as code. Parameterized queries send the query and the values separately, so input can never change the structure. Escaping depends on getting every case right for every database. In review I also search for raw SQL and string building inside ORM code, where it sneaks back in.
You are reviewing code that uses JSON Web Tokens for sessions. What do you check?
Whether you can spot common token mistakes in a code review.
The signature is always verified with a fixed algorithm, nothing secret sits in the payload, lifetimes are short, and tokens can be revoked.

First, that the server verifies the signature and pins the expected algorithm, so a token with alg set to none or a swapped algorithm is rejected. Second, nothing sensitive in the payload, since it is only encoded, not encrypted. Third, expiry is checked and short, with a way to revoke, because a stolen token works until it expires. And the signing key is strong and not in the repo.
A tester changes the invoice number in an API call and sees another customer's invoice. How do you fix it?
Whether you fix broken access control at the root, not by hiding IDs.
A server-side check, on every request, that the caller may see that object. Random IDs alone do not fix it. Then look for the same pattern elsewhere.

This is an insecure direct object reference. The fix is on the server: before returning the invoice, check that it belongs to the caller's account, every time. Random IDs make guessing harder but are not a fix. Then I search other endpoints for the same pattern, move the check into a shared layer, and add a test that uses a second user's ID and expects a denial.
A cloud access key with admin rights was pushed to a public code repository an hour ago. What do you do?
How you act in the first minutes of a credential leak.
Revoke the key first, then check logs for use, then clean up and stop it recurring. Deleting the commit is not enough; bots scan public repos within minutes.

I disable the key right away and issue a new one to whatever needs it. Bots find public keys within minutes, so I assume it was used. I check the cloud audit logs for activity by that key since the push: new users, new keys, new machines. Then the history gets cleaned, secret scanning goes into the commit checks, and we ask why an admin key was in code at all.
Our app fetches an image from any URL the user enters. What worries you, and how do you lock it down?
Whether you see server-side request forgery and its cloud risk.
The server can be pointed at internal systems, such as the cloud metadata service that hands out credentials. Use allowlists and network blocks, not just URL checks.

That is server-side request forgery. Someone can make our server call internal addresses, including the cloud metadata service at 169.254.169.254, which can return temporary credentials. I would allowlist domains if possible, resolve the name and block private and link-local ranges, not follow redirects blindly, and require session tokens on the metadata service.
The team wants to release tomorrow, and you found a medium-severity flaw that takes a week to fix. What do you do?
How you balance risk against delivery without being the blocker by default.
Judge real exploitability, look for a quick mitigation, and if the business accepts the risk, get it in writing from an owner with a fix date.

First I check how reachable it is: is it behind login, is the data sensitive. Often a quick control, like a feature flag, a web application firewall rule or a rate limit, cuts most of the risk. If they ship, the product owner signs a written risk acceptance with a fix date, and I track it. I block only if it exposes sensitive data or is easy to exploit from the internet.
Tell me about a security change you made that broke something. What did you learn?
Whether you own mistakes and roll out controls carefully.
An honest story: quick rollback, clear communication, and a changed process such as staged rollout or report-only mode first.

I tightened our content security policy, the browser rule for which scripts may load, and pushed it to everyone at once. The payment page used a script from a domain I had missed, and checkout failed for about 20 minutes. I rolled back, told the team, and fixed the list. Now I run new policies in report-only mode for a week and read the reports before enforcing.
What does CORS protect, and what does it not protect?
Whether you know what the browser enforces and what the server must still enforce.
CORS relaxes the same-origin policy; it is not access control. Reflecting any Origin while allowing credentials is the classic mistake.

CORS is how a server tells browsers which other origins may read its responses. It relaxes the same-origin policy; it does not stop requests from being sent, and tools outside a browser ignore it. So authorization still lives on the server. The bug I look for is echoing back any Origin header while allowing credentials, which lets any website read a logged-in user's data.
We are adding profile picture uploads. What do you check in the code review?
How you review a feature that has several well-known attack paths.
Type checked by content against an allow list, size limits, server-chosen file names, and files served so they cannot run script on the main site.

I check that the server picks the file name, so no one can use ../ to write somewhere else. The type is checked from the file content against an allow list, not from the extension. There is a size limit, and images are re-encoded. Files are served from a separate domain, so an uploaded SVG or HTML file cannot run script on our main site.
Walk me through how you threat-model a new feature.
Your method for finding design flaws before any code is written.
A data flow diagram with trust boundaries, a structured pass such as STRIDE, and ranked findings that become tickets with owners.

I sit with the team and draw the data flow: users, services, data stores, and where trust changes, like the internet edge. At each boundary I walk through STRIDE: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege. We rank what we find, agree on fixes, and file them as tickets with owners, not a report nobody reads.
How would you roll out a Content Security Policy on a large existing site without breaking it?
Whether you can deploy a strong control on old code without causing an outage.
Start in report-only mode, study the violations, use nonces or hashes instead of unsafe-inline, then enforce in stages.

I start with the Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only header, which logs violations without blocking anything. The reports show which scripts load from where. I replace inline scripts with nonces, a random value per page load, rather than allowing unsafe-inline, which would undo most of the protection against cross-site scripting. Then I enforce one section at a time.
A one-time discount code was redeemed fifty times in one second by the same account. What happened, and how do you fix it?
Whether you can spot a race condition in business logic.
A check-then-act race. The fix is one atomic operation in the database, not a faster check in the app.

The code read “is the code used?” and later wrote “used”. Fifty parallel requests all passed the read before any write landed. I would make it one atomic step: an update that only succeeds where used is false, checking the rows affected, or a unique constraint on the redemption. Then I test with parallel requests, because normal tests send them one at a time.
In a code review you see AES-GCM encryption where the nonce is a fixed value. Why does that matter?
Your grasp of how applied cryptography fails in real code.
Reusing a nonce under the same key in GCM leaks the XOR of the plaintexts and lets an attacker forge authentication tags.

GCM needs a unique nonce for every message under the same key. With a fixed nonce, two ciphertexts XOR to the XOR of their plaintexts, and an attacker can recover the authentication key and forge messages. The fix is a fresh random 96-bit nonce per message, stored with the ciphertext, or a counter, and a key rotation plan. I would also move the team to a vetted library.
We have two hundred cloud accounts. How do you make sure no one can make a storage bucket public?
Whether you think in preventive guardrails at scale rather than one-off fixes.
Prevention at the organization level that account admins cannot override, one approved path for public content, and detection for drift.

Checking buckets one by one does not scale. I would turn on the provider's public access block at the account level and add an organization policy that denies anyone, even account admins, the right to turn it off. Public content goes through one approved path, such as a CDN in front of a private bucket. A config rule then alerts on drift, in case a guardrail has a gap.
How do you harden a build pipeline that deploys to production?
Your understanding of the software supply chain as an attack path.
Short-lived credentials, pinned dependencies and build steps, no secrets for untrusted code, and deploys only from reviewed, protected branches.

The pipeline holds the keys to production, so I treat it like production. It gets short-lived credentials through OIDC federation, where the cloud trusts a signed token from the build, instead of stored keys. Third-party build steps are pinned to a commit hash, not a tag that can move. Pull requests from forks never run with secrets. Deploys need a reviewed merge to a protected branch.
You turn on a static analysis scanner and it reports 400 findings across the codebase. What now?
How you bring in a tool without burying developers in noise.
Triage and tune first, block only new high-confidence findings, and work down the old backlog by real risk.

I would not dump 400 tickets on the teams. I triage a sample to see which rules are mostly false positives, and turn those off or tune them. Then the scanner blocks only new findings from rules we trust, in the pull request, where fixing is cheap. The old backlog gets ranked by reachability and exposure, and we fix it over a few sprints.
A penetration tester finds a serious flaw in code you approved in review. How do you handle it?
How you own a miss and fix the process, not just the single bug.
Fix it and check for exploitation first, then find why review missed it and add a control that catches the whole class of bug.

First the fix, and a check of the logs for signs it was used. Then I say plainly that I approved it. I look at why I missed it: say, the authorization check lived in a file outside the diff. So I add a test or scanner rule for that pattern, search the codebase for the same bug, and walk the team through the case so others learn from it too.

semiconductor-fab.heading: Semiconductor fab engineer questions
qs: Walk me through the main steps of photolithography on a wafer.
Whether you know the core patterning flow and where it can be reworked.
The steps in the right order: prime, coat, soft bake, expose, post-exposure bake, develop, measure. Also that resist can be stripped and reworked before etch.

First the wafer is cleaned and primed so the resist sticks, often with HMDS. Then resist is spin-coated and soft baked to drive off solvent. The scanner exposes the pattern through the mask, then comes a post-exposure bake and develop. We measure critical dimension and overlay. If they fail, we strip the resist and rework before etch makes the pattern permanent.
What is the difference between control limits and spec limits?
Whether you understand the basis of statistical process control.
Spec limits say what the product needs. Control limits describe the stable process. A point can be in spec and still out of control.

Spec limits come from the design or the customer: what the product needs to work. Control limits come from the process itself, usually the mean plus or minus three sigma of stable data. A point can be inside spec and still out of control, which tells me something changed. I act on that signal before it turns into scrap.
When would you choose a wet etch over a dry plasma etch?
Your grasp of etch basics and their trade-offs.
Wet etch is isotropic, selective and cheap. Dry etch can be anisotropic for vertical walls on small features. The choice follows the feature.

Wet etch uses liquid chemicals. It is cheap and very selective, but it etches in all directions, so it undercuts the mask and is poor for small features. Plasma etch, like reactive ion etch, drives ions toward the wafer, so it can cut nearly vertical walls. I use dry for fine patterns and wet for cleans or film strips where undercut does not matter.
What does Cpk tell you, and what do you do if Cp is high but Cpk is low?
Whether you can read process capability and act on it.
Cpk accounts for centering; Cp does not. High Cp with low Cpk means a tight process that is off center, so you recenter it.

Cpk compares the spec window with the process spread and accounts for centering. It is the distance from the mean to the nearer spec limit divided by three sigma. A Cpk of 1.33 means that limit is four sigma away. If Cp is high but Cpk is low, the process is tight but off center, so I recenter the target rather than try to cut variation.
A tool just came back from preventive maintenance. How do you decide it is ready for production?
How you qualify a tool before it touches product.
Data, not a verbal OK: particles, rate and uniformity on test wafers compared to the pre-maintenance baseline, then a logged release.

I never release on a verbal OK alone. If a plasma chamber was opened, I run seasoning wafers first. Then particle monitor wafers, then rate and uniformity on test wafers, compared to the baseline from before the maintenance. If everything sits inside the control charts, I release it and watch the first production lot closely. All of it goes in the tool log.
An etch rate point lands above the upper control limit but still inside spec. What do you do?
How you respond to an out-of-control signal.
Hold the tool, confirm the measurement is real, look for what changed, check the lots run since the last good point, follow the written action plan.

I put the tool on hold so no more lots go through. Then I check the data is real: remeasure and check the metrology tool. If it holds up, I look for what changed: recent maintenance, a new gas bottle, chamber hours, recipe edits. I review lots run since the last good point and follow the out-of-control action plan, writing up what I found.
Yield drops and the failing dies form a ring near the wafer edge. How do you find the cause?
How you use wafer maps and lot history to trace a yield loss.
A pattern means a systematic cause, not random defects. Commonality analysis across tools and chambers, then confirmation with data or a split.

A ring says systematic, not random particles. I run a commonality analysis: which tools, chambers and recipes did the bad lots share that the good lots did not. Edge rings often point to a step with uneven results from center to edge, like etch, deposition or edge bead removal. I check that step's uniformity data and confirm with a split lot before changing anything.
You find that a lot was run with the wrong recipe on your tool. What do you do?
How you handle a misprocessing mistake, including your own.
Hold and report at once, find out how far it went, rework only where possible, send the rest to disposition, then fix the cause.

I hold the lot and tell my supervisor and the lot owner right away, not after I have a fix. Then I find which step went wrong and how far the lot got. If it was a litho step, the resist can usually be stripped and reworked. If it went through etch or implant, it goes to disposition. Then I fix what allowed it, like a recipe selection with no check.
A lot is slightly out of spec and production is pushing you to release it. How do you handle it?
Your judgement under schedule pressure.
It goes to formal disposition with the facts, not a quiet release. The decision is documented by the people who own it.

It is not my call alone, and it should not be. I put the facts in front of the review board or whoever owns disposition: how far out it is, what it may do to yield or reliability, and any past data on similar lots. They may approve a waiver or scrap it. What I will not do is release it quietly because the line is waiting.
You want to change an etch recipe to improve uniformity. How do you get from idea to production?
How you run a process change with data and proper control.
A designed experiment, a split lot through to yield, then the formal change process with sign-offs. No undocumented recipe edits.

I start with data showing the problem and a theory for it. Then a designed experiment on test wafers, changing pressure, power and gas flow together so I can see how they interact. The best setting goes on a split lot, half old recipe and half new, through electrical test and yield. Only then do I file the change through the formal change process, with sign-offs.
Besides a point outside the control limits, which patterns on an SPC chart make you act?
Whether you know the run rules that catch a shift before a point leaves the limits.
Names run rules such as a run of points on one side of the center line or a steady trend, and knows that more rules also mean more false alarms.

I use Western Electric style rules: two of three points beyond two sigma on the same side, four of five beyond one sigma on the same side, or eight in a row on one side of the center line. A steady trend also gets a look. Each rule I add catches shifts sooner but raises false alarms, so I choose the set per chart.
Before you put a new metrology recipe on an SPC chart, how do you know the gauge is good enough?
Whether you check measurement error before trusting the data it produces.
A gauge R&R study comparing measurement spread to the tolerance and process spread, with common guides like under 10% good and over 30% not acceptable.

I run a gauge R&R: the same wafers measured several times, on different days and by different operators or tools. I compare the measurement spread to the spec window and to the process spread. Under about 10% of tolerance is good. Over 30% means the chart would mostly show gauge noise. I also check bias against a reference wafer.
Why does a large die yield worse than a small die on the same process?
Your grasp of how defect density turns into yield.
Random killer defects hit bigger dies more often. The simple Poisson model gives yield as e to the minus die area times defect density.

If killer defects land at random, the chance a die escapes them falls as its area grows. The simple Poisson model says yield equals e to the power of minus area times defect density. Double the area and the yield is squared: 90% becomes 81%. Real defects cluster, so other models fit better, but the lesson holds: cutting defect density helps big dies most.
How do you run a particle monitor on a process tool, and what number do you look at?
Whether you know how tool cleanliness is measured in practice.
Bare monitor wafers scanned before and after a pass through the tool, judged on adders, not the total count, at a set size threshold.

I scan clean bare wafers on a laser surface inspection tool, run them through the chamber or the handler, then scan again with the same recipe and size threshold. The number that matters is the adders: particles after minus particles before. I chart adders per chamber, and the map often points to the source, like a cluster near a robot contact point.
A lot sat past its queue-time limit between pre-clean and the furnace. What do you do?
How you handle a time-sensitive process window when it is missed.
Knows why the limit exists, such as native oxide regrowth and contamination, holds the lot, and follows the approved rework rule instead of running it as is.

The limit exists because after the HF clean the bare silicon starts growing native oxide and picking up contamination, which hurts the film that comes next. I put the lot on hold, check the spec for the allowed rework, often a repeat of the pre-clean, and get it done. Then I find out why it waited: a tool down, dispatch, or a limit nobody could see.
Why would you add center points to a two-level factorial experiment?
Your understanding of how a DOE is built, not just run.
Center points test for curvature and estimate pure error, and spreading them through the run order shows drift during the experiment.

A two-level design assumes the response is a straight line between the low and high settings. Center points check that: if their average sits far from the average of the corner runs, there is curvature. Repeating them gives me pure error without replicating every run, and spreading them through the run order shows whether the chamber drifted during the test.
You need to screen six recipe factors and you have about sixteen wafers. How do you design it?
Whether you can trade experiment size against what the results can tell you.
A fractional factorial with a clear grasp of resolution and aliasing, a randomized run order, and a follow-up plan for the factors that matter.

A full two-level factorial on six factors needs 64 runs. A 16-run quarter fraction gives resolution IV: main effects are clear of two-factor interactions, but those interactions are confounded with each other. I randomize the run order, then do a small follow-up on the two or three factors that matter to untangle their interactions.
Your run-to-run controller keeps etch depth on target, but the etch time it sets has crept up for weeks. Is that a problem?
Whether you see what an automatic control loop can hide.
Yes: the controller is masking chamber drift. Chart the controller outputs with their own limits, then find and fix the cause.

Yes. The output looks fine because the controller compensates, but a rising etch time means the etch rate is falling, maybe from chamber wall buildup, a worn part or a gas flow change. I put the adjustments themselves on a chart with limits, so a drifting chamber alarms early, and I schedule the clean or part check now rather than when it runs out of range.
Five lots fail final test with the same signature. How do you find the step that caused it, and which other lots do you hold?
How you run an excursion: finding the source and containing the material.
Commonality analysis across tool, chamber, reticle and time, then holding every lot that passed the suspect tool since its last good check, not just the five.

I pull the process history of the bad lots and the good lots around them and look for what only the bad ones share: a tool, a chamber, a reticle, a time window. Say it is chamber B on one etcher since Tuesday. I hold every lot that ran there since the last good monitor, including lots still in process, and check them inline before release.
A split showed a 3% yield gain, you released the change, and production yield did not move. What could have gone wrong?
Whether you can find the flaw in your own experiment.
Looks at sample size, confounding, wafer selection and differences between the test tool and the fleet, and admits the first result may have been noise.

First I ask if the gain was ever real: with one lot, 3% can be wafer-to-wafer noise. Then confounding: did the split wafers sit in better slots, or run on a chamber the rest of the fleet does not match? Was the change applied the same way on every tool? Next time I spread splits over several lots and chambers and size the test for the gain I need to see.

senior-accountant.heading: Senior and staff accountant questions
qs: A December utility bill arrives in January. What entries do you book, and when?
Whether you know accrual entries and cutoff in practice, not just in theory.
Accrue the estimate in December, reverse it in January, and let the real invoice settle the difference.

In December I debit utilities expense and credit accrued liabilities for my best estimate, based on recent bills or usage. I set the entry to reverse on January 1. When the invoice arrives, AP books it to expense as usual, and the reversal cancels the accrual, so only the small true-up lands in January.
A vendor bills $12,000 in January for a one-year software subscription. How do you record it?
Your handling of prepaid expenses and their monthly amortization.
Book it to a prepaid asset, expense it evenly over the service period, and keep a schedule that ties to the balance sheet.

I debit prepaid expenses and credit accounts payable for $12,000. Each month I debit software expense and credit prepaid for $1,000. I keep a prepaid schedule by vendor, with start and end dates, and at close I check that its total matches the general ledger balance.
How do you decide whether a purchase is capitalized or expensed?
Whether you apply a capitalization policy with judgement.
Future benefit beyond a year, above the policy threshold, including costs to get it ready for use; repairs are expensed, improvements capitalized.

I capitalize it if it benefits more than one year and is above our capitalization threshold. Cost includes shipping and installation, not just the invoice. Routine repairs that keep an asset working are expensed; upgrades that extend its life or add capacity are capitalized. Depreciation starts when the asset is placed in service.
How do you record the allowance for credit losses and a write-off?
Your grasp of receivable reserves and their journal entries.
Expense hits when the allowance is set or adjusted; a write-off against the allowance has no new expense.

Under the current standard I estimate expected losses using history, current conditions and reasonable forecasts, often by aging bucket. I debit credit loss expense and credit the allowance. When a customer account is written off, I debit the allowance and credit receivables, so there is no new expense. If cash later comes in, I reverse the write-off and record the receipt.
Walk me through the five steps of revenue recognition under ASC 606.
Whether you know the revenue standard well enough to apply it to a contract.
All five steps in order, with control transfer as the trigger, and an example of splitting a bundle.

Identify the contract, identify the performance obligations, set the transaction price, allocate it to each obligation by relative standalone selling price, and recognize revenue when or as control passes. For a license sold with a year of support, I usually recognize the license part at delivery and the support part evenly over the year.
How does a lessee account for an office lease under ASC 842?
Your knowledge of lease accounting, which every close now touches.
Right-of-use asset and lease liability on the balance sheet; straight-line cost for operating leases, interest plus amortization for finance leases.

For a lease longer than 12 months I record a right-of-use asset and a lease liability at the present value of remaining payments, using the rate in the lease if known, otherwise usually our incremental borrowing rate. An operating lease shows one straight-line lease cost. A finance lease splits into amortization and interest.
Intercompany balances between two subsidiaries do not eliminate at month-end. How do you find the cause?
How you troubleshoot a consolidation problem methodically.
Compare both sides transaction by transaction and check the usual causes: timing, currency rates and miscoding.

I pull both entities' intercompany detail for the month and match them line by line. The usual causes are timing, where one side booked a charge the other has not; different exchange rates on each side; or an entry coded to the wrong entity or account. I fix the entries, then push for one cutoff date and one rate source so it does not recur.
The auditor proposes an adjustment you believe is wrong. How do you handle it?
How you work with auditors when you disagree.
Ask for their reasoning, answer with documentation and the standard, involve the controller, and stay professional.

First I ask them to walk me through their logic, because sometimes they have seen something I missed. If I still disagree, I write a short memo with the facts, the support and the guidance I relied on, and review it with my controller before we meet the auditor. The goal is the right answer, not winning the argument.
You find a $40,000 expense that was missed in last quarter's reported numbers. What do you do?
Your judgement on prior-period errors and whether you escalate them.
Confirm the facts, tell the controller quickly, assess materiality together, correct properly and fix the root cause.

I confirm the error and gather the invoice and dates, then tell my controller the same day. We assess materiality, both the size and qualitative factors. If immaterial, we usually correct it in the current period with a clear memo; if material, the prior statements may need revising, which leadership and the auditors decide. Then I fix the step that let it slip.
On the last day of close, a manager asks you to reverse a $50,000 accrual to hit the forecast, with no support. What do you do?
Your integrity and how you handle pressure on journal entries.
No entry without a documented basis; ask for the reason, explain the risk calmly, and escalate if pushed.

I ask what changed, because if the obligation really went away there should be support, like a credit memo or a canceled order. If there is, I document it and post. If there is not, I explain that I cannot book it and why, since an unsupported entry is a control failure. If the pressure continues, I take it to the controller or CFO, or the ethics line.
What is a reversing entry, and when would you set an accrual to auto-reverse?
Whether you use reversing entries to keep accruals clean from one month to the next.
A clear definition, a typical use like accrued expenses, and the risk of double counting when a reversal is missed.

A reversing entry undoes an accrual on the first day of the next period. If I accrue $8,000 of December legal fees, I set it to reverse on January 1. When the invoice is posted to expense in January, the reversal offsets it, so January carries only its own cost. The main risk is a manual accrual nobody reverses; then the expense is counted twice.
Three years into a 10-year life, management decides a $70,000 machine will last only 7 years in total. How do you account for that?
Whether you know a change in estimate is handled going forward, not by restating.
Treats it as a change in accounting estimate, spreads the remaining book value over the remaining life, and does not touch prior periods.

That is a change in estimate, so it is prospective. With straight-line and no salvage, book value after three years is $49,000. The new remaining life is four years, so depreciation becomes $12,250 a year from now on. I do not restate past years. I document the basis for the new life and disclose the effect if it is material.
We owe a European vendor 100,000 euros, booked at 1.08 dollars per euro. At month-end the rate is 1.10. What do you record?
Your understanding of remeasuring foreign currency payables under US GAAP.
Revalues the payable at the month-end rate and books the $2,000 transaction loss to income, assuming the dollar is the functional currency.

The payable was recorded at $108,000. At the month-end rate it is $110,000, so I debit foreign exchange loss $2,000 and credit accounts payable $2,000. The loss goes to the income statement. When we pay, any further rate difference is booked as a gain or loss on settlement.
How do you review a reconciliation prepared by a staff accountant?
How you review someone else's work with care rather than just signing it.
Ties both sides to their sources, questions old or unsupported reconciling items, looks for plugs, and gives feedback the preparer can learn from.

I tie the balance to the general ledger and the other side to its source, like the bank statement or subledger. Then I read every reconciling item: does it have support, and how old is it? Anything older than about 60 days needs a reason and a plan to clear it. I look for round-number plugs. If I find a problem, I send it back with a note on what to fix, not fix it silently.
The accrued liabilities balance has grown every month for six months, but activity has not. What do you check?
How you trace a balance that drifts upward without a business reason.
Pulls the detail by accrual, looks for stale or unreversed items and invoices posted to expense instead of against the accrual, then fixes the process.

I pull the accrual detail line by line and age it. Usually I find accruals that were never reversed, or invoices that were coded to expense while the accrual stayed open, so the cost hit twice. Sometimes a recurring accrual continued after a contract ended. I release the stale items with support, and I make those accruals auto-reverse going forward.
The auditors picked 25 payables for testing, and you cannot find the invoice for one of them. What do you do?
Your honesty and resourcefulness in audit support when evidence is missing.
Tells the auditors early, looks for other valid evidence, and never creates or alters documents to fill the gap.

I tell the auditors right away rather than letting it sit until the deadline. Then I look for other evidence: the purchase order, the receiving report, the payment record and the vendor's statement, and I ask the vendor for a copy of the invoice. If the liability still cannot be supported, I treat it as a possible error and look at the vendor's other entries.
Our books close December 31. In February, before the statements are issued, a customer who owed us $90,000 goes bankrupt, and a fire destroys a warehouse. How do you treat each?
Whether you know the two types of subsequent events under ASC 855.
Adjusts the December statements for the bankruptcy, since the customer's weakness existed at year end; discloses the fire, a new condition, without adjusting.

The bankruptcy usually reflects a financial condition that existed at December 31, so I adjust the allowance for credit losses in the December numbers. The fire is a new event after year end, so I do not adjust the balances. If it is material, I disclose what happened and an estimate of its financial effect, or say that one cannot be made.
Legal counsel says we will probably lose a lawsuit, and the loss will be between $200,000 and $500,000, with no amount more likely than another. What do you book?
Your knowledge of loss contingency rules under ASC 450.
Accrues because the loss is probable and estimable, uses the low end of the range when no best estimate exists, and discloses the possible extra loss.

A loss that is probable and can be reasonably estimated must be accrued. When no amount in the range is a better estimate, US GAAP says to accrue the minimum, so I book $200,000. I disclose the nature of the case and that the loss could be up to $300,000 more. If the loss were only reasonably possible, I would disclose it without an accrual.
You notice that one person can create, post and approve manual journal entries. What is the risk, and what do you propose?
How you think about internal controls over journal entries and management override.
Names the risk of undetected error or fraud and proposes segregation of duties, required support, and a review that fits the team's size.

The risk is that an error or a fraudulent entry goes through with nobody else seeing it. I would set the system so a preparer cannot approve their own entry and require support attached to every manual entry. In a small team where full separation is hard, the controller reviews a monthly report of all manual entries, including those posted late or by unusual users.

senior-software-engineer.heading: Senior software engineer questions
qs: What does owning a feature end to end mean to you?
Whether you see ownership as more than writing the code.
Covering the problem, design, rollout, monitoring and follow-up fixes, and telling people when plans change.

It starts before code: I make sure I understand the problem and who it is for. Then come design, the work plan, tests, rollout and the dashboards that tell me it works. It ends weeks after launch, when the numbers look right and the bugs are fixed. If a date slips, I am the one who tells people.
What goes into a design document, and when is one worth writing?
Whether you can make a technical decision clear to others before building it.
The problem, goals and non-goals, options with trade-offs, and the choice. Worth writing when a change is costly to reverse or touches other teams.

I write one when a change is hard to undo or affects other teams. It states the problem, what is in and out of scope, two or three options with their costs, the chosen one and why, plus the rollout plan and risks. I keep it short and send it to the people affected, because a review catches mistakes while they are cheap to fix on paper.
How do you split a large feature into pieces your team can ship?
How you plan big work so it delivers value early and stays low risk.
Thin slices that each work and can be released, often behind a flag, with the riskiest unknown tackled first.

I look for thin vertical slices: each one goes from the screen to the database and works on its own, even if it does little. I put the riskiest unknown first, like a new payment provider, so surprises come early. Unfinished parts stay behind a feature flag, so we merge small changes every day instead of one huge branch at the end.
How do you release a risky change to production?
Your habits for limiting the damage when a release goes wrong.
Small steps behind a flag or a canary release, clear health metrics, and a rollback planned before launch.

I decide in advance which metrics say it is healthy, like error rate and response time, and how I will roll back. Then I ship it switched off behind a feature flag, turn it on for internal users, then for a small percentage of traffic, and widen it step by step. If the numbers move the wrong way, I turn the flag off first and investigate after.
A test fails now and then for no clear reason. What do you do about it?
Whether you treat flaky tests as real bugs rather than noise.
Reproducing it and finding the cause, often timing, shared state or test order. Quarantining it with an owner if needed, never just rerunning forever.

A flaky test teaches people to ignore red builds, so I take it seriously. I run it many times in a loop, alone and with the full suite, to find the pattern. Usual causes are timing, data shared between tests, or a dependence on order or the clock. Sometimes it is a real race condition in the code. If the fix takes time, I quarantine it with a ticket and an owner.
A junior engineer on your team has been stuck on a task for three days and has not asked for help. What do you do?
How you support less experienced colleagues without taking the work away from them.
Reaching out early and privately, asking questions that guide them, and making it normal to ask for help, without taking over the task.

I would ask them to walk me through where they are, in private and without blame. I ask questions instead of giving the answer, so they find the next step themselves.
