PowerShell by itself is normal admin work. Word, Excel or Outlook launching it is the classic sign of a malicious macro or exploited document. I pull the full process tree, the document that was open, where it came from, and what the child process did next: network calls, files written, new scheduled tasks.
What traces does PsExec-style lateral movement leave on the target host?
Your knowledge of how lateral movement looks in Windows logs.
A network logon from the source host, use of the ADMIN$ share, and a new service installed, logged as event 7045, right after.

On the target I expect a type 3 network logon in event 4624 from the source host, a file copied through the ADMIN$ share, and a new service in the System log, event 7045, often named PSEXESVC. Attackers rename it, so I key on a service created right after a remote admin logon, not on the name.
What is Kerberoasting, and how would you detect it?
Whether you understand a common Active Directory attack and its signals.
Requesting service tickets to crack service-account passwords offline; watch event 4769 for RC4 tickets and one user asking for many services.

Any domain user can request a Kerberos service ticket for an account with a service principal name. Part of it is encrypted with that account's password hash, so the attacker cracks it offline. In event 4769 I look for RC4 encryption, type 0x17, and one account requesting many services in minutes. Long passwords or managed service accounts cut the risk.
Event 1102 shows up on a domain controller. What does it mean, and what do you do?
How you treat signs that someone is covering their tracks.
The Security log was cleared; treat it as high severity, identify the account, and rebuild the timeline from copies already forwarded elsewhere.

1102 means the Security audit log was cleared, and the event records the account that did it. On a domain controller that is serious unless a planned change explains it. I confirm with the admins, use the copies already forwarded to the SIEM to rebuild what happened before the clear, and review that account's other activity.
You see vssadmin deleting shadow copies on a file server at 2 a.m. How do you respond?
Whether you recognize a ransomware precursor and act fast.
Treats it as ransomware about to run: contains at once, then scopes other hosts and the account used, and protects backups.

Deleting shadow copies removes easy recovery, and ransomware often does it just before encrypting. I isolate the server through the EDR, disable the account that ran the command, and wake the incident lead. Then I search for the same command and account on other hosts, and make sure backups are out of the attacker's reach.
The owner of a revenue-critical server refuses to let you isolate it during an active incident. How do you handle it?
Your judgement when security risk and business impact pull apart.
States the risk plainly, offers partial containment, escalates through the incident plan, and documents who accepted the risk.

I explain what I see and what can happen if we wait, in business terms. If full isolation is off the table, I propose partial steps: block the bad IPs, disable the compromised account, restrict outbound traffic. If we still disagree, I escalate through the incident plan, since a named owner must make that call, and I write down who accepted the risk.
Walk me through how you would build a threat hunt from scratch.
How you turn an idea into a structured, repeatable hunt.
Starts with a testable hypothesis tied to a technique, confirms the data exists, defines normal, and ends with a detection or a documented gap.

I start with a hypothesis, like: an attacker is using scheduled tasks for persistence on our servers. I confirm we log task creation, pull 30 days of it, and stack it by name, author and command to find rare entries. I check the outliers with system owners. Either way, the hunt ends with a new detection or a note on a logging gap.
How would you prove that a detection rule actually catches what it claims to?
Whether you test detections instead of trusting them.
Safely simulates the technique in an approved setting, confirms the alert fires end to end, tries variations, and retests after changes.

I run the technique itself, in a lab or on an approved host, with a known test script that mimics it safely. Then I check the whole path: the log was created, reached the SIEM, the rule fired and the ticket landed in the queue. I try a simple variation, like a renamed binary, and rerun the test after any rule or log source change.

social-media.heading: Social media manager questions
qs: What is the difference between reach and impressions, and which do you put in a report?
Whether you know the basic numbers and use them honestly.
Reach counts unique accounts and impressions count total views. You pick the metric that fits the goal and say how it is defined.

Reach is how many different accounts saw a post. Impressions count every view, so one person seeing it three times is three impressions. For awareness I lead with reach, because repeat views can make impressions look big. Each platform defines them a little differently, so I compare within a platform, not across platforms.
Walk me through how you build a month's content calendar.
How you plan content instead of posting day to day.
Starts from goals and key dates, sets content pillars and a mix of formats, and leaves room for trends and approvals.

I start with the business dates: launches, sales and holidays that matter to our audience. Then I map three or four content pillars, like product, how-to and community, across the weeks for each platform. I plan formats and who makes what, and set approval deadlines a week ahead. I also leave a few open slots each week for trends or posts that react to the news.
How do you plan the first three seconds of a short video?
Your craft with short-form video, where viewers decide in seconds.
A clear hook up front, made for viewers who watch with the sound off, and a payoff that is delivered rather than teased forever.

Many people swipe away in the first seconds, so the hook goes first. I show the result, ask the question or start in the middle of the action, not with a logo. I put a short line of text on screen and add captions, because plenty of people watch with the sound off. Then I check the retention graph. If people drop at second two, the hook is what I test next.
We want to use a trending song in a post on the brand account. Can we?
Whether you know the music rights rules for business accounts.
Knows that popular songs on an app are often not licensed for brand use. Uses the platform's commercial library, licensed music or original audio instead.

Not always. Many trending songs are licensed for personal accounts, not for brand marketing. A business account can get the post muted or face a claim from the rights holder. I check the platform's commercial music library first. If the song is not there, I use licensed stock music or original audio and copy the trend's format instead of the track.
A creator we paid posts about our product without saying it is sponsored. What do you do?
Whether you know the FTC disclosure rules and act on them.
Asks for a clear, up-front disclosure right away, knows the brand shares responsibility, and fixes the process so it does not happen again.

I contact the creator the same day. I ask them to add a clear disclosure, like #ad or the platform's paid partnership label, at the start of the caption or in the video itself, not hidden in a pile of hashtags. Under FTC guidance the brand is responsible too. So I log it, put disclosure terms in every brief, and check each post before we share it.
A customer tags us in an angry post: their order is two weeks late. How do you reply?
How you handle a complaint in front of everyone.
Replies fast and like a person in public, moves personal details to private messages, and comes back to close the loop.

I answer publicly within the hour, in plain words: we are sorry, we are looking into it now, please send us your order number by direct message. I never ask for personal details in the comments. Then I work with customer service to get an answer and reply in private. Once it is solved, I add a short public note so others can see it was handled.
When do you hide or delete a comment, and when do you leave it up?
Your judgement in moderating a community.
Follows a written policy: removes spam, hate, threats and private data, and leaves honest criticism up and answers it.

I work from a written moderation policy. Spam, scams, slurs, threats and anyone's personal information come down, and serious threats go to the right team. Honest criticism stays up, even when it is harsh. Deleting it looks like hiding and often makes it louder. I answer it instead, and I keep a log of what we removed and why.
Our engagement fell by 40% this month. How do you find out why?
How you diagnose a drop in numbers instead of guessing.
Checks tracking and definitions first, then splits by platform, format and post, compares reach with engagement rate, and looks for outside causes.

First I check the drop is real: same metric, same date range, no tracking change. Then I split by platform and format. If reach fell but the rate per viewer held, the problem is distribution, maybe fewer posts or fewer videos. If reach held and the rate fell, it is the content. I also check outside causes, like the season or a news cycle, before I change the plan.
A major tragedy is in the news, and we have cheerful posts scheduled for today. What do you do?
Whether you think about timing and tone when the world changes.
Pauses all scheduled posts and ads at once, reviews them with leadership, and resumes only when the tone fits.

I pause every scheduled post right away. I check paid ads too, because those keep running on their own. Then I go through the queue with my manager and ask: could any of this look careless today? We usually hold for a day or two. We only post a statement if the event really touches our company or community. Otherwise, staying quiet is the respectful choice.
What do you make sure is in a creator contract before anything is filmed?
Whether you protect both the brand and the creator with clear terms.
Deliverables and dates, review rounds, disclosure, usage rights and how long they last, paid amplification, exclusivity and payment terms.

The deliverables, posting dates and how many rounds of review we get. Clear disclosure requirements. Usage rights: can we repost the video or run it as an ad, on which channels and for how long, and can we run ads through the creator's handle. Any exclusivity with competitors and how long it lasts. And payment terms, plus what happens if a post is late or taken down.
How do you calculate engagement rate, and what do you divide by?
Whether you know the metric well enough to compare posts and accounts fairly.
Names the denominator and why: reach for post quality, followers for comparing accounts, and the same formula every month.

I add up likes, comments, shares and saves, then divide by the post's reach. That shows how the people who saw it reacted. To compare our account with a competitor I divide by followers, since their reach is private. Whichever I use, I write it in the report and never switch mid-year, or the trend means nothing.
How do you make a post work for people who use screen readers or watch with the sound off?
Whether accessibility is part of how you publish, not an afterthought.
Concrete habits: alt text, checked captions, CamelCase hashtags, few emojis, and key information never only inside an image.

Every image gets alt text that says what matters in it, not just “photo.” Videos get captions I check by hand, because auto captions miss brand names. I write hashtags in CamelCase so a screen reader says the words separately, keep emojis few and at the end because each is read aloud by name, and never put key details only inside an image.
Who should have access to the brand accounts, and how do you set that up?
How you protect the accounts from lockouts, leaks and former staff or agencies.
Role-based access through each platform's business tools, two-factor on every login, no shared passwords, and access removed the day someone leaves.

People get access through each platform's business settings with the lowest role they need, so an agency can draft posts but not change ownership. Two-factor authentication is on for every login, recovery goes to a company address, and passwords live in a password manager. When someone leaves, I remove access that day, and I review the list every quarter.
A post with the wrong sale price has been live for three hours and has 200 comments. What do you do?
How you fix a public mistake without making it bigger.
Acts fast, gets a business decision on honoring the price, corrects openly, and closes the gap in the approval process.

First I ask the sales lead whether we honor the price for people who already bought, because that shapes every reply. Then I post a clear correction, pin a comment on the original and answer the top questions plainly. I would rather correct in public than quietly delete a post people have already screenshotted. Afterward I add a price check to our approval step.
We want a giveaway: follow us, comment and tag a friend to win. What do you check first?
Whether you know the basic legal and platform rules for promotions.
Knows that prize plus chance plus required payment is an illegal lottery, that official rules are needed, and that each platform has promotion terms.

In the US, a prize plus chance plus a required payment makes it an illegal lottery, so entry must be free. I draft official rules with eligibility, dates, how the winner is picked and the prize value, and legal reviews them. I follow the platform's promotion terms, such as stating it does not sponsor the giveaway. Some states also require registration for large prizes.
Our CEO wants every employee to post about the new product on their personal accounts. Any concerns?
Whether you know that FTC disclosure rules cover employees, not only creators.
Employees have a material connection and must disclose it in the post; posts must be honest opinions, voluntary, and free of unproven claims.

It can work, but under the FTC's Endorsement Guides an employee praising our product has a material connection, so they must say clearly, in the post itself, that they work here. I would give staff a short guide: disclose, say only what you really think, and do not repeat claims we cannot back up. I would keep it voluntary and keep staff off review sites.
Legal wants to approve every reply we post, and replies now take a full day. How do you fix that?
How you balance speed and risk in community management.
Proposes tiers agreed with legal: pre-approved answers for common cases, team replies for routine ones, legal only for defined high-risk topics.

I would sort a month of comments by type together with legal. Common questions like shipping or returns get approved answers we can post at once. We agree on a short list that must go to legal, such as injury claims, lawsuits or data issues, with a one-hour target. The team answers everything else. I report response times monthly so both sides see it working.
Leadership thinks organic social does not drive sales. How do you show what it does?
How you connect social to business results when click tracking misses much of it.
Combines several signals, such as tagged links, codes, checkout surveys and before-and-after tests, and is honest about what each one misses.

Last-click reports miss people who see a post, share it in a private message and buy days later. So I add UTM tags, the tracking codes on links, to every link, use a social-only discount code, and ask “how did you hear about us” at checkout. I also compare sales in weeks with and without a push on one product. Together they give a fair range, not a guess.
A video claiming our product made someone sick is spreading fast. Walk me through your first hour.
How you lead in a crisis: facts first, the right people, one clear voice.
Does not argue or delete; pauses scheduled posts, escalates, saves evidence, and posts a short holding statement while facts are checked.

I pause scheduled posts and alert the crisis group: communications, legal, product safety and customer care. I save copies of the video and comments. We do not call it false until product safety has checked. Within the hour we post a short holding line: we have seen it, we take it seriously, we are looking into it, and here is how to reach us. Then I track how it spreads.

software-architect.heading: Architect (software and systems) questions
qs: What is an architecture decision record, and what goes in one?
Whether you write decisions down so teams can follow the reasoning later.
A short record of one decision: the context, the options, the choice and its consequences, kept with the code and replaced by a new record when the decision changes.

It is a one-page note about one significant decision. I write the context, the options we weighed, what we chose and what it costs us. It lives in the repository next to the code. If we change our mind, I write a new record that supersedes the old one, so a new engineer can see why things are the way they are.
When would you keep a monolith instead of splitting it into microservices?
Whether you choose an architecture for the problem, not for fashion.
Microservices buy independent deployment for many teams at the cost of network failures, split data and more operations. Without that need, a modular monolith wins.

If one or two teams own it, it deploys fine and the domain boundaries are still moving, I keep it. I make it modular inside, with clear module borders and no reaching into another module's tables. When one part needs its own release pace or scaling, or teams keep stepping on each other, that module is the first candidate to split out.
A stakeholder says the system must be fast and secure. How do you turn that into something you can design for?
How you turn vague wishes into measurable quality requirements.
Concrete scenarios with numbers: which action, under what load, measured how, and a ranking for when two goals pull against each other.

I ask for scenarios. Fast becomes: the search page answers in under 300 milliseconds for 95% of requests with 2,000 users at peak. Secure becomes: who may see a customer's address, and how we would know if someone else did. Then I rank them with the stakeholder, because they often conflict, and I check the design against each one.
What does Conway's law mean for how you draw service boundaries?
Whether you see that team structure and system structure shape each other.
Systems tend to copy the communication lines of the organization, so boundaries should match how teams are split, or the teams should change to fit the design.

Conway's law says a system's design tends to mirror how the people building it communicate. If two teams must coordinate on every change to one service, that boundary will hurt. So I draw services around business areas one team can own end to end. When the design I want does not fit the teams, I raise the team structure with leadership instead of fighting it in code.
Two services want to read and write the same database tables. What do you do?
How you handle data ownership between services.
One owner per piece of data. Others go through its API or keep a copy fed by events, so a schema change does not break teams that never agreed to it.

I push back on shared tables. A shared schema ties the two teams together: one renames a column and the other breaks at runtime. I pick the service that owns that data's rules and make it the only writer. The other reads through its API, or keeps its own read copy updated from events if it needs speed or must keep working when the owner is down.
When would you use events between services instead of direct calls, and what does it cost you?
Whether you know the trade-offs of asynchronous messaging.
Events decouple teams and absorb load spikes, but bring delayed consistency, duplicate or out-of-order messages, and harder tracing of one request.

I use events when the sender does not need an answer right away, such as telling billing and email that an order was placed. The sender keeps working even if a consumer is down. The cost: data is briefly out of sync, consumers must handle duplicates and messages that arrive late or out of order, and following one request across services needs correlation IDs.
The business wants data written in two regions to stay consistent and always available, even when the link between regions fails. What do you tell them?
Whether you understand the CAP trade-off and can explain it to non-engineers.
During a network split you must pick: refuse some writes to stay consistent, or accept them and reconcile later. The choice can differ by type of data.

I tell them we cannot have both while the link is down; that is the CAP trade-off. So we choose per kind of data. Account balances should accept writes in only one region until the link is back. A shopping cart can accept writes in both and merge later. I show what each choice means for users during an outage, so the business decides knowingly.
A team brings a design to review that you think is wrong, and they ship in three weeks. How do you handle it?
How you use review authority without blocking teams or rubber-stamping.
Separating what is risky and hard to undo from personal taste. Blocking only the first, offering a fix that fits the deadline, and recording the rest.

First I ask questions to understand why they chose it; sometimes they know something I do not. Then I sort my concerns. Preferences I mention and let go. If something is hard to reverse, like a public data format or a security gap, I say clearly it must change, offer the smallest change that fits their date, and write the decision down.
Walk me through replacing a large legacy system piece by piece while it stays in use.
Whether you can plan an incremental migration instead of a risky big-bang rewrite.
A routing layer in front, one slice moved at a time, old and new run side by side with results compared, and old code removed only once traffic has moved.

I put a proxy in front of the old system so callers do not care which side answers. Then I pick one slice, say invoice lookup, build it new, and send a small share of traffic to it while comparing results with the old path. When they match, I move all traffic and delete the old code. Each step can be rolled back, and the old system shrinks until we switch it off.
Tell me about an architecture decision you made that turned out wrong. How did you find out, and what did you do?
Whether you own your mistakes and change course without sunk-cost thinking.
A real decision, the signal that showed it was wrong, a measured fix, and what you changed in how you make decisions.

I once split a reporting module into five services because I expected separate teams to own them. One team ended up owning all five, and every change meant five deploys. Time from commit to release roughly doubled. I proposed merging them back, wrote a record explaining why, and now I ask who will own a service before I draw it.
What is the difference between an SLI, an SLO and an SLA, and who should own each?
Whether you can turn reliability into numbers that teams and the business agree on.
Clear definitions, and an SLO set stricter than the SLA so the team acts before a contract is broken.

An SLI is the measurement, like the share of requests answered in under 300 ms. The SLO is the target we set for it, say 99.9% over 30 days. The SLA is the promise in a contract, with penalties. Engineering owns the SLI and SLO, and the business signs the SLA. I keep the SLO tighter than the SLA so we see trouble before we owe credits.
A checkout call depends on four services, each at 99.9% availability. What availability can checkout promise?
Your grasp of how hard dependencies multiply failure.
In series the availabilities multiply, giving about 99.6%. Then ways to cut the number of hard dependencies.

If all four must answer, the chances multiply: 0.999 to the fourth power is about 99.6%. That is roughly three hours of downtime a month instead of about 43 minutes. It also assumes failures are independent, and shared infrastructure can break that. To do better I make some calls optional, like loading recommendations later, add fallbacks, or move work to a queue so checkout does not wait on it.
How do you bring security into a design review before any code exists?
Whether you treat security as part of the design, not a scan at the end.
A structured threat model on the data flow, such as STRIDE, with each finding turned into an owned design change.

I ask the team for a data flow diagram with the trust boundaries marked. Then we walk each flow through STRIDE: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. For a new upload service that found missing audit logs and no file size limit. Each finding gets an owner and a fix in the design, not a ticket for later.
A service saves an order to its database and then publishes an “order created” event. What can go wrong, and how do you fix it?
Whether you spot the dual-write problem and know a reliable pattern for it.
The two writes can diverge on a crash. A transactional outbox writes both in one transaction, and consumers handle duplicates.

If the process dies between the two steps, the order exists and nobody hears about it. If we publish first, we may announce an order that was rolled back. I use an outbox: the order and the event go into the same database in one transaction, and a relay publishes from the outbox table. Delivery is then at least once, so consumers skip duplicates by event ID.
A team orders events coming from different servers by their timestamps. What is your concern?
Your understanding of time and ordering in distributed systems.
Clocks drift even with NTP, so wall-clock time cannot order close events. Use one sequencer, version numbers or logical clocks.

Server clocks drift apart, even when synced with NTP, and a clock can jump backward. Two updates a few milliseconds apart can land in the wrong order, and the older one wins. If order matters, one place assigns it: a version number checked on write, a partition key so one log orders each customer's events, or a logical clock. Timestamps stay for display.
An order needs payment, stock and shipping, each owned by a different service. How do you keep them consistent without one big transaction?
Whether you can design a saga with compensating steps and know its trade-offs.
Local transactions plus compensating actions, orchestration or choreography chosen on purpose, and visible in-between states.

I use a saga: each service commits its own local transaction, and if a later step fails, earlier ones are undone by compensating actions, like refunding the payment and releasing the stock. With several steps I prefer an orchestrator so the flow lives in one place. Users can see in-between states, so the order shows pending, and every step is idempotent because retries will happen.
You are designing a SaaS product for many small shops and a few very large customers. How do you isolate tenants' data and load?
How you weigh cost, isolation and operations in a multi-tenant design.
Knows shared schema, schema per tenant and database per tenant, and can mix them: pooled for small tenants, dedicated for large or regulated ones.

Small shops go in shared tables with a tenant ID on every row, enforced in the data layer, for example with row-level security, not left to each query. Large or regulated customers get their own database, which isolates load and makes restores and deletion simple. Per-tenant rate limits stop one noisy customer hurting the rest. A routing layer hides the model, so we can move a tenant later.
Teams say they have twenty microservices but cannot release one without releasing five others. What do you look at?
How you diagnose a distributed monolith and remove the coupling.
Finds the source of coupling, such as shared domain libraries, breaking contract changes or bad boundaries, and fixes it so teams deploy alone.

I map which releases move together and why. Usually it is a shared library carrying domain models, API changes that are not backward compatible, or boundaries cut so one feature touches five services. The fixes: contracts that only add fields, consumer-driven contract tests in each pipeline, and merging services that always change together. The goal is that any team can deploy on its own.
With thirty teams, how do you keep the architecture you agreed on from eroding over time?
Whether you make architecture rules checkable instead of relying on reviews alone.
Automated checks in the build, such as dependency rules and latency budgets, plus templates that make the agreed way the easy way.

Rules people must remember get forgotten, so I turn the important ones into automated checks, sometimes called fitness functions. A build test fails if the web layer calls the database directly, a check flags any service reading another's schema, and the load test has a latency budget. I also give teams a service template with logging, auth and deployment already done right.
You believe the company needs a two-year platform investment that will slow features for a while. How do you get leadership to fund it?
How you build technical strategy in business terms and deliver it in steps.
Ties the case to measured costs and risks, offers real options, and plans increments that pay off early instead of a big-bang rewrite.

I start with what the current state costs in their terms: we lost 11 days of releases last quarter to environment problems, and a new team takes six weeks to ship. I present two or three options with costs and risks, including doing nothing. The plan comes in quarterly steps, each with a result they can see, so if priorities change we stop with value already delivered.

software-engineer.heading: Software engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between a unit test and an integration test, and when do you write each?
Whether you know what each kind of test can and cannot catch.
Unit tests are fast and pin down logic. Integration tests prove the parts really work together. A sensible mix, not only one kind.

A unit test checks one function or class on its own, with its dependencies replaced, so it runs in milliseconds. An integration test runs real pieces together, like my code against a real database. I write many unit tests for business logic and fewer integration tests for the seams where things usually break: queries, serialization and calls between services.
Why should you not store money in a floating-point number?
Your grasp of a basic data mistake that causes real money errors.
Binary floats cannot hold most decimal fractions exactly. Use integer cents or a decimal type, and round by one stated rule.

A float stores numbers in binary, and 0.1 has no exact binary form, so 0.1 plus 0.2 does not come out as exactly 0.3. Over many sums the cents drift. I store amounts as whole cents in an integer, or use a decimal type in the database and the language, and round in one place with a clear rule.
A teammate sends you a pull request with 2,000 changed lines. What do you do?
How you keep a review useful when a change is too big to read well.
Talking to the author, asking to split it or walking through it together, rather than skimming and approving.

I would not skim it and click approve; nobody reviews 2,000 lines well. I would ask the author for ten minutes to walk me through it, then suggest splitting it: renames and generated files in one PR, the real logic in smaller ones. If it truly must go together, I review the risky parts first and say which parts I did not check closely.
A test passes on your machine but fails about one time in ten in CI. How do you handle it?
Whether you treat a flaky test as a real bug rather than something to rerun.
Finding the cause: timing, shared state, test order or the real clock. Quarantine with an owner if needed, never an endless retry.

First I check whether the code or the test is wrong, because sometimes the flake is a real race. Common causes are sleeps instead of waiting for a condition, tests sharing data, order dependence and the real clock. I run it in a loop and in random order to reproduce it. If the fix takes time, I quarantine it with a ticket and an owner.
How do you decide whether a database index is worth adding?
Whether you weigh what an index costs as well as what it speeds up.
Looking at the actual slow query and its plan, and weighing faster reads against slower writes and extra storage.

I start from a real slow query and read its plan with EXPLAIN to see if it scans the whole table. An index on the columns it filters or sorts by usually fixes that. But every index slows inserts and updates and takes space, so on a write-heavy table I add only what a frequent query needs, then check the plan again to confirm it is used.
What is a race condition? Give me an example and how you would fix it.
Whether you can spot bugs that appear only when two things happen at once.
A clear read-then-write example and a fix that makes the step atomic, such as a conditional update or a lock.

It is a bug where the result depends on timing. Two buyers load a product with one item left; both read stock as 1, both write 0, and we sell two. I would make the change atomic in the database: subtract one only where stock is above zero, and check that one row changed. A row lock also works, at some cost in speed.
How do you store and handle dates and times for users in different time zones?
Your care with a classic source of bugs: time zones and daylight saving time.
Past moments stored in UTC and converted for display. Future local events stored as local time plus a named zone, since zone rules change.

For things that already happened, like an order time, I store a UTC timestamp and convert to the user's zone only when showing it. For a future local event, like a 9 a.m. meeting in Chicago, I store the local time and the zone name, America/Chicago, not a fixed offset, because daylight saving and zone rules can change.
How do you merge a half-finished feature into the main branch without users seeing it?
Whether you know how to ship small changes safely with feature flags.
Code behind a flag that is off by default, rolled out gradually, with a plan to remove the flag once the feature is fully live.

I put the new path behind a feature flag that is off by default, so the code ships but does not run. That lets me merge small pieces daily instead of one big risky branch. When it is ready, we turn it on for staff, then a small share of users, and watch errors. Once it is fully on, I delete the flag and the old path.
You find that a change you merged last week has been quietly saving wrong data for some users. What do you do?
How you own a mistake and limit the damage before fixing the cause.
Stop the harm first, tell people at once, measure what was affected, repair the data carefully, then add a test so it cannot recur.

First I stop the damage: revert or switch off the change, and tell my lead and the on-call engineer right away. Then I find exactly which records were hit, say 3,200 orders between two dates. I write a repair script, test it on a copy and have someone review it before running it. Last, I add the test that would have caught it and write up what happened.
Walk me through finding a memory leak in a service whose memory keeps growing until it crashes.
Your method for a slow problem that no single error message explains.
Confirming the pattern on graphs, comparing heap snapshots over time, and knowing the usual causes: unbounded caches, listeners, growing lists.

First I confirm it on the memory graph: steady growth that a restart resets, often tied to traffic. Then I take two heap snapshots some time apart, on a test copy if I can, and compare which objects keep growing. Usual causes are a cache with no size limit, event listeners never removed, or a global list that only grows. After the fix, I watch for flat memory.
Our service has 95% code coverage. What does that number tell you, and what does it not?
Whether you understand what a coverage metric really measures.
Coverage shows which code ran during tests, not whether the tests checked the result. It is a tool for finding gaps, not a goal.

It tells me which lines ran during the tests, nothing more. A test with no assertions can still raise coverage. I use the report to find untested areas, like error branches. To judge test strength, I check that tests fail when I break the code on purpose; mutation testing tools automate that.
How should a system store user passwords?
Your grasp of a basic security rule that every engineer must get right.
Hashed, never encrypted or plain, with a slow algorithm built for passwords and a unique salt per user. A fast general hash alone is not enough.

Never in plain text, and not encrypted, because anything encrypted can be decrypted. I hash each password with a slow algorithm made for passwords, such as Argon2 or bcrypt, with a unique random salt. A fast hash like plain SHA-256 is wrong here, because attackers can try billions of guesses per second against it.
What is the difference between offset pagination and cursor pagination, and when would you pick each?
Whether you know how list endpoints behave on large or changing data.
Offset gets slow at deep pages and skips or repeats rows when data changes. A cursor on an indexed, unique sort key avoids both but cannot jump to a page.

Offset means skip N rows, take 20. The database still reads the skipped rows, so deep pages get slow, and new inserts shift rows between pages. A cursor says: give me 20 rows after the last created_at and id I saw, using an index. It stays fast and stable, but you cannot jump to page 50. I use offset for small admin tables, cursors for feeds and APIs.
A teammate tells you an API key for a payment provider was pushed to a public repository an hour ago. What do you do?
How you act on a leaked secret, and in what order.
Revoke and replace the key first, assuming it is already compromised. Then check for misuse, clean up, and stop it from happening again.

First I revoke the key and issue a new one, because bots scan public repositories for secrets within minutes. Deleting the commit does not undo the leak. Then I check the provider's logs for calls we did not make. After that we clean the history, move the key into a secrets manager, and turn on secret scanning so the next push gets blocked.
When do you use mocks in tests, and when do you avoid them?
Your judgement about tests that stay useful as code changes.
Mock slow or unpredictable boundaries like the network or the clock. Avoid mocking your own internals, which ties tests to the code's structure.

I mock things at the edge: an outside API, the clock, random numbers. I avoid mocking my own classes, because then the test repeats the code and breaks on every refactor while still passing when the logic is wrong. For database code I run tests against a real database in a container, since a mocked query proves nothing about the SQL.
Two support agents open the same customer record and both press save. How do you stop one from silently overwriting the other?
Whether you know optimistic and pessimistic locking and when each fits.
A version check on update that detects the conflict and tells the user, or a row lock when conflicts are frequent and edits are short.

I would add a version column. The update says: set the new values and version plus one, where id matches and version is still the one I read. If zero rows change, someone saved first, so I show the agent the newer data instead of overwriting it. Locking the row with SELECT FOR UPDATE also works, but holding a lock while a person types is a bad idea.
Users save their profile, the page reloads, and they see their old data for a second or two. We read from database replicas. What is going on, and how do you fix it?
How you reason about replication lag and read-your-own-writes consistency.
Replicas trail the primary, so a fresh read misses the write. Fix it for that user's reads without sending all traffic to the primary.

The write goes to the primary, but the reload reads from a replica that has not caught up yet. I would make that user's reads go to the primary for a short window after they write, or return the saved data in the save response so the page does not need to read again. Sending every read to the primary would fix it too, but it throws away the reason we have replicas.
Logs show the database killing a transaction with a deadlock error a few times a day. Walk me through what is happening and what you change.
Your understanding of deadlocks and practical ways to prevent them.
Two transactions lock the same rows in opposite order; the database aborts one. Lock in a fixed order, keep transactions short, and retry the aborted one.

Transaction A locks row 1 and waits for row 2, while B holds row 2 and waits for row 1. The database detects the cycle and aborts one of them. I would find the two queries in the logs, then make the code lock rows in the same order, for example sorted by id. I would keep transactions short, with no network calls inside, and retry a deadlocked transaction a couple of times.
Our mobile app reads a field called user_name from our API, and we want to rename it to display_name. Many users never update the app. How do you do it?
How you change a contract when you cannot control every client.
Add the new field next to the old one, move clients over, measure who still uses the old one, and remove it only when that number is acceptable.

I never rename in one step, because old app versions would break. I add display_name and keep sending user_name with the same value. New app releases read the new field. I track requests by app version, and only when old versions drop to a level product agrees on do we stop sending user_name, ideally with a forced upgrade prompt for the rest.
Your team wants to split our monolith into microservices. How do you decide whether that is a good idea?
Your judgement on a large architecture decision and its real costs.
Starts from the problem being solved, weighs network and operational costs, and prefers small, reversible steps over a full rewrite.

I first ask what hurts today: slow deploys, teams blocking each other, one part needing to scale alone. Services bring network failures, data spread across databases and more to operate. Often clean modules inside the monolith solve the problem. If not, I would pull out one piece with a clear boundary and its own data, run it for a few months, and measure before doing more.

solar.heading: Solar energy specialist questions
qs: Which way should a fixed solar array face in the US, and at what tilt?
Whether you know the basics of array orientation and when to break the usual rule.
True south, not magnetic south, with tilt near latitude for annual yield, and awareness that rates can favor west.

In the continental US a fixed array usually does best facing true south. That is not magnetic south, so I correct the compass reading for declination. A tilt near the site's latitude gives close to the most energy over a year. If the utility pays more in the late afternoon, a west-facing array can earn more money even though it makes fewer kilowatt-hours.
How does partial shade affect a module and a string, and what do bypass diodes do?
Your grasp of how cells, modules and strings behave electrically.
Series cells limit each other, bypass diodes skip a shaded section, and module-level electronics reduce the loss.

Cells are wired in series, so one shaded cell limits the current of its whole group. A bypass diode lets current flow around that group, usually one diode per third of the module, so you lose part of the module, not all of it. The string still loses voltage. Where shade cannot be avoided, I look at optimizers or microinverters.
How do you decide how many modules go in one string?
Whether you size strings for the cold-weather voltage peak.
Voc rises in the cold; uses record low temperature and the module's coefficient to stay under the inverter and system voltage limits.

Module voltage rises as cells get colder, so the highest voltage comes on a cold, clear morning. I take the record low temperature for the site, apply the module's voltage temperature coefficient to Voc, and multiply by the number of modules in series. That total must stay under the inverter's maximum input voltage and the system voltage limit. If it does not, I drop a module.
What is rapid shutdown, and how do you verify it works?
Your knowledge of a key rooftop safety requirement in the electrical code.
Its purpose for firefighters, the 30-second voltage reduction, how it is usually achieved, and a real test at commissioning.

It lets firefighters de-energize the conductors on a roof. When the initiator is operated, conductors both outside and inside the array boundary must drop to limited voltages within 30 seconds. On most roofs today that means module-level devices or microinverters. At commissioning I operate the initiator and measure the DC voltage at the inverter to confirm it drops in time.
Walk me through the checks you do on a string before you connect it to the inverter.
How methodical you are at commissioning and whether you catch wiring faults early.
Polarity, Voc against expected, Isc with a proper tester, insulation resistance, and written records; never opening connectors under load.

With the disconnect open, I check polarity with a meter, then measure open-circuit voltage and compare it with the expected value for that many modules at today's temperature. A string reading one module low has a problem. I measure short-circuit current with a proper PV tester, run an insulation resistance test to find damaged wire, and record every value on the commissioning sheet.
A homeowner wants panels on a shingle roof with about three years of life left. What do you advise?
Your judgement in protecting the customer from a costly problem later.
Recommends reroofing first, explains the removal and reinstall cost, checks structure, and documents the advice.

I would show them what it costs to remove and reinstall the array later, which can be a large share of the original labor, against reroofing now. My advice is to replace the roof first. I also want the rafters checked by someone qualified, because the array adds load. I put the recommendation in writing, so if they still go ahead, the risk is on record.
You find that a crew mated a DC connector from one brand with a look-alike from another. Is that a problem?
Whether you spot a common installation error that causes fires.
A clear yes, the heating and arcing risk, the code rule on intermating, and a fix plus a word with the crew.

Yes. Connectors that look the same can differ in tolerances and contact materials, and a poor fit heats up and can arc years later. The code requires mated connectors to be the same type and maker or listed for mating with each other. With the circuit off, I would replace them with matched pairs using the maker's crimp tool, then explain to the crew why.
Why would you put 120 kW of panels on a 100 kW inverter?
Your understanding of DC-to-AC ratio and inverter clipping.
Panels rarely hit nameplate, clipping losses are small, the extra DC adds energy at low cost, and inverter input limits still apply.

Panels rarely reach their nameplate power because of heat, sun angle and system losses. At a 1.2 ratio the inverter clips only around the peak hours, and the extra panels add energy in the morning, the evening and on cloudy days. I model the clipping loss in the design software and check the inverter's maximum DC voltage and current before I settle on the ratio.
How do you size the conductors for a PV source circuit?
Whether you can apply the code's current factors and derating correctly.
Isc times 1.25 for irradiance, then 125% for continuous duty, a separate check after derating, and voltage drop.

I start with the string's short-circuit current and multiply by 1.25, because sunlight can exceed test conditions. That is the maximum circuit current. I size the conductor at 125% of that for continuous duty, and separately check its ampacity after corrections for ambient temperature and conduit fill. The larger result wins. Then I check voltage drop on long runs.
An energy yield report gives a P50 and a P90. What do they mean, and who cares about the gap?
Your grasp of yield uncertainty and how it affects project finance.
P50 is beaten half the time, P90 nine times in ten. Lenders often size debt on P90, so a wide gap costs the owner money.

P50 is the annual yield we expect to beat half the time. P90 is the yield we expect to beat in nine years out of ten, so it is lower. The gap comes from weather variability and model uncertainty. Lenders often size debt on P90, so a weak irradiance dataset widens the gap and can shrink the loan the owner gets.
What is backtracking on a single-axis tracker, and why does it matter?
Whether you understand row-to-row shading on utility-scale tracker plants.
Rotating rows back toward flat when the sun is low so no row shades the next, trading a little angle to avoid a large shade loss.

Early and late in the day the sun is low. If every row pointed straight at it, each row would shade the one behind. Backtracking turns the rows back toward flat so no shadow falls on the neighbor. A small angle loss beats losing whole cell groups to bypass diodes. On sloped ground you need terrain-aware backtracking or shade comes back.
A house has a 200 A busbar with a 200 A main breaker. How much PV can you back-feed through a breaker in that panel?
Your command of the NEC load-side interconnection rules.
Applies the 120% rule correctly, places the breaker at the far end of the bus, and knows the options when more capacity is needed.

Under the NEC 120% rule, 125% of inverter output current plus the main breaker can't exceed 120% of the busbar rating. 240 minus 200 leaves 40 A, so the inverter can supply at most 32 A, with its breaker at the far end of the bus from the main. For more, I'd derate the main backed by a load calculation, use a supply-side connection or upgrade the panel.
What is islanding, and how do you make sure an inverter will not do it?
Whether you know the grid-safety rules that utilities enforce on interconnection.
Explains the hazard to line workers, IEEE 1547 and UL 1741 listing, and setting the grid profile the utility requires.

Islanding is an inverter keeping part of the grid energized after the utility has gone down, so a line worker could touch a wire he believes is dead. IEEE 1547 requires the inverter to stop energizing within two seconds. I check it is listed to UL 1741, with the SB supplement where required, and that the grid profile set at commissioning matches the utility's.
How do you decide the spacing of roof attachments on a house near the coast?
How you turn wind and snow loads into a safe, code-compliant mounting layout.
Site wind speed and exposure per ASCE 7, maker span tables by roof zone, tighter spacing at edges and corners, rafters verified.

I start from the site's design wind speed, exposure and ground snow load under ASCE 7. The racking maker's tables give the maximum span between attachments for each roof zone. Edges and corners see more uplift, so spans there are shorter. I check rafter size and spacing in the attic, and I get an engineer's letter when the tables don't cover the case.
A customer with an existing 8 kW string system wants a battery. AC-coupled or DC-coupled, and why?
Your judgement on storage architecture for retrofits versus new builds.
AC-coupled for retrofits to leave the working system alone; DC-coupled suits new builds and can capture clipped energy.

For an existing system I usually go AC-coupled. The battery gets its own inverter on the AC side, so I don't touch the working PV inverter or its warranty. DC-coupled fits new builds better: one inverter, fewer conversions, and it can store energy an oversized array would clip. I'd also recheck the panel, since a second inverter adds to the backfeed.
During commissioning you trace I-V curves. What do a step in the curve and a less steep slope near Voc tell you?
Whether you can read I-V curves to find defects before handover.
A step means mismatch with a bypass diode conducting; a softer slope near Voc means added series resistance, often a bad connection.

A step means part of the string makes less current, usually shade, soiling or a cracked cell, and a bypass diode is carrying current around it. A less steep slope near Voc means higher series resistance: a loose or corroded connector, a bad crimp or damaged cell ribbons. I compare to the expected curve corrected for irradiance and cell temperature first.
An inverter throws an insulation fault every morning and clears by noon. How do you track it down?
How you find an intermittent ground fault methodically and safely.
Links the timing to dew, tests strings isolated from the inverter while still wet, splits the bad string, and names the usual causes.

Clearing as things dry points to insulation that only leaks when wet. Early, with the dew still on, I isolate each string from the inverter and test positive and negative to ground with an insulation tester. I split the low string until I find the section. The usual causes are a wire pinched under a rail, a jacket cut on a sharp edge, or water in a connector.
Three months after commissioning, a 2 MW site is producing 12% below the model and the owner is upset. How do you find out why?
How you separate weather, equipment and modeling errors, and how you report the answer.
Reruns the model with measured weather first, then checks availability, strings, clipping and soiling, and reports honestly, even its own error.

First I compare like with like: I rerun the model with on-site irradiance and temperature, not typical-year weather. If a gap remains, I check inverter downtime logs, string currents for dead strings, clipping, soiling and tracker positions. Then I review the model inputs. I tell the owner what I found and the fix, even if the error was in our own model.

solutions-architect.heading: Solutions architect questions
qs: What is the difference between a functional and a non-functional requirement?
Whether you capture more than features when you gather requirements.
Functional is what the system does. Non-functional is how well it does it: speed, uptime, security, scale. Designs often fail on the second kind.

A functional requirement says what the system must do, like 'send an invoice when an order ships.' A non-functional one says how well: respond in under two seconds, keep data in the US, handle 5,000 orders an hour. Customers volunteer the first kind. I have to ask for the second, because that is usually where a design breaks.
What do RTO and RPO mean, and how do they change a design?
Your grasp of recovery targets and what they cost.
RTO is how long you can be down, RPO is how much data you can lose. Tighter targets cost more, so the business sets them.

RTO, recovery time objective, is how long the business can be without the system after a failure. RPO, recovery point objective, is how much recent data it can afford to lose, measured in time. An RPO of 24 hours allows nightly backups. An RPO near zero needs continuous replication, and that costs real money. I ask the business owner for both numbers before I draw anything.
Walk me through how you run a first technical discovery workshop with a new customer.
How you structure a workshop and get the facts a design needs.
The right people in the room, the business goal first, then current systems, constraints and the decision process, with a written summary sent back.

Before it, I ask who will attend and make sure someone owns the business goal, not only IT. I open with what problem they are solving and how they will measure it. Then we map their current systems on a whiteboard: data sources, integrations, identity, where it runs. I close with constraints, timelines and who signs off, then send a written summary within a day.
How do you set the success criteria for a proof of concept?
Whether your proofs of concept have a clear finish line.
A few measurable criteria agreed in writing before work starts, tied to the buying decision, with a fixed end date and owners on both sides.

I agree three to five criteria with the customer in writing before we start, each one testable: 'load 10 million records in under an hour,' 'single sign-on works with their identity provider.' Each maps to a concern in the buying decision. We set an end date, name who does what on their side, and agree that meeting the criteria means we move to the next commercial step.
How do you choose between a real-time API integration and a nightly batch file?
Your judgement on integration patterns.
You start from how fresh the data must be, the volume and what the other system supports. Real time is not automatically better.

I ask how stale the data can be before it hurts someone. If a sales rep needs a stock level during a call, it has to be an API call or an event. If finance reconciles once a day, a nightly batch is simpler, cheaper and easier to rerun when it fails. I also check volume, API rate limits on their side, and who will support it at 2 a.m.
Halfway through a proof of concept, the customer keeps adding new requirements. What do you do?
How you handle scope creep without losing the deal.
You go back to the agreed criteria, log new asks separately, and trade time or scope openly with the customer's sponsor.

I go back to the success criteria we signed off. I tell the team their new asks are useful and I log them, but ask which ones change the buying decision. If one truly does, I raise it with their sponsor and my account executive: we add it and extend the end date, or swap it for a criterion that matters less. Quiet scope growth turns a two-week test into a free pilot.
The customer asks for a capability the product does not have. How do you respond?
Your honesty and creativity when there is a product gap.
No bluffing. You find the need behind the ask, offer a workaround, partner or product feedback path, and say plainly what is not there.

First I ask what they want to achieve with it, because the request is often one way to solve a broader need. Then I am direct: we do not do that today. I offer what I can: a workaround through our API, a partner tool, or a way to route it to product management. I never promise roadmap dates I cannot confirm, and I write down exactly what I said.
The customer's security team pushes back on your design late in the deal. How do you handle it?
How you work with security reviewers instead of around them.
You treat them as stakeholders: get their specific concerns, answer with data flows and documented controls, and fix real gaps.

I ask for a meeting with the reviewer, not just an email thread, and get the concerns as a list. Usually it is where data is stored, how it is encrypted in transit and at rest, and who can access it. I bring a data flow diagram and our security documentation, and loop in our security team for questionnaire answers. If they find a real gap, I adjust the design rather than argue.
Tell me about a design of yours that caused trouble after go-live. What did you do?
Whether you own your mistakes and learn from them.
Clear ownership, a fix for the customer first, then a change in how you work so it does not happen again.

I once sized an integration for average daily volume and missed that the customer ran month-end imports ten times larger. The sync fell hours behind on day one. I joined the delivery team's call, we split the import into batches as a quick fix, then moved it to a message queue that absorbs spikes. Since then I ask for peak volume, not average, in every discovery.
Your account executive wants you to tell the customer the product fits, but you think it is a poor fit. What do you do?
Your integrity under sales pressure.
You raise it privately first with evidence, look for a smaller scope that fits, and never misrepresent the product to the customer.

I talk to the rep first, privately, and show the specific requirements we cannot meet and what that means after signing: a failed rollout and a lost renewal. Often a smaller scope fits well, and I propose that. If there is no fit, I say so to the customer. A deal that fails in implementation costs the company more than the one we walk away from.
The customer wants single sign-on and automatic user setup. What do you ask their identity team, and which standards come up?
Whether you know the identity standards that come up in almost every enterprise deal.
SAML or OpenID Connect for sign-in, SCIM for provisioning, and the practical questions: which identity provider, which attributes, who owns removing users.

I ask which identity provider they use and whether they prefer SAML or OpenID Connect. SAML passes XML assertions; OIDC sits on OAuth 2.0 and uses JSON tokens. For creating and removing users I check SCIM support. Then I ask which attributes map to our roles and what happens when someone leaves, because removing access is what auditors check.
In a SaaS deal, how do you explain the shared responsibility model to a customer's risk team?
Whether you can draw the line between what the vendor secures and what the customer must still own.
The vendor runs infrastructure and application security; the customer still owns its data, user access, configuration and who gets admin rights.

I say we secure the platform: hosting, patching, the application and its encryption. They still own who gets an account, how strong the sign-in is, what data they load and how sharing is set up. Many SaaS incidents start on the customer side, like an admin account without MFA, so I put the split in a one-page table for their risk file.
The customer says they process 2 million orders a month. How do you turn that into numbers your design can use?
How you size a design from business volumes instead of guessing.
Breaks the monthly figure into peak rates, asks about seasonality and growth, and sizes for the peak with headroom, with the assumptions written down.

Two million a month is about 67,000 a day, or under 50 a minute on average, which tells me little. I ask when the peaks are: a holiday sale can run ten times the average hour. I ask about growth over three years and how many API calls each order creates. Then I size for the peak with headroom and write the assumptions down so the customer can correct them.
Their middleware retries failed calls, so our system may get the same order twice. How do you design for that?
Whether you understand retries, duplicates and idempotency in integrations.
Makes the operation idempotent with a unique key, so a repeat is recognized and returns the first result instead of creating a second record.

I assume duplicates will happen, since most delivery is at least once. Each order carries a unique key from the source system, and our side stores it. If the same key arrives again, we return the original result instead of creating a second order. I also agree with them how long keys are kept and how a real update differs from a retry.
The customer wants to load 40 million historical records in one weekend, and our API has rate limits. How do you plan it?
How you plan a large data load around platform limits.
Does the math against the limit first, uses a bulk path if one exists, handles HTTP 429 with backoff, and runs a timed test load before promising the date.

First I do the math: at the allowed rate, how many hours do 40 million records take? If it does not fit, I use the bulk import path, or load older history early in batches and only the recent delta that weekend. The loader must back off on HTTP 429 responses and be restartable. I time a test load of a million records before anyone commits to the date.
The deal is signed. What goes into the design you hand to the implementation team?
Whether your pre-sales design survives the handoff to the people who build it.
Scope, integrations, data flows, volumes, decisions with their reasons, open risks, and what was promised to the customer, so nobody rediscovers it.

A diagram of systems and data flows, each integration with its direction, method and volume, and the performance and uptime targets we agreed. Then the key decisions with the reason for each, the open risks, and a plain list of everything the customer was told during the sale. I walk the team through it live, because the promises list is where surprises come from.
A prospect asks for a free six-week proof of concept. When do you say no, or offer something else?
Your judgement on when a proof of concept is worth the team's time.
A POC only for a real technical risk, with a sponsor, a decision date and agreed criteria; otherwise a demo, a reference call or a paid pilot.

I ask what question the POC answers that a demo or a reference customer cannot. If there is a real technical risk, a sponsor and a decision date tied to it, I run it, often shorter than asked. If it is a free trial with no buyer behind it, or they are using us to price another vendor, I offer a tailored demo or a paid pilot instead.
A competitor told the customer our product does not scale. How do you respond?
How you handle a competitor's claim without attacking the competitor.
Turns the claim into the customer's own numbers and answers with evidence at their load, open to checking, without running down the rival.

I do not argue about the competitor. I ask the customer what scale they care about: users, records, transactions at peak. Then I show evidence at that size, such as a reference customer of similar volume or a test on their data, with the method open so their engineers can check it. If we have a real limit at their size, I say so and show the design that works around it.
In a workshop you said a feature works with their setup. A week later you learn it does not. What do you do?
Whether you correct your own mistakes fast and honestly.
Confirms the facts, aligns with the account executive, then tells the customer quickly with the impact and an option, instead of hoping nobody notices.

I confirm the facts with product the same day. Then I tell the account executive and we call the customer's lead within a couple of days. I say plainly what I got wrong, what it affects, and what we propose: a workaround, a roadmap date in writing, or a changed scope. Correcting it myself keeps more trust than having their engineers find it in testing.
A healthcare customer says compliance requires an on-premises install, which we do not offer. How do you work through it?
Whether you can separate a real regulatory requirement from an assumption about one.
Asks which rule and which clause, knows HIPAA does not mandate on-premises hosting, and maps their actual controls to what the cloud offering provides.

I ask which rule they mean. HIPAA, for example, does not require on-premises hosting; it requires safeguards and a business associate agreement with vendors that handle patient data. So I map their specific controls, like encryption, access logs and data location, to what we provide, with our compliance team. If an internal policy truly bans cloud, I say we are not a fit.

solutions-engineer.heading: Solutions engineer questions
qs: In a deal, where does your job end and the account executive's begin?
Whether you understand how the sales team splits the work.
The AE owns the relationship, pricing and close. The SE owns technical fit and proof. Both share discovery and the plan to win.

The account executive owns the deal: the relationship, the forecast, pricing and the contract. I own the technical win. That means showing the product fits their systems and use case, and that their engineers believe it. We plan each call together so the customer never hears two different stories.
Explain what an API is to a finance buyer who is not technical.
Whether you can make a technical idea simple without making it wrong.
A plain analogy plus why it matters to them: systems share data automatically instead of people retyping it.

An API is a set of agreed requests one piece of software can send another, like a menu at a restaurant: you order from the list and get back what you asked for. For you, it means our product can pull invoices from your accounting system on its own, so nobody exports spreadsheets and retypes numbers.
What do you want to learn on a discovery call before you build a demo?
How you turn discovery into a demo that fits the buyer.
Business pain, current process and tools, who decides, what success looks like, and technical limits. Questions, not a pitch.

I want to know what problem costs them time or money today, how they handle it now, and which tools it touches. I ask who will use it, who signs, and what a win looks like in numbers. I note limits like single sign-on or an old system we must connect to. Then the demo follows their workflow, not our feature list.
How do you set up a proof of concept so it ends in a decision?
Whether you scope a proof of concept with clear success criteria and an end date.
Written, agreed success criteria, a short fixed timeline, named people on both sides, and an agreed next step if it passes.

Before anything is installed, I write down with the customer three to five success criteria they agree are fair, like 'syncs 10,000 records overnight without errors.' We set a two to four week window, name who does what on each side, and agree that if the criteria are met, we move to paperwork. Without that, a proof of concept turns into free consulting.
In a demo, the customer asks for a feature the product does not have. What do you say?
Your honesty when the product falls short in front of a buyer.
A clear no, a question about the need behind the ask, and a workaround or roadmap path only if it is real.

I say plainly that we do not do that today. Then I ask what they are trying to achieve, because often the need is covered another way, like an export or an API call. If it truly matters, I log it with product and tell them I will come back with an honest answer, not a promise of a date I do not control.
Your live demo breaks in front of six people from the customer. What do you do?
How you recover under pressure and keep the meeting on track.
Stays calm, names it briefly, switches to a backup environment or recording, and follows up on the cause.

I say something short like 'that is not what should happen, let me switch over,' and move to my backup: a second environment or a recorded clip of the same flow. I do not debug in front of the room. Afterward I find the cause and tell our champion what it was, so it does not linger as a doubt.
A customer's developer says every call to our API returns a 401 error. How do you troubleshoot it?
Your hands-on API debugging and your grasp of HTTP status codes.
Knows 401 means authentication failed, while 403 means not permitted. Checks the key, header format, environment and token expiry, then reproduces it.

A 401 means the server did not accept who they are, so I start with credentials. I ask for the request without the secret. Is the key in the right header and format, like 'Bearer' before a token? Is it a sandbox key hitting production? Has the token expired? Then I reproduce the call myself. If it were a 403, I would look at permissions instead.
Your account executive told a prospect we support something we do not. How do you handle it?
How you correct a teammate's mistake without losing the deal or the customer's trust.
Talks to the AE privately first, then corrects it with the customer before it ends up in the contract.

I go to the AE first, privately, and show where the gap is. Then we decide together how to correct it with the customer soon, ideally on the next call and with an alternative in hand. A wrong promise found after signing costs far more than one found now, and my name is on the technical answer.
The customer's security team sends a long questionnaire, and one question is about something you are unsure of. What do you do?
Whether you avoid guessing on security and compliance answers.
Never guesses. Uses approved answers, sends unknowns to the security team with the exact wording, and tracks the deadline.

I start from our approved answer library and any reports we can share under NDA, like a SOC 2 report if we have one. Anything I am unsure of, such as where backups are stored, goes to our security team with the exact wording. A wrong answer can become a contract promise, so I would rather be a day late than guess.
Three weeks into a proof of concept, it is clear the product is a poor fit for this customer. What do you do?
Your judgement on walking away from a deal and protecting the team's time and credibility.
Raises it early with the AE, with evidence, and gives the customer an honest read rather than forcing a win.

I bring it to the AE right away with evidence: which success criteria we cannot meet and why. If a setting or a partner closes the gap, we propose it. If not, we tell the customer honestly. Losing one deal cleanly beats a customer who leaves in six months saying we oversold, and it frees my time for deals we can win.
How do you structure a demo when the room has both executives and engineers?
Whether you can keep two very different audiences engaged in one session.
Starts from the customer's problem, shows the outcome first, goes deeper in layers, and moves heavy technical detail to a follow-up session.

I open with the problem they described on discovery, in their words, and show the end result first: the report the CFO wants. Then I go one level down for the engineers and park the deep questions for a technical session. I tell them what they will see, show it, then sum up what it means for them. I keep ten minutes free for questions.
When would you tell a customer to use webhooks instead of polling our API?
Your grasp of integration patterns and their trade-offs.
Webhooks for fast reaction to events with fewer calls, plus what they demand: a public HTTPS endpoint, signature checks, and handling of retries and duplicates.

Webhooks fit when they must react to events quickly, like an order status change, and polling would mean thousands of empty calls. But they need a public HTTPS endpoint, must verify the signature on each request, and must handle the same event arriving twice, since failed deliveries are retried. If their network cannot accept inbound calls, polling is the honest answer.
Their IT lead says they need SSO and SCIM. What is the difference, and why do they care about both?
Whether you know the identity questions that come up in almost every enterprise deal.
SSO handles login through their identity provider; SCIM automates creating and removing accounts. Removal of leavers is often the real concern.

SSO, usually through SAML or OpenID Connect, lets people log in with their company identity provider instead of a separate password. SCIM is a standard API that creates, updates and removes accounts automatically. IT cares most about removal: when someone leaves, disabling them in the identity provider should cut their access to our product without anyone doing it by hand.
The customer's integration runs as a nightly server job with no user present. Which OAuth 2.0 flow do you recommend, and why?
Your knowledge of API authentication beyond the basics.
Client credentials for machine-to-machine, with the secret stored safely and narrow scopes; authorization code with PKCE only when acting for a user.

Client credentials. The job authenticates as itself with a client ID and secret and gets a short-lived access token, with no user login involved. I would have them keep the secret in a secrets manager, not in code, and request only the scopes the job needs. If the app later acts for a specific user, that is the authorization code flow, with PKCE.
During a proof of concept, the customer's bulk data load fails with HTTP 429 errors. What do you tell their engineer?
How you diagnose a common API problem and guide the customer to a sound fix.
Knows 429 means too many requests; recommends honoring Retry-After, exponential backoff with jitter, bulk endpoints, and asking about a temporary limit.

A 429 means they are sending more requests than the rate limit allows, not that anything is broken. I would have them read the Retry-After header if we send one, retry with exponential backoff and some random jitter, and switch to a bulk endpoint if we offer one. If the one-time load still needs more, I ask our team about a temporary higher limit.
The customer's data sits in an on-premises database, and their security team will not open any inbound ports. How could the integration work?
Whether you can design around a real security constraint instead of fighting it.
Proposes an outbound-only design, such as an agent inside their network calling out over HTTPS, and gets security sign-off before building.

I would look for an outbound-only design. A small agent or connector inside their network makes outbound HTTPS calls to our service, so nothing has to listen for traffic from outside. Their firewall then only needs to allow outbound traffic to our addresses. I would draw it for their security team and get their sign-off before anyone builds.
The prospect asks you to tell them, honestly, how we compare with the competitor they are also testing. What do you say?
How you compete without losing the customer's trust.
No attacks on the competitor; ties the comparison to the customer's own requirements, admits real gaps, and suggests fair tests they can run.

I do not attack the competitor; it costs trust and buyers check. I go back to their top requirements and show, live, how we handle the ones where I know we are strong. Where the other product is better, I say so and explain why it matters less for their use case, if that is true. I may suggest test scenarios they can run on both products.
The deal has closed. What goes into your handoff to the implementation team?
Whether you protect what the customer was promised after the signature.
A written brief covering goals, success measures, people, technical design, anything custom or promised, and risks, reviewed live with the customer.

A short written brief: the business goal and how the customer will measure success, the people and who signs off, their systems and the integration design we agreed, anything custom or promised in writing, and the open risks. I walk the implementation lead through it on a call with the customer, so nothing they were promised depends on my memory.
In a proof of concept you wrote a custom script to make one workflow work, and the customer now thinks it is a standard feature. How do you fix that?
How you own a mistake that could become a broken promise.
Corrects it plainly before signature, explains the support impact, brings in services, and changes the habit so workarounds are always documented.

I tell them plainly before they sign: the script is custom, not part of the product, and here is what that means for support and upgrades. Then I bring in our services team to say whether it can be delivered and maintained, and at what cost. Since then I write every workaround into the POC summary as I build it.
We keep losing deals over the same missing capability. How do you get the product team to act on it?
