Your influence on the product, using evidence rather than anecdotes.
Brings deal data and the underlying customer need, uses the product team's process, and stays honest with customers about the roadmap meanwhile.

I bring evidence, not stories. I list the deals where it came up, their size, the stage where we lost or stalled, and what the customer was really trying to do, which is often narrower than the feature they asked for. I log it in the product team's system, review it with the product manager, and keep telling customers the truth about the roadmap meanwhile.

sourcer.heading: Sourcer questions
qs: Walk me through how you would build a Boolean search string for a backend Java developer in Austin.
Whether you can turn a job into a precise search.
Must-haves grouped with synonyms, correct use of AND, OR, NOT, quotes and parentheses, and a plan to test and adjust.

I list the must-have terms and their synonyms first. Then: (Java OR J2EE) AND ("Spring Boot" OR microservices) AND (Austin OR "Round Rock") NOT (intern OR recruiter). Parentheses group the synonyms, quotes keep a phrase together, and NOT drops noise. I run it, read twenty profiles, and adjust.
What is an X-ray search, and when would you use one?
Your knowledge of a basic sourcing technique.
Using a general search engine with the site: operator to search inside one website, and knowing when that beats the site's own search.

It means using a general search engine to search inside one website, by adding site: and the domain to the query, plus my keywords. I use it when a site's own search is weak, caps results, or needs a paid seat. For example, a code-hosting domain plus a language and a city finds developers who never update a job profile.
One search returns 4,000 profiles. Another returns 6. What do you do with each?
How you tune a search that is too broad or too narrow.
Specific ways to tighten and to loosen a search, aiming for a list you can actually review.

4,000 means my terms are too loose, so I add a must-have skill, search on titles, or narrow the area. 6 means I am too strict: I check for typos, drop a nice-to-have, add synonyms and nearby titles, or widen the location. I aim for a few hundred I can actually read, then pick the best by hand.
What goes into a first message to someone who is not looking for a job?
Whether you can write outreach that passive people answer.
Personal, short and honest, with a clear reason to care and a small, easy next step.

Their name and one real detail from their work, so they know it is not a mass email. Then the role in one sentence, why it might matter to them, such as scope, pay range or remote setup, and a small ask: a 15-minute call this week. I keep it under 100 words and never fake urgency.
What do you ask a hiring manager in the intake meeting before you start searching?
How you get the information a search depends on.
Must-haves versus trainable skills, sample profiles, target titles and companies, pay, location, off-limits companies and feedback speed.

I ask what the person must do in the first six months, which skills are must-have and which can be learned, and which titles and companies the best people come from. I ask for two or three profiles they like and why, the pay range, location rules and companies we must not approach. Then I agree how fast they will review profiles.
A strong candidate replies, "Thanks, but I'm happy where I am." How do you answer?
How you keep a relationship alive without pushing.
Respect for the no, a question that reveals what would make them move, a referral ask, and a planned follow-up.

I thank them and do not push. I might ask: "Makes sense. If that ever changes, what would a move need to offer you?" I note their answer. I also ask if they know someone the role might suit. Then I set a reminder to check in, maybe in six months, with something useful rather than the same pitch.
When a candidate agrees to talk, what do you pass to the recruiter?
Whether your handoff saves the recruiter and the candidate time.
A short, organized note on fit, gaps, what the candidate said and how to reach them, so nothing gets asked twice.

A short note with the profile, why I think they meet the must-haves, and any gaps I saw. What they told me: pay expectations if they shared them, notice period, location needs and what would make them move. How and when they want to be contacted. The recruiter should never ask something the candidate already told me.
Your outreach for a role gets a 5% reply rate after two weeks. How do you find what is wrong?
How you diagnose a weak campaign step by step.
Separating list, message and role problems, and testing one change at a time instead of guessing.

I check each step. Few opens points to the subject line or send time. Opens with no replies points to the message or the role itself, like pay below market. I also recheck the list: if the profiles fit poorly, no message will work. I change one thing, test it on a few dozen people, and compare before changing the next.
How do you build a more diverse pipeline without screening anyone on race, gender or age?
Whether you widen the pool in a fair and lawful way.
Broadening where you search and questioning needless requirements, while judging everyone on the same job criteria.

I widen where I look, not who I pick. I add sources like alumni groups of historically Black colleges, women-in-tech groups and veterans' networks, and I search nearby titles and skills. I ask the manager if a degree or a strict years count is truly needed, since those can shut people out. Everyone I send is judged on the same criteria.
A hiring manager asks you to skip anyone who graduated before 2005 "to keep the team young." What do you do?
Your judgement when asked to do something discriminatory.
You refuse the age filter, name the legal risk, steer back to job-related criteria, and bring in HR if pressed.

I would not build that filter. Screening out older people by graduation year is age discrimination, and federal law protects workers 40 and older. I tell the manager plainly I cannot do it, then ask what they actually need, maybe current skills or comfort with new tools, and search for that. If they insist, I bring in the recruiter or HR.
How do you search for people whose job title is different from the one in our posting?
Whether you know titles vary by company and can search beyond them.
You list title variants and search on skills, tools and work done, not just the title.

I list every title the work goes by, from the job description and from profiles of people who already do it here. One company says Site Reliability Engineer, another says Platform or DevOps Engineer. Then I search on the tools and tasks, like Kubernetes and on-call, so I catch people with odd or inflated titles.
What is a talent map, and how do you build one for a role?
Your grasp of talent mapping as a core sourcing method.
A map of where the target people work, how many there are, and who they are, built before outreach and shared.

It is a picture of the market: which companies employ people like the one we want, roughly how many, at what level and where. I start from the intake, pick target companies, count matching profiles in each, and note teams and names. Then I share it with the hiring manager so we agree where to fish before I send one message.
Which signals on a profile tell you someone might be open to a move?
How you judge timing for passive candidates.
Real signals like tenure, company news or a stalled title, used to prioritize outreach, not to assume anything.

I look at time in role, since people often think about moving after two or three years. Company news matters too: layoffs, an acquisition or a reorg. A title that has not changed in years can mean they want growth. I use these to decide who to contact first, never to rule someone out.
Someone has not replied to your first message. How do you plan the follow-ups?
Your outreach cadence and persistence without spamming.
A short planned sequence, spaced out, each message adding something new, possibly on another channel, then a clean stop.

I plan two or three follow-ups a few days to a week apart. Each one adds something: the pay range, a detail about the team, or a short note from the hiring manager. I may switch from InMail to email. After the last one I stop and note the date, so we can try again in a few months with a new reason.
You message a strong candidate, then learn another recruiter at your company is already talking to her. What do you do?
How you handle a mistake that makes the company look disorganized.
Own it fast, align internally on one contact, apologize to the candidate, and fix the process gap.

I call the other recruiter first and we agree they keep the lead. Then I write the candidate a short note: sorry for the double message, you are already in good hands with my colleague. Afterwards I check why I missed it. Usually I skipped the ATS search before outreach, so I make that step part of my routine.
You work at an agency and the best person for a search works at one of your clients. Do you call her?
Whether you respect off-limits agreements with clients.
No, not without checking the client's off-limits terms; protecting the client relationship comes first.

Not before I check. Most agencies agree not to recruit out of their clients, and some contracts say so in writing. I look at our off-limits list and ask my manager. If the client is off-limits, I leave her alone and use her profile only to learn which companies have people like her.
A candidate offers to send you his current employer's org chart and customer list. How do you respond?
Your judgement on confidential information and trade secrets.
Decline clearly, explain why, and never use confidential information from a current or former employer.

I say thanks, but no. I do not want anything that belongs to his employer, and taking it could put him and us at legal risk. I tell him to bring only his own skills. If something had been sent anyway, I would not open or share it, and I would tell my manager and our legal team the same day.
A candidate asks how you got her personal email and asks you to delete her data. What do you do?
Whether you handle data requests honestly and in line with privacy rules.
Tell her the source plainly, stop contact, and route the deletion request through the company's privacy process.

I tell her honestly where it came from, for example a contact data tool or her own website. I mark her do not contact right away and send the deletion request to whoever handles privacy, since laws like Europe's GDPR and California's privacy law give people rights over their data. Then I confirm back to her when it is done.
Your talent map shows about 40 people in the metro area who fit, and most earn above the budget. How do you take this to the hiring manager?
How you use market data to reset an unrealistic search.
Lead with the numbers and sources, then offer real options: pay, location, must-haves or level.

I show the map: 40 people, which companies, and the pay data from calls and salary reports. I say that at this budget we are fishing in a pond of maybe ten. Then I give options: raise the range, open to remote, drop one must-have, or hire one level down and train. I ask him to pick one so the search can move.

stablecoins-tokenization.heading: Stablecoin and tokenization specialist questions
qs: Walk me through how a fiat-backed stablecoin is minted and redeemed.
Whether you know the primary market flow behind a digital dollar.
Verified customers, dollars in before tokens out, burning on redemption, and the arbitrage that links the primary and secondary markets.

A customer who has already passed KYC wires dollars to the issuer's reserve account. Once the funds settle, the issuer mints the same number of tokens to the customer's verified address. To redeem, the customer sends tokens back, we burn them and wire dollars out. Everyone else buys on exchanges, and that mint-and-redeem arbitrage keeps the price near one dollar.
When a Treasury fund is tokenized, what does the token holder actually own?
Your grasp of the legal structure behind a tokenized asset.
The token stands for a fund share. What counts is the official register and the fund documents, not the code alone.

Usually a share of a fund that holds the Treasuries, not the bonds themselves. The key question is which record is official. In some structures the blockchain is the share register, kept by a registered transfer agent. In others the token mirrors an off-chain register. I read the offering documents to know which, because that decides ownership if the two disagree.
Why do most tokenized bonds and funds only move between approved wallets?
Whether you connect token design to US securities and anti-money-laundering rules.
They are securities sold under exemptions that limit buyers and resale, and the issuer must know its holders. The contract enforces an allowlist.

Most are securities, often sold under an exemption such as Regulation D, which limits who may buy and how the shares can be resold. The issuer also has to know its holders for anti-money-laundering rules. So the token contract checks an allowlist before every transfer, and a wallet is added only after its owner passes KYC and eligibility checks.
What is delivery versus payment, and why does it matter for tokenized bonds?
Your understanding of settlement, the main promise of tokenization.
Both legs settle in one transaction or neither does. That needs an on-chain cash leg, such as a stablecoin.

Delivery versus payment means the bond and the cash change hands together. On chain, one transaction can move the bond token to the buyer and the stablecoin to the seller. If either leg fails, the whole transaction reverts. That removes the risk of delivering and not getting paid, and it can settle in minutes instead of the usual one business day.
A tokenized money market fund earns daily income. Would you show it by growing balances or by a rising token price?
How you weigh a design choice that affects every integration.
Knows both models. Growing balances (rebasing) confuse many apps and pools; a rising price is easier to integrate but less intuitive for holders.

With rebasing, the price stays at one dollar and each wallet balance grows. Holders like it, but many lending pools and exchanges miscount a balance that changes without a transfer. With a rising price, the balance stays fixed and each token is worth more. If we expect wide integration I lean to the rising price, and I check tax reporting with the fund's advisers.
Our stablecoin contract can freeze addresses. Why have that power, and how should it be controlled?
Your judgement on a sensitive admin power.
Ties freezing to sanctions, court orders and theft, under a written policy, with several approvers, a multisig wallet and a log of every use.

Issuers need it to comply with sanctions rules, court orders and law enforcement requests, and to stop stolen funds from moving. The risk is abuse or a stolen admin key. So freezing follows a written policy, needs sign-off from compliance and legal, runs through a multisig wallet that requires several keys, and every action is logged and reviewable.
We want our stablecoin on a second blockchain. Would you issue it natively or use a bridge?
Whether you understand cross-chain risk.
Prefers native issuance or an issuer-run burn-and-mint transfer, and explains that a lock-and-mint bridge adds a contract that can be drained.

I would issue natively if the chain is worth supporting. A lock-and-mint bridge holds the real tokens in one contract and issues wrapped copies, so if the bridge is hacked the copies lose their backing. Bridge hacks have been some of the largest losses in crypto. Native issuance keeps one issuer and one pool of reserves behind every token.
Should the smart contract for a tokenized fund be upgradeable?
How you balance the need to fix problems against holders' trust.
Usually yes for a regulated asset, but only with a multisig, a timelock, an audit of each upgrade and advance notice to holders.

For a regulated fund I usually say yes, because rules change, bugs happen, and the issuer must be able to correct the share register. But an upgrade key can also change everything. So upgrades need several signers, wait behind a timelock so holders can see them coming, get a fresh audit, and are announced before they take effect.
Reconciliation shows 3,000 more tokens on chain than our reserve ledger says. What do you do?
How you handle a supply mismatch, the most serious problem an issuer can face.
Pauses minting, checks timing causes first, treats an unexplained mint as a possible key compromise, and escalates fast.

First I pause new minting and alert my lead and compliance. Then I check the simple causes: a deposit booked late in the ledger, or redeemed tokens we paid out but have not burned yet. I match every mint transaction to a ledger entry. If a mint has no matching request, I treat it as a possible key compromise and start the incident plan.
What is the difference between a reserve attestation and a full audit, and why does it matter to holders?
Whether you know what a reserve report really proves.
An attestation checks reserves against tokens at set dates. An audit gives an opinion on the full financial statements over a period, including liabilities.

An attestation is a CPA firm reporting on management's claim, for example that reserves covered tokens outstanding on certain dates. It says little about what happened between those dates. An audit gives an opinion on the full financial statements for a year, including debts that rank against reserves. Holders need both: frequent reserve checks and an audited balance sheet.
Why can a tokenized money market fund pass yield to holders while a payment stablecoin under the GENIUS Act cannot?
Your grasp of the legal line between a payment token and a security.
The fund token is a share in a registered fund that earns income. The GENIUS Act bars payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders interest or yield.

The fund token is a share in a registered investment company, sold as a security with a prospectus, so its income belongs to shareholders. A payment stablecoin is meant to work as cash, and the GENIUS Act bars the issuer from paying interest or yield just for holding it. If a product promises both a fixed dollar redemption and a yield, I ask which rulebook it is under.
On a tokenized fund, is the blockchain the official record of who owns the shares?
Whether you know where legal ownership is recorded.
Only if the issuer or its registered transfer agent has made it the record. Otherwise the chain mirrors an off-chain register, and the register wins in a dispute.

It depends on the setup. For a registered security, the official record sits with the issuer or its registered transfer agent. Some transfer agents keep that record on chain, and then the chain is the book. If not, the chain is a copy, and every transfer must be reconciled to the agent's register, because a court will look at the register, not the wallet.
Walk me through paying a coupon on a tokenized bond.
How you run a corporate action when the holders are wallets.
A snapshot at the record date, eligibility checks, payment in a cash token or by wire, and a plan for wallets that cannot receive.

At the record date I take a snapshot of balances at a set block. I match each wallet to the investor on the register, check none is blocked, and compute the coupon per holder. We pay in a stablecoin or by wire, as the bond terms say. Failed payments are held and logged, not lost, and I reconcile the total against the paying agent's figure.
A customer sends 5 million tokens to redeem. When do you treat that transfer as final and send the dollars?
Whether you understand finality and the risk of a chain reorganization.
Wait for finality as the chain defines it, not mere inclusion in a block. Scale the wait to the chain and the amount, and never pay on a pending transaction.

I wait for finality, not inclusion. On Ethereum that means the block's checkpoint is finalized, about 13 minutes, since a reorganization can still drop a newer block. On chains with only probabilistic finality, I set confirmation counts per chain and raise them for large sums. Once it is final, I burn the tokens, then send the wire.
How would you set up control over who can mint our stablecoin?
How you guard the most dangerous power in the contract.
Separate roles, a multisig with hardware keys, a cap per minter, minting tied to confirmed reserves, and an alert on every mint.

Minting sits in its own role, apart from the admin role that can add or remove minters. Mints need several signers on a multisig, with hardware keys held by different people. Each minter has a cap, so one stolen key cannot print unlimited tokens. No mint happens before the cash is confirmed in reserves, and each mint sends an alert checked against the ledger.
The fund's NAV feed on chain stopped updating yesterday, and subscriptions keep coming in. What do you do?
How you handle a stale price that lets investors trade at the wrong value.
Pause the flows that rely on the price, get the official NAV off chain, correct wrongly priced orders, and add a guard against stale prices.

First I pause mints and redemptions that use the feed, because a stale price lets someone buy or sell at a value we know is wrong. Then I get the official NAV from the fund administrator and check yesterday's orders against it. Wrongly priced orders get corrected under the fund's error policy. Last, I add a check so the contract rejects a price older than a set limit.
An approved investor lost the keys to a wallet holding $2 million of fund tokens. What can you do?
Whether you can recover a holding without opening a door to fraud.
Strong identity checks, the recovery process written in the fund documents, a forced transfer or burn and reissue, and a clean record.

Because the register, not the key, defines ownership, we can help. I verify the investor's identity again, with extra checks, since this is a common fraud story. The investor signs a request and an indemnity. Then, under the process in the fund documents, we force-transfer or burn and reissue to a new approved wallet, and the transfer agent records why.
A client wants to settle a tokenized bond trade on a Saturday night. How does the cash side work?
Whether you see that the asset moves around the clock but bank money often does not.
Fedwire is closed on weekends. Settle against an on-chain cash token for true delivery versus payment, or agree the trade now and settle on the next business day.

The bond token can move any time, but Fedwire is closed on weekends, so a normal wire leg would leave one side exposed until Monday. If both sides accept a stablecoin or a bank's tokenized deposit as the cash leg, one contract can swap bond for cash at once. If not, we agree the trade now and settle on the next business day, so nobody delivers before being paid.
On a Friday night, a bank holding part of our reserves fails, and redemptions jump. What do you do over the weekend?
How you lead during a run, when facts, speed and honesty all matter.
Measure the exposure, keep redemptions open from liquid assets, publish facts early, and never promise backing you cannot show.

First I confirm how much sat at that bank and how much is insured or likely recoverable. Then I check what we can pay out on Monday from other banks and from Treasury bills we can sell or repo. I publish the exact exposure early, keep redemptions open, and process them in order. I would not claim full backing until I can show it; a vague statement feeds a run.

storage-engineer.heading: Storage engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between block, file and object storage?
Whether you know the three basic kinds of storage and where each one fits.
Clear contrasts: raw disks for one host, shared folders over a network protocol, objects with metadata over HTTP, each tied to a real use.

Block storage gives a host a raw disk, like a SAN volume or a cloud disk, and is what databases want. File storage shares folders over NFS or SMB to many users. Object storage keeps whole objects with metadata, reached over an HTTP API. It scales cheaply for backups, logs and media, but you rewrite an object rather than edit part of it.
What are RPO and RTO, and how do they change your design?
Your grasp of the two numbers that drive every backup and recovery decision.
Correct definitions, how each one drives a different design choice, and that the business sets them.

RPO is how much data we can afford to lose, measured in time. An RPO of 15 minutes means a copy at least every 15 minutes. RTO is how long the service can be down before it is back. RPO sets how often we copy or replicate. RTO sets how fast the restore path must be. I get both numbers from the business instead of guessing them.
You have twelve large hard drives for a file server. RAID 5, RAID 6 or RAID 10, and why?
Whether you weigh rebuild risk, write speed and usable space when choosing a RAID level.
Sees the rebuild risk of RAID 5 on big drives, matches the level to the workload, and knows RAID is not a backup.

With large drives I avoid RAID 5. A rebuild takes hours, and a second failure or a read error in that window can lose the array. For a mostly-read file server I pick RAID 6, which survives two failed disks. For a busy database I would pay for RAID 10: half the capacity, much faster writes. And RAID is still not a backup.
Why is a snapshot not a backup?
Whether you understand what a snapshot depends on and what it cannot survive.
Explains that snapshots share the array and blocks with the source, names the failures they do not survive, and still sees their use.

A snapshot usually lives on the same array and shares blocks with the live volume. If the array fails, a bug corrupts data, or an attacker with admin access deletes the volumes, the snapshots go with them. Snapshots are great for a quick rollback. A backup is a separate copy on other hardware, ideally at another site, that survives losing the original.
An application team asks for a 10 TB volume by tomorrow. What do you ask before you build it?
How you gather requirements before you provision storage.
Asks about workload pattern, performance, growth, access and protection, not only the size.

I ask what runs on it and how it reads and writes: small random I/O like a database, or large streaming files. Then the latency and IOPS they need, expected growth, which hosts mount it, and what RPO and retention they need for backups. Ten terabytes of logs and ten terabytes of a transaction database belong on very different tiers.
The database team says storage is slow. How do you find out whether they are right?
How you tell a storage problem from a host or network problem using real measurements.
Compares latency at the host and at the array, checks IOPS, throughput and shared load, and uses a baseline.

I compare latency at the host with latency at the array. If the array shows 1 ms but the host sees 20 ms, the problem is in between: the host queue, the multipath setup or the network. If the array itself is slow, I check whether it is at its IOPS or throughput limit, or whether one noisy volume is eating the shared pool. I compare it all to last week.
A thin-provisioned pool is at 92% and still growing. What do you do?
How you handle an overcommitted pool before it runs out of space.
Treats a full pool as an outage for every volume on it, frees or adds space now, then fixes alerts and overcommit limits.

A thin pool that fills up can stop writes to every volume on it, so I treat this as urgent. I find what is growing, check for old snapshots I can safely expire, and move a volume to another pool or add capacity. Then I set alerts at lower levels that leave time to act, and agree a limit on how far we overcommit.
When would you use synchronous replication, and when asynchronous?
Whether you understand the trade-off between data loss, write latency and distance.
Sync gives near-zero data loss but adds round-trip delay and limits distance; async keeps writes fast but can lose recent changes.

With synchronous replication a write is confirmed only after both sites have it, so we lose nothing if one site dies, but every write waits for the round trip. That works only over short distances, like two nearby data centers. Asynchronous sends changes shortly after, so writes stay fast and distance matters less, but we can lose the last seconds or minutes.
How would you protect backups so that ransomware cannot destroy them too?
Your plan to keep at least one copy out of an attacker's reach.
Immutable or offline copies, separate accounts with MFA for the backup system, copies off-site, and tested restores.

Attackers go after backups first, so I keep at least one copy immutable, such as object storage with a retention lock, or offline. The backup system uses its own accounts with MFA, not domain admin, so stolen admin rights do not reach it. I follow 3-2-1: three copies, two kinds of media, one off-site. And I test restores regularly.
A restore fails during a real incident, but every backup job showed success. What went wrong, and what do you change?
How you handle a failed restore, and whether you know a green job does not prove a backup works.
Finds another restore point first, then the cause, and makes regular test restores the real measure of backup health.

First I look for another good copy: an older restore point, a replica or a snapshot. Later I find the cause. Often the job copied a database while it was being written, not in a consistent state, or skipped files it could not read. Then I add scheduled test restores that start the application and check the data, and report on those, not on job status.
What is the difference between zoning and LUN masking on a Fibre Channel SAN?
Whether you know the two layers that control which host can see which disk.
Zoning on the switch limits which ports can talk to each other. Masking on the array limits which hosts see which LUNs. Both are used together.

Zoning is set on the Fibre Channel switch and decides which ports, usually identified by WWPN, can talk to each other. LUN masking is set on the array and decides which host initiators can see which LUNs. I use single-initiator zones and masking together, so one mistake in one layer does not expose a volume to the wrong server.
What is ALUA, and what happens if a host ignores it?
Your grasp of how multipathing picks paths to a dual-controller array.
The array marks paths as optimized or non-optimized. The host should use the optimized ones, or latency rises and, on some arrays, LUN ownership flips.

ALUA means Asymmetric Logical Unit Access. The array tells the host which paths go through the controller that owns the LUN, called active/optimized, and which go through the partner, active/non-optimized. Non-optimized I/O must cross between controllers, so it is slower. If the multipath policy ignores this, latency goes up, and some arrays keep moving LUN ownership back and forth.
A vendor says their array does one million IOPS. What do you ask them?
Whether you can see through a benchmark number.
Asks for block size, read/write mix, random or sequential access, latency at that rate, and whether cache or data reduction made the test easy.

Under what test? A million 4 KB random reads served from cache tell me little about my 32 KB mixed workload. I ask for block size, read/write ratio, random versus sequential, the latency at that IOPS, whether data reduction was on and how full the array was. Then I ask to run my own test with a profile taken from a real workload.
What is the difference between a crash-consistent and an application-consistent backup of a database server?
Whether you know what a backup of a running system really captures.
Crash-consistent is like pulling the power. Application-consistent first has the app flush and pause writes, so the copy is clean without relying on crash recovery.

A crash-consistent copy captures the disks at one instant, like pulling the plug. The database will usually recover from its log, but what was in memory is lost. An application-consistent copy first tells the app to flush and pause writes, for example through the Volume Shadow Copy Service on Windows. For databases I prefer that or the database's own backup tool, and I test restores of both.
The vendor promises 4:1 data reduction. How do you use that number in capacity planning?
How you plan capacity when usable space depends on the data itself.
Plans on measured ratios per type of data, knows encrypted or already compressed data barely reduces, and keeps headroom in case the ratio drops.

I do not buy on the promised ratio. I run an assessment on our real data or test a sample. Databases, VMs and file shares reduce very differently, and data that is already compressed or encrypted on the host barely reduces at all. I plan with a conservative figure per workload and watch the real ratio monthly, because one team turning on host encryption can erase the savings.
A share must be used from both Windows and Linux clients. What problems do you expect, and how do you set it up?
Your experience with permissions and identity across SMB and NFS.
Knows SMB uses Windows accounts and ACLs while NFS uses Unix IDs, so user mapping and one permission style must be settled before go-live.

SMB clients arrive with Windows accounts and ACLs. NFSv3 clients arrive with Unix user and group numbers. If those are not mapped to each other, people get access denied or files end up with the wrong owner. I pick one security style for the share, set up name mapping through the directory, and test with a real user from each side before go-live.
Your object store can protect data with three copies or with 8+3 erasure coding. How do you choose?
Whether you understand the cost and performance tradeoff of protection in object storage.
Can work out the overhead (three copies stores 3x the data, 8+3 about 1.4x) and knows erasure coding costs CPU and rebuild traffic and suits large objects.

Three copies stores every byte three times and survives two lost copies. 8+3 splits data into eight pieces plus three parity pieces, stores about 1.4 times the data and survives three lost pieces. So erasure coding is much cheaper per terabyte. The cost is more CPU, more network traffic on rebuilds and poor efficiency for tiny objects, so I use it for large, colder data.
You have to move 300 TB of live volumes from an old array to a new one. Walk me through your plan.
How you plan a large migration with little downtime and a way back.
A full inventory, a copy method that syncs in the background, small waves, short cutovers with checks, and a rollback that stays possible.

I start with an inventory: every host, volume, multipath setup and owner. Then I choose the method per host, such as mirroring with the host's volume manager or the new array's migration feature, so data syncs while apps run. I move in waves, test systems first. Each cutover has a checklist, the app owner on the call, and the old volume left untouched until they sign off.
In a stretched cluster across two sites, the link between the sites goes down. What should happen, and how do you make sure it does?
How you prevent split-brain when both sites think they are in charge.
One site keeps serving and the other stops writing. A witness in a third failure domain decides, and the behavior is tested, not assumed.

If both sites keep writing to the same volumes, the copies diverge. That is split-brain, and one side's writes get lost. So one site must win and the other must stop I/O. I put a witness, or tiebreaker, in a third location that each site reaches on its own path. Then I test it in a window: cut the link and check that the right site stays up.
During a controller firmware upgrade, a few servers lost their disks while the first controller rebooted. What went wrong, and what do you change?
How you handle a non-disruptive change that disrupted, and the checks you add.
Suspects missing paths or unsupported drivers on those hosts, fixes the cause, and adds pre-checks of path health and the vendor support matrix.

A non-disruptive upgrade only works if every host can fail over. Most likely those servers had paths to one controller only, a broken zone, or host bus adapter drivers not on the vendor's support matrix. I check their path state and logs and fix them. Then I add a runbook step: every host shows healthy paths to both controllers before anyone starts.

store-manager.heading: Store manager questions
qs: Walk me through your first hour in the store on a normal morning.
How you set up the day before customers arrive.
A clear routine: floor, numbers, cash and schedule are checked, and the team hears the day's goal.

I walk the floor before opening: lights, fitting rooms, endcaps, anything left from close. Then I check yesterday's sales against plan, confirm the safe count and the deposit, and look at the schedule for gaps. Ten minutes before open I hold a short huddle: today's goal, one focus item, and who covers breaks.
Which numbers do you look at every day, and why?
Whether you run the store on numbers and know what each one tells you.
Sales against plan, plus the numbers that explain them: traffic, conversion, average sale, and labor against budget.

Sales against plan first. Then traffic and conversion, which is the share of visitors who buy, plus average sale and units per transaction. I also watch labor hours against budget. If sales dip, those numbers tell me whether fewer people came in or fewer of them bought, and those need different fixes.
How do you build a weekly schedule?
Your method for matching staff hours to customer traffic within a budget and the law.
Starts from the hours budget and traffic by hour, puts strong people at peaks, and checks breaks, minor rules and local notice laws.

I start from the hours budget and last year's traffic by hour, so my strongest people are on the floor at peak times. Then I fill in availability, breaks and the federal and state rules for minors. I post it as early as I can; some cities require advance notice, so I check local rules. Last, I make sure a key holder covers open and close.
A delivery arrives and the driver is waiting for a signature. Walk me through how you receive it.
Whether you protect the store from paying for stock it never got.
Counts against the paperwork before signing, notes any shortage on the driver's copy, and receives only what actually arrived.

I count the cases against the bill of lading, the shipping paper, before I sign, with the driver there. If two cases are short, I write the shortage on both copies and ask the driver to initial it. Then I receive only what arrived and report the gap to the vendor or distribution center the same day, so we are not billed for stock we never got.
An employee you like has been late four times this month. How do you handle it?
How you coach and hold people to the rules fairly, even friends.
A private talk, a clear expectation, written notes, and the same policy applied as to anyone else.

I talk to her privately, not in front of the team. I ask what is going on, because sometimes a schedule change fixes it. I state the expectation clearly, write down the conversation, and follow the same policy I would with anyone. If it keeps happening, the next steps are documented warnings. Liking someone cannot mean a different rule.
Two of your closers call out an hour before a holiday evening shift. What do you do?
How you cover a staffing gap fast without breaking budget or rules.
Works the call list, cuts tasks to what matters most, steps in personally, then follows up on attendance.

I go down my call list, starting with people who asked for more hours, and check nobody goes into overtime I cannot approve. While I wait I cut tasks: registers and the fitting room come first, restocking can wait until morning. If needed I stay and close myself. Afterward I talk to both callers and follow the attendance policy.
Halfway through the month, your store is 8% behind its sales plan. What do you do?
Whether you diagnose a sales gap before you try to fix it.
Breaks the gap into traffic, conversion and average sale, picks actions for the real cause, and tracks daily goals.

First I find where the gap is. If traffic is down, I look for outside causes and push events or local outreach. If traffic is fine but conversion fell, it is the floor: coverage at peak, greeting, product knowledge. If the average sale dropped, I coach add-ons. Then I set daily goals for the rest of the month and review them at each huddle.
Your last inventory showed shrink went up. How do you find out why?
Your understanding of where shrink comes from and how you investigate it.
Knows shrink includes theft, paperwork errors and vendor mistakes, and starts from data on which items and processes lose the most.

Shrink is the gap between what the books say we have and what we count. It comes from theft by customers or staff, paperwork errors and vendor mistakes. I pull the items with the biggest losses, then check receiving, damage logs, and void and refund reports by cashier. Often a big chunk is process, like damaged goods thrown out without being recorded.
Your district manager sends a planogram for this weekend's reset, and you think it will hurt your best-selling area. What do you do?
How you handle disagreeing with head office without ignoring direction.
Executes on time, raises the concern with specific data, measures the result, and asks for changes based on numbers.

A planogram is the diagram of what goes where. I set it as sent, on time, because other stores and the ad plan depend on it. Before the weekend I send my district manager last month's sales for that area and my specific concern, with a photo. Then I track sales for two weeks after the reset. If the numbers back me up, I ask for an adjustment with data, not opinion.
Your payroll budget is cut 10% for the next quarter. How do you keep service from slipping?
How you make hard labor trade-offs while protecting sales and customers.
Cuts hours where traffic is lowest, moves tasks off peak, cross-trains, explains the change, and watches conversion.

I look at sales by hour and cut where traffic is lowest, like the first hour after open, rather than across the board. I move restocking and price changes to quiet times so peak hours stay on the floor. I cross-train so fewer people can cover more. I tell the team why, and I check conversion weekly to see if service is slipping.
What is the difference between markup and margin, and why does it matter on the floor?
Whether you know the math behind pricing and profit.
Markup is profit over cost and margin is profit over price, so the same dollars give a smaller margin percent. Discounts eat margin faster than people think.

Markup is profit divided by cost. Margin is profit divided by the selling price. An item that costs $6 and sells for $10 has a 67% markup but a 40% margin. It matters when someone offers 20% off: on that item the discount eats half of the margin dollars, not a fifth of them.
Door counts are up 10% this month, but sales are flat. What does that tell you, and what do you check?
How you break sales down into traffic, conversion and average sale.
Sales equal traffic times conversion times average ticket. More traffic with flat sales means conversion or ticket fell, and you find out which before acting.

Sales are traffic times conversion times average transaction. If traffic rose and sales did not, fewer visitors bought or they spent less. I check conversion by hour against the schedule, since it often drops when the floor is thin at peak. I also look for out-of-stocks on key items. Then I fix the hours or the gaps I find.
The system shows 14 units of a fast seller, the shelf and backroom are empty, and no reorder is coming. What is going on, and what do you do?
Whether you understand phantom inventory and how it blocks replenishment.
Recognizes that a false on-hand count stops automatic reorders. Searches, corrects the count, gets stock ordered, and looks for the cause.

That is phantom inventory: the system thinks we have stock, so auto-replenishment will never order. I search the backroom, overstock and returns area first. If it is truly gone, I count it, adjust the on-hand to zero so an order triggers, and place a manual order if allowed. Then I look for the cause, like a receiving error or theft.
A dedicated hourly associate offers to clock out and finish the truck so you stay under your labor budget. What do you say?
Whether you know wage-and-hour rules and protect the company from breaking them.
A clear no. Non-exempt staff must be paid for all time worked, even if they volunteer, and a manager who allows it creates legal risk.

I thank her and say no. Under federal wage law, hourly employees must be paid for all the time they work, even when they volunteer, and that time counts toward overtime too. If the truck cannot be finished in the hours I have, that is my planning problem. I would rather explain an over-budget week than an unpaid-wage claim.
You see a man put two items in his jacket and walk toward the exit. What do you and your team do?
Whether you follow safe loss prevention practice instead of acting on instinct.
Safety over merchandise: follows company policy, no chasing or physical contact, uses customer service as a deterrent, and writes accurate notes after.

I follow our policy, which at most retailers means staff outside loss prevention never chase, block or touch anyone. Before he reaches the door I may greet him and ask if he needs help finding anything; that often makes people put items back. If he leaves, I let him go, note his description, the time and the items, and report it as our policy says.
An associate slips in the backroom, says she is fine, and asks you not to write it up. How do you handle it?
Whether you handle workplace injuries by the book.
Offers care, documents and reports it anyway, explains why, and fixes the hazard. Never discourages an employee from reporting.

I check on her first and offer medical care. Then I explain that I still have to report it: if her back hurts tomorrow, the report protects her workers' comp claim. I fill out the incident report the same day with the cause and any witnesses, and get the spill or whatever caused it fixed right away. I would never pressure anyone not to report.
You have a wall of seasonal stock selling slower than planned, with five weeks left in the season. How do you decide on markdowns?
How you use sell-through and weeks of supply to time markdowns.
Compares weeks of supply with the time left, checks placement first, and marks down early and in steps within company rules, not all at the end.

I look at sell-through so far and weeks of supply at the current rate. If 400 units are left and we sell 40 a week, that is ten weeks of stock for five weeks of season. Before cutting price I check that it is placed well on the floor. Then I take or request an early first markdown within our guidelines; a small cut now costs less than deep clearance later.
Which lines on your store P&L can you actually control, and which one do you manage hardest?
Whether you think like the owner of the store's profit, not only its sales.
Separates controllable lines like payroll, shrink and supplies from fixed ones like rent, and explains how they act on each.

Rent, depreciation and most utilities are largely set for me. What I control is payroll, shrink, supplies, damages and a lot of how sales and margin come in. Payroll is the biggest controllable line, so I manage it hardest: I schedule to traffic by hour and check labor against sales every week. Shrink is next, because every lost dollar comes straight off the bottom line.
You take over a store with high turnover, weak scores and a tired team. What do you do in your first 90 days?
How you diagnose a struggling store and set priorities before changing things.
Listens and measures before changing much, fixes a few visible basics fast, then sets clear standards, develops key people and follows up.

The first two weeks I mostly listen: one-on-ones with every leader and shifts across every part of the day. Then I fix two or three basics people feel right away, like posting schedules earlier or repairing broken equipment. By day 60 I set clear standards, coach the leads who can carry them, and act on those who will not. I track turnover and scores monthly.
Tell me about a management decision you made that turned out wrong. What did you change afterward?
Whether you own your mistakes and turn them into better systems.
A real mistake with a real cost, owned without blaming others, and a specific change in how they work now.

I once promoted my best sales associate to key holder because her numbers were great. She struggled to correct people she had worked beside, and two closers quit within a month. That was on me: I promoted for sales, not leadership. Now candidates run a few shifts with coaching before I promote, and I ask the team what they see.

strategic-sourcing.heading: Strategic sourcing manager questions
qs: What is total cost of ownership, and why does it matter more than unit price?
Whether you look past the price on the quote.
Names the costs beyond price, such as freight, duties, quality, inventory and switching, and shows how they can change a decision.

It is everything the item costs us over its life, not just the invoice. Freight, duties, payment terms, inventory we hold because of long lead times, scrap and returns, and the cost of switching. A part that is 8% cheaper overseas can cost more once I add ocean freight, a 12-week lead time and extra safety stock.
How do you use the Kraljic matrix to set a category strategy?
Your grasp of a standard tool for sorting spend into categories that need different handling.
The two axes, the four quadrants, and a different approach for each, not one playbook for all spend.

It sorts categories by profit impact and supply risk. Leverage items, high impact and low risk, I bid out hard. Strategic items, high on both, I build long partnerships with. Bottleneck items, low impact but high risk, I secure supply, even at a premium. Non-critical items I simplify with catalogs or purchasing cards.
When do you use an RFI, an RFQ or an RFP?
Whether you pick the right sourcing event for the need.
RFI to learn the market, RFQ when the spec is fixed and price decides, RFP when the solution and approach matter.

An RFI comes first when I do not know the market well: who can do this and how. An RFQ fits when the specification is tight, like a drawing for a machined part, and price and lead time decide. An RFP is for services or complex buys where suppliers propose their approach, scored on weighted criteria agreed with stakeholders in advance.
Walk me through how you start a spend analysis for a new category.
How you turn messy purchase data into a sourcing plan.
Pulls payables and purchase order data, cleans and classifies it, finds fragmentation and off-contract spend, then picks where to act.

I pull 12 to 24 months of accounts payable and purchase order data, then clean supplier names, since one vendor often appears five ways. I classify lines into categories and look at spend by supplier, site and buyer. If 40 suppliers share $3 million, consolidation is likely the first opportunity. I also flag off-contract spend to discuss with budget owners.
What is your BATNA going into a negotiation, and how do you build a strong one?
Your preparation and where your leverage really comes from.
Knows BATNA is the best option if no deal is reached, and builds it with real alternatives before talking, not with bluffs.

It is my best alternative if this deal does not happen. Before a renewal, I get at least one qualified alternative quoted, check whether we can split volume or delay, and set my walk-away point. If the incumbent knows I have a real second source, the conversation changes. I also estimate the supplier's alternative, since that shows how far they can move.
A supplier asks for a 12% price increase, blaming raw material costs. How do you respond?
How you test a price increase instead of accepting or refusing it outright.
Asks for the cost breakdown, checks it against published indexes and a should-cost view, and negotiates only the share that is justified.

I ask what share of their cost is that material and how much it really rose. If steel is 30% of the part and the index rose 15%, that supports about 4.5%, not 12%. I offer an index-linked clause so the price also comes down when the market falls. Then I look at volume, terms or spec changes to offset the rest.
How do you decide between single sourcing and dual sourcing a critical part?
Your judgement on balancing cost against supply risk.
Weighs volume leverage and tooling costs against disruption risk, and has a backup plan if single sourcing wins.

Single sourcing gives better pricing, but one fire or bankruptcy can stop our line. If the part is critical and a second source can be qualified at reasonable cost, I split it, maybe 70/30, so both stay active. If tooling or qualification costs too much, I single source but hold safety stock, track the supplier's health and keep a backup plan ready.
Finance says your savings are not real. How do you report savings so they hold up?
Whether your savings claims would survive a finance review.
Separates cost reduction from cost avoidance, uses a baseline agreed with finance, and counts savings on actual volume, not forecasts.

I agree the method with finance up front. Cost reduction is a lower price than we paid last year for the same item, and it shows in the budget. Cost avoidance, like blocking a requested increase, is real but reported separately. I calculate on actual purchased volume, not the forecast, and finance signs off on the baseline before I report a number.
Engineering keeps buying from a supplier outside the contract. What do you do?
How you handle off-contract spend without damaging internal relationships.
Finds out why first, fixes the real gap or brings the supplier in properly, and uses policy as the last tool, not the first.

First I ask why. Often the contract supplier is slow on prototypes, or engineers trust the other shop's quality. If that is true, I fix it: a quick-turn agreement, or adding that supplier under proper terms. If it is habit, I show the price and risk gap, like no liability or IP terms, and ask leadership to enforce policy only if that fails.
You learn that a key supplier is in financial trouble. What do you do in the first two weeks?
How you manage a supplier risk before it becomes a shortage.
Confirms the facts, measures exposure, protects supply quietly, and works with the supplier rather than pushing it toward collapse.

I confirm the facts through credit reports and direct talks with their leadership. Then I measure exposure: which parts, how much stock, how long a switch would take. I may build some inventory, secure the tooling we own, and start qualifying a backup. I avoid pulling all orders at once, which can push them under. Sometimes faster payment terms keep a good supplier alive.
What is the difference between buying FOB and buying DDP, and how does it change how you compare quotes?
Whether you know where cost and risk pass from supplier to buyer under common Incoterms.
FOB moves risk once goods are on board the vessel; DDP leaves cost, risk and duties with the seller to the destination. Quotes must be put on the same basis.

Under FOB the risk passes to us once the goods are on board the ship at the origin port, and we pay ocean freight, insurance, duties and inland moves. Under DDP the seller carries all of that to our door, duties included. So I never compare a FOB price with a DDP price directly. I add our landed costs to the FOB quote first, then compare.
When would you run a reverse auction, and when would you not?
Your judgement on when open price bidding helps and when it harms the supply base.
Use it for clear specs, several qualified suppliers and low switching cost. Avoid it for complex, strategic or relationship-driven buys.

It works for things like corrugated boxes or standard fasteners: a tight spec, four or five qualified suppliers, and little cost to switch. I avoid it for a single-source part, for engineered items where price is only part of the decision, or with a supplier we need to invest alongside us. Running an auction there can hurt trust for years.
How do you build a should-cost model for a machined part?
Whether you can estimate what a part ought to cost instead of accepting the quote.
Bottom-up: material, machine time, labor, setup, scrap, overhead and margin, with a source for each rate, used to ask better questions rather than to accuse.

I start with the drawing: raw stock weight times the current material price, plus scrap. Then cycle time per operation times a machine-hour rate for that region, plus setup spread over the lot size. I add overhead, packaging, freight and a fair margin. If the quote is 20% above my number, I ask the supplier to walk me through the gap line by line.
How do you design a supplier scorecard and run the quarterly review that goes with it?
How you manage supplier performance with data rather than complaints.
A few weighted measures agreed in advance, data both sides trust, and a review that ends with owners and dates for corrective actions.

I keep it to five or six measures: on-time delivery against the confirmed date, defects per million parts, cost, responsiveness, and one for the category, like lead time. The supplier sees the definitions and data before the meeting. We spend little time on the past and most on actions: who fixes what by when. Repeated red scores trigger a formal corrective plan.
How do you write a price adjustment clause tied to a commodity index?
How you share raw material risk with a supplier in a way both sides can audit.
A named public index, a base value, the material share of the price, a set review period and lag, and adjustment in both directions.

First we agree what share of the price is the commodity, say 40% for steel content. We name a published index, record its base value, and review every quarter using the average of the prior quarter. Only that 40% moves, and it moves both ways. I often add a small band, like plus or minus 3%, so we are not repricing for noise.
Beyond price, which clauses do you push hardest for in a multi-year supply agreement?
Whether you protect the company in the terms that matter when things go wrong.
Terms that matter in a crisis: liability limits, termination and exit help, continuity of supply, change of control and price mechanisms, worked out with legal.

I care most about what happens when things go wrong. I want a liability cap that fits the real risk, the right to terminate for poor performance, and help to move the work if we exit. I ask for notice before any change of owner or production site, and a continuity plan for critical parts. I agree the price mechanism up front and let legal own the final wording.
A supplier's rep emails you a competitor's price sheet, saying it came to them by mistake. What do you do?
Your integrity and how you handle confidential supplier information.
Do not use or share it, tell legal or compliance and follow their direction, and tell the rep plainly that this is not acceptable.

I stop reading, do not forward it, and do not use any of it. I report it to legal or compliance, keep a record of what came in and when, and delete it as they direct. I tell the rep plainly that we do not accept other suppliers' information. Our suppliers trust us with their pricing; if we used this, none of them should.
The lowest bid is 15% below the incumbent, but that supplier has never made this part for you. How do you make the award decision?
How you weigh savings against the real risk of changing suppliers.
Price the switch: qualification cost and time, quality risk and a fallback. Then phase the move instead of betting all the volume at once.

I first check the bid is complete: same spec, same terms, same Incoterm. Then I price the switch: tooling, qualification runs, engineering time, extra stock during the move. If the savings still hold, I visit the plant, run a trial lot, and move a share of volume first, say 30%, keeping the incumbent as backup until the new supplier proves itself.
We are a small customer to a supplier with few competitors. How do you get better service and terms?
How you gain leverage when the supplier holds most of the power.
Become a customer the supplier wants: steady forecasts, prompt payment, longer commitments, growth they value, while quietly building alternatives.

I find out what the supplier values: steady forecasts, fast payment, fewer rush orders, a longer commitment, or a reference in a new market. I offer those in exchange for capacity priority or better terms. I also pool volume with our other sites, and in the background I work with engineering to qualify an alternative, so our position improves over time.
Tell me about a contract term that came back to hurt you, and what you changed afterward.
Whether you learn from your own deals and own the result.
A real mistake told plainly, what it cost, how it was contained, and a specific change in how the person writes contracts now.

I signed a three-year deal with a firm volume commitment to get a lower price. In year two our product was cut and we fell 35% short, so we owed a shortfall payment. I contained it by moving another product line to that supplier. Now I commit to volume bands, tie them to our forecast, and include a review if demand drops sharply.

structural-engineer.heading: Structural engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between a dead load and a live load?
Whether you know the basic load types every design starts from.
Dead load is permanent self-weight; live load is from use and occupancy and can move or change. A clear example of each.

Dead load is the weight of the structure itself and anything fixed to it: the slab, beams, walls, finishes and fixed equipment. Live load comes from use, such as people, furniture and stored goods, and it can move or change. Because live load is less certain, the codes treat the two differently when we combine them.
Walk me through the load path for wind hitting the side of a low-rise building.
How you trace a load from where it lands down to the ground.
A continuous chain: cladding, framing, diaphragms, lateral system, foundation. Every connection along the way must carry the load.

Wind pushes on the cladding, which spans to studs or girts. Those deliver the load to the floor and roof diaphragms. The diaphragms carry it sideways to the shear walls, braced frames or moment frames, which take it down to the foundation and into the soil. I check every connection in that chain, because a missing link is where buildings fail.
What is the difference between LRFD and ASD?
Your grasp of the two design methods used in US steel and wood design.
LRFD factors loads up and strength down; ASD uses service-level loads against strength divided by a safety factor.

In LRFD, I multiply the loads by load factors and compare them with the nominal strength times a resistance factor below one. In ASD, I use service-level load combinations and compare them with the nominal strength divided by a safety factor. Both aim for safe members; LRFD sets the margin separately for loads and for resistance, so it is more consistent across load types.
What controls the strength of a slender column, and how can you raise it?
Whether you understand buckling and not only material strength.
Stiffness and effective length govern, not yield strength. Raise capacity with bracing, stiffer end fixity or a section with a larger moment of inertia.

A slender column fails by buckling before the steel yields. The Euler load depends on the modulus, the moment of inertia and the effective length squared, so a higher-strength steel barely helps. I would add bracing to cut the unbraced length, fix the ends better to lower the effective length factor, or pick a section with more inertia about the weak axis.
Why can a part that passes the static strength check still crack in service?
Your understanding of fatigue under repeated loading.
Cyclic stress well below yield can start and grow cracks at stress concentrations. Fatigue is checked by stress range and number of cycles.

Repeated loading can start a crack even when peak stress is well below yield. Cracks start at weld toes, holes and sharp corners, then grow a little each cycle. So for a crane runway or a vibrating mount I check the stress range at each detail against the fatigue curve for that detail, using the expected number of cycles, and I improve the detail if it falls short.
Your finite element model shows stress far above yield at a sharp inside corner. What do you do?
Whether you can tell a real stress from a modeling artifact.
Recognizes a likely singularity, checks mesh convergence, models the real fillet radius and compares with a hand calculation before acting.

A sharp inside corner with zero radius is a singularity: the stress keeps climbing as I refine the mesh, so the number means nothing. I refine the mesh to see if it converges, model the actual fillet radius from the drawing and read stresses a short distance away. I also check the overall load with a hand calculation. If the part sees cyclic loads, that local peak still matters for fatigue.
A contractor calls: the plumber wants to cut a 6-inch hole through a steel beam web. What do you tell him?
How you handle a field change without guessing on the phone.
No approval until the location and beam are known; explains where holes are least harmful and gives a written answer, adding reinforcement if needed.

I ask him not to cut anything yet and to send the beam mark, hole size and exact location with a photo. A hole near mid-depth of the web, away from supports and point loads, often works, because the flanges carry most of the bending and shear is lower there. I check the net section, add a reinforcing plate if needed and send a sketch in writing.
Two days before a design review, the margin of safety on a flight bracket comes out at minus 0.02. What do you do?
Your judgement when the numbers say no and the schedule says yes.
Treats a negative margin as a fail, reports it right away, and looks for real conservatism or a fix, never a quiet tweak of inputs.

A negative margin means the part does not meet the required factor of safety, so I flag it to my lead that day. Then I look for honest conservatism: a crude load, a stress read at a peak that is not real, or a better material allowable. If none holds up, I propose a thicker flange and show the mass cost. I do not change inputs just to get a positive number.
An owner wants to put a large air handling unit on the roof of an existing building. How do you approach it?
How you assess an existing structure for a new load.
Finds the original drawings, verifies conditions on site, checks members and connections down the load path, and considers vibration and future loads.

I start with the original drawings and visit the roof to confirm the framing matches and to look for rust or damage. I get the unit's operating weight and footprint, then check the deck, joists, girders, connections and columns down to the footing. If something is short, I look at dunnage spanning to stronger members or local reinforcement. I also check vibration isolation with the mechanical engineer.
After drawings are issued, you find a mistake in your own beam calculation. What do you do?
Whether you own a mistake fast, even when it is embarrassing.
Tells the lead and engineer of record at once, finds out if it is built, quantifies the effect and issues a documented fix.

I tell my lead and the engineer of record the same day, before anything else. Then I rerun the beam to see how far off it is and ask the contractor whether it is fabricated or erected. On one job a beam was 12% overstressed; we caught it before erection and swapped to the next size up through a formal revision. I also added that check to my template.
Why do we want a reinforced concrete beam to be tension-controlled, and how does the code reward it?
Whether you understand ductility in concrete design, not just the formulas.
The steel yields well before the concrete crushes, so the beam cracks and sags visibly before it fails. The code allows a higher strength reduction factor.

In a tension-controlled section the rebar yields long before the concrete crushes. The beam cracks and deflects a lot, which warns people before collapse. ACI 318 rewards that with a higher phi factor than a compression-controlled section gets. If a beam comes out over-reinforced, I make it deeper or add compression steel.
What is lateral-torsional buckling, and what do you do on a beam where it controls?
Your grasp of stability in steel beams beyond simple bending strength.
The compression flange buckles sideways and the section twists. Strength depends on unbraced length, so you brace the compression flange or pick a more stable section.

When a beam bends, its compression flange acts like a column and can buckle sideways, twisting the section. Under AISC 360 the strength drops once the unbraced length passes Lp. If it controls, I brace the compression flange closer, credit the moment gradient with Cb, or choose a section with a wider, stockier flange.
How does the choice of a rigid or flexible diaphragm change how you distribute lateral load to the walls?
Your understanding of how lateral force gets from floors into the vertical system.
Flexible shares by tributary width; rigid shares by stiffness and adds torsion. When unsure, model it semirigid or envelope both.

With a flexible diaphragm, like many wood roofs, each wall takes load by its tributary width. With a rigid one, like a concrete slab, walls share by relative stiffness, and any offset between the center of mass and center of rigidity adds torsion. ASCE 7 also requires accidental torsion for non-flexible diaphragms. When unsure, I model it semirigid or envelope both.
When do you specify slip-critical bolted connections instead of bearing-type connections?
Whether you know connection behavior and when slip matters, not just bolt strength.
Where slip would hurt: fatigue with reversing load, oversized holes, slots parallel to the load, or joints where movement is harmful. It costs surface prep and inspection.

In a bearing connection the plates can slip until the bolts bear on the holes, which is fine for most static joints. I go slip-critical for reversing fatigue loads, oversized holes, slots parallel to the load, or where movement would hurt the structure. It costs more: the contact surfaces need a specified slip class and pretension must be verified.
On an unshored composite floor beam, what do you check before the concrete hardens?
Whether you design for construction stages, not just the finished condition.
The bare steel beam must carry wet concrete and construction load alone, with its own bracing and deflection, and you allow for extra concrete from sag.

Until the concrete cures, the steel beam works alone. I check it for wet concrete, deck and a construction live load, braced only by the attached deck. I also check deflection during the pour: the beam sags, a slab screeded flat gets thicker at midspan, and that adds weight. So I specify camber or allow for the extra concrete.
Why is a flat roof with long, light framing at risk of ponding, and how do you design against it?
Whether you see the feedback between deflection and load on low-slope roofs.
Deflection collects water, which adds deflection. Check stiffness, give the roof slope, and design for rain with primary drains blocked, per ASCE 7.

Rain makes the framing sag, the sag holds more water, and that water adds more sag. If the framing is too flexible, the loop does not settle and the roof can collapse. I check stiffness with the AISC ponding provisions, slope the roof to drains, and design for the water depth that builds when primary drains are blocked, as ASCE 7 requires.
On a pre-pour site visit, you find the top bars of a cantilevered balcony slab lying on the bottom of the form. What do you do?
How you act on a serious field error when schedule pressure pushes to pour anyway.
Stop the pour for that area, explain why, require the bars raised on chairs to the specified cover, recheck before release, and document it.

A cantilever's tension is at the top, so bars lying on the bottom do almost nothing and the balcony could fail. I tell the superintendent that area cannot be poured, and why. The bars go up on chairs at the cover shown on the drawings, and I or the special inspector check them before the pour is released. It goes in my field report the same day.
A junior engineer hands you a finite element model of a transfer girder. How do you decide whether to trust it?
How you review analysis you did not build, with checks that do not depend on the software.
Reactions against applied loads, units, supports and releases, deformed shape, mesh refinement where it matters, and a hand calculation that lands close.

First I check that the reactions add up to the applied loads, which catches missing loads and unit errors. Then I look at supports, releases and the deformed shape: does it bend the way I expect? I refine the mesh where stresses matter to see if results settle. Last, a hand calculation of the girder as a simple beam must land in the same range, or I want to know why.
Why does a special steel moment frame get a much higher R value than an ordinary one, and what does that cost you in design?
Whether you understand that a lower seismic design force is paid for with ductile detailing.
A higher R assumes controlled yielding, so you owe AISC 341 detailing: strong column weak beam, protected zones, and prequalified or tested connections.

R lowers the design force because we expect the frame to yield and absorb energy instead of staying elastic. That works only if yielding happens where we planned. So under AISC 341 I make columns stronger than beams, keep protected zones at the hinges free of welds and attachments, and use AISC 358 prequalified or tested connections. Drift often ends up controlling sizes.
Why do thin-walled cylinders in rocket structures buckle well below the classical theory, and how do you design for it?
Your depth on shell stability, where theory and test results disagree badly.
Buckling is very sensitive to small imperfections, so you use empirical knockdown factors, as in NASA SP-8007, or imperfection analysis backed by test.

A perfect cylinder in axial compression has a high theoretical buckling load, but tiny dents and out-of-roundness cut it sharply, and tests scatter widely. The classic approach applies an empirical knockdown factor from NASA SP-8007, which is conservative. Newer work uses nonlinear analysis with measured or assumed imperfections, validated by test, to justify a milder factor.

summer-intern.heading: Summer intern questions
qs: Our interns present their project to senior leaders in the last week. How would you prepare for that?
Whether you plan for the end of the summer from the start.
Starting early, building the story as the work goes, and practicing with real feedback before the day.

I would ask in week one what past presentations looked like and who will be in the room. I would keep a running slide of results each week, so the deck is not a rush at the end. Two weeks out I would do a dry run with my manager and one teammate, then cut anything a leader would not need to make a decision.
How would you get feedback during the summer, not just in the final review?
How you seek feedback in a short internship where there is little time to adjust.
Asking early and on a set schedule, asking specific questions, and showing the feedback was used.

In my first week I would ask my manager for a short weekly check-in. Instead of asking how I am doing, I would ask something specific, like whether my status notes have the right level of detail. At the midpoint I would ask directly what would stop me from getting a return offer, so I have five weeks to fix it.
Your project brief is one vague paragraph. What do you do in your first week?
How you turn an unclear assignment into a project you can finish in ten to twelve weeks.
Clarifying the goal, who uses the result and what done looks like, then writing it down for the manager to confirm.

I would meet my manager and ask three things: what problem this solves, who will use the result, and what a good outcome looks like in August. Then I would write a one-page plan with goals, milestones by week and open questions, and ask them to confirm it. That page becomes what we both measure the summer against.
Halfway through the summer, you see your project is too big for the weeks left. What do you do?
Whether you raise scope problems early and offer options.
Telling the manager right away with a clear trade-off, instead of working nights and hoping or delivering half of everything.

I would tell my manager that week, not in week ten. I would bring two options: finish the core piece well and write up the rest as next steps, or keep the full scope with a simpler version of each part. I would say which I recommend and why. Then we agree and I update my plan.
You finish your assigned project two weeks early. What do you do next?
Your initiative and judgement about how to use extra time.
Checking the quality first, then asking for or proposing useful work tied to the team, not quietly coasting.

First I would make sure it is really done: tested, reviewed and documented. Then I would go to my manager with a short list of ideas, such as extending the analysis to another region or helping a teammate with a deadline, and ask which matters most. I would rather pick from their priorities than invent busywork.
Your manager is out for two weeks in July. How do you keep your work moving?
How you work independently without stalling or going off track.
Agreeing on a plan and a backup contact before the leave, then keeping a clear log of decisions to review on return.

Before they leave, I would ask what I can decide on my own and who to go to if I am blocked. While they are out I would follow the plan, keep a short daily log of progress and decisions, and check in with the backup person once a week. On their first day back I would send a one-page summary so they catch up in ten minutes.
You and another intern share a project, and they keep missing their part. How do you handle it?
How you deal with a peer problem fairly and without drama.
Talking to the other intern first and directly, offering help, and going to the manager only if the work is at risk.

I would talk to them privately first and ask what is getting in the way; maybe they are stuck or have unclear instructions. We would split the next tasks again with dates we both write down. If deadlines still slip and the project is at risk, I would tell our manager the facts, without blaming, so we can fix the plan in time.
You want to post about your summer project on LinkedIn. What do you check first?
Whether you understand confidentiality at work.
Knowing that company work is often confidential and asking before sharing any details, numbers or screenshots.

I would assume the project details are confidential until told otherwise, especially if I signed a confidentiality agreement.
