I would ask my manager what I can say, and keep the post general: the skills I used and what I learned, with no client names, data or screenshots. The same rule applies to my resume and portfolio.
How will you make sure your work is still useful after you leave in August?
Whether you plan a proper handoff when the internship ends.
Documentation, a named owner and a walkthrough, so the work does not die when the intern leaves.

From the middle of the summer I would ask who will own the work after I go. In my last two weeks I would write a short guide covering what it does, where the files are, how to run or update it, and known limits. Then I would walk the owner through it once and let them try it while I am still there to answer questions.
Suppose we make you a return offer, but you have other interviews this fall. How would you handle that?
Your honesty and judgement about offers and timelines.
Being open about the situation, respecting the deadline, and never accepting an offer while planning to back out later.

I would thank you and be honest that I have other processes going. If I needed more time, I would ask for it before the deadline rather than letting it pass. I would compare the team, the work and what I learned this summer. Once I accept an offer, I stop interviewing; backing out later would be unfair to you and to the next candidate.
How do you decide when to ask a question and when to keep digging on your own?
Whether you can balance independence with not wasting time stuck.
A time limit for digging, a check of the obvious sources first, and a question that shows what you already tried.

I give myself a set window, say 20 to 30 minutes, and check the docs, past files and team chat first. If I am still stuck, I ask, and I say what I tried and where I got lost. That way the answer takes two minutes, not twenty.
What would you put in a weekly update to your manager?
How you keep a busy manager informed without being asked.
Short and the same shape each week: done, next, blocked, and decisions needed, with problems raised early.

Four short parts: what I finished, what I am doing next week, what is blocking me, and any decision I need from them. I keep it to a few lines and put bad news at the top. If something slips, they should hear it from me on Friday, not find it in the final review.
Your manager and a lead from another team both send you an urgent request on the same morning. What do you do?
How you handle competing demands when you do not own the priorities.
You do not quietly pick one. You tell your manager, give an honest time estimate, and let them set the order.

I would estimate how long each takes, then message my manager: two requests, here are the times, which comes first? My manager owns my time, so they make the call. Then I tell the other lead when to expect theirs, so nobody is left guessing.
You are paid hourly and stayed late three evenings to finish an analysis. A full-timer says interns usually do not log extra time. What do you do?
Whether you know how hourly pay works and act honestly about it.
You record every hour actually worked, since off-the-clock work for hourly staff is not allowed, and you ask before working extra next time.

I would log the hours I actually worked. If I am paid hourly, the company has to pay me for all of it, and hiding hours can cause them a legal problem. I would also tell my manager, and next time I would ask before staying late, since overtime may need approval.
You want to use a free online AI tool to clean up the data for your project. What do you check first?
Whether you protect company data when using outside tools.
You check the company policy and what the data contains before pasting anything, and you ask if unsure.

First, the company policy on outside tools. Many firms ban putting internal data into public AI tools, because the text may be stored or used outside the company. I would also check whether the data has customer names or other private details. If I am unsure, I ask my manager or use an approved tool.
You find an error in a spreadsheet a senior analyst built, and the numbers are already in a client deck. What do you do?
How you raise a problem in someone else's work with tact and speed.
You confirm the error, go to the owner privately and quickly, show the evidence, and let them decide on the fix.

I would double-check it, then go to the analyst directly, that day, not to the group. I would say: I think this formula pulls the wrong column, here is what I see and the number I get. Maybe I am missing something. A client deck is time-sensitive, so I would not sit on it to avoid an awkward moment.
You think your manager's approach to your project is the wrong one. How do you raise it?
Whether you can disagree respectfully and still commit.
Evidence, a clear alternative, an open question about what you might not know, and full effort on their decision.

I would ask for ten minutes and bring a short comparison: their approach, mine, and what each costs in time. I would ask what I might be missing, since they know context I do not. If they keep their plan, I do it well and do not relitigate it in week eight.
How would you meet people outside your team this summer without wasting their time?
How you build a network in a way senior people respect.
A specific reason to talk, short meetings booked around their calendar, prepared questions, and a follow-up note.

I would ask my manager who works near my project, then request 20 minutes with a clear reason, like how their team uses the data I am building. I come with three questions, keep to time, and send a thank-you note with one thing I took away. That turns a name into someone who remembers me.
In your final presentation, a vice president asks a question you cannot answer. What do you say?
How you stay credible under pressure without bluffing.
An honest "I do not know," what you do know that is related, and a promise to follow up with a set time.

I would say: I did not look at that, so I do not want to guess. What I can tell you is the related number I did check. I will find the answer and send it to you by tomorrow. Then I actually send it. A senior leader forgives a gap far faster than a made-up number.
Your analysis shows a process your team built does not work as well as they think. How do you present that?
Your judgement in delivering unwelcome findings to the people who hired you.
You share it with your manager before any big audience, lead with evidence and limits, and frame it as a way to improve.

I would show my manager first, privately, well before the final week, so nobody is surprised in front of leaders. I would lay out the data, how sure I am and what I could not test. Then I would offer a next step, like a small pilot of a fix. Hiding the result to please people would make my summer worthless.

superintendent.heading: Construction superintendent questions
qs: What goes into your daily report, and why does it matter?
Whether you keep the record that protects the project later.
Manpower by trade, work done, weather, deliveries, inspections, visitors, delays and incidents, written the same day as plain facts.

I log each sub's headcount, what got done and where, weather, deliveries, inspections, visitors, and any delay or incident with photos. I write it the same day and stick to facts. Months later, when someone argues about a delay or a claim, that log is often the best evidence we have.
What is the critical path, and what is float?
Your grasp of how a schedule actually drives the job.
The longest chain of linked tasks sets the finish date; float is how long a task can slip without moving that date.

The critical path is the longest chain of linked activities from start to finish; any day lost on it moves the end date. Float is how many days a task can slip without that happening. I watch float shrink on near-critical work, because a task with two days of float can become critical after one bad week.
How do you run a three-week lookahead with your subcontractors?
How you turn the master schedule into work crews can actually plan for.
Updated weekly from the master schedule, built with the foremen, with materials, submittals and inspections cleared ahead of time.

Every week I break the next three weeks of the master schedule into tasks by area and go through it with each foreman. For each task we ask: is the material here, are submittals approved, is the area ready, is an inspection needed? Anything not ready gets an owner and a date, so problems show up two weeks out, not the morning of.
Walk me through your checks before a concrete slab pour.
Whether you catch the things that cannot be fixed once concrete is placed.
Inspections signed off, under-slab work done, rebar and embeds per drawings, grades checked, weather, trucks and the testing lab lined up.

I confirm required inspections are signed off and under-slab plumbing and electrical are done and tested. I check rebar size, spacing, chairs and cover, plus embeds and sleeves, against the drawings, and shoot the form grades. Then I confirm the mix, trucks, pump, finishers, weather plan, and that the testing lab is coming for slump and cylinders.
A utility trench on your site needs to go 7 feet deep. What has to be in place before anyone gets in?
Whether you know the OSHA excavation rules a superintendent is responsible for.
811 locates, a protective system at 5 feet or deeper, a competent person inspecting, a ladder to get out, and spoils kept back from the edge.

Utilities are located through 811 before we dig. At 7 feet we need a protective system: sloping, shoring or a trench box, since 5 feet or deeper needs one unless it is stable rock. A competent person inspects it daily before work and after rain. There is a ladder within 25 feet of each worker, and spoil piles sit at least 2 feet back from the edge.
The owner's representative walks the site and asks your carpenter foreman to add a wall. What do you do?
How you handle scope changes without giving away work or upsetting the owner.
Polite, but the work does not start until it goes through the change order process with price, schedule impact and written approval.

I tell the foreman not to start, then talk to the rep myself, politely. I say we can look at it, but extra work goes through the project manager with a price and schedule impact, and needs written approval. If it touches the design it may need an RFI to the architect first. A wall built on a hallway promise usually ends up unpaid and argued over.
A drywall sub is ten days behind and their foreman keeps saying they will catch up. How do you handle it?
How you hold a subcontractor to the schedule before it becomes a crisis.
A specific recovery plan with manpower and dates, tracked daily, written notice per the subcontract if missed, and protecting the trades that follow.

Catching up is not a plan. I sit down with the foreman and ask for one: how many more hangers, which areas, by what date. I track their headcount daily against it. If they miss it, our project manager sends written notice under the subcontract, and I look at resequencing so the painters and ceiling crew are not sitting idle.
Your excavator hits a buried concrete foundation that is not on any drawing or in the soils report. What do you do?
How you handle a differing site condition and protect the company's right to be paid for it.
Stop at that spot, make it safe, document with photos and measurements, and get written notice out within the contract deadline.

I stop digging at that spot and make sure nobody is hurt and no utility is involved. Then I photograph it, measure it, and note the time and crew in the daily report. I tell the project manager right away so written notice goes to the owner within the contract deadline. Meanwhile I move the crew to other work and track the extra hours and equipment separately.
You find out the drywall crew closed up a wall before the electrical rough-in inspection was signed off. What now?
Whether you own a sequencing failure and fix it the right way, not the easy way.
Tell the inspector honestly, open the wall as they require, and fix the sign-off check so it does not happen again.

I stop them closing anything else and call the inspector to explain. Usually they want the board removed or inspection holes cut, and we do whatever they ask. Tearing out costs little next to failing a final. Then I fix the cause: no area gets board until I have walked it and the inspection is signed, and I say that at the next foremen meeting.
The job is three weeks behind and the project manager asks you to get it back. How do you decide what to do?
Your judgement on recovering schedule without wrecking cost, quality or safety.
Start from the critical path, weigh resequencing, extra crews and overtime, and know that long overtime cuts output and raises risk.

First I find which critical path activities caused the slip and which can still overlap. Resequencing or splitting areas costs least, so I look there first. Then extra crews on critical work. I use overtime in short bursts only, since weeks of long days lower output and raise injury risk. I give the PM options with cost and days gained for each, not one guess.
What does dry-in mean, and why does it matter so much to your schedule?
Whether you understand the milestone that opens up interior work.
The building is closed to weather. Interior finishes and moisture-sensitive materials wait for it, so it gets protected in the schedule.

Dry-in is when the building is closed to weather: roof membrane or underlayment down, windows and exterior doors in, and the weather barrier on. Until then I cannot hang drywall, stock cabinets or start finishes without risking water damage. So I push hard on roofing and window deliveries, because a late dry-in pushes every interior trade.
What is the difference between an RFI and a submittal?
Your grasp of the two documents that keep design questions and products on record.
An RFI asks the design team to clarify the documents; a submittal shows what will be installed. Neither one changes the contract; that takes a change order.

An RFI is a written question to the architect or engineer when the drawings are unclear or conflict. A submittal is the sub showing what they will install: shop drawings, product data, samples. I review it against the specs before it goes to the architect. If either one adds cost or time, I flag it for a change order, because an approval alone does not change the contract.
A new subcontractor mobilizes Monday. What do you cover with them before they start?
How you set up a sub to work safely and to plan from day one.
Scope and exclusions, schedule, site logistics, safety rules and orientation, submittal status, inspections and who to call.

I sit down with their foreman, not just the office. We go over scope and what is excluded, their dates in the lookahead, where they park, stage and get power, and the site safety rules. Every worker gets orientation before they touch tools. I confirm their submittals are approved, which inspections they need, and that I get their daily manpower count.
A crane is coming on Monday to set steel. What do you have in place before the first pick?
Whether you know the main controls for crane work on a site.
Certified operator, ground checked, power lines located and cleared, lift plan and rigging checked, a qualified signal person and a barricaded swing radius.

I confirm the operator is certified and the crane's inspection is current. I check the ground and the mats under the outriggers, since OSHA puts that on the controlling contractor. Power lines are located; up to 350 kV we stay at least 20 feet away and treat them as live. The rigger checks slings, a qualified signal person is named, and the swing radius is barricaded.
A crew is cutting concrete openings indoors with a handheld saw. What do you expect to see?
Whether you know the OSHA silica rule for construction in practice.
Water at the blade, ventilation indoors, respirators per OSHA Table 1, no dry sweeping or blowing dust, and a written exposure control plan.

That cut makes silica dust, so water must feed the blade the whole time, and indoors I want air moving to clear it. OSHA's Table 1 says when a respirator is required; indoors it is required however long the cut lasts. Cleanup is wet or with a HEPA vacuum, never dry sweeping or compressed air. The company also needs a written exposure control plan and a competent person.
The plumber and the HVAC sub both say the same ceiling space above a corridor is theirs. How do you settle it?
How you coordinate trades in tight space and which systems get priority.
Gravity lines first because their slope is fixed, then large duct; pressure pipe and conduit route around. A ceiling height change goes to the designer by RFI.

I get both foremen in the corridor with the drawings and a tape. Gravity drain lines win because their slope is fixed, then the big duct, since it has the fewest options. Sprinkler, water and conduit can usually offset around them. If it still does not fit at the ceiling height shown, I write an RFI with dimensions instead of letting someone drop the ceiling on their own.
A slab is close to the drawings but slightly out of tolerance. How do you decide whether to accept it?
Your judgement on quality when work is close but not right.
Measure against the spec or the standard it references, think about what goes on it next, and take anything outside tolerance to the design team in writing.

First I measure and check the spec; for concrete it often points to ACI 117. Then I ask what comes next: an out-of-level slab matters a lot under a long run of tile or racking. Inside tolerance, I note it and move on. Outside, I do not quietly accept it. I send it to the architect with the numbers and options, like grinding or a topping, and the fix goes on record.
A laborer cuts his hand and the clinic closes it with stitches. What happens next on your end?
Whether you know what follows an injury: care, recordkeeping and learning from it.
Care first, then a written incident report and investigation. Stitches are medical treatment, so the case is recordable on the employer's OSHA 300 log.

First he gets care and someone goes with him. I secure the area and take photos and statements the same day. Stitches count as medical treatment, so it is a recordable case on his employer's OSHA 300 log. If he were admitted to the hospital, OSHA would have to be told within 24 hours. Then we find the cause, like a dull blade or missing cut gloves, and fix it.
The owner is two weeks late approving a change to the lobby, and your finishes are stalled. How do you protect the job's time and money?
Whether you document an owner delay so a time extension can be claimed.
Written notice inside the contract's window, daily records of the impact, a schedule showing the critical path effect, and other work moved forward meanwhile.

I make sure the PM sends written notice within the window the contract sets, because a late notice can lose the claim. Every day I log what is stalled, who is affected and what we did to work around it. I show the impact on the schedule against the critical path. Meanwhile I move crews to other areas so we are not just waiting, and I document that too.
Two weeks before substantial completion you have 500 punch list items and the owner wants to move in early. How do you handle it?
How you drive closeout and what must be true before people occupy the building.
Substantial completion means usable for its purpose; life safety and the certificate of occupancy come first, and early use is agreed in writing.

Substantial completion means the owner can use the building for its purpose, not that every item is done. I split the punch list by trade and area with dates and walk it daily. Life safety and the inspections for the certificate of occupancy come first; nobody moves in without it. Early use of any area gets agreed in writing: utilities, damage and insurance.

supervisor.heading: Supervisor questions
qs: What do you do in the first fifteen minutes of a shift?
How you set up a shift before the work starts.
A routine: read the handover, check who is in, hold a short huddle on goals and safety, then walk the floor.

I read the handover notes from the last shift and check who called out. Then I hold a five-minute huddle: today's volume, who is on which station, one safety point and any problem left over. After that I walk the floor to see that every station is staffed and the equipment is running before I go to my desk.
What goes into a good shift handover?
Whether you pass on what the next shift needs to know.
Written and spoken: open work, problems, equipment down, people issues, and anything promised to someone else.

I write it down and then say it face to face. Open orders and where they stand, any machine that is down or acting up, quality holds, who left early or is on light duty, and anything I promised a customer or another department. The next lead should not need to call me at home to understand the shift.
How do you decide who works which station on a shift?
How you match people to the work.
Training and restrictions first, then skills and the day's load, plus cross-training so the shift does not depend on one person.

First the hard limits: only trained and certified people go on equipment like forklifts, and I check restrictions such as light duty. Then I put my strongest people where volume is highest. I also rotate one or two people into stations they are learning, with a trained person nearby, so I am not stuck when someone calls out.
You were promoted over people who were your coworkers last week. How do you handle the first month?
Whether you can move from peer to boss without losing the team.
Talks to each person, stays friendly without favoritism, and applies the rules the same way to everyone from day one.

I would talk to each person one on one in the first week, ask what works and what gets in the way, and say plainly that my job has changed. I can still be friendly, but I cannot cover for anyone. The first time a friend breaks a rule, I handle it exactly as I would for anyone else, because the whole team is watching that moment.
One of your workers has been slow and making errors for two weeks. How do you handle it?
How you coach and correct someone who is falling behind.
A private talk with facts, a question about the cause, a clear expectation, a follow-up date, and notes kept in case it goes further.

I talk to him privately with the facts: his numbers and the errors I found, with dates. Then I ask what is going on, because it could be training, a scanner problem or something at home. We agree on what good looks like and when we will check again. I write down what we discussed. If nothing changes, I bring in my manager or HR with those notes.
A worker offers to finish a task after clocking out so the shift stays under budget. What do you say?
Whether you know that hourly work must be paid, even when the worker offers.
A clear no: hourly workers must be paid for all time worked. Then fix the real problem, the workload or the plan.

I thank him and say no. If he is working, he is on the clock, even if he volunteers; letting it slide can break wage law and the company pays later. If the task really must be done today, I approve the time or move it to the next shift. Then I tell my manager the plan was short on hours so we fix it, not hide it.
Two people on your shift start shouting at each other on the floor. What do you do?
How you handle conflict as it happens.
Separates them calmly, gets work going again, hears each side in private later, and follows policy if it crossed a line.

I step in calmly, ask them to stop, and send one to a different task so they are apart. If anyone threatens violence, I call security and my manager right away. Once things cool down, I talk to each of them alone, then together if it helps. I note what happened, and if it broke the conduct policy I follow the policy, whoever started it.
An employee tells you a coworker keeps making sexual comments, but asks you to keep it between the two of you. What do you do?
Whether you know a supervisor must report harassment, even when asked not to.
Does not promise secrecy, reports to HR promptly, protects the employee from retaliation and keeps the matter as private as possible.

I thank her for telling me and say honestly that I cannot keep it secret: once a supervisor knows, the company has to act. I promise to share it only with the people who need to know, and I report it to HR that day. I do not question the coworker myself. I also watch that nobody treats her worse for speaking up, because that is retaliation.
You signed off on a batch, then find out it had a defect and part of it has already shipped. What do you do?
How you own a mistake and limit the damage.
Tells the manager right away, stops more from shipping, helps trace what went out, and fixes the check that missed it.

I hold everything still in the building and tell my manager right away, with the lot numbers and what I know. I help pull the shipping records so customer service can reach the customers who got it. Then I look at my own check: maybe I only looked at the first few units. I change it to sample through the whole run, and I tell the team what changed and why.
Walk me through how you train a new hire on a station.
How you pass on a job so it is done right without you standing there.
Show, then watch them do it, then check the work. One step at a time, with the reason behind each safety and quality point.

First I show the task at normal speed, then slowly, and explain why each check matters. Then they do it while I watch and correct right away. I give them a few hours alone with spot checks. Before I sign them off, they show me the whole task, including what to do when the machine jams or a part is wrong.
A worker eats lunch at the station so she can keep answering the phone. Is that a problem?
Whether you know when break time counts as paid work time.
Yes. A meal break can be unpaid only if the worker is fully relieved of duty, and answering calls makes it work time.

Yes. Under federal wage rules, an unpaid meal break means she is completely off duty. If she is answering the phone, that time is work and has to be paid, even if she offered. Some states also require breaks. I would cover the phone or rotate it so she gets a real break, and make sure her time record is right.
How do you build a weekly schedule that covers the work and stays fair?
Your method for scheduling around volume, skills, overtime and people's lives.
Starts from expected volume and skills, watches overtime, rotates unpopular shifts and posts the schedule early.

I start from the forecast volume and how many trained people each station needs. I place the people with rare skills first, then fill. I track hours so no one goes past 40 in the week without approval, since nonexempt staff get overtime pay after that, and some states count daily overtime too. Weekend and late shifts rotate, and I post the schedule as early as I can.
A forklift nearly hits a worker on your shift, but no one is hurt. Walk me through what you do.
Whether you treat a near miss as a warning and dig for the cause.
Make the area safe, get the facts while they are fresh, look for the cause rather than a culprit, fix it and report it per policy.

I stop traffic in that aisle and check that both people are fine. Then I talk to the driver, the worker and anyone who saw it, separately, while it is fresh. I look at the layout: a blind corner, a blocked mirror, a walkway crossing a travel lane. I write it up per our near miss procedure, fix the cause, such as a mirror or a marked crossing, and share it at the next huddle.
An operator wants to clear a jam with the machine idling because it only takes a minute. What do you say?
Whether you hold the lockout rule when it costs time.
No. Hands in the machine means the energy is isolated and locked out per procedure, with each person using their own lock.

I say no, and I stay while it is done right. Idling is not off; a sensor can restart it. We shut it down, isolate the energy, put on locks and tags, and try the start button to confirm it is dead before anyone reaches in. Everyone working on it puts on their own lock. If jams happen so often that people want to skip this, I raise that as a problem to fix.
A worker cuts his hand, wraps it, and asks you not to write it up because he does not want to hurt the team's safety record. What do you do?
Whether you know injuries must be reported and that discouraging a report is not allowed.
Care first, then a report anyway, and a clear message that no one is punished for reporting an injury.

First he gets proper first aid or medical care, depending on the cut. Then I tell him I have to report it, and that he will not get in trouble for that; federal rules forbid retaliating against someone for reporting an injury. Whether it goes on the OSHA log depends on the treatment, and the rules decide that, not us. A hidden injury also hides the hazard that caused it.
Your best performer keeps skipping safety glasses because they fog up. How do you handle it?
Whether you apply rules the same way to everyone, and fix the real cause.
The same rule for the top performer as for a new hire, a private talk early, and a fix for the fogging so following the rule is easy.

I talk to him privately the first time I see it, not after the fifth. I tell him the rule applies to him like everyone, and that others watch what he does. Then I deal with the reason: anti-fog lenses, a different style, or a check of the ventilation. If he still skips them, it goes through the same discipline steps as for anyone.
You think a worker driving a forklift may be impaired. What do you do?
How you act on a suspicion safely and fairly, without accusing or diagnosing.
Takes them off the equipment at once, notes specific behavior, brings in a witness and HR, follows policy and keeps them from driving home.

I take him off the forklift right away and move him somewhere private. I write down what I saw: slurred speech, unsteady walk, a smell, the time. I bring in another supervisor or HR as a witness and follow our reasonable suspicion policy, which may mean a test. I do not diagnose or accuse; it could be medical. And I make sure he does not drive himself home.
An employee says she will need several days off over the next few months for a medical condition. What do you do?
Whether you know when a request must go to HR under leave and disability law.
Does not ask for the diagnosis or refuse; sends it to HR because it may fall under the FMLA or the ADA, and keeps it confidential.

I thank her, and I do not ask what the condition is or say we cannot spare her. I tell her I will involve HR today, because this may be protected leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act or an accommodation under the ADA, and HR decides that. I keep it between her, HR and me. I plan coverage and do not count her absences against her until HR answers.
Your manager wants 15% more output next month with the same crew. How do you respond?
How you push back with data and commit only to what is real.
Not a quick yes or no: finds the bottleneck and lost time, offers a realistic number with what it needs, and will not buy it with safety.

I would not promise it on the spot. I look at where we lose time now: downtime, changeovers, waiting on material, rework. If those add up to 10%, I come back with a plan for 10% and say what the other 5% would take, like one more trained person or a second shift on the bottleneck machine. What I won't do is get it by skipping checks or rushing safety steps.

supplier-quality.heading: Supplier quality and development engineer questions
qs: What is PPAP, and what does a Level 3 submission include?
Whether you know the core approval process for new production parts.
PPAP proves the real production process makes good parts. Level 3 means the warrant, sample parts and full supporting data go to the customer.

PPAP is the Production Part Approval Process. It shows that the supplier's real production process can make parts that meet every requirement. Level 3, the usual default, means the supplier sends the Part Submission Warrant, sample parts and the full data: dimensional results, material reports, PFMEA, control plan, capability studies and gauge studies.
Walk me through a process audit at a supplier you have never visited.
How you run an audit that finds real risks, not just missing paperwork.
Preparation from the drawing and history, following the part on the floor, and comparing the control plan with what operators actually do.

Before the visit I read the drawing, the control plan, the PFMEA, which is their risk analysis of the process, and our complaint history. On the floor I follow one part from incoming material to shipping. At each step I compare the control plan with what the operator really does, check gauge calibration, and ask how they handle a bad part. I close with findings, evidence and agreed due dates.
A supplier's Gage R&R on a critical diameter comes back at 35% of tolerance. What does that tell you?
Whether you check the measurement system before trusting the data.
Over 30% is unacceptable under common MSA guidance, so capability numbers built on that gauge cannot be trusted until it is fixed.

It means about a third of the tolerance is taken up by measurement error, which is over the usual 30% limit. Any Cpk they report on that diameter is not reliable. I would find out whether the problem is the gauge itself or how operators use it, ask for a better gauge or method, and have them rerun the study before I accept capability data.
Our line finds cracked housings from a supplier this morning. What do you do in the first 24 hours?
How you contain a problem before you look for its cause.
Protect the customer first: quarantine and sort suspect stock everywhere, set a clean point, then start the root cause work.

First I make sure the line stops using suspect parts, and we tag and quarantine what we have. I ask the supplier to hold or sort stock at their plant and in transit, and to mark certified good shipments so we know the clean point. Once the customer is protected, I open an 8D and get cracked samples to start the root cause.
A supplier's 8D names operator error as the root cause and retraining as the fix. How do you respond?
Whether you can push a supplier past a weak root cause.
You send it back and ask why the process allowed the error and why it was not detected, looking for error-proofing over retraining.

I send it back. Operator error says what happened, not why the process let it happen. I ask two things: why the error could occur, and why their checks did not catch it. Retraining fades in weeks. I want a fixture, a sensor or other error-proofing that makes the mistake impossible or catches it at once, plus proof that it works.
You learn a supplier moved one of our parts to a new press line without telling you. What do you do?
Your knowledge of change control and how you enforce it.
Treat the unapproved change as a risk: hold affected lots, require requalification, and get a corrective action on their change process.

A move like that should have come to us as a change request first, and it usually needs a new PPAP or first article inspection. I identify which lots came off the new line and hold them until we check them. Then I ask for the requalification data and a corrective action on why their change process failed, because the next unreported change could be worse.
Production is short and a buyer wants you to accept a lot that is slightly out of tolerance. What do you do?
Your judgement when schedule pressure meets a nonconforming part.
No informal yes: a written deviation approved by design engineering, limited to that lot, plus a corrective action from the supplier.

I do not say yes on the spot, or no without looking. I get the measurements and ask design engineering whether the feature affects fit, function or safety. If they approve, it goes on a written deviation for that quantity only, and the supplier owes a corrective action. If the feature is critical, the answer is no and we sort or find another source.
A supplier sends material certificates where every lot shows exactly the same test values. What would you do?
Whether you spot warning signs of copied or false documentation.
Real test data varies, so identical results suggest copied certificates. Verify independently and escalate it as an integrity issue.

Real test results vary a little from lot to lot, so identical numbers suggest the certificate is copied, not tested. I would send retained samples to an independent lab and ask for the raw test records and the mill's original certificates. If the data were invented, that is an integrity issue, so I escalate it to management rather than treat it as a normal corrective action.
A key supplier runs at 4,000 PPM defective and we cannot switch soon. How would you develop them?
How you lead improvement at a supplier, not just audit it.
A data-driven plan: a Pareto of defects, work on the top few causes on the floor, agreed targets and regular reviews.

PPM means defective parts per million. I start with a Pareto of their defects, both what reaches us and what they catch inside. Usually two or three causes make most of it. I work on those with their team at the stations, checking capability and controls. We agree a target and a monthly review. At one supplier this took us from about 3,500 to 600 PPM in six months.
What is the difference between Cpk and Ppk, and when does it matter?
Whether you understand what a capability index really measures.
Cpk uses within-subgroup variation and Ppk uses overall variation. A big gap means the process shifts over time, and Cpk means little without stability.

Cpk estimates sigma from the variation inside subgroups, so it shows what the process can do short term. Ppk uses the standard deviation of all the data, so it includes drift between shifts, lots and setups. If Cpk is 2.0 and Ppk is 1.1, the process moves over time. I look at the control chart before I trust either number.
In an 8D, why do you ask for two root causes instead of one?
Whether you separate why the defect was made from why it escaped.
One cause for occurrence and one for non-detection, each with its own fix, plus a look at why the system allowed both.

One answer explains why the part was made bad. The other explains why nobody caught it before it shipped. A burr from a worn tool is the occurrence cause. A visual check under poor light that missed it is the escape. If I only fix the tool, the next burr ships too. I also ask what let both happen, like no tool-life limit in the control plan.
When you review a supplier's PFMEA, what do you look for?
How you judge whether a risk analysis is real or written only for the file.
Links to the process flow and control plan, honest ratings, special characteristics covered, and real actions on the high-priority items.

Every step in the process flow should appear in the PFMEA, and every control in it should appear in the control plan. Then I check the ratings: a visual check rated as good at detection as an automatic gauge is a red flag. Under the AIAG-VDA method I want actions on high action-priority items, and I compare the last update date with recent changes and complaints.
A supplier inspects a safety characteristic by AQL sampling. Why does that worry you?
Whether you know what an acceptance sampling plan does and does not guarantee.
AQL plans accept lots that contain some defects. For a safety feature you want prevention, error-proofing or an automatic check on every part.

An AQL plan is built to accept lots at a certain defect level most of the time, so by design it lets some bad parts through. For a crimp height on a brake harness that is not acceptable. I would ask for the defect to be prevented at the source or checked on every part by an automatic method, with sampling kept only as an extra audit layer.
What is the difference between Controlled Shipping Level 1 and Level 2, and when would you use each?
Your knowledge of the escalation tools for a supplier that keeps shipping defects.
CS1 is extra inspection by the supplier's own people. CS2 adds an independent third party at the supplier's cost, used when CS1 fails or the risk is high.

In Level 1 the supplier adds a redundant inspection, run by its own staff, on top of normal controls, and reports results to us. Level 2 adds a third-party inspection company paid by the supplier, usually because Level 1 did not stop the escapes. I set exit criteria up front, such as a period of clean data plus a verified permanent fix, so it does not drag on.
Our incoming inspection rejects a bore that the supplier's report shows as good. How do you sort it out?
How you handle a measurement dispute without taking sides too early.
A correlation study on the same marked parts, checking datums, fixturing, method and temperature before deciding who is right.

I would not argue over numbers. We pick ten parts, number them, and both sides measure the same pieces. If results differ, I compare the datum setup, how the part is held, the gauge or probe used, the temperature, and how each side reads the GD&T callout. Most often it is a datum or fixturing difference. We then agree the method in writing so it does not come back.
A PPAP shows a Ppk of 1.9 from 30 parts from one run of a four-cavity mold. Do you approve it?
Whether you can see when a capability study proves less than it seems to.
Not yet: each cavity must be measured and studied, the sample must reflect real conditions, and capability should be confirmed in early production.

Not on that data. With four cavities I need results per cavity, because one cavity can run off and hide in the mix. Thirty parts from one short run also miss material lots and shifts. I would ask which cavities the parts came from, get a study per cavity with more parts, and plan a follow-up check after the first weeks of production.
How do you assess capability for runout, where the data cannot go below zero?
Whether you handle non-normal data correctly instead of forcing a normal formula.
A one-sided limit, a check of the distribution, a fitted model or transformation, and only the upper-side index reported.

Runout has only an upper limit, and the data bunch up near zero, so the distribution is skewed. A normal Cpk would mislead. I check the shape with a probability plot, then use a fitted distribution such as Weibull or lognormal, or a transformation, and report only the upper-side index. If no model fits well, I say so and look at the actual spread against the limit.
The root cause sits at your supplier's plating sub-supplier. How do you handle it?
How you manage quality two levels down without taking ownership away from your supplier.
The direct supplier stays responsible and leads. You may join a visit, but you also check why the supplier's own sub-tier controls missed it.

Our supplier owns its sub-tier, so it leads the 8D with the plater and I hold it to the dates. I usually join one visit to see the line, for example how they check the bath and how often they test thickness. I also ask why the supplier's incoming checks and sub-tier audits missed it, because that is a gap in their system, not only the plater's.
A supplier has had four clean weeks under containment and asks to stop the extra inspection. How do you decide?
Your judgement on when a corrective action is proven and containment can end.
Exit on evidence: the fix seen in place, production that covered the risky conditions, solid containment records, and an updated PFMEA and control plan.

Four clean weeks alone is not enough. I want to see the permanent fix in place on the floor, and to know those weeks covered the conditions that caused the defect, like a tool change or a new material lot. I check that the containment records are complete and that the PFMEA and control plan are updated. Then I approve a step down, such as reduced inspection, not a full stop at once.

supply-chain.heading: Supply chain and logistics questions
qs: How do you use ABC analysis to decide where to spend your time?
How you focus control on the items that matter most.
Ranks items by annual usage value, tightens control on A items, and adds criticality so a cheap but vital part is not ignored.

I rank items by annual usage value, which is units used times cost. Usually a small share of items, the A items, carries most of the value. I count them more often, review their forecasts weekly and watch their suppliers closely. C items get simple rules and bigger buffers. I also flag cheap parts that can stop a line, because value alone misses those.
What is the bullwhip effect, and how do you reduce it?
Whether you understand how demand signals get distorted up the chain.
Small shifts in end demand grow larger upstream. Fixes include sharing real sales data, smaller and more frequent orders, steady pricing and shorter lead times.

It is when a small change in what end customers buy turns into bigger and bigger swings in orders as you move up to distributors, plants and suppliers. Each step adds its own buffer and batching. I fight it by sharing actual sales data with suppliers, ordering smaller amounts more often, avoiding price deals that cause buying spikes, and cutting lead times.
If you built a supplier scorecard from scratch, what would be on it?
Your ability to measure suppliers fairly and use the results.
A few clear measures like on-time in-full, quality and lead time, agreed with the supplier, reviewed on a set schedule and tied to actions.

I keep it to four or five measures: on-time in-full against the date we agreed, defect rate at receiving, lead time, price against contract, and how fast they respond to problems. I agree the definitions with the supplier first so nobody argues the math later. We review it quarterly, and a red score leads to a written corrective action plan, not just a grade.
One supplier quotes FOB at their port and another quotes DDP to our warehouse. How do you compare the two prices?
Whether you understand Incoterms and landed cost.
Converts both to landed cost: under FOB the buyer pays ocean freight, insurance, duties and inland transport; under DDP the seller covers them.

I build a landed cost for each. With FOB, the seller's job ends once the goods are loaded on the ship, so I add ocean freight, insurance, customs duties, broker fees and the truck to our dock, and the risk is ours from loading. DDP already includes all of that up to our door. Then I compare lead times and how much control over the freight I give up.
Sales tells you a promotion will double demand for one product for six weeks. Walk me through what you do.
How you turn a demand change into a supply plan.
Gets firm dates and volumes, checks supplier, warehouse and carrier capacity against lead times, and plans for the dip and leftovers after the promotion.

First I pin down the dates, the expected volume and which stores or channels. Then I check our supplier's capacity and lead time, our warehouse space and carrier capacity. If the supplier needs eight weeks, I order now and may build ahead. I also plan for the drop after the promo, since customers stock up, and agree with sales who owns any leftover stock.
A part is late and the plant will stop in three days unless you pay for air freight at ten times the normal cost. How do you decide?
Your judgement on cost against the risk of a stoppage.
Compares the air cost with the real cost of downtime or lost sales, checks cheaper options first, and fixes the cause so it does not repeat.

I compare the numbers. If air freight costs $12,000 and a stopped line costs $40,000 a shift, the call is easy. But first I check other options: a small air shipment to cover a few days, stock at another site, or an alternate part engineering has approved. Afterward I find out why it was late and whether the supplier should pay part of the bill.
You find $200,000 of stock that has not moved in a year. What do you do?
How you handle excess inventory and its root cause.
Recovers what value it can, works with finance on the write-down, and fixes the planning setting or ordering habit that created it.

First I sort it into what is still sellable and what is truly obsolete. Then I look for value: return it to the supplier for a restocking fee, use it in another product, sell it at a discount or to a liquidator. Finance needs to know so the write-down is booked right. Last, I find why it built up, like a big minimum order or an old forecast, and change that.
Leadership asks you to cut inventory by 20% without hurting service. How would you approach it?
Whether you can lower inventory with a plan instead of cutting every item the same.
Separates excess and obsolete stock first, resets safety stock item by item, shortens lead times or lot sizes, and tracks fill rate weekly.

I would not cut every item by 20%. I start by splitting stock into healthy, excess and obsolete, since excess is often a big share. Then I recalculate safety stock item by item, because many settings are years old. I push suppliers for shorter lead times and smaller lots. I track fill rate every week, so if service starts slipping we see it early.
What is the difference between cycle service level and fill rate, and which one do you report?
Whether you know two service measures that people often mix up.
Cycle service level is the chance of no stockout in a cycle; fill rate is the share of demand shipped from stock. The candidate says which one fits the audience.

Cycle service level is the share of replenishment cycles with no stockout at all. Fill rate is the share of units ordered that we shipped from stock. A 95% cycle service level usually gives a higher fill rate, since most stockouts are small. Customers feel fill rate, so I report that and use cycle service level to set safety stock.
Walk me through how you set safety stock for one item.
Your grasp of the math behind buffer stock and what drives it.
Uses demand variability, lead time and its variability, and a service target. Knows the buffer grows with the square root of lead time, not in line with it.

I pick a service target and turn it into a z value, about 1.65 for 95%. I measure how much weekly demand varies and multiply: z times demand variation times the square root of lead time in weeks. If the supplier's lead time also varies, I add that term, because late deliveries often cost more buffer than demand swings do.
When does the economic order quantity formula give you a bad answer?
Whether you know the assumptions behind a classic tool, not just the formula.
Names the assumptions: steady demand, fixed order cost, known holding cost, no price breaks, and no limits on space, shelf life or pack size.

EOQ is the square root of two times annual demand times order cost, divided by the yearly holding cost per unit. It assumes steady demand, a fixed cost per order and no quantity discounts. It breaks for seasonal or lumpy items, when price breaks exist, when shelf life is short, or when the supplier only ships full pallets. Then I treat it as a starting point.
How do you measure forecast quality, and why is one number not enough?
Your ability to judge a forecast on both size of error and direction of error.
Separates accuracy from bias, knows MAPE fails on low or zero volumes, and uses a weighted measure across items.

I track two things. Error size, as weighted absolute error: the sum of absolute errors divided by total actual demand, so slow items do not distort it the way plain MAPE does. And bias, the sum of forecast minus actual, which shows if we lean high or low. A forecast can look accurate on average and still be biased high every month, which quietly builds stock.
What goes into the cost of carrying inventory?
Whether you see the full cost of holding stock, not only the warehouse bill.
Lists cost of capital, storage, handling, insurance, taxes where they apply, shrink, damage and obsolescence, and says the rate should be built for the business.

The biggest piece is usually the cost of the money tied up. Then storage and handling, insurance, property tax on inventory in states that charge it, shrink, damage, and obsolescence. I build the rate with finance for our business instead of using a rule of thumb, because a fashion or electronics item goes stale far faster than a steel fitting.
Finance wants to improve the cash-to-cash cycle by pushing supplier payment terms from 30 to 90 days. What do you tell them?
How you weigh a working capital gain against supply risk.
Knows the formula, days of inventory plus days receivable minus days payable, and flags the risk to small suppliers and price, with alternatives.

Cash-to-cash is days of inventory plus days receivable minus days payable, so longer terms do shorten it. But for small suppliers that is a loan from them to us. Some will raise prices, cut service or fail. I would segment: extend terms with large suppliers, offer a supply chain finance program to smaller ones, and look at cutting days of inventory too.
A supplier's scorecard shows 98% on time, but the plant keeps running short of their parts. What is going on?
Whether you can spot a metric that is measured wrong.
Checks the definition: promised vs. requested date, line vs. order level, partial shipments, and receipt date vs. ship date.

I would check how on time is defined. Often it is measured against the date the supplier promised, not the date we asked for. Or a partial shipment counts as on time, or it uses ship date, not receipt at our dock. I would rebuild it as on time in full, by line, against our requested date at receipt. The real number is usually much lower.
Walk me through a monthly sales and operations planning cycle that actually works.
Your experience running the process that links demand, supply and finance.
Clear steps: data, demand review, supply review, reconciliation, executive decision, with gaps and options brought to leaders, not just numbers.

Week one, we close last month and update the data. Week two, sales and marketing agree the demand plan in units and dollars. Week three, operations checks it against capacity and suppliers and flags gaps. Then a pre-meeting builds options with costs. The executive meeting decides on those options. The plan is one number everyone works to.
A key part comes from a single supplier in one region. How do you assess and reduce that risk?
How you judge supply risk and pay only for the protection that is worth it.
Maps the risk by impact and time to recover, looks below the first tier, and chooses mitigations like a second source, buffer stock or redesign by cost.

I ask two things: how long it would take to recover if they stopped, and what we lose per week meanwhile. I also check their own suppliers, since the real weak point can sit one tier down. If recovery takes longer than our stock covers, I qualify a second source. If that takes a year, I hold extra buffer meanwhile and ask engineering about an alternate part.
We ship from one distribution center. Leadership wants a second one to get closer to customers. How do you evaluate it?
Your grasp of network trade-offs between transport, service and inventory.
Weighs lower outbound freight and faster delivery against more fixed cost, more safety stock and split volume. Knows the square root effect on safety stock.

A second site cuts outbound freight and delivery days, but adds rent, labor and inbound freight. Inventory rises too: with demand split evenly and independent, total safety stock grows with the square root of the number of sites, so about 41% more going from one to two. I would model total landed cost and service for each option before we decide.

supply-chain-planner.heading: Supply chain manager and planner questions
qs: What is the difference between safety stock and a reorder point?
Whether you know the two basic numbers behind every replenishment decision.
Safety stock is the buffer for uncertainty. The reorder point is expected demand over the lead time plus that buffer.

Safety stock is the extra I hold to cover demand or supply that turns out worse than expected. The reorder point is the stock level that triggers a new order: average demand during the lead time plus the safety stock. If I use 100 a week, wait 3 weeks for delivery and keep 120 as a buffer, I reorder at 420.
How would you use ABC classification to decide where to spend your planning time?
How you focus your attention across thousands of items.
Ranking by annual usage value, with tighter control on A items and simple rules on C items. Critical cheap parts still get flagged.

I rank items by annual usage value, which is units used times unit cost. Usually a small share of items, the A items, carries most of the value. I review those weekly, forecast them carefully and count them more often. C items get simple min-max rules. I also flag cheap parts that can stop a line, because a 50-cent bolt can still shut down production.
Walk me through how MRP turns a production schedule into purchase orders.
Your grasp of the logic inside the planning system, not just the screens.
Gross needs come from the master schedule through the bill of materials, are netted against stock and open orders, then offset by lead time.

MRP starts with the master production schedule: how many finished units, and when. It explodes that through the bill of materials to get gross needs for each part. Then it subtracts on-hand stock and scheduled receipts to get net needs, applies lot-size rules, and offsets each order by its lead time. I review the planned orders before releasing them.
How do you measure whether a forecast is any good?
Whether you track both the size and the direction of forecast error.
An error measure such as weighted MAPE plus bias, measured at the lead-time horizon where buying decisions are actually made.

I track error size, usually weighted MAPE: the average percent miss, weighted by volume so big sellers count more. And bias: are we always over or always under? A 25% error with no bias is noise I can buffer. A steady 15% over-forecast builds excess every month, so I fix bias first. I measure at the lead-time lag, the forecast we actually bought against.
Sales plans a promotion in six weeks on a product whose supplier lead time is ten weeks. What do you do?
How you handle a demand change that arrives inside the lead time.
Getting the lift in units, finding every source of supply that can still be reached, and telling sales the real gap early instead of promising.

First I get the expected lift in units and by week, not just “big promo.” Then I check what I have: on-hand, open orders I can pull in, stock at other sites, and whether the supplier can expedite or ship by air at a cost. If there is still a gap, I tell sales the number we can support so they can shrink the promo or limit it to some regions.
How would you set safety stock for an item whose supplier lead time swings between four and nine weeks?
Whether you account for supply variability, not only demand variability.
Including lead-time variation in the buffer, setting it by a target service level, and working on the root cause with the supplier.

A buffer based only on demand swings would be too small here. I use a formula that includes both demand variability and lead-time variability, set to a service level that fits the item's importance. With lead time swinging five weeks, that term will likely dominate. So I also go after the cause: share forecasts with the supplier, track on-time delivery, and look for a second source.
A supplier's minimum order is 5,000 units and you use 800 a month. How do you decide what to do?
How you weigh purchase price against the cost of holding stock.
Comparing total cost: price, holding cost, space, cash and the risk of the part expiring or changing, plus trying to negotiate the terms.

That order is about six months of supply. I compare total cost: the unit price at 5,000 against a smaller lot from a distributor, plus holding cost, often estimated at 20 to 30% of item value a year, and the risk the part changes or expires. If it still looks bad, I ask the supplier for a blanket order with monthly releases.
What is the bullwhip effect, and how can a planner make it worse?
Whether you understand how ordering behavior amplifies swings up the supply chain.
Small swings in end demand grow into larger swings upstream, driven by batching, planning from orders instead of usage, and padding orders in shortages.

It is when a small change in what consumers buy turns into bigger and bigger swings in orders the further you go up the chain. Planners feed it by forecasting from incoming orders instead of real sales, ordering in big batches, and padding orders when supply is tight. I counter it by planning from actual sales or usage data and sharing forecasts with suppliers.
You find $400,000 of excess and obsolete inventory in your area. Walk me through what you do.
How you clean up a costly problem and stop it from coming back.
Separating dead stock from slow stock, recovering value where possible, working with finance on the write-off, and fixing the planning cause.

First I split it: items with no demand, and items with demand but far too much stock. For slow items I cancel open orders and let usage burn it down. For dead stock I check other sites or products that can use it, supplier returns, and liquidation. Finance books any write-off. Then I find the cause, such as a big minimum order or a stale forecast, and fix it.
Fourth-quarter demand is 20% above what the plant can build. How do you decide what gets made?
Your judgement when demand and supply cannot both be met.
Pricing out the options to add supply, then proposing a clear allocation rule agreed with sales and leadership, not decided alone.

First I check what can close the gap: overtime, extra shifts, building ahead in slower months, or a contract manufacturer. Each has a cost I put in numbers. For what is left, I propose an allocation rule, for example by contract commitments and margin, and bring it to the S&OP meeting, where sales, operations and finance agree one plan. Leadership decides, then we tell customers early.
What is the difference between a 95% cycle service level and a 95% fill rate?
Whether you know which service measure your safety stock math is really aiming at.
Cycle service level counts replenishment cycles without a stockout; fill rate counts units shipped from stock. Same number, different promise.

Cycle service level is the share of replenishment cycles that end without a stockout. Fill rate is the share of demand units shipped from stock. A 95% cycle service level usually gives a fill rate well above 95%, because a stockout often hits only the last few units of a cycle. So I ask the business which promise they mean before I size safety stock.
An item was out of stock for five weeks last year. How do you use its sales history in the forecast?
Whether you know that recorded sales are not the same as true demand.
Sales during a stockout understate demand, so the candidate cleans or replaces those periods before forecasting.

Those five weeks show what we shipped, not what customers wanted. Feeding them in would teach the model to expect less and set up the next stockout. I would flag the periods, replace them with an estimate from the weeks around them or from backorder and lost-order data, and note the change so the next planner knows why the history was adjusted.
How do you forecast a new product that has no sales history?
How you build a forecast when the usual inputs do not exist.
Uses similar past launches, the sales plan and early sell-through, plans for a range, and updates fast once real data comes in.

I find one or two similar past launches and scale their first months by expected distribution and price. I check that against the sales plan and any customer commitments. Then I plan for a range, not one number: long-lead parts covered, finished goods kept lean. For the first couple of months I review sell-through weekly and adjust quickly.
Most months a spare part sells zero, then someone orders 40. How do you plan it?
Whether you know that slow, lumpy demand needs different methods and measures.
Knows standard methods and MAPE break on zero months, looks at order size and frequency separately, and asks who buys before deciding whether to stock.

Simple averages mislead here, and MAPE does not work because you divide by zero in empty months. I look at how often orders come and how big they are, separately, which is the idea behind Croston's method. I also ask who buys it; a 40-unit order may be one customer's yearly maintenance we can plan with them. Then I decide whether to stock it or make it to order.
Walk me through the steps of a monthly S&OP cycle you have run or would run.
Whether you know S&OP as a full process, not just one monthly meeting.
Data, demand review, supply review, reconciliation with finance, executive decision, each with an owner and an output, ending in one agreed plan.

Week one, we close the month and refresh data and forecast accuracy. Week two, sales and marketing agree the unconstrained demand plan. Week three, operations checks it against capacity and materials and flags gaps. Then a pre-meeting with finance builds options with their costs. The executive meeting picks one plan, and those decisions feed the master schedule.
Sales wants to swap a product into next week's production, which is inside the frozen zone. How do you respond?
How you protect schedule stability while staying open to real business needs.
Knows why the frozen zone exists, works out the true cost of the change, and puts the decision with its owner instead of a flat yes or no.

The frozen zone exists because materials are staged and lines are set, so changes there cost real money. I ask what is driving it: a big customer order or just a preference. Then I check materials, changeover time and what gets bumped, and put that cost in front of whoever owns the decision. If it goes ahead, I log it so we can see how often the fence is broken.
The sales team overrides the statistical forecast every month. How would you find out whether that helps?
Whether you can measure each step of the forecast process instead of trading opinions.
Forecast value added: compare the error of a naive, statistical and final forecast; keep the overrides that help and coach or drop the rest.

I would run a forecast value added check. Store the naive forecast, the statistical one and the final one with overrides, then compare each to actual sales over several months. If overrides lower the error, good. If they add error, often by running high, I show it by product family and agree to override only where they have real information, like a new account.
A part ran out because the system had its lead time as 4 weeks when it is really 12. How do you handle it?
How you deal with a master data error: the short-term fix and the lasting one.
Works the shortage and protects customers first, then checks how many other records are wrong and sets up a regular review against actual receipts.

First I work the shortage: expedite with the supplier, look for substitutes or stock at other sites, and give customer service dates we can keep. Then I fix the record and pull a report comparing planned lead times with actual receipt times for all purchased parts. Anything off by more than a set margin gets reviewed with the buyers, and I make that review quarterly.
Finance wants inventory down 20% this year without hurting service. How do you approach it?
Whether you know which levers lower inventory without simply raising stockout risk.
Splits stock into cycle, safety and excess, then works on the drivers: order sizes, lead time and its swings, forecast error and slow movers.

I split the inventory into cycle stock, safety stock and excess. Cycle stock averages about half the order quantity, so smaller, more frequent orders help where ordering costs allow. Safety stock falls if forecast error or lead time swings fall. Excess needs a disposal plan. I show finance the service versus inventory curve so the 20% is a choice, not a guess.
One critical part comes from a single supplier overseas. How do you decide how much to spend reducing that risk?
How you weigh supply risk against cost at a senior level.
Puts a number on impact and recovery time, compares options like buffer stock, a second source or redesign, and gets a business decision on the cost.

I start with impact: how much revenue stops per week if the part is gone, and how long recovery would take. Then I compare options: extra buffer stock, qualifying a second source, or a redesign. Each has a cost and a lead time, and a second source can take many months to qualify. I bring these to leadership as insurance choices with prices attached.

support-engineer.heading: Technical support engineer questions
qs: What is the difference between a 401 and a 403 error?
Whether you know the HTTP status codes you will read every day.
401 means the request is not authenticated; 403 means the caller is known but not allowed. Each points to a different fix.

A 401 means we could not confirm who is calling: the key or token is missing, wrong or expired. A 403 means the server knows who is calling, but that account or key lacks permission for the action. So for a 401 I check the credentials first. For a 403 I check the user's role, the plan or the key's scopes.
A customer's integration suddenly gets 429 errors. What do you tell them?
Whether you understand rate limits and how a client should respond to them.
429 means too many requests. Honor Retry-After when it is sent, back off with growing waits, and find out why the call volume jumped.

A 429 means they hit our rate limit. I check our logs for their request volume; often a new deploy or a loop is sending far more calls than before. I tell them to wait as long as the Retry-After header says when it is present, retry with growing delays plus some randomness, and batch or cache calls. If they truly need more, I explain how to request a higher limit.
Walk me through how you read a log file to find the cause of an error.
Your method for finding the one line that matters among thousands.
Start from an exact time and a request ID, check the time zone, and look for the first error, not the last.

I get the exact time, the account and, if possible, a request ID from the customer. I convert the time to the log's time zone, usually UTC, and filter to that window and ID. Then I read forward to the first warning or error, because later errors are often side effects. I compare with a request that worked to see what differs.
A page breaks for one customer but works fine for you. How do you narrow it down?
How you isolate a fault on the customer's side.
Change one thing at a time: private window, another browser, extensions off, and read the console and the network tab.

I ask them to try a private window first, which rules out cached files and most extensions. Then another browser or device. If it still fails, I have them open the developer tools and send a screenshot of the console and of the failing request in the network tab. Ad blockers and company proxies are common causes, so I ask about those too.
A customer writes, "Your API is down." What do you check first?
Whether you verify the facts before you agree or disagree with the customer.
Status page and monitoring first, then the customer's own calls: endpoint, status codes, error text. Separate a wide outage from one account's problem.

I check our status page and internal monitoring to see if others are affected. Then I look up their recent requests: which endpoint, what status codes, what error messages. If only they fail, it is often an expired key, a wrong base URL or a network block on their side. I ask for one failing request with its timestamp and full response so I can match it in our logs.
Webhooks stopped reaching a customer's server yesterday. How do you troubleshoot it?
Your ability to follow one request across two systems.
Read the delivery attempts on your side first; the response code or timeout usually shows whether the fault is yours or theirs.

I open our delivery log for their endpoint. Timeouts mean their server is slow or unreachable; 4xx or 5xx codes mean their app rejected the call. Common causes are an expired SSL certificate, a firewall blocking our IP addresses, a changed URL, or a failed signature check after they rotated a secret. If we sent nothing at all, the problem is ours and I escalate.
A customer pastes a log into the ticket that contains their API key. What do you do?
Whether you treat customer secrets as a security issue, not a detail.
Redact the secret from the ticket, tell the customer to revoke and replace the key, and follow the company's data handling rules.

I redact the key from the ticket right away, or ask an admin to if I cannot. Then I tell the customer politely that the key was exposed and they should revoke it and create a new one. HAR files are similar, since they can hold cookies and tokens: I ask customers to remove those first, and I never forward a raw file to a chat channel.
A customer's script retried a payment request after a timeout, and now they have duplicate charges. What do you explain?
Whether you understand why retries can create duplicates and how APIs prevent it.
A timeout does not mean the request failed. Explain idempotency keys where the API supports them, and check the first request's real outcome.

A timeout only means they did not get the answer in time; the first request may have gone through, so the retry made a second charge. First I help them find and reverse the duplicates. Then I show them how to send an idempotency key, a unique ID per payment, so a retry with the same key returns the first result instead of charging again.
Five customers report the same error within one hour this morning. What do you do?
Whether you spot a possible incident early and raise it the right way.
Treat the pattern as a likely incident: alert the incident channel with evidence, link the tickets, and give customers one consistent update.

Five matching reports in an hour is a pattern, not five problems. I check monitoring and recent deploys, then raise it in the incident channel with ticket links, times, the error text and what the accounts share. I link the tickets to one parent so updates go out together, and I tell customers we are investigating, without guessing at a cause or a fix time.
A large customer asks you to fix their data with a quick change in the production database. How do you handle it?
Your judgement about access, risk and process when a customer pushes for speed.
No one-off writes to production. Confirm the problem read-only, get the fix reviewed and run through the change process with a backup, and keep the customer informed.

I would not run a write on production on my own, even with access. I would first use a read-only query to confirm exactly which records are wrong and why. Then I write up the fix, have an engineer review it, and run it through our change process with a backup. I give the customer an honest timeline; a fast wrong update can damage far more records.
What is the difference between a 502 and a 504 error, and what does each tell you to check?
Whether you know where in the request path a gateway error comes from.
Both come from a proxy or gateway: a 502 means the upstream sent an invalid response, a 504 means it did not answer in time.

Both mean a proxy or load balancer in front of the app had trouble with the server behind it. A 502 says the upstream gave an invalid response, often because it crashed or refused the connection. A 504 says it never answered within the timeout, so I look for slow queries or long jobs. In both cases I check the upstream server logs, not just the proxy logs.
A customer's names show up as “Ã©” where there should be “é”. What is happening?
Your grasp of character encoding, a common cause of garbled data.
Text stored as UTF-8 is read as Windows-1252 or Latin-1 somewhere. You find the step that assumes the wrong encoding.

That pattern is UTF-8 read as a single-byte encoding. In UTF-8 the é is two bytes, and a system reading them as Windows-1252 shows two characters. I check where the text crosses a boundary: the CSV import, the charset in the HTTP Content-Type header, the database column. I fix that step, and I flag that data already saved wrong may need a separate cleanup.
A customer's front-end code calls our API from the browser and gets a CORS error, but the same call works in curl. Why?
Whether you understand that CORS is enforced by the browser, not by the server.
The browser blocks the response unless the server allows that origin, and curl ignores CORS. You also check that no secret key sits in browser code.

CORS is a browser rule. The browser only lets the page read the response if the server sends an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header that matches the page's origin. Curl does not check that at all. If our API is not meant for browser calls, the fix is to call it from their backend. I also check they are not putting a secret API key in front-end code, where anyone can read it.
A customer changed a DNS record to point at our service an hour ago, and some of their users still reach the old server. What do you explain?
Your understanding of DNS caching and TTL.
Resolvers cache the old record for its TTL. You check the authoritative answer directly and give a realistic wait.

DNS answers are cached by resolvers for the time-to-live, or TTL, set on the record. If the old record had a TTL of a day, some users can see it for up to a day. I query their authoritative name server with dig to confirm the new record is right, then check the old TTL to say how long to expect. Next time, lowering the TTL a day ahead makes the switch faster.
When would you ask a customer for a HAR file, and what do you warn them about?
Whether you can collect browser evidence without creating a security problem.
A HAR records every network request in the browser. It can hold cookies and tokens, so you ask them to sanitize it and you treat it as sensitive.

I ask for one when a problem happens in the browser and I need every request, status code and timing. I send short steps for their browser's developer tools. I warn them the file can include session cookies, tokens and form data, so they should remove those or log out right after recording. On our side I keep it only in the ticket and delete it when the case closes.
A customer says every event in our reports is five hours off. How do you work it out?
How you handle time zones and timestamp formats.
You suspect UTC versus local time, confirm with one known event, and check whether the gap changes with daylight saving time.

A whole-hour gap almost always means time zones. Say our API returns UTC: I ask for one event whose real time they know and compare. Five hours fits US Eastern in winter. If their code drops the offset from the timestamp, UTC gets shown as local time. I also warn that the gap becomes four hours in summer, so subtracting a fixed five is the wrong fix.
Signed API requests fail from one of a customer's servers but work from all the others. What do you suspect?
Whether you think of clock drift when only one machine fails authentication.
Signatures and tokens often carry a timestamp. A server with a drifted clock falls outside the allowed window, so you check its time and time sync.
