We pick a low-traffic window, support is on standby, and afterward we run an agreed checklist before calling it done.
A customer's production system is down and the ticket has sat for two hours without engineering. What do you do?
How you manage an escalation when the normal process stalls.
Right severity, the defined escalation path to a named owner, a fixed update rhythm for the customer, and staying on it until service is back.

First I confirm the impact and that the ticket has the right severity. Then I use our escalation path to get a named engineer and an incident lead, not a queue. I tell the customer who is on it and that I will update them every 30 minutes, even with no news. I stay on the bridge call until service is restored.
The customer asks you to promise a date for a bug fix engineering has not committed to. What do you say?
Whether you protect trust by not promising what you do not control.
No invented dates. You share what is known, offer a workaround if there is one, and commit to when the next real update will come.

I tell them I will not give a date I cannot stand behind. I share what I know: the bug is confirmed, it is prioritized, and here is the workaround we tested. I commit to a date for my next update, and I take the business impact back to engineering so the priority reflects it.
In a review you see the customer runs everything on one server with no backup. They have had no problems. How do you raise it?
How you give architecture advice the customer did not ask for.
The risk named in business terms, options with rough effort, the advice in writing, and their decision respected but kept on the risk list.

I say it plainly: one hardware failure would take them down, and with no backup they could lose data. I put it in their terms, like hours of downtime. I offer two options, a backup schedule now and a second server later, with rough effort for each. If they wait, I note the risk in the account plan and raise it at each review.
After an outage, the customer wants a root cause analysis. What makes a good one?
Your understanding of what a post-incident report must contain.
A timeline, the impact, the real cause and not just the trigger, how service was restored, and preventive actions with owners, without blame or spin.

It has a clear timeline, the impact on the customer, the real root cause and not just what set it off, how we restored service, and actions to stop a repeat, each with an owner and a date. I check it with engineering for accuracy, then walk the customer through it so they can ask questions instead of just getting a file.
Three of your accounts opened tickets about the same odd behavior this month. What do you do?
Whether you look for patterns across accounts instead of treating each ticket alone.
Find what the setups share, raise one linked problem with engineering with the evidence, and warn other exposed accounts before they hit it.

I compare versions and configurations to find what the three have in common. I link the tickets and open one problem record with engineering, with the evidence, because three customers carry more weight than one. Then I check which other accounts share that setup and warn them before they run into it.
The customer's own configuration change caused the outage, but their manager blames our product. How do you handle it?
How you handle blame with facts while keeping the relationship intact.
Facts from the logs shared privately and without blame, a focus on preventing a repeat, and honesty if the product made the mistake easy.

I get the facts first: logs showing the change and when it happened. I share them with the manager privately, not in front of the admin's peers. I keep it about the system, not the person, and suggest a guard like a change review step. If our product made the mistake easy to make, I say so and log it as feedback.
What is the difference between an SLA, an SLO and an SLI?
Whether you can speak precisely about reliability commitments.
The SLI is the measurement, the SLO the internal target, the SLA the contract with consequences. The SLO is usually stricter than the SLA.

An SLI is what we measure, for example the share of requests that succeed. An SLO is the target we set for it, say 99.95% a month. An SLA is the promise in the customer's contract, often looser, with service credits if we miss it. I keep the SLO tighter so we see trouble before the contract is breached.
A customer asks for advice on disaster recovery. How do RPO and RTO shape what you recommend?
Your grasp of recovery targets and how they turn into architecture choices.
RPO is how much data loss, in time, is acceptable; RTO is how long restoring may take. Tighter targets cost more, so the business sets them first.

RPO is how much data, measured in time, they can afford to lose. RTO is how long they can be down. I ask the business owners for those numbers before we talk design. An RPO of 24 hours can live with nightly backups. An RPO of minutes needs replication, and a short RTO needs a warm standby and a tested failover, which costs more.
The customer's integration gets HTTP 429 errors every Monday morning. What do you look at and what do you advise?
Whether you can diagnose a rate-limit problem and advise a sound fix on the client side.
Reads 429 as too many requests, checks the traffic pattern, and advises backoff with jitter, honoring Retry-After, plus spreading or batching the load.

A 429 means they are over a rate limit, so I pull their request counts by minute. Usually a weekly job fires everything at once. I advise retries with exponential backoff and random jitter, respecting the Retry-After header, and spreading or batching that job. If their real volume needs more, we discuss a higher limit.
We are retiring an API version that your largest customer depends on, in six months. How do you manage it?
How you run a forced migration without surprising the customer.
Early written notice, an inventory of everything calling the old version, a plan with test dates and buffer, and an early warning if the date is at risk.

I tell them within days, in writing, with the date and the reason. Then we find every call to the old version, using our logs as well as their list, since a list always misses one. We agree on a plan: test environment in month two, production by month four, two months of buffer. I check progress every two weeks and raise slips early, while options remain.
Your main contact at the customer, the one who championed us, leaves the company. What do you do?
Whether you protect an account when the relationship rests on one person.
Fast outreach to the successor and other stakeholders, a fresh summary of value and open items, and wider contacts from then on.

Before they leave, I ask the champion who takes over and for a warm introduction. I meet the successor in the first two weeks with a one-page summary: what they run, open issues, planned upgrades and what we delivered last year. I also reach their manager and the engineers who use us daily. After that, no account of mine depends on one name.
During handoff you learn sales promised a feature that does not exist. The customer expects it next month. What do you do?
How you handle an inherited overpromise honestly and without blaming colleagues.
Confirms the facts internally, tells the customer the truth early, offers a workaround or a confirmed roadmap view, and fixes the handoff gap.

I check with the account executive and product what was said and whether anything is planned. Then I tell the customer early, on a call, not buried in email: the feature does not exist today. I bring what I can offer, a workaround or a roadmap view product has confirmed. I do not blame sales in front of them, but internally I push for promises to be written into handoffs.
The customer wants to upgrade production Friday at 4 p.m., skipping staging, to meet a deadline. What do you say?
Your judgement on change risk when the customer is pushing hard.
States the risk plainly, offers a safer path that still meets the deadline, and records the decision and rollback plan if they go ahead.

I tell them what can go wrong: if the upgrade fails, both teams are thin all weekend. I offer options, like a quick staging run Thursday or a Saturday morning window with our engineer on call and a tested rollback. If they still choose Friday, it is their call, so I write down the risk and the rollback steps and make sure I am reachable.
A critical security vulnerability is published in a component of our self-hosted product. Walk me through your first 48 hours with your accounts.
How you act in a security event: fast, accurate and within what security has approved.
Shares only the official advisory, finds which accounts run affected versions, contacts the most exposed first, and tracks each to patched.

I share only what our security team's advisory says, so I do not spread guesses. I check which accounts run affected versions and whether the component faces the internet. Those I call first, then I email the rest. For each I note the patch or mitigation plan and a date, follow up until it is applied, and report status daily to our security lead.
How do you get product to prioritize a feature one of your customers needs?
Whether you advocate with evidence rather than volume.
Frames the problem, not the solution, adds accounts affected, revenue at stake and workaround cost, and reports back honestly either way.

I write up the problem, not their proposed solution: what they are trying to do, what breaks, and how many hours a week the workaround costs them. I add other accounts with the same need and the revenue involved, so product can compare it. Then I tell the customer what I heard back, including a no, so they can plan.
Tell me about architecture advice you gave that turned out wrong. What happened?
Whether you own your mistakes and changed how you advise.
A specific case, a quick admission to the customer, a working fix, and a changed habit such as testing at real scale or stating assumptions.

I advised a customer to move a reporting job to our bulk export feature. I had not checked their data volume, and the exports hit a size limit and failed at month end. I told them the same day it was my call, helped split the job by region, and it ran that night. Now I ask for real volumes and test at that size before I recommend a pattern.

technical-product-manager.heading: Technical product manager questions
qs: Why would you track p99 latency rather than the average for an API?
Whether you read performance numbers the way engineers do.
Averages hide the slow tail. p99 shows what the slowest 1% of requests feel, which often hits the heaviest users.

An average of 80 ms can hide a tail where one request in a hundred takes two seconds. p99 means 99% of requests are faster than that number. A page or job that makes many calls is likely to hit the slow tail, so customers feel p99 more than the mean. I watch p50 and p99 together, broken down by endpoint.
Explain idempotency to a sales lead, and why a payments API needs it.
Whether you can turn an engineering idea into plain business terms.
A repeated request has the same effect as one. With an idempotency key, a client can retry after a timeout without charging twice.

Idempotent means doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Networks drop replies, so a client that times out does not know if the charge went through. If it sends a unique key with the request, we recognize the retry and return the first result instead of charging the card again. That protects customers from double charges.
Which API changes count as breaking, and which are usually safe?
Your knowledge of how changes hit the people who integrate with you.
Removing or renaming fields, changing types or making inputs required break clients. Adding optional inputs or new fields is usually safe.

Removing an endpoint or field, renaming it, changing its type or format, or making an optional parameter required will break someone. Adding a new optional parameter, a new endpoint or a new response field is usually safe, if clients ignore unknown fields. Even a new enum value can break a client with strict parsing, so I flag those in the changelog too.
How do you test an API design with developers before it ships?
How you get real user feedback when your users are engineers.
Spec and docs first, a few design partners building against it, and watching where they get stuck before the contract is frozen.

I share the spec and draft docs with three to five design partners and ask them to build a small real task against a beta or mock server. I watch where they read twice, what they guess wrong and how long the first working call takes. Fixing names and error messages then is cheap; after general release, every change is a migration for someone.
Walk me through retiring an old API version that customers still call.
Whether you can run a deprecation without breaking trust.
Usage data, a clear timeline and migration guide, direct outreach to top callers, warnings in responses, and a sunset date you keep.

First I pull usage by customer to see who still calls v1. Then I publish a notice with a sunset date months out, a migration guide and code samples. We add a deprecation header to v1 responses and email owners of active keys. I call the top accounts myself. Near the end we may run short planned brownouts so stragglers notice, then turn it off on the date.
A large customer keeps hitting your rate limits and wants them raised today. What do you do?
How you balance one customer's request against platform stability.
First learn why they hit limits. Fix their pattern, or grant a scoped temporary raise if capacity allows, then decide on a lasting policy.

I ask engineering to look at their traffic first. Often it is a retry loop without backoff, or polling that a webhook could replace. If the load is real and we have headroom, I agree a temporary higher limit on their key with an end date. Then I bring the pattern back to the team: maybe our tiers are wrong, or we need a bulk endpoint.
Product teams are building their own tools instead of using your internal platform. How do you respond?
Whether you treat an internal platform as a product that must earn its users.
Treating the bypass as user feedback: finding the gap and cutting the cost of adoption before reaching for a mandate.

I take it as a signal, not disobedience. I sit with two or three of those teams and ask what they needed that we lacked: a missing feature, slow onboarding, a support queue that took a week. Then I fix the biggest gap and track time to onboard. A mandate can come later, but forced users of a bad platform just find quieter workarounds.
Engineering wants a quarter for a database migration with no visible features. How do you make the case to leadership?
How you justify platform work in terms leadership can act on.
Tying the work to cost, risk and speed with numbers, and cutting it into phases that deliver value along the way.

I translate it into outcomes. For example: the current database caps us below next year's expected peak, incidents from it cost us 20 engineer days last quarter, and two planned features need the new schema. I ask for a phased plan so the first slice lands in six weeks, and I name what we will not ship meanwhile so the trade is clear.
You shipped a fix and a customer's integration broke because it relied on the old, undocumented behavior. What now?
How you handle a breaking change you did not see coming.
Restore service first, communicate plainly, then decide openly whether to keep the old behavior, and add tests so it is caught next time.

First I get them working: roll back, or add a flag that restores the old behavior for their account, and tell them what happened and when. Then I check logs for others with the same pattern. With enough users, someone depends on any behavior you expose. So we add a test for it and decide openly: support it, or deprecate it with notice.
When would you choose cursor-based pagination over offset pagination for a list endpoint?
Your grasp of API design choices that affect integrators at scale.
Offset paging breaks when data changes and gets slow at deep offsets. Cursors fix both but give up jumping to a given page.

Offset paging says skip 200, give me 50. If rows are added or deleted while someone pages, they see duplicates or miss items, and deep offsets get slow because the database still walks past the skipped rows. A cursor points at the last item seen, so pages stay stable and fast. The cost is that you cannot jump to page 40, which most API users do not need.
What does time to first successful API call tell you, and how would you shorten it?
How you measure and improve developer experience.
It measures onboarding friction from sign-up to a working call. Shorten it by removing concrete blockers: key approval, unclear auth, quickstarts that fail.

It measures how long a new developer takes from sign-up to a real successful response. Long times usually mean friction: waiting for keys, confusing auth, or a quickstart that does not run. On one product the median was 40 minutes. We issued test keys at sign-up and added a copy-paste example with the key filled in, and it fell to under 10.
How do you decide between REST, GraphQL and gRPC for a new API?
Whether you match the interface style to who calls the API and how.
Starts from the callers. REST for broad public use, GraphQL when clients need varied slices of linked data, gRPC for internal service-to-service calls.

I start with who calls it. For a public API I default to REST: every developer knows it and HTTP caching works. GraphQL fits when many clients need different slices of related data, but caching and rate limiting get harder since queries vary in cost. gRPC suits internal service calls; browsers need a proxy layer such as gRPC-Web to use it.
How would you design webhook delivery so integrators can trust it?
Your knowledge of event delivery guarantees and what receivers need.
Honest at-least-once delivery, unique event IDs for deduplication, signed payloads, retries with backoff and a way to recover missed events. No promise of strict ordering.

I would promise at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once, and say so in the docs. Each event gets a unique ID so receivers can drop duplicates, plus a signature, usually an HMAC of the body with a shared secret, to prove it came from us. Failures retry with backoff for a set window, and an events endpoint lets them catch up on anything missed.
Your API has used its whole monthly error budget with ten days left. What changes for the team?
Whether you treat the error budget as a real decision rule, not a dashboard number.
Follows a policy agreed in advance: risky releases pause, work shifts to reliability, stakeholders hear what slips. Repeated burns trigger a review of the SLO or the system.

We follow the policy we agreed before this happened. Risky feature releases pause and the next sprint goes to what burned the budget, such as a flaky dependency or a weak deploy process. Security fixes still ship. I tell stakeholders which features slip and why. If we burn the budget every month, either the SLO or the system needs a real conversation.
An engineer proposes making a new read endpoint eventually consistent to cut cost. What do you need to know before you agree?
How you turn a technical tradeoff into user impact and requirements.
Explains the stale-read risk, asks how long the lag is and which flows read right after writing, then plans a strong-read option or clear documentation.

Eventually consistent means a read right after a write may return old data for a short time. I would ask how long that lag is at p99, and which flows read right after they write, like creating a resource and fetching it. If integrators will hit that, we offer a strongly consistent option for those calls or document the lag with a pattern to handle it.
One tenant's heavy workload is slowing down everyone else on your shared platform. How do you handle it now and for good?
How you handle a noisy-neighbor problem across ops, customers and roadmap.
Contains the impact fast, talks to the heavy customer directly, then builds per-tenant limits, isolation options and per-tenant monitoring.

Now, I work with on-call to throttle or move that tenant so others recover, and I call the customer before they find out on their own. For good: per-tenant quotas so no one can take the whole shared pool, and isolated capacity for the biggest workloads, maybe as a paid tier. I would also add per-tenant metrics, since we learned this from complaints, not dashboards.
Your API was down for two hours. Walk me through your role that day and the week after.
Your role in incidents: communication, learning and follow-through.
Owns accurate, regular customer updates and shields engineers during the incident. Afterward, a blameless postmortem and action items that get real roadmap priority.

During the incident I am not debugging. I keep the status page and customer messages accurate and regular, and I field questions so engineers can work. After, I help run a blameless postmortem focused on causes, not people. I make sure the action items get real priority on the roadmap, and I send key customers a plain write-up of what happened and what changed.

technical-program-manager.heading: Technical program manager questions
qs: What is the critical path, and why does it matter on a program?
Whether you know the basic scheduling idea behind every date you commit to.
The longest chain of dependent work sets the earliest finish. A slip on it moves the date; a slip elsewhere may not.

It is the longest chain of tasks that depend on each other, from start to finish. Its length is the shortest time the program can take. A task on that path has no slack, so a two-day slip there is a two-day slip at launch. I watch those tasks closely and look for parts I can run in parallel.
How does your job differ from the product manager's and the engineering manager's on the same program?
Whether you understand where the TPM role starts and stops.
Product owns what and why. Engineering managers own people and technical choices. The TPM owns how the pieces come together across teams, and when.

The product manager decides what we build and why it matters to users. The engineering manager owns the team, its hiring and its technical choices. I own the execution across teams: the plan, the dependencies between them, the risks and the dates. If the product manager changes scope, I show what it does to the schedule.
Walk me through how you build a dependency map for a program that touches eight teams.
How you find and record the links between teams before they cause trouble.
Sessions with each team, every dependency with a provider, a consumer, a need-by date and named owners, and a map reviewed often.

I start from the end state and work backward: what has to exist on launch day. Then I meet each team and ask what they need from others and what others need from them. Every dependency gets a provider, a consumer, a need-by date and a named owner on each side. Both teams confirm it in writing. I review the map weekly, because it changes.
A team tells you their API will be ready “in a sprint or two.” How do you turn that into something you can plan on?
How you turn a vague estimate into a date you can schedule against.
Asking what drives the range, setting an interim milestone, and planning on the later date with a set point to confirm it.

I ask what makes it one sprint versus two. Usually it is an unknown, like a design review or a schema decision. I get a date for that unknown to be settled and an interim milestone, such as a stub endpoint other teams can build against. I plan on the later date and tell the consuming teams when I will confirm it.
What do you look at before a go or no-go decision on a release?
Your release readiness criteria and whether you set them before the meeting.
Criteria agreed in advance: open bugs by severity, test and load results, a tested rollback, monitoring and on-call ready, support briefed.

I agree the criteria with engineering and product weeks before, so the meeting checks facts, not opinions. I look at open bugs by severity, test results, load test numbers, whether rollback has actually been tested, dashboards and alerts, on-call staffing, and whether support is briefed. If a criterion fails, we openly decide to waive it or to slip.
How would you plan the rollout of a risky change to a service millions of people use?
Whether you reduce release risk with staged exposure and a way back.
A feature flag or canary, a small share of traffic first, stop thresholds agreed in advance, a tested rollback, and timing away from peak hours.

I would ship the code turned off behind a feature flag, then enable it for internal users, then for 1% of traffic as a canary. We agree in advance which metrics stop the rollout, like error rate or latency above set limits. Rollback is one switch, and we test it first. We widen in steps, during working hours, with the owning team watching.
Your status report says green, but you hear engineers saying privately that the date is impossible. What do you do?
Whether your status reporting reflects reality and how you surface hidden schedule risk.
Going straight to the engineers, testing their concern against the plan, and changing the status quickly with a cause and a path back to green.

I sit down with those engineers and ask what they see that the plan does not. Often it is work nobody estimated, like a data migration or a security review. If it holds up, I change the status to yellow or red that week, with the cause and the options. A status that turns red the week before launch means I was reporting hope, not progress.
After a major outage, how do you run the follow-up?
How you turn an incident into fixes that actually get done.
A blameless review with a timeline and contributing causes, a short list of owned and dated action items, and tracking them to closure.

Within a few days I hold a blameless review. We build the timeline from logs and chat, then ask why the system allowed the failure, not who caused it. We agree a short list of action items, each with an owner and a due date, and separate urgent fixes from longer work. I track them in the teams' own backlogs and report open items until they close.
Three teams need the same platform team, and the platform team can only take on one of them this quarter. What do you do?
How you settle a dependency conflict between teams with competing priorities.
Making the trade-off visible with impact and dates, looking for workarounds, and escalating to the priority owner with a recommendation.

First I check that each ask is real and sized; sometimes one can be met with an existing feature or a workaround. Then I lay out each request with its business impact and what slips if it waits. If the teams cannot agree, I take that one page to the leader who sets priorities across them, with my recommendation. Then I give the waiting teams their new dates.
Two weeks before launch, you learn that a team you depend on never put your work on their roadmap. How do you handle it?
How you recover from a missed dependency and what you change afterward.
Quick facts, options with their costs, a decision by the right people, honest updates, then closing the process gap that let it happen.

I meet that team the same day to learn what is needed and what it would take. Then I bring options: they pull it in and something of theirs slips, we launch without that feature behind a flag, or we move the date. Leaders decide with the costs in front of them. Afterward I add a written confirmation step to my dependency map, so a hallway yes never counts again.
What goes into a RAID log, and how do you keep it from going stale?
Whether you track the right things and keep the tracking alive.
Risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies, each with an owner, a date and a next step, reviewed on a fixed rhythm.

RAID stands for risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies. Each line gets one owner, a due date and the next action, not just a description. I review it in the weekly program sync and close what is done. When an assumption looks shaky, I turn it into a risk that day. If a line has not changed in three weeks, I ask the owner whether it is still real.
What is an error budget, and how does it change your release planning?
Your grasp of how reliability targets shape what ships and when.
The amount of failure the SLO allows, with a policy agreed in advance on when feature releases slow down.

It is the room for failure that an SLO, the reliability target, leaves. With 99.9% availability over 30 days, that is about 43 minutes of downtime. While budget remains, teams ship normally. If a service burns through it, the policy we agreed ahead of time kicks in: risky launches wait and reliability work moves up. I plan releases with that rule in view.
Your burn-up chart shows completed work climbing, but the total scope line is climbing faster. What does that tell you, and what do you do?
Whether you can read a progress chart and see what a busy team hides.
The finish line is moving away. You find where the new scope comes from and force a scope or date decision.

It says we will never finish at this rate, even though the team looks busy. I break the added scope down by source: new requests, discovered work and bugs. A lot of discovered work means our estimates were thin. New requests go to the product owner with a choice: swap something out or move the date. I show the projected finish so the trade-off is visible.
Feature flags keep piling up after each launch. Why is that your problem, and what do you do about it?
Whether you see cleanup as part of shipping, not an afterthought.
Old flags leave untested code paths and real risk. Removal is planned work with an owner and a date.

Every flag left in place adds paths the code can take, and nobody keeps testing the old ones. A stale flag flipped by mistake can bring back dead behavior. I make flag removal part of the launch plan: each flag gets an owner and a removal ticket dated a few weeks after full rollout. I also report open flags by age in the program review.
How do you estimate a part of the program that nobody on the team has built before?
How you plan around real uncertainty without faking precision.
A time-boxed spike to learn first, then a range instead of a single date, narrowing at named checkpoints.

I don't guess a date. I ask for a spike, a short time-boxed experiment, say one week, to build the riskiest piece and learn what we don't know. Then I get a best, likely and worst case from the engineers and plan to a range. I tell leadership the range will narrow at named checkpoints, and I put the first checkpoint early.
Walk me through the plan for moving a live service to a new database without downtime.
Your knowledge of how zero-downtime migrations are staged.
Staged steps: dual writes, backfill, verification, gradual move of reads, then retiring the old store, with rollback possible at each step.

First the service writes to both databases. Then we backfill old records into the new one and compare the two, often by reading from both and logging mismatches. When mismatches are near zero, we move reads over gradually. Only after a stable period do we stop writing to the old one and retire it. Each step can be rolled back, and I set dates around those checks.
You are retiring an old internal API. Most callers have moved, but the last 10% won't. How do you finish?
How you close out the long tail of a migration.
Name every caller and owner, remove their blockers, set a dated shutdown with leadership backing, and flush out hidden callers early.

I pull traffic logs to name every remaining caller and its owner. I sort them: blocked by something we can fix, low priority, or abandoned. We fix the blockers, sometimes by making the change for them. Then leadership agrees a shutdown date. Before it, we run short planned outages, called brownouts, so hidden callers show up while we can still help.
Two senior engineers from different teams disagree on a design, and the program is blocked. What do you do?
Whether you can unblock a technical decision without pretending to make it yourself.
Options written down against agreed criteria, a deadline and a named decider, then the decision recorded so it stays made.

I ask each of them to write their option in one shared doc: cost, risk and effect on the timeline. We agree on the criteria first, so the debate is about facts, not taste. I set a date and confirm who decides, often the lead architect. Once it is decided, I record the decision and the reasons, so it does not reopen next month.
Three days before a launch with a fixed external date, a security review finds an issue. What do you do?
Your judgement when risk and a hard date collide.
Get the severity from security, lay out fix, mitigate or delay, and have the accountable leader accept any risk in writing.

First I get the security team's rating and what an attacker could actually do. Then I lay out options: fix in time, ship with a mitigation such as keeping the feature switched off, or slip. I don't accept the risk myself. If we ship, the accountable leader signs off in writing with a dated fix plan. If it is serious, we move the date and tell partners early.
A launch you ran caused an incident, and the cause was a checklist step you had dropped to save time. How do you handle it?
Whether you own your own mistakes in the same blameless way you expect from others.
Saying it plainly in the postmortem, fixing the process so the step cannot be skipped silently, and seeing the fix through.

I say it in the postmortem in plain words: I cut the step, here is why, and here is what it cost. A blameless review looks at the process, so I ask why one person could skip a safety step alone. The fix might be turning that step into an automated check in the deploy. Then I track that action to done, because owning it only counts if something changes.

technical-recruiter.heading: Technical recruiter questions
qs: What is the difference between a frontend, a backend, and a DevOps or platform engineer?
Whether you know the roles well enough to search and screen for them.
Clear, correct lines between the roles, and what each changes in how you search and screen.

Frontend engineers build what the user sees in the browser or app, mostly in JavaScript or TypeScript. Backend engineers build the servers, APIs and databases behind it. Platform or DevOps engineers own deployment, cloud infrastructure and uptime. So for a platform role I look for automation and on-call experience, not UI work.
Looking at a résumé, how do you tell a senior engineer from a mid-level one?
How you read engineering experience beyond titles and years.
Scope and ownership: design decisions, systems owned end to end, mentoring. Not title or years alone, since titles mean different things at different companies.

Titles vary too much, so I read the bullets. A senior person describes owning a system, choosing between designs, handling scale or reliability problems and mentoring others. A mid-level résumé lists features built on a team. Then I confirm it on the call by asking what they decided themselves.
Walk me through the Boolean search you would build for a backend engineer who writes Go.
Your hands-on sourcing skill with search strings.
Correct use of AND, OR, NOT, quotes and parentheses, with synonyms covered and noise removed.

I would start with (Go OR Golang) AND (backend OR "back end" OR "server side") AND (engineer OR developer). Go alone pulls junk, so Golang matters. I add NOT (recruiter OR sales) to drop noise, then narrow by location. If results are thin, I widen the titles before loosening the skill.
What goes into a first message to an engineer who is not looking for a job?
Whether you can write outreach that engineers actually answer.
Short, specific to the person, says what is technically interesting about the role, and makes replying easy.

Three or four lines. Something specific I saw in their work, the real technical problem the team is solving, the level and pay range if I can share it, and an easy ask like a 15-minute call. No buzzwords. Engineers ignore mass messages, so if I cannot say why it fits them, I do not send it.
What do you ask a hiring manager in the intake meeting for a new engineering role?
How you turn a vague request into a search you can run.
Must-haves versus nice-to-haves, level, the team's real problems, the interview plan, and sample profiles to calibrate.

What will this person build in the first six months, and what level is it really. Which two or three skills are must-haves and which can be learned. Who is on the panel and what each interview tests. Then I ask them to react to three sample profiles, so we agree on what good looks like before I source.
A résumé says the candidate led a migration to microservices. What do you ask on the screen?
Whether you can probe technical claims without being an engineer.
Questions on their personal role, the why, the tradeoffs and what went wrong; vague or team-only answers are a flag.

I ask why they moved off the monolith, what their own part was versus the team's, how they split the services, and what broke along the way. Someone who did it talks about data ownership, deployment pain and things they would redo. If every answer is "we" with no detail, I note it for the technical interviewer.
When and how do you ask a candidate about work authorization and visa sponsorship?
Whether you handle sponsorship early and lawfully.
Ask early, ask only whether they are authorized and whether they will need sponsorship, never national origin; involve immigration counsel.

On the first call, because it decides whether we can move forward. I ask two questions: are you authorized to work in the US, and will you now or in the future need sponsorship. I do not ask about citizenship or where they are from. If sponsorship is needed, I check our policy and loop in immigration counsel before promising anything.
Your top candidate has a competing offer above your pay band and asks you to match it. What do you do?
How you negotiate offers within real limits.
Learns the full competing package and what the candidate values most, works with the manager on level and non-salary terms, stays honest.

I ask what the other offer includes and what matters most to them, cash, equity, title or the work. Then I go to the manager and comp team with facts: is the level right, can we use a sign-on bonus or more equity. I tell the candidate exactly what is possible and by when. I never bluff about a number I cannot get.
A candidate accepted your offer, then calls to say their current employer made a counteroffer. How do you handle it?
Your judgement in a late-stage risk most recruiters face.
Calm, asks what drove the search in the first place, does not pressure, and has prepared for this risk before the offer.

I thank them for telling me and ask what made them start looking. Usually it was the work, growth or the manager, and money does not fix that. I remind them of what they said they wanted, answer any doubts, and ask for a decision date. I raise counteroffers in the first screen, so this call is rarely a surprise.
The panel says a candidate you screened was far below the level you presented. How do you handle it?
How you own a screening miss and fix your process.
Takes responsibility, finds where the screen failed, recalibrates with the manager, and tells the candidate kindly and promptly.

I own it with the manager first. Then I compare my notes with the panel's feedback to see what I missed, often depth on system design. I add a probing question to my screen and ask an engineer to review my next few submittals. I close the loop with the candidate within a day or two, politely, so the miss does not cost them a bad experience.
What can a GitHub profile tell you about an engineer, and what can it not tell you?
Whether you read technical signals without overrating them.
Real signals, like contributions to shared projects and how they handle code review, plus the limit: most professional work sits in private repos.

It can show which languages someone uses, whether they contribute to projects other people rely on, and how they write pull requests and respond to review. It cannot show their day job, because most company code is private. An empty profile is not a red flag. A strong one is a good reason to start a conversation.
A candidate has a competing offer with RSUs, and ours has stock options. How do you explain the difference?
Whether you can explain equity clearly and honestly.
RSUs become shares when they vest. Options are a right to buy at a fixed strike price and are worth only the gap above it. No promises about future value.

An RSU turns into a share when it vests, so it keeps value even if the price drops. An option is the right to buy a share at a set strike price. It is only worth what the share price is above that strike, and exercising costs money. I walk through our vesting schedule and suggest they ask a tax advisor about their own case.
A hiring manager wants to post a remote engineering role without a salary range. What do you say?
Your knowledge of pay transparency rules for job postings.
Several states require a good-faith pay range in postings, a remote role can fall under them, and legal or HR should confirm what applies.

I would explain that states such as Colorado, California, Washington and New York require a pay range in job postings, and a remote role open to people there can be covered. Leaving it off risks penalties and puts off engineers who filter by pay. I would bring in our legal or HR team to confirm the rules and agree on a range we can stand behind.
The hiring manager asks you to find out what the candidate earns now. How do you handle it?
Whether you know salary history rules and still get the information you need.
Many states and cities ban asking about pay history. You ask about expectations and share the range instead.

Many states and cities, including California and New York, do not let employers ask about current or past pay, so I do not ask. I tell the manager I will ask what the candidate is looking for and share our range early. That answers the real question: whether we are in the same place on pay.
You start a new search for a staff engineer. How do you calibrate with the hiring manager in the first week?
How you avoid spending weeks on the wrong profile.
Sending a small set of real profiles early, getting a yes or no with reasons, and adjusting the search before scaling outreach.

Within a few days I send the manager five to eight real profiles, some I think fit and a couple that test the edges. I ask for a yes or no and the reason on each. The reasons tell me more than the job description, for example that scale matters more than the language. Then I adjust my searches before I reach out to a hundred people.
A strong senior candidate refuses to do a four-hour take-home assignment. What do you do?
Your judgement on interview design versus candidate experience.
Takes the objection seriously, offers options that test the same skill, and keeps the bar the same for everyone.

I would not just say it is required. I would go to the hiring manager with options that test the same skill: a time-boxed live exercise, or the candidate walking us through code they already wrote. Busy senior engineers often drop out over long take-homes. If it keeps happening, I bring the data and suggest a shorter task for everyone, so the process stays fair.
A candidate is Head of Engineering at a 15-person startup, but the panel sees a senior engineer, not staff. How do you handle the leveling talk?
How you handle a down-level without losing the candidate.
Explains that titles vary with company size, ties the level to evidence from the interviews, and talks about pay, scope and the path up.

I call before any offer goes out. I say that titles mean different things at a 15-person company and at ours, and that the panel saw strong senior skills, with specific examples. Then I focus on what matters to them: pay for the level, the scope of the work, and what it takes to get promoted here. A surprise in the offer letter is how you lose people.
In a remote technical interview, the person on camera does not seem to be the one from your phone screen. What do you do?
How you handle possible interview fraud fairly.
No accusation on the spot. Notes what was seen, checks identity the same way for everyone, and escalates to the hiring team and HR or security.

I would not confront them during the interview. I would write down exactly what I noticed, like a different voice or answers that lag as if read, and compare notes with the panel. Then I would ask for an identity check on camera at the next step, the same one every candidate gets, and bring in HR or security. A bad hire is costly, but so is a false accusation.
A hiring manager says they want someone “young and hungry” who fits the team’s vibe. How do you respond?
Whether you spot age bias and steer the manager to lawful, job-related criteria.
Names the risk: federal law bars age discrimination against workers 40 and older. Turns “hungry” and “vibe” into skills on a scorecard.

I would say it plainly but privately: asking for someone young can be age discrimination, and federal law protects workers 40 and over. Then I ask what “hungry” means for this job. Usually it is shipping fast or picking up new tools. I put those skills on the scorecard so every candidate is judged the same way, and I keep a note of the conversation.
You told a candidate a base salary on the phone that was higher than what the manager approved, and they said yes. What now?
How you own a mistake in an offer and fix it honestly.
Tells the manager the same day, pushes to honor the number if possible, and if not, calls the candidate personally, apologizes and fixes the process.

I tell the hiring manager the same day and own it as my error. I ask whether we can honor the number, since the gap is often small next to restarting the search. If we cannot, I call the candidate myself, apologize, explain, and see what else we can offer, like a sign-on bonus. Then I change my process: no number goes out until it is approved in writing.

technical-writer.heading: Technical writer questions
qs: What are the main topic types in structured writing, and why keep them separate?
Whether you know how technical content is organized.
Concept, task and reference, each answering a different reader question, kept apart so they are easy to find and reuse.

Concept explains what something is and why it matters. Task gives numbered steps to get one thing done. Reference holds the facts people look up, like parameters or settings. I keep them apart so a reader in the middle of a task is not slowed by background, and so one reference table can be reused in several guides.
How do you write a good numbered step?
Your craft at the level of a single instruction.
One action per step, an imperative verb, the condition before the action, and the expected result where it helps.

One action per step, starting with the verb: Click Save. If there is a condition, it comes first: If the file is open, close it. Where the reader needs reassurance, I add the result: The status changes to Active. I keep explanations out of the step itself, or put them in a short line underneath.
In safety messages, what is the difference between DANGER, WARNING, CAUTION and NOTICE?
Whether you know the US signal words for hazards in product documentation.
Matches ANSI Z535.6: severity and likelihood of injury decide the word, and NOTICE covers property damage, not injury.

Under ANSI Z535.6, DANGER means a hazard that will cause death or serious injury if not avoided. WARNING means it could cause death or serious injury. CAUTION means it could cause minor or moderate injury. NOTICE is for equipment or data damage with no injury risk. I place the message before the step it applies to, not after.
What does a complete reference entry for a REST API endpoint include?
Your knowledge of API documentation.
Method and path, authentication, every parameter with type and required flag, request and response examples, and error codes.

The method and path, a one-line purpose, and how to authenticate. Then every parameter with its type, whether it is required, its default and allowed values. A full request example and a real response, then the error codes the call can return and what each means. If there are rate limits or pagination, I say so on the same page.
What does docs-as-code mean, and how have you worked that way?
Whether you can work inside an engineering team's tools and process.
Docs kept as plain text in version control, reviewed like code, published by an automated build, ideally shipped with the feature.

It means treating docs like software: plain-text files with simple markup, stored in version control next to the code, changed through pull requests that engineers review, and published by an automated build. On my last team the docs change went into the same pull request as the feature, so the two shipped together and nothing was forgotten.
How do you check that a procedure actually works before it is published?
How you verify accuracy instead of trusting the draft.
Running every step yourself in a clean setup, copying commands from the draft, and noting the version tested.

I run it myself, step by step, in a test account or a clean environment, not on a machine that already has everything set up. I copy every command and code sample from the draft instead of typing my own. Where I cannot run it, I ask an engineer to run it with me, and I note which version I tested.
The style guide has no rule for a term that engineers spell three different ways. What do you do?
How you make and record a style decision.
Choosing a form based on the interface and the base style guide, recording it with a reason, and fixing old uses in one pass.

I check which form the product interface and the code use, since readers will see that, and what our base style guide suggests. I pick one, add it to our word list with the reason, and tell the team. Then I search the docs and fix the old forms in one pass, so consistency does not depend on anyone's memory.
A feature ships Friday and engineering says the docs can wait. How do you respond?
Your judgement when a deadline squeezes documentation.
Defining the minimum users need on day one, getting a short technical review, and naming the risk plainly.

I ask what users need on day one: usually setup steps, any change in behavior and known limits. I write that minimum now and ask for 20 minutes of an engineer's time to check it. Fuller guides follow, with a date. I also name the risk: support tickets in launch week cost more than a short review.
After a release, users report that a code sample in your guide fails. Walk me through what you do.
How you handle an error in published docs.
Reproduce, fix or flag the page fast, find the root cause, and change the process so it does not recur.

First I reproduce it against the current version to see whether the sample or the product changed. I fix the page or add a clear note right away, so no one else hits it. Then I find the cause, say a renamed parameter missed in review, and propose a fix such as testing samples in the build or a docs check on every API change.
How do you know your documentation is working?
Whether you measure docs by reader outcomes, not page count.
Signals tied to reader goals, such as support tickets, failed searches and time to first success, checked against real users.

I look at signals tied to what readers are trying to do: support tickets on topics we documented, site searches that return nothing, page feedback, and for an API how long a new developer takes to make a first successful call. I pair numbers with a few user sessions, because high traffic on a page can just mean people keep coming back lost.
An engineer asks you to review the product's error messages. What makes a good one?
Whether you can write short text that helps a user recover from a problem.
It says what went wrong in the user's terms and what to do next, without blaming the user or showing only an internal code.

A good error message says what happened, why if we know, and what the user can do now. "Invalid input" is useless. "Enter the date as MM/DD/YYYY, for example 03/15/2025" fixes the problem. I keep the tone neutral and never blame the user. If there is an error code, I put it after the plain sentence so support can search for it.
The manual will be translated into eight languages. How does that change the way you write?
Whether you write source text that is cheap and safe to translate.
Short sentences, one term per concept, no idioms, no text baked into images, and room for longer translated text.

I keep sentences short and use one term for one thing. Each synonym looks like a new concept to a translator and breaks matches in translation memory, the database of sentences already translated. I drop idioms and jokes, keep text out of screenshots, and warn the UI team that translated strings often run longer than English. Identical meanings get identical sentences.
What goes into a good code sample, and what do you keep out of it?
Your judgement about samples that developers will copy and paste.
Complete enough to run, small enough to read, with clear placeholders and no real secrets or unrelated logic.

It should run as shown once the reader fills in clearly marked placeholders, like YOUR_API_KEY. It shows one task, includes the imports it needs, and handles the error a reader is most likely to hit. I keep out real keys and tokens, unrelated business logic and clever shortcuts. If a sample needs more than a screen, I link to a full example project instead.
How would you document rate limits for a public API?
Whether you know what a developer needs in order to handle limits in code.
The limits and how they are counted, the 429 status code, any headers that report usage or wait time, and a recommended retry pattern.

I state the limit and its scope: per key or per user, per second or per minute. I show the response when it is exceeded, usually HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, and document any headers, such as Retry-After, that say how long to wait. Then I give a short pattern: wait as told, or back off with growing delays, instead of retrying in a tight loop.
Walk me through how you would explain the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow to a developer who has never used it.
Whether you can explain a hard security concept accurately and in the right order.
The roles first, then the steps in order: redirect, user approval, code, token exchange, and API calls made with the token.

I start with the roles: the user, your app, and the authorization server. Then the steps: your app sends the user to the server's login page; the user approves; the server redirects back to your app with a short-lived code; your app exchanges that code at the token endpoint for an access token. The token, not the password, is what your app sends with API calls.
Engineering hands you an OpenAPI file. What can you generate from it, and what still needs a writer?
Whether you know where generated reference ends and written guidance begins.
Reference pages can be generated; the writer improves descriptions and examples in the spec itself and writes the guides around it.

From the OpenAPI file, a tool can render the endpoint reference: paths, parameters, request and response schemas, status codes. But it is only as good as the descriptions in the file, so I edit those in the spec, not in the output. What still needs me: getting started, authentication, concepts, realistic examples, and guides that combine several calls into one real task.
The company supports version 2 and version 3 of the product at the same time. How do you organize the docs?
How you handle versioned content without confusing readers or doubling the work.
A clear version switcher with the newest as default, shared content single-sourced, and a firm rule for freezing and archiving old docs.

Each version gets its own docs set with a visible version switcher, and search defaults to the current one. Content that is the same in both comes from one source, so a fix lands in both. Differences go in a migration guide, not scattered notes. Version 2 gets fixes only, and when support ends I archive it rather than delete it, because some customers stay on old versions.
An API endpoint is being deprecated. Walk me through the documentation work.
Whether you can plan the docs side of a change that will break customers' code.
Confirmed dates and replacement, a visible notice, a migration guide, and updates across reference, samples and changelog.

First I confirm the facts with engineering: the deprecation date, the removal date, and the replacement. Then I mark the endpoint deprecated in the reference, add a notice with both dates, and write a migration guide that maps old calls to new ones with before-and-after code. I update every sample that uses the old endpoint, log it in the changelog, and give support the same text.
A product manager asks you to leave a known limitation out of the docs because it looks bad. What do you do?
Your judgement when accuracy and business pressure pull in different directions.
Documents the limitation plainly and neutrally, explains the cost of hiding it, and escalates only if needed.

I explain that users will hit it anyway, and when they do, missing docs turn into support tickets and lost trust. Then I offer a fair way to write it: a neutral sentence under Known limitations, with a workaround if one exists. No apology, no spin. If the manager still says no, I raise it with my lead, because accuracy is the one thing docs cannot give up.
You inherit a docs site with 600 pages, and many are out of date. Where do you start?
How you plan a large cleanup with limited time and people.
A content audit ranked by traffic and risk, fixing the pages that matter first, and retiring or redirecting the rest.

I start with a content audit: a spreadsheet of every page with its traffic, last update, owner, and the support tickets that cite it. The busiest pages and the ones that could cause data loss or security mistakes get fixed first. Pages nobody visits or needs get removed, with redirects so links do not break. Then I set review dates so the site does not drift again.

technician.heading: Technician questions
qs: What is lockout/tagout, and when do you use it?
Whether you know the basic rule that keeps you from being hurt by live or stored energy.
You isolate every energy source, put your own lock and tag on it, and prove zero energy before any work starts.

It means shutting a machine off, isolating every energy source, putting my own lock and tag on each disconnect, and then proving it is dead before I work. I use it any time I service a machine or clear a jam where I could be hurt if it started up. That covers electrical, gas, air pressure, springs and stored energy in capacitors.
How do you prove a circuit is dead before you touch it?
Your habit of testing your tester instead of trusting a switch or a breaker label.
The live-dead-live check: confirm the meter on a known live source, test the circuit, then confirm the meter again.

First I lock out the breaker or disconnect. Then I check my meter on a known live source, test the circuit phase to phase and phase to ground, and check the meter on the live source again. If the meter failed in between, the dead reading means nothing. Breaker labels are wrong often enough that I never trust them alone.
On a wiring schematic, what does a normally open contact mean?
Whether you can read the drawings you will use to find faults.
Schematics show devices at rest with no power; a normally open contact is open until its coil or switch is actuated.

Drawings show every device in its resting state, with no power and nothing pressed. A normally open contact is open in that state and closes when its relay coil is energized or the switch is pushed. So if a motor starter does not pull in, I look at which contacts in that line of the drawing should be closed and measure across them to find the open one.
Walk me through how you find the fault on a machine that has stopped.
How you find faults in a logical order instead of swapping parts.
Ask the operator, check the simple things first, then narrow it down with the schematic and a meter before replacing anything.

I ask the operator what happened just before it stopped and whether there was an error code. Then I check power, fuses, breakers, door switches and resets. If those are fine, I take the schematic and measure along the circuit, splitting it in halves until I find where the voltage stops. I only order a part once I have measured that it is the cause.
A walk-in cooler is running warm in the middle of service. What do you check?
Your practical refrigeration knowledge and your sense of what matters to the kitchen.
Tell the manager at once so food can be protected, then check the simple causes before the sealed system.

First I tell the manager so they can check product temperatures and move food if needed. Then I check the easy things: the thermostat setting, the door closing and its gasket, the evaporator fans running and the coil not iced over. Outside, I see if the condenser coil is clogged and the compressor and condenser fan run. Refrigerant work comes only after those are ruled out.
How would you set up a preventive maintenance schedule for a store's equipment?
How you plan maintenance so equipment fails less often.
Start from the manufacturer's manuals and the most critical equipment, adjust by repair history, and record every task.

I list every piece of equipment and rank it by what it costs the store when it fails; refrigeration and ovens come first. I take the intervals from the manufacturer's manuals, like cleaning condenser coils or checking belts, and write a short checklist for each. Every task gets logged, and if a unit keeps failing between checks, I shorten its interval.
A unit is low on refrigerant. Can you just top it up?
Whether you know the federal rules on refrigerant and why a top-up is not a repair.
Only an EPA Section 608 certified technician may open the system; venting is illegal, and the leak should be found and fixed.

Only if I hold the right EPA Section 608 certification, because federal rules require it to service the sealed system. And refrigerant does not get used up; if it is low, there is a leak. I find it with an electronic detector or soap bubbles, repair it, then charge the system properly. A top-up alone just leaks out again, and venting refrigerant on purpose is illegal.
A manager asks you to bypass a safety interlock so a machine can run until the part arrives. What do you do?
Your judgement when pressure to keep running meets a safety rule.
A clear no, the machine tagged out of service, and a practical workaround offered so the store can keep going.

I say no, politely and plainly: that interlock is there so nobody loses a hand, and a bypass tends to get forgotten. I tag the machine out of service, tell the manager when the part will arrive and see if I can rush it. Then I help find a workaround, like moving the work to another machine or doing it by hand for a day.
Tell me about a repair that did not hold. What did you learn?
Whether you own your mistakes and look for the root cause.
An honest story: what failed, how you found the real cause, and what you now do differently.

I replaced a blown fuse on a conveyor and it ran fine. Two days later the fuse blew again. This time I traced the wiring and found a cable rubbing on the frame, worn through and shorting now and then. I fixed the cable and added a protective sleeve. Now when a fuse blows, I always find out why before I call the job done.
You have a fault that comes and goes and never shows up while you are there. How do you track it down?
How you handle the hardest kind of fault, the intermittent one.
Gathering patterns from staff and logs, checking connections and heat, and monitoring until the fault shows itself.

I ask staff to note the time and what was running each time it happens, and I check any error log. Then I look for patterns: only when hot, only at opening, only when another big load starts. I check connections for looseness and burn marks, wiggle wires while watching readings, and if needed leave a recording meter on the circuit until it catches the event.
When you measure motor current with a clamp meter, why do you clamp only one wire?
Whether you know how your meter actually works.
Currents flowing in opposite directions cancel, so clamping a whole cord reads near zero. You clamp one conductor at a time.

The clamp reads the magnetic field around a conductor. If I put it around a cord with both the hot and the neutral, the currents run in opposite directions and their fields cancel, so I read close to zero. I clamp one leg at a time. On a three-phase motor I check all three legs and compare them.
You are about to change a condenser fan motor. The disconnect is off and locked. What else do you do before touching the capacitor?
Whether you know that stored energy remains after the power is off.
A capacitor can hold a charge with the power off. Discharge it with a proper resistor tool and confirm zero with a meter.

Lockout removes the supply, but a run capacitor can still hold a charge. First I verify zero volts at the unit with a tested meter. Then I discharge the capacitor across its terminals with an insulated resistor tool, not a screwdriver. I check it with the meter on DC volts before I take the wires off.
A fuse on a food warmer keeps blowing, and you find someone put in a bigger one. What do you do?
How you handle a dangerous shortcut and the fault it was hiding.
Put back the rated fuse, because it protects the wiring. Then find out why it blows: a short, a failing element or a bad connection.

I lock it out and put back the fuse the nameplate or the diagram calls for, with the same amps, voltage and type. The fuse protects the wire, and a bigger one lets the wire overheat. Then I look for the cause. I check the elements and wiring for a short to ground and look for burnt terminals. I tell the manager what I found so it does not happen again.
You have just reconnected a gas fryer after cleaning. How do you check the connection?
Your gas safety habits on kitchen equipment.
Leak test with solution or a gas detector, never a flame. Put the restraint cable back on, then light the fryer and watch the burners.

With the gas on, I brush leak detector solution on every joint I touched and watch for bubbles, or I use a combustible gas detector. Never a lighter. I make sure the quick disconnect is fully seated and the restraint cable is clipped back, so the fryer cannot roll and strain the hose. Then I light it and watch for a steady, mostly blue flame.
Why would you do a voltage drop test instead of just checking resistance with the power off?
Whether you can find a bad connection that hides when the power is off.
A corroded or loose connection can read fine on ohms with no current flowing, but it drops voltage under load. Measuring across it while running shows it.

An ohmmeter pushes a tiny current, so a corroded terminal or a contactor with pitted contacts can read almost zero ohms and look fine. Under real load, that same spot drops voltage and gets hot. With the machine running and proper PPE, I measure across each contact or connection. A good one shows close to zero volts. A few volts across one switch tells me where the problem is.
On a walk-in cooler, what do superheat and subcooling tell you?
Your understanding of how a refrigeration system is charged and working.
Superheat is suction-line temperature above saturation. Subcooling is liquid-line temperature below saturation. Together they point to charge, metering or airflow faults.

Superheat is how many degrees the suction line is above the boiling temperature at the suction pressure. It shows how well the evaporator is fed. Subcooling is how far the liquid line is below the condensing temperature. It shows how much liquid backs up in the condenser. High superheat with low subcooling points to an undercharge. I read both, plus airflow, before I touch the charge.
A mixer motor trips its breaker. How do you test the motor's insulation, and what do you disconnect first?
Whether you can test a motor without damaging the electronics around it.
Lock it out, isolate the motor leads from drives and controls, test each lead to ground with an insulation tester, and compare with past readings or the maker's guidance.

I lock it out and disconnect the motor leads at the starter or drive. An insulation tester puts out hundreds of volts or more and can destroy a drive or a control board. Then I test each lead to the motor frame. A low reading means the winding insulation has broken down, often from moisture or heat. I compare with earlier readings if we have them, and I discharge the winding after the test.
A conveyor bearing has failed three times in a year. What do you look at besides the bearing?
How you go after the root cause instead of swapping parts.
Read the old bearings for clues, then check alignment, belt tension, lubrication amount and type, and contamination such as washdown water.

First I look at the failed bearings: the wear pattern, any discoloration from heat, any rust. Then I check shaft alignment and belt tension, because a belt that is too tight overloads the bearing. I ask how it is greased, since too much grease causes heat just like too little. In a food area, washdown water getting past the seals is common, so I may move to a sealed bearing made for washdown.
Your shift ends with a machine half repaired and locked out. How do you hand it over?
Whether you know how lockout continues across a shift change.
The incoming tech locks on before the outgoing one removes their lock, as the written procedure says, with a clear spoken and written handover.

The equipment must never be left without a lock. The tech coming on puts their own lock on before I take mine off, following our written procedure. I walk them through which energy sources are isolated, what I have taken apart and what I found. I write it in the work order too. If nobody is taking over, my lock stays on and the supervisor knows why.
When is it acceptable to work on equipment while it is energized?
Your grasp of the rules for live electrical work, not just your habits.
Under NFPA 70E, only when shutting down adds a greater hazard or is infeasible. Testing needs a qualified person and PPE, and other live work needs a permit.

Turning it off is the default. Under NFPA 70E, live work is justified only when shutting down would create a greater hazard, like cutting power to life-safety equipment, or is truly infeasible. Lost sales are not a reason. Live testing and troubleshooting are allowed for a qualified person with the right PPE and approach distances. Actual repair work done live needs a written energized work permit.

technology-consultant.heading: Technology consultant questions
qs: What goes into total cost of ownership when a client compares two systems?
Whether you look past the license price.
Licenses plus setup, integration, migration, training, support, internal staff time and exit costs, compared over several years.

I count the subscription or license, setup and configuration, integrations, data migration, training and ongoing support. Then the hidden parts: internal staff time, modules priced later, renewal increases and the cost to leave. I compare both options over three to five years, not just year one.
Walk me through how you run discovery with a new client.
How you learn the business before proposing a solution.
Starts from the business goal, talks to the people doing the work, maps current process and systems, and confirms understanding before recommending.

I start with the business goal and who owns it. Then I interview the people who do the work, not only managers, and watch the process live if I can. I map the current process, list pain points with rough costs, and list systems and data. I end with a short readback so the client confirms I understood before I propose anything.
What is a fit-gap analysis, and what do you do with the gaps?
Your method for matching requirements to a product.
Mapping each requirement to standard, configurable or missing, then choosing per gap: change the process, configure, integrate, customize or accept.

I list each requirement and mark whether the product meets it as standard, with configuration, or not at all. For each gap I first ask if the process can change, since custom code costs money at every upgrade. If not, I look at configuration, an add-on or an integration, and customize only when the gap is core to the business.
How do you build a vendor scorecard for a software selection?
Whether your selection process is fair and hard to sway with a good demo.
Weighted criteria agreed before demos, scripted scenarios from the client's real cases, independent scoring and reference checks.

I agree weighted criteria with the client before we see any demo, so a slick pitch cannot move the goalposts. Weights cover fit, integration, security, cost, vendor stability and support. Vendors get scripted scenarios built from the client's real cases, several people score on their own, and I call references from customers of similar size.
The client asks how secure a SaaS vendor is. What do you check?
Whether you know the practical due diligence on a cloud vendor.
Reads the SOC 2 Type II report and its exceptions, checks login, encryption, data location and contract terms, and involves the client's security team.

I ask for their SOC 2 Type II report, which tests how controls worked over a period, and read the exceptions and the controls the customer must handle itself. I check single sign-on and multi-factor login, encryption, where data is stored, and contract terms on breach notice and getting our data back at exit. The client's security team makes the final call.
Plan a data migration from an old system. What are the steps?
Whether you treat migration as its own workstream with testing.
Profile and clean data, map fields, run trial loads, have business users validate, and cut over with a freeze and a rollback point.

First I profile the source data: duplicates, blanks, odd formats. The client decides what to clean, archive or leave behind. We map old fields to new ones, run at least two trial loads into a test environment, and have business users check record counts and spot-check real records. Cutover follows a written plan with a data freeze and a rollback point.
Midway through a fixed-fee project, the client asks for a 'small' extra integration. How do you handle it?
How you manage scope without hurting the relationship.
Sizes it honestly, writes a change request with cost and schedule impact and options, and waits for sponsor approval before building.

I thank them and size it honestly. Even a small integration needs design, testing and support. I write a change request with effort, cost and schedule impact, plus options: add it now, swap out a lower priority item, or move it to phase two. Nothing is built until the sponsor signs. Doing it quietly for free sets a pattern that sinks the budget.
A vendor offers you a referral fee if your client signs with them. What do you do?
Your independence and honesty with the client.
Follows firm policy, declines or discloses in writing before any decision, and never lets it shape the recommendation.

I would not let it near the recommendation. I follow my firm's policy, which usually means declining it or disclosing it to the client in writing before they decide. The client pays me for advice they can trust. If they learned later that the vendor I recommended was paying me, every past recommendation would look suspect.
Three months after go-live, half the staff still use spreadsheets instead of the new system. What do you do?
How you handle adoption, not just installation.
Finds the real reasons first, fixes the top blockers, gets managers to rely on system data, then retires the workarounds.

I find out why before pushing harder. I sit with a few users and look at usage data. Often a report they need is missing, or entry takes twice as long. I fix the top two blockers fast, get managers to run their meetings from the system's data, and retire the spreadsheets on a set date once the gaps are closed.
You recommended a system, and after signing you find it cannot do a feature the client counted on. What do you do?
How you own a mistake and recover the client's trust.
Tells the sponsor quickly and plainly, brings costed options, and changes the selection process so it does not happen again.

I tell the sponsor quickly, in person, with what I missed and why. Then I bring options: a configuration workaround, a partner add-on, a vendor roadmap date written into the contract, or a fallback process, each with its cost. Afterward I add that scenario to my demo scripts, so a vendor has to show a feature, not just say it exists.
What is the difference between configuring a system and customizing it, and why should the client care?
Whether you understand the long-term cost of changing a packaged system.
Configuration uses settings the vendor supports; customization adds code. Custom work costs more to test, upgrade and support, so it needs a real business case.

Configuration means using the options the vendor built in, like fields, workflows and roles. Customization means writing code the vendor does not maintain. On SaaS, a vendor release can break custom code, so the client pays to retest it each time. I push for configuration first and ask for a business case before any custom build.
Besides features, what requirements do you capture that clients usually forget?
Whether you cover non-functional requirements, not only what the screens do.
Performance, availability, recovery, security, access roles, data retention, accessibility and integration limits, each written so it can be tested.

I ask how many users work at peak, how fast a screen must load and what uptime they need. I ask for recovery targets: how much data they can afford to lose, called RPO, and how long they can be down, called RTO. I also cover user roles, audit logs, data retention rules and accessibility. Each one gets a number so we can test it.
Why do you write a demo script for vendors instead of letting them show their standard demo?
How you keep a software selection fair and based on the client's real work.
Scripted demos with the client's scenarios and sample data, the same for every vendor, scored live against the requirements by the people who will use the system.

A standard demo shows what the vendor does best. I send every vendor the same five or six scenarios from the client's day, like a returned order with a partial refund, plus sample data. Users score each scenario during the demo. If a vendor says a step is coming in a future release, we score it as missing.
The client hands you 300 requirements, all marked must-have. What do you do?
How you get a client to set real priorities.
A clear method like MoSCoW, each must-have tied to a business outcome or a legal need, and the business owners making the final calls.
