Tell me about a loss that came from a risk you had not modeled. What changed afterward?
Whether you learn from losses and turn them into better risk controls.
Owns a specific loss, explains the gap in the model clearly, and names the concrete control added afterward.

We ran a funding carry: long spot on one exchange, short perp on another. A sharp rally pushed the short close to liquidation while the gain sat in spot elsewhere, and moving collateral took too long. We lost about $80,000 closing in a thin book. Since then I model margin per account, not net, and keep enough buffer on each leg for a set move.

trading-systems-engineer.heading: Trading systems engineer questions
qs: How does a matching engine decide which resting order fills first?
Whether you know the core rule of a central limit order book.
Price first, then time at that price; the trade prints at the resting order's price.

Best price wins: the highest bid or the lowest ask trades first. At the same price, the order that arrived earlier fills first. That is price-time priority. The trade prints at the resting order's price, so a buy at 101 against a resting ask at 100 fills at 100. Some venues split fills pro-rata at a price level, but price-time is the common default.
What is the difference between an IOC, a fill-or-kill and a post-only order?
Your grasp of the order types traders rely on every day.
IOC fills what it can and cancels the rest; FOK fills fully or not at all; post-only is rejected or repriced if it would take liquidity.

Immediate-or-cancel takes whatever is available right now and cancels the remainder. Fill-or-kill must fill the whole size at once or it is canceled entirely. Post-only must rest on the book as a maker. If it would cross the spread and trade, the venue rejects it or, on some venues, reprices it. Market makers use it so they never pay taker fees by accident.
Why would you avoid floating-point numbers for prices and quantities?
Whether you know how small number errors creep into trading code.
Floats cannot store most decimal values exactly; use scaled integers tied to tick size and the asset's smallest unit, and check the range.

A double cannot store 0.1 exactly, so sums drift and prices that should match compare as unequal. I store prices as integers counted in ticks, and sizes in the asset's smallest unit. Crypto adds a twist: many tokens use 18 decimals, so a signed 64-bit integer holds only about 9 whole tokens at full precision. There I use 128-bit integers or a coarser unit.
Your average order latency is 20 microseconds. Why does that not tell me the system is fast?
How you measure latency in a way that matters for trading.
Averages hide the tail; look at p99, p99.9 and max under realistic load, with timestamps taken at consistent points.

The average hides the slow orders, and slow orders cluster in bursts, exactly when the market moves. I want the full distribution: median, p99, p99.9 and the max, under realistic load. I check where timestamps are taken, wire to wire if possible. I also watch for coordinated omission: the test tool stops sending while the system stalls, which hides the stall.
You send a new order, the connection drops, and no acknowledgement ever came. What do you do?
How you handle an order in an unknown state without doubling your risk.
Treat the order as possibly live, query it by client order ID, never blindly resend, and count it as open risk until resolved.

I assume the order might be live. I do not send a fresh one, or I could double the position. When I reconnect, I query its status by the client order ID I assigned, and check open orders and fills. If the venue offers cancel-on-disconnect, it may already be gone, but I confirm. Until it is resolved, the risk system counts that size as open.
Your market data handler sees a gap in sequence numbers. Walk me through what happens next.
Whether you can keep a local order book correct when updates are lost.
Mark the book stale, stop trading on it, resync from a snapshot plus buffered updates, then go live and log the gap.

A gap means my book may be wrong, so I mark that instrument stale and strategies stop quoting on it. I buffer new updates, fetch a fresh snapshot, drop buffered messages older than the snapshot's sequence number, and apply the rest in order. Only when the sequence lines up again do I mark it live. Frequent gaps point to a slow consumer or network loss.
What pre-trade risk checks would you put between a strategy and the exchange?
Your sense of the guardrails that stop one bad order from becoming a large loss.
Size and value limits, price bands, position and loss limits, message rate limits and a kill switch, all checked fast before sending.

Per order: a maximum size and value, and a price band that rejects a buy far above the market as a fat-finger error. Per account: position limits, a daily loss limit and a cap on open orders. A message rate limit to stay inside the venue's rules. And a kill switch that blocks new orders and cancels open ones. These run on every order, so I keep them simple and in memory.
How would you take latency out of the hot path of an order gateway?
Your hands-on knowledge of low-latency engineering.
Measure first, then cut allocation, locks, system calls and cache misses; pin threads and consider kernel bypass where it pays.

I profile first. Then I take allocation out of the hot path with preallocated pools, so there are no garbage collector or malloc pauses. I pass messages through single-producer, single-consumer ring buffers instead of locks, pin busy-spinning threads to isolated cores, and keep data compact so it stays in CPU cache. If the network stack is still the bottleneck, kernel-bypass networking is next.
How would you design a matching engine so it recovers from a crash without losing or changing trades?
Whether you understand determinism, journaling and replay in an exchange core.
A deterministic engine fed by a sequenced, durable input log; state is rebuilt from a snapshot plus replay, and a standby replays the same stream.

I keep the engine deterministic: one thread per order book, no wall-clock reads or randomness inside, so the same inputs always give the same outputs. Every input gets a sequence number and is written to a durable journal before its results are released. After a crash I load the last snapshot and replay the journal. A hot standby replays the same stream, so failover gives the same book.
A bug just sent the same order to the exchange hundreds of times. What do you do in the first ten minutes, and after?
How you act in a live trading incident and stop it from happening again.
Stop it with the kill switch, get the true position from the venue, bring in the desk and risk, then fix the root cause and add a guard.

First I hit the kill switch: block new orders, cancel everything open, and confirm with the venue that nothing is resting. I alert the desk and the risk team and pull fills from the exchange, not our own records, to get the true position. They decide how to flatten it. Then I write a blameless postmortem, fix the cause and add a duplicate-order check with a test.
What data structures would you use for a limit order book, and why?
Whether you know how a book is built for fast inserts, cancels and best-price lookups.
Sorted price levels, a FIFO queue per level, and a hash map from order ID to its node so a cancel does not need a search.

I keep bids and asks as sorted price levels, either a tree or an array indexed by tick if the price range is bounded. Each level is a doubly linked FIFO queue. A hash map from order ID to its queue node makes a cancel constant time, and I cache the best bid and ask so reading top of book costs nothing.
What is self-trade prevention, and what modes would you offer?
Your knowledge of a matching rule that exchanges and their regulators care about.
Stops one account trading with itself, which looks like wash trading, and offers clear modes such as cancel newest, cancel oldest or cancel both.

It stops an incoming order from matching a resting order from the same account or group, because that trade moves no real ownership and looks like wash trading. I would offer cancel the incoming order, cancel the resting one, cancel both, and decrement the larger by the smaller. The mode is set per order or per account and logged.
What is cancel-on-disconnect, and how far would you trust it?
Whether you treat an exchange safety feature as a backstop and not a guarantee.
Knows the exchange cancels open orders when the session drops or a timer expires, and still reconciles orders after reconnecting.

The exchange cancels my open orders if my session drops, or, with a dead man's switch, if I stop refreshing a timer. I turn it on for quoting. But it is best effort: a fill can happen in the gap. After reconnecting I query open orders and recent fills before quoting again, and only then trust my state.
An exchange gives you a REST snapshot and a WebSocket stream of book changes. Walk me through building a correct local book.
How you sync a snapshot with a live stream without losing or double counting updates.
Subscribe first and buffer, take the snapshot, drop updates it already covers, check continuity, then resync on any break.

I open the stream first and buffer updates. Then I fetch the snapshot, which carries a last update ID. I drop buffered updates at or below that ID and check the first one I keep starts right after it. From then on each update must follow the last one. If not, I mark the book stale, stop quoting from it and redo the whole sync.
Your strategy is close to an exchange's API rate limit during a volatile minute. What do you do?
How you protect your ability to cancel when request budget runs short.
Tracks usage locally, keeps headroom for cancels, throttles new orders first and backs off instead of retrying in a storm.

I track request weight on our side from the limit headers, not just by waiting for errors. I reserve a share of the budget for cancels, because being unable to pull a stale quote is the real risk. New orders and amends get throttled first. On a rate-limit error I back off with jitter; repeated violations can get the key or IP banned for a while.
How would you measure latency between a tick arriving on one server and the order leaving another?
Your grasp of clock sync and timestamping when a measurement crosses machines.
Knows one-way timing needs synced clocks, that PTP with hardware timestamps beats NTP, or that a single capture point avoids the problem.

Comparing two hosts' clocks is only as good as their sync. NTP is usually too loose for microseconds; PTP with hardware timestamping on the network cards gets far closer. Better still, I tap both wires into one capture device so the same clock stamps the tick and the order. Then I report percentiles, not one number.
A market maker says other firms react to their fills before they get the execution report. What is wrong, and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand fairness in the order of private and public messages.
The owner's execution report must leave no later than the public trade print; fix the publish order and prove it with timestamps.

If the public trade goes out on market data before the private fill reaches its owner, everyone else learns of their trade first. I would check where each message is sequenced and sent, and make the engine release the execution report no later than the public print. Then I would show the market maker timestamps from both feeds proving the order.
Why do perpetual futures venues trigger liquidations on a mark price instead of the last trade price?
Your knowledge of how a crypto derivatives engine resists manipulation.
Mark price comes from an index of several spot venues, so one trade in a thin book cannot set off forced liquidations.

The last trade can be pushed by one large order in a thin book, and that could liquidate many accounts in a cascade. The mark price is built from an index of spot prices on several venues, with any gap to the futures price limited. Someone would have to move many markets at once to trigger liquidations, which is much harder.
Your internal position in one coin no longer matches what the exchange reports. What do you do?
How you handle a state break where real money is at risk.
Stops adding risk in that market, treats the exchange's record of fills as the truth, finds the missing event and fixes the cause.

I stop new orders in that market and alert the desk. Then I pull open orders, fills and balances from the exchange and compare them with our log by order ID. Last time it was one dropped fill report after a reconnect. We corrected the position, then added a check that reconciles fills after every reconnect.
How would you test a change to the matching engine before it goes live?
Whether you can prove a change keeps matching results exactly as they should be.
Deterministic replay of recorded production input, comparing every output event, plus targeted tests for the changed rule.

The engine must be deterministic: the same input sequence always gives the same output. I replay recorded production input through the old and new builds and compare every fill and book event. Any difference must be one we intended. I add unit tests for edge cases of the changed rule and roll out to one market first.

training.heading: Training and enablement questions
qs: What is ADDIE, and how do you use it in practice?
Whether you know the standard design model and use it with judgement.
The five phases named correctly, plus a sign that you test and revise early instead of running it as a rigid one-pass sequence.

ADDIE stands for Analyze, Design, Develop, Implement, Evaluate. I use it as a checklist more than a strict sequence. I pilot a rough version with a few learners early, fix what they struggle with, and loop back. If you run it start to finish only once, you find the problems after launch, when they cost the most to fix.
How do you write a good learning objective?
Your ability to turn a vague topic into something you can teach and test.
An observable action verb, the conditions, and a standard of success. Not words like 'understand' or 'know', which cannot be observed.

I start from what the person must do on the job. 'Understand the refund policy' cannot be observed. 'Given a customer request, process a refund in the billing system with no errors' can. The action verb, the conditions and the standard tell me what to practice and how to assess it.
A manager asks you for a training because her team keeps making mistakes. What do you do first?
Whether you check that training is the right fix before building anything.
A needs analysis that finds the gap and its cause. Mistakes can come from tools, process, workload or incentives, which a course will not fix.

I ask what the mistakes are, how often they happen, and what doing it right looks like. Then I watch a few people work and talk to them. If they know the steps but the form is confusing, the fix is the form, not a course. I train only the real skill or knowledge gap, and I tell the manager what else I found.
How do you decide between e-learning, a live session and a simple job aid?
How you match the format to the task, the audience and the budget.
The task drives the choice: job aids for rare or step-heavy tasks, live practice for skills that need feedback, e-learning for scale and stable content.

If people do a task twice a year and just need the steps, a one-page job aid at the point of work beats any course. If they need practice and feedback, like handling a difficult call, I run live sessions with role-play. Self-paced e-learning fits stable content that thousands of people need. Often the answer is a mix of the three.
A subject matter expert wants every detail of the product in your course. How do you handle it?
How you work with experts while protecting learners from overload.
Respect for the expert, with content cut to what learners need to do the job; the rest goes into reference material.

I thank them, because their detail is valuable, then bring us back to the objectives. For each topic I ask: what goes wrong if a new user does not know this? If nothing, it moves to a reference guide or a knowledge base article. Then I show them a short draft and pilot results; seeing learners succeed usually settles it.
How do you run a 90-minute virtual workshop differently from an in-person one?
Your facilitation skill in the format many teams now use.
Shorter segments, frequent interaction, breakout practice, a co-host for the technology, and a backup plan when a tool fails.

I cut the talking into chunks of about ten minutes, each followed by a poll, a chat question or a breakout task. A co-host handles links, access problems and the chat so I can focus on teaching. I test every tool the day before and keep a simple slide version of each activity, in case a tool fails during the session.
A product launches in three weeks and 200 sales reps must be ready. Walk me through your plan.
How you prioritize enablement under a hard deadline.
Focus on what reps must say and do on day one, involve sales managers, keep materials short, and plan deeper content after launch.

Week one, I agree with product marketing and sales managers on what reps must do at launch: the pitch, the top objections and the demo. Week two, I build a short video, a one-page cheat sheet and a practice session. Week three, managers run role-plays and sign off their reps. Deeper content comes after launch, based on real customer questions.
Learners rate your course highly, but managers say nothing changed on the job. What do you do?
Whether you understand transfer: getting learning used at work, not just enjoyed.
Looking for the barrier between class and job, such as no practice, no manager support or mismatched tools. Then adding reinforcement, not more content.

Good ratings tell me people liked it, not that they use it. I would talk to a few learners and managers to find where it breaks: no chance to use the skill soon, a manager who does it the old way, or a system that does not match what we taught. Usually the fix is follow-up practice, a manager coaching guide and a job aid, not a longer course.
After launch, you find your course teaches a step that changed in the last product release. What do you do?
How you own and fix a mistake that is already in front of learners.
A quick fix and an honest notice to everyone trained, plus a process change so training content keeps up with product releases.

First I post a correction where learners will see it and send a short note with the right step to everyone who completed the course. Then I update the module and the job aid, and check other courses for the same step. Last, I ask to join release reviews or get release notes early, so changes reach training before they reach customers.
What is the difference between SCORM and xAPI, and when would you use each?
Whether you know the technical standards behind learning platforms.
SCORM packages courses for an LMS and tracks basics; xAPI records learning anywhere as statements sent to a Learning Record Store.

SCORM is an older set of standards for packaging an e-learning course so any compliant LMS can launch it and track completion, score and time. xAPI records learning as simple statements, like “Maria completed the pricing simulation,” sent to a Learning Record Store. I use SCORM for standard courses and xAPI when I need to track learning outside the LMS, like in an app or a simulation.
Walk me through how you write a multiple-choice question that tests skill, not memory.
How you build assessments that measure real performance.
A realistic scenario, a clearly best answer, and wrong options based on mistakes people actually make.

I start with a short, realistic scenario, like a customer email, and ask what the learner would do next. The right answer is clearly best to an expert. Each wrong option is a mistake I have seen new hires make, so it is plausible. I keep options similar in length, avoid “all of the above,” and never test a fact they could look up in two seconds.
A stakeholder asks you to design the course for visual, auditory and hands-on learners. How do you respond?
Whether you know the research on learning styles and can push back politely.
Matching teaching to a person's preferred style is not supported by research; match the method to the content instead, without making the stakeholder wrong.

I would say, kindly, that studies have not found people learn better when teaching matches their preferred style. What helps is matching the method to the content: a diagram for a process, hands-on practice for a software task, audio for a call script. Most people benefit from a mix. So we still get the variety they want, for a better reason.
How do you make sure an e-learning course is accessible?
Your working knowledge of accessibility in course design.
Accessibility built in from the start, specific checks against WCAG, and testing with assistive technology before launch.

I design to WCAG at level AA from the start. That means captions and transcripts for video, alt text for images that carry meaning, enough color contrast, nothing that relies on color alone, and every interaction usable by keyboard. I test with a screen reader before launch. Fixing it at the end costs far more than building it in.
Reps forget most of a two-day bootcamp within a few weeks. How would you redesign it?
How you design for retention, not just for the day of training.
Shorter core session, spaced retrieval practice over weeks, manager reinforcement, and job aids for rarely used details.

I would cut the bootcamp to the essentials and spread the rest out. Short practice questions come back at growing intervals: two days, a week, a month later. Managers get a one-page guide to run a ten-minute practice in team meetings. And I would add job aids for what people only need now and then, so they do not have to memorize it.
Your product certification exam has a 98% pass rate. Is that a problem?
How you judge whether an assessment actually measures anything.
Not automatically: check item data, retake patterns and on-the-job performance before rewriting the exam with experts.

Not by itself, so I check first. Questions almost everyone gets right tell us nothing. I see whether people pass by retaking until they remember the questions. Then I compare scores with field results: if certified people still struggle on the job, the exam is too easy or tests the wrong things. If so, I rewrite items around real tasks and set the pass mark with experts.
Support tickets dropped 15% after your training launched. How do you know it was the training?
Whether you can separate training's effect from everything else that changed.
Checking other causes, using a comparison group or staggered rollout, and reporting a likely contribution with honest caveats.

I would not claim it yet. I check what else changed: a product fix, fewer new customers, a new help article. Best is a comparison: if we rolled out region by region, I compare trained and not-yet-trained teams over the same weeks. I also check whether the drop is in the ticket types the course covered. Then I report it as a likely contribution, with caveats.
You must roll out a program through 30 managers who will teach it themselves. How do you keep quality consistent?
How you scale delivery through other facilitators.
A solid facilitator guide, practice with feedback before they teach, fixed core activities, and follow-up based on learner results.

I give them a facilitator guide with timings, key messages and the questions learners usually ask. Each one sees the session run once, then teaches a short part back to me and gets feedback. I keep the core activities fixed and let them adapt the examples. After the first sessions I review learner results by facilitator and coach the ones who need it.
You inherit a learning platform with 400 courses, many of them outdated. Where do you start?
How you manage a content library at scale.
Usage data first, safe retirement with compliance in mind, fixing high-traffic courses first, and named owners with review dates.

I pull usage data first: launches, completions, last update and owner. Usually a small share of courses gets most of the traffic. I retire what nobody has opened in a year, after checking none is required for compliance, and I keep the completion records. I fix the busiest courses first. Then every course gets a named owner and a review date.
Your team of three gets twelve training requests this quarter. How do you decide what to build?
Your judgement in setting priorities and saying no to stakeholders.
Same questions for every request, a visible scoring on impact and effort, leaders sharing the tradeoffs, and lighter solutions where they fit.

I ask each requester the same things: what business problem, how many people, what it costs if we do nothing, and whether training is even the fix. I score requests on impact and effort and share the list with leaders so we make tradeoffs together. Some get a job aid or a short video instead of a course. The ones we decline hear why and when we might revisit.

treasury.heading: Treasury questions
qs: What is the difference between a direct and an indirect cash forecast, and when do you use each?
Whether you know the two main ways treasury forecasts cash.
Direct lists actual receipts and payments for the short term; indirect starts from net income and the balance sheet for longer horizons.

A direct forecast lists the cash I expect in and out: customer receipts, payroll, vendor runs, tax and debt payments. I use it for the next few weeks, often a 13-week view. An indirect forecast starts from projected net income and adjusts for noncash items and working capital. It suits quarters and years, where line-by-line detail would be guesswork.
When would you send a payment by wire instead of ACH?
Your knowledge of US payment rails and their trade-offs.
Wires settle one by one and are final the same day but cost more; ACH is cheap and batched, suits routine payments, and can be returned in some cases.

I use a wire when the money must arrive today and be final, like a loan closing, an urgent supplier or a large intercompany move. A wire cannot be pulled back once sent, so it gets extra checks. Payroll and regular vendor runs go by ACH: it costs far less and handles volume well. Same-day ACH covers some urgent cases if the amount is within the network limit.
What is a zero-balance account, and why would a company use one?
Whether you understand how cash is concentrated across accounts.
Sub-accounts are swept to zero each day into a master account, so cash sits in one place and is easy to see, invest or use.

A zero-balance account is a sub-account that the bank brings back to zero at the end of each day. Deposits are swept up to a master account, and payments are funded from it. We might keep one per business unit for clean tracking, while all the cash sits in one concentration account. That gives one balance to watch, less idle cash and fewer overdrafts.
The company has more cash than it needs for the next few months. How do you decide where to put it?
Your priorities when investing surplus cash.
Safety first, then liquidity, then yield, inside a board-approved investment policy; no chasing return with operating cash.

I follow the investment policy, and the order is safety, liquidity, then yield. First I split the cash: what the forecast says we may need soon stays in the bank or a government money market fund. Money we clearly will not need for months can go into short Treasury bills. I would not reach for extra yield with cash that pays salaries next quarter.
You get an email from a supplier asking you to change their bank details before the next payment run. What do you do?
Whether you know how payment fraud works and how to stop it.
No change based on the email alone: a call to the supplier on a number already on file, then a second person approves the change.

I treat it as possible fraud until proven otherwise. I do not reply to the email or use any phone number in it. I call the supplier on the number we already have on file and confirm the change with someone I know. Then a second person approves the update in the system, and I watch the first payment to the new account. If anything is off, I alert our bank and security team.
We sell to a customer in Germany and will receive 2 million euros in 90 days. How would you hedge that, and what do we give up?
Whether you understand a basic currency hedge and what it costs.
Sell euros forward to the expected date to lock the dollar amount; you give up the gain if the euro rises, and hedge only what is fairly certain.

The risk is that the euro falls before we convert. I would sell euros forward with a bank for about the payment date, which locks the dollar amount today. The forward rate reflects the interest rate gap between the two currencies; it is not a forecast. We give up any gain if the euro rises. If the amount or timing is unsure, I would hedge only part of it.
Our term loan pays a floating rate based on SOFR. The CFO is worried about rates going up. What can treasury do?
Your grasp of interest rate risk and how a swap or cap manages it.
Explains a pay-fixed swap or a cap, what each costs, and sizing the hedge to the debt that will really be outstanding.

SOFR is the benchmark most US floating loans now use. One answer is an interest rate swap: we pay a fixed rate to a bank and receive floating, which offsets the loan, so our net cost is fixed. If rates fall, we pay more than we would unhedged. Another option is a cap: we pay a premium up front and are covered above a set rate. I would match the hedge to the debt we expect to keep.
Most of our cash sits at one bank. Is that a problem?
How you weigh bank counterparty risk against convenience.
Knows deposit insurance covers only a small part of corporate balances, and spreads cash and services across sound banks with a backup plan.

It can be. Deposit insurance covers only a small slice of a company balance, so above that we are an unsecured creditor of the bank. The bank failures of 2023 showed how fast deposits can be frozen. I would keep operating accounts at a main bank, hold surplus in Treasury bills or government money market funds, and keep a second bank ready to run payroll.
Your 13-week cash forecast missed and an account almost went overdrawn. What do you do?
How you handle a forecast error and fix the process behind it.
Secure the cash position first, then find the cause line by line, and change the process so it does not happen again.

First I cover the account with a transfer from the concentration account or a draw on the credit line, and I tell my manager. Then I compare forecast to actual line by line. Last time it was a large customer paying 20 days late, and our receipts were based on invoice terms. I switched those lines to each customer's real payment history and added a weekly check with collections.
Your forecast shows the company may break a leverage covenant in two quarters. What do you do?
Your judgement with lenders when bad news is coming.
Confirm the numbers against the credit agreement, tell leadership with options, and go to lenders early for an amendment or waiver.

I check the math against the credit agreement definitions, since adjusted EBITDA there often differs from ours. If the problem holds, I tell the CFO right away with options: paying down debt, cutting spending or asking for an amendment. Then we talk to the lenders early. Banks respond far better to a plan two quarters ahead than to a surprise breach. A waiver may cost a fee, far less than a default.
What is the cash conversion cycle, and which parts of it can treasury actually move?
Whether you connect working capital to the cash that ends up in the bank.
The formula (DSO plus DIO minus DPO) and realistic levers such as payment timing, collections and supplier finance, with their limits.

It is days sales outstanding plus days inventory outstanding minus days payables outstanding: how long a dollar is tied up between paying suppliers and collecting from customers. Treasury mostly works the edges. We pay on the due date, not early, speed up cash application and may run a supplier finance program. Inventory belongs to operations, so I bring them the numbers.
How does positive pay work, and what does payee positive pay add?
Your knowledge of the bank's basic fraud controls on outgoing checks.
The issue file, the daily exception decision before the bank's cutoff, and the name match that catches an altered payee.

We send the bank a file of every check we issue, with number, amount and date. When a check is presented, the bank matches it against the file. Anything that does not match comes back to us as an exception, and we decide to pay or return it before the cutoff. Payee positive pay also checks the payee name, so it catches a check that was washed and rewritten to someone else.
Our bank account analysis statement shows an earnings credit rate. What is it, and what do you look for in that statement?
Whether you can read bank pricing and spot idle cash or overcharges.
The ECR offsets fees but is not interest, and you check fees against the agreed pricing and look for balances held only to earn credits.

The earnings credit rate is an allowance the bank applies to our balances to offset service fees. It is not interest, and credits beyond the fees usually are not paid out. So I check each fee against the agreed price list and look for services we no longer use. If our balances earn more credit than we have fees, that extra cash could earn real interest elsewhere.
Why is the 90-day forward rate for a currency different from today's spot rate?
Your understanding of how FX forwards are priced.
Interest rate parity: the forward reflects the interest rate gap between the two currencies, not a forecast of where the rate will go.

It reflects the difference in interest rates between the two currencies, not the bank's view of the future. If dollar rates are higher than euro rates, the euro trades at a forward premium. Otherwise someone could borrow one currency, lend the other and lock in a free profit. The forward points are that rate gap for the period, plus the bank's spread.
How would you set up the payment process so that no single person can send money out alone?
How you design segregation of duties and controls around outgoing payments.
Separate set-up, creation and approval, limits by amount, personal bank credentials and regular reviews of user access.

I separate the steps. One person sets up or changes vendor bank details, and another verifies them. One person creates a payment, and a different person approves it in the bank portal, with approval limits by amount. Bank tokens are personal and never shared. I review user rights in the portal every quarter, and anyone who leaves is removed the same day.
What is the difference between physical and notional cash pooling, and when would you choose each?
Your knowledge of structures for concentrating group cash.
Physical pooling moves cash and creates intercompany loans; notional pooling only offsets balances for interest and is not available or practical everywhere.

Physical pooling actually moves balances, usually daily, into a header account. That creates intercompany loans, which need documented terms and arm's length interest. Notional pooling leaves cash where it is, and the bank calculates interest on the net position. It saves transfers, but it is not offered everywhere and banks charge for it. For US entities I would usually use physical sweeps.
A wire for 400,000 dollars went out twice by mistake. What do you do in the first hour?
How you handle a costly payment error under time pressure.
Fast action, knowing a wire is final: a recall through the bank, direct contact with the payee, escalation, then a fix to the cause.

I call our bank right away and ask them to send a recall request to the beneficiary bank. A wire is final once it is received, so the recall only works if the other bank and the payee agree. At the same time I call the supplier's finance contact and ask for the refund in writing. I tell my manager and accounting, then find out why our duplicate check failed and fix it.
We hedge forecasted euro purchases with forwards. How does hedge accounting change what shows up in earnings?
Your grasp of the accounting behind hedging under US GAAP.
Cash flow hedge under ASC 815: derivative value changes go to other comprehensive income and reach earnings with the hedged item; documentation is needed at inception.

Without hedge accounting, the forward is marked to market through earnings every quarter, so profit swings before the purchases even happen. As a cash flow hedge under ASC 815, the change in the forward's value goes to other comprehensive income. It moves into earnings when the purchases affect earnings. We need formal documentation at inception, and the purchases must be probable.
Cash is building up in a subsidiary in a country with currency controls. How would you think about getting it out?
How you handle trapped cash across tax, legal and FX limits.
Learn the local rules first, compare repatriation routes and their tax costs with the tax team, and use the cash locally if nothing works.

First I learn the actual rules: what the central bank allows and what paperwork it needs. Then I compare routes: a dividend, repaying an intercompany loan, or charging for real services or royalties at arm's length prices. Each route has a tax cost, often withholding tax, so I work it through with tax. If none works, I use the cash for local costs and stop sending more there.
Markets are stressed and the CFO asks whether we should draw our whole revolver now. What do you advise?
Your judgement on liquidity in a crisis, weighing cost against access to cash.
A view based on a downside forecast, the cost of drawing versus the commitment fee, the borrowing conditions in the agreement, and possibly a partial draw.

I would first run our forecast under a bad case. Drawing means paying the drawn interest rate instead of the smaller fee on unused commitments, and the cash must be held somewhere safe. The case for drawing is that a bank under stress might not fund, or a borrowing condition might fail later. I would check those conditions in the credit agreement, maybe draw part, and explain it to our banks.

trust-safety.heading: Trust and safety questions
qs: What makes a content policy easy for reviewers to enforce the same way every time?
Whether you know how good rules are written, not just how they are applied.
Clear definitions, examples on both sides of the line, and a focus on what reviewers can see, not on guessing intent.

Each rule names what is banned in observable terms, like a direct threat against a named person, not vague words like offensive. It gives examples that break the rule and close calls that do not. If ten reviewers read the same post, the rule should lead them to the same answer.
Besides removing a post or leaving it up, what other actions can a platform take?
Your knowledge of the full range of enforcement options.
Names several steps, such as labels, reduced reach, age gates, warnings, feature limits and suspensions, and matches them to severity.

We can add a warning screen or a context label, limit how widely a post is shown, put it behind an age gate, or block sharing. On the account side there are warnings, temporary limits on posting, and suspension or a permanent ban. I pick the lightest action that removes the harm, and save bans for severe or repeated violations.
A post contains a slur, but the user is quoting a message they received to show they were harassed. How do you rule?
How you weigh context instead of matching keywords.
Reads the whole post and its purpose; knows most hate speech policies allow quoting to condemn or raise awareness.

I read the full post and the caption, not just the flagged word. If the user is clearly sharing abuse they received to call it out, most policies allow that, so I leave it up, maybe with a warning screen. I would also check whether the original sender broke the rules, because that account may be the real case.
A user appeals a ban for spam and says their account was hacked. How do you check that?
Whether you investigate account signals before deciding an appeal.
Looks for signs of takeover such as new logins, password or email changes and a sudden change in behavior, then restores and secures the account if they fit.

I look at the account history: a login from a new device or region, a recent password or email change, and a sudden burst of posts that do not match years of normal use. If the pattern fits a takeover, I restore the account, remove the spam, and require a password reset and two-factor setup. If nothing changed, I uphold the ban and explain why.
How would you spot a network of fake accounts working together?
Your ability to see patterns across accounts, not just single posts.
Names shared signals like creation dates, devices, identical text and timing, and treats one signal alone as weak.

I look for accounts created in the same short window, sharing devices or network details, posting the same or near-identical text within minutes, and liking each other's posts. One signal alone proves little, since families share a home network. When several line up, I document the links and escalate the whole cluster to the investigations team.
Two reviewers on your team reached opposite decisions on the same case. What do you do?
How you handle inconsistency and keep the team calibrated.
Finds the cause, either an unclear rule or a misread case, fixes the decision, and shares the answer with the team.

First I settle the case itself, using the policy and a lead if needed. Then I ask both reviewers how they read it. If one missed a detail, that is coaching. If the rule honestly allows both readings, I send it to the policy team and add the case to our next calibration session so everyone lands the same way.
Walk me through how you would run a quality audit on a reviewer's decisions.
Whether you know how QA sampling and scoring work in moderation.
Random sample plus targeted checks, a clear score against policy, error types tracked, and feedback with examples.

I pull a random sample of decisions, plus extra from high-risk queues. Each one is graded against the policy version in force that day, and I log the error type: wrong action, missed violation, or over-enforcement. I share results with the reviewer using their own cases, and watch whether the same error repeats across the team.
You see a post where someone says they plan to hurt themselves tonight. What do you do?
How you act when someone may be in immediate danger.
Treats it as urgent, follows the emergency escalation path, and makes sure the person is shown crisis resources such as 988.

I stop working the queue and escalate right away through our imminent-harm process, which can involve contacting emergency services. I make sure the user gets our crisis resources, like the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. I do not remove the post in a way that erases the details responders need. Then I write down exactly what I saw and when.
While reviewing a queue, you come across what appears to be child sexual abuse material. Walk me through your next steps.
Whether you know the legal escalation path and handle this material safely.
No downloading, forwarding or digging further; escalate to the dedicated team, which reports to NCMEC as US law requires providers to do.

I do not download it, screenshot it or forward it, and I do not investigate on my own. I use our dedicated escalation tool so the specialist team can act fast. They remove it, preserve it under legal guidance, and file the report with NCMEC's CyberTipline, which US law requires of online providers. Then I take a short break if I need one.
You realize you applied an outdated version of a policy to about 200 cases last week. What do you do?
How you own a mistake that affected many users.
Tells the lead quickly, sizes the impact, helps fix wrongly actioned cases, and finds why the old version was in use.

I tell my lead the same day, with the date range and case count. Then I pull the 200 cases and recheck each against the current rule. Users who were wrongly actioned get their content or accounts restored, and any real violations I missed get handled. Last, I check why I had the old version, like a saved link, so it cannot happen again.
A user reports that a video uses their music without permission. Why is that handled differently from a hate speech report?
Whether you know copyright claims follow their own legal process.
Names the DMCA notice-and-takedown process, the need for a valid notice, and the counter-notice that can lead to restoring the content.

Copyright goes through the DMCA process, not our community rules. We need a valid notice from the rights holder or their agent, we remove the content promptly, and we tell the uploader. If they send a counter-notice, we can restore it after 10 to 14 business days unless the claimant tells us they have filed a lawsuit.
What does Section 230 protect a platform from, and what does it not?
Your grasp of the US law that shapes moderation decisions.
Covers liability for users' content and good-faith removals; no shield for federal criminal law, intellectual property or certain sex trafficking claims.

It generally stops a platform from being treated as the publisher of what its users post, and it protects good-faith decisions to remove objectionable content. It does not cover federal criminal law, intellectual property claims or certain sex trafficking claims. So it lets us moderate, but it never replaces our duty to report child abuse material.
Why is the number of posts we removed a weak measure of how safe the platform is?
Whether you can pick metrics that reflect the harm users actually see.
Removals rise with both more abuse and better detection; prevalence from sampled views, plus appeal overturn rates, tells the real story.

Removals can go up because abuse grew or because we got better at finding it, so the number alone tells me little. I prefer prevalence: take a random sample of content views, label it, and estimate what share broke the rules. I pair that with the share of removals overturned on appeal, so we see our mistakes too.
An account gets 500 reports in an hour, all for the same rule. How do you treat that?
How you separate real harm from a coordinated reporting campaign.
Judges the content on its merits, not the report count, and looks at who is reporting to spot brigading.

Report volume tells me to look fast, not what to decide. I review the content against the policy as if there were one report. Then I check the reporters: new accounts, the same wording, a post elsewhere telling people to report. If it is a campaign, I protect the target and may act against the organizers.
Users start spelling a banned slur with numbers and symbols to get past our filters. How do you respond?
How you handle evasion without blocking innocent speech.
Adds the variants to detection, tests for false matches first, and uses behavior signals, not just a longer keyword list.

First I collect the variants from recent cases and add them to detection, but I test the new rules on a sample of normal posts before turning them on, since some strings match real words. I send matches to human review instead of auto-removing at first. I also watch accounts that keep evading, because repeat evasion is a stronger signal than any one spelling.
A news outlet posts graphic footage of a shooting, and people are discussing it as news. What do you do?
Your judgement when public interest and harm pull in different directions.
Weighs context and purpose, uses middle options like warning screens and age limits, and removes reposts that glorify the attack.

Footage shared to inform is different from footage shared to celebrate. For the news post I would add a warning screen and limit it to adults, and keep it up if our policy allows a news exception. Copies that praise the shooter or target the victims come down. I would also check whether any clip is the attacker's own recording, which needs stricter handling.
We want a classifier to remove hate speech automatically. How do you decide where to set its threshold?
Whether you understand precision, recall and the cost of each kind of error.
Explains the trade-off, demands high precision for automatic removal, and sends the uncertain middle to human review.

Precision is how often a removal is right; recall is how much of the real hate speech we catch. Raising the threshold lifts precision and lowers recall. For automatic removal I want very high precision, checked on a fresh labeled sample, since wrong removals hit real users. Scores in the middle go to human review, and I recheck as language shifts.
A police officer emails asking for a user's messages and IP addresses for a case. What do you do?
Whether you know how legal requests for user data are handled in the US.
Routes it to the team that handles legal requests, verifies the sender, and knows message content generally needs a warrant, with an emergency exception.

I would not send anything myself. I forward it to our law enforcement response team, which checks that the request is genuine. Under federal law, message content generally needs a search warrant, while lesser legal process can cover basic account records. The exception is an emergency involving danger of death or serious injury, which that team handles under its own rules.
How would you protect reviewers who see graphic content every day?
How you lead a team exposed to harmful material over long periods.
Concrete tool and schedule measures, confidential counseling, and a culture where stepping away is normal.

I would start with the tools: blur and grayscale by default, audio off, and still frames before video. Then the schedule: time limits on the worst queues, rotation onto lighter work, and real breaks. Counseling should be available and confidential. Leads take breaks openly, so nobody feels they must prove they can take more.
After a policy update you wrote went live, the appeal overturn rate for that rule doubled. What do you do?
How you own and fix a policy that does not work in practice.
Reads the overturned cases, finds where the wording fails, clarifies fast, restores wrong removals and tells reviewers what changed.

I would pull a sample of the overturned cases and read them myself. Often one phrase is being read two ways. If wrong removals are doing real harm, I pause that part of the rule or send a clear note with examples that day. Then I fix the wording, retrain with the edge cases, restore content removed in error, and watch the overturn rate weekly.

ui-designer.heading: UI and visual designer questions
qs: What is the difference between a vector and a raster asset, and when do you export each?
Whether you know how assets reach the screen and stay sharp.
Vectors for icons and logos, raster for photos, exported at the right densities for high-resolution screens and kept light.

Vectors are paths and math, so they scale without blurring. I use SVG for icons, logos and simple illustrations. Raster images are pixels, so I export photos at 1x, 2x and 3x for high-density phone screens, or one large source the developer can resize, and I compress them so pages load fast.
How do you build a type scale for a new product?
Your grasp of typography as a system, not single font choices.
A base size, a ratio to step up, rounded values, set line heights and a small number of sizes and weights.

I start from the body size, usually 16 pixels on the web, and pick a ratio like 1.2 or 1.25 to step up to the headings. I round to whole numbers and set line heights, around 1.4 to 1.5 for body text and tighter for big headings. Then I limit myself to a few sizes and two weights so the hierarchy stays clear.
Why do many teams use an 8-point spacing system?
Whether you understand why spacing rules help both design and code.
Fewer, predictable values, consistent alignment and easier handoff, with a smaller step for tight spots.

Spacing in multiples of 8, with 4 for tight spots, gives a short list of values everyone can remember. Layouts line up, engineers stop guessing between 13 and 15 pixels, and 8 divides cleanly on common screen densities, so nothing lands on half pixels when it scales.
Walk me through every state you design for a button.
Your attention to the interaction details that are easy to forget.
Default, hover, focus, pressed, disabled and loading, with a visible focus style and no layout jump.

Default, hover, focus, pressed, disabled and often loading. Focus gets its own visible ring, not just the hover color, because keyboard users rely on it. Disabled looks clearly inactive but stays readable. Loading keeps the button's width, so the layout does not jump when a spinner replaces the label.
What makes a set of icons feel like one family?
Your eye for visual consistency and optical correction.
A shared grid, stroke, corners and detail level, plus optical adjustments where the math looks wrong.

The same grid, say 24 by 24 with padding inside it, one stroke width, matching corner radius and line ends, and the same level of detail. I also correct by eye: a play triangle gets nudged right so it looks centered, and a circle is drawn a bit larger than a square so they look the same size.
What are design tokens, and why separate primitive tokens from semantic ones?
Whether you can build designs that scale across a product and a codebase.
Named shared values; primitives hold raw values, semantic tokens name the purpose, so theming changes stay small.

Tokens are named values for color, spacing, type and radius that design and code share. Primitives are raw values, like blue-600. Semantic tokens name the job, like color-action-primary, and point to a primitive. Components use the semantic ones, so a rebrand or dark mode means remapping a few tokens instead of editing every screen.
How do you approach a dark theme for an existing light interface?
Whether you treat dark mode as a design job rather than a color swap.
No straight inversion: dark gray surfaces, elevation through lighter tones, adjusted brand colors and rechecked contrast.

I don't just invert the colors. I use a dark gray background rather than pure black, show elevation with lighter surfaces instead of shadows, and tone down saturated brand colors, which can look like they vibrate on dark. Then I recheck every text and icon pair for contrast and test on a real phone in a dark room.
A screen looks perfect with your sample data. What do you test before calling it done?
How you design for real content instead of ideal mockups.
Long, missing, empty and huge content, error and loading states, translation, larger text and narrow screens.

I swap in real and ugly content: a 40-character name, a missing photo, zero items, 500 items, a failed load. I check text that runs about a third longer in languages like German, a large system font size and the narrowest phone width. Most layouts break on one of those, and it is cheaper to find in the file than in a bug report.
A stakeholder asks for three equally prominent primary buttons on one screen. How do you respond?
Your judgement on visual hierarchy and how you defend it.
You ask about the main user goal, show the options side by side and treat a true tie as a structure problem.

I ask which action most users need here and bring data if we have it. Then I mock two versions: three equal buttons, and one primary with two secondary. Side by side, the equal version usually reads as noise. If two actions truly matter equally, that tells me the screen may need splitting, not more emphasis.
A week before launch the built screens don't match your designs: spacing, font weights and colors are off. What do you do?
How you handle quality gaps under deadline pressure.
A review on the real build, gaps listed and ranked by impact, agreed with the lead, and root causes fixed.

I review the real build on real devices and list every gap with a screenshot and the expected value. I sort them: broken or confusing first, visibly off-brand second, small polish last. I agree with the lead what fits before launch and file the rest. Often the cause is a missing token, so I fix that once instead of 30 single values.
What do you look for when you choose a typeface for a product interface?
Whether you judge a typeface by how it works on screens, not only by how it looks in a specimen.
Practical criteria: legibility at small sizes, distinct letterforms, enough weights, tabular figures and language coverage, tested in real screens.

I test it at 12 to 14 pixels first. I want a generous x-height, open shapes, and a capital I, lowercase l and number 1 that look different. Then I check the weights, tabular figures and the languages we ship. I set a real dense screen with it before I decide.
How do you set line length and line height for long body text in an interface?
Your command of the type details that decide whether people can comfortably read a block of text.
A sensible line-length range in characters, line height tied to font size and line length, and limits set in the layout, not left to the screen width.

I aim for roughly 45 to 75 characters per line, so I cap the text column with a max width instead of letting it stretch on wide screens. Body line height usually lands around 1.4 to 1.6 times the font size. Longer lines need a bit more, short labels need less.
A play icon sits exactly in the middle of a circle, but users say it looks off-center. Why, and what do you do?
Whether you understand optical adjustment versus mathematical alignment.
Explains that visual weight differs from the bounding box and that designers nudge shapes by eye; the same idea applies to overshoot on round letters and icons.

The triangle's bounding box is centered, but most of its visual weight sits on the left, flat side. So it reads as shifted left. I move it right a little, until it looks centered, and check at real size. It is the same reason round shapes overshoot a line slightly to look the same size as square ones.
Walk me through how you design a data table full of numbers.
How you handle dense, data-heavy screens where reading speed and accuracy matter.
Right-aligned numbers, tabular figures, consistent decimals, headers aligned with their data, and restraint with lines and color.

I right-align numbers and their headers so digits line up by place value. I turn on tabular figures, which give every digit the same width, and keep the same number of decimals in a column. I use light row dividers or spacing instead of a full grid, and keep text columns left-aligned.
Why can't you build a color palette just by changing the lightness value in HSL?
Your understanding of color beyond picking swatches, and how you build ramps that behave predictably.
Knows HSL lightness does not match how bright colors look, and uses a perceptual space or contrast checks to build even ramps across hues.

HSL lightness is not perceptual. A yellow and a blue at the same lightness look very different in brightness, so the steps in each ramp feel uneven. I build ramps in a more perceptual space like OKLCH, then check contrast ratios for each step, so step 600 works the same way in every hue.
The brand's signature orange fails contrast with white text on the main button. Marketing will not change the brand color. What do you do?
How you solve a conflict between brand and accessibility without giving up either.
Knows the AA text ratio, offers concrete options like a darker interactive shade or dark text, and keeps the bright orange for uses where it does no harm.

Normal-size text needs a 4.5 to 1 contrast ratio for WCAG AA. I would test dark text on the orange, which often passes, and a slightly darker orange used only for interactive elements. The original orange stays in illustrations and accents. I show both options in context so marketing sees the brand still reads clearly.
A dashboard you inherited has bold headings, colored badges and icons everywhere, and nothing stands out. How do you fix it without adding more color?
Your skill at visual hierarchy and your willingness to remove rather than add.
Starts from what users need first, then uses size, weight, spacing, grouping and muted styling; tests whether the key number is found faster.

I ask what users must see in the first few seconds, usually one or two numbers. Those get size and weight. Everything else steps down: regular weight, grey text, icons only where they help. I group related items with spacing instead of boxes. Then I run a quick test to see if people find the key figure faster.
A product team wants a one-off variant of a design system component for their feature. How do you decide whether to add it?
Your judgement in running a design system: consistency versus the real needs of product teams.
Asks about the underlying need and reuse, checks existing options, and chooses between adding, extending or a local exception with a clear record.

I ask what problem the variant solves and whether other teams have it too. Often an existing option covers it. If the need is real and likely to repeat, I design it properly as part of the system. If it is truly local, they build it as a documented exception, and I revisit it if a second team asks for the same thing.
You need to change the padding and structure of a component used in dozens of screens across several products. How do you roll it out?
How you manage a breaking change in a design system without breaking products or trust.
Audits usage, plans with engineering, versions the change, communicates and gives a migration path and deprecation period rather than a silent swap.

First I audit where it is used and which screens would shift. I agree the plan with engineering: a new version, the old one marked deprecated with a removal date. I write a short changelog with before and after images and migration notes, and I review the riskiest screens with each team before the old version goes away.

underwriter.heading: Underwriter questions
qs: What is adverse selection, and how does underwriting protect against it?
Whether you understand why underwriting exists at all.
Higher-risk applicants seek coverage more eagerly. Underwriting gathers and checks facts, then prices or declines so the pool stays sound.

Adverse selection means the people most likely to have a claim are the most eager to buy coverage, often because they know something we don't. If we priced everyone the same, the pool would get riskier and rates would spiral. Underwriting asks the right questions, verifies the answers and sets a price that matches each risk.
What are the five Cs of credit, and which one do you look at first?
Your grasp of the basic framework for judging a borrower.
Character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions. Capacity to repay usually comes first, since collateral is a fallback, not the source of repayment.

Character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions. I start with capacity: can the cash flow actually cover the payment? Collateral matters, but it is the second way out. A loan that only works if we take the property back is a loan I should not make.
How do you calculate a debt-to-income ratio, and what can it miss?
Whether you know the core affordability measure and its limits.
Monthly debt payments divided by gross monthly income, plus awareness that it ignores savings, living costs and how stable the income is.

I add up the monthly debt payments, including the new housing payment, and divide by gross monthly income before taxes. It is a quick test of capacity. But it says nothing about savings, how stable the income is, or a family's real living costs, so I read it next to the credit report, assets and job history.
What does a loss ratio tell you, and how is it calculated?
Your understanding of how an insurance book of business is judged.
Incurred losses divided by earned premium. A rising ratio signals pricing or selection trouble, and it is read together with expenses.

It is incurred losses, often with loss adjustment expenses, divided by earned premium. If we earn 1 million dollars of premium and incur 650,000 in losses, the loss ratio is 65%. Add the expense ratio and you get the combined ratio; above 100% means we lose money on underwriting before investment income.
Which factors are you not allowed to consider in a credit decision?
Whether you know fair lending law and keep it out of your decisions.
The protected traits under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, and awareness that rules that look neutral can still discriminate.

Under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, I can't base a decision on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status or age, or on income coming from public assistance. I also watch for proxies, like a rule tied to a neighborhood, that can hurt a protected group. I judge the file on income, credit, assets and collateral, and I write down why.
A commercial property submission shows a 1920s building with what looks like original wiring. How do you handle it?
How you turn a red flag into a clear decision.
Getting facts before deciding: an inspection or electrician's report, then accept, add conditions, adjust the price or decline within guidelines.

Wiring that old may be knob-and-tube, which is a real fire risk. I would not quote on the building's age alone. I would ask the broker for an electrician's report or order an inspection. If it was fully updated, I write it normally. If not, I make the upgrade a condition with a deadline or decline, depending on our guidelines.
A broker wants you to bind a policy today, but the loss runs have not arrived. What do you do?
How you hold your standards under sales pressure.
A firm but helpful answer: say what is missing and why, offer a fast path, and never bind blind or beyond your authority.

I'd tell the broker I want to help meet the date, but I can't price a risk without its loss runs, the claim history from the prior insurer. I'd ask if the prior carrier can email them today. If nothing arrives and our guidelines offer no other route, I don't bind. A missed deadline is easier to fix than a bad risk on the books.
A self-employed borrower's income fell from 120,000 to 90,000 dollars over the last two tax years. How do you treat it?
Whether you can judge income that is not stable.
No blind averaging: use the lower, recent figure at most, find the cause and judge whether the decline has stopped.

Averaging would give 105,000, which overstates what the borrower earns now. I would use 90,000 at most, then find out why it dropped: a lost client, a new competitor, a one-time cost. I'd ask for a year-to-date profit and loss statement and bank statements. If income is still falling, I may not be able to count it as stable at all.
When would you approve a file that falls outside the guidelines?
Your judgement on exceptions and your respect for authority limits.
Only with real, documented compensating factors, within your own authority, and escalated when it goes beyond it.

Only when strong compensating factors offset the weak spot and I can write them down. For example, a debt-to-income ratio slightly over our limit, but with a year of cash reserves, a long job history and a large down payment. I document the reasoning in the file, stay within my approval authority, and send it up when it goes beyond that.
After a policy is issued, you learn the applicant left out two prior claims. What do you do?
How you handle a serious problem fairly and by the rules.
Verify the facts, judge whether they are material, involve your manager and compliance on state rules, and document every step.

First I confirm it: I pull the claims history and make sure the claims belong to this insured. Then I ask whether the facts are material, meaning we would have priced or written it differently. If so, I take it to my manager and compliance, because cancellation, nonrenewal and rescission each have state rules on timing and notice. I document every step.
When a loss run arrives, what do you look at beyond the total incurred?
How you read loss runs in detail, not just the bottom line.
Valuation date, paid versus reserved, open claims, frequency, large losses and their causes, and whether every year asked for is there.

First the valuation date and whether every year is there. Then paid versus incurred, because incurred includes reserves on open claims that can still grow. I count claims per year, pick out the large ones, and read the cause of loss. Three slip-and-falls at the same store tell me more than one total.
Two accounts have the same five-year losses: one has a single 200,000 dollar claim, the other has forty small ones. Which worries you more?
Whether you understand frequency and severity as different signals.
Frequency usually predicts future losses better. A single large loss still needs its cause checked, not ignored.

Usually the forty small claims. Frequency shows a pattern in how the place is run, and small losses often grow into a large one. The single big claim may be a one-off, but I would still ask what caused it and what was fixed. If the answer is nothing, it worries me just as much.
A workers' compensation submission shows an experience mod of 1.35. What does that tell you, and what do you ask?
Your knowledge of experience rating in workers' compensation.
Past losses ran well above what is expected for that payroll and class mix. You ask what drove it and what has changed.

It means the account's past losses were about 35 percent worse than expected for its class codes and payroll, and the manual premium is multiplied by 1.35. The mod uses about three completed years, so I ask for the worksheet and loss runs to see what drives it, many claims or one big one, and what safety changes the insured has made since.
A building that would cost 1,000,000 dollars to rebuild is insured for 600,000 with an 80 percent coinsurance clause. A 100,000 dollar loss happens. What gets paid?
Whether you understand insurance to value and the coinsurance penalty.
The right formula, insurance carried over insurance required times the loss, and why low values hurt both the insured and the insurer.

The clause requires 800,000 of coverage. They carried 600,000, so they get 600 over 800, or 75 percent: 75,000 dollars, less the deductible. That is why I check values at submission. An underinsured building also means we collect too little premium for the risk, so I push the broker for a current valuation.
The most recent policy year on a loss run looks almost clean. Why might you not trust it?
Whether you understand loss development and claims not yet reported.
Recent years are immature: claims are still being reported and reserves still move. You compare years at the same age or allow for development.

A year that ended a few months ago is not mature. Some claims have happened but have not been reported yet, and open reserves often rise as claims develop, especially in liability. I compare years at the same age, look at how earlier years grew after their first valuation, and ask the broker for an updated run before binding.
A commercial real estate loan request shows a debt service coverage ratio of 1.05. How do you look at it?
Your grasp of cash flow coverage in commercial lending.
Net operating income over annual debt service. At 1.05 there is almost no cushion, so you test the income and the loan structure before deciding.

DSCR is net operating income divided by annual principal and interest. At 1.05, a small vacancy or a repair bill means the property cannot cover the loan. I check that the income uses real rents and a vacancy allowance, then look at fixes: a smaller loan, a longer amortization, or a guarantor. If it still cannot reach our minimum, I decline.
A risk is acceptable except for one exposure you do not like. What tools do you have besides declining?
How you shape a risk with terms, not only with a yes or a no.
Deductibles, sublimits, exclusions, conditions, required improvements with deadlines, and price, each chosen to fit the exposure.

I can raise the deductible on that peril, sublimit it or exclude it, or add a condition such as a working sprinkler or a kitchen hood cleaned on a schedule. I can require fixes by a set date after a loss control visit. Then I price what remains. I tell the broker why, so the insured knows what to fix to earn better terms.
A broker tells you a competitor quoted your best renewal 20 percent lower. What do you do?
How you keep rate discipline while protecting a broker relationship.
You check what the other quote really covers, decide on the account's own merits, and tell the broker honestly where you can go.

I ask what is in the other quote: limits, deductible, exclusions, the carrier's rating. Often it is not the same coverage. Then I rerun my pricing. If my rate was high, I adjust and say why. If the account needs that rate, I hold, tell the broker plainly and thank them. Buying business below cost hurts the book at the next renewal.
Tell me about an account you wrote that turned out badly. What did you change afterward?
Whether you own your mistakes and turn them into a better process.
A specific case, what was missed, honest ownership, and a concrete change to how you underwrite now.

I wrote a small contractor with clean loss runs, but I did not ask how much work went to subcontractors. They used uninsured subs, and a fall injury landed on our policy. Since then I ask for subcontractor spend and certificates of insurance on every contractor file, and I check them again at the premium audit.
Your book's loss ratio rose from 58 to 71 percent in two years. How do you work out why?
How you diagnose a portfolio problem instead of reacting to one number.
You split the change into large losses, frequency, business mix, rate adequacy and reserve changes, then act on the cause you find.

First I take out large and catastrophe losses to see if the core changed. Then I split by class, state and new versus renewal, because new business often runs worse. I check whether rate kept pace with claim cost trends and whether reserves were raised on old years. Once I know the cause, I fix that piece: rate, a class, or a broker.

university-recruiter.heading: University recruiter questions
qs: What does a full recruiting year look like for you, from the start of fall to the end of summer?
Whether you know the campus hiring calendar and when each step has to happen.
A clear cycle: planning, fall events and interviews, offers, a smaller spring round, then the summer internship and return offers.

Late summer I plan the school list and train interviewers. Fall is career fairs, info sessions and interviews for next summer's interns and new grads, with most offers out by late fall. Spring is a smaller round to fill gaps. Summer the interns are on site, and at the end we decide on return offers.
How do you decide which campuses to visit in person?
How you use data to spend a limited travel budget.
Choices based on past hires, performance and acceptance, plus matching programs and a wider pipeline, with virtual events for the rest.

I look at where our past hires came from, how they performed, and how often offers were accepted at each school. I add schools with strong programs in the roles we need and some we have overlooked. Schools that make the list but not the budget get virtual sessions and résumé reviews.
Walk me through how you would prepare for a career fair at a large university.
Your planning and how you turn a busy booth into real candidates.
Clear roles at the booth, trained staff, a fast way to capture candidates, and follow-up within days.

I confirm the roles we are hiring for and brief the engineers or managers who will staff the booth. We use a QR code so students apply on the spot instead of handing us paper. Each evening we tag strong candidates, and I send interview invites within a week, while they still remember us.
A student at your booth asks whether you sponsor work visas. What do you say?
Whether you handle sponsorship questions accurately and without discriminating.
A straight answer on company policy, the same sponsorship question for everyone, and no questions about nationality or national origin.

I tell them our policy for that role plainly, so they do not waste their time. In the process we ask every candidate the same thing: will you now or in the future need sponsorship to work here. I do not ask where they are from or about their citizenship; national origin is not something we screen on.
A hiring manager wants to interview only students with a GPA of 3.7 or higher from five schools. What do you do?
How you push back on narrow screens with data and keep the manager on side.
Asks what the manager is really looking for, shows how the filter shrinks the pool, and proposes job-related screens instead.

I ask what the cutoff is meant to predict. Usually it is coding skill or follow-through. I show how few candidates the filter leaves and that our best interns last year included people outside it. Then I suggest a short skills exercise for everyone, and we compare results after one cycle.
How do you set deadlines for offers to students?
Your judgement on giving students fair time while protecting your hiring plan.
Reasonable time to decide, respect for school policies, no pressure tactics, and extensions handled case by case.

I give enough time for a student to finish their fall interviews, and I check each school's career center policy first. I avoid exploding offers; a forced yes often turns into a renege later. If someone asks for more time, I ask what they are waiting on and extend when it is reasonable.
A student accepted your internship offer in October and calls in February to say they took another job. What do you do?
How you handle a renege calmly and recover the hire.
Stays professional, learns the reason, moves to backup candidates fast, and follows the school's reporting policy if it has one.

I thank them for telling me directly and ask what made the difference, because that tells me if our offer has a gap. I do not threaten or guilt them. That afternoon I go back to our strong runners-up. If the school asks employers to report reneges, I do that factually.
What numbers do you track to know if an internship program is working?
Whether you measure the program by results, not by activity.
Return offer rate, offer acceptance, first-year retention and performance, by source school, plus intern feedback and cost per hire.

I track how many interns get return offers and how many accept them, then how those hires perform and stay after a year. I break it down by school to guide next year's list. I also run an end-of-summer survey; last year it showed managers who skipped weekly check-ins had lower acceptance.
Halfway through the summer, a manager tells you an intern is not performing. What do you do?
How you handle a struggling intern fairly before the return offer decision.
Gets specifics, makes sure the intern hears clear feedback and gets support, documents it, and keeps the final decision fair.

I ask the manager for specific examples and whether the intern has heard them. Often the goals were never made clear. We hold a midpoint talk with two or three concrete targets and weekly check-ins. I write it down so the return offer decision at the end is based on the same facts everyone saw.
