We have almost no name recognition at a school we want to hire from. How would you build our brand there over two years?
How you build a presence on a campus starting from nothing.
A multi-year plan with faculty, clubs, career staff and real employees from the school, plus a way to measure progress, not just a bigger booth.

In year one, I would meet the career center and two or three faculty in the right departments, sponsor a club project, and send alumni who work here to speak. In year two, I add a case event and bring interns back as ambassadors. I would measure applications from that school, event turnout, and how many first-round candidates come from it each year.
You need 40 new graduates to start next summer. How many offers do you make?
Whether you plan offer volume from your own acceptance and renege history.
Working back from past acceptance rates and late reneges, releasing offers in waves, and holding back in case yield runs high.

I start from our history. If about 65% of our offers are accepted and about 5% of acceptances back out before the start date, I need 40 divided by 0.65, then divided by 0.95. That is about 65 offers. I would release them in waves, watch acceptances, and hold the last wave so we do not overshoot if yield comes in high.
A manager wants to bring on unpaid summer interns. What do you tell them?
Your grasp of federal wage rules for interns at for-profit companies.
That the Department of Labor uses the primary beneficiary test, and that an intern doing productive work for the team will usually need to be paid.

At a for-profit company, the Department of Labor asks who is the primary beneficiary, the intern or the employer. It looks at factors like whether the work is tied to the student's education and whether the intern replaces paid staff. If the intern does real work for the team, I would pay them. Some states are stricter, and paid programs also recruit better.
You have 60 engineers interviewing interns this fall. How do you keep their ratings consistent?
How you run structured, fair interviews at high volume.
The same questions and scoring guide for each role, short training, calibration on sample answers, and watching each interviewer's pass rate.

Each role gets a set question bank and a scoring guide that describes a weak, solid and strong answer. New interviewers take a short training and shadow once. Early in the season we all score the same recorded mock answer and talk through the gaps. Then I watch pass rates by interviewer; anyone passing 90% or 10% of candidates gets a conversation.
A new graduate with our standard offer asks for $10,000 more and shows a competing offer. How do you respond?
How you balance fairness across a new grad class with winning one candidate.
Knowing your pay policy before the call, applying it the same way to everyone, and selling the whole offer honestly.

I thank them and ask what matters most besides pay. Our new grad salaries are set by level and location, so I cannot move one person's base pay. If we have a set lever, like a sign-on bonus within a range, I use it the same way for anyone in this spot. Then I talk honestly about the team, training and growth, and give them time to decide.
Leadership wants a more diverse intern class. How do you do that within the law?
Whether you know where outreach ends and illegal selection begins.
Wider outreach is fine; hiring decisions must use the same job-related criteria for everyone, never race or sex, which Title VII prohibits.

I widen the pool, not the rules. I add schools we skipped, such as HBCUs, Hispanic-serving institutions and state schools, recruit transfer students, and keep events open to every student. Then everyone goes through the same screen and structured interviews. Nobody is picked or rejected because of race or sex; that would break Title VII.
An F-1 student intern wants to start Monday, but their curricular practical training is not on their I-20 yet. What do you do?
Whether you know a student cannot start work before the school authorizes it.
No start until the school's designated official records CPT on the I-20 for this employer and these dates; you move the start date instead.

They cannot start, not even for orientation. CPT is approved by the school's designated school official, and it has to show on the I-20 with our company and dates before the first day. I would move the start date, tell the manager why, and help the student get the school what it needs, usually an offer letter with dates, hours and duties.
A finalist's background check comes back with something that may disqualify them. Walk me through the next steps.
Your knowledge of the federal steps before acting on a background report.
A pre-adverse action notice with the report and the summary of rights, time to respond, then a final notice, plus a check of state and local rules.

Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, before we decide, I send a pre-adverse action notice with a copy of the report and the summary of rights, and give the candidate reasonable time to respond. The report may be wrong or need context. If we still decide against them, I send an adverse action notice. I also check state and city fair chance laws, which can add steps.
You find out 40 new grad offer letters went out with the wrong salary. What do you do?
How you handle a costly error that candidates have already seen.
Getting the facts fast, deciding with leadership whether to honor the figure, calling each person before any new letter, and fixing the process.

First I find out which way it was wrong and how many people signed. If the number was too high, I push leadership to honor it; taking money back from 40 new grads costs more in trust than in salary. If it was too low, we correct it right away. Either way I call each person before the new letter goes out, and I add a second check on letter data.
Mid-winter, the business cuts next year's new grad hiring in half, and offers are already accepted. How do you handle it?
Your judgement when offers may be pulled and trust with campuses is at stake.
Pushing to keep accepted offers through other teams or deferrals; if some are rescinded, doing it fast, by phone, with real support, and telling career centers.

I first argue for keeping accepted offers: place people on other teams, defer start dates with a payment, or slow experienced hiring instead. If some offers must be pulled, it happens now, not in May, by phone, with a payment and job search help. I call the career centers myself. Students talk, and schools remember which employers pulled offers.

ux-designer.heading: UX designer questions
qs: How would you explain the difference between UX and UI design?
Whether you understand where your work starts and ends.
UX covers the whole experience: needs, flows and structure. UI is the visual and interactive layer. They overlap but are not the same.

UX is whether the product makes sense for the person: what steps they take, in what order, and whether they reach their goal. UI is how each screen looks and behaves: type, color, buttons, spacing. A beautiful screen can still sit in a confusing flow. On many teams I do both, but I start with the flow before I touch the visuals.
When do you use a low-fidelity prototype instead of a high-fidelity one?
How you match the tool to the question you need answered.
Low fidelity early, to test structure and flow cheaply. High fidelity when details, interactions or visual cues matter, or for final checks.

Early on, I use paper sketches or gray wireframes. They are fast, and people comment on the flow instead of the colors. Once the structure holds up, I move to a clickable high-fidelity prototype to test labels, button states and anything where the look changes behavior. I do not polish what I may throw away next week.
Besides the main path, what states do you design for a screen?
Whether you think past the happy path.
Empty, loading, error, partial and too-much-content states, plus permission cases, each with a clear next step for the user.

For a list screen I design the empty state for a new user, with a clear first action. Then loading, an error with a way to retry, a partial state when some data fails, and the case with very long names or hundreds of items. I also check what a user without permission sees. Engineers will build these states anyway; if I skip them, they get invented on the spot.
How do you write a task for a usability test without leading the participant?
Your skill at running research that gives honest results.
A realistic goal in the user's own words, no interface labels or hints, and neutral follow-up questions.

I give a goal, not instructions. Instead of “Click Transfer Funds,” I say “You owe your roommate $40 for groceries. Pay them back.” I avoid the words on the buttons, since that turns the test into word matching. During the session I stay quiet, and if they ask what to do, I say “What would you do if I were not here?”
What is the difference between card sorting and tree testing, and when do you use each?
Your knowledge of the methods for organizing navigation and content.
Card sorting shows how users group content and helps build a structure; tree testing checks whether people can find items in a proposed structure.

In card sorting, people group topics into piles that make sense to them, and in an open sort they name the groups. It tells me how users think about the content. Tree testing comes after: I give a text-only menu, no visual design, and ask people to find specific items. Card sorting helps me build the navigation; tree testing tells me whether it works.
How many people do you test with in a usability study, and why?
Whether you understand the tradeoffs of small qualitative tests.
Small rounds of about five per user group find the major problems, and several rounds beat one big one. Measuring numbers needs a much larger sample.

For a qualitative test, I usually run about five people per distinct user group. By then the same big problems keep showing up. I would rather fix them and run another round of five than test fifteen at once. If I need numbers, like a success rate to compare two designs, that is a different study and needs a much larger sample.
In interviews, users say they love a feature, but analytics show few people use it. What do you believe?
How you combine what users say with what they actually do.
Behavior outweighs stated opinion, but you dig into why: the feature is hard to find, needed rarely, or praised out of politeness.

I trust behavior more than opinion, but I do not stop there. The gap is a question. Maybe people cannot find the feature, maybe they need it twice a year, or maybe they were being polite to me. I would check where it sits in the flow, look at who does use it, and watch a few sessions. Then I decide whether to move it, explain it, or cut it.
You have one week and no research budget before a design goes to development. How do you get evidence?
How you do useful research under real limits of time and money.
Cheap, fast methods aimed at the riskiest assumption: support tickets, analytics, quick tests with real users, and a clear note of what stays untested.

I pick the one assumption that would hurt most if wrong. On day one I go through support tickets and analytics for that flow. Then I run quick tests with three to five people who fit the user profile, recruited through support or sales, using a clickable prototype over video. I share a one-page summary and list what we still have not tested, so the risk is known.
Your redesign ships and sign-ups drop 10% in the first week. What do you do?
How you own and work through a design that made things worse.
Check the data is real, find where in the funnel the drop happens, watch sessions, decide on a rollback with the team, and share what you learn.

First I check it is real: a tracking change, a bug or a seasonal dip can look like a design problem. Then I find the step where people drop off and watch session recordings or run quick tests on it. If the cause is clear and serious, I propose rolling back or fixing that step while we learn. I tell the team early; hiding a bad result costs more than the drop.
A product manager asks you to hide the cancel button to cut churn. How do you respond?
Your judgement when business goals push toward a dark pattern.
You refuse the trick, name the risks to trust and the legal exposure, and offer honest ways to keep customers.

I would say that hiding cancel does not cut churn; it delays it and turns leaving customers into angry ones who complain and dispute charges. Regulators also act against subscriptions that are hard to cancel. Then I offer real options: ask why people leave, offer a pause or a cheaper plan, and fix the top reasons from the exit survey. Cancel stays easy to find.
What does Fitts's law mean for how you size and place buttons?
Whether you know a core law of interaction and can apply it to a screen.
Time to hit a target grows with distance and shrinks with size. So key actions are big and close, and risky ones are kept apart.

Fitts's law says the time to reach a target depends on how far away it is and how big it is. So I make the main action large and place it near where the thumb or cursor already is. I also use it the other way on purpose: a destructive action like Delete goes away from Save, so a slip does not cost someone their work.
When should a form show an error message, and what should the message say?
How well you design the small moments where users get stuck.
Errors appear when the user leaves a field or submits, not on every keystroke. The message sits by the field and says how to fix it.

I validate when the person leaves the field or submits, not while they are still typing. A red error on the second letter of an email is just noise. The message goes next to the field and says what is wrong and how to fix it, like “Enter a date as MM/DD/YYYY.” I keep what they typed, and on submit I move focus to the first error.
You finished 12 user interviews. Walk me through how you turn the notes into findings.
Your method for synthesis, not just for collecting data.
A traceable process: notes broken into observations, clustered into patterns, and each finding backed by how many participants showed it.

First I write each observation on its own note, keeping quotes and behaviors apart from my guesses. Then I cluster them with affinity mapping and name each group as an insight, not a topic. For each finding I note how many of the 12 showed it, with a quote or clip as proof. A pattern seen in only two people becomes a question to check, not a finding.
What can a heuristic evaluation catch that a usability test cannot, and the other way round?
Whether you know the limits of expert review compared with watching real users.
Expert review is fast and finds breaks of known principles. Only real users show which problems actually stop people, and why.

A heuristic evaluation is a few designers checking the interface against principles like Nielsen's ten heuristics. It is cheap and catches things like inconsistent labels or missing feedback. But experts guess at severity and miss problems tied to the user's own words and context. A usability test shows what really blocks people. I use the review to clean up first, then test.
How do you write a screener so you recruit the right participants for a study?
Whether you can get real users into a study instead of people who say what you want to hear.
Questions about past behavior, not opinions, with no hint of the qualifying answer, and filters that screen out industry insiders and frequent testers.

I ask about behavior, not opinion: “How many times did you book a flight online in the past year?” with ranges, not “Do you travel often?” I hide which answer qualifies by mixing in other options. I screen out people who work in design or research, and anyone who took part in a study recently. Then I confirm a few by phone before the sessions.
When would you run an A/B test instead of a usability test?
Whether you match the research method to the question you need answered.
A/B tests show which version performs better at scale; usability tests show why people struggle. A/B needs enough traffic and a clear metric.

An A/B test answers “which one wins” on a metric like completion rate, using real traffic. It needs enough users to reach a reliable result, and it will not tell me why. A usability test with a handful of people tells me why someone fails, but not how often. So I usually test first to find and fix problems, then A/B test the finalists if traffic allows.
Your team ran the System Usability Scale and the product scored 62. What does that tell you?
Whether you can read a standard usability score without misusing it.
SUS runs from 0 to 100 but is not a percentage. About 68 is the average across studies, so 62 is below average. It shows how users feel, not what to fix.

SUS is ten statements rated on a five-point scale, turned into a score from 0 to 100. It is not a percentage. Across many published studies the average is about 68, so 62 is somewhat below average. It tells me perceived usability is weak, not what causes it. I would pair it with task success and session notes, and track it across releases.
A senior stakeholder watched one test session and now wants to redesign checkout around what that one participant did. How do you respond?
How you protect research quality while keeping a stakeholder engaged.
Thanks them for watching, puts the session in context with the other participants, and turns their concern into something to check.

I am glad they watched; that is how research gets used. I would show what the other participants did on the same step, side by side. If the issue showed up for others too, we act on it. If it was only one person, I add it as a question for the next round to see if it repeats. Either way, they see their concern taken seriously.
A product team wants a custom component that breaks the design system. How do you decide?
Your judgement on consistency versus a real user need.
Asks whether existing patterns fail a real user need. If so, proposes a change to the system with the use case rather than building a one-off.

I first ask what user problem the existing components fail to solve, and I look for proof. Often a variant of an existing pattern works. If the need is real, I do not make a one-off. I bring it to the design system team with the use case, so it gets built accessible, tested and available to others. One-offs pile up into an inconsistent product.
You must change the main navigation of a product that millions of people use every day. How do you plan the change?
How you change a product without breaking the habits of current users.
Tests with existing users, not only new ones, measures a baseline, and rolls out in stages with a way back and clear signals to watch.

Current users have muscle memory, so I test the new navigation with them, not just with newcomers, using tree testing and tasks on common paths. I measure a baseline first. Then we release to a small share of users and watch task completion and support tickets. We explain the change inside the product and keep the option to roll back.

ux-researcher.heading: UX and market researcher questions
qs: When would you run interviews instead of a survey?
Whether you match the research method to the question being asked.
Interviews to learn why and to discover unknowns; surveys to measure how many, once you know what to ask.

I run interviews when we do not yet know the problem. I need stories, reasons and the words people use. I use a survey when we know the options and need to know how common each one is. Often I do both in that order: eight interviews to find the themes, then a survey to size them.
How many participants do you need for a usability test?
Your grasp of sample size in qualitative testing.
It depends on the goal: about five per distinct user group to find problems, tested in rounds; many more to measure task success rates.

For finding problems, I plan about five people per distinct user group, then fix what we saw and test again. The most common problems show up early and repeat. If the goal is a number, like a task completion rate to compare with the last release, five is far too few. That needs a larger quantitative study.
How do you keep from asking leading questions in an interview?
Whether you can get honest answers rather than the ones the team hoped for.
Open, neutral questions about past behavior instead of guesses about the future, shown with a concrete rewrite.

I ask about what people did, not what they would do. Instead of “Would you use a feature that saves your receipts?” I ask “Tell me about the last time you needed a receipt. What happened?” I work from a discussion guide, avoid words that hint at an answer, and let a pause sit instead of filling it.
What is wrong with the survey question “How satisfied are you with the speed and design of our app”?
Your eye for survey questions that produce data you cannot use.
Spotting that it asks two things at once and splitting it, with a balanced scale for each part.

It is double-barreled: it asks about two things at once. Someone who finds the app fast but ugly has no honest answer, and we cannot tell which part the score reflects. I would split it into two questions, each with the same balanced five-point scale from very dissatisfied to very satisfied, plus a “not sure” option.
During a test, a participant stops and asks you, “Am I doing this right?” What do you say?
How you moderate a session without steering the participant.
You stay neutral, hand the question back, and remind them that the design is being tested, not them.

I say something like, “There is no right way here. What would you do if I were not in the room?” If they seem anxious, I remind them we are testing the design, not them, and that getting stuck shows us what to fix. I only step in if they would otherwise give up, and I note exactly where that happened.
Walk me through how you turn twelve interview transcripts into findings.
How you do synthesis, the step between raw notes and a clear conclusion.
A visible method from notes to clusters to insights, with support counted and tied back to the research question.

I put each observation on its own note with the participant ID, then group notes by what they share, not by my interview questions. I name each cluster as a statement, count how many participants support it, and keep the quotes that show it best. Then I tie each theme to the decision the team has to make, so it becomes a finding with a recommendation.
Your usability test found fifteen problems. How do you present them so the team fixes the right ones first?
How you rate and present findings so they lead to action.
A severity rating based on impact and how many people hit it, the worst few first, each with evidence and a suggested fix.

I rate each problem by how badly it blocks the task and how many participants ran into it. Anything that stopped people from finishing goes to the top. I open with the three most severe, each with a short clip, the count, such as four of five participants, and a suggested fix. The rest go in a table the team can work through later.
A product manager asks you to run a study to “validate” a feature they have already decided to build. What do you do?
How you handle pressure to confirm a decision instead of testing it.
No refusal, but a reframe: agree in advance what result would change the plan, and design a study that could show it.

I ask what we would do if the study showed people do not need it. If the answer is “build it anyway,” I suggest we test how to build it well instead, with usability tests of the flow. If the decision can still change, I agree on success criteria up front, in writing, so the result counts whichever way it goes.
In interviews people said they love a feature, but analytics show almost no one uses it. How do you explain the gap?
How you handle conflict between what people say and what they do.
Trusting behavior data on usage, then finding the cause: hard to find, an unrepresentative sample, or polite answers.

What people say they like and what they do often differ, so on the question of use I trust the analytics. Then I look for why. Maybe people cannot find the feature, maybe my participants were heavy users unlike most customers, or maybe they were being polite. I would check who I recruited, then watch a few people try to find it in a quick test.
A senior leader asks for the raw session videos, with participant names, to show at a company-wide meeting. How do you respond?
Your handling of consent and participant privacy.
Using recordings only as participants agreed, and offering a safe alternative such as anonymized clips or asking for new consent.

I check the consent form first. If it said only the research and product team would see the videos, a company-wide meeting goes beyond that, and names should not travel with clips in any case. I offer a short highlight reel with names removed, or I ask participants for consent to the wider use. People speak openly to us because we keep that promise.
What is the difference between generative and evaluative research, and how do you decide which one a team needs?
Whether you can match the type of research to the stage of the product.
Generative research finds needs before a solution exists; evaluative research tests a solution. The choice follows the decision the team faces.

Generative research asks what problems people have and how they work today, before we have a design. Evaluative research checks whether a design we already have works. I ask the team what decision they face. If they are still choosing what to build, testing a prototype is too early. If the direction is set, I test it.
When would you use a card sort, and when a tree test?
Your knowledge of the methods for organizing navigation and content.
A card sort shows how people group content, to shape a structure. A tree test checks whether people can find items in a proposed structure, without visual design.

I run an open card sort early, when we need to learn how people group our content and what they call the groups. Once we have a draft menu, I run a tree test: people see only the text hierarchy and pick where they would go for a task. The card sort helps build the structure; the tree test tells me if it works.
When is a diary study worth the time and cost?
Whether you know a method for behavior that unfolds over days or weeks.
For behavior over time or in moments you cannot observe, with short regular prompts and a plan to keep participants engaged to the end.

When the behavior spreads over time, like how people plan meals across a week or use an app on a commute I cannot watch. I keep entries short, prompt at set times or after a trigger event, check in early to fix confusion, and pay in stages so people finish. A kickoff call and an exit interview help me read the entries.
How do you run a contextual inquiry, and how is it different from a regular interview?
Whether you can observe work where it happens, not just hear about it.
You watch people do real work in their own setting and ask about it as it happens, like an apprentice with a master, instead of relying on memory.

I go to where the person works and ask them to do their real tasks while I watch, like an apprentice learning from a master. I ask about what I see in the moment: why they printed that, what the sticky note is for. In a normal interview people describe an ideal version of their work. On site I see the workarounds they forgot to mention.
How do you write a screener that gets the right participants and keeps out people who game it?
Your skill at recruiting, which decides whether a study's findings are worth anything.
Questions about recent behavior, a hidden study topic, answer options that do not reveal the right choice, and a quick recheck at the start of the session.

I ask about recent behavior, not opinions: 'In the last month, which of these have you done?' with real options mixed with decoys, so the right answer is not obvious. I do not name the product or topic up front. I add one open question to see if they can explain themselves clearly, and I recheck key answers in the first minutes of the session.
How is the System Usability Scale scored, and how do you read a score of 72?
Whether you know a standard usability questionnaire and avoid misreading its score.
Ten items on a five-point scale, converted to a 0 to 100 score that is not a percentage, read against benchmarks or your own earlier rounds.

It has ten statements rated 1 to 5, alternating positive and negative. For odd items you subtract 1 from the answer, for even items you subtract the answer from 5, then multiply the total by 2.5. So 72 is not 72 percent. It is a bit above the often cited average of about 68, and it means most next to our own earlier score.
In a test, 4 of 5 participants finished the task. The PM writes “80% success rate” in the launch deck. What do you do?
How you keep small-sample numbers from being presented as precise metrics.
You explain that five people reveal problems, not rates. The true rate could be far lower, so you offer honest wording or a larger study if a rate matters.

I would talk to the PM before the deck goes out. With five people, a confidence interval around that result runs from roughly a third to nearly everyone, so 80% sounds far more exact than it is. I would suggest '4 of 5 participants completed the task' plus what blocked the fifth. If leaders need a real success rate, that takes a larger test.
Halfway through a study, you realize your screener let in the wrong kind of user. What do you do?
How you handle a mistake in your own study openly.
Pause, fix the screener, tell the team at once, and keep data from the wrong users apart instead of mixing it into the findings.

I would pause the remaining sessions, find the screener question that failed, and fix it. Then I tell the team right away what happened and what it changes. Sessions with the wrong users I keep separate: they may still show general usability problems, but they do not count toward findings about our target users. Then I recruit replacements and share the new date.
Product managers want to run their own customer interviews. How do you handle that?
Your judgement on sharing research work while protecting its quality.
Support it with guardrails: training, templates, review of their guides, clear limits on what non-researchers run, and one shared place for notes.

I welcome it, because more customer contact is good. I give a short training, an interview guide template, and offer to review their questions before sessions. I draw a line: PMs can run feedback and simple usability sessions, while sensitive topics, research with children, or studies behind big bets stay with research. Notes go into our shared repository.
Leadership needs an answer in two weeks on a question that would normally take two months of research. How do you scope it?
How you trade rigor for speed and say plainly what a faster study can and cannot tell.
Narrow the question to the decision, use what is already known, pick a fast method, and state the confidence and limits of the result up front.

First I ask what decision they will make, which usually shrinks the question. I check what we already know from past studies, support tickets and analytics. Then I pick something fast, like six remote interviews or an unmoderated test, and say up front what it will and will not show. I deliver a clear answer with its confidence level and what to study next.

value-engineer.heading: Value engineer and business value consultant questions
qs: Walk me through how you build a business case, from discovery to the number the CFO sees.
How you structure the work and whose numbers go into the model.
Starts from the customer's problems and data, ties each value driver to a metric, includes all costs, and is reviewed with the customer before finance sees it.

I start with discovery: what hurts, what it costs today and who owns that budget. I pick three or four value drivers and tie each to a metric the customer already tracks. I build the baseline from their data, add our full cost including implementation and their staff time, then walk the champion through it line by line before it goes to finance.
The customer will not share their baseline numbers. How do you build the model?
How you work with incomplete data without making numbers up.
Uses benchmarks or ranges as clearly labeled placeholders and asks the customer to confirm or correct each one.

I start with ranges from published benchmarks or similar customers, clearly marked as estimates. Then I ask narrow questions they can answer, like whether it is closer to 10 or 30 hours a week. People who will not share a spreadsheet will often react to a number. Every assumption gets a source column, so finance can see which ones are theirs and which are mine.
Why should a business case not show full benefits from month one?
Whether you model the realistic timing of costs and benefits.
Costs come early while benefits ramp up with rollout and adoption. Ignoring this inflates ROI and shortens payback on paper only.

Costs land early: licenses, implementation, training and the customer's own staff time. Benefits arrive as people adopt the product, often over several months. I model a ramp, for example a quarter of the benefit in the first quarter rising to full by month nine. It lowers year-one ROI, but the payback date is one the customer can actually hit.
How do you show a CFO how solid your numbers are?
Your use of sensitivity analysis and conservative cases.
Shows which assumptions drive the result, gives a conservative and an expected case, and shows the deal still works on the cautious one.

I run a sensitivity check: move each key assumption up and down and see which ones swing the result most. Usually two or three drivers do most of the work. I show a conservative case and an expected case, and I aim for a deal that still pays back on the conservative one. Then the CFO debates two numbers, not twenty.
A CFO says, “These are your numbers, not ours.” How do you respond?
How you earn trust from a skeptical finance buyer.
Does not defend the model. Invites the CFO to change inputs, uses their own figures and cost of capital, and makes the case theirs.

I agree that it should be their numbers. I open the model, show every input with its source, and ask which ones they would change. I swap in their cost of capital and their labor rates on the spot. Once a CFO has edited the assumptions, it becomes their case, and they tend to defend it in their own approval meeting.
The champion asks you to raise the numbers so the case clears their approval bar. What do you do?
Your judgement when pressure to close meets an honest model.
Refuses to inflate, looks for missed value or a scope that truly clears the bar, and protects the champion's credibility.

I explain that an inflated case hurts them most: they own it in front of finance and again at renewal. Then I look for real value we missed, check whether a phased rollout pays back sooner, or adjust scope and price with my sales lead. If it still does not clear, I would rather know now than sell a case that fails in a year.
At renewal, the value review shows the customer got half the savings you projected. What do you do?
How you handle a shortfall honestly when the account is at stake.
Finds the cause first, shows the gap openly before the customer raises it, and brings a plan with owners and dates.

First I find out why: low adoption, a missed integration, or an assumption that was wrong. I show the customer the gap myself. Then I bring a plan, for example retraining two teams and turning on a feature they skipped, with a target and a date. If my original assumption was too high, I say so and fix it for future cases.
After a deal closes, you find your model counted the same saving twice. What do you do?
Your honesty and how you repair a mistake in your own work.
Sizes the error, tells the account team and the customer promptly with corrected figures, and adds a check so it does not recur.

I recalculate first so I know the real size of the gap. Then I tell my manager and the account lead, and we tell the champion with corrected figures before their finance team finds it. The deal may still pay back; if not, we discuss it openly. Afterward I add a check to my template: each saving must map to one budget line and be claimed once.
What goes into a TCO model besides the subscription price?
Whether you know total cost of ownership beyond the price on the quote.
All costs over the full term on both sides: implementation, internal time, training, run costs and exit, compared with the full cost of the status quo.

I count everything the customer spends over the term, usually three to five years. Beyond the license: implementation and integration, their staff time on the project, training, ongoing admin, extra infrastructure, and the cost to switch away later. I do the same for their current setup, which has its own run costs. Two full totals make a fair comparison; our price against zero does not.
ROI, NPV, payback: which do you lead with for a CFO, and why?
Your grasp of the finance measures and what each one hides.
Lead with the measure their finance team uses. Know that payback ignores time value and later years, NPV discounts all cash flows, and ROI alone hides timing.

I ask what their finance team uses and lead with that. Payback says how fast the money comes back, which matters when cash is tight, but it ignores time value and everything after that date. NPV discounts all cash flows at their rate, so it is the best test of whether the deal creates value. ROI is easy to read but hides timing and scale, so I never show it alone.
Your model shows $2 million in new revenue as a benefit. What is wrong with that line?
Whether you separate revenue from profit in a benefit line.
Revenue is not the benefit; the margin on the extra sales is. Revenue lift can be shown as a driver, but the ROI uses profit.

Revenue is not the benefit; the profit on it is. If extra sales carry a 30% gross margin, $2 million of revenue is about $600,000 of benefit, before any extra selling costs. I show the revenue lift as an input so sales leaders see it, but the ROI uses margin. A finance team spots that gap at once, and then trusts nothing else in the model.
The biggest benefit in your case is hours saved. How do you treat it?
How you handle productivity gains that may never reach the budget.
Hours count as money only when something changes: hiring avoided, overtime cut, or time moved to revenue work. The rest is shown as capacity, not dollars.

Hours saved only become money if something changes: hires they no longer need, overtime cut, or people moved to work that earns revenue. I ask which one applies and count only that, often a share of the hours. The rest I show as capacity freed, not dollars. A CFO who sees 40,000 hours turned into full payroll savings knows no one will be let go and discounts the whole case.
What discount rate do you use in an NPV, and where do you get it?
Whether you use the customer's cost of money rather than a number that flatters the case.
The customer's hurdle rate or cost of capital, asked for in discovery; if not shared, a stated, reasonable rate with a higher-rate check.

I use the customer's own rate, usually their hurdle rate or weighted average cost of capital, and I ask finance for it in discovery. If they will not share it, I use a rate in line with their industry, state it clearly, and show the result at a higher rate too. Picking my own low rate would make the case look better, and it would be the first thing a CFO changes.
How do you put a value on a risk the product reduces, like a major outage?
Your method for valuing risk reduction without overstating it.
Expected value: yearly chance times cost of the event, and only the reduction the product brings counts, based on the customer's own history.

I use expected value. Say a major outage costs them $500,000 and their history suggests a 20% chance a year: that is $100,000 of yearly exposure. If we cut the chance in half, the benefit is $50,000 a year, not $500,000. I base the chance on their own incident records where I can, and I keep risk on its own line so it never props up the hard savings.
How do you find which assumptions matter most in a model, and how do you show it?
Whether you use sensitivity analysis to focus discovery and the CFO talk.
Vary key inputs over realistic ranges, rank their effect, show break-even points, and spend validation effort on the few drivers that carry the value.

I change each key input over a realistic range, one at a time, and see how much NPV moves. A tornado chart ranks them, and usually two or three drivers carry most of the value, like adoption rate and time saved per task. Then I show a break-even: adoption can fall to 40% and the deal still pays back. That points the talk, and my discovery time, at the inputs that matter.
A year after go-live the metric improved, but the customer also hired staff and changed a process. How do you show what the product did?
How you attribute results honestly when other changes happened at the same time.
Start from the agreed baseline, find a comparison group or prior trend, agree the method with the sponsor, and credit other causes openly.

First I go back to the baseline we agreed before go-live. Then I look for a comparison: a team or region that went live later, or the trend before launch. If handling time fell 25% where we launched and 5% where we had not, about 20 points is a fair claim. I agree the method with the sponsor and say plainly which part came from their hiring and process change.
Sales leadership wants a business case on every deal, and your team is three people. How do you decide where to work?
Your judgement in spending scarce value engineering time where it changes outcomes.
Clear rules agreed with sales: deep work where a case changes the result, self-serve tools for the rest, and regular review of the rules.

I rank deals by where a business case changes the outcome: large deals, a CFO or board that must approve, or a competitive evaluation. Smaller or clearly won deals get a standard calculator reps run themselves, with locked defaults so numbers stay sane. I agree these rules with the sales leader up front, so we do not argue deal by deal, and I review them each quarter.
How would you prove that the value engineering team itself is worth its cost?
Whether you can measure your own impact without fooling yourself.
Compare like-for-like deals with and without the team on win rate, discount, size and cycle time, and allow for the fact that the team picks the big deals.

I compare deals with and without us on win rate, discount, deal size and cycle time. The trap is selection: we choose the big, strategic deals, so a raw comparison is misleading. I match deals by size, segment and stage, and track renewal and expansion where we ran value reviews. Sales leaders' views on which deals we changed help, but I treat them as color, not proof.

video-editor.heading: Video editor and producer questions
qs: What is the difference between a J-cut and an L-cut, and when would you use each?
Whether you know the basic editing grammar that makes dialogue feel smooth.
Correct definitions (audio leads in a J-cut and trails in an L-cut) plus a real reason to use each.

In a J-cut the audio of the next shot starts before its picture, so you hear someone before you see them. In an L-cut the audio of a shot carries on over the next picture. I use J-cuts to pull the viewer into a new scene and L-cuts to show a listener's reaction while the speaker keeps talking.
You're shooting at 24 frames per second. What shutter speed do you set, and why?
Your camera basics and how they shape the look of motion.
The 180-degree shutter rule: about double the frame rate, so 1/48 or 1/50. Also when and why you would break it.

I'd set 1/50, or 1/48 if the camera offers it. That's the 180-degree rule: the shutter is open for half of each frame, which gives the motion blur people read as natural. Under some lights in the US, 1/50 can flicker, so I use 1/60 there. If it's too bright I add ND filters instead of raising the shutter speed, unless I want a crisp, choppy look on purpose.
Walk me through how you offload camera cards on a shoot.
Whether you protect footage that can't be shot again.
Verified copies on at least two drives before any card is formatted, with a clear naming and logging system.

I copy each card to two separate drives with software that does checksum verification, so I know every file matches the original. I name folders by date, camera and card number, and log it. A card only gets formatted in the camera once both copies are verified. Back at the office a third copy goes offsite or to the cloud.
When do you edit with proxies, and what can go wrong with them?
How you manage heavy footage without slowing the edit or hurting the final file.
Lightweight copies for smooth editing, then a relink to the full-quality originals before color and export.

With 4K or raw footage I make lower-resolution proxy files so playback stays smooth on any machine. The risk is exporting from the proxies by mistake, which gives a soft master. Before color and the final export I switch back to the original media and check a few shots at full size. I also keep the same file names so relinking doesn't break.
What's the difference between color correction and color grading?
Your grasp of the finishing order and the tools you use to judge color.
Correction comes first and makes shots accurate and consistent. Grading adds the look on top. You judge with scopes, not just your eyes.

Correction comes first: I set exposure and white balance and match shots so a scene doesn't jump between cameras. If the footage is log, I convert it to standard color first. Grading is the creative look on top, like warmer skin or cooler shadows. I check with the waveform and vectorscope, because my eyes adjust to a bad monitor and the scopes don't.
A client wants a 9:16 vertical version of a 16:9 interview piece. How do you approach it?
Whether you can adapt one edit for social platforms without losing the story.
Reframing shot by shot, keeping text and faces clear of on-screen buttons, and burning in captions for silent viewing.

I don't just crop the center. I reframe each shot so the face or action stays in frame, and I shorten the cut because vertical viewers scroll fast. I keep titles and captions out of the areas where the app puts its buttons and text. I burn in captions, since many people watch with the sound off. Next time I'd shoot wider so there's room to reframe.
The client wants a hit pop song under their brand video. What do you tell them?
Your knowledge of music rights and how you protect the client.
That it needs a sync license for the song and a master use license for the recording, and realistic options if that doesn't fit.

I explain that buying the song or crediting the artist isn't permission. For a video we'd need a sync license from the publisher for the song and a master use license from the label for the recording. For a hit that can take weeks and cost a lot, if they agree at all. I'd ask the budget, and if it doesn't fit, pitch two or three tracks from a licensed music library with a similar feel.
In a documentary interview, you could cut two answers together so the subject seems to say something stronger. Would you?
Your ethics when editing real people's words.
Cuts can tighten an answer but must not change its meaning. Check each edit against the full transcript and raise doubts with the director.

Not if it changes what they meant. I tighten answers all the time, removing ums and repeats, and I cover the cut with B-roll so it isn't jarring. But joining two answers to make a claim they never made is putting words in their mouth. I check each edit against the full transcript, and if I'm unsure, I show the director the original take.
You get to the edit and the lav mic on the main interview has loud rustle and dropouts. What do you do?
How you solve a technical problem in the material you're given.
Check backup audio first, then repair tools, then cut choices. Tell the producer early if a re-record is needed.

First I check what else was recorded: the camera's mic or a boom track. Often the backup is clean enough for the bad sections, and I sync it and match its tone with EQ. For rustle I try repair tools on short spots. Where nothing works, I pick other answers or cover with B-roll. If a key line is lost, I tell the producer the same day so they can plan a re-record.
A video went live and the client spots a misspelled name in a lower third. How do you handle it?
How you own a mistake and fix it without making it worse.
A fast fix and replacement, honest ownership, and a new checking step so it doesn't happen again.

I'd tell the client it's my error and I'm fixing it now. I correct the title, re-export, and watch the new file through before sending. Then I'd check how to swap it: some platforms let you replace the video, others need a new upload that starts at zero views, so the client decides. After that, every name and title gets checked against a written list from the client.
You're shooting in a log profile. How do you set exposure, and how do you monitor the image?
Whether you understand what log footage needs on set.
Exposure is set with a tool such as false color or the waveform, not by eye on the flat image. Monitoring uses a viewing LUT that is not baked into the recording.

Log looks flat, so I never judge exposure by eye on it. I use false color or the waveform and place skin where the camera maker recommends. On many cameras I lean a little bright to keep noise down, without clipping highlights. I monitor through a Rec.709 viewing LUT but record clean log, so the grade stays open.
You're filming an interview next to a window, and the room has warm tungsten lamps on. How do you deal with the mixed light?
How you control color temperature on location instead of leaving it to the grade.
You pick one color temperature and bring the other sources to it with gels or different bulbs. Then you white balance for the key light.

Daylight is around 5600K and tungsten around 3200K, so one white balance can't make both look neutral. I swap the lamps for daylight-balanced bulbs or put CTB gel on them. If I want a warm look, I gel the window with CTO instead. Then I white balance for the key. Fixing two color temperatures in one shot later is slow and rarely clean.
Your A and B cameras are different brands, and the skin tones don't match. How do you match them in the grade?
Your method for matching cameras with scopes, not guesswork.
You use the waveform and RGB parade for levels and balance and the vectorscope for skin. A final check by eye on a calibrated monitor finishes the match.

I grade the A camera first as the hero. On B, I match black and white levels on the waveform, then neutralize on something gray using the RGB parade. I check that skin on both sits near the skin tone line on the vectorscope. Then I play them side by side on a calibrated monitor. Scopes get you close, and your eye finishes it.
You shot at 59.94 fps for slow motion, and the timeline is 23.976. How do you get clean slow motion, and how slow will it play?
Whether you understand frame rate conforming.
You conform the clip to the timeline rate so every frame plays once. That gives 40% speed with no blended or repeated frames.

I conform the clip to 23.976, so each recorded frame plays exactly once. 23.976 divided by 59.94 is 40%, so the action runs at 40% speed and stays smooth. If I just slow it with a speed effect, the software may blend or repeat frames, and it looks soft. I also mute or detach the audio, since it no longer matches the picture.
A spot is going to US broadcast and to the web. How do you handle loudness for each version?
Whether you mix to a measured delivery spec.
You mix by meter to the integrated loudness and true peak in the spec. US broadcast follows ATSC A/85, while web targets vary by platform.

I mix by meter, not by ear alone. US broadcast follows ATSC A/85, which targets -24 LKFS integrated, and the CALM Act makes that binding for commercials. Web platforms normalize to their own levels, so I read each delivery spec and often make a separate web mix. I also check true peak, so nothing clips after encoding.
Walk me through turning a locked cut over to a colorist and a sound mixer.
How you prepare a clean handoff for finishing.
A simplified timeline, an XML or AAF, media with handles, and a reference export with burned-in timecode. Notes cover anything that won't translate.

First I clean the timeline. I delete disabled clips, put video on as few tracks as possible and note effects the colorist must rebuild. Color gets an XML or AAF and a reference movie with burned-in timecode. Sound gets an AAF with handles, with dialogue, music and effects on separate tracks, plus the same reference. Then I check one conform before signing off.
You have 20 hours of documentary footage and need a 10-minute film. How do you find the story?
Your process for shaping a story from a lot of raw material.
Transcripts, selects, a paper edit and a long string-out cut down in passes. You don't start at clip one and hope.

I get transcripts and read all of them, marking moments that surprise or move me. I pull selects into bins by theme. Then I write a paper edit with a beginning, a turning point and an end, in the subject's own words. I build a 40-minute string-out from it and cut down in passes, each time asking what the viewer truly needs to know.
You're shooting a brand video in a public park, and a child walks into a great shot. What do you need before you use it?
Whether you know the release rules for commercial work.
Anyone recognizable needs a signed release for commercial use, and for a minor, a parent or guardian signs. Without it, you cut, blur or reframe.

For a brand video, anyone recognizable needs a signed release, and a child's own signature isn't enough. A parent or guardian has to sign. If the parent is there and agrees, I get it signed on the spot. If not, I don't use the shot, or I blur or reframe so the child can't be identified. I also confirm the park permit covers our shoot.
The client says your export looks washed out on their Mac, but it looked right on your reference monitor. What's going on, and what do you do?
How you diagnose a display problem before changing the grade.
You know Mac players often show Rec.709 files with a lighter gamma than a 2.4 reference monitor. You fix it with tags or a web version, not a guessed regrade.

Often it's gamma, not my grade. A reference monitor shows Rec.709 at gamma 2.4, while many Mac players use a lighter curve, so dark areas look lifted. I check the file's color tags and compare in the same player the client uses. For web-only delivery, I may make a version prepared for that viewing. I show the client a side-by-side so they see the cause.
Mid-project, the client asks for a second shoot day and two extra cutdowns, but the budget and deadline stay the same. How do you handle it?
How you manage scope, money and time as a producer.
You name the change, put cost and time in writing, offer options and get approval before the extra work starts.

I say it plainly and politely: this is outside the scope we agreed. Within a day, I send a short change order. The extra day costs this much, and the cutdowns add two edit days. I offer options, like one cutdown now and the rest later, or a smaller crew. Nothing extra starts until they approve in writing, so the invoice holds no surprises.

video-motion.heading: Video and motion questions
qs: What shutter speed would you set when shooting at 24 frames per second, and why?
Whether you know how shutter speed shapes the way motion looks on camera.
The 180-degree rule: about 1/50 second at 24 fps for natural motion blur, plus when and why you would break it on purpose.

Around 1/50 of a second, about double the frame rate. That is the 180-degree shutter rule, and it gives the motion blur viewers read as natural. A much faster shutter makes movement look choppy, which can suit an action scene. In bright sun I add ND filters, which cut light like sunglasses, rather than raise the shutter speed.
What is the difference between a J-cut and an L-cut, and when do you use them?
Your command of basic editing technique.
Correct definitions, with the audio leading or trailing the picture, and why it makes edits feel smoother.

In a J-cut the audio of the next shot starts before its picture, so you hear someone before you see them. In an L-cut the audio of the current shot keeps going after the picture changes, like an interview answer running over cutaway footage. Both hide the cut and make the edit flow like a conversation instead of a slideshow.
A client says your logo animation looks stiff. What is the first thing you check?
Whether you understand easing and timing in motion design.
Easing first: linear keyframes look mechanical, so you shape the speed curves. Timing next, since a move that runs a few frames long also reads as stiff.

The easing. Real objects speed up and slow down, so linear keyframes look robotic. I open the graph editor, which shows speed over time, and shape the curves so the logo eases out of its start and settles into its end, maybe with a small overshoot. Then I check timing; a move a few frames too long often feels stiff too.
Why would you build an animatic before animating a two-minute explainer video?
How you use storyboarding to control time, cost and client approval.
The animatic tests timing and structure cheaply, and client sign-off on it keeps later notes about polish, not about rebuilding scenes.

An animatic is the storyboard frames cut to a scratch voiceover and music with rough timing. It shows whether the script fits two minutes and where a scene drags, before I spend days animating. Changing a sketch takes minutes; changing a finished scene takes a day. I get client sign-off on it, so later notes are about polish, not structure.
On an interview shoot, what do you do for sound besides clipping a mic on the speaker?
Whether you protect audio on set, where most fixes are cheaper than in the edit.
Constant headphone monitoring, a backup audio source, controlling background noise, and recording room tone for the editor.

I monitor on headphones the whole time, not just at the start. I run a second source, a boom mic or a backup recorder, in case the clip-on lav mic rustles on clothing. I turn off fridges and air conditioning where I can, and before we wrap I record 30 seconds of room tone so the editor can fill gaps without the background going dead.
The client wants one video for a 16:9 website player and for 9:16 vertical social feeds. How do you plan it?
How you plan for several aspect ratios from the start instead of fixing it in the edit.
Planning both formats at the storyboard stage: centered framing, room to reframe, text in safe zones, and graphics rebuilt per format.

I plan for both at the storyboard stage, not in the edit. I keep key action near the center so a vertical crop still works, and shoot at a higher resolution than delivery to leave room to reframe. Text stays inside the safe zone so app buttons and captions do not cover it. Titles and graphics I rebuild for each format instead of cropping them.
A training video needs captions. Do you burn them in or deliver a caption file?
Your grasp of open and closed captions and of accessibility.
It depends on the platform: a sidecar file for closed captions in players, burned-in open captions for muted social feeds, and always a proofread.

It depends where it plays. A sidecar file, a small SRT or VTT text file with timestamps, gives closed captions viewers can turn on or off in the player or learning platform. On social feeds, where many people watch muted, I often burn in open captions in the brand style. Either way I proofread against the audio, because auto-captions get names and terms wrong.
The client says the music drowns out the narrator. How do you fix the mix?
Your sound mixing method and whether you mix for how people will actually listen.
Dialogue set first, music ducked and EQ'd under it, checks on small speakers, and loudness measured against the delivery spec.

Dialogue comes first. I set the voice level, then bring the music under it and duck it, meaning lower it further while the narrator talks, with a small EQ cut where the voice sits. I check on laptop speakers and a phone, not just good headphones. Then I measure the mix in LUFS, the standard unit of perceived loudness, against the target in the delivery spec.
The marketing manager wants a hit pop song under the new product ad. What do you say?
Whether you understand music licensing and protect the client from legal and platform problems.
A commercial use needs a sync license for the song and a master use license for the recording; you explain the risk and offer licensed options.

I explain that an ad needs two licenses: a sync license from the publisher for the song itself and a master use license from the label for the recording. For a hit that is often slow and expensive, and an unlicensed track can get the ad muted or taken down. I offer stock music licensed for ads, or a composer, and keep the license paperwork with the project.
Two days before launch, after the cut was approved, a VP sends notes that contradict the approved version. How do you handle it?
How you manage late, conflicting feedback without losing the deadline or the client.
Sorting notes by impact, estimating time, sending the decision back to the client, starting quick fixes, and agreeing what gives on big changes.

I do not just pick a side. I list the new notes, mark which change the approved structure and which are small fixes, and estimate the time for each. I send that to my main contact and ask them to settle it with the VP. Small fixes I start right away. If the big changes go ahead, we agree on what gives: the deadline, the scope or the budget.
Why do many editors cut with proxies or transcoded files instead of editing camera H.264 or H.265 footage directly?
Whether you understand how codecs affect editing performance.
Long-GOP files store most frames as changes from other frames, so they are slow to decode when scrubbing. Intraframe codecs store every frame whole.

Camera H.264 and H.265 are long-GOP. Most frames only store what changed from nearby frames, so the computer has to rebuild them on the fly and playback stutters. I make lightweight proxies in an intraframe editing codec, where every frame is stored whole. I cut with those and relink to the originals for color and export.
You are filming in an office with LED panels, and the footage shows rolling dark bands. What is happening, and how do you fix it on set?
Whether you can diagnose light flicker before it ruins a shoot.
US power runs at 60 Hz, so many lights pulse 120 times a second. A shutter speed that matches that cycle, such as 1/60 or 1/120, removes the bands.

The lights pulse with the 60 Hz power, which means 120 flashes a second, and my shutter is catching them out of step. At 24 fps I move from 1/50 to 1/60, which covers whole light cycles, or I fine-tune the shutter until the bands vanish. If one fixture still flickers, I turn it off and light with my own panels.
You need 40% slow motion in a 23.976 fps edit. How do you shoot and conform it?
Your grasp of frame rates and true slow motion versus software retiming.
Shoot at 59.94 fps and conform the clip to 23.976, so every recorded frame plays once. 23.976 divided by 59.94 is exactly 40% speed.

I shoot at 59.94 frames per second, then set the clip to play at the timeline rate of 23.976. Each recorded frame is shown once, so motion stays smooth, and 23.976 over 59.94 is exactly 0.4. If I simply slowed down normal 23.976 footage, the software would have to repeat or invent frames, which looks choppy or warped.
Walk me through how you offload camera cards on a shoot day.
How you protect footage that cannot be shot again.
Copying with checksum verification to at least two drives, clear labeling, and never formatting a card until the copies are confirmed.

I copy each card with software that verifies by checksum, to two separate drives, into folders named by date, camera and card. I log what is on each card and mark it done only after both copies verify. Until then the card stays unformatted. After the shoot, a third copy goes offsite or to the cloud, so one lost bag cannot lose the project.
How do you set the loudness of a final mix for delivery?
Whether you mix to a measured target rather than by ear alone.
Measuring integrated loudness and true peak with a meter against the destination's spec, such as ATSC A/85 for US broadcast.

I ask for the delivery spec first. For US broadcast that is the ATSC A/85 practice of -24 LKFS integrated; for web or a streaming platform I use their published target. I mix by ear, then run a loudness meter over the whole program, check integrated loudness and true peak, and adjust the dialogue and music levels rather than crushing everything with a limiter.
The marketing team wants to update lower thirds themselves in their editing software. How do you hand off your animation?
Whether you can build graphics others can use without breaking them.
A locked template with only the needed controls exposed, tested with long text, delivered with fonts and short instructions.

I export the lower third as an editable template their editing software can open. I expose only the text fields and maybe a color choice, and lock timing and layout. I test it with the longest name and job title they might use, so the box resizes cleanly. I include the font files or license notes and a one-page guide with screenshots.
Your export looks washed out on the client's laptop but fine in your editor. How do you track down the problem?
How you troubleshoot color across apps and screens.
Checking the file's color tags, how each player reads them, and a calibrated display before changing the grade.

First, I do not regrade. I check the export's color tags, which should say Rec. 709 for a standard HD video, and play the file in two or three players, because some read the gamma tag differently. I compare it on my calibrated monitor and on a phone. If only one player shifts, it is a playback issue, and I explain that rather than bending the grade to one screen.
After final approval, the client asks for a few quick cutdowns for social. How do you respond?
How you protect scope and budget while keeping the client happy.
Saying yes to defined work: how many versions, lengths and formats, priced as a change order before starting.

I say yes and ask for specifics: how many cuts, what lengths, which formats and platforms. Three 15-second vertical cuts with new captions can take a full day, so they are not really quick. I send a short change order with cost and dates before I start. They get what they need, and nobody is surprised by the invoice or the schedule.
A week after a video goes live on several channels, you spot a misspelled name in a lower third. What do you do?
How you own a mistake and fix it everywhere the video lives.
Telling the client right away, fixing the project, re-exporting every version, and adding a check that prevents a repeat.

I tell the client the same day, with a fix plan, before they hear it from someone else. I correct the project, re-export every version with a new version number, and list each place the video runs so none is missed. Then I add a step to my checklist: names and titles are checked against a written source and signed off by the client before final export.

vip-relationship.heading: VIP and institutional relationship manager questions
qs: How do the needs of a fund differ from those of a very active individual trader?
Whether you know who you are actually serving on an institutional account.
A fund means many people and roles: traders, operations, compliance, auditors. A good answer names them and what each needs.

An active trader wants fast answers, good fee terms and someone who picks up when the market moves. A fund also needs the entity onboarded, several authorized users, API access, reports its auditors accept and clear answers on custody. So with a fund I work with traders, operations and compliance staff, not just one person.
Explain maker and taker fees and how volume tiers work.
Your grasp of the fee model your biggest clients care about most.
Maker adds liquidity, taker removes it. Tiers usually follow volume over a rolling period. Clients are never pushed to trade just to reach a tier.

A maker order rests on the book and adds liquidity. A taker order fills right away against a resting order and removes it. Most exchanges charge takers more. Tiers usually depend on volume over a rolling period, often 30 days. If a client is close to the next tier I show the numbers, but I never push extra trading just to reach it.
When would you send a client's order to the OTC desk instead of the order book?
Whether you understand market impact on large orders.
When the size is large next to the book's depth. The answer weighs the quoted spread against the slippage and information leak on the book.

When the order is large compared with the depth of the book. Selling a big block on the book would walk the price down and show the market what the client is doing. The OTC desk quotes one price for the whole size and settles it in one trade. I check the depth first and explain the trade-off: a quoted spread against the slippage.
A new fund says the API keeps rejecting their orders during busy periods. What do you do?
How you handle a technical problem for a client without dropping it on them.
Gets error codes and times, suspects rate limits, brings in API support, and follows through until it works.

First I get the exact error codes and timestamps. Rejections in busy periods are often rate limits: too many requests per second on one key. I check their limits, see whether their code retries too fast, and bring in our API support. If their volume justifies it, I ask whether a higher limit is possible. Then I follow up until fills are clean.
Walk me through onboarding a new hedge fund as a client.
Your knowledge of entity onboarding and how you keep it smooth for the client.
Covers entity documents, beneficial owners and controllers, authorized users, compliance review and account setup, with one clear checklist.

I collect the formation documents, the fund structure, the beneficial owners and the people who control it, and who may trade and withdraw. Compliance screens them and reviews the source of funds. Meanwhile I set up sub-accounts, API keys and withdrawal address whitelists. The client gets one checklist and one timeline, so nobody asks twice for the same paper.
You told a fund their withdrawal would settle the same day, and it did not. What now?
How you own a mistake you made with an important client.
Tells the client first, with confirmed facts, escalates any harm, and changes the habit that caused the error.

I call before they find out. I say what I told them, what actually happened and when the funds will arrive, based on what operations confirms, not a guess. If it caused a missed trade or a margin problem, I escalate it. Then I fix my side: I stop quoting times I have not checked against current processing.
A top client asks you whether a certain token is about to be listed. How do you answer?
Whether you protect confidential information even under pressure from a big client.
A clear no, no hints, a friendly tone, and a word to compliance if the client keeps pushing.

I say I cannot share that, and nobody on our side can, because listing decisions are confidential until they are announced. Tipping one client would be unfair to everyone else and could be treated as trading on inside information. I keep it friendly, point them to our public announcements, and tell compliance if they keep pushing.
A large client asks you to split a big withdrawal into smaller ones so it does not get flagged. What do you do?
Whether you recognize structuring and refuse to help with it.
Says no, gives no tips on thresholds, informs compliance per policy, and never tells the client whether a report was filed.

I say no, plainly. Splitting amounts to stay under reporting thresholds is called structuring, and it is a federal crime even if the money is clean. I do not coach anyone on thresholds. I tell compliance about the request as our policy requires, and I never tell the client whether a report was filed, because that is confidential.
Our platform went down during a sharp market move and a fund lost money. They want compensation. How do you handle it?
How you balance client loyalty with the firm's rules on losses.
Gathers facts, makes no promises on the call, routes the case to whoever decides, gives a timeline, and explains the outcome in writing.

I listen, then get the facts: their order IDs, times and what they expected to happen. I do not promise money on the call. I pass the case with our logs to the team that decides and tell the client when they will hear back. If our system failed, I push for a fair answer under our terms. Either way I explain the decision in writing.
A fund's due diligence team asks how they can be sure their assets are safe with us. What do you tell them?
Whether you can explain proof of reserves and custody honestly, limits included.
Explains what proof of reserves shows and does not show, and adds segregation, custody controls and independent reports instead of overselling.

Proof of reserves shows that wallets we control held certain assets at one moment, and a Merkle tree lets each client check their balance was counted. It is not a full audit and does not prove there are no hidden debts. So I also show how client assets are kept apart from company assets, our custody controls, and any independent reports we can share under NDA.
What is the difference between cross margin and isolated margin, and which would you suggest to a fund running several strategies?
Whether you understand how collateral and liquidation risk work on a derivatives account.
Cross margin shares collateral across positions. Isolated margin caps the loss at the margin set aside. The choice depends on how the fund wants risk separated.

With cross margin, all the collateral in the account backs every position. A winner can keep a loser alive, but one bad move can drain the whole account. Isolated margin puts a fixed amount behind one position, and liquidation only takes that amount. For separate strategies I would suggest separate sub-accounts, so one strategy cannot pull down another.
How do funding rates on perpetual futures work, and why does a basis trader watch them closely?
Whether you know the mechanics behind a common institutional trade.
Funding is a regular payment between longs and shorts that keeps the perpetual near the index price. For a basis trader it is the main income or cost.

A perpetual has no expiry, so the exchange keeps its price near spot with funding. When the perp trades above the index, longs pay shorts. When it trades below, shorts pay longs. A fund that buys spot and shorts the perp collects funding while it stays positive. If funding turns negative, the trade starts costing money, so they need accurate, timely funding data from us.
A fund wants to trade with us but keep its assets with a third-party custodian. How does off-exchange settlement work?
Your grasp of the custody setups institutions ask for after exchange failures.
Assets stay at the custodian, the exchange mirrors them as trading collateral, and gains and losses settle on a set schedule. You also name the risks that remain.

The fund's assets stay in a segregated account at the custodian. The custodian confirms the balance, and we show it as trading collateral on the exchange. Profits and losses are settled between the custodian and us on an agreed cycle, often daily. The fund cuts its exposure to us failing, but it still carries risk on the unsettled amount and on the custodian itself.
A top client says a rival exchange offered them fees 30% lower than ours. How do you respond?
How you negotiate on value instead of matching every price.
You compare total cost of trading, not just the fee line: spreads, depth, slippage, uptime. Then you make a measured offer within your approval limits.

First I ask what exactly they are comparing, then I run their real fills from last month against both venues. Fees are often small next to slippage on a thin order book. If our total cost is still higher, I take a case to pricing, maybe a better tier tied to a volume commitment. I would not cut fees on the spot beyond what I am allowed to approve.
A fund's volume with us fell 40% this month, and they have not said why. What do you do?
Whether you spot and investigate a client problem before it becomes a lost account.
You check the data first, separate a market-wide drop from a client-specific one, then ask the client directly and act on what you learn.

I first check whether volume fell across the market or only with them. If only with them, I look at their rejected orders, latency and fills in our data. Then I call the trader, not just the operations contact, and ask plainly what changed. Once a fund had moved flow because a new pair of ours lacked depth, and we fixed it by bringing in a market maker.
A market-making firm asks for a rebate on maker fees. How would you structure that deal?
How you tie a fee concession to obligations the exchange can measure.
The rebate is paid against clear duties: quote uptime, maximum spread, minimum size, measured over a fixed period, with a step down if they miss.

I would offer a rebate only in return for obligations: two-sided quotes on set pairs for a high share of trading hours, within a maximum spread and at a minimum size. We measure it monthly from our own data. If they miss the target, they drop to the standard schedule the next month. The rebate should cost us less than the extra trading a tighter book attracts.
What makes you open an early risk review on an existing institutional client?
Whether you know client review is ongoing, not a one-time onboarding step.
Changes in ownership, trading pattern, flows or news. You escalate to compliance and document what you saw rather than deciding alone.

A change in who owns or controls the firm, a move to a new jurisdiction, flows from addresses our screening tool flags as high risk, trading that no longer fits the strategy they described, or bad news about the fund or its directors. I write up what I saw and send it to compliance. I do not warn the client about a possible review; I keep serving them normally.
You notice a client trading heavily between their own sub-accounts near the end of the month. What do you do?
Whether you recognize possible wash trading and handle it without shielding the client.
You see that self-matched trades can fake volume to reach a fee tier, flag it to surveillance, and do not count that volume in fee talks.

Trades between accounts with the same owner do not change who holds the risk, and at month end it looks like a push for the next fee tier. That can be wash trading, which is market manipulation.
