I apply the fee the same way to every tenant, send a written notice and note it in the ledger. If a tenant warns me about a problem early, I ask the owner about a payment plan.
Three requests come in on a Monday morning: no heat in one unit, a dripping faucet and a broken mailbox lock. How do you prioritize them?
Whether you can sort maintenance by safety, habitability and risk of damage.
Emergencies first, meaning safety, habitability or active damage, then urgent items, then routine ones, with every tenant told when to expect someone.

No heat comes first, especially in winter, because it is a habitability issue and can lead to frozen pipes. I get a technician out that day and tell the tenant when to expect them. The mailbox lock is next, since mail security matters, and I schedule it within a day or two. The faucet goes into the routine queue for that week. Every tenant gets a reply with a time frame.
Walk me through a move-out inspection and how you decide what to deduct from the security deposit.
Whether you separate damage from normal wear and tear and document deductions.
Compare with the move-in report and photos, deduct only for damage beyond normal wear and tear, itemize costs, and follow the state's deadline and notice rules.

I walk the unit with the move-in checklist and photos and take new dated photos of every room. Faded paint and worn carpet from normal use are wear and tear, not deductions. A hole in the wall or a burned countertop is damage. I itemize each deduction with the invoice or estimate and return the balance. Deposit rules and deadlines vary by state, so I follow the ones for that property.
What does fair housing mean in your day-to-day work as a property manager?
Whether you apply fair housing rules consistently in screening, showings and requests.
The same criteria and process for every applicant, no steering, careful ads, and a proper process for accommodation requests. State and local laws may protect more groups.

It means every applicant gets the same written screening criteria, the same application and the same answers. I don't steer people toward or away from units, and our ads describe the property, not who should live there. Accommodation requests, like an assistance animal in a no-pets building, go through our process, not an automatic no. Many states and cities protect more groups than federal law does.
A tenant has paid only half the rent for two months and stopped answering calls. What do you do?
Whether you follow a fair, documented process before anything legal.
Written notice as the lease and law require, an attempt at a payment plan, everything documented, the owner updated, and eviction only through counsel and the courts.

I send a written notice the way the lease requires and try other channels, like email and a note at the door. If I reach them, I ask what happened and whether a payment plan could work, with the owner's approval. Everything goes in the tenant file. If nothing changes, the owner and our attorney decide the next steps. I never change locks or shut off utilities. The court process is the only route.
An owner wants a big rent increase on every renewal in the building. How do you handle it?
Whether you balance owner goals with market data, vacancy risk and local rules.
Comparable rents, the real cost of turnover and vacancy, any local rent rules and notice periods, and a recommendation backed by numbers.

I pull current rents for comparable units nearby and show the owner where we stand. Then I estimate what turnover costs: a vacant month, cleaning, paint and leasing fees. Often a $75 raise with most tenants staying beats a $250 raise with several moving out, and I show that math. I also check any local rent rules and the notice period required before renewal offers go out.
A leak from an upstairs unit is coming through the ceiling below at 11 p.m. on a Saturday. What do you do?
Whether you can run an after-hours emergency calmly.
Stop the water first, protect people and property, get the emergency vendor out, document everything, and notify the owner and insurer as needed.

First I make sure the water to that unit is shut off, either by the tenant or our on-call tech at the valve. I call our emergency plumber, and a water mitigation company if it is spreading. I tell both tenants what is happening and take photos and video. The next morning I update the owner, start an insurance claim if needed and plan repairs. The ceiling can wait a day; the leak cannot.
Two tenants in the same building complain about each other's noise every week. How do you deal with it?
Whether you handle disputes between tenants fairly and through the lease.
Listening to both, checking the lease and house rules, a written reminder to the right party, and a record of each complaint, without taking sides on hearsay.

I talk to each tenant separately and ask for dates and times. Then I check the lease and our quiet hours rule. If the facts point to one unit, I send a polite written reminder that cites the rule. If both have a point, I suggest simple fixes like rugs or felt pads. I log every complaint, so if it keeps happening, we have a record to act on under the lease.
A vendor you have used for years sends an invoice 30% higher than their quote. What do you do?
Whether you protect the owner's money and manage vendors firmly.
The invoice compared with the quote and work order, an explanation requested, payment of what was approved, and new bids if overruns keep happening.

I compare the invoice to the quote and the work order and ask the vendor what changed. Sometimes there is a real reason, like a hidden pipe problem, but they should have called me before doing extra work. If someone on site approved it, I find that out first. Otherwise I pay the approved amount and discuss the rest. If overruns keep happening, I get new bids for the next job.
An applicant has a low credit score but strong income and good references. How do you decide?
Whether you apply written screening criteria the same way to everyone.
The written criteria applied as to anyone else, only the alternatives the policy allows, a written notice if denied, and the reason kept in the file.

I go back to our written screening criteria, because every applicant has to be judged the same way. If our policy allows an alternative for a low score, like a qualified guarantor, I offer it exactly as I would to anyone else. If the application doesn't meet the criteria, I send the written notice the law requires when a credit report was used. I document the reason either way.
Tell me about a time you had to give a property owner bad news.
Whether you keep owners informed early and honestly.
Early contact, the facts and costs, options with their risks, and a recommendation instead of hiding the problem until the monthly report.

At a 40-unit building, an inspection found the roof needed replacing two years earlier than planned. I called the owner that day instead of waiting for the monthly report. I sent three bids, explained what a patch would buy us and what it would risk, and recommended replacing it before winter. They weren't happy about the cost, but they said they valued hearing it early with options.
How do you keep track of lease renewals, inspections and compliance dates across several properties?
Whether you have a reliable system for dates that carry legal or financial risk.
One system for all dates, reminders well ahead of deadlines, a weekly review, and notes others can follow if you are out.

Everything with a date goes into our property management software: lease ends, renewal notice dates, fire inspections, boiler certificates and insurance renewals. I set reminders 90 and 30 days ahead. Every Monday I review the next month for all six of my properties. I keep notes in the system, not in my head, so my backup can see what is due if I'm out sick.
Tell me about a time you calmed down an angry tenant and solved the problem.
Whether you stay calm with upset people and fix the real issue.
Listening first, admitting what went wrong, a clear next step with a time frame, and following through until it is done.

A tenant came into the office shouting because his air conditioning had been out for four days and two vendor visits had failed. I let him finish, agreed four days was too long, and called a different HVAC company while he was there. They came the next morning. I brought him a portable unit that night and, with the owner's approval, credited part of his rent. He renewed six months later.
Tell me about a property you took over from another manager. What did you do first?
Whether you learn a property methodically before changing things.
A review of leases against the rent roll, open work orders, vendors and budget, a walk of the property, then priorities agreed with the owner.

When I took over a 60-unit complex, I spent the first two weeks checking every lease against the rent roll and walking every vacant unit. I found eight tenants on expired leases at old rents and 30 open work orders, some months old. I cleared the urgent repairs first, then sent renewal offers. By the third month, open work orders were under ten and the owner had a clear list of capital needs.

hr-generalist.heading: HR generalist questions
qs: When does a new hire's Form I-9 have to be completed, and what do you watch for?
Whether you know the basic I-9 timing and avoid common document mistakes.
Section 1 by the first day of work, Section 2 within three business days, original documents the employee chooses from the lists, and secure storage.

The employee completes Section 1 no later than their first day of work. We complete Section 2 within three business days of the start date after examining their original documents. I let the employee choose which documents to show from the lists, because asking for a specific one can be discrimination. I keep I-9s apart from personnel files and check the current USCIS instructions.
An employee asks if they qualify for FMLA leave to care for a parent. How do you work it out?
Whether you know how FMLA eligibility is checked and that state leave laws may also apply.
A check of employer coverage, the employee's length of service and hours, the reason for leave, and any state leave law, then the required notices on time.

I confirm we are a covered employer and that their worksite meets the size rule, then check their length of service and the hours they worked in the past year. Caring for a parent with a serious health condition is a qualifying reason. I also check our state's leave law, since some states cover more people or reasons. Then I send the eligibility notice and certification form on time.
What makes good documentation of an employee's performance problem?
Whether you know how to document performance so it is fair and holds up later.
Specific facts, dates and examples, the expectation that was missed, the support offered, the consequences, and the employee's response, written at the time.

Good documentation is specific and written when it happens. Instead of 'bad attitude', it says that on March 3 and March 10 the client report was two days late and the client complained. It states the expectation, the help we offered, like a weekly check-in, and what happens if it doesn't improve. The employee reads it, can add comments and signs to show they received it.
An employee tells you a coworker keeps making sexual comments to her. What are your first steps?
Whether you know how to take a harassment complaint and start a fair investigation.
Taking it seriously, written notes, honesty about confidentiality limits, protection from retaliation, interim steps if needed, and a prompt, impartial investigation.

I thank her for telling me and take notes on what happened, when, where and who saw it. I explain that I'll keep it as private as I can, but I can't promise full secrecy because we have to investigate. I tell her retaliation is not allowed. Then I decide with my manager or counsel whether we need interim steps, like separate schedules, and start the investigation right away.
A manager wants to fire someone for poor performance tomorrow, but nothing is documented. What do you advise?
Whether you can push back on a risky termination and offer a better path.
Questions about the facts, a check for risk such as a recent complaint or leave, a documented improvement plan unless the conduct is serious, and legal advice if unsure.

I ask what happened and what the employee has been told. If nothing is in writing, they may not know there is a problem, and a sudden firing looks unfair. I also check whether the person recently complained, took leave or asked for an accommodation, because that raises the risk of a retaliation claim. Usually I suggest a written improvement plan with clear goals. Serious misconduct is handled differently.
An employee asks you to promise to keep something confidential before telling you what it is. What do you say?
Whether you are honest about the limits of confidentiality in HR.
No blanket promise. HR keeps things as private as possible but must act on issues like harassment, safety or legal violations.

I tell them I'll keep it as private as I can and share it only with people who need to know, but I can't promise total secrecy before I hear it. If it involves harassment, safety or something illegal, I have to act. Most people still go ahead. Being honest at the start is better than breaking a promise later.
You discover a new employee has been paid below their offer letter rate for three pay periods. What do you do?
Whether you fix pay errors quickly, honestly and in line with wage rules.
The correct rate confirmed, payroll fixed, the back pay paid promptly, the employee told directly, and the cause found. Timing rules vary by state.

I compare the offer letter to the payroll setup and confirm the error with payroll. Then I tell the employee before they find it themselves, apologize and say when the difference will be paid. We pay it in the next run, or sooner if state rules require. Last time the gap was $1.50 an hour, about $360 in total. Now a second person checks every new pay rate.
During the review cycle, two managers gave very different raises to people in the same role with similar ratings. What do you do?
Whether you spot pay consistency risks and raise them before raises are final.
A look at the data and the reasons, a check for any pattern linked to a protected group, a talk with the managers, and a flag to HR leadership before letters go out.

I put the numbers side by side with ratings, start dates and current pay. Sometimes there is a good reason, like one person already being high in the range. If not, I ask each manager how they decided. If I see a pattern, like women or older workers getting less, I raise it with my HR manager before any letters go out. Fixing it now is much easier than after a complaint.
A manager posts a job ad that says 'recent graduates only'. What do you do?
Whether you catch discriminatory language in hiring before it causes harm.
The age discrimination risk explained, the ad pulled or edited quickly, and a rewrite around the skills and experience level the job really needs.

I ask the manager to let me edit the ad right away. 'Recent graduates only' can screen out older applicants, which creates an age discrimination risk. I ask what they really need, usually someone at entry level who learns quickly, and we rewrite the ad around those skills. Then I check the manager's other open ads for similar wording.
An employee has called in sick three Mondays in a row, and their manager wants to start discipline. What do you advise?
Whether you consider leave laws and policy before discipline for absences.
The attendance policy and any state or local sick leave law checked, a thought for FMLA or an accommodation, and a private talk with the employee first.

I first check our attendance policy and whether a state or local sick leave law protects those days, since many places have one and the rules vary. A pattern like this can also point to a health condition, so FMLA or an accommodation might apply. I suggest the manager have a private, neutral talk and ask if anything is going on. If it is protected leave, we can't count it against them.
Tell me about a time you disagreed with a manager about how to handle an employee issue.
Whether you can influence managers while staying firm on policy and law.
A specific case, the facts and risk explained calmly, an alternative offered, and the outcome, without giving in just to avoid conflict.

A manager wanted to cut an employee's hours right after she complained about scheduling. I explained that even with other reasons, the timing would look like retaliation. I asked him to write down the business reason and wait until the complaint was resolved. He was annoyed but agreed. Two weeks later the complaint was settled, and her hours stayed the same.
How do you keep up with changes in employment law in the states where your employees work?
Whether you have a reliable way to stay current on rules that vary by state.
Named sources like state labor department sites and employment counsel updates, a tracker by state with effective dates, and a check with counsel before acting.

I get updates from our employment law firm and from the labor departments in the four states where we have people. I keep a simple tracker of changes, like new sick leave rules or minimum wage dates, with the effective date and what we need to update. Each quarter I review it with my manager. When something is unclear, I ask counsel before we change a policy.
Tell me about a time you made a mistake in an employee's benefits or leave paperwork.
Whether you own errors that affect people's pay or coverage and fix them fast.
Quick disclosure to the employee, a fix with the carrier or payroll, fair handling of any cost, and a change to the process.

I once missed adding a new employee's spouse to the medical plan, and they found out at a doctor's office. I called the carrier that afternoon, and since the signed election form was on file, they backdated the coverage. I called the employee to apologize and explain. Since then I check every enrollment against the carrier's confirmation within a week.
How do you handle a week when a dozen employees need answers from you about benefits, leave and payroll at once?
Whether you can manage a heavy flow of employee questions without dropping any.
Every request tracked, sorted by urgency and impact, a quick reply with a time frame, and an FAQ for questions that repeat.

I log every question in our ticket system so nothing lives only in my inbox. Pay problems and urgent leave go first, because they affect people's money and health. Everyone gets a reply the same day saying when I'll have an answer. If I get the same question five times, like during open enrollment, I write a short FAQ and send it to everyone.

real-estate-agent.heading: Real estate and leasing agent questions
qs: Walk me through how you price a home using comparable sales.
Whether you can build a price from market evidence, not from what the seller hopes.
Recent nearby sales of similar homes, adjusted for differences, plus active and pending listings as competition and expired ones as a warning.

For a three-bedroom ranch last spring I pulled sales within a mile from the past six months, same size range and age. Four were close matches. I adjusted for a finished basement and a newer roof, then checked the six active listings it would compete with. The range came to $340,000 to $355,000. We listed at $349,000 and had two offers in the first week.
A seller gets four offers in one weekend. How do you handle them fairly?
Whether you protect your seller and treat every buyer the same way.
Every offer goes to the seller, compared on net proceeds and terms, not price alone, and every buyer's agent gets the same deadline and information.

I put all four in a side-by-side sheet: price, financing, down payment, contingencies, closing date and what the seller nets after costs. The highest price had the weakest financing, so the second offer was stronger. When my seller asked for best and final offers, I sent every agent the same deadline in writing. I don't share one buyer's terms with another unless the seller approves.
A buyer asks whether a neighborhood is safe and what kind of people live there. How do you answer?
Whether you know how fair housing rules shape what an agent can say about an area.
No opinions about who lives there or whether it is a good area. Point the buyer to objective sources and talk about the property, not the people.

I tell them I can't steer anyone toward or away from an area, so I don't describe places by who lives there. I give them sources to check themselves: the police department's crime map, the school district's website, and a drive through at different times of day. Federal law sets the baseline and many states and cities protect more groups, so I stick to facts about the home.
What do you check before you approve a rental applicant?
Whether you screen tenants thoroughly and the same way for everyone.
Written criteria applied to every applicant: identity, income, rental history, credit and, where the law allows, background, with consent on file.

We have written criteria from the owner, and I apply them to everyone in the same order. I verify identity, confirm income with pay stubs or an employer call, and call the last two landlords about payment and the condition they left. Then credit and, where local law allows it, a background check, with signed consent. Rules on criminal history and application fees vary by state and city, so I check ours.
A seller wants to list 10% above what the comparables support. What do you do?
Whether you can tell a client an unwelcome truth and still keep the listing.
The comparables shown plainly, what overpricing usually costs, and a written plan with a date to review the price if the market says no.

I show them the same sales a buyer's agent and the appraiser will use. Then I explain that a home priced too high gets fewer showings early, when interest is highest, and often sells for less in the end. If they still want to test the higher price, we agree in writing to review it after two weeks or 15 showings without an offer. Last year that review led to a cut and a sale within a month.
The appraisal comes in $12,000 below the contract price. What happens next?
Whether you know the options when an appraisal gap threatens a deal.
Checks the contract deadline, then lays out the options: challenge with better comparables, renegotiate the price, the buyer covers the gap, or a split.

First I check the appraisal contingency date, because that sets how much time we have. Then I read the report for errors and look for sales the appraiser missed, in case the lender will accept a reconsideration. If the value stands, the lender lends on the lower figure, so someone has to close the gap. On my last one the seller came down $6,000 and the buyer brought $6,000 more in cash.
Two applicants both meet the criteria for the same apartment. How do you decide who gets it?
Whether you follow a consistent, documented rule instead of a gut feeling.
A written rule, usually the first complete application that meets the criteria, applied every time and documented, so the choice can be explained.

Our policy is first complete qualified application, with time stamps. Last month the second applicant was friendlier and offered to sign a longer lease, but the first one applied an hour earlier with everything in place, so she got the unit. I wrote down the times in the file and told the second applicant about a similar unit opening the next month. Gut feelings are how fair housing complaints start.
A buyer you are working with wants to make an offer on your own listing. How do you handle it?
Whether you understand dual agency and protect both clients.
Knows dual agency is banned in some states and allowed with written consent in others, follows brokerage policy, and offers to refer one side out.

First I check what our state and my brokerage allow, because some states ban dual agency and others allow it only with written consent from both sides. If it's allowed, I explain to both that I can't advise either of them against the other on price. In my last case the buyer preferred her own advocate, so I referred her to a colleague in my office and kept the seller.
The seller tells you the basement flooded two years ago and asks you to keep it quiet. What do you do?
Whether your honesty holds when the client asks you to hide something.
A clear refusal, an explanation that known material defects must be disclosed, and a way to present it well, such as repair records.

I tell the seller I can't hide a defect I know about, and that it belongs on the disclosure form. What exactly the form requires varies by state, but hiding water damage is the kind of thing buyers sue over after closing. I ask for the repair invoices and any waterproofing warranty, because a fixed problem with paperwork scares buyers far less than a surprise. If the seller still refuses, I take it to my broker.
Your listing has had 20 showings and no offers in a month. What do you do?
Whether you diagnose a stalled listing with evidence before you talk to the seller.
Reads showing feedback, compares new sales and competing listings, and comes to the seller with a specific change to price, condition or marketing.

Twenty showings means the marketing works and buyers are coming, so the price or the house is the problem. I collect feedback from every buyer's agent and check what sold nearby since we listed. On a listing like this last fall, eight agents mentioned the dated kitchen. I showed the seller the feedback and two newer sales, and we cut the price by $10,000. It went under contract nine days later.
A caller you have never met wants to see a vacant listing tonight. How do you handle it?
Whether you take your own safety seriously when meeting strangers at empty properties.
Verifies identity before the showing, tells someone where they are going, keeps daylight or a colleague where possible, and stays near the exit.

I ask for their full name and number, and for a photo of their ID or a lender preapproval before I book. I suggest meeting at the office first or showing it in the morning. If it has to be tonight, I bring a colleague, share my location with the office, and walk behind the client in the house. Real buyers rarely mind. The one caller who refused all of that never called back.
Tell me about a deal that fell apart close to closing. What did you do?
How you handle a setback and what you change afterward.
Fast, honest communication with the client, a quick plan to recover, and a specific lesson the candidate now applies on every deal.

A buyer's loan was denied eight days before closing because he changed jobs. I called my seller that hour, not by email, and we put the house back on the market the same day. A backup buyer from the first open house signed two weeks later. Since then I ask buyers up front not to change jobs or open new credit before closing, and I check in with the lender every week.
How do you keep track of deadlines when you have several deals under contract at once?
Whether you have a system that prevents missed contingency dates.
Every date from the contract goes into one calendar with reminders, plus a checklist per file and regular check-ins with lender, title and the other agent.

The day a contract is signed, I enter every date into my calendar: inspection, appraisal, loan approval, final walk-through and closing, each with a reminder three days ahead. Each file has a checklist, and every Monday I email the lender and title company on each open deal. Last spring I had seven under contract at once and didn't miss a date.
How would you find your first ten clients in a market where you know few people?
Whether you have a realistic plan to build a pipeline on commission.
Specific, steady activity: hosting open houses, following up every lead within a day, and a simple system to track contacts over months.

I would ask agents in the office if I can host open houses at their listings, two every weekend, and follow up with every visitor within a day. I would also join one local group, like the chamber of commerce, and show up regularly. When I moved two years ago, that brought 11 clients in my first nine months. Most came from open houses.

physician-assistant.heading: Physician assistant questions
qs: A 52-year-old comes in with chest pain. How do you build your differential?
Whether you think about dangerous causes first and narrow the list with history and exam.
Life threats first, such as heart attack, pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection and pneumothorax, with an early ECG, then common causes as evidence allows.

Vitals and an ECG come first, within minutes. Then I list what could kill him today: heart attack, pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection, collapsed lung. The history narrows it: when it started, what it feels like, what makes it worse, risk factors. Reflux or a strained muscle moves up only after the dangerous causes are reasonably ruled out. If one stays possible, I bring in the physician early.
When do you bring your supervising or collaborating physician into a case?
Whether you know the limits of your role and escalate at the right time.
Knows that scope and supervision rules vary by state and practice agreement, and escalates for instability, uncertainty, cases outside their experience or policy.

It depends on the state and our practice agreement, so I learn those rules first in any new job. Beyond that, I call the physician when a patient is unstable, when I'm not sure of the diagnosis, when a case is outside what I've managed before, or when the plan isn't working. Last month a patient's headache didn't fit any pattern I knew, and the physician saw her before she left.
What goes into a good note for a clinic visit?
Whether your documentation is clear, complete and useful to the next clinician.
A clear structure such as SOAP, the reasoning behind the assessment, the plan, what the patient was told, and when to follow up, written the same day.

I use SOAP. The subjective part has the complaint in the patient's words and the pertinent negatives. Objective has vitals, exam and results. The assessment shows my reasoning, not just a diagnosis code, so the next clinician sees why I thought what I thought. The plan lists tests, treatment, what I told the patient, warning signs to return for, and the follow-up date. I finish notes the same day.
How do you explain a new diagnosis and plan to a patient so they actually follow it?
Whether you can turn a medical plan into something a patient understands and acts on.
Plain words, a few key points, written instructions, and teach-back to confirm understanding, plus asking about barriers like cost or schedule.

Last week I diagnosed high blood pressure in a 48-year-old truck driver. I kept it to three points: what the numbers mean, the one pill to take each morning, and a recheck in four weeks. Then I asked him to tell me the plan in his own words. He mixed up the timing, so I explained it again. I also asked what might get in the way, and he mentioned cost, so we picked a generic.
A patient insists on antibiotics for what looks like a viral cold. What do you do?
Whether you hold to good prescribing while keeping the patient's trust.
Listens to the worry behind the request, explains why antibiotics will not help, offers a symptom plan, and gives clear reasons to come back.

I ask what worries them most. Often it's missing work or a past infection that turned bad. I explain that antibiotics don't work on viruses and can cause side effects like diarrhea. Then I give them a plan for the symptoms and tell them exactly what should bring them back, such as trouble breathing or getting worse after getting better. Most patients accept that once they feel heard.
A lab calls with a critical potassium result for a patient who went home two hours ago. What do you do?
Whether you act quickly and safely on a critical result after the visit.
Reaches the patient promptly, asks about symptoms, considers whether the result could be wrong, arranges a repeat or emergency care, informs the physician, documents.

I call the patient right away and ask about weakness, palpitations or other symptoms. I check the lab comment for hemolysis, but I don't assume it's an error. With symptoms or a very high value, I send them to the emergency department. Without, I arrange an urgent repeat. Either way I tell my supervising physician and document every call. Last time the repeat was normal.
At the end of a rushed visit, the patient mentions chest pain on the stairs. You are 40 minutes behind. What do you do?
Whether you put patient safety ahead of the schedule.
Stops and assesses the new symptom now, with vitals and an ECG as needed, involves the physician if concerning, and lets the front desk manage the delay.

The schedule waits. I sit back down and ask about the pain: when it happens, how long it lasts, what eases it. We get vitals and an ECG. Last time this happened, the ECG was abnormal and I brought in the physician, who sent the patient to the emergency department. I asked the front desk to tell my next patients I was running late and to offer to reschedule anyone who couldn't wait.
A patient says they would rather see the doctor than a PA. How do you respond?
Whether you can handle doubts about your role calmly and without ego.
Respects the request, briefly explains the PA role and the team, and offers the physician or a later appointment without taking it personally.

I tell them that's completely fine. I explain in one or two sentences that I'm a physician assistant, licensed to examine, diagnose and treat, and that I work with Dr. Patel on the same team. Then I offer two options: I start the visit and bring her in if needed, or the front desk books her next opening. Most choose to stay. The ones who don't usually see me next time.
After a patient leaves, you realize you forgot to order a test you meant to order. What do you do?
Whether you own mistakes openly and fix them quickly.
Contacts the patient, explains honestly, arranges the test, tells the supervising physician, documents, and follows the practice's reporting process.

I call the patient the same day and say plainly that I meant to order a test and missed it. Last year it was a thyroid panel for a woman with fatigue. I ordered it that afternoon, told my supervising physician, and wrote an addendum to the note. I also changed my habit: I now read the plan back to myself before the patient leaves the room. Patients forgive honesty far more than surprises.
A patient arrives speaking little English and brings her 12-year-old son to interpret. What do you do?
Whether you know to use a qualified interpreter and why family members are a poor substitute.
Uses a qualified medical interpreter by phone, video or in person, explains why children should not interpret, and documents the interpreter used.

I thank the son and tell the mother, through a phone interpreter, that we have professional interpreters at no cost to her. Children can miss medical terms, and a mother may not share everything in front of her son. The phone line took two minutes to connect. In the note I recorded the interpreter's ID number and the language. Her son waited outside for the exam.
Tell me about a case where your first diagnosis turned out to be wrong.
Whether you reflect honestly on your clinical reasoning and learn from it.
A specific case, what led them astray, how it was caught, and a concrete change in how they work, without blaming others.

A 30-year-old came in with back pain after moving furniture, and I called it a muscle strain. She returned three days later with a fever, and her urine showed a kidney infection. I had anchored on the furniture story and skipped a urine test. Now, for back pain, I ask about fever and urinary symptoms every time, even when the cause seems obvious.
Tell me about a time you disagreed with your supervising physician about a plan.
How you raise a clinical concern with someone senior and work it out.
Raises it privately and with evidence, listens to the physician's reasoning, and puts the patient's safety first, whatever the outcome.

The physician wanted to start a patient on a new medication, and I had noticed in the chart that her kidney function had dropped. I asked to talk for two minutes outside the room and showed him the lab trend. He had not seen it, and we chose a different drug. Another time I was the one missing context, and I said so. The point is the patient, not who was right.
How do you keep your clinical knowledge current?
Whether you have a steady habit of learning, not just meeting minimum requirements.
Regular, specific sources, continuing education beyond what certification needs, and learning tied to real cases seen in practice.

I complete the CME I need to keep my NCCPA certification, but most of my learning comes from my own cases. When a patient raises a question I can't answer well, I note it and read the current guideline that evening. I also join our monthly case review with the physicians. Last year that habit changed how early I screen adults for diabetes.
You have 24 patients booked and 60 results in your inbox. How do you get through the day safely?
Whether you can manage a heavy workload without letting anything unsafe slip.
Triages the inbox for abnormal and urgent items first, uses short gaps during the day, asks for help before falling behind, and does not skip documentation.

Before the first patient I scan the inbox for abnormal and critical results and handle those first. Normal results go out in batches between visits with a short template message. I chart during the visit where I can, so notes don't pile up. If I'm more than 30 minutes behind by noon, I tell the office manager so they can move a few routine visits. Nothing abnormal waits until tomorrow.

product-owner.heading: Product owner questions
qs: Write a user story for a password reset feature, with acceptance criteria.
Whether you can write a clear, testable story from the user's point of view.
A story that names the user, the need and the reason, and criteria that are specific and testable, covering the main path and key failure cases.

As a registered user who forgot my password, I want to reset it by email so that I can get back into my account without calling support. Criteria: the reset link arrives within five minutes; it works once and expires after one hour; an unknown email gets the same message as a known one; the new password meets our existing rules; other sessions are signed out after the reset.
How do you decide the order of the product backlog?
Whether you order work by value and risk rather than by who asks loudest.
A clear basis: value to users and the business, cost of delay, risk and learning, dependencies and size, with reasons visible to stakeholders.

I look at the value to users and the business, what it costs us to wait, risk, and effort from the developers' estimates. Items that teach us something important or remove a big risk often go near the top even if they're small. Last quarter a quick pricing test went ahead of a larger reporting feature because it answered a question blocking three other items. I share the reasons so stakeholders can challenge them.
What is the difference between acceptance criteria and the definition of done?
Whether you understand two quality checks that people often mix up.
Acceptance criteria are specific to one item. The definition of done is a shared quality standard that applies to every item, such as tested, reviewed and documented.

Acceptance criteria belong to one story and say what it must do, like the reset link expires after one hour. The definition of done applies to every item the team delivers: code reviewed, tests passing, documentation updated, deployed to staging. A story is done only when it meets both. On my last team we added an accessibility check to the definition of done after a release failed an audit.
What makes a sprint review useful?
Whether you know the sprint review is a working session, not a status presentation.
Working product shown to real stakeholders, honest discussion of what was and was not done, and feedback that changes the backlog.

We show working software, not slides, and the stakeholders try it themselves where possible. I say plainly what we didn't finish and why. Then we talk about what we learned and what should come next, and I update the backlog in the room. At one review a sales lead tried the new export and pointed out that customers needed CSV, not PDF. That changed the next sprint.
A vice president asks you to add a feature to the current sprint. What do you say?
Whether you can say no to a senior stakeholder and still protect the sprint goal and the relationship.
Understands the urgency first, protects the sprint goal, offers the next sprint or a trade, and involves the developers in any change to the sprint backlog.

I ask what is driving the request and what happens if it waits two weeks. Usually it can wait, and I offer to put it at the top of the backlog for the next sprint. If it truly can't, I talk to the developers, since the sprint backlog is theirs, about whether it fits without hurting the sprint goal. Something else comes out, and I tell the vice president plainly what that costs.
On the last day of the sprint, a story meets every acceptance criterion except one small one. Do you accept it?
Whether you hold the line on done, even when bending it feels harmless.
No partial credit: the story goes back to the backlog, the gap is fixed or rewritten as a new item, and the team discusses why it slipped.

No. A story that misses a criterion isn't done, even if the gap looks small. Last time it was an error message that didn't show on mobile. We left the story out of the increment, the fix took half a day in the next sprint, and in the retrospective we agreed to test on mobile earlier. If a criterion turns out not to matter, I remove it openly instead of quietly accepting the story.
Two department heads each say their feature must come first. How do you decide?
Whether you can make a priority call between stakeholders and explain it.
Gets the evidence behind each request, compares them on the same basis, makes the call as product owner, and explains the reasoning to both.

I meet each one and ask for the evidence: how many customers, how much revenue, what happens if it waits. Then I compare both on the same terms. Last year support's request would cut about 300 tickets a month, while marketing's was for a campaign that could move. Support's went first. I told marketing why in person and gave them a date for theirs, which we hit.
Halfway through the sprint, the developers tell you the sprint goal is at risk. What do you do?
Whether you respond to bad news with scope decisions, not pressure.
Learns what changed, works with the developers to renegotiate scope while keeping the goal, informs stakeholders early, and cancels only if the goal is obsolete.

I thank them for telling me early and ask what changed. Last spring an outside API was slower than anyone expected. We kept the goal, which was letting users book online, but moved the reschedule option to the next sprint. I told the stakeholders that same day. Pushing the team to work late would have hidden the problem until the end of the sprint.
Sales promised a customer a feature by next month without asking you. What do you do?
Whether you handle an outside commitment calmly and protect the team's plan.
Learns what exactly was promised and why, checks with developers what is realistic, agrees a clear answer with sales, and fixes the process so it does not recur.

First I talk to the salesperson to learn what exactly the customer was told and what the deal is worth. Then I ask the developers for a rough size. Last time the full feature would take three months, but a smaller version covered the customer's real need in four weeks. Sales and I went back to the customer together. Afterward we agreed that any date promise goes through me first.
The developers ask for a sprint to pay down technical debt. How do you decide?
Whether you weigh invisible technical work against features fairly.
Takes the request seriously, asks what the debt costs in speed, bugs or risk, and plans it into the backlog, often as a steady share of each sprint.

I ask them to show me the cost: how much slower changes are, how many bugs come from that area, what could break. On my last team the payments code caused about half our production bugs. We didn't take a whole sprint, but we agreed to spend about a fifth of every sprint on it for a quarter. Bugs in that area fell, and so did the time to ship small changes.
The team keeps stopping mid-sprint to ask you what stories mean. What do you change?
Whether you prepare backlog items well before the sprint starts.
Better backlog refinement: stories discussed with the developers ahead of time, clear acceptance criteria, examples, and the product owner reachable during the sprint.

That tells me the stories reach planning before they are ready. I set up a weekly refinement session where the developers question the next sprint's stories while there is still time to find answers. I add examples and mockups to the criteria. Questions during the sprint are still welcome, and I sit with the team most mornings, but within a few sprints they dropped to one or two a week.
Tell me about a feature you pushed for that users barely used. What did you do next?
Whether you measure outcomes and admit when you were wrong.
Owns the decision, finds out why with data and user conversations, then improves, changes or removes it, and adjusts how ideas are tested first.

I pushed for saved searches in our scheduling app. Three months after release, fewer than 3% of users had saved one. I called eight users, and most didn't know the feature existed or why they'd want it. We moved the button next to the results and added an email alert, and use roughly tripled. Now I test interest with a simple prototype before we build the full thing.
Tell me about a time the developers pushed back on a story you wrote.
How you handle disagreement with the team and use their expertise.
Listens to the technical concern, looks for a smaller or different way to deliver the same value, and changes the story when they are right.

I wrote a story for real-time notifications, and the developers estimated it at three sprints. I asked what made it big. Real-time meant new infrastructure. Then I asked what users actually needed: to know about a change within a few minutes. A check every two minutes did that in four days. I learned to describe the problem in stories, not the solution, and to let the team suggest how.
How do you stay close to real users when the team is busy delivering?
Whether you keep direct contact with users instead of relying only on stakeholders.
A regular habit, such as a set number of user conversations each month, joining support calls, reading feedback, and sharing what they learn with the team.

I book at least four user calls a month and protect that time like a sprint event. I also listen to two support calls a week and read every piece of feedback tagged to our area. Every couple of sprints a developer joins a call with me. After one of those, a developer rewrote an error message on the spot because she heard a user read it aloud and get confused.

claims-adjuster.heading: Claims adjuster questions
qs: A homeowner reports water damage. How do you decide whether the policy covers it?
Whether you read the policy in order instead of guessing from the type of loss.
Declarations, insuring agreement, exclusions, conditions and endorsements read in order, the cause of loss confirmed, and a reservation of rights if coverage is unclear.

I start with the declarations page to confirm the policy was in force and who is insured. Then I read the insuring agreement, the exclusions that fit, like gradual leaks or flood, and any endorsements. I confirm the cause on site. Once a stain looked like a sudden pipe burst, but the plumber found a slow leak over months, which that policy excluded. If coverage is unclear, I send a reservation of rights letter.
What is a reserve, and when do you change one?
Whether you see a reserve as an honest estimate that moves with the facts.
The expected total cost of the claim, set early on the best facts available and updated as soon as new information changes the picture, not at closing.

A reserve is my best estimate of what the claim will cost in the end. I set it early from the first facts and change it as soon as something material changes. On an auto injury claim I raised the reserve the same week the MRI showed a herniated disc, instead of waiting for the demand letter. Big late jumps in reserves surprise management and make the numbers hard to trust.
How do you take a recorded statement from a claimant?
Whether you get a fair, usable statement that will hold up later.
Permission on the record, date, time and names stated, open questions in time order, no leading, and a closing question about anything missed.

I tell the person why I am recording and get their permission on the recording. I state the date, time, claim number and everyone present. Then I ask open questions in time order, like where were you going and what did you see first. I don't lead or argue. At the end I ask if they want to add anything. A 20-minute statement done this way rarely needs a second call.
What is subrogation, and what do you do early on a claim to protect it?
Whether you spot recovery chances and keep the evidence that makes them possible.
Recovering paid amounts from the party who caused the loss, plus early steps: identify that party, preserve the failed part, send notice and document everything.

Subrogation is when we pay our insured and then recover that money from whoever caused the loss. On a kitchen fire I saw that a new dishwasher had started it. I told the insured to keep the unit, had it tagged and stored, and notified the manufacturer before anything was thrown away. The recovery came a year later and also returned the insured's $1,000 deductible.
Which signs make you look harder at a claim for possible fraud?
Whether you know common fraud indicators and handle them by the book.
Indicators like recent policy changes, late reporting, shifting stories or pressure to settle fast, treated as reasons to check facts and refer to the SIU, not as proof.

I watch for a policy bought or increased shortly before the loss, a story that changes between calls, missing receipts for expensive items, or strong pressure to settle fast. None of these proves fraud. When I saw three of them on an $18,000 electronics theft claim, I documented the facts and referred it to our special investigations unit, then kept handling the file fairly while they looked.
An insured is angry that their claim is partly denied and threatens to call the state insurance department. What do you do?
How you stay calm and clear when a customer escalates.
Listening first, the policy language explained in plain words, the decision put in writing, and respect for their right to complain to the regulator.

I let them finish, then walk through the exact policy wording that limits the payment and show what we are paying and why. I send the same explanation in a letter that quotes the policy section. I tell them they have every right to contact the department, and I note the call in the file. If a complaint does come in, a clear letter and a complete file usually answer it quickly.
You have 140 open files and five new losses come in after a storm. How do you organize your week?
How you prioritize a heavy caseload without missing required deadlines.
Fast first contact on new losses, unlivable homes first, deadlines checked against state rules, which vary, and an early word to the supervisor if the load is too much.

On day one I call all five new insureds, because first contact sets the tone and states set their own deadlines for acknowledging claims. Anyone who can't live in their home gets help with temporary housing that day. Then I check my diary for open files due this week and block two afternoons for inspections. If I see I will fall behind, I tell my supervisor by Wednesday, not Friday.
A contractor's estimate for a roof is $9,000 higher than yours. How do you handle it?
How you settle a scope or price dispute on facts instead of splitting the difference.
A line-by-line comparison, a joint reinspection if needed, agreement on scope before price, and clear notes on what changed and why.

I ask for the contractor's itemized estimate and compare it with mine line by line. Usually the gap is scope, not price. On one claim he had included tearing off a second layer of shingles that I had missed. We met on the roof, I confirmed it and revised my estimate. Two other items were upgrades the policy did not cover, and I explained that in writing. We settled $4,000 below his first number.
Both drivers in an auto claim say the other one ran the red light. How do you decide liability?
How you gather evidence and reach a fair liability decision.
Statements from both drivers and witnesses, the police report, photos, damage patterns and any video, with fault rules that vary by state applied to the evidence.

I take recorded statements from both drivers and any witnesses, get the police report and look at where each car is damaged. I also ask nearby businesses for camera footage right away, because it is often recorded over. On one claim a gas station video showed our insured entered on yellow. Where it stays unclear, I apply the state's fault rules, which differ by state, and explain the split in writing.
A claimant's attorney sends a policy limits demand with a 10-day deadline. What do you do?
Whether you treat time-limited demands seriously and involve the right people.
The deadline calendared at once, the supervisor told, damages and liability reviewed quickly, missing records requested in writing, and claims counsel involved early.

I put the deadline in my diary the same hour and tell my supervisor, because missing a time-limited demand can expose our insured beyond the policy limits. I review the medical records and liability to judge whether the claim is worth the limits. If records are missing, I ask for them in writing before the deadline. I involve our claims counsel early and keep the insured informed in writing.
Tell me about a claim you had to deny. How did you deliver the news?
How you give a hard answer clearly and with respect.
A phone call before the letter, the policy reason in plain words, what the person can still do, and a letter that quotes the exact policy language.

A homeowner had mold from a leak that had gone on for more than a year, and the policy excluded long-term seepage. I called her before the letter went out, explained the exclusion in plain words and went over the photos that showed the slow leak. I told her she could send more information if she disagreed. The letter quoted the exact wording. She was not happy, but she said she understood.
Describe a time you found a mistake in your own estimate after payment. What happened?
Whether you own errors and fix them quickly.
Quick disclosure to the supervisor, a correction in the file, a call to the insured, and a changed habit so it does not happen again.

After paying a water claim I noticed I had measured one bedroom at 10 by 12 instead of 12 by 14, so the insured was underpaid about $600 for flooring. I told my supervisor the same day, issued a supplement and called the insured to explain. Since then I photograph my measurements with the tape in the frame, so I can recheck them at my desk.
How do you keep good relationships with appraisers and contractors without losing objectivity?
Whether you can work closely with vendors and still make neutral decisions.
Prompt, professional contact, no gifts or favors beyond company policy, the same review standard for every vendor, and decisions based on the file.

I return calls within a day and give clear assignments, so vendors like working with me. I turn down gifts beyond what our policy allows. I review every estimate the same way, whoever wrote it. Once a body shop I trusted sent a bill with labor hours that looked high, and I questioned it like any other. They corrected it, and we still work together.
How do you keep your adjuster licenses and policy knowledge current?
Whether you take licensing and continuing education seriously.
Renewal dates and continuing education tracked for each state license, since rules vary by state, plus reading new endorsements and claim guidelines as they come out.

I hold licenses in three states, and each has its own renewal date and continuing education rules, so I track them in one spreadsheet with reminders 90 days out. I take courses on the lines I handle most, like a recent one on hail damage to roofs. When the company issues a new endorsement, I read it that week and note how it changes what I check on a claim.

mortgage-loan-officer.heading: Mortgage loan officer questions
qs: How do you explain debt-to-income ratio to a first-time buyer?
Whether you understand DTI and can explain it in plain words.
Monthly debt payments divided by gross monthly income, which debts count, and that the acceptable limit depends on the loan program and the lender.

I say it is the share of your monthly income before taxes that goes to debt payments. We add the new house payment with taxes and insurance, plus car loans, student loans and minimum card payments. If you earn $6,000 a month and those payments total $2,400, your DTI is 40%. Then I explain that the limit depends on the loan program and our guidelines, and we look at it together.
What are the main differences between conventional, FHA and VA loans?
Whether you know the major loan types well enough to match them to a borrower.
Conventional loans are not government backed, FHA loans are insured by the FHA and allow lower down payments, VA loans are for eligible veterans and service members.

A conventional loan is not backed by the government and usually needs mortgage insurance with less than 20% down. An FHA loan is insured by the Federal Housing Administration and allows a lower down payment, with its own insurance premiums. A VA loan is guaranteed by the Department of Veterans Affairs for eligible veterans and service members and often needs no down payment. I compare total cost for each borrower.
A borrower asks what a rate lock is and whether they should lock today. What do you tell them?
Whether you explain rate locks accurately without predicting the market.
A lock holds a quoted rate for a set period, the period should cover closing, extensions may cost money, and no promises about where rates will go.

I explain that a lock is our agreement to hold a specific rate and points for a set number of days, as long as the loan details stay the same. If closing slips past the lock, extending it may cost money. I don't predict rates. I show the lock periods we offer and suggest one that covers their closing date with a few days to spare. When to lock is their decision.
What does NMLS licensing mean for your work as a loan officer?
Whether you understand the licensing basics that let you originate loans.
A unique NMLS ID shown on documents, registration for bank employees or a state license for others, education and testing where required, and yearly renewal.

Every loan originator has a unique NMLS ID that goes on applications and disclosures. I work for a nonbank lender, so I need a state license in each state where I originate. That meant pre-licensing education, the national test and a background check, and I renew every year with continuing education. Rules differ by state, so before helping a borrower in a new state I confirm my license covers it.
A borrower's credit report shows a late payment from six months ago that they say was a bank error. What do you do?
How you handle a credit issue with documents instead of assumptions.
A written explanation, proof from the creditor or bank, a check of how the guidelines treat it, and no promises until underwriting reviews it.

I ask the borrower for a letter of explanation and any proof, like the bank's letter admitting the autopay error. If the creditor agrees it was their mistake, the borrower asks them to correct it with the credit bureaus, and I check with our processor whether a rapid rescore makes sense. I don't promise approval. I send the full package to underwriting and tell the borrower what we are waiting on.
Two weeks before closing, the appraisal comes in $15,000 below the purchase price. How do you help the buyer?
How you guide a borrower through a low appraisal calmly and with options.
A clear explanation of what it means for the loan, realistic options like renegotiating or more cash down, a review of the report for errors, and quick updates to both agents.

I call the buyer the same day and explain that the loan is based on the lower value, so keeping the same terms takes $15,000 more in cash. Then we go over options: the seller lowers the price, they split the gap, the buyer adds cash, or they use any contingency in the contract. If the report has factual errors, I request a reconsideration of value. I update both agents that afternoon.
A self-employed applicant's income dropped last year. How do you approach the application?
How you handle harder income files honestly and early.
Full tax returns reviewed up front, income calculated the way the guidelines require, the effect explained, and a realistic price range before they make an offer.

I ask for two years of personal and business tax returns at the start, not after they find a house. If income fell from $90,000 to $70,000, the guidelines look closely at the decline and may require the lower figure. I calculate qualifying income that way and tell them what price range it supports. It is better they hear a lower number from me now than from underwriting after an offer.
A real estate agent who sends you a lot of business asks you to adjust a borrower's numbers so the deal works. What do you do?
Whether you keep loan files honest under pressure from referral partners.
A firm no, no changes to income, assets or occupancy, a search for legitimate options, and a report to compliance if the pressure continues.

I say no and keep it simple: I won't change income, assets or how the borrower plans to use the home, because that is mortgage fraud and it puts the borrower at risk too. Then I look for honest options, like a different program, a co-borrower or a lower price. If the agent keeps pushing, I tell my manager and compliance. Losing one referral source is better than losing my license.
A borrower stops returning calls, you still need their bank statements, and closing is in ten days. What do you do?
How you keep a file moving when the borrower goes quiet.
Contact through more than one channel, an exact list of what is missing and why it matters, help from the buyer's agent, and an early warning about the closing date.

I send a short email and a text with the exact items missing: two months of checking statements, all pages. I explain that underwriting can't clear the loan without them and that the rate lock ends on the 28th. I also call the buyer's agent, who often knows what is going on. Once a borrower was simply traveling. We got the documents in two days and closed on time.
A borrower asks whether they should use their 401(k) for the down payment. How do you answer?
Whether you stay inside your role when a question touches taxes or financial planning.
How the lender would treat and document the funds, a clear note that tax effects are a question for a tax professional, and the decision left to the borrower.

I explain what the lender needs: if they withdraw or borrow from the 401(k), we document where the money came from, and I check how our guidelines treat any loan repayment. I don't tell them whether it is a good idea, because there can be taxes and penalties that depend on their situation. I suggest they talk to a tax professional or their plan administrator before deciding.
Tell me about a loan that almost did not close. What did you do?
How you solve problems and communicate under deadline pressure.
A specific problem, the steps taken, honest updates to everyone involved, and what the person changed afterward.

Four days before closing, the title search found an old contractor's lien on the seller's property. I called the title company and the seller's agent that morning. The seller paid it off and the title company had the release two days later. I kept the buyer updated each afternoon, and we closed on the original date. Since then I order title the day the purchase contract comes in.
How do you build a steady flow of borrowers without relying on one or two agents?
Whether you can build your own pipeline in a referral-driven business.
A mix of sources such as past clients, several agents and builders, regular follow-up, and marketing that goes through the company's compliance review.

I keep in touch with past clients twice a year with a short, useful note, like when it might make sense to review their loan. I work with about eight agents, not two, and I run a monthly homebuyer class at the local library. Every flyer or post goes through our compliance review first. About a third of my loans last year came from past clients and people they sent me.
How do you keep a borrower informed during a 30-day loan process?
Whether you update borrowers before they have to chase you.
A set update rhythm, milestones in plain words, same-day news when something changes, and the borrower's preferred channel.

At application I ask whether they want updates by text or email, and I send one every Monday even if nothing changed. I explain the milestones in order: disclosures, appraisal, underwriting, conditions, clear to close. When something changes, like an extra condition, I tell them that day. Most borrowers stop calling to check once they know a Monday update is coming.
What do you do when you think a borrower would be better off not buying right now?
Whether you put the borrower's long-term interest ahead of a quick loan.
Honest numbers, a clear explanation of the risk, a plan to get ready, and respect for the borrower's own decision.

I show them the numbers plainly. Last spring a couple qualified, but the payment would have left them with almost no savings after closing. I showed them what paying off a $300 car payment and six more months of saving would do. They waited, paid off the car and bought in the fall with a cushion. They have since sent two friends to me.

hr-coordinator.heading: HR coordinator questions
qs: What goes on your onboarding checklist for a new hire?
Whether you can run onboarding so nothing falls through the cracks.
Steps before day one, on day one and in the first weeks: forms, systems access, equipment, policies, benefits information and a check-in, each with an owner.

Before day one: signed offer, background check if the role needs it, equipment ordered, accounts requested and a welcome email. On day one: I-9, W-4, any state tax form, direct deposit and the handbook acknowledgment. In the first 30 days: benefits enrollment before the deadline, required training and a check-in with the manager. Each item has an owner and a date in our tracker.
When does the Form I-9 need to be completed, in general terms?
Whether you know the basic I-9 timing and handle it without overstepping.
Section 1 by the employee by the first day of work, Section 2 by the employer within three business days of the start, and no telling employees which documents to bring.

The new hire completes Section 1 no later than their first day of work. We examine their documents and complete Section 2 within three business days of the start date. I send the list of acceptable documents ahead of time but never tell people which ones to bring. I keep I-9s apart from personnel files and check our tracker every Friday so none is late.
How do you keep personnel files confidential?
Whether you protect employee records and know who may see them.
Access limited to people with a business need, medical information kept separately, secure storage, and a check with HR leadership or counsel on access requests.

Paper files stay in a locked cabinet, and in our HRIS only HR and payroll see the full record. Medical notes and leave paperwork go in a separate confidential file. When a manager asked to see an employee's whole file, I gave him the performance documents he needed and nothing else. If an employee or a lawyer asks for copies, I check with my manager, since access rules vary by state.
How do you keep data in the HRIS accurate?
Whether you treat HR data as something payroll and benefits depend on.
Changes only from approved requests, a second check on pay data, regular audits against payroll, and fixes to the cause of errors, not only the record.

Every change needs an approved form or ticket, and pay changes get a second person's review before payroll runs. Each month I compare a report of active employees with payroll and the benefits carrier file. Last quarter that found 11 people with the wrong work location, which affected their state tax withholding. We fixed them and added work location to the new hire checklist.
A manager wants a new hire to start Monday, but the background check is not back. What do you do?
Whether you follow the hiring process when a manager pushes to skip a step.
A check of company policy, a call to the screening vendor, a clear explanation to the manager, and escalation to HR leadership instead of a quiet exception.

I call the screening company first to see what is holding it up. Often it is a county court search. Then I tell the manager where it stands and what our policy says. If the offer depends on the check, the start date moves unless HR leadership approves an exception in writing. Once I moved a start date by three days, and the manager was fine once he knew the reason.
An employee asks you for a copy of a coworker's offer letter to compare pay. How do you respond?
Whether you protect other employees' records while staying helpful.
A polite refusal to share someone else's documents, no discouraging employees from talking about pay, and a route to the right person for their own pay question.

I reply that I can't share another employee's documents, the same way I would not share theirs. I don't tell them they can't talk about pay with coworkers, because that is their choice. I offer to set up a conversation with their manager or HR business partner about how their own pay was set. Then I let my manager know, in case a pay concern is coming.
Three people start on the same day and one laptop has not arrived. How do you handle day one?
How you solve practical onboarding problems without spoiling a new hire's first day.
An early equipment check, a heads-up to IT and the manager, a loaner or a schedule that starts with non-computer tasks, and follow-up until it arrives.

I check equipment two days before each start, so I would know on Thursday, not Monday. I tell IT and the manager and ask for a loaner. If none is free, I rearrange the person's day: paperwork, a building tour and team meetings in the morning, then shadowing a teammate in the afternoon. I tell the new hire honestly what happened and follow up with IT until the laptop arrives.
A manager asks you to quietly change an employee's start date in the system to last month. What do you do?
Whether you keep records accurate when asked to change them without a reason.
A question about the reason, no change without approval and documents, and a route to HR leadership or payroll if the change has a real basis.

I ask what is behind it. Sometimes there is a real reason, like a contractor who was hired as an employee, and then I need approval and documents before I touch the record. A start date affects pay, benefits eligibility and length of service, so I never change it on a verbal request. If it is not a real correction, I politely say no and tell my manager about the request.
During a routine paperwork call, an employee says their manager keeps making comments about their religion. What do you do?
Whether you recognize a possible complaint and route it correctly.
Careful listening, notes of what was said, no promise of full secrecy, a mention that retaliation is not allowed, and a same-day report to the HR manager.

I stop the paperwork and listen. I write down what they say, with dates and examples. I tell them I need to share this with our HR manager so it can be looked into, and that the company does not allow retaliation for raising it. I don't promise to keep it secret, because I can't. I pass it to my HR manager the same day and leave the investigation to them.
Open enrollment, 20 new hires and a payroll audit all land in the same month. How do you plan?
How you plan around HR's busy peaks so routine work does not slip.
One calendar of fixed deadlines, a list of what can wait, batched repeat tasks, and an early talk with the manager about priorities or help.

First I put every fixed deadline on one calendar: the enrollment window, the start dates and the audit dates. Then I group the 20 new hires into two orientation days instead of 20 separate sessions. I prepare the audit files in the first week, before enrollment questions peak. In week one I tell my manager which tasks could slip, like filing, so we agree on what waits.
Tell me about a time you found an error in an employee's paperwork after it had been processed. What did you do?
Whether you own and fix mistakes in records quickly.
A quick correction, a word with whoever is affected, notes on what changed, and a process change to stop it happening again.

A week before a new hire's first payday, I noticed two digits swapped in her direct deposit account number. I called her that day, had her confirm the right number in writing and updated it with payroll before the cutoff. She was paid on time. After that we had new hires enter their own bank details in the self-service portal instead of on a paper form.
How do you handle the same question from 40 employees during a busy week?
Whether you answer repeat questions efficiently and still kindly.
One clear written answer or FAQ, a shared place to find it, patience with each person, and a fix for whatever caused the confusion.

When 40 people asked how to find their W-2 online, I wrote a five-step guide with screenshots and posted it on the intranet. I replied to each person with the link and a short personal line. The questions dropped off within a day. Then I suggested we email the guide every January, so people have it before they need it.
Which HR systems have you used, and how do you learn a new one quickly?
Whether you can pick up the HR tools a team already uses.
Specific systems named, an example of learning one, use of vendor training and test entries, and a short guide that helps the next person.

I have used Workday and BambooHR, plus Greenhouse for hiring. When my last company moved to a new HRIS, I took the vendor training and practiced in the test site with ten fake employees before touching real data. Then I wrote a two-page guide for the most common tasks, like address changes, and the team still uses it.
What does good service to employees look like in an HR coordinator role?
Whether you see HR coordination as service to people, not only paperwork.
Quick, accurate replies, clear next steps, respect for privacy, and follow-through until the request is closed.

It means people get a reply within one business day, even if the answer is that I am checking. I tell them exactly what happens next and when. I keep their information private and close the loop when it is done. At my last job I kept a simple request log, and we cut the average time to close a request from four days to two.

benefits-specialist.heading: Benefits specialist questions
qs: How do you run open enrollment so employees make informed choices?
Whether you can plan and run open enrollment from start to finish.
Early, clear communication, plan changes explained, help sessions, reminders before the deadline, and a check that elections reach payroll and carriers correctly.

I start six weeks out with a short summary of what changed, like a higher deductible on one plan. Then I hold live sessions, record one for the night shift and send reminders at two weeks and two days. After the window closes, I check elections against payroll deductions and the carrier files. Last year that check found 14 dependents missing from a carrier file before January 1.
What counts as a qualifying life event, and how do you handle a mid-year change request?
Whether you know when employees can change benefits outside open enrollment.
Common events like marriage, birth, adoption or loss of other coverage, a check of the plan's deadline and proof rules, and a change that fits the event.

Common events are marriage, divorce, birth or adoption, and losing other coverage, like a spouse's job ending. When someone asks, I check the plan document for the deadline and the proof needed, like a marriage certificate. The change has to fit the event and the plan's rules. If they miss the plan's deadline, I explain that they usually wait for open enrollment.
How would you explain COBRA to an employee who is leaving?
Whether you can explain COBRA accurately in plain, general terms.
Continued group health coverage after events like leaving the job, usually at the full cost plus a fee, with notices and deadlines from the plan or its administrator.

I explain that COBRA may let them and their covered family keep the same group health coverage for a limited time after they leave. They usually pay the full premium, including the part we used to pay, plus a small administrative fee. Our administrator mails the election notice with the deadlines. I tell them to read it closely and compare other options, like a spouse's plan or the marketplace.
How would you explain a 401(k) employer match and vesting to a new hire?
Whether you understand 401(k) basics and can explain them without giving advice.
The match formula from the plan, the difference between their own money and employer money, the vesting schedule, and no personal investment advice.

I use our plan's numbers. We put in 50 cents for each dollar they save, on up to 6% of their pay. Their own contributions are always theirs. Our match vests over three years, so if they leave after one year, they keep only part of it. I show them where this is in the plan summary. If they ask what to invest in, I point them to the plan's education tools or a financial advisor.
An employee's claim was denied by the health insurer and they come to you upset. What do you do?
How you help employees with insurer problems while staying within your role.
Listening, a look at the explanation of benefits, a call to the carrier with permission, help with the appeal steps, and privacy for health details.

I ask them to show me the explanation of benefits and read the denial reason with them. Often it is a coding issue or a missing prior authorization. With their permission I call our carrier rep. In one case the provider had used the wrong code, and a resubmission fixed it. If it is a real denial, I explain the plan's appeal steps and deadlines. I keep health details out of email.
