A new hire missed the enrollment deadline by two days and wants coverage. How do you respond?
Whether you apply plan rules consistently and explain them kindly.
A check of the dates and plan rules, no exceptions the plan does not allow, a clear explanation, and the next chance to enroll.

I check the hire date and the plan's enrollment window first, in case our notice went out late or the window started on a different date. If the deadline really passed, I can't make an exception the plan does not allow, because that causes problems with the carrier and is unfair to others. I explain this kindly and tell them about the next open enrollment and the life events that would let them enroll sooner.
An employee asks whether to pick the high-deductible plan with an HSA or the PPO. What do you tell them?
Whether you help employees compare plans without making the choice for them.
A side-by-side of premiums, deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums, worked examples for low and high use, and the decision left to the employee.

I don't choose for them, but I make the comparison easy. I show the yearly premiums, deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums for both, plus any HSA contribution from the company. Then we run two examples: a year with a few doctor visits and a year with a surgery. Seeing both totals side by side usually makes the choice clearer. For tax questions about the HSA, I suggest a tax professional.
A manager asks you why an employee has been on leave for three weeks and what is wrong with them. How do you reply?
Whether you protect medical information while giving managers what they need.
Only what the manager needs, such as the expected return date, no medical details, a short reminder about confidentiality, and help planning the work.

I reply that the employee is on approved leave and give the expected return date, which is what the manager needs to plan. I don't share the reason or any medical details, and I explain briefly that leave and medical information is confidential. Then I offer to talk through how to cover the work, like a temporary assignment. If the manager keeps pressing, I bring in my HR manager.
Payroll finds that an employee has had the wrong medical deduction for four months. What do you do?
How you investigate and fix a benefits deduction error fairly.
The cause found in elections, carrier and payroll records, a fair correction agreed with payroll, a written explanation to the employee, and a process fix.

I compare the employee's election, the carrier enrollment and the payroll setup to find where it broke. In one case a plan change never reached payroll, so we under-deducted $45 a month. I worked out the total with payroll, explained it to the employee in writing and offered to spread the catch-up over several paychecks, following our policy and state wage rules. Then we added a payroll check after enrollment.
An employee asks you whether they qualify for FMLA leave. How do you handle it?
Whether you handle leave requests through the process instead of guessing.
Eligibility checked against the rules, the required notices sent on time, state leave laws checked too, and the leave administrator or counsel asked about unclear cases.

I start the process instead of answering off the cuff. I check whether they meet the eligibility rules, such as time with the company and hours worked, and whether the reason may qualify. Then I send the required notices and certification forms on time. Many states have their own leave laws with different rules, so I check ours as well. If something is unclear, I ask our leave administrator or counsel.
Tell me about a time you explained a complicated benefit to someone who was confused or worried.
Whether you can make benefits clear to people under stress.
A specific example, plain words without jargon, a written follow-up, and a check that the person understood.

An employee whose wife was expecting their first child was worried about the cost of the birth. I sat down with him and walked through the deductible and the out-of-pocket maximum: the most they would pay in network that year was $4,000. I wrote the numbers on one page for him to take home and reminded him to add the baby within the plan's deadline. He did, and it was done in a day.
Describe a time you found a problem with a benefits carrier or vendor. How did you resolve it?
How you manage vendors and hold them to what they agreed.
A clear record of the problem, escalation through the account manager, a fix with dates, and follow-up until employees were made whole.

After a carrier change, 30 employees got ID cards with the wrong group number, and two were turned away at the pharmacy. I sent the carrier a list of every affected person and asked for corrected cards and a system fix within 48 hours. I called our account manager daily until it was done. I also gave employees a temporary coverage letter and helped the two get their money back.
How do you keep up with changes in benefits rules and plan options?
Whether you keep your knowledge current in a field where rules change often.
Regular sources such as broker updates, Department of Labor and IRS guidance and professional groups, plus checking unclear changes with the broker or counsel.

I read our broker's compliance updates each month and the Department of Labor and IRS news on benefits. I keep a list of yearly changes, like new contribution limits, and update our employee guides when they are announced. I am working toward a benefits certification. When a change is unclear for our plans, I ask the broker or our counsel instead of guessing.
How do you handle the sensitive personal information you see in benefits work?
Whether you can be trusted with employees' health and financial details.
Need-to-know sharing, secure systems instead of email for medical details, no casual talk, and quick reporting of any mistake.

I see diagnoses, family situations and salaries, and I treat all of it as need-to-know. I use our secure portal instead of regular email for anything medical, and I lock my screen when I step away. Once I sent an enrollment file to the wrong internal address. I reported it to my manager and our privacy officer within the hour, and it was deleted the same day.

chef-cook.heading: Chef and cook questions
qs: How do you keep hot food and cold food safe while it sits on the line during service?
Whether you understand temperature control for food that is being held.
Hot food kept hot and cold food kept cold, temperatures checked with a probe thermometer on a schedule and logged, and food out of range reported to the chef.

I keep hot food in the steam table at 135°F or above and cold food in the reach-in at 41°F or below, or the temperature our local code sets. I probe every pan when it goes out and every two hours after that, and write it on the log. If something has dropped out of range and I cannot tell for how long, I tell the chef and we throw it out.
How do you prevent cross-contamination between raw meat and ready-to-eat food?
Your habits for keeping raw proteins away from food that will not be cooked again.
Raw meat stored below ready-to-eat food, separate boards and knives or cleaning and sanitizing between tasks, and hand washing with a glove change when switching.

Raw proteins go on the bottom shelves of the walk-in, under produce and cooked food, so nothing can drip down. I use color-coded boards, red for raw meat and green for vegetables. If I switch tasks on the same station, I wash, rinse and sanitize the surface and change gloves. Last month I caught a new cook slicing tomatoes on the chicken board, and we started that prep over.
What do you do in the kitchen when an order comes in flagged with a food allergy?
Whether you treat allergy orders as a separate, careful process.
Checking every ingredient including sauces and labels, clean tools and surfaces, fresh gloves, no shared fryer or grill, and asking the chef when unsure.

I read the ticket and check every ingredient, including sauces, marinades and anything someone else prepped, against the label or the recipe book. I wash my hands, change gloves and use clean pans and utensils on a sanitized surface. Nothing goes in the shared fryer. If I am not sure about one item, I ask the chef before cooking, not after. Then I hand the plate to the server myself.
What does FIFO mean in a walk-in, and how do you keep it working during a busy week?
Whether you rotate stock and label food so older product is used first.
First in, first out: new deliveries go behind older stock, everything is labeled with the item and date, and expired or unlabeled food is thrown out.

FIFO means first in, first out. When a delivery comes in, I move the older product forward and put the new cases behind it. Every container I prep gets a label with the item, the date and my initials. On Mondays I check dates in the walk-in and pull anything past its use-by date. At my last job that cut our weekly spoilage from about three cases to one.
What does your mise en place look like before a dinner service, and how do you decide how much to prep?
How you organize your station and plan prep for the expected volume.
A station set the same way every time with everything in reach, and prep based on par levels, booked covers and recent sales.

I start from the prep list and the par sheet, then check how many covers are booked. On a Friday with 180 covers I prep to par plus a little extra on the fast movers. My station is set the same way every night: proteins in the lowboy, sauces left to right in plating order, towels and tongs in the same spot. If I have to look for something during service, my setup was wrong.
The printer keeps firing, you are three tickets behind, and the expo is calling for a table that is not ready. What do you do?
How you stay organized and communicate when you fall behind on the line.
Staying calm, reading the rail, giving the expo honest times, firing in order, and asking another station for help before the window falls apart.

I stop for two seconds and read the rail so I know what I have. I tell the expo the real time on that table, like four minutes, not a guess. Then I fire in order and group the same items where I can. If I am still behind, I ask the cook next to me to drop the fries or plate the sides. On a 220-cover Saturday that kept our ticket times under 15 minutes.
A plate comes back because the guest says the steak is overcooked. How do you handle it?
Whether you can take a sent-back plate without ego and fix it fast.
No arguing, a new steak fired right away with priority, a thermometer check, and a look at why it happened so it is not repeated.

I do not argue with the plate. I fire a new steak right away and tell the expo the time, usually about eight minutes for a medium-rare strip. I check the new one with a thermometer to be sure. Then I look at what went wrong. Last time it was a section of the grill that was too hot after a rush, so I moved the steaks to the cooler side.
Halfway through service you notice the walk-in cooler reads 48°F. What do you do?
Whether you act fast on an equipment problem that puts food safety at risk.
Telling the chef at once, checking food temperatures, moving the riskiest food, writing down times and readings, and letting the chef decide what to discard.

I tell the chef right away. I check whether the door was left open or the fan is iced up, then probe a few items like the dairy and raw chicken. We move the most sensitive food to the reach-ins and the other cooler. I write down the time I found it and the readings. The chef decides what is thrown out based on how long it was warm, and the manager calls the repair company.
During prep you find out the delivery is two cases of chicken short for a banquet of 150. What do you do?
How you solve a supply problem early instead of hiding it.
Telling the chef early, counting what is on hand, offering options like another supplier or a menu swap, and never quietly cutting portions.

I tell the chef as soon as I know, not at plating time. I count what we have and work out how many portions it covers. Then I bring options: a run to the restaurant supply store, borrowing from a sister kitchen, or switching some plates to the pork we have in stock. For a 150-person wedding once, we had the extra chicken in the kitchen within an hour.
You see a coworker taste a sauce with a spoon and put the same spoon back in the pot. What do you do?
Whether you speak up about food safety with a coworker.
Speaking up right away and calmly, a clean spoon, the chef deciding about the sauce, and going to the chef if it happens again.

I say something right then, quietly: grab a clean spoon, that one goes in the dish pit. Then I let the chef decide about the sauce. Most of the time it is a habit, not carelessness, so I show them the cup of tasting spoons we keep on the station. If it keeps happening, I tell the chef, because one sick guest is worse than one awkward talk.
Tell me about the last new dish you had to learn quickly. How did you get it right?
How you learn a new dish fast and keep it consistent.
Reading the recipe, a test plate for the chef, asking about plating and portion, and a station set up so the dish is fast to put out.

Last month the chef added a seared scallop special the afternoon before service. I read the recipe, asked him to walk me through the plating and portion, and made one test plate for feedback. I set up the parts in plating order and weighed the first few portions. We sold 40 that night, and I only had to adjust the sauce once, after the first plate.
Tell me about a time a dish you made did not come out right. What did you do?
Whether you own mistakes and fix them before they reach a guest.
A real example, catching it before it left the kitchen, telling the chef, and changing a habit so it does not happen again.

At a hotel banquet I salted a batch of soup for 80 twice because I did not mark the pot after seasoning. I tasted it before it went up, and it was too salty to serve. I told the chef right away. We stretched it with unsalted stock and cream, and it went out fine. Since then I put a piece of tape on the lid as soon as a pot is seasoned.
How do you keep up your pace and your standards on a double shift?
Whether you can handle long hours on your feet without letting quality slip.
Practical habits like water, a real meal, good shoes, prep done early, and the same checks on the last plate as the first.

I drink water all day and eat a real meal at family meal, not just bites from the line. I wear good shoes and change socks between shifts. I do as much prep as I can before the first service so the second one is easier. And I keep the same rules on the last plate as the first: taste it, check the temperature, wipe the rim. Twelve-hour Saturdays are normal for me.
How do you take feedback from a chef who is blunt with you in the middle of a rush?
Whether you can take direct criticism during service and keep working.
Taking the note without arguing in the moment, fixing the plate, and talking it through after service if something needs clearing up.

During service I say yes, chef, fix it and move on. A rush is not the time to discuss it. If I think the note was unfair or I did not understand it, I ask after close when things are calm. One chef told me sharply that my plating was sloppy. After service he showed me what he wanted, and within a week I was getting it right every time.

food-service-worker.heading: Food service worker questions
qs: When do you wash your hands during a shift, and how do you do it?
Whether you know when and how to wash your hands in food service.
Washing at the hand sink with soap and warm water for about 20 seconds: at the start, after the restroom, trash or raw food, after touching the face, and before new gloves.

I wash at the start of my shift, after the restroom, after taking out trash or touching raw food, after touching my face or phone, and every time before I put on new gloves. I use the hand sink only, never the prep sink, with soap and warm water, and scrub for about 20 seconds before drying with a paper towel. On a breakfast shift that can be 15 times or more.
Do gloves replace hand washing? When do you change them?
Whether you know gloves are not a substitute for clean hands.
Gloves go on clean hands and get changed when torn or dirty, when switching tasks, after raw food, and after touching money, trash or the face.

No. Gloves go on after I wash my hands, not instead of it. I change them when they tear, when I switch from raw food to ready-to-eat food, after I touch trash, money or my face, and when I have been on one task for a long time. At the deli station I go through several pairs an hour at lunch, and that is normal.
What is the difference between cleaning and sanitizing a surface?
Whether you know the two steps and why both are needed.
Cleaning removes food and dirt; sanitizing reduces germs to a safe level. Clean first, then sanitize at the right strength, checked with test strips.

Cleaning takes off the food, grease and dirt with soap and water. Sanitizing kills most of the germs that are left, and it only works well on a surface that is already clean. So I wash, rinse, then sanitize. I check the sanitizer bucket with a test strip at the start of the shift and change it when it gets cloudy or tests weak, usually every couple of hours.
A customer asks if the cookies have nuts in them. How do you answer?
Whether you handle allergen questions carefully and never guess.
No guessing: checking the label or ingredient list, asking a cook or supervisor, and being honest about shared equipment.

I never guess. I check the label or the ingredient binder we keep at the register. If the cookies are baked in house, I ask the cook about the recipe and whether they were baked on the same trays as anything with nuts. If I cannot be sure, I tell the customer I cannot promise they are nut-free. Last week that happened with a muffin, and the customer thanked me for being honest.
The lunch line is 30 people long and the hot food pan is almost empty. What do you do?
How you keep service moving and food stocked during a rush.
Calling for a refill early, swapping whole pans instead of adding new food on top of old, keeping portions steady, and telling people about the wait.

I call back to the kitchen for a new pan before the old one runs out, ideally when it is a third full. When the new pan comes, I swap the whole pan instead of pouring fresh food on top of the old. I keep the same portion size even when the line is long. If there is a wait, I tell people it will be about two minutes, so they can choose something else.
You notice the salad bar feels warm and its thermometer reads higher than it should. What do you do?
Whether you act on a temperature problem instead of ignoring it.
Telling the supervisor right away, checking the food with a probe, moving food to a working unit, and letting the supervisor decide what to throw out.

I tell my supervisor right away and check the food itself with a probe thermometer. If it is above 41°F, or the temperature our local code sets, I move it to the walk-in or a working unit and put a sign on the bar. The supervisor decides what gets thrown out based on how long it was warm. I write down the time and the readings on the temperature log.
A student in the dining hall tells you the food made them sick last time. What do you do?
How you handle a possible foodborne illness report calmly and correctly.
Listening without arguing, taking it seriously, getting the details, and passing it to the manager who handles reports.

I listen and do not argue or promise anything. I say I am sorry they felt sick and that I want to pass it on properly. I write down what they ate, when they ate it, and how they can be reached. Then I give it to my manager right away, because the manager decides whether the health department needs to know. I do not guess about the cause.
A coworker comes in with vomiting and diarrhea because they cannot afford to miss a shift. What do you do?
Whether you know sick workers should not handle food and will speak up.
Telling the person kindly that they should not work with food while sick, and telling the supervisor so they can be sent home.

I tell them kindly that they should not work with food with those symptoms, because it can make dozens of people sick. Then I tell the supervisor, who decides whether to send them home. I understand the money worry, so I offer to swap a shift with them later in the week. Keeping a whole dining hall healthy matters more than one shift.
You drop a tray of plates in the dining room during a busy meal. What do you do?
How you handle breakage safely while service goes on.
Keeping people away from the glass, a broom and wet floor sign, a quick and safe cleanup, and checking that no food near it was contaminated.

First I make sure nobody is hurt and ask people to step around it. I put out a wet floor sign and use the broom and dustpan, never my hands, for broken china. If any pieces flew toward the serving line, I tell the supervisor so we can check and replace food that may have glass in it. It takes about five minutes, then I go back to clearing tables.
A catered lunch for 200 starts in one hour and the van with the hot food has not arrived. What do you do?
How you stay useful and calm when an event is running late.
Telling the lead right away, finishing everything that can be set without the food, and keeping the client informed through the lead.

I tell the event lead right away and let them call the kitchen or the driver. While we wait, I finish everything that does not need the food: tables, linens, chafing dishes, utensils, drinks and signs. I light the chafing fuel only when the food is close so it is not wasted. Last fall the van came 20 minutes late, and because the room was ready we still served on time.
Tell me about a time a customer was angry that their order was wrong. What did you do?
How you stay calm and fix a problem with an upset customer.
Staying calm, apologizing, fixing the order quickly, and calling a supervisor if the person stays abusive.

At a hospital coffee shop a visitor got a sandwich with cheese he had asked us to leave off, and he started yelling at the counter. I kept my voice low, said sorry and remade it right away, ahead of the line. He calmed down once he saw it was being fixed. If someone keeps yelling or uses insults, I call my supervisor to take over.
Tell me about a time you noticed something unsafe in a kitchen or serving area and spoke up.
Whether you act on safety problems even when it is not your task.
A specific example, fixing it or speaking up, telling the right person, and what changed afterward.

At my last job a coworker propped the walk-in door open with a milk crate during a delivery and left it for almost an hour. I closed it, checked the thermometer, and told the shift lead. The readings were still fine. After that the lead set a rule that the door closes between trips. Nobody got in trouble, and it did not happen again.
Which part of food service do you like best: the serving line, prep, dish or catering events?
Whether you know the work and where you will do your best.
An honest preference with a reason, plus a willingness to work any station when the team needs it.

I like the serving line best because I enjoy talking with people, and I am fast and steady with portions. I have also done dish and prep, and I do not mind them. At my last job I covered dish two days a week when we were short. I would rather the team run smoothly than stick to one station.
How do you use the slow time between meal periods?
Whether you find useful work without being told.
Cleaning and sanitizing, restocking, checking dates and labels, and helping prep for the next meal.

Between breakfast and lunch I clean and sanitize my station, restock cups, lids and napkins, and check dates on what is in the cooler. Then I ask the cook what prep I can help with, like cutting fruit or setting up the salad bar. I keep a short list in my head so I am not standing around. On a slow day that is about an hour of work.

janitor-cleaner.heading: Janitor and cleaner questions
qs: Why should you never mix bleach with ammonia or other cleaners?
Whether you know that mixing chemicals can create toxic gas.
Bleach mixed with ammonia or acid cleaners can release toxic gases. One product at a time, labeled bottles, and rinsing between products.

Bleach mixed with ammonia, or with acid cleaners like some toilet bowl cleaners, can give off toxic gases that hurt your lungs. So I never mix chemicals, I use one product at a time, and I rinse the surface before switching. I keep every product in its labeled bottle. If someone mixes something by mistake, I get everyone out, open doors if it is safe, and call my supervisor.
What do you look for on a safety data sheet before using a new chemical?
Whether you know how to read a safety data sheet and use it.
The hazards, the protective gear needed, first aid steps, safe storage, and spill cleanup, plus knowing where the sheets are kept.

I check the hazards first, then what gear I need, like gloves or goggles. I read the first aid section so I know what to do if it splashes in my eyes, and how to clean up a spill and store it. Our binder of sheets is in the supply closet on the second floor, and I know where it is before I open any new product. If something is unclear, I ask my supervisor.
How do you mop a busy hallway without someone slipping?
Whether you know how to keep people safe around wet floors.
Signs out before starting, mopping one half at a time to leave a dry path, low-traffic times when possible, and signs left until the floor is fully dry.

I put wet floor signs at both ends of the hallway before I start. I mop one side at a time so people have a dry path, and I try to do it when traffic is low, like after 7 p.m. in an office. I wring the mop well so I do not leave puddles. The signs stay out until the floor is fully dry, not just mostly dry, and then I pick them up myself.
Walk me through how you clean a public restroom.
Whether you clean in an order that avoids spreading germs.
Sign out and gloves on, trash and restocking, top to bottom and clean to dirty, separate cloths for toilets, the label's contact time, and floors last.

I put out the closed sign and put on gloves. I empty the trash and restock paper and soap first. Then I go from top to bottom and from cleaner areas to dirtier ones: mirrors, sinks and counters, then toilets and urinals with their own color of cloth. I let the disinfectant sit for the time on the label. The floor is last, working toward the door. A six-stall restroom takes me about 20 minutes.
You find a used needle in a trash can while emptying it. What do you do?
Whether you handle sharps safely and follow procedure.
Not touching it with bare hands, not pushing the trash down, using the sharps procedure and container, and reporting it.

I stop and do not reach in or push the bag down. I tell my supervisor and follow our sharps procedure: heavy gloves and tongs, and the needle goes into a sharps container, never the regular trash. I never try to recap it. Then I write down where it was found. That is also why I always hold trash bags away from my body and never press them down with my hands.
Someone reports a spill of an unknown liquid in a hallway. What do you do?
Whether you are careful with a spill you cannot identify.
Blocking off the area, not touching it until it is identified, checking with the supervisor, and using the right kit and gear.

I block the area with cones or wet floor signs so nobody walks through it. I do not touch it or smell it up close until I know what it is. I ask around and call my supervisor. If it turns out to be a chemical, we check the safety data sheet and use the spill kit and gloves. If it is just coffee, I clean it up and dry the floor. Either way, the signs stay until it is dry.
You are behind schedule with four floors left and one hour until the building opens. What do you do?
How you set priorities when there is not enough time.
Restrooms, trash, break rooms and entrances first, telling the supervisor what will be skipped, and writing it down for the next shift.

I do what matters most first: restrooms, trash, break rooms and the lobby, because those affect health and are what people see first. Vacuuming low-traffic offices and dusting can wait a night. I text my supervisor so they know what will be skipped. I write it down so it is done first the next shift. It has happened maybe twice in a year, usually after an event on a floor.
While cleaning an office at night, you see a laptop left open and papers on a desk. What do you do?
Whether you respect privacy and property in the places you clean.
Cleaning around private things without reading them, putting anything moved back exactly, and following the client's rules on reporting.

I clean around them and do not read anything or touch the laptop. If I have to move papers to dust, I put them back exactly where they were. Some clients want open offices or unlocked cabinets reported, so I follow the building's rule and note it on the shift log. People trust us with their spaces at night, and that trust is a big part of the job.
A client in a home you clean asks you to also clean the oven, which is not on the work order. What do you say?
How you handle extra requests outside the agreed work.
Being polite, checking with the office about scope and cost, and not doing unapproved work that delays the rest of the day.

I say I am happy to check. I call or text the office to see if it can be added today and if there is an extra charge. If they approve and I have the time, I do it. If not, I tell the client the office will call to schedule it. Once I did an oven without asking and ran 45 minutes late for my next house, so now I always check first.
During your rounds you notice a loose handrail in a stairwell. What do you do?
Whether you report safety hazards instead of walking past them.
Reporting it right away with the exact location, marking the hazard if possible, and following up to make sure it was fixed.

I report it right away to my supervisor or the building engineer, with the exact stairwell and floor, and a photo if that is allowed. If it looks like it could fail, I put a cone or caution tape at the top until maintenance comes. I write it on my shift log. The next night I check whether it was fixed, and if not, I report it again.
How do you make sure your work is consistent when no one is checking it?
Whether you keep your own standards on night or solo shifts.
Working from a checklist, a last walk-through, and treating each area as if the client will inspect it in the morning.

I work from a checklist for each floor and tick things off as I go. Before I leave, I do a last walk-through and look at what people notice: mirrors, sink counters, trash cans and the corners of the floors. I clean as if the client will walk in first thing, because sometimes they do. At my last building we went 11 months without a single complaint ticket.
Tell me about a time a client or tenant complained about your cleaning. How did you respond?
How you take criticism and fix the problem.
Listening, no excuses, a quick fix, and a change in routine so it does not happen again.

An office manager said the conference room tables were sticky in the mornings. I did not argue. I found out the polish I was using left a film, so I switched to the right cleaner and wiped the tables twice that week. I left a note asking her to tell me if it was better. She said it was, and later she asked for me by name.
Which kind of building do you prefer to clean: offices, hotels, schools or homes? Why?
Whether you know what each setting demands and where you fit best.
An honest answer with a reason, a clear picture of what that setting demands, and flexibility to work elsewhere.

I prefer offices on the night shift. I like working on my own with a clear route, and I know what each floor needs. I have also cleaned hotel rooms, about 14 rooms a shift, which is faster and more detailed. I have done summer deep cleans in schools too. I can work anywhere, but offices are where I am most efficient.
How do you look after your body in a job with a lot of lifting, bending and walking?
Whether you work safely so you stay healthy and reliable.
Lifting with the legs, using carts and the right tools, asking for help with heavy loads, and reporting even small injuries.

I lift with my legs and keep loads close to my body. I use the cart and long-handled tools instead of bending over all night. For anything heavy, like full trash bins or furniture, I ask a coworker or use a dolly. I stretch before my shift. In six years I have not missed work from an injury, and I report even small strains so they are written down.

hotel-guest-services.heading: Hotel and guest services questions
qs: The hotel is oversold and a guest with a confirmed reservation arrives after the last room is gone. How do you handle it?
Whether you know how to relocate a guest with care and follow hotel policy.
An apology away from the line, the truth told plainly, a comparable nearby room and transport arranged per policy, and a follow-up.

I apologize and explain it quietly, away from the line. Following our policy, I have already called nearby hotels earlier in the evening, so a comparable room is ready. We pay for that night and the taxi, and I offer to bring them back the next day with a note to the manager. Last summer I relocated three guests in one night, and two of them came back to stay with us.
A caller says he is a guest's husband and asks for her room number. What do you do?
Whether you protect guest privacy and safety.
Never giving out a room number or confirming who is staying, and offering to connect the call or take a message instead.

I do not give out room numbers or even confirm that someone is staying with us. I say I can connect the call if there is a guest by that name, or take a message. If he comes to the desk, the same rule applies. A guest's safety can depend on it. If he gets pushy or upset, I tell the manager on duty and, if needed, security.
A guest at the desk says she lost her key card and asks for a new one. What do you check first?
Whether you follow room key security.
Checking photo ID against the registration before making a key, never saying the room number out loud, and making a new key that cancels the old one.

I ask for her photo ID and check it against the name on the room. If she is not on the registration, I do not make a key, even if she knows the room number. I write the number on the key sleeve instead of saying it out loud in the lobby. I make a new key that cancels the old one, in case the lost card was stolen. It takes a minute, and most guests thank us for it.
How do you offer a room upgrade without sounding pushy?
Whether you can upsell politely and honestly.
Listening first, offering one upgrade that fits the guest with the price said clearly, and taking a no without pressure.

I listen first. If a guest mentions it is their anniversary or that they will work in the room, I offer one upgrade that fits, like a king with a view or a room with a desk, and I say the price per night clearly. I ask once. If they say no, I move on with a smile. At my last hotel I upsold about four rooms a week that way, and nobody complained of being pushed.
What does a good check-in include, from hello to handing over the keys?
Whether you know the steps of a smooth, accurate check-in.
A warm greeting, confirming dates, room type and rate, ID and payment with the hold explained, the key facts of the stay, and a question about special requests.

I greet the guest by name if I have it and confirm the dates, room type and rate. I check ID and the card for incidentals and explain the hold amount. I tell them the three things they will want: Wi-Fi, breakfast hours and checkout time. Then I ask if they need anything, like extra pillows or a late checkout. A smooth check-in takes me about three minutes.
A guest calls the front desk at 2 a.m. to complain about loud noise from the next room. What do you do?
How you handle a noise complaint fairly and calmly.
Apologizing, contacting the noisy room or sending security, calling the guest back, and offering a room move if the noise does not stop.

I apologize and tell the guest I am on it. I call the noisy room first and ask politely to keep it down. If it continues, security goes up to knock. Then I call the guest back within about 15 minutes to see if it stopped. If not, I offer a room move, and I note it so the manager can decide about a gesture in the morning.
A guest arrives at noon and asks to check in early, but no rooms of that type are ready. What do you do?
How you balance a guest request with what housekeeping can deliver.
An honest time, asking housekeeping for a priority room, storing luggage, and contacting the guest when the room is ready.

I ask housekeeping if a room can be done first and give the guest an honest time, like 1:30 instead of 3. I store their bags, give them the Wi-Fi password and point them to the restaurant or the pool. I take their cell number and text them when the room is ready. If another room type is ready now, I offer it at the same rate if my manager approves.
A guest is upset about a charge on the bill they say they did not make. How do you handle it?
Whether you look into billing disputes fairly and calmly.
Listening, going through the folio and the source of the charge, adjusting within your authority, and explaining clearly.

I listen and go through the folio with them line by line. If it is a restaurant charge, I pull up the signed check. If it is the minibar, I ask housekeeping when it was recorded. If it looks like our mistake, I take it off within my limit and apologize. If it is above my limit, I call the manager. Last month a $40 minibar charge turned out to belong to another room.
A housekeeper tells you a guest has had the Do Not Disturb sign up for three days. What do you do?
Whether you follow welfare check rules and take guest safety seriously.
Checking the guest's notes, calling the room, then a manager and security checking in person per policy, with respect for privacy.

I check the notes first to see if the guest asked not to be disturbed during a long stay. Then I call the room. If there is no answer, I tell the manager on duty, and the manager and security do a welfare check in person, following our policy. Most of the time the guest is fine and just wants privacy. Once in a while a guest needs help, so we do not skip it.
During the evening rush, with eight people in line, a family asks for a crib, extra towels and a late checkout. What do you do?
How you handle several requests at a busy time without losing track.
Writing requests down, sending them to the right department at once, giving a realistic time, and confirming they were done.

I write all three down while they talk. Late checkout I can answer right away, so I give them noon or 1 p.m. based on how full we are. The crib and towels go to housekeeping through the system at once, with the room number, and I tell the family about 20 minutes. Once the line clears, I call the room to confirm everything arrived.
Tell me about a time you turned around a guest's bad experience.
How you recover a stay after something went wrong.
A specific story, listening and taking ownership, a fix that fits the problem, and a follow-up.

A guest's air conditioning broke on a 95-degree night, and she came down furious. I apologized, moved her to a room on another floor within ten minutes, and sent up water and fruit. The next morning I called to check on her and, with my manager's approval, took one night off her bill. She mentioned me by name in her review.
How do you keep your patience at the end of a long shift with a demanding guest?
Whether you stay friendly and professional when you are tired.
Practical ways to stay calm, not taking it personally, and knowing when to ask a coworker or manager for help.

I remind myself the guest does not know it is my ninth hour, and the problem is real to them. I slow down, listen and repeat back what they need. If I feel myself getting short, I ask a coworker to cover for two minutes or bring in the manager. Then I write a clear handover for the next shift so nothing gets lost.
Tell me about a time you made a mistake with a reservation. What happened?
Whether you own errors and fix them before they reach the guest.
An honest example, how it was caught and fixed, and a change in routine to prevent it.

I once booked a guest for the wrong dates, Friday to Sunday instead of Thursday to Saturday. I caught it when I ran the arrivals report the day before. I called him, fixed the booking and kept the same rate. Since then I read the dates back to every caller before I end the call. It adds ten seconds and has saved me more than once.
What does good teamwork between the front desk and housekeeping look like to you?
Whether you work well with the department that gets rooms ready.
Early, accurate updates on arrivals and room status, respect for housekeepers' time, and quick action on problems they report.

It means I tell housekeeping early which guests are arriving early or have special needs, so they can plan. I keep the room status accurate and never send a guest to a room that has not been inspected. On a heavy day with 180 departures, I bring them coffee and thank them. When they flag a problem, like a broken lamp, I put in the maintenance request right away.

mental-health-counselor.heading: Mental health technician and counselor questions
qs: A patient on the unit is pacing, shouting and moving toward a staff member. How do you de-escalate?
Whether you know the basics of verbal de-escalation and keep everyone safe.
A calm voice, space and a clear exit, one person talking, listening for the need behind the anger, and calling for the team early as the unit's protocol says.

I keep my voice low and stand at an angle, about two arm lengths away, with the door behind me. One person talks, so I ask others to step back. I use the patient's name and ask what happened. Once a man was angry about a missed phone call to his mother. I offered to set up the call in 10 minutes, and he sat down. If it escalates, I call for the team as our protocol says.
A client says, almost in passing, that sometimes they wish they would not wake up. What do you do?
Whether you take passing comments about death seriously and act on them.
Asking directly about suicidal thoughts, staying with the person, following the safety protocol, telling the clinician or supervisor at once, and documenting.

I do not let it pass. I sit down and ask plainly: are you thinking about killing yourself? Asking does not put the idea in their head. I ask if they have a plan or access to means. Then I follow our safety protocol, which here means staying with them and telling the nurse or clinician on duty at once. I write down their exact words and what I did.
How do you explain confidentiality and its limits to a new client?
Whether you set clear expectations about privacy from the first meeting.
Plain words at the first session: what stays private, the general exceptions such as serious risk of harm or abuse, that rules vary by state, and a check the client understood.

In the first session I say that what they tell me stays private, with a few exceptions. If I believe they or someone else is in serious danger, or a child or vulnerable adult is being harmed, I have to act. A court can also order records. I explain that the exact rules depend on state law and our policy, and I give them the written notice. Then I ask them to say it back in their own words.
What goes into a useful progress note after a session or a shift?
Whether your documentation is factual, timely and useful to the next person.
Objective observations, the client's own words in quotes, what you did and how they responded, any risk and the action taken, written promptly in the setting's format.

I write what I saw and heard, not my opinion. So I write that the patient stayed in his room for 3 hours and said “I don't see the point,” not that he seemed depressed. I note what I did, how he responded, any risk and who I told. I use our format, often DAP or SOAP, and finish my notes before I leave, because memory fades by the next day.
A client arrives at group clearly under the influence. How do you handle it?
How you protect the group while treating the client with respect.
A private, calm talk, a safety and medical check, following program policy on taking part, no shaming, and a note and handoff to the clinician.

I do not confront them in front of the group. I ask them to step out with me and check that they are safe, including whether they drove. If they seem very sedated, I get medical help. Our policy was that they could not join group that day, so I said that calmly and told them we wanted them back tomorrow. I told the clinician and documented what I saw.
A mother calls and asks how her adult son is doing on the unit. What do you say?
Whether you protect privacy while staying kind to worried families.
Not confirming anything without a signed release, explaining why kindly, offering to pass on a message, and checking the release in the chart per policy.

Without a signed release I cannot even confirm he is here, so I say that kindly: I'm sorry, privacy rules mean I can't share whether someone is a patient. I take her name and number and offer to pass on a message. Then I check the chart. If he has signed a release for his mother, I share only what it allows. I note the call either way.
A patient refuses to attend group and says the whole program is useless. What do you do?
How you engage a resistant patient without a power struggle.
Curiosity about the reason, respect for the patient's choice, a small next step, and letting the treatment team know, instead of arguing or forcing.

I ask what makes it feel useless instead of arguing. One woman told me group made her relive her trauma in front of strangers. That was fair. We agreed she would sit in for 15 minutes and only listen. I passed her concern to her therapist, who adjusted her plan. A week later she was speaking in group. Forcing her would have ended that.
During a routine safety check you find a patient's room and bathroom empty. What do you do?
Whether you act fast and follow procedure when a patient may be missing.
An immediate alert to the charge nurse, a search as the protocol says, following the missing patient procedure, and exact times in the notes.

I tell the charge nurse right away, not after looking around for 10 minutes. Then I follow our missing patient procedure: we check the unit, the common areas and the exits, and call security if the patient is not found. I give the time I last saw them and what they were wearing. Afterward I document the times and actions exactly as they happened.
A client tells you their partner hits their young child. How do you handle it?
Whether you know your mandated reporting duty and follow the process.
Staying calm and supportive, no promise of secrecy, telling the supervisor, reporting as state law and agency policy require, and documenting.

I stay calm and thank them for telling me. I do not promise to keep it secret, because I explained the limits at intake and I remind them now. I tell my supervisor the same day, and we make the report the way our state law and agency policy require. When it is safe, I involve the client in the call. I document what they said and what we did.
A client you have seen for months sends you a friend request on social media. What do you do?
Whether you hold professional boundaries without hurting the relationship.
Declining the request, explaining the boundary warmly in person, following agency policy, and raising it in supervision.

I do not accept it, and I bring it up at our next session instead of ignoring it. I say I value our work, and keeping it in this room is part of what makes it safe. Our agency does not allow social media contact with clients, so I mention that too. I raise it in supervision. Most clients take it well when it is said warmly.
Tell me about a time you noticed a change in a patient before anyone else did. What did you do?
Whether you observe closely and pass on what you see.
A specific change, why it mattered, quick reporting to the nurse or clinician, and a clear outcome.

On a night shift a patient who usually chatted with me at every check gave away his headphones and snacks to others. It seemed small, but giving away belongings can be a warning sign. I told the charge nurse within minutes. The clinician did a risk assessment and he was moved to closer observation. He later said he had been planning to hurt himself that night.
Tell me about a hard session or shift that stayed with you afterward. What did you do about it?
How you handle the emotional weight of the work and use supervision.
Honesty about the impact, use of supervision or debriefs, steady self-care habits, and keeping the effect away from other clients.

A teenager I had worked with for 6 weeks relapsed and was readmitted. I kept replaying what I could have done differently. I asked my supervisor for a debrief, and she helped me see what was mine and what was not. I also kept my usual walk after shifts. Talking about it early is what keeps me fair to the next client.
Describe a time you disagreed with a nurse or clinician about a patient's care. How did you handle it?
How you speak up for a patient while respecting the team.
Raising the concern privately with facts, respecting roles and the final decision, and going up the chain of command if safety is at stake.

A nurse wanted to take a patient off close observation because he seemed calm. I had heard him tell another patient he was saving pills. I asked to speak with her privately and told her exactly what I heard. She called the psychiatrist, and his room was searched. If she had disagreed, I would have gone to the charge nurse, because safety comes first.
How do you work with a client whose choices or values you personally disagree with?
Whether you can stay nonjudgmental and focused on the client's goals.
Awareness of their own reactions, focus on the client's goals, respect for the client's right to choose, and supervision if feelings start to affect the work.

I notice my reaction and keep it out of the session. One client planned to go back to a partner I thought was bad for her. My job was not to decide for her, so we worked on a safety plan and her own goals. When my frustration grew, I took it to supervision. She came back to us 4 months later because she trusted we would not judge her.

clinical-research-coordinator.heading: Clinical research coordinator questions
qs: Walk me through how you obtain informed consent from a new participant.
Whether you treat consent as a process, not just a signature.
The current IRB-approved form, a private setting, a plain explanation, time for questions, a check of understanding, signing before any study procedure, and a note.

First I check that I have the current IRB-approved version. I meet the person somewhere private and go through the purpose, visits, risks, and that joining is voluntary and they can leave at any time. I offer to let them take it home. I ask them to explain the study back to me. They sign before any study procedure, get a copy, and I write a note on how consent went.
What is a protocol deviation, and what do you do when you find one?
Whether you recognize deviations and report them instead of hiding them.
Any departure from the approved protocol, told to the PI promptly, logged, reported to the sponsor and IRB under their rules, with a fix to prevent repeats.

It is any time we did not follow the approved protocol, like a visit outside the window or a missed lab. When I find one, I tell the PI the same day and log it. Then I check what the sponsor and our IRB require, because their reporting rules differ. Once a visit fell 4 days out of window, so we added reminder calls a week ahead for every participant.
A participant mentions a new rash at a study visit. How do you handle it?
Whether you know the basics of recording and reporting adverse events.
Records it as a possible adverse event, has the investigator assess it, checks whether it is serious, and follows protocol and sponsor reporting timelines.

I ask when it started, what it looks like and whether they took anything new. I tell the investigator before the participant leaves, because judging seriousness and any link to the study drug is their call, not mine. I record it in the source and the AE log. If it meets the protocol's definition of serious, I follow the much shorter reporting timeline for that.
What does Good Clinical Practice mean in your day-to-day work?
Whether you see GCP as daily habits, not just a training certificate.
Participant safety and rights first, following the protocol, accurate and traceable data, proper consent, and current training and records.

For me it means three habits. Participant safety and rights come before enrollment numbers. I do exactly what the protocol says, and when we cannot, I report it. And every data point traces back to a source someone could check years later. I keep my GCP training current, and I only do tasks the PI has delegated to me on the delegation log.
What makes a good source document, and how do you correct a mistake in one?
Whether your records would hold up at a monitor visit or an audit.
Records that show who wrote what and when, legible, made at the time and accurate. Corrections with a single line, initials, date and reason, never hiding the original.

A good source document shows who recorded what and when, it is readable, and it was written at the time, not rebuilt later. To fix an error on paper, I draw one line through it so it stays readable, write the correct value, and add my initials, the date and the reason. I never use correction fluid. In an electronic system, the audit trail does this job.
A good candidate for your study speaks limited English. How do you approach consent?
Whether you include people fairly while following consent rules.
An IRB-approved translated form or the IRB's approved short form process, a qualified interpreter rather than a relative, and full documentation.

I do not skip them, and I do not ask a family member to translate. I check what our IRB allows. If there is an approved translated consent form, I use it with a qualified medical interpreter. If not, I follow the IRB's short form process, which often needs a witness. Last year this let us enroll 6 Spanish-speaking participants we would have missed.
Halfway through the study, your site has enrolled 40% of its target. What do you do?
How you improve recruitment without bending eligibility.
Finding where candidates drop off, working with clinicians and referral sources, using only IRB-approved materials, and keeping the PI and sponsor informed.

I look at the screening log to see where people drop out. At one site most were lost because study visits were only on weekday mornings. With the PI's approval we added two late afternoon slots, and I met the clinic nurses so they knew the criteria. Any new flyer went to the IRB first. We reached 85% of target by the end.
A monitor visit is in three days and you find missing signatures in the regulatory binder. What do you do?
Whether you fix gaps honestly instead of backdating.
Gets missing signatures dated today, writes a note to file where needed, never backdates, tells the PI and the monitor, and adds a routine check.

I list every gap and take it to the PI that day. Missing signatures are signed now with today's date, never backdated. Where needed I write a note to file explaining what happened. I tell the monitor at the start of the visit instead of hoping they miss it. Then I add a monthly binder check to my calendar so it does not happen again.
An investigator asks you to enroll a patient who misses one eligibility criterion by a small margin. What do you say?
Whether you protect the protocol under pressure from senior staff.
A respectful no, an explanation that eligibility cannot be waived, and options such as rescreening if the protocol allows it or asking the sponsor about the criterion.

I say I can't enroll them, and I explain why: eligibility is set by the protocol, and enrolling someone outside it is a deviation that can put the patient and the data at risk. Then I offer options. Some protocols allow rescreening later. If the criterion keeps excluding good candidates, the PI can raise it with the sponsor. I keep it about the protocol, not about who is right.
A participant tells you they want to leave the study. How do you handle it?
Whether you respect a participant's right to withdraw.
Accepting the decision without pressure, explaining follow-up and data options as the consent form describes, telling the PI, and documenting per protocol.

I thank them and make clear it will not affect their regular care. I ask, without pressure, if they want to share why, because sometimes it is a fixable problem like parking costs. I explain the options in the consent form, such as a final safety visit. I tell the PI, record the date and reason in the source, and complete the withdrawal steps the protocol lists.
The sponsor needs 60 open data queries resolved by tomorrow. How do you approach it?
How you meet data deadlines without cutting corners.
Sorting queries by type and effort, answering only from source, sending medical questions to the investigator, and flagging any that cannot be closed honestly.

I sort them first. Many are quick, like a missing date that is in the source. I clear those first, always checking the source rather than my memory. Queries that need a medical judgment go to the investigator as one short list. If some cannot be answered by tomorrow, I tell the sponsor which ones and why, instead of guessing to close them.
Tell me about a time you caught an error before it reached the sponsor or the IRB.
Whether you check your own work and the systems around you.
A specific error, how it was found, how it was fixed with proper documentation, and a change that stops it from happening again.

Before a continuing review submission I compared our enrollment count with the screening log. The tracker showed 23 participants, but the log showed 25. Two people consented on a busy clinic day had never been added. I fixed the tracker, told the PI and submitted the right number. Now I reconcile the two logs on the first of every month.
How do you keep several studies on track when each has its own visit schedule?
Whether your organization holds up when the workload grows.
One calendar or tracking system, visit windows worked out in advance, a weekly review, and handoff notes so nothing depends on memory.

I put every participant's visit windows into one calendar as soon as they enroll, not one visit at a time. Each Monday I review the next two weeks across all studies, which was 5 studies at my last site. I prepare kits and lab requisitions two days ahead. I also keep a one-page summary for each study so a colleague can cover if I am out.
Describe a time you had to tell a principal investigator something they did not want to hear.
Whether you speak up clearly to senior people when it matters.
Facts in hand, a prompt and private conversation, a focus on participant safety and compliance, and follow-through.

Our PI wanted to delay reporting a deviation until after a sponsor meeting. I asked for 10 minutes with him and showed him the IRB's reporting deadline and the sponsor's. I said a late report would look worse than the deviation itself. He agreed, and we submitted it that afternoon. I kept it short and factual, and I offered to draft the report.

healthcare-administrator.heading: Healthcare administrator questions
qs: How do you make sure the clinic has enough staff for every shift, including when people call out?
Whether you plan coverage ahead instead of reacting every morning.
A schedule built from patient volume and published early, a clear call-out process, cross-trained staff or a per diem list, and tracking of overtime.

I build the schedule from expected patient volume by day, not from habit, and publish it four weeks out. Call-outs go to one phone number by 6 a.m. so I hear early. I cross-trained two front desk staff to room patients, which covered most gaps. For the rest I keep a short list of per diem staff. I review overtime every two weeks to spot burnout.
What does HIPAA mean in practice for the front desk and the back office?
Whether you turn privacy rules into everyday habits.
Access limited to what each job needs, private screens and conversations, identity checks, regular training, and a clear way to report possible breaches to the privacy officer.

At the front desk it means screens turned away from the waiting room, quiet voices at check-in, and verifying identity before giving out information. In the back office, people see only what their job needs. Everyone gets training at hire and every year. When something goes wrong, staff tell the privacy officer at once, and we assess it under our policy and the law.
Claim denials have gone up for three months in a row. How do you find and fix the cause?
Whether you go to the root cause of revenue problems.
Sorting denials by reason and payer, tracing each back to the step that caused it, fixing that step with training or checks, and tracking the rate monthly.

I pull the denial report and sort it by reason code and payer. At my last clinic most denials were for eligibility, so the problem started at scheduling, not billing. We added an insurance check two days before each visit and trained the front desk on it. I tracked the denial rate monthly, and within a quarter it was back to its old level.
Walk me through how you handle a formal patient complaint.
Whether you resolve complaints fairly and learn from them.
Quick acknowledgment, listening, facts from staff and records, a clear reply, any formal steps the payer or state requires, and fixing the process behind it.

I call the patient within one business day and mostly listen. Then I get the facts from staff and the record. I reply with what we found and what we will change. If the complaint is about clinical care, I bring in the medical director. Some complaints have formal steps under payer or state rules, so I check those. Every month I review complaints for patterns.
About one in five appointments at your clinic end in a no-show. What would you try first?
Whether you tackle no-shows through causes and data, not just penalties.
Finding who misses and why, reminders and easy rescheduling, a waitlist to fill gaps, and measuring the effect before trying anything stricter.

First I find out who misses and why. I sort no-shows by visit type, how far ahead they were booked and day of week. Often it is new patients booked far out. I add text reminders two days and two hours before, with a way to cancel by reply, and keep a short-notice waitlist to fill gaps. I check the numbers after 60 days before trying anything stricter.
A senior physician regularly runs 45 minutes behind and patients are complaining. What do you do?
How you raise operational problems with physicians tactfully.
Data on the delays, a private and respectful talk, looking for causes in the schedule template or support, and a shared plan with a follow-up date.

I bring two weeks of data, not stories, and ask for a private conversation. With one doctor the cause was new patient visits booked in 15-minute slots. We changed them to 30 minutes and moved his refill requests to a nurse. His average delay dropped to about 10 minutes. If the talk had gone nowhere, I would have involved the medical director.
Next year's budget is cut by 8% while patient volume is expected to grow. How do you approach it?
Whether you can make tradeoffs without hurting safety or quality.
A review of every cost line, protection for safety and core staffing, savings in supplies, contracts and scheduling, and clinical leaders involved in the choices.

I go through every line with finance and mark what is fixed, what is safety-critical and what is flexible. I protect clinical staffing first. At one practice we closed most of the gap by renegotiating a supply contract and turning regular overtime into planned part-time shifts. I share the options with clinical leaders before deciding, so the cuts make sense to them.
A staff member posts a photo from the clinic, and a patient's name is visible on a screen behind them. What do you do?
Whether you handle a privacy incident quickly and by the book.
Getting the post removed, telling the privacy officer, a breach assessment under policy and law, any required notices, discipline per policy, and retraining.

I ask the employee to take it down right away and keep a copy of what was posted for the record. I report it to our privacy officer the same day. They decide, under our policy and the law, whether it counts as a breach and whether the patient must be notified. HR handles any discipline under our policy. Then I remind the whole team about photos in clinical areas.
Two of your three medical assistants resign in the same month. How do you keep the clinic running?
How you protect patient care during a staffing crisis.
Short-term cover from agency or float staff, a safely trimmed schedule, fast hiring, support for the remaining staff, and finding out why people left.

First I protect the remaining assistant from burning out, so I bring in agency staff and trim the schedule where it is safe. I post both jobs that week and ask the team for referrals. I also hold exit conversations with both people. At my last job that showed our pay was below nearby clinics, and the raise cost less than constant turnover.
Your practice is switching to a new electronic health record system. How do you lead the change?
Whether you can run a big operational change with clinicians on board.
Clinical champions, training before go-live, a lighter schedule in the first weeks, extra support on site, and a clear way to report and fix problems.

I pick a doctor and a nurse as champions to test workflows and speak for their colleagues. Everyone is trained before go-live, with practice logins. For the first two weeks we cut the schedule by about a quarter and have vendor support on site. We meet for 15 minutes each morning to log problems and assign fixes. The old system stays read-only for lookups.
Tell me about a decision you made that clinical staff did not like. How did you handle it?
Whether you can hold a decision and still keep people's trust.
An open explanation of the reason, listening to concerns, adjusting details where it makes sense, and following up on how it worked.

I moved lunch breaks to staggered times so the phones were answered all day. The nurses hated losing their shared lunch. I explained that we were missing about 40 calls a day at noon, and I asked them to help design the rotation. They chose the groups themselves. After a month missed calls had dropped sharply, and I shared that number with them.
Describe a time you used data to change how a clinic or department ran.
Whether you base operational changes on evidence.
A clear problem, the data gathered, the change made, and a measured result, explained simply.

Patients complained about long waits at check-in. I timed check-in for two weeks and found it averaged 12 minutes, mostly because of paper forms. We moved the forms to a link sent with the reminder text. Two months later check-in averaged about 5 minutes, and front desk complaints fell. I posted the before and after numbers for the staff.
How do you build trust with physicians and nurses when you are not a clinician yourself?
Whether you can lead clinical people without clinical authority.
Respect for clinical judgment, time spent on the floor, quick follow-through on their problems, and asking before changing anything that touches care.

I spend time on the floor, not just in my office. In my first month I shadowed each role for half a day and asked what slowed them down. They named a broken printer and a slow fax line. I fixed both within a week. Small wins like that earn trust for bigger changes. I never change anything that touches patient care without asking the clinical leads first.
Tell me about a time a conflict between staff members started to affect patients. What did you do?
How you deal with team conflict before it harms care.
Acting quickly, hearing both sides privately, a focus on behavior and patient impact, clear expectations, and follow-up.

Two front desk staff stopped speaking, and patients noticed the tension at check-in. I met each one privately to hear their side, then both together. The issue was who covered the phone during breaks. We wrote a simple coverage schedule, and I made clear that how they treat each other in front of patients is part of the job. I checked in weekly for a month.

rehab-therapist.heading: Physical and occupational therapist questions
qs: How do you structure the evaluation of a new patient?
Whether your evaluation is thorough and leads to a clear plan.
History and the patient's own goals, a screen for red flags, standardized tests and functional measures, and a plan of care with goals and frequency.

I start with the history, the referral, and what the patient wants to get back to. I screen for red flags that need a doctor first. Then I test what matters for their goals: strength, range of motion, balance, and a real task like standing up from a chair or getting dressed. I use at least one standardized measure so I can retest it. I finish with a plan we agree on.
How do you write a goal that is actually measurable?
Whether your goals are functional, specific and testable.
A functional task, a measurable level such as distance, time or amount of help, the conditions, and a target date, written so any therapist could test it.

I tie it to something the patient does in daily life and make it testable. Instead of improve balance, I write: patient will walk 150 feet with a cane on level ground without loss of balance within 4 weeks. An OT goal might be: patient will put on a shirt independently, sitting at the edge of the bed, within 3 weeks. Anyone on the team could check it.
What does your documentation need to show for a payer to keep covering therapy?
Whether you know the general basis of documenting medical necessity.
The need for skilled care, objective measures, progress toward functional goals, and why therapy should continue, following each payer's own rules, which vary.

It has to show that the patient needs a therapist's skills, not just supervised exercise. In each progress note I record objective measures, like gait speed or how much help they need with toileting, compared with the start. I link them to the goals and explain what is left and why. The exact rules differ by payer, so I check each plan's requirements.
During a session, when do you stop or change an exercise?
Whether you recognize warning signs and keep patients safe.
Stopping for chest pain, unusual shortness of breath, dizziness, confusion or sharp new pain, checking vital signs against facility limits, alerting the team, and documenting.

I stop for chest pain, unusual shortness of breath, dizziness, new confusion, or sharp pain that differs from normal effort. I check vital signs against our facility's limits and get the nurse or doctor if anything is off. For milder problems I change the exercise by reducing range or load. Once a patient's heart rate kept climbing during a walk, so we stopped and I called his nurse.
A patient after knee replacement says therapy hurts too much and wants to skip today. What do you do?
How you balance pain, motivation and recovery.
Listening and assessing the pain, checking for warning signs, working with nursing on pain control timing, adjusting the session, and explaining why movement matters.

I ask where it hurts and how it compares with yesterday, and I look at the knee for anything unusual. If the pain seems expected, I talk with the nurse about timing pain medication before our session. I explain that bending the knee now is what lets them climb stairs later. Then I offer a shorter session. Most patients agree once they feel heard.
A patient keeps skipping the home exercise program you gave them. How do you respond?
Whether you look for the reason instead of blaming the patient.
Curious questions about barriers, a shorter program tied to daily routines, clear handouts or videos, and checking understanding with a teach-back.

I ask what gets in the way, without judgment. One man had 8 exercises on a sheet and could not remember how to do them. We cut it to the 3 that mattered most, linked them to brushing his teeth and making coffee, and I filmed him doing them on his phone. He started doing them most days, and his range of motion began to improve again.
A stroke patient's family wants you to push walking every session, but the patient is not ready. How do you handle it?
How you manage family expectations while keeping care safe.
Listening to the family, explaining the plan and the safety reasons in plain words, showing small gains, and giving them a useful role.

I meet with them and listen first, because their hope is a strength. Then I explain that he cannot yet control his trunk while sitting, and walking now would risk a fall. I show them his progress in sitting balance with numbers from last week. I give them tasks they can help with, like practicing reaching while seated. Families usually relax once they see a path.
Insurance approves 8 visits, but you think the patient needs more. What do you do?
Whether you advocate for patients within payer rules.
Planning the visits for the most impact, documenting need clearly, requesting more visits through the payer's process, and building a strong home program.

I plan the 8 visits with the end in mind and teach the home program early. I document objective progress and what still limits function. Before the last visits I request more, with that evidence, through the payer's process. If it is denied, I explain the appeal options and make sure the patient leaves able to keep progressing at home.
A patient with a high fall risk insists on going home alone. What do you do?
Whether you respect a patient's choice while reducing risk.
Respect for the patient's right to choose, a clear explanation of risks, equipment and home changes, the case manager involved, and documentation.

It is their choice, so my job is to make home as safe as possible. I explain the risks plainly and listen to why home matters. I recommend a walker, grab bars and a shower chair, and we practice getting up from the floor. I ask the case manager about home health visits and a medical alert device. I document my recommendations and the patient's decision.
You have 12 patients today and two urgent new evaluations get added. How do you prioritize?
How you manage a heavy caseload safely and fairly.
Priority by medical need and discharge timing, clear communication with the team, shorter or moved visits for stable patients, and no skipped documentation.

I look at who is going home soonest and who has a safety question, like a patient who needs clearance to walk before discharge. Those come first, along with the new evaluations. I tell the charge nurse and my lead which visits move to tomorrow. Stable patients may get a shorter session that day. I still finish every note before I leave.
Tell me about a patient whose progress stalled. What did you change?
Whether you reassess and adapt instead of repeating the same plan.
Retesting, looking for new causes or barriers, changing the approach or referring back when needed, and showing the result.

A woman with shoulder pain stopped improving after 4 weeks at the same range of motion. I retested and saw she was guarding because she feared the pain. I spent time explaining that hurt does not always mean harm, and we graded the movements in small steps. Within 3 weeks she could reach a high shelf. If she had not improved, I would have sent her back to her doctor.
How do you work with nurses, doctors and the other therapy discipline on a shared patient?
Whether you coordinate care instead of working alone.
Clear updates in notes and huddles, safety recommendations shared at once, goals aligned with other disciplines, and asking others for input.

I share safety changes right away, like telling nursing a patient now needs two people to transfer. In team meetings I keep updates short: function now, goal, barrier. With the PT or OT on the same patient, we avoid repeating tests and split goals, so one of us takes walking and the other takes dressing. I also ask nurses how the patient manages at night.
Tell me about a time you trained a family member to help with care at home.
Whether you can teach caregivers safely and clearly.
Simple steps, a demonstration, practice with feedback, a teach-back, written or video reminders, and a check on how it goes after discharge.

A man was taking his wife home after a hip fracture. I showed him how to help her from bed to chair, then had him do it three times while I watched. He kept bending his own back, so we practiced with his knees bent until it felt natural. I gave him a one-page sheet with photos and called the next week. They had managed every transfer safely.
Tell me about a time a patient's own goal changed your treatment plan.
Whether your care is built around what matters to the patient.
Asking what matters to the patient, adapting goals and activities to it, and showing how that improved effort or outcome.

An 80-year-old man with Parkinson's did not care about my balance goals. He wanted to get back to his garden. So we practiced kneeling and getting up, carrying a watering can and stepping over a hose. He came to every session after that. His balance scores improved, but what he talked about was picking tomatoes in July.

estimator.heading: Cost estimator questions
qs: How do you do a quantity takeoff, and how do you make sure nothing is missed?
Whether you have a method for measuring quantities from drawings.
Works through the drawings by trade or CSI division, marks items as counted, reads the specs and addenda, and has a second person check the big totals.

I go sheet by sheet in CSI division order and color each item on the plan as I count it, so gaps stand out. Then I read the specs and every addendum, because a lot of scope hides there. On a 40,000 square foot school, the spec called for a floor sealer the drawings never showed. A second estimator checks my largest quantities before I price them.
What is the difference between contingency and escalation in an estimate?
Whether you know what each allowance covers and why they are kept apart.
Contingency covers unknowns in scope and risk. Escalation covers prices rising over time. Each has its own basis and its own line.

Contingency is for things we expect but cannot define yet, like design gaps or unknown site conditions. Escalation is for prices rising between the estimate date and when we actually buy. On a job that bids now but buys steel in 18 months, I carry escalation on that package with the index and rate written down, and keep contingency as a separate line.
In plain terms, how does earned value tell you whether a project is on track?
Whether you understand earned value well enough to explain it to a project team.
