I say I can't share anyone's contact details, because people gave them to us for the program only. Then I offer to pass their number on, so the other person can reach out if they want to. Most people are fine with that. It keeps the trust of everyone in the group, including the person asking.
Your program director and a partner organization give you different instructions about the schedule. What do you do?
How you handle conflicting directions without picking a side on your own.
Both requests written down, the conflict raised quickly with the director, and the people with authority deciding before anything is announced.

I don't pick one and hope. I write both versions down, including what each one affects, like room bookings or staff time. Then I take it to my director the same day and ask who should decide. Usually a short call between the director and the partner settles it. I only send the schedule to participants once it's agreed, so they don't get two versions.
Tell me about a tracking system you set up that other people actually used.
Whether you build tools that make the team's work easier.
A real problem, a simple tool, getting people to use it, and a visible result.

Our case notes were in four different spreadsheets, so no one knew who had finished intake. I built one shared sheet with drop-down fields and a column for the next step. I sat with each coordinator for 15 minutes to set it up with their own cases. Within a month, missing intake forms went from about 20 to 3, and our funder report took a day instead of a week.
How do you keep volunteers informed and coming back?
How you manage people you do not pay or supervise directly.
Clear roles, schedules sent early, specific thanks, and a quick way for volunteers to raise problems.

I send the schedule two weeks ahead with a short note on what each role does, so nobody arrives unsure. I text a reminder the day before. After each event I thank people by name for something specific. Every few months I ask what would make it easier. One group asked for shorter shifts, and we kept more of them once we cut shifts to three hours.
Describe a time a mistake of yours reached a participant or a funder. What did you do?
Whether you own errors and fix the process behind them.
Quick ownership, a direct fix, an honest note to the people affected, and a change that stops it happening again.

I once sent a quarterly report with last quarter's attendance numbers in one table. The funder's program officer noticed. I called her that afternoon, said it was my error and sent the corrected report within the hour. Then I added a second-person check on every report before it goes out. It takes ten minutes per report, and we haven't had a repeat.
Three programs need your attention in the same week. How do you decide what comes first?
How you prioritize when everything feels urgent.
Fixed deadlines and anything affecting participants first, an honest talk with the director about trade-offs, and clear updates on what will wait.

I list everything with its real deadline. Funder deadlines and anything that affects participants that week come first, like an event or a stipend payment. Internal tasks can usually move a few days. If two things truly clash, I ask my director which matters more instead of guessing, and I tell people what will be late and when they will get it.

construction-laborer.heading: Construction worker questions
qs: What do you check at the start of a shift before you begin work?
Whether daily safety checks and PPE are a habit for you.
PPE in good shape, tools and ladders inspected, the day's hazards from the toolbox talk, and a look at what changed on site since yesterday.

I put on my hard hat, safety glasses, vest, gloves and boots, and check none of it is damaged. I look over my tools, cords and any ladder I'll use. At the toolbox talk I listen for what's happening that day, like a crane lift or a new trench. Then I walk my work area, because things change overnight, and I report anything off to the foreman before starting.
How do you stay safe working near heavy equipment like an excavator or a loader?
Your awareness of blind spots and swing areas around machines.
Staying out of blind spots and the swing radius, eye contact with the operator before getting close, and never walking behind a moving machine.

I assume the operator can't see me unless we have made eye contact. I stay out of an excavator's swing radius and never walk behind equipment that's backing up. If I need to get close, I signal and wait for the operator to stop and give me the okay. I wear my vest, and I never stand between a machine and a wall or a truck.
When should you stop work, and how do you do it?
Whether you will speak up when something is unsafe.
Stopping when there is a clear hazard, making the area safe, telling the foreman right away, and restarting only once the hazard is fixed.

If I see something that could hurt someone, like a trench wall cracking or a load swinging over people, I stop and tell the people near me to step back. Then I tell the foreman right away. On the sites I've worked, anyone could stop work for safety, and I've done it twice. We start again only when the problem is fixed, not when it's just been talked about.
How do you use a set of plans to find where something goes?
Whether you can read basic plans and layout marks.
The right sheet and the latest revision, written dimensions used instead of measuring the drawing, reference points, and questions when something is unclear.

First I make sure I have the latest set, since old revisions cause rework. I find the right sheet, like the foundation plan, and read the written dimensions instead of measuring off the paper. I measure from the gridlines or control points the surveyor marked. If two numbers don't add up, I ask the foreman before cutting or pouring, because concrete is hard to undo.
What did you take away from OSHA 10 or OSHA 30 training?
Your general knowledge of construction safety training.
A basic grasp of common hazards like falls and struck-by, workers' rights, real examples from site work, and awareness that some states and employers require the card.

I did the OSHA 10 for construction. The big points for me were the main causes of serious injuries: falls, being struck by objects, electrical hazards and getting caught in or between things. It also covered my right to raise safety concerns. Some states and many employers require the card, but for me the value was learning what to look for on a site every day.
The concrete truck shows up early and the forms are not fully braced. What do you do?
Whether you resist pressure to rush when the work is not ready.
No pour until the forms are checked, a quick word with the foreman, and help getting the bracing finished fast.

I tell the foreman right away that the forms aren't ready. A form that blows out during a pour is dangerous and costs far more than waiting. I jump in to finish the bracing with the crew. The driver can usually wait a little, and if not, the foreman decides what happens with the load. I don't start placing concrete in forms I'm not sure about.
You see a coworker working near a roof edge without being tied off. What do you do?
Whether you look out for others even when it is awkward.
Speaking up at once in a calm way, getting the person back from the edge, and telling the foreman if it continues or equipment is missing.

I tell him right then to step back from the edge and tie off. I keep it calm, not a lecture, something like: hey, clip in before you go back out. If he says there's no anchor or harness available, I tell the foreman so it gets fixed. A fall from a roof can kill someone, so I'd rather be annoying for a minute than see that happen.
You are the signal person for a crane lift and lose sight of the operator. What do you do?
Whether you know a lift stops when communication is lost.
The stop signal given, the load held until contact is back, and a move to a better spot or a second signal person added.

I give the stop signal and call stop on the radio if we're using one. The load should not move while the operator and I can't see or hear each other. Then I move to a spot where we can see each other, or the foreman puts a second signal person in place. Only someone qualified as a signal person for that site and lift should be doing this job.
It is 95 degrees and the crew is pouring concrete all afternoon. How do you handle the heat?
Whether you know how to prevent heat illness for yourself and others.
Water often, breaks in the shade, watching for signs like dizziness or confusion, and acting fast when someone shows them.

I start drinking water before I'm thirsty and keep a jug close. We rotate the hardest jobs and take short breaks in the shade. I watch my crew too. If someone gets dizzy, sick or confused, I get them out of the sun, cool them down and tell the foreman, and we call 911 if it looks serious. Heat can drop a strong person fast.
Your foreman asks you to run a skid steer you have never been trained on. What do you say?
Whether you will turn down an unsafe task politely and offer a way forward.
An honest no to running it untrained, a clear reason, and a request for training or for a trained operator.

I tell him I haven't been trained on that machine and I'm not comfortable running it yet. I offer to do something else, like spotting or hand work, while a trained operator runs it. Then I ask if I can get trained, because I'd like to run it later. Most foremen respect that more than someone who tips a machine on day one.
You find a frayed sling or a cracked ladder in the gang box. What do you do?
Whether you take damaged equipment out of use.
Tagging it out of service, setting it apart so no one grabs it, and telling the foreman so it gets replaced.

I don't use it and I don't put it back. I tag it do not use, set it apart from the good gear and tell the foreman so a replacement gets ordered. A frayed sling can fail under load, and a cracked ladder can fold under you. It takes two minutes, and the next person who reaches into that box won't get hurt.
Tell me about a day the work fell behind schedule. What did you do?
How you help the crew catch up without cutting corners.
Pitching in where needed, staying organized, honesty about what can be done safely, and no skipped safety steps to save time.

We were setting forms for a footing and the lumber delivery came three hours late. I staged the next section's materials while we waited, so we could move straight on. When the lumber came, we split into two teams. We finished about an hour past the normal end of the day. We didn't skip bracing or checks to make it up, because rushing that part only makes a longer day later.
How do you learn a new task, like tying rebar or rigging a load, from an experienced worker?
Whether you are coachable and learn safely.
Watching first, asking questions, doing it under supervision, and admitting when you are not sure yet.

I watch them do it a few times and ask why they do each step, not just how. Then I do it while they watch and correct me. On my last job a rebar worker showed me a faster tie, and it took me about a week to get quick at it. If I'm not sure about something like a rigging hitch, I ask before the load goes up, not after.
How do you keep up a steady pace through a long, physical day without getting hurt?
Whether you know how to work hard and stay safe all day.
Good lifting habits, help or equipment for heavy loads, water and breaks, and steady work rather than rushing.

I lift with my legs and keep loads close, and if something is heavy or awkward, I get a second person or a dolly instead of being a hero. I drink water all day and eat at lunch, even when we're busy. I keep a steady pace instead of rushing in the morning and fading by three. That way I'm still careful at the end of the shift, when I'm tired and mistakes are easier to make.

automotive-sales.heading: Automotive sales questions
qs: Walk me through how you run a test drive.
Whether you follow the dealership's test drive process.
A valid license checked and copied, the store's rules on insurance and ride-alongs followed, a planned route, and the drive used to show what matters to the buyer.

I ask for the driver's license, check it's valid and not expired, and copy or scan it as our policy says. Some stores also ask for proof of insurance. I ride along unless our policy says otherwise, and I use a set route with highway, city streets and a parking lot. On the way I show the features they said mattered, like lane assist, and I let them drive quietly for a while.
How does a trade-in appraisal work, in general terms?
Your basic understanding of how a trade value is set.
Condition, mileage, history report, local market data and reconditioning costs considered, with the appraiser or used car manager setting the final number.

The used car manager or appraiser looks at the car's condition, mileage, options and history report, and drives it. They compare what similar cars are selling for at auction and locally, then take off what it will cost to recondition it. My job is to collect good information, like service records, and explain the number honestly. I don't promise a value before the appraisal.
A customer asks what interest rate they will get on a loan. How do you answer?
Whether you explain financing honestly without promising rates.
No promised rate, a clear explanation that it depends on credit and the lender, and a hand-off to the finance office for real numbers.

I tell them honestly that I can't promise a rate. It depends on their credit, the loan term, the car and the lender who approves it. If there's a manufacturer offer on that model, I can show them the advertised terms. Then I explain that the finance manager will give them real numbers once they apply. I'd rather they hear that now than feel misled later.
An internet lead asks about a specific car at 9 p.m. How do you follow up?
Whether you know how to answer and follow up on leads.
A fast, direct answer to the question asked, a clear next step, everything logged in the CRM, and a steady follow-up plan that respects the customer's time.

If our store allows after-hours replies, I answer that night. If not, first thing in the morning. I answer exactly what they asked, like whether the blue one is still in stock and its price, and suggest a time to see it. I log everything in the CRM. If I don't hear back, I follow up by call and text over the next few days, then slow down, so I'm helpful, not a pest.
A customer says the same car is $1,500 cheaper at a dealer across town. What do you do?
How you handle a price objection without bluffing or panicking.
Asking to see the offer, comparing the full out-the-door price and equipment, and bringing it to the manager honestly.

I ask if they can show me the quote, and I look at it with them. Often the cars differ in trim or options, or the other price leaves out fees. If it's truly the same car, I take it to my sales manager and see what we can do. I also remind them what we offer, like our service department being closer. If we can't match, I tell them so plainly.
A couple arrives for a test drive, and the only license they have expired last month. What do you do?
Whether you follow the license rule even when it costs you a drive today.
No drive on an expired license, a friendly explanation, and other ways to keep the visit useful, like a sit-in walkthrough or a booked drive later.

I tell them kindly that I can't let anyone drive on an expired license, because it's against our policy and our insurance. Then I keep the visit useful. I walk them through the car, let them sit in it, pair a phone and price it out. I offer to book a drive once the license is renewed. Most people understand, and some come back the same week.
A customer only wants to talk about the monthly payment. How do you keep the deal clear and honest?
Whether you explain total cost instead of hiding it in a payment.
Price, term, down payment and trade shown together, an explanation of how a longer term changes total cost, and the customer left to decide.

I ask what payment they're comfortable with, because that's a real limit. But I show it next to the price, the term, the down payment and the trade value. If the payment only fits with a longer loan, I show what they would pay in total over that term. Then they choose. People trust you more when they see the whole picture, and they come back for the next car.
A customer's trade-in appraisal comes in $3,000 below what they saw online. How do you handle it?
How you explain a disappointing number without losing trust.
Acknowledging the gap, explaining what the appraisal found, showing local market comparisons, and asking for a second look if there is new information.

I say I understand, because $3,000 is real money. Then I explain what the appraiser found, like tires that need replacing or past damage on the history report. I show what similar cars sell for locally. Online tools give estimates before anyone has seen the car. If they have service records we missed, I take them to the manager for a second look.
At delivery, the customer notices a scratch on the bumper. What do you do?
How you handle a problem at the most important moment of the sale.
Owning it instead of brushing it off, a clear written plan to fix it, and a proper handover that keeps the customer's trust.

I look at it with them and say they're right. I don't tell them it's nothing. I ask the detail team if it can be buffed out right then. If not, I write up a repair promise with a date, signed by my manager, so they have it on paper. Then I finish the handover properly. Since then I walk around every car myself before the customer arrives.
A customer who bought last week calls upset because the check engine light came on. What do you do?
How you take care of customers after the sale.
Calm listening, a fast service appointment, follow-through until it is fixed, and staying the customer's main contact.

I listen first and say I'm sorry it happened. Then I walk over to service, book them the soonest slot, and ask about a loaner or a ride if our store offers one. I call them after the visit to make sure it's fixed. Often it's something simple, but they don't know that yet. How I handle this call decides whether they buy from me again.
Tell me about a month when you were behind your sales target. What did you change?
How you respond to a slow month with action, not excuses.
A look at where deals were lost, more follow-up and prospecting, and specific changes with a result.

Two years ago I was at 6 cars by the 20th with a target of 12. I went through my CRM and found 15 people who had driven a car and not heard from me in over a week. I called every one. Four came back in and two bought. I finished at 10. Since then I block an hour each day for follow-up, even on busy days.
How do you keep up with new models, trims and features, including EVs and hybrids?
Whether you keep learning about the product you sell.
Manufacturer training, driving the cars, knowing how features work in daily use, and honest answers when you do not know something.

I finish the manufacturer training modules when a new model comes in, and I drive every new trim myself. For EVs I learned how home and public charging work in plain terms, because that's the first thing buyers ask. If a customer asks something I'm not sure of, like exact charging times, I say I'll check and get back to them that day, rather than guess.
Describe a time you steered a customer to a cheaper car because it fit them better.
Whether you put the customer's needs ahead of a bigger commission.
Listening to how the customer will use the car, a recommendation that fits, and the long-term result of that honesty.

A young couple came in for a large SUV, but they had one child and a long commute. I showed them a smaller crossover with better fuel economy and the safety features they wanted, about $7,000 less. They bought it. A year later they sent her parents to me, and they bought two cars. A smaller sale that fits beats a big one they regret.
How do you use the slow hours on the showroom floor?
Whether you stay productive without a customer in front of you.
Follow-up calls, CRM updates, learning the inventory, and reaching out to past customers instead of waiting for walk-ins.

I work my CRM first: calls and texts to recent leads and people who drove a car but didn't buy. Then I check new arrivals so I know what's on the lot. I also send short notes to past buyers about a service reminder or a model they asked about. Walk-ins are a bonus. Most of my sales come from people I followed up with.

react-developer.heading: React developer questions
qs: A useEffect that fetches data runs in an endless loop and keeps hitting the API. How do you find and fix the cause?
Whether you understand how React compares effect dependencies between renders.
Spots an object, array or function recreated on every render in the dependency list, or state the effect both sets and depends on, and fixes the dependencies instead of silencing the linter.

After a refactor, a dashboard sent about 40 requests a second. The effect depended on a filters object built inline in the parent, so it was a new object on every render, and the effect set state that re-rendered the parent. I changed the dependencies to the two primitive values the effect actually used, and the loop stopped. The exhaustive-deps lint rule now stays on.
A table of 2,000 rows lags on every keystroke in the search box above it. How do you approach it?
Whether you measure render cost before reaching for memoization.
Profiles first with the React DevTools Profiler, then applies memo, stable props, useDeferredValue or list virtualization depending on what the profile shows.

I record a profile in React DevTools first. In one app every keystroke re-rendered all 2,000 rows because the parent passed a new onSelect function each time. I wrapped the row in React.memo, made the handler stable with useCallback and used useDeferredValue for the filter text. A keystroke went from about 300 ms to under 20 ms. If that had not been enough, I would have virtualized the list.
Two sibling components need the same value, and someone keeps two copies in sync with useEffect. What would you change?
Whether you know when to lift state up instead of syncing copies.
Moves the state to the closest common parent or derives it, deletes the syncing effects, and only reaches for context or a store when passing props gets deep.

Syncing copies with effects costs an extra render and leaves moments where one copy is stale. I move the state to the nearest common parent and pass the value and a setter down. In one checkout form this removed two effects and a flicker where the total showed the old price for one frame. If the props had to pass through five layers, I would consider context, but not before.
A user types fast in a search field and sometimes sees results for an older query. Why does that happen and how do you fix it?
Whether you can handle race conditions when fetching data in effects.
Explains that responses can arrive out of order, and fixes it with an AbortController or ignore flag in the effect cleanup, or a library like TanStack Query that caches by query key.

The request for "re" can come back after the one for "react" and overwrite the newer results. In the effect I create an AbortController, pass its signal to fetch and abort in the cleanup, so only the latest request can set state. On a larger project we moved to TanStack Query, which keys the cache by the search term and handles this for us.
A child component loses what the user typed every time its parent re-renders. What are the likely causes?
Whether you know how React decides to keep or reset component state.
Names a component defined inside another component's body, a key that changes on every render, or a condition that swaps the element type at that position.

The most common cause I have seen is a component declared inside the parent's function, so each render creates a new component type and React remounts it. On one settings page that wiped a half-filled form every time a toast appeared. Moving the inner component to module level fixed it. I also check for keys built from Math.random() or from indexes in lists that reorder.
How would you organize server data, global UI state and form state in a mid-sized React app?
Whether you pick the right tool for each kind of state instead of one global store.
Keeps server data in a cache like TanStack Query or framework loaders, small global UI state in context or a small store, and form state local, with reasons for each.

Server data goes in TanStack Query, because caching, refetching and loading states are already solved there. The theme and the current user go in context, or Zustand if they change often. Form state stays in the form, usually with React Hook Form. On my last project this let us delete about 1,500 lines of Redux code that only mirrored API responses.
When would you use useLayoutEffect instead of useEffect, and what does it cost?
Whether you know when effects run relative to the browser paint.
useLayoutEffect runs after React updates the DOM but before paint, so it suits measuring layout to avoid a visible jump. It blocks painting and does not run during server rendering.

I use useLayoutEffect when I must measure something, like a tooltip's height, and position it before the user sees it. It runs before the browser paints, so heavy work there makes the page feel slow. In a popover component, switching to it removed a one-frame flicker at the wrong position. Everything else stays in useEffect.
What changed about batching state updates in React 18, and how can it affect existing code?
Whether you know automatic batching and what it changes in practice.
With createRoot, React 18 batches updates inside promises, timeouts and native event handlers too, not only React events. flushSync opts out when a DOM read must see the update.

Before React 18, two setState calls after an await or inside a setTimeout caused two renders. With createRoot they are batched into one, as in click handlers. After our upgrade, one test that counted renders failed, and one function read the DOM right after setState and expected the new value. For that rare case I wrapped the update in flushSync.
In development your effect runs twice and sends two analytics events. Is that a bug, and what do you do?
Whether you understand what StrictMode does in development and why.
Knows that StrictMode in React 18 and later mounts, unmounts and remounts components in development to expose missing cleanup, and fixes the effect instead of removing StrictMode.

It is StrictMode in React 18 and later. In development it mounts each component, unmounts it and mounts it again, to show effects that do not clean up. Production is not affected. For a subscription or a timer I add a proper cleanup. For a page-view event I leave it, because the double call only happens in development and we do not send dev events to the real analytics project.
What can and cannot go inside a React Server Component, for example in the Next.js App Router?
Whether you understand the split between server and client components.
They run only on the server, can be async, read data directly and ship no JavaScript, but cannot use state, effects or browser APIs. Props passed to client components must be serializable.

In the App Router, components are server components by default. They can be async, query the database directly and add nothing to the client bundle, but they cannot use useState, useEffect or window. When I need interactivity, I make a small component with the "use client" directive and pass it serializable props. On one product page this cut the JavaScript we shipped by about 40%.
Tell us about a bug you shipped to production in a React app. How was it found, and what changed afterward?
Whether you own mistakes and improve the process after them.
A specific bug, how it was noticed, how it was fixed or rolled back, and a lasting change such as a test, a lint rule or a review habit.

During a cleanup I removed type="button" from a shared IconButton. Buttons inside a form default to submit, so on the address page every icon click saved a half-filled address. It ran for about two hours before a support ticket flagged it. I reverted, added a test for the button inside a form, and now I search all usages before changing a shared component's defaults.
How do you review a React pull request, and what do you look for beyond style?
Whether your code reviews catch real problems and stay respectful.
Runs the change, checks effects and cleanup, state placement, loading and error states, accessibility, tests and bundle impact, and writes clear comments marked as blocking or optional.

I run the branch and try the unhappy paths: slow network, an empty list, an error from the API. In the code I look at effects and their cleanup, where state lives, labels and keyboard access, and new dependencies that grow the bundle. Formatting is Prettier's job. I mark which comments block the merge, and if a thread passes three replies, I suggest a short call.
Describe a major React upgrade you did, such as 17 to 18 or 18 to 19. How did you plan it?
How you plan risky upgrades without stopping feature work.
Reads the release notes, checks third-party libraries first, uses the official codemods, works in small steps behind tests, and keeps feature work going.

We moved a 200-component app from React 17 to 18. First I checked our libraries; two were not compatible, so we upgraded them on their own. Then I switched to createRoot in a branch, fixed the effects that the StrictMode double mount exposed, and ran our tests and a manual pass of the main flows. It shipped in two weeks alongside feature work, with no rollback.
What does your testing strategy for a React app look like, and what do you deliberately not test?
Whether you test what users see rather than implementation details.
Component tests with React Testing Library that query by role and label, mocked APIs with a tool like MSW, a few end-to-end tests for key flows, and no tests of internal state.

Most of my tests use React Testing Library and find elements by role and label, the way a user would. I mock the API with MSW so components get realistic responses. About 10 Playwright tests cover sign-up, checkout and other paths that touch money. I do not test internal state or large snapshots, because they break on every refactor without catching real bugs.

nodejs-developer.heading: Node.js developer questions
qs: After a release, API latency jumps from 50 ms to 2 seconds for everyone, and one CPU core sits at 100%. How do you find what is blocking the event loop?
Whether you can find and remove synchronous work that blocks the event loop.
Measures event loop delay, takes a CPU profile under load, looks for sync crypto, fs or zlib calls, huge JSON or bad regex, and moves heavy work off the main thread.

I take a CPU profile with node --cpu-prof under load. In one case a new endpoint called bcrypt's hashSync with a cost of 12 on every login, which blocked the loop for about 250 ms each time. Switching to the async hash, which runs in the libuv thread pool, brought p95 latency back to 60 ms. For CPU-heavy work like PDF generation, I use worker threads or a queue.
Your Node process crashed in production with an unhandled promise rejection. What happened, and how do you prevent it?
Whether you know how Node treats unhandled rejections and how to handle async errors.
Knows that since Node 15 an unhandled rejection exits the process by default, finds the missing await or catch, and adds a process handler that logs and exits cleanly.

Since Node 15, an unhandled rejection crashes the process by default. In our case a fire-and-forget call to send a welcome email had no catch, so when the mail provider timed out, the whole API restarted. I added a catch with logging, turned on the typescript-eslint no-floating-promises rule, and added an unhandledRejection handler that logs and shuts down cleanly.
Memory on a Node service grows by about 100 MB a day until the container is killed. How do you track down the leak?
Your method for finding memory leaks in a long-running Node process.
Compares heap snapshots taken hours apart, looks for growing maps, caches, listeners or timers, fixes the cause with limits or cleanup, and confirms with memory metrics.

I take two heap snapshots a few hours apart, with --inspect or v8.writeHeapSnapshot, and compare them in Chrome DevTools. Last time the growth was a plain object used as a cache keyed by request ID that was never cleared. I replaced it with an LRU cache capped at 10,000 entries, and memory stayed flat at about 300 MB for a week.
One client is hitting your public API at 500 requests a second. How do you add rate limiting?
Whether you can design rate limiting that works across several server instances.
Picks an algorithm like token bucket or sliding window, keeps counters in Redis or at the gateway when there are several instances, limits per key and returns 429 with Retry-After.

With several instances, in-memory counters do not work, so I keep them in Redis or set the limit at the API gateway. I limit per API key with a sliding window, for example 100 requests a minute, and return 429 with a Retry-After header. For one partner we raised the limit in their plan instead of blocking them. A dashboard shows who hits the limit.
How do you make a Node service shut down gracefully when Kubernetes sends SIGTERM?
Whether you avoid dropped requests and broken jobs during deploys.
Handles SIGTERM, fails readiness, stops new connections with server.close, lets in-flight work finish, closes pools and consumers, and forces exit before the grace period ends.

On SIGTERM I first make the readiness probe fail so no new traffic arrives, then call server.close and let in-flight requests finish. After that I close the database pool and the queue consumer. A timer forces exit after 25 seconds, before the default 30-second grace period ends. This took our 502 errors during deploys from a few hundred per release to zero.
A route has to process a 2 GB CSV upload. How do you design it so the server does not run out of memory?
Whether you use streams and backpressure instead of loading everything into memory.
Streams the upload instead of buffering it, parses row by row with stream.pipeline, writes in batches, and moves long processing to a background job with progress status.

I never read the whole file into memory. The request body streams to object storage, then a background worker reads it as a stream, parses it with a streaming CSV parser and inserts rows in batches of 1,000. I connect the steps with stream.pipeline so errors and backpressure are handled. Memory stayed under 150 MB for a 2 GB file, and users saw a progress bar.
What runs in the libuv thread pool and what does not, and why does it matter for performance?
Whether you know what actually runs off the main thread in Node.
File system calls, dns.lookup, zlib and some crypto like pbkdf2 and scrypt use the pool of 4 threads by default. Network sockets do not. UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE can raise the pool size.

Network I/O does not use the thread pool; the operating system notifies libuv through epoll or kqueue. File system calls, dns.lookup, zlib and crypto functions like pbkdf2 do, and the pool has 4 threads by default. I once saw slow logins because pbkdf2 calls queued behind file reads. Raising UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE to 16 helped, and so did caching those reads.
In what order do process.nextTick, promise callbacks and setImmediate run, and when does that matter?
Whether you understand microtasks and event loop phases in Node.
nextTick callbacks and promise callbacks run before the loop moves on, setImmediate runs in the check phase after I/O, and recursive nextTick or microtasks can starve I/O.

process.nextTick callbacks run right after the current operation, usually before promise callbacks, and both run before the event loop moves on. setImmediate runs in the check phase, after I/O callbacks. I prefer setImmediate for yielding, because a recursive nextTick can starve I/O. I saw that once in a retry helper that kept a socket from ever being read.
When would you use worker threads, child processes or the cluster module in Node?
Whether you pick the right tool for parallel work in Node.
Worker threads for CPU-heavy JavaScript in a small pool, child processes for running other programs or isolating crashes, and cluster or more containers to use more cores for HTTP.

Worker threads are for CPU-heavy JavaScript like image resizing, with a small pool rather than one worker per request. Child processes are for running other programs, like ffmpeg, or when a crash must stay isolated. To use more cores for HTTP in Kubernetes, I run more pods with one process each instead of cluster. On a resize service, a pool of 4 workers tripled throughput.
How do you handle configuration and secrets in a Node service, and what does the --env-file flag change?
Whether you handle config safely and fail fast on bad values.
Reads config from environment variables, validates it at startup with a schema, keeps secrets in a secret manager, and knows Node 20.6 and later can load .env files with --env-file.

All config comes from environment variables, validated at startup with a zod schema, so a missing DATABASE_URL stops the service at boot instead of at the first request. Locally I use a .env file, and since Node 20.6 I load it with --env-file instead of the dotenv package. In production, secrets come from AWS Secrets Manager and never sit in the image or the repo.
Tell us about an incident in a Node service that you caused. What did you change afterward?
Whether you own production mistakes and fix the process, not just the bug.
A concrete incident, how it was detected, the fix, and a lasting change such as a test, an alert, a timeout or a review rule.

I added a call to a third-party tax API without a timeout. When their service slowed down, our requests piled up, the connection pool filled and checkout failed for about 20 minutes. I added a 3-second timeout with AbortSignal.timeout, a fallback rate and an alert on pool usage. Our review checklist now asks about a timeout on every new outbound call.
How did you plan a Node.js upgrade across major versions, for example from 18 to 22?
How you handle runtime upgrades safely, since Node majors reach end of life on a fixed schedule.
Follows the LTS schedule, adds the new version to CI first, checks native modules and deprecations, tests in staging under load, and rolls out one service at a time.

Node 18 reached end of life in April 2025, so we moved 12 services to Node 22. I added Node 22 to the CI matrix first, which showed two native modules that needed new versions. We updated the base Docker image in staging, ran load tests to compare latency, then rolled out one service at a time over three weeks. Only one service needed a code change.
How do you review a pull request for a Node API? What do you look for?
Whether your reviews catch reliability and security problems.
Input validation, awaited promises and error handling, timeouts on outbound calls, N+1 queries, personal data in logs, and tests, with comments marked as blocking or optional.

I check that every input is validated, every promise is awaited or handled, and outbound calls have timeouts. I look for N+1 queries, missing indexes for new filters and logs that print tokens or emails. If the change touches money or auth, I run the tests locally. I mark which comments block the merge, and I approve quickly when the code is good.
How do you test a Node API, and where do you draw the line between unit and integration tests?
Whether your tests give confidence without being slow or brittle.
Unit tests for pure logic, HTTP-level integration tests against a real database in a container, stubbed external APIs, and as few mocks of your own code as possible.

Pure logic, like pricing rules, gets fast unit tests. For routes I run integration tests over HTTP with supertest against a real Postgres started by Testcontainers, because a mocked database once hid a bug for us. External APIs are stubbed with nock. The suite has about 600 tests and runs in under 3 minutes in CI, so people actually run it.

javascript-developer.heading: TypeScript and JavaScript developer questions
qs: A teammate typed an API response as any, and a renamed field caused a crash in production. How would you type it instead?
Whether you know the difference between any and unknown and validate data at the edges.
Uses unknown at boundaries so the compiler forces a check, validates with a schema library like zod or a type guard, and infers the type from the schema.

any turns off checking, so the code still compiled after the backend renamed userName to username. I typed the response as unknown, which forces a check before use, and parsed it with a zod schema. The TypeScript type is inferred from the schema, so there is one definition. Now a changed field fails at the boundary with a clear error instead of showing undefined in the UI.
You have a union type for an API result that is either success or error. How do you narrow it, and how do you make sure every case is handled?
Whether you can use discriminated unions and exhaustiveness checks.
Adds a literal field like status to each variant, narrows with switch or if, and assigns to never in the default branch so a new variant fails to compile.

I give each variant a literal field, like status: 'success' or status: 'error', and switch on it. TypeScript narrows the type in each branch, so data only exists where it should. In the default branch I assign the value to a variable of type never. When a teammate added a 'pending' state, the compiler pointed to the four places we had not handled.
A quantity of 0 shows as missing, and an ID check fails for some records. Which equality and coercion bugs do you look for?
Whether you can spot coercion bugs with falsy values and mixed types.
Checks for truthy tests that drop 0 or an empty string, || defaults that replace valid falsy values, and comparisons between strings and numbers, fixed with ??, === and explicit conversion.

The zero bug was a check written as if (item.qty), which treats 0 as missing, plus qty || 1 further down. I changed them to an undefined check and ??. The ID bug came from comparing a number from the API with a string from the URL using ===, which is correctly false. I convert the URL value with Number once, at the edge, and the eqeqeq lint rule keeps == out.
A method passed as a callback loses this and throws "Cannot read properties of undefined". Why, and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand that this is set by how a function is called.
Explains that passing a method detaches it from its object, so this is undefined in strict code, and fixes it with an arrow function, bind or a class field arrow.

this is decided by how a function is called, not where it is written. Passing this.save to promise.then or array.map calls it without an object, and class bodies are strict mode, so this is undefined. I fix it with an arrow function at the call site or a class field defined as an arrow. I avoid bind inside code that runs often, because it creates a new function each time.
Your package works with require but breaks when imported from an ES module, or the other way around. How do you handle ESM and CommonJS?
Whether you understand the practical differences between ESM and CommonJS in Node.
Knows the type field and .mjs or .cjs extensions set the format, uses the exports field with import and require conditions, and knows newer Node versions can require ESM.

The format depends on the type field in package.json and on the .mjs or .cjs extension. For a library I publish both builds and map them in the exports field with import and require conditions, plus types. I watch for two copies of the package holding separate state. Since Node 20.19 and 22.12, require can load an ES module that has no top-level await.
A loop that awaits one API call per item takes 40 seconds for 200 items. How would you speed it up without overloading the API?
Whether you can run async work concurrently with limits and handle partial failures.
Replaces sequential awaits with limited concurrency using a limiter or batches, uses Promise.allSettled so one failure does not sink the rest, and respects the API's rate limit.

Each call took about 200 ms, and awaiting them one by one added up. I ran them with a concurrency limit of 10 using p-limit and Promise.allSettled, so one failed item did not reject the whole batch. The job went from 40 seconds to about 4. I picked 10 after checking the API's rate limit, and failed items are logged and retried once.
What does turning on strictNullChecks change in a TypeScript project, and how would you enable it in a large existing codebase?
Whether you know what the strict flags catch and how to adopt them gradually.
Knows null and undefined stop fitting every type, plans a gradual rollout by folder with error tracking, and avoids mass fixes with any or the ! operator.

With strictNullChecks, null and undefined no longer fit into every type, so the compiler finds places that can crash. In a 300-file app turning it on gave about 1,200 errors. We fixed them folder by folder, tracked the count in CI so it could only go down, and did not allow new non-null assertions without a reason. We found three real crashes along the way.
What does the satisfies operator do in TypeScript, and when is it better than a type annotation?
Whether you know newer TypeScript features and how type inference works.
satisfies checks a value against a type but keeps the narrower inferred type, while an annotation widens it to the declared type. It was added in TypeScript 4.9.

With an annotation like const routes: Record<string, Route>, TypeScript forgets which keys exist, so a typo like routes.hmoe compiles. With satisfies Record<string, Route>, the object is still checked, but the type keeps the exact keys, so the typo fails. It came in TypeScript 4.9. I use it for config objects and lookup tables where I want both checking and autocomplete.
How do microtasks and tasks interact when you mix setTimeout, promises and async/await in the browser, and when has that surprised you?
Whether you understand microtasks versus tasks in practice.
Code after await and promise callbacks run as microtasks before the next task such as setTimeout, and the browser cannot paint until the microtask queue is empty.

Code after an await runs as a microtask, so it runs before any setTimeout callback, even one with a 0 ms delay. The browser also cannot paint until the microtask queue is empty. I hit this when a loop chained 10,000 promises to process data, and the spinner never appeared. Splitting the work into chunks with setTimeout, so the browser could paint between them, fixed it.
How do you choose between a Map and a plain object, or a Set and an array, in JavaScript?
Whether you pick data structures for behavior and performance, not habit.
Map for dynamic or non-string keys and frequent changes with no prototype keys, Set for fast membership checks, plain objects for fixed shapes and JSON.

For a fixed shape, like a user record sent as JSON, I use an object. For a lookup filled at runtime, I use a Map: keys can be any type, size is built in, and a key like constructor cannot clash with the prototype. For membership checks I use a Set. Replacing array.includes over 50,000 IDs with a Set cut a sync job from 9 seconds to under 1.
Tell us about a bug you shipped that TypeScript did not catch. Why did it slip through?
Whether you understand the limits of static types and learn from mistakes.
A real case such as unchecked JSON, a type assertion, array index access or a time zone issue, plus a concrete step that prevents the same class of bug.

I wrote items[0].price in a cart summary, and TypeScript allowed it because index access is typed as always defined by default. An empty cart crashed the page for about 30 minutes. I added a guard and a test for the empty cart, and we turned on noUncheckedIndexedAccess. It flagged 40 more places, and two of them were real bugs.
How did you migrate a JavaScript codebase to TypeScript, or how would you plan it?
Whether you can plan a gradual migration without freezing feature work.
Starts with allowJs, converts shared modules and API clients first, requires new files in TypeScript, tracks progress, and limits any with clear rules.

We had about 400 JavaScript files. I turned on allowJs so both could live together, then converted shared utilities and API clients first, because everything depends on them. New files had to be TypeScript. We tracked the remaining JS files and converted them when we touched them. It took five months alongside feature work, and any was allowed only with a comment.
When you review TypeScript code, which patterns make you ask for changes?
Whether your reviews keep the type system honest.
as casts on outside data, any without a reason, unneeded non-null assertions, generic types nobody can read, and floating promises, each explained calmly.

I push back on as casts on data from outside, any without a comment, and the ! operator where a simple check would do. I ask to simplify generic types that take five minutes to read, because someone else has to maintain them. A floating promise blocks the merge for me. I explain the reason in each comment and link to our guidelines, so it does not feel personal.
How do you decide what to test in a TypeScript codebase when the types already catch a lot?
Whether you balance types and tests instead of duplicating effort.
Skips tests the compiler already proves, focuses on business logic, edge cases and integration points, and keeps a small set of end-to-end tests for key flows.

I do not write tests that only check a function gets a string; the compiler does that. Tests go to business logic, edge cases like empty input or time zones, and the integration with the API. We use Vitest, and about 1,500 tests run in 40 seconds. A few Playwright tests cover login and payment. A bug that reaches production gets a test first, then the fix.

angular-vue-developer.heading: Angular and Vue developer questions
qs: In an Angular component with OnPush, the data changes but the view does not update. What do you check?
Whether you understand Angular change detection with OnPush.
Knows OnPush reacts to new input references, events, the async pipe and signals, finds mutated objects or updates from outside Angular, and fixes them with immutable updates or signals.

With OnPush, Angular rechecks a component when an input reference changes, an event fires inside it, the async pipe emits or a signal it reads changes. In our case a service mutated an array with push, so the reference stayed the same. I changed it to create a new array and later moved that state to a signal. markForCheck is my last resort, for third-party callbacks.
In Vue 3, a value changes but the template keeps showing the old one. What are the common causes?
Whether you understand how Vue 3 reactivity tracks changes.
Destructuring a reactive object, reassigning a variable that held reactive(), or changing nested data in a shallowRef, fixed with toRefs, ref or replacing the whole value.

The most common cause I see is destructuring a reactive object, which copies plain values; toRefs fixes that. Props destructured from defineProps stay reactive only since Vue 3.5. Another cause is reassigning a variable that held reactive(), so the template keeps the old object, which is why I prefer ref. With shallowRef, a nested change is not tracked, so I replace the value.
A component subscribes to an observable in ngOnInit, and memory grows as users navigate. How do you fix it, and how do you clean up in Vue?
Whether you clean up subscriptions and watchers to avoid leaks.
Uses the async pipe, toSignal or takeUntilDestroyed in Angular, and in Vue knows watchers made synchronously in setup stop on their own while others need manual cleanup.

Each visit added a subscription to an interval that never ended. In Angular I prefer the async pipe or toSignal, and for manual subscriptions takeUntilDestroyed, added in Angular 16. In Vue, watchers created synchronously in setup stop on unmount, but one created in an async callback, or a window listener, needs cleanup in onUnmounted. After the fix, memory stayed flat over 50 navigations.
A component deep in the tree needs to tell a distant component that the cart changed. How do you set up the communication?
Whether you choose the right communication pattern for the distance between components.
Inputs and outputs or props and emits for parent and child, a shared service with signals or a store like Pinia or NgRx for distant parts, and no global event bus.

For parent and child I use inputs and outputs in Angular, or props and emits in Vue. For distant parts I put the cart in shared state: a service with a signal in Angular, a Pinia store in Vue. The header reads the count, and the product page calls addItem. I avoid global event buses, because in one Vue 2 app nobody could tell who listened to a cart-updated event.
The first load of your Angular or Vue app downloads 3 MB of JavaScript. How do you use lazy loading to fix it?
Whether you can split bundles by route and measure the result.
Lazy loads routes with loadComponent or loadChildren in Angular and dynamic imports in Vue Router, defers heavy widgets, and checks the result with a bundle analyzer.

I look at the bundle analyzer first. In one Angular app the admin area and a charting library were in the main bundle. I moved admin routes to loadChildren and the chart into a @defer block, which Angular has had since version 17. In Vue I use dynamic imports for routes and defineAsyncComponent for heavy widgets. The initial bundle went from 3 MB to about 900 KB.
A Vue watcher or an Angular effect updates state and keeps triggering itself until the page freezes. How do you untangle it?
Whether you can avoid reactive loops and prefer derived state.
Replaces the watcher or effect with a computed value for derived data, keeps raw input separate from output, and uses watch or effect only for side effects like API calls.

Usually the watcher sets a value it also watches. In a Vue form, a watcher rounded a price and wrote it back, which fired the watcher again. I replaced it with a computed value for display and kept the raw input separate. In Angular I use computed signals for derived values and keep effect for side effects, like saving to localStorage, not for setting other signals.
What do Angular signals change compared with change detection driven by Zone.js?
Whether you follow how Angular is moving toward signals and zoneless apps.
Zone.js patches async APIs and triggers broad checks, while signals tell Angular exactly which value changed and which views read it, which makes zoneless apps possible.

Zone.js patches browser APIs and tells Angular that something async happened, so it checks the tree, or the OnPush parts that are marked. Signals say exactly which value changed and which views read it. With signals and zoneless change detection, stable since Angular 20.2, the app does less work and drops Zone.js. I build new features with signals first.
How do the Options API and the Composition API compare in Vue 3, and when would you move a component over?
Whether you know both Vue APIs and can judge when a migration pays off.
Both are supported in Vue 3. The Composition API groups logic by feature and allows composables and better TypeScript. Migrate when logic is shared or a component is hard to follow.

Both are fully supported in Vue 3, so I do not rewrite working components just to switch. I move a component to script setup when its logic is reused elsewhere or it has grown to 500 lines spread across data, methods and watch. Then I pull the shared parts into composables, like useOrderFilters. TypeScript also works much better with the Composition API.
How does dependency injection scope work in Angular, and what goes wrong when a service is provided in the wrong place?
Whether you understand the injector hierarchy and service lifetimes in Angular.
providedIn root gives one app-wide instance. Providing it in a component or a lazy route creates new instances, which splits state by accident or isolates it on purpose.

providedIn: 'root' gives one instance for the whole app. If someone also lists the service in a component's providers, that component and its children get their own copy. We had a cart service that showed 0 items in the header because a feature component provided it again. Removing that provider fixed it. I do provide services per component on purpose, for example for a wizard's state.
What is the difference between switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap and exhaustMap in RxJS, and where have you used each?
Whether you can pick the right RxJS flattening operator for real cases.
switchMap cancels the previous inner observable, concatMap queues in order, mergeMap runs in parallel, and exhaustMap ignores new triggers while one is running.

I use switchMap for type-ahead search, so an older request is canceled when the user keeps typing. concatMap fits saves that must happen in order, like autosave of a document. mergeMap runs things in parallel, for example loading 20 thumbnails. exhaustMap ignores clicks while a request runs, which is how we stopped duplicate orders when users double-clicked Pay.
Tell us about an Angular or Vue major version upgrade you did. What broke and how did you handle it?
How you plan big framework upgrades and deal with breaking changes.
Uses official tools like ng update or the Vue migration build, upgrades step by step, deals with third-party libraries first, and keeps tests passing throughout.

I led a Vue 2 to Vue 3 migration of about 150 components. We used the migration build, @vue/compat, to run the app on Vue 3 with warnings, then fixed them module by module. The hardest part was a UI library with no Vue 3 version, which we replaced. Filters and the global event bus also had to go. It took four months alongside feature work, with two weeks of testing in staging.
Describe a production bug you caused in an Angular or Vue app and what you changed afterward.
Whether you own mistakes and leave the code safer.
A specific bug, how users were affected, the fix, and a lasting change such as a test, a lint rule or a review habit.

I put v-if on a component holding a multi-step form. When a background refresh briefly set the data to null, the form unmounted and users lost what they had typed. About 200 users hit it in one day before support flagged it. I kept the form mounted and showed a loading overlay instead, added a test for a refresh during editing, and now I check what unmounts when data reloads.
What do you look for when you review an Angular or Vue pull request?
Whether your reviews catch framework-specific problems early.
Subscriptions and watchers cleaned up, no heavy functions in templates, state in the right place, props not mutated, accessibility, tests and bundle size of new imports.

In Angular I check for manual subscriptions without takeUntilDestroyed, functions called in templates, which run on every change detection pass, and services provided in the wrong place. In Vue I look for watchers that should be computed values and props mutated in a child. In both I check keyboard access and the size of new libraries. I say which comments block the merge.
How do you test Angular or Vue components, and how much do you rely on end-to-end tests?
Whether your testing strategy is balanced and focused on behavior.
Unit tests for services and stores, component tests through the DOM with Testing Library or Vue Test Utils, mocked HTTP, and a small set of end-to-end tests.

Services, stores and pure functions get unit tests with Vitest or Jest. I test components through the DOM with Testing Library, clicking and reading text like a user would, with HTTP mocked. About 15 Playwright tests cover login, search and checkout and run on every merge. I keep end-to-end tests few, because each one is slow and flaky ones quickly lose the team's trust.

sql-developer.heading: SQL developer questions
qs: A monthly sales report that ran in 4 seconds now takes 3 minutes after the orders table grew to 40 million rows. How do you find the cause?
Your method for diagnosing a query that slowed down as data grew.
Measure first, read the actual execution plan, check indexes, statistics and predicates, and test one change at a time against realistic data.

First I capture the actual execution plan and the reads, not just the time. In one case the plan showed a full scan of orders because the filter wrapped order_date in a function, so the index could not be used. I rewrote it as a plain date range, added an index on order_date that included the columns the report needed, and the report dropped to 6 seconds.
In an execution plan, one operator shows 12 estimated rows and 2 million actual rows. What does that tell you and what do you check?
Whether you can read a plan and spot a bad row estimate.
The optimizer planned for a tiny input. Likely causes are stale statistics, a hidden column in a function or conversion, or a table variable. Fix the estimate before reaching for hints.

It means the optimizer planned for a tiny input, so it likely chose nested loops and a small memory grant. I check when statistics were last updated, whether the predicate hides the column in a function or implicit conversion, or uses a table variable, since older SQL Server versions guess one row for those. A full-scan statistics update once turned a nested loop over 2 million rows into a hash join.
A stored procedure is fast for most customers but takes minutes for your largest one, and recompiling it helps for a while. What is going on?
Whether you understand plan caching and parameter sensitivity.
A plan compiled for one parameter value is reused for very different data sizes. Names fixes like recompiling, optimizing for a value or splitting the procedure, with their costs.

This is parameter sniffing. The plan is compiled for the first value passed, say a customer with 50 orders, and reused for a customer with 3 million. In SQL Server I confirm it by comparing the compiled parameter values in the cached plan with the slow call. The fix depends on call volume: OPTION (RECOMPILE) for a report run a few times a day, OPTIMIZE FOR, or a separate path for the largest customers.
Two nightly jobs keep failing with deadlock errors on the same tables. How do you investigate and fix it?
How you diagnose deadlocks instead of only adding retries.
Captures the deadlock graph, finds the resources and lock order, then fixes access order, indexing or transaction length. Retries are a safety net, not the fix.

In SQL Server I pull the deadlock graph from the system_health extended events session. In one case job A updated invoices then payments, while job B did payments then invoices. I changed B to touch the tables in the same order and added an index so its update stopped scanning and locking extra rows. Deadlocks went from about 3 a week to none, and I kept a retry for the rare one.
A revenue report shows totals three times higher than finance expects after you joined orders to shipments. What happened and how do you fix it?
Whether you catch row multiplication from one-to-many joins.
Recognizes that the join multiplies rows, checks the grain of each table, and aggregates before joining or uses EXISTS instead of summing duplicated rows.

An order with three shipments appears three times after the join, so its amount is summed three times. I check the grain by counting rows per order_id on each side. The fix is to aggregate shipments per order in a CTE first, then join, or use EXISTS if I only need to know the order shipped. I also add a check that the report total matches the orders table alone.
You need to add a NOT NULL column to a 200-million-row production table that is used around the clock. How do you do it safely?
Whether you can change a large live table without long locks or downtime.
Knows the engine and version matter, adds the column nullable or with a fast default, backfills in batches, enforces NOT NULL last, and rehearses with a rollback plan.

It depends on the engine. In PostgreSQL 11 and later, and SQL Server 2012 Enterprise and later, adding a column with a constant default is a quick metadata change. Otherwise I add it as nullable, backfill in batches of 10,000 rows with short pauses, then enforce NOT NULL. I rehearse on a restored copy of production, run it in a quiet hour and keep a rollback script ready.
When do you reach for a window function instead of GROUP BY? Give a report where it made the query simpler.
Whether you know how to keep detail rows while computing aggregates.
Window functions keep each row while adding running totals, ranks or comparisons, which removes self-joins. A strong answer mentions partitions and the default frame.

When I need the detail rows and an aggregate side by side. For one sales report I needed each order plus the customer's running total and rank in the month. With GROUP BY that took a self-join; with SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) it was one pass. I set the frame to ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING, because the default RANGE frame lumps orders with the same date together.
How do you decide the key columns and included columns for a new index on a busy table?
Whether you design indexes around real queries and their write cost.
Starts from the queries: equality columns first, then range columns, included columns to cover the output, and a check for overlapping indexes and write cost.

I start from the queries, not the table. For WHERE status = 'open' AND created_at > a date, I put status first, then created_at, and include the few columns the query returns so it never goes back to the base table. Before adding it I look for an existing index with the same leading columns, because every index slows writes. On one table with 9 indexes I dropped 3 that had no reads in a month.
Why can NOT IN with a subquery return no rows at all, and what do you use instead?
Whether you understand how NULL behaves in filters.
Explains that one NULL in the subquery makes NOT IN unknown for every row, and uses NOT EXISTS or filters out NULLs.

If the subquery returns even one NULL, x NOT IN (...) is unknown for every row, because comparing anything to NULL is unknown, so nothing comes back. I hit this when a list of excluded customers had one row with a NULL customer_id and the report went empty. I switched to NOT EXISTS with a correlated subquery, which handles NULLs the way people expect and usually gets an anti-join plan.
A report reading live order data shows a summary and a detail section that do not add up. How can isolation levels cause that, and what would you change?
Whether you know how isolation levels affect consistency in reports.
Separate statements under read committed can see different moments. Fixes include snapshot isolation, one statement, or a replica or snapshot copy. Warns against NOLOCK.

Under read committed each statement sees data as of its own start, so the summary and the detail can run seconds apart and disagree. In SQL Server I would run the report under snapshot isolation so every statement sees one point in time; in PostgreSQL, repeatable read does the same. I would not add NOLOCK, because it can skip or double count rows while pages move.
Tell me about a time a script you ran changed production data you did not mean to change. What do you do differently now?
Your honesty about mistakes and the safeguards you built after one.
A real, owned mistake, fast communication and recovery, and lasting habits like transactions, row-count checks and a second reviewer for data fixes.

Early on I ran an UPDATE on the customer table with a WHERE clause on the wrong column, and 4,200 rows got the wrong region. I told my lead within minutes, and we restored the old values from the previous night's backup into a side table and fixed them. Since then every data fix runs inside a transaction, I check the row count before committing, and a second person reads the script.
How do you review another developer's stored procedure or report query before it goes to production?
What you look for in SQL code review beyond style.
Correctness on edge cases, the plan on realistic data volume, set-based logic, transaction and error handling, safe dynamic SQL, and a respectful tone.

I read it for correctness first: NULL handling, join grain and date boundaries like the end of the month. Then I run it on a copy with production-sized data and look at the plan and reads. I flag cursors that could be set-based, dynamic SQL built by string concatenation, and transactions with no error handling. Where I am unsure, I write the comment as a question.
How do you test SQL code like stored procedures and report queries?
Whether you test database code with the same care as application code.
Repeatable tests on known data with tricky cases, a framework like tSQLt or pgTAP run in CI, and reconciliation of report totals against the source.

I keep small fixture datasets with the tricky cases: NULLs, duplicates, month boundaries and a customer with zero orders. For SQL Server procedures I use tSQLt, and pgTAP on PostgreSQL, run in CI against a database in a container. For reports I also reconcile totals with the source system; one check caught a 0.4% gap from orders placed around midnight UTC.
A junior developer on your team writes cursors for almost everything. How do you help them move to set-based SQL?
How you mentor someone toward set-based thinking.
Pairs on a real case, shows before and after numbers, explains the way of thinking, gives practice, and follows up in later reviews.

I pick one of their real procedures and we rewrite it together. In one case a cursor that updated prices row by row took 25 minutes for 300,000 rows, and the set-based UPDATE with a join took 9 seconds. Seeing the numbers did more than any rule. Then I ask them to describe the result they want before writing a loop, and I review their next few procedures closely.

dotnet-developer.heading: .NET and C# developer questions
qs: An ASP.NET Core endpoint stalls under load and the thread pool keeps growing. You find .Result calls on async methods. What is happening and how do you fix it?
Whether you understand sync over async and thread pool starvation.
Blocking on tasks ties up threads the async work needs, causing starvation in ASP.NET Core and deadlocks in UI apps. The fix is async all the way up.

Each .Result blocks a thread pool thread while the async call needs another thread to finish, so under load the pool runs dry and requests queue. ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, so it is starvation rather than the classic deadlock you get in WinForms or old ASP.NET. I made the call chain async all the way up, and p95 latency went from 8 seconds back to 120 ms.
A page listing 50 orders with their customers takes 2 seconds, and the SQL log shows 51 queries. What is wrong and how do you fix it in EF Core?
Whether you can spot and fix N+1 queries in EF Core.
Identifies lazy loading or queries in a loop, fixes with a projection or Include, knows when split queries help, and confirms with the logged SQL.

That is an N+1: one query for orders, then one per order for its customer, usually from lazy loading or a query inside a loop. I replace it with a projection, a Select into a small DTO with the customer name, which becomes one SQL join. If I need full entities I use Include, and AsSplitQuery when several collections would multiply rows. Then I check the log to confirm it is one query.
A background worker using EF Core gets slower and uses more memory every hour it runs. What do you look at?
Whether you know how change tracking and DbContext lifetime affect memory.
A long-lived DbContext tracking every entity it loaded. Fixes: a new context per batch, AsNoTracking for reads, ChangeTracker.Clear, sensible batch sizes.

My first suspect is one DbContext kept alive for the whole job, so the change tracker holds every entity it ever loaded and each SaveChanges gets slower. I create a new context per batch of 1,000 rows through IDbContextFactory, use AsNoTracking for read-only queries, and call ChangeTracker.Clear if a context must live longer. In one worker memory went from 3 GB to a flat 200 MB.
A singleton service takes a scoped DbContext in its constructor, and you start seeing errors about a disposed context under load. Explain and fix it.
Whether you understand DI lifetimes and captive dependencies.
Explains the captive dependency, knows scope validation catches it in Development, and fixes it by making the consumer scoped or creating a scope per operation.

The singleton captures the first DbContext and keeps it, so it is shared across requests and threads, which DbContext does not support. ASP.NET Core catches this at startup in Development through scope validation, so I keep ValidateScopes on in integration tests too. The fix is to make the consumer scoped, or inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope for each unit of work.
Memory in a long-running .NET service grows about 100 MB a day, and a dump shows thousands of objects kept alive through an event. How did that happen?
Whether you can trace a leak from event subscriptions with dump tools.
Short-lived objects subscribe to a long-lived publisher and never unsubscribe. Uses dumps and GC roots to prove it, and unsubscribes in Dispose.

A publisher holds a reference to every subscriber through the event's delegate list. If short-lived objects subscribe to a singleton's event and never unsubscribe, they can never be collected. I take two dumps with dotnet-dump a few hours apart, compare type counts, and run gcroot on a leaked object to see the chain. The fix was unsubscribing in Dispose and making sure those objects were really disposed.
How do you set up configuration so the same build runs in development, staging and production with different settings and secrets?
Whether you know the .NET configuration system and keep secrets out of source control.
Layered appsettings per environment, environment variables, user secrets locally, a vault in production, and typed options validated at startup.

I build once and let configuration layer: appsettings.json, then the file matching ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT, like appsettings.Staging.json, then environment variables, which win. Secrets sit in user secrets locally and Azure Key Vault in production, never in the repo. I bind sections to options classes with ValidateDataAnnotations and ValidateOnStart, so a missing setting fails the deploy, not the first request.
When do you choose a record over a class in C#, and what surprised you about record equality?
Whether you understand value equality and its limits in C# records.
Records fit immutable data with value equality. Knows equality is member by member, so collection properties compare by reference, and that entities need identity instead.

I use records for DTOs, messages and small value objects where two instances with the same data should be equal. The surprise is that equality is member by member, so a List property is compared by reference, and two records with equal lists are not equal. I avoid records for EF Core entities, because an entity needs identity, not value equality.
What is the practical difference between passing IQueryable and IEnumerable around in an EF Core app?
Whether you know where a LINQ query actually runs.
IQueryable is translated to SQL; IEnumerable runs in memory on loaded rows. Calling ToList or AsEnumerable too early loads too much. Careful about exposing IQueryable.

With IQueryable, Where and Select still become SQL, so filtering happens in the database. Once it is IEnumerable, everything after runs in memory on rows already loaded. I once found a repository returning IEnumerable of all invoices, and the caller filtered to 20 in C# after loading 600,000 rows. I also avoid returning IQueryable from public APIs, since callers can build queries that do not translate.
How do you use CancellationToken in an ASP.NET Core API, and what happens if you ignore it?
Whether you stop wasted work when a request is abandoned.
Takes the token in actions, passes it to EF Core and HttpClient calls, treats cancellation as normal rather than an error, and links tokens for timeouts.

I take a CancellationToken parameter in the action, which ASP.NET Core binds to the request's abort token, and pass it to every async call: EF Core queries, HttpClient and so on. If I ignore it, a user who closes the page still costs us a full 10-second report query. I do not log OperationCanceledException as an error, and for timeouts I use a linked token source.
Why is creating a new HttpClient for every request a problem, and how do you manage HttpClient in a modern .NET service?
Whether you know HttpClient lifetime pitfalls like socket exhaustion and stale DNS.
A client per call can exhaust sockets; one static client ignores DNS changes. IHttpClientFactory or a pooled connection lifetime solves both, with timeouts and retries.

Creating and disposing one per request leaves sockets in TIME_WAIT, and under load we ran out of ports. One static client fixes that but never sees DNS changes. I use IHttpClientFactory with typed clients, which pools and rotates handlers, or a shared client with SocketsHttpHandler and PooledConnectionLifetime of a few minutes. Retries and timeouts come from Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience.
Tell me about a bug you shipped to production in a .NET service. How was it found and what did you change afterward?
Your ownership of mistakes and the changes that followed.
A specific bug, owned plainly, quick mitigation, a clear root cause, and a lasting change such as a test, an analyzer rule or an alert.

I shipped a change that parsed dates with the server's culture, and on one server set to en-GB about 300 orders got day and month swapped. Support found it the next morning. I fixed it with CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, wrote a script to correct the rows and added tests for both cultures. We also turned on analyzer rule CA1305 so culture-less parsing gets flagged in the build.
What do you look for when reviewing a C# pull request, beyond the formatting the analyzers already catch?
What you focus on in a .NET code review.
Behavior over style: async misuse, disposal, EF Core query shape, exception handling, DI lifetimes, tests that prove the change, and comments that teach.

Formatting is the build's job, so I spend my time on behavior. I look for async void outside event handlers, blocking calls on tasks, IDisposable objects never disposed, EF queries that load more than they need, and catch blocks that swallow exceptions. I check that a test fails without the change. I mark which comments block the merge and which are only suggestions.
How do you test an ASP.NET Core API that uses EF Core and calls two external services?
How you balance unit and integration tests in a .NET service.
Unit tests for business rules, integration tests through WebApplicationFactory with a real database in a container, and stubbed HTTP for the external services.

Business rules get plain xUnit tests with no framework involved.
