I answer each comment in the review system, not in side emails. After approval, nothing changes without a new review. On my last project this kept us to two review rounds.
The primary endpoint was not met, but the study team wants the discussion to focus on a positive secondary endpoint. What do you do?
Whether you report results honestly when the team wants a better story.
The primary result stated plainly and first, secondary results described with their limits, and any disagreement taken to the medical lead and statistician.

I write the primary result first and plainly: the study did not meet its primary endpoint. The secondary result can go in, described as a secondary finding with its limits. If the team pushes for more, I take it to the medical lead and the statistician and refer to the protocol. Readers need to see what was planned and what was found.
Two reviewers give you opposite comments on the same paragraph. How do you resolve it?
How you handle conflicting feedback without guessing.
Both reviewers brought together or the document owner asked to decide, a choice based on data and guidance, and the decision recorded.

I do not quietly pick one comment. I send both comments to both reviewers in one message and suggest wording that might work for each. If they still disagree, I set up a 15-minute call or ask the document owner to decide. I record the decision in the comment log, so the next review round does not reopen it.
A key author sends comments a week after the deadline, and the submission date is fixed. What do you do?
How you protect a timeline while respecting the authors.
Quick sorting of the comments, accuracy fixes always taken in, a clear talk with the lead about what else fits, and the rest recorded for later.

I read the comments the same day and sort them into accuracy fixes, important clarifications and style. Accuracy fixes go in no matter what. For the rest, I tell the project lead what we can do without missing the date. On a recent clinical summary, 30 late comments came in and 8 really mattered. We took those and logged the rest for the next version.
You notice a number in the draft report text does not match the statistical tables. What do you do?
Your attention to data accuracy and checking against the source.
The source tables checked first, the text corrected or a query sent to the statistician, and the whole document searched for the same error.

I check the number against the final tables and listings, because they are the source. If my text is wrong, I fix it and search the whole document for the same number. If the tables look wrong, I query the statistician with the table number. Once a patient count was off by 2 in the synopsis, and we found the same error in three other places.
A sales manager asks you to write a slide saying the drug is safer than a competitor's, based on one small study. How do you respond?
Whether you keep claims within the evidence and the rules.
A clear explanation that the claim needs strong evidence and formal review, accurate alternative wording offered, and no unsupported claims written.

I explain that a comparative safety claim needs strong evidence, usually head-to-head data, and one small study is not enough. I offer wording that describes what the study actually found, with its limits. Anything I write goes through medical, legal and regulatory review anyway. I would rather have that talk now than see the slide rejected a week before the meeting.
You are asked to write a training module for nurses in a therapy area you know little about. How do you start?
How you get up to speed on unfamiliar science.
Reading from reliable sources such as guidelines and the label, time with experts, learning objectives set first, and review by a clinical expert.

I start with recent review articles, treatment guidelines and the product label. Then I book an hour with a medical science liaison or a nurse who works in the area. I write the learning objectives before the content, so I know what nurses need to do differently. A clinical expert reviews the draft. For an oncology module last year, this took about a week before I wrote a word.
Tell me about a document you wrote under a tight regulatory timeline. How did you manage it?
How you plan and deliver under submission pressure.
Key messages agreed early, fixed review rounds and comment deadlines, risks raised as soon as they appear, and a concrete outcome.

I wrote a clinical summary for a submission with six weeks to go. I agreed the key messages with the team in week one, so reviews were about accuracy, not direction. I set two review rounds with fixed dates and a comment deadline. When the safety data came late, I told the lead the same day and drafted around placeholders. We submitted on time.
Describe a time you pushed back on an expert's wording.
Whether you can disagree with senior experts respectfully.
A concern based on accuracy, guidance or clarity, a suggested alternative, and respect for the expert's final say on the science.

A principal investigator wanted to call a result a breakthrough in an abstract. I explained that the journal and our policy avoid that kind of word, and that the data speak better on their own. I offered a sentence with the actual effect size, and he agreed. On the science I defer to the expert, but on clear and fair wording it is my job to speak up.
Tell me about a month when several of your documents were due at once. How did you organize your work?
How you plan and prioritize several documents at the same time.
All deadlines and review dates in one plan, protected writing time, early warning when something slips, and honest talk about capacity.

Last spring I had a study report, a manuscript and a congress poster due within four weeks. I put every review date in one calendar and worked backward. I kept mornings for writing and afternoons for reviews and calls. When the poster data came late, I told the lead and moved the manuscript by a week with the authors' agreement. Everything else landed on time.
Why medical writing, and which kinds of documents do you most want to write?
Whether your interest fits the type of medical writing this role covers.
A specific reason, an honest preference among regulatory, publication and education work, and willingness to do the parts they enjoy less.

I did a PhD in immunology and enjoyed writing the papers more than running the experiments. I like regulatory documents most, because the structure is strict and accuracy matters. I am also happy to write patient materials, since turning a complex result into plain words is a skill I want to keep. Formatting and QC are not exciting, but I do them carefully.

bioinformatics.heading: Bioinformatics scientist questions
qs: Walk me through the main steps of a bulk RNA-seq differential expression analysis.
Whether you know the standard RNA-seq workflow.
Read QC, alignment or pseudoalignment, gene counts, sample-level QC, normalization, a count-based model with covariates, multiple testing correction, then interpretation.

I start with read QC and trim adapters if needed. Then I align to the reference genome or use pseudoalignment and get gene-level counts. I check the samples with PCA and correlation plots to find outliers. For differential expression I use a count-based model like DESeq2 or edgeR, with known covariates in the design. Then I correct for multiple testing and look at pathways.
What are batch effects, and how do you deal with them?
Whether you can spot and handle technical variation in data.
Technical variation explained, prevention through study design, detection with PCA, and batch included in the model rather than blindly removed.

Batch effects are differences caused by processing, like the date, the lab or the sequencing run, not by biology. The best fix is design: spread conditions across batches. To find them I color a PCA plot by batch. If batch is known, I include it as a covariate in the model. Once all treated samples ran on one day, so batch and treatment could not be separated, and I told the team so.
You test 20,000 genes for differential expression. Why can't you use p < 0.05 directly?
Whether you understand multiple testing correction.
Many tests produce many false positives by chance, so the false discovery rate is controlled, for example with Benjamini-Hochberg, and effect size is also considered.

If I test 20,000 genes at 0.05, I expect about 1,000 to look significant by chance even if nothing changed. So I control the false discovery rate, usually with Benjamini-Hochberg, and report adjusted p-values. I also look at effect size, because a tiny change can be significant with enough samples and still not matter biologically.
How do you make an analysis pipeline reproducible?
Whether you build pipelines that others can rerun and trust.
Version control with review, a workflow manager, pinned software in containers or environments, recorded reference versions and parameters, and automated tests.

All code goes in Git, with reviewed pull requests. I write the pipeline in a workflow manager such as Nextflow or Snakemake. Software runs in containers with pinned versions, and every run records the genome and annotation versions. Small test data runs automatically on each change. Last year a colleague reran a two-year-old analysis and got the same results.
A biologist asks you to remove three samples because they do not show the expected result. What do you do?
Whether you protect the integrity of an analysis under pressure.
Samples removed only for documented technical reasons, QC checked objectively, results shown both ways if unclear, and every exclusion recorded.

I explain that I can only remove samples for a technical reason, like low read depth or a failed QC metric. I check the QC for those three samples. If they pass, they stay. If the case is unclear, I run the analysis with and without them and show both results. I write down every exclusion and the reason in the analysis report.
Your differential expression results show thousands of significant genes, far more than expected. What do you check?
How you debug a surprising result before believing it.
Sample labels and metadata, the design matrix, confounding with batch or depth, normalization and outliers, all checked before anything is reported.

First I check that the sample labels and metadata are right, since one swapped label can do this. Then I look at the design matrix and whether condition is confounded with batch or sequencing depth. I check the PCA for outliers. Once this happened because the control samples came from a different tissue prep. We reported it as a confound, not a finding.
A scientist asks for a quick single-cell analysis for a leadership meeting in two days. How do you handle it?
How you balance speed with honest caveats.
Scope narrowed to the one question that matters, a standard workflow, limitations stated on the slides, and a proper analysis planned afterward.

I ask what single question leadership needs answered and focus on that. I use our standard workflow for QC, clustering and cell type annotation, with no custom steps. On every slide I note that the analysis is preliminary and what has not been checked. Then I schedule the full analysis for the next few weeks. A fast answer is fine if everyone knows how firm it is.
A pipeline that ran fine last month now gives different results on the same data. What do you do?
Whether you can trace changes in code, software or reference data.
Code, software versions, references and parameters compared using logs and version control, the cause found and fixed, and a check added.

I compare the run logs and the Git history for both runs. Common causes are a changed package version, a new annotation release or a different parameter. In one case a container was rebuilt without a pinned version and a tool updated silently. I pinned it, reran both jobs to confirm, and added a check that fails if versions change without review.
A collaborator sends you patient sequencing data to your personal email. What do you do?
Whether you follow data protection rules for patient data.
Files not opened or forwarded, a switch to the approved secure transfer under a data agreement, and the privacy or compliance team informed per the SOP.

I do not open or forward the files. I reply that we need to use the approved secure transfer and confirm a data agreement covers it. Then I tell our data protection or compliance team, as our SOP says, because it may need to be logged. It is not about blame. Patient data has rules, and they protect both the patients and the project.
Your team wants to use a newly published tool that claims better accuracy. How do you decide whether to adopt it?
Whether you evaluate methods with evidence before using them.
A benchmark against the current tool on data with a known answer, checks on maintenance and license, and a team decision before switching.

I read the paper and check whether its benchmarks look like our data. Then I run it next to our current tool on a dataset where we know the answer, like spike-in controls. I also check whether it is maintained and whether the license allows our use. If it is clearly better, I propose the switch with the results and update the pipeline under version control.
Tell me about a time you explained a statistical result to biologists who disagreed with it.
Whether you communicate analysis clearly to non-specialists.
A plain explanation with simple plots, real listening to their biological knowledge, a joint check of the data, and an honest outcome.

A team expected a gene to go up, and my results showed no change. I showed them the normalized counts per sample in a simple plot, so they could see the spread. They pointed out that two samples came from a different time point, which I had missed in the metadata. We fixed the design and reran. The gene still did not change, but now everyone trusted the result.
Describe a piece of code you wrote that other people now rely on.
Whether you write maintainable code for a team, not just for yourself.
A specific tool with documentation, tests and code review, evidence that others use it, and a plan for maintaining it.

I wrote an internal package that builds QC reports for RNA-seq runs. I added documentation, example data and tests, and every change goes through a pull request. Now about 15 scientists use it for each new dataset. When someone finds a bug, they open an issue and we fix it in a tagged release, so older reports stay reproducible.
Tell me about an analysis that turned out to be wrong. What happened, and what did you change?
Whether you own mistakes and improve your process.
An honest account of the error, a quick correction and clear communication, and a concrete change that prevents it from happening again.

I once used the wrong genome annotation version for a variant analysis, and two gene names were off. A colleague noticed a week after I shared the results. I told the team the same day, reran everything and sent a corrected report listing the changes. Since then my pipelines write the reference version into every output, and the report fails if it is missing.
Why do you want to work on drug discovery data rather than academic research?
Whether you understand and want the pace and goals of industry work.
Motivation tied to real medicines, comfort with team priorities and deadlines, and an honest view of what they give up compared with academic freedom.

In my postdoc I spent three years on one question. I enjoyed it, but I want my analysis to feed decisions on real medicines. I like working with chemists and biologists who need an answer this month. I know I will have less freedom to follow side questions, and I am fine with that. Seeing a target I helped choose enter a drug program would mean a lot.

cross-platform-mobile.heading: Cross-platform mobile developer questions
qs: When do you write a native module instead of staying in JavaScript or Dart?
Whether you know where the cross-platform layer should end.
Native code only for what the framework cannot reach or do fast enough, like a vendor SDK, behind a thin, typed and tested bridge.

I go native when there is no maintained package for a platform API, or a vendor ships only iOS and Android SDKs. Last year we needed a card reader SDK, so I wrote a small module with three methods and kept all business logic in TypeScript. Both platforms got the same interface and the same tests. If a good package already exists, I use it, after reading its open issues.
What makes a long list slow in React Native or Flutter, and how do you keep it smooth?
Whether you understand list virtualization and the cost of each rendered item.
Builds only visible items with FlatList, FlashList or ListView.builder, uses stable keys, light items and sized images, and profiles before tuning.

Usually it is too much work per item, or building every item at once. On a feed of about 3,000 posts we switched to ListView.builder so only visible rows were built, decoded images at thumbnail size instead of full photos, and moved date formatting out of the build method. The profiler on a mid-range Android phone went from regular dropped frames to steady scrolling.
How do you decide between local state, a server data cache and a global store in a cross-platform app?
Whether you keep state as close as possible to where it is used.
Local state by default, server data in a query cache or providers, and a global store only for truly shared app state like the signed-in user.

I start local. A text field's value or whether a sheet is open stays in the screen. Server data goes in a query cache, so refetching and loading states live in one place. Only things many screens need, like the current user and settings, go in a global store. In one app, moving server data out of Redux cut the store code by about half and removed several stale-data bugs.
What can and cannot be changed with an over-the-air update?
Whether you know the limits of over-the-air updates and app store rules.
JavaScript and assets only, never new native code or permissions, within current store guidelines, with a staged rollout and a way to roll back.

An over-the-air update can change the JavaScript bundle and assets, not native code. A new SDK, a new permission or a native bug fix needs a store release. Apple and Google both have rules on what an update may change, so I read the current guidelines and never use it to add a feature review has not seen. I ship to a small share of users first and keep the previous bundle ready.
A screen works on iPhone, but on some Android phones the keyboard covers the input field. What do you do?
How you handle platform differences in layout.
Reproduces on the reported devices, checks the Android keyboard resize setting and the framework's keyboard handling, and tests on several devices.

I reproduce it on the phones in the report, because keyboard behavior varies by Android maker and version. In one case the manifest used adjustPan while the screen relied on resizing. I set it to adjustResize, wrapped the form in a scroll view that brings the focused field into view, and tested on four Android phones and two iPhones before shipping.
Crash reports jump after a release, and almost all of them come from one Android version. How do you handle it?
Whether you can triage a platform-specific crash calmly and fast.
Halts the staged rollout, reads the stack traces and device data, reproduces on that version, ships a fix, and adds the version to the test matrix.

I halt the staged rollout in the Play Console first so it stops spreading. The stack traces pointed to a native module calling an API that older Android versions do not have. I reproduced it on an emulator, added a version check with a fallback, and shipped a hotfix. The crash-free rate was back to normal in two days, and that version joined our test matrix.
The app takes 6 seconds to start on older Android phones. Where do you look?
Whether you measure startup time instead of guessing.
Profiles cold start on a low-end device, defers work the first screen does not need, checks bundle size and engine settings, and measures again.

I measure cold start on a real budget phone, not my own. In one app we initialized analytics, three SDKs and the full translation file before showing anything. I moved the SDKs to after the first screen rendered, loaded only the current language and made sure Hermes was on. Cold start on that phone dropped from about 6 seconds to under 3.
Apple rejects your release two days before a planned launch. What do you do?
How you handle app review under time pressure.
Reads the cited guideline carefully, warns stakeholders about the date, fixes or replies in App Store Connect, and never hides features from review.

I read the rejection note and the guideline it cites. Once it was an app that let users create an account but not delete it in the app. I told the product manager that morning the date was at risk, we built the delete flow in a day, and I resubmitted with a note on the change. If I think the reviewer misread something, I reply with screenshots instead of arguing.
A designer wants a custom control that looks identical on iOS and Android, but it breaks the back gesture. How do you handle it?
Whether you balance one shared design with what users of each platform expect.
Keeps the shared look but respects platform behavior like back navigation and accessibility, and shows the designer the problem on real phones.

I show the designer the control on both phones, because a demo settles it faster than a debate. In one case a custom header blocked the iOS swipe back and ignored the Android back button. We kept the shared visual style and used native navigation underneath. I also tested it with VoiceOver, TalkBack and large text sizes, since those break custom controls often.
Two screens show different cart totals after the user goes offline and comes back. How do you find the cause?
Whether you can debug state that has drifted out of sync.
Finds the two sources of truth, makes one the owner and derives the rest, and decides how offline changes are queued and synced.

The usual cause is two copies of the same data. In our app the cart screen read from the server cache and the header badge from a local store with its own update logic. Offline, only one got the change. I made the query cache the single owner, derived the badge from it, and queued offline edits to replay in order. The mismatch stopped and the code got shorter.
Tell me about a time you had to choose between a cross-platform framework and fully native code for a feature.
Whether you make technology choices on evidence, not preference.
Names the real constraints, runs a short spike or prototype, decides with data, and is honest about the tradeoffs and the outcome.

We had to add video calling to a React Native app. I built a two-day spike with a maintained package and tested it on older phones, and audio drifted on Android. We kept the app in React Native but wrote the call screen natively on both platforms behind a small module. It cost about three extra weeks, and the call quality complaints we feared never came.
Tell me about a time a release went out with a bug that affected many users.
How you own a mistake and what you change afterward.
Owns it, describes fast mitigation and honest updates, and a lasting change to testing or the release process.

I shipped a change that logged out iOS users with saved sessions and blocked them from signing back in. Support had 40 tickets within an hour. I paused the phased release, shipped a fix the same day and posted updates every hour. Afterward I added an upgrade test that installs the old build, signs in and then updates. It has caught two similar bugs since.
Tell me about a time you worked with backend developers to change an API because of mobile needs.
Whether you speak up for mobile constraints like slow networks and old app versions.
Explains mobile limits in concrete terms, proposes a specific change backed by measurements, and keeps older app versions working.

Our home screen made seven API calls on launch, which was slow on mobile data. I recorded a request waterfall on a real phone, showed it to the backend team and proposed one endpoint for that screen. We kept the old endpoints, since some users never update. Load time on 4G went from about 4 seconds to 1.5, and now the backend team asks us early about new screens.
Tell me about a time you had to support users on an old app version you could not force them to update.
Whether you plan for many app versions running at the same time.
Keeps old API paths working, adds a minimum version check with a friendly prompt, tracks version share, and gives notice before switching off.

We had to change how payments worked, but about 15% of users were on versions over a year old. We kept the old API path working, added a minimum version check that showed a polite update screen, and watched version share in analytics. After three months the old share was under 2%, and only then did we switch the old path off, with notice in the app.

desktop-developer.heading: Desktop application developer questions
qs: Why does a desktop app freeze when work runs on the UI thread, and how do you keep it responsive?
Whether you understand the UI thread and how to move work off it.
Explains the single UI thread and message loop, moves slow work to background tasks or async I/O, and returns results to the UI thread safely.

The UI thread handles all input and painting, so a long task there stops repaints and the window shows as not responding. I move file reads, network calls and heavy parsing to background tasks and post results back to the UI thread. In a WPF app, opening a 200 MB log file went from a 10-second freeze to a progress bar with a working cancel button.
What does code signing protect, and what happens if you ship an unsigned app?
Whether you understand code signing and how operating systems decide to trust an app.
Signing shows who published the binary and that it was not changed; unsigned apps get warnings or blocks, and macOS also expects notarization.

Signing ties the binary to our company and shows it was not changed after we built it. Without it, Windows SmartScreen warns users, and macOS blocks the app by default unless it is signed and notarized. I keep signing keys in a hardware module or a cloud signing service, never on a laptop, and sign in the build pipeline so every release is signed the same way.
How should an auto-updater work so users and IT teams can trust it?
Whether you know what makes an update channel safe and reliable.
HTTPS downloads, signature checks before install, no interruption of user work, rollback, gradual rollout, and a way for admins to turn it off.

The updater checks over HTTPS, downloads in the background and verifies the package signature before it touches anything. It installs on the next restart, never in the middle of someone's work, and keeps the previous version so a failed update can roll back. We roll out to 5% first and watch crash rates. Enterprise admins can turn auto-update off and deploy with their own tools.
Where should a desktop app store settings, caches and user files on Windows and Mac?
Whether you follow each operating system's file conventions and permissions.
Per-user locations like AppData or Application Support, never the install folder, documents where the user chooses, and sandbox rules respected.

Settings and caches go in the per-user locations: AppData on Windows, and Application Support or Caches on Mac. The install folder is read-only for normal users, so writing there fails without admin rights. Documents go where the user picks in a save dialog. In one app, moving the cache out of Program Files fixed a whole class of errors for users without admin accounts.
After an update, some users report that the app crashes on launch, but you cannot reproduce it. What do you do?
Whether you use crash data to debug problems you cannot see yourself.
Pauses the rollout, reads symbolicated crash reports, looks for common factors like OS, GPU or security software, and talks to an affected user.

I pause the rollout and open the crash reports. With symbols uploaded, the stacks pointed to our graphics code, and almost every report came from one older GPU driver. I got an affected user on a call, confirmed it, and added a software rendering fallback for that driver. We resumed the rollout two days later, and launch crashes went back to the usual level.
Antivirus software flags your new installer as malware. How do you handle it?
How you deal with false positives without telling users to drop their protection.
Confirms the build is clean, checks every binary is signed, uses each vendor's false-positive process, and never advises turning antivirus off.

First I make sure it really is a false positive: I rebuild from a clean pipeline and compare hashes. Then I check that the installer and every binary inside it are signed. I submit the file through each vendor's false-positive form and give support a short note for users. I never tell users to turn antivirus off. Last time, two vendors cleared it within about two days.
Mac users say the app cannot open files in their Documents folder after an OS update. What do you check?
Whether you understand macOS privacy permissions and sandboxing.
Checks privacy prompts and sandbox entitlements, gets access through the system file picker, shows a clear message, and tests on the new OS.

I test on the new OS version with a fresh user account and check our sandbox entitlements. Newer macOS versions ask before an app reads folders like Documents, and a denied prompt looks like a broken app. We switched to opening files through the system picker, kept access with security-scoped bookmarks, and showed a clear message pointing to the right settings page.
A large customer wants to deploy your app to 5,000 machines with no user prompts. What do you need to support?
Whether you know what enterprise IT needs from an installer.
Silent MSI or PKG installs with documented options, per-machine installs, settings by policy, auto-update that can be turned off, and clean uninstall.

IT teams need a silent install they can push with their management tools, so we ship an MSI for Windows and a signed PKG for Mac with documented command-line options. Settings like the license server come from policy, not a first-run wizard. Auto-update can be switched off, since they test versions first. I also test a clean uninstall, because leftovers cause tickets.
The app's memory use grows by a few hundred megabytes over a long day of use. How do you find the leak?
Whether you track down leaks with tools and a repeatable test.
Finds a repeatable action, compares heap snapshots, looks for handlers, caches or native handles never released, and confirms with a long run.

I look for a repeatable action that makes memory grow, like opening and closing a document 50 times, and compare heap snapshots before and after. In one app each closed document stayed alive because a global event handler still pointed to it. I unsubscribed the handler on close and added a test that opens and closes 200 documents. Memory stayed flat over an eight-hour run.
Your crash reporter collects thousands of reports, but most have no useful stack traces. What do you change?
Whether you can make crash reporting actually useful.
Uploads symbols for every build, adds version and breadcrumb data without personal details, groups by signature, and ranks fixes by users affected.

Usually the cause is missing symbols, so I make the build pipeline upload them for every release automatically. I add the app version, OS version and a few breadcrumbs, like the last screen opened, without file names or other personal data. Then we group crashes by signature and fix them by number of users affected. In one quarter that cut our crash rate by about half.
Tell me about a time you had to keep supporting an old operating system version longer than you wanted.
How you balance user needs against engineering cost.
Uses data on who is affected, talks to product and support, plans a deprecation with notice, and keeps a way to test that version.

About 8% of our users were still on an older Windows version when a new UI library needed a newer one. The usage data showed most of them were at one large customer. We kept the old version on a maintenance branch for security fixes only, gave six months of notice, and helped that customer plan their upgrade. Nobody was cut off without warning.
Tell me about a time you made a slow desktop app feel fast.
Whether you measure what users feel and pick the right fix.
Measures user-visible delays like startup or typing lag, finds the real bottleneck with a profiler, and gives a before and after number.

Users said our editor felt sluggish when opening projects. I profiled startup and found we scanned every file in the project before showing the window. I showed the window first, scanned in the background and loaded the file list in batches. For large projects the window now appears in under a second instead of about 7, and the complaints about it stopped.
Tell me about a time a code signing certificate was about to expire or was at risk.
Whether you treat signing keys and certificates as critical assets.
Tracks expiry dates, renews ahead of time, limits who can sign, and writes down the renewal and revocation process.

Our Windows signing certificate was close to expiring, and I noticed only because of a build warning about three weeks before. Only one person knew the renewal steps. I renewed it with the security team, wrote down the process, set a reminder 60 days ahead and moved signing into the build pipeline with restricted access. The next renewal took one afternoon.
Tell me about a time you worked closely with support to fix a problem users kept reporting.
Whether you treat support tickets as a source of real bugs.
Listens to support, collects logs and steps, fixes the root cause, and closes the loop with support and users.

Support kept tagging tickets about lost work after crashes. I sat with two agents for an hour and read 30 tickets. Autosave ran only every 10 minutes and wrote to a temp folder that some cleanup tools wiped. We switched to saving every minute in the app data folder and offering recovery on the next launch. Lost-work tickets fell sharply, and support got a short note to share.

compiler-engineer.heading: Compiler engineer questions
qs: Why do compilers use an intermediate representation instead of going straight from source code to machine code?
Whether you understand how an IR separates front ends, optimizations and back ends.
One IR lets many languages share optimizations and many targets share front ends, SSA makes analysis simpler, and passes can be tested alone.

An IR lets us write each optimization once and use it for every language and target. With LLVM, a new language needs only a front end that emits IR, and a new chip needs only a back end. SSA form makes many analyses simpler, because each value has one definition. It also lets me test a single pass on a small IR file instead of a whole program.
In general terms, what is register allocation, and what happens when there are not enough registers?
Whether you understand register pressure and spilling.
Maps many virtual values onto few physical registers using liveness, spills to memory when they run out, and tries to keep hot loop values in registers.

The IR uses as many virtual values as it needs, but the chip has a fixed number of registers. The allocator looks at which values are live at the same time and assigns registers. When too many are live, it spills some to the stack and reloads them later, which costs memory traffic. A good allocator spills values used rarely, not the ones inside a hot loop.
How do you test a compiler beyond unit tests for each pass?
Whether you know fuzzing, differential testing and test case reduction.
Fuzzing for crashes, differential testing against other compilers or optimization levels, real programs built often, and automatic reduction of failures.

Unit tests on small IR files catch most regressions in a pass. On top of that I run fuzzers that generate random programs and look for crashes. Differential testing compiles the same program at different optimization levels or with another compiler and compares outputs. When something differs, a reducer like C-Reduce shrinks it to a few lines. We also build large open source projects nightly.
What does a framework like MLIR add compared to a single fixed IR?
Whether you understand multi-level IR and dialects in general terms.
Dialects at several levels of abstraction, gradual lowering that keeps high-level information long enough to optimize, and shared infrastructure.

MLIR lets you define dialects at different levels, like tensor operations, then loops, then hardware instructions, and lower step by step. For an AI accelerator that matters, because fusing two operations is easy to see at the tensor level and very hard after lowering to loads and stores. It also gives shared tools for passes, verification and printing, so a team does not rebuild them.
A user reports that their program gives a wrong result at -O2 but works at -O0. How do you hunt it down?
Whether you can find a miscompile step by step.
Rules out undefined behavior first, reduces the test case, bisects passes and commits, finds the bad transform, then fixes it and adds a regression test.

First I check the program for undefined behavior with sanitizers, because that explains many of these reports. If it is clean, I reduce it to a few lines with a reducer, then turn passes off one at a time to find the guilty one. In my last case a loop optimization assumed two pointers could not alias. I fixed the alias check and added the reduced program as a regression test.
A fuzzer finds 300 crashes overnight. How do you handle them?
How you triage a large batch of fuzzer findings.
Deduplicates by assertion or stack, reduces each unique case, ranks wrong-code bugs above crashes on invalid input, and files each with a reproducer.

Most of them are duplicates, so I group them by the assertion and the top stack frames. Last time, 300 crashes became 11 unique bugs. I reduce each one to a small reproducer, then rank them: anything that suggests wrong code goes first, crashes on valid input next, and crashes on invalid input last. Each gets a ticket with the reduced file and the commit where it started.
A new optimization speeds up one benchmark by 15% but slows two others by 5%. Do you merge it?
Whether you judge performance changes on the whole picture.
Reruns to rule out noise, checks the full suite and code size, finds why the slowdowns happen, and limits the transform with a cost check if needed.

Not yet. I rerun all three several times to rule out noise, then look at why two got slower. In a similar case the pass raised register pressure in large loops and caused spills. I added a cost check that skipped the transform when too many values were live. The gain on the first benchmark stayed, the slowdowns disappeared, and then we merged it.
After an LLVM upgrade, your out-of-tree back end fails to build and dozens of tests fail. Where do you start?
How you handle upstream changes in a large codebase.
Fixes build breaks first, reads the upstream commits behind each change, groups test failures by cause, and writes down what changed for next time.

I fix the build first, using the upstream commits that changed each API we call. Then I group the test failures, because a few upstream changes usually explain most of them, like a renamed intrinsic or a new default. I read the related commits and reviews before changing our code. Last upgrade, 40 failures came down to 4 causes, and I wrote them up for the next person.
A model runs correctly on a new AI chip but is three times slower than expected. How do you investigate?
Whether you can connect compiler output to hardware performance.
Profiles on the hardware, compares kernels to expected throughput, inspects generated code for missed fusion, poor tiling or extra memory traffic.

I profile the model on the chip and rank kernels by time. In one case a few matrix multiplies took most of it. Reading the generated code, the tiles did not fit in on-chip memory, so data moved back and forth to main memory. Changing the tile sizes for that shape closed most of the gap. I added that shape to our performance tests so it would not regress.
Two engineers disagree on whether a transformation is legal under the language rules. How do you settle it?
Whether you reason about semantics carefully instead of by opinion.
Goes to the language standard and IR semantics, writes the smallest program that would behave differently, and tests it.

I ask both of them to write the smallest program where the transform would change the result. Then we read the relevant parts of the language standard and the IR reference together. In one case the question was whether a load could move above a function call. The example showed the call could change that memory, so the move was illegal there. Writing it down ended the debate.
Tell me about the hardest miscompile you have tracked down.
Your persistence and method on a long investigation.
A concrete story with reduction, bisection and the root cause, plus what changed afterward, like a new test, verifier check or fuzzer.

A customer saw a wrong checksum about once in every thousand runs. It depended on a rare register allocation path. I reduced their program from 20,000 lines to 30 and found a spill reload placed after the value had been overwritten. The fix was small. I also added a check to our machine code verifier, and it later caught two similar bugs.
Tell me about a time you reviewed a compiler change and pushed back on it.
How you give hard review feedback on correctness.
Specific feedback backed by a counterexample, a respectful tone, and a path forward like a guard condition or a test.

A colleague sent a patch that folded some floating point expressions. It looked fine, but I wrote a small example where the result changed for negative zero. I posted the example in the review instead of a vague worry, and suggested applying the fold only when fast-math flags allowed it. They updated the patch the same day and added my example as a test.
Tell me about a time you worked with hardware designers on a new instruction or feature.
Whether you can work across the hardware and software boundary.
Gives early feedback on what the compiler can really use, backs it with data from real workloads, and speaks the hardware team's language.

The hardware team proposed a new fused instruction for an AI chip. I prototyped the pattern match in our compiler and ran it over the 20 models we cared about. It matched in only a few kernels, because it needed a rare data layout. I showed them the data, and they changed the operand order to fit our usual layout. The final version was used in most of the models.
Tell me about a time you made the compiler easier for other engineers to debug or work on.
Whether you care about tooling and the team, not only your own code.
A concrete improvement like better dumps, a verifier, a bisect script or docs, and evidence that others used it.

New team members spent days finding which pass broke something. I wrote a script that runs the pipeline one pass at a time and stops at the first output that differs from a reference. I also made our IR dumps print source locations. A new engineer used it in their first week to find a bug in about an hour, and it is now the first step in our debugging guide.

cryptographer.heading: Cryptographer questions
qs: Why should a product team not design its own encryption scheme, even if its engineers are strong?
Whether you know why vetted algorithms and libraries matter.
Crypto fails silently and subtly, trust comes from years of public analysis, so products use standard algorithms through reviewed, high-level libraries.

Custom crypto usually passes every test, because a broken scheme still encrypts and decrypts. The flaws show up only when someone attacks it. Standard algorithms have had years of public analysis. So I steer teams to a well-reviewed library with a high-level API, like libsodium or the platform's crypto library, and keep our own code to choosing settings and handling keys.
What goes wrong if a nonce is reused with AES-GCM under the same key?
Whether you understand the real consequence of nonce reuse.
Keystream reuse leaks the XOR of plaintexts and lets an attacker recover the authentication key and forge messages; prevented by design, not hope.

Reusing a nonce with the same key reuses the keystream, so the XOR of the two plaintexts leaks. Worse, an attacker can recover the authentication key and forge messages. To prevent it I use a counter that cannot repeat, or random nonces kept well under the safe message limit per key, and rotate keys. Where nonces are hard to manage, I consider a misuse-resistant mode like AES-GCM-SIV.
What does constant-time code mean, and why does it matter?
Whether you understand timing side channels.
Time and memory access must not depend on secrets: no secret-based branches, table lookups or early-exit compares, checked with tools and review.

It means the time and memory access pattern do not depend on secret values. A classic bug is checking a MAC with a normal compare that stops at the first wrong byte, so timing shows how many bytes matched. I use a constant-time compare, avoid branches and table lookups indexed by secrets, and test sensitive code for timing leaks, since compilers can undo careful source code.
In general terms, how should an organization prepare for post-quantum cryptography?
Whether you can describe a sensible migration without hype.
Inventories public-key crypto use, puts long-lived secrets first, follows NIST standards like ML-KEM and ML-DSA, considers hybrids, and builds agility.

Start with an inventory of where public-key crypto is used: TLS, VPNs, code signing, stored data. Data that must stay secret for many years matters most, because it can be recorded now and decrypted later. NIST has standardized ML-KEM for key exchange and ML-DSA for signatures. Many teams start with hybrid key exchange next to the current one, and make algorithms easy to swap.
In a code review you find a service encrypting stored customer data with AES in ECB mode. What do you do?
How you handle a real crypto flaw in a product.
Explains the risk plainly, moves to an authenticated mode through a standard library, plans re-encryption of existing data, and looks for other uses.

ECB encrypts identical blocks the same way, so patterns leak, and it has no integrity check. I explain that to the team with a short example, not a lecture. Then I propose AES-GCM or a library's sealed box API, plus a migration: decrypt old records and re-encrypt them with a version tag. I also search the codebase for other ECB uses, and found two more the last time.
A developer wants to store user passwords encrypted so support can read them back. How do you respond?
Whether you know passwords should be hashed with a slow function, not encrypted.
A clear no, hashing with Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt or PBKDF2 and unique salts, and a reset flow so support never needs the password.

I say we should never be able to read a password back. If the database leaks along with the key, every password is exposed, and people reuse them. We store a hash from a slow function like Argon2id or bcrypt with a unique salt. Support gets a reset flow instead. When I explained this once, the real need turned out to be account recovery, which the reset link covered.
A team finds that a signing private key was pushed to a public code repository an hour ago. What do you do?
How you respond to key exposure.
Treats the key as compromised: revoke and rotate, clean history, check for misuse, follow the incident process and add secret scanning.

I treat the key as compromised, even after one hour, because public repositories are scanned all the time. We revoke it, issue a new key and update everything that trusts the old one. Deleting the commit is not enough, so we clean history and ask the host to purge caches. Then we check for anything signed with it, follow the incident process and turn on secret scanning.
A product manager asks you to approve a vendor that promises "military-grade, unbreakable encryption." How do you evaluate it?
Whether you judge vendor crypto claims on evidence.
Asks for algorithms, modes, libraries, key handling, independent audits or FIPS 140-3 validation if required, and treats marketing words as no evidence.

Those words tell me nothing, so I send the vendor specific questions: which algorithms and modes, which library, where keys are generated and stored, who can access them, and whether there is an independent audit or a FIPS 140-3 validation if we need one. Once a vendor answered that keys were stored in the same database as the data. That answer settled it.
A constant-time compare in your library shows a small timing difference after a compiler upgrade. How do you investigate?
Whether you know compilers can break side-channel protections.
Reads the generated assembly, confirms with a statistical timing test, uses barriers or vetted primitives, and adds a regression check to CI.

I look at the generated assembly first, because a new compiler can turn careful branch-free code back into a branch. In one case it added an early exit to our compare loop. I confirmed the leak with a statistical timing test, then rewrote the function with a value barrier the optimizer cannot see through. That function now has a timing test and an assembly check in CI.
A team wants to encrypt data in a new service. How do you design the key management?
Whether you know keys matter as much as algorithms.
Envelope encryption with a KMS or HSM, no keys in code, least-privilege access, rotation, logged key use, and tested recovery.

I usually use envelope encryption. A key in a managed KMS or HSM wraps data keys, and the service gets data keys only through an API with logged access. Keys never go in code or config files. Only the service role can use the key, rotation runs on a schedule, and we test restoring from backups. Most real failures I have seen were key handling mistakes, not broken algorithms.
Tell me about a time you explained a cryptographic risk to people without a math background.
Whether you can make risk clear to non-specialists.
A plain demo or comparison, a focus on impact and the decision needed, little jargon, and a clear next step.

Leadership wanted to delay fixing a weak random number generator used for session tokens. Instead of explaining entropy, I showed a demo where I predicted the next token after seeing a few, in under a minute. Then I explained what an attacker could do with it and what the fix cost, about two days of work. They approved the fix that afternoon.
Tell me about a time you found a flaw in a design you had approved earlier.
Whether you own mistakes in security-critical work.
Raises it quickly, assesses the impact honestly, fixes it with a plan, and changes how reviews are done.

I had approved a token design that used the same key for encryption and for signing. Months later, while reviewing something else, I saw that one use could help an attack on the other. I told the team that day, wrote up the real risk, which was low but not zero, and we split the keys in the next release. Key separation is now on my review checklist.
Tell me about a time you had to choose between a stronger security design and a deadline.
How you balance security with delivery.
Separates must-haves from later work, makes the remaining risk explicit and written, and has the right owner accept it.

We were launching a file sharing feature with two weeks left, and full end-to-end encryption would have taken months. I listed what launch needed: encryption in transit and at rest with managed keys, access logging, and short-lived links. End-to-end went on the roadmap. The product owner signed off on the remaining risk in writing, and we shipped on time.
Tell me about a time you reviewed someone else's protocol and found a problem.
How you review carefully and give useful feedback.
Checks the assumptions, shows a concrete attack or counterexample, and gives respectful, actionable feedback with a fix.

A partner team sent a protocol for pairing devices. Walking through the messages, I saw one value was not covered by the signature, so an attacker in the middle could swap it. I wrote a short attack sketch with the exact messages and a suggested fix, signing the whole transcript. They agreed in one meeting, and the fix added only a few lines to their code.

ot-security.heading: OT and product security questions
qs: How do security priorities in OT differ from those in a typical office IT network?
Whether you understand that safety and availability come first in OT.
Safety and availability first, long-lived equipment, legacy protocols without authentication, changes planned with operations, no unapproved scans.

In IT, protecting data often comes first. In a plant, the first questions are whether a change could hurt someone or stop production. Controllers may run for 20 years and use protocols with no authentication. So I never run an active scan on a control network without operations approving it, and every change goes through the same planning as a process change.
What does good network segmentation look like between the business network and a plant's control systems?
Whether you know how to design zones and the paths between them.
Zones by function and risk, a DMZ between IT and OT, no direct paths, explicit allow rules with owners, controlled remote access and monitoring.

I split the plant into zones by function and risk, like safety systems, control and supervision, and put a DMZ between the office network and the plant. Nothing goes straight from an office PC to a controller. Data like historian copies cross through the DMZ, and remote access goes through a jump host with MFA. Every firewall rule has an owner and a reason, and we review them on a schedule.
What does secure boot protect on a device, and what does it not protect?
Whether you understand the chain of trust and its limits.
Verifies each boot stage from a hardware root of trust; does not fix bugs in signed code, protect stolen keys, or stop downgrades without anti-rollback.

Secure boot checks that each stage of the boot chain is signed by a key the device trusts, starting from a root in hardware. It stops someone loading modified firmware. It does not fix bugs in signed code, protect a stolen signing key, or stop a downgrade to an older signed version with known flaws. That is why I also want anti-rollback counters and well-guarded signing keys.
How do you threat model a connected device, such as a smart meter or an industrial sensor?
Whether you can analyze a device step by step.
Maps interfaces, data flows and trust boundaries, lists assets and attackers, uses a method like STRIDE, includes physical access, ranks by safety impact.

I start with a diagram: the device, its interfaces, the cloud service and the phone app, with trust boundaries marked. Then I go through each interface with STRIDE and ask what an attacker with the device in hand could do, like reading the debug port. For a smart meter, the remote disconnect command was the top risk, so it got strong authentication and server-side limits.
A critical vulnerability is announced for controllers that run a production line nonstop and can only be restarted in the annual shutdown. What do you do?
How you manage risk when patching right away is not possible.
Checks real exposure, adds compensating controls like tighter firewall rules and monitoring, confirms the patch with the vendor, and plans it for the outage.

First I check whether we are exposed: which controllers, which firmware, and what can reach them. Then I add compensating controls, like blocking the affected service at the zone firewall and alerting on any traffic to it. I confirm with the vendor that the patch is approved for our setup, and we schedule it with operations for the next planned shutdown, with a tested rollback.
The IT team wants to run its standard vulnerability scanner across the plant network next week. How do you respond?
Whether you protect fragile equipment from well-meant IT practices.
Explains the risk to older devices, offers passive monitoring and config-based inventory, and allows active checks only on a test bench or in a window.

I explain that some older controllers can crash from scan traffic, and a crashed controller can stop a line. Then I offer what they need in a safer way: a passive monitoring tool that builds the asset list from traffic, plus vendor and config data. If we need active checks, we try them on a spare controller first and run them in a maintenance window with operations present.
During a walk-through you find a cellular modem attached to a controller so a vendor can connect remotely. What do you do?
How you handle unmanaged remote access without disrupting operations.
Documents it, finds the owner and purpose, does not pull it mid-shift, moves the vendor to controlled access with MFA and logging, then removes it.

I do not unplug it on the spot, because I do not know what depends on it. I photograph it, find out who owns it and which vendor uses it, and report it to the plant manager and security lead. Then we give the vendor access through our remote access system, with MFA, approval for each session and recording. Once that works, the modem comes out in a planned change.
Your company's field devices accept firmware updates that are not signed. How do you fix the update process?
Whether you can design a safe firmware update path.
Signed images checked on the device before install, signing keys in an HSM, anti-rollback, an A/B or recovery path, and a staged rollout.

The device should install only images signed with our key and check the signature itself before writing anything. Signing keys go in an HSM with approval steps. I add a version check against rollback and an A/B layout, so a failed update boots the old image. We roll out to a small group first. For devices already in the field, we plan the move to signed updates carefully.
A plant reports that operator workstations are acting strangely and the historian is sending unusual outbound traffic. What do you do?
How you respond to a possible incident without creating a safety problem.
Follows the OT incident plan, involves operations before isolating anything, preserves evidence, checks safety systems, and escalates as required.

I follow the OT incident plan and call the shift supervisor first, because isolating systems can affect the process. Together we decide whether the plant can run safely in manual or a reduced mode. Then we block the outbound traffic at the DMZ, preserve logs and disk images, and check that the safety systems are separate and normal. Reporting duties vary by sector and region, so legal handles that.
A product team wants to ship a device with its debug port open on production units to help field repairs. How do you handle it?
Whether you can balance serviceability with device security.
Learns what repairs really need, then locks the port and offers an authenticated service mode with per-device credentials.

I ask the repair team what they actually do through the port. Usually it is reading logs and reflashing. We can give them a service mode that needs a signed, per-device unlock token and keep the raw debug port locked in production. On one product that took about three weeks. Repairs still worked, and every unit no longer had an open port with access to memory.
Tell me about a time you had to convince plant operators to accept a security change.
Whether you can earn trust from operations teams.
Listens to operator concerns, tests the change with them, shows it will not slow their work in an emergency, and starts small.

Operators pushed back on removing shared logins from the HMIs, because they feared being locked out during an alarm. I spent a night shift watching how they worked. We used badge login with fast switching between users and kept a sealed break-glass account for emergencies. We piloted it on one line for a month, and then the operators asked for it on the other lines.
Tell me about a time a security control you added caused a problem in production.
How you own operational impact and learn from it.
Owns the problem, restores operation fast, finds why testing missed it, and changes the change process.

I tightened a firewall rule between two zones and blocked a weekly report the historian sent to the quality system. Nobody noticed until a quality engineer asked where Monday's report was. I restored the rule within the hour and found the flow was missing from our traffic capture, which covered only a few days. Now we capture at least a full month before changing rules.
Tell me about a time you worked with an equipment vendor that was slow to fix a security issue.
How you manage vendor risk when you do not control the fix.
Clear, documented requests, interim controls, escalation through contracts or account contacts, and security terms in future agreements.

A vendor took months to respond about hard-coded credentials in a gateway we used at five sites. I documented the issue, put compensating controls in place, and escalated through our purchasing contact, who had leverage at contract renewal. We also asked for security update terms in the next contract. The vendor released a fix about four months later, and we rolled it out site by site.
Tell me about a time you built an asset inventory for an environment that had none.
Whether you can create the basics that OT security depends on.
Combines passive monitoring, walk-throughs and engineering documents, records firmware, owners and criticality, and keeps it current through change control.

At one plant the only list was an old spreadsheet. I combined passive network monitoring, the engineering drawings and walk-throughs with maintenance staff. We found about 30% more devices than the spreadsheet listed, including two unmanaged switches. Each asset got an owner, firmware version and criticality, and updating the inventory became a step in every change request.

telecom-engineer.heading: Telecommunications engineer questions
qs: In general terms, what do you consider when planning radio coverage for a new site?
Whether you understand the main factors in RF planning.
Coverage and capacity goals, terrain and buildings, frequency band, antenna height, tilt and direction, interference with neighbors, and drive test checks.

I start with what the site must do: fill a coverage gap, add capacity or both. Then I look at terrain, buildings and the band, since lower bands reach farther and higher bands carry more capacity. In the planning tool I set antenna height, tilt and direction, check overlap with neighbor cells, and plan drive tests after launch, because models are never exact.
How do you approach capacity planning for a mobile network?
Whether you plan capacity from data, not guesses.
Uses busy-hour trends and utilization thresholds, adds business forecasts, and compares options like carriers, sectors, small cells or new sites.

I look at busy-hour traffic per cell, how it has trended, and how close each cell is to the utilization threshold we set. I add forecasts from marketing, like device launches or big events. For cells that will cross the threshold, I compare adding a carrier, splitting sectors, small cells or a new site. Each has a cost and lead time, so the longest ones get planned first.
What changes in the core network when an operator moves from non-standalone to standalone 5G?
Whether you understand 5G architecture beyond marketing.
Non-standalone uses the 4G core with 5G radio; standalone uses a 5G core of service-based network functions, split control and user planes, and slicing.

Non-standalone 5G adds 5G radio but still relies on the 4G core. Standalone uses a 5G core built from network functions like AMF, SMF and UPF that talk through service-based interfaces. The user plane can sit closer to users for lower latency, and slicing lets one network serve different needs. For operations, it means more software, cloud platforms and automation.
What are common causes of dropped calls, and how do you tell them apart?
Whether you know how to read the evidence behind dropped calls.
Coverage holes, interference, handover failures, missing neighbors, congestion and core or transport faults, told apart with counters and traces.

The usual causes are weak coverage, interference, failed handovers, missing neighbor definitions, congestion and sometimes a core or transport fault. I tell them apart with data: drop reasons in the counters, signal and quality at the moment of the drop, and where drops cluster. Drops at one cell's edge point to coverage. Drops on a border between two cells point to handover settings.
Dropped calls on one cluster of cells doubled since yesterday. What do you do?
How you troubleshoot a sudden drop in performance.
Checks recent changes and alarms first, compares counters before and after, isolates the cells, rolls back a bad change, and confirms with tests.

I check what changed in the last day first: software upgrades, parameter changes, new sites or alarms. In one case a neighbor list was overwritten during a planned change, so handovers failed between three cells. The counters showed handover failures jumped at the exact time of the change. We restored the old neighbors, drops were normal within hours, and the change script got a check.
You lead a core network change in a midnight to 4 a.m. window, and at 2:30 the test calls fail. What do you do?
Whether you follow the rollback plan under pressure.
Uses the go or no-go time in the plan, rolls back if the cause is not clear by then, keeps everyone informed, and records everything for review.

Our plan had a go or no-go point at 3:00 and a tested rollback that took 40 minutes. I gave the team until 3:00 to find a clear cause. When we could not, I called the rollback, told the operations center, and we confirmed service with test calls before 4:00. The next day we found a configuration mismatch in the lab, and we redid the change two weeks later.
A stadium will host a large event next month. How do you prepare the network?
Whether you plan ahead for known traffic peaks.
Uses data from past events, adds temporary capacity, tunes parameters, coordinates with the venue, watches live, and reviews afterward.

I pull the data from the last big event there: peak users, traffic per cell and where it congested. Then we plan extra capacity, like a portable cell site or temporary carriers, and tune parameters for many users close together. I coordinate access and power with the venue. On the day, an engineer watches those cells live, and afterward we compare results to the plan.
Customers in one suburb complain about slow mobile data, but your dashboards show the cells are fine. How do you investigate?
Whether you take customer reports seriously and look past averages.
Looks at the exact streets and times, checks busy-hour and per-user numbers, transport links and devices, and confirms with a field test.

Averages hide problems, so I look at the streets and times in the complaints. In one case the cells looked healthy on daily averages, but at evening peak the backhaul link to that site was full, and throughput per user fell sharply between 7 and 10 p.m. A drive test confirmed it. We upgraded the backhaul, and complaints from that area stopped within weeks.
A field team reports that a new antenna was installed with a different tilt and direction than planned. What do you do?
How you handle installation quality issues.
Checks the impact with data, logs the gap, has it corrected in a planned visit, and adds checks to installation sign-off.

I check the impact first: are coverage and interference different from the plan? In one case the antenna pointed about 20 degrees off and overlapped a neighbor cell. I logged it, scheduled a crew to fix it during low traffic hours, and compared counters before and after. We then added photos and an alignment tool reading to the installation sign-off.
A regulator asks your company for details about an outage that affected emergency calls. What is your role?
Whether you handle regulatory matters carefully and through the right channels.
Builds an accurate timeline, hands it to the regulatory or legal team, does not guess, and knows reporting rules vary by country and regulator.

My job is accurate facts, not the reply itself. I build a timeline from alarms, logs and tickets: start, scope, cause and restoration. I give it to our regulatory and legal team, who know the reporting rules, since they differ by country and service. If I do not know something yet, I say so instead of guessing. Afterward I make sure the fix and lessons are tracked.
Tell me about a time a network change you made caused an outage.
Whether you own mistakes and improve the process.
Owns it, describes fast restoration and a blameless review, and names a concrete change to procedures or checks.

I pushed a routing change that I had tested in the lab, but production had an extra filter the lab did not. Traffic for one region dropped for about 12 minutes before I rolled it back. I wrote the incident review myself, and we added a step to compare lab and production configs before every routing change. That check has caught three differences since.
Tell me about a time you worked with another operator, vendor or utility to solve a network problem.
How you work with people outside your own company.
Brings clear evidence, builds the relationship, troubleshoots together, and leaves a documented fix and a contact for next time.

We had interference on several sites near a border, and our data suggested it came from another operator's equipment. I collected spectrum scans and the times it happened, and reached their engineers through our spectrum management team. We compared data and found a misconfigured filter at one of their sites. They fixed it in a week, and we now have a direct contact for next time.
Tell me about a time you automated a repetitive network task.
Whether you reduce manual work and risk with automation.
Picks a task with real time cost or error risk, automates it safely with checks and dry runs, and measures the result.

Engineers spent hours each week checking neighbor lists by hand after new sites went live. I wrote a script that compared each new site's neighbors with the planning tool and flagged missing ones, with a dry run before any change. It cut the check from about three hours to ten minutes per site, and missing neighbors at launch, a common cause of drops, mostly disappeared.
Tell me about a time you explained a network problem to non-technical people, such as customer care or managers.
Whether you can turn a network issue into impact and actions others can use.
Plain words, a focus on customer impact, what is being done and when, and what customer care can tell callers.

During a long fiber cut, customer care was getting angry calls and had nothing to say. I joined their morning briefing and explained it simply: a cable was cut, traffic was rerouted, service worked but was slower in three towns, and crews expected to finish by evening. I gave them a short script and updated it twice that day. Their calls on it got shorter and calmer.

reporting-analyst.heading: Reporting analyst questions
qs: What makes a metric definition clear enough to put in a recurring report?
Whether you know a number is only as good as its written definition.
A plain name, the exact formula, what is in and out, the source, time zone and cutoff, an owner, and a dated note whenever the definition changes.

I write each metric on one line of a shared glossary: name, formula, filters, source, refresh time and owner. For example, net revenue excludes refunds and tax, comes from the billing system, and closes at midnight Eastern. When we changed how trials counted, I added a dated note, so anyone comparing March to April knew why there was a 3% step.
How do you reconcile a report to its source before it goes out?
Your routine for proving the figures are right, not just plausible.
Control totals against the source or ledger, row counts, a few records traced end to end, a comparison to last period, and written reasons for any gap.

I tie the totals to the source of record, usually the ledger or the system's own report, and check row counts after each join. I trace three or four records from source to final line. Then I compare with last month and flag any move over 5% for a reason. The checks live in a tab of the workbook, so a reviewer can repeat them in ten minutes.
Why can the same figure differ between a dashboard and the finance system when neither is wrong?
Whether you understand the timing, cutoffs and definitions behind numbers.
Different refresh times, cutoffs and time zones, posted versus pending entries, currency rates, filters, and whether adjustments or refunds are included.

Most often it is timing. The dashboard refreshes nightly and counts orders when placed, while finance books revenue when it is recognized and posts adjustments at month end. Time zones matter too: one month our UTC dashboard showed $40,000 more than finance because late Pacific orders on the 31st fell into the next day. I put the cutoff rules in the report footnote.
When is a manual report worth automating, and when is it not?
Whether you weigh effort, risk and stability before you build.
Automate when it is frequent, stable, rule-based and error-prone. Hold off when the source or definitions are still changing or the report runs only once.

I look at how often it runs, how long it takes and how often hand steps cause errors. A weekly report that took six hours and had copy-paste mistakes twice a quarter was an easy yes; I rebuilt it as a scheduled query and it now takes 20 minutes to review. A one-off board pack with shifting asks stays manual, with a checklist, until the asks settle.
A regional manager says a number in this week's report is wrong. What do you do?
How you respond to a challenge without getting defensive or giving in.
Ask what they expected and why, check the definition and source, reply with a clear answer either way, and correct and notify everyone if it was wrong.

I ask what number they expected and where it came from. Last time, the manager's figure came from their CRM, which counted deals at signing, while our report counted at first invoice. Both were right, so I sent a short note explaining the difference with the 12 deals behind it. If I find a real error, I fix it, reissue and tell everyone who got the report.
A total in last month's published report changes when you rerun it a week later. How do you handle it?
Whether you manage late data and restatements openly.
Find why it moved, such as late or corrected source data, follow the team's restatement policy, tell readers the size and reason, and snapshot published runs.

First I find the cause. Usually it is late transactions or a corrected source record. If the change is above the threshold our team agreed, 1% in my last job, I restate with the old number, the new number and why. Below that, I keep the published figure and log the difference. After this happened twice, I started saving a snapshot of each published run.
Your report total is $18,400 lower than the general ledger for the same month. How do you find the difference?
Your method for tracking down a reconciliation gap.
Break both sides down by account, entity and date until the gap is isolated, look for timing items, manual journals, filters and duplicates, and document the bridge.

I break both sides down by account and day until the gap sits in one place. In a similar case, the whole difference was in one account on the last day of the month. It turned out to be two manual journals posted directly in the ledger that never touched the billing system. I added them as a reconciling line, documented it, and asked accounting to flag those journals to me.
You inherit a weekly report that takes a full day of copying between spreadsheets. How do you approach automating it?
How you plan an automation so people can trust the new version.
Document the current steps and hidden fixes, confirm what readers use, rebuild from source, run old and new in parallel until they match, then retire the old one.

I first shadow the person who builds it and write down every step, including the hand fixes they make. Then I ask readers which tabs they actually use; in one case it was 4 of 11. I rebuilt those from the source tables, ran both versions side by side for three weeks until totals matched to the dollar, and then switched off the manual one.
Sales and finance each want their own definition of active customer in the executive report. What do you do?
How you settle a definition conflict without picking a side yourself.
Show both definitions and their numbers side by side, explain the gap, have the report owner decide, then document the choice and label any alternative clearly.

I put both definitions on one page with the counts they produce, 8,200 and 7,100 in a case like this, and what drives the gap. Then I take it to the executive who owns the report, since it is not my call. Once decided, I record it in the glossary and, if useful, keep the other version in an appendix with a clear label.
A regulatory report is due in three days and a reconciliation check fails for one region. What do you do?
Whether you escalate early and protect accuracy on a fixed deadline.
Tell the report owner and compliance at once, work the gap, never force numbers to tie, and let compliance decide how to handle it under that regulator's rules.

I tell my manager and the compliance contact the same day, with the size of the gap and what I know so far. Then I work the gap with the regional team. I never plug a number to make it tie. If it cannot be resolved in time, compliance decides how to handle it under that regulator's rules, and I document every step so we can explain it later.
Tell me about a time you found a mistake in your own report after it had been sent.
Whether you own errors quickly and fix the process behind them.
Prompt disclosure, a corrected version that says what changed, a check of who relied on it, and a new control so it does not happen again.

I once sent a monthly churn report where a filter dropped one product line, so churn looked 0.8 points better than it was. I found it two days later, told my manager, and reissued it that afternoon with a note on what changed. I checked whether anyone had used the number in a decision. Then I added a row count check by product line before every send.
Tell me about a time an upstream system change broke a report you owned.
How you handle data you depend on but do not control.
Fast detection, clear word to readers, a fix, and a lasting arrangement with the system owner, such as change notices or automated checks.

Our CRM team renamed a status value without notice, and the pipeline report dropped $2 million overnight. A volume check caught it before the report went out, so I held it and told readers it would be a day late. I mapped the new value, then asked the CRM team to add our reports to their change checklist. We have had no surprises like it since.
Tell me about a time you retired or merged reports nobody was using.
