Whether you manage the report catalog instead of only adding to it.
Usage evidence, a conversation with each requester, a notice period, and fewer, clearer reports as the result.

We had 64 scheduled reports and nobody knew who read them. I pulled three months of open and download logs and found 20 with no views. I emailed each requester, gave a month's notice, and switched off the ones nobody claimed. Five more were merged into one sales pack. It freed about a day a week of maintenance.
Describe a time you held a report back because you did not trust the numbers yet.
Whether you protect accuracy under deadline pressure.
A clear reason, early notice to the reader, a new time, and no hiding the delay.

One Monday the weekly operations report showed orders down 30%, which made no sense given what the warehouse was seeing. I told the VP it would be four hours late and why. The cause was a load job that had run for only half the stores. Once it was rerun, the drop disappeared. The VP said a late correct report beat an early wrong one.

itsm.heading: IT service management questions
qs: How would you explain the difference between an incident, a problem and a change to a new service desk analyst?
Whether you understand the ITIL practices well enough to teach them simply.
Incident: restore service fast. Problem: find and remove the cause behind one or more incidents. Change: a controlled modification, often the fix. A real example helps.

I use one example. A floor of printers stops working: that is an incident, and our job is to get people printing, even with a workaround. If it keeps happening, we open a problem to find the cause, say a driver that crashes. Replacing the driver on 300 machines is a change, so it is planned, risk assessed and approved before anyone touches production.
What makes an SLA useful instead of just a number on a dashboard?
Whether you design SLAs around what the business needs and can measure.
Targets by priority tied to business impact, clear start, stop and pause rules, OLAs with resolver teams behind them, targets tested on real data, and regular review.

It has to match what matters to users and be measured the same way by everyone. I set priority by impact and urgency, then response and resolution targets per priority, with clear rules for when the clock pauses, like waiting on the user. Behind each one I agree OLAs with the resolver teams. Before signing, I check six months of data to see if it is achievable.
What is a change advisory board for, and which changes should not need to go through it?
Whether you see change control as risk management, not paperwork.
The CAB weighs risk and timing for normal changes. Low-risk repeatable work becomes pre-approved standard changes, and emergencies take a fast path with review after.

The CAB looks at risk, timing and conflicts for normal changes that could hurt the business. It should not see routine work. Adding a user to a group or a tested monthly patch should be standard changes, pre-approved with a template. Emergencies go to a small emergency group and get reviewed at the next meeting. A CAB that reviews 200 items a week reviews none of them properly.
What makes a knowledge base article actually get used by the service desk?
Whether you know what makes knowledge useful at the moment of need.
Titles in the words people search with, short tested steps, an owner and review date, links to the tickets it solved, and retirement of articles nobody uses.

It has to show up in the first search, so the title uses the words people type, like 'Outlook keeps asking for my password', not a system name. Steps are short and tested. Each article has an owner and a review date. We link articles to the tickets they resolve, so we can see which ones work and which need rework. Articles nobody uses get retired.
Email is down for the whole company at 9 a.m. and you are the major incident manager. What do you do in the first 30 minutes?
How you take control of a major incident and keep people informed.
Declare it, open a bridge with the right resolvers, assign roles, set an update rhythm, keep interruptions away from engineers, and log decisions with times.

I declare a major incident in the tool, open a bridge, and pull in the messaging team, network and the vendor if it is hosted. I assign a scribe and a comms lead. A first notice goes to staff within 15 minutes saying what we know and when the next update comes, then every 30 minutes. I keep managers off the bridge so engineers can work, and I log every decision with a time.
The same VPN connection error has been logged 40 times this month, and each ticket was closed as fixed. What do you do?
Whether you move recurring incidents into problem management.
Link the incidents to a problem record with an owner, look for patterns, publish a workaround as a known error, and track the permanent fix through change.

I link all 40 tickets to one problem record and give it an owner in the network team. Then I look for patterns; in a case like this it was one client version on laptops updated the month before. We published the workaround as a known error article, so the desk could fix it in two minutes. The permanent fix, a client rollback, went through change the next week.
A team keeps making production changes without raising change requests. What do you do?
How you get compliance without only policing people.
Find out why they skip the process, make the right path the easy one with standard changes, show the cost of unrecorded changes, and escalate if it continues.

I talk to the team lead first to find out why. Usually the process is too slow for small, routine work. In one case we turned their five most common changes into pre-approved standard changes they could raise in two minutes. I also showed them two incidents last quarter where nobody knew what had changed. If it had continued, I would have raised it with their director.
The business wants every priority 2 ticket resolved within four hours, but the team averages eleven. How do you respond?
Whether you negotiate SLAs with data rather than agreeing to fail.
Show current performance and where time goes, ask what business impact drives the ask, consider staffing, triage or a narrower scope, and agree a target the team can meet.

I do not agree to a target we will miss on day one. I show six months of P2 data and where the time goes; often it is waiting in a second line queue. Then I ask which services really need four hours. We might agree four hours for payroll and eight for the rest, with an OLA for the queue handoff. Everyone signs off on what we can actually deliver.
An outage was caused by a change the CAB approved last week. How do you run the review?
Whether you run a blameless review that improves the change process.
A blameless timeline, how the risk was judged, what testing and the backout plan missed, actions with owners and dates, and fixes to the process rather than to people.

I run a blameless review within a few days with the implementer, the approver and the service owner. We build a timeline and ask what we knew at approval. In one case the backout plan had never been tested and the risk rating missed a shared database. The actions were tested backouts for that class of change and the database added to the impact checklist, each with an owner and a date.
Ticket categories in ServiceNow are so messy that the reports tell you nothing. How do you fix it?
How you clean up the data that drives ITSM decisions.
A shorter category list that matches how resolvers think, category confirmed at closure, training and sampling audits, and accuracy tracked over time.

In one instance we had 380 categories and a third of tickets in 'Other'. I pulled a year of data, kept the 40 categories that covered almost all volume, and mapped the rest. We made resolvers confirm the category at closure, since the desk often guesses at intake. I sampled 50 tickets a month for accuracy. Within a quarter 'Other' was under 5% and we could see real trends.
Tell me about a time you cut the time it took to resolve a common type of ticket.
Whether you improve service with data, not just effort.
A specific ticket type, data showing where the time went, the change made, such as self-service or automation, and before and after numbers.

Password resets were 18% of our tickets and took an average of six hours because they sat in a queue. I worked with the identity team to roll out self-service reset with multi-factor checks and put the link on the portal's front page. Within three months reset tickets fell by about two thirds, and the desk had more time for harder work.
Tell me about a time a senior leader wanted their request moved ahead of everyone else's.
How you keep prioritization fair while staying helpful to executives.
Respect for the leader, priority set by impact under the agreed rules, a clear explanation, and any executive support process used openly rather than quietly.

A vice president wanted a new laptop set up the same day, ahead of a P2 that had 30 sales staff unable to work. I explained that and gave her a firm time the next morning, with a loaner that afternoon. She accepted it. Afterward we wrote a short executive support process, so requests like hers had a clear, visible path.
Tell me about a time you got engineers to write and keep up knowledge articles.
How you build a knowledge habit that lasts.
Knowledge built into the workflow, low effort, visible value and credit, measured by reuse and first contact resolution rather than article counts.

Engineers saw articles as extra work. I changed the process so that when they closed a ticket, they could create a draft article from the resolution notes in one click, and the desk tidied it up. Each month I shared which articles had solved the most tickets and named the authors. Over six months first contact resolution rose from 58% to 67%.
Tell me about a major incident that did not go well and what you changed afterward.
Whether you learn from incidents and fix the process, not just the outage.
An honest account of what went wrong in the handling, such as slow escalation or poor updates, and the specific process changes made after the review.

During a payroll outage we found the cause in two hours, but users heard nothing for the first 90 minutes and the desk took 400 calls. The review showed nobody owned communication. We added a comms lead role to every major incident, a template for the first notice, and a 15 minute target for sending it. The next major incident brought a fraction of the calls.

process-improvement.heading: Process improvement questions
qs: How would you use DMAIC on a slow invoice approval process?
Whether you can apply DMAIC to real work rather than recite it.
A clear problem and goal, a cycle time baseline, causes backed by data, tested fixes, and controls such as a chart and an owner to keep the gains.

Define: invoices take a median of 19 days to approve and we pay late fees; the goal is under 7. Measure: pull timestamps for every step for three months. Analyze: find where the waits are, often one approver or invoices bounced for missing purchase orders. Improve: pilot fixes like approval limits by amount. Control: a weekly cycle time chart with an owner who acts on it.
How do you map a current process so the map shows what really happens, not what the procedure says?
Whether you go to the work instead of trusting documents.
Walk the process, talk to the people doing it, follow real items end to end, capture waits, rework and handoffs, and check the map with the team.

I go where the work happens and follow a few real cases end to end, like five customer returns from arrival to refund. I sit with the people at each step and ask what they do when something is missing. The map always has steps the procedure does not, such as a side spreadsheet someone keeps. Then I review the map with the team so they can correct it.
When do you use 5 whys and when a fishbone diagram, and what goes wrong with each?
Whether you understand the limits of the root cause tools you use.
5 whys fits simple problems with one causal chain. Fishbone helps when many causes may contribute. Both fail when answers are guesses, so causes must be checked with data.

I use 5 whys for a fairly simple problem with one likely chain, like a missed shipment. Fishbone is better when many things could contribute, such as high scrap on a line. The risk with both is that people stop at an opinion or at blaming a person. So I treat each cause as a hypothesis and check it with data before we fix anything.
How do you show an improvement really worked and is not just normal variation?
Whether you measure before and after with enough care.
A stable baseline, the same measure before and after, enough data points, a run or control chart, and a check for other changes that happened at the same time.

I make sure we have a baseline of several weeks, measured the same way we will measure after. I plot it on a run chart or control chart to see if the shift is beyond the usual ups and downs. I also ask what else changed, like volume or staffing. In one project handle time dropped 12%, but half came from a seasonal mix change, so we reported the smaller number.
A department head asks you to 'implement Lean' in their team next quarter. What do you do first?
Whether you start from a business problem rather than a method.
Ask what problem they want solved and how they will know, agree a measurable goal and scope, then pick the tools that fit instead of rolling out a toolkit.

I ask what is hurting them. In one case the real issue was that new client setups took 30 days and sales was losing deals. So we agreed on one goal, setup under 15 days, and one process to start with. Tools came in as needed: a process walk, a value stream map, then a few pilot changes. Starting with a goal kept it from becoming a training program with no results.
The team you are working with says their process is fine and the delays are all caused by another department. What do you do?
How you handle blame between teams with facts.
Listen, follow the work across the boundary with data, bring both teams to the same map, and focus on the handoff rather than on who is at fault.

I take it seriously and look at the handoff with data. When I traced 50 orders, about half the delay was waiting on the other team, but a third came from orders sent over incomplete, so they bounced back. I brought both teams together with the same map and numbers. We agreed on a short handoff checklist, and the back and forth dropped by more than half.
Three months after your project closed, the team has slipped back to the old way of working. What do you do?
Whether you understand why gains fade and how to make them stick.
Find out why without blame, check whether the new way is harder, unowned or unmeasured, fix that cause, and give the process owner a simple control.

I go and ask the team why, without blaming anyone. Often the new way is slower in cases nobody planned for, or the supervisor who backed it has left. Once the reason was that a form we designed did not work for rush orders. We fixed the form, gave the process owner a weekly check of two measures, and added the standard to new hire training. I now check in at 30, 60 and 90 days.
Leadership wants to announce savings from your project, but the change has only run for one week. What do you do?
Whether you protect credible results under pressure to show wins.
Share early signs with clear caveats, explain what data is needed to confirm, agree a date for the real number, and avoid overstating savings.

I give them what we know, clearly labeled as early: rework is down from 9% to 5% in week one, but one week cannot separate real change from noise. I propose a date, after six weeks of data, to confirm the savings, and agree the calculation with finance. An inflated number that later shrinks hurts the credibility of every project after it.
Your root cause analysis points to a software system that another department owns. What do you do?
How you drive a fix you do not control.
Bring clear evidence and impact to the system owner, agree a fix and timing through their process, and use a workaround or process check in the meantime.

I put a number on the impact first; in one case a system default caused about 400 hours of manual rework a year. I took that to the system owner with examples, and we raised a change through their normal request process. It was scheduled for the next quarter, so we added a simple check in our process to catch the bad records until then. My sponsor followed up at director level.
An approval process has 14 sign-off steps and nobody can explain why most of them exist. How do you approach it?
Whether you remove waste carefully rather than cutting blindly.
Trace each step to a purpose, owner and risk, involve control owners such as audit or compliance, then remove, combine or set thresholds with their agreement.

I list each step and ask who added it and what risk it covers. Some are real controls required by audit or policy, and those stay or get simplified with the control owner's agreement. Others were added after one bad event years ago. In a purchasing process I worked on, we went from 14 steps to 6 by setting approval limits by amount, with finance and audit signing off.
Tell me about a project where the root cause turned out to be different from what everyone assumed.
Whether you let data overturn opinions, including senior ones.
A clear assumption, the data that disproved it, how it was shared with the people who held the view, and the better fix that followed.

Everyone believed late deliveries were the carrier's fault. When I matched 600 orders to scan times, most were late before the carrier picked them up, because orders after 2 p.m. missed the last pick wave. I showed the operations director the chart rather than arguing. We added a second afternoon wave, and on-time delivery went from 87% to 95% in two months.
Tell me about a time frontline staff owned an improvement instead of having it done to them.
Whether you involve the people who do the work.
Staff involved in mapping, finding causes and testing fixes, their ideas used, and signs they kept improving after the project ended.

On a claims team I asked the processors to map their own process on a wall and mark where they waited. They found that 20% of claims came back for one missing document. Their idea was a simple intake checklist, which they tested for two weeks. Because it was their fix, they kept using it and later added two more checks on their own.
Tell me about an improvement project that did not work and what you learned from it.
Whether you reflect honestly on failure and change your approach.
A specific failure, an honest view of their own part in it, and a concrete change to how they run projects now.

I once redesigned a warehouse layout that cut walking distance by 25% on paper. I had not involved the night shift, who handled most bulky items, and the new layout made their work harder. Within a month they had moved things back. Now I include every shift in mapping and pilot on one shift before any full rollout.
Tell me about a time you chose a quick fix instead of a full DMAIC project, or the other way around.
Whether you match the method to the size of the problem.
A clear reason for the choice based on how well the cause was known and the risk, and the result, showing they do not force every problem into a big project.

A billing team had a 3% error rate on one invoice type. A quick look showed one field defaulted to the wrong code, an obvious and known cause. We fixed the default and watched results for two weeks, no project needed. In the same team, heavy overtime had many possible causes, so that one got a full DMAIC project with a sponsor and a baseline.

spend-analyst.heading: Procurement and spend analyst questions
qs: How do you build a spend cube from raw accounts payable data, and where does it usually go wrong?
Whether you know the practical steps and pitfalls of spend analysis.
Pull AP and PO data, group suppliers into parents, classify to a taxonomy, add business unit and time. Weak supplier cleanup and a big unclassified bucket are common failures.

I pull 12 to 24 months of invoices and POs, clean supplier names into parent groups, then classify each line to a category taxonomy, by supplier first and by line description where a supplier sells many things. The three sides are who we buy from, what we buy and who buys it. It usually goes wrong when a big share lands in 'other' and nobody checks the top suppliers by hand.
What is the difference between hard savings and cost avoidance, and why does it matter to finance?
Whether you report savings in a way finance will trust.
Hard savings lower spend against a baseline and can come out of the budget. Cost avoidance stops an increase. Both are real, but they are reported separately.

Hard savings mean we pay less than before for the same thing, like a price cut from $40 to $36 a unit, so the budget can actually come down. Cost avoidance means we stopped an increase, like holding the price when the supplier asked for 8% more. Both have value, but only hard savings free up money. I report them separately, using the baseline method finance has agreed.
What is maverick spend, and how do you find it in the data?
Whether you can spot off-contract buying and its causes.
Buying outside contracts or the approved process. Find it through non-preferred suppliers in contracted categories, no-PO invoices and card data, then ask why it happens.

It is spend that goes around the agreed process, like buying from another supplier when a contract exists, or paying invoices with no purchase order. I look for spend in contracted categories going to other suppliers, POs raised after the invoice, and card transactions. Then I talk to the buyers, because often the contract supplier is slow or the catalog is hard to use.
How do you decide whether consolidating suppliers in a category makes sense?
Whether you weigh savings against risk and service.
Look at the spread of spend, prices, quality and service, supply risk, switching costs and user needs. Consolidate where volume buys leverage without a single point of failure.

I start with the spread: in one category we had 60 suppliers, but 8 held 80% of spend. I compare prices for similar items, service records and how critical the category is. For office supplies, moving to one or two suppliers was low risk. For a critical raw material, I would keep at least two qualified suppliers even if one is cheaper, because one failure can stop production.
In the supplier master you find the same company listed 23 different ways. What do you do?
How you clean vendor data and keep it from getting messy again.
Normalize names, match on tax ID and address, map records to one parent, fix the master with its owner, and add a duplicate check to new supplier setup.

For the analysis I normalize names and match records on tax ID and address, then map all 23 to one parent. In one cleanup that changed our top ten list and showed a supplier we had underestimated by $1.5 million. For the long term, I work with the team that owns the vendor master to merge or block duplicates and to require a duplicate search before any new supplier is created.
A category manager reports $2 million in savings, but budget owners say they cannot see it in their budgets. How do you sort it out?
Whether you can reconcile savings claims with what actually hit the budget.
Check the baseline, volume changes, timing and savings type, trace each line to actual spend, and agree one method with finance.

I take each savings line and trace it to actual invoices. The gaps usually come from a few places: some of it was cost avoidance, volume went up so total spend rose even though unit prices fell, or the contract started later than planned. In one review, $2 million claimed became $1.1 million of hard savings in the year. I then agreed one savings method with finance for all categories.
Marketing buys from dozens of agencies outside the preferred contract. What do you do?
How you reduce maverick spend while keeping the business on your side.
Learn why they go elsewhere, show the cost of fragmentation, adjust the contract or supplier panel to fit their needs, then make the compliant route the easy one.

I sit with the marketing leads first. In one company they used 45 agencies because the preferred agency could not do video or quick-turn social work. So we ran a small sourcing event and built a panel of six agencies covering those needs, with agreed rates. We made the panel the default in the buying tool, and off-contract agency spend fell from about 60% to 20% in a year.
In your spend analysis, 15% of the total is coded to miscellaneous. What do you do?
Whether you push classification until the data is usable.
Sort the unclassified spend by supplier and value, classify the largest pieces by hand or with rules, fix coding at the source, and track coverage over time.

I sort the miscellaneous spend by supplier and start at the top, since a small number of suppliers usually make up most of the value. I classify those by hand or with rules on supplier and line description. In one case 40 suppliers explained 85% of it, and the biggest was an IT reseller coded wrong at the PO stage. I then asked for that code to be removed from the requisition form.
Leadership asks you to take 10% out of indirect spend this year. Where do you start?
How you prioritize savings work across many categories.
Use the spend cube to rank categories by addressable spend, levers and ease, check contract end dates, and build the plan with budget owners and finance.

I rank indirect categories by addressable spend, how fragmented they are, and when contracts end. That shows where the realistic levers are, like consolidating facilities suppliers or cutting unused software licenses. I build a short list with an estimate per category, agree it with budget owners and finance, and say plainly if 10% needs cuts in demand, not just better prices.
A business unit resists moving to a single supplier because they worry about supply risk. How do you respond?
Whether you take risk concerns seriously instead of chasing savings.
Explore the actual risk, consider a primary supplier with a qualified backup, compare savings against the cost of disruption, and let the business decide with clear facts.

I ask what failure they are worried about, like a late shipment stopping a line. Then I look at the numbers: the saving from one supplier against the cost of a disruption. Often the answer is a primary supplier with 70 to 80% of the volume and a qualified backup with the rest. In one case that kept most of the saving and gave the plant a second source it could scale up.
Tell me about a time your analysis found a savings opportunity others had missed.
Whether you dig into data beyond the obvious categories.
A specific finding, how it showed up in the data, how they checked it, and the money or result it produced.

While cleaning card and invoice data, I saw we paid for the same design software through 14 separate team subscriptions, all at list price. Nobody saw it because each was small and on a card. I added up about 300 seats and worked with IT to move them to one enterprise agreement, which cut the cost by roughly a third and gave IT control of access.
Tell me about a time you had to correct a savings figure that had already been reported.
Whether you put accuracy ahead of looking good.
A quick, open correction with the reason, how the error happened, and a change to the method so it does not happen again.

We reported $800,000 in savings on a logistics contract in the first quarter. When I checked actual invoices, volume had shifted to a lane the contract did not cover, and real savings were about $500,000. I told my manager and the finance partner that week with the details, and we restated it in the next report. We then started tracking savings from invoices, not from the bid sheet.
Tell me about a time you worked with finance to agree how savings would be counted.
Whether you build shared rules that make savings credible.
A real disagreement about method, a jointly agreed definition of baselines and savings types, and more trust in the numbers afterward.

Procurement and finance argued every quarter about savings. I proposed a one-page method: the baseline is the last price paid, hard savings count for 12 months from contract start, and cost avoidance is shown separately. I tested it on last year's projects with the finance controller, and we adjusted two rules. After that, savings reviews took an hour instead of weeks of email.
Tell me about a time a stakeholder disagreed with how you classified their spend.
How you handle challenges to your data openly.
Listening, checking the facts, adjusting where they were right, explaining the rule where they were not, and keeping the taxonomy consistent.

The facilities director said $1.2 million we had put in facilities was really IT, because it was data center cooling. He was partly right. We agreed a rule that equipment serving the data center goes to IT infrastructure, and I moved the $700,000 that matched. The rest was general building work and stayed. I added the rule to our classification guide so the question would not come up again.

workforce-management.heading: Workforce management questions
qs: How do you build an hourly volume forecast for a support team, and what do you check before you trust it?
Whether you forecast from patterns and known events, not a single average.
Clean history, weekly and daily patterns, trend and seasonality, known events such as launches or billing runs, and accuracy checks against actuals and business input.

I take at least a year of history, remove odd days like outages, and build volume by week, then split it into days and half hours using recent patterns. I layer in known events, like a billing run that adds 30% on the 1st. Before I publish, I compare it with the same weeks last year, ask product and marketing what is planned, and review error by interval every week.
In plain terms, what does Erlang C tell you, and where can it mislead you?
Whether you understand the staffing model and its limits.
Given volume, handle time and a service goal, it estimates agents needed. It assumes no one hangs up and one contact at a time, so it can overstaff voice and fits chat poorly.

Erlang C takes contacts per interval, average handle time and a service goal like 80% answered in 30 seconds, and estimates how many agents you need taking contacts. It assumes callers never hang up and each agent handles one contact at a time. So for chat with several sessions, or email backlog, I use other methods or simulation, and I always add shrinkage on top.
What goes into shrinkage, and what happens when you get it wrong?
Whether you understand the time agents are paid for but not available.
Planned items like breaks, training, meetings and leave, plus unplanned absence and lateness. Underestimating it leaves intervals short even when volume is on forecast.

Shrinkage is paid time when agents cannot take contacts: breaks, lunches, meetings, coaching, training, vacation, sick time and system downtime. I track planned and unplanned separately and by month, since summer vacation and winter illness differ. Once we planned at 30% while the real figure was 36%, and we missed service most afternoons even though volume was on forecast.
How do you balance service level against occupancy when deciding staffing?
Whether you understand the trade-off between speed of answer and agent workload.
Higher occupancy saves cost but lengthens waits and raises burnout. Small teams need lower occupancy for the same service. Targets should fit the queue size and the work.

If occupancy runs very high, agents go from contact to contact with no breathing room, waits grow fast with any spike, and burnout and attrition follow. Small teams also cannot run as hot as large ones for the same service level. I agree a service target with the business, then watch that occupancy stays in a range the team can sustain, and flag it when it creeps up for weeks.
At 10 a.m. volume is running 25% over forecast and the queue keeps growing. What do you do?
How you manage intraday changes in a structured way.
Confirm the cause, reforecast the rest of the day, pull back off-phone work, move breaks within the rules, offer voluntary overtime, and keep leaders informed.

I first check why, since an outage or a bad customer email can mean a spike that keeps growing. Then I reforecast the rest of the day. I move training and meetings that can wait, shift breaks within the rules, and offer voluntary overtime. Team leads and the operations manager get a short update every hour. Afterward I record the cause so the next forecast can include it.
A team lead says your schedules are unfair because the same agents always get the late shifts. What do you do?
Whether you treat schedule fairness as a real issue and fix it with data.
Check the data, explain how shifts are assigned, then fix it with rotation or bidding under agreed rules, within any labor laws or union terms that apply.

I pull six months of shift assignments by agent. In one case the complaint was fair: newer agents had 70% of late shifts because the tool filled gaps by start date. We moved to a quarterly schedule bid under rules the team leads agreed, with everyone rotating through some late shifts. Before changing patterns I check any local scheduling laws or union terms with HR.
Real-time adherence shows an agent out of adherence for 40 minutes. What do you do?
How you use adherence data without treating agents as suspects.
Check for a good reason first, go through the team lead, log exceptions properly, and look at patterns over time rather than reacting to every minute.

I check the obvious first: a long call, a system issue or an approved exception nobody logged. Then I message the team lead rather than the agent, since the lead manages the person. If there was a real reason, I log the exception so the report is accurate. I look at trends over weeks rather than single events, and I bring patterns to the lead with the data.
A new product launches next month and there is no contact history for it. How do you forecast it?
Whether you can forecast with little data and plan for uncertainty.
Use drivers like expected customers and contact rate, borrow from similar launches, build low, likely and high cases, and agree how to cover the high case.

I build it from drivers: expected new customers times a contact rate from a similar past launch. If we expect 20,000 sign-ups and a past launch had 12 contacts per 100 customers in its first month, that is about 2,400 contacts. I make low, likely and high cases, staff to likely, and agree in advance how we would cover the high case, like overtime or a partner team.
Your volume forecast was accurate last week, but service level still missed every afternoon. How do you find out why?
Whether you look beyond volume to the other staffing inputs.
Compare actual handle time, shrinkage, schedule fit and adherence to plan by interval, find which one drove the gap, and fix that input.

Volume is only one input, so I compare plan to actual for handle time, shrinkage and staffed agents by half hour. In one case handle time was 15% higher in the afternoons because a new process added steps, and team meetings were booked at 2 p.m. We updated the handle time assumption and moved the meetings to the morning dip.
Finance wants to cut 10 agents from the support team. How do you show what that does to service?
Whether you can turn a budget decision into clear service impact.
Model service level and waits by interval with fewer agents, show the trade-offs plainly, and offer options such as changed hours or deflection work.

I run the model with 10 fewer agents against next quarter's forecast. In a similar case, service level fell from 80% to about 60% in peak hours and average wait went from under a minute to several minutes. I showed that with options: cut fewer agents, shift hours, or invest in self-service first. Finance chose a smaller cut tied to a deflection project.
Tell me about a time your forecast was badly wrong and what you changed afterward.
Whether you learn from forecast misses and improve the method.
A specific miss, its cause, how the day was handled, and a lasting change to data, process or how other teams share plans.

We forecast a normal Monday, but volume came in 40% high because marketing had sent a promotion email on Sunday night that nobody told us about. We pulled training and offered overtime, but still missed service. Afterward I set up a weekly 15 minute call with marketing and product to review their calendar, and I added known campaigns as an input to the forecast.
Tell me about a time you changed a schedule pattern that agents disliked.
Whether you balance service needs with agents' lives.
Listening to agents, using data to find options, testing a change, and improving both satisfaction and coverage where possible.

Agents hated split shifts, and exit interviews kept mentioning them. I looked at the intervals those shifts covered and found we could use part-time staff and later start times instead. We piloted it with one team for six weeks. Coverage held within 2 points of target, so we rolled it out, and split shifts stopped coming up in exit interviews.
Tell me about a time you had to say no to an operations manager who wanted a schedule change.
How you hold firm on service needs while staying a partner.
An explanation of the impact with data, an alternative that meets their goal, and a relationship that stays good.

A manager wanted his whole team off the phones for a two hour meeting on Monday morning, our busiest time. I showed him the model: service would drop below 50% for those two hours. I offered Wednesday afternoon, our quietest period, or two one hour sessions. He took Wednesday, and later started checking with me before booking big meetings.
Tell me about a time you found room in the schedule for coaching or training without hurting service.
Whether you plan off-phone time into the schedule on purpose.
Using interval forecasts to find low-volume slots, planning off-phone time ahead, and protecting it unless service really needs the people.

Team leads said coaching kept getting canceled. I looked at the forecast by half hour and found steady quiet slots on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons. I scheduled coaching there, 30 minutes per agent a week, and only canceled it if volume ran 10% over forecast. Coaching completion went from about half to over 90%.

coo.heading: COO questions
qs: What does a good operating cadence look like, and what belongs in each part of it?
Whether you know how to run a company's rhythm of reviews and decisions.
A short weekly metrics review, monthly business reviews by function, quarterly planning against goals, clear owners and actions, and meetings that end in decisions.

Weekly, a 45 minute review of a small set of metrics, with owners explaining misses and next steps. Monthly, each function reviews its numbers and risks in depth. Quarterly, we reset goals and budgets against the annual plan. Every meeting has a purpose, a fixed pack and a decision log. In my last company this replaced about a dozen recurring meetings.
How do you choose the few metrics you watch every week as COO?
Whether you focus on the measures that drive results.
A small set tied to company goals, leading and lagging measures, one owner each, written definitions, and paired metrics so one is not gamed at another's cost.

I start from the few outcomes the company must hit this year, then pick the inputs that drive them. For a delivery business that might be orders, on-time rate, cost per order, contacts per order and staff turnover. Each has one owner and a written definition. I pair metrics that pull against each other, like speed and quality, and I keep the list under 12.
What usually breaks first when operations scale quickly, and how do you get ahead of it?
Whether you anticipate scaling problems instead of reacting to them.
Informal processes, handoffs, onboarding, systems and decision rights. Get ahead with documented core processes, capacity planning and leaders hired before they are needed.

What breaks first is anything that relied on a few people knowing everything: handoffs, approvals, onboarding and data in spreadsheets. When we went from 80 to 250 staff in a year, I wrote down the ten core processes, set clear decision rights, and hired two operations leads a quarter before we needed them. I also planned capacity six months ahead instead of hiring after queues grew.
How should a COO and CEO divide the work, and what makes the partnership hold up?
Whether you understand the COO role as a partnership that differs by company.
The split depends on the CEO and the company. Clear ownership, no surprises, regular one-on-ones, disagreement in private and one voice in public.

It depends on the CEO. Some want a COO who runs all operations so they can focus on product, investors and customers; others want a partner on a few big programs. I agree in writing what I own and what we decide together, and we meet weekly. We disagree in private and give the team one view. I never let the CEO hear bad news from someone else first.
The CEO sets a goal to double revenue in 18 months. How do you turn that into an operating plan?
How you translate strategy into capacity, budgets and milestones.
Break the goal into drivers, work out the people, capacity, systems and cash needed and when, set quarterly milestones with owners, and raise trade-offs with the CEO early.

I break it into drivers: how many customers, at what order size, and what that means for each team. Then I work out what each function needs and when, like support headcount, warehouse space and system upgrades, so we are ready before demand arrives. I set quarterly milestones with owners and a budget, and tell the CEO early where the plan needs cash or trade-offs we have not agreed.
The board asks for a 15% cut in operating costs without hurting customers. Where do you start?
How you reduce cost while protecting service.
A full cost baseline, levers ranked by size and customer risk, vendor and process waste first, service guardrails tracked weekly, and honest reporting of remaining risk.

I build a full cost baseline by function and vendor, then rank levers by size and risk to customers. The first money usually comes from vendor contracts, unused software, duplicate work and processes we can automate. I set guardrails, like on-time delivery and support wait times, tracked weekly during the cuts. Headcount comes last and only with a plan for the work. I tell the board what risks remain.
Sales keeps promising delivery dates operations cannot meet, and the two teams blame each other. What do you do?
How you resolve cross-functional conflict through shared facts and rules.
Both leaders looking at the same data, the root cause found, a shared rule such as a capacity check before commitments, and goals aligned where needed.

I get both leaders in a room with the data; in one case 35% of orders were promised faster than our standard lead time. We agreed that sales could see live capacity in the CRM, that anything faster than standard needed an operations check within four hours, and we added on-time delivery to sales leaders' goals. The blaming stopped because both teams owned the same number.
Your head of fulfillment resigns three weeks before peak season. What do you do?
How you keep operations stable when a key leader leaves suddenly.
Secure their knowledge, name an interim, step in personally where needed, protect the peak plan, tell the team calmly what changes, and start the search.

First I make sure the peak plan, vendor contacts and open decisions are written down before they go, and I ask them to help with the handover. I name an interim, often their strongest deputy, and join the daily stand-up myself through peak. I tell the team what is changing and what is not. Then I start the search, but I do not rush a permanent hire during peak.
The CEO commits to a major customer on a timeline operations cannot deliver. What do you do?
How you handle a CEO decision you think is wrong without undermining them.
A quick private talk with the CEO with facts and options, a plan agreed together, and a realistic message to the customer rather than a quiet miss.

I go to the CEO the same day, in private, with the numbers: what we can deliver by the promised date and what it would take to do more, like overtime or delaying another client. We pick an option together. If we cannot meet it, I would rather we tell the customer now with a credible new date than miss quietly. Then we agree how big commitments get checked in future.
Your weekly metrics all look on track, but customer complaints are rising. What do you do?
Whether you check that your metrics measure what customers feel.
Read the complaints, find where the metrics miss the customer's view, check for averages hiding problems, and fix both the issue and the metric.

I read a sample of complaints myself, about 50. In one case our on-time delivery was 96%, but we measured it at the carrier handoff, not the customer's door, and a new carrier was losing a day in one region. The average hid it. We fixed the carrier issue and changed the metric to delivery at the customer, by region, so we would see the next one early.
Tell me about a time you scaled an operation through very fast growth.
Whether you have actually led operations through rapid growth.
Specific scale, the constraints they hit, what they built or changed in people, process and systems, the results, and what they would do differently.

At a meal kit company we went from 5,000 to 40,000 weekly orders in 14 months. I opened a second facility, hired its site leader six months before launch, and standardized pick and pack across sites. Cost per order fell 18%. What I would change: I left customer support tools too late, and wait times spiked for two months before we caught up.
Tell me about a time you disagreed with the CEO on a major decision.
How you challenge the CEO and then commit to the outcome.
Clear, private disagreement backed by data, real listening, a decision made, and full public support afterward, whichever way it went.

The CEO wanted to enter two new states in the same quarter. I thought our hiring and training could support only one well, and I showed the numbers in our one-on-one. We agreed to launch one state, with the second three months later if we hit service targets. We did, and the second launch went faster because we had fixed the training gaps first.
Tell me about a time a cost-saving decision went wrong and what you did about it.
Whether you admit mistakes and reverse course quickly.
An honest account of the decision, how the problem was spotted, how fast they acted, and what they changed in how cost decisions are made.

To save about $400,000 a year, I moved tier one support to a new outsourcing partner. Within six weeks customer satisfaction dropped 9 points and repeat contacts rose. I brought part of the volume back in house, put the partner on an improvement plan, and told the CEO and board plainly what had gone wrong. Now any cost change that touches customers gets a pilot with service guardrails first.
Tell me about a time you shut down an initiative that was not working.
Whether you stop failing work instead of letting it drag on.
Clear criteria, the evidence it was not working, how the decision was made and shared, and what happened to the people and the lessons.

We spent eight months building an in-house routing tool to replace a vendor. It was behind schedule and handled only half the cases. I set a review with the team and laid out the cost to finish against the vendor's price. We stopped it and moved the engineers onto inventory work. I thanked the team publicly and wrote up what we learned about build versus buy.

legal-intern.heading: Legal intern questions
qs: How do you check that a case you plan to cite is still good law?
Whether you verify authority before anyone relies on it.
A citator such as KeyCite or Shepard's, reading the later treatment yourself, checking the court and jurisdiction, and flagging anything doubtful.

I run every case through a citator, KeyCite or Shepard's depending on what the firm uses, and I read any negative treatment myself instead of trusting the flag color. I also check that the court binds ours. Last summer a case I liked had been distinguished twice on facts close to ours, so I told the associate and found a stronger one.
How do you structure a research memo for a partner?
Whether you write for a busy reader who needs the answer first.
Question and short answer up front, the facts relied on, analysis with authority, the strongest counterarguments, and open issues stated plainly.

I put the question and a short answer in the first paragraph, so the partner can stop there if she wants. Then the facts I relied on, the analysis with citations, and the best arguments against us. I end with what I could not confirm. My last memo was four pages, and the partner told me the first paragraph was all she needed for her client call.
In general terms, how is attorney-client privilege different from the duty of confidentiality?
Whether you understand that these are related but not the same thing.
Privilege shields certain lawyer-client communications from disclosure; confidentiality is a broader duty covering client information generally. Details vary by jurisdiction.

In general terms, privilege protects confidential communications between lawyer and client made to get legal advice, and it can be waived. Confidentiality is a wider ethical duty that covers almost everything I learn about a client's matter, wherever it came from. So even public facts about a client are not mine to chat about. When a specific question comes up, I ask a supervising lawyer.
You get a research question in a state whose law you have never worked with. Where do you start?
Whether you research efficiently instead of jumping straight into case databases.
Secondary sources first to learn the framework, then the controlling statutes and cases read in full, with the current version and the right court confirmed.

I start with a secondary source, like a state practice guide or a treatise, to learn the vocabulary and the leading cases in an hour instead of a day. Then I go to the statute and the controlling cases and read them myself. I confirm I have the current version of the statute and the right court, because secondary sources can be a year behind.
At 4 p.m. you realize you will not finish a research assignment due at 9 a.m. tomorrow. What do you do?
Whether you warn early instead of missing a deadline quietly.
Tell the assigning lawyer now, share what is done, propose what can be ready by the deadline, and ask what matters most for their use.

I tell the associate right away, not at 8:55. I send what I have, say which part is unfinished and what I can deliver by 9, like the answer for our home state with the other two states by noon. Then I ask what matters most. Once an associate told me she only needed the short answer for a call, which saved me hours.
A partner returns your memo covered in edits with the note 'not what I asked for.' What do you do?
How you take blunt feedback and learn what the reader actually needed.
No defensiveness, a short follow-up to understand the real question, a fast revision, and a habit change such as confirming scope at the start.

I read every comment first, then ask the partner for five minutes to make sure I understand what she needed. In my case she wanted a yes or no on one issue, and I had written a survey of three. I rewrote it to two pages that afternoon. Since then I repeat the question back in one sentence when I get an assignment and ask how the answer will be used.
You find a case that hurts the argument your supervising attorney wants to make. What do you do?
Whether you report adverse authority instead of burying it.
Report it promptly with a view on whether it can be distinguished. Lawyers can have a duty to disclose directly adverse controlling authority to the court.

I tell the attorney the same day and put it at the top of my notes, not in a footnote. I explain how it differs from our facts, if it does, and how the other side will use it. Bad news found early is useful; found by opposing counsel, it is a problem. Whether it must be cited to the court is the attorney's call, and I make sure they have what they need.
A friend asks what you are working on, and one of the firm's matters has been in the news. What do you say?
Whether you protect client information outside the office.
Nothing about the matter, even what is public. A polite deflection, and care with phones, social media and conversations in public places.

I say I can't talk about client work and change the subject, even if the case is in the news. Confirming that the firm is involved, or saying how I feel about it, can already be too much. I am careful where I take calls and never discuss a matter on a train or in a coffee line. If I am unsure what is allowed, I ask before I speak.
You think you may have sent a document with client information to the wrong email address. What do you do?
Whether you report a mistake at once instead of hoping nobody notices.
Tell the supervising lawyer immediately with the facts, do not try to fix it alone, and follow the firm's process; the lawyers decide on next steps.

I tell my supervising lawyer within minutes, with the exact facts: what was sent, to whom and when. I do not email the recipient on my own, because what to say has legal and ethical sides that the lawyers and the firm's general counsel must decide. Then I follow their instructions. It is uncomfortable, but hiding it for even a day makes everything worse.
Two associates each give you an urgent assignment due the same afternoon. How do you handle it?
Whether you manage competing demands openly rather than guessing.
Tell both about the conflict with realistic estimates and ask them, or whoever coordinates the work, to set the order. Never let one slip silently.

I tell both associates about the conflict right away, with my estimate for each task. If they cannot agree, I ask the person who coordinates our program or a senior associate to set the order. Last summer one task turned out to need only a list of cases, so I did it in 40 minutes and spent the afternoon on the other. Guessing who matters more is not my job.
Tell me about a time you made a mistake in your research or writing and how you handled it.
Whether you own errors and change your process.
A specific mistake, prompt disclosure, the fix, and a concrete change in habits afterward.

In my first internship I cited a statute section that had been amended six months earlier. The associate caught it before anything went out, but it was my job. I apologized, corrected the memo that day, and since then I check the effective date of every statute and note when I checked it. That habit has caught two outdated citations since.
Tell me about a time you explained a legal issue to someone without legal training.
Whether you can make the law clear without oversimplifying it.
Plain words, the practical consequence first, honesty about what is uncertain, and a check that the listener understood.

At a law school clinic I helped explain a lease issue to a tenant, with the supervising attorney in the room. Instead of the doctrine, I said what it meant for her: the landlord had to give written notice first, and we would check whether he did. I asked her what she would bring next time. She came back with the notice and the envelope, which turned out to matter.
Tell me about a time you got feedback on your writing that was hard to hear. What changed afterward?
Whether you can take criticism and act on it.
A real piece of criticism, no excuses, a specific change, and evidence that it worked.

A legal writing professor told me my memos buried the answer on page three. It stung, because I thought thoroughness was the point. I started writing the short answer first and cutting every paragraph that did not support it. My next memo went from nine pages to five, and the grade went up a full letter. I still use her checklist.
Tell me about a time you asked for help when you were stuck on an assignment.
Whether you know when to ask instead of spinning your wheels.
A real attempt first, a focused question showing what was already tried, and a rule for when to ask next time.

On a choice-of-law question I spent three hours and found nothing useful. I wrote down what I had searched and took one specific question to a senior associate. She pointed me to a treatise chapter in two minutes. Now I set myself a limit: if I am stuck after about an hour, I ask, because my time costs the firm too.

corporate-governance.heading: Corporate governance questions
qs: What makes good board minutes?
Whether you know minutes are a record of decisions, not a transcript.
Attendance and quorum, materials considered, discussion summarized at the right level, resolutions and votes recorded accurately, recusals noted, counsel review.

Good minutes show who attended, that a quorum was present, what materials the board received, that directors discussed each item, and exactly what was resolved and how they voted. They are not a transcript. I keep discussion summaries short and neutral and note any recusal. Drafts go to the general counsel and the chair before the board approves them at the next meeting.
How do you keep track of filing deadlines for a group with entities in many states and countries?
Whether you rely on a system rather than memory.
One entity system holding each requirement, owner and due date, early reminders, rules confirmed with agents or local counsel since they vary, and regular reconciliation.

Every entity sits in our entity management system with its jurisdiction, officers, registered agent and filing due dates. Rules and deadlines vary by state and country, so we confirm them with the registered agent or local counsel instead of assuming. Reminders go to a named owner 60 days ahead. Each quarter I reconcile the system against the agents' reports, which once caught a missed annual report.
What does a director conflict of interest look like, and how should it be handled?
Whether you know the process when a director has a personal interest in a matter.
Early disclosure, a note in the minutes, recusal where policy or law requires, a decision by disinterested directors, and counsel's advice, since rules vary.

A typical case is a director whose family company wants to become our supplier. The director discloses the interest before the item comes up, and I record it in the minutes. Depending on our policy and the law that applies, they leave the room for the discussion and the vote, and the disinterested directors decide. I flag these to the general counsel in advance.
What goes into a good board book, and when should directors receive it?
Whether you know how to prepare materials directors can actually use.
An agenda marking items for decision or discussion, short cover memos, draft resolutions, prior minutes, and delivery early enough for directors to read it.

The agenda comes first, with times and whether each item is for decision, discussion or information. Each decision item has a two-page cover memo saying what we are asking and why, then the detail and a draft resolution. Last meeting's minutes are included for approval. We aim to send it a week ahead through the board portal. When a paper arrives late, I tell the chair so she can decide whether to defer it.
A director asks you to change the draft minutes to show they opposed a decision they voted for. What do you do?
Whether you keep the record accurate under pressure from senior people.
A polite refusal to record what did not happen, a check of notes, the general counsel and chair informed, and corrections only to reflect what occurred.

I thank the director and check my notes. If they show a vote in favor, I explain that minutes must reflect what happened, though I can note concerns they actually raised in the discussion. I tell the general counsel and the chair before the minutes go for approval. Minutes are a legal record, and changing them to suit one person puts the company at risk.
You discover that a subsidiary missed its annual report and is now listed as not in good standing. What do you do?
Whether you fix a compliance gap calmly and find its cause.
Status confirmed, legal leadership and deal teams told, the filing and any reinstatement completed under local rules, and the reminder process fixed.

First I confirm the status on the state's records and with our registered agent. Then I tell the general counsel and check whether any contracts or financing with that entity close soon, because a good standing certificate is often required. I file the overdue report and whatever reinstatement the state requires. Last, I find why the reminder failed and fix it.
The CEO needs a board decision before the next scheduled meeting. How do you get it done properly?
Whether you know the options and follow the bylaws.
The bylaws and governing law checked for written consent or a special meeting and their notice and vote rules, then papers prepared and filed in the minute book.

I check the bylaws and the law of the state of incorporation to see what is allowed. Often it is a unanimous written consent, or a special meeting called with the required notice. I draft the consent with counsel, send it with a short explanation, and track signatures. Once fully signed, it goes in the minute book. If even one director wants to discuss it, I set up a call instead.
An officer who signs for twelve subsidiaries leaves the company on Friday. What do you do?
Whether you see every record that one personnel change touches.
Resolutions to accept the resignation and appoint replacements, bank mandates and powers of attorney updated, filings made as each jurisdiction requires, and the system updated.

I pull every entity where he is an officer, director or bank signatory from our system. Then I prepare resolutions to accept his resignation and appoint replacements, work with treasury on bank mandates, and revoke any powers of attorney he held. State and foreign filings get updated as each jurisdiction requires. I keep a checklist per entity until all twelve are closed.
A business leader wants a new entity set up in another country within a month. How do you handle the request?
Whether you slow down the right parts of a rushed request.
The business purpose first, tax and legal sign-off, local requirements and timing from local counsel, directors and bank accounts lined up, and the entity recorded from day one.

I ask what the entity is for, because hiring staff, signing contracts and holding IP can need different structures. Tax and legal must approve the structure. Local counsel tells us the steps and the realistic timing, which in some countries is longer than a month, and I say so early. I line up directors, an address and a bank account, and add the entity to our system the day it is formed.
Before an audit, you find that signed minutes for three past meetings are missing from the minute book. What do you do?
Whether you repair records honestly without backdating anything.
A search of drafts, the board portal and email, a check of whether they were approved, counsel's advice on approval now with current dates, and no backdating.

I search the board portal, email and my predecessor's files for drafts and any record that the board approved them. If I find approved versions, I file them with a note on how they were found. If not, I ask the general counsel how to have the board approve them now, dated as of today. I never backdate a signature. Then I add a rule: signed minutes filed within 30 days.
Tell me about a time something went wrong during a board or committee meeting you were supporting.
Whether you stay calm and keep the record accurate when logistics fail.
A real problem, a quick and proper fix, an accurate record of what happened, and a change that prevents it next time.

At one meeting the video link failed for two of seven directors just before a vote. We still had a quorum, but the chair chose to pause for ten minutes while IT reconnected them. I recorded the break and who rejoined when. Afterward we added a dial-in backup to every meeting invitation, and we have not lost a director since.
Tell me about a time you had to tell a senior executive that something could not be done the way they asked.
Whether you hold a governance line with tact.
The reason explained in business terms, an alternative that gets them most of what they want, and escalation to counsel when needed.

A division president wanted to sign a contract for a subsidiary where he was not an authorized signatory. I explained that the counterparty or a court could later question it. I offered two options: a director with authority signs this week, or the board grants him a limited power of attorney. He chose the first, and the contract was signed two days later.
Tell me about a time you improved how your team keeps entity records.
Whether you can turn scattered records into a reliable system.
The starting point, a clear plan, cleanup with owners, a measurable result, and a habit that keeps records current.

When I joined, our 80 entities lived in spreadsheets and shared folders. Over four months I moved them into an entity management system, starting with those that had filings due soonest. For each entity I checked officers and directors against signed resolutions. By year end every record had a source document attached, and the auditors' request for a director list took ten minutes.
Tell me about a time you handled highly confidential board information.
Whether you are discreet and careful with sensitive material.
Limited distribution, secure tools, no hints to colleagues, and calm handling of people who ask questions they should not.

Before a CEO succession was announced, I prepared the board materials. Only the chair, the general counsel and I had the drafts, and we used the board portal, not email. When colleagues asked why the chair was in the office so often, I said I couldn't discuss board business. The announcement came out on schedule, and nothing leaked before it.

government-contracts.heading: Government contracts questions
qs: In general terms, what is the FAR, and how do you use it day to day?
Whether you treat the FAR as working rules rather than trivia.
The FAR governs most federal agency buying and agencies add supplements such as the DFARS. Day to day you work from the clauses actually in your contract.

The FAR is the Federal Acquisition Regulation, the rulebook most federal agencies follow when they buy. Agencies add their own supplements, like the DFARS for defense. Day to day I start from our contract: which clauses it includes, in full text or by reference, and which dates they carry, because the version matters. When a clause question could cost money, I bring in counsel.
How do you build a compliance matrix for an RFP?
Whether you can turn a long solicitation into a checklist nobody can miss.
Every requirement from the instructions, evaluation criteria and statement of work, with its reference, proposal section, owner and status, checked before submission.

I go through the whole RFP, mainly Sections L and M and the statement of work, and put each requirement in a row with its paragraph reference. Each row gets the proposal section that answers it, an owner and a status. Page limits and format rules go in too. Before submission, someone who did not write the proposal checks every row, which on my last bid caught a missing form.
What is the difference between a bilateral and a unilateral contract modification?
Whether you understand who can change a government contract and how.
Bilateral: both parties sign, as in a supplemental agreement. Unilateral: only the contracting officer signs, as in an administrative change or a change order.

A bilateral modification is signed by both sides, for example a supplemental agreement that adds work at a price we negotiated. A unilateral one is signed only by the contracting officer, such as an administrative change or a change order under the changes clause. With a change order we may be owed an equitable adjustment, so I track the cost from day one and meet the notice deadlines in our contract.
Why must some clauses be flowed down to subcontractors, and how do you decide which ones?
Whether you treat flowdowns as real obligations, not boilerplate.
Some clauses require flowdown by their own terms, often depending on dollar value or type of work. Read each one, check thresholds, and ask counsel about unclear cases.

Some prime contract clauses say themselves that they must go into subcontracts, often above a dollar threshold or for certain work, like cybersecurity or labor clauses. I read each clause rather than pasting the whole list, because flowing down everything confuses suppliers and some clauses do not fit. I keep a flowdown matrix for each prime contract and ask counsel about unclear ones.
A program manager says the customer asked the team for extra work that is not in the contract. What do you do?
Whether you protect the company from unauthorized work.
Only the contracting officer can change the contract. Pause or document the work, write to the contracting officer, and get a modification before spending more.

I explain that only the contracting officer can change the contract, not the technical representative who asked. I ask the program manager to pause the extra work or carefully document it, and I write to the contracting officer that week describing the request and asking for direction. If they want the work, we price it and get a modification. Otherwise we risk doing it for free.
A government auditor asks for the timesheets and records behind your last six invoices. How do you prepare?
Whether you handle an audit with order and honesty.
Scope confirmed against the contract's audit clause, finance and counsel involved, records gathered and indexed, accurate answers to what is asked, and errors corrected.

I confirm the scope in writing and read the audit clause in our contract. Then I bring in finance and our counsel, and we gather timesheets, invoices and supporting documents in one indexed folder. We answer what is asked, accurately and on time, and log everything we provide. If we find an error before they do, we raise it and correct it, because credibility is worth more than one invoice.
You notice an invoice billed an employee's hours at a labor category they do not qualify for. What do you do?
Whether you correct billing errors quickly and through the right people.
Stop billing that way, size the error, tell management and counsel the same day, correct or credit the invoice, and follow company policy on disclosure.

I check the employee's qualifications against the labor category requirements to confirm the error. Then I stop future billing at that rate and work out how many hours and dollars are affected. I tell my manager and our counsel the same day, because billing errors on government contracts can have serious consequences. We correct or credit the invoice and fix the step where the category was assigned.
A subcontractor refuses to accept a cybersecurity clause your prime contract requires you to flow down. What do you do?
Whether you hold a compliance requirement while keeping the supply chain working.
Understand their concern, explain the clause, confirm with counsel that it applies, offer practical help, and do not issue the subcontract without it if required.

I ask what worries them, since small suppliers often fear costs they do not understand. I explain the clause in plain terms and confirm with counsel that it applies to the work and data they will handle. If it applies, we cannot drop it, so I offer help, like pointing them to official guidance or limiting the information we share. If they still refuse, I tell the program manager we need another supplier.
Two days before a proposal is due, you find an RFP amendment that changed the page limit. What do you do?
Whether you react quickly and keep the proposal compliant.
The full amendment read, the proposal manager told at once, the plan and matrix adjusted, and every amendment acknowledged exactly as the RFP requires.

I confirm the amendment on the official posting and read all of it, since it may change more than pages. I tell the proposal manager at once and we decide which sections to cut. I update the compliance matrix and make sure we acknowledge every amendment the way the RFP requires, because a missed acknowledgment can sink an offer. Then I check the posting daily until the due date.
A contract is near the end of its period of performance and the program team assumes an option will be exercised. What do you do?
Whether you plan for the government's choices instead of assuming them.
The option clause and its timing checked, an early conversation with the contracting officer, realistic expectations set, and plans ready for both outcomes.

I read the option clause for the exercise window and any preliminary notice the government is to give. A few months ahead I ask the contracting officer about their plans, and I remind the team that options are the government's choice. If no modification is signed by the end date, staff should not keep working on an assumption. I plan for both outcomes with the program manager.
Tell me about a time you found a compliance problem others had missed.
Whether you read carefully and raise issues without drama.
A specific issue, how it was found, how it was raised, and what changed in the process afterward.

In a contract modification I noticed a newer version of a clause had been incorporated, with a changed reporting requirement. Nobody had updated our process. I wrote a one-page note for the program manager and counsel, and we set up the new report before its first due date. Afterward we added a clause comparison step to every modification review.
Tell me about a time you explained a contract restriction to an engineer or program manager who saw it as red tape.
Whether you can make rules make sense to the people who must follow them.
The reason behind the rule in business terms, a practical way to comply, and a working relationship that survives.

An engineer wanted to buy a part from a source our contract did not allow. Instead of quoting the clause, I explained that a violation could cost us the contract and future bids. Then I helped him find an allowed supplier with the same part and a lead time two weeks longer. He planned around it, and later he started checking with me before ordering.
Tell me about a time you negotiated a modification with a contracting officer.
Whether you can work with the government firmly and respectfully.
Facts and documents first, a clear position, respect for the contracting officer's authority, and a fair outcome or a well-documented disagreement.

The government added a reporting task and our program team estimated 400 hours. The contracting officer thought it was minor. I sent a short proposal with hours by labor category and sample reports. We met, she questioned two assumptions, and we agreed on 320 hours. Keeping it factual, and conceding where she was right, made the next modification easier.
Tell me about a time a bid or contract deliverable deadline was at risk.
Whether you plan backward and escalate early.
An early warning, a recovery plan with owners, a backup option, and a lesson applied to the next deadline.

On one proposal, the pricing volume was waiting on a subcontractor quote with four days left. I called their contracts lead, agreed on a firm date, and prepared a backup estimate with our program team. The quote came a day late, and we submitted six hours before the deadline. Since then I ask for subcontractor quotes in the first week of every bid.

public-administration.heading: Public administration questions
qs: Walk me through a public budget cycle in general terms.
Whether you understand how public money gets planned, approved and spent.
Department requests, executive review, a proposed budget, public hearings, adoption by the legislative body, spending with monitoring, then audit. Details vary by government.

In general terms, departments prepare requests, budget staff review and balance them, and a proposed budget goes to the council or legislature. There are public hearings, changes and adoption. Then we spend within what was approved, track it monthly and request amendments when needed. An audit closes the loop. The calendar and rules vary, so I work from our own charter and budget calendar.
How do you measure whether a public program is working?
Whether you look at outcomes, not just activity.
Outcomes tied to the program's purpose, a baseline, honest data with known limits, and results used to change the program.

I separate outputs from outcomes. For a job training program, classes held is an output; participants employed six months later is an outcome. I set a baseline, agree on a few measures with the program team, and report them every quarter with the caveats. When our placement rate stayed flat for two quarters, we used the data to change how we recruited employers.
Why do public procurement rules exist, and how do you work within them when a department needs something fast?
Whether you see procurement rules as protection rather than obstacles.
Fairness, competition, value and public trust. Use the fast options your rules allow, never split purchases, and fix the cause through planning.

The rules protect public money and give vendors a fair chance, which keeps the public's trust. When a department needs something fast, I check what our rules allow: an existing contract, a cooperative contract we can join, or the emergency process if it truly is one. I never split a purchase to stay under a threshold. The real fix is planning, so I meet departments each quarter about upcoming needs.
How do open meetings and public records laws affect your daily work?
Whether you work as if your records and meetings are public, because they often are.
Agendas posted on time, no deliberation outside meetings, records kept where they can be found, and email treated as a possible public record. Rules vary by state.

Most states have open meetings and public records laws, and the details vary, so I learn ours. Day to day that means agendas posted on time, no side discussions among a quorum of board members, and records kept where they can be found. I write every email assuming it could be requested, because it often can be. When I am unsure whether something is exempt, I ask the city attorney.
A resident submits a public records request for emails between two department heads. What do you do?
Whether you follow the process instead of deciding alone what to release.
Log it, acknowledge on time, gather every responsive record, have legal review exemptions and redactions, and respond within the deadline your law sets.

I log the request with the date received, because response deadlines vary by state and often start right away. I send an acknowledgment and ask IT to search both mailboxes for the terms and dates.
