The records go to the city attorney's office to review exemptions and redactions. Embarrassing is not an exemption. We release on time and keep a copy of what we sent.
During public comment at a council meeting, a resident gets angry about a program you run. How do you handle it?
Whether you stay calm and respectful in public.
Listen without interrupting, follow the meeting rules, avoid debating from the dais, offer to follow up, and actually follow up.

I listen and take notes. The chair runs public comment, so I do not argue from my seat. If staff are asked to respond, I acknowledge the concern and give the facts briefly. Afterward I find the resident, give my card and set a time to talk. Last year a man upset about delays in a home repair program turned out to have a lost application. We fixed it within a week.
A council member asks you to move a constituent to the front of a waiting list. What do you do?
Whether you serve residents fairly under political pressure.
A respectful explanation of the rules, a check of whether the case qualifies for priority under policy, the director informed, and the contact documented.

I thank them and look at the constituent's case. If our policy gives priority, for example for an emergency repair, I apply it as I would for anyone. If not, I explain that the list follows the published criteria, and I tell my director about the request. I document the contact. Being fair to the people who have no one to call for them is the job.
Halfway through the fiscal year, your program is on pace to overspend its budget by 10%. What do you do?
Whether you manage public money with early warning.
Find the cause, tell the budget office early, look for savings inside the program, and request an amendment or transfer through the proper process if needed.

First I find out why: higher demand, a price increase or a coding error. Then I tell the budget office and my director now, not in month eleven. I look for savings inside the program, like delaying a vehicle purchase. If we still need money, I prepare a budget amendment or transfer request with the numbers and the impact of not funding it. Spending past what was approved is not an option.
A vendor who lost a bid calls you to complain that the process was unfair. How do you respond?
Whether you handle a bid complaint by the book.
Listen, do not discuss the evaluation informally, point to the formal protest process and its deadlines, and inform procurement and legal.

I listen politely and take notes, but I do not discuss how scores were reached over the phone. I tell the vendor about the formal protest process in our procurement rules, including the deadline, and how to request a debriefing if we offer one. Then I tell the procurement officer and our attorney about the call. If they file, the record we kept during evaluation speaks for itself.
Data show that residents who do not speak English use one of your services far less than others. What do you do?
Whether you work to serve everyone, not just the easiest to reach.
Confirm the gap in the data, talk to community groups, remove barriers like language and office hours, and measure whether use changes.

I check the numbers by neighborhood and language first, to be sure the gap is real. Then I meet a few community groups to learn why. Often it is simple: forms only in English, office hours during work time, no interpreter. In one program we translated the application into the two most common languages and added an evening each week. Use from those neighborhoods rose by about a third in a year.
Tell me about a time you had to carry out a policy you did not personally agree with.
Whether you can implement decisions made by elected officials professionally.
Concerns raised through the right channels before the decision, full implementation after it, and honest reporting of results.

Our council cut walk-in hours at a permit counter to save money, and I had argued for keeping them. Once it was decided, I made it work: we added online booking and posted the new hours everywhere. I tracked wait times and complaints and reported them honestly after six months. The data led the council to restore one evening a week.
Tell me about a time you made a process easier for residents.
Whether you see services from the resident's side.
A real pain point, a change that cut steps or time, and a measure showing it worked.

Residents needed three separate visits to get a block party permit. I mapped the steps with police, streets and permit staff and found that two signoffs could happen by email. We built one online form that routed to all three. Average time from application to permit went from 15 days to five, and in-person visits for that permit almost stopped.
Tell me about a time you worked with another department or agency to get something done.
Whether you can get results across organizational lines.
Shared goals made clear, a specific agreement on who does what, follow-through, and credit shared.

Our housing program and the health department visited many of the same families, each with its own forms. I proposed a shared intake form and a monthly call. We agreed on what each side could share under the privacy rules, with our attorneys' review. Within six months, families answered one set of questions instead of two, and both teams cut visit time.
Tell me about a time you explained an unpopular decision to the public.
Whether you can communicate clearly and honestly with residents.
Plain language, the reason behind the decision, honest trade-offs, and a way for people to ask questions and get answers.

When our water rates went up, I prepared the community meeting presentation. Instead of the full rate study, I showed one typical household bill before and after, and what the money paid for: replacing old pipes under three main streets. I answered every question or wrote it down and posted answers online the next week. People were not happy, but nobody said we hid anything.

organizational-development.heading: Organizational development questions
qs: How do you diagnose a team problem before proposing a fix?
Whether you gather evidence before choosing an intervention.
Interviews, data and observation, looking at structure, roles, processes and leadership as well as people, then sharing findings before agreeing on action.

I start by asking the leader what they see and what success would look like. Then I interview most of the team one to one, look at data like turnover and missed handoffs, and sit in on a few meetings. I look at roles, processes and decision rights, not just behavior. I share the themes with the team before we choose a fix, so they own it.
How do you measure the impact of a leadership development program?
Whether you look beyond satisfaction scores.
Several levels: reaction, learning, behavior on the job and results, with a baseline, input from managers, and honesty about cause and effect.

Satisfaction scores only tell me whether people liked it. I use the four Kirkpatrick levels as a guide: reaction, learning, behavior on the job and results. Before the program we take a baseline, such as 360 feedback and team engagement scores. Six months after, we repeat them and ask participants' managers what changed. I say openly that other things also affect results.
What makes an engagement survey worth running?
Whether you see a survey as the start of action, not the end.
A clear purpose, protected confidentiality, fast results to managers, action planning with teams, and visible follow-through before the next survey.

A survey is worth running only if we will act on it. I keep it short, protect confidentiality by not showing results for groups below a minimum size, and get results to managers within a few weeks. Each manager discusses them with the team and picks one or two actions. If people see nothing change, the next response rate drops, and they would be right to stop answering.
What makes a performance review process useful rather than a yearly ritual?
Whether you understand what reviews are for and where they usually fail.
Expectations set early, regular check-ins, evidence-based ratings with calibration, real development conversations, and a process light enough that managers do it well.

Reviews work when nothing in them is a surprise. That means goals set early, regular check-ins and notes through the year. Ratings should rest on evidence and be calibrated across managers to reduce bias. When I can, I separate the development conversation from the pay conversation. At my last company we cut the form from six pages to two, and both completion and quality went up.
Leadership will announce a reorganization in six weeks and asks for your help. Where do you start?
Whether you can help design and land a structural change.
Clarity on the goal, design options tested against it, roles and decision rights, the people impact, managers prepared to communicate, and support after launch.

I start by asking what problem the new structure must solve, because a reorganization is a means, not a goal. I help leaders compare two or three options against that goal. Once one is chosen, we define roles and decision rights, map who is affected, and prepare managers to talk to their people first. I plan check-ins at 30 and 90 days, because the real work starts after the announcement.
Engagement scores in one department dropped 15 points, and the manager is defensive. What do you do?
Whether you can use difficult data with a defensive leader.
A private conversation, curiosity over blame, a look at the comments and other data, help sharing results with the team, and a few agreed actions.

I meet the manager alone first and treat the results as information, not a verdict. We look at which items fell and what the comments say. Often there is a clear cause, like a role nobody refilled. I help them plan how to share the results with the team and ask for ideas. If the issue is the manager's own behavior, I offer coaching and agree on what we tell their leader.
A senior executive wants an off-the-shelf leadership course for every manager by next quarter. How do you respond?
Whether you push for the right solution while respecting the deadline.
The business need clarified, the course checked for fit, a design that meets the deadline, and agreement on how results will be measured.

I ask what they want managers to do differently and why now. If the need is basic people management for new managers, a good external course may fit, and I can launch it by next quarter, adding practice on our real situations and involving their bosses. If the need is something else, like decisions stuck at the top, I say a course will not fix it and show what will.
Halfway through a culture change program, managers stop attending the sessions. What do you do?
Whether you treat low participation as information.
Ask managers why, check sponsor support, adjust the design, and bring senior leaders back in visibly.

I talk to five or six of them to find out why. Last time it was simple: the sessions clashed with month-end close, and their own leaders never came. We moved the dates, cut the sessions from three hours to ninety minutes, and asked a senior leader to open each one. Attendance went back above 80 percent. Low attendance is usually a message about priorities.
After a reorganization, two teams keep arguing over who owns a process. How do you help?
Whether you fix role confusion with structure, not just goodwill.
Both leads in one room, the process and decisions mapped, ownership agreed with a tool such as a RACI chart, and the shared leader confirming it.

I sit with both team leads and map the process step by step. For each decision we agree who does the work, who approves, and who only needs to know, using a simple RACI chart. Where they cannot agree, their shared leader decides. We publish the result and check back after a month. Most of these fights are about unclear decision rights, not personalities.
A manager asks you to coach an employee with a 'bad attitude,' but you suspect the manager is part of the problem. What do you do?
Whether you handle a sensitive situation honestly and fairly.
Facts gathered before taking sides, candid feedback to the manager with evidence, sources protected, and the HR partner involved if conduct issues appear.

I ask the manager for specific examples, then, with the employee's agreement, talk to them too. If I hear that the manager changes priorities daily and criticizes people in public, I tell the manager what I heard, with examples and without naming anyone who asked not to be named. I offer coaching to the manager as well. If there are conduct issues on either side, I bring in the HR business partner.
Tell me about a program you designed that did not work as planned.
Whether you learn from failure and adjust.
A specific program, what went wrong, how it was noticed, what changed, and what you do differently now.

I built a mentoring program with 60 pairs, and by month three half had stopped meeting. Feedback showed mentors had no guidance and pairs had no goals. For the second round, we trained mentors in one session, asked each pair to set three goals, and checked in monthly. Pairs still meeting at month six went from about half to over 80 percent.
Tell me about a time you helped a leader change how they lead.
Whether you can influence senior people.
Trust built first, feedback grounded in evidence, small specific changes, and support until the change stuck.

A director made every decision himself, and his team waited for him. His 360 feedback showed it clearly, and I went through it with him. He agreed to try one change: managers would decide anything under a set budget. We met every two weeks for three months. His team's score on empowerment rose 12 points the next year, and he said he finally had time to think.
Tell me about a time you used data to change a leadership team's mind.
Whether you use evidence persuasively.
Clear data, a story that ties it to business results, the right audience, and a decision that followed.

Leaders believed people left for pay. I analyzed exit interviews and turnover by manager and found that 40 percent of departures that year came from teams under five managers. I showed it on one slide with quotes from exit interviews. The team agreed to a manager coaching program before a pay review, and turnover in those teams fell the next year.
Tell me about a time employees resisted a change you were supporting.
Whether you treat resistance as information and work with it.
Listening to the reasons, separating valid concerns from fear, changing the plan where needed, and involving people in the solution.

When we moved to a new performance review process, a group of engineers pushed back hard. I held three listening sessions and learned their concern was real: the new goals format did not fit long projects. We changed it to allow project milestones. A few of the loudest critics joined the pilot, and their feedback made the launch smoother.

industrial-security.heading: Industrial security questions
qs: In general terms, what is the NISPOM, and how does it shape a cleared contractor's security program?
Whether you understand the framework a facility security program is built on.
The rule setting how cleared contractors protect classified information, now in federal regulations, with oversight usually by DCSA, turned into the company's own procedures.

The NISPOM sets out how cleared contractors protect classified information. It is now in federal regulations, at 32 CFR Part 117, and for most contractors DCSA provides oversight. It covers personnel clearances, reporting, safeguarding, visits and self-inspections. I turn it into our own procedures and training, and when a requirement is unclear I check the rule and ask our DCSA representative instead of guessing.
In general terms, what do cleared employees have to report, and how do you make sure they do?
Whether you know the reporting obligations and how to make them easy to meet.
Personal status changes, certain foreign travel and contacts, and information affecting eligibility, as the rules set out, supported by training and a simple process.

In general terms, cleared employees report things like changes in personal status, certain foreign travel and contacts, and information that could affect their eligibility. The exact requirements are in the rules and agency guidance, so I point people to them instead of quoting from memory. I make reporting easy: a short form, one contact, and a reminder in training that reporting is part of keeping a clearance.
How does a classified visit get approved and controlled at a cleared facility?
Whether you understand visit control in general terms.
Clearance verified through the proper channel and need-to-know confirmed before the visit, identity checked and logged, access controlled, and disclosure limited to what was approved.

Before a classified visit, the visitor's clearance is verified through the official system or the sending organization's security office, and the host confirms need to know for the specific information. On the day, we check identity, log the visit, and escort or control access. Hosts are told what can be discussed. A clearance alone never means someone gets to see everything.
What is a self-inspection for, and how do you make it more than a checklist exercise?
Whether you use self-inspections to find real weaknesses.
The program tested against the requirements, employees interviewed, records sampled, findings fixed with owners and dates, and results reported to senior management.

A self-inspection is our own check that the program meets the requirements before anyone else checks it. I use the oversight agency's self-inspection aids as a guide, but I also interview employees, sample records and walk the secure areas. Findings get an owner and a date, and I brief our senior management official as the rules require. Last year we found three people overdue on training.
An employee tells you they left a classified document on their desk overnight in an open area. What do you do?
Whether you handle a possible security incident by the process.
Secure the material, thank them for reporting, conduct a preliminary inquiry, decide whether loss or compromise is possible, and report to the government as the rules require.

First I make sure the document is secured and accounted for. I thank the employee, because prompt reporting is what we want. Then I start a preliminary inquiry: who had access to the area overnight and whether anything is missing. Based on what I find, I report to our cognizant security agency as the rules require and document everything. Retraining and corrective action follow.
A foreign national arrives at the front desk for a meeting with an engineer, and nobody told security in advance. What do you do?
Whether you control access without causing a scene.
A polite wait in a public area, a call to the host, a check of visit and export control requirements, and a controlled visit only once cleared, or a new date.

I welcome the visitor and ask them to wait in the lobby. I call the engineer to find out what the meeting is about. Foreign national visits may need advance approval and an export control review, so I bring in our export compliance lead. If it cannot be cleared today, the meeting moves to a public space with nothing sensitive, or gets rescheduled. Afterward I remind the engineer of the notice process.
A cleared employee mentions in passing that they have large debts and fear losing their home. What do you do?
Whether you handle sensitive personal information with both care and compliance.
Respect and privacy, a check of whether it must be reported under the rules, help with the process, support such as an employee assistance program, and only required records.

I thank them for telling me and keep it private. Depending on the facts, financial trouble can be reportable, so I check the guidance and make sure it is handled as required, and I help them through the process. I also point them to our employee assistance program for financial counseling. I record what is required and nothing more. Treating people decently is what makes them come forward.
An engineer wants to email a file to a customer but is not sure whether it contains classified information. What do you do?
Whether you stop a possible spill before it happens.
Do not send it, check the security classification guide or ask the government program office, use only approved channels for classified, and treat any sent copy as an incident.

I tell him not to send it yet. We check the security classification guide for the program and, if it is still unclear, ask the government program office. If it is classified, it can only move over an approved classified system or channel. If it turns out he already sent a similar file, that is a possible spill, and I follow our incident procedure and report as required.
Two weeks before the deadline, only 70% of cleared employees have finished required security training. What do you do?
Whether you drive compliance steadily and without drama.
Names sent to managers, easy ways to finish, leadership involved for holdouts, and consequences applied as company policy states.

I send each manager the names on their team who are not done, with the deadline. I offer short in-person sessions twice a week for people who struggle with the online course. A week out, our senior management official gets the list. Under our policy, people who miss the deadline lose access to classified work until they finish. Next year I start reminders a month earlier.
You inherit a security program from a predecessor who left suddenly, and a government review is a month away. How do you prepare?
Whether you can take over and stabilize a program quickly.
Inventory of classified holdings and records, clearance and reporting status checked, past findings reviewed, gaps fixed by risk, and open contact with the government representative.

I start with an inventory: classified holdings, accountability records, personnel clearance status and open reports. I read the last review and self-inspection and check that past findings were fixed. I call our industrial security representative, introduce myself and ask what they will focus on. Then I fix gaps by risk, starting with safeguarding. What cannot be fixed in a month gets a documented plan.
Tell me about a time you enforced a security rule with a senior person who did not want to follow it.
Whether you can hold the line with leaders respectfully.
The rule and its reason explained, respect for the person, escalation to the right official if needed, and no exception without authority.

A vice president wanted to bring his personal phone into a closed area for an urgent call. I said no, explained that it was a written restriction for that area and that a violation would be an incident I had to handle. I offered him the office phone just outside. He was annoyed but used it. Later he asked me to brief his staff on the rule.
Tell me about a time you handled a security incident from start to finish.
Whether you are thorough and calm under pressure.
Containment, facts gathered without blame, required reports made on time, the root cause found, and corrective action that held.

An employee found a security container unlocked one morning. We checked the contents against our records, talked to the last people who used it, and found nothing missing. The cause was a new hire who did not know how to fully lock the dial. I reported as required, retrained the team with a hands-on demonstration, and added a second-person check at closing for 60 days.
Tell me about a time you improved how employees report things they are required to report.
Whether you can build a culture where people come forward.
The barrier identified, a simpler process, trust built through how reports are handled, and a measurable improvement.

Our foreign travel reports were often late, and people told me the form was confusing and they feared questions. I wrote a one-page guide, set up a simple online form and spoke at team meetings about why reporting protects them. Within a year, late reports dropped from about one in four to almost none. Being calm and quick with each report mattered more than any reminder.
Tell me about a time you rolled out a new security requirement across a company.
Whether you turn new rules into everyday practice.
The source read closely, interpretation confirmed with the oversight agency where unclear, a practical rollout with training, and a check that it worked.

When the NISPOM became a federal regulation, 32 CFR Part 117, I compared the new text with our procedures line by line. Where I was unsure, I asked our DCSA representative. I updated our procedures, briefed managers in 30 minutes each, and changed our reporting form to match. At the next self-inspection I tested the changed areas first, and they held up.

industrial-designer.heading: Industrial designer questions
qs: How do you decide a sketch direction is ready to move into CAD?
Whether you know what sketching is for and when to commit to a direction.
Wide exploration first, a few directions tested as quick foam or paper models, key dimensions and internal parts checked, and team agreement before detailed CAD.

I sketch broadly first, often 40 or 50 thumbnails, then narrow to three directions. I make quick foam models of those, because proportions that look right on paper often feel wrong in the hand. Once one direction works in the hand and fits the internal parts the engineers gave me, I move to CAD. Starting CAD too early locks in decisions nobody has tested.
What do you check in a plastic part before it goes to an injection molder for a quote?
Whether you design parts that can actually be made at a reasonable cost.
Even wall thickness, draft on vertical faces, no needless undercuts, sensible ribs and bosses, a parting line that suits the look, and an early review with the toolmaker.

I check that walls are an even thickness, since thick spots cause sink marks and warping. Every face that pulls out of the tool needs draft. I look for undercuts, because each one can add a side action to the tool. Then I review the parting line and gate location with the toolmaker early. On a speaker housing, that review removed two side actions before we cut steel.
How do you choose the color, material and finish for a product people handle every day?
Whether you think about how materials wear, feel and cost, not just how they look.
Choices tied to the use, physical samples tested for scratches, fingerprints and grip, cost and supplier ability checked, and a clear spec the factory can match.

I start with how the product is used. A kitchen tool gets wet, greasy and dropped, so I test real samples for grip, scratches and how easily they clean. I avoid high gloss on surfaces that get handled, because every fingerprint shows. I check cost per part with sourcing and then write a finish spec with approved color chips so the factory has a clear target.
What can a rough prototype tell you that a polished rendering cannot?
Whether you use physical models to learn, not just to present.
Scale, weight, grip, reach and how parts fit together, learned early and cheaply, plus honest reactions from users who are not distracted by a perfect finish.

A rendering can make anything look good. A foam or 3D printed model shows whether it is too big for a small hand, whether the button sits where the thumb lands, and how it balances. People also give more honest feedback on rough models because they do not feel the design is finished. On one handheld scanner, a $30 print showed the grip was 8 mm too thick.
In a user test, most people pick up your handheld device the wrong way round. What do you do?
Whether you treat user behavior as information about the design, not as user error.
Accepting that the form gives the wrong cue, finding what signals which way is up, testing fixes with new models, and not relying on a label to explain it.

I take it as a design problem, not a user problem. If 7 of 10 people hold it upside down, the shape is telling them to. I watch the videos to see what they grab first, then make two or three quick models with a clearer cue, like a thumb rest or more weight toward the base. I test those with new people. A printed arrow is a last resort.
The toolmaker says a detail you care about needs an extra side action and raises tooling cost. What do you do?
How you balance design intent with manufacturing cost.
Asking what the detail does for the user, looking for ways to keep the effect without the undercut, getting the cost in numbers, and deciding with the team.

I ask myself what the detail actually does for the user. If it is only a styling line, I look for another way to get the same effect, like moving it to the parting line or changing the draft direction. If it matters, such as a snap that makes assembly easy, I get the extra cost in writing and show the team the trade-off. Then we decide together.
Late in development, the unit cost target drops by 15%. What do you do?
Whether you can cut cost without wrecking the product.
A cost breakdown by part, the biggest cost drivers tackled first, the features users touch protected, options with savings shown, and quick checks with users.

I ask sourcing for a cost breakdown by part, because guessing wastes time. Usually a few parts drive most of the cost. On a lamp project, the metal base was 30% of the cost, so we switched to a weighted plastic base with a metal-look finish and tested it with five users. I protected the parts people touch most and cut where they would not notice.
Marketing wants a high gloss finish on a product that will be handled all day. What do you do?
How you settle a disagreement about finish with evidence, not opinion.
Understanding why marketing wants it, showing physical samples after real use, offering options like gloss on low-touch areas, and agreeing on what users will see over time.

I ask what they want gloss to say, usually premium. Then I bring samples: a gloss part and a fine texture, both handled for a week on my desk. The gloss one shows scratches and prints. I suggest gloss on a low-touch area like the top ring and texture where hands go. Seeing the samples side by side usually settles it faster than any argument.
First production samples arrive with sink marks and a color that does not match the approved chip. What do you do?
How you handle quality problems with a factory calmly and clearly.
Defects documented against the spec, tool problems separated from process problems, fixes worked out with engineering and the factory, and approval only against the agreed standard.

I photograph the defects next to the approved chip under the agreed light and mark the sink locations on the drawing. Sink marks are often a wall thickness or process issue, so I review them with the mechanical engineer and the factory. Color goes back with the chip and the spec. I do not approve a near match to save time, because it becomes the new standard.
An engineer moves a button to simplify the circuit board, and now it is hard to reach. What do you do?
How you protect usability while working with engineering constraints.
Understanding the engineering reason, showing the usability cost with a model or quick test, exploring options like a mechanical extension, and deciding together with cost clear.

I ask why it moved; maybe the board got smaller or a part had to shift. Then I make a quick print with the button in the new place and have a few people use it. If reaching it is awkward, I show that clip to the engineer. We look at options together, like a longer plunger or a small flex cable. Sometimes the extra cost per unit is worth it and sometimes it is not.
Walk me through one project in your portfolio from the brief to production.
Whether you can explain your process, your decisions and your own role clearly.
The problem and constraints, research and early ideas, why one direction won, trade-offs with engineering and cost, what shipped, and their own role made clear.

My strongest piece is a cordless drill grip for a tools brand. The brief was less hand fatigue at the same cost. I watched 6 contractors work, made 20 foam grips, and tested the top three. Engineering needed the battery lower, so I reshaped the grip around it. It shipped in 14 months. I led the form and finish; the mechanical team owned the motor and gearbox.
Tell me about a time a design you liked failed in user testing.
Whether you let evidence change your mind.
A real example where they set aside their own preference, what the test showed, how the design changed, and what they do differently now.

I designed a sleek bottle warmer with a hidden touch control. I loved it. In testing, 5 of 8 parents could not find the control at night with one hand. We added a raised physical dial with a clear click. It looked less clean, but it worked half asleep. Now I test controls in the real setting, like a dark room, before I fall for a shape.
Tell me about a time you solved a problem with an overseas factory.
How you work with suppliers across distance, time zones and language.
Clear documentation with photos and marked-up drawings, patience with time zones, a direct fix rather than blame, and the lesson built into the next project.

On a lamp project, the factory kept sending shades with a visible seam. Calls went in circles. I sent a marked-up drawing with photos of the seam, an acceptable sample and a reject. I also asked what was causing it. It was the tool parting line, so we moved it 5 mm into a groove. Since then I send visual quality standards with every new part.
Tell me about a time you had to defend a design decision to engineers or executives.
Whether you can argue for the user with evidence and still listen.
Evidence like test results or cost data rather than taste, real attention to the other side's concern, and an outcome they can explain, even a compromise.

Our VP wanted to drop the rubber overmold on a handheld meter to save $1.20 a unit. I brought drop test results and a short video of users gripping it with wet gloves. I also offered a cheaper option: overmold only on the grip zone. He agreed to that. It works better to show what the user loses than to say the design will look worse.

customer-advocacy.heading: Customer advocacy questions
qs: How do you find customers who would make good advocates?
Whether you know where advocates come from and check before asking.
Several signals like survey scores, usage, support history and CSM input, a check on account health before any ask, and a request that gives the customer something too.

I start with signals: high survey scores, strong usage, good results, and people who already post about us. Then I always check with the customer success manager, because a promoter in the survey may have an open escalation. I ask what the customer would value, like visibility for their team or a speaking slot. Last quarter that gave me 25 new advocates from a list of 60.
How do you run a reference program that does not wear out your best customers?
Whether you protect advocates while still meeting sales demand.
A large enough pool matched by industry and size, limits per customer, a request process that checks the deal, every use tracked, and real thanks.

Every reference request goes through a short form with the deal stage and size, so we use references late in real deals. I track every call in the CRM and cap each customer at about two calls a quarter unless they offer more. I keep growing the pool so there are matches by industry and size. After each call, the rep and I thank the customer and tell them how the deal went.
How do you measure the influence of advocacy on pipeline and revenue?
Whether you measure honestly without overclaiming.
References and content tracked against opportunities in the CRM, win rates and deal speed compared, results called influence rather than credit, and a consistent method.

I log every reference call and case study send against the opportunity in the CRM. Then I compare deals that used advocacy with similar deals that did not. Last year, deals with a reference call won about 10 points more often. I report it as influence, not as revenue we created, because many things win a deal. Finance trusts the number more when I say that.
What makes a case study useful to a sales team, not just pleasant to read?
Whether you write customer stories for how they will actually be used.
A specific problem, a clear before and after with numbers the customer approved, a quote that sounds human, tags by industry and size, and short versions for slides and email.

Reps need to find a story that matches their prospect, so I tag each case study by industry, size and use case. The story needs a real problem, the numbers the customer agreed to share, and a quote that sounds like a person. I also make a one-slide version and a three-line email version, because most reps will never send a four-page PDF.
A sales rep asks for the same star reference for the fourth time this month. What do you do?
How you protect a key advocate while still helping the deal.
Checking the deal stage, offering a similar alternative, explaining the limit to the rep, and asking the customer again only in a way that makes a no easy.

I check the deal first. If it is early stage, I offer a case study or a video instead. If it is late and large, I look for another customer in the same industry and size. If the star customer is truly the only fit, I ask them directly and make it easy to say no. I tell the rep why we cap requests: if we burn this customer out, nobody gets them.
A customer agreed to a case study, but their legal team wants all numbers and their name removed. What do you do?
How you handle case study approvals and still get something useful.
Understanding the concern, offering options like percentages or an anonymous version, our own legal checking claims, and accepting the customer's final decision.

I ask our contact what legal is worried about. Often it is exact figures or being seen to endorse a vendor. I offer options: percentages instead of dollar amounts, an anonymous version like a regional bank, or a quote with title only. Our own legal team checks the claims. If they still say no, I thank them and keep the relationship. A pushed customer stops being an advocate.
An advocate due to speak at your conference now has an open escalation and an unhappy CSM. What do you do?
Whether you put the customer relationship ahead of the event.
Talking to the CSM first, being honest with the customer, offering to step back without pressure, helping move the fix along, and a backup speaker ready.

I talk to the CSM first to understand the problem and the timeline to fix it. Then I call the customer myself and say plainly that I know things are rough and they can step back without any awkwardness. Some still want to speak because the issue is being handled well. I keep a backup speaker ready either way, and I help push the escalation along inside the company.
Your CMO asks whether the advocacy program is worth its budget. What do you show?
Whether you can tie advocacy to outcomes leaders care about.
Full program cost, pipeline and win rates for deals that used advocacy, content use by sales, advocate account retention, and an honest view of what to cut.

I show the cost, including tools, gifts and my team's time. Next to it I show pipeline that used a reference or case study, win rates for those deals, and how often reps used our content. I add retention for advocate accounts, but I say plainly that happy customers both renew and advocate. I end with what I would cut. Last year that was a gift program nobody valued.
A rep promised a customer a discount in exchange for a case study, without telling you. What do you do?
How you handle incentives that could cause approval or credibility problems.
Finding out exactly what was promised, bringing in sales leadership, checking policy and any disclosure needs with legal, documenting the outcome, and a clear process going forward.

First I find out exactly what was promised and whether it is in writing. Then I bring it to the sales manager, because discounts have approval rules. I ask legal whether this kind of exchange is allowed under our policy and whether it would need to be disclosed with the story. Whatever we decide, I write up a simple rule so reps come to me before offering anything.
Your main contact approved the case study, then left the company before it was published. What do you do?
How you handle approval risk when a champion leaves.
Holding publication, finding the new owner of the relationship, getting approval again in writing, and using it to start a relationship with the new contact.

I hold the publication. The approval came from a person who no longer speaks for the company, so I need a new one. I ask the CSM who owns the relationship now and send them the draft with a short note on why the story is good for their team. It cost us six weeks once, but the new contact became an advocate too. Publishing without consent could lose the account.
Tell me about a case study you took from the first ask to publication.
Whether you can run the whole approval process from start to finish.
How the customer was chosen, the interview, the draft, customer and legal approvals, what changed, how long it took, and how sales used it afterward.

I asked a logistics customer after their CSM said they had cut onboarding time by half. I ran a 30 minute interview with the operations lead, drafted the story in a week, and sent it with the quotes highlighted. Their legal asked to change a cost figure to a percentage. Approval took five weeks. Sales used it in about 40 deals that year, and the customer spoke at our event.
Tell me about a time a customer said no to being an advocate. What happened next?
Whether you respect a no and learn from it.
Accepting the no gracefully, asking whether a lighter option would work, keeping the relationship, and changing how they ask in future.

A healthcare customer said no to a case study because their policy blocks vendor endorsements. I thanked them and asked if anything lighter was possible. They agreed to take one peer call a quarter, with no public mention. I learned to check such policies before asking, and now I offer a menu of options, from a quote to a private call, instead of starting with the biggest ask.
Tell me about a time you worked with customer success to recruit advocates.
How you partner with the team that owns the customer relationship.
Shared goals with customer success, a light process that respects their time, credit for their help, and no asks without their go-ahead.

CSMs saw my requests as extra work, so I asked their manager for 15 minutes in their weekly meeting. I showed how references helped renewals and expansion, not just new sales. We added one field in the CRM where CSMs flag possible advocates, and I do the outreach. I share wins in their channel and credit them by name. Nominations went from 3 to 20 a quarter.
Tell me about an advocacy activity you stopped because it was not working.
Whether you judge your own programs honestly.
Clear evidence it was not working, the decision to stop, how stakeholders were told, and where the time or budget went instead.

We ran an online advocate points platform where customers earned rewards for reviews and shares. After six months, the same 15 people did most of the activity, and the reviews felt forced. I showed the numbers to my manager and we did not renew it. We used the budget for a small customer advisory board, which gave us better references and product feedback.

sponsorships.heading: Sponsorships questions
qs: How do you put a value on a sponsorship package?
Whether you value a deal on what it delivers, not on a price list.
Audience size and fit, each asset priced from comparable deals and delivery cost, rights like exclusivity priced separately, and the sponsor's goals taken into account.

I list every asset in the package: signage, digital posts, hospitality, naming, and rights to use the marks. I price each from comparable deals in our market and from what it costs us to deliver. Then I look at the sponsor's goals, because a package worth $200,000 to a beer brand may be worth half that to a bank. Exclusivity adds value, so I price it separately.
What is activation, and why do many sponsorships fail without it?
Whether you understand that the rights fee is only the start.
Activation is what the sponsor does with the rights, like campaigns, experiences and offers. Without a plan and a budget for it, a logo alone rarely changes anything.

Activation is everything the sponsor does with the rights they bought: an on-site experience, a promotion, content with the athlete, hospitality for key clients. A logo on a banner alone rarely moves sales. When I sell a deal, I ask what budget the sponsor has to activate and help plan it, because a sponsor who never activates usually does not renew.
What should a sponsorship contract spell out about deliverables?
Whether you know how to prevent disputes before they start.
Each asset with quantities, dates and specs, creative approval, exclusivity terms, make-goods for misses, reporting, payment schedule and termination, reviewed by legal.

Every asset should be listed with how many, when and where: two LED rotations per game, four social posts, eight hospitality seats. It should say who approves creative and by when, what category is exclusive, and what happens if we miss something, usually a make-good of equal value. Payment dates, reporting and termination go in too. Legal reviews the terms; I make sure the list is complete.
How do you measure the return on a sponsorship?
Whether you set goals first and measure against them.
Objectives agreed before the deal starts, metrics that match them like leads, sales, brand lift or client meetings, a baseline, and an honest recap report.

I agree on goals before signing. If the sponsor wants leads, we set up a tracked offer and a lead scanner at the booth. If they want awareness, we run a brand survey before and after. For hospitality, we count client meetings and the deals that followed. Media exposure goes in the recap, but I do not lead with it, because it says little about business results.
A sponsor says their logo was missing from the stage backdrop and wants money back. What do you do?
How you handle a delivery failure without making it worse.
Checking the facts fast, owning the miss if it happened, offering a fair make-good under the contract, fixing the process, and confirming it all in writing.

I check photos and the production order the same day. If the logo really was missing, I call the sponsor and say so plainly. I check what the contract says about make-goods, then offer something of equal or higher value, like extra digital posts or a feature at the next event. I confirm it by email and add a logo check to our production checklist.
A new sponsor wants category exclusivity, but an existing partner is in a nearby category. What do you do?
Whether you protect existing contracts while trying to close a new deal.
Reading the existing exclusivity language, defining categories clearly, asking legal when unclear, talking to the current partner if needed, and never selling what is already sold.

I read the existing contract first. If our current partner has exclusivity for sports drinks and the new sponsor sells energy drinks, the definitions matter a lot. If it is unclear, I ask legal. Where there is overlap, I either narrow the new category or talk to the existing partner before signing anything. I would rather lose a new deal than break a promise to a current partner.
An athlete your brand sponsors is suddenly in the news for a scandal. What do you do?
How you protect the brand with a calm, careful response.
Pausing scheduled activations, getting the facts, bringing in legal and communications, checking the contract's conduct terms, and deciding with leadership.

I pause any scheduled posts and ads with the athlete that day, because a cheerful post next to bad news is the worst outcome. Then I bring in legal and communications. Legal reviews the conduct clause in the contract. We agree on a short holding statement if press asks. Leadership decides whether to suspend or end the deal once we know the facts, not on the first headline.
Final attendance at an event you sold comes in 30% below the number in your sponsor deck. What do you do?
Whether you are honest with sponsors when numbers fall short.
Telling sponsors before they hear it elsewhere, explaining the cause, checking what each contract guaranteed, offering fair added value, and fixing future forecasts.

I tell the sponsors myself, before the recap, with the real number and the reason. Then I check each contract to see what was guaranteed and what was an estimate. Where we promised a number, we offer a make-good. Where we did not, I still add value, like extra content or a booth upgrade next year. I also change how we forecast attendance in our decks.
Your sponsorship budget is cut mid-year and you must drop one of three deals. How do you decide?
Whether you decide on results and contract terms, not habit.
Each deal's results compared against its goals, termination terms and costs reviewed, relationships and timing weighed, and a professional exit.

I compare all three against the goals we set: leads, sales lift, client meetings. Then I read each contract's termination terms, because ending some deals mid-term costs money. Last year one deal drove most of our leads and another mainly gave executives tickets. We kept the first. I told the other partner in person that we were exiting, and we honored the notice period.
Mid-season, the sponsor's marketing lead changes and the new person questions the whole deal. What do you do?
How you protect a deal when your contact changes.
Meeting the new person quickly, showing results so far against goals, learning their priorities, adjusting activation within the contract, and building more than one contact.

I ask for a meeting in the first two weeks. I bring a short recap of what the deal has delivered so far against the goals their predecessor set. Then I mostly listen, because the new lead has their own targets. If their focus is leads, not awareness, I shift the remaining assets toward that within the contract. I also make sure I know at least two other people on their team.
Tell me about a sponsorship deal you negotiated that you are proud of.
How you structure and close a deal that works for both sides.
A real deal with the starting positions, what was traded instead of discounted, how value was shown, and results after signing.

A regional bank wanted naming rights for our 10K race but had a small budget. Instead of discounting, I built a three-year deal with a lower first-year fee rising each year, plus a financial literacy booth for activation. They hit their goals and we got stability. They renewed after year three at a higher level, and their booth signed up over 300 new customers.
Tell me about a time a sponsorship did not deliver what you expected.
Whether you own results and learn from them.
An honest account of the gap, the cause they found, what they did with the partner, and what changed in how they buy or sell deals.

We bought a festival sponsorship expecting leads, but the booth was in a corner and we got 80 scans against a goal of 500. I had not asked for the site map before signing. I talked to the organizer, and they moved us for day two, which helped a little. Now I get booth placement and expected foot traffic written into the contract before we commit.
Tell me about a time you turned a first-year sponsor into a renewal or a bigger deal.
Whether you manage partners all year, not just at signing.
Regular check-ins, early reporting, help with activation, a recap tied to goals, and a renewal proposal built on what worked.

A local car dealer took a small game-day package as a test. I sent a short report every month with photos and numbers, and helped them run a test-drive offer for fans. At season end, I showed 120 test drives traced to the offer. They renewed and doubled the deal. I started the renewal talk three months before the end, not in the last week.
Tell me about a time you had to say no to a sponsor's request.
Whether you can hold limits and keep the relationship.
A clear reason for the no, such as brand fit, contract or safety, an alternative offered, and the relationship kept intact.

A sponsor asked to hand out free energy drinks to kids at our youth tournament. Our policy and the venue rules did not allow it. I said no on the phone and explained why, then offered a family zone with water stations under their brand and a coupon for parents. They took it. Saying no with an option ready kept them happy, and they renewed.

fundraising-grants.heading: Fundraising and grants questions
qs: What does good donor stewardship look like between asks?
Whether you keep donors close when you are not asking for money.
Prompt, personal thanks, regular reports on what the gift did, chances to see the work, contact matched to giving level, and every contact logged in the database.

It starts with a fast, personal thank you, within a few days. Then the donor hears what the gift did: a short update with a story and a number, like 40 families housed this quarter. Major donors get a call or a site visit. I log every contact in the database so the next person knows the history. The next ask should never be the first thing they hear from us since the last one.
How do you build a grant budget that matches the proposal?
Whether your budget and narrative tell the same story.
Every activity in the narrative costed, staff time and direct costs shown, indirect costs per the funder's rules, a budget justification, and a review with finance.

I build the budget alongside the narrative, not after. Every activity in the plan, like training 50 teachers, has its costs: staff time, materials, travel. Indirect costs follow the funder's rules, which vary, so I check their guidelines and our rate with finance. I write a short justification for each line. Then finance reviews it so we never promise what we cannot track.
How do you write outcomes a funder can actually check?
Whether you know the difference between activities and results.
Outcomes that describe change for people rather than activities, with a baseline, a target, a timeline and a realistic way to collect the data.

I separate what we do from what changes. Running 20 workshops is an activity. Seventy percent of participants passing a job skills test within six months is an outcome. I check that we have a baseline and can collect the data with the staff we have. I would rather promise a smaller target we can measure than a big one we cannot prove at report time.
How would you explain restricted and unrestricted funds to a new board member?
Whether you understand donor restrictions in plain terms.
Restricted gifts must be used as the donor specified, unrestricted gifts keep operations running, and finance tracks the two separately under accounting rules.

I would say a restricted gift comes with conditions from the donor, like use only for the after-school program or only next year, and we must honor them. Unrestricted gifts can go where the need is greatest, including rent and salaries, which keep every program running. Our finance team tracks the two separately under accounting rules, and our auditors check it.
Three months before a report is due, the grant-funded program is well behind its targets. What do you do?
Whether you are honest with funders early.
The facts from program staff, a call to the program officer before the report, causes and a recovery plan explained, and a request for a change or extension if needed.

I meet with the program lead to understand why: staffing, enrollment, a partner delay. Then I call the program officer before the report, not in it. I explain where we are, what caused it and what we will change. If the targets cannot be met, I ask how they handle changes or no-cost extensions. A surprise in the final report is what damages trust.
A donor you have cultivated for a year is ready for a major gift ask. How do you prepare and run the meeting?
Whether you can plan and make a major gift ask with care.
A specific amount and purpose based on research and past conversations, the right people in the room, a clear ask, then silence, listening and an agreed next step.

I prepare a specific ask based on their giving history, interests and what they have told me, like $50,000 over two years for the reading program. I decide who attends; often the executive director. In the meeting we talk about the work first, then I make the ask plainly and stop talking. Whatever they say, I listen, answer questions and agree on a next step and a date.
A donor offers a large gift restricted to a project your organization does not run. What do you do?
Whether you protect the mission from gifts that pull it off course.
Thanking the donor, understanding their interest, checking with leadership whether it fits the mission and can be done, and offering an aligned alternative or a polite no.

I thank them and ask what draws them to that project. Then I talk to the executive director, because a new program needs staff, space and money beyond the gift. If it does not fit our mission, I go back and suggest a program we do run that meets the same interest. If that does not work, I may point them to a group that does that work. Mission drift costs more than the gift.
Two grant deadlines and the annual gala fall in the same week. How do you handle it?
How you plan and prioritize under heavy deadlines.
Planning backward from each deadline, finishing proposals early, handing off defined gala tasks, and telling leadership early if something is at risk.

I map all three on one calendar and plan back from each date. I aim to submit the grants a few days early, since portals can fail on the last day. Reusable parts, like the organization background and budget notes, I prepare first. For the gala, I hand defined tasks to a volunteer lead. If one proposal cannot be done well, I tell my director early so we decide together.
A loyal donor's annual gift drops from $10,000 to $1,000 with no explanation. What do you do?
Whether you respond to a change with care rather than pressure.
Sincere thanks for the gift, a personal call to reconnect, listening for what changed, and a note in the database without pushing for more.

I thank them warmly for the $1,000, the same as any year. Then I call to check in, not to ask why. Often I learn something: a change in their finances, a concern about us, or a gift moved elsewhere. If it is a concern, I take it to leadership. If it is their circumstances, I respect it. I note what I learn in the database so no one makes an awkward ask later.
Finance tells you some grant money was spent on costs the grant does not allow. What do you do?
How you handle a compliance problem with a funder.
Facts confirmed with finance, the grant agreement checked, costs moved to an allowable source where possible, leadership told, and the agreement followed on telling the funder.

I sit down with finance to see exactly what was charged and how much. Then I read the grant agreement again. Usually the fix is to move the expense to unrestricted funds and charge allowable costs instead. I tell my director the same day. If the agreement or the funder's rules require us to report it, we do, with a clear explanation. Then we fix the coding process so it does not repeat.
Tell me about a grant proposal you wrote that was funded. What made it work?
Whether you understand what makes a proposal win.
Research on the funder and fit, a clear need with data, a credible plan and budget, any contact with the program officer, and what they reuse now.

I wrote a $150,000 proposal to a regional foundation for a youth jobs program. Before writing, I called the program officer to check fit, and she said they cared most about employer partners. So I got letters from four local employers and built the plan around them. The budget matched each activity. We were funded, and she later told me the employer letters made the difference.
Tell me about a proposal that was declined. What did you do next?
How you learn from a rejection.
Asking for feedback, accepting it, improving the proposal or the fit, and a clear decision on whether to reapply.

A national funder declined our food access proposal. I emailed to ask for feedback, and the program officer said our evaluation plan was weak. I worked with our program team to add a simple pre and post survey and a university partner to help analyze it. We reapplied the next cycle and were funded at $75,000. Now I build evaluation into every proposal from the start.
Tell me about a major gift you helped close.
Whether you can grow a relationship into a significant gift.
The cultivation over time, how the ask was shaped, who was involved, the outcome, and how the donor was thanked and kept informed after.

A retired teacher gave $500 a year for a decade. I visited her, learned she cared most about literacy, and invited her to see our tutoring program. Over 18 months we talked many times. When she asked how she could do more, our executive director and I asked for $100,000 over five years for tutoring. She said yes. We send her a letter from a student every term.
Tell me about a time you had to get data from program staff for a grant report.
How you work with busy colleagues to meet reporting deadlines.
Asking early with a clear template, explaining why it matters, making it easy, following up kindly, and fixing the process for next time.

Program staff saw my data requests as paperwork. For one report, I sent the template a month early with only the fields the funder needed, and I joined their team meeting to explain that this grant paid for two of their positions. I followed up once a week. We submitted on time, and then I set up a shared tracker so the numbers go in monthly, not all at the end.

business-continuity.heading: Business continuity questions
qs: How do you run a business impact analysis, and what should come out of it?
Whether you know how to find what matters most to keep running.
Interviews with process owners, impacts over time, dependencies on people, systems, sites and suppliers, ranked recovery priorities with targets, and leadership sign-off.

I interview each process owner with the same questions: what happens if this stops for an hour, a day, a week? We look at money, customers, legal or regulatory duties and reputation. We map dependencies on systems, people, sites and suppliers. Out of it comes a ranked list of processes with recovery time and data loss targets. Leadership signs off, because it drives spending.
Explain RTO and RPO, and who should set them.
Whether you understand recovery objectives and who owns them.
RTO is how fast a process must be back; RPO is how much data loss is acceptable. The business sets both through the BIA, and IT confirms what is achievable.

RTO, the recovery time objective, is how long we can be down before the damage is unacceptable. RPO, the recovery point objective, is how much data we can afford to lose, measured in time. If the RPO is one hour, backups or replication must run at least hourly. The business owner sets both through the BIA. IT tells us what the current setup can actually achieve.
How do you design a tabletop exercise people actually learn from?
Whether you can run an exercise that tests plans, not people.
Clear objectives, a realistic scenario with timed injects, the real decision makers present, a neutral facilitator, a no-blame tone, and an after-action report with owners.

I start with two or three objectives, like testing who can declare a disaster and how we reach staff without email. The scenario is realistic for us, with injects every 15 minutes that add pressure. The people who would really decide must be in the room. I keep it no-blame. Within two weeks I send an after-action report, and each gap gets an owner and a due date.
What makes a crisis communications plan work in the first hour?
Whether you know what has to be ready before a crisis starts.
Named roles and backups, pre-approved message templates, contact lists that work without the main systems, a set update rhythm, and one source of truth for facts.

The first hour goes well only if most decisions were made before. That means named roles with backups, contact lists stored outside our main systems, and templates for staff, customers and media that legal has already reviewed. We commit to an update at a set time, even if it says we know little yet. One person owns the facts so nobody shares different versions.
During a tabletop, it becomes clear nobody knows who can declare a disaster. What do you do?
How you handle a governance gap found in an exercise.
Noting it without blame, letting the exercise go on with a temporary choice, then getting leadership to name the authority and backups, and updating the plan.

I note it on the board and let the group pick someone for the rest of the exercise, so we keep learning. In the debrief I make it the top finding. Then I take it to the executive sponsor with a proposal: the COO declares, with two named backups and clear criteria. Once approved, I update the plan, tell everyone involved, and test it in the next exercise.
The BIA says order processing needs a 4-hour RTO, but IT says recovery takes two days. What do you do?
Whether you can turn a recovery gap into a business decision.
Both numbers checked, the cost of the gap and of closing it shown to leadership, options like manual workarounds offered, and the decision and any accepted risk recorded.

First I check both numbers: is four hours really needed, and is two days tested or a guess? Then I lay out options for leadership: invest in faster recovery, use a manual workaround for urgent orders, or accept the risk. I show rough costs for each with IT and finance. Leadership decides, and I record the decision. An unspoken gap is worse than an accepted one.
Ransomware takes down email and file shares at 9 a.m. You lead continuity. What do you do in the first hour?
Whether you can run the business response alongside IT security.
The crisis team activated on backup channels, security leading the technical response, workarounds started for critical processes, and communications begun with legal involved.

I activate the crisis team using our backup channel, a text alert and a bridge line, since email is down. Security leads the technical response; my job is the business. I check which critical processes are hit and start their workarounds. Legal and communications join early, because notification duties vary by law and contract. We set hourly updates and log every decision.
A hurricane is forecast to hit the city with your main call center in 48 hours. What do you do?
Whether you act early on a warning instead of waiting for the impact.
The plan activated early, staff safety first, work shifted to other sites or remote staff, suppliers and backups checked, and customers kept informed.

I bring the crisis team together that day. Staff safety comes first, so we follow local official guidance and give people time to prepare their homes. We start moving calls to our other site and confirm remote agents have laptops and connectivity. I check the generator fuel contract and data backups. We prepare a customer message about longer waits. Then we meet twice a day until it passes.
A department head says they have no time for continuity planning. What do you do?
How you get busy leaders to take part.
Understanding their workload, showing the risk in their own terms, making the work light and fast, and going to the executive sponsor only if needed.

I ask what is on their plate and listen. Then I show them one scenario in their terms: if your system is down for three days, what happens to your customers and targets? I offer to draft the plan from a one-hour interview, so they only review it. Most say yes to that. If they still refuse, I tell the executive sponsor, because the risk belongs to the business.
A key supplier has a fire and cannot deliver for six weeks. What do you do?
Whether you plan for supply chain disruption.
The impact and stock on hand confirmed, alternate suppliers worked through with procurement, customers and products prioritized, and early, honest communication.

I work with procurement to confirm what we have: stock on hand, orders in transit, and how many weeks that covers. Then we check alternate suppliers from our list and what it takes to qualify them. If supply runs short, we agree with sales which customers and products come first. Customers hear from us early. Afterward, I push to add a second source for that part.
Tell me about a real outage or incident you helped manage.
Whether you have handled a real disruption and what you learned from it.
The situation, their role, the decisions made, how communication went, recovery time against targets, and what changed afterward.

A power failure took our main office offline for 11 hours. I ran the crisis call, moved 200 staff to remote work, and sent updates every hour. Our payment process recovered in 3 hours, inside its 4-hour target. The phone system did not fail over as planned, which took 2 hours to fix. The review found a missed configuration change, and we now test failover every quarter.
Tell me about a time you got leadership to fund a continuity improvement.
Whether you can make a business case for resilience.
A clear risk tied to the BIA, costed options, a recommendation in business terms, and the decision they secured.

Our BIA showed our customer database could lose up to 24 hours of data, but the business needed one hour. I worked with IT on two options and costs, and with finance on what a day of lost orders would cost. I presented it to the CFO on one page. She approved the cheaper option with hourly replication. A year later a storage failure cost us under an hour of data.
Tell me about a time you had to communicate bad news during a crisis.
Whether you communicate honestly under pressure.
Clear, timely facts, no guessing, what is being done, when the next update comes, and coordination with legal and communications.

During a data center outage, our recovery estimate slipped from 4 hours to 12. I told the executive team within 10 minutes of knowing, with the reason and the new estimate. With communications, we updated the customer status page and said plainly it would take longer. We gave the next update time and kept it. Customers were unhappy about the delay, not about being misled.
Tell me about a time you kept continuity plans current after a big change in the business.
Whether you maintain plans instead of writing them once.
Seeing that the change affected plans, updating the BIA and contacts, retesting key steps, and a trigger so future changes reach them in time.

When we moved to a new cloud provider, half our recovery steps became wrong overnight. I worked with IT to rewrite the runbooks and redid the BIA for the affected processes. We ran a short test to prove the new recovery times. Then I asked the change board to add a continuity check to every major project, so I hear about changes before they go live, not after.

visual-merchandiser.heading: Visual merchandiser questions
qs: What makes a planogram work for both the customer and the store team?
Whether you see a planogram as a selling tool and a work instruction.
Logical groupings, key items at eye level, facings based on sales, a fit with the real fixtures, easy restocking, and clear visuals the team can follow.

For the customer, items need to be where they expect, grouped the way they shop, with best sellers and new items at eye level. Facings should follow sales, so fast movers do not run out. For the team, it must fit the actual fixture, be easy to restock, and come with a clear photo and item list. If a planogram needs an hour to understand, stores will skip it.
How do you plan a window display on a tight budget?
Whether you can create impact with simple means.
One clear message, a strong focal point, scale and repetition, color and lighting, props reused or made cheaply, and the product as the hero.

I pick one message, like one new color story, and build around it. Repetition and scale do a lot cheaply: 30 of the same paper shape in one block of color reads from across the street. I reuse risers and forms we already have and spend on lighting, because a dark window shows nothing. On one $300 budget, the featured sweater sold through in two weeks.
How do you measure whether a new display changed sales?
Whether you test displays fairly instead of guessing.
Test and control groups of similar stores, a before and after period, sales of the featured items, notes on promotions and season, and enough time to see a pattern.

I set the display in a group of test stores and match them with similar control stores that keep the old setup. I compare sales of the featured items over the same weeks, before and after. I also note any promotion, weather or staffing change that could explain it. On one test, featured items rose 18% in test stores and 6% in control, so I credited about 12 points to the display.
How do you decide where products go on a new store floor?
Whether you plan layouts around how customers really move and shop.
Watching traffic flow, keeping the entrance uncluttered, key items on main paths and focal points, related products grouped, and changes made from sales data.

I start by watching how people actually walk the store, not just the floor plan. I keep the first few steps inside the door open so people can slow down. Key and new items go on the main path and at aisle ends where people look. Related items go together, like phone cases next to chargers. After a few weeks, I check sales by zone and move what is not working.
You roll out a new set to 200 stores, and photo checks show half set it wrong. What do you do?
How you fix a rollout problem and its cause.
Finding the common errors, checking whether the instructions caused them, a clear correction with photos, follow-up with the worst stores, and a better next guide.

I sort the photos to see what went wrong most often. If 100 stores made the same mistake, the guide is probably the problem, not the stores. I send a short correction with a photo of the right set and the top three fixes, with a date to resubmit photos. I call the district managers for stores still wrong after that. Then I test the next guide in two stores before sending it out.
A store manager says your planogram does not fit their fixtures. What do you do?
Whether you listen to stores and adapt sensibly.
Asking for photos and measurements, checking the fixture records, sending an approved alternative quickly, and correcting the store's records for next time.

I ask for photos and measurements of the fixture. Often the store has an older gondola than our records show. I send an approved version that fits, keeping the key items and adjacencies the same. Then I update the fixture record for that store so the next set is right. I thank the manager, because those calls stop the same problem in other stores.
A product featured in your window sells out in three days. What do you do?
How you react quickly when a display works too well.
Telling buying and replenishment fast, swapping in a related item so the window keeps selling, not featuring what customers cannot buy, and sharing the result.

I tell the buyer and replenishment team the same day with the sales numbers, because they may be able to get more stock. Meanwhile I do not leave a window selling something we cannot sell. I swap in the closest related item or another color. I send the store a simple update so staff know what to say. I also share the result, since it helps plan stock for the next display.
A vendor sends a branded display that clashes with your store's look. What do you do?
How you balance vendor agreements with brand standards.
Checking what was agreed with the vendor, talking to the buyer, a placement or adjustment that meets both needs, and standards shared for future displays.

I check with the buyer what we agreed with the vendor, since some deals require their display to be used. If it is required, I look for a spot where it works, like an aisle end away from our main focal point. If it is not, I suggest our own fixture with their product and a small sign. Then I share our display standards with buying so vendors see them before they build.
A holiday display is narrowing an aisle and customers keep bumping into it. What do you do?
Whether you put safety and access ahead of looks.
Fixing it right away, checking the company's aisle and safety standards, redesigning the display for the space, and updating the guide for other stores.

I move it that day, even if it means a smaller display. Safety and access come first, and aisle width and fire rules can apply, so I check the company standard and ask facilities or loss prevention if unsure. Then I redesign it for the space, perhaps going taller instead of wider. If the same guide went to other stores, I send a correction to all of them.
Head office sends a new promotional set two days before launch, and stores are short-staffed. What do you do?
How you get a rollout done under time pressure.
Prioritizing what customers see first, simplifying where allowed, a short clear guide for stores, and flagging stores that cannot finish before launch.

I split the set into must-do and nice-to-have. The window and the front table are must-do, because that is what customers see. I send stores a one-page guide with photos and a time estimate for each part. I call the busiest stores to agree on what they can finish. Anything that will not be ready, I flag to my manager before launch, not after.
Tell me about a display you created that clearly moved sales.
Whether you can connect your work to results.
The goal, the idea, how it was set up, how results were measured, the numbers, and what they learned.

Our candles sold poorly on a back wall. I moved them to a table near the entrance, grouped by scent family with testers out, and added soft lighting. Over six weeks, candle sales rose 25% compared with similar stores that kept the old setup. The testers mattered most, so we added them to the chain standard.
Tell me about a time you won over a skeptical store manager.
How you build working relationships with stores.
Listening to their concerns, involving them in the plan, showing results, and giving their team credit.

One manager ignored our guides because they took his team too long. I visited, worked a shift on the floor, and saw his stockroom was tiny. We adjusted the set so it could be restocked without moving the whole fixture. His sales in that category went up, and I praised his team on our regional call. After that, he sent me ideas from his staff.
Tell me about a time you had to rework a display after it launched.
Whether you admit mistakes and fix them quickly.
What went wrong, how they noticed, how fast they fixed it, and what changed in their process.

We launched a back-to-school wall with notebooks up high and backpacks below. Store photos and first-week sales showed kids could not reach the notebooks, and sales were flat. I flipped the layout and sent a correction to 40 stores within three days. Sales picked up the next week. Now I think about who the shopper is, including their height, before I set shelf heights.
Tell me about a time you changed a display because of what you saw customers do.
Whether you learn from watching real shoppers.
Specific observations, the change made, and the result measured or seen.

I spent two afternoons watching our shoe wall. Customers picked up a shoe, looked for their size, and gave up because the size range was only on the boxes in the back. We added a small size chart next to each style and a call button for staff. Fewer people left the wall without help, and shoe sales in that store rose about 10% over the next month.
